en: Karnakagomin’s Commentary on Dharmakīrti’s *Pramāṇavārttikavṛtti*
Homage to the Buddha.
1. Homage Verse:
To him whose form is profound and vast, having shaken off the web of conceptual construction—*Pramāṇavārttika*...
Homage to Samantabhadra, whose radiance pervades everywhere! (1)

The glorious Lord Mañjunātha, the all-pervading one, whose course has destroyed all bonds, who abides in perfect mastery, in whom arises a continuous stream of stainless wisdom that extends to all objects of knowledge,
and whose mind is ever intent on the welfare of sentient beings— may he long protect us.
Having bowed to that [work], I shall now speak somewhat regarding the Vārttika, which has been thoroughly examined.
This entire merit belongs to the author of the commentary, that he speaks here even regarding this profound subject;
for once the obstacles [in the form of] Dignāga’s tusks have been removed by the elephant-goad [of the commentator], young elephants proceed with ease along the paths they have found.
If anyone who prides himself on his virtues disregards me, let him know that this effort is not directed toward him;
for there may yet come someone in the world who seeks this through various means, for there is no end to the diverse inclinations of those born in this world.

For although, at the commencement of a treatise, even without the presentation of a verse of salutation, the completion of the work may occur without obstacles due to the accumulation of merit through performing a salutation to one's chosen deity by means of body, speech, and mind;

Nevertheless, the Master has introduced this verse of worship to a distinguished deity, considering that the activity of both expounders and listeners preceded by such praise generates a superior merit and ensures the observance of the conduct of the virtuous.
He begins with the words, "With conceptual constructions shaken off," and so forth.

When the term *Samantabhadra* is not understood through conventional usage as referring to a bodhisattva, then this is an offering to the Buddha, the Blessed One. And that [offering] is twofold: by way of praise and by way of prostration. By the word *namaḥ*, it is by way of prostration;

by the remaining [words], it is by way of praise. Praise, moreover, is [threefold]: by way of the perfection of one's own welfare, by way of the perfection of the welfare of others, and by way of the welfare of others—
And it is threefold by way of the perfection of attainment: one who has attained their own welfare becomes capable regarding the welfare of others.
(RT 420b–zb2a)

First, the perfection of one's own welfare (*svārthasaṃpat*) is stated by means of the first half [of the verse]. And this perfection of one's own welfare, characterized by the three bodies (*kāya*), is manifested as distinguished by three specific qualities:
by the distinction of the abandonment of obscurations (*āvaraṇaprahāṇa*), by the distinction of profundity (*gāmbhīrya*), and by the distinction of magnificence (*audārya*).

In this context, "conceptual constructions" (*kalpanā*) refers to the minds and mental factors belonging to the three realms that function in the form of "self" and "mine," as well as those that function in the form of "grasped object" and "grasping subject. Because these are of the nature of being bound by a net, they are so designated. Those forms whose [nature] has been shaken off—that is, destroyed along with their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) and brought to a state of non-arising—are described in that way. By this, the abandonment of the obscurations—

The distinction has been stated. However, the specific qualities of profundity (*gāmbhīrya*) and magnificence (*udārya*) are expressed by the terms "profound" and "magnificent. They are profound because they have shaken off the web of conceptual construction (*kalpanājāla*), being beyond the scope of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others. They are magnificent because they pervade all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the welfare of all sentient beings. The three embodiments (*mūrti*) are the three bodies (*kāya*): the essential (*svābhāvika*), the enjoyment (*sāmbhogika*), and the emanation (*nairmāṇika*).

Of that Blessed One, whose form is profound and sublime, having shaken off the net of conceptual construction; from whose presence there arises for all supplicants, without exception and according to their capacity, *bhadra*—that which is auspicious, characterized by worldly prosperity and the ultimate good—he is therefore *Samantabhadra*. By this, the perfection of the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpat*) has been stated. And of this perfection of the welfare of others...

By the phrase "having light that radiates everywhere" (*samantasphuraṇatviṣa*), the means for attaining accomplishment (*siddhi*) is stated. Here, "light" (*tviṣ*) refers to the rays [of cognition] which consist precisely in the apprehension of things as they truly exist. Thus, the teaching of the Dharma is analogous to this. These "lights" are so called because they are like rays, having as their object the means for achieving both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). "Everywhere" (*samanta*) means without exception; the means for accomplishing the welfare of others (*parārtha*) is made to radiate.
Because they are spoken in their entirety from the Vinayas, those [teachings] by which [the world] is pervaded are "all-pervading radiations" (*samantaspharaṇī*);

he whose light of Dharma-teaching is of such a nature is "one whose light is all-pervading" (*samantaspharaṇatviṭ*). And because of its connection with the word *namaḥ*, the dative case is used everywhere.
When, however, conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is taken into account, this term "Samantabhadra" is conventionally established in the Mahāyāna as referring to a particular type of bodhisattva;
thus, this is an offering to a bodhisattva. The meaning of the word (*padārtha*), however, should be applied as before. This, however, is the distinction:

the state of having shaken off the web of conceptual construction (*kalpanājāla*) is to be understood from the abandonment of the obscurations (*āvaraṇa*) of the bodhisattva stages. Profundity [is that of] the Śrāvakas—

[Because it is not the domain of Pratyekabuddhas or ordinary beings; its vastness, however, arises from the greatness of the Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, the three bodies (trikāya) indeed exist in accordance with the Bodhisattvas, but they are established as belonging to the Buddhas because of their attainment of the ultimate excellence.]

Indeed, there certainly exist those who will grasp this treatise known as the *Śāntisiddhi*; nevertheless, because of the abundance of defects in listeners, one might render even an existing benefit as if it were non-existent. Therefore, demonstrating that the very state of having a mind cultivated by the practice of well-spoken words (*sūktābhyāsa*) is the cause for undertaking the treatise, [the author] indicates—by means of an indirect statement—that this defect of a cause which leads to the loss of great purpose is fit to be abandoned.
To explain this, he states the second verse regarding the purpose of the treatise: "Generally, people are attached to the vernacular and possess neither strength nor wisdom; they are merely—"

Though surrounded by well-spoken words that are useless to him, and possessed of the stains of hatred and envy, my mind has long harbored not even the thought that this [work] is for the benefit of others; yet, because my addiction has been increased by the practice of sublime sayings, my longing for it remains firmly bound.

"Generally, the vulgar," and so forth. Here, four kinds of defects in the listener are brought to light: poor discernment (*kuprajñatva*), ignorance (*ajñatva*), lack of purpose (*anarthatva*), and lack of impartiality (*amādhyasthya*). The word *prāyaḥ* ends in the vowel *o* and signifies "for the most part" or "in abundance. *Prāyo janaḥ* means "the majority of people. *Prākṛtasaktiḥ* refers to one whose attachment (*sakti*) is toward the "vulgar"—that is, toward external treatises (*bahiḥ-śāstra*). (1)

Because it conveys meaning, the *bahuvrīhi* compound has different grammatical referents (*vyadhikaraṇa*); or, it may be taken as having the same referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*), namely: "one whose attachment is natural" (*prākṛtā vā saktir yasya*).

Furthermore, because its object is the natural state, the attachment is called "natural. By this, the defect of the listener—namely, their poor intelligence—is stated. One whose intelligence is "unbalanced" (*apratibala*)—that is, incapable (*aśakta*) regarding the grasping of the treatise—is one of "unbalanced intelligence"; such a person is common among the populace.

This is the connection [of the words]. By this, ignorance is expressed: [the person] not only does not praise well-spoken words, but being overwhelmed by the impurities of envy, he even hates the speaker of well-spoken words. The meaning is that he both disregards them and hates them. By this, lack of interest and lack of impartiality are stated respectively. Here too, the phrase "generally people" (*prāyo janaḥ*) should be connected [to the preceding].

Others, however, explain that there is also a particle *prāyaḥ* ending in the letter *s*; and by its very nature, it functions in the sense of the instrumental case (*bāhulyena*) in this context. Envy (*īrṣyā*) is the mental resentment toward the excellence of others. That itself is a "stain" (*mala*) because it defiles the mind. The plural number is used because of the multiplicity of individual instances. Since this is so, therefore...
For what reason has this work, titled *Vātikā*, been undertaken? It is for the sake of benefiting others (*paropakāra*).

The term *upakāra* is derived from the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe ghañ*), meaning "that by which one is benefited. Alternatively, it is *paropakāra* in the sense of "one who benefits others," according to Pāṇini’s rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (3.2.1).
As for this "benefiting of others," we have not even the slightest concern [for reward]. How then [is it undertaken]?

He states that there is an inclination toward the composition of this treatise: "The mind, for a long time," and so forth. For a long time—that is, over a vast period—the mind has had its attachment (*vyasana*)—meaning its devotion and dedication—augmented by the practice of well-spoken verses (*sūktābhyāsa*).
Thus, it is described as such. For this reason, the mind has developed a longing—that is, an arisen desire—for the composition of this *Vārttika*.
Thus some explain it;

others, however, otherwise. At this point of inquiry—namely, why this teacher Dharmakīrti provides a commentary on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* according to the method of a *vārttika* rather than composing an independent treatise (*śāstra*) himself—he says: "For the most part... (*prāyaḥ*).

And so forth. This is the summarized meaning of this verse: "By means of reflection and compassion, my mind has conceived a desire for the commentary on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*. Reflection and compassion arise because the treatise composed by the Teacher [Dignāga] provides only limited benefit; and its limited benefit is due to the fault of his kinsmen. [The word] *padārtha-*...

It is stated: "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) means that, for the most part, the connection is with "people who are attached to the ordinary" (*prākṛtasaktirjana*). The "ordinary" (*prākṛta*) is said to be [the one characterized by] (1) investigation of the reason (*hetucintā*) and (2) the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

(2) The definition of the reason (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) is stated in order to establish it, because the discernment of what is meaningful and what is meaningless relies upon inference, and because there are misconceptions regarding that [reason].

In the world, one is considered base if their positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is faulty. Likewise, the treatises of the non-Buddhist sects (*tīrthika*) and those composed by others [regarding] the teacher’s system—

2b Refutations of the Treatise: Because they arise from perverted cognition and because their logical connection (*anvaya*) is corrupted, [the treatises] are "prākṛta" (vulgar). One who has attachment—that is, affection—for them is so described. Why, then, does he have attachment to the vulgar? He says: "because his wisdom lacks power. Therefore, taking even what is poorly spoken to be well-spoken, he becomes attached to the vulgar. [He is] powerless...

Furthermore, because he lacks both strength and wisdom, he is unable to understand the well-spoken words of the Teacher correctly by himself; instead, grasping them as faulty, he finds no benefit in those well-spoken words of the Teacher and becomes hostile toward the Teacher. Thus [the author] says "merely," and so forth.
Not only does he find no benefit from the well-spoken words of the Teacher, but being possessed by envy and malice, he even hates the Teacher.
What is it that has become a passion for the practice of well-spoken words (*sūktābhyāsa*)? Even when separated by distance, a connection certainly exists, according to the maxim:
"Whatever has a relationship with something, it belongs to that thing even if it stands far away.
Well-spoken words (*sūkta*) are the teachings of the Blessed One; therein lies the practice, therein the cultivated passion, and therein indeed the extreme devotion.

He to whom attachment belongs—that is, to the teacher Dignāga—is thus described. By this, [the author] states that the teacher Dignāga has accumulated merit and knowledge; for only those who have accumulated merit and knowledge become devoted to the practice of well-spoken words. Because he possessed wisdom beyond compare, was not indifferent to the teacher’s elegant sayings, and was attached to the ordinary [truth], for that reason, this *Pramāṇasamuccaya*...

The accumulation [of merit] is for the sake of helping others (*paropakāra*). "Upakāra" means assistance; it is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (Pāṇini 3.3.18). It is called "not helping others" because no superior assistance arises from it; however, there certainly is some small assistance, and that is precisely what is indicated by the word "mostly" (*prāya*). The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason (1): for this reason, we have this concern. [It is] of great significance—

"This treatise has not yet become beneficial to many; how then shall I bring it to complete fruition?"—this is the form [of his thought]. Furthermore, even the slightest malice toward a teacher who is like a Bodhisattva is a cause of misfortune; therefore, by elucidating the teacher’s system without error, I shall generate great respect for the teacher and, thereby, turn people away from that cause of misfortune. Thus, [he acts] out of compassion for suffering...

The word "also" (*api*) implies that compassion (*karuṇā*) likewise takes the form of a desire for yoga. Thus, by the second word "thus" (*iti*), he states that reflection (*cintā*) and compassion are the causes [of the work]. Through these two—reflection and compassion—the mind has for a long time, over a prolonged period, maintained a continuous desire (*anubaddhaspṛham*) here for the composition of the *Pramāṇavārttika*, which is a commentary on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.
"Desiring to flow forth."

If one asks why the Master Dharmakīrti, desiring to compose a commentary on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, establishes inference independently [of Dignāga], the author states "arthān... and so forth to dispel this doubt. The analysis of the compound is: he whose aim (*artha*) is the investigation of the cause (*hetu*) of welfare (*hita*).
The discernment of benefit and harm depends upon inference, because it has inference as its basis.

For, having ascertained benefit and harm through inference, one establishes them in their respective categories—either for attainment or for avoidance—by means of a continuous stream of knowledge that follows after inference. Therefore, [the treatise] has inference as its basis.

The discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful [is established] because of the disagreement regarding that [inference]. Some explain this as follows: "Because there is disagreement concerning that inference, [the author] states [this] in order to establish it.
However, in this regard, the following must be considered: 6.
If it is first determined that "this is because the discernment of what is beneficial (*artha*) and what is harmful (*anartha*) alone rests upon inference," that is not so;
for the discernment of a third object, which is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*), distinct from both the beneficial and the harmful, is also [dependent] upon inference.

Because [the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful] depends upon [perception], and because that discernment is not restricted [to inference alone], it is not precluded that perception is its basis.
What excellence, then, is proclaimed for inference such that it is explained first? Alternatively, even if it is determined thus:

"Precisely because the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful depends upon inference"—even so, this restriction is incorrect, for the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful...

This is also because [the determination of] benefit and harm (*artha-anartha*) is based upon perception (*pratyakṣa*). For in this way, objects appear in perception precisely with their distinct forms.

And that perception—having attained proficiency through the excellence of repeated practice (*abhyāsātiśaya*) and having removed the causes of error—generates the subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that discriminates between what is beneficial and what is harmful. Indeed, this alone is the [function of] perception in the discrimination of benefit and harm.

The state of being a basis for desire and aversion consists in the production of a determination regarding an object after one has experienced it through the distinction between what is beneficial and what is harmful;

nor can it be said that this distinction between benefit and harm occurs only subsequently, because [the distinction] is made by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) with respect to the real entity (*vastu*).

Because the intrinsic nature [of the object] is not apprehended, or because it would be conceptual if it were apprehended; for there is a contradiction in the clear manifestation of an object to a cognizer who is bound by conceptual construction.
However, in some cases, perception may be incapable of removing the causes of error due to a lack of clarity regarding the object.

In that regard, certainty is sought through inference, but not in every case. Therefore, the determination of validity—both intrinsically and extrinsically—applies to perception. Furthermore, this matter will be established in the second chapter, so it is not elaborated upon here.

Furthermore, it must necessarily be accepted that perception—which has had the causes of error removed through the power of repeated practice—serves as the basis for the discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful, because it generates a certainty in accordance with its experience; otherwise, there would be no established validity even for inference, since the inferential mark (*liṅga*), such as smoke, would not be certain. If the cognition of smoke and so forth were itself to be apprehended through inference, there would be an infinite regress.
In that case as well, it is because another mark (*liṅga*) is ascertained through another inference.

And if perception were not the basis for discriminating between what is beneficial and what is harmful, then that which was stated by the author of the treatise in another section— namely, "Because the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful are invariably preceded by correct knowledge," and so forth— would be untenable.
That [position] would be contradicted; likewise [it is said], "For its object is not determined," and so forth. Furthermore, it has been stated:
"In the case of perceived objects, there is recollection and so on, which arise from the capacity of consciousness," and so forth.
Therefore, others maintain that it must be explained otherwise. [This concerns] the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa) composed by the teacher Dignāga.
The meaning [of the treatise] is valid because it is logical; that which is composed by non-Buddhist outsiders is not the true meaning because it is illogical.

The discernment of these two—the establishment of them as being either logical or illogical—is based upon inference (*anumāna*), for it is by relying solely on inference that the definition [of the treatise] is established.
[The opponent argues: "In establishing the validity or invalidity of definitions (*lakṣaṇa*), perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not [the means], because it is non-discursive (*avicāraka*).

This too is incorrect. For it is not by their own nature that definitions are valid or invalid, but rather through their object (*artha*). And just as that object is understood to be valid by means of inference (*anumāna*), so too is it by means of perception. And thus:
He will say:
(1) "Perception, which is free from conceptual construction, is established by perception itself" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.123).
Likewise...
"The determination of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is through perception," and so forth.
Even for one who thinks: (1) "It is true that the discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful is indeed performed by means of perception and inference;
however, as for the claim that this discrimination relies upon inference, there is no dispute regarding its being an object of perception."

"If [direct perception] were possible, there would be no basis for definitive determination other than inference; therefore, because of the primacy of inference, it was stated that [the treatise] relies upon its analysis.
This too is incorrect, because only that object which is ascertained is established as the domain of direct perception.
Furthermore, it is incorrect to say that dispute cannot occur regarding what has been ascertained.

However, another [author] says: (1) The discernment of what is beneficial (*artha*) and what is harmful (*anartha*) arises from inference alone, not from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is because those things beneficial or harmful whose results have already been experienced or are currently being experienced are not objects of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*), since their result has already been accomplished.

Therefore, activity toward objects—whether beneficial or harmful—is directed toward those things capable of performing a future causal function (*arthakriyā*). Furthermore, that capacity is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) within those [objects] such that they would constitute the objective domain of activity. This is because the causal function to be accomplished by the activity is yet to come, and thus the capacity [for it]—that is, its state of being "productive" (*kurvadrūpatā*)—is also yet to come. Consequently, [activity is directed toward] that which was previously experienced as a means of accomplishing a causal function...

Because of the similarity of entities, even regarding objects that are directly perceived, there is no determination of their fitness for future results through perception; therefore, the discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful arises solely from inference.
This too is incorrect, because if that fitness (in the form of *kurvadrūpatā*, or causal efficacy) were present in objects at the time they exist in the present...

Then it would be ascertained by perception, even for one possessing an excellence of practice, just like [an object known through] a logical mark (*liṅga*). Alternatively, if that [object] were indeed future, then it could not be ascertained even by inference; for he will state later that there is an absence of inference regarding a future object.
By this, the claim that "the attainment of the object which is the domain of activity is indistinguishable for both perception and inference" is refuted.

That too must be regarded as refuted. For the object of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti-viṣaya*) is that which is capable of future causal efficiency; however, it has been stated that such capacity is not ascertained by either perception or inference. Furthermore, the object of purposeful activity is held to be something delimited (*paricchinna*), and since the continuum (*santāna*) is not delimited by a single moment of perception or the like, how could it be the object of purposeful activity? 1. Investigation of the Cause (*hetu-cintā*).

Now, it is argued that even though perception operates at a single moment, because it is determined by conceptual ascertainment (*niścaya*), it is improper to say that its object is a single continuum, since its object would then be a universal (*sāmānya*) of moments. For it is by virtue of ascertainment that perception is established as having a universal for its object through the very object that appears; this is not so in an ultimate sense, because [perception] has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object. Just like a logical mark (*liṅga*).

The object of perception is the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). For instance, this appearing particular characteristic of smoke may be produced by grass, by cow-dung, or something else; and because there is no ascertainment of its specific qualities at that moment, and because it is determined for only a single instant, perception—though having the particular as its object—is established as having the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. This is due to the determination that arises subsequent to the perception.

Because it follows upon the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, it is not possible to establish direct perception as having a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) as its object; for that moment which appears in direct perception is not ascertained, nor is it possible for it to be of the nature of a preceding or a succeeding moment, since they belong to different times. Therefore, how could there be [ascertainment] regarding a moment through the non-determination of its specific qualities?
And by means of the ascertainment [produced by] perception, perception would be established as having the generality of moments as its object.

Even though the ascertainment "this is that very same thing," which arises subsequent to perception, has the generality as its object, it does not have the continuum as its object— [for it apprehends] what was already perceived and is now being perceived.
Because future moments are not ascertained by being made the objects of these two [means of knowledge], and because their object is a form excluded from those of a different class,
for this very reason, even when a moment appears, there is the ascertainment that informs one "this is a jar.
Now, if it is argued that a real continuum of things capable of causal efficiency is not determined by either perception or inference—
How, then, do those two [perception and inference] function as motivators? We reply: by determining the mere essential nature of the thing (*vastu*).

For instance, when one determines through perception that a thing such as fire, existing in a continuous series at one location, is capable of performing a purposeful action such as burning, one then determines—upon perceiving it elsewhere—that even in another place it performs such an action precisely because it exists in a continuous series.

Furthermore, at another time, that same person, seeking the result and investigating its nature, perceives fire and so forth through both perception and inference; preceded by the ascertainment that "this is that very thing," he proceeds to act. Therefore, the function of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in the determination of the mere nature of that object, not in the determination of its continuous occurrence, nor in the determination of its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*). As before—
This is not so, because all of this [the object] is delimited (*paricchinna*). Therefore, it is indeed logical that perception and inference function as the motivators [of action].
How then was it stated that the discernment between what is beneficial and what is harmful depends upon inference? [...]
...it is not the self (*ātman*) that is intended here, but rather the four noble truths (*catur-ārya-satya*).

For it has been stated by the Blessed One that we are those for whom liberation is the goal, and that liberation arises from the vision of the four noble truths. Furthermore, that vision is accomplished through the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and engagement in cultivation occurs through certainty regarding the four noble truths. 42

And since the ascertainment of that [truth] occurs through inference alone because it is beyond the senses, inference alone is the basis for the discrimination between what is beneficial (*artha*) and what is harmful (*anartha*).

"Beneficial" refers to Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*), because they are to be adopted; "harmful" refers to Suffering (*duḥkha*) and Origination (*samudaya*), because they are to be abandoned. Alternatively, "beneficial" is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and "harmful" is conventional truth (*saṃvṛttisatya*); the discrimination between these two—their establishment according to their own nature—is [the function of inference].

Because it is based on conceit (*māna*). Furthermore, all cognition that effects the discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful does not grasp the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), but rather determines it; thus, it is indeed erroneous (*bhrānta*). Therefore, if the cognition of words and so forth is held to be the basis for the discrimination between benefit and harm, it too is invalid (*apramāṇa*) precisely because it is erroneous. For this very reason, there is no possibility of its being explained here [in this treatise]. As for inference (*anumāna*)... [51]
(3) The reason is threefold;
(4) fallacious reasons.
A reason is a property of the subject that is pervaded by a part of it; it is indeed of three kinds.
Because they cannot be established [as valid reasons]; therefore, others are fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa). || 3 ||

Even though it is erroneous, the validity [of perception] exists by virtue of its necessary connection; however, if the validity of cognitions such as those derived from verbal testimony is accepted in this manner, they would be included within inference.

Since that which does not possess the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) cannot be a means of proof, the capacity to distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful belongs to inference alone.

Now, if the validity of inference were due to its connection [with the object], then conceptual cognitions such as "eternal" and so forth would also be valid, because they too are connected to objects such as momentariness. Alternatively, if validity were due to a connection with the object as it is determined [by the cognition], then the cognition of a gem in the luster of a gem would be valid; for that too is indeed connected with the gem as it is determined.

Therefore, even though there is an obstruction [to the object], inferential cognition is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when it causes one to attain that very object which was determined as being connected to a particular place and so forth, because of the determination of the identity of the continuum (*santāna*) with respect to that place and so forth. Not every cognition is [valid].

Furthermore, the discernment between what is beneficial and what is harmful consists in the form of apprehension; inference is a valid means of knowledge because its aspect is such. Or rather, [it is so] because of the mark (*liṅga*).
Therefore, inference is the basis for the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful, because there is disagreement regarding it;
that is, because of confusion concerning that inference. To establish it—that is, to establish that inference by removing the disagreement—the author of the Sūtras says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*):

if one asks why, when inference itself is to be established, [the author] establishes only the logical reason (*hetu*) by means of "the property of the subject" and so forth, this is not a fault; for since there is disagreement regarding inference by way of disagreement regarding the logical reason, [it is established] precisely by way of explaining that [reason].

Its establishment is as follows: inferential cognition (*anumānajñāna*) arising from a mark possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpaliṅga*) is indeed well-known in the world; therefore, any misconception regarding it is refuted by means of that very common understanding.
Alternatively, when the word "inference" (*anumāna*) refers to the mark itself, then its establishment serves as the very reason for refuting misconceptions concerning it.
Thus, there is no fault.

In this verse, the definition of the logical mark (*liṅga*), the restriction of its number, the cause for that restriction of number, and the exclusion of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) have been stated. The definition is: "the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) which is pervaded by that [property] in view of it."
The property intended to be proven is necessarily pervaded by that [reason];

this restriction is expressed by the phrase "only threefold" (*tridhaiva*), which establishes the rule of number. The reason for this rule of number is "because of the necessity of inseparable connection" (*avinābhāvaniyamāt*);

the meaning is that inseparable connection is restricted exclusively to these three. The phrase "fallacious reasons are other than these" (*hetvābhāsāstato'pare*) effects the exclusion of the counter-example (*vipakṣanivṛtti*).
Therefore, other [reasons] than these three are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). [1. Investigation of the Reason:

Now, if the pervasion by that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*) is apprehended only in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then inference would not arise, because the pervasion of the reason by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) would not be apprehended in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). And in that case, the definition "the reason is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) would be useless.
The definition [of inference] is not [valid] because it lacks the capacity to produce cognition; for even if the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is grasped by means of a universal induction,
inference does not possess validity, since its object is already established by the very means of valid cognition that grasped the pervasion.

It might be argued: "The definition 'the reason is a property of the subject' need not be stated, because it is already understood through the very statement of its pervasion by that part [of the subject]. By the force of that pervasion by the part... 4b

Furthermore, it is not by its mere presence in the subject (*pakṣa*) that a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) functions as a means of cognition, because a donkey or similar entity residing therein does not function as such a means. Therefore, the definition "the reason is a property of the subject" must be stated separately [from the definition of the thesis],
because it has the nature of a recollection (*smṛti*).
As it has been said:
"Where there is the condition of being otherwise impossible, what is the use of the three [criteria]?
Where there is no condition of being otherwise impossible, what is the use of the three?"

Furthermore, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) cannot be a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), because the apprehension of something else is a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*). Moreover, since a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is itself the form of the subject, and a reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*) is likewise independent and does not depend upon a subject, it must be stated that a reason which is a property of the subject cannot be an effect-reason or an essential-nature reason, nor can there be a pervasion by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpti*) for such a constructed property of the subject. Thus, [non-apprehension] is not a reason that is a property of the subject.

Likewise, if the state of being a cause (*hetutva*) were pervaded by the state of being threefold (*tritva*), then because the state of being a cause is not restricted [to those three], its status as a cause would remain unprevented in other cases as well, such as in the case of conjunctions (*saṃyogin*); thus, the restriction "only threefold" (*tridhaiva*) would be untenable.

On the other hand, if the state of being a cause were pervaded by the state of being threefold, then because the state of being threefold is not restricted to causes, it would follow that effects (*kārya*) and so forth would also [be threefold].
Furthermore, it is not tenable that the causehood of the effect and so forth exists ultimately [only] in the effect itself.

Moreover, if there were no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between non-perception and the probandum, then even an unconnected reason would be a prover; thus, the rule that "the reason is of only three kinds" would not hold.

If there is an obstacle [to the relationship], then because it would be included within either the effect (*kārya*) or the essential nature (*svabhāva*), that reason would still be only of three kinds;

yet even so, this is not tenable. To say "the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are other than those" is not logical, because since another type of reason is entirely beyond perception (*atyantaparokṣa*), its absence cannot be ascertained through perception or other means; thus, what was said is incorrect. 3.

The reason (*hetu*) is that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and is pervaded by a part of it; it is of only three kinds due to the rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*); others than these are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).

To this it is replied: although the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is apprehended through a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), nevertheless, from the mere grasping of that pervasion, there does not arise here a specific certainty that "the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) now resides in this subject (*sādhyadharmī*). This certainty, however, must come from inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, regarding the object to be proven (*sādhyārtha*) which is connected to a specific place and so forth as already apprehended—
Inference is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of its being a demonstrator, and that occurs only when there is the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*),
and not otherwise. Since a probans (*sādhana-dharma*) located in one place cannot be connected with a probandum-locus (*sādhya-dharmin*) located in another place,
the cognition of the probandum as delimited by a specific location and so forth [is what constitutes inference].

Inference arises precisely from the capacity to understand the means of proof (*sādhana*) as delimited by [the property to be proved]; however, the cognition of mere fire does not arise from the mere presence of the property (*dharma*) alone, because that [cognition] is the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Nor does it arise even when there is an understanding, without qualification, that "wherever the property of the means of proof exists, there the property to be proved exists."

The property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is established because, although it is not perceived as a specific feature of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), it is expressed in a general sense.
Therefore, in order to bring about the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) as delimited by a specific location and so forth, the property of being a feature of the subject must be demonstrated.
Consequently, as for what was stated—that "since the property of the subject is already expressed by the statement 'wherever there is smoke, there is fire,' [the mention of] the location..."
The objection that "one need not state 'there is smoke here' for the sake of establishing a specific fire, because its meaning has already been expressed" is thereby refuted.

Now, if inference were thus valid as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then even an inference whose property is not located in the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*) would be a valid means of knowledge, since it provides the comprehension of what was previously unapprehended.
For example, having seen rain upstream, one infers rain downstream; likewise, [one might infer] "this child is a Brāhmaṇa."
"Because of the Brahminhood of the parents. As it has been said: "Even a river-flood seen in the lower region [necessarily] causes the rain that occurred above to flow down, acting as its regulator."
Thus, it is accepted that "having dharma as its object through direct perception" (*pratyakṣadharmatva*) is the primary member of the reason (*hetvaṅga*).
It is, however, rendered inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) by the observation of other properties previously mentioned.
The inference that the son is a Brāhmaṇa based on the Brāhmaṇahood of his parents is well-known to all the world; it does not depend upon the property of the subject (pakṣadharma).

If one were to imagine that the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) exists even there [in the case of a fallacious reason] due to a flaw, then his definition would not coincide with the object to be defined.

"Just as that which is well-known in the world is followed by its characteristics, so too would the characteristic of the characterized be [established]; thus, that which is unprecedented would not be proven.
To this it is replied: Why is there inference of rain only above and not elsewhere? [Because] of the flood's connection with that...

If you say [it is] like that, then [we reply]: if this is so, one may infer rain from the fact that this river flood has come from such-and-such a place, but not elsewhere, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Furthermore, for another person, there is the capacity to indicate [the conclusion] only when there is certainty regarding its connection [to the subject]; otherwise, it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Likewise, in the case of the argument "this child is a Brahmin because his mother and father are Brahmins," it is only for that specific child—[that the inference holds].

The *brahmaṇya* (the state of being a Brahmin) belonging to his very father and mother— characterized by the *dharma* of being a Brahmin— is the indicator (*gamaka*) [of his status], not merely the *brahmaṇya* of his parents [or the *brahmaṇya* of others related to them], because that alone does not indicate [his own status].
Therefore, for him as well...

Since the capacity to prove [the probandum] exists when there is the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), there is no need for the laborious postulation of *pakṣadharmatva*. Alternatively, that alone which is the cause of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) is the logical reason (*hetu*).

For example, the fact that smoke is an effect of fire, and the fact of being born from parents who are Brahmins, are the causes for a child’s status as a Brahmin; therefore, that alone is the proper reason. To postulate anything else would involve unnecessary labor.

Likewise, there can be no inference of the rise of the ocean from the rising of the moon, because that would entail the possibility of such an inference occurring both before and after the moonrise. If it is argued that the inference occurs only at the very time of the moonrise, because it is only then that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been apprehended; [we reply:]...

If this is so, then the connection with that very time is what constitutes the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). In that case, that same time would be the locus (*dharmin*), and the inference of the probandum would occur therein; since the rising of the moon is connected to it, how could there be a lack of "property-of-the-subject" (*apakṣadharmatva*)? Alternatively, if time is not accepted, then this inference is fallacious due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Now, as for this inference of the Buddhists—

"It does not exist because of the absence of time"—this is incorrect. For it is accepted that "time" is a designation for a specific great element (*mahābhūta*) which is the object of cognitions such as "forenoon" and so forth. In the same way, the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) should be applied in other cases as well.

[Objection: Let it be granted that inference possesses validity when the reason is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). Nevertheless, the definition "property of the subject" need not be stated separately, because that is already included by the statement of its pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the probandum. [Reply: True.

However, it was formulated for the purpose of excluding as a reason even that which is not a property of the subject, provided it is pervaded by the probandum. For example, [the presence of] smoke on a mountain...
This refers to the inference of fire in the ocean from previously perceived smoke and the like.
Now, it may be argued that a probans (*liṅga*) must be pervaded (*vyāpta*), yet the smoke found in the kitchen and such places is not pervaded by the fire to be proven (*sādhya*) in the ocean.

The statement of the definition that "the reason is merely pervaded by the probandum" alone does not secure the understanding that the inference of the pervading property (*vyāpaka-dharma*) occurs only where the pervaded property (*vyāpya-dharma*) exists. Therefore, in order to eliminate the suspicion that the inference of the probandum might occur elsewhere as well, the statement of the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) is required. Even in the case of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), the property of being a feature of the subject is indeed present; for when [the non-perception] belongs to another...

The non-apprehension of another [object] is simply the fitness for producing a cognition of the ground and so forth; since that fitness is the very nature of the other ground and so forth, how could it not be a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) for the non-apprehension? In the same way, properties such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) are properties of sound and the like. Even though non-apprehension has the form of a property of the person [who perceives], its ultimate status as a property of that [ground] is simply its being an effect of the other ground and so forth, because it is dependent upon it. As with smoke—

In this way, although the effect possesses properties such as spatial location and so forth, it is merely by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that their very nature as related entities is established for the subject (*pakṣa*) as "this is its property.

Furthermore, the status of being a logical reason (*hetutva*) is pervaded by invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*); for one who does not know the invariable concomitance, [the mark] is not a prover, and thus [it is not] a reason. (T) 5b

Because inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is pervaded by the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*). Furthermore, when there is a thesis consisting of either an affirmation or a negation, the affirmation of another thing is [the province of] the effect-reason, while the negation is [the province of] the nature-reason and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*); thus, the reason is pervaded by these three types, and therefore it is of exactly three kinds. It is not that only the threefold reason is [pervaded], for even the effect-reason and the others [are included].

Because that which is already known lacks causal efficacy. Furthermore, the capacity of the non-perception of a cause and the non-perception of a pervader to produce cognition arises solely from their necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
For it is precisely because of that same necessary connection that the effect and the pervaded indicate the cause and the pervader;

likewise, it is because of that very same necessary connection that the non-perception of the cause and the pervader indicates the absence of the effect and the pervaded. [This applies to] the non-perception of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*)...

In both cases, when the nature of a jar or the like— which is capable of producing its perception— is called "perception," and since perception is not deviant from existence when all other causes are present, perception is its very being (*sattā*); then, because of this identity between the two, even in this position— 1 421a— [the same fault applies].

The subject (*pakṣa*) is the locus of the property (*dharmin*). If it is argued that there is no figurative usage [of the term "subject"] because there is no purpose for it, we say no; for the capacity to prove (*gamakatva*) is based solely on the exclusion of all properties belonging to the subject. Furthermore, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not included within the category of effects (*kārya*) and other such reasons, because it does not depend upon a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with its own probandum (*sādhya*). And the cognition of the probandum from the reason would only occur if it were dependent upon that [connection].

(1) Furthermore, there is no dependence on [the cause] when conjunction exists, because those things not in conjunction lack conjunction; nor is there dependence on conjunction even for those things that are conjoined, since their being conjoined arises from something else entirely. The same should be said regarding inherence (*samavāya*). Therefore, dependence consists only in identity (*tādātmya*) or origination therefrom (*tadutpatti*); thus, conjunctions—which fall outside the categories of effect-nature (*kāryasvabhāva*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*)—[do not establish dependence].
Fire and the like are not causes [of smoke], because, in the absence of dependence upon them, there is no invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
If, however, there is dependence upon them, then that very dependence is the basis for the capacity to indicate [the probandum]; thus it is established that a cause is of only three kinds.
Now, even so, how does inference arise? Through non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), the property (*dharma*), the locus (*dharmin*), and their relationship—

Because two things are apprehended independently through the act of grasping, it is said that even by conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), the apprehension of the relationship between property and locus (*dharmin-dharmabhāva*) regarding smoke, location, and so forth, is nothing other than the appearance of one being "upon" the other (*uparyuparibhāva*). And this [appearance] exists even in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*); the only difference is between the two types of cognition—conceptual and its opposite.

The distinction between [perception] with and without conceptualization is as follows: (1) That non-conceptual cognition is accepted as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it produces affirmation and negation—such as "this exists here" or "this does not exist"—precisely regarding the object as it has been apprehended. Consequently, the determination of the intrinsic nature of both the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), as well as the determination of their relationship, occurs solely through perception (*pratyakṣa*).

It has been stated that [the reason] is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). In the Sūtra, however, the property of the subject is defined as a collection of both the property and the substratum (*dharmadharmasamudāya*).

Since the status of being a property of such a collection is not established for the opponent with respect to the reason, every such reason would consequently be unestablished (*asiddha*). Alternatively, if it were established, inference would be rendered useless; thus he says:

"The subject (*pakṣa*) is the property (*dharma*)," because the term for the whole is applied metaphorically to its part. And since being a "part" is the basis for this metaphorical application of the whole, the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) is not called the "subject" (*pakṣa*). Īśvarasena said: "One should state only that 'the reason (*hetu*) is a property of the subject' (*dharmidharma*); there is no need [to mention the word *pakṣa*]."

Regarding the phrase "the metaphorical designation of the subject" (*vādanupacāra*), he says: "For a purpose," and so forth. He refutes [the objection] with the words "no," and so forth. It is not that there is an absence of purpose; rather, it is expected because the metaphorical designation has the purpose of negating both the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*). If the metaphorical designation were absent, the instruction "the property of the property-bearer" would have to be used. And in that case, the reason (*hetu*) would also be a property of the example-property-bearer (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*). [This is avoided] by means of the metaphorical designation.
However, the property is negated for every subject (*dharmin*). If one asks how this is so, he says: "Because it is a part of that" (*tadekadeśatvāt*).

And because the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) is a part of the thesis (*pakṣa*)—that is, because it is a constituent member of the thesis—it is fit to be treated as the thesis through figurative designation (*upacāra*). The application of such a figurative designation is for the sake of understanding its property (*dharma*). Thus, when there is an understanding of the subject fit for figurative designation, [properties such as] visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so forth [are understood].
The rebuttal: [The word] "etc. (*ādi*) includes such cases as "the crow's blackness" and so forth.

This is because [the property] is for the sake of that [the object], because it is a part of that, and for the purpose of understanding properties suitable for metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) with respect to that. Thus, the rebuttal regarding "being visible to the eye" (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so forth is also resolved.

If it is argued that even by the statement of the property (*dharma*), the locus of the property (*dharmin*) is established, and that the establishment of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) follows from proximity due to the inherent capacity of the statement of the property-locus (*dharmidharmavacana*), we say: no. For there is also proximity to the property-locus of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*). Since its existence in the example-locus is established by the "pervasion by a part of that" (*tadaṃśavyāpti*), the statement of the property-locus results in the inclusion of the property-locus of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) alone.

Now, if the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) "because it is visual" (*cākṣuṣatvāt*) is "because it is an object of visual consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñānaviṣayatvāt*), then this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); thus, it is already refuted by the statement regarding its lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*). So what is the point of this figurative usage (*upacāra*)? Alternatively, if the meaning of the reason is "because it is a producer of visual consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñānajanakatvāt*), even then, that quality of being a producer is simply existence (*sattva*) itself; and that [existence] is present in sound—
Some might argue that this is merely a property of the locus within which something exists, such that "it exists" does not refer to the object itself.
That is incorrect. For being a generator of visual consciousness is a specific characteristic of existence (*sattvaviśeṣa*), and that belongs only to things such as jars, not to sound;

therefore, the employment of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is for the purpose of excluding [sound from being considered existent]. However, even in the absence of metaphorical designation, that which is pervaded [by the property] possesses the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
(1) Nor is visibility pervaded by the non-eternality of sound; how then could it serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*)?
This is not a fault. For it is indeed pervaded by non-eternality in general, and since that [non-eternality] exists in sound as well, how could it be a non-reason (*ahetu*)?

"By the statement of the property," and so forth. Since the property is pervaded by its locus, even by the mere statement of the property, because the property is dependent upon the subject (*dharmin*), it necessarily implies that subject. Therefore, when the mere recourse to—that is, the acceptance of—the subject is established, the inclusion of the term "subject" in the expression "the property of the subject" follows from its functional necessity.

It is understood that "proximity" (*pratyāsatti*) is intended here; for if pervasion (*vyāpti*) were intended, the mention of the locus (*dharmī*) would be purposeless. Therefore, proximity is established by the force of the expression "the locus. And this proximity belongs specifically to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), because the reason is first presented in relation to it. By means of that proximity, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is grasped.
It will be so. The inclusion of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) does not arise from proximity; why?

(1) Because it applies to the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*) as well, not only to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmī*); for sometimes, in an application preceded by the observation of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the existence of the reason (*hetu*) is first demonstrated even in the case of the subject of the example.

If the property-bearer (*dharmin*) is not established through proximity, then it will be established by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). For, by means of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of a portion [of the subject] which serves as the reason (*hetu*), the existence of the property (*dharma*) in the instance (*dṛṣṭānta-dharmin*) is established. It is thought that without an instance, the pervasion of the reason by the probandum (*sādhya*) cannot be demonstrated. Therefore, [the term *dharmin* is used] because of the exclusion from the instance...

The subject (*dharmin*) is understood precisely from that which is being excluded [as the locus of the probandum]. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "by its part" (*tadaṃśena*), since the subject is already implied by the word "that" (*tat*)—which denotes the property (*dharma*)—it should not be suspected that the mention of the "subject" (*dharmigrahaṇa*) is intended for the sake of connecting [the part] with it.
That for which no other purpose is possible is the domain of the *pāriśeṣya* (method of elimination); however, the mention of the subject serves another purpose.

Even when [the negative concomitance] is established, a statement is expected for the sake of restriction (*niyama*). This is because, although the absence [of the reason] from the dissimilar instance (*vijātīya*) is already established by the fact that the reason exists only among similar instances (*sajātīya*), there is a statement regarding its non-existence in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).
Furthermore, it is also for the purpose of avoiding the burden of explaining the meaning through mere implication (*sāmarthya*).

Thinking that even the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) might have some purpose, the proponent of the established tenet (*siddhāntavādin*) says: "Since its existence in the locus of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*) has already been established through its pervasion by that [property], the further mention of the subject is for the sake of showing that only that which is a property of the locus of the example is the logical reason (*hetu*)."

It is suspected that [the term] is used for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Consequently, only reasons such as "being visible" (*cākṣuṣatva*) would be valid, and not reasons such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*); thus, an undesirable conclusion would follow. Therefore, a figurative application (*upacāra*) must be made.
Furthermore, has it been seen anywhere in a treatise that a statement is made for the purpose of restriction? To this, he says: "of the same class" (*sajātīya*).

"Thus," and so forth. In that regard, concerning the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*)— namely, "that which exists in the similar class (*sajātīya*), and is of two kinds [present and absent] in its absence (*tadatyaya*)"— although the exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar class (*vijātīya*), i.e., the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), is already established by the restriction "existence only in the similar class," the Master [Dignāga] stated "its absence in its absence" (*asaṃstadatyaye*) as a statement of non-existence in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) for the purpose of establishing that very restriction.

It has been explained that non-existence [is established] only when [the locus] is non-existent, and not otherwise, nor is it contradictory. Likewise here as well, the mention of the subject (*dharmin*) is suspected to be for the purpose of establishing a restriction (*niyama*).

But surely, since that which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) is not a valid reason (*ahetu*), there can be no suspicion regarding a restrictive purpose? For a reason is that which is pervaded (*vyāpta*), and nothing else.

Since the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), which resides in the subject (*dharmī*), is pervaded by the proving property (*sādhanadharma*) residing in another [subject], the inclusion of the property to be proven will occur precisely through the force of stating the reason (*hetu*) that is pervaded by that part (*tadaṃśavyāpta*); therefore, he says: "By implication" (*sāmarthyāt*), and so forth.
From the implication just mentioned, there arises the cognition characterized by the inclusion of the property to be proven.
However, for listeners of sharp intellect who pursue the meaning themselves without relying on words, there would be a burden in comprehension.

Therefore, by avoiding the mere figurative expression that leads to one's own independent inference of the wordless meaning, and by using the identical designation "property of the subject" (*dharmidharma*) instead of "property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharma*), this burden of comprehension is avoided. By the word "and" (*ca*), he says this: those who are...

Those who seek peace in the [logical] categories (*pada*) should understand this matter through the statement of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Since it is understood according to its definition, how could there be such a doubt as "that which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) is not a reason (*hetu*)"? Therefore, for the sake of removing the doubt regarding the restriction for those who follow the definition, the use of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is employed here, because [the definition] has the function of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).

The application of the word "only" (*eva*) must necessarily be determined [as follows]: since it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), namely *pakṣadharma*, no other compound is possible. And thus, because of the restriction that it is "the property of the subject alone," the pervasion by its own part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*) is contradicted; pointing out this state of having the definition of a contradictory reason (*viruddha*), he says:

If it is argued that since the property must belong to the subject (*pakṣadharmitva*), the qualification of the subject requires exclusion from others; and thus, a property that depends on such a qualification does not recur elsewhere—namely, in any other similar instance (*sapakṣa*) than the one made the subject—and that consequently, because it depends on that qualification as its subject-property, it would fail to recur elsewhere and thus become "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇatā*); [we reply: so be it.

No; because it is a qualification by way of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), as in "Caitra is an archer. We shall explain later that it is not by way of excluding connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), as in "Pārtha is the archer. For in that case, depending on the speaker's intention, it is not qualified by the subject (*pakṣa*); rather, it belongs to the subject itself, as in "Devadatta’s son. Therefore, [the definition] does not apply elsewhere.

The uniqueness of the occurrence would not be common; that is to say, there would be a contradiction with the "pervasion by that part" (*tadaṃśavyāpti*). This is because [the definition] establishes pervasion by that part through its being common. Therefore, if it is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), there is no pervasion by that part;
or if there is pervasion by that part, it is not a property of the subject—thus the definition is contradictory.

Now, if the pervasion of the probans by the probandum has not been apprehended in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*), then the reason (*hetu*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). On the other hand, if it has been apprehended, what is the use of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason in the example? Furthermore, how could the pervasion of the "portion of that" (*tadaṃśavyāpti*)—namely, the pervasion of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)—be contradicted, since pervasion is already established even in the case of the subject (*sādhyadharmin*)? [This is so] because all things are momentary.

Or rather, what positive concomitance (*anvaya*) could there be for a reason characterized by existence (*sattva*) in the case of the probandum? Therefore, because of its necessary connection with its own probandum, the reason is established as being pervaded by it; and since that [pervasion] is also established in the subject of the probandum through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the opposite case, there is no need for anything else, such as positive concomitance elsewhere. So how can this doubt be raised: "Is there not [concomitance] elsewhere"?
Regarding the phrase "the uniqueness of the occurrence":
it is true that although inference cannot arise without the reason's possession of the pervasion by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpti*) in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*), nevertheless,

the probandum cannot [be established] without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum and the probans in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

The pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established even for the subject (*dharmin*); it is for this purpose that this [objection] was raised. As for what is said—that this was raised with respect to the specific nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*) in view of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*)—that, however, refers to the case of the inference of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) in view of existence (*sattva*), because that [inference] functions as a means of cognition precisely through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

We shall examine this point further below. Therefore, for the sake of recollecting the means of valid cognition that establishes the necessary connection (pratibandha) previously grasped, the occurrence of the reason in something other [than the subject] must be required. He refutes this with the words beginning "no" (na): "There is no non-occurrence elsewhere; why? Because of non-connection (ayoga)."

The connection [of the reason] is due to the qualification of the subject (*pakṣa*) by means of its exclusion from that [other]. For a qualification does not occur solely through the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*), but also through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*). This is because where the existence of a property in a given subject is doubted, the exclusion of non-connection is logically required. An example of this is: "Caitra is an archer."

(1) For, regarding Caitra, there is doubt as to whether he possesses archery or not; consequently, when it is said, "Caitra is an archer," this exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*)— which negates the alternative possibility of non-archery raised by the listener's expectation— is what is logically required here.
Desiring to refute the position held by others, he says: "It is not by the exclusion of connection with another that there is a qualification;
for a part is a portion of that [whole], since the word 'pakṣa' does not denote the aggregate. (The term 'pervaded' refers to pervasion.)"

For in that case, there is the presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) alone, nor is there the necessary presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) therein. By this, the determination of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is also [implied].
The connection is as follows: because it does not extend elsewhere, it is "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*). Here too, the example is as follows: "Pārtha is the archer..."

Thus, although this word "archer" (*dhanurdhara*) is a general term, by the force of the context and other factors, it functions here as a term for one possessing pre-eminent qualities; for Pārtha’s status as an archer is already established, so there is no suspicion of non-application (*ayoga*). However, when the listener wonders whether such excellence exists elsewhere or not—this being the suspicion of application to another (*anyayogaśaṅkā*)—and it is then said, "Pārtha is the archer," at that time [the word] refers to that which is pre-eminent.
It is understood that Pārtha alone is the archer, and no other; therefore, in this case, the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is logically established.

Likewise, when there is a doubt as to whether this property belongs to the subject (*pakṣa*) or not, upon saying "it is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), it is understood that it is indeed a property of the subject and not a non-property. And because a property is dependent [on its locus], it functions as a qualifier; thus, non-connection (*ayoga*) is excluded, but not connection with another (*anyayoga*). This is the pervasion by its part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*).
Because there is no doubt regarding the example through the demonstration of the other [type of] connection (*anyayoga*), we shall address this:

in the fourth chapter (4.110), when it says "that part is its property" (*tadaṃśas taddharmaḥ*), does the word "that" (*tat*) refer to the subject (*pakṣa*) and not to the property (*dharma*)? For a property cannot possess another property.

The "part" (*aṃśa*) of that subject (*pakṣa*) is the property (*dharma*) to be proven (*sādhya*) of that very [subject]. If it is asked how the word "part," which is conventionally established as referring to a single portion (*ekadeśa*), can denote a property (*dharma*), he replies: "By virtue of the speaker's intention. The denotative power of words does not arise from the force of objective reality (*vastubala*), but rather from the speaker’s desire to speak (*vivakṣā*). Thus, the connection with the context is that "that part of it" is its "part" (*tadaṃśa*). (1)

If it is asked, "Why is it so?", he says: "Because the word *pakṣa* does not denote the aggregate. If the word *pakṣa* were to express the aggregate, then a part of the *pakṣa*—which consists of the aggregate of the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*)—would be the property itself.
However, by means of the word *pakṣa* used figuratively, only the locus (*dharmin*) is denoted; and since that [locus] is a single entity, how [could there be a part]?
[A portion:

He explains [the term] *pada* as "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) and so forth. Of that which exists as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), there is pervasion—that which pervades and that which is pervaded—because it is cognized as having the nature of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the pervaded (*vyāpya*). When [it is cognized] as having the nature of the pervader...

When it is intended to be expressed, the connection is that there is the existence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) precisely where the pervaded (*gamya*) exists. In the word "there" (*tatra*), the locative sense (*saptamy-artha*) is primary;
this is not primarily the sense of a substratum (*ādhāra*), because properties (*dharma*) do not possess other properties. Therefore, the meaning is as follows:
(1) wherever the pervaded exists in a given property-bearer (*dharmin*), there the pervader necessarily exists; thus, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the property of the pervader.

However, it is not determined that the pervader alone exists there, because that would entail the absence of the reason (hetu). This is because even non-pervaders, such as corporeality (mūrtatva) and the like, exist there. Nor is it determined that [the pervader] exists only there, for that would result in the fallacy of "effort-immediacy" (prayatnānantarīyakatva) and the like being non-reasons; furthermore, the reason would become "over-common" (sādhāraṇa), since eternality exists among all knowable objects (prameya). But when [it is considered as] the pervaded—

When the pervasion of the nature of things (*dharmatā*) is intended, then wherever the pervader exists, there alone does the pervaded exist, and not elsewhere. Here too, the restriction "the existence of the pervaded alone" [is implied], because the consequence of the absence of the reason would otherwise follow; it is not based on the fact that the non-pervaded also exists there. Nor is it restricted to mean that "the existence of the pervaded is only there."

For [otherwise] there would follow the consequence that a reason which exists in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) would not be a valid reason; furthermore, even a common property (*sādhāraṇa*), such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*), would become a valid reason because it necessarily exists in eternal things. By the phrase "the presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) therein," the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is implied; and by the phrase "the presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) only therein," the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is implied.

Alternatively, the description of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) properties serves to demonstrate the necessity and non-necessity [of their relationship]. By this, the reason (*hetu*) is that which is pervaded, but not the pervader, because the latter is non-necessary (*aniyata*). Now, how can a property that exists without the pervaded be a pervader? For, being unconnected with the pervaded, it would not be a pervader.
Because it is natural.

True; however, it is only the general relationship of pervader and pervaded between two properties that is ascertained. And that general impermanence which has been ascertained as the pervader of being produced immediately after an effort is [present] even in that which is not produced immediately after an effort.

That which is observed is called the "pervader" (*vyāpaka*) and is thus indefinite. Now, if impermanence can be ascertained as having the very nature of being immediately following upon effort (*prayatnānantarīyaka*), then these two possess a mutual relationship of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*); thus, the reason (*hetu*) becomes truly pervaded.
And this is the rule: that upon which there is disagreement is the probandum (*sādhya*), while the other is the means of proof (*sādhana*).

If, then, the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) were merely "a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) that is pervaded by a part of it (*tadaṃśena vyāptaḥ*)," then the reason would have only two forms—being a property of the subject and being pervaded by a part of it—whereas elsewhere it is stated to have three forms; how then is there no contradiction? To this, he says:
By this statement regarding the pervasion of that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are stated;

the meaning is that [this follows] because of the pervasion consisting in the nature of form (*rūpatva*). For instance: (1) whatever is positively concomitant with something, and whatever ceases when that thing ceases.

That very [subject] is said to be pervaded by that [reason], because pervasion consists in having that as its nature; thus, through the statement of pervasion, there is the expression of both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Consequently, since two aspects are expressed by the statement of pervasion, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, these two are ascertained within the context of the "indicative reason" (*jñāpaka-hetu*); and their ascertainment does not occur through a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather through whichever [cognition] is appropriate for each.

[The reason is that] by whatever means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) one's own [reason] is ascertained; and for whichever [subject] there is a particular means of valid cognition, that will be explained later.

Now, since the logical mark (*liṅga*) is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), how can there be its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)? If it is argued that its nature consists in the absence [of the mark] when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent, we say no.
For that very existence of the mark which occurs only when the probandum exists is itself [the mark's absence] when the probandum is absent.

This is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Thus, although there is identity between both positive and negative concomitance, their distinction is merely constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpakalpita*).

Others maintain that negative concomitance is the property of the logical mark (*liṅga*) being absent when the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is absent. Positive concomitance (*anvaya*), on the other hand, consists in the form: "wherever the property of the means (*sādhana*) exists, there the property to be proven exists. Therefore, as for what was stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kumārila:
And the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is ascertained by its respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
"The sunrise that is yet to come is not accompanied by today’s sunrise;
nevertheless, from today’s sunrise, it is inferred that it too will occur tomorrow."
When the tip of smoke is seen in the sky, fire is inferred on the ground; yet the tip of smoke follows the fire, while [the observer] remains situated on the ground.
Thus, it has been refuted [by some] that "in this way, the mark (liṅga) follows the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) by means of place and time;
