therefore, no relation called 'concomitance' (anvaya) is perceived as a constituent part of it. For the reason that the logical mark (hetu), as previously described, exists as being concomitant with the probandum (sādhya), by that very fact, this [objection] is also [refuted].
It has been replied:
"In this case, the postulation of a pervasion-relationship must likewise be rejected;
for how could that which is not concomitant with another be pervaded by it?"

For this very reason, in order to refute such a pervasion (*vyāpti*) imagined by others, the Master [Dharmakīrti] demonstrated the worldly pervasion with the words "the existence of the pervader there" (*tatra bhāva*), and so forth. The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the relationship is that which grasps the dependence of the logical mark (*liṅga*) upon the probandum (*sādhya*). And that which grasps this dependence is precisely what constitutes positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

The apprehension of pervasion belongs to that [inference] which consists of a single [negative] instance, because the very nature of pervasion is dependence upon the probandum. Therefore, from that very means of valid cognition which grasps the pervasion, there arises the certainty—even in the absence [of a positive instance]—that "wherever the pervaded is impossible, there is the absence of the pervader; wherever there is the absence of the pervader, there is the absence of the pervaded. By this, [it refutes] what is said...
By Bhaṭṭa Kumārila:
"And because it has a universal as its object, positive concomitance (anvaya) is not possible in perception;
nor is it inferred, since there is no prior knowledge of another instance of positive concomitance."

Now, if there were an inference based on positive concomitance (anvaya) that is devoid of any other positive concomitance, then since this [inference] would be established without depending on it, what would be the use of positive concomitance elsewhere?
Furthermore, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the logical mark (liṅga) with the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) cannot be established at all;
for even with great effort, that absence would not be understood due to a lack of cognition.
"As long as the limit of all opposing factors has not been determined, who is able to know from that [limit] the non-occurrence of the reason?"— this too is refuted.

The connection [of the sentence] is to be understood as follows: it should be known that the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is stated as being ascertained by its respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And thus, since the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) has been stated by the very mention of the property of the subject, there is no contradiction.
Therefore, as for what was said by Diṅnāga: "It is true that we do indeed accept inference as a means of valid cognition..."

The objection that "the definition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) is improper because it is merely well-known in the world" is refuted; for the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) of the logical mark is also well-known in the world, as in the case of smoke and so forth. [Objection: But how is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) ascertained by its respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), given that the logical mark is a universal (*sāmānya*)? (1)

Furthermore, it is not apprehended by perception because perception has only the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object; nor is that which is unapprehended a logical mark (*liṅga*). Nor is the particular, once apprehended, a logical mark because it lacks concomitance (*anvaya*). Nor is there an apprehension of the universal (*sāmānya*) by means of inference, since the inferential mark (*liṅga*) itself is of a universal nature and is not apprehended by perception; for if it were apprehended by inference, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Thus he says: "Because signs, the objects signified, and inferences are infinite, comprehension of even a single object possessing a sign would not occur even in many thousands of yugas."

Now, it might be argued that the universal (*sāmānya*), which appears as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the nature of an effect and so forth, is called the "reason" (*hetu*)—such as the reason of an effect—because it is the basis for the perception of effects and the like, and because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of it [as such].

This is incorrect; for that [universal] also is not distinct from the conceptual construction, and thus, like the conceptual construction itself, it does not exist elsewhere than in the conceptual construction.

Since it does not follow through [all instances], how could a universal (*sāmānya*) be the logical mark (*liṅga*)? Therefore, it is the very nature of smoke and so forth—excluded from what is of a different class—which, being ascertained by perception due to the context of the "informative cause" (*jñāpaka-hetu*), is called the "mark characterized as a universal" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-liṅga*) because its specific particulars are not determined.

It is not, however, either the exclusion from the dissimilar (*vijātīyavyāvṛtti*) or the form of the conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*), because these are not real entities (*avastutvāt*). Thus, this is the meaning.

By means of the ascertainment following upon direct perception— which determines the form as excluded from non-smoke— and by means of the non-determination of specific qualities such as "this appearing particular characteristic of smoke is sometimes derived from grass or from leaves," the inferential mark (*liṅga*), which is a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) consisting of multiple particular characteristics, is established within the domain of direct perception. And just as [there is] of the inferential mark's specific qualities...
In the same way, the probandum also possesses a general form because it is established by means of ninefold determination. Thus he said:

"Because it establishes merely the thing as excluded from what does not possess that nature, the logical mark is said to have a general object, since it is not established in particular distinctions."

And for such a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) which serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*), its being an effect of the probandum (*sādhyakāryatva*) and its being of the same nature as the probandum (*sādhyasvabhāvatva*) are not contradictory, because it is a real entity (*vastu*). Furthermore, since that logical mark is ascertained through perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means, everything is well-established.
With the words "these, namely," and so forth, he explains the phrase "that [reason] is of three kinds.

These three reasons are characterized as effect (*kārya*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). For example: "There is fire here because of smoke," and "This is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*."

"These are those [reasons]" means that effect-reasons (*kāryahetu*), nature-reasons (*svabhāvahetu*), and non-perception-reasons (*anupalabdhihetu*) are so described because they possess the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharman*) and are conjoined with the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Their "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*)—that is, their essential nature—is such; thus they are so called. "Smoke, etc. is the statement of the effect-reason. "Fire is here" is the statement of the result to be proven (*sādhya*). But is this not an application of the subject (*pakṣaprayoga*)? (1)

But surely, that portion of space which is in contact with fire is imperceptible; and that which is perceptible—consisting of light and so forth and appearing as a part of the sky—is not possessed of fire when it is seen as having smoke. Therefore, how is the existence of smoke established in that location through perception?

Therefore, smoke alone is properly the subject (*dharmin*). As Udyotakara stated: "The relationship between the probandum and the probans is as follows: 'This smoke possesses fire because it is smoke.

For even in that case, the constituent part of the smoke that possesses fire is not perceptible; and as for the visible portion situated in the lower part [of the smoke], it is [not possessed of fire] by means of fire.

How can there be a perceptual determination of smoke-in-general on the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) based on co-occurrence? If it is argued that "the whole (*avayavin*) consisting of smoke is perceptible," we say no; for that [whole] does not exist apart from its parts. Even if there were a worldly consensus regarding its unity, the imagined singleness of such an extent of space would not be prevented. And it is precisely this space which...

The world resorts to fire as the subject (*dharmin*), not to smoke; therefore, if an inference of fire is desired, let the inference be made with respect to that very spot as the subject—this is the intended meaning of this [statement]. However, some hold that this does not avoid the previously mentioned fault. Alternatively, the visible spot itself is the subject (*dharmin*).

The property to be proven (sādhyadharma) here is "possessing fire in the lower part," not merely "possessing fire. Since the pervasion has already been established with such a property to be proven, and since smoke is established here by direct perception, why is this not an inference? As for the claim that the probans as an effect (kāryahetu) functions as a means of cognition only in relation to a specific location and so forth—that is entirely inconsistent, because the qualification [by location]—

Because it is already established; for this probandum is established by the mere sight of smoke. Alternatively, when one has seen fire in a certain location and then removes the doubt as to whether it is *kiṃśuka* wood or something else by means of seeing smoke—this should be understood as the illustrative example. For in that case, both the locus (*dharmin*) and the property to be proven (*sādhanadharma*) are established through perception.
As for what is said—that inference [occurs] only when the subject (*dharmin*) consists of both perceptible and imperceptible aspects—that is incorrect.

Even if the reason (*hetu*) is established in the perceptible portion, there can be no inference of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) therein, because it is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādhitatvāt*).

However, while there might be an inference regarding the imperceptible portion, the reason is simply unestablished (*asiddha*) there. Furthermore, perception does not [apply to] a subject that is of a perceptible nature.

Dharma is established through perception when its locus (dharmin) is perceptible, because perception does not operate upon that which is imperceptible. Alternatively, when there is an inference of impermanence regarding sound—which is grasped by hearing—how then could the locus possess both perceptible and imperceptible natures? This [objection] is trivial. "Because it is a *śiṃśapā*" is an example of a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*).
"In a certain specific location, there is no jar, because it is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception.

Regarding this, Uddyotakara says: "The capacity of an essential nature (*svabhāva*) to function as a logical reason is utterly discarded, because the relationship between the signified and the signifier is based on difference. For there can be no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in that which is non-different. [It is not the case that] a *śiṃśapā*..."
It is of the nature of a tree, because it is excluded from that [which is not a tree]. For whatever is excluded from something else is not of the nature of that thing;

just as a cloth is not of the nature of a jar. And since the *śiṃśapā* is excluded from *khadira* and other trees, it is not of their nature. If it were of their nature, then at the very moment the logical mark (*liṅga*) is perceived, there would be no distinction [between the mark and the subject], and consequently, just like the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*), the logical mark itself could not be perceived.

Since the probandum (*sādhya*) has already been apprehended, there would be a loss of the status of being an object of inference (*anumeya*). Furthermore, if *śiṃśapā*-ness were the indicator (*gamaka*) by virtue of identity (*tādātmya*), then because identity is no different [in both cases], it would follow that *vṛkṣa*-ness (tree-ness) is also an indicator of *śiṃśapā*-ness. If it is argued that [the latter] is not an indicator because it is not invariably concomitant (*aniyata*), then invariable concomitance (*niyatatā*) alone must be the cause for being an indicator, and not identity, since identity is found even in cases of deviation (*vyabhicārin*).

Because identity is observed in the case of a tree; for if the *śiṃśapā* were not of that very nature as the tree, then there could never be a relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) between the two.

"In the case of difference, however, there is an absence of identity; thus, the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamya-gamaka-bhāva*) between the exclusions of 'non-śiṃśapā' and 'non-tree', or between the two cognitions of exclusion, must be rejected. (9a)

That is incorrect. For the *śiṃśapā* has the nature of being a particular kind of tree, and that particular kind of tree also has the nature of being a *śiṃśapā*; thus, there is identity (*tādātmya*) between both. Even given this identity, someone might be confused regarding the nature excluded from non-trees, but not regarding the nature excluded from non-*śiṃśapās*. Therefore, because the mark (*liṅga*), such as the *śiṃśapā*, is apprehended, there is no loss of its status as an object of inference (*anumeya*). And since...
A *śiṃśapā* tree does not have "tree-ness" as its intrinsic nature; therefore, "tree-ness" is not a means of cognition (*gamaka*) for the *śiṃśapā*.
Furthermore, the author of the treatise himself will refute the fault of the absence of the probandum and the probans, so this [objection] is trivial.

"Location" (*pradeśa*) is stated as the [locus] where there is non-perception. "A specific location" refers to the place indicated. "Somewhere" means in a place established for both the proponent and the opponent. "There is no jar" indicates that the conventional usage of the absence of a jar is the probandum (*sādhya*). By the words "perception," etc., the reason (*hetu*) is pointed out. The "instruments of perception" (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇāni karaṇāni*), such as the eyes and so forth, are those whose capacities are unimpeded. "Perception" (*upalabdhi*)...
The characteristics [of non-apprehension]: they consist in a specific nature that, having been attained, is capable of producing a cognition bearing its own appearance;

the meaning is that the object is included within the causal complex for the production of its own cognition. From the non-apprehension of such an object, the conventional usage of "non-existent" is established.

But how can that which does not exist in a certain place meet the conditions for perception there? For meeting the conditions for perception means being an object of cognition; and if that is the case, how could there be non-existence?
It is said: when a thing has previously been established [as existing] within a certain causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it remains so within that very same complex.

If it were to exist, it would have to be exactly like that which possesses the nature of being perceptible, and not otherwise. Therefore, it has been stated that its existence is characterized by perceptibility. Among these, two are reasons for establishing a positive entity, while one is a reason for negation.

If [an object] were to exist when the causal complex is present, it would be perceived just as it was at a previous time; having thus mentally reflected upon the fact that the object meets the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*), one establishes its negation by saying "it does not exist" because the entity does not appear. However, this does not apply to that which is invisible, because there is no means to reflect upon its appearance, and because it is never apprehended.

If it is asked: "In the absence of the visible object, how is that very causal complex apprehended? We reply: "Because of the perception of one of two entities that are objects of a single cognition. Furthermore, the fact that the negated object meets the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*) is determined by its own nature alone. This very [nature] constitutes the condition for perceptibility through its fitness for generating a cognition.

In order to demonstrate that [the object] has been attained, he says: "If it were so"—that is, if its existence were such that it is perceivable—then it would necessarily be of that very nature; not otherwise. Thus, it is never ungraspable; rather, being of that nature, it does not fail to produce cognition. This is the meaning. "Since this is so" means for that reason.

Regarding the qualification "of that which has reached the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya*) which was stated, it follows by implication that it means "of an existent thing that has reached the conditions for perception.

Here, however, the external meaning is as follows: that by which something is characterized is a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). Perception itself is the characteristic; that which has reached this is "having reached the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), meaning that its connection with cognition is non-deviant.

That which possesses such a nature is described as "of such a kind. The meaning is that when the subject (sattva) is of such a nature, knowledge necessarily ceases along with it. All proof is pervaded by affirmation and negation; and the object to be proven (sādhya), when being affirmed, is divided by two types of logical connection (pratibandha). Thus, showing that affirmation and negation depend upon three types of reasons (hetu), he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth:

among those three types of reasons, two—the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*)—are proofs for a real entity (*vastusādhana*), meaning they are proofs for an affirmation (*vidhisādhana*). The restriction "only two" does not mean that they are exclusively proofs for a real entity; for by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), through these two, the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is also established.

"One [reason] is the reason for negation. This means that non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), as defined by the previously stated characteristics, is indeed a reason for negation; however, it is not restricted to being the *only* one, because exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is understood through the two preceding reasons as well.
Someone says: "Is every kind of exclusion established by words and logical marks? It is so.
"The phrase 'precisely because of the non-apprehension of everything' means that non-apprehension alone is the single reason.

This is incorrect; for this is not stated with reference to the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because the operation of the means of valid cognition pertains only to a real entity (*vastu*). As it has been said: "Therefore, the validity of both [perception and inference] has as its object a real entity. Nor does it refer to conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*)...

This is stated on account of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), because the object itself is determined; furthermore, it is because there is no connection of the logical mark (*liṅga*) with exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).

When there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibaddhatva*), this object does not deviate [from the conclusion], because that [mark] has that [object] as its nature (*tadātmatva*). Regarding this state of having that as its nature:

If it is argued that there is no distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*), we say: no, because the distinctions between properties (*dharma*) are merely conceptualized (*parikalpanāt*).

Furthermore, even for one who maintains that in the case of non-perception (*anupalambha*), what is being proved is the fitness for the conventional usage of "non-existent" (*asad-vyavahāra-yogyatā*) and not a negation (*pratiṣedha*), and that this fitness is indeed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); likewise, when a location possessing fire is the probandum, the possession of fire by that location is simply its own intrinsic nature.

And the reason "because it possesses smoke" [proves] that the locus is non-different from the fire; thus, every reason is merely a *svabhāvahetu* (essential identity reason). This is incorrect. For if that were the case of being a prover (*gamaka*), then even donkey-hood and the like would be provers.

If you argue that it is not so because the donkey lacks the state of being an effect of fire, then in that case, the fact that smoke is an effect of fire is precisely what constitutes its status as a prover.
"How is it that the basis (*nibandhana*) is not a reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*)?
Another, however, thinks: "Non-perception (*anupalambha*) is the effect of a location; thus, when the conventional usage of 'non-existent' is to be proven, it is indeed a reason based on effect.
Furthermore, the conceptualization of being produced is the effect of the word 'impermanent'; therefore, every such reason is a reason based on effect."

That too is incorrect. For the conceptualization of "produced" (*kṛtaka*) would, by virtue of being the cause of what is produced, lead to the inference of that [product] alone, not of impermanence. If it is argued that it establishes impermanence because the nature of the produced is itself impermanent, then in that case, the cognition of impermanence would arise from "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) alone, and not from the conceptualization of the produced. It is precisely through the nature of being produced that—

Because [the capacity] indicates permanence; or else, since there would be the alternative of being produced or not being impermanent, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). The capacity to produce the conceptualization of being produced is not distinct from the produced thing itself, and that [capacity] exists neither before nor after [the production]; therefore, it is impermanent.
If, on the other hand, the capacity is non-distinct [from the produced thing], then how is it not an essential nature (*svabhāva*) as a logical reason (*hetu*) for proving impermanence?
This is of no consequence.
Furthermore, why are there only two means of establishing a real entity (*vastu*)? He says: "The connection by way of essential nature (*svabhāva*)," [which forms] the compound *sādhanakṛta*.
This means being connected by way of essential nature; that is to say, having an essential nature that is connected. When that exists, the object [is established].
The mark (*liṅga*) does not deviate from the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), which is the object.

And why is that [invariable relation] a connection by way of essential nature (*svabhāvapratibandha*)? He says: "Because of being of that nature" (*tadātmatvāt*), meaning because it has the nature of the probandum (*sādhyasvabhāvatvāt*). When there is identity with that—that is, when the means of proof (*sādhana*) has the nature of the probandum—whatever is the probandum, that very thing is the means of proof.

Regarding the phrase "(namiti)," which refers to the non-difference between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*): having raised the objection that the reason (*hetu*) is therefore a part of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñā*), he says "no," and so forth. This is because the various properties (*dharma*) that constitute the probandum and the probans are conceptually constructed and superimposed through their distinct exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*).

This is what is meant: a distinction between properties (*dharma-bheda*) is superimposed, and by that, a distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) [is established]. For it is said that the certain indicator is the "indicator" (*gamaka*), and that which is to be ascertained is the "indicated" (*gamya*). Since the object of ascertainment is precisely that which has been superimposed, the distinction between properties is superimposed through the distinction of ascertainment. We shall explain this further in the section on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
And thus it has been stated [in *Pramāṇavārttika* 3:163–73]:

"Indeed, this entire conventional practice of inference and the object of inference is constructed by the intellect; for the distinction between property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) exists only as mounted upon the intellect. The distinction in terms of property and property-bearer is produced by the form of the intellect (*buddhyākāra*), not by the object itself. The intellect—

(Conceptual construction) Because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) follow merely one's own whim and are based on what is not the [actual] object, when there is a cognition of an object through that which has a constructed object, there would be the attainment of only what is not the object. Even in the case of an effect, there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with its own nature, because that nature arises from it. These two—[the essential nature and the effect]—are cognitions of the inferable even though they do not manifest as that [inferable itself], because they do not arise directly [from the object].

The Master Dignāga also did not state this, as he says: "And likewise," and so forth. "All indeed" means that even in cases where there is a real distinction between the probandum and the probans—such as fire and smoke—since conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is impossible through the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is the conventional usage of the inferential mark (*anumāna-liṅga*), which is that by which one infers; the object of inference (*anumeya*), which is the subject of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*); and the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). These constitute their conventional usage.

It corresponds to diversity. That is to say, the linguistic convention of difference [is established] by means of a distinct form—[namely,] the distinction between the property and the property-bearer—which is mounted upon the intellect and has entered into the appearance of the intellect. If, then, all properties and property-bearers were merely conceptual constructs of the intellect, then Bhaṭṭa says: [2]

Or, even if a distinction exists, it is conceptually constructed by the intellect (buddhiprakalpita) and postulated for the sake of conventional usage based on the properties of the probandum and the probans.
Therefore, regarding this proof (*sādhana*) employed by you—namely, that "cognition arises everywhere"—it would constitute a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
To this, he says: "Difference," and so forth. Or rather, it is the meaning itself that conveys the meaning; it is merely a property (*dharma*)...

This distinction—the multiplicity consisting of "this is the property" (*dharma*) and "this is the property-bearer" (*dharmin*)—is created by the form of cognition and is merely imagined by the intellect; it is neither the object nor the logical mark (*liṅga*). [Objection: Why does the comprehension of the object not arise from a logical mark that is itself constructed by conceptualization? [Response: He says, "By conceptualization," and so forth. [It is because] of the distinctions among conceptualizations... [of conceptualization].
The meaning is as follows: because words (*viśeṣāṇām*) follow merely the speaker’s intention (*icchāmātrānurodhitvena*), they do not by themselves depend upon external objects;

since [the object] does not arise directly [from them], they lack a real objective basis. Therefore, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is imagined by those [words] which have non-existent things as their basis, and this is the "object" (*viṣaya*);
thus, it is an "imagined object. If one accepts that the cognition of an object arises from such a cause...
In measuring [the object], there would only be the acquisition of what is useless and never the acquisition of what is useful;

thus he states the second characteristic of an obstacle: "of the effect as well," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of that nature" (*tatsvabhāvasya*), which refers to the nature of the effect, he says this in response to one who does not accept the validity of inference based on its arising from that [cause] (*tadutpatteḥ*).

The connection is that these two—the [inference based on] essential nature and the [inference based on] effect—are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the object to be inferred. He says "these two" because non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is included within the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Alternatively, he says "two" with reference to what has been introduced [in the preceding discussion].

Because there is no necessary rule [that they must appear as such]. "Cognitions of the inferable" (*anumeya-pratyaya*) refers to the two types of cognition—[those arising from] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and [those arising from] a cause (*kāraṇa*)—which have the inferable as their object. "Even though they do not manifest that" (*atat-pratibhāsitve 'pi*) means even though they do not manifest the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the inferable. They do not manifest that because they do not arise directly from it. How, then, is this...?

He states that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Because of "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*), [the mark] arises indirectly from the two inferable things, namely the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the cause (*kāraṇa*). "Non-deviating from that" (*tadavyabhicārin*) means non-deviating from the inferable object. For this reason, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, as for what was said by Vidyākara: "A valid means of knowledge is the determination of an object not yet known; therefore, inference is not [a valid means of knowledge]."... [omitted] ...it is not so. This is because the determination of an object not yet known occurs through inference as well. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "inference is not a valid means of knowledge because it is dependent on other means of knowledge," that too is incorrect. For even in the case of perception, since one acts toward an object after having ascertained its nature through the recollection of a previously experienced connection, it would follow that perception is not a valid means of knowledge. Thus, it is established that inference is indeed a valid means of knowledge. It is stated: "Inference is the cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses], which arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is itself perceived and possesses three characteristics. Regarding this, the word "perceived" (*dṛṣṭa*) is used to exclude [marks] such as the horns of a rabbit (*śaśaviṣāṇa*), which are not perceived. The word "logical mark" (*liṅga*) is used to exclude the object itself, the person who knows the object, and the means of knowledge. The phrase "possessing three characteristics" is used to exclude those marks that have only one or two characteristics. The word "cognition" (*jñāna*) is used to exclude the physical body (*deha*), sense organs (*indriya*), and so forth. The phrase "not in contact" (*asaṃnikṛṣṭa*) is used to exclude perception. "Object" (*artha*) is used to exclude the cognition of the mark itself. "Arises" (*utpanna*) is used to exclude the latent impression (*saṃskāra*). "Inference" (*anumāna*) is used to exclude the result of inference (*anumiti*). Now, the three characteristics of a logical mark are as follows: (1) being present in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), (2) being present in the similar class (*sapakṣasattva*), and (3) being absent in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣāsattva*). Among these, the "subject" (*pakṣa*) is the locus where the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is intended to be demonstrated.
