The claim that "it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it lacks the capacity to determine an object" is refuted; for every discerning person desiring purposeful action (*pravṛtti*) seeks a means of valid cognition precisely because it presents an object that serves as the locus of such action, and the object that is the locus of action must indeed be capable of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*). Furthermore, the capacity of a thing for the causal efficacy to be accomplished through action—pertaining to the future—is not determined by perception.

Since it has been stated that [cognition] is "known," how can its validity consist merely in the determination of its object? Therefore, perception is a means of valid cognition because, by arising with respect to its own object, it produces the ascertainment—"This is that very same thing which was previously apprehended by me as functioning effectively in a continuous stream"—and thus prompts action;
likewise, inference is also a means of valid cognition.

With the words "of perception as well," etc., he states the pervasion (*vyāpti*). "Only non-deviation from the object" means that the validity of perception exists only when there is the presence of an object previously determined to be capable of performing its intended function; otherwise, in the absence of such an object, the perception that arises would be deceptive, because it would not correspond to the determined object. This—

What is the case? When direct perception does not determine an object that is capable of causal efficiency, and if the means of valid cognition were to deviate even from such an object, it would not be a valid cognition at all. Furthermore, what else could non-deviation from another thing consist of if not its arising from that [object]? Whatever non-deviation there is of one thing with another distinct entity, that is nothing other than its arising from that; it is not anything else. (10b)
The meaning is that "non-deviation" consists precisely in being produced from that [object].

Why? Because there is no necessity of non-deviation due to the absence of a rule of coexistence for those things whose forms are not dependent—that is, whose natures are unconnected. Therefore, perception is precisely the production from an object ascertained by its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
The sense is that non-deviation constitutes validity, and since that [non-deviation] exists in inference as well, both are equal.
By this, the following view is also refuted: "Because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not secondary (*agauṇa*), the ascertainment of an object from inference is difficult to obtain.
If "not secondary" is said to mean being non-figurative (*anupacarita*), then inference is also certainly non-figurative, because its nature consists of unerring cognition (*askhaladbuddhi*).

If the collection of both the property and the substratum (*dharmidharmin-samudāya*) were the object to be proven (*sādhya*), it would be impossible for the reason (*hetu*) to possess the property of being present in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) or to have a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the presence of the reason in the subject, the status of being the *sādhya* must be figuratively attributed to the substratum; and for the sake of establishing the positive concomitance, it must be so attributed to the property (*dharma*).
Thus, because its object is figurative, inference itself is figurative.
Therefore,
if the effect were to indicate [the cause] solely by virtue of its arising from it, then a relationship of indicator and indicated would obtain in every respect;
that is incorrect, because in the world, mere smoke— pervaded by mere fire— is seen only in that locus (*dharmin*) where fire exists.

Since cognition occurs [in this way], what here is merely a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*)? And thus, the status of the whole (*samudāya*) as the probandum (*sādhya*) is established. As it has been said:

"When the property (*dharma*) alone is to be proven in respect to the locus (*dharmin*), the establishment of the intended whole is thereby accomplished. Nor does the application of the term "probandum" to the object of inference (*anumāna-viṣaya*) imply that the inference itself is metaphorical.
Now,
it might be argued that direct perception (pratyakṣa) is a valid means of knowledge because it is non-figurative and non-erroneous, whereas inference (anumāna) lacks validity because it is erroneous.

That is incorrect. (1) For even in the case of an erroneous inference of fire, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is observed in the world because it arises from that [perception] and determines an external fire, just like perception. If, on the other hand, perception were not accepted as a valid means of knowledge, it would contradict worldly consensus; for both perception and inference are recognized as valid means of knowledge by the world.

Now, it is not that the validity of perception and inference as means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is being denied. Rather, when one objects that a logical mark (*liṅga*)—whether characterized by three features (*trilakṣaṇa*) or four features (*caturlakṣaṇa*)—is not established by any means of knowledge, if inference is then stated as the proof for that [mark], the same objection applies there as well. Thus, all the sūtras are merely intended to provide such counter-objections. And so:

As for the Sūtra statement: "(1) 'The absence of a specific [reason] following [the probandum] is a case of proving what is already established by the general [reason],' (1)" that too is incorrect; because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) has already been implied by the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Nor is the opponent questioned by means of what is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇaka*), because [such a means] is unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent. Now,

if the inference consisting of the verbal expression is not a valid means of knowledge for the speaker, yet he nevertheless communicates it to the opponent through that speech, then in that case, questioning is carried out by means of what is not a valid means of knowledge.

That too is incorrect. For from the speech of both [the speaker and the listener], the cognition of the object arises as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it determines the object; however, since the speaker’s own comprehension has already been established, it is not a valid means of knowledge for him. But if it is not a valid means of knowledge for him, then it is not a valid means of knowledge for either of them. How, then, could this cognition arise from that?

As for what was also said— that "an inference is negated by means of an inference established for the opponent"— that too is refuted by this [very argument]. For if [the fire] were a signifier by virtue of conjunction, [it would follow that] "fire is not non-conjoined with any part whatsoever."

"Or rather, smoke is in every respect [the sign] by which the manifestation [of fire] is apprehended from smoke. This objection—which was raised against another by the Master Dignāga regarding the undesirable consequence of a universal relation between the signifier and the signified—is here also anticipated as a concern regarding the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), beginning with the words "If... and so forth, on the grounds that the effect arises from the probandum.

If it is argued that [the relationship between cause and effect] exists in every respect because of the relation of producer and produced, we say no; for in the absence of that [relation], there would be no necessity regarding the arising of one from the other.
For thus:
"A result is invariably concomitant with as many essential natures as exist in its cause."

The cause is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); it is the cause because of the necessity of being its effect. Those [things] which do not exist without those [others] are [the indicators]. The word "of the cause" (*kāraṇasya*) is to be supplied as the indicator (*gamaka*). In every respect, the relationship between the indicated (*gamya*) and the indicator (*gamaka*) is established. Of fire, the generality (*sāmānya*)—11a.

Like the general property (*dharma*), specific properties such as "arising from grass" or "arising from leaves" would also be [inherently] cognizable. Furthermore, just like the specific properties of smoke, its general properties such as "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and "earthiness" (*pārthivatva*) would also become indicators (*gamaka*). Why? Because there is a relationship of produced and producer in every respect. For instance, just as fire is a producer by virtue of its general properties such as "fireness," "substantiality," and "existence," [so too would its specific properties be producers].

Likewise, [it is produced] by specific qualities such as being made of reeds or leaves; and just as smoke, when produced, is endowed with its own specific, restricted properties such as "smokeness" and "pale-white," it is likewise endowed with general properties such as "existence" (*sattva*) and "substantiality" (*dravyatva*).
Therefore, since the relationship of effect and cause exists between these two, the relationship of the signifier and the signified would likewise exist. To this, he says:
"Not so," and so forth. There is no relationship of produced and producer in every respect; therefore, how could there be a relationship of signifier and signified?

If one asks why, it is because in the absence of those—namely, in the absence of those specific properties such as being produced from fuel (*tārṇa*, *pārṣṇa*, etc.)—there would be smoke in general, and thus the restriction of its production (*tadutpatti-niyama*) would consist in the fact that it arises from those very specific properties.

Because of its absence; that is to say, in the absence of that [fire], there is an absence of the universal property (*sāmānyadharma*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) which occurs when fire is absent—a restriction of origination (*tadutpattiniyama*) consisting in the form "this belongs to fire alone. How could there be a relationship of producer and produced in every respect, from which a relationship of signifier and signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*) would follow in every respect?

Since this is so, therefore the effect—such as smoke—is "inseparable" (*avinābhāvi*) by means of its own inherent natures (*svabhāvaiḥ*), such as being smoky (*dhūmatva*), etc.; here the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇā*). "Inseparable" means that which does not exist without [the cause]. In what is it inseparable? In the cause; that is, within the domain of the cause. Alternatively, "in the cause" (*kāraṇe*) is the locative case of the substratum (*ādhārasaptamī*); [it refers to] the inherent natures belonging to the cause.

The meaning is that the effect is the indicator (*gamaka*) of those general properties residing in the cause with which it is invariably concomitant, such as "fire-ness" (*agnitva*), "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), and so forth. Why is this? Because of the restriction to being its effect;
for there exists a restriction of this nature: that the effect belongs only to those very general properties residing in the cause.
For that effect never deviates from its general property. Thus far, it has been explained that the general properties residing in the cause are what is to be known (*gamyā*).
Now, demonstrating that the specific properties residing in the effect are the indicators (*gamaka*), he says: "By those very [properties]," and so forth. The effect, too...

It is by those very properties inherent in themselves that they indicate the properties considered to be the causes. If it is argued that this would entail a relationship of produced and producer between smoke-ness and the part [of the mountain]—since [smoke-ness] does not occur in anything other than fire—[the answer is]: no, because what is intended is the apprehension of the specific limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of the mark (*liṅga*) produced by that [fire]. When [properties] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) are intended without qualification, then for them...

Specific properties such as solidity and so forth, which reside in the effect, do not exist without the general properties residing in the cause; for here too, it is understood that there is a rule of being an effect [only] in dependence upon those very specific properties residing in the effect in relation to the general properties residing in the cause.
This is because there is a rule of being an effect based on those specific properties residing in the effect in relation to the general properties residing in the cause.

If the relationship of the signifier and the signified were to exist solely through the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between general properties residing in the cause and specific properties residing in the effect, then there would be a partial relationship of producer and produced. In that case, only the general properties of fire would be the producers, while only the specific properties of smoke would be the produced. Yet, the relationship of producer and produced is intended to be absolute in every respect.
Thus, there is a contradiction with one's own tenet. He addresses this [objection]: (1) "There is no consequence of a part-whole relationship between producer and produced;

for we maintain that the entity is partless and that the relationship of producer and produced exists in its entirety. Furthermore, the relationship of signifier and signified is also intended to exist in its entirety. He states this in the passage beginning with "tajjanya" (produced by that). For if the effect were [produced] by them...

The specific quality produced by the specific qualities residing in the cause can be apprehended, because it is accepted that there is an apprehension of the specific quality produced by a probans-based reason. For indeed, when smoke is apprehended as not being heavy, there occurs the inference of its fire. Likewise, there is a specific quality of the mark (*liṅga*).

The specific characteristic (*liṅga*) itself is the particularity, namely the defining mark of smoke; for it is intended that the capacity to indicate [the probandum] belongs to those [categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, which have that [smoke] as a qualifying adjunct (*upādhi*). Indeed, substantiality and the like, when qualified by smoke, do not deviate from fire.
Because of that [reasoning], at that time,
smoke alone is the indicator (*gamaka*) there, and not properties such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) qualified by it; just as in the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*).
"In the case of 'because it is knowable' (*prameyatvāt*), it is precisely 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*) that is the indicator, not 'knowability.

This is true. However, some say that this statement was made merely for the purpose of demonstrating non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). But another says: smoke is not subject to deviation here; rather, the mention of the universal (*sāmānya*) is for the sake of all cognizers who have perceived [it]."

Cognition occurs first with respect to the general form (*sāmānyākāra*) of an object, followed by the determination of its specific features (*viśeṣa*). In that process, the general form that has been apprehended is not at all abandoned. Therefore, by virtue of the cognizer’s determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*), it is the general form as qualified by the specific feature that becomes the probans (*liṅga*), and not the specific feature itself, because the latter is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

This is quite young [in its reasoning]. For if this rule holds—that the apprehension of a particular must be preceded by the apprehension of a universal—then how can there be a cognition of smoke-in-general alone, devoid of properties such as substantiality (*dravyatva*)? Furthermore, the objection previously stated remains entirely unavoidable. Therefore, this is the correct position here: that the particular characteristic of the mark (*liṅga*) is employed precisely as a qualifier of the universal.
(d) As for the state of being a non-reason (*ahetutva*): indeed, the state of being a reason would exist only upon the inclusion of [the property of] being a reason, and not otherwise.

When, then, do the general properties residing in the logical mark (*liṅga*) fail to be indicative? To this he says: "unqualified," and so forth. When properties such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) are intended as unqualified, then, because they are deviant (*vyabhicāra*), their status as indicators is not accepted.
2. Consideration of non-apprehension:
Even an entity [is not established] when [the cognition] conforms merely to the existence of the entity itself. //4//

The term "cause" (hetu) carries over [from the previous context]. The identity (tādātmya) of a cause exists only in that which conforms strictly to it, and not in that which depends on something else;

for there is no necessity that what arises from the existence of that [cause] must necessarily exist subsequently, since causes can deviate from their effects. Thus, [identity] is not accepted as the means of cognition (gamaka).

(1) The result of the non-perception of the perceptible is the non-occurrence [of means of knowledge]; when [an object] is absent, the result of the non-occurrence of the means of knowledge is the cognition of its absence, depending on certain distinctions of causes. //5//

Non-occurrence of the means of valid cognition is non-apprehension. Regarding non-existence, non-occurrence is like an effect. [In the margin: Concerning the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), he says: "The application of existence, cognition, and verbal designation..."

"Essential nature" (*svabhāva*), etc. The word "reason" (*hetu*) is understood [to carry over] from the phrase "the reason for those. When essential nature is the probandum (*sādhya*), what kind of thing is it? It is that which conforms to the mere existence of the entity; that is, the reason is the mere existence of the entity. [In this context,] "essential nature" is the reason. The inclusion of the term "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of demonstrating independence from any other object. Why is it that essential nature conforms only to that [mere existence]?

He states the reason: "For the identity (*tādātmya*) of an object consists solely in its conformity to that [object]; it exists only in that which is of the nature of the means of proof (*sādhana*), not in what depends on something else. Identity does not exist in what occurs later and is dependent upon another cause. If one asks why, he says: "In the existence of that," and so forth. [It refers to] the existence of that cause, whether it is about to be or has already become [the effect], [and not] from another cause...

Because there is no necessary rule regarding that which exists subsequently to a dharma that possesses a cause; for it is not necessarily the case that something existing later, being dependent on other causes, must come to be. What is the reason? Because causes can deviate from their effects. Since causes are subject to the possibility of obstruction, how could the effect necessarily arise from them?

But surely, no one accepts that the nature of the probans (*sādhana*) is identical to that of the probandum (*sādhya*); so how can it be said that identity consists solely in following the existence of that [probandum]? The intention is as follows: even by those who accept the two properties (*dharma*) of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) as distinct, it must necessarily be admitted that there is the coming into being after not having existed, and the ceasing to exist after having existed.

Otherwise, producedness (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*) would not belong to cloth and other things, just as they do not belong to the self (*ātman*) and so forth. Therefore, let that very coming-into-being after having not existed be producedness, and let that very non-existence after having existed—non-abiding—be impermanence; what is the use of postulating another universal (*sāmānya*)? He says: "[Because it is] unperceived... and so on.
It is like the negation of a necklace [which is established] by means of its effect. For their perception exists because they exist.

Indeed, this is the nature of the reasons that establish the negation of existence and non-existence, which is similar to the case [of the necklace]. Thus, it is not the case that perception itself is the entity;

rather, it is either the characteristic of a thing's fitness [for perception], or the operation of the cognition that takes that [thing] as its object. This is because from that [fitness or cognition] proceeds the application of the terms "existence," "cognition," and "linguistic convention."

The non-existence of entities is established through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), depending on a distinction in the logical reason (*hetu*). In some cases, because it is the effect of the cognition of non-existence, non-apprehension is the reason; for its "distinction" (*bheda*) is indeed its qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*). [An entity] does not possess existence characterized by perceptibility. Here, if non-existence is to be proven by the mark (*liṅga*) of non-apprehension, then non-apprehension itself—
If it were argued that there must be another apprehension to establish the [first] apprehension, an infinite regress would follow, and thus no comprehension would be possible.

Alternatively, if non-apprehension could exist even in the absence of apprehension, then the absence of existence itself would be established; thus, non-apprehension would be useless. Or, if non-apprehension is established through the apprehension of something else, then non-apprehension is established by perception.

"Non-occurrence," and so forth. Of what is there non-occurrence? Of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The plural number is used because there is a multiplicity of means of valid cognition due to the distinction between individual instances. [This refers to] that which depends upon scripture (*āgama*).
"It is said that [the means of knowledge] is established.

He thinks as follows: because there is no distinction between the cognition and the object of cognition insofar as they both consist of the nature of awareness (*bodharūpatva*), the means of knowledge—such as perception and the rest—which consist of the nature of awareness, are established by themselves (*svataḥ*). However, the object of knowledge, such as a jar and so forth, being insentient (*jaḍarūpatva*) by nature, depends upon a means of knowledge.

Since there is no distinction between the absence of cognition and the absence of the object of cognition due to their both being formless (*nīrūpa*), how can it be said that the absence of cognition is established intrinsically (*svataḥ*) while the absence of the object of cognition is established through the absence of cognition? Now, if it is argued that the absence of cognition is not established by another [cognition], because cognitions, being self-cognizing in nature, lack the property of co-occurring within a single cognition; then, if [the absence of cognition were] merely...
In one's own continuum, knowledge would exist and should be perceived; since it is not perceived, its non-existence is established by itself as a matter of course.
Likewise, the absence of existence would also be established. For in that case too, if existence were present, it would be perceived; [but it is not].

From the perception [of the locus], it is determined that "the object does not exist"; therefore, non-apprehension of the object is the means for establishing its absence. Now, in order to refute the position that consciousness itself is the other entity, [the author says] "Now," and so forth. Through the apprehension of the ground as distinct from the jar and other objects, the non-apprehension of the jar is established; this is non-apprehension established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

This is what is meant: because the state of being a grasper of a jar and the state of being a grasper of the ground are conjoined within a single cognition, when that cognition occurs as a grasper of the ground alone, it then determines the absence of the state of being a grasper of a jar;
thus, the non-apprehension of the jar is established by perception itself through this very experience.
In the same way, why is non-existence not established by the existence of another? Just as [non-existence is established] through non-perception, so too is it for both.

The intention is that the jar and its location are connected to a single cognition. Why would the existence of the object to be negated—such as the ground as distinct from the jar—not be established by the establishment of the existence of that other [ground]?
Now, one might ask: since non-existence is of the nature of the cessation of an entity, how can it be said to be established by perception?

He thinks as follows: Non-existence (abhāva) does not exist at all; rather, it is merely that perception, which has existence as its object, causes the ignorant to engage with the non-existence of other things. Therefore, what was stated—that non-existence is apprehended through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)—is incorrect.

For, first of all, the mutual non-existence of jars and the like is not identical [to those things], because if it were, it would follow that when a jar is destroyed, a cloth or some other thing would arise.

Because the absence of cloth and so forth would have already perished. Alternatively, if the absence were distinct [from the entities], then there would be no mutual distinction between jars and the like. For when the cloth—which is of the nature of the absence of the jar—does not exist, then the cloth would be the jar itself. Or, just as the jar possesses the nature of a jar because it is distinct from the absence of the cloth, so too would it be for the cloth and other things; [for they too would be distinct] from the absence of the jar.
Precisely because they are distinct.

Nor can difference be produced in the absence of these things which are mutually non-distinct, since difference is incapable of effecting a distinction between what is distinct and what is non-distinct. Furthermore, mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) is not possible among things that are non-distinct. Nor...

Difference is not produced by the non-existence of mutually distinct things, because they arise from their own causes as already distinct. Nor is the conventional usage of "difference" produced [by that non-existence]. For the very arising of entities in their respective individual forms is difference per se;
and that, precisely because it appears in direct perception, is the cause for the conventional usage of difference.
Therefore, that which is stated—"the establishment of the non-confusion of entities depends upon the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence"—is refuted. Furthermore:

(1) The distinction between existence and non-existence is not based on non-existence, for that would lead to an infinite regress. If, on the other hand, the distinction exists by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), then that same [distinction] would apply to existent things as well; so what is the use of postulating non-existence? Nor, in the absence of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), could there be... [of an effect].
The consequence of beginninglessness does not follow, because there is no arising in the absence of a cause.

But is it not the case that, when prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) exists, arising occurs from the cause, whereas it would not occur if prior non-existence were absent, since [the effect] would already be present?
If this were so, the production of an effect would never occur, because the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the contrary [effect] would be constantly present.

Nor can the production of the effect result from the destruction of that [non-existence], for that would entail the undesirable consequence of admitting the production of an effect even in the absence of its prior non-existence.
Furthermore, the production of the effect itself cannot be the destruction of the prior non-existence, since such production is impossible due to the presence of the contrary [effect].

Because prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not destroyed at the time when the cause exists, yet it is destroyed at the time of the production of the effect— just like the destruction of the cause itself— therefore, prior to its production, the effect possesses neither existence nor non-existence, because its properties do not exist and because a real entity is partless. Rather, when it is produced, it is conventionally designated as "existent," and at other times, it is designated as "non-existent."

Therefore, it is said that "the non-existent arises. Furthermore, the Master himself will later state that the nature of destruction is non-existence. And whatever arises from something is called its effect and its cause. Since these exist for only a single moment, they are perishable by their very nature.

The mutual distinction [of things] is established precisely by their form (*rūpa*) as they arise; therefore, even in the absence of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) occurs indeed through the differentiation of causes and so forth. Furthermore, no mutual distinction among prior non-existence and the others is perceived, because only the cessation of a jar or similar object—whether before, after, or elsewhere—is perceived as non-different. Even if...
A difference in time is perceived; for the universal "cowness" (gotva), though perceived as related to many different times and so forth, does not thereby become manifold.
Furthermore, since cessation is formless, how can there be multiplicity in non-existence? This is because non-existence consists in the negation of existence.
This is stated only with reference to that fool who desires the existence of an effect prior to its production, after its destruction, or elsewhere.
(1) By stating that "the effect is non-existent before, after, and elsewhere," one merely negates the superimposition of existence;
therefore, what was said—that these forms could not belong to a non-entity—is refuted.

Furthermore, this should be seen as refuted by the fact that there is no relation whatsoever between an entity and the two states of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).

The relationship characterized by origination from that (*tadutpatti*) or characterized by opposition (*virodha*) does not exist because [the two terms] do not coexist and thus do not reside together. For this very reason, there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).

Nor is there a relationship of qualifier and qualified precisely because of non-coexistence, since the nature of being a qualifier and a qualified does not exist in the entity itself. This [relationship] exists only [by means of another relationship].

It is conceptualized [as such], like the relationship between a staff and its bearer. Furthermore, if the cognition "the prior non-existence of an entity" occurs by virtue of the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), then there would likewise be a cognition "the existence of prior non-existence and so forth," since the relation is no different. Therefore, the cognition of prior non-existence and the like as being related to an entity when they are actually unrelated is nothing but an error.

Furthermore, there is no mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) among entities. For the cessation of a jar is not the cessation of a cloth, as it is not so perceived; nor is it logical that such [cessation] belongs to the cloth simply because it exists within it. If this were the case, then prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the like would also constitute mutual non-existence, since they exist in their respective causes and so forth. Therefore, there is only absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), and nothing else.

Since there is no other absence [than non-existence], there is no distinction between prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the others; how then can it be said that there are four kinds of non-existence? Furthermore, the refutation of the perception of non-existence has already been stated in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*, so it is not discussed here. [Objection: But since non-existence is experienced as being non-existent, how can its ascertainment be through perception? [Response: This is not a fault. *Note: The bracketed portions indicate textual fragments or clarifications based on the context of the original Sanskrit fragments.*

The apprehension of its absence [is established] because its apprehension is impossible when it is present; as it has been said: "Existence is perception, provided there is no deficiency in other causes and there is no deviation from that [object]; non-existence is non-perception, and non-perception is the perception of something else. Therefore, this is the meaning: [the statement] "perception determines non-existence" does not mean that it determines it [directly]. That...

And the ascertainment of the non-existence of the perceptible is simply the ascertainment of its absence. Thus, it is established that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising in the wake of perception conforms to the object of that perception. Therefore, since the conventional usage regarding the non-existence of an object is established by perception—just like the conventional usage regarding the non-perception [of a cause]—this [non-existence] is not proven by means of an inferential mark (*liṅga*). Thus far, for one who is not deluded...

Furthermore, when non-apprehension itself is the [means of establishing] the non-existence of such things, then—even though the object is established—one who, due to delusion, does not understand the linguistic usage of the term "knowledge" as referring to the subject, proceeds to establish the convention by demonstrating the object. For example:
"This is indeed a cow, because it consists of a collection of [features] such as the dewlap. And thus, even the objection regarding the unestablished nature of the example [is resolved].

It is countered: because we observe that even when an object is apprehended, there are those who do not apprehend the subject [of that apprehension]. Thus, for these two, the non-perception of the perceptible does not deviate from absence; therefore, the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding absence is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Nor can it be said that there is a deviation of non-perception due to the existence of absences that are not perceived, even though they are capable of being perceived.

Thus, it is correct to say that [non-existence] cannot be treated [as an object] in this way; for if this were so, even perception would not be a determiner of non-existence. Since there is doubt, it is not logical that one thing which determines [an object] should be something other than a factor for conventional usage.
Therefore, because it determines through perception, it brings about the conventional usage of the non-existence of the perceptible, just as it does for existence.

[The author] asks: "How, then, can this conventional usage of existence (*sadvyavahāra*) be that which is to be proven? He says: "But when," and so forth. For in such a case, the non-existence of non-existent objects is simply the non-apprehension of what is capable of being apprehended, and nothing else. Even though the object of the conventional usage of absence has been established by perception, [there may still be] delusion regarding the subject—that which is non-existent yet appears as if existent.

Knowledge has the form "it does not exist. And the word "it does not exist" refers to a person's activity or conventional usage characterized by the absence of doubt regarding coming and going. A person who does not apprehend those [objects]—by means of pointing out the object, namely, the perception of a place devoid of a jar which is the locus for the conventional usage of non-existence—at that time, during the conventional usage of non-existence...

[They] are being applied. He states an example: "Just as," and so forth. A cow is nothing other than the collection of [features] such as the dewlap; therefore, it is not "cowness" (*gotva*) that is to be proven there, but rather the linguistic convention (*go-vyavahāra*) of "cow. When this dull-witted person—who has already applied the convention of "cow" to a brindled cow (*śābaleya*)—does not apply the convention of "cow" to a spotted cow (*bāhuleya*) because he perceives it as lacking the form of the brindled cow, he is shown the underlying cause [for the application].

By this [means], the conventional usage of "cow" is set in motion. For the conventional usage of "cow" is based on the collection of features such as the dewlap and so forth; it is not based on the specific form of Śābaleya (the brindled cow). Since that same basis exists in Bāhuleya (the black cow) as well, why should the usage not be applied there too?
Similarly, even in a place devoid of a jar, one is led to the conventional usage of "non-existent" by demonstrating the basis for its non-perception.

And likewise, by that very [reason] through which this conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is established, even the objection regarding the non-establishment of the example (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*) is warded off and rejected. For when non-existence is to be proven from the mark (*liṅga*) of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), if the non-existence of the probandum (*sādhya*) were not [established] in the subject (*pakṣin*) by that very mark, then it would also not be [established] in the subject of the example; in that case too there would be another example, and thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). (1) [Conventional usage...]

But there is no infinite regress when the *hāra* (the means of apprehension) is what is to be proven, because it is simply the application at a later time of that very linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) which was previously set in motion.

[Objection: Surely, one who perceives an object also perceives the subject; how then can the linguistic usage itself be something yet to be proven? [The author] says: "The object," and so forth. For in the world, such persons are indeed seen who—regarding the object—...

[This applies] even to those whose objects are not yet engaged in practice. For example, a Sāṃkhya who has set out [with the thought] that "there is no *rajas* in *sattva*"—because of the presence or absence of the cause of his own error—he has stated that the result is the negation of the conventional usage of "existent. This is because in one case there is doubt, while in the other there is error. Among these, the former is said to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the negation of the conventional usage of "existent."

But there is no utility for [the perception of] the absence [of the reason] in cases such as the observation of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), because of doubt. However, the second [type of non-apprehension] is appropriate here as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, even the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) does not proceed with respect to a lump of clay due to the absence of certainty regarding its cause; rather, it proceeds toward the linguistic convention of the absence of a jar once the non-perception has been shown to be the cause.

The conclusion is stated with the words "In this way" and so forth. In the manner thus described, these two non-apprehensions—the apprehension of the perceptible and the non-apprehension of the imperceptible—are equal in having the negation of the conventional usage of existence as their result.
How so? By means of the presence or absence of the cause for its own opposite; by the word "own" (*sva*), the essential nature of the conventional usage of existence is grasped.

By the word "contradiction" (*viparyaya*), the discourse of non-existence (*asad-vyavahāra*)—which is opposed to the discourse of existence—is understood. Their causes are their own contradictory causes (*svaviparyaya-hetu*). Among these, the cause of its own [existence] is perception (*upalabdhi*), while the cause of its contradiction is the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*). Their absence and presence are the absence and presence of their own contradictory causes. By means of those two...

This is what is meant: (1) In the case of the non-apprehension of the imperceptible (*adṛśyānupalabdhi*), since apprehension—which is the cause for the linguistic convention of existence (*sadvayavahāra*)—is absent when perception and inference have ceased, there is the cessation of the linguistic convention of existence. However, in the case of the non-apprehension of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), because the cause for the linguistic convention of non-existence (*asadvyavahāra*)—which is contrary to the linguistic convention of existence—is present, that [convention] proceeds; thus, by that means, there is the cessation of the linguistic convention of existence.

The result—the prohibition of the conventional usage of "existent"—is the same in both cases. Now, one might ask: since there is doubt regarding the existence of an object even when its perception has ceased, how can the conventional usage of "existent" be precluded? To this he says: "In one case," meaning that because there is doubt regarding existence in the case of non-apprehension whose object is invisible, the conventional usage of existence—which consists of certainty—[cannot arise from it].

The [logical] reason (*hetu*) indeed ceases [to apply], but the doubtful application of existence (*sattva-vyavahāra*) does not cease. However, in other cases, since there is a reversal in the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*), there is certainty through the reversal of doubt; that is to say, because there is certainty regarding non-existence.

If there is doubt regarding the non-perception of the imperceptible (*adṛśyānupalabdhi*), how can it be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this he says: "In that case, first," and so forth. In that regard:

Between the two types of non-apprehension, the first—perceptual non-apprehension—is stated to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it functions effectively in negating the conventional usage of existence.
But where, then, does it lack validity? To this he says: "But not... and so forth. [It lacks validity] regarding the observation of absence (*vyatireka*), which is non-existence.

This is the determination [of non-existence]. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), both verbal expression (*chanda*) and conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) are understood. Since a determination of non-existence does not arise from doubt, it is therefore not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As for the second [type], it is the non-perception of an object that is perceptible.

Here, because it results in a determination—given that it is seen to have the result of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), etc.—it is considered that determination itself is its result. That [non-perception]...

And the non-perception of perceptible objects is fourfold due to the differences in formal application (*prayoga*); this is the connection [of the terms]. "The contradictory" (*viruddha*) and "the effect of the contradictory" (*viruddhakārya*) constitute a singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) based on their dissimilarity (*virūpa*). The phrase "establishment (*siddhi*), [which is] perception (*upalabdhi*), of that which has a perceptible nature" should also be connected here. 2. An Examination of Non-Perception (*anupalabdhicintā*).

(2) Non-apprehension is fourfold: the establishment of the contradictory and the effect; the establishment of the cause and the nature [of the thing]; and non-apprehension due to the absence of those things whose natures are perceptible. Thus, non-apprehension is fourfold. ||6||

Whatever negation-convention there may be, it is all indeed by means of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). For that [negation] is twofold: it would be effected either through the affirmation of something or through its negation. Even in the case of affirmation, either what is contradictory would be affirmed or what is not contradictory. If what is not contradictory is affirmed, there is no negation because there is no contradiction with coexistence. As for what is contradictory, even if it is not apprehended—

The understanding of negation occurs through the absence of attainment. For instance, there is the understanding of contradiction because that which has an unlimited cause is absent when another thing is present. That [contradiction] also arises from non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).

By this, two types of evidence are indicated: the perception of what is contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāva-viruddhopalabdhi*) and the perception of an effect contradictory [to the probandum] (*viruddha-kāryopalabdhi*).

"The non-establishment of the cause and the [object] possessing the nature of being visible" means the non-perception of the cause and of the essential nature when they have reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
By this, both the non-perception of the cause and the non-perception of the essential nature are indicated.

It is fourfold. It is "non-existence as the noble object" (*abhāvāryā*), meaning that its object (*artha*)—in the sense of purpose (*prayojana*)—is non-existence (*abhāva*) and the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*).
[Objection: But in the case of the establishment of two contradictory effects, it is not stated that this is "non-perception" (*anupalabdhi*); so how can these two...?

To [the objection that] non-apprehension itself [is not established], he says: "Whatever there may be," and so forth. By the phrase "whatever there may be," this pervasion (*vyāpti*) is stated. There is no conventional usage of negation based on a logical mark (*liṅga*) that can be performed without non-apprehension; however, the conventional usage of absence (*abhāva*) is not something to be accomplished by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

And this has already been refuted; [the author] says "tathā hi" (for it is thus) in order to demonstrate that very same pervasion (*vyāpti*) which was mentioned previously. "Saḥ" (that) refers to the negation.
It would be made twofold—that is, it would be treated as either the affirmation or the negation of some object. 15a. Of some [object], by way of affirmation or by way of negation.

Even when [the thing] is being produced, whether a contradictory [thing] is enjoined or a non-contradictory one, in the case of enjoining a non-contradictory [thing], there is no contradiction regarding the coexistence of that which is being prohibited and that which is being enjoined; therefore, there is no negation of that which is intended to be prohibited. As for the phrase "of the contradictory also," etc.:
for this [thing] would indeed be contradictory only if its own contradictory were not perceived therein. For instance...
To this, he says: "Of that which has an unlimited cause" means of that which has an unexhausted cause, such as cold touch and the like, as it arises in a continuum;

"prior to the proximity of fire and so forth" is how it should be understood. The comprehension of contradiction arises from its non-existence—that is, its non-arising—when another [cause] is present, namely when fire and so forth are present. It does not arise from non-existence [in general], because destruction would then be causeless.

This is what is meant: when each preceding cold touch ceases by its own inherent nature, there is a contradiction characterized by the non-coexistence of each subsequent one with the other, like the relationship between the eternal and the non-eternal.
Furthermore, as the cold touch undergoes a gradual diminution through varying degrees of heat, it arises sequentially.

Until, in every respect, there is the non-arising of that which is characterized by the sensation of heat; therefore, even though destruction is causeless, when fire is present, the sensation of cold that had been proceeding in a continuous stream ceases by its own nature, and another [sensation] that was about to arise in the stream does not arise due to the presence of fire. Thus, in the world, the opposition between fire and cold is understood, but not ultimately.
In reality, there is a contradiction; for this very reason, he says that it is the "comprehension of contradiction.
Furthermore, as for what is said: "There is no such thing as a 'remover' of fire and so forth without the removal of its cause."

That is incorrect, because destruction is causeless; how, then, could it be the remover of a cause? If it is argued that this is said while accepting that destruction has a cause, then why does it not remove the effect as well as it removes the cause? And if it is impossible to remove the effect without first removing the cause, then that [remover] must be the cause itself.

Furthermore, how could that [destruction] be a remover [of the entity], as long as it does not remove its cause? And if the same applies to the cause of that [cause] as well, then due to this infinite regress (*anavasthā*), nothing would ever be the remover of anything. Nor is it appropriate to speak of this in reference to a continuum (*santāna*), because if destruction were causeless, the very notion of a continuum would be non-existent; thus, this argument is trivial. And as for "it [is] non-existence when another exists" (*sa cet*... *anyabhāve satyabhāvaḥ*)— [The text continues: ...that is, the absence [of the entity] when something else is present. This is what is meant by "destruction. For example, when a jar is absent in a place where a cloth exists, that absence is called the "destruction" of the jar. It is not that the jar has been destroyed by the cloth; rather, the jar simply does not exist there. Therefore, this so-called "destruction" is merely the non-existence of the entity in relation to another thing. Consequently, since destruction is not a distinct entity, it cannot be produced. And because it is not produced, it cannot be momentary. Thus, the claim that all things are momentary because they possess destruction is refuted. Furthermore, if destruction were a distinct entity, it would follow that even a permanent entity, such as space, would be momentary, because it too would possess destruction. Therefore, this [position] is untenable. Moreover, if destruction were a distinct entity, it would lead to the absurdity of a single object being both existent and non-existent simultaneously, because the existence of the entity and the existence of its destruction would occur at the same time. Hence, this is also illogical. Furthermore, if destruction were a distinct entity, it would have to be either eternal or non-eternal. If it were eternal, then since it would always exist, no entity would ever appear. If it were non-eternal, then it would itself be subject to destruction, and thus one would have to postulate yet another destruction for it, leading again to an infinite regress. Therefore, this is also untenable. Consequently, the theory that destruction is a distinct entity is rejected. On the other hand, if destruction is not a distinct entity, then the statement "destruction is the non-existence of the entity" is established. In that case, since non-existence is not a positive entity, it cannot be produced. And since it is not produced, it cannot be momentary. The cause of contradiction characterized by non-arising is conventionally expressed on the basis of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
By this, the contradiction characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) has been explained.
Showing the second type of contradiction, he says: "mutual apprehension," and so forth. Mutual apprehension...

Mutual apprehension is its [the contradiction's] opposite; exclusion (*viveka*) is the avoidance of that. Those two whose characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), i.e., their own-nature (*svarūpa*), are established through that [exclusion] are described as such. The state of those two—the fact that they are characterized by the exclusion of mutual apprehension—is "the state of being characterized by the exclusion of mutual apprehension. That, or rather, is contradiction. The word "or" (*vā*) is used for conjunction. "Like permanence and impermanence" is the example.

But is it not the case that even in the first type of contradiction there is mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*), and in the second as well there is non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*)? For indeed, the second type of contradiction applies only to those two properties for which there is no coexistence in a single locus. Thus, this [second type] is not admitted in the case of color and taste. If one asks why two types of contradiction have been stated: (1)

It is true that [the distinction between the two types of contradiction] was stated for the sake of distinguishing their respective objects. Some hold that the first contradiction concerns only perceptible entities (*dṛśyavastu*), whereas the second concerns both non-entities (*avastu*) and imperceptible entities (*adṛśyaviṣaya*). Alternatively, the former is a contradiction with another by way of the cognition of the absence of one in the other, while the latter concerns the essential nature (*svarūpa*) by way of the absence of identity with another; such is the difference between these two contradictions.

Furthermore, the contradiction between impermanence and permanence consists precisely in their mutual exclusion; it resides in their own essential natures (*svarūpa*). And even in the case of blue [and non-blue], it is simply the non-perception of the other that is expressed by the perception of one. Otherwise, for one whose perception is not negated, there would be no cessation; for yellow is of the nature of the cessation of blue, and blue is of the nature of the cessation of yellow, since both are positive entities (*bhāva-rūpa*), and thus [the presence of] yellow would follow in the absence of blue.

Furthermore, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence [of over-extension], there is no such contradiction between these two. Nor is this contradiction due to their non-deviation from mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), because that is not perceived. For this very reason, the affirmation of what is non-contradictory is stated. Even in the case of blue, its contradiction with "non-blue" is by way of non-blue being the negation of blue, not with a non-blue that is necessarily defined by the absence of blue; for such a thing is a non-blue entity [in its own right].

Because there is no existence [of yellow and so forth] apart from [the cognition of] yellow and the rest. How then is there a negation of identity with yellow and the rest when blue and so forth are being perceived?
This is not a fault, because upon the perception of a single blue object, there is the non-perception of another [color], even though it might otherwise be perceived.

If it possessed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would be perceived exactly as such; thus, having considered that it meets the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*), identity (*tādātmya*) is negated through the non-perception of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*). And here too, regarding this contradiction, that [contradiction] is [established] through non-perception—

Since there is no need for further dependence, the meaning is as follows: (1) This mutual exclusion (*anyonyaparihāra*), which is a form of contradiction, must be determined solely through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
For instance, the contradiction between contradictory things is defined precisely as the non-appearance of one when the other appears.
And when the nature of an entity (*bhāva*) appears, its absence (*abhāva*) does not appear. Therefore, [the contradiction] between an entity and its absence—
Contradiction is determined because the two [states] do not appear as identical. In this same way, it is to be determined in cases such as "permanent" and "impermanent.
And non-appearance is said to be simply the appearance of one [of the two]. Thus he says: "In that case also," and so forth. In that case also—

Regarding the contradiction just mentioned: by the "perception of one," that is, by the perception of one contradictory thing, the non-perception of the other is indeed what is called the non-perception of the object to be negated. "Otherwise" means if the non-perception of the other were not stated by the perception of one; then, since the non-perception of that object to be negated would remain unestablished, its absence would not be proven even when the one is perceived. And therefore—
There would be no contradiction at all for that which is being perceived. Therefore, since both types of contradiction are produced by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*),
even those [reasons] such as the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) which are formulated in a positive manner (*vidhimukhena*), are in their essential nature non-perceptions.

Now, it may be argued that in the case of two contradictory things, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is observed in the example as the means of grasping the relationship characterized by contradiction; yet, the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps a relationship does not itself become one of the two related entities. For [the nature of] the [means of grasping the relationship] of fire and smoke— [is not the same as their relationship].

The nature of perception belongs to smoke, not to fire. Therefore, how can the apprehension of the contradictory be a non-apprehension, given that it appears in the form of an apprehension? Consequently, having perceived fire and so forth—which have been established as contradictory [to cold]—in a particular instance, one infers the absence of cold and the like upon seeing them in another location.

To this it is replied: if the relationship of the signifier and the signified is established through the relation of contradiction, then [the absence of one] is ultimately not established by means of the contradictory. For when the negation of one thing does not establish the absence of another, it is simply the establishment of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), since negation is of the nature of non-apprehension. As for the negation of "another," even there, in the case of cause and effect—

Or [it may be] of that which is neither. 5. In that case, because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) for that which is neither, how can it be established that "in the absence of that, the other must not exist"? Even in the case of the non-perception of an effect, its absence [is not certain], because causes do not possess [the effect] by necessity;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of deficiency or obstruction. Therefore, how could there be an absence [of the effect] from that? Thus, [it follows that] there is no non-perception of the cause...
Only deafness makes one fail to perceive [the sound]. However, non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is itself a state of non-existence; it does not involve an external object.

For instance, the cognition of cold might arise from the sight of fire because those two are produced through a relationship of contradiction (*virodha*). It is not, however, due to a relationship with the absence of cold. And when the cold is dispelled by the fire, how then—
Contradiction is not a relationship because it lacks the property of residing in two things. Nor is there a contradiction between fire and the absence of cold, since they can coexist.

Furthermore, there is no inference of the absence of cold from fire, because fire does not invariably entail the absence of cold; for cold is observed even when fire is present. Therefore, to the extent that cold is not perceived while fire is present, to that same extent...
Because the absence of that [cold] is established in the example, in other cases as well, the absence of cold from fire is likewise a non-perception;

at that very time, it constitutes a state of opposition to fire, and not at any other time. Since its capacity to indicate [the absence] is due to this state of opposition, it follows that it indicates by means of the non-perception of something else. Therefore, the perception of the contradictory is a form of non-perception, because it is invariably determined by non-perception.

The nature of form (*rūpatva*). Just as the non-perception of a jar consists in the perception of the bare ground, so too, even in the case of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*), the perception of the contradictory is nothing other than non-perception. For example, [in the case of the Jains]: "A jar may be impermanent; it may be permanent. In this case, the perception of impermanence is itself the non-perception of permanence; therefore, there is no [simultaneous] permanence and impermanence.
Form (*rūpa*) is the entity (*vastu*).

Having thus established that even in the case of the affirmation of another object, the non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) of the object to be negated is the means of cognition (*gamika*), he says "of one," etc., in order to establish it also in the case of the negation of another object. Why? [He says] "of the negation," etc. And not [is it] of the object—

There is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the negation] would be the negation of something else (*arthāntaraniṣedha*), because even in that case, when the negation of another is to be proven, the reason would have to be the negation of cause and effect;

or the reason would have to be the negation of that which is neither, i.e., that which is neither an effect nor a cause. In those cases, there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between that which is to be negated and that which consists of neither an effect nor a cause.

"In its absence" means in the absence of that which is not restricted by the presence of the other. "By another" refers to that which is intended as the object of negation. "It must not exist"—from what [source] is this known? Even in the case of the non-perception of an effect, from what is its absence known? This is the connection [of the argument]. "Its absence" refers to the absence of the cause. For causes are manifold; they possess their effects, yet due to the possibility of deficiency or obstruction, [the effect may not appear].

And this was stated by taking "cause" in its general sense: the absence of a cause whose capacity is unimpeded is indeed understood from the absence of the effect; for it is the non-perception of both [the cause and the effect] that serves as the means of cognition. Therefore, the absence of another cause is established; however, in that case, only the object [of negation] is established. In this [case of non-apprehension] as well, when the pervader—

By the non-apprehension of the property (*dharma*), he states the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*); at that time, there is also the absence of [the probandum]. For this is the non-apprehension of that which has a contradictory object; it is fourfold through the division of its application: by the establishment of the contradictory. As in: "There is no sensation of cold here, because of fire.
By this, the establishment of the contradictory of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhasiddhi*) should be understood as stated. As in: "There is no sensation of frost here, because of fire."

For [it is] by means of the establishment of a contradictory effect; as in: "There is no cold touch here, because of smoke. It is understood that it is the effect itself that makes known the absence, due to its connection with the word "effect" (*kāryasya*).

If it is argued that the restriction is improper because non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is also a reason for absence, he says: "Non-perception of the essential nature..."

In this case, however, there is simply non-existence itself; it is not the absence of some other entity that is being proven here. Furthermore, when the negation of another nature (*svabhāvāntara*) is the probandum, it is restricted to the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) alone; therefore, there is no contradiction.
To the question, "What then is being proven there? he says: "Only," and so forth. "There" refers to the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

The subject (*viṣayin*) consists of non-existent cognition and so forth. In this case as well—that is, in the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*)—when one states the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) through the non-perception of a property that is its pervader (*vyāpaka*), such as "there is no *śiṃśapā* here because of the absence of trees," then by the word "also" (*api*), the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) is also established for the pervaded. For when two mountains are elevated...
In one region, a forest of trees is seen, but because it is extremely dense, the specific species of the trees cannot be determined.

In that case, regarding another part of the mountain where a *śiṃśapā* tree is not perceived, its absence cannot be ascertained because the *śiṃśapā* is not visible; however, since a tree in general meets the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), it is possible to ascertain the absence of that [tree]. Thus, when the pervader—
The absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is established from the presence [of its contradictory].

With the words "this," etc., he explains the portion of the verse beginning with "the meaning of non-existence. Regarding "by the establishment of the contradictory": by the perception of that which is contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāva*). As for "for example," etc.: in a given locus (*dharmin*), where cold touch is imperceptible, and fire...

This application is seen even when [the object] is at a distance. By this example of the perception of what is incompatible with the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), it should be understood that the establishment of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhasiddhi*) has been stated. The example beginning with "for instance" (*yathā*) refers specifically to a particular cold touch.
Frost is accompanied by snow; its pervader is cold, and that which is incompatible with it is fire. In that regard, fire—

By excluding the cold [temperature] which is contradictory [to fire], one also excludes its pervaded [quality], namely the touch of frost; thus, this [inference] is included within the perception of what is contradictory by nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*). Furthermore, this formulation should be understood as applicable where fire is perceptible, while the touch of cold and the touch of frost are imperceptible, through the non-establishment of the effect of that which is contradictory. For example, etc.
"There is no sensation of cold here because of smoke"—here, fire is the opposite of cold, and smoke is its effect;

that [fire] brings about its own presence, and it removes the cold. And where the sensation of cold is imperceptible while both fire and smoke are perceptible, this formal argument (prayoga) is to be seen. Thus, the establishment of the effect of what is contradictory has been explained.
Now,
(1) even the non-existence of that [is established]...
[text fragment].

By way of the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*): as in "there is no smoke here because of the absence of fire. By way of the non-establishment of the essential nature (*svabhāvāsiddhi*): as in "there is no smoke here because fire is not perceived.
By this, the non-establishment of the essential nature of the pervader (*vyāpakasvabhāvāsiddhi*) is stated: as in "there is no *śiṃśapā* tree here because of the absence of trees."

In all cases, the non-existence [of an object] is established through non-apprehension; furthermore, for those things that are perceptible by nature, the establishment or non-establishment of their opposites should be understood [as grounds for non-existence]. For others, non-existence is established [through other means].
If the non-existence [of a cause] is established even by the apprehension of an effect opposed to it, why is it not established by the apprehension of its cause?
When the perception of a cause that is contradictory to [the object to be negated] is employed, it is fallacious because of the absence of contradiction between the two causes. ||7||

“Non-establishment of the reason and its presence [in the subject]”—this he explains by means of the following illustration: (1) "by the non-establishment of the reason" means by the non-perception of the cause; "for example," and so forth.
When there is doubt regarding whether the steam and such rising above a great lake are actually smoke and the like...
In that case, the following formal argument (*prayoga*) is to be observed: For if there were fire in a great lake that is perfectly still, it would necessarily be perceived due to its luminosity;
since it is not perceived, there is an absence of the effect [of fire] precisely because of the absence of fire.

It is established by the non-apprehension of its own nature (*svabhāvāsiddhi*), that is, by the non-apprehension of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), [in the form]: "there is no smoke there, because it is not apprehended.

It should be understood as referring to that which has met the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). By this—namely, by the formal argument (*prayoga*) of the non-apprehension of own-nature—it is shown that this [smoke] is the pervader (*vyāpaka*).

And when that very nature is not established, its non-perception has been stated [as a reason for negation], as in: "There is no *śiṃśapā* here, because of the absence of trees. For tree-ness is the very nature of *śiṃśapā*-ness; therefore, the *śiṃśapā* is pervaded by tree-ness.

But is it not the case that the negation of a perceptible object occurs through the non-perception of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), and not through the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth? For instance, the negation of a cold touch—which is itself imperceptible—and of its effect, which is likewise imperceptible, is what is being established. Indeed, if they were perceptible, there would simply be a case of the non-perception of their own nature. Therefore, just as there is a negation of an imperceptible cold touch, so too [is there a negation] of a *piśāca*.
Since it might be argued that this [non-perception] would apply even to words such as "and" (*ca*) and so forth, he says: "In all cases," and so on.

This is what is meant: just as in the case of the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the absence of a jar or similar object—which has been perceived elsewhere—is established in a particular location, so too is the absence of cold touch—whose contradiction with heat is known elsewhere, and whose being an effect is known—[established].

Furthermore, the absence [of the probandum] in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) is established through the perception of what is incompatible with the effect (*kāryaviruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth, but not for that which is always unperceivable.

The word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) refers to when the proof of non-existence is employed both in the affirmative mode (*vidhimukha*) and the negative mode (*pratiṣedhamukha*); and by the term "non-existence," both the absence itself and the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding absence are intended.

Furthermore, regarding those causes and so forth whose absence establishes the non-existence [of something else], their very non-establishment—being of a perceptible nature—is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). And there is the non-apprehension of things contradictory to that, as well as of things contradictory to the object to be negated, such as those with contradictory natures and so forth. For example: "There is no sensation of cold here, because of wood. This applies when there is a contradiction between two causes and when one serves as an indicator of the other. For example:
There are no specific qualities such as horripilation in this person because of the presence of a specific cause for killing.

By this, it is stated that the absence of an effect contrary to that [cause] is understood even from its effect; for example: "This place does not contain a person endowed with specific qualities such as horripilation, because there is smoke."

Success (siddhi) is to be understood as being by way of apprehension (upalabdhi). And here, it is not to be construed as "the success of those things whose nature is perceptible," because the state of having a perceptible nature is already obtained from the very mention of "apprehension. Rather, the connection should be made thus: "the success of those things which are the opposites of those intended to be negated, [provided they] have a perceptible nature. Why? Because—

(1) Because the non-existence of other [entities]—such as causes and so forth—whose nature is invisible, is not established; for there is no establishment of contradiction based on the "contradiction of nature" (*svabhāvaviruddha*) regarding those invisible things that are intended to be negated.

The opponent [objects] with the words "If... and so forth: Even by the perception of smoke, which is the effect of fire that is opposed to cold, the absence of cold is established. Why is the absence of cold not likewise established by the perception of the cause of that fire opposed to cold—namely, the perception of fuel such as wood?

"Of that which is contrary to it," and so forth, says the Teacher. By this, the perception of wood or other fuel—which is the cause of fire and is contrary to that cold touch—is employed [as a reason], yet it is fallacious (*vyabhicāriṇī*). When? (1) When there is no cessation of the two causes; that is, when there is no contradiction between the causes of fire and cold. He provides an example:

"Yathā" and so forth. For here, there is no contradiction between mere wood, which is the cause of burning, and coldness, such as frost and the like, which is the cause of its non-burning. However, as for that wood whose capacity to produce fire is unimpeded and which generates fire—although there is indeed a contradiction between such wood and the cause of coldness, nevertheless, because the effect [fire] is actually observed from such wood, it is a case of contradiction with the effect (*kāryavirodha*) alone.

It may be so. Furthermore, when there is a contradiction between two causes, there is the non-perception of the cause that would make [the effect] known. For example: "This person does not have specific symptoms such as horripilation.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), trembling of the teeth, shivering, and so forth are included. The inclusion of the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) is for the purpose of excluding those effects of cold; for even those [symptoms] caused by the transformations of *piśācas* and the like are possible. [The cause] is present...

One whose fire is of a specific kind is "one characterized by that"; [the word] "from that" refers to the state of being such. Here too, the inclusion of the term "specific" is for the purpose of including only that kind of fire which is capable of removing horripilation and the like. For in this case, there is a contradiction between the fire, which is the cause of intense heat, and the cold, which is the cause of horripilation and the like. Therefore, it is fire.

By removing its own opposite, cold, it also removes its effects, such as horripilation and so forth. This application of the argument is to be understood when the cessation of horripilation and the like is intended to be proven through the removal of the cause of cold, on the basis of observing that [the effect] is not seen while the cold sensation and its effects— namely horripilation and so forth— are imperceptible.

By this example of the contradictory cause (*kāraṇaviruddha*), it is shown that [the reason] may also be contradictory on account of its effect (*tatkāryāt*). Even in the case of a contradictory effect, dependence on place, time, and so forth is required;
otherwise, it would be inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), like ashes used to prove the absence of cold. (8)

The apprehension of the absence of the effect of that which is contradictory [to another] has been stated. When the effect of a certain contradictory thing is perceived, that which is its second contradictory counter-correlative (pratiyogin) is "contradictory to that"; the apprehension of the absence of its effect is what has been stated. For example:
a person who is possessed of specific symptoms such as horripilation caused by cold, in whatever place—

It exists in that manner. The mention of "a location" (*pradeśa*) is for the purpose of establishing the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharma*) of the reason "because of smoke. For if the subject were "a person," the reason would not be a property of the subject, since smoke is a property of a location. And this formal argument is to be understood as being employed in order to prove the absence [of fire] in a case where fire is imperceptible, while cold touch and specific effects such as horripilation are present.

For in that case, by the perception of smoke—which is the effect of fire, the opposite of cold—one intends to establish the absence of horripilation and the like, which are the effects of cold, the opposite of fire; therefore, such [an absence] alone is the probandum (*sādhya*). Indeed, smoke brings fire into proximity, and that fire removes the cold; as that [cold] is being removed, it removes its own effects, such as horripilation.
In effect, this is the "perception of what is incompatible with the cause.
The connection is that "this is the perception of its opposite" (1.32); the meaning is "the perception of what is incompatible with the cause."

It has already been pointed out that this is indeed due to the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*), which is itself the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*). Since, in these two applications as well, the understanding of the absence of the effect is derived solely from the non-perception of the cause, this [non-existence] is stated by means of the non-perception of the cause alone.
"Thus this," and so forth: although it is fourfold according to its primary divisions, it becomes manifold through the distinctions of intermediate applications.

It is of eight kinds.
