For it has been stated that from the perception of what is contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) follows the perception of what is contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). From the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) follows the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). From the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) follow the perception of what is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*) and the perception of the effect of what is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*). And the perception of the contradictory effect (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*) is of one kind; thus, there are eight types.
It comes to be.

[Objection: But surely, since smoke may still exist in a dwelling house or similar place even after the fire has long since perished, how is there no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the perception of a contradictory effect? To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth. In that regard, regarding the perception of a contradictory effect, there is a requirement for consideration of place, time, and other factors; [it is not the case that] here, in some [place], there is no cold.

When fire is present at a particular time, there is dependence on time; when smoke [indicates fire] in the sky, there is no dependence on any specific location. There is dependence on place when one thinks, "In such-and-such a place where cold is absent, fire is present and this smoke has arisen. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), dependence on a specific state is included—that is, having regard for that specific state of smoke which was observed when fire was in proximity.

Even in the present time, the absence of cold is inferred; for even in the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), such as "there is fire here because of smoke," dependence on place, time, and so forth is accepted. The word "even" (*api*) serves to include this very point.
Now, if dependence on place, time, and so forth were a qualification of the effect-reason, the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the subject (*dharmin*).

If it is argued that [the reason] is not established because of its existence [in other cases], we say no. For it has been stated that the indicator-status [of the reason] exists precisely within the locus (*dharmin*) itself, by virtue of its dependence on place, time, and so forth. 2. Investigation of Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi-cintā*):
Now, how is that production of an effect which is inferred from a complete causal complex (*kāraṇakalāpa*)—[provided it possesses] equal qualities—subsumed under the threefold [classification]?
It is included within the reason (*hetu*).

When the production of an effect is inferred from a complete set of causes, that [inference] is described as being based on essential nature (*svabhāva*), because it does not depend on any other factor. (9)
This [effect] also does not depend on any object other than that which is proximate; thus, its nature is invariably concomitant with just such [a cause].

In that regard, one merely infers the possibility of the production of the effect from the collection of causes. If there were no dependence on place and so forth for the complete causes, then the contrary effect would be erratic (*vyabhicārin*). For example, ash—

That which disregards place and time is inconclusive when the absence of cold is to be proven by a means of proof that is not [actually] cold. In this same way, it has been established that the perception of the contradictory and so forth is non-perception. As for the opponent’s words beginning with "But that... and so on: "Equal quality" refers to that which is present and unobstructed, as in the case of earth and a seed.

Having observed the collection of causes such as water and so forth, the effect, namely the sprout, is inferred. How does that [cause], being termed a "cause," subsume within the three types of reasons—namely, those called essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*)? It cannot be included in non-perception, because it is a means of establishing an affirmation (*vidhisādhana*). Nor can it be included in the reason of effect, because it is the essential nature of the cause. Since one thing is not inferred from another distinct thing, it must be included in the reason of essential nature.
In the case of the essential nature as a logical reason (svabhāvahetu).

He states the inclusion [of the effect within the cause] with the words "by the cause," and so forth. By "complete" is meant that from whatever collection of causes an effect is seen to arise, it arises from that much;
it does not arise from those [causes] when they have reached their final state, because the sign (liṅga) is apprehended even before the effect is perceived. If [the effect] were unperceived...

Nor can there be inference for the sake of ascertaining the final state; for one who would be able to ascertain those [final moments] cannot do so through inference, since they are beyond the perception of one with limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*). That which is inferred from the production of an effect has been described as the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the cause. Why? Because it does not depend on anything else. Therefore, the meaning is this: because it is invariably concomitant (*anubandhin*) with the mere capacity for producing an effect.
It is of the nature of intrinsic being.

[Objection: But when the production of the effect depends upon the final state, how can it be said to be independent of anything else? [Reply: He says: "This too," namely the production of the effect. "As it is present" means of whatever kind it is present. The "assemblage of causes" is such that from its being present in that manner, it does not depend on any other thing; thus, its nature is invariably concomitant with just that. (Of what is this the nature? Of the cause.

This refers to the entire collection of causes (1) with respect to the continuum (*santāna*), not with respect to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). "Productive" means that the continuum of the collection of causes is independent [of other conditions].

Although the production of the effect is independent [of anything else], one might ask: "Since it is a different entity, how can it be the nature [of the cause]? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.

Because, in that context, when the causes are complete, the possibility (*sambhava*) of the production of the effect is inferred from the complete cause as its mark (*liṅga*). "Possibility" (*sambhava*) means that which occurs from this; the meaning is that the capacity for producing the effect is inferred.

He clarifies this very point: "Because there is an inference of the capacity of the complete causal complex to produce the effect. And this capacity is inferred from its being inherent in the nature [of the complex], since it is invariably concomitant with the mere presence of the causal complex.
But why, then, is it that the effect itself is not inferred from the causal complex?

[It is because] when there is a continuous transformation of the potencies that constitute the fruit of the causal complex, there is the possibility of an obstruction; thus, [the inference of] the effect is inconclusive. || 10 ||

For causal substances do not produce their own effect merely by being present as a complete collection (*sāmagrī*). This is because the production of an effect depends upon the transformation of the potencies generated by that collection. During this interval, since an obstruction may occur, there can be no inference of the effect.
However, because the capacity (*yogyatā*) does not depend on any other substance, inference is not contradicted. [This concerns] the successive potencies—

By means of transformation, it is capable of producing various effects, because there is no other requisite condition for the transformation of its capacity; for it is produced by a capacity whose cause consists solely of its own preceding homogeneous moments. Indeed, the fitness of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is dependent on the causal complex alone and requires nothing else, as it does not depend on any other cause.

The opponent asks: "If, then, the capacity to produce an effect is necessarily concomitant with that [cause] alone, and the production of the effect is thus certain, why is that very [capacity] not itself inferred? To this he replies: "But rather, is it the effect itself that is inferred from the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)? He states: "The causal complex," and so forth. [The compound means: both the fruit of the causal complex and those capacities.

The potencies of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) are as follows: from a preceding complete complex, there arises a subsequent capable moment, and its specific excellence is its potency; thus, the causal complex is the result, and the potency is its transformation (*pariṇāma*). The production [of the effect] occurs through a continuous succession of successive moments, in a result that is connected to and dependent upon that [complex]. [If one were to argue that] the cause must be inferred [from the effect], this would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

What is the reason? Because an obstruction is possible. He explains this with the words "for not," and so forth. Only when complete—that is, only when present—do causal substances produce their own effect. What is the reason? "Because of the totality," and so forth. [The effect arises] from the totality (*sāmagrī*).

Regarding those powers, there is a successive transformation; for the arising of an effect depends upon that production of a subsequent, more distinguished moment from each preceding moment. "In this interval" refers to the time of the transformation of the continuum (*santāna-pariṇāma*);
[it is said so] because an obstruction is possible.

[Objection: But surely even "capacity" (yogyatā) is restricted by the successive transformation of subsequent moments, and since a restriction is possible there as well, how can there be an inference of it? [The author] says: "But as for capacity," and so forth. Because it does not depend on another substance—that is, because it does not depend on any other cause apart from the collection of causes already present—an inference of it is not contradicted.

He states that very inference: "The successive," and so forth. Taking each preceding moment as the material cause (*upādāna*), the arising of a subsequent efficient moment is the transformation of successive potencies (*uttarottara-śakti-pariṇāma*). With that [transformation] as the reason, the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is: "capable of producing an effect. The subject (*dharmin*) is "this causal complex" (*kāraṇa-sāmagrī*). This is because there is no other condition (*pratyaya*) to be depended upon for the transformation of potency.

The reason for this is that there is no other auxiliary condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) to be depended upon for the transformation of the capacity; therefore, it is said to be "non-apprehension. 2. This is called the investigation of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi-cintā*).
If that perception of color-form and so forth by means of another factor, such as taste and so forth— which is neither its cause nor its effect— is thus [admitted],
then it is likewise [the case that] there is the perception of color-form and so forth, which are non-existent, depending upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*).
[One knows] the causes [of phenomena] by means of inference, like [the inference of] a transformation of fuel through smoke. ||11||

To the question, "From where, then, is the production of the capacity? he says: "The preceding," and so forth. "Preceding" means similar; "of the same genus" (pūrvasajāti) refers to that which has as its cause merely that much—a preceding collection of causes. The state of being such is "tadbhāva";
from that reason, that fitness is said to be independent of anything else.

Now, if it is said that the capacity of a cause with respect to its effect is "power" (*śakti*), then since the capacity would also be subject to deviation when the effect deviates, how can this be an inference? Alternatively, if it is said that there is merely the possibility of capacity, then the meaning would be: "the effect may or may not occur. Even so, how can this be an inference, given the doubt?

To this it is replied: How indeed can the opponent object that this inference is produced from three kinds of reasons? If this inference is validated by the opponent, then the Teacher demonstrates that it is indeed produced from a threefold mark (*liṅga*). Some say that this [objection] is not intended to show that this is not inference in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). Alternatively, if [the opponent argues that] the production of an effect occurs exclusively...

Capability is inferred. If that were so, there would be no inference due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). However, when it is rather "possibility" (*sambhava*)—in the form "it might at some time produce an effect"—that is inferred, how could there be deviation in this case? Therefore, the meaning is as follows: if there is an absence of continuity in the successive transformations, then an effect may occur; otherwise, it does not. But in the case of the opponent's [view], it is absolute—
In the inference from effect (kāryānumāna), there is indeed deviation (vyabhicāra).

Others, however, maintain that when the causal complex (sāmagrī) possesses transformation and there is an absence of obstructions, there arises an absolute capacity for the production of the effect; it is this very capacity that is inferred. Furthermore, the cognition of the capacity for producing the effect is itself a specific [form of] the effect.

They maintain that because [the absence of an obstacle] is implied by its nature as a non-existence, no separate inference of the effect is made. It is argued that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) when one infers an effect from the mere causal complex (*sāmagrīmātra*) alone. If it is asked, "How is the absence of an obstructing factor (*pratibandhakābhāva*) apprehended?"—[the reply is:
True. This inference belongs to one who is capable of knowing it; for just as one must know that smoke is produced by fire, so too must one know this.

Just as one is able to infer fire from its smoke, but not another [who lacks that connection], so too [the author] again states the contradiction of the claim "it is of three kinds" by means of the passage beginning with "yā tarhi" (but that which...). This refers to [an inference] based on something other than the object to be inferred, which is neither its effect nor its cause, such as taste (*rasa*) or the like; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), smell (*gandha*) and other such qualities are included.

The cognition of form and so forth. Here too, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), touch and the rest are included. For in the dark, having tasted a citron fruit and the like, having smelled the fragrance of a *campaka* flower, and having experienced the sensation of heat, one infers their common property of form;
likewise, having seen the form of fire, one [infers] its touch. How, then, does that [inference] fall within the three types of logical reasons (*hetu*)?

Regarding the subject at hand: he says "that too," etc., to show that there is no lack of authority [for this inference] and thus no contingency of having to posit another logical mark (*liṅga*). The connection is: "that too is a means of cognition" (*gati*).
Of what kind is the form (*rūpa*) and so forth? It is that which is dependent on the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*). That which is the producer of taste...

The cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, which depends upon that very causal complex (*sāmagrī*), arises from the taste; this is by means of the inference of the property of the cause (*hetudharmānumāna*). That which is the cause of the taste—namely, the prior substratum (*apādāna*)—has the property of being the producer of color (*rūpa*);

it is by the inference of that property that this meaning is established: from the taste, there is the determination of the producer of color belonging to its cause, which exists at the same time as the taste.

For in this way, its capacity to produce a color that exists at the same time as the taste is determined; provided that there is also a determination of the color existing at the same time. Thus, for past things belonging to a single moment, there is only one mode of inference, namely that arising from the mark of an effect. [Objection: But surely, the inference of the simultaneously existing color occurs after the cause of the taste has been apprehended, and thus it arises from a cause.

Because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in an inference from an effect; and in the case of an inference of the capacity to produce an effect, there would be no inference of a color that exists at the same time as the taste. Furthermore, because there is no cognition resulting from an inference based on an [already] inferred [reason]. Therefore, as it is said: (1) "When there is the movement of past [entities], then the effect is both that [entity] and its mark (*liṅga*); therefore, it is 'born from the mark of the effect' (*kāryaliṅgajā*)."

But when movement occurs at the same time [as the object], then that which has an effect as its mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the inference of the property of the cause—is "that which has an effect as its mark" (*kāryaliṅga*);
that which arises from this is "born from the mark of an effect" (*kāryaliṅgajā*). Thus, that [objection] is refuted. [In that regard, others [maintain...

that in a composite substance (*avayavidravya*), qualities such as color (*rūpa*) are established; therefore, it is logical that there is movement of color and so forth within that [substance] even while it is non-existent [in another location]. However, for the Buddhists, color and...

Because we do not admit a whole (*avayavin*) apart from its parts, there is no absence of a subject (*dharmin*). Furthermore, if inference were possible without a subject, it would follow that one could infer color and so forth from taste everywhere. Moreover, the collection as a whole would become the probandum (*sādhya*), and the reason (*hetu*) would fail to be a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*).
Nor is it logical to infer a property of the cause, because taste and the like are not recognized as being the effects of color and the like.

Nor is this stated without having first determined the position of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). For if form (*rūpa*) and so forth were momentary, they would produce effects of their own kind and not effects such as taste (*rasa*), because there would be no means of apprehending a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Furthermore, among moments, there can be no conventional usage of inference and the object of inference (*anumānānumeya-vyavahāra*), because no relationship can be ascertained. However, if the conventional usage of inference and so forth is based upon a continuum (*santāna*), then for the continua of form and so forth, [there is no such problem].
Since a mutual relationship of cause and effect is established, how can there be the conventional usage of inference and the object of inference?

It is thought as follows: (1) it is not the case that in all instances there is an inference of color and so forth from taste and so forth; rather, it occurs in a locus such as a mango. And in that case, the rule of the mutual inseparability (*avinirbhāga*) of color and the other qualities is indeed perceived. And that is the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

Otherwise, how could there be the rule of mutual inseparability even for things such as jars and cloths? Furthermore, their necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is neither identity (*tādātmya*), because they are perceived as distinct, nor is it origination from that (*tadutpatti*), because they exist simultaneously. Nor can there be inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*) for them, since inherence in a single substrate cannot arise through the power of inherence for those things that do not already inhere [in something else], precisely because of the nature of inherence itself.

Because it would exist [independently], and because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For even in the case of things that are inherent (*samaveta*), they are produced as such from their own causes by means of inherence. Since they are designated as such precisely through being produced in that way, they possess the capacity to indicate [their cause]. Therefore, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) consists in dependence upon the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*). And for one who has ascertained the necessary connection, there is inference regarding another [instance] at a different time. Even though, in this case, a whole (*avayavin*) [is postulated]...
Nevertheless, since the subjecthood (*dharmitva*) of the object of the cognition of a mango and so forth does not exist [independently], there is an inference of color and so forth from the taste.

But even so, how can these [qualities] depend on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*)? For it is not by the same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that form produces form that it produces taste and so forth, because otherwise those [qualities] would result in being non-different from one another; nor does it produce the other by means of a different [nature].
[If it were so,] it would entail a difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*).

This is not a fault, because in that case, form does not previously possess the capacity to produce a single effect—such that this fault would arise—but rather possesses the capacity to produce multiple effects simultaneously; for it is observed that [the effect] arises from that very [form].
It might be so.
However, the causality of a cause does not consist in the mere absence of its effect—such that it would follow that a plurality [of causes] could produce a single [effect] from one;
rather, in the world, its causality consists simply in its existence prior to the arising of the effect. And just as it functions for the production of a single effect, so too...

Furthermore, the state of being an antecedent cause is observed even in the production of a collection [of qualities], because it is seen that by whichever very same nature a substance produces color, by that same nature it also produces taste and so forth; the difference in their own natures, however, is caused by a difference in their material causes (*upādāna*), not by auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*).

For instance, although touch exists in air, there is no production of color and so forth due to the absence of color and the rest; and likewise in fire, [there is no production of touch] due to the absence of color and the rest.

Even when [the other qualities] are present, because of the absence of taste (*rasa*), there is no production of taste. Likewise, even though smell and the rest exist in water, because of the absence of smell, there is no production of smell. Therefore, it is determined that the specific cause of taste and so forth is taste itself. And a specific cause is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), which is of the same genus or exists within an undifferentiated continuum. Consequently, due to the difference in their material causes, [there is a difference between] form (*rūpa*)...

This is the distinction in the nature of the [causal] factors (*dīna*). Furthermore, it is said that there is a conjunction of multiple potencies therein; thus, by means of one potency, the form produces form, while by another, it produces taste and so forth.

That is incorrect. (1) Even if one accepts that a single entity produces multiple effects by means of multiple powers (*śakti*), the consequence of its being multiple remains unavoidable, because the multiple powers themselves constitute the multiple intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of that entity. Furthermore, since the powers are non-different [from the entity], if there were a distinction between the powers, it would follow that the nature [of the entity] itself must be distinct. Alternatively, if the powers were distinct, the nature [of the entity] would lack causal efficiency.

This follows as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). Nor can something that is incapable become an agent (*kāraka*) through a connection with power (*śakti*), because that which is incapable lacks a connection with power. Furthermore, what is the use of a connection with power for that which is already capable?

It is by its very nature (*svarūpa*) alone that it is an agent; otherwise, power itself would not be an agent, as it lacks a connection with [another] power. If you argue that, being power itself, it does not require another power, then an entity (*bhāva*) likewise, being capable, [does not require power].

Why, then, does one depend upon power (*śakti*)? Even the Mīmāṃsaka who holds this view [must explain it]: Power is simply an excellence of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of an entity (*bhāva*), and it is both distinct and non-distinct from that entity. Since power is not perceived when the entity is being perceived, it is distinct from the entity; yet, because the effect would otherwise not occur...
If it were identical with the entity through its production, then the entity would not be an agent [of that action]. As it has been said:

(1) "The potencies of all entities are postulated through the presumption of their effects. This too is refuted, because there is a contradiction in a single potency having both a distinct and non-distinct nature. Furthermore, as for the [argument from] presumption—

One might argue that since the power (*śakti*) must be postulated as non-different from the very entity that exists prior to the effect, this prior existence itself is the power; and since that [prior existence] is established by perception, why is the power not perceptible? It is simply that it is ascertained through the observation of the effect. Therefore, because one infers the properties of the cause from the effect—such as taste and so forth—this is a case of the "effect-as-reason" (*kāryahetu*).

[This is] an inclusion. "Like the transformation of smoke into clouds": just as when fire and other causal complexes are inferred from smoke, the ash—being of that very nature—is inferred there as the cause; such is its cause.
For indeed, without the operation of potency (*śakti*), there is no taste; that [potency] itself is the other cause.
Thus, the cognition of past and future times arises from the mark of their effects.
The auxiliary condition (sahakāri-pratyaya) produces taste from the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) which possesses the capacity for activity;
this is just like the production of smoke by an auxiliary condition acting upon the material cause that is a specific modification of fuel. For instance:
It is set in motion by its own capacity (*śakti*). Without the inclination of its own cause toward the production of the effect, the flavor (*rasa*) does not arise.

That [inclination] itself is the cause for other causes. It is the cause for the activity of the material causes of form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, the activity of the material causes of flavor is also a cooperative condition (*sahakārin*) for the activity of the material causes of flavor. Therefore, from a cause that has arisen in such a manner, [the effect] arises in such a manner.
Inferring the person, one infers the form;
just as there is an inference of the transformation of fuel such as embers, so it is in this case.

But is it not the case that this is an inference of a contemporaneous effect from a cause inferred through the effect of taste, rather than an inference of the property of the cause? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). When there is the cognition of color (*rūpa*) from taste, the cause itself is of such a nature; thus, the relation of producing color is inferred, in the inference of which another effect [such as taste] is also [inferred].

That [cause] becomes determined by its specific qualification. However, another effect is not to be inferred from a cause that has already been inferred. Why? He says: because (*hi*) that whose power (*śakti*) has been set in motion and is unimpeded is called "possessing active power" (*pravṛtta-śakti*).

That which is such and is also the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) is described as "so-called. Being an auxiliary condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) for that, it produces the taste (*rasa*) from the cause of taste.

[The cause] produces [the effect]. And when the cause is of such a nature, the inference of form follows by implication from the inference [of taste], because form and taste are dependent upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatvāt*).

A specific transformation of fuel, such as ashes, charcoal, and so forth, has wood as its material cause (*upādāna*) and fire as its cooperative condition (*sahakāripratyaya*). Just as smoke is produced by that [fire], it is similar to that case: form and taste are likewise dependent upon a single causal complex.
He establishes this with the words beginning "for it is so," which constitute the sūtra: "The power proceeds. Its explanation begins with "of its own cause" and so forth.

"Of its own cause" refers to the juice (*rasa*); without the manifestation—that is, the conformity—of that which is its own cause toward the production of the fruit, namely the production of the juice, the juice does not arise. Thus, it is said: "the power proceeds."
The explanation of the phrase "another cause" (*anyakāraṇa*) begins with "the material cause of form" (*rūpopādāna*), and so forth.

The material causes of form are the atoms of form (*rūpaparamāṇu*) comprised within the preceding definition; the "activity" (*pravṛtti*) is their orientation toward the production of form, and [the other cause] is the cause of that activity.

This is because the material cause of form is oriented toward its own effect only when accompanied by the auxiliary cause that is the cause of taste. That [activity] also belongs to the cause of taste—

The activity of the material cause of taste is so described because it has the nature of acting in conjunction with the activity of the material cause of form toward the production of form. Since this is so, [taste arises] from such a cause—that is, from the material cause of form whose power is activated, which is accompanied by the activity of the preceding moment and which subsumes [the causal factors]. From taste—
Thus, even in that case, there is a movement [of inference] regarding past and simultaneous [factors], but not regarding future ones, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Therefore, this too is born from the mark of the effect (*kāryaliṅga*). Consequently, no other reason is a means of cognition (*gamaka*), because for that which lacks a restricted nature (*apratibaddhasvabhāva*), there is no necessity of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva-niyama*).

The *rasa*, which is intended as the logical mark (*liṅga*), by making known the cause exactly as it is, makes known the form that exists at the same time [as itself]. Therefore, this meaning is simply the ascertainment of the cause in such a manner, and nothing else;
it is not, however, an inference of an effect subsequent to a cause that has already been inferred. And because [the cause] functions precisely as the producer of the effect...

The determination of the nature of causes is not otherwise; for this very reason, he said: "In that case also," and so forth. By means of this method, even there—in the inference of color and other qualities from taste and other qualities—there is the cognition of past and simultaneous [factors]. Those factors existing at the same time as the material cause of the taste are the "past" ones; those coexisting with the taste which serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*) are the "simultaneous" ones; there is the cognition of these. Not of the future.

Inference based on a currently existing mark (*liṅga*) is fallacious due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). For that which is yet to come may indeed fail to occur because of the possibility of an obstruction to its causes;

since such an obstruction might be deficient, [the effect] might not arise. Furthermore, the inference of tomorrow’s sunrise from today’s sunrise is not a valid inference, as it lacks a restrictive mark (*niyāmaka-liṅga*); it is like inferring tomorrow’s sunrise from seeing a donkey today.

Therefore, this cognition of color and so forth from taste and so forth is also an inference based on an effect as the logical mark (*liṅga*). And since a reason (*hetu*) is that which makes [the object] known by being dependent upon the probandum (*sādhya*), for that reason there is no other type of reason—such as "conjunction" (*saṃyogin*) and so forth—that makes [the object] known than the threefold reason. Why?

Because there is no rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva-niyama*) for a nature that is not restricted to the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) through identity (*tādātmya*) or origination (*tadutpatti*).

This is what is meant: first of all, there is no conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between things that are not in contact. Even for those that are in contact, what is the use of conjunction, since they arise in that state of contact from their own causes? Therefore, the capacity to signify [the probandum] does not depend on conjunction, because it is not invariably concomitant with it, as in the case of a jar and a cloth. Likewise, there is no inherence (*samavāya*) between things established separately (*pṛthaksiddha*). Nor is there inherence even for those that are not established separately (*apṛthaksiddha*).

Since [the property] arises from its own causes through a successive sequence by way of inherence (*samavāya*), it does not possess the capacity to indicate [the probandum] even by means of that inherence; for there is no dependence upon the probandum, and he will state later that inherence itself does not exist. For this very reason, it was stated previously in the context of the inference from taste that there is no such thing as "inherence in the same object" (*ekārthasamavāyin*). Furthermore, the contradictory (*virodhi*) is included within non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
And as for what was stated by the Naiyāyikas: "Inference is of three kinds—*pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [Nyāya-sūtra 1.1.5].

Among these, *pūrvavat* is the inference of an effect from a cause; and it has been demonstrated that this is subject to deviation (*vyabhicārin*). As for *śeṣavat* inference, which is the inference of a cause from an effect, that is indeed accepted by the author of the treatise. As for *sāmānya-*...

Inference based on what has been seen (*pūrvavat*) is that which, having observed the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) in one locus (*dharmin*), results in an inference regarding another [locus].

For example, having observed that Devadatta’s arrival at another location was preceded by movement, one infers movement in the case of the sun as well, because of its arrival at another location. This too is indeed produced from the mark of an effect (*kāryaliṅgaja*), since arrival at another location is the effect of movement. All of this—
The Master himself will state in the third chapter that inference is indeed only *sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*.
Furthermore, as for the example of *sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa* cited by Uddyotakara—namely, [the inference] of water from a crane...
[text fragment].
By this, the inference of rain from the emigration of ants and the leaping of fish is also explained.
In that case as well, it is precisely the transformation of the elements (bhūtapariṇāma), which is the cause of rain, that serves as the cause for the emigration of ants and so forth.

When an effect is inferred from a complete set of causes, that is "like the remainder" (*śeṣavat*); because [otherwise] there would be no capacity [for the inference], just as passion is inferred from the body. (13)
That inference as well is born solely from the mark of an effect (*kāryaliṅga*), as stated in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*.
Therefore, it is established that there is no other probans (*hetu*) that makes [the object] known apart from these three types of reasons.
By this—namely, by stating that the inference of color and so forth from taste and so forth is born from the mark of an effect—the [inference] of ants ascending...

The movement elsewhere of those [birds] who have taken their eggs; the leaping of fish, which is a transformation of the fish; by the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the flashing of lightning, the croaking of frogs, and so forth. Regarding the inference of rain and so on, here too, by the word "etcetera," the inference of wind and so on is stated. Just as that too is an effect, it arises from the inference of the property of a cause produced by a mark (liṅga).

He states this very point with the words "tatrāpi" and so forth. "Tatrāpi" means even in the case of the swarming of ants and the like. "The transformation of the elements (*bhūtapariṇāma*) alone is the cause of rain"—here, the particle *eva* (alone) is displaced in its syntactical order. It means that the transformation of the elements is indeed the cause of rain. [Furthermore,] it is the cause of the agitation of ants and so forth, characterized by their swarming and the like. Therefore, from such a transformation of the elements as it actually occurs...

The transformation of ants' eggs is the cause of rain; from the inference of such a cause, there is an inference of rain occurring at that same time. In other cases, however, only the capacity [for rain] is inferred, but not rain itself, because of the possibility of deviation due to the presence of obstacles. Therefore, even from a complete collection of causes, there is no inference of the effect; there is only the inference of its capacity.
That is indeed inference.
However, those such as the Mīmāṃsakas who infer an effect even from an incomplete cause are utterly excluded from the path of logic; demonstrating this, he says:
"(1) But by a cause that is not complete... and so forth. "Incomplete" means deficient. The *śeṣavat* inference is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

This is the meaning. Why? By implication (*sāmarthyāt*). The explanation of this is "for [the causes] must be complete," and so forth. First of all, there is no inference of the effect in any way whatsoever. By the word "also" (*api*), he states that even when they infer capability, they infer only those [causes] that are complete. Because that which is incomplete is absolutely incapable, and because it is incapable even through subsequent transformation, it is not even a partial [cause].
Inference from effect (*kāryānumāna*). This is the explanation of the example: "like the inference of passion from the body. Regarding the phrase "as follows" (*yathā*) and so forth:

"the body, the sense organs, and the cognitions" form a *dvandva* compound. "This person possesses passion and so forth, because he possesses a body, because he possesses sense organs, and because he possesses cognition. In this way, passion and so forth are inferred from the body and other factors. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), hatred, delusion, and the rest are included.

In the Sūtra, however, the mention of "attachment to the body" (*deharāga*) is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). For it is not the sense faculties (*indriya*) and so forth alone that are the cause of attachment and the rest; rather, attachment and the others are preceded by the clinging (*abhiniveśa*) to a self and what belongs to a self (*ātmātmīya*). That clinging which consists of the notions of "I" and "mine" (*ahammama*) with respect to the self and what belongs to the self is the primary cause of attachment and the rest; therefore, they are described as such. The phrase "improperly" (*ayoniśas*) and so forth is an elaboration of this very point. "Yoni" refers to the [true] objects (*padārtha*).

It is not impermanent, suffering, non-self, and so forth, because it is the cause for the arising of right vision (*samyagdarśana*). One praises and relies upon that [object]. This is the consideration of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*):
for only when causes are complete do they allow one to infer their capacity; for an incomplete set lacks efficacy by necessity.

For example, the inference of passion and so forth from the possession of a body, sense faculties, and intellect; these are preceded by the deep-seated attachment (*abhiniveśa*) to a self and what belongs to a self.
Passion and the other [afflictions] arise because all faults originate from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*).

Even though the body and so forth serve as causes, since they lack the specific capacity [to produce them], and because their presence in the absence of the [afflictions] has not been observed, doubt arises through inference *śeṣavat*. Likewise—

The cognition of a cause based merely on its non-observation in the contrary instance, due to the observation of a general effect, is a fallacy of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*), just like [inferring] passion from speech. (14)

For movement, speech, and so forth are not the effects of passion (*rāga*) alone, because they have the desire to speak (*vaktukāmatā*) as their cause. If it is argued that this very [desire] is passion, we say: since this is accepted, nothing is contradicted. For passion arises from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) based on the view of a permanent self, pleasure, and what belongs to a self (*ātmātmīya*). Regarding the term *yoni*, it is derived from the rule: "From a numeral and a word in the singular, when repetition is intended. (*saṃkhyaikavacanācca vīpsāyām*). Thus, "one attends to the source again and again" is expressed as *yoniṃ yoni manasikaroti*. *Note: The grammatical rule cited corresponds to Pāṇini 5.4.43.*

Alternatively, the suffix *śas* is applied. Thus, that mental attention (*manaskāra*) which is of such a nature is "appropriate mental attention" (*yoniśomanaskāra*), which is the knowledge of selflessness (*nairātmyajñāna*). Its opposite—the knowledge of a self and so forth—is "inappropriate mental attention" (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), because all faults such as passion arise with that as their precursor.

[Objection: But surely the body, sense organs, and intellect are also causes of attachment and so forth, since attachment and so forth are not observed in those who lack them. [Reply: He says: "Even though the body and so forth are causes... The term "of the mere ones" means of those devoid of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*). Regarding the probandum, which is attachment and so forth, the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) are things such as stone fragments, which are devoid of attachment and so forth. In that case, there is the occurrence of the reason—namely, "possessing a body and so forth"—in those [dissimilar instances]. [The argument follows: ...of that [occurrence]...

Even when [the reason] is not observed in the absence [of the probandum], because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary, this is an inference "from the remainder" (*śeṣavat*); and from this, doubt arises, not certainty. Just as this which was just mentioned is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so too is the cognition of a reason based merely on its non-observation in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), due to seeing a general effect—that is, a mere effect—[whereas it would require] an inference of a specific cause.
"Resembling a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābha*) means appearing as a means of valid cognition; that is to say, it is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). How is this so?
Like [the inference of] passion and so forth from speech.
But if every speech is indeed an effect of passion and so forth, how can it be said to be a "commonality of effects"? To this, he says:

"Not [present]," and so forth. "Tremor" (*spanda*) refers to the movement of the lips, since it necessarily occurs at the time of speaking. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), other modifications of the face and the like that occur at the time of speaking are also included. "The mere desire to speak" (*vivakṣāmātra*) without distinction is the general [cause]; those tremors and so forth for which that very thing is the cause are described as such. Therefore, it is because of their existence [as being caused by that].

If it is argued that this desire to speak is attachment (*rāga*), because attachment is of the nature of clinging—so the opponent thinks—the Master says: "Because it is desired, nothing is contradicted. Since the desire to speak is the desire for the effect, which is speech, there is nothing undesirable about it. Furthermore, the desire to speak is not attachment; rather, it is that vision which takes the form of a permanent self, pleasure, and what belongs to the self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*).
They say that [the mind] projected by attachment has as its object contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena;
however, compassion and the like are not so, because they can occur otherwise—as we shall explain. For example, one who is attached...

Likewise, one who is detached also speaks. Thus, there is no comprehension [of a person's state] from mere speech, nor even from specific [speech], because the underlying intention is difficult to discern; for all [speech] is subject to deviation due to the confusion of worldly usage. If it is argued that one does not speak when there is no purpose, we say no, because [speech] is for the sake of others.

If it is argued that [the arising of compassion] is not logical because [the Buddha] is free from passion (*vītarāga*), we say no; for it arises through compassion (*karuṇā*) as well. If it is argued that this very compassion is itself passion, we accept this. There is no fault, however, because it arises from non-perversion (*aviparyāsa*). Compassion is projected and produced even in the absence of the clinging to a self (*ātma-abhiniveśa*); its object is impure phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), meaning it takes the five aggregates of grasping (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) as its objective support.
The wise say that mental attachment is passion (*rāga*).

It might be thought: (1) loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth are admitted for those considered to be free from passion; yet, because they take sentient beings as their object, they proceed from the view of a self and so on, and by proceeding through an inclination toward sentient beings, they are of the nature of attachment. Therefore...

Since even those free from passion (*vītarāga*) appear to be impassioned (*rāgin*) [when they exhibit compassion], he says: "Compassion and the like are not thus" (1). This means that for those free from passion, compassion and the like do not have sentient beings as their object (*sattvālambana*), because they can also occur otherwise—that is, by having phenomena as their object (*dharmālambana*).
We shall explain this immediately hereafter. In this context, if one were to infer passion based on these words...

The connection is with the phrase "no understanding from mere speech. For just as one who is impassioned speaks, so too does one who is dispassionate—that is, even one whose passion has been destroyed. Inference of passion is not based on mere speech, but rather on a specific kind of speech, namely that which is produced by passion alone; thus he says: "Nor [is there inference] from a specific [speech]. This refers to the intention (*abhiprāya*).
Because it is difficult to understand. For one who is dispassionate may act as if passionate, and one who is passionate may act as if dispassionate; this intention is difficult to discern.

Furthermore, because of the statement "for all [beings] through the influence of worldly convention," there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in using mere speech or a specific utterance—such as passion and so forth—as a logical mark (*liṅga*). Therefore, even from a specific [utterance], there is no inference of passion and the like. As it has been said:
Anticipating the objection that one who is dispassionate does not speak, he offers the following response: "For a purpose," and so forth. "Speech" refers to the utterance of words.

For there is no fruit in the utterance of words for one who is free from passion; thus, the point is that there is no deviation between passion and speech. [The author] says "No," meaning: there is no absence of purpose, because speech is for the sake of others.

The opponent says, "This is not logical," and so forth. The meaning is that one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) is not attached to others, and there can be no engagement for the sake of others without attachment. [The author replies: This is not so, because engagement occurs even through compassion (*karuṇā*).

If it is argued that this very compassion is itself passion, then we accept this naming of compassion as "passion," since it arises from the cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*) of perceiving a self in sentient beings.

If it is argued that compassion (*karuṇā*) is also a fault consisting of attachment (*rāga*), he says: "Because it arises from non-perversion," and so forth. He explains precisely how it arises from non-perversion: "Even in the absence of grasping at a self," and so forth. [He states] "merely by seeing a particular kind of suffering," which refers to the perception of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Suffering...

[This state] arises merely from the perception of distinction through the power of cultivation; for instance, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others are held to have sentient beings and their qualities as their objects. These [virtues], functioning through the repeated practice of their own kind, do not depend upon passion (*rāga*). Passion and the like are not so, because they do not exist in the absence of cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*). For one who is compassionate, an undertaking that is free from distortion is not fruitless.
If it is argued that this is correct, we say no; for it is only the benefit of others (*parārtha*) that is intended as the fruit. Indeed, the definition of a fruit is established by intention.

Since there is in no way any superimposition of what is unreal, he is faultless. In proving that one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) possesses faults by means other than that [intention], there is nothing undesirable.

By mere investigation. "Aroused by the power of practice" means that compassion indeed arises from preceding moments of a similar nature. Corroborating this with scripture (*āgama*), he says: "For it is thus," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those [compassions] without an object (*anālambana*) are included.

Compassion having sentient beings as its object belongs to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); that having phenomena as its object belongs to the noble ones (*ārya*); and that without an object refers to the [grasped]—

For the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who are free from the attachment to a grasper, loving-kindness and the others—namely, loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—are accepted as such in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). But are these not practiced by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) only with sentient beings as their object? How then can they have phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth as their objects?
To explain why they are so called, he says:

"And these—loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—function through the cultivation of their own kind, because they arise by the power of preceding similar moments. However, this much is the distinction: as long as one perceives sentient beings, they have sentient beings as their object; as long as [one perceives] phenomena (*dharma*)..."

They do not have phenomena as their object; the meaning is that they do not operate toward sentient beings through a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) with the thought, "I shall not be dependent on passion.
Now, was this point not already stated immediately before—that [compassion] arises through the power of practice merely by seeing specific instances of suffering?
True; however, the distinction here is that now all [compassions] arise by relying specifically on compassion (*karuṇā*). This remains so even when the view of self (*ātmadarśana*) has ceased.

To this, he says: "In that case, passion and the like arise from habituation, just as compassion does. It is not so; passion and the like do not function through habituation to their own kind, such that they would continue to operate even when the view of a self has ceased. This is because they are absent whenever there is an absence of the misconception regarding a self and so forth. For one who is compassionate, the undertaking for the sake of others is fruitless [in terms of personal gain] because, due to the absence of misconception, there is no clinging to a self and the like.

Because there is no such thing as a self-interest (*svārtha*). This is not a fault, because it is precisely the interest of others (*parārtha*) that is accepted as the fruit. If it is asked: "Granted that it is the interest of others, how can it still be a fruit? He replies: "By desire," and so forth. It is characterized by desire;
the meaning is that it is defined by being the object of desire. In short, whatever is desired is the fruit.
If it is asked, "How can there be activity even for the sake of others in one who is devoid of the cognition 'I am'?"—(1) No;

some say that activity occurs because of the presence of non-afflicted knowledge (*akliṣṭajñāna*). Others say it is due to the manifestation of pure mundane consciousness (*śuddhalaukikacitta*) through the power of yoga (*yogabala*). Still others say it is because [the Buddha] appears in such a way to those to be trained (*vineya*).

"By all means" (*sarvaśaḥ*) is the conclusion. If the desire to speak in one free from passion (*vītarāga*) is established on the basis of his speech, then he would be called "one with passion" (*sarāga*) because of that compassion. In every respect, however, he is faultless as one free from passion and so forth, because there is no superimposition of what is unreal; for passion and the like, which are by nature defects, must necessarily be present [if they existed]. Therefore, for one free from passion, the desire to speak and so forth are distinct from passion and the like.

For if one were to infer [passion and so forth] in another based on seeing passion and so forth in the speaker himself, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Since there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*), what certainty is there that there is no deviation in other cases? Speech might lead one to infer the speaker’s desire to speak due to the excellence of the instruments [of speech], because speech is not observed in one who lacks the capacity to produce passion. Even in that inference, there would be an over-extension.

Thus it has been said: for if passion (*rāga*) itself is not employed, how could its power (*śakti*) be employed? Indeed, if the power were employed, then passion itself would be employed; therefore, it was stated that such [independent power] does not exist.
In establishing the subjection to defects (*doṣavaśyatva*), there is nothing undesirable.

One might think: "Since passion and other such qualities are observed in the self of the speaker, there will be an inference [of passion] even regarding those regarded as free from passion, merely by observing their presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*). To this he says: "In the self of the speaker," and so forth. There would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in inferring passion and the like in one regarded as free from passion; for whatever specific quality exists in the self of the speaker—

In every case where [a property] has been observed [in one instance], there follows the undesirable consequence of inferring it elsewhere. This is because the specific qualities observed in the self—such as being dark or fair—are subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Regarding the phrase "inference of what is not other": if one were to infer another quality residing in the self that is distinct from passion (*rāga*), then what certainty could there be that there is no deviation even in the case of passion and so forth, which are here intended as the probandum (*sādhya*)? None at all.

Because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between passion (*rāga*) and speech. Since inference does not [proceed] from the observation of oneself, therefore [the compound] *karaṇa-vaktukāmatā* is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound; this is indeed a dual form in the accusative case. Because speech is not observed in stones and the like, which lack the capacity to produce passion, [the author] says "passion," etc., to show that it is inferred from that very speech. That is the inference.

Thus, there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the inference of capacity. For instance, just as there is an absence of the capacity to produce passion in stones and the like, so too [there would be an absence] of all human attributes; therefore, if one were to infer the capacity to produce passion from the non-perception of such speech, the same would apply to all human attributes.

Now, if it is thought that (1) the capacity for the production of passion is the single cause for both passion and speech, and that when this [capacity] is inferred, passion is also inferred by implication— therefore,

the inference is only of the capacity and not of all personal attributes— to this he replies with the words beginning "of passion" (*rāgasya*). If passion were of no use regarding speech, [speech would arise] from the activity of the palate and other organs alone.

Regarding the production of sound: how is the power of passion (*rāgaśakti*) employed toward the utterance? If it is maintained that at the time of the activity of the palate and other [articulatory organs], the power of passion is also employed toward the utterance, then at the time of the production of the first phoneme, passion itself must also be produced, because both depend upon the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatvāt*). And of that passion, there is a continuum (*santāna*).
Furthermore, in the production of the second and subsequent phonemes, it would be passion (*rāga*) alone that is employed. Thus he says:
"For if there were employment of the capacity, then that [capacity] itself would be employed. And it has already been stated previously that there is no employment of passion.

Alternatively, for those who are free from the attachment to a self and what belongs to a self (*ātmātmīyābhiniveśa*), passion (*rāga*) has no application with respect to speech. How then could that power—the power of passion characterized by the attachment to a self and what belongs to a self, which is called "latent disposition" (*vāsanā*)—be applicable to speech? [This is] the consideration of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). Therefore, only an effect that is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) with its cause can lead to the inference of that cause, because it is dependent upon it; not any other.
Even when there is no perception [of an object], for one who perceives everything (*sarvadarśin*), the absence [of that object] is ascertained through the cessation of its perception.

This is because things seen in a certain way at some time may later be seen otherwise due to differences in place, time, or processing (*saṃskāra*). For example, *āmalaka* fruits, when sprinkled with milk, produce sweet fruit; yet such cases are not commonly observed. Therefore, it is appropriate for a speaker like me to say that [the Buddha is free from passion and so forth]—[whereas others cannot].

Because there is an absence of attachment to a self and so forth among those who possess passion. For speech depends upon the application of capacity; that very passion would be applied [to speech] because all those who possess attachment to a self and so forth are indeed passionate. And it has been stated that such passion has no utility with respect to speech. This is because the desire to speak is a general cause, as was explained in the intervening discussion.

Therefore, the conclusion beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore) is indeed inseparable; by virtue of that causal connection, it is necessarily non-deviant from the cause, because it is dependent upon that cause. Nothing else is [non-deviant] if it lacks such a connection, even if the reason is not observed in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). For one of limited vision, certainty does not arise from mere non-observation; however, for an omniscient being, certainty would arise through the cessation of observation.

For he possesses knowledge that pervades all objects of knowledge. This very point is stated in the passage beginning with "all-seeing" (*sarvadarśana*). To the question, "How can there be a certainty of non-existence based merely on non-perception? he replies with the passage beginning with "in some cases, thus" (*kvacittathā*). Regarding those things previously seen in that manner, the word "difference" (*bheda*) is to be connected with each term: "by difference of place," "by difference of time," and "by difference of mental disposition" (*saṃskāra*). Mental disposition (*saṃskāra*)...
The sprinkling of milk and so forth would be different from the manner previously observed. To ask "In what way? he says: "Just as in the case of a mango.

This is an illustration of the difference in latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and it is not as if this is common; for sweet fruits are not seen in abundance, since bitter fruits are seen in great numbers. Nor is it the case that sweet fruits are not seen at all now, because they are seen frequently.

In some cases, there is the rejection of a sweet fruit that is otherwise possible; likewise, there is the occurrence of the *piṇḍakharjūra* (date palm) due to a difference in location, and of flowers and so forth due to a difference in time. He states this by means of the example of the *āmalakī*: just as *āmalakī* fruits become otherwise through processing with milk and other substances, so too the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*), which is susceptible to passion and the like, [becomes otherwise] through the practice of reality (*tattvābhyāsa*).

Through cultivation, one becomes fit; and through repeated practice, consciousness that has selflessness (*nairātmya*) as its sole object is said to be "clearly manifest" and "dispassionate" (*vairāgya*), because through the vision of selflessness, attachment and other afflictions do not arise due to the disappearance of the clinging to a self and so forth. Furthermore, knowledge that has the momentariness and other characteristics of all phenomena as its object is said to be "clearly manifest" and "omniscience" (*sarvajñatva*), because of the total removal of all ignorance.

Therefore, it is precisely the increase in clarity resulting from the practice of reality (*tattva*) that, by means of the direct perception of reality, brings about its manifestation and subverts the nature of cognition as being susceptible to passion and the like. Consequently, even if something has been observed otherwise, it may yet become otherwise through the power of causes; thus, even if a statement free from passion is not observed in some instances, that does not mean it is so in all cases.

There is no certainty that one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) cannot possess speech; therefore, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not ascertained, one cannot infer passion and so forth from speech alone. For this very reason, it is possible for someone like me to speak even while being free from passion, due to improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*). He states this very point in the passage beginning with "In the arising of passion," etc. He asks: "But what is this [improper mental attention]? and then says:

"Self," and so forth. The view of a self (*ātmadarśana*) is the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). The perversions of permanence, pleasure, and so on, are improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*). This is a copulative compound (*dvandvasamāsa*). [The phrase] "the view of a self itself is improper mental attention" is a qualification;
it is joined with the specific condition for the arising of passion because of possessing both the view of a self and improper mental attention. At that time—
To say this is a meaningless utterance; therefore, non-observation in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is not a [valid] reason.
Nor is there non-deviation from the counter-example (vipakṣa) by mere non-perception, because deviation is possible, as in the case of rice cooking in a pot. (15)

For even when cooked things are seen in abundance, cooking is not established merely by their being inside a pot, because deviation is observed. Thus, it is correct to say that those things which have such a nature and share the same cause of cooking are "cooked.
Otherwise, however, that inference would be "residual" (śeṣavat) and fallacious.
What, then, is the *śeṣavat* [type of inference]?
(a) The refutation of *śeṣavat* inference: that in which the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is demonstrated merely by the non-observation [of the probans in the absence of the probandum].
Because it is a cause of doubt, that [inference] is illustrated as *śeṣavat* (the remainder-based). ||16||

Or [it may be taken as] a compound. Even if "one like me" is specified as the speaker by the word *tadā* (then), the citation of the statement is useless; that is to say, the citation of the reason "because of the statement" is purposeless. For in that case, the reason would simply be: "One who is like me, being endowed with a specific condition for the arising of passion, is passionate—just as I am. Since this is so, [the object] does not exist merely because it is not perceived.

Therefore, the certainty regarding the absence [of the reason] in the counter-example consists in the non-observation of the reason in the counter-example; this non-observation of the reason in the counter-example is the cause for the ascertainment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the logical mark.

One might think: (1) there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason (*hetu*) due to its observation in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), and since speech is not observed in one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)—is established by that non-observation. To this, he says: "And not by mere non-observation" is the non-deviation of the reason in the counter-example. Why? Because [deviation] is possible...

Because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). That which has a possible deviation is so described; it is because of that state [of possibility]. Even if [the reason] is not observed in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), nevertheless, since its presence there is not contradictory, deviation is considered possible.
It is like the cooking of rice grains contained within a pot (*sthālītaṇḍula*).

In order to support this very example, he says: "For not," and so forth. Even when those things placed inside a pot are seen to have been cooked in abundance, cooking is not established by the mere fact of being inside the pot. The inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding a specific [qualification]. As he will say later: "But it might be thus. Why is there a lack of proof? Because of the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Thus—

"Those of the same nature" means those which have been seen to be ripe are of a nature identical to them. What is the reason that they are called "ripe" based on being equal to these very ripe ones? Otherwise, if that qualification were non-existent, it would be false. "The remainder exists" (śeṣavat) means that there is an undetermined object; and that is fallacious.

Now, it has been stated that "residual inference" (*śeṣavat-anumāna*)—which consists in the inference of a cause from an effect—is intended here; thus, the refutation of Īśvarasena’s position follows:
his negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is uncertain, and therefore its occurrence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) might be suspected.
For the mere observation of the establishment of negative concomitance is a cause for doubt. Indeed, not every non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is a means of certain knowledge. Therefore—
By one who desires the exclusion of another through the exclusion of this [the probans], a necessary connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) between the two must also be established;
otherwise, the reason would be non-probative.

(kha) The ascertainment of the three-fold reason: The ascertainment regarding the three aspects of the reason is described by him [Dignāga] through the exclusion of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viparītārtha*), and the deviant (*vyabhicārin*) reasons. (17)
—The investigation of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is what is intended by Dignāga;

for indeed, in the absence of a necessary connection, there can be no certainty regarding positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Therefore, demonstrating that very [connection], [one achieves] certainty.

He asks, "What then? and so forth. He states the nature of the *śeṣavat* [type of inference] with the words "of which" (*yasya*) and so on. That reason for which the exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa-vyatireka*) is established by mere non-perception—which is not a means of valid cognition—is called *śeṣavat* inference because that reason is a cause of doubt, that is, because it produces doubt. What is the reason? Because that exclusion of the reason is uncertain.

Thus, even in the case of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the occurrence [of the reason] might be suspected. Why, then, is it not certain? To this he says: "The absence... and so forth. How can there be doubt even when there is non-perception? To this he says: "Not all... and so forth. It is only the non-perception of what is perceptible that is indicative [of absence]. Since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) does not result from mere non-observation, therefore, by the exclusion of one [the reason], the exclusion of the probandum is established as the means of proving the exclusion of the other [the counter-example].

One who desires the cessation of those two—the probandum and the probans—must accept some essential connection (*pratibandha*) between them, characterized either by identity (*tādātmya*) or by causality (*utpatti*). It is not merely non-perception (*adṛṣṭi-mātra*). Otherwise, the reason would fail to communicate the understanding of the non-existence of the connection, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) would remain unascertained.

For this reason, he [Dignāga] has described the ascertainment of the three forms—the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* and other works, by means of the passage beginning with "But that which is unestablished for both is not a proof. He asks, "By the exclusion of what? and replies with the words "unestablished" (*asiddha*), etc.; since it belongs to the *ādi*-class, it is used in the sense of the instrumental case.
The meaning is: "by its opposite" (tadvipakṣeṇa).

In that regard, by the opposite of the unestablished (asiddha), the ascertainment of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) is described; by the opposite of the contradictory (viruddha), which has a contrary meaning, the ascertainment of positive concomitance (anvaya) is described; and by the opposite of the inconclusive (anaikāntika), which is erratic, the ascertainment of negative concomitance (vyatireka) is described.

Furthermore, by one who describes the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is indeed shown by implication; for there is no ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance when a necessary connection is absent. For that reason, that very [connection], namely identity (*tādātmya*)—

Demonstrating the necessary connection characterized by origination from that [cause], and thereby challenging [the opponent's position], he states the certainty: "When a certain defect has been eliminated... [The rest of the passage is illegible]. This concludes the *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (1917).

He said: "In that regard, by the ascertainment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), there is the exclusion of those [reasons] that are contradictory (*viruddha*) or belong to that same class; by the non-ascertainment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), there is the exclusion of those such as the *śeṣavat* which belong to that same class."

"But it is well-known that" [the phrase] "in both" refers to the negation of what has been established in one case. By the expression "well-known," there is likewise no doubt regarding the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), just as in the case of the *śeṣavat* and the *asādhāraṇa*. Otherwise, if there were no necessary connection (*pratibandha*), then even if there were merely non-observation in the dissimilar instance, [the reason would be fallacious] in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Furthermore, as for the statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-vacana) by means of a counter-example that deviates [from the probandum],

both of these— the statement of similarity and the statement of dissimilarity— should be stated as the counter-arguments to the contradictory (viruddha) and the inconclusive (anaikāntika) reasons; and that statement of dissimilarity serves as the counter-argument to the inconclusive reason.

If that which is the result of non-perception (*adṛṣṭiphala*) is explained by that [statement of dissimilarity] as the non-observation [of the reason] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), he explains the certainty (*niścaya*) that was stated [in the previous verse] with the words beginning "In that case" (*tatra*). Regarding the phrase "of those contradictory to it and its class" (*viruddhatatpakṣyāṇām*): "contradictory" (*viruddha*) refers to...

And regarding those with contradictory loci (*viruddhapakṣya*): for those whose presence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is certain, but whose presence in the similar example (*sapakṣa*) is doubtful, these are indeed "inconclusive due to doubt" (*sandigdhānaikāntika*). This designation is made according to what is established by others (*paraprasiddhi*). The connection is with the current context: "due to the non-ascertainment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). The connection is "the exclusion of the inconclusive. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: [this refers to] the common (*sādhāraṇa*)...

"Of the non-conclusive [reason]" means: of that position, and of the position of the inconclusive [reason]. "And of the rest," such as *śeṣavat* and so forth; by the word "etcetera," there is the exclusion of that which is doubtful regarding both the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). That which possesses presence in the similar instance and whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established merely through non-perception in the dissimilar instance is *śeṣavat*.

Now he explains the Master’s text beginning with "But [what is] well-known belongs to both. Regarding the words "of both" and so forth: by the term "of both," there is the exclusion of that which is established for only one party, whether the proponent (*vādin*) or the opponent (*prativādin*). The connection is as follows: by the expression "well-known" (*prasiddha*), there is the exclusion of those two types of reasons—the *śeṣavat* (probans based on remainder) and the *asādhāraṇa* (uncommon)—which are both doubtful. He asks: "Doubtful of what? and says:

The phrase "also in the case of the similar and dissimilar instances" implies that for the *śeṣavat* [inference], there is doubt regarding the absence of the reason in the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*). For the *asādhāraṇa* [reason], however, there is doubt regarding both the similar and dissimilar instances.
Therefore, by stating "certainty," the Teacher also certainly accepts a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

Otherwise, if no such connection existed between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), then even if there were merely a non-observation [of the probans] in the dissimilar instances, [the inference would be invalid].

The intended meaning is that when the Teacher [Dignāga] was seeking to exclude the inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) by means of a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), his statement regarding the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-vacana*) was purposeless.
To the question, "Where, then, did the Teacher state this? he says: "When... and so forth; this was stated in the *Nyāyamukha*.

That which is to be stated as both is similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). To the question, "In opposition to what has each been stated? he says: "The contradictory," and so forth. The statement of the proof (*sādhana*) is [stated] in opposition to the contradictory; the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is in opposition to the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, that which has non-perception as its result—that is, that which has mere non-perception as its result—is the statement of dissimilarity. 3. Investigation of Pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Even though that is not explicitly stated, it is understood. ||18||

For his prior visual error is certainly not something that is to be removed by a verbal statement. If it is argued that memory regarding non-perception is produced by speech, it is logical to establish such a recollection only in cases where perception is not being experienced, since perception itself is not a factor there. However, non-perception is simply the absence of perception; it is sublated by perception. Since that absence is already established in the absence of perception, [the recourse to memory] is useless.
The statement is for the sake of establishing that.

He explains this very point with the words beginning "yadi" (if). By that—that is, by the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—the non-observation of the reason (*hetu*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is made known. That non-observation is understood even when the dissimilarity has not been explicitly stated, because non-observation is characterized by the absence of observation.

Because it is already established even prior to the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the statement of dissimilarity is therefore purposeless. If it is argued that the statement of dissimilarity is for the sake of removing the error regarding the perception of the reason (*hetu*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), he replies: "Not indeed," and so forth.
