"Of him" refers to the person to be instructed; [it means] prior to the statement of dissimilarity, there is no error regarding the perception of the reason in the counter-example.

If it is argued that there exists something which is excluded by the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), and therefore— just as when the reason (*hetu*) is observed in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), there is no error but rather [the reason] has been forgotten,

and thus it is remembered by the statement of similarity (*sādharmya*); likewise, memory is produced by the verbal statement of dissimilarity even when [the reason] is not observed— [the author] says "Observation," etc., in order to refute that very example.

It is logical that perception which is neither being perceived nor remembered is not a factor for the comprehension of the probandum; thus, in the case of such perception, the application of memory through speech—that is, the production of recollection—is appropriate. However, this is not appropriate for the purpose of non-perception (*adarśana*). For non-perception is the absence of perception in the heterologue (*vipakṣa*) of the reason; it is sublated by perception. In its absence—that is, in the absence of perceiving the heterologue—it is indeed established as perception.
The statement "existence" is redundant for the sake of establishing that [non-existence], namely, for the sake of establishing the non-existence of perception. This is the intended meaning:

since perception might be forgotten because it is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), a statement is appropriate for the purpose of remembering it. However, the non-existence of perception consists in the cessation of perception;
and that manifests precisely from the absence of the experience of perception. And for that which is manifesting, what need is there for memory?
[Objection: For the sake of establishing that [absence], the statement is useless.

[Response: Indeed, for a person who does not perceive [something], there can be no certainty that "the reason is absent in the counter-example" based on mere non-perception alone; for even when things are remote in terms of space and so forth, they may exist despite being unperceived. Therefore, [one cannot conclude] "it does not exist."

If it is argued that the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is for the purpose of producing certainty, that is not so; because a thing being negated does not thereby cease to exist simply by the statement "it does not exist," which is itself devoid of valid means of cognition (*apramāṇaka*). Then how is it understood that "it does not exist"?
To this he says: "Just as... and so forth.

This is what is meant: the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of the reason with its own probandum is what apprehends its dependence upon the probandum;

and it is this "observation" (*darśana*) that is intended here. Furthermore, the observation of the reason only in the presence of the probandum is itself the non-observation of the reason in all counter-instances (*vipakṣa*).

Therefore, for that person alone who has previously engaged in the observation apprehending the connection between the probandum and the probans but has since forgotten it, [the absence of the reason in the counter-instance does not establish the pervasion].

The meaning is that when perception and non-perception are cognized, recollection is produced by means of statements of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), and not by any other means.
As it has been said: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are demonstrated by means of two types of examples. Just as, if [something] does not exist, it is explained [by its absence].
Vépha.
"Whatever one does not perceive, by that very fact one makes known its non-existence, [saying] 'it does not exist'."

Nor does it follow that something is non-existent simply because of the statement "it does not exist"; for if it were the case that whenever something is said to be non-existent, it is thereby understood to be non-existent according to logic, [then the statement would be valid]. //19//
If it is argued that non-existence follows from non-apprehension, then even by means of a verbal expression, there would be no cognition [of existence];
for that verbal expression is itself nothing but non-apprehension.

Moreover, the non-apprehension of one thing does not establish the absolute non-existence [of another], because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor can it be said, "It does not exist" on that basis alone.

It becomes so merely because it was stated; this would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Therefore, how can the exclusion of the inconclusive (anaikāntika) be achieved by a statement of dissimilarity alone?
Consequently, one who desires [the reason's] exclusion must state the logical justification (*nyāya*) whereby there arises the certainty that "it is excluded from here."
[Objection: But surely, since it is not perceived in the absence of that [property], the exclusion is unestablished. [Reply: It is so;

for in whatever manner—namely, by way of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with its own probandum—if the reason does not exist in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), then if that principle is made known or remembered through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the connection, it is understood that "it does not exist. But not otherwise.

He states the first portion of the verse beginning with "If," namely: "If, while not perceiving [something], one does not understand that it does not exist based on mere non-perception, then one will not understand it even from a statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) that lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*). For that statement of dissimilarity is likewise [without a basis]."
By that [statement], he indicates only non-perception (*anupalambha*) and not some further distinction.

It might be thought: "The absence of the reason caused by the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is indicated by the statement of dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*); therefore, there is a distinction. To this, he says: "And not one," and so forth. "One non-perception" refers to the non-perception of the probandum; "the other"—

The existence [of the reason] would entail the absence of the means of proof; the sense is that there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*). [He says] "because of over-extension" (*atiprasaṅgāt*): if cessation occurred without a necessary connection, then by the cessation of a cow, there would necessarily follow the cessation of a horse as well.
Now, it might be thought: since the Master Dignāga stated, "The reason does not exist in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)," certainty [regarding its absence] follows from that very fact.
To this he says: "And not," and so forth. Because that statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) stating "it does not exist" was made by that Venerable One, it follows accordingly;

that is, there would be the non-existence of the thing itself due to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For if that statement were authoritative, the probandum (*sādhya*) would be established by the mere thesis (*pratijñā*) alone. Therefore, how could the statement of dissimilarity avoid being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)?

Not at all [is it] a necklace. Therefore, by one who desires the exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), the logical justification for that exclusion must be stated, because of the principle:

"from which [reason] the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) grasping the necessary connection (pratibandha) between the probandum and the probans [arises]. "Of this" refers to the person to be instructed. Thus, there arises the certainty that the proof is indeed an exclusion.

The opponent [objects] with the words "nanu" and so forth. He thinks that because there is no perception [of the reason] in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāve*), the exclusion of the reason is unestablished; this is precisely the logical principle [he relies upon]. If the exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) were established through non-perception, then would the *śeṣavat* inference be fallacious? It would not be fallacious at all. But what kind of [inference] is it? To this he says: "Just as... and so forth. 3. Investigation of Pervasion (*vyāpticintā*).
If cessation were to occur through non-perception (*adṛṣṭi*), would the remaining six [reasons] not be fallacious?

For example: "These fruits are ripe" and "they are sweet," because their color is indistinguishable, or because they originate from the same branch, like those already consumed. Here too, if the entirety of what is intended to be expressed is made the subject (*pakṣa*).

If there is non-perception of the reason (*hetu*) in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*), how can there be deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? Some say that deviation consists precisely in the suspicion of sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*). This is not so; for such sublation does not exist within the domain of the subject (*pakṣa*) under consideration. If it were to occur [there], then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because there is no rule that sublation must occur elsewhere; rather, it is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) that has already functioned which constitutes the sublation. As for the sublation of what has not yet functioned...
There is no confidence in anything.

These are the fruits other than those already consumed. And this is the instruction on the nature of things (*dharmanirdeśa*): "They are ripe and thus possess such flavors" is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). "Possessing such flavors," meaning sweet or sour, is the reason (*hetu*), because there is no difference in their appearance (*rūpa*). Upa-

Because it is similar to that which is the nature of the connected fruit—such as its redness and so forth—the reason is "originating from the same branch. "Like that which has been consumed" is the example. He states "In this case also," etc., because if one were to desire the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based on mere non-perception, there would be a lack of invariable concomitance (*vyabhicāritva*) in the case of the *śeṣavat* inference. Here, in this *śeṣavat* inference, the intended [meaning is as follows].

If one were to take as the subject (pakṣa) the entirety of that fruit which is distinct from what has been consumed and is endowed with specific qualities such as form, then— since the reason consisting of those specific qualities of form and so forth is not observed in the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva)— there would be an exclusion from the counter-example (vipakṣavyāvṛtti), and consequently, there would be non-deviation (avyabhicāritā). For instance, apart from the fruit that is made the subject and that which has been consumed and taken as the similar example (sapakṣa), in that which constitutes the counter-example...
In the third group, there is no occurrence of the stated reason.

Regarding the phrase "contradiction by perception" (*pratyakṣabādha*) and so forth: since it is possible for one to experience through direct perception a fruit that has arisen from a single branch which is either unripe or lacks its [expected] taste, there is indeed a suspicion of contradiction by perception regarding the *śeṣavat* [inference], which constitutes its deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Some, such as Īśvarasena and others, say: "The meaning of this is that a logical reason (*hetu*) is not a means of cognition through mere positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) alone; rather, it is so provided that its object is unsublated (*abādhitaviṣayatva*). He refutes this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*).

For, regarding that imperceptible object which has been made the subject (*pakṣa*), there is an absence of sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*); thus, there is no suspicion of sublation by an operative perception.

But if it is argued that there might sometimes be sublation by the perception of odor, [the author] says: "In that way," and so forth. If one suspects that there might thus sometimes be sublation by perception, there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is because, in another case where a reason is intended, there is no rule that sublation by perception must be absent. For indeed, even when a relationship is accepted, the opponent's suspicion of sublation does not cease.

This is the intended meaning. Therefore, for one who does not accept the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), a valid cognition that has already occurred (*vṛtta-pramāṇa*) must be accepted as the sublater (*bādhaka*). If there were sublation by a cognition that has not occurred—that is, by a cognition that has not even arisen—there would be a lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) everywhere; there would be no confidence, which is to say no certainty regarding the indicative power (*gamakatva*), in any logical reason (*hetu*), because a sublater might always be suspected. This is not the case for the proponent of the necessary connection (*pratibandhavādin*); in every logical reason—

There is no lack of confidence when the reason (*hetu*) is connected with the probandum (*sādhya*), because there is also an absence of any suspicion of sublation (*bādhā*). However, prior to the formulation of the reason, there might be a suspicion of sublation; for this very reason, it is said that the statement of the reason is made regarding what is doubted. Furthermore, there exists no established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates the "remainder" (*śeṣavat*). Therefore, it remains established that even for the *śeṣavat* [reason], there is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) based on mere non-perception (*adarśanamātra*) regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is indeed established as a means of proof, yet it requires certainty regarding the existence of that [concomitance] in such a manner. For even if non-existence is established in some instances through non-perception (*anupalambha*), non-existence is not established everywhere in the absence of that [probans], because that which is not invariably connected [to the probandum] lacks such necessity.
Due to doubt, there is indeed no exclusion [of the probandum from the heterogeneous instances]; this is the deviation of the *śeṣavat* [reason]. ||16||
Furthermore, there would also be a negative (vyatireka) reason:
"This living body is not soulless, because [otherwise] it would follow that it lacks breath and so forth. [In the case of] soulless things such as jars—

Because breath and so forth are not observed in all things—both those seen and those unseen—and because the self is established through their cessation; for if non-existence were not established by the non-perception of the invisible, then the absence of a self in jars and the like would not be established, and thus breath and so forth would not cease [therein]. Consequently, there would be the possibility of their functioning.

[Objection: But surely, by the force of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), when there is the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) and the exclusion of the reason (*hetuvyatireka*), that exclusion would be a means of cognition (*gamaka*) by its mere existence. To this, he says: "But the exclusion... and so forth. That exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is indeed established—that is, certain—as the proof. Thus, the certainty of the reason being of such a nature [is required] regarding that which is the absence of the probandum.

The absence of the reason depends upon the ascertainment of that [absence]. This is what is meant: for us, unlike for you, exclusion (*vyatireka*) does not consist in the mere absence of perception. Rather, when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum and the probans, the property inherent in the reason (*svagato dharmaḥ*) is its exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) when the probandum is absent. Furthermore, whatever is the nature of the reason must necessarily depend upon its own ascertainment, because it is a means of cognition (*jñāpaka*).
If it is asked, "How is it that, according to your view, the *śeṣavat* [inference] is subject to deviation? he says: "But because of non-perception," and so forth.

Even if the absence of the reason (*hetu*) is established in some part of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there remains doubt regarding the unconnected reason with respect to the probandum (*sādhya*). This is because its absence in every instance of the counter-example—where the probandum is absent—is not established; therefore, that very lack of exclusion from the counter-example is what constitutes the deviation.
There is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the *śeṣavat* [inference] (1);

the word "and" (*kiṃca*) serves to aggregate another fault. If non-existence [of the probandum] were established merely through non-perception, then even a purely negative (*vyatirekin*) reason would be valid. An example of such [a reason] is: "This is not soulless," and so forth. This was stated by way of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) concerning the lack of breath and other [vital signs].

By way of a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*): because it possesses breath and so forth, [the body] is endowed with a self (*sātmaka*). This reason is said to be "non-deviant" (*avyatirekin*)—meaning it possesses the property of being absent when the probandum is absent—because it is not observed in any instance possessing a self, and it is excluded from all things devoid of a self. For indeed, since breath, inhalation, and exhalation are not observed in things devoid of a self, such as jars and the like, whether perceived or unperceived, [it follows that they must possess a self].

Because blinking and non-blinking are not observed. Regarding those things that are seen, their non-observation occurs precisely through the non-perception of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), since breath and so forth have reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). Regarding those that are not seen, it is by virtue of belonging to that same class. Therefore, selflessness (*nairātmya*) is pervaded by the absence of breath and so forth. In the case of a living body, however, because that [absence] is excluded—namely, the exclusion of the absence of possessing breath and so forth—there follows the exclusion of selflessness, which constitutes the cognition of a self (*ātman*).

[Objection: It might be so. [Question: Then how is it a cause for doubt in your view? [Response: He says: "Because of the non-perception of the invisible self," and so forth. Since the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in jars and the like is not established due to the non-perception of the invisible self, the property of being devoid of self (*nairātmya*) is not established in jars and the like. For this reason, there is no exclusion of breath and so forth from that which is devoid of self. By means of the absence of breath and so forth, even the property of being devoid of self—which is itself doubted—is [not established]; this is the consideration of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*).

If it is argued that [the self] is established through acceptance (*abhyupagama*), then how is the self established [otherwise]? Otherwise, how could the absence of a self (*nairātmya*) be established for another [opponent] who lacks such acceptance? For by means of acceptance, one distinguishes between those things possessing a self and those lacking a self;

yet, even while stating that [the reason] is indicative (*gamakatva*) by its presence therein, one has admitted that the self is known through scripture (*āgamika*) and not through inference (*anumeya*). Therefore, in the case of non-perception—
Nor is there a cessation [of the self] from anything, because the cessation of the self itself is unestablished.

Even if there were a cessation of the vital breaths and so forth, it would not be indicative [of the self's cessation], because their connection [to the self] is absent and thus their cessation is unestablished in all cases.

As for the application of the "unestablished" (asiddhi) fallacy in cases such as "existing in the similar class (sapakṣa), both existing and non-existing," and so forth— which should be illustrated accordingly according to the circumstances— that too is not to be stated as an application of the unestablished fallacy. //20//
This means "establishment.

If it is argued that because the Buddhist has accepted selflessness (*nairātmya*), the absence of a self in jars and other things is thereby established by virtue of that acceptance—then if the Buddhist's own acceptance is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can the existence of a self in a living body be established now? That too [must be established] by the Buddhist.

[The opponent claims: "Selflessness is accepted [only] for the living body; therefore, since the acceptance of selflessness regarding the living body lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*), its self is being established.
[The respondent replies: If that is so, then for the other [party], how could selflessness be established even for a jar or the like, which is distinct from the living body?
For the Buddhist's own acceptance cannot be a means of valid cognition in one instance and not in another. Furthermore, by means of mere acceptance...
By distinguishing between those things that possess a self (*sātmaka*) and those that do not (*anātmaka*), both you and we agree that jars and the like are devoid of a self;
therefore, they are *anātmaka*. However, while we accept the living body as possessing a self, you maintain it to be devoid of a self.

Having thus distinguished them, by asserting that the absence of breath and other signs in those things devoid of a self establishes their nature regarding the self, you [demonstrate] their probative capacity with respect to the self.

The opponent has accepted that the self is known through scripture (*āgamika*), not through inference. Therefore, even though the self is not perceived in things such as a jar, its absence cannot be established because the self is by nature imperceptible; thus, there is no exclusion [of the self] from anything such as breath, which would be devoid of a self. Consequently, [the reason] is non-probative (*agamaka*). To begin with, the exclusion of the self from anything is not at all established. Having granted this for the sake of argument...

It is replied: even if that [breath] ceases and the self ceases in some instances—such as in the case of a jar where it is observed that although [the breath] has ceased, the vital functions (*prāṇa*) and so forth do not necessarily follow because there is no connection with the self; and since, even in all unobserved cases such as jars, the cessation of the vital functions is not established by the cessation of the self—the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful, and therefore [the reason] is not a means of valid cognition.

He states that if one accepts the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based merely on non-perception, there is this further fault, beginning with the words "And also... (*yāpi* etc.). He asks, "What is that? and replies, "Likewise, [the reason] exists in the similar instances" (*tathā sapakṣe san* etc.). This passage belongs to the Master [Dignāga]. In that context, having raised a doubt, he specifies that the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is understood as being ascertained by both the proponent and the opponent; therefore, [the reason] which is unestablished for either or for both is excluded.

This excludes [the fallacies of] the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) and so forth. Just as the four types of the unestablished (*asiddha*) are excluded by the ascertainment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), so too are the various kinds of the unestablished—such as "existent in the similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) or "non-existent in the similar instance"—eliminated by the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

This is because the categories of the unestablished, such as the "unestablished for one party" (*anyatarāsiddha*), cannot possibly occur within the similar instances and so forth. He states that these should be illustrated accordingly.
Nor can it be said that there is a connection with non-establishment;

for when there is a cognition of the contrary (*vipakṣa*), since there is doubt regarding non-perception, there is an absence [of certainty] even when there is perception. Therefore, from non-perception, there is negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

no. For one who considers that the non-cessation of doubt persists even when there is non-perception—on account of the fact that [the reason] expresses certainty regarding both [sides], as stated in the passage beginning "that which expresses certainty regarding both"—states its refutation.

the exclusion of a particular [property] would be the cause [of exclusion] because of its non-observation.

Since there is doubt regarding the presence of the reason (*hetu*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) when there is only non-perception as a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*), how [could there be certainty]? Because that [doubt] is impossible when there is perception [of the reason] in the counter-example; for when the reason is perceived in the counter-example, that doubt does not exist. Therefore, by implication, the exclusion of the reason from the counter-example is based on non-perception. Thus, it is doubtful.

This is not so; for immediately following that, there is the statement beginning with, "But that very word which expresses what is certain for both [parties]," and so forth. That very word which denotes the three-fold nature (trairūpya) as being certain for both, or [denotes] non-establishment (asiddhatva) and so on, is itself the proof (sādhana) or the refutation (dūṣaṇa). The passage, "Nor does a word expressing what is established or doubtful for only one [party] constitute [proof], because it requires further proof," etc., is the illustration here. For [the word of] only one...
Whether it be the proponent or the opponent, that which states what is unestablished (*asiddha*) or doubtful (*sandigdha*) is neither a proof (*sādhana*) nor a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
A reason whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful is itself doubtful for both parties; therefore, its statement is not a proof.

Since only a reason certain for both has been declared as such, even when there is non-perception (*anupalambha*), because of the doubt regarding its absence from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), [the reason remains uncertain].

Considering that the reason would not cease [to apply] because of this, he states the negation of the probative status of that reason whose negative concomitance is doubtful, by means of an application of non-establishment (*asiddhi*).

Furthermore, if exclusion were intended to occur through non-perception, then a specific property such as audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*), which is uncommon [to both categories], would become a cause for exclusion. Why? Because it is not observed in either the eternal or the non-eternal. He explains this with the words "of audibility also," and so forth. For in that case, exclusion is held to result from mere non-perception.

Furthermore, the non-perception of audibility in both the eternal and the non-eternal would constitute its reason for exclusion from them; it would become a reason for the negation of both eternality and non-eternality. If, indeed, by virtue of that non-perception, it were excluded from those two, [then it would follow].

Then [the opponent] asks: "How is it that audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is the cause for the exclusion of those two? To this he says: "For not... For there is no exclusion other than the exclusion of those two, namely the exclusion of the eternal and the non-eternal. If it is asked, "Even for you, how is it that audibility is not the cause of exclusion?", he says: "Because there is no exclusion..."

Because it is for the sake of exclusion (vyavaccheda). 3. There is no consideration of pervasion (vyāpti) other than the exclusion of what is not that [the probans]. For how could something which is ascertained as "not existing" in a certain place—not being an exclusion from that—fail to indicate its absence? Since there is no determination of exclusion from anything else, [pervasion] is nothing but the exclusion from that [where the probandum does not exist].
How could that which exists where it is ascertained as "not being" fail to make known its non-existence?
If it is argued that its non-existence is established by another means of valid cognition, then [we reply: no, for that which is not perceived [cannot be so established]. (21)

Furthermore, even if there were another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublated the exclusion of both, [the following would apply]: for among things whose nature consists in mutual exclusion, the affirmation of one through the exclusion of the other constitutes a non-negation; this is because affirmation and negation are contradictory [if they occur simultaneously].

It is not the case that non-existence [is established] by mere non-perception. This being so, non-perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because there is the possibility of sublation (*bādhā*).
(kha) Refutation of the Master’s view:
Likewise, in other cases as well, sublation by another means of knowledge is possible.
"‘dastu’ and so forth. Because there is no certainty regarding exclusion based merely on non-perception from something permanent or impermanent [respectively].

And this lack of certainty arises because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established in either case. And this must necessarily be so; otherwise, if a property is ascertained to be absent in a certain locus, how could that same property, while existing, be said to be absent in some other locus?
How could that which is ascertained not lead to its non-existence?

If it is suspected that there would be sublation by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when audibility—though excluded from both the permanent and the impermanent—is used to prove the exclusion of both, [the author says: "Or even so," etc., which is an explanation of the very same point: namely, regarding the exclusion of both by means of audibility.

When the exclusion of both the eternal (*nitya*) and the non-eternal (*anitya*) is to be proven, there exists another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that serves as a sublater (*bādhaka*). He states this with the words "mutually exclusive," and so forth.

Those whose nature consists in mutual exclusion are "such" (*tathā*). For instance, the exclusion of the eternal is itself impermanence (*anityatva*), and the exclusion of that [impermanence] is itself eternality (*nityatva*); likewise, the exclusion of existence (*bhāva*) is itself non-existence (*abhāva*), and the exclusion of non-existence is itself existence.
Because one [property] is excluded by the affirmation of another; and because the second, being contradictory, is affirmed, there is no negation [of the first].

This is what is meant: when "audibility" is excluded from the eternal—meaning it is differentiated from it—that very [fact] would establish impermanence; and since that same [audibility] is excluded from the impermanent, it would exclude impermanence.

And if one were to enjoin [something] eternally, there would be both injunction and prohibition for that same single thing at one and the same time; and that is improper. Because injunction and prohibition are mutually contradictory, there can be no prohibition of anything whatsoever. For an injunction is characterized by the cessation of prohibition, and a prohibition is simply the cessation of an injunction. How could those two, being mutually opposed, exist simultaneously in a single entity?

(1) Therefore, there is no certainty regarding exclusion from anything whatsoever on account of audibility; this is the position of the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*). "Now" (*idānīm*) refers to the absence of sublation (*bādhā*). From the non-perception of such [a reason] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the non-existence of the reason therein is established. Consequently, under these circumstances, non-perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because sublation is possible.

If it is argued that "let there be no means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) regarding audibility itself, but not elsewhere, because there is no sublation (*bādhā*) [there]," he says: "In that way," and so forth.

Even elsewhere, the sublation by another means of valid cognition is possible for the reason (*hetu*), namely for the non-perception that establishes the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Why? He says:
"By the definition," and so forth. Audibility is endowed with that definition which is the basis for the exclusion [of the reason] from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) through its non-perception.

If there were no sublation (*bādhā*) regarding that which possesses such a characteristic (*tallakṣaṇa*), then that very characteristic would be undermined, resulting in a lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) everywhere.
If it is argued that even in the domain of inference, a lack of confidence would follow because contradictions between perception and inference are observed; [we reply:]...

This is not so, because [the definition] is impossible as stated; and because that which is possible does not possess those characteristics. If it is argued that "the non-deviant contradictory" has been mentioned, [we reply: its scope within the domain of inference has not been specified; therefore, its scope must be pointed out. || 21 ||
Furthermore:
"The observed inconsistency and the unobserved [inconsistency] would be non-contradictory to touch. (22)

Since there is the possibility of sublation regarding that non-perception which constitutes the [probans], the very definition—that is, the essential nature—of that non-perception which is intended to establish the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) would be undermined as being applicable to all cases. Consequently, there can be no confidence in non-perception everywhere as a means of establishing negative concomitance; nor can there be any certainty regarding its capacity to produce knowledge.
If this is so, then even regarding the object of inference, since contradictions between perception and inference are observed in some cases—

for instance, when it is argued that "sound is eternal because it is audible, like the nature of sound" (*śabdatva*), its eternity is sublated by inference; and likewise, when it is argued that "sound is inaudible because it exists, like a pot," it is sublated by perception— therefore, in all such instances, inference must be [qualified] by a definition that excludes those [cases].
If it is argued that this leads to the consequence of non-respiration, this is not so.

For, as stated, in an inference produced by the non-perception of an effect or an essential nature (*svabhāva*), there is no contradiction with perception or inference; moreover, since that which is subject to contradiction with perception and so forth does not possess the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of such [valid] inference, it lacks the definition of that inference.

[This is] because [of its being a reason]. If there is no sublation (*bādhā*) in an inference possessing the characteristics as previously described, then two reasons endowed with the characteristics of a reason that establish mutually contradictory objects, having descended upon a single subject (*dharmin*), would be called "contradictory non-deviants" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*); such is the statement of the Master [Dignāga]. By this, he states the abandonment of his own accepted position (*abhyupetahāni*). Regarding the object of inference, the contradictory non-deviant—...

Since this has been stated by the Teacher (*ācārya*) in his words and so forth, how can there be an abandonment of what was accepted? To the question, "Where then did the Teacher say [this]?", he says: "And the object," and so forth. This refers to the *viruddhāvyabhicārin* (the contradictory non-erroneous reason). Regarding "Furthermore," and so forth: here, the Vaiśeṣika, for the sake of proving the existence of wind (*vāyu*), uttered the sūtra: "And touch [is perceived], but [it is not seen] among those things that are visible. The meaning of this is as follows: (1)

Whatever is a quality (guṇa) is dependent upon a substance (dravyāśrayī), such as color-form (rūpa) and so forth. Furthermore, the tactile sensation (sparśa) that is not produced by heating (apākaja) and is neither hot nor cold is a quality; therefore, there must be a substance that serves as its substratum (āśraya). This [quality] is not a quality of the perceived [elements] such as earth and the rest, because they possess qualities such as tactile sensations produced by heating, being hot, or being cold. Consequently, when it is stated that the substance to which this quality belongs must be air (vāyu):
Regarding the Vaiśeṣika [position], the teacher Dignāga stated there that "if a negation were made regarding things seen merely on the basis of non-perception, that too would not be logical.

Showing that this contradicts what was previously stated, Vārttikakāra says "dṛṣṭa... and so forth: "If cessation [of doubt] were to occur through non-perception, then likewise, because of the cause which is the non-perception of the unseen..."

If it is argued that "the establishment of cessation [of doubt] occurs through non-perception," and if it is asked, "How is it that what was stated—namely, that 'if a negation is made regarding things already seen based on mere non-observation, that too is not tenable'—is untenable? [It is not untenable], because the absence [of a thing] is established through non-perception. (17)
The negation of that which is characterized by the qualities of tangibility and verbal expression is indeed appropriate.

It is not inappropriate, because there is no negation regarding the mere object that is its visible intrinsic nature. However, since one states the negation after having grasped [the category] "earth" and so forth in a general sense, [it is appropriate], for even when that [nature of earth] exists in cotton, stones, leaves, and the like, a difference in tangibility is observed.
Since there must be a suspicion that this [property] might also occur in some particular case, it is improper to exclude it based merely on its non-observation everywhere;

for the Vaiśeṣikas' argument—that the touch which is neither hot nor cold is not observed in earth and the other elements—is illogical. That inconsistency described by the Vaiśeṣikas regarding the perceived elements, of which the Teacher has stated the impropriety, would indeed be consistent and logical [if applied to the case at hand].

The meaning is "it might be so. He explains that with the words beginning "yadā" (when). As the Teacher said in the section on Air (*vāyu-prakaraṇa*): "If, by the mere non-perception [of touch], a prohibition of touch were to be made regarding earth and the other elements which are [otherwise] perceived—this would not be logical for the Vaiśeṣika."
Thus [it is said]. If the teacher also intends the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by mere non-perception, then how could the prohibition of touch be improper?
It would indeed be proper. What is the reason? Because here too, it is accepted that the absence [of the probandum] is established through the non-apprehension of the reason.

"Is it not so? and so forth says the opponent. "Because of the attainment of the conditions for perception, the negation of a touch that is neither hot nor cold—which is not produced by fire and is not perceived—in earth and the other elements is indeed logical.
"It is not logical," says the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī). "For what reason? Because [a substance] such as earth, which is other than that which is neither hot nor cold..."

That which is conjoined with touch is perceptible and visible; and elsewhere, even though it is imperceptible in respect of place and so forth, earth and the like are of that same nature, being conjoined with such touch. The compound *dṛśyastatsvabhāvaśca* is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound meaning "the visible and its nature. That very thing is the object; that alone is the "mere" (*tanmātra*), formed by the rule *sup supā*. Because there is no prohibition of touch in that case; for if there were a prohibition therein—

This would indeed be a certainty, provided that this Vaiśeṣika, having grasped earth and the other elements in their general nature without any distinction, were to state a negation of touch, saying: "Whatever there is of earth and so forth, all that is devoid of neither-hot-nor-cold touch. However, touch does not possess the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpti*) in earth and the others taken merely as such; nor does it [belong] to a single...

The restriction of touch belongs to earth and the other elements because, although the general category of earth and so forth persists across its various particulars—such as cotton, stones, and leaves—even while that [category] exists and earth and so forth exist, a difference in touch is observed. For instance, the touch of cotton is of one kind, characterized by softness, while that of a stone is of another kind, characterized by hardness and so forth. This refers to the touch that is neither hot nor cold.
In some cases, thinking that there must be a possibility of its occurrence due to a particular earthly substance, one should [investigate] everywhere regarding earth. 428b. [End of section].
Refutation:
Thus, any master whatsoever who asserts non-existence on the basis of non-perception is [himself] perceived.
Moreover:

"The potencies of substances are seen to differ according to differences in place and other factors. Therefore, the determination of a certain property observed in one instance is not logically applicable elsewhere. (23)
The denial of a touch that is neither hot nor cold based merely on the observation of a forest fire is illogical.

As for what is said— that because earth and the other elements are uniform everywhere, their touch must likewise be uniformly neither hot nor cold— whereas the distinction between smoothness and so forth, which occurs despite the presence of earth and the other elements, is due to the dense or non-dense conjunction of the atoms of earth and the others.
As for the argument "because it has been produced," that is incorrect. For in the case of non-dense [substances], there is an absence of conjunction due to the lack of contiguity.
Therefore, just as there is density of conjunction among the atoms of stone, so too is it for the atoms of cotton; how then could there be a distinction such as smoothness and so forth?

It may be so. Therefore, even though conjunction exists, the atoms of iron are of one nature and the atoms of cotton are of another; and it is precisely this that causes the difference in smoothness and so forth. This difference is not produced by the density or lack of density of the conjunction.
And thus, just as there is a difference in touch such as smoothness due to the difference between earth and other elements, so too is there a difference in the quality of being neither-hot-nor-cold.
It might be argued:

"Granted that there may be no inference of air regarding an unperceived object; however, in the case of a perceived object, since a touch that is neither hot nor cold—which is visible—is not perceived as being connected with earth or other elements, an inference of air from that [touch] would be possible."

He thinks as follows: if the quality-nature of touch were established, then there would be an inference of the substance wind; however, that very [quality-nature] is unestablished. Because it is perceived independently, for us, it is merely a specific kind of touch that is called "wind. But the Master Dignāga, having accepted a wind distinct from touch, [declared] the inference of others regarding it to be incorrect.
Thus, there is no fault in saying it is "liberated.

Therefore, this remains established: by stating that there is an absence of negation based merely on the non-observation of positive and negative concomitance, the Teacher has intended the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

If it is asked, "Who was censured for this [objection]? he says: "In this way," and so forth. "In this way" means by the arguments just mentioned. A certain disciple of the Teacher, who was ignorant of the Teacher’s treatises and who asserted non-existence on the grounds of non-perception, was censured.

Furthermore, he says "deśādi-bhedāt" (due to differences in place, etc. in order to show the contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa-bādhā*) that would arise if non-existence were accepted merely because something is not seen.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), differences in time and processing (*saṃskāra*) are included. Even among substances belonging to a single genus, powers (*śaktayaḥ*) characterized by taste (*rasa*), potency (*vīrya*), post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*), and so forth, are seen to be diverse and manifold according to differences in place and other factors. In that regard, among substances possessing multiple powers, [one might argue] based on the observation of only one.

Because a substance that possesses a single nature is observed in one place, it is not logical to determine its existence in another location and so forth [simply by that]. 3. Regarding the consideration of pervasion (*vyāpti*): if, merely by observing [the probans] in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), there were non-deviation from it even for that which is unconnected [to it], then how is it that certain substances are observed in a certain way in a certain place, yet are observed otherwise elsewhere? For example:

Certain medicinal herbs possess specific tastes, potencies, and post-digestive effects due to the particularity of their soil, and not otherwise; likewise, this is also due to differences in time and processing. However, because those [effects] are not observed to be so by people in that region, it does not follow that all such herbs exist as they are described in reality. This is because other qualities depend upon other causes. But in the absence of a specific cause for variation, it would be so.

Inference: Even that which has an unseen author is preceded by human refinement (*puruṣasaṃskāra*), because there is no distinction among sentences; because all types [of texts] are seen to have humans as their cause; and because a distinction is observed among all qualities [of authors]. This is not possible, just as there is no determination of the nature of a substance based on what is not perceived.

With the words "yadi" and so forth, he explains this very point: if the non-deviation from the probandum (sādhyāvyabhicāra) of a reason that is unconnected to its own probandum is desired merely because it is not observed in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), then the form of a substance perceived in one place would have to be inferable in another place as well, on the basis of the commonality of being a substance; for at that time, [that form] exists there too.
It is merely the non-observation [of the reason] in the counter-example (vipakṣa),

and this is not logical. Because certain substances are observed in some places in a certain way by virtue of having specific tastes and so forth, yet they are seen elsewhere in a different way— that is, with a reversal of the form as previously observed.

With the words "yathā" and so forth, he states the subject matter. *Vīrya* is the power to remove defects; *pariṇāma* is the transformation or maturation. The analysis of the compound is: those [plants] whose tastes, potencies, and maturations are distinguished (*viśiṣṭa*). "Not elsewhere" means not in a location other than that specific field (*kṣetra-viśeṣa*). Just as they become possessed of distinguished tastes, potencies, and maturations due to a particular place, so too do they arise from differences in time and processing (*saṃskāra*). Processing (*saṃskāra*)...

[This refers to] the sprinkling of milk and so forth. Nor [can it be established] on the grounds that "those persons whose specific locations have been observed to possess such particular tastes and so forth—therefore, all [plants], even those not in those locations, must be identical in reality by virtue of having similar forms and so forth, and thus possess the same nature as those previously apprehended. What is the reason? Because other qualities, namely the specific variations of taste and so forth, [are not necessarily concomitant].

Because it depends on other causes; however, in the absence of a specific cause, there would be an inference of a single nature. That Vedic [text] which has an unseen author is likewise preceded by human refinement and caused by human effort. And this is the probandum. Since there is no distinction between sentences intended to be human and those intended to be non-human, the reason has been stated by this [argument].

Furthermore, the application [of the reason] is as follows: whatever entity has an undifferentiated nature (*abhinnasvabhāva*) possesses the same cause; for example, one instance of smoke is of the same genus as another instance of smoke. And sentences regarded as non-human (*apauruṣeya*) have an undifferentiated nature from human sentences;
thus, this is a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*). Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*); for by those very modes [of operation], such as the removal of poison and so forth...

A distinction is maintained for the Vedic [texts], because all types of those [Vedic texts] are observed by persons to have a cause. For instance, even in the case of mantras such as the *śabarādi*, effects such as the removal of poison are observed.
If, on the grounds of the similarity of the nature of the words, the human authorship of even that which has no visible author is inferred, then in that case—
By seeing the continuum of one's own mind, all mental phenomena are known: (1) therefore, as long as there is the nature of awakening, [so long... (Indian text:
*pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* 1.23).

If there were no specific causes for the distinctions among persons by which one might infer total identity on the basis of some slight similarity such as speech and so forth—since specific cognition arises from specific mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and since such [causes] are possible for others as well;

and because, if they were impossible, there would be no reason to infer them; and because dispassion (*vairāgya*) is not perceived; and because that which is unperceived cannot function as either the sublated or the sublator—[then your position would fail].

Everything that is dependent on the five sense-faculties and conceptual, and which contains within it the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that generate passion and so forth—just as it is now, so too will it be in the future state; and just as it is for me, so too for others. (1) Therefore, by virtue of being of the nature of mind, being dependent on the sense-faculties, and being the cause of speech and so forth, the mind of every person is always associated with passion and the like, and grasps at fixed objects.

Anticipating the objection, "Why is it not inferred that [the Veda] has a non-universal scope? he says: "Not so," and so forth. Just as sentences do not have possible specific causes [for their production], persons do not likewise have possible specific causes—by which [absence of specific causes] [the inference would be established].

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "speech etc.," there is the inclusion of being dependent on sense organs, having a mind, and so forth. [The argument is: by a mere portion of speech etc. itself...

Therefore, based on a partial similarity with that mark (*liṅga*), one might infer a complete identity in all respects—whether by way of possessing passion and so forth, having restricted objects, or by some other quality—among men.
To the question, "How can there even be the possibility of a distinguishing cause? he says: "Because a distinction is observed among all mental qualities."
For desire, wisdom, and the like, although their functions in grasping their respective objects are extremely sluggish, become more acute over time;
and it is observed that their respective objects become clearer to them—this is the distinction seen. To the question "From what does this [distinction] arise?", he says:

"From cultivation (*saṃskāra*), which is practice (*abhyāsa*)," because a distinction in wisdom and the other faculties is perceived through a distinction in that [cultivation]. Let it be granted that wisdom and the others belong to the mind (*manas*).
Since excellence is observed through repeated practice, but omniscience and such qualities have not been observed, how can their existence be established?

To this he says: "In the same way," and so forth. For it is possible for another person to possess the specific quality of omniscience and the like; moreover, by the power of practice, there arises a vivid appearance of the mental image (*ākāra*) of selflessness and of a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) that grasps all objects as universals (*sāmānya*).

That alone would be dispassion and the state of omniscience. Therefore, there would be an inference of the impossibility of the specific qualities of dispassion and omniscience based on these three reasons: if conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) regarding the object of selflessness or regarding all objects were impossible;
or if, even when possible, there were no distinction among the qualities of the mind (*manoguṇa*); or if, despite the existence of such a distinction, the cause of that distinction were not known.

It might be so; however, since conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) having selflessness (*nairātmya*) and so forth as its object is possible, and the specific cause—namely, repeated practice—is known, it is therefore like the inference of capacity: just as this causal complex of seeds is capable of producing a sprout provided there is no obstruction or deficiency, so too [is it capable] even after a long time, provided there is no obstruction or deficiency.
Furthermore, because of the specific nature of practice and the intensity of cultivation, it is possible for knowledge—whether its object is selflessness or all phenomena—to possess a vivid clarity;
thus, there is an inference of the possibility of both dispassion (*vairāgya*) and omniscience (*sarvajñatva*). Such, then, is our inference of possibility.
As for an inference of impossibility, you possess no valid reason that could subvert that property [of omniscience]. Therefore—
The connection is that "men do not possess non-existent specific causes" because of their existence. But how is there an absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*)?

He says: "Because dispassion (*vairāgya*) is not observed. And this is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative mark), because omniscience (*sarvajña*) is also not observed. And since dispassion is not established by its non-observation, for there is no effect that deviates from passion and the like. Even if specific [causes] were possible...

Because they are impossible to perceive. Sentences are not subject to such rejection in the same way as persons are, because they are specific instances of what is perceptible. If they were imperceptible, it would contradict the admission that there is a difference in kind (*vijātīyatva*) among those whose specific qualities (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) are unperceived; for those specific qualities [would have to exist] elsewhere.
Because it is possible [to prove it]; because there is no contradiction between perceptible [statements] and that which has an imperceptible nature;
and because the relationship of sublation and sublated cannot be established between a reason and an object of error.
He said:

It might be thought that the impossibility of dispassion and so forth in [the Buddha] is not directly inferred from his mere speech, such that a subverting reason (*bādhaka-hetu*) would have to be sought; rather, passion and the like are inferred in those who are considered to be free from passion, and once they are so inferred, by implication—

The phrase "due to passion" (*rāga*) and so forth refers to the contradiction between passion and detachment, even though detachment has not been perceived, because it is prohibited for those who have transcended the three [types of] passion and so on.
Indeed, there is no effect that is invariably concomitant with passion and the like. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), non-omniscience is also encompassed.
For instance, starting from the acquisition of linguistic convention, to the extent that there is thorough knowledge of an object, to that same extent...

Since the capacity for speech has that [knowledge] as its object, if someone were to possess a cognition whose object is everything, who could prevent their capacity for speech from also having that as its object?
This might be argued: "If he possesses a distinction characterized by dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth, why is it not perceived by us?"
Thus he says: even if those specific qualities characterized by detachment (*vairāgya*) and so forth were possible, they cannot be perceived in the mental continuum of another.
Nor can there be a rejection [of their existence] simply because such things are not perceived; for he says that such remote things do not deserve to be rejected.

This might be so: [the opponent argues that] just as persons are not subject to refutation, so too are their statements. To this, he says: "Not so," and so forth. What is the reason? Because they possess observable distinctions (*dṛśyaviśeṣatvāt*). For it is held that a distinction in Vedic statements is indeed observable. Now, if such a distinction is not accepted—if one were to admit a distinction even while it remains unobservable—[then the following would ensue].
For, since that specific quality is not perceived, it would contradict the admission that Vedic sentences—which have unperceived specific qualities—are of a different genus from worldly sentences.

It might be thought: (1) the specific qualities of the Vedic [sentences] are indeed perceptible, such as their being difficult to hear (*duḥśravaṇatva*) or difficult to pronounce (*durbhaṇatva*), by means of which...

[The author] says "of those specificities" (*tadviśeṣāṇām*) and so forth, [anticipating the objection]: "They will be distinct from those produced by human agency" (*pauruṣeyebhyaḥ*). The word "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) refers to those produced by human agency. It is not only because it would contradict the acceptance of their being of a different genus (*vijātīyatva*) that the invisibility of these specificities is untenable; for this further reason as well: because there is a contradiction between being perceptible and having an imperceptible nature. Indeed, a single thing cannot possess two natures.

A contradiction arises. [The opponent argues: "The particulars are indeed directly perceived; however, because of the presence of a cause for error, they are not ascertained, just like the potency of poison and so forth. To this, he replies: "Because there is no cause for error. For in the case of poisons and the like, the perception of a similarity in form is the cause of error; but this is not the case with Vedic [words]. If it is asked how this is known, he says: "Because there is no sublation."
"Because error is unestablished": if, for the Vedic [texts], no specific error is perceived, then [the claim that they are] dependent on something else [is untenable].
ISTĪ, TAKEN HERE FROM YOUR ASANA, GO, GO, EAT!

Because there is an absence of a cause [for error], because there is an absence of a subverting factor, and because error is not established; whereas in the case of persons, the perception of specific differences acts as a subverting factor, so it is not the same. Nor is there a distinction among sentences, because that which exists as a state dependent on another is not a specific quality of those [sentences].
Therefore, for all things whose nature is non-different from that [sentence], either all are produced by a person, or none at all.
ga. Refutation of the Vaiśeṣika View:
Furthermore, that which does not establish the non-existence of the self, clay, consciousness, and so forth—
Is that very non-perception the prover of the absence of a cause? ||24||

For one who takes its non-apprehension as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the doctrine of a self (*ātmavāda*) would be without support; a means of valid cognition for the self would arise that contradicts error, whereby there would be certainty regarding the error and its cause—but that does not exist. Therefore, when it is to be proven that Vedic words are no different from worldly words, there is no proving evidence (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*).

If that is so, then what is the subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) regarding persons (*puruṣa*) based on the mere non-perception of such a teacher, by virtue of which there would be a fault in proving the equality of all qualities? To this he says: "In persons," and so forth. The very fact of observing excellence—such as wisdom and the like—which is preceded by practice, is itself the subverting evidence.
If the mind of a person were such that detachment were impossible for it, then no excellence could be produced through practice; yet such excellence does exist.

Therefore, because the perception of this excellence acts as a sublater [of the contrary], the case is not the same. As for what was said regarding the inference from Vedic statements—that there is an absence of a non-perceptible nature in words that are themselves perceptible—this would be a fault only if the distinction were a matter of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

It would have to be [of its own nature]; however, [the author] says it is "of the nature of another" (*parabhāvabhūta*). Regarding the phrase "of that which has become the nature of another": having gone to the nature of another is "become the nature of another"; the meaning is "having another intrinsic nature" (*anyasvabhāva*). "Because there is no distinction from that" means because there is no distinction from the sentence.
Since there is no distinction among sentences, therefore all [sentences], whether considered human or non-human, possess an identical intrinsic nature.
Human action (*puruṣakriyā*) means acting by means of persons; or rather, it belongs to no one at all. The meaning is that even in worldly [activity], there is no such thing as human action.

Having stated the contradiction with the treatises and the contradiction with the means of valid cognition for one who desires the exclusion [of the probandum] from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*) as the reason, he describes the mutual inconsistency among the non-Buddhist schools (*tīrthika*), beginning with "Furthermore," and so forth. "Earth is sentient"—this is the Lokāyata view. "The self and earth-sentience" is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). "And so forth"— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*

From the word [“non-perception”], [one understands] substance and so forth in the case of milk and the like. Even though non-perception has been stated by the opponent as a means to establish the non-existence of those [entities], it is held by the proponents of the self (*ātmavādin*) and others not to be a prover of that non-existence, because mere non-perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatvāt*).

That very same non-perception is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge for the negation of the self and so forth; why? Because of the absence of a reason (*hetvabhāva*), [that is,] because of the absence of a reason [that would exclude it] from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

It is the establisher of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). For those such as the Vaiśeṣikas who employ non-perception (*anupalambha*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the absence of a cause, the doctrine of the self would become baseless and unsupported; this is because, in that case, non-perception—which establishes non-existence—is possible. To explain: there is no perception of the self through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since it is admitted to be eternally beyond the senses (*nityaparokṣa*). Now, if...

One might argue that there is indeed perception [of the self] through inference itself; to this, he says: "Because its effect," and so forth. Precisely because the self is not perceptible (*apratyakṣatvāt*), there is no perception [of it] through inference, since the logical mark (*liṅga*)—which would consist of the nature of its effect—is not ascertained. Regarding the consideration of pervasion (*vyāpti*), because its effect is unestablished (*asiddhatvāt*): for the sense faculties and so forth, consciousness alone is the effect, and that [consciousness] is occasional.
Because it is conscious (*citkatvāt*). Its establishment is said to be through dependence;
that is, it is established that it has some cause, though not necessarily of such a nature [as previously imagined]. In this way, the effect consisting of pleasure and so forth is proven.

It does not establish any point whatsoever, because it accepts [the self] as having a cause by means of some reason or other. And this being the case, there would be no non-perception of the self at all. Therefore, why is one who rejects it through non-perception countered?
How could such a person establish a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)?

And someone, desiring to establish the consciousness of clay despite its being unperceived, might argue that—just as there is inference for the sense faculties and so forth even though they are eternally beyond perception—there will likewise be [inference] for the self.
To this, he says: "Of the sense faculties," and so on. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the seeds of memory and the like are included. Consciousness itself is the effect.

Because it is occasional; for instance, even when form, light, and attention are present, consciousness is absent in states such as when the eyes are closed, whereas it occurs again in states when the eyes are open. Thus, the effect that is consciousness is established as being dependent on other causes; therefore, by the establishment of this dependence, the existence of the sense faculties and so forth is proven.
It is said:

this is what is meant. That which is dependent and occasional consciousness is inferred to have some cause; that very thing is conventionally designated as the "sense-faculty" (*indriya*). However, it is not [the sense-faculty] in the manner [described by the opponent]. Thus it is not [the case].

The meaning is that the sense organ is inferred as being endowed with a specific form, such as corporeality (*mūrtatva*) and so forth. "In this way" means that just as the inference of the sense organ is based on the impossibility of explaining the occasional nature of the effect, which is cognition, in any other manner; likewise, by the inference that there must exist some entity for which pleasure and so forth are effects—namely, that "that of which pleasure and so forth are the effects is something"—it has been established that this [entity] is the very nature of the self (*ātman*). 28b.

The proponent of the self does not support his position; for he accepts that pleasure and so forth possess a cause by means of some unspecified, unqualified cause. Yet such a self is not [the object of inference], because it is accepted as being characterized by such attributes as being an eternal agent and enjoyer. And since there is no effect-sign (kāryaliṅga) for the self as it has been thus accepted, it follows accordingly:

The non-perception of the self would simply be a non-perception; therefore, why has the proponent of the self been refuted—that is, rejected—by one who denies that self by means of that very non-perception characterized by the cessation of perception and inference? [The opponent asks:

"Is it not the case that the non-existence of the self does not follow from mere non-perception? [The respondent replies: How can that which is not a proof [be a reason]? [For] the vital breaths [are not a reason] for the opposite side...

One would thereby establish the exclusion [of consciousness] from being an object of cognition and so forth. For the Cārvākas maintain that consciousness is the very power (*śakti*) of the primary elements (*bhūta*), and that this nature of the elements is like that of clay; thus, the Lokāyata, even while desiring that consciousness is not perceived in clay, says:
"From those elements, consciousness arises, just as the power of intoxication [arises] from grain. Furthermore, from that...

Thus, from this very lack of perception as a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka-anupalambha*), he states the exclusion [of the reason] from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)— namely, that speech and so forth, which have been presented as a logical mark (*liṅga*) to prove non-omniscience and the like, because they are not observed [in the case of an omniscient being]. He does so even while acknowledging that curds and the like, though not perceived within milk and other substances, do indeed exist.

The author replies: For one [instance], such as curd and so forth, exists within milk and so forth; another [instance] refers to those that are purposeless (*aparārtheṣu*), because the state of being a composite is not observed there, he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). What rule is there here that composites must necessarily exist for the sake of another?
The perception of curd and so forth within milk and so forth is indeed an inference, because [the effect] does not arise from that which lacks the capacity [to produce it].

Now, is that very entity the power, or is it something else entirely? If it is the same, it would be perceived in exactly that same way, because there is no difference [between them]. If it is something else, how could it exist in the absence of the other? It would be a mere metaphorical designation.
This is their mutual contradiction.

Therefore, either an essential nature (svabhāva) connected with that alone, or the entity itself, would be excluded; as for the other [reason], the Sāṃkhya says it is that very same one: "The eyes and so forth exist for the sake of another, because they are composites. Thus it is stated.

He states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) because the state of being a composite (*saṅghātatva*) is not observed in things for the sake of others, such as a rabbit’s horn and the like. Thus, first of all, there is a mutual contradiction in this [argument]. Furthermore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this reason is not established by mere non-observation alone. For what necessity is there here that composites must necessarily exist for the sake of another, such that the fact of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) would be established for the eyes and so forth on account of their being composites?

The Sāṃkhya doctrine of *svārthatva* (having its own purpose) would be established. As for what was said—that curd and so forth are not perceived even within milk and so forth—the reason is that there is indeed perception of curd and the like within milk and the like. To the question "What is this [perception]?", he says: "Inference. And as for inference, he says: "Because there is no production from that which lacks the capacity. For if the capacity for curd and the like did not exist in milk and so forth...

Otherwise, curd and the like would not arise from milk and the like, even though they possess [the capacity for it]. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is incapable of producing something does not arise from that thing, just as a barley sprout does not arise from a rice seed; yet curd and the like do arise from milk and the like;
therefore, the capacity for curd and the like exists in milk and the like. This is a *vaidharmya* (negative) argument that resembles the *kāryahetu* (effect-reason).

The argument is as follows: [the opponent] thinks that curd and so forth are indeed the capacity itself, because of the non-difference between cause and effect. To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies with "Now" (atha) and so forth: Is that very entity which is later perceived as curd and so forth [identical to the previous state]?

Is "being" (bhāva) power (śakti), or is it something else entirely distinct from curd and so forth? If it were the former, then just as with curd and the like in their perfected form, it would be perceived even during the state of milk, because there would be no difference [between the two states]. If, on the other hand, it is the latter—that is, if power is a thing distinct from curd and the like—then how can there be the existence of one thing (the entity called power) through the existence of another (curd)? For in that case, that curd and so forth would not exist.
This is the intended meaning: because of the capacity to produce curd and so forth, there would be a mere metaphorical designation of "curd" and so on for milk and the like.

To disregard non-apprehension as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and then, conversely, to accept it as such—this is the mutual contradiction of these proponents of the self and other [categories]; such is the conclusion.

Since there is no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based on mere non-perception, therefore the connection is with that alone. A nature (*svabhāva*) that is connected by the mere existence of the reason (*hetu*), when intended as the probandum (*sādhya*), would—by its very presence—exclude the very state of being which has been brought forward as the reason, since it is of the same nature. The word "or" (*vā*) refers to the alternatives to be mentioned later. For example, a tree, when being excluded...

Just as a tree [proves] a *śiṃśapā*, because that specific entity possessing branches and so forth is well-known by that word, for it is indeed its own nature (*svabhāva*). How could an entity exist while abandoning its own nature? Since the very nature is its form, there is no deviation [from the probandum] precisely because of that essential connection (*pratibandha*).
Or the cause [is inferred] from the effect, because of their non-deviation. ||25||
The cause, upon ceasing, causes the effect to cease.

Otherwise, that would not indeed be its effect at all. Once the causal relationship is established, it restricts the essential nature [of the entities]. In both cases, the exclusion [of the cause] occurs solely through the essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*).
Otherwise, how could the cessation of one thing result in the cessation of another? [If so,] would one who does not possess a horse necessarily not possess a cow as well? (26)
Just as there is proximity for one [element], how can there be proximity for another? Would one necessarily be a possessor of cattle simply because of that, even if he also possessed horses? (27)

The tree is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that entity called "śiṃśapā. How could an entity called "śiṃśapā" exist while abandoning its own intrinsic nature, the tree? For what reason? Because the very essence of the tree is itself the existence of the śiṃśapā-form. Therefore, because of this essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), the proof-reason (*sādhana*), such as the śiṃśapā, which is identical with that [tree], [establishes the probandum] through its very intrinsic nature.

In the case of a tree or other object intended as the probandum (*sādhya*), there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*) precisely because of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in the manner previously described. The word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is to be supplied [to the phrase] "or, being withdrawn," while "it would withdraw the effect" (*kāryaṃ nivarttayet*) is the subject under discussion. Why? Because of non-deviation; that is to say, because the effect does not deviate from its cause. He explains this with the words beginning "the cause."

"Otherwise" means: if the effect were not to cease when the cause ceases, then that which is considered the effect of that cause would not indeed be its effect. Therefore, the cause, in ceasing, necessarily causes the effect to cease. Even though, for instance, in a bedroom or similar place, smoke does not cease even when the fire—the cause—is absent, nevertheless—
The meaning is that its production from anything other than the observed cause is not intended. For this very reason, he says:

"But the established," and so forth. The established causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva), however, restricts the nature of the effect to the cause; by means of the principle that "when [the cause] exists, [the effect] occurs, and when it does not exist, it does not occur," it makes that [effect] non-deviant. "In both ways" means through identity (tādātmya).

Or rather, it is precisely because of that essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) arising from the production of that [effect] that there is the cessation of the reason through the cessation of the probandum. "Otherwise" means if no such connection is admitted; then, by the cessation of one thing—the probandum which lacks a connection—there would be no cessation of the other. How could there be the cessation of a probative property (*sādhanadharma*) that is not connected? It could not at all. Because:
One should not think, "He is horseless" simply because he lacks a horse; likewise, why should one not think, "He possesses a cow"? [The opponent replies:

"Because of the proximity of one. [The author asks: How can there be the proximity of another probandum merely through the proximity of a reason that is by its very nature unconnected to it? For: (1) [The verse follows...]
“Must a mortal necessarily possess cattle, or even horses?

Therefore, it is solely through an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) that the reason makes known the probandum. And that [connection], termed "inseparable relation" (*avinābhāva*), characterized either as identity (*tadbhāva*) or as origination from that (*tadutpatti*), is demonstrated by those two [types of reasons]. || 27 ||

Therefore, in the case of a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), a substratum is not necessarily required here; for even when that [substratum] exists, the [property] is understood from the statement "when that is absent, this is absent. (28)
For this reason: "Indeed, the presence of the probandum and the presence of the reason are demonstrated in the example for those who do not know them."

For in an example, the presence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is demonstrated as being of the same nature (*tatsvabhāvatva*) through its necessary connection (*tanmātrānubandha*) with that [property].
