Therefore, it is precisely because of this essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), and because the reason is connected to the entity intended as the probandum, that the reason brings about its own probandum; it does not do so through a mere relationship. This is because [in the case of] cause and effect, there is no coexistence, and thus no pervasion—

Furthermore, because there is an absence of a relation residing in two [distinct] things due to the oneness of the two pervaders, that [relation]— namely, the essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*)— is characterized by either the nature of the probandum (*sādhyasvabhāva*) or its origination from it (*tadutpatti*). This very essential connection, known as inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), is demonstrated through examples of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

This is what is meant: the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is the apprehender of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
For by that very [cognition], one grasps the dependence of the probans upon the probandum; thus, the absence [of the probans] when the probandum is absent is already grasped.

It is only because that means of valid cognition which apprehends their inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) has been forgotten that it is demonstrated by means of the two examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). And since that means of valid cognition—
By the mere mention [of the absence], through the recollection of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), the absence of the probans in the absence of the probandum becomes ascertained;

this occurs in the case of the example by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). In that context, for this reason, a real substratum (*dharmin*) characterized as an effect or an essential nature (*svabhāva*) is not required as a basis for the logical reason (*hetu*). However, in the case of the non-perception of an essential nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*), such a basis is indeed accepted.
For in that case, the perception [of the reason] through its opposite must be demonstrated. What is the reason? He says: "Because the substratum is not accepted," and so forth.

In the absence of that—that is, in the absence of the pervader and the cause—the mark known as the effect pervaded by them does not exist; thus, because of this statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the understanding of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) follows from that which is devoid of a substratum. (28)

What is the reason? [It is] because, and so forth. In the case of an essential nature as a logical reason (*svabhāvahetu*), the existence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is established as being pervaded by that [reason].

In the case of an effect as a logical reason (*kāryahetu*), the state of being the cause (*hetubhāva*)—that is, causality—is established for the probandum. "For one who does not know that" refers to that...

[The author] explains this for the person who understands the existence of the cause of the [probandum’s] presence: "In the example," and so forth. The presence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—namely, its being of the same nature as the probans (*sādhanasvabhāvatva*)—is made known through its necessary connection with that alone; that is, through its necessary connection with the probans alone. This occurs precisely upon the production of the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*).

By means of that very nature of the probans—which is the fact that the established impermanence is invariably concomitant with the mere quality of being produced, and thus possesses that as its own nature—the existence of that [impermanence] is established. It is not, however, produced later from some other cause. Through the example, the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is made manifest: "That which produces the nature of being produced produces it precisely as having the form of impermanence."
Otherwise, because there would be no rule that the existence of one property must necessarily entail the existence of another,

there would be a suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). By that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the necessary concomitance (*tanmātrānubandha*) of the property to be proven with that [probans] alone is demonstrated.
It is produced as such from its own causes alone, being perishable and having the nature of existing for only a moment; for its existence [otherwise] is negated by another [cause].
Or rather, it is demonstrated through the meaning of a different [exclusion], namely that the state of being a cause exists only when [the effect] exists.

Thus, when the state of being a cause for that [effect] is established, there is an absence of "producedness" in the absence of "impermanence," just as there is smoke in the absence of fire. If this is the nature of the reason (*hetu*), how could it exist without its own nature and its own reason, namely impermanence—as some who are mistaken claim? Demonstrating that it possesses only that [essential property], he says: "ya... [whoever...]

And so forth. The meaning is that the reason which produces something produced (*kṛtaka*) in its own nature produces it as being precisely of an impermanent form. By this means, the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the object of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is established by means of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and not merely through observation and non-observation. "Otherwise" means if such valid cognition is not demonstrated; then, because of the existence of a single property, [the proof]—*sādhana*—[would fail].

Because of the actual existence of the property (*dharma*), there would be no certainty that it must also exist in another instance, namely the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); thus, there would be a suspicion of the probans (*sādhana*) deviating from the probandum (*sādhya*).
Even if a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed to be demonstrated by means of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), he asks: "What is established thereby? and replies: "And by that..."

"Concomitance with that alone by means of the valid cognition" means concomitance with the mere probans (*sādhana*). How is this made known? He says: "Whatever is the cause of the produced, from that very [cause] the produced is so born; being born, it is perishable, having the nature of lasting for only a moment.
The meaning is that it is perishable precisely by virtue of its momentariness, and not after having endured for another period of time.

But how is it that [the thing] has arisen in such a way from its own cause alone? To this he says: "from another," meaning from a cause of destruction other than its own cause. This is because the existence of that produced thing is denied—that is, its nature as impermanent is denied—by what will be stated later.
Or, it refers to the state of being a cause. And the connection is that it is made manifest by that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [This concerns] the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).

Either the state of being a cause (*hetubhāva*) or the state of being a reason (*kāraṇatva*) with respect to the proof (*sādhana*) is explained by this manner: "Because the proof exists only when that [other thing] exists.

In this way, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is demonstrated by means of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*). To the question, "Of which probandum (*sādhya*), then, is the state of being a cause being demonstrated?
he says: (1) "Of another object (*arthāntara*)," meaning distinct from the proof. Thus, by means of the example shown, [the relationship is established].

When the existence [of the effect] and the causal status [of the cause] have been established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and when the essential nature of the probandum has been established as being that very [cause], that is, when the probans is of the same essential nature; and when the causal status of the cause has been established—then, in connection with the subject at hand, the phrase "in the absence of fire, smoke does not exist" applies. The word "that" refers to the impermanent essential nature and to fire. The word "of that" refers respectively to the essential nature of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and of smoke.

Or the cause (*hetu*). The word "or" (*vā*) is used for conjunction. Since this is so, how could that smoke—which is produced—or its own nature, which is impermanent, exist without fire as its cause? It could not exist at all. Thus, it is with respect to the object of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), whose form has not been explicitly stated, [that this is shown]. *Second Chapter, Second Section* (*dvitīyam āhnikam*)
Thus,
even in the absence of a positive instance (*anvaya*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established through a heterogeneous example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
For those for whom the existence of that [effect] and its being caused by that [cause] are well-established, for those wise ones, indeed, only the reason itself needs to be stated. //29//

Thinking that since the purpose for which the statement of an example is made is already established, what is the use of that statement? And even if it were to demonstrate that, why rely upon a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta)?—the Teacher rejects such reliance.
When the relationship has been known by that very [means], through the statement of either one of the two, a recollection of the second also arises by implication. (30)

As it has been said: "By implication (*arthāpatti*), or by the demonstration of either one [of the two], both are shown. In that case as well, when stated by means of an example, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established even in a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) without requiring a substratum (*āśraya*).
Therefore, as for what was stated by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara:

“Furthermore, even the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) cannot be obtained from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). If [the mark] were absent [there], it would not be understood despite efforts, because of lack of cognition; thus [the objection] is refuted.

Thus, first of all, (1) an example must be stated for those who do not know the relationship between the existence of the probandum and the existence of the reason, in order to demonstrate that relationship.

However, for those who already have the existence of the probandum and the existence of the reason established beforehand—such as when the fact that [the reason] is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) alone has been ascertained by their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—for those who are knowledgeable regarding that relationship between the existence of the probandum and the existence of the reason, there is simply the reason itself. For what purpose? [It is] for the sake of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

For the sake of certainty: since that very object is established for the person being instructed by themselves, what is the use of stating it? "Then" (*tadā*) means at the time when positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) have been ascertained.
Furthermore, even when an example is presented for the sake of one who is deluded, even upon that presentation of the example...

[Objection: There is a dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Even without a substratum (*āśraya*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is indeed established by the method already stated. Therefore, what is the point of relying on an example? Thinking thus, the Teacher rejects the substratum in the *Nyāyamukha* and other works.
For it is objected there as follows: "In that case, when the opponent accepts that space (*ākāśa*) and so forth are eternal..."

(1) "In that case, how can there be the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of 'being produced' from the 'eternal'? To this, the Master (*Ācārya*), rejecting the [notion of] a substratum (*āśraya*), says: "In that case, there is no doubt at all, because in the absence of that [eternal thing], the [reason] does not occur there.
This is what is meant: for one who has grasped the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), since the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is absent in that [locus] such as space (*ākāśa*), the pervaded (*vyāpya*)—

Because the existence [of the probandum] is established; that is to say, the non-existence of the impermanent is established by virtue of the non-existence of the permanent. Since the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is stated by means of two examples, for that reason, when the logical reason (*hetu*) has its relation [to the probandum] already known, through the statement of either one of the two examples—whether by similarity (*sādharmya*) or by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—[the proof is complete], even if the other of those two is not stated.

Memory arises through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*). Regarding the consideration of pervasion (*vyāpti*), thinking that it consists in demonstrating the relation of identity (*tadbhāva*) and the relation of causality (*hetubhāva*), [the author] states the establishment of the second by means of the statement of the one through presumptive implication.

For instance, when it is said, "Whatever is produced is necessarily impermanent," it is clearly understood that this is its very nature (*svabhāva*), even though no other object is explicitly mentioned.
"It is certain that [the reason] is observed through valid cognition as being invariably concomitant with that [property to be proven], because it is restricted to its existence.
Connecting this also with the words of the Teacher (*ācārya*), he says: "As it has been said," and so forth. This passage is found in the *Nyāyamukha*.

Therein, the word "or" (*vā*) refers back to the previous alternative. "By one or the other" means by either the example of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) or the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

Or by means of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*). This is because both [positive and negative concomitance] are demonstrated, that is, because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are shown. Regarding that very text as well, the Master [Dignāga], considering that in the case of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) and the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the demonstration of the existence of the effect when the cause exists (*tadbhāva*) and the existence of the cause when the effect exists (*hetubhāva*) is performed respectively by means of an example, [proceeds] by implication (*arthāpatti*) through the statement of either one—the positive or the negative concomitance—to indicate the second respectively.
He states the establishment of either the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) or the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). He says this very thing: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).

When it is stated that "whatever is produced is necessarily impermanent," it is clearly and necessarily ascertained by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that this property called impermanence is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of this produced thing, and that it is invariably concomitant with it—that is, invariably concomitant with mere production.

[Objection: But surely, even in the case of an effect, the cause necessarily exists; yet that [cause] is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that [effect]. To this he says: "not a different thing" (*anarthāntara*). How is it that [the effect] is invariably concomitant with that alone? He says: "because of the necessity of its existence" (*tadbhāvaniyamāt*). This means that when there is the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), impermanence necessarily exists.

That is incorrect. For even if destruction were causeless, it would be causeless only at the very moment when the destruction of a jar or the like is perceived, and not at any other time. How, then, could there be momentariness? Or, if [you argue that] because the jar arises as lasting for only a single moment, its destruction exists even prior to its production—

Now, one might object: just as production occurs from its own causes with the property of lasting for only a single moment, so too could it occur with the property of lasting for multiple moments; for causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) are observed to possess diverse potencies. Furthermore, if destruction were to occur only occasionally and in certain places, then because it would depend on time and substance, its independence [from causes] would be lost. [This is not the case,] because destruction does not depend on a cause of destruction.

Otherwise, there would be no destruction even in the second moment, because it would depend on that time and so forth. Now, existence characterized by causal efficiency is pervaded by succession and simultaneity; and since succession and non-succession are excluded from eternal things, existence—being excluded from them—is restricted to momentary things alone. Thus, being produced, when conjoined with existence, serves as a probans [for momentariness].

That too is incorrect. For if there is momentariness, there can be no apprehension of succession; indeed, the preceding object is not apprehended by the same momentary cognition that [apprehends] the subsequent one, nor is the subsequent [object apprehended] by that which [apprehends] the preceding one. Thus, how could there be an apprehension of succession? For that which is prior—

Immediately after the apprehension of one object, if there were an apprehender of another, it would have to be an apprehender in succession; or else, this [apprehender] would have to be momentary. For that Buddhist for whom time itself does not exist, how could there be an apprehension in succession? Because there is no apprehension of objects at different times. And in the absence of time, succession is merely the nature of multiple objects. Thus, even for something eternal, there could be the capacity to act in succession.

There is no contradiction. Just as a permanent entity might possess multiple forms due to its capacity for successive action, so too might a momentary entity. If it is argued that, like a momentary entity, the permanent entity would also cease to exist in the second moment because of the absence of an effect, that is incorrect, because there is no such thing as time [independent of causal efficiency]. Or, even if there were a perception of succession, how could existence [be established] through both succession and non-succession?
Pervasion [is established] because causal efficiency is impossible through any mode other than succession or simultaneity.

Nor can there be a certainty of non-existence regarding another mode based on the non-perception of the perceptible; for if that were so, the certainty of non-existence would apply only to specific places and times, and not at all times. Furthermore, there can be no certainty of non-existence based on the non-perception of the imperceptible, due to the presence of doubt. Therefore, in the case of eternal things...
Śaṅkarasvāmin and others argue: "Even if succession and simultaneity are impossible, since existence is not excluded [from eternal things], how can existence have momentary nature?

Or, even if existence were pervaded by succession and simultaneity because there is no other alternative, nevertheless, the impossibility of succession and simultaneity in eternal things is not established by perception and so forth, because eternal things are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Since that [pervasion] is not established...

Furthermore, the establishment of the cessation of sentient beings (*sattva*) does not occur within those [entities], and if that is not established, the momentary nature (*kṣaṇikasvabhāvatva*) of sentient beings is not established.

Moreover, from existence (*sattva*), there would be an inference of succession and simultaneity, because [existence] is pervaded by those alone; however, there is no inference of momentariness therein, because the capacity for successive agency is impossible.

To this it is replied: succession and simultaneity are indeed established by perception. For simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is the coexistence of entities, whereas succession (*krama*) is their relation as prior and posterior. This [succession] belongs to successive [moments], and its manifestation is a single manifestation. However, that is the manifestation of the subsequent immediately after the manifestation of the preceding. It is not the manifestation of a single [entity] alone, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

True. Even in that case, when there is the appearance of one [object], there is not [at that time] the appearance of the other; for if it were present, there would be a simultaneous appearance. Therefore, when two successive [objects] are grasped by preceding and succeeding cognitions, the succession is indeed grasped, because they are non-different from it. It is merely that, through the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the previously experienced object, [the cognition arises]: "this follows immediately after that."

The apprehension of sequence is established through the arising of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding succession. Even when there is an apprehension of successive things, if conceptual constructions of succession do not arise in some way, the non-apprehension of sequence is established; for this very reason, it is said that there is no apprehension of sequence even when there is an apprehension of a single [successive] thing.
Furthermore, how could there be an apprehension of sequence even for one who maintains the existence of time (*kāla*), since all effects would exist simultaneously?

Now, it might be argued that the sequence of effects arises from the sequence of limiting conditions (upādhi) consisting of causes occurring at different times; however, that is incorrect because time is unitary. For this very reason, there can be no such thing as an eternal entity [possessing temporal sequence].
Alternatively, one might argue that time possesses sequence because it consists of prior and posterior forms.

Now, if its sequence also depends on another time, there would be an infinite regress. If, however, its sequence exists by its own nature, then likewise there would be a sequence for many effects even when they are devoid of auxiliary causes. For us, however, time—which is the object of cognitions such as "prior" and so forth—is indeed a specific great element (mahābhūta) well-known in the world; and because of its differentiation...

The perception of succession and so forth is indeed logical. Nor is it possible for an eternal entity to be an agent in any other way. For: 3. [In the] investigation of pervasion (*vyāpti*), if it were to produce a single effect at once through another mode, or if it were to produce many effects, then at other times it would be a non-entity because of the absence of an effect. Furthermore, if it produces the effect again and again, there is only succession; no other mode is possible. Now, if it were not to produce [the effect] all at once through another mode...
Furthermore, if it were to perform an action repeatedly and then not perform it again, it would follow that it is a non-entity (*avastu*), because it would never be an agent.

Therefore, since a jar or similar object is established by perception as performing no action through either succession or simultaneity, and because it is recognized as "this is that very same thing," it is indeed perceived as non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*). Moreover, when it possesses the capacity for the performance of a single effect, that capacity exists only at that time, neither before nor [after].

Because that effect does not exist subsequently. Furthermore, capacity (*sāmarthya*) is non-different from that [entity]; this should be understood in the same way regarding the production of each successive effect. Since there is a distinction between entities based on the distinction of their capacities, the restriction of succession and simultaneity applies only to that which is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Therefore, wherever there is existence, even when succession and simultaneity are perceived, there is indeed the perception of momentariness. Thus, in that which is momentary, succession—

This very [principle] is the rule of succession and simultaneity; it is absent in eternal things. Therefore, whatever permanence is perceived in such things as a jar is contradicted by existence (*sattva*). Thus, it is stated that for an eternal entity, there is a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) due to the impossibility of both succession and simultaneity.
And just as existence is pervaded by momentariness in perceived things like jars, so too is it in unperceived things, because there is no distinction between them.

Having apprehended the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), to the extent that existence (*sattva*) is ascertained in those [things], to that same extent there is the inference of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). However, if existence is not ascertained, then—just as in the case of a rabbit's horn—there would be no cognition of momentariness due to the suspicion of non-existence in them.
Nor is there any need for an inference in that case either, since momentariness is established solely by a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*).

It is redundant; for once a person has grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the object to be proven is understood by the mere ascertainment of existence alone, and thus the raising of an objection is pointless. However, this method of grasping the pervasion has been explained in detail in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*, so it should be understood from that very source.

However, those who, having established the pervasion of momentariness by existence throughout all things through the absence [of existence] in the case of the subject (*sattva*), infer momentariness in that very [subject] from its existence—for them, the very arising of the inference would be impossible. This is because momentariness would already be established everywhere by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting in the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, the locus (*dharmin*) is not established, since it comprises the entire threefold world.

Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) because [the subject] is directly perceived. Moreover, if the absence of any counter-example (*vipakṣābhāva*) is established for the entire subject (*dharmin*) under consideration due to the force of a sublation (*bādhaka*), then since the probandum (*sādhya*) would also be established, there could be no arising of an inference. And since no other subject is established, how could a sublation occur? Thus, this [argument] is trivial. (1)

Therefore, it is established that for this "producedness" (kṛtakatva) which is qualified by existence, the property called momentariness is its essential nature (svabhāva) and is necessarily concomitant with it alone; or else, the essential nature of this momentariness is necessarily concomitant with producedness alone,
as is observed through valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Alternatively, even for a reason such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) that is devoid of the qualification "existent," there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) when proving momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).

This is because if the very same nature (*svabhāva*) that exists in the first moment were to exist in the second moment, then it would necessarily be a case of "coming into being after not having existed," just like the first moment; and from that, momentariness follows. Now, regarding the produced thing in the first moment... [41b]

In the second moment, there would be existence alone and no origination; yet even so, momentariness would follow, because of the non-difference between origination and that which originates, as well as between existence and that which exists. Furthermore, there can be no existence in the second moment without origination;
for one who has thus cognized its nature, it follows by implication (*arthāpatti*) that in the absence of impermanence, there is an absence of being produced (*kṛtakatva*).
For when its own [cause] is absent, the effect does not exist, because there is no difference [between them]. Otherwise, the statement "it exists when that exists" would not even be possible.

Thus, it has been said that "in the absence of that, there is an absence. In this way, when the state of being that [cause] is known, one realizes, "this is its intrinsic nature (svabhāva)," and thus it does not exist in the absence of that; for otherwise, it would be impossible. Therefore, through the realization of its being that intrinsic nature, there arises the recollection of the positive concomitance (anvaya).

[Objection: It is joined [with existence]. [Response: If it is birth, then it is not "abiding," because that [birth] occurs in the first moment and subsequent moments. Since it is the same in those cases as well, there is only origination everywhere and no abiding; thus, there is indeed momentariness. And since origination is produced by causes, "being produced" (kṛtakatva) applies only to that [origination], not to abiding. Therefore, because being produced is contradictory with non-momentariness, there is no inconclusiveness [of the reason]. This has been explained in detail.

The pervasion of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) by "momentariness" was stated during the proof of selflessness (*nairātmya*); it should be understood from that very context. Therefore, although "being produced" is not included within [the category of] "existence," its pervasion is seen through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As it has been said: "Its nature is necessarily concomitant with that alone, as seen by valid cognition, because of the necessity of its existence. For whenever there is the state of being produced, there is necessarily impermanence.
"Because of the rule of its non-existence. Thus,
for a person who has understood that the state of being known possesses the nature of impermanence and is produced, there arises— by way of logical necessity—
the certainty that "in the absence of the probandum, namely impermanence, the produced does not exist," because [the property] does not belong to itself.

In the absence of the impermanence of an entity, its existence occurs; thus, being produced (*kṛtakatva*) becomes identical with that [impermanence]. What is the reason? Because there is no difference between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). "Otherwise" means: if being produced were to exist even in the absence of impermanence, then it would not necessarily follow that when that [being produced] exists—that is, when being produced exists—impermanence must exist. "In that way" means as follows:

The connection with what is to be stated later is as follows: "In a formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya-prayoga*), there is an understanding of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*); likewise, in a formulation based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-prayoga*), there is a recollection of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Regarding the phrase "in the absence of that" (*tadabhāve*): when it is stated that "if there is an absence of eternity (*nityatva*), being produced (*kṛtakatva*) necessarily does not occur," then from that very formulation of dissimilarity, for a person who understands the nature of that [absence]—that is, for a person who understands that the probans (*sādhana*) has the same nature as the probandum (*sādhya*).

If it is asked, "How does one know that it is its nature?", he says: "For thus," and so forth. This property called impermanence is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this produced thing (*kṛtakatva*), by virtue of which, in the absence of that [impermanence], producedness does not occur. Otherwise—that is, if impermanence were not the intrinsic nature of the produced—then it would be illogical to say that producedness does not exist in the absence of that [impermanence].

For this reason, through the realization that [the probans] has that [probandum] as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), and through the realization that the produced has impermanence as its intrinsic nature, there arises the recollection of the positive concomitance (anvaya).
This is what is meant: that very existence of the probans only where the probandum exists is itself its non-existence in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa); such is the positive concomitance.

The identity of the two absences and their mutual pervasion means that, in this case, the cognition of the positive concomitance (anvaya) within the reason leads to the cognition of the negative concomitance (vyatireka), and the cognition of the negative concomitance leads to the cognition of the positive concomitance; this is indeed inference itself.
Therefore, as for what is said:

Likewise, when it is stated that "where there is smoke, there is fire," smoke is the effect of the fire; therefore, when smoke exists, fire necessarily follows. Otherwise, because there would be no necessary connection (*anubandha*) with another entity, the existence of the thing would be independent. Consequently, even in its absence, there would be no non-existence [of the effect], since the nature of the cause would remain unimpaired. When the effect exists, [the cause] necessarily...
This is the reason. This very thing is the causality of the cause: the presence of its own nature when another entity is present;
and for the effect as well, its existence is only when that [cause] exists. And that [causality] exists in smoke.

Therefore, for one who has understood through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that smoke is the effect of fire, the realization occurs through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that "in the absence of fire, smoke does not exist"—this constitutes negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
This is the comprehension of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Likewise, from the statement "where there is no fire, smoke does not exist," one necessarily understands through implication that "where there is smoke, fire exists"; for otherwise, in the absence of that [fire], why would [smoke] not occur?

But surely, even if there is no causal efficacy regarding eternal or non-eternal objects, the knowledge arising from hearing [the scripture] remains; as it is said in the *Nyāyamañjarī*: "For one who desires the capacity [of words], what is not established? The determination of duality [is established]. That [objection] is refuted.

Alternatively, this is not a [valid] means of knowledge at all; rather, there is no fault because a single sentence, employed either through the method of agreement (*anvayamukha*) or the method of difference (*vyatirekamukha*), conveys both [meanings] solely by virtue of convention.
This is indicated by the pronoun "where" (*yatra*).

Having explained the comprehension of both [the presence and absence of the probandum] through the application of either one in the case of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) as the reason, he states [the rule] for the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) with the words "In the same way," and so forth.

When it is stated therein that "fire is necessarily present" [wherever smoke is], from this very statement of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the certainty arises that smoke is the effect of fire. What is the reason? [It is because] by virtue of which fire is necessarily present when smoke is present.

Otherwise, if fire were not the cause of smoke, then because there would be no necessary connection (*anubandha*) between that [smoke] and another entity [fire], there would be no necessity for its pervasion (*vyāpti*) in smoke. Consequently, the nature of smoke would possess independence; therefore, due to that independence, even in the absence of that [fire], the nature of smoke would exist even when fire is absent.

There would be no absence of the effect; nor is this the case, therefore smoke must be accepted as the effect. For when smoke is admitted as the effect, fire necessarily exists there as its cause. This is the justification for the phrase "this very thing. "The existence of another entity" means that upon the presence of what is intended as the effect, there is the imposition of its own nature—that is, the manifestation of its essential form. The effect also possesses that existence.

The very state of being the cause is the state of being an effect; and that state of being an effect exists in smoke precisely because it exists only when the cause is present. Therefore, for a person who has understood through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that smoke is an effect [of fire], it follows by implication that smoke does not exist in the absence of fire.

Now, he explains the process of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*), beginning with the words "In the same way" (*tathā*). When it is stated that "where there is no fire, smoke does not exist," from this statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), for one who has recognized smoke as the effect of fire, there arises an understanding of positive concomitance to the effect that "in smoke, fire necessarily exists. Otherwise, if it were not stated by the statement of dissimilar instance that "smoke is the effect of fire," [the understanding of concomitance would not occur].

In the absence of that [fire], if fire were absent, why would smoke not be present? [One might argue it] would indeed be present; thus, there would be no certainty regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Therefore, this remains established: (1) when there is a distinct entity, that which necessarily does not occur in the absence of another is the effect of that [other]; and thus, from the statement of negative concomitance, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is understood. [The text here marks a break with "a" and "Pat"].

It either exists or it does not exist; for from those two alone arises doubt. Otherwise, if its non-existence were certain, how could there be doubt through the consideration of its existence? It is merely said that "it does not exist" because of the absence of a determination of its existence.
Here, the opponent states an objection: "But surely," and so forth. The meaning is as follows: the effect of eternal and non-eternal objects is the "effect of eternal and non-eternal objects";

its existence is their "nature" (*tattva*). Even in the absence of that [nature], for instance, auditory cognition—because it is a property of sound alone—is unique to it; yet it is not known whether auditory cognition is the effect of sound as something eternal, or [the effect] of something non-eternal.
Thus, the knowledge arising from hearing (*śravaṇajñāna*) does not have a permanent object as its effect, nor does it have an impermanent object as its effect;
nevertheless, that knowledge of hearing does not occur even in the absence of permanent or impermanent objects. Therefore, it is excluded when those [objects] are excluded.
[The opponent says: "As long as [the property] does not exist when there is the absence of the eternal, so long it does not exist in impermanent things such as jars, because it is absent from them.

Furthermore, even when there is the absence of the impermanent, it does not exist, because it is absent from eternal things such as space. The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) replies: "It is certainly not the case that it does not exist.
It cannot be understood in this way—that audibility (śrāvaṇatva) does not exist in the absence of both the eternal and the impermanent. However, if by its absence..."

If there were the certainty that "it exists," then its being an effect would necessarily follow; however, there is no such certainty that "it does not exist when that [cause] is absent. Why? Because from that very quality of audibility, there arises doubt regarding those two states of permanence and impermanence. Otherwise, if audibility were ascertained through the absence of both permanent and impermanent things, how could there be doubt regarding sound upon the consideration of its existence?
It might be so. Therefore, there is indeed no exclusion of audibility from both the permanent and the impermanent.
How then is it said that audibility does not exist in either the permanent or the impermanent because of its being "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*)? To this he says: "But merely," and so forth.
This is because there is no certainty regarding the existence of audibility among things that are permanent or impermanent. Audibility [is thus] permanent—
It is said that [the reason] does not exist in both [the similar and dissimilar instances].

Now, if audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) were observed in both the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) when proving impermanence and so forth, there would indeed be doubt regarding sound because of its audibility, just as in the case of knowability (*prameyatva*) and the like. However, this [audibility] is not observed in either the similar or the dissimilar instance; therefore—
Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara state: "It is a non-apprehension. Now, [the opponent argues]: "The object of the word is sometimes eternal and sometimes non-eternal;

and audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is a property of that object. Therefore, doubt is said to arise from this. That is incorrect. For in that case, it would be the status of being a property of the object itself that is the cause of doubt, not audibility.

To this it is replied: For if it were established that wherever there is audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*), there is the absence of both the eternal and the non-eternal, then there would indeed be a non-apprehension of the eternal and the non-eternal. However, it is not the case that audibility is absent in things like jars which are joined with non-eternality and so forth; therefore, its absence in sound [is not proven], and thus, because of its audibility, there remains only doubt regarding it.

[Objection: But surely audibility is the capacity for auditory cognition, and a permanent entity lacks such capacity because it is contradictory for it to perform a causal function; so how can there be doubt from this, since there is indeed the certainty of impermanence? [Reply:
He thinks as follows: if mere capacity were the reason, then that would be nothing other than existence (*sattva*), and thus there would be no fault whatsoever.

(1) Because it is common to the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), the same should be understood regarding [reasons] such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth. Now, the capacity that exists with respect to auditory cognition is the [proposed] reason; and since that has not been established anywhere as being pervaded by impermanence, how could impermanence be established from this? Because it is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), this very sound is not established as being pervaded by impermanence. For indeed, by that very subverting proof (*bādhaka*), the investigation of pervasion [is negated].

Furthermore, when the causal relationship between fire and smoke has not been demonstrated by means of an example, then the principle "where there is smoke, there is fire" would not even hold, because of the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). However, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—that "in the absence of fire, smoke does not exist"—is established by implication; thus, since the absence [of the probandum] is not established through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the recollection of positive concomitance (*anvaya-smṛti*) constitutes the negative concomitance.

It may be so; for when one exists, the other is established because it is impossible in its absence. By means of this example, this very essential connection (svabhāvapratibandha) as previously described has been demonstrated.
When there is the absence of the nature of the cause,

that is the reason for the negation of something; for those two [the cause and its nature], when they themselves are excluded, exclude what is connected to them, thus effecting the negation of some object.
One who desires to establish even this must state the absence of the pervader and the absence of the essential nature as the reason;
for if there is no necessary connection, how can the absence of one thing prove the absence of another?
[It is only] when that [object] is perceptible that its non-perception is logical. (31)

Since impermanence is established there by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), audibility would be redundant. In this way, it should be understood that those [reasons] which are "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) are non-probative.

Therefore, this is established: (1) in the case of a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*), the relationship of cause and effect between the probandum and the probans is demonstrated by means of two examples.

It is not merely a matter of seeing or not seeing that must be explained; for in that case, the cognition of the second [term] would occur through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) based on one of them, since otherwise it would not exist. Thus he says: "But when," and so forth. At that time, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) itself—namely, "wherever there is smoke, there is fire"—would not exist, because of the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). And when the positive concomitance itself is not established, then...

In the absence of fire, how can smoke not exist? Thus, by implication, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established. Likewise, since mere non-perception is demonstrated through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the absence of the reason in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is not established; how then could there be a recollection of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of that? "As stated" refers to the characteristics of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*). When one [of these] exists—that is, when the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of an effect or an essential nature (*svabhāva*) exists—[the other] is established.

This is for the sake of establishing the object of inference—the nature of the cause—and for the sake of establishing the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*); because in the absence of that [establishment], that is, when the aforementioned necessary connection (*pratibandha*) does not exist, it is impossible to establish the other when one is present.

"The absence of the nature of the cause" means both the absence of the cause and the absence of the nature of the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Therefore, for this reason just mentioned, when there is a negation of some effect or of that which is pervaded (*vyāpya*), and by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), when the conventional usage of negation is to be established, the reason (*hetu*) is the logical mark (*liṅga*). For what reason? Because those two alone—namely, the cause and the pervader—[are the basis].

When one intends to establish the negation of some object— whether it be an effect (*kārya*), a pervaded (*vyāpya*), or an essential nature (*svabhāva*)— by means of two [types of] evidence currently present, namely the cessation of the cause (*hetu*) and the cessation of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), the word "also" (*api*) implies that conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is likewise established by the cessation of the cause and the cessation of the essential nature as the logical reason (*hetu*).

It is not to be explained. What is the reason? Because there is no obstruction, and so forth. The meaning is that there is no obstruction other than those two. "Proper" means logical; "of which there is a proper perception" refers to the object of perception (*dṛśya*). It is the cause for its negation. It is called "the cause of that" because it is the cause for the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the object of negation. Likewise—
Since the non-perception of an entity is itself of the nature of a negation, both types—non-perception of the cause and non-perception of the pervader—are logical reasons.

Thus, this threefold non-apprehension is said to be of many kinds, through the application of various distinctions such as the non-cognition of that which is contradictory [to the object], and so forth. (32)

The probans for negation (pratiṣedhahetu) is indeed threefold: the non-apprehension of the cause, the pervader, and that which exists as its own nature. This very [probans] is declared to be threefold according to the application [of the syllogism], through the distinction between the non-cognition of that [object] itself, the cognition of what is contradictory to it, and the cognition of its contradictory effect. These are precisely the non-cognition of that, the cognition of what is contradictory to it, and the cognition of its contradictory effect.
And thus, the non-perception of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the reason for negation (*pratiṣedhahetu*). This is not a reason for negation itself;

rather, it is called the "reason for negation" because it is the reason for the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that constitutes the object of negation. What is the reason? It is because such a non-perception—that is, the non-perception of what is perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*)—is itself the negation.
"Of that too" refers to the negation and the linguistic usage of negation.

Thus, this non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), though stated briefly in three ways, is further stated in many ways—just as it was previously divided into eight types in this very context. By what method? He says: "That which is opposed to each of those," and so forth. By the word "that" (*tat*), the triad of essential nature (*svabhāva*), cause (*kāraṇa*), and pervader (*vyāpaka*) under discussion is grasped. It is that which is opposed by those three, such as essential nature, and so on.
The contradictory [reason] is of three kinds:
namely, the contradictory of the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddha*), the contradictory of the cause (*kāraṇaviruddha*), and the contradictory of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddha*).

That which has "the contrary of that" (*tadviruddha*) as its beginning is called "that which begins with the contrary of that" (*tadviruddhādi*). By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the effect of the contrary (*viruddhakārya*) and the effect of what is contrary to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakārya*). That is "that which begins with the contrary of that. "The non-comprehension and comprehension of those two" means the non-comprehension of that [object] and the comprehension of that which begins with the contrary of that. The distinction between those two is the "distinction of application"; therefore, it is stated in many ways due to this distinction of application. In that regard:

Thus, by way of non-perception, three types are subsumed: non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), and non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). By way of perception of the opposite of those, there are likewise three: perception of the opposite of the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), perception of the opposite of the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*), and perception of the opposite of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). From the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should understand the perception of the effect of the opposite (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*).
And [the eighth is] the perception of an effect that is incompatible with the cause. In this way, there is a summary of the eightfold non-perception mentioned previously.
He states the meaning of the verse with the words "only threefold," etc.; "of that which has an existence capable of being perceived" means of that which is fit for perception.

The connection is: "the non-perception of the reason. This refers to the fact that the pervader and one's own self possess a perceptible existence. The connection is that this threefold probans for negation has been described in many ways according to its application (*prayoga*). To the question, "In what way is it according to its application?", he says: "by means of the application of the distinctions between the non-apprehension and apprehension of each respective contradictory [factor] and so forth. This very point is expressed by the phrase beginning with "by its non-apprehension" (*tasyāgatyā*).

It is analyzed as follows: "by the non-perception of its own nature, cause, or pervader" (*svabhāva-kāraṇa-vyāpakānupalabdhi*); "by the perception of something contradictory to its own nature, cause, or pervader" (*tadviruddha-svabhāva-kāraṇa-vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*); and "by the perception of a contradictory effect" (*viruddha-kāryopalabdhi*). Such are the various applications [of the reason], as previously stated.
3. Investigation of Pervasion (vyāpticintā).

Section g: The restriction of inseparable connection (avinābhāvaniyama) arises either from the relation of cause and effect (kāryakāraṇabhāva) or from an essential nature (svabhāva) that acts as the regulator.

"By such varieties of formal arguments" refers to the application of various types of arguments, such as the perception of an effect that is incompatible with the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*), as previously stated in the investigation of the varieties of non-perception (*anupalabdhiprabhedacintā*) at [verse] 116.

Since it is thus a signifier by virtue of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), therefore: either from the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), which acts as a regulator by establishing the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) between the probandum and the probans; or from the essential nature (*svabhāva*), which acts as a regulator characterized by identity (*tādātmya*).

The meaning is that the inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the mark—whether it be an effect or an essential nature—does not exist without the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). It is not [otherwise].

Furthermore, for that which is unique [to the subject], there is no invariable concomitance with the probandum, because it is a cause of doubt. If, however, there were invariable concomitance, then by the very same means of valid cognition that ascertains it, the probandum would already be established in that subject; how then could this [unique property] be a prover?
Therefore, as for what is said by that Bhaṭṭa:
The term *avinābhāva* (inseparable relation) also encompasses all meanings;
it does not, for us, bring about the apprehension of a relationship suitable for inference.

If, first of all, that absence [of the reason] in the dissimilar instance is not subsequently distinguished [from its presence in the similar instance], then it would exist even in the case of the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) reason; thus, it would be a non-reason.
As for the claim that "a property which is unique [to a subject] is made its own by that [subject] alone;

therefore, it follows that the reason is known only as something that does not exist without [the probandum]," that is refuted. For the very absence of separation (*avinābhāva*) is the restriction (*niyama*), because it is established as "not existing without the probandum" (*sādhya*). (33b)

If this is so, for what purpose is the restriction (niyama) stated once again? [Response: True; it is for the sake of refuting the opinion of others. For he [the opponent] maintains a restriction other than inseparable connection (avinābhāva). As Bhaṭṭa has said:
"Thus, having refuted the relationship as stated by others,
the relationship called 'restriction' (niyama) is now set forth according to our own view."
There are two possible courses for relations such as that of cause and effect:
they must be either determinate or indeterminate; it is the determinate relation that serves as a constituent of inference.
All these non-restrictions (aniyama) are indeed not the cause for the arising of inference;
for nothing whatsoever fails to be inferred due to restriction alone.

Therefore, in this context, only a restrictive relation (niyama) is determined as the connection; and that is intended to be between the indicator alone and the indicated, as has been previously established.
"The cognition of the whole [the probandum] from the perception of a single part [the reason], based on the correct recollection of the rule after having properly restricted [the observation]—
that is inference"— this [definition] is refuted.
The restriction of invariable concomitance does not arise from non-observation, nor from observation. 33.
Otherwise, what necessity would there be for the restriction of the inevitable [arising] of one thing by others?
Or, if it were caused by a different entity, it would be like the color on a cloth. (34)

In the absence of a relationship such as that of cause and effect, there would be no necessary rule at all; for there is no necessity of coexistence among things that are unconnected. Furthermore, mere paleness and the like are not the effects of fire. Moreover, since a logical mark (*liṅga*) functions as a means of cognition only in dependence upon place, time, and so forth, how could there be a necessary rule even when a relationship of cause and effect exists?

Two courses are stated. Now, it might be argued: even for one who accepts a relationship such as that of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), as long as the necessity (*niyama*) of the probans with respect to the probandum has not been ascertained, it cannot be a factor for the cognition of the probandum; therefore, even when the relation of cause and effect exists, it is only necessity itself that is accepted as the relationship, because that alone is a factor for cognition. To state that...

Thus, only one [of these] is a constituent part of inference, while the remainder are merely causes for its manifestation. That is incorrect. For restriction (*niyama*) consists precisely in that [invariable concomitance], and that [restriction] has as its very nature identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*). Therefore, the ascertainment of restriction is nothing other than the ascertainment of identity and causality; restriction is not ascertained through observation and non-observation, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

[Objection: "But surely, just as there is deviation regarding the determination of necessity based on perception and non-perception, so too would there be deviation regarding the determination of the causal relation.
[Reply: That is incorrect; for it is only through specific perceptions and non-perceptions that the determination of the causal relation is admitted.
Because of the [logical] fallacy of circularity (*itaretarāśraya*). This very point will be stated right here.

Furthermore, as it is said by Umveka: "The observation of smoke in fire hundreds of times gives rise to a cognition of necessity—that 'this smoke is restricted to fire'—by way of the impossibility of otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*).
The observation of smoke in what is not fire is the sublater (*bādhaka*) of that [cognition]."
"And since that [fire] does not exist, there is no necessity of smoke with respect to fire.

This is incorrect. For if smoke were not an effect of fire, then the non-perception of smoke in what is not fire would be a mere non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*); as such, being a non-authoritative means of knowledge, it could not serve as a sublater. Since smoke would thus be suspected of existing in what is not fire, how could there be a necessity of smoke with respect to fire? Therefore—
This is established:

(1) "The rule of inseparable connection [is determined] either from the relation of cause and effect or from an essential nature as the regulator. And because the relation of cause and effect and so forth is ascertained, the rule of inseparable connection is established.

Regarding the objection that [invariable concomitance] is established "neither from non-perception nor from perception": (1) there is no certainty regarding the rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) based merely on the non-perception of the reason when the probandum is absent;
nor is it established "from perception," meaning neither from the mere perception of the coexistence of the probandum and the probans.
Therefore, the inseparable connection of one thing with another thing is established solely through the relation of origination from that (*tadutpatti*).

Otherwise—that is, if there were no production from that [cause]—what necessary connection (*avaśyambhāvaniyama*) could there be for a mark (*liṅga*) that is not of the same nature as the other, which is intended by opponents to be the probandum? However, if the mark is not a separate entity, then the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) must be admitted to be invariably concomitant with that [mark] alone;
otherwise, for instance, the cause of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) would have a different cause, such as a hammer or the like, and it would also be non-eternal.
3. Consideration of Pervasion (Vyāpticintā):

For a property (dharma) caused by a different object would be something entirely other. Indeed, even when that [cause] has been accomplished, it is not logical for something to be unaccomplished or to have a different cause while possessing the same intrinsic nature (svabhāva). 16a. This—
The difference between entities must consist either in a difference of cause, or in the superimposition of contradictory properties, or in a difference of the causes of such superimposition.
If these two were not differentiators, then there would be no difference for anything from anything at all; consequently, the entire universe would be a single substance.
From that, it would follow that all things arise and perish simultaneously, and everything would be applicable everywhere. Otherwise, [the following would occur]: 4322...

It would not be so; for it is merely another name, since it is designated as such by accepting the same underlying object. Or rather, [if you say] that [the nature] is accepted in this [entity], then what is the rule of necessary concomitance regarding that property? It is like dye on a cloth: the color produced by safflower and the like is something that occurs subsequently once the cloth has already been completed.

In that case, just as there is no rule of necessity, so too, if impermanence is intended to have a different entity as its cause, not only is this fault present, but there is another fault as well; thus he says, "Moreover," and so forth. A property called "permanence" caused by a different entity would be something entirely other than that which constitutes the essential nature, such as being produced (*kṛtaka*); for [otherwise] the probandum—

If it is admitted that a property (*dharma*) has a distinct cause (*arthāntara-nimitta*), two things are entailed: its non-production despite the production of the means of proof (*sādhana*), and its having a different cause. And this is not possible without a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*). For, even when that intrinsic nature of the means of proof has been produced, it is not logical for the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) to be unproduced or to have a different cause; [otherwise] it would not be consistent with that [proven] intrinsic nature, since it was already produced previously.
Furthermore, it is logical for a mark (*liṅga*) that has distinct causes to possess a distinct nature (*svabhāva*), because this indeed is the world-renowned distinction between entities:

namely, the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) or the connection with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmayoga*). Here, completion and non-completion are the two contradictory properties. Likewise, this very cause of distinction—the distinction in causes (*kāraṇabheda*) and the distinction in causal complexes (*sāmagrībheda*)—is what generates the distinction. In this context, "cause" refers to...
The distinction is to be observed; by this, both the nature of the distinction and the cause of the distinction have been stated.

The appearance of difference, however, is that which apprehends difference. If those two—the superimposition of contradictory properties and the cause of difference—are not themselves differentiated from the object, then no entity would have any difference from any other thing; consequently, the entire world would be a single substance. If it is argued that oneness is indeed accepted for everything because there is no distinction in the three *guṇas*, the author replies: "And therefore... (tataśca).

Because [all things] are identical, there would be simultaneous arising and destruction; that is to say, upon the arising of one thing, there would be the arising of all, and upon its destruction, the destruction of all. Furthermore, everything would possess efficacy (*upayoga*) and causality (*kāraṇatva*) with respect to every effect. If one does not accept simultaneous arising and so forth, it would follow that no entity whatsoever could be singular. Alternatively, if they were distinct from one another by virtue of differences in efficacy and so on, [the claim of identity would be lost].

It is intended that there may be another name for those distinctions; a single designation would have been applied to many. What is the reason? Because, having accepted objects that are mutually distinct, they are designated in such a way; that is, by being designated as "one."

1. It is not different [from the entity]. [Objection: Even if it is not a separate object, since impermanence is not yet accomplished at the time the entity exists, its nature would be the same [as that of permanence].
[Response: No; "accomplishment" is said to be the acquisition of a previously non-existent nature. For that very entity is [the impermanent one].

Impermanence (*anityatā*) is the property of abiding for only a moment (*kṣaṇasthitidharma*). We shall explain later the reason for the difference in expression based on the distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*).

Now, it might be argued that impermanence is the connection with existence (*sattā*) occurring within prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and subsequent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*); and that [existence] belongs to what is produced (*kṛtaka*).

At the time of its completion, it is already completed and would simply perish; it does not manifest at a later time—this too is untenable. For as long as destruction has not arisen, how can there be impermanence existing in the interval? And even when destruction has arisen, how could this [impermanence] exist in the interval? Or else, what would be the nature of the entity (*bhāva*) that is produced?
Because that very [non-existence] does not exist.

The opponent says, "But surely," and so forth. Even if it is a cause for no other object (*anarthāntara*), and even if it does not depend on a cause of destruction according to your own view, impermanence (*anityatā*) is not established at the time of the entity's existence; that is, at the time when the entity has its being, that impermanence— [...is not established.]
One might think that impermanence arises at a later time because the entity was previously unproduced; however, [the reason] is equivalent to "not having that as its nature" (*atatsvabhāva*).
Just as there would be production even when [the cause] is a different object (*arthāntara*), so too there is a difference between those two even when [the cause] is not a different object;
thus, the state of "not having that as its nature" is equivalent.

He responds with the words beginning "no" (na), etc.: "The acquisition of a previously non-existent nature is called 'accomplishment' (*niṣpatti*); impermanence consists in the cessation of an entity. Therefore, since there is no such thing as accomplishment at all, how could there be a conjunction of contradictory properties? If, then, impermanence is not an existing real entity (*vastu-sat*), how can there be a relationship characterized by identity between the probandum and the probans? To this he says: "That very [same...]"

Regarding the phrase "for existence" (*hi bhāva*): it refers to that whose property (*dharma*) is stability within a moment. Impermanence is said to be the very nature (*svabhāva*) characterized by the property of cessation; that alone is the probandum (*sādhya*). Therefore, there is identity (*tādātmya*) between the reason and the probandum. Since the meaning is not distinct, impermanence is not formless (*nīrūpa*); thus, through such statements as "impermanence belongs to existence," no separate form whatsoever is attributed to existence.

However, it is not that the perceived form itself is being enjoined; rather, the meaning expressed is that "it does not exist," because if one were to designate a different property (*dharma*), there would be the undesirable consequence of failing to demonstrate the cessation of existence.
If impermanence were simply the existence [of the thing] itself, then how could there be this difference in expression, namely, that "eternality" is a property of the substratum, the sound?

Therefore, he says: "Even though there is a difference in expression," and so forth. Even regarding that difference in expression—the distinctness of the denoters—by way of being the property (*dharma*) and the possessor of the property (*dharmin*), we shall state the underlying cause later on.
By this, [he addresses] what was also said by Adhyayanavidha, Karṇa, Dyotakara, and others: "If..."
Just as there is the simultaneous sinking and rising of the two ends of a balance scale, the destruction of the cause occurs at the very moment of the production of the effect.

If that were not so, the relationship of cause and effect would not exist; for since the destruction of the cause is the very arising of the cause, according to the statement that "destruction is indeed existence," it follows that the effect has arisen together with the cause. And if destruction is indeed existence...

Even at the first moment, the existence of the entity would not be [permanent]; for the cessation of the entity is due to its destruction, and destruction arises from its own cause because it is produced in such a way. Although one perceives that nature of abiding for a single moment as its very essence, the person of dull intellect—either because of the suspicion that it might always remain so due to the perception of its existence, or because of being deceived by the production of similar subsequent moments—does not ascertain this.

It is not the case that existence itself is perceived [as non-existent]. Furthermore, because destruction exists at all times, the existence of an entity would have to persist [forever]. If, on the other hand, the destruction of the cause were distinct from the production of the cause, then impermanence would not have "being produced" as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Moreover, if destruction were something separate, then even when that destruction had arisen, that moment (*kṣaṇa*) would not have ceased; so how could there be momentariness? (1)
That is refuted: for destruction is held to be twofold—consisting of the cessation of an entity and the entity itself.
Therefore, an arisen entity performs its function, and at the time of that function, the destruction consisting of the cessation of the cause is indeed recognized by the world.
This [destruction] is not held to be of the nature of an entity (*bhāva-svabhāva*), nor is it [held to be] non-different or different from the arising of the cause.

Because it is formless (*nīrūpa*), only the negation of its difference and non-difference is thus performed. And so he will say: "(1) 'For this conceptual distinction would exist regarding an entity, because affirmation conforms to a real thing' (1.281). Therefore, the claim that when a destruction distinct [from the entity] arises, the moment does not cease, is refuted; for from the second—
Cessation occurs at the very moment of its arising, that is, in the first instant; therefore, an entity that persists for only a single moment is designated by the term "destruction" (*vināśa*).

And since this destruction is of the nature of an entity, it is essentially identical with the means of production itself. Furthermore, because it ceases at the time the effect arises, it exists at a time distinct from the effect; nor does it exist at all times, because the entity [itself] is non-existent [at that later stage].

Alternatively, by means of these two terms denoting both property (*dharma*) and the possessor of the property (*dharmin*)— namely, "this is perishable" (*vinaśvara*) and "its destruction" (*vināśo'sya*)— one and the same entity, which is excluded from non-perishing, is expressed through the exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions; thus, it is entirely consistent that the entity itself is called "destruction."

If, then, impermanence is indeed the very nature of the entity, then since that [impermanence] is also directly perceived when the entity is perceived, why is it not ascertained in exactly that same way? To this he says: "That," and so forth. The connection is: although one sees—that is, although one directly perceives—the nature called impermanence, which is the property of existing for only a moment, one does not ascertain; one does not determine it.

Why is it said that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the property of momentary existence? Because it arises from its own cause (*svahetu*) precisely as something whose nature is to exist for only a single moment. Furthermore, why does one not determine this even while perceiving it? He says: "because of dull intellect" (*manvabuddhi*). One whose intellect is dull due to the latencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the form of permanence and so forth, which have been cultivated throughout beginningless saṃsāra, is thus described; otherwise, [one would perceive it correctly].

Why would there not be certainty regarding the nature of all things when they are directly perceived? By this, it is stated that for yogins, even though there is the perception of similarity, certainty regarding momentariness arises because they lack dullness of intellect.
If, then, due to ignorance there is no determination of impermanence, let there be no impermanence even when an entity has perished.

Anticipating the objection that this is a mere mental determination (*adhyavasāya*), he states that even external factors are the seeds of error, beginning with the words "by the perception of existence" (*sattopalambhena*). This means:
by that perception of existence alone which is not a perception of non-existence.
What is intended is this: because the preceding moment perishes at the very time the succeeding moment arises, there is [no simultaneous existence] of the preceding and succeeding moments.

Because there is no interval due to the non-existence of [separate] moments, and because otherness is not perceived through continuity, one always perceives only existence even in the second and subsequent moments. Thus, "the state of being such" (*tathābhāva*) refers to the existence (*sadbhāva*) of that which was previously seen; the doubt regarding that is whether it might perhaps... [be otherwise].

He says that even for one who is mistaken, there arises a doubt in the form "this is indeed that," because of the perception "this is that very same thing. Deceived and cheated by that [doubt], one does not reach a firm determination.

In that case, there would also be no certainty regarding the causal relationship between fire and smoke, because [the relationship] would not be established through the absence of any intervention by another.

He says this because of the apprehension of "you" (*tvāgraha*). [The phrase] "due to the arising of another similar [moment]," and so forth, means that the perception of another similar [object] is observed to be the cause of the delusion of non-difference even in cases such as mother-of-pearl. This has been analyzed in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*; it should be understood there. Therefore, one who is deceived by the arising of another [moment] entirely similar to the preceding moment does not [perceive] the preceding moment—

Even when one determines that [the subsequent moment] is distinct from the preceding moment of protection, because of the thought "this is that very same thing," there is no cognition of the destruction of the preceding moment nor the cognition of the arising of the subsequent one. However, in the case of fire and smoke, because they are absolutely dissimilar, the determination of their causal relationship occurs through the apprehension of their distinctness even when they are in immediate succession. The word "or" (*vā*), however, is used in the sense of "not being possible."
This is for the purpose of indicating [the following].

By this, the meaning is as follows: if there were deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the perception of existence, or if there were deception due to the arising of a similar subsequent [moment], then there would always be deception; such is the purport [of the opponent].

Alternatively, [the author] asks: why is it that one does not determine [an object] even while seeing it? He says: "Because of the apprehension of existence" (*sattopalambhena*). Previously, one who was deceived by the apprehension of existence—meaning, by the superimposition of a previously seen state upon what is being perceived, which gives rise to the doubt of its existence—does not determine it.
If this were the case, then determination would occur only at the perception of the first moment, because prior to that there has been no apprehension of existence. Thus [he says]:

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Or else, [one] is deceived by the production of a subsequent [moment] similar [to the preceding]. The word *vā* (or) has the sense of *ca* (and). Because of the production of a second moment similar to the first moment, one is deceived and does not reach a definitive determination (*vyavasyati*). To the objection that in that case even yogins would lack certainty, he says: "[It is only] one of dull intellect. This is because of the existence of causes for deception, both external and internal.
Therefore, this is the certainty of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). For yogins, however, even though there is a perception of similarity, certainty certainly arises because of their sharp intellect.
Therefore, it is established that even while perceiving the nature of momentary existence, [one may fail to realize it] due to the arising of subsequent similar [moments].
"One who is deceived does not determine [the object]," it is said.

But if an entity is momentary, there should be an appearance of the preceding and succeeding moments as distinct; since they do not appear as such, how can it be said that one "does not determine" even while seeing? Furthermore, [if the object were] non-different from blue and so forth...
From this, the apprehension of momentariness [would follow] upon the apprehension of blue.

This is logical; however, the following must be examined here: (1) Is this blue non-momentary, or is it of the nature of a moment, or is it a continuum? In that regard, if it were non-momentary, then how could there be an appearance of momentariness within the appearance of blue?
