Now, as for the nature of the moment: [an objection]—is it not the case that this very [momentary nature] is unestablished? How, then, can it be said that there is the manifestation of a moment within the manifestation of blue?
(Pramāṇavārttika 1.225.3). This is the investigation of pervasion (*vyāpticintā*).

Furthermore, because a single moment does not appear [to perception], there is no appearance of blue in the form of a continuum (*saṃtāna*). Now, if it is argued that when there is the appearance of mere blue, there is the appearance of its momentariness—that is incorrect. For the apprehension or non-apprehension of a perception occurs through appearance or non-appearance, and not otherwise. Thus it is said: "Whatever it apprehends, it does so by means of that appearance."
And it has been stated that there is no appearance of moments.

Furthermore, if momentariness were non-different from blue and so forth, then since momentariness would be ascertained at the very time of the ascertainment of blue, inference would be rendered useless. As for the one who says: "Momentariness is simply the state of being the object of a single cognition,"

Since what appears now as the object of a present cognition is precisely that which is excluded from being the object of preceding and succeeding cognitions, the moment is indeed distinct from the preceding and succeeding moments; it is determined through perception, while inference merely refers back to what has already occurred in perception.
Thus, inference is not redundant.

That is incorrect. For if a single cognition were non-momentary, then the object as well would have to be non-momentary. If, on the other hand, that [cognition] is momentary, how is this known? If you say it is because that too is an object of a single cognition, then the realization of momentariness would result in an infinite regress. If, however, the manifestation of the moment of cognition is admitted, then that same [manifestation] must belong to the moment of the object.
Why is this not accepted? Otherwise, even a single moment would possess multiplicity because it would be the object of multiple cognitions.
Bhaṭṭa Vāsudeva, however, says: "The non-appearance [of an entity] due to the destruction of preceding and succeeding moments is itself the appearance of its non-momentariness;
therefore, every perception is indeed a grasper of non-momentariness, and [the claim that it grasps momentariness] is merely [contradicted] by the inference of momentariness."
The claim that "error is being established" is also untenable; for since the thesis is sublated by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no possibility for an inference to arise.

Furthermore, even if non-conceptual perception were erroneous, one could not grasp the [logical] relation (*sambandha*). This is because of the passage beginning with "even while seeing... [paśyannapi].
And as for the contradiction [in the claim] that "even though seeing, one does not determine," it is replied here:
Just as there is a sequence of prior and posterior among the moments of the object, so too there is a sequence among the moments of cognition.

Therefore, by that preceding moment of cognition, only the preceding moment of the object is grasped, not the subsequent one; and by the subsequent [moment], only the subsequent [object] is grasped, not the preceding one.

It is objected: "Since those two do not appear within a single cognition, how could there be an appearance of distinction such as 'this is different from that previous one'? [The reply is: The very appearance of a thing's own nature (*svarūpa*) is its appearance as distinct from others, just like the appearance of Sumeru as distinct [from other mountains]. And since that [own-nature] exists even for a momentary entity (*kṣaṇa*), why would it not have an appearance of distinction?

And because of the cognition that "the seen is being seen," [it follows that they are distinct]; for the nature that was previously seen is one thing, and the nature currently being seen is another. To explain:
the first observer perceives only the presently appearing nature of the entity, and not the previously seen one; thus, there is indeed a difference between these two.
It is only because the preceding and succeeding moments are entirely similar and lack any interval—unlike a jar and a cloth—that their distinction is not perceived.

Nor does identity [of the two] exist, because they do not appear as distinct. For when one proceeds toward mother-of-pearl with the thought, "This is that very silver of ours," there is no appearance of a distinction between the mother-of-pearl and the silver;
therefore, even identity does not exist. Thus, in this case, within non-conceptual cognition, there is the appearance of the mother-of-pearl’s own nature.

In this way, there is the appearance of distinction from another; likewise, it could apply even to a single moment. If the only objection were to be raised as to why the preceding moment is not remembered with its distinctions, the answer has already been stated: it is not remembered because people are deceived by the production of subsequent moments that are similar [to the preceding ones].
But even so, the moment (*kṣaṇa*) does not appear, because an entity is perceived only as the duration of the passage of a single atom, and not as a moment.

However, if it is argued that a moment does not appear, how then can there be an appearance of the non-momentary? For [the non-momentary] does not appear at every moment. Moreover, an entity as it arises is apprehended by perception as being devoid of prior and subsequent forms.

How is momentariness apprehended? Nor is a non-momentary thing perceived, precisely because it does not appear in the earlier and later times. Since its connection with those [times] appears now in perception, the non-appearance now of the nature connected with the earlier time is itself destruction, and the appearance of another nature is itself origination. Thus, how can it be said that there are earlier and later moments?

It is not non-momentary because destruction and origination do not appear [to perception]. Nor does it have the form of multiple moments; for if this present time were composed of multiple moments, it would possess a nature such as having already been grasped and so forth, which would not be purposeless.
Indeed, a certainty arising from direct perception does not determine that "this exists only at this very moment"; rather—

"It exists now"—this is what is established by inference as "it exists at this very moment. Therefore, it is established that [the verse] beginning with "even though seeing, one does not determine" is valid.
Now, if there were a certainty through direct perception that [an object] is eternally similar, then the cognition "this is that very same thing" would occur.
Since the cognition "this is that very same thing" arises with a firm form at all times, how can it be an error? To this, Bhaṭṭa says:
“Where the mind has become firmly settled on the idea that ‘it is always exactly the same,’ it is only in such a case that the recognition ‘this is that’ can be considered an error.”
In this case, a firm cognition arises that "this is indeed the same [entity] eternally";
and because it exceeds the mere existence of that [object], its status as a valid means of knowledge is appropriate.
"In that case, due to differences in place, time, and so forth, there is a limited occasion [for such a claim];
for the existence of the present has not been grasped by prior cognitions.
Nor is there always a certainty of similarity through inference, because it is sublated by perceptual recognition (pratyabhijñā)."
Because there is no arising of inference in the absence of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Nor can it be argued that recognition lacks validity due to the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*);

for as long as its invalidity is not established, there is no arising of inference, and as long as there is no arising of inference, there is no invalidity of recognition—thus, there is the fault of mutual dependence.

To this it is replied: by the word "that" (*sa*), the nature associated with a prior time is made the object; and by the word "this" (*ayaṃ*), that associated with the present time is made the object. There is a difference between these two, and not a difference in any way whatsoever, since [their] being present has been established. (3) 3. Examination of Pervasion (*Vyāpticintā*)

Because there is certainty for those who perceive the final moment, and subsequently, through the non-perception of that [same thing], there is the cognition of non-persistence; thus, at the time of that certainty, impermanence is established. This is because an entity possesses a single nature consisting of the form existing at the time of the cause's capacity to produce an effect. Therefore, it is precisely difference that appears when there is recognition.
Thus, by this [argument], there is a sublation of the inference of momentariness.
Alternatively, the connection of an entity with a prior time is simply non-existent now, because that prior time no longer exists. If it were existent...
It has been stated that for this [cognition], there would only be a connection with the present time, and not a connection with a prior time, due to contradiction.

Therefore, that portion of the cognition which apprehends a non-existent connection with a prior time is erroneous; otherwise, it would have to apprehend the object in its clearly manifest state of childhood and so forth, yet it does not do so. Consequently, from that erroneous [portion], the form previously seen—

How can there be sublation by inference based on the cognition "this is that very same [thing] by means of the rope"? Perception arises as the apprehender of that object only where there is the operation of the sense organ. Now, regarding existence at a prior time, what operation could there be now? For it is not present, being non-proximate. Nor can there be [perception] through non-difference from that [prior state]; so how could the cognition that apprehends the identity between existence at the prior and subsequent times be perception? And when...

That which is perceived in the state of childhood is recognized in the state of old age; yet, neither in that object nor in the recognition itself does permanence manifest. Rather, one merely determines the identity as "this is that very same thing. And this identity does not exist because of the difference between the states of childhood and old age, nor [does it exist] otherwise.
Nor can permanence and so forth be postulated on the grounds that the apprehension of reality would otherwise be inexplicable;
for such an apprehension can arise even from the delusive cause of the production of successive similar moments, as in the case of hair that has been cut and grown back again.

Furthermore, in this case, recognition does not proceed from a distinct universal of "hair-ness," because that would entail the absurd consequence of the cognition "this is that" arising [even when the hair is different].

Nor can there be a continuous perception of something other than what is non-different, given that the forms of "persistence" (*anugata*) and "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtta*) are either mutually exclusive through a chain of connections or absolutely distinct. Consequently, the recognition "this is that very same hair" is caused solely by the production of a similar subsequent [moment] and is therefore an illusion. Thus, because this [recognition] is suspected of being illusory in the case of jars and the like, the arising of inference is indeed justified.
Nor is there the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), because it is not by means of inference that the invalidity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is produced;
rather, it is simply known [to be invalid] because it arises from its own causes as something inherently invalid. This is because of the apprehension that "what was seen is being seen now.

For the state of having been previously seen does not exist at that time, since at that moment the object has only the nature of being currently perceived. Nor does it exist now, for the very same reason.

Nor can there be a connection with a prior time for that which is being perceived now, since it did not exist previously. Therefore, recognition—which functions as a grasper by superimposing the quality of "having been seen"—arises as invalid precisely because it is erroneous. Furthermore, the emergence of inference is not caused by the invalidity of this [recognition], but rather by its necessary connection with the probandum; thus, inference serves as the sublater of recognition.
This detailed analysis of the refutation of recognition has been set forth in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*; therefore, it should be understood from that very work.

Consequently, this remains established: (1) even though one perceives that very nature which is the property of momentary existence, one does not ascertain it because one is deceived by the production of a similar [subsequent] moment and fails to determine the destruction of the preceding moment.

But how is it understood that one who is deceived by the arising of a similar [moment] does not determine [the object]? To this he says: "In the final," and so forth. The "final moment" (*antyakṣaṇa*) is a moment that does not connect with another similar moment; for those who perceive it, it is "lost," which means it is determined as such. Even when the effect is not seen, although the cause is seen, because the effect is seen through that impermanent nature, it is thus.

[Otherwise, there would be] the cognition [of it as such]. Or, if it were caused by something else, it would be logical that it is causeless. Impermanence would then be a separate entity altogether; and in that case, there would be no connection with existence for those things that are independent. If, however, it does depend [on something else], then since that very impermanence belongs to its own self, what is the use of another? For how could that which is inherently immobile [be affected] by a separate entity?
Furthermore, it is because it is improper for that which possesses such an intrinsic nature to coexist [with its opposite].

Whether impermanence (*anityatā*) is a distinct entity (*dharmāntara*), if that too were produced from another object, it would have to be either a cause or an effect; for there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) for anything other than cause and effect, and because its existence cannot be established through inference. In that regard:
"Because it occurs later, it cannot be the cause; how then could there be certainty regarding the effect? (35)

Since that object has already been established, if it were to arise from another entity [subsequently], that [other] would be its cause. And because an effect necessarily exists in its cause, that [cause] is an uncertain indicator (*gamaka*) and motive (*nimitta*). Therefore, because a property (*dharma*) whose motive is other than that [object] does not necessarily exist in the object, there is no inference. Now, if [it is argued that] it is seen—
"In perception, there is no locus for the cognition of positive and negative concomitance; how then can there be the cognition of knowledge that smoke does not deviate from fire?"
Thus:
smoke is the effect of fire because it follows the nature of an effect;
[it is known] from the non-perception of that which has become its characteristic, provided there is perception [of the conditions].
And because of that, even when one [of the two] is absent,
this is understood; it perishes at every moment from the very beginning, solely due to the aforementioned deception.
The reasons are ascertained.
[Objection: But even for one who perceives the final moment, how can there be an ascertainment of impermanence, since at that time the apprehension of existence still persists?
For one who perceives only existence itself does not understand its absence. To this he says: "Afterwards," etc. It is not so.

They say that certainty arises from the mere perception of the final moment; however, having seen the final moment, [the certainty] occurs afterwards. At that time, it is no longer perceived, and thus it cannot be its effect. Furthermore, when smoke arises in the presence of fire, wood, and so forth, its non-perception does not occur even when horses and other things are removed. But when the fire and such are removed, its non-perception does occur. Thus...

When perception and non-perception are combined, the status of being a cause is established without doubt regarding those very things accepted as causes. And that aforementioned definition of an effect exists in smoke; therefore, smoke arises from fire alone.

Furthermore, since smoke occurs whenever fire is present, its not being produced by what is not fire is established, because that which exists or does not exist at any time cannot be produced by something other than its cause.

[The cause] is non-perception; that is its effect, and that exists in smoke. It is called such either because it has fire as its cause or because it has an invisible cause. Regarding this, first of all, it is not the former position, as we shall explain in the third chapter, in the section beginning with "If [it is argued] that everything is incapable" (*Pramāṇavārttika* 3.4). Nor is it the case that it lacks a cause, for which reason it is stated in that very same place.
He will say: "Nor is smoke caused by an invisible factor, because it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of fire and so forth.

Now, it might be argued: "(1) This is the nature of the invisible factor, that it produces smoke only when fire and so forth are present, and makes it endowed with fragrance and the like at the time of burning camphor and such, but not otherwise. [To this we ask: Then, does it ever produce smoke without fire?

If it is argued that smoke is observed to arise from consciousness (cit), and thus it is so stated; if this is denied, then how is it that smoke is not an effect of fire, given that it exists when fire is present? Furthermore, to claim that at the time of smoke's production, fire—though always perceived—is merely present by way of the "crow-and-palm-fruit" (coincidental) maxim, is an extraordinary (alaukika) designation.

Alternatively, that very nature of the invisible [entity] is such that if it were not assisted by fire, why would it produce smoke only when fire and other conditions are present, and not before or after? Therefore, its very nature as a producer of smoke exists only when fire and other conditions are present, and not otherwise; thus, even in that case, smoke is ultimately produced by fire alone.
It may be so; furthermore, just as smoke is perceived to depend on [its causes] because it does not arise in the absence of place, time, and so forth, so too...

Since it is observed that smoke never arises in the absence of fire, by whom can its dependence on fire be denied? That dependence is nothing other than being its effect. Just as the fact that smoke exists only when an invisible entity [fire] is present leads to the acceptance of its being produced by that [entity], why is it not likewise accepted that smoke is produced by fire because it is observed to exist at all times only when fire is present? And as long as [the cause] is in proximity...

To the extent that an entity is seen arising, all those [preceding factors] possess the status of being its cause, because their prior existence is equal. Thus, since smoke is produced by a causal complex including fire, fuel, and so forth, how could there be any deviation from fire?
Another, however, says: "Let it be that fire and smoke stand in a cause-and-effect relationship; nevertheless, they are not [produced] by a single [cause]."

Apprehension by means of cognition [is impossible] because of the difference in time. Nor can it be apprehended by this preceding non-conceptual [cognition], for that [cognition] grasps only the prior object and not the cause-form of the effect, since the latter is not perceptible due to its future existence. Likewise, the subsequent [non-conceptual cognition] also grasps only the subsequent object and not the effect-form of the cause, because the former has passed away and thus cannot be grasped. Nor can it be apprehended by a conceptual [cognition].

In that case as well, this objection is equally applicable: "Therefore, no one perceives that 'this has arisen from that'; for that very reason, it is not perceived even by memory, because there was no prior experience.
To this it is replied: First of all, in its unarisen state, the effect does not possess a relationship with the cause simply because it is non-existent.

It is the same even in the state of completion. Because it is independent, the cause as well is unrelated to the effect during both the states of the effect’s production and non-production. Furthermore, there is no relationship of causality between these two because they exist at different times; rather, this designation—“this is the effect of that” and “this is the cause of that”—is merely conceptual. Therefore, from the perspective of the cause...

In this way, the very acquisition of its own nature (*svarūpalābha*) constitutes being an effect. For the cause as well, causality with respect to the effect consists simply in its prior existence; and since that acquisition of self-nature and that prior existence are non-different from the entity itself, they are indeed apprehended by perception. Thus, how could the relation of cause and effect not be graspable by perception? It is merely when the effect is observed that one employs the conventional designation: "this is the effect of that" or "this is the cause of that."

For since the relation of cause and effect is not possible between that which is not a cause and that which is not an effect; nor can their causality be made non-different from the relation of cause and effect due to contradiction; nor can it be different, because that would entail that they lack the nature of cause and effect by their very essence. If even for those things that are cause and effect by their very essence, what [is the cause and what is the effect]?

Because [the cause] possesses the nature of cause and effect by its very own essence, rather than through some imagined distinct entity, the causal relation between those two is simply the state of being prior and posterior. Therefore, when the preceding thing is apprehended, the cause—which consists in the immediate proximity to the effect—is already apprehended; and by the subsequent cognition, the subsequent thing, which is immediately after the cause, is apprehended as the effect.

Only its own nature is apprehended, because immediate succession (*ānantarya*) has a nature non-different from that [nature]. For this very reason, there also arises the recollection, "this occurs immediately after that," because the immediate succession has been experienced.
However, Aviddhakarṇa said: "When one perceives the state of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) upon seeing the first [instance], and then sees the second and subsequent instances..."

"It is established that for the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), there is no persistence of a seer; nor is there recollection of the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) of one person with an object experienced by another, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)," [they argue]. This is incorrect, because the first momentary object is apprehended by the first momentary cognition, and so on for those belonging to a single continuum (*ekasantati*).

Furthermore, memory is possible by way of the relationship between cause and effect. How the relationship of cause and effect exists in the case of momentariness has already been stated and will be stated again.
[Objection: Even so, since the moments themselves are not ascertained, how can the relationship of cause and effect be ascertained? Nor [can it be ascertained] by means of a continuum (*santāna*).
Since that [continuum] does not exist as something distinct from its constituent members (*santānin*), it is merely the members themselves that exist in earlier and later moments.

In that case, since when one moment exists another does not, there is only the appearance of a single moment; how, then, can there be the appearance of a continuum? And in the absence of that [continuum], how can there be a causal relationship?

That is incorrect. (1) Since there exists no entity consisting of a single atom, the appearance of a continuum (*santāna*) is merely the appearance of gross entities in immediate succession. In that case, because one determines unity through similarity—failing to discern the distinction between moments—the causal relationship between the moments occurring within a single continuum cannot be ascertained. [Distinct...]

However, as for those [entities] existing within a continuum, because they are of a different class from the progression of the continuum itself, that determination [of identity] does not occur; therefore, the claim that the determination of the causal relationship between the fire-continuum and the smoke-continuum arises from the cognition of a smoke-continuum preceded by a fire-continuum is merely a trifle.

Furthermore, [the opponent] says: "When the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between two specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) has been apprehended, how can there be a relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) between two universals (*sāmānya*), given that they are distinct?
This too is incorrect, because it is accepted that a universal consists of many specific characteristics. As it has been said:
Even when in the state of being praised, one should not transgress against those who possess malice. ||36||
The effect is accomplished even by seeing [the cause] once, because it does not occur even once without its cause. As it is said:

"Because it establishes merely the thing as excluded from what is not of that nature, and because it does not rest upon particulars, the logical mark (*liṅga*) is declared to have a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. (Pramāṇasamuccaya)

Therefore, the apprehension of the relation between universals is nothing other than the apprehension of the relation between their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); it is not something else. Now, for the Buddhist who maintains the theory of inference, one must apprehend all the specific characteristics existing in the three worlds as being pervaded by fire; for if even a single one were not apprehended, the logical reason (*hetu*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Yet, perception does not function in this manner.

It is capable [of establishing the pervasion] because its object is present; nor can the pervasion of other particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) be grasped through inference, as that would lead to an infinite regress.
This is incorrect, because perception apprehends the smoke-particular only when the fire-particular is present.

In these cases, one determines that the nature of smoke—which is excluded from non-smoke—is exclusively the effect of fire, which itself is excluded from non-fire. (1) Just as it is here, so it is in other places and times; one determines that this very nature is produced solely by fire, for otherwise its connection with fire would not be apprehended through perception. Thus, regarding its being the effect of both fire and non-fire, [it would have to be] connected to both.

The cognition would not arise solely through connection with fire; yet it is so cognized. Therefore, because there is a certainty that this very form occurs from fire alone even in other instances, how could there be any deviation of smoke from fire? Furthermore, this inference belongs only to one who is able to discern that form as distinct from vapor and the like, and not to anyone else. This is the view of those who maintain that the universal pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) is grasped.

Nor is there an inference [of fire] based on the determination of the generality of smoke as being invariably concomitant with fire— due to the apprehension of the generality of smoke in cases such as a cowherd’s water-pot even in the absence of fire—

because that very determination of the generality of smoke as being invariably concomitant with fire is itself preceded by the determination of individual instances of smoke connected with fire. Furthermore, it is not the case that in every instance, such as in all locations and so forth, there is a connection with fire...
The apprehension of the universal "smoke" as qualified by specific instances of smoke is not possible through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Nor has the universal "smoke" been perceived in the kitchen or elsewhere as qualified by specific instances of smoke connected with fire, because there is no concomitance (*anvaya*) with those specific instances that persist elsewhere. Furthermore, that universal "smoke" which does persist is not invariably concomitant (*avyabhicārin*) with fire.

Therefore, even for one who maintains that the universal concomitance is grasped, the same objection applies: how is it that the specific universal of smoke is understood to be pervaded by fire everywhere?

Now, if there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against smoke being produced by fire in other instances, and because of the cognition "this is that very same [smoke]," [the pervasion is established].

"That which is apprehended as a universal is accepted by us as well, because the cognition 'this is that very same thing' arises; since it is accepted by both of us, what is the difference between us?"—this is trivial. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "That smoke exists [only] in the absence of that, namely, the absence of fire."

If it were causeless, one could transcend its possession of a cause. Alternatively, if that smoke were perceived as being connected with fire, yet it were to exist in the absence of that [fire]—that is, in the absence of fire—it would not be perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as possessing a cause, namely, as being connected with fire. Yet it is so perceived.
Therefore, even though it exists, it is not [known] merely from repeated observation; rather, it is known from the aforementioned direct perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). 100.

For if an effect were to exist in the absence of its own cause, it would simply be causeless; indeed, that in whose absence something occurs cannot be the cause of that thing. Thus, because smoke exists even without fire, fire would not be its cause.

If it is argued that [fire] is not causeless because it has another cause, this is not so; for the same logic applies there as well. Even in the absence of that [fuel], since fire still exists, that [fire] would also be something else [than the fuel]. Because its nature is not to produce that [fuel], it would exist only in such a way. Since that which lacks the nature of producing it does not produce it, that [fuel] would be causeless.

What is the reason? Because fire does not exist even when present [without fuel], let alone because it is absent more frequently. Indeed, oil never arises from sand, even once. With the words "of the effect" (*kāryasya*) and so forth, he states the meaning of the verse. The phrase "for indeed" (*na hi*) and so forth is the justification for that very point.
By this, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is stated; otherwise, for one who asserts deviation, smoke would exist even without fire. By this—

And the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) has been stated. The meaning is that "of that" [smoke]—since it exists even without fire—it is not caused by that [fire], nor is it caused by fire; thus, it would be causeless.
As for the phrase "having another cause," since fire has something else, such as grass or wood, as its cause, smoke cannot be causeless because it is produced from that [other cause].
If this is argued, it is not so; for even in that case, the same difficulty applies when another cause is postulated. To explain:
(1) since fire occurs again even in the absence of that [cause] and in the absence of other causes, that other cause would likewise not be a cause. Furthermore, as for that which...

39b. Furthermore, that which is distinct from fire—what is its nature? Is it the nature of producing smoke, or is it not? If it is not the nature of producing smoke, then how could smoke arise from that, or from something else such as a thunderbolt (*śata-krauda*), since they lack the nature of producing it? Smoke would simply not come into being from that which lacks the nature of producing smoke. Why is this? Because that which does not possess that nature is itself incapable of producing smoke.

Because its own nature would not be produced, that smoke would lack a cause. Alternatively, if there were another [fire] whose nature is to produce smoke, then both would possess the status of fire, because fire is characterized by having the nature of producing smoke. This will be explained later.

The proponent of deviation does not indeed say, "It is that very same [smoke]," and so forth; nor is it said that smoke produced from fire arises from something else. For if that very same [smoke] were to arise from elsewhere, there would be the consequence of its being causeless, because such a thing—being identical in nature to the property produced by fire—would exist from another source.

Or [the verse beginning with] "from something of a different kind" (*anyādṛśāt*) may be the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). [Objection: Is it then intended that the cause is similar to its effect, such that it is said:
"How can that which arises from something of a different kind be of that same kind? [Response: No, because the meaning is different.

For when fire is seen as the producer of smoke, if smoke arises from something dissimilar to that [fire], how could it be "produced by fire"? [It would not. Thus, the point is not that the cause must be similar to the effect.
It possesses a nature equal to the *dharmatā*.

This is what is meant: just as various types of smoke—such as that produced from grass, leaves, and so forth—are considered "similar" (*tādṛśatva*) in relation to one another, so too are the various types of fire that produce those smokes—such as fires from grass, leaves, and so forth—considered "similar" only in relation to one another. 3. Examination of Pervasion (*vyāpti*).
If it is argued that "it is indeed [the same] because such a thing exists," [we ask]: how can something arising from what is unlike [itself] be of that very nature?

For only by arising from what is like itself could it be of that nature. If it were to arise as such even from what is unlike it, then, due to the absence of a restriction on its causal capacity (*śakti*), the difference in causes would not be a differentiator; consequently, the manifold variety of the universe would be without cause, or else everything [would be identical].
Everything would arise from everything. Therefore, through the difference or non-difference of the cause, the difference or non-difference of the effect would not occur;
for if an object were produced from a dissimilar thing possessing a form different from that observed in smoke, it would follow that it is causeless.
This is not so;
for [a cause] would be either eternally existent or eternally non-existent, because it does not depend on anything else.
Therefore, just as a particular instance of smoke is seen to arise from a particular instance of fire, such a particular instance of smoke—[would likewise arise from that same fire].
The production [of smoke] arises from a specific distinction of fire; however, that which is produced from what is not fire is of a different kind altogether, like steam and the like.

If it is argued: "But surely, by means of a moment of smoke produced by fire, there is a moment of smoke produced by that [same] moment of smoke; thus, even from something of a different kind, something of that same kind comes into being," we say: No. For of a moment of smoke produced by fire, there is another [moment] produced specifically by fire.

A moment of smoke is of such a nature and not otherwise; for even when there is a determination that steam and the like are of such a nature, they do not actually become so. Furthermore, a moment of smoke produced by another moment of smoke is of such a nature only if it is produced by a moment of smoke, and not otherwise. Therefore, since such an effect arises only from such a cause, how can there be any deviation? By this [it is established].
If things are momentary, how could their modes of existence ever depend upon anything else,
given that their occurrence arises from something other than well-known causes?
"Therefore, just as the production of smoke from smoke that is not produced by fire [is impossible],
who could prevent the production of that [smoke] from the head of Śakra?"—
this is refuted; for the subsequent moment of smoke produced by fire is of the same nature as the first moment of smoke produced by fire.

A second moment of smoke produced by a moment of smoke is indeed of such a nature as to be produced by another moment of smoke; likewise for the third and subsequent moments. Thus, even with respect to the moments, there is no deviation for that which is of such a nature. He says this very thing: "For from that which is of such a nature, what is of such a nature would arise; even if it were from something else, that is, from something dissimilar to fire."

It would be of such a nature as smoke produced from fire; for there is an absence of a restriction on its causal capacity (*śakti*). Since there is no restriction on the capacity of causes—whether similar or dissimilar—such that a similar cause produces only a similar effect and a dissimilar cause produces something distinct, it follows that the difference in the cause does not constitute a differentiator of the effect. Thus, [the opponent argues].

The cause of the universe would indeed possess a universal form (*vaiśvarūpya*). If it is argued that because [things] arise from some cause or other, they are not without a cause, he replies: "Or else everything would arise from everything," and so forth. If there were production even from that which lacks the capacity, then everything would be born from everything; but this is not the case. Therefore, and so on. "That is not smoke": "that" means "therefore," since smoke is produced [only from a specific cause].
That fire has been seen as having a perceived form; the meaning is that it is distinct from what is not fire.
For it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible. ||37||

For if that smoke were to exist without a cause, then, due to the absence of any dependence, it would never fail to exist, because there would be no deficiency [in its conditions], just as at the time it is desired. Or else, it would not exist even then, because there is no distinction between that time and the time of its non-existence. Indeed, it is through dependence that entities occur only occasionally; for [otherwise] there would be no difference between the times of their existence and non-existence.

Because of the connection with the fitness or unfitness for that state; for if space and time were equally fit or unfit, there could be no restriction regarding that which possesses them and that which does not.
And if that fitness were something other than the state of being a cause, then [there would be] in some cases [a restriction] of space and time.

And likewise, if there were causelessness (*ahetukatva*), smoke would have to be either eternally existent or non-existent. Why? Because an entity that lacks a cause does not depend on anything else for its own production; that is, it does not depend on other causes. If it is argued that even in the absence of dependence on other causes, it might occur only occasionally by way of its own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), [the author] says: "For [it arises] from dependence."
This is what is meant: since that which is unestablished is non-existent by its very nature, how could it have occasional occurrence (*kādācitkatva*) through intrinsic nature (*svabhāvataḥ*)?
On the other hand, that which is established does possess an intrinsic nature; however, the objection is raised as to how that very establishment occurs only at certain times.
He explains this very point with the words beginning "sa hi" [he, indeed...]: "It would never not exist" means it would exist at all times.

What is the reason? Because when that [fire] exists, the smoke-nature exists; since it does not depend on other causes, there is no deficiency, as in the case of the time [when fire is present]. Furthermore, "even then" means that even at the time when it is observed, smoke would not exist, because there is no distinction from the time when smoke is absent.

Dividing the latter half [of the verse], he says: "Indeed, by way of dependence. This means by way of dependence on a suitable place and time. For, since there are two times—the time of existence and the time of non-existence of the effect—there is a connection with the suitability and unsuitability of that existence, namely the production of the effect, respectively. The mention of "time" is intended as an illustration; in this same manner, it should also be stated for place and substance. Now, if this is so...

It is not accepted [that this is so]. For, when two points of time—one possessing the effect and one lacking it—are equal in terms of their capacity and incapacity, it is impossible to establish a restriction (*niyama*) regarding which possesses that [capacity] and which does not. Only the time of the effect possesses it; "possessing the effect" means having the effect, while for the other, it is the opposite—namely, not possessing the effect. Since such a restriction is untenable, both those times—the time of the presence of the effect and the time of its absence—would possess the effect.

They might [be considered causes] due to suitability (*yogyatā*) or similarity; or rather, they are not, because unsuitability is equal [in both cases]. Therefore, suitability belongs only to the time of that [effect’s] existence. Or, depending upon that [suitability], entities become occasional.
Let it be granted that there is suitability for the desired place, time, and so forth; yet, by that much alone, the status of being a cause is not established. To this, he says:
"And that," etc. Since, if there were thus no cause, there would be either eternal existence or non-existence, and yet this is not the case;
therefore, "from that," etc. That by the avoidance of which something proceeds is independent of it; and that wherein it exists is dependent upon it.
If it is asked, "Even if it indeed exists in some place or time, how is it dependent on that?", he says: "For it is so."
"Functioning in such a manner" means functioning elsewhere by way of excluding [the former].

If it is argued that while an entity indeed depends on place and so forth, no assistance (*upakāra*) is rendered to it by that place and so forth, he says: "By the assistance produced by that," and so on. By way of that restriction, because of its presence in other places and times, it becomes dependent upon them. For instance, functioning in such a manner—

[The fire] indeed depends [on its cause], for it is impossible for that which is independent of the assistance provided by its cause to be restricted to it. This is because of the restriction of place and time.

For where smoke has been observed once, and is not observed when there is a deficiency [of its causes], its nature is produced by that [fire]. Otherwise, since it would never exist at any time, how could that which is restricted to that [cause] occur elsewhere? Or, if it were to occur, it would not be smoke. (433b)

Smoke is a specific nature produced by that [fire]. Likewise, the cause also possesses a nature that produces such an effect. If it were to arise from something else as well, then it would not possess that nature, and thus it would not produce smoke even once. Nor would that be smoke, because it would have arisen from an entity whose nature is not to produce smoke. And if it did possess that nature, it would not be anything other than fire; thus, there is no deviation.
The movement.
If the head of Śakra were non-different from fire, being fire itself, then how could smoke exist there, since its nature would be that of fire? (38)
"Because of the impossibility of restriction (*niyamāyogāt*). This means that it is impossible to maintain a restriction such as "it must not exist in that very place and so forth.

(1) The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the mention of place and time; it is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes substance (*dravya*) as well. "Where" refers to the place and so forth where [the object] was previously seen. "Once" means:
by the aforementioned perception, it was seen when those [causes] were present, but it is not seen again when any one of them is deficient.

"Otherwise" means: if its nature were not produced by that [cause], then this smoke would not be restricted to that specific causal complex consisting of fire and so forth. How could it arise elsewhere than from fire? It simply would not arise. Or, if it did arise, it would not be smoke.
For smoke is a specific nature produced by that—that is, produced by fire. The same applies to the logical reason (*hetu*) as well.

Likewise, fire possesses the nature of producing an effect consisting of the elements, which is the nature of being capable of producing smoke; this capacity, being the cause, certainly exists even in the state devoid of smoke. Therefore, the definition is not too narrow (avyāpi) in the case of fire and smoke. 17 Thus [is it] for fire and smoke. 4cb.
When their mutually dependent and fixed natures have been established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),

if it were admitted that this smoke could arise from something other than fire, then that nature of producing smoke would not belong to that non-fire. For in that case, when smoke arises from what is not fire, the nature of producing smoke would have arisen in that very non-fire.

And how could that which is the nature of non-fire be the nature of fire? Consequently, because fire would lack the nature of producing smoke, it would not produce smoke even once. Furthermore, smoke itself would not possess the nature of smoke; thus he says: "Nor... and so forth. That smoke does not arise from something other than fire—what is the reason? Because [fire] lacks the nature of producing smoke...

Because smoke exists only when fire exists— that is, because it arises from it— and because its nature is such that even if one were to admit that what is not fire possesses the nature of producing smoke, fire alone is the producer of this smoke by virtue of having that very form; thus, through this means, smoke is non-deviant [of fire].
For the sake of easy comprehension, he states two verses beginning with "having the nature of fire" (*agnisvabhāva*).
"For fire has the nature of being the cause of smoke and possesses a specific capacity for that; if it were present in the absence of smoke, it would be without a cause. (39)
These are the summary verses.
Now, how can an effect arise from a distinct auxiliary cause? For example, visual consciousness [arises] from the eye and visible form.

Indeed, not even a single one of those things possesses that nature as an individual producer; rather, it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that is the producer. The meaning is this: when [the mountain peak] has the nature of fire—that is, the nature of producing smoke—then that very Śakra’s peak is fire because it has the nature of producing smoke. Alternatively, if that Śakra’s peak does not have the nature of fire, then [it is not fire] in that case, namely, on Śakra’s peak.

He asks, "Why would it not be so? and replies with the words beginning "dhūma" (smoke), etc. For [the word] "hi" means "because. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has smoke as its causal nature. Why is this so? Because it possesses a distinction of capacity (*tacchaktibhedavān*). By that capacity for producing smoke—which functions as the instrument—it is distinct from, or dissimilar to, other things such as fireflies (*khadyota*), etc. If smoke were to arise from a non-smoke cause—that is, from something whose nature is not fire—[it would follow that it arises] without a cause.

If its arising were admitted, that smoke would be causeless, as was stated previously. "How? and so forth asks the opponent. "Now" means if one does not admit the arising of a single effect from something of a different genus, such as smoke.
How [could it arise] from distinct things that are mutually of a different genus? [The answer is: the production of a single effect from the presence of auxiliary causes.

"How so? he asks. "For example," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), light, mental attention (manaskāra), and the like are included. This being the case, consciousness arises from the nature of the eye and also from the nature of form, mental attention, and so on; yet it is not without a cause. Likewise, smoke may arise from fire and also from the head of Śakra, which is not fire; yet it will not be without a cause—so argues the objector.

[The opponent] thinks [as follows]. [The author] refutes this with the words beginning with "na khalu kiṃcit" (not at all, nothing...). [He argues: Among the eye and other [causes], that nature which is productive does not exist as something single and independent of the others. For if it were so, then there would be a deviation from the cause in each individual case.

It would follow that [the cause] is the cause of the result itself; however, it is the totality (*sāmagrī*) that is the producer. That which has the nature of producing is the producer by its very nature.

Since the state of having that nature is already obtained simply by saying "the totality is the producer"—for that which does not have that nature is not a producer—why is it stated separately as "what is its nature"? True; however, it is stated for the sake of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). It means that the state of having that nature exists only in the state of the totality, and not otherwise.

"Neither before nor after, nor separately. The collective meaning is that all other causes, whose presence is determined by the capacity of their own respective causes, constitute the "cause" with respect to a single effect.
Some, however, read the word *vā* (or), [interpreting it as]: "The causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is the producer, or its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is so. But in this context...

The word "or" (*vā*) serves no purpose; thus, this is simply a corrupt reading. If, after stating that it is the "assemblage" (*sāmagrī*), one were to claim that visual consciousness could arise even from another assemblage, then because it would arise from something distinct, it would follow that it is causeless. That very assemblage is what is inferred by means of the effect. The point is that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), for the effect does not arise from any individual cause other than [the complete set].

It might be argued as follows: the very first moment of smoke is produced by the causal complex (sāmagrī) consisting of fire and other factors, yet there is no consideration of its being a logical mark (liṅga) or its pervasion (vyāpti). That very [complex] is what is inferred. And that same complex is the basis for the persistence of the nature of the non-effect. For this very reason, there is no simultaneous production by the auxiliary causes.
Because its end is uncertain. Furthermore, the connection with smoke that is apprehended is simply the cause of the preceding smoke;

how, then, can there be an inference from the causal complex consisting of fire and so forth? To this he says: "And that very [complex]... and so on. Because the continuity of the effect is established by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*), the basis is the primary cause. For without the causal complex, the continuum of smoke itself would not exist.

Then, having unified the series of smoke with the effect of fire, there is an inference of the causal series consisting of the burning [fire] and so forth; for empirical observation (*arvāgdarśana*) cannot function through the distinction of individual moments. It might be argued: "Only the fire itself is inferred, and that does not serve anything for one who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)."
This objection, namely "yojanam" (the joining), has already been answered by the very act of raising it. At that time, the meaning is as follows:

(1) That same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), proceeding in a continuous stream, is the cause for the persistence of the nature of the effect and for the occurrence of the continuity of the effect; for, in dependence upon each preceding moment of fire and so forth, each subsequent moment of smoke arises. Indeed, there is no such rule that only a single moment of smoke [is produced] by fire.

There is no other [effect] to be produced. As long as the fuel has not been completely reduced to ashes, the production of moments of smoke is not contradictory. Therefore, just as a continuous series of smoke of a certain nature has been produced by a fire that functions as a continuum through the generation of successive moments of burning, and this has been determined by direct perception, one should determine it to be of that same nature elsewhere as something capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

The inference of a burning continuum for one who desires it is not contradictory; for the nature of smoke from a broken burning continuum is one thing, while that of smoke from a house or similar place where the burning continuum has been interrupted is quite another. Since the world clearly perceives the distinction between these two, how can there be any deviation [in the logical mark]?
Alternatively, it is explained otherwise:
Is it not the case that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is distinct from its constituent parts (*samagra*)? And because that [complex] is a single unity, only a single effect is produced;
otherwise, due to the individual capacity of each constituent, there would be a multiplicity of effects, or else they would produce a single effect only successively, which is not what occurs.
Thus, having raised the doubt as to how there can be a single producing cause, he says:

"And that very [collection]," and so forth. "And that very collection" means that it is precisely the complete factors that are designated by the term "collection. For what reason? Because, by virtue of their abiding in their own nature—that is, through the presence of their own essential form—they serve as the basis for the effect.

He thinks as follows: if the production of the effect were due to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) alone, then the individual members of that complex would lack causal agency. This would contradict empirical experience. Furthermore, even if those members were indeed causal agents, there would either be a multiplicity of effects, or they would produce a single effect only in succession. Moreover, their uniformity does not arise from the power of the causal complex; rather, it belongs to the complex itself.

Because it would entail the consequence [of their being] entities. Therefore, those factors, produced as restricted to performing a single effect by their own causes when complete, are designated by the term "causal complex" (*sāmagrī*). And there is no sublation regarding many things performing a single effect. Nor is it our view that the cause itself becomes the effect, such that the multiplicity [of causes] having a single effect would be contradictory. And just as there is a single effect—

Since it is observed that the causal status belongs precisely to the prior existence of those [factors], so too it must belong to multiple [factors] as well. Or, just as those very same [factors], when complete, produce a single collection characterized by conjunction, why should they not likewise produce a single effect?

Even though the production of lotus roots (*śālūka*) and the like from heterogeneous sources such as cow dung is observed, even in that case, despite being described in such a way, there is indeed a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) because of the difference in the nature of the cause, just as in the case of the plantain tree which arises from seeds and bulbs. Thus, in the world, the distinction is clearly made by means of their different forms. In this manner...
For an effect whose form has been well-discriminated does not deviate from its cause.

That which is observed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as following another is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of that [other]; therefore, it cannot arise from something different. (40)

Therefore, since the relationship of cause and effect is established even by a single instance of observation and non-observation— otherwise, because positive and negative concomitance would depend upon exhaustive observation and non-observation—
this is the summary verse.
Therefore,
that [notion] is entirely baseless; for it is precisely from the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces [an effect] that the simultaneous production by the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) occurs.
The meaning is that there is no production through a sequential process.

With the words "And as for... and so forth, he raises the objection regarding production from a heterogeneous cause and refutes it; the meaning is that he demonstrates here precisely what was stated previously, namely, that a thing of such a nature cannot arise from something of a different nature. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [he includes] an arrow from a cow's horn.

41b. "From cow dung, a scorpion [arises]"—the phrase "even there" refers even to the case where an effect arises from something of a different genus (*vijātīya*). "Even when designated as such" means that even though a lotus root (*śālūka*) and so forth produced from something of a different genus is designated by the term "lotus root" and so on, it nonetheless exists precisely because it originates—that is, its production (*prabhava*)—is from its own seed characterized as a lotus root; thus, it exists by virtue of originating from its own seed.

There is a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*). What is the reason? (1) Because of the difference in the intrinsic nature of the causes. This is because of the difference in the intrinsic nature of the causes, which are characterized by two distinct sets of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*). A plantain tree that arises from a seed and from a bulb is such [a case];
and it is mutually distinct due to the difference in its causal status.
And this distinction is not something to be proven; thus he says, "clearly," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "or [he] discerns the entity in its difference":
it means that the form is well-discriminated—that is, the form is ascertained through a distinction from causes that possess similar forms, which would otherwise lead to error.

Existence only when that exists is positive concomitance (*anvaya*); non-existence only when that is absent is negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). From these two, positive and negative concomitance, [the following follows]: whatever nature of an effect is observed to follow a particular persisting cause, that persisting nature is the cause of that [effect]; thus, that persisting [nature] is the cause from which it arises.

This is the analysis of the compound *tasya* (*of that*). When, however, it is stated with reference to the cause, then the "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) of that which is to be followed—such as fire—is the "cause" (*hetu*) of that which is intended as the effect—such as smoke; that is, it is the cause of that [effect]. And since, in this way, there is a restriction of the intrinsic natures of cause and effect through their mutual dependence, for that reason, there can be no arising from something different—that is, from a heterogeneous cause.

Therefore, because the causal relationship is established through the aforementioned perception and non-perception—namely, by seeing [the effect] once and not seeing it [in the absence of the cause]—it follows from that establishment of the causal relationship. From that establishment of the causal relationship comes the comprehension of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and the comprehension of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) does not occur otherwise; thus, apart from the certainty of the causal relationship, [these two do not arise] from mere [perception and non-perception] alone. This is the consideration of universals (*sāmānyacintā*).

Even when permanence is observed, it is seen otherwise elsewhere; for in some cases, that which was not observed in the absence of permanence is now observed. [In the section on] the Examination of Universals:
Granted that there may be an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the cause because an effect arises from it, how can there be an inseparable connection with the essential nature (*svabhāva*)?
Intrinsic nature has an inseparable connection with that which follows upon mere existence;
in the absence of that [existence], the intrinsic nature itself would be absent, because of their non-difference. (41)

The understanding of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) does not arise from mere observation and non-observation. Why is this? Because the understanding of positive and negative concomitance is dependent upon exhaustive observation and non-observation, whereas [mere] observation is restricted to what is actually perceived.

For observation establishes positive concomitance only if the reason (*hetu*) is observed in every instance of the similar class (*sapakṣa*); likewise, non-observation would establish negative concomitance.

If there were no observation of the reason (*hetu*) in all instances where the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent— just as the fact that smoke is once produced in a single instance establishes its nature as an effect everywhere— then it might be argued that likewise, through observation in some cases of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and non-observation in others of the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*),

there would be a certain determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) everywhere. This too is false, because [in the case of] immateriality (*amūrtatva*) in some instances...

Regarding the observation of permanence in space and so forth, this is stated by way of what is established for the opponent. In other cases, such as pleasure and the like, it is otherwise; that is, because the reason—formlessness—is observed [to coexist] with impermanence, the observation in one instance does not prove the existence of that same state everywhere. Therefore, observation is fallacious with respect to positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Likewise, in some cases, such as a jar, it is not observed even though permanence is absent.

Furthermore, since non-eternality is observed in pleasure and the like—which lack permanence—the mere non-observation [of the reason] in one part of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is not a proof for the ascertainment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Therefore, the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance arises solely from the ascertainment of the causal relationship (*hetu-phala-bhāva*).

[The opponent objects: "As for 'essential nature' (*svabhāva*) and so forth... [The author replies: "Now," meaning that since the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) has been established in the case of the effect-reason (*kārya-hetu*), at this point...
How is there an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) in the case of a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*)?

But was it not already established previously that there is an inseparable connection in the case of an essential identity reason, by means of the statement beginning: "Indeed, existence itself is a reason when it follows upon mere existence"?

True. However, [the opponent] thinks as follows: "If the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is described as existing only in that which has the nature of being exactly as it is (*yathābhūta-svabhāva*), then it follows that [the reason] is a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*). The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*), considering that the charge of being a part of the proposition's meaning is avoided by the subsequent proof of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), [asserts] the inseparable connection as that which conforms to "only that" (*tanmātrānurodhin*).

He restates what was said previously: "The inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) exists even in the case of essential nature (*svabhāva*)," and so forth. Even in the case of essential nature—that is, even in the case of an essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*)—there is an inseparable connection. In respect to what probandum (*sādhya*)? In respect to that which follows upon mere existence (*bhāvamātrānurodhin*). The phrase beginning with "For that which... is the explanation of this very point. "The inseparable connection of existence" refers to [the property] such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*). Because in the absence of that [probandum], there is no mere existence...

In the absence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) which follows [the presence of] the subject (*anurodhi*), there would be an absence of that which has been presented as the reason (*hetu*). What is the reason?

For one who desires an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of an entity even when its nature merely follows the existence of another entity—indeed, in the absence of that [other], there would be an absence of the nature itself, because of their non-difference. That very entity which follows the mere existence of another entity [is what is meant].
It is called "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva); that very thing is, by its own nature, an entity (bhāva). And how could that exist while abandoning itself?
In that case, because there is no difference [between them], the reason would be a part of the meaning of the thesis itself, namely, "whatever is produced is impermanent.
This is not a fault.
All things, by their very nature, are established in their own individual natures;
for they partake in exclusions from both intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature. (42)

Because there is no difference between the probandum and the probans, he explains this very non-difference with the words "that which... and so forth. That very entity, such as the impermanent, which conforms solely to the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), is called its "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). That same entity, by virtue of not depending on any other cause, is in reality—that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth—the produced thing itself; and that entity [is] its own self, namely impermanence, which constitutes its intrinsic nature.

"How could it be [the reason] without abandoning that?"—thus the opponent asks. "The statement of the subject is the thesis (*pratijñā*). Its object is the aggregate of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*); one part of that aggregate would be the reason (*hetu*), consisting of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). For instance, as much as has been stated: "Sound is impermanent; sound is impermanent..."
The sense is that [the argument] "sound is non-eternal because it is produced" is likewise unestablished (*asiddha*) as a reason.

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) says, "This is not a fault," beginning with the words "because all entities... Here, by the first verse, the seed for the conceptualization of a property (*dharmakalpanābīja*) is shown; by the second, the conceptualization of the property itself; and by the third, the fact that [the reason] is a mere part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*).

The collective meaning is that the rebuttal is now being stated. [The suffix] *ghinuṇ* is used because all entities (*bhāva*) possess a distinction from both their own nature (*svabhāva*) and the nature of others (*parabhāva*). All entities are excluded from those of the same class and those of a different class by way of their own nature—that is, by way of their own form—and not by way of the form of another. This is because they are established in their own nature; that is, because they abide in their own nature.

Is it not the case that a cow is distinct from a horse and so forth by way of its genus (*jāti*); that a horned cow is distinct from another individual cow by way of its substance (*dravya*); and that a white cow is distinct from another horned individual cow by way of its quality (*guṇa*)? In this manner, the differentiation of all entities down to the atom is produced by qualifiers such as genus and the like, and not by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

To this it is replied: (1) First of all, a distinction is not produced by means of a genus (*jāti*) and so forth for entities that are already non-distinct, because in the case of making a distinction between what is distinct and non-distinct, the genus is ineffective therein. Nor [is it applied] to those that are already distinct, because it would be redundant. Nor is the conventional usage of "distinction" (*bhedavyavahāra*) produced for these [entities], because the establishment of the conventional usage of distinction follows simply from their appearing as distinct in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by virtue of their own nature.

Furthermore, the distinction of universals (*jāti*) and so forth from one another and from their possessors cannot be established through anything other than those [universals] themselves, as that would lead to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If distinction exists by way of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), why is it not accepted as belonging to entities (*bhāva*) alone?
What is the purpose of postulating universals and the like?
Even the Digambara who maintains: "(1) 'If there were no exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), there would be one [entity] consisting of all things;

therefore, difference itself would not exist, unless there were mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) among entities'—he too is refuted by this [same argument], because it is impossible for difference among entities to be produced by non-existence. Nor can there be [difference] among things that are not distinct."
Mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is possible for things that have arisen from causes. If they have arisen as distinct entities, how could there not be mutual non-existence?

[Objection: But surely all things are distinct. [Response: If this is an inference, then the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished with respect to its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because all things are not objects of perception (*pratyakṣa*). For this very reason, this is not considered to be a function of perception.

But another says: although entities are distinct by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they nonetheless possess properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, because these are indeed perceived. Nevertheless, non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-vijñāna*) apprehends only the mere existence (*sattāmātra*) in cows and the like, not their distinction. For the apprehension of distinction is precisely the apprehension of a specific property (*viśeṣa*), and a specific property cannot be grasped without conceptualization (*avikalpya*).
It is grasped; thus, it is the object of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), not of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*). As it has been said:
“Particularities, however, are apprehended by conceptual cognitions;
and some of these reside in each individual substance, while others are established in many.”
"It conceptualizes that which has arisen through its nature of both exclusion and inclusion; moreover, [this cognition] arising with respect to a cow and a horse is not distinguished from perception.
Therefore, there is no manifestation of the distinction between objects in indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*).

As for the one who says: (1) "Even by conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), difference is not apprehended; for the apprehension of the difference between entities is caused by the apprehension of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). And this mutual non-existence, which is the difference, is not an absence (*abhāva*) that can be apprehended by perception (*pratyakṣa*). For perception does not determine that 'there is no horse in the cow'; therefore, perception is the apprehender of mere existence (*sattāmātra*) alone."
This has been stated by Maṇḍana:
"The wise say that perception is a positive [means of knowledge] and not a negator;
therefore, scripture is not contradicted by that perception regarding oneness.
Both of these [statements] are untenable, because mere existence does not manifest [in perception], [just as it is not perceived] in the case of cows, horses, and so forth, each in its own...
Because it appears precisely as a form (rūpa). As it has been said:
“Because a distinct form is perceived for each substance endowed with its own reality (*tattva*), one cannot conclude that there is no difference simply because it is impossible to describe.
As for the one who says: (1) “There is no difference at all among entities; for instance, when a horse is not produced from a cow, [the cow remains] as it was...”
Even when a horse is produced, its own nature remains exactly as it was; nothing else additional has arisen. Thus, how can there be any difference [between the two]?
Or, even if there were a difference, it is not something graspable by perception in the form "this is different from that," because such an operation [of cognition] does not exist.

[The objection] that [difference] is absent in perception has been refuted by the statement: "For this [perception] is not capable of performing such extensive operations. Furthermore, the very arising of cows, horses, and so forth in their own specific forms (*svarūpa*) is what constitutes difference. And these appear in perception precisely as their own specific forms. To claim that such an appearance is what we call the "appearance of difference" in the world is trivial. Therefore:

Because things situated before one are established in their own respective natures, one who perceives difference through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) perceives it by way of universal inclusion (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*); therefore, the result of the means of valid cognition that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is that "all entities participate in exclusion. Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that universals (*jāti*) and so forth do not exist as separate entities.
(1) Therefore, it is stated that there is no ultimate reality to the status of being a property or a possessor of properties (*dharmadharmin*).

Now, [it may be argued: "Is it not the case that things are called 'homogeneous' (*sajātīya*) due to their connection with a universal (*sāmānya*)? And if the universal does not exist, how can one speak of 'exclusion from the homogeneous' (*sajātīyavyāvṛtti*)?"
This is not so. It is not because of a connection with a universal (*sāmānya*) that things which have already arisen as similar possess a similar form;

rather, they are produced as such by their own causes alone. Therefore, as for what Uddyotakara says: "Cowness does not exist in the cow, such that prior to its connection with cowness it would not be a cow... [this is incorrect].

The universal "cowness" would be useless; rather, a thing is connected with cowness at the very moment it exists as a thing. Prior to its connection with cowness, the thing does not exist. And that which does not exist cannot be designated as either "cow" or "non-cow."
That has been refuted. For at the very moment an entity exists, it is already established in its form as a cow; what, then, is the use of a connection with "cowness" (*gotva*)?

Nor does the uniformity of dissimilar things arise from their connection with a universal (*sāmānya*), because for them, the universal itself does not exist. Furthermore, it is accepted that a universal is the state of being similar among those things that are already similar. If the uniformity of entities were derived from a universal, [it would lead to an infinite regress].

If [the connection with a universal] were admitted, then as long as there is no connection with a universal, things would not be similar; and as long as things are not similar, there would be no connection with a universal—thus there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). Therefore, they are produced as similar from their own causes alone. For that reason.
(1) "The difference from a brindled cow is the same for both a black cow and a horse;

if no other universal (*sāmānya*) is admitted, then where could 'exclusion' (*apoha*) be postulated?"— this is refuted, because exclusion is postulated precisely among universals, and because those that are not similar possess the nature of being excluded.
Because of conceptual construction (*prakalpanāt*).

As for what is also said: (1) "They are similar" [is known] precisely from the appearance [in cognition]; otherwise, in non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), there would be no appearance of a universal (*sāmānya*), just as [there is none] between a *bāhuleya* cow and a horse. Furthermore, there would be a perception of difference even between a *śāvaleyā* cow and a *bāhuleya* cow.
Because there is a difference in every respect [between individuals], yet there is the cognition "it is the same," therefore this very thing is the universal (*sāmānya*).

As it has been said: "By non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-bodha*), there is the apprehension of the object as having a dual nature. Alternatively, if the universal were not apprehended by conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), then it would have been apprehended by non-conceptual cognition as well. [This concludes] the investigation of the universal.

Because they have distinct appearances. For instance: (1) those very things such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*) which are grasped by the cognition "this is a cow" appear in that same way in non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition. The only difference is that one [the conceptual] grasps them by not conceptualizing their unity, while the other [the non-conceptual] grasps them by conceptualizing something else. Thus, there is a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*), but not a difference in their appearance (*pratibhāsa*). Therefore, even in non-conceptual cognition, the universal (*sāmānya*) appears.
Thus,
that [objection] is also refuted; for certain similar things appear precisely from their own causes,
and the nature of a universal is dependent upon its manifestations (*vyakti*), yet non-conceptual cognition does not grasp the dependence of a real entity.
