Since it grasps the object through its own independence, how can it be said to grasp a universal (*sāmānya*)? Furthermore, because a recurring form does not appear simultaneously in many [individuals] in the same way that it appears in each one individually, for this very reason, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—grasping a recurring form among things that are entirely distinct yet similar—is erroneous, as it is sublated by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*). Nivi-...

Alternatively, a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) that apprehends a universal (*sāmānya*) as grasped by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would itself be non-valid (*apramāṇa*), because it apprehends what has already been apprehended. If, on the other hand, you argue that it is not "apprehending what has already been apprehended" because it apprehends [the object] through conceptualization, then even memory and the like would not be "apprehending what has already been apprehended," since their objects are things being remembered.

Furthermore, if you claim that conceptual cognition possesses the quality of "apprehending what has not yet been apprehended" because it apprehends an entity qualified by a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, even so—

If the state of being qualified by genus (*jāti*) and so forth were an ultimate property (*pāramārthika-dharma*) of the object, then it would necessarily be apprehended even by non-conceptual [perception]; how then could there be the status of "apprehending what was not previously apprehended"? On the other hand, if it is conceptual, then how can that which apprehends it possess validity (*prāmāṇya*), since its object is superimposed? Therefore, it is established that genus and so forth do not exist at all.
How, then, is it said that entities possess exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)? There is no fault, for this designation is made by way of an imagined property (*kalpitadharma*). Therefore:
"Those who imagine that the universal to be expressed is the exclusion of the non-cow (*agonivṛtti*)," [it is said].

The claim that "by the term 'non-cow' (agopoha), the very entity of cowness (gotva) was clearly expressed by them" has been refuted. He will state later that what is being negated is the ultimately real (pāramārthika) cowness, not the imagined (kalpita) one.
[Objection: If the relationship between property and property-bearer does not exist in an ultimate sense, how then can it be said that "sound is produced and impermanent"?
The distinction between cognitions arises because their object is solely the nature of the word.
[Objection: "If these [cognitions] are indeed without objects, being merely the seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), how can there be comprehension and activity regarding external things?"

Now, if activity proceeds from the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the external object, even so, since the very determination of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is non-different from "impermanence" (*anityatva*), how can there be a difference in cognition? [The opponent argues: Since "the produced" and "the impermanent" are non-different, there is no real difference in cognition because there is an absence of a difference in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of those [two]. To this, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "yasmāt": because all things are excluded from everything else, therefore, those [cognitions] are based upon that from which objects such as sound and so forth are excluded—namely, from the permanent, the unproduced, and so on. They are based upon those limits of exclusion (*vyāvṛttyavadhi*).
Therefore, [the verse states]: "(those [cognitions] are based upon that from which objects are excluded)."
Distinctions of genus are conceptualized as those which penetrate into its specific differences. ||43||

The distinctions of properties, such as impermanence, being produced, and so forth, are conceptualized—that is, they are superimposed by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)—as being based on the functional mode (*vṛtti*). What are they characterized as? They are "those which penetrate its specific features. This means they are those which penetrate the specific features of that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), whose nature consists in the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of what is unproduced and so forth; their habit is to penetrate these, meaning their habit is to manifest them as non-different [from the particular].

This is what is meant: by means of this gateway—"it is not unproduced"—the latent impression (*vāsanā*) for the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of "produced" is awakened; it is precisely the nature of that [impression] that, when a conceptual construction arises from it as "produced," it apprehends the specific individual characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound as excluded from the non-produced, being non-different from its own form, but not as "impermanent. Likewise, [it does not apprehend it] as "permanent."
Even by this door [of the statement] "it does not exist," it is the power of the very impression of impermanence (*anityavāsanā*) that has been awakened which functions;

thus, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from it apprehends the specific characteristic of the word (*śabdasvalakṣaṇa*) as being non-different from its own form and as excluded from the permanent, but not as "produced" (*kṛtaka*). Therefore, there is a difference in cognition. And because it is sublated, [the conceptual construction is]—

An external object does not exist as the referent of speech; therefore, the appearance of an external object occurs solely through the power of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and it is that very conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which is called the "own-form" (*svākāra*), because the object appearing as an external form is [in fact] its own form. It is not, however, a superimposition of externality upon the own-form due to similarity. As it is said in the *Nāmanimittaprakaraṇa*: (1)
If it is argued that the occurrence [of cognition] with respect to an object is due to similarity and error, it would not occur at all times; furthermore,
there is no error regarding place in cognition,
because consciousness arises in such a way as to manifest an external object.

By this, it is said: (1) "When there is the apprehension of a form that is absolutely dissimilar to an external object as being of that same nature, that refers to a similarity produced by the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*). For example, although a cloth is dissimilar to a jar, when it is determined as being qualified by the absence of trees, it is determined as being similar to a jar in the sense of 'not a tree,' because the exclusion of trees is common to both the jar and the cloth."

The object of conceptual construction is entirely dissimilar even to that which is similar; it is nevertheless apprehended as similar because of the grasping of a resemblance produced by the exclusion of others.
(1) Likewise:

That is rejected, because the conceptual cognition appearing as an external object arises from its own causes alone. Nor is similarity produced among dissimilar things by means of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because in that case, such exclusion would be ineffective in producing either difference, non-difference, or similarity.
Furthermore, no similarity exists within the exclusion of others itself. How, then, could similarity be produced even among similar things by means of the exclusion of others?

Because there is similarity by way of its very own nature (*svarūpa*). Nor does it appear that first there is the manifestation of its own form, and subsequently there is the superimposition (*bāhyāropa*) of the external, which is intent upon grasping a similarity produced by the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) therein. For, if the own-form had not previously manifested in the case of a mirage, the superimposition of water caused by the grasping of similarity would not be possible; and prior to the superimposition of the external, there is no [manifestation] of its own form.

There is no superimposition of an object of apprehension, because conceptual construction itself does not exist. Even if it were to exist, it would be of the singular nature of pure awareness and thus not similar to an external object.

Consequently, since there is an absence of similarity produced by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), how could it be perceived as having an external form? Furthermore, the operation of inference does not presuppose the grasping of the exclusion of others, because the logical mark (*liṅga*) is established through its connection with that [exclusion]. And when—

When the penetration of the specific features of that [object] by conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) is perceived, then activity occurs precisely through the form of affirmation (*vidhi*), because there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the nature of the thing as being affirmed; thus, by implication, the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) is understood. Therefore, for us as well, the meaning of a word is indeed affirmation; and the connection with both affirmation and negation belongs to that which is superimposed as being external.

But surely, conceptual cognition (vikalpa) appears as grasping a determinate form; therefore, by conceptualizing [an object] as devoid of any other form, it conceptualizes a specific object. Consequently, since the determination of a determinate form has the exclusion of others (anyanivṛtti) as its object, how can it be said that the word-meaning is purely a positive injunction (vidhi)?

That is incorrect, because there is no cognition [of the form] "I am conceptualizing the exclusion of another. Furthermore, that which does not appear as being conceptualized cannot be the object of a conceptualization. If one were to conceptualize a specific object while conceptualizing only the exclusion of other forms, there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): for the other form would also have to be a specific form by way of the exclusion of another.

Because it would follow that this is merely a [positive] practice (*pratipatti*). Now, if one conceptualizes the form of the other by way of a positive injunction (*vidhirūpeṇa*), then the determination of a specific form is not preceded by the ascertainment of the exclusion of others.
Furthermore, as in the case of "I see an object possessing a universal," there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified between the universal and its possessor.

*Pratibhāsa*: (1) Furthermore, just as the Naiyāyikas and others have postulated the perception of an individual qualified by a universal (*sāmānya*) in accordance with specific cognitions (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*), so too do others postulate "exclusion" (*nivṛtti*). Even though there is no such [direct] cognition, since the superimposition of something external and similar [to it] would otherwise be inexplicable, the form of the external object is superimposed upon the aspect of the conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*) for the sake of excluding other things.
This is logical, because a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone, even in the absence of similarity, having determined an external form.

As it has been said: "Its nature is such that it originates from the latent impression deposited by the experience of that [object], and its essential character is the determination of that [external] state; likewise, the nature of the latent impression of conceptualization is such that it appears in this way."

Nor can a cognition that superimposes an external form have as its object the exclusion of others, even if its cause is a similarity produced by the cognition of something else. For instance, the cognition of water in a mirage does not have similarity as its object, because its object is the superimposed water. Furthermore, the fixed nature of entities is not produced by the exclusion of others; for that [exclusion], being a non-entity, lacks any form.
Because it is produced from its own causes alone,
and because there is no determination of a restricted form that has the exclusion of others as its object, since this [perception] has a restricted form as its object;
for this very reason, it is not apprehended by perception itself as being preceded by the exclusion of others.

Furthermore, he will state that it is not logical for the exclusion of "that" to be a distinct entity. Nor is it logical for it to be inexpressible in terms of identity or difference; for if it were so, it would be a mere non-entity like a rabbit's horn.

Moreover, it could not be accessible through direct perception because it lacks any form. Nor could it be accessible through inference, because a logical mark (*liṅga*) cannot be established due to the absence of a relationship.
Therefore, whatever specific property is perceived by means of one [cognition], it cannot be [perceived] by another; thus, the establishment [of objects] is distinct. (44)

Nor can there be a conceptualization of that [exclusion] based on the impossibility of its having a restricted form otherwise; for there is no absence of exclusion from others in the case of things whose forms are not restricted.

And as for those things whose forms are restricted, how could their state of having a restricted form arise through the exclusion of others? This is because they arise with restricted forms from their own causes alone.
Therefore, the exclusion of others is perceived only as preceded by the determination of a restricted form. For instance, when "pot" is said, [the non-pot is excluded].
"It does not exist" is understood by implication; therefore, this [negation] is merely constructed through conceptualization and does not exist in the ultimate sense.
Consequently, it is established that while a real entity is presented in a positive form by means of words and logical marks, the negation of other things follows by implication (*arthāt*).
As he will state: "The exclusion of others is understood from those very words [denoting the object]" (1.128), and so forth.
Therefore, as for that which was stated by Kumārila:
“However, on your position, it has not been described that a word effects the exclusion of others; for here, nothing is understood from the negation itself, other than a mere mental appearance.”
However, from words such as "cow," "gavaya," "elephant," and "tree," verbal cognition proceeds by determining them in a positive form.

"Therefore, only in those words where there is a connection with the negative particle (*nañ*) does the exclusion of another (*anyanivṛtti*) become a subordinate factor; it is understood elsewhere as its own self.
(1) This, which is already established, is here proven, because the meaning of a word is accepted even as having a positive form (*vidhirūpa*). How then [is this different] from the view of others?
(1) What is the internal division of the Buddhist doctrine? Or how is it said that the object of both word and logical mark is *apoha*?

Surely there is indeed a great difference [between us], since for our opponents conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) is held to have an ultimate reality as its object, whereas for the Buddhists it is held to have a mentally constructed (*kalpita*) object. Furthermore, a constructed form is called "exclusion" (*apoha*) because it is based upon exclusion, or because it is that by which [other things] are excluded. Alternatively, mere negation of others (*anyanivṛtti-mātra*), being implied by the sense of the object, is called "exclusion" (*apoha*). (1)
However, it is called "exclusion" (*apoha*) because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is excluded therein.
Therefore, in dependence upon various objects that are mutually differentiated, properties whose distinctions are conceptually constructed are made the objects of conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*).
Consequently, conceptual cognitions have distinct objects, and words that share those same objects are also not synonyms.

To demonstrate this, he says: "Therefore," and so forth. Since the various properties (*dharma*) are thus conceptualized, therefore that specific particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇaviśeṣa*) which is established in dependence upon the eternal as that which is to be excluded is the characteristic of the non-eternal (*anityalakṣaṇa*). By which property, by which word—just as by the word "non-eternal. The word itself is also called a "property" because it denotes a property. It is not...

It can be distinguished by another [term]: by a term such as "produced" (*kṛtaka*), which is other than the word "impermanent," through the addition of another object to be excluded. Therefore, the determination is distinct. For that reason, there is no single [referent] for conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
*Slokavārttika* 4. *Sāmānyacintā* (Investigation of Universals) 1.208–209.

For all entities indeed abide in their own nature and do not mix themselves with another, because that would entail the consequence of [the entity] being non-other. That form which is non-different and constitutes their very self is not [identical to] those [entities], because at that time the entities are absent;
for it would be that alone, since there exists only the non-different.
Because there is no existence of the undifferentiated; because there is no existence of a differentiated [entity] for that which has not been apprehended;
and because differentiation is contradictory to that very [undifferentiated entity]. Furthermore, that which is established in its own nature is precisely unmixed.
This is the state of being an object. And thus, words are not synonyms.

Therefore, what was stated—that (1) there is no relationship of the cognized and the cognizer between two things that possess identity (*tādātmya*), and that there is no connection between two conceptualized forms (*vikalpitarūpa*) that stand in the relationship of the cognized and the cognizer—is refuted; for it is precisely the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as excluded from the non-produced (*akṛtaka*) that falls within the scope of the indicative reason (*jñāpakahetu*). [The term] "produced" (*kṛtaka*)...

Because that which is known possesses the capacity for signification (*gamakatva*), and because that [known object] consists of a reality that is eternally excluded [from others], there is identity (*tādātmya*).

With the words "For all... and so forth, the author states the meaning of the verse while refuting Advaitavāda. Those things whose stability is in their own nature (*svarūpa*)—that is, within themselves—are "so [stabilized]. For indeed, all entities are stable in their own nature and do not mix themselves with another.
They make them one. What is the reason? Because that which is being mixed would result in the status of being other than itself; that is, it would incur the state of being the self.
This might be the thought:
"And with respect to all things, cognition arises as having both an exclusive and an inclusive nature;
and that [cognition] would not be possible without a dual nature.
(1) Therefore, particulars have a universal nature and universals have a particular nature; thus, an entity possesses a dual form.

In this case as well, there must be either (1) the non-difference of a single form from distinct things, or the non-difference of a distinct thing from a single [form]. To refute the first position, he says: "Of those"—it is impossible to say that the form, which is non-distinct, meaning of one essence or not separate, belongs to those entities. Why? Because at that time, the expectation arises: "To what does it belong? (45a)

Because that non-different form does not exist for them, precisely due to its non-difference. Now, if there were non-difference [of those things] from a single [form] that is different [from them], he says regarding that as well: "For that very [single form] would be [the nature] of the non-different, because it exists. If the form is one, then the absence of difference [among them] is established; that very same non-different form would belong to them, not a different one. Why is this so? Because of that—
Because there exists a nature that is non-different [from them].

Now, it might be argued: "Their difference is indeed admitted. To this, he says: "Therefore, because there is no other entity distinct from that non-different self which possesses a differentiated and manifold nature."
Now, it might be argued: (1) "The very distinction that belongs to the particular is itself the non-distinction of the universal. As it has been said:

"But for one who asserts a distinction within the universal, [that distinction] must be demonstrated through its particulars and accepted as such. To this, he replies: "Furthermore, because distinction is contradictory to that very [universal]; for it is impossible for that single entity to possess multiplicity."

Now, it might be argued: (1) the distinction of the universal occurs through its specific features (*viśeṣa*) and not by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*). In that case, [the universal] would be neither inclusive (*anugata*) nor exclusive (*vyāvṛtta*). Furthermore, even if it were a different entity (*arthāntara*), it could not be the universal of those [particulars] because it inheres in many of them; for it is not of their nature. This would lead to the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even dualities (*dvitva*) and other such qualities, as well as effect-substances (*kāryadravya*), would be universals. Moreover, things that are not identical with one another are not made identical merely by another related thing; rather, they remain distinct while simply possessing that [relation].

Because two forms cannot be conjoined with one another, there would necessarily be a difference between them. Thus it is said: (1) And that [form] is of a single nature, established within itself in its own essence as something entirely unmixed in its manifest form; and when that which is unmixed is perceived as having a mixed nature, it is nothing but falsity.
Now, if it is argued that this [cognition] is not false because the universal is somehow non-different from the individual, he says:
"This is not so, because superimposition and the like are impossible for cognitions such as 'horse' and so forth;
for the difference of the genus and so on from the individual is certainly not established."

That is incorrect: (1) because it is contradictory for that very form by which [an object] is distinct to be non-distinct from it; furthermore, difference and non-difference do not appear together in a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Moreover, if non-difference is apprehended by one [cognition] while difference is apprehended by another, how could the cognition apprehending [the latter] not be erroneous? For it would be apprehending [the object] otherwise, and yet the object possesses a single nature.

Alternatively, due to the very fact of non-mixture, a single form could not possess the nature of a universal, because it would be a distinct entity, like a jar. However, Uddyotakara says: "The cognition of recurrence in cows and the like must have as its cause something distinct from the individual bodies and so forth, because it is a specific [cognition], like the cognition of blue and the like. And that cause [is the universal], because it produces uniform cognitions."

"It is called a universal. Regarding this as well, it is not the case that a commonality of form is produced for things that are already similar by means of some distinct entity, because they are already established as such. Showing this, he says: "A distinct entity" refers to existence (*sattā*), cowness (*gotva*), and so forth; these do not [produce] those [similarities].

The universal belongs to the individual instances because it does not possess their specific form; for those instances are of a dissimilar nature, and the state of being similar is what is intended by the term "universal."

Alternatively, [the universal] is distinct from individuals because it does not possess their form, just as unity is. Now, if you argue that even though it is a distinct entity, it is the universal of those [individuals] because it inheres in many, then the same consequence would apply to duality and other effect-substances; for duality also inheres in multiple substances.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), plurality and the like are also included. Likewise, conjunction also inheres in multiple substances.

Furthermore, since a product-substance (kāryadravya), designated as a whole (avayavin), inheres in its constituent substances (ārambhakadravya), it follows that [this substance] would entail the status of being a universal (sāmānyarūpatā) with respect to duality and so forth. To this, he says: "That alone is a universal in which, when another entity exists, the particulars become similar, and not everything. He replies: "No; because by another related entity characterized by oneness, others—"

They are neither identical nor different; they are not identical because they do not occupy a single location, since they function as distinct, non-distinct, and identical entities. Furthermore, because they appear in different locations and so forth, how could they be identical? At most, these particulars (*bhedāḥ*) would merely possess that [quality], meaning they would possess a single attribute. As for the elements, the planets, and the constellations, there is a long quality (*guṇa*) upon their necks—

The elements (bhūtas) would be like a quality (guṇa) in the throat; they would not have a common object of cognition, just as the elements [do not]. Thus, the intellect (buddhi), while constructing its own self, appears to have a universal (sāmānya) as its object. It is not as if there were two things related to a single entity, as in the case of the elements. This is stated for the sake of worship: by means of that single quality in the throat, the elements possess it, yet they do not become one.
The same applies to the individuals as well. [Objection:

But surely, since a quality possesses corporeality (*mūrttatva*), it is appropriate to perceive it as possessing that [quality]; however, this is not the case for universals in individuals, because a universal lacks corporeality. [Response: No, because we accept that [the universal] is inherent (*samaveta*) in them, and because it exists as a distinct entity (*arthāntarabhāva*). And since—

Even when there is a connection with something else, individual instances (*vyakti*) are not identical; for that very reason, they are not the objects of a non-different cognition, nor are they the objects of a single-formed (*ekākāra*) non-erroneous cognition. This is because they exist as such [distinctly]. Just as the elements (*bhūta*), which possess natures devoid of [specific] qualities, are not the objects of a cognition having the form of a single quality—so it is here. Thus, even when connected with many things, a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) is not their universal (*sāmānya*).

It is established that [otherwise] there would be the consequence of [the universal being] duality and so forth; and yet, they are perceived as identical. Therefore, it is precisely the nature of those two differences, their very essence, which the intellect—unifying them through its own internal aspect by thinking "this pair is of a single form"—manifests as having a common object, namely the universal. It does not manifest as "two things related to one" merely because they are connected to a single universal.

The cognition does not appear in such a way that "these two are possessed of this [universal]," whereby a universal as a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) would be established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The phrase "like the elements" (*bhūtavat*) is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); the meaning is that it is not like the case where cognition grasps the elements as being connected by a single quality.

Or rather, it might be argued that the cognition whose object is the universal appears in such a way that, just as the individual entities are related to a single [universal], so too the two distinct [individuals] are related to a single [universal]; but this is not the case.
Now, it might be thought: (1) the universal is indeed the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the individuals, and a qualifier [conveys its own]... in the particular.
Because it produces the cognition of redness, it does not appear to this [cognition] as a separate entity from the individuals.

Now, even if it is a qualifier, it cannot be identical with the qualified object, just as a staff is not identical with the staff-bearer; so how can there be an appearance of non-difference? Since they are one even in their aspect of non-difference, the relationship of qualifier and qualified does not exist.

Therefore, the cognition of non-difference between the universal and the individual is indeed an error. If it is argued that this is not an error because such a cognition occurs at all times, he says:
"That which is perceived as having one form and is then perceived otherwise is false; however, that which is always understood by means of itself [is not false]"—this is incorrect.
For [if that were so], it would follow that the universal is non-different from the individual. This is because there is a difference in cognition, such as "this is a cow" versus "cowness."
And because of [your] own admission. Furthermore, the cognition of a relation between a universal and its possessor is not non-erroneous in the manner of lac and crystal;
for the cognition of a crystal that is not red as being red due to lac is erroneous. Thus, there would be oneness of the universal and its possessor.
If it is argued that this [cognition] is an error for one who perceives that [universal], then from what does the perception of that [universal] arise?
If it is argued that an error cannot be without a seed (cause), then those very things which produce that single effect are the seed of the error.

This is because [the universal] is absent even in cases such as number, conjunction, and substances that are effects, since they are real entities. Therefore, because it is not situated in a universal in that manner, there is no other [entity called] a "universal."

Or, because it too abides in its own self, there is no mixing with anything else. Therefore, these entities are not grasped as belonging to the same class; rather, it is an error that the intellect perceives only the universal (*sāmānya*). If it is argued that this error—namely, the apprehension of individuals as non-different from the universal—occurs because the inherence (*samavāya*) linking the intellect to that [universal] is subtle, then [the response is: for one who sees that...

Thus, from where [does this follow]? (1) From what source is there certainty that this cognition perceives an ultimate universal? Because it always has as its object the non-difference from the individual instance (*vyakti*). It is "seedless" because it lacks a seed; and thus it would be an error, since that [lack of a seed] is impossible. For an error arising without a cause is not tenable—[as seen in the case of] errors regarding water and so forth.
[Objection: This error, which combines even entities that are not combined, must therefore have a cause;

that which is its cause is the universal (*sāmānya*). [Response: To this he says: "Those very particulars themselves, which produce a single effect such as the cognition of that universal—they, being the cause of that single effect, are the seed of the error. And this will be demonstrated later.
Furthermore, it is not tenable that a uniform error regarding individuals occurs through the superimposition of a universal upon what has been perceived;

for (1) resemblance is a cause of error, yet a universal is absolutely distinct from individuals, since the universal lacks the form of color and configuration while individuals possess the form of color and configuration.

Now, it might be argued: (1) "The superimposition upon particulars is not caused by similarity; rather, even among things that are absolutely distinct, there is an error consisting in the determination of identity—'this is that very same thing'—which cannot occur without a single form. We reply: if this were so, then simply because they share a single related entity, even in the absence of any cause for error, the objects of an error regarding a single form would [arise].

[They] exist. Then, in those elements (*bhūta*) which possess number, conjunction, the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), and—by the word "etcetera"—disjunction and so forth, and which are endowed with a single quality, there would be an illusion of a single form; yet it does not occur. Therefore, even for individuals (*vyakti*), the illusion is not caused by oneness. "That" means for that reason.

Just as a universal is intended to be distinct from individuals, so too, because it does not enter into the cognition of the universal and because it does not appear [therein], there is no other universal. Or, even if a universal existed, that universal would abide in its own self—that is, in its own intrinsic nature—and thus it would not be mixed with anything else in the form of an individual. This is because it does not abide within individuals.

The meaning is that its nature consists of the dharma itself. Therefore, because of the establishment of their own intrinsic natures (*svasvabhāvavyavasthānāt*), these entities—such as pots and so forth—are distinct and separate from what is considered similar by virtue of having an identical form, and from what is considered different, namely those of a dissimilar class; this is because they possess a single form by way of their own nature and primordial essence (*prakṛtyā*). This is due to the establishment of their own intrinsic natures.
...up to ...
He states the meaning of the second verse: "Since those entities are distinct from this or that [other thing], their distinction is *tadbheda* (distinction from that).

Therefore, for the purpose of communicating those distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), a word is applied with a specific arrangement to indicate each distinct nature. This is the investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*).
[These natures] are excluded from what is intended and from other things as well, because by their very nature they possess a single form.

From whatever [particular] things they are differentiated, the word—having been applied for the purpose of conveying that differentiation—takes up those various differentiations and causes objects possessing manifold properties to be cognized as non-different even though they are distinct. Although those words do not imply all possible differentiations, because they enjoin only one particular differentiation, they nonetheless terminate in the specific individual (*svalakṣaṇa*). Thus, even from a single [word], there is a differentiation of that [object].
Thus it is said.

Therefore, for a single entity, there are as many exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) as there are forms of other things, in relation to those [other things]. This is because that [entity] is distinct from them due to its not being the cause or effect of what is impossible in them. And as many as are the exclusions, so many are the verbal expressions;

by means of words—acting as instruments—that have established conventions based on non-common effects, entities possessing multiple properties, such as the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), are cognized as having specific natures.

Even though there is differentiation, for a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) there is no plurality of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). How then can it possess multiple properties? To this he says: "By taking its differentiation from this and that" (1). That is to say, by relying upon and taking as a basis its differentiation from whatever [other things] it is excluded from; those words which have been established by convention to manifest each of those various differentiations—that is, each distinct intrinsic nature—are applied to it.

Since their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are distinct, words are restricted to being denoters [of those specific natures]. Therefore, no single word denotes all distinct intrinsic natures; nor do those words, even though each one does not denote all distinctions, denote a single distinct intrinsic nature when they express one particular distinction. Consequently, they are based precisely upon that specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), the intrinsic nature of which is expressed. The intrinsic nature of which [particular]—
That which is determined by the word as distinct from other things—that is both [the conceptual object] and the particular (svalakṣaṇa). They are established in that very thing;
they have that alone as their object.
But surely, the object appearing in the word, which is determined as being external, is one thing—namely, the universal (sādhāraṇa)—and the particular is another?

Regarding the question, "How can that [conceptual cognition] have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object? he says: Since an object is made the referent of a word by being excluded from even a single thing—whether it be that which is not its cause or that which is not its effect—there exists a differentiation of that particular characteristic, which is itself differentiated from many [other things]. Therefore, those [cognitions] are said to have that [particular characteristic] as their object, but they do not have it as their object exclusively. Or rather, of that...

The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property that serves as the basis for exclusion is precisely what those [cognitions] are established upon; they culminate in the attainment of that very [characteristic]. What is the reason? It has already been explained that there is a distinction of that [object] even from a single instance of it.
Concluding, he says: "Therefore. Because exclusion from both the similar and the dissimilar—

Therefore, for a single entity, there are as many exclusions from other forms as there are those other forms; these are conceptualized as distinct properties (*dharmabheda*) in relation to those other forms. They are so called because "by means of these, the dissimilar is excluded.
Why is this? Because, with respect to that excluded object—the substratum (*dharmin*) which serves as the limit—there is no occurrence of its effect or its cause [within that dissimilar thing].

That [property] belongs to the intended subject because it is the effect or cause of that which is impossible for it; this is due to its exclusion from what is not its effect and what is not its cause. As many as there are exclusions, so many are the verbal expressions (śrutis) employed for the sake of conventional usage by way of excluding other causes. For example, sound is "produced immediately after effort," "audible," and "not its own effect."
This is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of being a non-reason (*akāraṇa*).

Therefore, even though there is no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) or differentiation that is perceived by the subject through its name cannot be perceived by anything other than that; thus, all words do not have the same referent. Consequently, the reason is not a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) in this manner.

How is it that this very exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is conveyed by word and logical mark (*liṅga*) through affirmation (*vidhi*), and not the actual form of the thing? [The answer is: For the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), [words] function by excluding what does not have that effect or cause. That which has the intended effect or cause is "that-effect-cause" (*tatkāryakāraṇa*). For example, sound has auditory cognition as its effect and effort as its cause; that which is not so [is excluded].

It becomes that which does not have those [qualities] as its cause; the analysis of the compound is: "those whose purpose (artha) is practical activity (vyavahāra)—characterized by engagement and withdrawal—is for the sake of worldly transaction.

He states the object: that which has effort as its cause is called "immediately following from effort" (*prayatnānantarīyaka*). By that, it is not [the case that] those... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the definition of sound as non-eternal, specifically discussing the *prayatnānantarīyakatva* argument. The translation reflects the available portion.)

The term "produced by effort" (*prayatnānantarīyaka*) is intended to exclude [sounds] such as lightning, which have causes other than effort. The term "audible" (*śrāvaṇa*)—meaning that whose effect is auditory cognition—is intended to exclude sounds that do not have that as their effect. Furthermore, because all conventional transactions (*vyavahāra*) are based on causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and because causal efficiency is characterized by the relationship between cause and effect, this applies even to words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*).
The exclusion of that which is its effect and that which is not its cause should be applied.

With the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth, he explains the third verse. Because distinct exclusions (*vyāvṛtti-bheda*) and verbal expressions (*śruti*) are each restricted to their own respective distinctions, therefore—even though there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this subject (*dharmin*)—the "difference" (*bheda*) characterized by being produced (*kṛtaka*) and so forth, which is the meaning of the phrase "whatever distinction," [is established]. The explanation of the word "subject" (*dharmiṇaḥ*) is "by name" (*nāmnā*), which means "by the word" (*śabdena*).

A property (*dharma*) is perceived as being conceptually constructed; it cannot be [perceived] by anything other than that. Therefore, it cannot be made known by a word such as "impermanent" that is different from the intended word such as "produced. Consequently, the reason is not a part of the meaning of the thesis, because the words "impermanent" and "produced" have distinct meanings.

"How so? and so forth begins the opponent's [objection]. "By word and by mark" (śabdaśca liṅgaśca tābhyām). Although the mark (liṅga) is the subject under discussion here, the mention of the word (śabda) is for the purpose of demonstrating that, like the mark, it lacks a real object; by this, the authority of the Veda is refuted.

Now, it has been stated that an object is communicated by a word or a logical mark (*liṅga*) in a positive form; so how can this doubt be raised—that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is what is communicated—and how is this understood?
This is not the case. "Exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*) is that by which something is excluded; it is simply the mental aspect (*ākāra*) superimposed as having an external form.

It is said: By that [word], it is precisely that [exclusion] which is conveyed by means of the word and the logical mark (*liṅga*) through the operation of injunction (*vidhi*), and not the nature of the real entity (*vastu-rūpa*). How is this known? Or rather, "exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*) is so called because things are excluded therein; it refers to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). That alone is what is apprehended, because other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not operate [upon it]. For instance:
When a single object-entity is itself directly perceived, what other unperceived part could there be that would need to be examined by means of other instruments of knowledge? (45)

For the nature of an object is one; it is directly perceived. Since proof is impossible regarding properties that are not established, as for example when "sound" is the subject in the proof of its being "eternal," there is an establishment of all its aspects simply through that direct perception, because there is no other part of it that remains unestablished. If such a part were to exist, it would follow that it does not possess the nature of that very object.

For it is not logical that what shares a common destiny (*ekayogakṣema*) with something else should not be of the same nature as it. How is it understood that [the object] is presented and determined through a positive formulation (*vidhi*)— by means of words and logical marks (*liṅga*) based solely on that [commonality]— and that the actual form of the thing, characterized by a relationship between ultimate property and property-bearer (*dharma-dharmin*), is not being presented?

The response beginning with "of another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntarasya*) and so forth has this meaning: if the relationship between property and property-bearer (*dharma-dharmin-bhāva*) were ultimately real and entirely non-distinct, then, because the object would be fully delimited by a single means of valid cognition or by a word once it had been apprehended, there would be no further application of another means of valid cognition or another word, as that would merely involve the grasping of what has already been grasped (*gṛhītagrāhitva*).

Because of its validity. Furthermore, since activity proceeds from other words and so forth, the relationship between property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) is indeed merely conceptual (*kalpita*). Although the conceptual nature of the relationship between property and property-bearer has already been established by the refutation of the previous [real] universal (*sāmānya*), there is no fault here, as it is established once again by this author through a different method. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "For instance," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of one": since the nature of an object—the reality of the thing itself—is partless and devoid of any distinction between property and possessor of properties, and since it exists as something directly perceived by its own very form, what other unperceived portion could there be? What other nature, distinct from the nature already seen through direct perception, could there be that would need to be examined by means of instruments of knowledge known as inference? [This is not so] because of the difference between individuals.
The plural form [is used] because the whole is indeed perceived, since an entity is partless; therefore, it should not be examined by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The passage beginning with "one" is the explanation: for the single nature of an object is partless, and that must first be admitted as being directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) where inference (*anumāna*) operates. What is the reason? Because a proof (*sādhana*) is impossible when the subject (*dharmin*) has not been previously established by a means of valid cognition.
Since the logical mark is impossible due to the unestablished nature of its locus, there must therefore be a well-known subject (dharmin).

This is what is meant: there would not even be the operation of the mark (*liṅga*) itself, let alone the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the ascertainment of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*). For example, when "impermanence" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), sound is established by perception;

because its own nature is established by the very means of valid cognition that is perception, it follows that all its aspects are established. Why? Because anything other than that [sound] remains unestablished.

Because there is no nature other than the nature of sound that is unestablished; or, if such an unestablished nature were to exist, it would follow that it is not of that nature—that is, it would not have the nature of sound—because of the contradiction between being established and unestablished having a single nature. He says this very thing with the words "For not," and so forth. Yoga is the persistence of a property not yet acquired; kṣema is the persistence of a property already acquired.

"One who has a single *yoga* and *kṣema* is thus [described]; that is to say, one whose properties are identical. That intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) which does not always share the same *yoga* and *kṣema* with something else is one of "different *yoga* and *kṣema*" (*bhinnayogakṣema*). Because its intrinsic nature is such that it possesses different *yoga* and *kṣema*, [it is distinct]."
"Because the conventional usage of difference [arises] from that [cognition], otherwise there would be the consequence of non-existence; thus it has been stated. Therefore, in perception..."
Because the subject is determined in its entirety as having that nature, there is no scope for the operation of another means of valid cognition.

If another quality were not joined [to it] by means of a cause of error—just as the form of silver is [superimposed] upon mother-of-pearl due to the perception of a similarity in appearance—[then there would be no error]. (46)

An intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not tenable; for the linguistic convention of difference is based solely on that [exclusion], and it is through this that the distinction of the system is established.

"Otherwise" means that if this cause of differentiation is not accepted, then—as was stated in the context of the discussion regarding "this indeed is the cause of difference and non-difference"—it would follow that the linguistic convention of non-difference would be impossible. Therefore, in the case of a perceptible subject (*dharmin*) such as sound and so forth...

Because of the complete determination of its intrinsic nature; that is, because the intrinsic nature of the subject (*dharmin*) is understood in its entirety, there is no scope for the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as inference, regarding that subject, as it would be devoid of an object.

If it is argued that the same fault applies to you as well, he says: "(1) No," and so forth. By means of a cause for error—such as the arising of a similar subsequent [moment]—another quality, such as stability, would be joined with or superimposed by a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*). The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "just as" (*iva*); just as the form of silver is superimposed upon mother-of-pearl, how could [stability] be joined to silver?

Regarding the similarity (*sādharmya*) between the form of a mother-of-pearl shell and [the form of silver], such as their whiteness and so forth— it is because of the perception of that [similarity] that the very form of the mother-of-pearl shell, when its specific qualities are not determined, is called "similarity of form" (*rūpasādharmya*), since it is the basis for a cognition of resemblance. However, there is no such thing as "similarity" existing as a common property (*sādhāraṇa*) belonging to both.

This is what is meant: if another quality were not superimposed by means of a cause of error, then even my position would be subject to the same fault; however, it is indeed superimposed. Therefore, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates for the purpose of excluding that superimposition. Consequently, regarding an object already experienced and ascertained, another means of valid cognition would not operate because it would be grasping what has already been grasped (*gṛhītagrāhitva*), due to the presence of superimposition.
Some maintain that, once an object has been experienced but not yet ascertained, another means of valid cognition—inference—proceeds for the purpose of excluding superimpositions upon that object.

This is incorrect, because the logical mark (liṅga) lacks an established connection with such exclusion. Furthermore, as long as the exclusion of the opposing position is not effected by the reason, the cognition of the probandum would remain doubtful, since the reason is connected with the probandum.

And where there is no probandum, there its opposite cannot exist due to contradiction. Therefore, the logical mark (liṅga), while ascertaining its own pervader in a positive form, by implication negates the superimposition of anything else.

[Objection: Even so, how can there be a negation of that [non-momentary nature], since even when the inference of momentariness has occurred, there is still the superimposition of non-momentariness? [Reply: True. However, once the negation of the object "non-momentary" has been effected by means of inference, it is demonstrated that this cognition with the form of non-momentariness is not produced by that [object], but rather is superimposed due to the production of a similar subsequent [moment]. Therefore...

Inference for the sake of ascertainment proceeds regarding that very object which has been experienced and ascertained, such as its momentariness. Even in cases where there is no superimposition of the contrary—and where, due to the absence of repeated practice and so forth, the experience is not capable of producing ascertainment—there too, the operation of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) results in ascertainment; for by the ascertainment of one aspect, it is ascertained in its entirety. And it is not the case that...
That object appears whose own nature is not determined in any way; therefore, even in that case,
regarding the investigation of the universal (sāmānyacintā),
if there were an obstruction to certainty— just as the form of silver [appears] even in mother-of-pearl whose entire true nature has been perceived— then [the universal would be established].

By means of a non-delusory cause, another quality would not be superimposed. For it is not possible for both a common and a specific form to exist simultaneously in a mother-of-pearl shell; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence [of such a confusion] occurring at all times. Alternatively, if there were no cognition [of the distinction], the conceptualization of duality through discrimination would be impossible, and this would lead to an over-extension [of the principle].

One who perceives the form of mother-of-pearl perceives it as something specifically qualified. Because of the commonality with a determinate cognition (*niścaya-pratyaya*), when a non-determinate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has proceeded, there would necessarily be no proceeding of another [cognition].
This is the explanation beginning with the word "yadi. The analysis of the compound is: that whose entire reality (*tattva*)—that is, its own nature (*svarūpa*)—has been seen. Likewise...

By a cause of error characterized by the production of a subsequent [cognition] similar [to the first], which obstructs certainty and hinders the determination of things as they are perceived—such as the stability of other qualities—it would not be joined; it would not be superimposed. Just as, even when mother-of-pearl is perceived in its specific form, the form of silver might be superimposed due to its similarity with white [objects]. At that time...
There would be no room for the operation of another means of valid cognition.

(1) It might be thought: "It is not that there is a superimposition of silver upon the mother-of-pearl due to the perception of a specific form; rather, because one perceives a universal form belonging to silver, there is this determination. To this, he says: "Not indeed" (na hi). For two forms cannot possibly exist in the mother-of-pearl.

The form is identical to that of silver, yet another [form] is distinguished, and there is a restriction. What is the reason? Because otherwise, there would always be the consequence of a cognition appearing as variegated (*śabalābhāsā*) by way of both universal and particular forms. Or, regarding non-cognition:

"by way of distinction" means that if there were no cognition through such a distinction or separation—namely, "this is the universal" and "this is the particular"—then the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of duality would be impossible.

For it is illogical to conceive that there are two forms in the mother-of-pearl; for if one were to conceive duality without a difference in appearance, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), whereby one might as well conceive duality even in other things intended to be singular. Furthermore, it would entail the non-arising of the sublating cognition, "This is not silver. Therefore, because two forms are impossible in the mother-of-pearl...
Seeing the form of mother-of-pearl, a person sees only its specific unique particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*), not a universal (*sāmānya*).
Because the conditions for certainty—such as repeated practice and so forth—are absent, he fails to ascertain it;
nevertheless, seeing that specific form of mother-of-pearl, he thinks, "I am seeing its universal, namely the universal of the form of silver. From that [arises] "silver"—

The superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl occurs for the observer due to the conceit of grasping a commonality of form. Alternatively, one thinks, "I perceive that which is the common, identical form of both the mother-of-pearl and the silver"; thus, from the perception of that form, the superimposition of silver arises for this observer. For indeed, the very same form of silver as was previously apprehended by me is perceived in this [mother-of-pearl] as well.

Therefore, the cognition "this is that very same silver" arises from form [alone]. Just as there is the superimposition of silver upon a mother-of-pearl shell, so too, with respect to a perceived substratum such as sound, due to the arising of successive similar moments— specifically, the arising of a second moment similar to the first— there occurs a superimposition of existence (*sattā-samāropa*) by a person who, because of the cause of delusion, fails to perceive the difference between the preceding and succeeding moments, and thus superimposes that state [of silver] upon them.

One thinks, "Indeed, I see that universal. Consequently, there arises for him the superimposition of silver; because the difference [between the two] is not perceived due to the production of similar subsequent moments, there is the delusion of stability through the superimposition of that state. As many as are its extrinsic states...

Since there are exactly as many superimpositions as there are things arising from their respective causes, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) serve to exclude them and thus become fruitful. However, for those [cognitions] whose fruit is exclusion, there is no activity directed toward making known a portion of a real entity that has not already been cognized; for it is impossible to perceive a partless [entity] through a single portion, since it has already been seen in its entirety.
Therefore, when an entity is perceived, all its qualities are indeed perceived; [the claim] that "it is not so determined due to error" is the basis upon which the proof proceeds. (47)
This is the summary verse:
therefore, there is no operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to what has already been seen, for the purpose of apprehending what is already seen.
And because one ascertains a single property through inference by grasping the object-entity, this fault does not apply when all [other] properties are excluded. (48)

[This is] the delusion regarding stability. Therefore, as many as there are extraneous states—such as permanence and so forth—of this [object], such as sound and the like, which has a momentary and selfless nature, so many are these superimpositions (*samāropa*), each arising from its own respective cause; that is, they arise from whatever cause corresponds to them. These [cognitions] are the exclusions (*vyavacchedaka*) of that superimposition, because they exclude it from the object by implication.

What are they? They are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that arise under the designation of inference (*anumāna*). The plural number is used because of the distinction between individual instances.

"They would be fruitful" means they would be purposeful. However, there is no activity—no engagement in making known or revealing—an unapprehended portion of a thing (*vastvaṃśa*), a part of the object, for those means of valid cognition whose fruit is exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) and whose fruit is the negation of superimposition (*samāropa-pratiṣedha*).
Because that part of the object is seen when the partless substratum (*dharmī*) is being perceived. What is the reason? Because it is impossible for a partless thing to be seen in part.

Since this is so, therefore, although every quality—that is, the entire nature—of an entity perceived by direct perception is indeed seen, it is not ascertained because of the presence of error; thus, for the sake of that ascertainment, the means of proof, namely inference, operates precisely in a positive form (vidhi-rūpeṇa). This has been clearly stated.

Therefore, the purpose of the mention of "the unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*) is not for the sake of grasping what is already seen through perception; rather, by stating that "activity proceeds only from the ascertainment of what is seen," the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) is clearly expressed, while the negation of other [means] follows by implication.

"Grasping the entity," and so forth. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction with respect to perception. And when an entity is accepted through inference, because the subject (*dharmin*)—such as sound—is determined to be partless by virtue of the ascertainment of even a single property (*dharma*), such as its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), there follows the ascertainment of all properties; consequently, other inferences, such as [the inference] of permanence (*nityatva*), would be rendered futile.
[One] conceives [it] as being eternal. 1. Regarding the consideration of the universal (*sāmānya*):

it is not only the case that another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not operate toward what is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). When inference (*anumāna*) also [operates] toward a real entity (*vastu*) by way of affirmation (*vidhi*),...

When that which is intended does not perform an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), then, because of its non-difference from it, the determination of all dharmas follows from the determination of a single dharma; thus, there is no operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
For it is not logical that when one thing is determined, that which is its very self (*tadātman*) would not be determined.

When, however, the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa*) is effected by means of inference, since the exclusion of one superimposition has been accomplished, the exclusion of another has not yet been accomplished; therefore, another [inference] proceeds for that purpose.
Now, it might be argued that the ascertainment of what is not yet cognized is necessarily preceded by error (*viparyāsa*); but this is not an invariable rule. For example:

Apoha is the form superimposed as something external, so called because "by means of this, [the other] is excluded" (*pohyate*). If that which is to be established by inference is accepted as such, then apoha is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)— so called because "in this, [the other] is excluded"—
and if it is admitted that this particular characteristic is grasped by inference as non-different from its own form (*svākāra*), then the fault just mentioned does not apply.
The phrase "not merely," and so forth, is an elaboration. The connection is with the words "in some case, upon a subject perceived through direct perception" (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭe dharmiṇi*);

the meaning is "upon some subject perceived through direct perception. The term "in some case" (*kvacit*) is used because not every subject is perceptible. By the reasoning just stated, there is no operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

In that case, inference is also held to cognize a real entity such as sound through affirmation; it does not effect the exclusion of superimpositions by means of the determination of the object as a real thing. "In that case" (*tatra*) refers to the grasping of the nature of the real entity in the form of an affirmation. When there is the ascertainment of one property, because of its non-difference from that [entity]—that is, because of the non-difference of the ascertained property from the entity—there is the ascertainment of all properties; thus, there is no operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
There is no occurrence of another inference even when there is non-exclusion (*avyatireka*). If it is argued that "there is no certainty regarding all properties," he says:

"For not," and so forth. "In that" refers to the property ascertained by the first inference. "Having that as its nature" means that it is not logical for something to be unascertained while having the nature of a property already ascertained.
Explaining how the fault does not follow in the case of *apoha*, he says: "But when," and so forth.

When, however, inference—while performing a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of a real entity (*vastu*)—effectively brings about the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*) by implication, rather than directly, because its function is that of a cognizer (*jñāpaka*), then this [objection] is refuted: that the exclusion of superimposition alone constitutes the object other than conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). 48b.

There would be no engagement [with the world] because [the object] would not be ascertained by inference. This is because, according to you, since one inference of "producedness" does not effect the exclusion of another superimposition—namely, the superimposition of "eternality"—another inference, such as that of "impermanence," must proceed for the sake of excluding that other superimposition. Therefore, it is not [the case that there is no engagement].
Although the external object is grasped by conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) in its own form, it is in fact apprehended only as unified with the cognition's own internal aspect (*svākāra*).
That [unified] external object, being unreal, is called "exclusion" (*apoha*) because other things are excluded by it.

And while this is the case, another person, not having understood the intention, says: "But surely," and so forth. First, error (*viparyāsa*) proceeds by superimposing a contrary form [upon an object]. Thereafter, based on that error, there arises a determination of an unperceived object through a logical mark (*liṅga*). Thus, this restriction—that [determination] must be preceded by error—is not absolute, because inference is possible even in one who is free from error. He states this as follows: "Just as..."

"Why is there the cognition of fire? For in that case, the superimposition of non-fire is not possible. If it is argued that therefore exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is not performed in all cases, [we reply]:

in this case, since the substratum (*dharmin*) is cognized, everything is cognized because of its non-difference from it. Therefore, if there were difference, that which is unconnected would not be cognized."

Thus it has been said: "Therefore, even in that case, how could there be a determination of its nature for one who perceives it? It is precisely due to error. And that [error] occurs when one perceives that place as distinct from it—that is, with a cognition free from the conceptualization of the presence of fire—distinct from it.

And so forth. “Accidentally” (*akasmāt*) means from that which has arisen without [prior] deliberation. For instance, there is the cognition of fire in a certain place due to smoke all at once (*sahasaiva*). Indeed, in that case, when there is an accidental cognition of fire, the superimposition (*samāropa*) of non-fire is not possible.
Therefore, it is not the case that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is performed everywhere by implication through inference.
The Master has said: "For regarding the operation of inference as apprehending the essential nature of a real entity (*vastu-svarūpa*), the following answer has been stated:

if *dharma* were apprehended by perception, then because those *dharmas* are non-different from their locus (*dharmin*), everything would be perceived, rendering inference futile. Or, if a difference between the *dharma* and its locus (*dharmin*) is admitted, [then] together with the locus..."

The relation characterized by identity does not exist, because difference is admitted. Furthermore, impermanence and other such properties do not arise from the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*), nor does the substratum arise from impermanence and the like. Consequently, it has already been stated that there can be no cognition of a property (*dharma*) in its substratum when the two are unrelated; for, as was argued in the interim, inference is impossible in a case where there is no relationship of cause and effect.

Therefore, in that case as well, when fire is cognized from the sudden sight of smoke, there is indeed for the person observing that place— namely, the observer of the location— an ascertainment of its nature, which is an ascertainment of its nature as possessing fire. And that [ascertainment] is rendered indeterminate solely through error, precisely because of the apprehension of similarity with a place that lacks fire.
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "And that... (1).
Alternatively, why would there be no determination of its intrinsic nature? Rather, there would surely be a determination because of the absence of error.
Yet, there is indeed non-determination. Therefore, the apprehension of the subject (*dharmin*) does not grasp the actual nature of the thing; thus, it has exclusion (*apoha*) as its object.
Furthermore: "And he," and so forth. "And he" refers to the person (*puruṣa*). "By means of its exclusion" (*tadviviktena*) means by means of the exclusion of fire (*vahnivivekena*).
Even though that place contains fire, he determines it through his intellect (*buddhyā*) by means of its form as excluded from that [fire]. By what kind of intellect?

By one that is "devoid of the cultivation of the existence of fire" (*agnisattābhāvanāvimuktayā*), meaning devoid of the possibility of the existence of fire. How is he not mistaken? He is indeed not mistaken.

Because of the apprehension of that [fire] in this [place], for it is thus: as long as one does not see smoke in that location, one determines that very place to be similar to another location devoid of fire. Even if there were some experience [of fire] elsewhere such that a certainty arises here, one must still have doubt regarding that [specific case]; and doubt rests upon both sides [of the alternatives].

And since that [sign] touches upon what is contrary to its own side, therefore, even when doubt is excluded, how could there not be an exclusion of the other by means of the sign? Furthermore, one who apprehends the object of inference solely through the sign must necessarily be possessed of error and doubt regarding that object of inference; for it is only when one is free from the superimposition of the form of "existent" and from doubt that there can be no superimposition of the form of "non-fire. (127)
And how can one who ascertains [the object] by way of a universal (sāmānya), while being free from superimposition and doubt regarding that aspect,
be said not to be mistaken?
In its realization, one should not follow a logical mark (liṅga); nor should one pay heed to its positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka).
Therefore, the logical mark (liṅga) is proclaimed to have exclusion (apoha) as its object;
otherwise, since the locus (dharmin) would already be established, what further [unestablished] could there be? (49)
This is the summary verse.

Furthermore, a person who is free from doubt would not follow a logical mark (*liṅga*) in order to apprehend that [object], just as one would not follow a mark to apprehend fire; nor would he rely upon the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). Likewise, he would not take heed of the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that mark. To the extent that he would follow it—

And one perceives [it]. Therefore, the cognizer who possesses superimposition and doubt regarding that form removes the superimposition by the power of the logical mark (*liṅga*), and in some cases, the doubt; thus, in all instances, the exclusion of superimposition is effected through the cognition of its own pervader (*svavyāpaka*).
Consequently, it has exclusion (*apoha*) as its object—that is, the exclusion of others as its object—in the manner described, but not directly.

"Otherwise" means: if the apprehension of inference were desired to occur without superimposition (*samāropa*), then, given that the subject (*dharmin*) is established by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what other nature (*rūpa*) could there be for that unestablished subject— distinct from its already established intrinsic nature— for the sake of communicating which the inferential mark (*liṅga*) would operate?

But surely, if doubt and error were to arise, there would be a partial [realization]. As it has been said: "(1) Nor do these conceptual constructions arise and perish entirely without being cognized. Furthermore, even in the position where no certainty arises, one cannot postulate a doubt consisting of a superimposition of that form by following a logical mark (*liṅga*) for its apprehension; for even in the case of the non-arising of certainty regarding the probandum (*sādhya*)—
Because it is possible to follow the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for that purpose;

otherwise, by the statement, "If the subject (*dharmin*) is established, what remains unestablished beyond this? (1), even by this [statement], the cognition whose object is the subject would have a conceptualized object, and not [an object] in the subject itself.

If superimposition (*samāropa*) is established, how can there be the exclusion of superimposition (*vyavaccheda*) by means of that inference? True; however, this is the intended meaning: as long as there is no certainty regarding the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), there is no arising of the inference, because the reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished (*asiddha*). And in a location possessing fire, [the reason] exists merely as a connection with that location.

The certainty that "this is smoke" is itself an error, because it is a determination contrary to reality. For the error here is not merely of the form "there is no fire here," but rather, even the cognition of the form "this place is different from one possessing fire" is an error.
Therefore, in this inference as well, there is indeed a negation of superimposition in the form: "This place possesses fire; it is not merely a place."
Let it be granted, then, that an inferential mark (*liṅga*), which operates upon its own object in order to exclude superimposition (*samāropa*), effects the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
But as for this conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*) that arises subsequent to perception—since it occurs even when there is no superimposition, how can it effect the exclusion of others?

Furthermore, it must necessarily be admitted that its object is the exclusion of others, because its object is a universal (*sāmānya*) and because the definition of [the universal] is the exclusion of others.
According to your view, regarding the universal:

"Even when something is perceived, that cognition which conceptualizes it as a universal has as its object the exclusion (*apoha*) of only those [features] upon which other parts have not been superimposed. (50)

Therefore, he says: "In some cases," and so forth. Even when some [object] such as a form (*rūpa*) is seen through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the cognition that arises subsequent to it has a universal as its object—that is, it has the universal as its domain—and for that very reason, it is conceptual (*vikalpaka*). It functions toward an object in which no other aspect—the form of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*)—has been superimposed; thus, even that [cognition] is [a cognition of] that alone.

[The phrase] "having the external as its object" means this: (1) conceptual cognition, while grasping the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) devoid of superimposition through the differentiation of its own form, is erroneous; therefore, it merely determines the external as being devoid of that superimposition, but it does not grasp the actual nature of the external.
Consequently, that [cognition] alone is the determination of the external as restricted, whereas for another [cognition], there is superimposition.
Conceptual cognition has exclusion (*apoha*) as its object.

Alternatively, that which is both non-superimposed and other-particulars—conceptual cognition, when it operates in the presence of such [an object], has as its object the exclusion of only that [part]. That which is non-superimposed and other-particulars becomes the object of the differentiation (*vyavaccheda*) of only that.

This is what is meant: even where a superimposition has occurred, the negation of that superimposition is not established by means of words or logical marks (*liṅga*), because of the absence of a [necessary] relationship; for this very reason, it is not produced [by them], and because destruction is causeless. Rather, [the superimposition ceases] simply due to the natural cessation of the preceding superimposition when there is certainty regarding impermanence and so forth through words and logical marks. As for the other...

When there is no arising of superimposition (*samāropa*), the negation of superimposition is accomplished. Likewise, even when something is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), who can prevent the exclusion of superimposition by another conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? Therefore, it is not the case that there is a discrepancy in the statements, such that a different kind of exclusion of superimposition was stated previously and now a different kind is being stated.
By this, the following [objection] is refuted:
"If one hears the word 'cow,' there would first arise the cognition 'it is not a cow'; it is for the sake of excluding what is not a cow that the sound 'cow' is employed."

When it is postulated that words and logical marks function to exclude others by producing certainty regarding their own objects, then it is established that their operation occurs solely in the form of affirmation. Therefore:
(1) "If this word 'cow' is capable of excluding others..."
Janaka’s claim that the cognition of "cow" arises from the word "cow," while another sound [the word "elephant"] is excluded, is refuted.
Likewise, as for what is also said:
"Even if the operation of words and logical marks is not tenable when [the object] is devoid of exclusion (*apoha*),
nevertheless, the cognition of the knower does indeed rely upon a real entity.
(1) How then is it that this certain knowledge arises regarding the operation of perception toward that which lacks marks such as form and so forth?

If it is argued that [the cognition] has exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) as its object, [we reply: because there is an absence [of the object] in the domain of superimposition (*samāropa*).
