For where this [cognition] has a superimposition, there is no certain determination (*niścaya*) regarding the particularity (*bheda*) that it is "endowed with a self" (*sātmaka*).
That is exactly what we desire. Furthermore, it is not the function of the word or the logical mark (*liṅga*) to negate other things once an object has been established by them;
therefore, as Kumārila says:
Nor is there a relationship of indicator and indicated (*liṅga-liṅgibhāva*), nor is there expressibility by words;
for negation is formless and lacks differentiation.
“There would be no relationship of signifier and signified between the two exclusions (*apoha*), because they are non-entities,
just as in the world there is none between a sky-flower and a rabbit’s horn according to your own position.
Furthermore, if the meaning of a word is conceived as being merely of the nature of a negation,”

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is expressed by the word "non-existence," would be of a different nature [from the object]. (36) If exclusion (*apoha*) were the denotable object, then all words expressing distinct universals (*sāmānya*) would be synonyms based on their reliance on the particular (*viśeṣa*). (42) 2

Likewise, if the differentiation of the exclusion (*apoha*) were due to the differentiation of the objects to be excluded (*apohya*), then that would be merely figurative. Furthermore, since an exclusion that is devoid of intrinsic form (*nīrūpa*) cannot be differentiated by a difference in its properties (*dharma*), how could it be differentiated by external exclusions? Thus he says:
"But surely, the differentiation of the exclusion will be established through the differentiation of the objects to be excluded."

"There is no distinction in it either by itself or from another; [any such distinction] is merely figurative. Furthermore, since even the substrata that are associated with it do not differentiate it in reality, the claim that 'it would be differentiated by the excluded objects (apohya) situated externally' is an excessive conceptual construction. (47, 52)

This is rejected, because mere exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is not an object of words and the like. He explains the verse beginning with "yah" and so forth. By the word "ādi," sound and the rest are included. "It has no mark" (*aliṅga*) refers to the certain cognition that "this is such-and-such a form and so forth. This occurs when there is no superimposition (*samāropa*); for [it does not occur] otherwise.

Regarding form and so forth perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there exists at that time the superimposition (*samāropa*) of a contrary aspect (*viparītākāra*). How, then, can it have exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) as its object? With this much, the first half of the verse has been explained. To explain the second half, he says: "The superimposition..."

Because that person lacks determinate knowledge regarding the object of superimposition, it follows—connected with the present context—that [the cognition] has the exclusion of that [superimposition] as its object.

He states this very point: "In whatever distinction there is no superimposition for this person, in that distinction which is the object of superimposition, there arises either an unstable certainty or [the realization that it is] devoid of self."

Because of the relationship of sublated and sublator between the cognitions of determination and superimposition, an entity that is perceived as distinct from everything else is not recognized as being exactly so [identical] through recognition; rather, there is some distinction.

Because an intervention is possible, as in the case of the whiteness of a conch shell. Where there is a cause for error, the cognizer’s ascertainment arises as a mere recollection even though the perception itself is no different; this is because of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator between error and ascertainment.
It is understood that its activity occurs within the isolation from superimposition. ||51||

The exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is precisely that discrimination (*viveka*). Therefore, even that [conceptual cognition] has as its object only the exclusion of that [particular], and does not, by its own nature, determine the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the real entity (*vastu*). For it is observed that even when there is such a determination, there is still no actual apprehension [of the thing]. What is the reason for this? It is because of the relationship of sublation and sublated between the conceptual determination and the superimposing mind. This is because of the [nature of] the determinative cognition.

And because there exists a relationship of sublated and sublator between knowledge that superimposes [an attribute] contrary to reality and [the object itself], he says the following while establishing precisely that relationship of sublated and sublator: "For not... [The connection is as follows: even if an entity is perceived as distinct from everything—both from its own kind (*sajātīya*) and from other kinds (*vijātīya*)—it is not recognized through every aspect exactly as it was seen; it is not determined as being "just so. For what reason?

In some cases, such as [the determination of] momentariness and so forth, there is the possibility of an intervention. This occurs when one has reached the cause of error; for example, even though one perceives a piece of mother-of-pearl as distinct from everything else, there is no certainty regarding its being mother-of-pearl because the cause of error—the similarity to silver—is possible. However, in that aspect where the cause of error does not exist, it is precisely there that the experience of this perceiver occurs.

A subsequent determinate cognition (*niścaya*) arises which is of the nature of recollection (*smārta*). Although there is no difference in the perception of that [object], and although perception is non-distinct with respect to all its aspects (*ākāra*), it is called "recollection" because it takes the form of memory.
But how can it be of the nature of recollection, given that it does not arise with the explicit mention of "that" (*tad*)?

It is true that [this cognition] is called "of the nature of recollection" because it takes as its object by unifying it with its own form that which was the object of non-conceptual [perception]. And since, even though there is no difference from direct perception, the ascertainment occurs only regarding an object free from superimposition—therefore, the relationship of sublated and sublater between superimposition and ascertainment is understood. From that relationship of sublated and sublater...

It is understood that this [cognition] proceeds from the cause of the ascertainment of the absence of superimposition (*samāropa*) when there is the exclusion of superimposition. Granted that it proceeds toward the exclusion of superimposition, nevertheless, its object is not "other-exclusion" (*anyāpoha*) by way of a positive form (*vidhi-rūpeṇa*), because it proceeds [toward the exclusion]. He says: "The exclusion of other is precisely that exclusion; the exclusion of superimposition is precisely other-exclusion. Therefore...

"By virtue of its occurrence in that which is devoid of superimposition, even that [is such]"— meaning that not only is the determinative cognition "sound is impermanent," but even this determinative cognition arising subsequent to perception has as its object the exclusion of that alone (*tanmātrāpoha*), and does not determine the intrinsic nature of the real entity by its own form. Why is this so?

For it is observed that even when there is ascertainment of a certain aspect, such as "form-ness" (rūpatva), there is no apprehension of another aspect, such as "momentariness," and [furthermore,] such ascertainment would be impossible [if they were identical].

4. Consideration of the Universal: (As many as are the superimpositions of parts, so many are the determinations for their exclusion; and there are just as many words. Therefore, they have distinct domains. ||52||
(Otherwise, if a single object were pervaded by one word or by one cognition, it would not have other objects [of words or cognitions], and thus there would be synonymy. || 53 ||
This is an intermediate verse.

However, if the determination of the nature of a thing is effected by a certainty arising subsequent to perception, then, because that thing is partless, such [subsequent] determination of its nature would be impossible; consequently, no other aspect of it could be determined.
Because of connection.

Since the activity of a determination or of a word occurs solely through the conceptual ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) of an object, and not by way of grasping the actual nature of the object itself, therefore, for as many superimpositions of one part or superimpositions of another form as have occurred or have not occurred, there are exactly that many determinations and words for the purpose of excluding them— that is, for the purpose of removing those superimpositions.

They indeed operate only within their own respective domains. For that reason, those determinations and words have distinct spheres and distinct objects; because, by virtue of their own respective causes, they have as their object an external reality that is non-different from their own determined forms. Therefore, this [is said]: "That which is established by the intellect and resides in the intellect does not follow after another object or another cognition."
Furthermore, that [cognition] which does not produce the intended object cannot be said to be [the word's meaning] in reality.
Moreover, if even mental intuition (*pratibhā*) has external objects as its domain,
then how could there be diverse intuitions regarding an external object that is fixed in a single nature?
Now, if these [cognitions] are devoid of objects because they exist as mere mental impressions (*vāsanā*),
how can there be cognition or activity regarding external objects?
If it is held that activity always occurs through a conviction (*adhimokṣa*) toward externality with respect to one's own part [of the cognition], [then...]
The argument that "the object of a word is unreal because it functions through delusion" has been refuted, since conceptual construction is accepted as having a constructed (kalpita) object.

"Otherwise" means when the intrinsic nature of a thing is apprehended by means of cognition and verbal expression. When [the object] is pervaded by a single word and made the object of [that word] in all its aspects, then, because it is pervaded by a single cognition—specifically one consisting of ascertainment—there is no other aspect as its object.
"Another object" (*anyaviṣaya*) refers to that which is both another aspect and an object; there is no further aspect of that thing [other than what has been grasped].

The object to be communicated exists as the objective domain (*viṣaya*). Alternatively, there is the differentiation of another word or cognition that communicates that very thing— a cognition which, though having a single essence, grasps its object through various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) as if it were manifold.
When the capacities of the various auxiliary factors that provide assistance are apprehended as non-different from the [single] self, [the cognition is unitary]. (54)

For that which is to be assisted by its entire self, how could there be any indeterminate distinction? Even for one who thinks: "The limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are indeed distinct from one another and from their substratum;
thus, the scriptural texts based upon them also apply to that very substratum. For him as well—

If the self, which is non-different from the powers that constitute the auxiliary causes of various limiting adjuncts (upādhi), were grasped in its entirety, what unascertained difference could there be for the beneficiary?

Or else, [the object] would not be the domain [of the word]. For this reason, since the object is already cognized, words that subsequently function toward it would become synonyms, like the words *vṛkṣa*, *pādapa*, and so forth. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of a single object for cognitions that proceed by following different objects, such as "the taste is sweet," "it is oily," "it is heavy," "it is cold," and so on; [such cognitions] would not occur.
Introducing [the following] in order to refute the ultimate reality of the distinction between property and property-bearer, he says: "yasyāpi" and so forth.

Even for that Vaiśeṣika, for whom a certain object—such as a jar—possesses manifold adjuncts (*upādhi*), that is, qualifiers such as "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and so on, because they are distinct from one another and from their substratum; that [object] which possesses these manifold adjuncts is differentiated precisely by that difference of adjuncts.
By that very same rule, the cognition which apprehends the universal is of the nature of a determination; and it is distinct with respect to each limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
And by demonstrating the difference in objects for cognitions, the difference for words is also shown by implication.

He explains this with the words "He who... and so forth: (1) limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like, are mutually distinct from one another and distinct from their substratum—that is, distinct from that which possesses the adjuncts. Based on those—meaning based on distinct limiting adjuncts—is the verbal expression (*śruti*).

The mention of "grasping" (grahaṇa) is merely an illustration; the same applies to cognitions (buddhi). [The terms] reside in their respective substrates—the substrates of the limiting conditions (upādhi) for persistence—and they exist precisely within those very objects of cognition as limiting conditions. They function by way of denotation. Therefore, there is no contingency of synonymy—characterized by the mutual interchangeability of words and cognitions—among these various terms and cognitions.

He states the reply: "Of that too," and so forth. When there is a grasping—that is, a determination—by a single determinate cognition (*niścayajñāna*) of the possessor of attributes (*upādhimat*), whose nature is non-different from those potencies which are the causes (*aṅga*, *kāraṇa*) for the assistance provided by various kinds of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
and when this has been performed in its entirety, what distinction remains? What specific attribute (*upādhiviśeṣa*) is left for the collection of adjuncts (*upādhikalāpa*) that is to be assisted?
It might be that [the subject] is uncertain; (1) [but rather] everything must be certain.

Now, even though there is a connection between fire and smoke, it is observed that when fire is not ascertained, smoke is not ascertained; likewise, when a property (*dharma*) is not ascertained, the locus (*dharmin*) will remain unascertained.
But would this not itself be non-perception? For when the nature of fire is grasped in its entirety by a determinate cognition,
even though the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are indeed distinct, nevertheless—

It is the cause of the objects for all subsequent verbal cognitions; yet it is only that which possesses those [attributes] which is apprehended by them. Since that [entity], whose nature consists of powers that serve as the substratum for the assistance of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), lacks any internal differentiation, if it were grasped in its entirety, what single limiting adjunct could possibly remain undetermined?—indeed, none at all.

Because it is ascertained solely by virtue of being the cause of smoke and so forth, and because smoke and the like are themselves ascertained; therefore, there is no apprehension of its own nature through ascertainment. In that case, even by means of non-conceptual [perception], there would be no apprehension in its entirety, since the fact of being its effect is not apprehended simply because smoke does not appear [to it].

This is not so. (1) The causality of fire with respect to the production of smoke is stated as its mere prior existence (*pūrvabhāva*). And since that [prior existence] appears in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could there not be a cognition of fire as the cause of that [smoke]? Therefore, the meaning is this: in reality, there is no mutual dependence between fire and smoke; for a relationship does not exist between a state that has already been produced and one that has not yet been produced.

Because [the smoke] exists only when fire exists, these two are called cause and effect. However, since the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*) are mutually dependent, if the property-bearer were ascertained in its entirety, there would be a direct ascertainment of all its properties;

it would not be a case of implication (*ākṣepa*) through the object. But when the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is one that determines an external object and is not a grasper [of the internal form], then—

Since the exclusion of others is possible for a property that has already been established, it is logical that another property is implied by implication. Furthermore, if there were mutual dependence—

such that as long as there is no determination of the property (*dharma*), there is no determination of the substratum (*dharmin*), and as long as there is no determination of the substratum, there is no determination of the property— then there would be the fallacy of circular reasoning (*anyonyāśrayatva*).

But surely, the relationship between the qualifier (*upādhi*) and the qualified (*upādhimat*) is said to be nothing other than the relationship between the locus (*āśraya*) and the located (*āśrayin*). And that [relationship] exists only between two things that exist at the same time;

for there can be no relationship of beneficiary and benefactor (*upakārya-upakāraka-bhāva*) between those two because this [relationship] requires a difference in time. So how can it be said that "there is the apprehension of everything as qualified by a single qualifier"?

True; however, others maintain that the relationship between producer and produced (*janyajanakabhāva*) is one thing, while the relationship between beneficiary and benefactor (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*) is another. For instance, although the substance of a jujube fruit is produced by its own causes, it is nevertheless assisted by the bowl; therefore, this relationship of beneficiary and benefactor is asserted to exist between two things occurring at the same time. It is with this intention that this was stated. Alternatively:

When a property (*dharma*) is being determined, because it necessarily depends upon a substratum (*dharmin*), it implies the cognition of that substratum; and since this applies to all properties that depend [on a substratum], there is a determination of everything. Therefore, because it functions through a means of knowledge other than verbal testimony, the relationship between property and substratum is merely conceptualized (*kalpita*).

Furthermore, in this view, since [the distinction] is not a real entity, there is no redundancy in employing another means of knowledge when postulating the difference or non-difference of properties.

This is because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no such thing as difference or non-difference among them; and since other attributes must be postulated by means of other valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*), how could one postulate a difference or non-difference of attributes in the absence of those [cognitions]? This is merely a triviality.

With the words "even though" (*yadyapi*) and so forth, he explains the meaning of the verse: although it is admitted that for other words— that is, for other cognitions— the objects, which consist of substrata possessing limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), have distinct limiting adjuncts as their respective causes, nevertheless...

The object possessing those [attributes], being endowed with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is apprehended—that is, made an object—by verbal cognitions. For that possessor of attributes, which has as its very nature the powers that serve as the substratum for the assistance provided by the various adjuncts, there is no differentiation within its own self, its essential form. Consequently, [the cognition] of a single adjunct... [omitted].

Because it is apprehended as being an auxiliary (*upakāraka*) to the object. For when that [auxiliary] is apprehended in its own form, its status as an auxiliary is not something else that remains unapprehended. Therefore, whatever is the apprehension of this [auxiliary] by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), that very same is its apprehension by way of its being an auxiliary as well.
Because they are related to the self, both are apprehended in a single cognition. ||55||

Since the relationship of mutual assistance between the substrate (*upādhi*) and that which possesses it (*upādhimat*), which constitutes their very nature, is grasped in a single cognition, there must be a grasping of both possessors of attributes (*upādhimantau*) within that same cognition.

Thus, even when one thing qualified by a single attribute is being grasped, all attributes are grasped, because their grasping is inseparable from the grasping of that [qualified object]. Otherwise, even in that case, it would not be grasped; for it is not [the case that] another...
Furthermore, O All-Self, if there is apprehension even through the door of cognition, what distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) could remain uncertain for it?
Rather, everything would be certain. Why? Because it is apprehended as the benefactor of all limiting adjuncts.

If it is argued that by means of a single attribute (*upādhi*), it is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the substrate (*upādhimat*) that is apprehended, and not the fact of its being assisted by the attribute, [the author] replies with the words "For not," and so forth. This connects to the phrase "not indeed something else unapprehended" [referring to the assistance]. For there is no difference between the nature of the substrate—which is being apprehended in its own form—and the fact of its being assisted; since...

Thus, for this reason, regarding "this" which possesses adjuncts (*upādhi*): that very apprehension [of it] by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*), that is, its essential form (*svarūpa*), is itself the apprehension [of it] as being the benefactor (*upakāraka*) [of those adjuncts].
Let it be granted that through one adjunct there occurs the apprehension of the possessor of adjuncts, which consists of its own nature as the benefactor of all adjuncts.
To the question, "How then can there be a perception of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) which are distinct from that [substratum]? he says: "Of those two," and so forth.

This means that between the collection of limiting adjuncts and the possessor of the limiting adjuncts—which stand in a relationship of the benefited and the benefactor—there is a mutual connection within the self by way of its own nature; that is to say, because the relationship of the benefited and the benefactor is essentially identical with the self. And therefore, the benefactor—

When there is cognition of a single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is the apprehension of the two [related entities] by virtue of their connection; that is, the apprehension of the qualifier (*upādhi*) and the qualified (*upādhimat*). He explains this with the words "of that which has become its own essence" (*ātmabhūtasya*), and so forth. For instance, when the possessor of the qualifier (*upādhimat*) is apprehended, its status as a benefactor (*upakārakabhāva*), which has become its very essence, is first apprehended; and when that is apprehended, the status of being the beneficiary (*upakāryabhāva*) of the qualifiers is also [apprehended] as its essence.

Since both the attribute (*upādhi*) and the substratum (*upādhimat*) are apprehended in a single act of cognition, when that substratum qualified by even one attribute is apprehended, there is the apprehension of all attributes, because their apprehension is inseparable from its apprehension—that is, because the apprehension of the attributes is inseparable [from it]. Otherwise, if the attributes were not apprehended, it would likewise not be apprehended; for the attributes [are essential to it].
Even in this way, it would not be apprehended as "the agent possesses an adjunct.

If it is argued that at that time, the subserviency of the possessor of the adjunct is apprehended only with respect to that very adjunct which is the cause for the application of the term "cognition," and not with respect to the subserviency toward other adjuncts—the author replies: "For it is not another," and so forth. [It is] subservient to another.

Thus, while no other nature that assists an external adjunct (*upādhi*) is grasped, rather, the entirety [of the object] is grasped because the entity is partless. Even if some nature that assists another were grasped, [the cognition] would not be [an apprehension of] the effect of that assisting factor when the assisting factor itself is not grasped.

There would be non-apprehension [of the self], because it would follow that even that [the relation] is not apprehended. It is like the case of ownership and the owner. Therefore, the same consequence applies even to the theory that [the relation] is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of a distinct entity.
Now, it might be thought: those powers by which [the substance] assists its limiting conditions (upādhi) are indeed distinct; therefore, this undesirable consequence does not apply. [If one objects:
"If there is a difference between the powers that assist the properties (dharma), what does that matter to the [substance] itself?"
There would be no benefit for them from that, and likewise, there would be an infinite regress. ||56||

It might be thought: (1) that there is a perception of the possessor of attributes as being merely "beneficial" without regard for its relation [to the subject], but not as "the benefactor of this"; therefore, the attributes themselves are not perceived. To this, he says: "And also not," and so forth. "Perceived in such a way" means perceived simply as "the benefactor. Why is there a non-perception of the attribute, which is the effect of the benefaction? What is the reason?

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even for that which is the "helper" (*upakāraka*), there would be no apprehension [of it as such]—that is, the term "helper" would not be grasped. This explains that (1) because it is a relational entity, the apprehension of something as a "helper" does not occur without the apprehension of a second related entity.

He provides an illustration of such a case: "like the relationship between property and owner. For indeed, there is no apprehension of "property" (*sva*) without the apprehension of the "owner" (*svāmin*).

There is the apprehension of ownership (*svāmitva*). For this reason, even though a single cognition or word functions by means of a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there occurs the apprehension of all limiting adjuncts and of the substratum of those adjuncts in its entirety. Therefore, even in the theory that limiting adjuncts are distinct entities (*arthāntara-upādhivāda*), the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) applies; namely, that other words and cognitions would become synonyms (*paryāyatā*).
"It follows [that there would be no distinction].

Now, with the words "But even if... and so forth, the opponent raises a further objection: those powers by which the possessor of power (śaktimat) assists its limiting adjuncts (upādhi)—those powers are distinct from the possessor of power; therefore, because of that distinction, this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) does not apply.

If there were a grasping of the non-difference of the power that assists a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), then there would be a grasping of all powers; and from that grasping, there would be a grasping of all limiting adjuncts—this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) does not occur.
He states the answer: "In the assistance of the properties," and so forth. The "properties" (*dharma*) are the limiting adjuncts; those which are the powers of their assistance—of those [powers]...
If a difference [of the powers] from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) is admitted, what do those powers become in relation to that possessor of power?

They become nothing at all; the meaning is that they are not related to it. This is because if there is no benefit (*upakāra*) conferred by them upon the possessor of power, then [they are unrelated]. Now, if benefit is desired for the sake of establishing a relationship, then [the powers] would be benefactors of the powers.

Further powers distinct [from the entity] must be admitted; and for those powers by which it is assisted, another assistance must be postulated in order to establish their status as relations. In that case, there would be the postulation of further powers, and thus an infinite regress would result.

If the capacities for assistance belonging to that [entity] with respect to each limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) are neither identical to its own nature nor do they experience assistance from it, then what are those [capacities] to it? On the other hand, if this single entity assists by means of powers that are identical to its own nature, then upon the apprehension of one limiting adjunct, there would be the apprehension of it in its entirety. For indeed, when the limiting adjunct is apprehended, the assistance provided by it—

The apprehension of a substance (*dravya*) is the apprehension of its power (*śakti*). When that [power] is apprehended, the entity (*bhāva*) which assists it—namely, that which consists of the assistance of all its inherent powers—is apprehended, and thus it causes all the powers to be apprehended. And since those [powers] cause the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) to be apprehended, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains in that state. Alternatively, if those powers that assist the [primary] power are indeed distinct from the entity itself, then [the same problem applies] to the limiting adjuncts.
And because those powers are manifested through an endless succession of ever-newer powers, that single [entity] is explained by them as such;

this is what is meant by the words beginning with "yadi" and so forth. With respect to each limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the capacities for providing assistance belong to that possessor of limiting adjuncts; they are not identical with its own self, nor are they its essential nature (*svabhāva*), but rather distinct from it.

Nor do they experience any benefit from that substrate (upādhimat), nor do they assimilate it as their own; what then are they called? They are called the "powers" (śakti) of the substrate. Why are they so called? Because of the absence of a [direct] relationship. If, for the sake of establishing a relationship, one were to admit that those powers which assist the substrate receive assistance from the substrate itself, then by means of which...
Regarding the powers that assist the limiting adjuncts: this possessor of adjuncts assists the powers.

If those powers are held to be identical with its own self, then this possessor of adjuncts is one and partless by virtue of its own inherent powers; thus, while assisting the powers that assist the adjuncts, it remains undivided.
Thus [it is said].
Of what nature [is it]?

By the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and so forth, he establishes the apprehension [of the object] in its entirety. When one limiting attribute (*upādhi*) is apprehended, the assistance provided by that...

The apprehension of a power distinct [from the substrate] occurs through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that provide assistance; upon that apprehension—namely, the apprehension of the power assisted by the limiting adjuncts—that which assists it is what assists the power assisted by the limiting adjuncts.
This results in the impairment of all powers that constitute its own self, [namely] all the powers that constitute its own self and assist the limiting adjuncts.

An entity (*bhāva*) that possesses well-functioning capacities (*śakti*) is apprehended in such a way that it grasps all its auxiliary and supportive capacities (*upādhy-upakārikā-śakti*). And these capacities, once apprehended, cause their own supported adjuncts (*upādhi*) to be apprehended; thus, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains as before. What difference would there be from what was stated [earlier], namely, "what would be the distinction if [the object] were not determined"?

Now, lest this fault should arise, those powers that assist the power [of the substrate] are themselves held to be distinct from the entity possessing the adjuncts (*upādhi*). In that case, one must further postulate powers distinct from those [adjunct-assisting powers], and likewise powers assisting those, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding both the adjuncts and their powers. This concerns the assistance rendered by the adjuncts—

And because there is no finality regarding the powers of the *kṛt* suffixes, which results in an undesirable infinite regress (*aniṣṭhā*) due to their being connected—that is, joined—to one another; for indeed, the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are connected to distinct powers, and those [powers] are likewise [connected] to yet other distinct ones. Thus, each subsequent power is connected to preceding powers that are themselves distinct, resulting in an infinite regress.

[The universal] is connected with this [particular], but not with the substrate of the limiting adjunct (*upādhimat*). Consequently, that single substrate of the limiting adjunct—because it is characterized by being assisted by those [adjuncts]—is such that its nature as assisted by them has never been grasped at any time.
[This concludes] the investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*). 4. Because it is indicated by being assisted by those [adjuncts].
5. The nature of being assisted by them has never been grasped at any time.
Because those [entities] are not apprehended as possessing that [universal].

If, on the other hand, words and cognitions were to apply to the mere limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), even then, because there would be no connection [between the word and the universal], there could be no comprehension of all [particulars] by means of the communication of that [adjunct]. If this is argued:

Even then, because words do not imply [the exclusion], the application of words to that which lacks the connection with a word would be futile. All worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which rests upon purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), proceeds by way of affirmation and negation. Since limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are incapable of that [action] there, and yet that which is capable is not expressed at all, what is the point of employing a word? Consequently, even the limiting adjuncts themselves would not exist. At times...

By which powers (*śakti*) has it never been grasped even at any time as having the nature of being assisted by them? That is to say, [it is not grasped] as having the nature of being assisted by those powers;

that is, as having the nature of the powers belonging to those powers that assist the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), because those powers are distinct from the [substratum] itself. Therefore, [to speak of it] as possessing those [powers], i.e., as possessing the power that assists the limiting adjuncts, and consequently as possessing the limiting adjuncts themselves, is likewise useless.

The sense is that there is the conceptualization of an adjunct (*upādhi*). Thus far, the fault has been stated regarding the case where the application of cognition and the word occurs in that which possesses the adjunct. Now, another fault must be stated for the case where they occur in the adjuncts themselves. To state that, he introduces the position of the adjuncts with the words "If, however," and so forth.

How could words and cognitions apply themselves to adventitious attributes (*upādhi*)—that is, to distinct qualifiers—that are devoid of any basis other than [the thing itself] and are purely impermanent? They would have to rely upon them as being the conveyors [of meaning]. This is because those possessors of attributes (*upādhimat*) are not included within, nor made objects of, the words and cognitions. [This applies] by way of the cognition of that [attribute], which is to say, by way of the cognition of the possessor of the attribute. Even by means of a single word or cognition, [there would be the cognition] of every attribute.

Regarding practice (*pratipatti*), he states the fault here as well, beginning with "even then" (*tadāpi*) and so forth. "Of that" refers to that which possesses limiting conditions (*upādhimat*). "Because of non-implication" means because of its non-demonstration. Regarding the phrase "therein," i.e., in that which possesses limiting conditions, he asks how it is redundant and replies with "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*) and so forth. Purposeful action...

That conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) for which purposive activity (*pravṛtti*), as the basis of efficacy (*arthakriyā*), is the support and objective basis (*ālambana*), is so described. Whatever conventional practice there may be among those who act with foresight, it concerns what is beneficial or harmful. And that [practice] occurs in two modes—affirmation (*vidhi*) and negation (*pratiṣedha*)—since there is no third mode. This is an instance of the *itthambhūtalakṣaṇā* (the instrumental case used to denote a characteristic mark).

The third [alternative]: universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth are incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in that regard; yet it is the particular individual (*vyaktibheda*), which is capable, that is expressed by the word. Thus, what is the point of employing the word? And since this particular individual, which is capable of causal efficiency, is not expressed by words, then those intended universals such as "cowness" are not [true] adjuncts (*upādhi*).

They would not be qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). Because when a word or a cognition functions with respect to something possessing an adjunct (*upādhimat*) by way of that adjunct—in the case of some possessor of an adjunct, namely the primary object (*pradhāna*), which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—due to the absence of a limb [i.e., the absence] of the qualifier in relation to that, namely in relation to the primary, they are so called; they are called "adjuncts" (*upādhi*). This...

The determination of the adjunct (*upādhi*) according to logic: When, however, it is the adjuncts themselves that are expressed by the word, then, since there is no primary entity (*pradhāna*) for whose occurrence those [adjuncts] would be subordinate members (*aṅga*), they are designated as such only in relation to that [primary]. Since they are not implied by the word, they are not subordinate members of anything; how then can they be called "adjuncts"?

If it is argued that there is no fault because [the object] is characterized by the cognition of its characteristics, the same undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) follows. For as long as that [object] is being characterized by those limiting adjuncts (upādhi) through necessary concomitance, it is characterized in its entirety even by a single adjunct; thus, the same undesirable consequence remains in that state.
For what distinction is there here? Would it be the words themselves that characterize this [object], or would the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) characterized by them be characterized?
In any case, since it is at that time the benefactor of everything, it makes no difference whatsoever. 56.
Therefore:
"When one thing that provides assistance is apprehended, no other assistances [are apprehended].
When that [one] is seen, those [others] which are unseen are [also seen]; thus, upon the apprehension of that [one], there is the apprehension of the whole. (57)
—This is the summary verse.
Since they are neither implied nor expressed by the word, those adjuncts (*upādhi*) do not constitute limbs (*aṅga*) of any primary entity;
that is to say, they are not adjuncts at all. Even if only the mere existence of adjuncts is questioned, nevertheless, as for those adjuncts indicated by the word—

If it is argued that there is no fault because [the object] is delimited by those qualifiers (*upādhi*) through their defining characteristic, and thus the fault of the uselessness of employing words does not apply—then that same consequence follows: the necessity of grasping all qualifiers. He states this very point: "He [is] that," and so forth. "He" refers to the possessor of the qualifiers (*upādhimat*). "By way of being inseparable" means that because of the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) between the qualifier and the qualified, even by means of a single qualifier, [the object] is indicated.

Since [the universal] is partless, it is characterized by its entire self through the word; thus, the consequence of grasping all adjuncts (*upādhi*) remains exactly as before. It might be thought: "This consequence applies where there is a direct denotation (*codana*) of the possessor of the adjunct by the word, but not where it occurs by virtue of the sense (*arthavaśāt*. To this, he says: "For what difference is there here? Whether the words directly [denote] this possessor of the adjunct...

They would cause [the object] to be conveyed; or rather, the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), whether characterized by that [object] or characterized by the word, would indicate the possessor of the adjuncts (*upādhimat*). What difference is there? None at all. For instance, at the time of indication, the possessor of the adjuncts is ascertained through the power of the adjuncts as "the benefactor of all," meaning "the benefactor of all the adjuncts. And thus...

As before, there is the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) would have to be grasped; therefore, what was said—that [the cognition] arises from a "characterization by characterization" (lakṣitalakṣaṇā)—is of no consequence, because it is vitiated by the previously mentioned defects. Since there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā) if the powers (śakti) that assist the adjuncts were distinct [from them], those powers are not distinct.

Therefore, when it is accepted that a single substrate possessing an adjunct (*upādhimat*) is assisted by one particular adjunct, there must be distinct capacities (*śaktibheda*) that assist the other adjuncts; consequently, those [capacities] which assist other adjuncts do not arise from the same nature as that which assists the first adjunct.
Chapter 4: An Examination of the Universal (Sāmānyacintā).
Section (ka): Refutation of the Views of the Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā Schools.
(ka) Entities have an excluded nature (*vyāvṛttasvabhāva*).
If it is held that even when one part is grasped, another remains ungrasped due to error, this might be so:

when a partless entity is apprehended, what else could there be that is not then apprehended? [One might argue: "But because it is not determined due to error, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) proceeds. If this is the case, [then we reply: [The opponent continues: If it is so...
That [cognition] is established as having that exclusion as its object; therefore, the other is likewise [established]. (58)

Because it functions even with respect to an object that is free from superimposition, and because it functions with respect to an object that is free from superimposition; [it is] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for one who has engaged in activity for the sake of removing error.
Those [conditions] which are not seen when that [object] endowed with conditions is seen, are indeed not other [than it]. For this reason, they are included within what is to be grasped by it.
When that which possesses attributes (*upādhimat*) is apprehended, there is the apprehension of its nature as the benefactor of all its attributes.

As for the Bhaṭṭa who thinks: "(1) Attributes are indeed distinct; therefore, when a substratum (*dharmin*) is determined by means of one attribute, there is no determination of all attributes because of their difference," he says this:
“That which persists through things characterized by appearance and disappearance is the substratum (*dharmin*),

or else it is the cognition [of it] that occurs prior to the apprehension of its attributes (*dharma*). (152) When a single attribute is determined within a substratum possessing infinite attributes...”
"The word would be merely a means, but not a definitive determination of everything"—
this [position] is also refuted precisely because it entails the faults inherent in both sides.

With the words "If," etc., he anticipates the opponent's intention. Even when an object has been grasped in its entirety by a single determinate cognition (*niścayajñāna*), another [cognition]—meaning another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)—might exist for the purpose of removing error.
He explains this very point with the words "This might be so," etc.: namely, when there is the apprehension of an object that is partless (*nirbhāga*) and without components (*niraṃśa*).
At that time, when an indivisible entity is being apprehended, what other part could there be that is not apprehended? Indeed, everything is apprehended.
However, although it is apprehended, it is not ascertained due to error; thus, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) proceeds [to function].

To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) replies with the words beginning "If it is so": "That subsequent means of valid cognition which is desired for the purpose of removing the error... (532).

That [cognition] is established as having exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) as its object—that is, having the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object—by the reasoning previously stated; it is like the subsequent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, another determination-knowledge (*niścayajñāna*) occurring at a prior time, which arises from a subsequent means of valid cognition, also has exclusion as its object. What is the reason? Because it operates upon an object free from superimposition (*asamāropa*).
"That is so.
"In that case, it is established that the result is the exclusion of the superimposition of other [entities]; likewise, the other [entity], which is non-existent, is also [established]."

Because mental superimposition functions with respect to an object, wherever there is such superimposition, there is an absence of certainty; thus, that which exists in the absence of superimposition is established as the object of *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others).
Moreover: "By means of determinations (niścaya), that form which is determined therein—how can that be their object? (59)

This alone is the apprehension of its own object by determinate cognitions. If that [object] were as indeterminate as other forms, then how could it be said to be "grasped" even by perception while remaining undetermined?
No; for perception is not the determiner of anything; rather, it grasps that which is already determined, and it does not determine it.
By what? Not by that [external object], but by the appearance (*pratibhāsa*). Therefore, the apprehension or non-apprehension of perception does not depend on certainty or uncertainty.

He explains the verse beginning with "tatsatyādi": since it has the exclusion of the superimposition of another form as its result, it is established that [perception] has the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object, by way of negating the superimposition that is about to arise. It is the same for other [cognitions] as well.

Previously, it was stated that determinate cognition (*niścayajñāna*) has the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object. What is the reason? Because it operates upon an object where there is no superimposition (*samāropa*). This very point is expressed [in the verse]: "Because of the apprehension of this form. For this reason, it is established that the preceding determinate cognition, which operates in the absence of superimposition, has the exclusion of others as its object.

Furthermore, (1) for one who desires another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even regarding an object already grasped by ascertainment in order to eliminate error, it would have to be admitted that the object of ascertainment is not ascertained; otherwise, error would be impossible.
And that is incorrect, as he says: "Moreover," and so forth. That form which is not ascertained by ascertainment belongs to them...

How could there not be an object for determinations? What is the reason? Because this very apprehension of an object by determinations consists in the ascertainment of that object. If that [object] which is intended as the object of determination were unascertained—just like any other aspect (ākāra)—then that which is not intended as the object of determination would likewise be grasped in that ascertainment.

"How so? and so forth begins the opponent's objection: Even for the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), who desires another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the purpose of excluding superimpositions regarding what has been grasped by perception, must either accept that an aspect which is not being ascertained is grasped by perception, or else maintain that grasping occurs only by virtue of ascertainment. How, then, can a form that is not being ascertained be said to be grasped even by perception?
The same consequence [applies].

He refutes this with the words "No," and so forth; the intention is that [the object] is distinct from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). As for that which is called "perception" (*pratyakṣa*)—even though it is said to grasp the form of blue and so on—that grasping does not occur by way of a determinative judgment (*niścaya*).

Rather, it is by way of appearance (*pratibhāsa*). For a partless entity, there is no appearance whatsoever; thus, there are no certainties in every respect. Even for one who ascertains something, there is grasping and non-grasping due to the difference in activity caused by uncertainty regarding other things. Therefore, that which is a certainty is itself the grasping of that [object]. Otherwise, even if the form were single, it would not be so.
It may be so.

But why is it that, even when an experience arises regarding an object whose nature is distinct from all else, a corresponding conceptual ascertainment (*niścaya*) does not likewise occur? Because of the deficiency of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). And therefore:
"Even though a particularity devoid of parts has been grasped by perception..."
That which exists as a cognition when there is a determination of a particularity is what is cognized. ||60||

(1) "Grasping" refers to that [perception]; therefore, the grasping or non-grasping of perception occurs not by virtue of certainty or uncertainty respectively, but rather by virtue of appearance or non-appearance. Consequently, even when there is no certainty, the establishment of something as grasped by perception through mere appearance is not contradictory. It is not the case that for certainties, as it is for perceptions, there is [an object] that is not certain.
The connection is as follows: apprehension occurs merely through the manifestation of a form, while non-apprehension occurs merely through its non-manifestation.

If one asks why this is so, he says: "For instance," and so forth. Just as, upon seeing a person, even though one determines that it is a person, there is a difference in activity and a difference in conventional usage due to the lack of certainty regarding other things such as a thief; for it is by means of the determination of "personhood" [that this distinction arises].

A course of action such as placing one's trust is observed to correspond to the certainty regarding a person; and because there is no certainty of his being a thief, a corresponding course of action such as fear is not observed. Therefore, that specific activity which corresponds to a certainty is apprehended by means of that certainty, while that specific non-activity which corresponds to a lack of certainty is not apprehended. Because this is so, [the author says] "therefore," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of this" (*asya*), which refers to the form (*ākāra*): (1) "otherwise" means that if its apprehension were not established by virtue of a definitive cognition (*niścaya*).

Then, even in the case of a single form—even in a form intended to be definitively cognized—there would be no apprehension of it "as such" (*tad*) by means of a definitive cognition. Why is that so? The opponent asks: because [the object] is "different from everything," that is, because it is excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes.

"It is just so" means that, in accordance with experience, there is no conceptual determination (*niścaya*) regarding any of the particulars (*bheda*). For this reason, the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others) maintains that another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must function regarding other particulars in order to exclude other forms. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) states: "Because of the deficiency of auxiliary causes. For mere experience is not the cause of determination; rather—

Habitual practice (*abhyāsa*) and other such factors are also auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). Determination occurs only with respect to that aspect where these [causes] exist, and not elsewhere. But surely, since there is always perception even of the momentary aspect, habitual practice must indeed exist there, and thus determination should arise? No; for here, "habitual practice" is intended to refer to that which has an experienced and determined object, and a momentary thing cannot be so, because of the possibility of causes for error.

Since it is already certain regarding the real object, how can there be cultivation (abhyāsa) therein? Therefore, this remains established: wherever there is cultivation with respect to a mental aspect (ākāra), there alone is certainty.

He says that very thing: "Then, whiteness," and so forth. Even though a particular—characterized as blue or the like, distinguished from everything else, unproduced by conceptual construction (*avikalpita*), and partless—is grasped by perception in its entirety, that particular for which there exists a cooperative condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) for the determination (*avasāya*) or ascertainment (*niścaya*) is what is cognized—that is, what is ascertained.

Although experience indeed consists of an entity devoid of parts distinct from everything else, nevertheless, by that much alone, there would be no ascertainment regarding all its differences, because it depends upon other causes. For experience generates an ascertaining cognition in accordance with the habitual practice of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), just as, despite there being no difference in the perception of a form, there arise the conceptualizations of it as a corpse, a lover, or food.

In that case as well, the acuity of the intellect, the intensity of the habitual practice of passion (*rāga*), and so forth, are also cooperative causes for the arising of the determination of difference based on experience. And it is due to differences such as proximity among these very factors that there is a sequence of priority and posteriority. For example, even though there is no distinction between being a progenitor and being a teacher, upon seeing one's father approaching, one determines, "My father is coming."
"Not [my] teacher"—this certainty also occurs only when there is no cause for error. Therefore, there is no certainty regarding all aspects of that which has not been experienced.

He explains this with the words beginning "Even though" (*yadyapi*). Regarding all distinctions, such as momentariness and so forth, [the cognition] arises by means of mere experience (*anubhava-mātreṇa*).

This is because the knowledge of experience depends upon other causes for the production of certainty. He states that very point with the words beginning "For experience... (*anubhavo hi* etc.). "According to the habituation to conceptual construction" (*yathā-vikalpābhyāsam*) means that it functions together with whatever kind of habituation to conceptual construction one possesses as its auxiliary cause.

The meaning is that it produces [the conceptual construction] through habituation (*vāsanā*). He provides an example, beginning with "Just as," and so forth. Although there is no difference in the perception of the form of a dead woman, the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of a wandering mendicant, a lustful man, and a dog arise respectively as a corpse, a beloved, and food, according to the habituation to those respective conceptualizations.
And it is not only the habituation to conceptualization that acts as the auxiliary cause; rather, there is another as well. He says: "In that regard..."

And so forth. Even in that case, despite there being no difference in the perception of form (*rūpa*), "clarity" (*pāṭava*) refers to the sharpness of the intellect (*buddhi*). Just as for yogins, through the clarity of their intellect, there is a determination of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) and other such qualities by mere perception; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), desire, capacity, and the like are included.
"And so on" means beginning with these. [This occurs] from experience—that is, from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—which serves as the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).

Regarding the auxiliary causes for the arising of the certainty of existence: when, then, among many certainties the aforementioned causes are not present, how can there be a sequential occurrence of those certainties? To this he says: "And of those very [causes]," and so forth.
"Of those" refers to the causes of certainty; [the sequence arises] due to the differences in the degrees of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) [of the causes]. Of whichever certainty the proximity—

First of all, that which causes the ascertainment of the object arises; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is a sequence of certainties based on the distinctions in the degrees of intensity. He provides an illustration with the words "Just as," etc. When the teacher is like a father, then, although there is no difference between one person’s being a progenitor and his being a teacher, upon seeing the father approaching, [one thinks] "my father is coming."

[Objection: Even when there is cultivation of the conceptualizations of momentariness and selflessness, for those who do not perceive reality, the ascertainment of momentariness and so forth does not arise from perception; therefore, he says "that too," and so on. [It arises] when the cause of error is absent, but not from the mere presence of an ascertainment-condition. Since this is so, when the cause of error is absent and the auxiliary conditions are complete...

And when [the conceptualization] exists, the ascertainment arises from perception, not from [perception] alone. Therefore, it is said: "it is not experienced," and so forth. [In the context of] the investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*), there too [one speaks of] "exclusion of others" (*anyavyāvṛtti*) and "excluded from others" (*anyavyāvṛtta*).
And both words and determinate cognitions conform to convention. (61)
Even for a positive entity (*vṛtti*), there is no such thing as a "subject" (*dharmin*) that is distinct from what is excluded (*vyāvṛtta*).
For if that which excludes [the other] were to cease, it would follow that it possesses the nature of that very thing [it excludes]. Consequently, even the exclusion itself would be non-existent.
Therefore, this remains established: the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*) is what is conveyed by words and logical marks (*liṅga*).
Now, if exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) were non-different from the object (*padārtha*), then when that object is apprehended by a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or word,
other [means or words] would be redundant, because it would be ascertained in its entirety. Alternatively, if it were different, then since it is dependent upon that [object],
when the object characterized by one exclusion is ascertained by a single means of valid cognition, [the same problem follows] by the logic previously stated.

Since all exclusions (*vyavaccheda*) would be certain, there would be no application of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth; therefore, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) follows.
That is not so, because for entities (*bhāva*), there is no mutual exclusion that is either non-different or different. It is merely...
It has been stated that they have arisen as distinct from their own respective causes, and this will be explained further.

To the question, "How then do designations such as 'exclusion of others' and so forth, as well as cognitions, operate? he says: "In that case also," and so on. Even in that case, where the word-meaning is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), those words which express properties and their possessors—such as "exclusion from others" or "this is excluded from others"—as well as the determinate cognitions (*niścaya*) whose objects are both [the property and the possessor], conform to linguistic convention (*saṃketa*).

The distinction between property and property-bearer among these is imagined through conformity with linguistic convention; however, in the ultimate sense, there is no exclusion at all—this is the meaning.

He explains this with the passage beginning "In that regard, 'exclusion of others' (*anyāpoha*)," [showing that] the cow's exclusion from the horse is one thing, while the property [of exclusion] is another.
The substratum (dharmin) as excluded from the horse does not exist as "the cow" qualified by that exclusion;
rather, he will state that the exclusion itself is what is excluded.
And if the exclusion from the horse were something other than the non-horseness of the cow-substance, then [there would be a problem] even with the exclusion from the horse.

A cow must be distinguished from the category of "divine substance" (godravya) because of their difference. Consequently, if the cow were not excluded from non-horseness (anaśvatā)—that is, if it did not turn away from that—then it would follow that the cow possesses that very state [of being a horse], just as a horse possesses its own nature. For a cow is excluded from the exclusion of the horse, which is characterized by non-horseness, only if it were itself a horse. And thus, the cow would incur the status of being a horse.
The exclusion of the horse from the cow is its non-existence [in the horse], because the cow and the horse are one [in terms of their shared nature].
Therefore, as for what was stated by the followers of Jaimini:
"If there were an over-extension of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), then everything would be of the nature of everything else."
Regarding this, the following has been said: "If the exclusion of others were a distinct entity, then cows, horses, and so forth would possess identity.
Therefore, that which is the exclusion is itself the excluded.

Nor is the cow's exclusion of the horse non-different from the cow, because it would follow that there would be no cognition of "this is a cow" when the horse is excluded. Furthermore, [if they were non-different], upon the destruction of the cow...

Furthermore, because it would follow that the horse arises [along with the exclusion], and because the negation of the horse would have perished; therefore, there is no such thing as exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) at all. Consequently, as stated by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara: "Is this non-exclusion of the cow (*agopoha*) a distinct entity from the cow?
If it is distinct, is it dependent or independent? (1) If it is dependent, then, because of its dependence, it is a quality (*guṇa*)."

Thus, at that time, by the word "cow" (go), the possessor of the quality (guṇin) is denoted, and not the substance "cow" (godravya). [Otherwise] there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the cow stands. Now, if it were unattached, by what meaning would there be the sense of the genitive case in "the exclusion of the cow" (*gor apohaḥ*)? Furthermore, if this exclusion (*apoha*) were non-different [from the cow], it would simply be the cow itself; thus, nothing undesirable would follow. And if this exclusion were one with respect to each individual object and yet related to many, then that very thing [is what we maintain].
The claim that "it is 'cowness'" is refuted;

for there is no such thing as the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*). Rather, an entity, produced from its own causes in its own specific form, is excluded from others, and it is this exclusion from others that is conceptually constructed. Furthermore, since [the universal] is not a separate...

Exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) exists. Therefore, that which is the exclusion is itself that which is excluded (*vyāvṛtta*), because both [terms] refer to one and the same object. Furthermore, that very thing which is excluded from others possesses the status of being a logical mark (*liṅga*), the status of being the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), the relation [between them], and the state of being an object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For conceptual construction, having superimposed [the external object] as non-different from its own internal form upon that which is excluded from others, causes the person to act toward it.
Because it performs that function, therefore that very external object, excluded from others, is the meaning of the word.
As for what was said by Kumārila— that exclusion might sometimes occur from only one thing,
or from all things— if it were from only one, then just as the substance "cow" is designated as "cow" by way of the exclusion of the horse—

Otherwise, this would apply to the lion and so forth as well, because the exclusion of horses (*aśvāpoha*), which is the cause for the application of the word "cow," exists [in them]. Thus he says: "Therefore, since they consist of the exclusion of horses, all those [beings] such as lions, by possessing that non-exclusion of cows as their cause, could be called 'cows'."

Now, the exclusion (*apoha*) of the substance "cow" must be from everything else. In that case, if horses and so forth were to be excluded individually, then because the objects to be excluded (*apohya*) are infinite, the exclusion itself could not be established. Furthermore, because the objects to be excluded are distinct, a differentiation of the exclusion would follow as a consequence. And thus, even with respect to a single individual (*piṇḍa*), there would arise the cognition of multiple universals (*jāti*) due to the multiplicity of universals, [and] in another universal—
[It would be] like [the exclusion] in the case of horses and so forth. "Therefore, a single universal denoted as 'cow' is not established.
Nor is it possible for all of them to be excluded in the form of a collective aggregate (*samudāya*), for an aggregate exists either as a part or—
It might be argued that it is not possible for the objects to be excluded (*apohya*) to possess a single location or the like; nor does there exist a distinct aggregate of them;
and if they were not distinct [from the aggregate], their infinity remains as it was before. Furthermore, those objects cannot be excluded in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*).
(Ibid., 604. *Sāmānyacintā*)
For the difference in the comprehension of words arises from the difference in convention; there is no difference in the denotatum itself.

But is it not the case that a distinction in convention is untenable? Because [the term] denotes only one of the two, and because, in that case, the negative (vyatirekin) would be a non-entity; furthermore, if it were an object of exclusion (apohya), it would follow that it is a real entity.
This is incorrect, because (1) all things, arising each with its own specific form, [are distinct] from everything else—
Exclusion (apoha) is indeed established by its own causes.

Now, if it is asked how this is known, [we reply: does the nature of the cow—whether past, future, or present—appear in perception? If you say no, then how is it that the exclusion of all [non-cows] is not established by perception in that case?

For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not exclude other things by grasping them with its two hands; rather, its exclusion of others consists precisely in the manifestation of an object of a determinate form. Therefore, the apprehension of the exclusion of everything else by perception is simply the appearance of an object of a determinate form. And that [perception], while ascertaining its own object, ascertains everything that is not thus as being "other"; hence, all [exclusions] are [apprehended] simultaneously.

A negation is made of another [thing] in a general and undifferentiated manner, because a generality (*sāmānya*) consists in a form that has not been determined as a particular. As it has been said: "(1) Because it establishes merely the thing itself as excluded from what does not have that nature. (1)
"It is stated that [the word] has a universal as its object because there is no establishment of a distinction of gender" (*Praśastapādabhāṣya*).

Therefore, it is indeed accepted that whatever is to be excluded (*apohya*) possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastu*). Nor is there any proof for the claim that "being a real entity follows from being something to be excluded," since even a non-entity (*abhāva*) can be something to be excluded.

And it has been stated that this [exclusion] possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastu*). Therefore, because of the exclusion of all [other things] simultaneously—namely, the exclusion of non-cows (*agopoha*)—there is "cowness" (*gotva*) even in a single individual (*piṇḍa*). Furthermore, through the exclusion of each [specific] horse and so forth, various conceptualized classes (*jātibheda*) such as non-horseness, non-lionness, and non-buffalooness are postulated;
and by means of these, the words denoting them function. Thus, this [objection] is trivial.

If there is no difference between the excluded [object] and that which is excluded by the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)—the referent of the expression—how can there be a distinction between the word and the cognition, such as "exclusion" and "excluded"? For instance, "exclusion" is one word, while "excluded" is indeed another word. Likewise, there is also a distinction in cognition: when "exclusion" is stated, only the property (*dharma*) is perceived; when "excluded" is stated, the property-bearer (*dharmin*) is perceived.

Then he says: "(1) *śabdetyādi*. The cognition (*pratīti*) that arises from a word (*śabda*) which denotes a property (*dharma*) or its possessor (*dharmin*) is "verbal apprehension" (*śabdapratipatti*). The compound *śabdaśca śabdapratipattiśca* is a *virūpaikaśeṣa* (an elliptical compound consisting of dissimilar members). The meaning is: "the difference in words" (*śabdabheda*) and "the non-difference of that [cognition] which arises from a word. The convention (*saṃketa*) is the establishment of the relationship between a name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*); [the phrase refers to] the difference of that convention. And the difference of convention has just been explained immediately below.

This will be demonstrated by the passage beginning with "the rejection of other distinctions" (*bhedāntara-pratikṣepa*) and so forth. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "there is no difference in the denotation (*vācya-bheda*) of the two words 'dharma' and 'dharmin'."

The opponent objects with the words "But surely," and so forth. If it is asked, "Why is a difference in convention not appropriate when there is no difference in the object to be denoted? he replies with the words "Of the two," and so forth. This genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). [If it were otherwise,] according to the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti*, since both [agent and object] would be applicable, the rule *karmaṇi* would apply, and thus the use of the genitive case would be improper. If it is argued that this is because the distinctions [of the convention] depend upon that [genitive], then:

(Although there is a single designation for two things,) the case-ending appears as if it were distinct; it follows the meaning as though it were different, due to a slight distinction in what is expressed.

Indeed, the application of words is never dependent upon the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of their objects; for if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that they could not function according to [the speaker's] intention. Just as they are employed by the will of the user regarding difference or non-difference, so do they manifest that object without obstruction. Therefore, although "cow" and "cowness" denote the same object, for someone...

When a linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) is established for the purpose of conveying a distinction (*viśeṣa*), even though there is no difference in meaning, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) appears as if it were expressing a separate referent (*arthāntara*), because it is observed to be used in that way through repeated practice. This is due to the rule of optionality (*vikalpa*) stated as "there is an option regarding the remainder" (*niyamasya śeṣe vibhāṣā*). Thus, by means of the two words *dharma* and *dharmin*, a single object—

The meaning is: because [the two] are denoted [by the same word]. If there were only one [entity], then a convention expressed by two [words] would be redundant. "And likewise" refers to the case where there is no difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*); thus, in the case of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the expression "the cowness of a cow" (*gorgotvam*), which expresses a distinction (*vyatireka*). This is because that genitive case, being a marker of distinction, functions by relying on a real difference (*vastubheda*), just as in the case of "Devadatta's [cow]."

Regarding the term *kamaṇḍalu*: thus, when it has been urged that there is an absence of convention and an absence of a case-ending expressing distinction (*vyatireka*), he first addresses the fault regarding the absence of the case-ending by saying "of the two," and so forth. Even though two words—one denoting the property (*dharma*) and one denoting the substratum (*dharmin*)—express a single object, the case-ending is distinct; that is, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expresses distinction, as if [there were a difference].

The word *bhinna* is displaced [in the compound]; it follows and shows the object as if it were distinct. This is due to a slight (*leśena*) or minimal (*mātrayā*) distinction caused by a difference in convention regarding the denoted meaning (*vācye*), but not from an ultimate difference in the thing itself (*paramārthato vastubhedāt*).
As he explains with the words "Indeed, for words... and so forth: "dependent on the nature of the object" refers to the external particular (*bāhya-svalakṣaṇa*).

[The words] are not dependent [on external objects]. What is the reason? Because, if it were by the power of desire—that is, by the influence of a person's wish—there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [words] could apply even to non-existent things. "Those" refers to words whose application is restricted by desire. In whatever manner they express a distinction, [they may apply] to something distinct, as in "the king's man"; or to something non-distinct, as in "for the self alone is the seer of the self. In the same way...

Words are employed by being applied (*niyukta*) as if they possessed differentiation, even though their referent is non-different; thus, they manifest that referent as if it were differentiated without obstruction. Although, in reality, there is no difference in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), for this reason—by virtue of that cause—he states "cow" (*gauh*) as denoting the substratum (*dharmin*) and "cowness" (*gotva*) as denoting the property (*dharma*). Even though these two express a single [referent], [they indicate] that which is excluded from non-cows (*agovyāvṛtta*).

Even when the word "cow" is employed for the purpose of conveying a certain object, it is for the sake of manifesting "cowness" (*gotva*), which has the exclusion of non-cows (*agovyāvṛtti*) as its cause. When the convention (*saṃketa*) is established such that the word "cowness" denotes merely the exclusion of non-cows, there is a distinction [between the two]. Consequently, the case-ending does not denote a separate meaning; thus, the genitive case occurs in the form "its cowness" (*asya gotvam*), because its meaning is distinct [from the base].
The analysis of the compound is *ssab* (the *s* and *b*). It appears as if it were presenting a property (*dharma*) as something distinct from the substratum (*dharmī*), such as ether;

however, this does not imply that there is a difference everywhere. For even elsewhere, there is no restriction on the application [of a term] based on the whim of the speaker. Just as a single thing is expressed in the singular number in some cases, even though there is no distinction [in the object], due to the desire for respectful designation.
It is made known by means of the plural number.

If it is argued that there would be no distinction between conventions due to the absence of a purpose, that too certainly exists. Thus: "The exclusion and non-exclusion of other differences in those two [terms] are the basis for the distinction of convention, which follows the desire of the cognizer. (63)
"Even in the case of a different object"—that is, even when the property is non-distinct—what is the reason? It is because of the habitual observation of the use [of the genitive] in such cases.
When there is a difference in entities (*vastu*), there is the habitual observation of the use of the genitive, as in "Devadatta’s water-pot" (*devadattasya kamaṇḍaluḥ*) and so forth.
What is meant is this: whether the entity be distinct or not, in every case, the case-ending expressing distinction (*vyatireka-vibhakti*)—
It conforms merely to the requirements of the meter; it is solely through the habit of observing usage that it makes the word and its meaning appear as if distinct.

"To that extent" means simply by the employment of the case-ending. "In all cases" means even where there is no difference in meaning, as in "cow" (*gauḥ*) and "cowness" (*gotvam*), for there is no ultimate difference between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substrate (*dharmin*). Therefore, in other instances as well, even when there is no difference in meaning, [the distinction] proceeds by virtue of human intention.

Because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) for a word that expresses exclusion (*vyatireka*).
