Furthermore, he states that the application of words is observed to depend on human intention even when such an external denotatum does not exist, beginning with the words "For example" (*yathā*) and so forth. A single object is expressed by the singular number in a certain context, as in "you" (*tvam*); even though there is no difference in that [object], its singularity—

Even when there is a distinction, that same entity is expressed by the plural "you" (*yūyam*). Therefore, because the plural is observed even when referring to a single thing, it is understood that the application of words does not correspond exactly to the actual state of things. If it is argued that the plural occurs even for a single entity due to the extended rule (*atideśa*)—"some [grammarians] hold that [the suffixes] for *yuṣmad* [are used] in the sense of the singular"—this must be examined: does the extended rule produce plurality in what is actually one?

Or is it that the mere plural number, which was not previously established, is being prescribed? (1) It cannot be the first alternative, because it is impossible to establish real entities by means of mere words. Even in the second alternative, it is already established that the application of words occurs solely through the power of intention. Thus, for now, the fault regarding the absence of case-endings has been avoided.
He introduces that very point in order to avoid the fault of the absence of convention: "(1) 'But because there is no purpose,' etc.
There is no purpose because a single thing is denoted by both the word for the subject (*dharmin*) and the word for the property (*dharma*). Yet, that purpose certainly exists:
namely, the exclusion or non-acceptance of other differences relative to "cowness" (*gotva*), such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), earthiness (*pārthivatva*), and so forth.

Those two— rejection and non-rejection— are, respectively, the purpose (*pada*)— that is, the motive— of that distinction in convention (*saṃketabheda*) belonging to those two words which express either the property (*dharma*) or the substratum (*dharmin*), and which is characterized by conforming to the desire for knowledge, meaning it follows the intention of the cognizer.

This is what is meant: when a cognizer, having no further expectation regarding the form excluded from others, desires to know merely the exclusion of "horse" with respect to a particular individual object— without depending on the existence of that which is excluded from it— then he is awakened by a word for which a convention has been established to convey such knowledge, [with the understanding] that "there is no horse here."

Thus: when one desires to know that [cow] without any further desire for the exclusion of other [exclusions], then, in order to manifest it as such, one desires to know the cow-individual as something not excluded from others. At that time, as long as one does not speak—by means of a worldly word denoting a property (*dharma*) preceded by a convention—having superposed an exclusion from horses that is a distinct entity, the listener’s desire to know [it] will not be satisfied.

The meaning [of the term] can be established; therefore, with respect to that, it is said that "it is not a horse. For in this way, because the subject (*dharmin*) is not primary, there is no implication of a form excluded from others, and there is exclusion from only one thing, namely, the horse.
It is not stated in that way as "not a horse," for by that [expression], there would be an implication of a form that is already excluded from others.

Furthermore, how could one who speaks of what has not been sought after by another— indeed, what has not even been inquired about— not be insane? Moreover, when someone desires to know a cow-individual as distinguished from a horse, insofar as its form is expectant of the exclusion of others, even then,
as long as one superimposes the individual as being of the nature of a property (*dharma*) characterized by the exclusion of horses, and likewise, based on convention, [speaks] to a worldly person...

As long as one does not speak by means of a term that denotes the subject (*dharmin*), the object desired to be known by another cannot be communicated; therefore, with respect to that [subject], it is said, "this is a non-horse. For in this way, through the predominance of the subject, there is an implication of a form excluded from others, and the mass of matter that is a cow is described as being excluded from horses. It is not, however, at that time explained as "non-horseness" (*anaśvatva*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of implying a form that is excluded from other things, which is not what the other person wishes to know. Furthermore, how could one who speaks of a matter not intended to be known not be insane? Moreover, all verbal communication is preceded by convention, and convention itself is necessarily preceded by an object constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*);
therefore, it is logical that even through conceptual thoughts, the cognition of the relationship between property and property-bearer occurs by this very same door.

Therefore, what was said—that while there may be an activity directed toward the exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions regarding the designations of properties (*dharma*) and property-bearers (*dharmin*), how is there a comprehension of the conceptual constructions of property and property-bearer?—is refuted.
Clarifying this very point through the commentary, he says: "When this," and so forth. "Comprehension" refers to the listener. Therefore...

That which is other than the horse and so forth—such as the buffalo and so forth—is the "exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*). Its nature, which is excluded from the buffalo and so forth, is independent of those [other] entities; it does not depend upon them. This occurs with respect to a specific individual, such as a cow. One desires to know merely the exclusion from the horse: "Does this [cow] possess a form that is distinct from the horse? It is for the purpose of making known that which is of such a nature, just as it is desired to be known by the cognizer.

In accordance with that [intention], for the purpose of making known the mere difference from a horse of such a [referent], the term "non-horseness" (*anaśvatva*) is awakened—that is, revealed—by a word whose convention has been established for the mere exclusion of horses, having set aside other differences, as in: "this particular object possesses non-horseness. This is in relation to the exclusion from horses; [it is] the differentiation from buffaloes and so forth.
There are other exclusions (*vyavaccheda*). The cognizer has no further desire regarding them. "That" refers to the whole (*piṇḍa*).
This means that he wishes to know the substance "cow" as being conjoined with the exclusion of "horse," while not rejecting other internal distinctions.

It is that in which other internal distinctions, such as the exclusion of "buffalo" and so forth, have not been abandoned; [it is] in that [substance] where other internal distinctions have not been abandoned.

In that very case of the exclusion of the horse (*aśva-vyavaccheda*), speakers employ a word denoting the subject (*dharmin*) as "this is not a horse" (*anaśvo 'yam*). To the question "How do they employ it?", he says: "For the sake of such manifestation. That is to say, [they employ it] for the sake of manifesting that which has other differences unexcluded, while having other differences excluded—namely, "this is not a horse. This is the investigation of the universal (*sāmānya-cintā*).

They employ grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on the function of words; for this very reason, there is no relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) with another difference that was previously rejected. [For example: "The cow-nature of this is white..."

It is like the case of "cow-ness" (*gotva*). Because the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the substratum of that [exclusion], does not appear as a unity due to the particularity of that [exclusion] alone, [the word] is for the purpose of manifesting the delimitation (*vyavaccheda*).

Others read: "The exclusion of the horse is manifested precisely as that which has its internal differences un-rejected. Even in that case, the meaning is this: the exclusion of the horse is precisely that which has its internal differences un-rejected.
They employ a form of exclusion; that is, they express it by means of a word denoting the substratum (*dharmin*), such as "this is not a non-horse. For what purpose?

It is for the sake of manifesting [the object] in that manner—that is, for the manifestation of that which has other differences excluded. Precisely because the word denoting the property (*dharma*) excludes other differences, for that very reason, in the previous case regarding the word denoting the property, the difference was excluded.

Regarding the phrase "by which there is another interval": one should form an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) by taking the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) in a general sense; subsequently, it is to be connected with the words "because of the function of the word. Otherwise, it would result in the statement "it is rejected because it is a different kind of distinction. In this same way, the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) should be understood for other words of this class as well.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the occurrence of two words with distinct causes [of application] in a single substratum. The relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*) is the relationship of that which is excluded and that which excludes. An example is: "His cow-nature is white" (*gotvam asya śuklam*).
Others read "white" (*śukla*) as masculine, [arguing] that the word for a quality possesses gender like its denoted object; thus, [the example would be] "his cow is white. In this way...

They explain as follows: (1) A word denoting a quality (*guṇaśabda*), when employed while referring to the quality alone by excluding other distinctions, takes the masculine gender—as in the case of words such as *śukla* ("white") which function solely to denote a quality. However, for those [words] that refer to the substratum possessing that quality (*tadvat*), the gender is that of the thing to be expressed (*abhidheyaliṅgatā*). Thus, there can be neither grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) nor a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between these two, as they both function solely to denote a property (*dharmamātra*).
Regarding the phrase "the state of being the qualified" (*viśeṣyabhāva*):

why is there no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? To this he says: "In that alone," and so forth. This explains that coreferentiality with the object and so on exists only within the appearance of the cognition; it does not exist in the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because the latter is inexpressible.

(1) Or rather, it is spoken of as being external merely by way of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). Furthermore, if a single cognition produced by two words were to arise with respect to a single object endowed with two properties, then there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). But in this case, the cognition—which has that [cow] as its substratum—is colored solely by the qualifier "cowness," wherein other differences have been excluded by that very [qualifier].

Thus, there is no relation of qualifier and qualified, because [the object] does not appear as a single substratum (*dharmin*) due to its lack of unity— which is the basis for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). The meaning is that it does not appear to the cognition after having grasped a single substratum conjoined with both "cowness" and "whiteness."

Or rather, [it refers to] "of that which has it as its substrate": that is, because the cow-individual does not appear as identical with that cognition—which has that very *gotva* (cowness) as its substrate—by means of that specific [aspect], namely *gotva* alone, which excludes other properties;
for in the usage "this has *gotva*," one perceives the property (*dharma*) in its abstracted form.
And because it is free from further expectancy.
But in the second case, it does occur; thus, in accordance with convention, there is a differentiation by means of a property that has withdrawn all exclusions (*vyavaccheda*).
Because it appears as if it were a single thing and because it depends upon the exclusion of others,
there is no difference whatsoever in the denotable object between two words— one expressing a substance and the other expressing a state— everywhere. (64)

Therefore, in all cases involving words denoting properties (dharma) or property-bearers (dharmin), cognition does not arise with respect to the expressed object as being the domain of a determinate conceptual cognition (*niścaya-pratyaya*). Consequently, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, because the cognition excludes other properties and is thus free from expectancy regarding other distinctions, there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*).

In the second case, however, regarding the position that words denote the substratum (*dharmin*), there occurs either grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), as in "the white cow. He states the cause for this coreferentiality with the words beginning "tathā" (in that way). "In that way" means according to convention (*saṃketa*); that is, by the cause which is the convention, the word denoting the substratum applies to a single object—a thing in which other distinctions have not been excluded.

"Conjunction in the locus (*dharmī*) is withdrawal. "Exclusion-properties" (*vyavacchedadharmāḥ*) are properties whose cause is exclusion; they are "withdrawn" (*saṃhṛtāḥ*), and being all such exclusion-properties, this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. By means of these [properties], which function as instruments, there is "that which possesses division"—namely, the locus (*dharmī*) which possesses many divided properties. This is because the single [locus] possessing many divided properties appears to the intellect through the presentation and manifestation of words. [Thus, it is] "possessing many properties" (*anekadharma-*)...

The meaning is that cognition appears as if it were displaying a single substratum (*dharmin*) possessing properties. However, the substratum displayed in the appearance of cognition is not actually one, because the distinction between property and substratum constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) is unreal. Some also read "of the one alone" (*ekasyaiva*); even in that case, it is logical [to understand it] solely by virtue of the determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) of the cognizer.

This is how it should be understood. Consequently, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established. Furthermore, because the word denoting the substratum (*dharmin*) functions without excluding other distinctions, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) arises for the cognition produced by it—since that cognition depends upon other distinctions not excluded—such as "the cow is white" or "blue. And the word "and" (*ca*) is used as before to indicate what has passed.
Dependent upon causes.

He states that this alone is the pervader of all linguistic usage, and not anything else imagined by others, such as universals (sāmānya), qualities (guṇa), and so forth, because those [entities] are sublated by valid cognition (pramāṇa). He says: "This very difference," and so on. This very difference between two words—one denoting a substance (dravya) and the other denoting an entity (bhāva)—is characterized by the exclusion or non-exclusion of other properties (dharmāntara). "Everywhere" means in both the universal (sāmānya) and the possessor of the universal (sāmānyavat).

In the case of "possessor of qualities" (*guṇavat*) and "quality" (*guṇa*), or "possessor of action" (*kriyāvat*) and "action" (*kriyā*), with respect to every object, the term denoting the substratum (*dharmin*) is a designator of substance (*dravya*),

while the term denoting the attribute (*dharma*) is a designator of state (*bhāva*). Since this is so, for that reason, there is in reality no distinction whatsoever between the expressed objects of those two terms, "substance" and "state."
He explains that [with the words] "Therefore," and so forth. By means of being the object of a determinative cognition (*niścaya-pratyaya*), there is no distinction whatsoever.

For instance, just as when "cowness" (*gotva*) is stated, there is a determination precisely regarding the exclusion of the non-cow (*agovyavaccheda*), so too, although when "cow" (*go*) is stated there is a denotation of that which is excluded from the non-cow while other differences remain unrepudiated, nevertheless, there is no distinct particular (*viśeṣa*) that effects the exclusion of the non-cow; it is one and the same.
"Make go"—this alone is the distinction.

4. The investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*) indicates that [the speaker], having set aside other distinctions, desires to make known another object by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) or a primary derivative (*kṛt*), without excluding [those other distinctions].
Or if one were to say it by means of something else, there would be no difference other than that. ||65||

One should demonstrate [the object] to such an extent for the purpose of making known its actual state (*tathābhūta*). It is equally appropriate to demonstrate it by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), as in "pāka" (cooking), or by means of a primary suffix (*kṛt*), as in "pacet" (one should cook), or even by means of one's own conventional terminology. By the mere act of denoting it in such a way, there is certainty regarding that very [object], while other distinctions are merely not excluded. And that alone is the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*) wherein the verbal [cognition] occurs.

Since certainty arises [in this way], there is no difference in the expressed object (*vācya*) between two words that denote an existent entity (*bhāva*) or a substance (*dravya*); rather, they differ merely in whether they exclude other distinctions (*bhedāntara*). This is stated here: "One [is] that very same," and so forth.
"One" refers to the word for the property (*dharmaśabda*); "that" refers to what is excluded from non-cows. That word for the property by which other distinctions are excluded is described as such.

The word "other" (*anya*) is a term denoting a substratum (*dharmin*); since it does not exclude that very same individual (*piṇḍa*), it conveys it through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Thus, there is no difference regarding the determination of the substance; the only difference lies in mere exclusion (*pratikṣepa*) or non-exclusion (*apratikṣepa*). In the same way, in the case of "the going of Devadatta" and "Devadatta goes," there is no difference whatsoever; this should be applied similarly in other cases as well.

He states that even the fourfold application of words—distinguished by genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and relation (*sambandha*)—is subsumed by this very same differentiation of properties inherent in the object, beginning with the words "desiring to make known" (*jijñāpayiṣu*), and so forth. One who desires to make an object known [employs a word] characterized by the exclusion or non-exclusion of other differentiations; [this occurs] by means of a *taddhita* [derivative], that is, one ending in a *taddhita* suffix, or also by means of a *kṛt* [suffix]. A *kṛt*...

Or if one were to express it by means of a word ending in a suffix denoting cognition (*jña*), or by any other word— whether a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) distinct from primary and secondary nominal suffixes (*kṛt-taddhita*), or an underived word (*avyutpanna*) such as "white" (*śukla*)— then there would be no further distinction [between these cases] than the specific characteristic of whether other distinctions are excluded or not excluded.
He explains this with the words beginning "to such an extent" (*etāvantam*). "To such an extent" refers to that which is characterized by the exclusion of other distinctions.
The connection is: "or even when it has been performed, he would show [it].
This applies when the root *pac* (to cook) occurs in reference to an action such as placing [the pot] on the fire, which resides in the agent, and the suffix *ghañ* is applied to that very [action].

In that case, since the relation between the action and its agent is denoted by the term "cooking-ness" (*pācakatva*) as inherence (*samavāya*), the word "cooking" (*pāka*) has the same meaning as the term "cooking-ness. Both of these convey an object that excludes the non-cooker, with no other distinction between them rejected. However, when the action of cooking, namely the softening (*viklitti*) residing in the object, is the meaning of the root *pac*, then...

How can the word *pācakatva* (the state of being a cook) denote a relation? For there is a difference in meaning between *pācakatva* and *pāka* (cooking). Or rather, it would denote something else entirely distinct from what was intended—namely, something other than a primary derivative (*kṛt*) or a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)—such as a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and so forth. This is because the word has been conventionally established (*saṃketa*) to denote such [an unintended] thing for the sake of making that known.

But is it not the case that there is no relationship between the cooker and the act of cooking? As it has been said: "Indeed, no one distinct from the act of cooking is designated as 'the cooker. Whatever is its [the act's] designatum, that alone is the designatum; that very same thing is also designated by the term 'cook-ness. These phenomena are false conceptual constructions lacking any foundation."

The connection is that one should demonstrate [the meaning] by means of a convention established by oneself for the purpose of making known other distinctions, as in the examples "Devadatta sleeps" and "the whiteness of the cloth. Here too, the very same meaning that belongs to the word *śāyaka* (the sleeper) is the same when it is [expressed as] *śayyate* (is slept), with other distinctions rejected. Likewise, in the case of "the white cloth," the very same [meaning] that is excluded from what is non-white has its other distinctions rejected.
The very same object that is [already] delimited is what is meant by "the whiteness of the cloth," once other distinctions have been excluded.

By the mere act of such a designation, that very entity—which is in reality nothing other than a distinct object—is simply differentiated into the forms of property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*). However, it does not actually become something else; this is the connection [of the argument]. What is the reason? Because for an entity that is already of such a nature, whether other distinctions are excluded or not excluded...
This is because the term *dharma-adharma* has been established as a convention for the purpose of making known that very single [entity];
or rather, it is by the mere mention of such a designation— that is,
by the mere mention of a property (*dharma*) that is distinct from the [substratum]— that its being a property of that [substratum] [is understood].

Form, in the ultimate sense, is indeed a distinct entity; for the word "property" (*dharma*) has been conventionally established to indicate that very same [form], which is independent of other distinctions and excluded from everything else.

"Now, [it might be objected]... and so forth—the opponent speaks. "A relation is expressed" means that the relation between the action of cooking and the agent, the cook, is characterized as inherence (*samavāya*). For it is observed that a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) following a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix expresses a relation, as it has been said: "In compounds, *kṛt* derivatives, and *taddhita* derivatives, there is the expression of a relation. And the word "cook" (*pācaka*) ends in a *kṛt* suffix.
Regarding the word *śabda*: (1) it is not the case that the action (*kriyā*) itself, which consists of cooking, is expressed by the word "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*).
What is meant is this: the action is indeed distinct from the agent, and the relationship between the two is likewise distinct.
Consequently, even though the action residing in the agent is denoted by the verbal root *pac* ("to cook"), [the word] "cooking" (*pāka*) and the word "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*) [are not identical].

Regarding the statement "the meaning is the same," he refutes it with the words "not indeed by cooking" (*na vai pākena*), and so forth. By "cooking" (*pāka*), there is no agent who is distinct from the action of cooking and called "the cooker" (*pācaka*)—as described by the Vaiśeṣikas and others as being independent and separate from the action—merely through a non-substantial operation residing in the agent. Rather, the word "cooker" denotes such an agent.

The meaning is this: where there would be a relationship between an agent (*kartṛ*) and an action (*kriyā*) that is a real entity (*vastubhūta*), [it would have to be so] because that independent agent is distinct from the action, and such an agent will be refuted. If the action is not distinct [from the agent], nor is the agent distinct [from the action], then how could there be a relationship whose expression by means of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is proposed? Furthermore, as for the word "pācaka" (cook) in the phrase "of this... [the following applies].

The denotable object (*abhidheya*) is that which is excluded from non-cookers (*apācaka*), not rejecting other distinctions, and is the mere thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*). Just as it is understood that the action is neither separate [from the agent] nor its inherence (*samavāya*).

Therefore, the description of the "possessor of that" (tadvat) position regarding the object of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) has been rejected; for if there were a difference [between them], the fault pertaining to the universal (jāti) and its possessor would arise. (66)

The objection that was stated—namely, that "even when there is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because a qualified object is denoted by words, all the aforementioned consequences would equally apply to the position [that the word denotes] that [qualified object]"—is also refuted by this [following argument]. For in that case, one must supply the phrase:
"the denotation of the word is also denoted as being a cook. This is because that very [denotation], from which other distinct differences have been rejected—

Because that [the universal] is denoted; however, the relation is not denoted, because it does not exist as a real entity. By the word "also" (*api*), it is meant that what is denoted by the word "cook" (*pācaka*) is indeed the same thing denoted by the word "cooking" (*pāka*). There is another explanation: "not indeed by cooking" means that, according to the position of those who advocate the theory of exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), it is something entirely different [from the individual] by means of the word "cooking."

A "cook" is designated as the substratum of a distinct action, such as it is described by the opponent—that which would be the substratum of the relationship between an action and its factors. Since that [distinct action] is unestablished, however, what is expressed is the exclusion of the non-cook (*apācaka*), by way of rejecting other differences. He states this very point with the words "But that which... and so forth. The word "that which" (*yat*) refers to the characteristic of the exclusion of the non-cook.

The object of denotation, which excludes other distinct entities, has been shown immediately following the word "pāka" (cooking); that very same object denoted by the word "pāka" is also denoted by the word "pācakatva" (the state of being a cook), but it is not a [real] relation, because such a relation is unestablished.
Indeed, these false conceptual constructions arise from unstable [minds] and do not derive from the power of real entities.

But how is it understood that there is no action distinct [from the substance], nor its inherence [in it]? To this he says: "Just as... and so forth. "Or its inherence" means the inherence of the action and the factors of action (*kāraka*). And because there is no difference between exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and that which possesses exclusion (*vyāvṛttimat*), for that reason, a word denotes that which possesses a universal (*jātimat*) as having the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object. (1) That—58a...

The objection raised against the position that [the word denotes] "that which possesses it" (tadvat) would also apply to the theory of exclusion of others (anyāpoha); thus, the description of that position is rejected.

For if the universal (jāti) and the possessor of the universal were admitted to be distinct, then the fault mentioned regarding the position of "that which possesses it" would indeed arise. However, since words denote an object qualified by that [exclusion], namely an object qualified by the exclusion of others (anyāpohaviśiṣṭa), the fault mentioned regarding the position of "that which possesses it" does not apply.

The same [objection] applies to the position that has been stated: namely, that if a word, having denoted a universal (*sāmānya*), were to apply to the possessor of that universal (*tadvat*), it would be non-independent; and consequently, because a word controlled by a universal—which serves as the ground for its application—would not imply the mutual differences residing in the individuals, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would not occur. Furthermore, the application of the word to the possessor of the universal would be merely figurative (*upacarita*).

Having thus stated the exclusion (*vyāvṣtti*)—namely, that the fault begins with "subsistence" (*vṛtti*) and so forth—it would follow that every sound (*dhvani*) existing in that which possesses it (*tadvat*) would be independent (*asvatantra*). That too is a description of the position of the "possessor" (*tadvat-pakṣa*). By this [statement], the objection is refuted and rejected on the grounds that there is no difference between the exclusion and that which possesses the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-vyāvṛtti-matoḥ*); for in that case, in the position of the "possessor," it would be a different object (*arthāntara*).

In the case of [the word] "cow," based on a real universal (*sāmānya*) existing in one thing, [the word] applies to another object that possesses it. Because it does not directly denote the possessor of the universal, it lacks independence. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the faults of non-co-referentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇya*) and metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) is intended.

However, in the theory of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), since there is identity between the exclusion and that which is excluded, a word does not apply to another object by taking up a different entity.

Because a word that functions by taking up a different referent lacks independence, there is no fault of contradiction; for it has been stated that the exclusion from another is not distinct from the excluded object itself, since both are denoted by a single term.
This may be so.

How, then, can the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) be a universal (*sāmānya*), given that one excluded thing does not follow into another? [The answer is: because it appears as such in the cognition thereof. Indeed, there is no universal at all. Rather, a cognition based on words arises through the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), joining together even those properties that are not actually conjoined. It is the appearance of an unreal objective form (*asadarthākāra*).

By means of this [exclusion], both the universal and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) are established, because there is no difference among the objects themselves. Therefore, he says "nor... and so forth, stating that there is no fault such as lack of independence (*asvātantrya*) regarding the occurrence [of the term], since the exclusion from another entity is not different from that which is excluded. Of the two words—one expressing the property (*dharma*) and the other the property-bearer (*dharmin*)—of one...

It was stated immediately prior that this is because of the expression of a distinction between exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). The opponent asks, "How so? and so forth. "Now" refers to the identity between the exclusion and its possessor (*tadvat*). Because a single excluded particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not inclusive (*ananugama*), and because it does not associate with other objects (*arthāntara-asamsarga*), how could [the universal] be of the nature of that particular?
If exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) were non-concomitant like a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it would not be a universal (*sāmānya*). This is not so; for it is observed as a universal.

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) states this with the words "In the cognition of that," and so forth. Since it appears in a conceptual cognition of a universal in a single form, it is precisely a single form that is excluded by this [cognition]; thus it is called "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*). It is called a "universal. This is what he says.

(1) Among distinct particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is no single exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) that constitutes their essence as a universal (*sāmānya*). Rather, it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising at a time subsequent to the experience of the distinct particular characteristics that, by its very nature, arises as if displaying a single form among entities that produce a single effect. On account of that conceptual construction, a universal is postulated—[though in reality] there is no universal among those [particulars].
And by this [verse], the object consisting of sound and so forth has been directly shown.
Clarifying this very point, he says: "Not anything at all," and so on. The intended meaning is that [the object] does not exist as a real entity (*vastubhūta*).

If so, how is there the conventional usage of universals (*sāmānya*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and so forth? To this he says: "Sound," and so on. Sound is the basis (*āśraya*) and the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*).

That conceptual cognition which arises by the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*anādivāsanā*), having as its cause the [non-existence] of [external] objects, brings about even properties that are not actually conjoined, making them appear as if they were of a single form. By virtue of the appearance of a single form in that cognition, there is a universal (*sāmānya*). And by virtue of the non-appearance of a single substratum (*ekāśraya*) endowed with two properties, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

It is established. Furthermore, this conventional usage of "universal" (*sāmānya*) and so forth is established as pervading what is non-existent. To the question "In what way does it have a non-existent object?
he says: "Of objects," and so on. Because there is no conjunction of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the conventional usage of "universal" has a non-existent object;
and because there is no difference in a single particular characteristic, the conventional usage of "coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has a non-existent object.
[Objection: But since this entire conventional discourse proceeds by way of dissimilarity (*virūpatā*), how can it have the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object?

To this, he says: [the connection is with the phrase] "the objects of all that conventional discourse, such as universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, are the common basis. Furthermore, its effect is "conformity" (*tatsamānatā*). This is the universal-cognition (*sāmānyabuddhi*).

And it is the common substratum for all of that. Objects, being distinguished from others by virtue of being its causes and effects, constitute the substratum. A word, moreover, operates by excluding what is undesired; therefore, it is said to have "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) as its object.
In that regard, disregarding the reality of external objects, [the word]—by the power of the mental appearance—is a single entity excluded from many.

By means of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)— which arise from the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by words and their corresponding experiences— and which have as their object that very nature [of the thing] as determined by them, things become the basis for all conventional usage such as "universal" (*sāmānya*) and so forth, because they are distinguished from others— that is, from those things which do not possess such causes and effects. For this reason, they are distinct from others.

It has been stated that [exclusion] has exclusion as its object: (1) however, exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) does not appear therein, because it is the external object itself, appearing in a single form, that appears as a positive entity (*vidhirūpa*). Furthermore, since a person impelled by a determinative cognition (*niścaya*) is led toward the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which is excluded from the undesirable—by avoiding what is undesirable, for this reason also it is said to have exclusion of others as its object, but [exclusion] itself does not appear.
[The word] is dependent [on its object], because it appears as an injunction.
Therefore, as stated by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara: "What is the nature of the referent of the word 'cow'—is it an existent or a non-existent?
If it is an existent, is it a cow or a non-cow? If it is a cow, there is no dispute. If it is a non-cow, then a non-cow is the referent of the word 'cow'."

Thus ends the discussion on the extreme skill [of the opponent]. Now, as for the claim that it is non-existence, that is incorrect. For upon hearing the word "cow," there is no comprehension by the person being addressed regarding non-existence. Furthermore, the meaning of a word is understood through comprehension, yet no one comprehends non-existence from the word "cow.
Likewise, regarding this exclusion (*apoha*) expressed as "a cow is not [non-cow]," does it have the cow as its object or the non-cow as its object? If it has the cow as its object, how...
Non-existence is indeed like a cow. Now, if it has the non-cow as its object, how can there be a cognition of one thing through an exclusion (*apoha*) that has a different object?

For when a *khadira* tree is being cut, the cutting does not occur in a *palāśa* tree. Or, if it is the negation of "cow" in the form "it is not a non-cow," [we ask: by what means was "non-cowness" attributed to the cow such that it must now be negated?
(1) [The objection] has been refuted: since the word "cow" has the actual cow as its object, the dispute arises solely because [the opponent] assumes it has a conceptualized object.
Or, just as the negation of "cow" occurs even in the absence of superimposition, so it has been stated; thus, the claim that "it is not so" is trivial.
Therefore, it remains established that the meaning of a word is indeed a positive injunction (*vidhi*).

Demonstrating this very point, he says: "In that regard," and so forth. That which is called "the subject" (*dharmin*) is that which, by its own nature, does not depend upon an external reality, but appears as a mental construct (*vikalpa-buddhi*). It is said to be "unitary and excluded from the manifold" by virtue of appearing to the mind; for it appears to the intellect through the presentation of a single subject that is excluded from many [other things]. By virtue of that [appearance], it is unitary.

The substratum (*dharmin*) is established as excluded from many [other things]. The sense is that since it is excluded from many, conceptual distinctions (*dharmabheda*) are imagined therein as exclusions from those [many things]. That very real substratum is made the object of words, because speakers utter words in order to produce a conceptual appearance (*vikalpapratibhāsa*) corresponding to such a [real] state of affairs. And because it is excluded from others...

The appearance in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is made the object of words; therefore, the status of being an object of affirmation (*vidhi*) is established—this is the intended meaning. [Objection: It is indeed so. And in that very context, the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) consists precisely in their being inexpressible as either identical or different from one another.
This is elaborated as follows:

A property (*dharma*) is certainly not other than the substratum (*dharmin*), because it would then be designated as a separate entity (*anarthāntara*). Nor is it identical to it, because that would entail the consequence that just like words denoting the substratum, words denoting the property would also imply the exclusion of other [properties]. And thus, [the desired] non-cognition would not be established.

From this [reasoning], there is no differentiation of conventions. Regarding the referent of a word, there is an inexpressibility of both the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*). In the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the real entity, the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is inexpressible because it does not exist [there].
He states that it is not only by words but also by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that it is not made an object: "The experience of that," and so forth. Of that...

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: the experience of that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is "that experience" (*tadanubhava*); the latent impression (*vāsanā*), which is a capacity, is "produced by that" (*tenāhitā*); its awakening is "the arousal of that" (*tasyāḥ prabodhaḥ*); and those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) whose birth is "conducive to the production of an effect" (*kāryotpādānuguṇya*) from that [awakening] are "those whose object is made manifest" (*tadviṣayīkriyante*).

What is the meaning of the phrase "having determined that state" (*adhyavasitatadbhāva*)? It means that in which the "state of being that" (*tadbhāva*), namely the external state, has been determined (*adhyavasita*).

"Those conceptual constructions for which the object is such that it consists precisely in the non-existence of that [external thing] within the appearance of the conceptual construction—this is what is meant by 'those [conceptual constructions] being thus'. In other words, this refers to proceeding by unifying the perceived and the conceptualized.

"Adhyavasita-tadbhāvārtha" is an alternative reading; it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that object which has the nature of being determined. The connection is that even a single [entity], when excluded from others, is the "object whose nature is determined.
Therefore, the linguistic convention of "universal" (*sāmānya*) and so forth arises by virtue of the appearance in cognition (*buddhipratibhāsa*). And precisely in that appearance in cognition—
The term "this" (*ayam*) is characterized by the exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions. "Linguistic usage" (*vyavahāra*)—derived as a *karmasādhana*—means that which is used.
Linguistic usage pertains precisely to the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*).
This is what is meant: those two, the property and the substratum, which are established within the appearance of cognition (*buddhipratibhāsa*), [are the objects of linguistic usage].
It is elaborated that [the self] is inexpressible in terms of identity with or difference from [its attributes]. Therefore,

it is implied that the fault previously stated regarding the positions of the ultimate reality of either identity or difference between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*)— namely, the futility of other means of valid cognition and the like, characterized by independence and so forth— does not apply here.

He states another fault regarding the two positions of identity and difference: "For it is not," and so forth. A property (*dharma*) is not other than the substratum (*dharmin*). Why? Because there is no designation of a different object; for by the two words "property" and "substratum," only one excluded [entity] is designated. Nor is that which is the substratum the very same as the property. Why? Because by the word denoting that...

[This is] like [the case of] words that denote properties (*dharma*). For even in the case of words denoting properties, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of implying another exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). And because it would not communicate what is intended; for by the word "property" (*dharma*), the specific difference (*bheda*) that is intended—namely, one from which other excluded differences have been rejected—is not communicated. Therefore, [the proponent] does not establish a distinct convention (*saṃketa*); rather, it communicates the exclusion that has rejected other differences.

The non-establishment of this particular convention, namely the word "dharma," refers to what was just stated: that the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) are inexpressible in terms of identity or difference with respect to the objects appearing in words and cognitions. As for the phrase "in reality" (*vastuni*), it refers to external particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Because they do not exist [externally], they are inexpressible as identical or different; however, the object of words and so forth functions according to how it appears.
[The term] is established. 4. Consideration of the Universal:

Now, if there is non-difference or difference between the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*), the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and others are observed [to be used]. In that case, when many properties are involved, a diversity of verbal expression is observed; however, it would not be logical for such a diversity of expression to occur with respect to a single property-bearer.
It has been stated here: "Indeed, words do not depend upon their own intrinsic nature. Moreover:
"For those for whom words are governed by the actual state of things, and not dependent on the speaker's intention,"
The objection regarding the difference in case endings, such as the genitive, is appropriate when directed against them. //67//

If these [words] were intended to be directed toward something specific, like smoke and so forth due to a necessary connection with an object, they could not indeed be employed by persons at will; in that case, how could there be the objection, "How is it that the sixth [case-ending] and so forth [are used]?"?
Furthermore:
"In whatever way a word is employed by speakers as a signifier, it is a signifying expression in that way, regardless of the reality of the external object. (68)
"Now, [it may be argued]... and so forth—the opponent says: "Seen" means observed in actual usage.

The genitive case in "the cowness of a cow" (*gorgotvam*) is used; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one includes such usages as "cowness is established in the cow," or "the word 'cow' applies to the cow on the basis of the cause that is cowness"—this is the inclusion of various case-endings. Furthermore, because there are many properties (*dharma*) such as cowness, substantiality, and so forth, [the question arises] regarding those many properties.

"The distinction observed in the expressions 'cowness,' 'substantiality,' and 'earthiness' would not exist" (1)— if there were no ultimate distinction between the property and the property-bearer, nor mutual distinction among the properties themselves—
thus says the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin). "Indeed, the [functioning] of words does not depend at all upon the intrinsic nature of their objects."
Because it has been stated [in the text] beginning with "the mode of subsistence" (vṛtti), etc.

Furthermore, he says "api ca" and so forth, in order to establish [the point] by means of an additional qualification. For those disputants whose words are "under the sway of the thing" (*vastuvaśāḥ*), that is, dependent upon the actual object (*vastvāyattāḥ*), and not "dependent primarily on the speaker's intention" (*vivakṣāparāśrayāḥ*)— that is,
those words for which the speaker's intention alone is the primary basis (*paraḥ pradhānaḥ āśrayaḥ*)— there would be no genitive case, nor the variation of number and so forth.

"‘They would not exist’—this is the objection regarding the genitive case, the difference in number, and so forth; that is, the objection concerning the genitive case, the difference in number, and so forth. By the word ‘and so forth,’ the objection regarding the absence of *taddhita* suffixes in expressions such as ‘the state of a cow is cow-ness (*gotva*)’ is included. Against those who maintain the reality [of external objects], this is logical: these words, beginning with the genitive, are intended to be applied in certain instances even when there is no difference in the underlying entity."

[The opponent objects: "They are sweet [i.e., logically flawed], because they are tied to real entities (*vastu*), that is, because they are dependent upon real entities, like smoke and so forth. For smoke, which is tied to fire, is capable of conveying fire; it cannot, by contrast, be employed to convey water. Thus, if words were tied to real entities, this objection would arise: 'If there is no exclusion (*vyatireka*), how can there be the genitive case and so forth?'"

He says that this very thing does not exist, starting with the words "But when," and so forth. Whatever word, in whatever manner—that is, by whatever mode—for the purpose of conveying either difference or non-difference; what is its specific quality? It is independent of an external object, insofar as it functions as a signifier.

For rules such as "the genitive is used in the sense of distinction" (*avyatireke ṣaṣṭhī*) or "the suffix *ka* is used when there is abundance" (*bāhulye karṇādi*) do not function by themselves merely through the proximity of an object, independent of human intention. Rather, people employ them in those ways, and from that, the corresponding cognition arises. Likewise in other cases, they are employed by them in some manner and become causes for cognition in exactly that way.

[Such things] occur. In that regard, there is a consideration of the application of words—which depend on human agency, which do not perceive real entities, and which serve as causes for the awakening of conceptual construction—to their referents according to habituation. To establish the nature of a real entity based on those [words] is nothing but a display of stupidity.

In cases such as the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), words are established through convention based on their mutual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); they are not, however, restricted by actual reality. That expression [of a word] as "that" is a denoter according to its appropriate application.

He explains this with the words beginning with "not indeed" (*na hi*). When there is a distinction (*vyatireka*)—that is, a difference in reality—the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*) is used for plurality.

The grammarians' established rule that suffixes such as *jas* and others occur in the plural number is likewise independent of human intention; it does not function by its own power through the mere presence of the object. Rather, it functions solely by the force of convention (*saṃketa*).
This is precisely what he says: "But they, there," and so forth. "They" refers to the grammarians and others, and "there" refers to the state of plurality (*vyatireka*) or multiplicity.

And likewise: since people employ the genitive case and the plural number according to convention, a corresponding understanding arises from the genitive and so forth. An understanding of exclusion (*vyatireka*) and other relations occurs for others as well, because such linguistic usage is observed.
However, the restriction of the genitive and other cases to a plurality of exclusions does not arise by the force of the thing itself (*vastubala*). The same applies elsewhere as well.

Even though there is no distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*), and even though the entity is a unity, [terms such as] "producedness," "impermanence," and so forth are used by speakers with the genitive case-ending, the plural number, and so on, respectively— by resorting to a distinction between property and property-bearer characterized by the exclusion or non-exclusion of other differences, and by resorting to a plurality in "producedness" and the like, which is indicated by the difference in their exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*).

In that same way, when applied appropriately, they become causes for cognition. This being the case—words being based solely on intention, their functioning dependent on persons, and thus proceeding by the force of those persons' intentions—they do not manifest the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) from words because they do not reveal the actual thing. Rather, conceptualization occurs according to habituation; that is, according to how one has practiced the convention (*saṃketa*).

"Awakening" (*prabodha*) means the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); that is to say, the causes of conceptual construction within the mental continuum of the listener, which corresponds to linguistic conventions (*saṃketa*). Regarding such words, there is this consideration of their application to the objects denoted (*vācya*), such as the use of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in expressions like "in the absence of [something else]," and so forth. For the Naiyāyikas and others, the determination of the reality of things (*vastuvyavasthāna*) is "by virtue of that," meaning by virtue of the word. In the absence of...
The acceptance of a distinct entity [is asserted] because of the statement "the cowness of a cow"; since there is a genitive case here, the universal (*sāmānya*) must be distinct, and so forth.
This is merely a display of stupidity, a demonstration of ignorance regarding the established system of word-meanings.

To this, the opponent replies with "In that way," etc.; [he means] that such an established system applies to the property (*dharma*), the substratum (*dharmin*), and so on, [and thus] there is no distinction between the property and the substratum.
The designations "property" (*dharma*) and "property-bearer" (*dharmin*) are established through the exclusion and non-exclusion of an interval [between them].

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), terms with plural endings—such as "substantiality," "earthiness," and so forth—are established through the differentiation of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). However, this is not because there is an actual ontological distinction between property and property-bearer, nor because of a real difference in substance such that properties like substantiality would exist in an ultimate sense due to a sixth-case [genitive] relation.

"The plural number is used because of such a distinction. From what [is this known]? From the reply beginning with "tathā" (so it is). Why is that? Because conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) would otherwise be impossible. This is the consideration of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*). Why is that? Because conventional usage would be untenable.

For we shall explain that if there were a difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), or if words functioned according to the actual state of things while possessing those respective forms, then the relations of universal and its connection, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and the relation of qualifier and qualified would not be tenable.
This applies to one for whom the differentiation in the application of words is held to be based entirely on the real object in every case. For such a person—

In cases such as "the wife" (*dārāḥ*) or "the six cities" (*ṣaṇṇagarī*), where there is an established distinction between difference and non-difference, what is the basis for [the usage] in such instances as "the nature of space is spaceness" (*khasya svabhāvaḥ khatvam*)? (69)

Because even for a single woman there is the linguistic usage "wife" (*dārāḥ*), and for a single grain of sand there is the usage "sand" (*sikatāḥ*); this is because, if the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*)— which are the objects of conventional usage— were in reality distinct, and if properties were mutually distinct from one another in ultimate reality, then conventional usages such as "universal" (*sāmānya*) and so forth would be impossible.

He explains this very introductory statement with the words "na hi" and so forth. He presents two alternatives—namely, that the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), which are the objects of conventional usage, must be either identical or distinct, because there is no other possible mode for a real entity (*vastu*)—in order to point out the defects in both positions: that they are different, and that they are identical in nature. Otherwise, by the opponent...

If the position of difference (*bheda*) is adopted on the grounds that "it is due to the distinction between the object and its representation," then the presentation of the position of identity (*tattva*) would not be appropriate for the context.

The phrase "connected with that" refers to the relationship between the universal (*sāmānya*) and its possessor (*tadvat*). Furthermore, if it is accepted that words function according to the actual state of things (*yathāvastu*), then universals and so forth are logically consistent. We shall explain this further below. [This is] established by the nature of the thing (*vastukṛta*).

Regarding the unity and plurality of things, there is a distinction in the application of words, such as the difference in the application of singular and plural endings. For instance, the word *dārāḥ* (wife/wives) is accepted as being always plural and masculine; when this word refers to a single woman, it does so because its conventional meaning is fixed as a plurality. Similarly, in the expression *ṣaṇṇagari*, many cities are expressed by means of a singular ending.

Since non-difference is established through the use of a single designation, what is the basis for [the claim that] the external object does not exist at all? By the word "etcetera" (ādi), one refers to the establishment of both difference and non-difference in cases such as "a palace-garland. Furthermore, regarding the expression "the nature of space" (*khasya svabhāvaḥ*)—specifically in the phrase "spatiality is the nature of space" (*khatvaṃ khasya svabhāvaḥ*)—what is the basis for the use of the genitive case of separation (*vyatireka-ṣaṣṭhī*)? Now, if [you argue] that by the term "reality" (*tattva*), [it is meant that] if [it belongs] to space...

Regarding the statement that the secondary derivative (taddhita) formation "svābhāvyam" occurs from the word "svabhāva," that is not the case. For the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) does not apply in the sense of "svabhāva"; rather, it applies in the sense of "being" (*bhāva*). Furthermore, there is no purpose in demonstrating a secondary derivative formation, since the distinction [between the two] is already established by one or the other.

On this point, some say that since every conventional usage is encompassed by both the grammatical operation (*vṛtti*) and the sentence (*vākya*), the pair [of examples] was stated for the purpose of demonstrating that such usage is so encompassed.
Others explain it differently: [they ask] what is the basis for the distinction [implied in the phrase] "the nature of space" (*khasya svabhāvaḥ*)? Likewise...

"What is the basis for the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) in the expression 'the state of being a pillar' (*khatvam*), which denotes a distinction? [The answer is: "The basis is the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). [Objection: "If that is so, how can there be plurality in such a case? [Reply: "If you say it is due to a difference in capacities (*śaktibheda*), [we reply] that this applies everywhere. *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (1966).

The use of the singular number would be abolished because there is a plurality of powers [in the object]; likewise, effort [toward linguistic convention] would be rendered futile. If it is argued that the singular is used elsewhere due to the non-difference of the entity, then it should also apply here. Therefore, this restriction, being established without a real basis, demonstrates the independence of one's own will in the employment of words. How, then, is "Ṣaṇṇagarī" used in the plural?

There would have to be a singular number. For cities are not some single thing; how then could there be a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) of them? This is because there is no commencement of a whole composed of heterogeneous elements such as palaces, men, and so forth. Furthermore, when these [parts] are combined or separated, there is no substance (*dravya*) [constituting a city], nor is there any conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
He explains this with the words beginning "when" (*yadā*): "when" means at which time. Others read the word *yat* as *yasmāt*.

This is the meaning: by virtue of this [distinction], the plural forms such as *dārāḥ* (wife/wives) and so forth come to be. The point is that because [the referent] is a single entity, one would expect only the singular case-ending. However, even for a single woman or for grains of sand (*sikatā*), there are many capacities (*śakti*);

therefore, the diversity of capacities is the cause of the plural number. The word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) refers even to cases where the singular is intended, such as in *vṛkṣaḥ* (tree) and so forth.

Because there is no object that possesses only a single power; for everything possesses manifold powers. If this were the case, the effort to establish the rule "the singular number is used when there is one" would be futile, because even though there is a difference in powers, there is no difference in the entity itself, as the substratum of the powers is non-different. If you argue that the singular number is used in other instances where the referent is a single entity, such as in "tree" (*vṛkṣaḥ*) or "cloth" (*paṭaḥ*), [we reply:]...

In this case, the singular number [used] for "wife" (*dārā*) and so forth refers to a single woman because there is no difference in the underlying entity (*vastu*). Since this is so, the differentiation in the application of words is neither based on the nature of the entity nor on its incapacity. Therefore, this restriction in the application of words, being established without a basis in reality and not depending on external entities, establishes the independence of human will in the employment of language.

If it is argued that the collection (*samāhāra*) of the six cities is either of the nature of an action or of the nature of a quality, and that because there is one such [collection], the singular number is used—[the author] replies: No, for the cities themselves are not anything [independent]; since a substance (*dravya*) that is a whole (*avayavin*) consisting of those cities is not admitted, how could there be a collection of those cities, whether of the nature of an action or a quality, from which it could be so designated as "action"?

Because qualities (*guṇa*) must reside in a substance (*dravya*). What, then, is that substance? He says: "The palace," and so forth. A city is a collection of houses and the like. Since it is not admitted that dissimilar things such as palaces and the like originate a [single] substance, how could their collection—the collection of palaces and so forth—be a substance called a "city"? For it is merely a collection of palaces, gateways, persons, and so on.
A city is not admitted [as a distinct substance]. Because there is no conjunction of all those constituent substances, such as palaces and so forth, there is no "city-substance.

It is maintained that substances which possess conjunction as an auxiliary cause are what initiate other substances. However, there is no conjunction among the palace, the person, the wall, and so on, when they are separated; by virtue of which a "city-substance" produced from the palace and the rest could exist.

It might be thought: (1) although there is no conjunction of palaces and so forth in their entirety, nevertheless, since there is a mutual conjunction among those things such as palaces and persons, the city will indeed exist as having that conjunction as its nature. To this, [the response is]:
it is not so.
It is because it is something that is observed as a whole (*spyi-lta-zig-rjas-pa*).

According to Pāṇini 1.4.22: "A conjunction [is not designated by a singular number]. A palace (*prāsāda*) is itself of the nature of a conjunction, and because it does not conjoin with anything else, for that very reason, its number—

If it is argued that a city is indeed existence (*sattā*) as qualified by its constituent entities (*bhāva*) and by the persons associated with them, then what could possibly qualify this [existence], which is itself devoid of any further distinctions? For existence is one; thus, even when there is a plurality of cities, the plural form "cities" (*nagarāṇi*) would not occur. If it is argued that it is the mutual accompaniment of these two [entities and persons], then how can there be such accompaniment between two things that neither benefit nor are benefited by one another?

The substantiality (*vastutva*) of the city is unestablished because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) belongs to the category of qualities (*guṇapadārtha*); therefore, he says: "It is not conjunction," and so forth. The city does not have the nature of conjunction. Likewise, since heterogeneous substances such as wood and bricks do not originate a new composite substance (*kāryadravya*), the palace (*prāsāda*) also is not of the nature of a substance; rather, it is held to have the nature of conjunction. And conjunction is a quality (*guṇa*), and [qualities] are devoid of further qualities (*nirguṇa*).
From what [source] would there be a "quality" (guṇa) of the palace, by virtue of which the city could consist of that conjunction?

This very point he states with the words "of the palace," and so forth. Furthermore, because there is no conjunction with anything other than the object of the master (pati), the city is not a conjunction; and by the word "and" (ca), it is also because there is no conjunction with the separate palaces and so forth mentioned immediately prior.

The term "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is conjoined with "city wall" (*nagarabhitti*). Thus, because there is an absence of conjunction in both ways for palaces and the like, the nature of the city as being a conjunction is refuted.
If it is argued that the city will consist of whatever number belongs to the palaces and so forth, he says: "For that very reason."

Regarding the phrase "the absence of number": for that very reason—that the palace consists of conjunctions—there is an absence of number in the palace, because numbers are qualities (*guṇa*) and qualities are devoid of [intrinsic] qualities. For number, too, has the nature of a quality. That which is both "that" and "conjunction" is *tatsaṃyoga*; the meaning is that it is a conjunction whose essence is the palace. It is distinguished by that conjunction and by the persons.

If it is argued that existence (*sattā*) is the city, then what qualification could there be for this existence, which is unitary, eternal, and unsurpassed? For palaces, men, and so forth do not qualify existence, because it is incapable of having any excellence added to it.
Therefore, existence is without qualification. If that [existence] were the city, then cityhood would apply everywhere; thus it is said—

"Generally," [it is said] "because existence (*sattā*) is one. This means that among substances, qualities, and actions, there is only one all-pervading existence. Even when there is a plurality of cities—meaning even when there is a plurality of collections of palaces and so forth that serve as the basis for the arrangement of cities—otherwise, if the city were essentially existence itself, how could there be a plurality of cities? "Of the two" refers to the palace, the person, and so forth, as well as existence.

If it is argued that the state of being mutually associated constitutes a "city," then in that case, the cognition of a city would not occur everywhere, because palaces and other such structures are not present in every location. Furthermore, the opponent maintains that the use of the plural number is established due to the multiplicity of palaces and so forth.

He states the reply: "That which is not assisted," and so forth. What kind of assistance can there be between two entities—such as existence (*sattā*) and a palace—that are neither assisted nor assisting? For the meaning of "cooperation" is twofold: either the production of a distinguished moment within a continuum through the imparting of mutual excellence, or the performance of a single effect by those things that have arisen already capable due to their own prior causes.

For those things that are not agents [of action], how could there be a singular number, as in "the city" (*nagaram*), for those which do not assist one another? If it is argued that the cause is a non-differentiated capacity (*śakti*) belonging to such things with respect to some object, we say no; for as for that capacity—
Because it would not be distinct from the nature of the entity itself.

Furthermore, even if it were distinct from the object, it could provide no assistance because it would lack dependence upon it. Or, if there were assistance through a power (*śakti*), then if that assisting power were also distinct [from the entity], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and thus no comprehension. Or, if it were not distinct from that [entity]...

The claim that this would lead to an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) regarding the first [definition] is trivial. Furthermore, the definition "the nature of space is spaceness" relies upon a distinction (*vyatireka*). First, it cannot be the former [definition], because existence (*sattā*) admits of no added excellence (*anādheyātiśaya*). Nor can it be the second, because just as pure existence is incapable of producing the cognition of a city, so too it would be [incapable] even when accompanied by palaces and the like; or else, it would possess such capacity.

Even a single [element] might produce [the city]. And if the city were the mutual conjunction of two [elements], then even a single city would consist of multiple parts, because it consists of palaces and so forth. Consequently, since there is a plurality of conjunctions with persons, there would have to be a singular form "city" (*nagaram*). By the word "conjunction," a conjunction consisting of palaces is meant. "Of such things" means of those that are mutually conjoined.

In the cognition of "a city" with respect to certain objects—such as the existence of men and their conjunctions—and in the production of the word itself, there exists a single, non-different capacity (*śakti*). If it is argued that this non-different capacity is the cause for the singular number, we say no. Why? Because the capacity is not distinct from the essential nature of the object; that is, because it is not distinct from the objective forms such as the men themselves.

In that very same way, since there is multiplicity, how could there be a singular number based upon it? Alternatively, if the power (*śakti*) were admitted to be distinct from the essential nature of the entity, then for that form of power—which cannot be assisted by the existence of the conjunction with the *puruṣa*—there would be no dependence on the *puruṣa* and so forth.
Consequently, the relationship expressed as "the power of the *puruṣa*" and so on would not exist; this is the intended meaning.

Now, if—even for a power that is distinct [from the person]—an assistance produced by the person and so forth is desired in order to establish the dependence of that power upon the person and so forth; then, when such an assistance to the power by the person and so forth is being posited, [we must ask]: by which power do the persons and so forth first assist that power? If there is another power that assists this first power, then, given the distinctness of that [second] power from the [first] power—

There would be an infinite regress, or else there would be non-distinction [of the power from the entity]. If the first case were accepted—namely, that the power is intended to be the basis for the singular number—then it would follow that there is no distinction [between the power and the entity]. And if there is no distinction, then because the power is as manifold as the entity itself, the consequence remains that the plural number must apply to many things; thus, this [argument] is trivial. Furthermore, in the conceptualization of a power, the expression "the nature of space" (*khasya svabhāvaḥ*) relies upon a relation of distinction.
The genitive case would not occur. Because it is the cause of the genitive, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is also designated by the word "genitive" through metaphorical usage.
Therefore, this is another meaning: [if it were not so], the formation of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) based on the relation of distinction (*vyatireka*)—as in *khatvam*—would not occur.
Since the abstract suffix arises through this etymological derivation, namely that "the nature of space is *khatva*," its basis is the relation of distinction.

Alternatively, the connection and the division of the text should be made according to what is appropriate: (1) [If it were so,] there would be neither the genitive case based on distinction (*vyatireka*) in the expression "the nature of space" (*khatvam*), nor would there be a universal (*sāmānya*) therein; nor would qualities such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and so forth be spoken of in that way, because it is impossible for another entity to have that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). And [this is so] because those [qualities] lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).

Because it would lead to an infinite regress (*atiprasaṅga*). If you argue that this [universal] also has the nature of another entity (*arthāntara-svabhāvatva*), then there would be an infinite regress; even so, there would still be no cognition [of the universal].
This should be stated likewise for the six categories (*ṣaṇṇāṃ padārthānām*) and for the groupings of the six categories and so forth; for in those cases, there is no universal (*sāmānyam*).

The ellipsis to be supplied is: "there would be no derivation of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*). [This means] that there would be no genitive case in the expression "the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of space (*khasya*)," because there exists neither a distinct intrinsic nature nor a distinct entity other than the referent denoted by the word "space" (*kha*), which could serve as the basis for either the genitive of separation (*vyatireka-ṣaṣṭhī*) or the secondary suffix respectively. There is indeed a universal (*sāmānya*) called "spatiality" (*khatva*); [but] its separation—
If it is asked what the basis for this designation is, he says: "Not there," and so forth. Because space is of a single nature, the universal "spaceness" does not exist in it.

Even though existence (*sattva*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*) do exist in space, nevertheless they are not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of space, because they are common to jars and other things as well. Nor are existence and substantiality the basis for the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) in the term "spaceness" (*khatva*). This is because of those two...

The word *śa* [is used] because it is not the cause of cognition (*pratyaya*). That which has the nature of being the basis for cognition and designation corresponding to itself is accepted as the cause of cognition. Nor are qualities such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*) [the cause]; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), oneness (*ekatva*), otherness (*paratva*), and so forth are included.

Thus it is said: "the nature of space" (*khasya svabhāvaḥ*). This refers to the nature of that [space], namely the quality of omnipresence and so forth, which is a distinct entity from substance (*dravya*).

Because it is impossible for them to be connected with you, and because it is impossible for them to have the nature of space. For it is not logical that one distinct entity should be the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of another distinct entity.

And if pervasiveness and so forth were the intrinsic nature of space, then since those qualities such as pervasiveness would have space as their intrinsic nature, it would follow that they are devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva). To explain: that which is the intrinsic nature of those qualities, if true, would mean that only space has arisen, and [the qualities themselves] would not exist.

The sense is that if there were another intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there would be a state of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). And if those [other natures] were themselves devoid of intrinsic nature, then space would have no distinct intrinsic nature of its own. If it is argued that even properties such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*) possess an intrinsic nature that is a different entity, he says: "Of that too," and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has an intrinsic nature that is a different entity from that [space]," namely, from omnipresence and the like.

Regarding the charge of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): whatever other entity (*arthāntara*) is intended as the nature of omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and so forth, that too must possess the nature of another entity. Otherwise, because it would not be distinct from omnipresence, it would likewise lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
And thus, by searching for further and further natures, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and consequently, not even a single [entity] would have a stable foundation.

Because of the non-existence of the entity. The intention is that there is no apprehension of the first [category], which has the nature of space, and therefore that itself constitutes the absence of exclusion (*vyatirekābhāva*).
Thus, there is the group of the six categories: substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence. The word "etcetera" (ādi)—
From the word [“palace”], expressions such as “palace-row” and so forth are denoted.
