[Objection: How can there be a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when there is no distinction? For in that case, neither a universal (*sāmānya*) nor a number (*saṃkhyā*) or a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is possible among the six categories of existence (*ṣaṭpadārtha*).

Now, how is it that in the absence of any differentiation one speaks of "the nature of space" rather than simply "space"? It is because the word "space" functions based on a form that does not refer to a specific entity distinct from space, but rather to a form common to other things; thus, it is spoken of precisely because of such a desire for knowledge (*jijñāsā*).
This is not, however, because a form excluded from all other things is being denoted.
That very form [of the object] is not presented to the intellect, for that would entail the consequence of it being beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*). Rather, this is the intended meaning:

by means of a word, the listener is presented with a conceptual reflection (*vikalpapratibimba*) upon which is superimposed that which is unconnected to the actual nature of the thing—namely, what is expressed by a class-term (*vargaśabda*). This is because universals (*sāmānya*) are admitted only in respect of substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karman*). The same applies to number (*saṃkhyā*) and conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Or [it] is not possible, because since those two are categories of quality (*guṇa*), they exist only within a substance (*dravya*). "How so? and so forth asks the opponent: if one does not admit that "now" has a nature distinct from the object itself, then since the referent denoted by the word *sva* (self) and the referent denoted by the word *bhāva* (being) are both ascertained to be non-existent, how can there be a designation of them as distinct, such as "its own nature" (*svabhāva*)? It is not, however...

"Kham" (space) alone. The meaning is that because there is no basis for differentiation, it is logical to designate it solely by way of non-differentiation. He refutes this with the words "of space," and so forth. "Of space" refers to the object denoted by the word *kha*; "by another object" means by excluding earth and the other elements. [The word] *kha*—

The common form of a disease—which serves as the basis for its occurrence when one does not reflect upon other unperceived specificities—is distinct from the form belonging to other substances. Likewise, in this case, there is an inquiry regarding that which is not conjoined with any other object;
thus it is said, "the nature of space," or "spatiality" (*khatva*), so that it may be understood that this belongs to space.
"The nature [belongs] to nothing else.

By this, through the rejection of other distinctions, because the form excluded from one [thing] is not being denoted, another very different basis for denoting exclusion (vyatireka) has been stated. By that, designations such as "the absence of a jar" are established.

Others, however, say: when the word "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is used to indicate the intrinsic nature of space (*kha*), it indicates it merely by the exclusion of [other] intrinsic natures, but not by the non-rejection of other intrinsic natures. The word "space," on the other hand, indicates that very same thing without rejecting other forms. Therefore, due to this slight distinction characterized by the rejection or non-rejection of other intrinsic natures, this is the intrinsic nature of space.

Thinking that by stating "the form which is the basis for the application of its own word, through the non-reflection upon a form common to other objects, is thus expressed," the opponent has actually stated that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself is the denotable object, [Dharmakīrti] says "But not all... and so forth.

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) replies with "No... and so forth: "That very form which is the particular characteristic, consisting of the exclusion from everything else, is [the denotable object]."

The connection is as follows: [the particular] is not presented by words in a cognition arising from words. Why? Because, just as in the case of sensory cognition, if that particular were to appear in verbal cognition, it would follow that it is beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*), and it would follow that it is perceptible (*pratyakṣatva*). If it is asked, "Then what is done by the word? he says: "Only," and so forth. "This" refers to the communicator.
Deceived by the determination of identity between the perceived object and the conceptual construction, one intends: "I shall cause [the listener] to understand such an uncommon object.

With this intention, by means of a word acting as an instrument, there arises in the listener a conceptual construction which is superimposed as being external, like a reflection. Regarding this, he says: "(1) 'For when the object is not perceived, there is merely a conceptual construction of the object. This is the consideration of the universal (*sāmānya*).

In this way, neither the person to be instructed nor the instructor has actually apprehended or communicated the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Even upon hearing of heaven and so forth, there is no difference in appearance for them compared to those who have experienced it. Therefore, although he does not truly apprehend the intrinsic nature of things, he is satisfied by determining that very [nature] within the reflection of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pratibimba*). Thus—

Precisely because the cognition of the word-meaning arises from its being real (*bhūtatva*), it is said that "the word expresses its own form" (*svarūpam āha*); this is not, however, because it generates a cognition in which only the [word's] own form appears.
How then can there be a universal (*sāmānya*) among entities that are absolutely excluded from one another? Because they do not coalesce (*asaṃsarga*).

If it is argued that [the universal exists] because of the absence of anything else, it has already been stated how a universal [could exist]. It is the non-connection of things that are unconnected by means of a single [cognition]. That very [non-connection] bestows its own form upon those things which are distinct from it. What is this [form]? It is the nature of being unconnected with them, having the form of the object not yet grasped. Thus says the Master:

He states that this is also the intention of Diṅnāga, saying "As it has been said," and so forth: when a word such as "heaven" (*svarga*), whose referent is unperceived, is uttered, there arises for the listener merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of an object; that is, a conceptual construction whose nature is determined by an external object, but which does not grasp the actual external form itself.

And by this [statement], he demonstrates that even according to the Grammarian (Vaiyākaraṇa), the meaning intended by the word is the object of the act of piercing (vidhi). For it is not the case that when a conceptual reflection is produced in the hearer by means of a word, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is— respectively for the speaker and the listener— either apprehended or communicated.

For if a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were conveyed by a word, then even upon hearing words such as "heaven" (*svarga*), there would be no difference in appearance for the listener compared to those who have experienced it, or compared to those who perceive heaven directly through sensory perception. Consequently, the listener would also possess a cognition of the specific form of the particular characteristic of heaven. Since, however, there is no cognition of a particular characteristic from a word...

Furthermore, even though this listener does not actually comprehend the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) from the word, he is satisfied, thinking, "I have indeed apprehended the particular characteristic itself," because he is one who determines (*adhyavasāyin*) that very thing within a conceptual reflection (*vikalpapratibimba*), which is of such a nature—that is, it is precisely the nature of an entity as it is, being a nature of an object unassociated [with other things], and he determines it as the particular characteristic. What is the reason? Precisely because it is of such a nature; for even when the particular characteristic is not grasped, [the determination occurs].

Because the comprehension of the word-meaning occurs precisely through the form of the determined particular (*adhyavasita-svalakṣaṇa*), and because the word-meaning is cognized by means of the determination of the particular, it is not said that "the word expresses its own form. This is because of the statement: "The unique form, which is the cause for the application of its own word, is expressed by not referring to a form common to other objects. However, it is not [the case that...].
Because it produces a cognition in which only its own form appears.

Therefore, this is established: the meaning of the word [in an injunction] is distinct from the position of the opponent because it is unreal (*alīka*). [The opponent asks: "How so? and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: "those things whose nature is exclusively excluded. Of those entities—
"Because of the non-association with another"—that is, because it is distinct from individual entities (*bhāva*)—[the universal does not exist].

"It has been stated," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*). To the question, "In what way has it been stated?", he replies: "Of those that are unassociated and mutually excluded...
It has been stated that they are equal.
Moreover:
"By means of that cognition which, relying upon distinct entities, brings about the concealment of their other forms by its own form, there arises the appearance of a single object. (70)
In this way, entities whose various meanings are concealed by conventional reality, though inherently distinct, appear as if non-distinct through some form. (71)
Due to the force of that [person's] intention, the universal is proclaimed as being existent;
yet it is non-existent in the ultimate sense, just as it was conceptualized. (72)

Non-connection with one heterogeneous entity is as follows: for example, the non-connection of individual cows with the single nature of being a non-cow (*agotva*)—that very non-connection is [the basis]. The commonality (*samānatā*) of the various cows, which are excluded from that non-cow nature—that is *gotva* (cowness). In this same way, other universals (*sāmānya*) are also to be understood.
This is what is meant: the genitive case in "of similar things" (*samānām*) is used in the sense of the agent; thus, the state of being similar is "generality" (*sāmānya*).

The meaning is that entities which have arisen with a common form, excluded from those of a different class, constitute the generality. Furthermore, this very generality possesses the nature of a logical mark (*liṅga*), the nature of that which is marked (*liṅgin*), and the relationship between them, because it is a real entity (*vastu*) and performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*).

Therefore, being the object of activity and the object of conceptual construction belongs to the external thing according to its determination (*adhyavasāya*), and not to the form of the cognition itself,
because it is the opposite of that.

Thus, having refuted the indirect criticism against the position of superimposition (*samāropa*), and having set aside the indirect criticism against the position of exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) precisely by not accepting such an exclusion, and having established that entities which are indeed excluded from others are determined as a unity and constitute the universal (*sāmānya*), [the author] says "api" in order to remove the criticism stated by others even regarding the universal that is the form of cognition (*buddhyākāra*).

And so forth. "Depending on distinct entities" means that a single cognition arises based on particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*) which are mutually excluded; by means of its own nature—that is, by a single form consisting of its own internal image—it conceals or covers the other nature, namely the particularity that is mutually excluded from others. By what kind of [cognition]? By a conventional one (*saṃvṛti*).

It is called *saṃvṛti* because by means of it one's own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is concealed. Those things whose various meanings are concealed—that is, whose various meanings are covered—appear as if non-different, as if mixed together, even though they are inherently distinct, by means of some form such as "cowness" (*gotva*) which is conceptually constructed through the exclusion of dissimilar things (*vijātīya-vyāvṛtti*). By that [means], (1)
"The form [of the object] resides in the cognition, yet it does not follow from the object to another cognition;
nor does it bring about the intended object; therefore, that too is not to be called [the object] in reality"—this and other such [arguments] are refuted.

Therefore, by the power of the intention of the intellect, and by the power of superimposing a single form, the universal (*sāmānya*) is proclaimed as a whole. That is to say, it is the very form superimposed by the intellect that is called the universal. As [stated] by him in the *Sāmānyacintā*: 404. [omitted].

The conceptualizing intellect (*buddhi-vikalpikā*), having arisen based on entities that are distinct from others, projects (*āropita*) that which is imagined (*kalpita*) by its own latent predispositions (*svavāsanā*). Thus, that universal (*sāmānya*) is non-existent in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
[Objection: If you admit that the appearance is undifferentiated (*abhinnapratibhāsa*), how can it be said that the universal is non-existent? [Response: No.

Because that which is intended to be distinct from individuals appears as non-distinct from them, and because if there were non-difference in every respect it would follow—as with the individuals themselves—that there could be no connection [of a universal], the cognition of a recurring [universal] is nothing but an error. Furthermore, if there were both difference and non-difference, there would likewise have to be an appearance of both forms simultaneously.
Yet, in whatever cognition there is the appearance "this is a cow," there is not at that very same time the appearance "the cowness belongs to this."

Now, it might be argued: (1) that which follows where another does not follow must be distinct from it, just as the non-blue is distinct from the blue. And since the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) persists in other individuals despite the non-persistence of the individual *śāvaleyā*, it is therefore distinct from that [individual].

In that case, however, the perception that grasps the cowness as non-different from the *śāvaleyā* would be erroneous, because it perceives as non-different what is actually distinct and has been apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Because they are perceived [as distinct]. Furthermore, it is not the case that a single entity possesses difference by one form and non-difference by that very same form, due to contradiction. Nor is it the case that things possess difference by way of their specific (viśeṣa) forms and non-difference by way of their universal (sāmānya) forms; for if this were so, the particulars would have to occupy the same location and so forth, which they do not. Moreover, there would be no distinction in appearance between the universal and the particular, since they would be non-different in every respect.

Alternatively, if there were a distinction [between the universal and the particulars], it would follow that they are absolutely distinct due to the lack of mutual connection between the inclusive (anugata) and the exclusive (vyāvṛtta) forms.

And if that [universal] were non-different from each individual instance, how could there be a single universal? Nor can it be argued that even though it was not grasped at the perception of the first individual, it is a single universal because of the cognition "this is that very same one" regarding the second and subsequent individuals. (632)
It is logical [to say] "it exists," because the component of memory as "that" cannot arise in the absence of a previously experienced universal as its object.
Consequently, just as it was not grasped in the first individual, so too it would not be grasped individually in the second and subsequent individuals;
how then could the cognition "this is that very same one" arise? Nor can the memory "that" be explained otherwise...

It is not logical to postulate the apprehension of a universal through either the first individual instance or through another non-conceptual cognition, because there is no appearance of a recurring form therein. Nor is its apprehension there as a property (*dharma*) logical, because a universal possesses a single recurring nature. Nor can it be apprehended by the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā-pratyakṣa*) as being related to preceding and succeeding individuals.

It cannot be said that there is "apprehension" [of the universal], because it would follow that perception itself arises in this very manner [i.e., as a conceptual apprehension]. Furthermore, since the previous individual instance is not present, perception is held to be characterized by the ascertainment of a present object.
Therefore, when another [individual] excluded from non-cows is being experienced, preceded by the experience of a single particular excluded from non-cows, that...

Since this erroneous cognition, which has a single form such as "this is indeed so," arises through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it is logical to postulate that very [cognition] itself as its cause, and nothing else. Furthermore, because the intellect is erroneous, this universal form (*sāmānyākāra*) is established as belonging to the cognition, not to the external object.
However, in accordance with how things appear, the universal is said to belong to external objects themselves.
He explains the meaning of the verse beginning with "buddhi" (cognition). It is connected with the phrase "buddhir vikalpikā" (cognition is conceptualizing).

Those which possess "differentiation from others"—that is, differentiation from those of their own class—are "tadanyavyatirekiṇaḥ" (distinguished from others); this means they are excluded from what is of a different class (*vijātīya*). [The term] "in distinct things" refers to those whose nature is the conceptualization of one's own latent impressions (*svavāsanāprakṛti*), that is, the inherent nature of conceptualizing tendencies.

Conforming to their own nature, this [cognition], by superimposing non-difference upon these entities, itself produces them as having a non-different form; thus, mixing them together, it presents them [as such].

And that [conventional reality] is the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of entities—which are distinguished by others precisely through the relation of the means and the end of a single goal;

its nature (*prakṛti*) arises from that. And this [predisposition], appearing in such a manner, is conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), because by it the intrinsic nature of another [entity] is concealed (*saṃvaraṇāt*). And those various forms of concealment, although distinct in essence, are [unified] by something...
They appear as if non-different from the form (*rūpa*). "Following" means conforming to the capacity for producing a single cognition. It is in this way that its own cause is imitated by it:
if a single form arises even with respect to distinct things. "Of these" refers to the objects (*padārtha*). "Superimposing" [is the sense].

Having superimposed upon objects the single form of entities themselves, she creates those entities; making them appear as if non-different, she displays them—meaning, she shows them as if they were of one and the same form. Therefore, it is said:

Now, an objection is raised: "If it is maintained that conceptual construction arises through the force of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of an object, how can a conceptual construction with a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*) arise, given that a universal has never been experienced? To this, he says: "And that," and so forth.

[This refers to] those entities whose single [property] is similar, whether it be the probandum (*sādhya*) or the probans (*sādhana*). For example, in the case of jars and the like, there is a single [function], such as the holding of water.

The object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), such as a lump of clay and so forth—those which possess a single object and means of accomplishment, the state of being that [is expressed] by that [instrumental case]. By means of that [instrumental factor], for discerning persons, that is the *prakṛti* (nature) or intrinsic character (*svabhāva*) of entities;
it is characterized by the production of a conceptualization of a single form, even though the entities are distinct by nature.

The impression (*vāsanā*) which is the cause of such a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and its nature (*prakṛti*) is such that it projects this very form onto another; this is what appears as cognition (*buddhi*). That is to say, it appears as grasping a universal (*sāmānya*) that is non-different from the individual (*vyakti*).

"The claim that 'this cognition [of identity] is based on memory (smārta) without distinction' is surely refuted by the fact that even the son of a barren woman possesses the capacity for recollection;
for it is precisely distinct [cognitions] that, by performing a single function, [produce] a non-distinct form regarding their own objects. Thus [the objection] is rejected.

It is like a magician. "Arising from that" means that which arises—either directly or through a succession—from the natures of the discerning ones, namely the latencies (*vāsanā*) for the conceptualization of phonemes; it is thus [described]. And this very cognition is called "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*).

It is a definition based on the instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), because by means of this cognition, the nature of another—the form of the actual object—is concealed by its own form, which is its own appearance.
Having established the [suffix] *ktin*, those entities are [conceived] by the cognition "they are such. Their distinctions are concealed, meaning their diversity is hidden.
"In some form" means by that which is superimposed by the conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*). They appear within the conceptualizing cognition.
(Sāmānyacintā) 160.4.4. The Investigation of the Universal.

Therefore, by grasping the specific forms of these entities as they appear within the intellect— appearing as if external while being the manifestations of the intellect— one synthesizes them, and their very form is called the universal (sāmānya).

If it is asked, "How then is 'exclusion of others' (*anyāpoha*) the universal (*sāmānya*)?"—it is that very exclusion of others. [The text continues: "Clinging to that very thing, they think 'this belongs to them,' and so forth. [It refers to] the appearance in cognition, the form of a conceptualizing thought (*vikalpabuddhi*). The connection is as follows: "The synthesis (*anusandhāna*) by persons of a single form presented by that cognition is called the universal. Of what things is this said to be the universal?

[This refers] only to those things that revolve within the intellect (*buddhiparivartin*). The connection is: "of these [things] revolving within the intellect. Having experienced particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), those indistinct pot-forms—which are the entities revolving within the intellect and which appear in conceptual cognitions (*vikalpabuddhi*) such as "this pot is white" or "another is black"—are what possess the universal (*sāmānya*) as their correlate. It is not the particular characteristics themselves that [possess the universal] in the cognition of the universal.

Because they appear [to consciousness] and because they lack [any real] connection [with external objects]. The qualification "of those revolving within the intellect" means "of those appearing as if external," even though they are flashing forth as if outside. And he states the cause for this external flashing forth: "because of the grasping of specific forms. (1)
Some maintain that there is an external determination (*bāhyādhyavasāya*) because of the imitation of the clear configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of the conceptualization of external objects.
This, however, is incorrect; for it has already been demonstrated that the attribution of externality is not caused by similarity.
Therefore, the specific form—the form of a jar or the like—is its apprehension, which is experience; from that [experience], it appears as if external.
Vibration.

This is what is meant: a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), arising through the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of a jar and so forth, determines its own form as non-different from the external jar and so forth, but it does not actually grasp it. (1)

Therefore, regarding the object prescribed by a word, a doubt sometimes arises because of non-apprehension. In that case, however, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), by its own causal nature alone, determines its own form as non-different from the external object;
it does not do so on account of similarity, because there is no such similar object and because of non-apprehension.
But surely, even for those forms revolving within the intellect, what other form appears apart from their own essential nature that could be the universal?
True.

Regarding this, some say that because they are not distinct from a single cognition, they possess oneness. Others, however, say that each of them has the nature of a universal in relation to its own individual manifestation. Both of these views are untenable, because there is no appearance of a single [universal] form. It is merely because others determine them as having a single form that they accept them as a universal.

It is stated [in this way] precisely with that intention. For the Teacher, however, what is intended is the appearance as "identical" (*samānāḥ*), not [the identity of] a single [entity]; and thus he will say later:
"Alternatively, let it be that the appearance is distinct from the cognitions; [nevertheless], because they are grasped as 'identical'... and so forth.

(1|106) Thus it is said. If the universal (*sāmānya*) is merely the form displayed by conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), which revolves within the intellect itself, and since that [form] is of a positive nature (*vidhirūpatva*), how can it now be called "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as the universal?
Because conceptual cognitions are by nature deluded, they appear as if they were grasping a real entity (*vastu*). For that [cognition], in relation to things distinguished from others...
It is understood that [the conceptual construction] occurs with respect to entities (*bhāva*) alone, having discrimination as its object.
But surely there are external discriminators; and yet, no activity of conceptual construction occurs with respect to them. How then can it be said to occur "with respect to them"?

It is precisely those who have explained [the system] who discriminate in this way, but not the ordinary practitioners (*vyavahartṛ*). They, however, [perceive] only their own objective support (*ālambana*) as [capable of] causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Considering [the object] as suitable, people act by conceptualizing distinct objects and unifying them. It is on account of this intention that the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) says, "That very same [object]. That very thing, which appears as determined by conceptual cognition, is called "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha), because it is derived through the perception of an entity as distinguished from others.
If the universal is merely the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*), how can there be a cognition of external things as having a common nature? As it has been said:
"(1) Now, if these [cognitions] are objectless because they exist solely as mental impressions (*vāsanā*), how could there be a comprehension or an engagement with external objects? (1)

To this he says: "That very [object]," and so forth. Grasping that which is the appearance (*pratibhāsa*) in a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), that non-conceptual cognition (*avikalpikā buddhiḥ*) appears as if it were grasping a real thing (*vastu*). Why? Because of the natural delusion (*prakṛtivibhrama*) of conceptual cognitions;
that is, because by their very nature they are deluded regarding the apprehension of an object as non-different from their own internal form (*svākāra*).

How, then, is it said that [conceptual cognition] has exclusion (*apoha*) as its object? To this he says: For conceptual cognition, by virtue of its determinative function (*adhyavasāya*), arises with respect to individual particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) which are distinguished from others; thus it is understood to have exclusion as its object. This is so by way of its effect (*kāryataḥ*), but not because it takes the nature of exclusion itself as its object.
But the opponent, having largely misunderstood [the intention], says "Now then" (*nanu*) and so forth. The meaning is that external things are [identical] due to their commonality with *svalakṣaṇas*.
For in this way, the inclusion of both external and internal [phenomena] is accomplished. [The opponent asks:

"How can there be a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) regarding those *svalakṣaṇas*, which are distinct from one another for a discerning person and do not [reside] within them? To this, it is said: [the following].

He refutes this with the words beginning "the commentators" (*vyākhyātāraḥ*). For they, while establishing the object exactly as it exists, distinguish them in this way: "The appearance in conceptual cognition is one thing; the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is another. However, those who engage in worldly transaction (*vyavahartāraḥ*) do not distinguish them in this manner. Rather, those practitioners of transaction [regard] the object as being precisely the appearance of conceptual cognition, which has itself as its objective support (*svālambana*).

Thinking that the external particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is capable of causal efficiency, [the author] clarifies this very point: (1) The object of perception is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), while the object of conceptualization (*vikalpya*) is the appearance of a universal (*sāmānyapratibhāsa*). By unifying these two, one conceives with conviction (*adhimucya*) that "this very particular characteristic is being made an object by conceptual cognition and is being expressed by a word," and thus proceeds to engage in purposeful action.

It is stated thus—namely, that "conceptual cognition arises regarding distinct entities"—solely by virtue of the intention of those who engage in worldly discourse, because they act by unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object. By saying this, it is implied that there is no superimposition of the external upon one's own internal form;
otherwise, it would follow that activity would occur toward the internal form alone. [This is illustrated by] the superimposition of water upon a mirage.

Nor is there a superimposition of its own form upon the external object; for that would entail the consequence of activity occurring solely through the desire for the result being superimposed, just as one desiring water acts toward a mirage of water. 4. Regarding the investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*):

it is said that [words] convey, by means of sound, things as distinct from those that do not perform that function, precisely because they perform that function. This is the investigation of reality (*tatvacintā*).

Who, indeed, would not perceive non-difference [of objects] due to the difference in their appearances and so forth? If one conforms to the intention of the cognizer, then even "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) should not be considered a universal (*sāmānya*). Now, what is meant by the "unification of the perceived and the conceptualized"? If it means that the perceived is non-different from the conceptualized in the external world—

There would be no cognitive engagement (*pravṛtti*). If there were non-difference between the object of conceptualization and the perceived, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) would be the referent of the word. Yet, there can be no unification of the perceived and the conceptualized, because perception does not have the conceptualized as its object, nor does conceptualization have the perceived as its object. Furthermore, since the perceived is absent in the case of the past and so forth, how could there be a unification of those two?

To this it is replied: When there is an experience of an object, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises—triggered by the awakening of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—bearing that object's form;

this construction determines its own internal form as non-different from the external object, but it does not actually make them non-different. Therefore, because the object of the conceptual construction is determined as having the nature of the perceptible (*dṛśya*), the unification of the perceptible and the conceptual is spoken of. (1) That which is fit for being seen is "the perceptible" (*dṛśya*); it is so called because it can be seen.

Or, that which is the object even of a conceptualized perception—such as "I shall see"—is also a visible object (*dṛśya*). By this, it is established that even a future object indicated by scripture is a visible object, and likewise non-existence (*abhāva*) is also a visible object. For this very reason, a cognition (*pratyaya*) is said to have non-existence as its object because it cognizes by superimposing its own form—which is of the nature of non-existence—upon the absence of a thing, rather than [cognizing] non-existence itself.
It apprehends [them] because all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) lack an objective referent (*nirviṣayatva*).

Regarding the phrase "by way of its being produced by that" and so forth: it is not merely said that the conceptual cognition arises with respect to the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and their exclusions (*viveka*) through the force of that [cognition’s] intention; rather, by way of its being produced by that—that is, by means of its being caused by that—it [apprehends] objects as distinct from those things which do not produce it.

It is said that speakers convey [their meaning] by means of words. If it is asked why commentators also do not realize the identity between the perceived object (*dṛśya*) and the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), he replies: "Because of the difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa-bheda*) and so forth.
For the appearance of the perceived object is indeed vivid (*spaṣṭa*).

Not [of] conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because for that which is bound up with conceptual construction, clarity is impossible. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is meant that even when the visible object has ceased, conceptual construction does not cease; and because [the former] performs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) while [the latter] does not. "Those who contemplate reality" (*tattvacintaka*) refers to the commentators who follow logic (*nyāya*). This is a genitive of residue (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*): "those who contemplate reality. They [belong to] reality.

The term *cintaka* [is used] because, when there is a requirement for the mere exclusion of other related entities, the relationship of action and agent (*kriyākārakabhāva*) is not intended to be expressed. Alternatively, having formed a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) of the word *tattva* with the word *cintaka*—derived from the root *cit* with the suffix *ac* (as in *pacādyac*)—the suffix *kan* is added as an affix denoting the same meaning (*svārthika*). Consequently, the prohibition of the genitive compound by the rule "with [words ending in] *tṛc* or *ka*" (*tṛjakābhyām*), etc., does not apply here.

It should not be suspected that [the opponent] does not perceive non-difference; for the subject under discussion is "between the perceived object and the conceptual construction. The challenger [objects] with the words "If," etc. The establishment of a universal (*sāmānya*) regarding external objects conforms to the intention of the cognizer.
In that case, let even "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) not be a universal. Why? Because it is not so. [The text continues: "Exclusion of others..."

There is no such understanding among those who engage in linguistic usage that "it is impelled by a word. If you argue that even the Teacher does not have such an understanding because [the universal] is equal [to all individuals], we reply: it is not only that there is no such understanding; there is likewise no understanding of [the universal] through such aspects as being distinct from or non-distinct from the individual, being unitary, or being pervasive. It is simply that [there is no understanding] of that which has a non-differentiated form.
The basis of this cognition is called "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha), because it occurs with respect to real entities, because it is not contradictory [to them],
and because linguistic usage is observed to function in that manner. Therefore, there is no such thing as a real universal (sāmānya) that appears to this cognition.
Explaining this, he says:
"Not indeed only... and so forth. "Thus there is no comprehension" means by way of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
Even though you accept a universal (*sāmānya*) through such forms as being distinct from individuals and so on, nevertheless, there is no comprehension at all.

[The view] that [the universal] is distinct from its substratum belongs to the Vaiśeṣikas and others, while [the view] that it is non-distinct belongs to the Sāṃkhyas and others; by the word "etcetera," [concepts such as] its presence in each individual and its pervasiveness are included. In that regard, first of all, no difference of the universal appears at all, because the cognition "this is the universal" does not arise here [in the object]. Even if there were non-difference, only the individuals would appear, and not [the universal].

Regarding the universal (*sāmānya*): if it were both different and non-different [from its instances], the faults pertaining to both positions would ensue. Nor is it logical for it to be fully present in each individual instance; for if that were so, it would be related to only one thing in a single individual, rather than being related to many. And this is not the case, because the universal is related to many, since it is defined by the statement: "the universal is the state of being common to those things that are alike."

Now, because that [universal] is recognized (*pratyabhijñāna*) in other individuals, it must be related to them; even so, like a quality of an element (*bhūtaguṇa*), it would be one and related to many, yet not fully present in each [individual]. This is because it is not perceived as being related to many within each single individual. Or, if it were so perceived, there would have to be an appearance of multiple individuals therein. Now, regarding other individuals—

Because it does not appear [in that way], it is said to be fully present in each individual instance. But does this much establish its connection with many [instances] in a single place? Furthermore, it has already been stated that recognition (pratyabhijñāna) is not tenable regarding a universal (sāmānya).
Therefore, it is established that neither its full presence in each individual instance, nor its eternity, unity, and omnipresence, appear [to consciousness].

If there is an equal absence of apprehension in conventional usage for both a real universal (*sāmānya*) and an exclusion (*apoha*), then what is the basis for this [latter]? To this he says: "Only," and so forth. The exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is the fact that particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are devoid of those belonging to other classes; this is stated to be the cause for a cognition that has a non-differentiated form. What is the reason? Because of its [the exclusion's] being distinct from those of other classes...

Because the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), characterized by the absence of non-yava, exists in all distinct entities, and because such an exclusion is not contradictory to being the cause of a universal cognition; for just as one perceives a single tree as excluded from non-trees, so too does one perceive another, and thus a cognition of a single form arises therein. Furthermore, there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in this case.

He states the third reason: "And of linguistic usage," and so forth. "Because it is seen to be so" means because it is seen to be based on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). And this will be demonstrated by the passage beginning with, "And it is called 'sound' (*dhvani*) because it functions by excluding what is other than that. "Just as" refers to how this conceptual cognition appears as having a single form.
4. Consideration of the Universal: Particulars do not follow [one another], nor does anything else that follows [them] appear.
For those particulars do not enter into one another; due to the absence of difference, the universal itself would be non-existent.
Because it would lead to an absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*). Furthermore, nothing other than those [particulars]—that is, something distinct and separate from them—appears in cognition.
And how could that which does not appear [in cognition] cause another to be grasped by itself, or be designated as such?
Nor can a universal (*sāmānya*) exist on the grounds of having a single relation, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); thus they have stated. Abhi-...

Thus, the meaning of the statement is that such an external universal does not exist; therefore, the intention is that a real entity as a universal cannot be the basis for conceptual construction and perception.
And he states the reason for the non-existence of a universal: "Because," and so forth. "Individuals" refers to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

They do not "follow" (anuyanti), that is, they do not intermingle. By this, the acceptance of a non-distinct universal is refuted. To refute a distinct [universal], he says: "something else that follows. That which is intended as following despite difference—
That other form, which is the universal (sāmānya), does not appear in perceptual cognition.

[Objection: But even regarding the universal appearing in conceptual construction, this same fault of non-continuity (*anvaya*) and so forth is equal whether one takes the position of difference or non-difference;
how then can a universal be accepted? [Reply: First of all, a common form indeed appears, as long as it...
It is not perceived as being devoid of difference and non-difference; rather, this is merely a poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*) because it establishes its lack of substantial reality (*avastutva*).
For this very reason, it is said that "this exists according to appearance" (*yathāpratibhāsam*).
They "enter into" (*anvāviśanti*) means they become intermingled. If there were mutual entry (*parasparam anvāveśaḥ*), then due to the attainment of a single form (*ekarūpāpatti*), difference—

This is the state of affairs. For that reason, it would follow that the universal itself does not exist. Therefore, the meaning is this: the universal is the property (*dharma*) that serves as the basis for a single-form cognition regarding distinct things that are similar; [the universal] would cease to exist through the absence of such distinctions. Furthermore, the phrase "other than" (*anyat*) is an explanation of "different from the individuals" (*vyaktibhyo 'nyat*), meaning "distinct" (*vyatiriktam*). Likewise, in that manner, within the cognition of the universal—

(1) By this, the non-apprehension of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) has been stated when proving the conventional designation of the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*) that meets the conditions for apprehension. Furthermore, one should not admit a universal that does not meet the conditions for apprehension; for how could a universal that is not manifest cause another—that is, a possessor of the universal—to grasp it by means of its own nature as a universal?

Or one might attribute it [to something else]. "In its own form" connects with the subject under discussion: "how could it be anything else? By the force of the universal (*sāmānya*), the occurrence of non-differentiated designation and cognition among individuals is desired. Therefore, the collective meaning is that the universal must indeed be accepted as meeting the conditions for perception. Thus, in this way, because there is no perception of that which meets the conditions for being perceived, there is no single [entity], nor is there a manifold [of such entities].
"Let it be called 'related to many' (*kasambandhin*); nevertheless, its nature as a universal (*sāmānyarūpatā*) is not tenable," he says with the words "And not... and so forth.

"By them" refers to the distinct individuals (*vyaktibheda*). "Has been stated" refers to duality and so on. Even in the case of substances that are effects of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), there is no nature of being a universal.

Because it has already been stated that such an undesirable consequence does not follow. If you argue that a universal (*sāmānya*) is not simply "that which is one and connected to many," but rather that a universal is specifically that single entity which serves as the cause for a non-verbal cognition and a non-designating expression—and that not everything [connected to many] is a universal—then how can a cognition arise with respect to one thing based on another? If you say it is "due to its connection" (*tatsambandhāt*), then it would follow [absurdly] even in the case of number, action, substance, and so forth, since these also exist [in connection with many]. This is incorrect.

If it is argued that [the universal] consists of being an object of cognition (*mānyātmaka*), then what is this "nature of being a universal" (*sāmānyātman*)? That very point has not yet been examined.

In that regard, when a relation exists, there occurs a cognitive application (*pratyayavṛtti*); from that, it is said to be a "universal. Since the cause for such a [cognitive] application exists even with respect to multiple related substances and so forth, there is a cognitive application [toward them as well], and thus they possess the nature of a universal.

Otherwise, let it not be so even elsewhere, for there is no distinction [between the cases]. And thus, if it is argued that there is a single universal (*eka-sāmānya*) which is the cause of the designation and cognition of "form" (*rūpa*) as distinct from substance, quality, and generality— but that this is not the case for all instances such as duality (*dvitva*) and so forth, because those do not serve as the cause for the aforementioned words and cognitions— then how could there be a uniform nature (*ekarūpa*) through a universal in another individual instance (*vyakti-bheda*) based on a different universal?
"In that which has not been produced": the occurrence of a cognition [as] having a single form.

"Due to its connection with that," says the opponent: because of the connection with those individuals, the occurrence of a cognition [in a single form] arises from another universal as well, in another [individual].

And this [term] "number" (saṃkhyā) is that which begins with it. This locative case is used in the sense of a defining characteristic (bhāva-lakṣaṇā). When number exists—that is, when there is a composite substance (avayavin) as an effect—then, because the suffix -vat occurs in connection with conjunction (saṃyoga) and so forth (indicated by the word "ādi"), these too would result in being universals (sāmānya);
such is the collective meaning. Because number and the rest do not have the nature of a universal, there is no single uniform cognition (ekākāra-pratyaya) regarding the substance through them.
If it is argued that this is the "function" (*vṛtti*), [we reply:

Is it not precisely this very nature of the universal (*sāmānyātman*) that is being investigated? What is this "nature of the universal"? Since the specific characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) itself has not been apprehended as distinct from number and the other categories, this is not yet clear. To that effect, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "Therein," etc.: when it was asked, "What is this nature of a universal (sāmānyātman) therein?", you replied that it is the occurrence of a non-different cognition among individuals when there is a relation of one [thing] with many. From that—that is, from the cause which is the occurrence of the cognition—the definition of a universal is: "A single universal is that which is related to many."

In this regard, we state the following regarding the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*): there exist multiple related entities, such as effects, substances, and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including duality and the like. From these [entities] as well, there would arise a single-form cognition (*ekākārapratyaya*) with respect to the substances that serve as their substrata. What is the reason? Because the cause [for such a cognition] is present. For indeed, there is a relation to multiple [entities].

"O King, it is accepted that a single cognition arises from a universal (*sāmānya*) as its cause. Furthermore, even in the case of substances (*dravya*) and so forth, there exists a state of being related to many things which serves as the cause for a single cognition. Consequently, because they give rise to a single cognition, number (*saṃkhyā*) and the rest possess the nature of a universal (*sāmānyātmatā*).
'Otherwise' means: if, despite possessing the aforementioned definition of a universal, the nature of a universal is not accepted for number and the rest."

Let it not be so even in other cases that are considered to be universals (*sāmānya*). What is the reason? Because there is no distinction [between them]. And thus, if substances (*dravya*) and the rest were to also attain the status of being universals, there would be a confusion of forms (*rūpa-saṃkara*) among substances, qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth. It is merely a confusion of appearances within cognition (*buddhi*). And if that is the case, then the appearance of cognition itself is the universal by virtue of its existence (*sattā*), because it consists of the knowledge of objects.
If that is so, it is not thus.
And how could that which is non-different from cognition proceed as a separate object? ||73||

How can the form of cognition be the universal (*sāmānya*) of external objects, given that it does not exist in them? If you say it is because there is a determination (*vyavasāya*) of its existence [in them], then if conventional usage proceeds through such an error, what is the basis for the arising of that appearance? If it were to arise without a basis, it would occur everywhere.

(Alternatively: How can there be a single cognition of a single form that is non-distinct [from the object], and yet [be] the manifestation of another cognition—that is, the conceptual cognition—as a single form?

This is the connection: the universal (*sāmānya*) is the appearance of a single form within conceptual cognition. And because it has the nature of cognition, it exists as a reality, just like cognition itself. As it has been said: (1)
“The universal is indeed the form of the thing; it will be the aspect of the cognition.
And that cognition, having the form of a real entity, arises with respect to the meanings of words.
Therefore, the real entity itself should be postulated as the denotable object, not a cognition devoid of exclusion (anapoha).”

He refutes this with the words "That is not so" (*tanna*) and so forth. That universal which is asserted to be of the nature of cognition—being non-different from that cognition, like the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of cognition itself—how could it become something else, namely an external [object]? The meaning is: "it is not their universal.
He explains this with the words "of cognition" (*jñānasya*) and so forth; because that which has the nature of cognition does not exist in those objects.

[Objection: It is true that there is no real inherence (*anvaya*) of the nature of cognition within individual instances; rather, because that [nature] is determined (*adhyavasāya*) to exist within the mental appearance (*buddhipratibhāsa*), and because the external object is determined [to exist], there is thus a uniform linguistic usage (*samānavyavahāra*) due to error.
[Response: ...if this is argued, [then we reply:]...

And this is exactly what we maintain as our established doctrine (*siddhānta*). It is simply that individual manifestations (*vyakti*), which by their very nature have a single effect, are excluded from those things that do not have that effect; such [manifestations] are the cause for a conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*). Thus, that cognition has "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as its basis.
This is the author’s own view.

However, the opponent does not accept such a cause. For this very reason, the proponent of the established doctrine interrogates the opponent regarding the cause itself, beginning with "In that case," and so forth.
In that context, since the various individuals are non-substantial entities, and because individuals by their very nature [are distinct]...
For those who do not accept that things excluded from others (vijātīyavyāvṛtta) have a single effect, what is the basis for the arising of cognition? None at all.

For the opponent does not accept that distinct entities excluded from others are the cause of a single conceptual cognition (*ekapratyaya*), nor does there exist any real entity (*vastubhūta*) such as a universal (*sāmānya*). Thus, [you must explain] the arising of a cognition of a universal that is without a basis—that is, without a cause.
If it were the case that [the universal] exists everywhere, then the single-form cognition "cow" would also occur in relation to trees.
He states another meaning of the passage beginning with "not distinct from cognition," starting with "Alternatively," and so forth. Previously, by the term "another object" (arthāntara), [he meant...

[Otherwise,] the form would belong to an intermediate state; and consequently, how could a universal be something that does not distinguish one individual from another individual through a different cognition?
Therefore, this apprehension of a single nature in objects is a false conceptual construction.

For indeed, there is nothing whatsoever—whether by way of difference, non-difference, or even by some capacity—that is equal to these objects; thus, the conceptual construction that apprehends them as such is also false.
The seed of this [conceptualization] is mutual differentiation, which is indicated by its designation. //74//

For the purpose of communicating that mutual distinction—so that, having understood that things to be accomplished are distinct from those not to be accomplished by it, one may act by avoiding the latter—a convention is established. This [distinction] belongs to that [cognition] which appears as a single unity; thus, its falsity has been explained. Now, another cognition is being pointed out. Therefore, he says: "(1) How, moreover, can there be another cognition?"

Of what kind of cognition? (1) Of that which arises from another individual instance; the meaning is: of the conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*) that has arisen from one cow-individual (*govyakti*) [and] from another cow-individual distinct from it. For in this way, a universal (*sāmānya*) might exist either by pervading multiple cognitions or by pervading external individuals. But as for the appearance within cognition...
Both are non-existent. Thus he says: "And therefore," and so forth. "Another individual" refers to the external [object].
"Therefore" is the conclusion.

He explains [the meaning] with the words "for not," and so forth. "By something" means by way of a general form (*sāmānyarūpeṇa*). "Thus their apprehension" means the apprehension [of objects] as being "similar."

[The opponent objects: "Surely even the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) must state the basis for this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its arising everywhere, since it would have no support. To this he says: "Mutual exclusion" (*itaretarabheda*), and so forth. That mutual exclusion is that which has the name (*saṃjñā*)—that is, the application of a convention (*saṃketa*)—as its purpose; and having considered that its object (*artha*)—meaning its result—is that which is to be communicated, such is this mutual exclusion.

The seed of this false conceptualization—which has the mutual exclusion of entities as its characteristic—is the application of designations (*saṃjñā*) and conventions (*saṃketa*). [The text asks: "For what purpose? [It answers: "For the sake of communicating that mutual differentiation. He explains this with the words beginning "of which," etc.: "For the sake of communicating that mutual differentiation, a convention is established."

Having cognized through differentiation those entities to be accomplished as distinct from those not to be accomplished—that is, from those things which do not have that [desired] effect—one forms a convention with the thought: "By excluding those [non-targets], one shall engage in those things which have that effect. This aforementioned mutual exclusion (*itaretara-bheda*) is the seed, the cause, of the false conceptual construction (*mithyā-vikalpa*) which appears as a single essence and possesses a single form.

"Grasping that very [object]" means grasping a differentiated particular as being distinct; this is stated by virtue of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). However, there is no actual grasping of a real entity (*vastu*) by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). This conceptual construction, which has the form of a universal (*sāmānyākāra*), arises from the nature of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
that is, it arises from the inherent character of the impressions of conceptualization. Thus, it appears as having a single, uniform form. (174)

But how can there be a non-different effect—consisting of a conceptualization of a single form—from particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) that have distinct natures? [This is explained in] the "Investigation of the Universal" (*Sāmānyacintā*): The seed of conceptualization, while grasping that very [particular], appears in this way due to the very nature of its own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
(kha) How can there be a non-differentiated effect from differentiated things? Since it is distinct from others, how can it be called "non-differentiated"? Such is the very nature of entities.

Although they are distinct, certain things—such as the sense organs and so forth—are restricted by their own nature to accomplishing a single purpose, such as a single unifying reflective cognition or the knowledge of an object. (75)

Just as the sense faculty (*indriya*), light, and attention (*manaskāra*)— or the self, the sense faculty, the mind, and the object, along with their contact— produce a single visual consciousness even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*) fixed to its existence; by this [reasoning], because they share a single effect, and because they are distinguished from other things that do not produce that effect, it is stated that there is non-difference among the individuals.

Because it is stated that "the association with one [thing] is the same for those that differ from it," he refutes this with the words beginning with "prakṛti. *Prakṛti* means intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "Single-formed recognition" (*ekākāra-pratyabhijñāna*) refers to a single conceptual determination (*ekapratyavamarśa*). "Cognition of experience" (*anubhavajñāna*) is the cognition of an object (*arthajñāna*). The term is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) consisting of "single conceptual determination" and "cognition of an object."

Because the rule regarding the prior placement [of a word] is subject to exceptions, the term *arthajñāna* (knowledge of the object) has not been placed first, even though it consists of fewer syllables. The analysis of the compound is: "that of which these are the beginning. By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), effects such as burning, houses, and so forth are included.

It is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning that the single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*) and so forth constitute a single object. Regarding its accomplishment or establishment, even if there is difference—that is, plurality—[the following applies].

"Fixed" (niyatā): some [hold that this is] by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) or primordial essence (prakṛti), like the sense faculties and so forth. Alternatively, even among things that exist, some are produced from their own causes as similar, while others are produced as dissimilar; this has already been stated there. Those which are produced as similar produce a cognition of a single form through that intrinsic nature, even without a universal (sāmānya), just like the sense faculties and so forth. In that regard, a single cognition—

The statement "they are restricted to the means of realizing reflective awareness" is presented as the point of application (*dārṣṭāntika*), whereas the statement "they are the means for accomplishing a single object, such as the knowledge of an object," is presented as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) because it is established for both parties.

For this very reason, it is analyzed at the beginning with the words "Just as the sense-faculties, light, and mental attention [are the causes] of form... and so forth. Just as the sense-faculties, light, and mental attention [are the causes] of form...

The connection is that [the sense-faculties] produce a single cognition. He illustrates this as established by the force of the facts (*vastubala-siddha*). The phrase beginning with "ātma" (self) is based on the tenets of another school. "Eternal, atomic, and swift" refers to the mind (*manas*) whose nature is atomic. "From their conjunction" refers to the conjunctions of the self, the sense-faculty, the mind, and the object. "The self is conjoined with the mind; the mind with the sense-faculty; the sense-faculty with... [and so forth].

From the statement "thena" (by that). It is a *dvandva* compound: "the self, the sense-faculties, the objects, and their contacts. [The compound is] "the self, the sense-faculties, and the objects. It is the opponent's accepted position that the self, the sense-faculties, and the objects, assisted by their respective contacts (*sannikarṣa*), produce consciousness.

Even in the absence [of one], it is determined by their existence; that is, it is restricted to having a single effect. For it is not the case that [the production of] visual consciousness [depends solely on] the eye and so forth.
The opponent maintains that "oneness" (*ekatva*) is a universal (*sāmānya*).

However, individual instances such as feet, though distinct from one another and lacking mutual inherence, naturally produce a single-form recognition or other purposeful actions—such as burning, carrying, or other functions accomplished by wood—according to their respective conditions. This occurs despite the fact that there is no difference in their being distinct particulars.
Water and so forth [are not causes] in the cognition of form and so forth, just as the ear and so forth [are not causes].
Just as certain medicinal herbs are observed to alleviate fever and other ailments either together or individually, while others are not effective even for various purposes; so it is here. (76)
Or, for example, it is like the individual instances of *guḍūcī* and so forth, which—whether together or individually—possess the characteristic of pacifying fever and the like;
they perform a single function, and in that regard they do not depend upon a universal (*sāmānya*). This is because, despite their difference, they possess that very nature (*tatprakṛtitva*).
It is not the case that even when there is no such distinction [of nature], things like curd and cucumber would [perform the same function].

If it is argued that even when those [individuals] are in such a state, there exists some commonality (*sāmānya*), for that very reason he now explains the example: "the *śiṃśapā* and so forth" means the *śiṃśapā*, *khadira*, *nyagrodha*, and so on; even though they lack mutual concomitance and even in the absence of a commonality of "treeness," there arises a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in a single form, namely "tree."

They proceed as follows: it is the subject at hand that, because they are recognized as being other [than fire], *śiṃśapā* trees and the like produce purposeful activities (*arthakriyā*) such as burning or building a house, which are accomplished by wood.

"According to conditions" means that when they obtain the cooperative condition of fire, they produce burning; when there is a convergence of conditions favorable for a house, they produce a house; and by the word "etc.," effects such as chariots and so forth are included.

However, although there is no difference in their being distinct entities, water and other such things are not by nature capable of performing the causal function (arthakriyā) accomplished by wood, because they do not have that as their effect.

Regarding this point as well, he provides an example: "like visual cognition in relation to the ear and so forth. Just as the ear, sound, and so forth are not capable when it comes to producing the cognition of form; and by the word "and so forth" (ādi), [he includes] the cognitions of taste and the rest.
It might be argued that (1) the fact that many [causes] each perform a single effect would not be established without a universal (*sāmānya*);
therefore, he says "each individually" (*pratyekam*), meaning those having an individual form. He says "together" (*saha*), meaning accompanied by other individuals.

Just as medicinal herbs are observed [to function] toward a single effect, such as the alleviation of fever; the word "or" (vā) is used with reference to the preceding example. Nor are other things, such as curd or *trapusa* (?), [effective in this way]. He explains by means of the phrase beginning with "just as" (*yathā*). In that case, regarding the task of alleviating fever and so forth, it is not the general property of being a "medicine" (*oṣadhitva*) [that is the cause].

They do not depend on a universal (*sāmānya*). What is the reason? Because even though they are distinct, they possess that same nature; that is, because their intrinsic nature consists in the causal activity of pacifying fever and so forth. If these particulars were incapable [of such action], there would be a dependence on a universal.

But this is not the case, for even when there is no difference in the universal and no difference among the particulars, we have things such as *dadhitrapusa*—that is, sour gruel (*dadhitrapusa*) which is simply curd (*dadhi*) that has become weakly fermented—and curd itself.
Others explain "trapuṣaśca" as a dvandva compound.

In those instances, such as the individual *guḍūcī* plants and so forth, which perform a single effect while being of such a nature, [if it is argued] that "there is something"—whether distinct or non-distinct—that produces it; this is what was stated: "(1) If it is thought that there would be an effect... (1).
That is incorrect; because there is no distinction, the universal does not perform that function.
Furthermore, there would be no distinction [between them] because of the consequence of their being indistinguishable;
for even though there is a difference in their fields and so forth, they remain constant and thus provide no assistance. ||77||

If it were argued that the effect of pacifying fever and so forth arises from the universal (*sāmānya*) because there is no distinction in it, then—even though there are differences among individuals such as their field of application and so on—there would be no distinction in the rapidity of pacification or in the pot and other objects, nor would there be a gradation in the quality (*guṇa*).

If, however, this distinction exists within the universal, then its own nature is lost due to the difference in its essential character (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, because it is eternal (*dhrauvya*), it cannot be assisted by anything else.

The universal (*sāmānya*) does not produce an effect. For if it were to assist [the particulars], then—since that which cannot have further distinctions added to it is independent of anything else—it would either produce its entire effect all at once, or it would not possess the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) to produce it. As for the individuals (*vyakti*), however:
"In the case of an action being brought about, the genus (*jāti*) therein is also a means of accomplishment."
"That action is the motivator for the accomplishment of its own substrate.

For that very reason, because it is a [single] universal, that effect—characterized by the subsiding of fever and so forth—is one; and thus, the meaning is that the example is unestablished (*asiddha*).

"That is incorrect," says the Siddhāntavādin. "Because the universal is without distinction. Since it is undifferentiated due to its unity and eternity, the universal does not perform that specific effect; that is, it does not perform the effect of pacifying fever. Otherwise, because the universal would remain without distinction even when those individual instances such as *guḍūcī* differ according to their soil and other conditions, its effect of pacifying fever and so forth [would likewise remain unchanged].

Because it would lead to the consequence of there being no distinction [between cases], such as "quickly" or "after a long time," and so forth: for those born in a distinguished field, there is quick pacification;
for those born in the opposite [conditions], there is pacification after a long time.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), terms such as "much longer" and "much faster" are included. Furthermore, there would be no gradation (*tāratamya*) in the quality characterized by health and so forth in the body resulting from the use of *gūḍūcī* and other substances that differ according to the preparation of the field (*kṣetra-saṃskāra*) and other factors; for the universal (*sāmānya*) is one and the same. Now, if it is claimed that the universal possesses a particularity (*viśeṣa*) due to the differences in the field and other factors...
In that case, if a particularity were desired within the universal, there would be a difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because difference is characterized by particularity.

Consequently, there would be a loss of its own essential form; for the single nature of the universal would be lost. Furthermore, due to the reason of permanence, since the universal does not provide any assistance to the individuals, it does not perform any function. For if the universal were to assist [the individuals], [it would be subject to change].

In that case, because it is eternal and thus possesses no specific quality to be imparted by auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), it would not depend on anything else; consequently, due to its independence from auxiliaries, that universal (*sāmānya*) would produce its effect all at once. Alternatively, if it does not produce it, then it does not possess the nature of producing it;
for since there is no difference between its non-producing state and its producing state, it would follow that it would not produce the effect even at the time of its occurrence. This is the sense.

He says that for individual [entities], which are impermanent, there is no such fault in their performing an action, beginning with the words "But the individuals... (*vyaktayas tu*). "Refinement" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the sprinkling of water and so forth. Those whose production is qualified are "thus" (*tathā*). [The suffix -mat] is used because one thinks, "This has a distinction" (*viśeṣo 'syāsti*).
