There is no contradiction, because [the entity], through the efficacy of place, time, refinement, and activity, produces a specific result characterized by a particular excellence. Similarly, in that case, even though there is [change in] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), certain things— such as the recognition of a single object— [are established].

Alternatively, they are "non-different" because they are distinguished from those that do not perform that action, or because they are distinguished from things not produced by that [cause] when a single entity produces a manifold effect.
Now, is the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) to be understood as being identical to the universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by differentiation, or is it something entirely different?

If [it is argued that it is the particular], what follows from this? If it is the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), how can it be the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? Or otherwise, how could there be causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)?

A specific effect—characterized, for example, by the alleviation of fever—is not observed in those individuals; nor is it reasonable to say that the intermediate generality (*avāntarasāmānya*), characterized by qualities such as rapid efficacy, which resides in them, is what produces the specific effect.
Because it would follow that the effect of those [plants] would arise even for a man who does not consume the medicinal herbs. "Like that" means like a specific individual.

"Some" refers to members of the same class, such as the single recognition [of them as the same species], and by the word "etcetera," [one includes] the fetching of water and so forth from a single source.

"From those that do not perform that function" means they are said to be non-different from the difference [between them] with respect to those things that do not produce recognition and so forth. It is not [the case that they are non-different in every respect].
[This is] because of their connection with a single commonality. Having established non-difference by way of the effect, he speaks by way of the cause, beginning with "or by one," and so forth.

Just as the various types of jars produced by effort are said to be non-different from those not produced by effort—that is, from things not produced by effort—because they are distinguished from them; even though [each individual jar]...

"Even though there is a difference in the effort regarding the jar, nevertheless, because it is the cause for a single act of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), that [effort] also possesses unity. This will be demonstrated later. But what then... and so forth is the opponent's objection. "By that universal (*sāmānya*) which has differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*)—that is, exclusion—as its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or cause (*nimitta*)."
That which consists in the manifestation of conceptual cognition is incapable of performing a causal function; therefore, by virtue of that characteristic of difference,
it should be understood as being "common" through its similarity with the universal, while being other than the particular (svalakṣaṇa).

But surely, since it was previously stated that a universal is spoken of because these [entities], which appear as external while actually revolving within the intellect, have their specific forms grasped by those who conform to the appearance in the intellect, the persistence of doubt remains exactly as before.
True; however, this is introduced for the purpose of establishing a further fault. He speaks in order to make known that fault: "What follows from this?

The other [the opponent] states the intention of the question with the words beginning "If [it is] a particular characteristic," and so forth: "If the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of cognition, how can it be the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? For, by the power of the intention of conceptual cognition, the universal (*sāmānya*), characterized by difference [from others], [is established]."
It is established by virtue of its intended meaning, because of the statement: "The universal is proclaimed as being existent.
If the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were to be perceived as identical with such a universal, it would always be the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
And this is not tenable. Alternatively, if it is the form revolving in the intellect (*buddhiparivarti-rūpa*) that is perceived as identical, he states the fault in this case as well:

Or how could causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) arise from anything else? For causal efficiency does not arise from a form that is merely a mental appearance (*buddhipratibhāsi*). [Objection: Since impermanence and so forth are not perceived in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), they lack that nature; moreover, those properties belong to non-entities (*avastu*). [Response:
This is not a fault, because [impermanence and so forth] pertain to the object appearing in cognition (*jñānapratibhāsī*).

The suspicion regarding the linguistic conventions of universals, co-referentiality, and the relationship between properties and property-bearers [is addressed as follows]: This conceptual cognition which has arisen by relying on the grasping of the intrinsic nature of things and upon the latent impressions (vāsanā) deposited by that experience— though it does not have that [intrinsic nature] as its object, yet appears as if it had that as its object— is produced from the power of those very latent impressions deposited by that experience.

[The cognition] has the nature of having determined that state [of the object], as if it were its own essence (*svabhāva*). It grasps an object that is non-different from those things which produce an effect that is non-different [from itself]. However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), it possesses a form identical to the exclusion of others (*tadanyabheda*). This means it has a form identical to the exclusion of other [objects]. In that regard, for those engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahārin*), the form of the object exists because their activity proceeds through such a determination (*adhyavasāya*)—namely, [regarding the object] as being external and as being one.

Therefore, since they are said to be non-different from those things that do not produce that effect, the establishment of a universal (*sāmānya*) by way of its effect is untenable. Furthermore, because the form [of the universal] is merely a mental construct (*buddhiparivartin*), and because universals such as impermanence (*anityatva*) are not perceived within the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), the particular would not possess that nature—that is, the nature of impermanence and so forth. And in the particular, impermanence—
Since [entities] such as "you" (tvadīna) are not perceived, and since qualities such as impermanence (*anityatva*) are properties of non-entities (*avastu*), [the opponent objects].

He refutes this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*). The position adopted here is that the conventional usage of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth applies only to forms appearing in cognition (*buddhipratibhāsin*). Thus he says: "The object appearing in cognition," and so on.

And this is the summary statement (*grahaṇakavākya*). Its explanation is as follows: it is connected with the phrase "this conceptual cognition. Although it does not have that [particular] as its object—meaning although its object is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the real entity—it is "as if having that as its object," that is, as if having the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object. It is "that whose own form has determined that state," meaning its own form has superimposed an external existence upon it. And because—

Therefore, [the opponent] considers that [the conceptual cognition] has as its object only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it has determined (*adhyavasita*) that [particular] as its own nature. If one asks how it is that it has the nature of having determined that [particular] as its own nature, he says: "Because its very essence (*prakṛti*) arises from the latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of that [particular].

That is to say, the experience of that particular characteristic deposits a latent impression; the arising or production of that universal (*sāmānya*) from that [impression] is its essence or intrinsic nature.

The meaning is that by means of which the nature of the determined object comes into being. Those entities such as jars and the like, which have identical effects and are the causes of a cognition characterized by a single form, appear as if they were grasping a non-different object because they are produced from them through a continuous succession.
However, there exists no such thing as a universal entity—whether distinct or non-distinct—that could be grasped by it.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), however, the analysis is as follows: "having a form identical to the exclusion of others" means that its nature—which is distinct from those things intended as similar (i.e., of the same class) because it is different from them—is precisely that which is identical in form in the ultimate sense. For that very reason, because it arises from that [exclusion] and because it excludes that [opposite], the exclusion of others is said to be its identical form.

In that regard, concerning the cognition just mentioned, "as if one" means as if it were following after all individual instances; "as if performing its function" means as if it were performing purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). If it is asked, "How does it appear in such a way? he says: "Of those engaged in conventional practice," and so forth.

"Having thus determined" means having determined the very portion of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—namely, [the aspect] as being external, as being one, and as being capable of performing purposeful action.

"By way of causal efficiency" (*kāritvena*) means that it appears as having that very efficiency; otherwise, its engagement [with an object] would not be logical. And that [efficiency] appears by virtue of performing a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), as if distinct from those things that do not perform such an action. For it cannot be said that even for that [appearance], there is an ultimate reality (*tattva*), because such investigation is not a factor in this context. Those objects residing in the intellect are apprehended as being identical to that [perceived object].
Because they appear as if excluded from something [else]. Nor is it the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because that does not appear therein.

Those very [particulars], though undifferentiated, appear as possessing exclusion when excluded from something [else], because activity occurs for those who do not themselves engage in linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*). Others read "by those who engage in convention" (*vyavahāribhiḥ*); this refers to the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) by those who engage in convention.

By this [statement], because of the prior connection, only the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is employed, and not the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). This is because of the prohibition of the sixth case in the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 2.3.69). "Otherwise" means that if there were no external determination (*bāhyādhyavasāya*) regarding the aspect of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*), then even when such a conceptual differentiation has arisen, there would be no activity directed toward that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*). That too is the reflection within the conceptual differentiation.

It appears as if it possesses causal efficiency by virtue of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the person who employs it in practical discourse (*vyavahartṛ*). Consequently, it appears as if distinct from those things that do not perform that function. If it is asked, "Why is it not the case that the conceptual reflection (*vikalpaprativimbaka*) itself is the reality (*tattva*)?", he says: "And not," and so forth. That conceptual reflection is neither reality nor a real entity (*vastu*). For what reason? Because it lacks causal efficiency (*anarthakriyā*).
Because deviation is not a factor in the examination by way of causal efficacy (*kāritva*). We shall demonstrate this immediately hereafter.

In that regard, those objective forms (*arthākāra*) which, having entered through the door of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), appear in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), are [the] objects.
They are apprehended as being "similar" by means of that universal characterized by difference, which appears to conceptual cognition.

[The phrase] "excluded from something" refers to exclusion from what is of a different class (*vijātīya*). For instance, although the various particular trees appear to conceptual cognition, because they possess an externally determined form, they appear as if excluded from non-trees. The same applies to others.
The connection is made by modifying the gender and number [of the words], as in: "the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not apprehended as being similar to that.
What is the reason? Because in that conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) in which the universal (*sāmānya*) appears, the specific characteristic does not appear.
Thus far, the conventional usage of the universal with respect to the object appearing in cognition has been explained. Now, regarding the common...
Co-referentiality arises from verbal expression.

Furthermore, this aforementioned conventional usage of co-referentiality among objects appearing as mental reflections is performed with a purely false object. Why? Because even though the forms of conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*) are themselves non-existent, [they appear as such].

It is not so, because [the universal] is followed by a single form. Since the nature of a dharma is followed by two exclusions (vyāvṛtti), even for those things that exist as bound to the verbal expression of conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), they are presented by the intellect; thus, the conventional usage of universals and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has only a false object.

And all this [conceptualization] proceeds from the impressions deposited by the perception of unique particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves. Even though mental conceptualizations do not have those [particulars] as their direct manifestation, they nevertheless engage with the real object—just as the error of perceiving a gem occurs in the luster of a gem—and not otherwise. This is so even though these [conceptualizations] arise from differences [between objects], provided that one does not abandon the pursuit of the specific features as they were perceived.

Because of the superimposition of another [object] through the apprehension of some slight similarity— just as there is the cognition of a gem in the light of a lamp— the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) does not belong to the objects of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
despite their appearing in manifold forms.

Because of perception: the convention of "generality" arises from appearing in a single form, and the convention of "grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) arises from the appearance of a single [entity].
If every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has only a false object, why do [properties] such as impermanence—arrived at through the gateway of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth—[apply]?

Conceptual constructions such as "self" and so forth are not valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), yet conceptual constructions are not eternal; therefore, he says: "And all this," and so on. The connection is: "all this is a distortion" (*viplava*). "Distortion" (*viplava*) means error (*bhrānti*). "This" refers to that which has the form of universals (*sāmānya*) and the like.

It is produced by the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) deposited by the very perception of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); thus, all conceptual constructions [are produced] through a causal succession.

This is because they do not arise through the medium of the perception of a real entity (*vastu*). For even conceptual constructions such as "permanent" and so forth arise only through the perception of a real entity, insofar as they depend upon the perception of a continuous succession of similar subsequent arisings. In that regard, although all conceptual constructions equally depend upon the perception of a real entity as their gateway, conceptual constructions such as "impermanent," whose production is bound to that [perception], do not have that [entity] as their objective appearance (*pratibhāsa*), even though they arise in dependence upon it.

Even though the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear [in conceptual cognition], there is no lack of correspondence (*avisamvāda*) with respect to the real entity (*vastu*), because the superimposed form—such as impermanence and so forth—actually exists in the real entity.

It is merely that it does not appear in the form of the particular characteristic; thus, conceptualization is called an error (*vibhrama*). Just as in the case of the illusion of a jewel in the luster of a jewel, even when the true nature of the jewel is not grasped, there is no lack of correspondence with the luster of the jewel.
Because [the light] is bound to the gem, and because the illusion of the gem arises by depending upon the light;

however, conceptual constructions such as "eternal" and so forth are not like this, for even though they are dependent upon the gateway of perceiving the object, they superimpose a form that does not exist in the object at all. Thus he says: "Not of others," and so forth. "Of others" refers to those [conceptions] such as "eternal."

The connection is with the phrase "the correspondence of conceptual constructions (vikalpa) regarding the object. "Even though they arise from its differentiation" means even though they are produced from the non-differentiation of the object. This refers to abandoning the certainty that follows the particular feature perceived—characterized by momentariness and so forth—and [apprehending] some generality, whether it be distinct or non-distinct [from the object].

Or, because of the apprehension of a generality (*sāmānya*), there is a superimposition (*samāropa*) upon that particular [object] of qualities such as stability; thus, just as in the case of the cognition of a gem arising from the similarity of brilliance and so forth in the light of a lamp, there is no correspondence with the actual gem-object. This is because even with respect to the gem determined through a causal chain (*pāramparya*), [the cognition] lacks a direct connection. And since conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have only false objects, therefore, by means of conceptual construction—

The capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) exists in objects (*viṣaya*) that are [real] entities; therefore, the point previously raised—namely, how there could be causal efficiency from anything else—is established as proven.
[Thus, things] have arisen.

If it is asked, "How then is the universal, characterized by the exclusion of what does not produce that [effect], established with respect to objects that are the referents of conceptual construction? We say:
No. For those things which appear as if external, because they perform a single causal function, are distinguished from those that do not perform that function. Is this not so?

Nor is there an absence of impermanence and so forth in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Thus, for a moving entity, there is no such thing as "impermanence" per se. Because they perceive that which exists in such a way—namely, as abiding for only a moment—the [cognitions] of those [beings] arise: "This is impermanent" or "Impermanence belongs to this. Entering into that very nature of phenomena, conceptual constructions do not demonstrate the exclusion of various other properties.

Nor are they without a basis, because they depend on the perception of that [object's] differentiation. Nor do they possess the nature of a non-entity, because it is precisely the intrinsic nature of that [object] which appears as if it were a name. Regarding what was stated—that because impermanence and so forth are not perceived in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is no identity of form (*atādrūpya*)—he says "nor also," etc., in order to refute that: because impermanence does not exist apart from the moving entity (*vastu*).

There is nothing by which the impermanence of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) would be unconnected [to it]. Rather, the very entity that is in flux is permanent, precisely because the particular characteristic itself has the nature of impermanence; in this same way, "selflessness" (*anātman*) and so forth are also to be understood. Therefore, when the particular characteristic is apprehended by perception, impermanence is indeed apprehended, but it remains undetermined solely due to the presence of causes for error.

(1) Therefore, the function of inference consists merely in the ascertainment of that [universal]; thus, it is established that the cognition of impermanence regarding the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is simply the ascertainment of that [impermanence].

If the particular itself is impermanent, how can there be such expressions as "this object is impermanent" or "impermanence belongs to this"? [This would be impossible] regarding the subject (*dharmin*) and its property (*dharma*).

Because there is a cognition [of the object] as having a form [of permanence], he says "momentary," and so forth. "Of such a particular characteristic" means of that which has a mobile nature because it does not persist for more than a moment. Because it is grasped as lasting for only a single moment, for those who perceive the final moment at a later time, this occurs: "This is impermanent," and so forth. When there is no intention to exclude other distinctions, [the cognition is simply] "this is impermanent."
When there is a desire to exclude other distinctions, the cognition of the relationship between a property and its locus (*dharmidharmabhāva*) arises in the form "this has impermanence.

Since this is constructed by conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one might ask how there can be a relationship between a property and its locus regarding an external object; to this, he says: "taddharmatām," etc.

The meaning is that conceptualizations, while not actually entering into the state of being a property of that [external object]—that is, the state of being a property of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇadharmitā*)—determine the particular characteristic.

The compound *vyatirekāśca* is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound meaning "various forms and single forms, as well as exclusions. Following words for which conventions have been established based on differences in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), they show various properties (*nānādharmān*) such as impermanence and being produced, as well as a single property—impermanence—in many things such as pots, and the exclusion [of non-impermanence] in pots and so forth. The word "in the object" (*vastuni*) is to be supplied.

[Objection: But is it not the case that the capacity to cut through [the notion of] manifold properties and so forth is established by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? [Response: No, because conceptual construction does not grasp real entities (*avastu-grāhitvāt*).
For this very reason, he says: "they show. [Objection:
If they do not grasp real entities, then it follows that they are without a basis (*nirāśraya*). [Response: To this he says: "And not those... [The word] "not" (*na*)...

Thus, because conceptual constructions (vikalpas) have as their basis that perception— the direct experience (*anubhava*)— of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which consists of impermanence and so forth, and which is the differentiation of the objects of conceptualization that reveals various phenomena and the like; for it is indeed the case that, having seen the particular characteristic in its ultimate form as impermanent and so forth, the conceptual constructions— which arise through the power of that seeing— proceed by way of determining (*adhyavasāya*) the perceived aspect.

And since conceptual constructions proceed by expressing exactly what has been perceived—such as the aspect of impermanence—and do not follow after something else, like the conceptualization of permanence and so forth, therefore that which was stated—that "their nature is non-existent" (*avastu-dharmatā*)—is refuted. He says: "No. These [constructions] of impermanence and so forth do not have a non-existent nature. Why? Because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)...

Because that very [object] appears as having such properties as impermanence and so forth; that is to say, because of its manifestation and subsequent conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). If [it is asked] why it appears thus: it is because of its appearing in that way. However, the apprehension of multiple exclusions (*vyatireka*) in a single real entity is an error. This is because that [entity], which performs a single function, is established in that manner in order to induce the appearance of suchness during investigations into its state of being so, for the purpose of [facilitating] the desire to know it as such.
Not due to a difference in the object (*vastu*), because it is impossible for that very same single thing to be manifold, and impossible for the manifold to be one,

since any distinct [entity] has been negated. Furthermore, if one accepts the word-meaning according to the object based on a difference in their primordial nature (*prakṛti*), then grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be impossible.

If it is argued that there is no fault because only one thing possessing those attributes is denoted, [we reply: even though [the attribute] does not assist [the substrate], the dependence [of the attribute upon it] appears as a real property of the object, such as impermanence and so forth. Then, what is the delusion produced by conceptual construction?
He says: "But of the object," and so on. It is the grasping of a single object in multiple forms, and of many [objects] as one. [This concerns] the property and...

The apprehension [of an object] as distinct from its generic nature (*jāti*) is an error; that is to say, it is a delusion. What, then, is the reason that the apprehension of oneness and so forth is an error? He says: "Of that, whether one or many," and so forth. This refers to the distinction between jars and other things that perform a single function—namely, performing functions such as carrying water—and likewise regarding the desire to know their existence. That is, regarding the desire to know their status as performers of a single function. Likewise...

For the purpose of explaining [the unity of the cause], that is, for the purpose of explaining the performance of a single function; because it has been established as such [a unity]; because it has been fixed in a single form, such as a jar, for the sake of simplifying conventional usage (*vyavahāra*); and likewise, even though a single thing performs multiple functions—just as a jar performs functions such as visual cognition and the occasional holding of water—there is an inquiry into its existence as such.

This is for the purpose of making known [the object], that is, for the purpose of making known its manifold nature, because it exists in such a state; that is, because it is established in forms such as being visible, being earthy, and being impermanent. The same should be stated elsewhere as appropriate. It is not from a difference in the thing itself that there is an establishment of multiple properties in a single entity. What is the reason? Because of those very many [properties] of that single thing.

Because of the impossibility of [the identity of] the one [with the many], it is stated that the apprehension of the one as being many is an error (*vibhrama*). Likewise, the establishment of the one in what is actually many occurs only by way of the exclusion of what is not its effect (*akāryavyāvṛtti*), and not due to any non-difference in the entity itself; for he says: "because of the impossibility of the one in what is many. Thus, the apprehension of the one in what is many is an error. In the same way, the apprehension of a distinction between property (*dharma*) and the possessor of properties (*dharmin*) is also [an error].

This is indeed an error. What is the reason? Because a universal (*sāmānya*) distinct [from the particular] has already been refuted by such statements as, "The particulars do not follow after another," and so forth.
Since properties (*dharma*) are indeed distinct from the substratum (*dharmin*), the referent of a word corresponds to the object as it actually exists.

He says, "It will be so," beginning with the words "of those," and so forth. Because of the difference in the nature—that is, the intrinsic essence (*svabhāva*)—of those properties such as impermanence and the like, if one accepts the referent of a word according to its actual state, then coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be impossible in cases such as "the blue lotus" or "sound is impermanent. This is because there is no mutual [identity] between qualities such as blue and the like, and the universals (*jāti*) such as lotus and the like, in terms of their intrinsic essence.

Because of their difference [in nature], words denoting those [distinct things] do not have a single substratum; thus, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible. Therefore, the point is that the determination of word-meanings does not correspond to the actual state of reality.
