First, I shall go to settle the matter and examine the difficulty for others;

there is no difference [in the case] of *gātna* (*gantṛ*). Even in a state of dependence, because of the relationship between the produced and the producer, the two do not exist simultaneously; thus, neither is denoted.

The mental superimposition (*adhyāhāra*) of one by means of the intellect (*buddhi*) would not be a verbal object (*śabdārtha*) concerning a real entity. This is a manifestation of the intellect (*buddhipratibhāsa*).

With the words "of that [substance's] adjunct" (*tadupādheḥ*) and so forth, he anticipates the opponent’s objection: "There is no fault because those qualities such as blue and so on are the adjuncts of a single substance; since that one [substance] is denoted by two [terms], namely, a quality and a genus, there is no fault regarding the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). He states the answer: "(1) *anupakāriṇi* etc. [This refers to] those things intended to be the adjuncts.

A substance provides no assistance to properties such as blue and so forth. For no assistance whatsoever is rendered by the substance to the quality of blue or to the universal of "lotus-ness. Consequently, since dependence upon another is impossible for blue and other properties whose occurrences cannot be imparted to a substance that renders them no assistance, properties such as blue are not adjuncts (*upādhi*). This is because they lack dependence on another; otherwise, this [following] would occur:

It would not even be possible for them to be "conditioned" (upādhi). Now, if it is accepted that the dependence of properties (dharmas) has substance (dravya) as its object, then even in that case of dependence, one must admit that they are produced by the substance;

otherwise, their dependence upon the substance would be untenable. Furthermore, the producer must be admitted to be momentary (kṣaṇika), because a non-momentary thing is incapable of causal efficiency (arthakriyā). Consequently, [there is a causal relationship] between the conditions (upādhis), which are considered effects, and that which is considered the cause.

Because of the impossibility of two substances coexisting, there is no simultaneous denotation of both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), since at that time the specific property intended as the cause has ceased. The term "of one" refers even to the qualified [entity] which possesses limiting conditions (*upādhi*). The mental supplementation (*adhyāhāra*) presented there does not have a real entity as its object; rather, the meaning of the word would be only that which is superimposed by the intellect.
Because the particular (*viśeṣa*) is denoted by the word.
It might be thought: (1) let that which has perished—the qualified (*viśeṣya*)—be the object of the mental appearance for the word whose referent it is;
however, as for that which is still existent, namely the adjunct (*upādhi*), let the word expressing it have the real entity (*vastu*) itself as its object.
He says: "The appearance in cognition," and so forth. That designation whose object is the appearance in cognition is "thus" (*tathā*);

when that state exists, let every designation—even that which is intended to have a particular as its object—be likewise only an object of the appearance in conceptual cognition. What is the reason? Because [it refers to] that which possesses distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in such a manner.

Because a single entity possessing various qualifiers appears in the cognition upon its apprehension; for in that case, one must admit a conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) that mentally supplies [the qualifiers] when the qualified entity has perished. And since the qualified entity is absent at that time, the qualifier is also absent, because there is no dependence [of the qualifier] [upon it]. How [could there be a cognition] when a single entity possessing distinct qualifiers does not appear?
Regarding grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*):

when it is accepted that both the qualifier and the qualified appear as objects of a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), then a single cognition arises which manifests a single substratum (*dharmin*) grasped by two imagined properties (*kalpita-dharma*). Thus, coreferentiality is not contradictory.
[The term] *adhikaraṇya* [is used].

With the words "the beneficiary" (*upakārya*) and so forth, he anticipates the opponent’s objection. The faultlessness [of the position] is that which was stated by the passage beginning with "this superimposition upon a single cognition" (*ekasya buddhyādhyāhāra*). Because an attribute (*upādhi*) that exists simultaneously with its possessor (*upādhimat*) and has an already established form lacks dependence (*pāratantrya*) [upon that possessor].

[Objection: "The state of being a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is precisely that dependence [on another] which exists prior [to the cognition]. To this, he says: “No,” and so forth. For it is not the case that because the objecthood [of the universal] is one, everything should be exactly like that; for when there is apprehension, a single thing possessing distinct limiting adjuncts appears as such.
If it is argued that there is no fault because the adjunct (*upādhi*) and the possessor of the adjunct (*tadvat*), as well as the benefactor and the beneficiary, exist simultaneously, we say:

no. Since there is an absence of dependence (*pāratantrya*) at the time of production, there can be no status as an adjunct. Nor is there non-production, because [the entity] is determined by its own nature (*svabhāva*).
Because there is an absolute absence of dependence, that very same cognition [of dependence] is superimposed through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) in all linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).

Why is it not followed [by other words]? Because when a thing is made an object by a single word and a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), all its particularities (*viśeṣa*) are implied by the force of the thing itself; thus, there would be no point in [employing] others. Since the appearance in cognition (*buddhipratibhāsa*) lacks a real entity (*nirvastuka*), there is no possibility of [particularities] arising through the power of the thing. Even when making an object of a single form that is non-different from that [thing], the form—

Because there is no certainty regarding one form [of the object], it must be grasped by a cognition that has expectations regarding another form. Since a distinct word-meaning—once established—is like the horn of a hare, its dependence (*pāratantrya*) or its status as a limiting adjunct (*upādhitva*) is in every respect non-existent, whether the thing itself be existent or non-existent.
For this reason, having made the dependence of limiting adjuncts a conceptual superimposition (*kalpanāropita*), [one speaks of] dependence...

Regarding conventional usage (*vyavahāra*): "in every way" means by every possible manner. Just as the intellect is followed in the conventional usage of dependence (*pāratantrya*), why is that same superimposing intellect not followed in the conventional usage of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*)? For it is logical to follow that [intellect], because it is impossible to engage in conventional usage without relying on the appearance of an object as presented by the intellect. This is so with respect to the real entity (*vastu*).

If an object were made the object of a single word and a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then by the force of the thing itself, there would be an implication of all properties that constitute the intrinsic nature of that thing; consequently, the [use of] other words and so forth would be redundant, as was previously stated regarding "the intrinsic nature of a single object being perceived," and so on.
Alternatively, in the case where the thing is the subject (*pakṣa*), it would have to conform to the appearance in the cognition thereof. Why? Because of the cognition—[text fragment].

Because the manifestation (*bhāsa*) is devoid of a real entity (*nirvastuka*), there is no occasion for those faults that arise from the causal efficacy of a real entity. By using the plural number, he says this:

not only is the fault of the other [terms] being redundant absent, but likewise, a separate universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist, because it is impossible for limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) to possess dependence on another.

The absence of the relation between qualifier and qualified, and the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—which you have stated [to apply] because a single entity possessing distinct limiting adjuncts does not appear in cognition—these too are impossible here; he states this very point in the passage beginning with "that appears as non-different" (*tad-abhinnam*). For indeed, the form appearing in that cognition appears as non-different; therefore, it is a universal (*sāmānya*).

Having modified the statement to "so that it does not contradict experience," the connection is made with what is to be said hereafter: although when "blue" is stated, the conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) takes as its object a single form, namely blueness, by way of the exclusion of non-blue (*anīlavyāvṛtti*), the removal of doubt occurs only regarding that very form of blue, and not regarding other forms. Therefore, the nature appearing to that cognition is—

Because there is no ascertainment of the form of the lotus—which is excluded from non-lotuses—within the form of the white [lotus] and so forth. The connection is as follows: since a cognition has arisen that does not ascertain a certain form, another form appears as the object to be grasped by that cognition, because the word "lotus" is employed with reference to it while still being expectant of that other form.
By this, the cause for the relationship of qualifier and qualified has been stated; [now] he speaks of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

[The verse begins with] "distinct," and so forth. Even when there is a presentation—that is, a communication—of distinct word-meanings characterized as "blue" and "lotus," they appear in a single cognition as non-distinct; thus, the general relationship of qualifier and qualified and [grammatical] coreferentiality [are established].

The co-existences [of properties] are not contradicted according to how they are perceived. Furthermore, although there is a distinction between property and property-bearer, even when that [object] is distinct from multiple things, it is that very same entity when there is an inquiry regarding the affirmation or negation of its distinction from one [specific thing]. This is because, after other distinctions have been set aside, it appears to the cognition in such a way when prompted by the word "property. It is distinct [from others].

Just as with the property (*dharma*), another [property] is established as the substratum (*dharmin*) without distinction and is thus demonstrated. On the basis of that alone, the two properties, being embraced within an undivided single substratum in the form of a mental appearance, appear in conceptual cognition; therefore, universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth are not contradicted according to how they are perceived.

Therefore, as for what was stated by Bhaṭṭa: "(1) By grasping apoha as merely the exclusion of others, since there is an absence of the exclusion of non-lotuses when there is the exclusion of non-blue things, and since there is an absence of the exclusion of non-blue things when there is the exclusion of non-lotuses, there can be no relationship of qualifier and qualified between those two properties; and because that [relationship] is absent, there can be no such relationship between the two words that denote them."
There is also no relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two words, nor is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), because the objects denoted by the words are distinct.

Nor can coreferentiality be mediated through the objects in which the two exclusions (*apoha*) reside, because exclusion, being a non-entity, lacks the property of being "located" (*ādheya*). Furthermore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not accepted as the object of the word, nor is any other substratum admitted. And it is not the case that...

The claim that "even though both the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and exclusion (*apoha*) exist, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between two words because their having a single object is not perceived" is refuted; for it is accepted that the word's own form (*svākāra*), which is distinct from the external [object], is the object of words and so forth. Therefore, in words such as "blue lotus," the denotation of the word-meaning is indeed accepted, and thus everything is well-established.

The connection [of the sentence] is through the transformation of the words: "the distinction between dharma and adharma of this mental appearance (*buddhipratibhāsa*) is not contradicted by its mode of perception. He expresses that very point with the words beginning with "from the manifold" (*aneka*). Because the mental appearance is unreal (*alīka*), how could there be a distinction of manifold objects? It is merely said thus on account of the person's conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*); such is his cognition.

Regarding the distinction of a single appearance from its object, when there is a desire to know its affirmation or negation—such as "Is sound impermanent? or "Does it not possess visual form?"—the connection is that the very object which has become the appearance of cognition is what is being demonstrated. To the question "In what manner?", he says: "Having rejected," and so forth.
Alternatively, the connection is that even the distinction between property (dharma) and its possessor (dharmin) is not contradictory for this entity. Why? He says:

when a distinction from multiple external objects is possible, regarding the distinction of that [entity] from one [object], in the inquiry as to its affirmation or negation—such as "Is sound impermanent? or "Does it not possess visibility?"—that very [distinction] is what is intended.
The connection is that "an external object is demonstrated. To the question "By what is it demonstrated?", he says: "Having rejected," and so forth.

The connection is: "having urged by means of the word 'dharma' (property), [one] establishes it as if it were a distinct property. For instance, when an urging is made by the word 'dharma' such as "impermanence is not visible," a property such as impermanence appears as if it were distinct [from the subject].

It is established. For what reason? He says: because it appears thus to the intellect (*buddhi*). Due to the distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*), the intellect appears as if possessing distinctions, but not due to an actual ontological distinction.
Furthermore, by the indication of the multiplicity of such distinctions, there is the distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).

(ga) Apoha functions as the differentiator from heterogeneous classes; the differentiation of the appearance of properties, which rests upon its own nature, is produced for the sake of cognizing that very nature.

The intellect, having that as its intrinsic nature (or the Great Door), arises as conceptualizing, devoid of even that object, and established in the differentiation of objects that do not possess that causal function. ||78||

In that [cognition], whatever form appears as if it were a single external object distinct from others— because the cognition, when prompted by a word, manifests as apprehending a property (*dharma*) that is indeed distinct [from the substrate]— "without distinction" means without rejecting all particular differences; thus, this other external nature, whose internal differences have not been rejected, is established as the substratum (*dharmin*).
It is indicated by the word "sthāpya" (having established).

This is what is meant: having prompted [the mind] with the word "dharma" and shown it as if there were a distinct property (*dharma*), and then again having prompted it with the word "dharmin" and established another intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as the substratum (*dharmin*), that very same external object is demonstrated.

The impermanence of sound is not its visibility; thus, "sound is impermanent and not visible. Regarding the phrase "by way of the presence and absence [of attributes]": because the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) are distinct when other differences are either excluded or not excluded, the conceptualizing cognition appears as if it were differentiated and as if it had distinct forms. However, there is no actual difference in the entity itself. It is not the case that the cognition is differentiated due to a difference in the entity.
Why? (1) Because of the aforementioned fault; for it is impossible for properties to be dependent upon a subject (*dharmin*) that provides no assistance.
Likewise, there would be a distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*), which is impermanence, and the probans (*sādhana*), which is "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*). Therefore, he says:
"In such a manner," and so forth. [This refers to] the manyness of the distinct properties (*dharmabheda*) that have rejected other intervening distinctions.
The connection [of the sentence] is that the distinction of words and the distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) are being made.

The meaning is: by means of those reflections in conceptual cognitions (*vikalpabuddhi*) which have as their basis the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that entity excluded from this and that, and which consist of the various appearances of properties (*dharma*); that is to say, by means of the various appearances whose essence is the properties. He asks: for what purpose are they made? [He replies:]
"Of that very nature," and so forth; for the sake of the realization or the attainment of that very excluded (vyāvṛtta) nature of the thing.
Because their connection to the object occurs through a causal sequence (*praṇālikā*), he states a summary verse for the sake of easily grasping the very subject at hand:
"Its own nature," and so forth. That cognition which is known as conceptual (*vikalpikā*) is the experience of that objective nature.

The word "also" (*api*) is displaced [in the verse]. Even though it does not possess [the object] directly, it has that very object as its referent; that is, it has the real entity (*vastu*) as its object. This is because of its determination (*adhyavasāya*).

The [cognition] is said to be "based on that" because it arises through the force of experiencing the exclusion [of others], and because there is correspondence with the object as excluded from those things which do not produce that effect. It is based on that [exclusion] because it resides in the difference from those things which do not have that effect.
It is said to be "based on that" because it arises through the power of experiencing that [exclusion] and because of the correspondence of the object that has been excluded.

In such a cognition as this, that objective form—which appears as if external due to the unification of the perceived object and the conceptual construction—appears as if identical across individuals of the same class, as if unitary, and as if excluded from others of a different class. Yet it is indeed excluded [from being real], because the nature of cognition is unreal. That form of cognition is devoid of reality (*nistattva*).
Bha 4Ad Maganda,
the same as the Yoga Mapā.
That [exclusion], being devoid of reality because it is not a constituent part of investigation, is as if it were excluded. (79)
Since those objects are established in cognition as having the nature of being excluded [from others], they appear as if distinct; yet they are further excluded from other things. (80)
It is precisely those [particulars]; through cognitions and designations whose objects are common and share a common substratum, false discourse (*vyavahāra*) is extended. (81)
Furthermore, all things depend upon mutual non-existence; therefore, one thing is the support of another, and that [other] is the support of the former. (82)

It is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). What is the reason? Because it lacks the status of being a factor for critical examination (*parīkṣānaṅgabhāva*). Only that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*) is a factor for critical examination; therefore, by virtue of lacking the status of being a factor for critical examination, it follows that it is incapable with respect to causal efficiency. And since the form appearing to cognition (*buddhipratibhāsi-rūpa*) is without reality (*nistattva*), the conventional activity (*vyavahāra*) directed toward it proceeds only with regard to a false object.
Thus he said.

"Objects," and so forth. "Qualified by cognition" means that they have ascended onto the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*); being thus qualified by cognition, they possess the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) because they consist of the form of exclusion from what is heterogeneous. For example, lotus-objects consist of the form of exclusion from non-lotuses. Therefore, by virtue of that ultimate form of exclusion—namely, "lotus-ness"—they appear as if they were non-different.
Not ultimately, because the nature of cognition is unreal. By this, the cause for the conventional usage of "universal" has been stated.

Furthermore, "those very [objects] are excluded from others" means that those very objects, as qualified by cognition, while possessing the form of being excluded from others, appear again as excluded even from others of the same class, just like those very particular instances of blue.
[It arises] from what is non-blue; and for this reason, because a single object, embraced by two exclusions, appears [in cognition].

The seed of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has been stated. He states that very point with the words "of them," and so forth. The connection is as follows: "the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of those objects appearing in cognition is extended. The genitive case in "of them" (*teṣām*) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) with respect to the linguistic usage. Of what nature is this false object? By what means is it produced? To this he says: "by the universal," and so forth.

"Having a common substratum" (*samānādhāratva*) means "that which has a common substratum" (*samānādhāra*). Because the designation emphasizes the state [of being], the linguistic usage regarding the universal (*sāmānya*)—which has the universal as its object—is extended by means of cognitions and designations whose objects are those having a common substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
By other [means], the linguistic usage regarding co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established.

Although in this context linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) consists solely of verbal cognition, nevertheless, by attributing to them an active operation (*savyāpāratā*), both cognition and the word are regarded as instruments (*karaṇa*). There is no fault in this, because it is precisely the activity characterized by the manifestation of the object that is intended to be the linguistic usage for those two—just as cognition may be designated as either the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or the result (*phala*). And all such linguistic usage is characterized by cognition and its expression.

The mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of things—that is, their individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)—is their mutual exclusion (*parasparavyavaccheda*). [The conceptual cognition] is based upon that, because it arises by way of the experience of excluded objects. Therefore, by virtue of being based on mutual absence, that linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is said to have "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as its object;
however, this is not because its object is the exclusion of others, for this convention has a positive entity (*vidhi*) as its object. (4) [Investigation of Universals]
Where there is a connection with a real entity, as in the aforementioned inference, [the cognition is valid];
it is not so elsewhere, even if there is an equality of error, just as the light of a lamp [is not the cause] for the perception of death.

(Therein, although it is manifold, it has a single effect; by means of designations and cognitions based on its difference from those things that do not produce that effect,) worldly transaction is extended through its being treated as a unity. (84)

Likewise, although it is a single entity produced by many [causes], when its various states are manifested, it is perceived as possessing manifold properties (*nānādharmā*) through the differentiation of its effects and purposes. (85)
This meaning of words, though non-existent, is stated according to common cognition;
yet, co-referentiality (sāmānyādhikaraṇya) is not possible for that which lacks reality. (86)

Conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*) is not the basis for the acquisition of a real entity (*vastu*) nor for the attainment of a real entity; nor is it all [such discourse]. Rather, it is that conventional discourse in which there exists an indirect connection with such a real entity as it truly is. He provides an example: "as in the aforementioned inference" (*yathoktānumitau yathā*). The "aforementioned inference" refers to the conceptualization of inference previously described. It does not apply elsewhere, such as in [the case of] permanence (*sthira*) and so forth.
Because in that conceptual construction, there is no connection to the actual object even through a causal succession; for the object possesses unstable and other such characteristics.

This is because both inferential conceptualization and other types of conceptualization are equally erroneous, insofar as they determine an external object through their own internal mental image (*svapratibhāsa*). Just as with the light of a lamp: just as the cognition of a gem in the light of a gem is an error, so too is it an error in the case of the light of a lamp.

Even though they are equally erroneous, the perception of the luster of a gem as being the gem itself is consistent with the gem that is to be attained, whereas the light of a lamp is not; likewise, the conceptual construction of [the object] as stable and so forth is consistent—this is the meaning.

If the linguistic usage of "universal" (*sāmānya*) and so forth applies only to objects that are established within cognition, then there would be no activity regarding external objects because the usage of "universal" and so forth would be absent there; therefore, he says: "In that regard," and so on. The word "therein" (*tatra*) introduces the sentence, or it functions as a term of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Therein, among the individuals (*vyakti*), those individuals which perform a single function are selected. [The text continues: "many..."

Just as specific jars, though distinct, perform the same function—such as carrying water—and thus do not perform what is not their function, so too there is an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from those things that are other than them. That exclusion is the basis (*āśraya*) for those cognitions and designations by which even a manifold object is led to be treated as one; that is to say, it attains the status of a universal (*sāmānya*) in conventional usage.

The word "tathā" (likewise) refers to the expectation of the immediately preceding generality. Even a single entity performs multiple functions; for example, a jar performs such functions as being perceived by visual consciousness, carrying water, and so forth. In the *Tadbhāvadīpana*, this is for the purpose of illuminating its status as a performer of multiple functions. By means of the reason of its distinction from other effects, it possesses various properties (*nānādharmā*), such as "the jar is visible," "it is earthen," and so on. By that, [there is] commonality—
Furthermore, the conventional usage of co-occurrence, qualifier, and qualified has been demonstrated only with respect to external objects.

If conventional usage regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth among external objects were ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), then [the aforementioned fault] would follow; therefore, he says: "as described according to cognition" (*yathā-pratīti-kathita*). In accordance with the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpa-buddhi*), the referent of a word (*śabdārtha*)—namely, the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—is described as it appears, even though it does not exist in ultimate reality. Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is also described as it appears.
Because this verbal meaning and its grammatical coreferentiality cannot possibly apply to a real entity:

"The distinction between property and property-bearer, as well as their non-distinction, is established in such a way that it is perceived in the world without regard for the true nature of reality. (87)
Relying precisely upon that [conventional reality], the establishment of the means and the goal is formulated by the wise for the purpose of entering into the ultimate truth. (88)
Ultimate objects are neither conjoined nor divided in themselves;
their appearance as one or many is merely a conceptual construction of the intellect. (89)

Therefore, this distinction—namely that "universal" and "particular" are both [aspects] of the mental object—is merely a conceptual differentiation of its properties through the exclusion of others. (10)

Because the perception of real entities is lost when one conceptualizes the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), [the author] says "dharma," etc., in order to summarize what was introduced in the statement: "The conventional usage of property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*) pertains to objects appearing in cognition. This is the establishment that "this is the property" and "this is the substratum," and the distinction between these two is such that "this is its property because it is produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*).
It has the characteristic of being a conceptual construct. It is a non-difference such as "this is produced. And this [non-difference] is superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
It does not examine the true meaning of reality; the analysis of the compound is: that by which the true meaning of reality—that is, the actual object—is disregarded.
As in common worldly usage:
Even when mounted upon the intellect, it is perceived as having that state through the process of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: that distinction between phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth is postulated exactly as it is perceived in the world, through the differentiation of the established relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). For what purpose? For the sake of entering into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), that is, for the sake of fathoming the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things such as impermanence.

Furthermore, he asks: what is the reason that linguistic conventions such as "oneness" and so forth are impossible with respect to a real entity? He says: "They do not conjoin," and so on. Ultimate objects do not conjoin by themselves; therefore, there is no conventional usage of a universal (sāmānya) with respect to a real entity.

They are neither merged nor differentiated by properties such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, because it is impossible for that single entity to possess [multiple] identities individually. Therefore, when among those many objects a single form is determined (*adhyavasīyate*) in one object, or multiple forms are determined in a single object, that is a delusion—an error—of conceptual cognition (*vikalpakā buddhiḥ*). For this reason, ultimate objects (*pāramārthikā arthāḥ*) are neither conjoined nor differentiated.

For that reason, this [conceptual] generality belongs to many [individuals]. Likewise, regarding the distinction between properties (*dharma*) and property-bearers (*dharmin*), this distinction—that is, the conventional usage of diversity—is based on the object of cognition (*buddhyartha*), not on the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). Since the appearance in cognition is unreal, one might ask: "How then can there be a distinction between properties such as 'being produced' and so forth within that particular? To this he says: "Of that very [particular]..."
And so forth. It is precisely that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is conceptually differentiated into distinct properties (*dharma*) through the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*).

Why is the relationship between the signifier (*gamaka*) and the signified (*gamya*) established through the distinction of imagined properties (*kalpitadharma*) rather than by the mere perception of the real entity (*vastu*)?

To this he says: "The probandum," and so forth. This is because, in the conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*) that "this is the probandum" and "this is the probans," there is a loss of the perception of the real entity.

Alternatively, why is it that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself, as qualified by the universal (*sāmānya*), is not apprehended by inference just as it is by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? To this he says: 4. *Sāmānyacintā* (Investigation of the Universal).
Difference [is that which is] associated with the universal; here, the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is not the object of cognition. || 91 ||
That [object] cannot be grasped in any way through forms such as "identical" or "different," because it is impossible for multiple distinct differences to reside in that single [entity]. (12)

That form is entirely distinct [from others], yet there exists neither scripture nor conceptual construction that establishes it as such, because [the term] functions solely by way of a universal (sāmānya). //93//
These are the summary verses.

If it is asked, "But why are words applied to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)? [the answer begins with] "In the conceptualization of the probandum and the probans," and so forth. Because of the abandonment of the perception of the real entity (*vastu*) in the conceptualization of the probandum and the probans, how could there be a universal (*sāmānya*) of the particular characteristic?

[The opponent claims: "There is the apprehension of the qualified; the particular (*bheda*) conjoined with the universal (*sāmānya*) is what is to be apprehended. Thus, [the author] speaks the words beginning with "particular" (*bheda*) in order to dispel the suspicion that masters such as Ācārya Dignāga have asserted the apprehension of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as conjoined with the universal.
Even in this statement, "the particular conjoined with the universal is perceived," that which is to be apprehended is not the particular itself.

The meaning is that it should not be understood as "it has been taught" [in that literal sense]. Rather, it should also be understood there that external particulars themselves, conjoined with the universal characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), are determined (*adhyavasīyante*), but they are not actually apprehended (*gṛhyante*).
Others, however, read the text with the masculine gender: "the particular conjoined with the universal is the object of apprehension" (*grāhya*). In that case, the meaning is as follows:
Even in this statement that "the object of apprehension is that which is conjoined with a universal," the particular (svalakṣaṇa) is not to be understood [as the object].

If it is asked, "What, then, is the reason that it must be understood as being in that very [particular]? he says: "Similar," and so forth. "Similar form" (*samānākāra*) refers to a single form existing in many things. "Different form" (*bhinnākāra*) refers to the state of possessing multiple properties (*anekadharmatva*) in a single thing. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the forms of property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) is intended. That particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not at all an object of apprehension (*grāhya*). What is the reason? Because in that [particular], which is a single [entity]...

Regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), since it is impossible for many distinct properties— such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*)— which are themselves distinct entities, to exist within that single specific characteristic; for it is not logical for a single entity to possess multiple forms, because a specific characteristic is partless (*niraṃśa*).

He says, introducing [the next point], "That form," and so forth. "That" means for that reason; "form" refers to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is distinct from everything else and unique. Thus, there is no verbal expression (*śruti*), that is, no word, nor is there any conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), that expresses that particular characteristic by way of its unique form. The word "no" refers to what is under discussion: [there is no such expression] for the particular characteristic by way of its own unique nature.
The meaning is that there is no grasper. What is the reason? (1) Because both the word and conceptual construction function only with respect to the universal.

By stating that there is no scripture (*śruti*) that establishes that [particular], he has said that words are not applied to the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); to this, he raises an objection with the words "But what then," and so forth. Words are "conventional" (*saṃketinaḥ*), meaning they have been made objects of convention; they express that [object]. They are... [the text continues with *vyava-*]

The convention is established for the sake of communication. However, at the time of practical usage, that specific particular (svalakṣaṇa) does not exist where the convention was originally made. Therefore...
[the object] is not perceived.
Words express that which has been conventionally designated; this is remembered as being for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*).
At that time, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not exist; therefore, no convention applies to it. (94)

For a convention does not exist at the time of indicating a conventionalized object by means of words; rather, it is as if one thinks, "A convention has been established at a later time such that from this word there is the comprehension of this object," and thus employs it for the sake of linguistic practice. However, it is not logical that a word whose convention was previously established regarding a particular (svalakṣaṇa) should be applied later [to a universal], because that [particular] lacks [the properties of] place and time.
Because it does not encompass particulars. If this is so, then there can be no application of convention (*saṃketa*) to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Now, if it is argued that a word is said to denote something that pervades both the distinct and the non-distinct, and thus there is no fault regarding the absence [of the object] at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), we say:
no; it is not so.
A person might act only after discerning things capable of purposeful action;
thus, denotative expressions are applied to objects for the sake of accomplishing those ends. (95)
Indeed, the world would not suffer distress or calamity if it did not employ words without conventional agreement.
If one asks why this is so: every undertaking worthy of attention is for the sake of a result; an undertaking that is fruitless is to be disregarded.

Furthermore, because even a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is momentary, there is no persistence of that very same form at a later time; nor, if it were non-momentary, [would such persistence be possible].

Or, because of the very absence of cognition [of such a universal], there is no persistence of its being the object [of a convention] even at another time, much less among particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) that are distinct in space and time. For this reason, the ellipsis is supplied: "Therefore, a convention is not made with respect to that particular characteristic.
He explains this with the words beginning with "for not" (*na hi*).
"Api nāma" means "how indeed might it be? "Prāk" (previously) refers to the connection established at the time of the convention with the word; this is the grammatical construction.

"Ekatra" means in a single, identical particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); "paścāt" means at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). Why is it not tenable? He says: "tasya," etc. "Tasya" refers to that which was perceived at the time of the convention during the state of linguistic usage.
Because it does not fail across differences of place and time, and because it follows [the object]; for a particularity observed in one place cannot possibly exist elsewhere.

According to the Vaiśeṣika system, it is distinct; according to the Sāṃkhya system, it is non-distinct. Because it pervades individual instances of the same class, the universal (*sāmānya*) is all-pervasive (*vyāpin*). Therefore, there is no fault regarding the absence [of the object] at the time of linguistic usage.
There is no fault of the absence of the word-referent at the time of linguistic usage, because the universal is the referent of the word, and that very universal is a single entity.
Because [the object] exists at both the time of the convention and the time of practical usage.

How so? Regarding this sense, the word *api* [is used]. (1) At the time of practical usage, having cognized objects capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) from a word that has been uttered, how indeed might one proceed toward their accomplishment—that is, toward the accomplishment of purposeful action?

With the intention expressed by the word "person" (*pumān*), expressive words are applied to objects. He explains this with the passage beginning "Indeed not," and so forth. "Indifference to the result" refers to a lack of intent or a mere whim; that is, when people, whether they are establishing a convention or using words for an object already conventionally established, do so entirely [without regard for a specific result]. 4. Examination of Universals (*sāmānyacintā*).

Because [human action] is purposeful, therefore this person, when employing a word in some context, ought to desire some result. And that result consists entirely of the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired. Thus, having determined what is a means to the desired and what is not a means to the undesired, he would attend to an injunction (*niyoga*)—thinking, "I shall perform or cause to be performed an engagement or a withdrawal therein"—or he would employ words accordingly.

Otherwise, because it would be something to be disregarded, the universal (*jāti*) therein is incapable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Indeed, the universal is never present in such things as carrying or drawing loads. Nor is there the employment of words in worldly transactions in the absence of such a context. Since the individual (*vyakti*) cannot be directly denoted [by the word], the universal is said to be expressed through "indication of that which is indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).

Another [type of] verbal [expression] is that which is worthy of attention, fit for apprehension, an undertaking, and a practical activity aimed at a result; it is not, however, fruitless. Why? Because an undertaking that is fruitless is to be disregarded by those who act with foresight, and thus it is not to be grasped. Therefore, this cognizer, while employing [a word] for some intended object or establishing a convention, seeks only a result.

"Engaged" (*yukta*) means that one ought to expect nothing other than the purpose (*prayojana*). "And that" refers to the fruit, characterized by the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired; this is to be connected accordingly. Since the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is intended to consist precisely in the acquisition of the desired and the removal of the undesired, this person [seeks] the means and the non-means for those two desired fruits.

Having understood this, one would engage in that which accomplishes the desired and desist from that which accomplishes the undesired; or, with the intention "I shall cause others to act," the speaker would employ words, and the listener would likewise attend to the injunction.
It is indeed reasonable to employ words with the thought, "I shall cause another to act," because the employment of words is for the sake of another.

But what is the utility of the word regarding the causes of engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*)? True; however, this presentation was made on the grounds that one who, through the habit of employing words, understands for himself alone, might sometimes understand in such a way; otherwise, [the word] would be something to be disregarded, as there would be no purpose for the application of the word.
Because it is to be disregarded. Since this principle is thus established, a universal (*jāti*) is incapable of performing a purposeful action; therefore, it is not an object of words.
He explains this with the words "for not," and so forth. A universal is not capable of performing such tasks as carrying or milking; and consequently—
For those seeking [results] such as carrying or milking, the injunction regarding the universal (*jāti*) is fruitless; therefore, the employment of words is not for its sake.

Furthermore, as for the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) characterized by one’s own cognition that is described as belonging to the universal, a person does not act for the sake of that, because it is already established through the very employment of the word. Will the employment of the word then be for the sake of the cognition of the universal alone?

If it is argued that [the universal is denoted], he says: "Not so," and so forth. "Such" refers to the context of carrying, milking, and so on; for it has been stated that the employment of a word for something fruitless is to be disregarded. Furthermore, if the universal were the denotation, there would be a cognition of the sentence-meaning from the sentence "Bring the cow," because the universal *gotva* (cowness) lacks connection with the action. Nor is it indicated (*lakṣita*)—

Or rather, the cognition of the sentence-meaning occurs through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because it is not [directly] perceived from the words themselves. For first there is no cognition of universals (*sāmānya*) from the words;

then from those [universals] comes the cognition of particulars (*viśeṣa*), and from the particulars comes the cognition of their mutual connection (*anvaya*). Thus, the cognition of the sentence-meaning is of a delayed nature. [Objection: Even if exclusion (*apoha*) is the denotable object, how can there be a cognition of the external object, given that exclusion is devoid of form? Nor [is it the case that the cognition arises] from a portion of the cognition itself...

If this is argued, [we reply: even if a relation exists that is not enjoined by words, how could one act upon it? For when someone says, "Cut the staff," no one cuts the person holding the staff. Nor can there be activity toward the individual because of impossibility; for it is logical that the application of a word be directed toward what is unrelated [to the intended action], since [the individual] does not perform the purposeful action [denoted by the word].
It will be demonstrated that it is indeed correct to apply a word to that [particular] because it appears solely as that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākāritva*).
Nevertheless, even so, since that aspect of cognition is a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), how can it be denotable by a word?

To this it is replied: First of all, a part belonging to itself (*svāṃśa*), which is non-different from the external object, indeed appears in conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*). It does not appear [in its entirety] simply because it is a conceptual cognition, for that would entail the consequence that it must be ascertained in its totality, and such is not admitted.
Nor is its apprehension merely the determination (*adhyavasāya*) by conceptual cognition of it as having the nature of an external object, according to its actual mode of being.

If [the object] is not apprehended because it is not grasped by a means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could there be an appearance (*pratibhāsa*) of it? However, if [it is held that] the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of cognition is such that its own part (*svāṃśa*) has the nature of consciousness (*samvit*), then an appearance is logical.

Therefore, if the nature of the specific characteristic of cognition is not admitted for the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—which consists of the part belonging to itself and is of the form of ignorance (*avidyā*)—then there would be no appearance at all. And how, then, could there be [an appearance] through a conceptual construction that is of the nature of non-cognition (*ajñāna*)?

The delimitation of its own aspect [belongs] to this [conceptual cognition] because it is of the nature of cognition. Therefore, precisely because it is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of cognition, the appearance of its own aspect in conceptualization is established as the object of conceptualization, being non-different from the external.

Since that which has a form known through experience is determined by conceptualization as non-different from the external, for this very reason conceptualization has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object.

It is said: [cognition] does not have the particular (svalakṣaṇa) as its object, because neither of the two parts [of the cognition] is apprehended in its own form. Therefore, even the particular nature of the cognition itself, when superimposed as having an external nature upon its own part, possesses the character of a universal (sāmānya). And so he will say:
"If it were an object by virtue of being the nature of cognition, then it would follow that it is a universal."
"Likewise, because it is desired [as such], it is considered equal by virtue of having the form of the object to be excluded" (PV 3.336).

And its being denotable by a word is indeed logical. [The opponent says: "It is a case of 'indication of the indicated' (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) and so forth. [The author replies: True; the universal (*sāmānya*) does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*), but rather the individual (*vyakti*) alone does.
73b. Because the individual (*vyakti*) alone cannot be denoted, the word is applied to the universal (*sāmānya*).
It indicates the universal; and by means of that universal indicated by the word, the individual is also indicated through its connection with it.

This is untenable. For when the word "cow" is uttered, neither "cowness" (*gotva*) nor the "cow" (*go*) is perceived; rather, [what is perceived is] the cow— *Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on Dignāga’s *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, specifically concerning the theory of the "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) of the individual by the word for the universal.*
It is being refuted: even if it were so, it is nevertheless stated [by the opponent] that "it is not prompted by words," and so forth.

Even if there were a relationship between the universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*), how could [the word] apply to a specific individual (*vyakti-viśeṣa*) that is not prompted by words? It could not at all. For even though a relationship exists between a staff and the bearer of the staff, no one who acts with foresight [would ever say "staff" when referring to the person].

When it is said, "Cut the staff," one cuts the person holding the staff; likewise, since the individual is not directly denoted by the word, it is not logical for the application [of the word] to occur toward the individual when the universal (jāti) is what is denoted.

Furthermore, because activities such as carrying or milking are impossible in the universal, the application [of the word] occurs toward the individual even though it is not directly denoted by the word. This is the consideration of the universal (sāmānyacintā).

It might be so; however, there is no application [of the word] to anything other than that [the primary meaning], just as in the case of an injunction to milk a bull. Furthermore, when there is an injunction regarding one thing, another thing is not indicated. Even though a relationship exists, there is no cognition of "one who possesses a staff" (daṇḍin) by means of the word [“staff”]. If it is argued that because the relationship is not fixed, there is no application [of the word] to that [secondary object], then that is the same in the case of the universal (jāti) as well. For the universal is manifested through the individuals.
It serves solely for the purpose of indicating the state of being. Words such as "bhrāma" (confusion) and the like, however, might imply something else because they are relative terms;

but words such as "boṣu" and so forth do not denote a relationship. If it is argued that even for universals (*jāti*) whose individuals have disappeared, [the action] would apply based on the hearing of those words, he says: "Nor indeed," and so forth. It is merely an effect possible in another object that is impossible in the actual object.

A speaker who urges [a listener] would become a person of incoherent prattle if [the listener] were to act upon something incapable because of that urging. However, it is not the case that from an incapable urging one proceeds toward what is capable—as in the urging to milk a bull. For when someone says, "Milk the bull," since milking is impossible there, the listener does not proceed to milk the bull; rather, he proceeds to milk a cow, which is other than the bull and where milking is possible.
For him alone it occurs thus: "This speaker is one who utters incoherent chatter.

It might be thought: "In the case of urging an ox, let there be no application [of the word] to a female cow due to the absence of a relation; however, when the universal (*jāti*) is what is expressed, there will be application to its individual (*tadvyakti*) because of the relation. To this he says: "And not," etc. [The meaning is: the object—

[This refers] to the exclusion of another [object], namely the universal (*sāmānya*) and the relation (*sambandha*), by means of the injunction; thus, it is the particular (*vyakti*) that is meant. [Objection:
But has this point not already been stated in the passage beginning with "even when the relation exists, though not enjoined by the word"?

[Response: True. However, this introduction is made again for the purpose of providing further exposition. He states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding that very point: "It is not fixed... (*aniyata*).

"tad" and so forth. That staff whose relation [to its possessor] is indefinite is described as such. For instance, even in the absence of the person with the staff (daṇḍin), the existence of that [staff] is found in the staff itself; therefore, "therein" means in the person with the staff. "If it is said 'no'" means that when the staff is prompted, no activity occurs [toward the person]. The point is that when the universal (jāti) is prompted, there is a cognition of the individual (vyakti) because the relation is fixed.
“*Tat*,” etc., from the *Siddhāntavāda*. “*Tat*” refers to the lack of a fixed connection [with a specific individual], which is equal even in the case of a genus (*jāti*).

If one asks how this is so, he says: “*vyaktīnām*,” etc. It might be argued that just as words such as “brother” (*bhrātṛ*), while denoting their own primary referent, imply a second [related entity], so too do words for a genus; therefore, he says: “words such as ‘brother’...”

"Such as 'father' and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," terms such as "son" are included. This means that because they are denotable by relative terms, their establishment depends precisely upon another related entity. "They would imply another" refers to a second [relative], such as a brother. And "implication" (ākṣepa) consists in the generation of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) having the form of a second relation.

But it is not merely the presence [of the relation] that [is required], for even when the related entity has perished, a conceptual construction (vikalpa) arises. "It is not so" is stated as a statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya). He says "if they were denoters of the related entity," etc., meaning that if they were denoters of the related entity, then this fault would arise; "apeta" means perished, and "vyaktayaḥ" refers to the individuals as related entities.

For those classes (*jāti*) such as "Pāṇḍu" and so forth, there would likewise follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that they are constantly accompanied by words denoting the class even when [the individuals] have departed, because of their connection with those words denoting the class. For in this way, those classes would be accompanied by [the words] through a connection with individuals that have departed only if there were an accompaniment of even those individuals who have departed. Or rather, [this would apply] to the classes through [their] relations.
Because there would be the undesirable consequence of those individual instances that have perished following [the word] eternally through those words.
If it is argued that this is indeed desired because the fitness for that connection is perceived at all times, then there would never be the application of the word "cow" [to a specific instance].
Because there is no specific implication regarding the states of being conjoined or unconjoined.

If it is argued that there is no fault because the injunction refers to the universal (*jāti*) as related to the individual (*vyakti*), then since that universal is also necessarily implied as a qualifier of the individual, the denotable object would have to be "that which possesses it" (*tadvān*).

Furthermore, there is no relationship whatsoever between a universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*), because they do not mutually assist one another through the relation of producer and produced. Consequently, even the definition [of a universal] is untenable. Thus, the word does not apply to the universal, as there would be no result [from such application]. However, it is the possessor of the universal (*tadvat*)—not the universal itself—that is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā-yogya*).

The opponent says: "At all times," and so forth. If it is argued that because the capacity for that [universal] relation is perceived at both times—when the individual is absent and when it is not absent—it is indeed accepted that the universal follows the individual; this explains as follows: just as words such as "brother" and the like, while denoting their own primary referent, imply the related person without qualification, so too do words denoting universals.

He states the answer: "At all times" (*sarvadā*). "At all times" means that there is no application of the word to a particular individual (*vyakti*) capable of performing functions such as carrying water or milking, based on the connection with the time when the individual's presence or absence occurs. If one asks for what reason, he says: "Accompanied," and so forth.

This is a locative dual. [It refers to] the state of the universal (*jāti*) being either accompanied by or unaccompanied by the individual, specifically regarding its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

"Because there is no implication of a distinction" (12). This is what is meant: just as there is an implication of past and future individuals by means of a word denoting a universal (*jāti*), because they possess the nature of the word's referent, so too there is no distinction in the manifestation of a present individual in both ways—as having the nature of the word's referent.
If it is argued that this is not a fault because the cognition of the individual arises from the injunction of the genus as related to the individual;

Let it be so; however, that individual (vyakti) is also necessarily implied when the universal (jāti) is enjoined, by virtue of being its qualifier—that is, as a qualifier of the universal. Thus, the universal alone is not the denotable object. Rather, the possessor of that [universal] (tadvān) would have to be the denotable object;
this would constitute the adoption of an alternative position. And we shall point out the fault in that immediately thereafter—this is the intended meaning.

This was stated [previously] while assuming a relationship between the genus (*jāti*) and that which possesses it (*tadvat*); however, he now states that such a relationship does not exist at all, beginning with the words "And not... Why? Because there is no mutual assistance, as they stand in a relation of neither being produced nor producing one another. Therefore, due to the absence of a relationship, it has also been stated that the individual (*vyakti*) is indicated by the expression of the genus; the meaning is that this is because there would be no result [of such an indication].

Because of the absence of action. Even for one who maintains that the universal is non-different from the individual, there would be an appearance of the individual in verbal cognition just as in perception. Furthermore, its definition [as a universal] is untenable even with respect to the aspect of difference. With the words "In this way," etc., he anticipates another position: "tadvān" (that which possesses it).
"Jātimān" means possessing a genus (*jāti*). "Alam" means capable. "Tatra" means in that which possesses it (*tadvat*). "Sa ca" refers to the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*).
The explanation of this very point begins with "sa ca śabdaḥ" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "tatra vyaktau," [the opponent asks]: "What is the use of another universal (*sāmānya*)?
If it is argued that "therein lies the connection with the word (*śabdayoga*),"—
Why is it not applied directly?
If [it is argued that] by means of the application of the word to the individual (vyakti), there is a result, then why is that very word not applied directly to the individuals? 448b
In that case, what is the use of another intervention—an imagined intervening factor? If [you argue] it is because of infinity, this is the same [for both sides]. (96)

It might be argued as follows: "Individuals possessing that [universal] are indeed incapable of being denoted by words because of their infinity. If this is so, then this infinity applies equally to the possessor of the universal as well. Since individuals qualified by the universal must be expressed in this way, a relationship [between the word and its referent] must necessarily be established there, for that which has not had a relationship established is not denoted. And that [relationship] is impossible."

If it is argued that because [the word] is applied to that which is related to it, it is therefore as good as applied to that [relation] itself, it has been said in this regard: "Even when a relation exists, since there is no cognition of what is produced in one place in another place, the relation does not exist [as a basis for such transfer]. (66)
Moreover: "And because of infinity," says the opponent;
"This infinity is equal," is the reply.
He explains this very point with the words beginning "It might be so" (*syādetad*). "Even in that which possesses it" (*tadvaty api*) means even in that which possesses the universal (*jāti*).

Because individuals (*vyakti*) alone—qualified by the universal and so forth—must be expressed, for that reason, the relation of the word must necessarily be established "there," that is, with respect to the individuals. Why? Because that which has not had its relation established is not denoted.

The genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). The meaning is that it refers to the word with which the relation has been established, because [the relation] is not denoted by that [word]. Alternatively, the genitive is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*), because the meaning whose relation has not yet been established is not denoted by the word. "That" refers to the relation.
It cannot be performed together with that which possesses it, because of its infinity. Therefore, this position is untenable.
If it is argued that because the word establishes a relationship with the universal (sāmānya) as related to the individual (vyakti),

a relationship is thereby already established with the individual through those two— the universal and its relation— [we reply: [this is not so,] because [the relationship] was established with respect to the universal.
Regarding the convention:

the answer to this has already been stated. (1) Even though a relation exists for the universal, it is not perceived in one individual while being absent in another; furthermore, it has been stated that there is no relation between the genus and its possessor. For even if [the relation] exists...

In the case of a relationship, there is a cognition of the possessor of the staff (*daṇḍin*) from the word "staff" (*daṇḍa*); however, no such relationship exists between a universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*), as has already been explained.
Thus, with the words "all entities," etc., the author of the Vārttika [Dignāga] sets forth his own intended position regarding the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of affirmative words.
Having thus explained the subject matter, [the author now addresses] the intention with which the teacher Dignāga stated that the universal is characterized by difference:
"Why was it not made based on the similarity of difference from those that do not perform that function, among those things that perform that function?

For one employs words toward objects with reference to a specific causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*); [therefore, the exclusion should be] from other things than those objects that perform that efficacy."
Since there is no difference among them in that very respect, why is the word not employed?
If it is argued that this is because the defect is equal [in both cases], then let it be so; there is no need for a further "universal" (jāti). //97//

It might be argued as follows: even if the word-referent (*śabdārtha*) is excluded from others, there is no distinction [between the two cases] compared to the subject (*pakṣa*), because that which possesses the exclusion (*tadvat*) is denoted as qualified by the exclusion. For what difference is there here between "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) and "that which possesses the exclusion" (*vyāvṛttimat*)? Likewise, the same fault would apply.

Let it be granted that the universal (*jāti*) is something distinct. For even by one who accepts the universal, particulars (*vastūni*) must necessarily be accepted, because in their absence, the universal itself would logically follow as being non-existent. He asks in order to demonstrate this from a single instance, beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*), etc. He thinks as follows: just as [the object] is not perceived from the word "cow" (*go-śabda*)...

Just as the word "cow" is conventionally designated for the universal *gotva*, so too [is it designated] for those things that perform that function—namely, those that perform the intended purposeful action (arthakriyā). From among those that do not perform that function—those which are not performers of the intended action—there is a distinction (*bheda*). Because all those things that perform that function are alike in being distinct from those that do not, why is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), characterized by this commonality of difference, not accepted? For what reason?

He asks another why no convention has been made; he says this very thing: "With regard to purposeful action," and so forth. With reference to the accomplishment—meaning the production—of an object characterized by burning, cooking, and so on, this person employs—that is, applies—the word "fire" to those objects that perform the intended purposeful action, [distinguishing them] from others that do not perform such action.
Because of the cause of differentiation, those things which perform that function are non-differentiated by virtue of being excluded from everything of a different class.

Therefore, since there is non-difference among these objects in that very [exclusion], why is the word not employed for that which is characterized by the exclusion of others? The intention of the question is that, by the force of convention, there could be a cognition even of that which is qualified by exclusion.

"Like that," and so forth. Regarding the fault stated by the teacher Dignāga in the position that [the word] possesses a universal (*jāti*), namely, "because that which possesses it is not independent," and so on—the fault arises because the same [logical] flaw applies to the expression "possessing that" (*tadvat*).
Therefore, the word is not employed to denote the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its defining characteristic. He accepts this fault, saying, "Let this fault be. It is certainly not...

This has been established; however, it was stated thus while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position]. The meaning is that a universal (*jāti*) is redundant, as another universal is not tenable.
He explains this with the words "it might be," and so forth: even though an entity is excluded from others—that is, from those that do not perform that function—words...

When [the property] is admitted [to exist], "possessing that" (*tadvat*) refers to that which possesses exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). There is no distinction between this position of possessing exclusion and the position of possessing that [property]. He states this very point with the words beginning "For who... and so forth. You have called it "exclusion," while the opponent has called it "universal" (*jāti*) and so forth.
What difference is there here in what is expressed? None at all, except for a difference in terminology.

"Let it be so," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*). [He asks: "Is the universal (*jāti*) something else, an entity in reality? Why, when the fault is equal, is exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) accepted, but not a real universal? To this he replies: "For even the universal... and so forth. [The meaning is: Let there be non-difference among those other than that [exclusion], and let there be cognition of objects qualified by that [exclusion]. In every way, this is for the sake of avoiding the fault. 449a. *Sāmānyacintā*, Chapter 4.
