Because it is impossible to do so; for if another object were admitted, there would be no purpose, since that object's meaning is already established by the other, and the admission of that [other] would necessarily follow as well.
Moreover, it is said that [the word] "dhvani" functions by excluding others;
therefore, how could there be an exclusion of this [word] from those [other things]? (98)
One employs words with the intention that the hearer might act toward objects by avoiding what is undesirable;
however, whether it be permission to act in this case or elsewhere, or permission to both act and desist from acting, the mention of "denotation" (*abhidhāna*) is redundant.

This is because, in the absence of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there would be no such thing as a "universal" (*jāti*) existing as a real entity (*vastubhūtā*). For if there were no distinction between entities, [this universal] too would not exist.

Because there is no such thing as a universal (*jāti*) that possesses a form inherent in multiple objects, and because it has already been stated that no non-difference is produced by a universal, one must necessarily admit difference. Now, let there be a cognition of non-difference among those things which possess that [non-difference]—namely, the non-difference of those other than that from what does not produce that effect, and the non-difference of those other things which do produce that effect from that same [non-producer]. Let this cognition occur with respect to those things qualified by that [non-difference], which are themselves qualified by non-difference.

It is called "practice" (*pratipatti*) because it is the objective support (*ālambana*) of practice; however, it is not itself the practice. Alternatively, the word "practice" is derived in the instrumental sense (*karaṇasādhana*), considering that entities are practiced by means of this exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "in every respect": if the object to be expressed were qualified by exclusion or qualified by a universal (*jāti*), then the faults mentioned regarding the position [of the opponent] would apply.

Just as there is the fault of infinite regress and so forth, because it is impossible to effect its avoidance; if it is argued that since the fault is equal, why is the universal (*jāti*) itself not accepted? To this he says: "In another object," and so forth. An "other object" is a universal existing as a real entity (*vastubhūtā*). If it is argued that the purpose of the universal is to produce a non-differentiated cognition regarding diverse things, he says: "Of that object," meaning of that which is to be accomplished by the universal.

"By another" means by a non-difference characterized as the exclusion of what does not have that effect. For that object is established even by a universal (*jāti*); so why, when abandoning the universal, is there an acceptance of exclusion? To this he says: "That," and so forth. "Of its acceptance" means of the acceptance of exclusion. For it has been stated that if that [exclusion] were not accepted, the conceptualization of a universal would not even exist.

Now, since exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) must necessarily be indicated by the word, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*), and so forth. It is called "articulation" (*dhvani*) by the speaker because the listener proceeds by means of excluding what is other than the intended object. The particle *ca* has the sense of the word *eva* (only) and its position is displaced; it should be understood as following immediately after the phrase "by the exclusion of that which is other than that. By that [word],...

By means of the *dhvani*. The meaning is that when there is no exclusion (*avyavaccheda*) of that intended object from those unintended ones, it is expressed without such exclusion. [The question is: "How would the listener act?

He explains this very point with the words beginning with "the word" (*śabdam*). This [word] [functions] toward objects which are intended and which perform the desired causal function (*arthakriyā*), while [excluding] the unintended...
With the intention that "how indeed might the listener proceed by means of exclusion— that is, by the delimitation of an unintended object?"— one employs [the word].
If the exclusion of others were not indicated by the word, then [the word] would apply both to the intended object to be communicated and to other unintended objects.
26. Indeed,
O Magas, the heat of the sun is truly fierce.
(Prasaṅga: Furthermore, if there were no expression of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), then because a single injunction would not be possible, there would be no expression at all.

Therefore, exclusion must necessarily be denoted. And if that [exclusion] pertains to things other than that [referent] on all sides, then the property of a universal (*jāti*) also exists. Having abandoned that which is accepted as necessary, that which is enjoined as necessary, and that which establishes the meaning of a universal, [one might instead resort to] another object—
Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is merely an insistence on what is meaningless, because it is impossible for [the object] to exist in the manner in which it is constructed.

Nor is it the case that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is not performed at all; rather, when those who state the object of engagement (*pravṛtti-viṣaya*) speak of a "universal" (*jāti*), engagement is thereby permitted. And when that [engagement] exists, there is a name—the designation—for that intended object.
Otherwise, the employment of the word [“fire”] would result in futility. For instance, when it is said “bring it,” a mere object is implied;

therein, the word “fire” is employed to exclude what is not intended, as in “bring fire. If, however, even when that word is used, the bringing of non-fire were not excluded, then there would be no purpose served by the utterance of the word “fire. The same applies to the word “bring.”

Because the bringing [of the fire] would not be rejected, it would follow that both bringing and non-bringing are permitted; and since both engagement and withdrawal would thus be authorized, the mention of its name would be rendered meaningless—this connects with what was stated previously. Thus, because there is disregard for the injunction regarding one desired object, such as fire, and one performance characterized by bringing and so forth, there is simply no statement [of the prohibition].
It would apply to words [only] when there is no denotation of the exclusion of others;

or rather, it should be connected with what will be stated later as "in the case of permission for engagement and withdrawal. This is because, according to the method already described, there is disregard for a single injunction regarding both engagement and withdrawal—that is, regarding that which is characterized by engagement and that which is characterized by withdrawal.
Or, because there is no injunction regarding an operation characterized by such [a nature]—the rest is to be explained as before.

And in this way, the linguistic usage of words would be annihilated; but it is not so. Therefore, "necessarily," and so forth. And that is the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*). "In those other than that" means in those things which have the same effect, being distinct from those that do not have that effect. For all of these, it is non-differentiated.
Because it is excluded from its own effects. Thinking thus, the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) possesses the property of a universal (*jāti*), namely, the exclusion from multiple objects.

"That" refers to the exclusion; what qualifies it? It is "that which has a fixed acceptance" (*niyatābhyupagama*). For if that were not accepted, it would follow that the universal does not exist. And "that which has a fixed expression" (*niyatacodana*) means that whose designation is fixed. For if that were not expressed by the word—

The application [of the term] would be fruitless. The meaning of the universal (*jāti*)—characterized by the conformity of cognition and verbal expression across individuals—is established by this [treatise], in the sense that "it is established by means of this. To abandon such an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) and instead postulate another entity, a universal, is merely a stubborn adherence to what is useless; it is nothing but an attachment to a non-entity, and there is no other reason for it whatsoever.
The meaning is that it exists. What is the reason? Because this universal cannot logically possess characteristics such as eternality and omnipresence according to [our] conceptualization;
thus, this is the intention of the teacher Dignāga in stating "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*).

"No," and so forth, says the opponent. "It is certainly not the case that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is not effected by the word; rather, it is indeed effected. For what purpose, then, was the universal (*jāti*) mentioned? To this he replies with the words beginning "pravṛtti" (activity): for the universal is the object of that activity of one who seeks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). It is the universal that we have mentioned while explaining that [object].

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) says: "Exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*), and so forth. If there is an exclusion that is the denotable object (*abhidheya*) of this word, then—considering the universal (*sāmānyacintā*)—if there is such an exclusion for it, then surely this much alone is the purpose of words. What need have you for another, separate universal in that case? (99)
But was it not said that the object of activity is being presented? Even though those words were spoken, the universal (*jāti*) was not stated;

for it has already been demonstrated that it is not fit to be the object of activity. By that very fact, activity toward that which is not enjoined has also been refuted. For in that case, there would be an intervention in the injunction.

If the universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*) are accepted as the objects of linguistic application, why are exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and its possessor not likewise accepted? If it is argued that this is not the case because exclusion, being a non-entity (*avastu*), cannot serve as a means of proof (*asādhanatva*), then this is equally true for the universal. If it is claimed that there is no fault because the possessor [of the universal] is the means of proof, or that the exclusion of this possessor of the universal is what is expressed by the word, then surely this much [exclusion of others]—

Since the purpose of words is the incitement toward what is desired, "therein" refers to the act of incitement toward the desired object through exclusion; or else, "therein" refers to the object of activity—what further need have you for a [separate] universal?

The opponent begins with "nanu" (but surely) and so forth; the Master replies with "uktam" (it has been said) and so forth. The phrase "for thus" (*tathā hi*) serves to demonstrate the lack of logical consistency.

"That" (*sā*) refers to the universal (*jāti*). Because it lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), the universal is not fit for purposeful activity. Nor is the universal cognized from the word "cow. This has already been explained in the passage beginning with: "In that regard, the universal is incapable of causal efficiency" (*tatrānarthakriyāyogyā jātiḥ*, *Pramāṇasamuccaya*).
If it is argued that a person’s activity toward a substance capable of causal efficiency will occur by means of the universal (*jāti*), he says:
"By means of that," and so forth. [He asks: "Even though the connection exists, how could one act when it has not been enjoined by words? and so on.
If it is argued that the possessor of that [universal] alone is enjoined by means of the universal, he says: "Enjoining that which possesses it," and so forth. [There is] an intervention...
The word "released" (*muktam*) is connected through a change of gender (*liṅgapariṇāmena*). It was stated that there is an intervention (*vyavadhānam*) therein by way of generality (*sāmānyena*).
Why is it not applied directly? [It is asked: "But why is there an intervention by another thing there? and so forth. It might be thought:
neither the universal (*jāti*) alone nor the individual (*vyakti*) alone is the basis for the application of words, because [the application] depends on both.

An individual born [of its causes] lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and a mere individual cannot be the object of a linguistic injunction. Therefore, the universal (*jāti*) and the possessor of that universal (*tadvat*) together constitute the object of engagement; it is these two taken together that are the meaning of a word. To this end, he says: "Of the universal and its possessor," and so forth. This means, having accepted that they are the objects of engagement—that is, the objects of engagement based upon words—...

Regarding the word *māne*: the ellipsis to be supplied is "why are exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and that which possesses it (*tadvat*) not accepted as the objects of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti-viṣaya*)? The underlying intention is that exclusion and its possessor are established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that because exclusion—which is of the nature of a word—is a mental construction, it is not a real entity (*avastu*), and therefore, being incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) such as carrying or milking, it cannot be an object of purposeful activity; [the response is: this incapacity for causal efficiency...

If it is argued that the individual (sāpi) is equal to the universal (jāti) in being incapable of such functions as carrying or milking, and therefore—since the possessor of the universal possesses the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyāsādhana)—the fault characterized by the absence of purposeful activity does not arise; ... [then the response follows].

If it is argued that [the object] exists, that is equally true for that which possesses the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). For those who maintain the theory of exclusion, verbal cognition is a grasper of a non-entity; by virtue of error, it determines as a cause that which is not a cause. Concordance with the real entity (*vastu-saṃvāda*) would occur only if there were a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with it, through the production of the real entity, and not otherwise.

If it is argued that there is no error because the object arises [as it appears], this is not so; for there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of something as being that which does not appear in that way.

The illusion of a gem in a light is an error because of its appearance. If it is argued that there is no correspondence (*saṃvāda*) for an error, we say no; for, as already stated, there would be a lack of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Indeed, the definition of error is a false appearance (*vitatha-pratibhāsa*).
For, because it is invariably concomitant with that [cognition], correspondence does not depend upon appearance.
"It is the same," and so forth, is from the *Siddhāntavāda*. "That" refers to the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsādhanatva*).
Thus far, having accepted the existence of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), even though it is non-existent, by way of the principle of the necessary connection (*pratibandhaka-nyāya*).

Having explained that the word-meaning was stated by the teacher Dignāga, he again states that the word-meaning is indeed a positive entity (*vidhi*), beginning with "And it apprehends a non-entity" (*avastugrāhī ca*). If it is asked, "If its object is a non-entity, how does it cause a person seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) to engage [with it]? he replies, "That [is] through delusion" (*sa vibhrama*), and so forth. "That" refers to the verbal cognition (*śābdapratyaya*). It causes the person to engage through the power of delusion; for it is delusion itself [that prompts engagement].

To the question "How so? he says: (1) Even though [the object] is not an agent (*akāraka*), because it is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) within its own appearance, the external object is considered an agent since it is what is being determined (*adhyavasāyin*). If one asks, "In that case, how is there correspondence with a real entity (*vastu-saṃvāda*) in the case of inference and the like? he says: "Correspondence with a real entity," and so forth.

When there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), from where does that very connection arise? It arises from the production [of the cognition] from the real entity (*vastu-utpatti*) which is the thing to be proven.
By way of its production as a cause, that is, otherwise when there is no obstruction, there is no correspondence whatsoever for a cognition such as that derived from words.

If it is argued that "the production from a real entity constitutes non-delusion," this would be the case if one considers that verbal and other cognitions which correspond to a real entity must arise from that very entity—thereby implying the perception of something incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). But this is not so; for even when there is production from a real entity, [the cognition] does not correspond to it.

The point is this: because it manifests as the form of a real object, yet through the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [manifestation]—that is, through the conceptual determination of a real object—it is erroneous.
Consequently, since there is no contradiction between the production of the form of a real object and error, the reason (*hetu*) is one whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.

For instance, the illusion of a jewel in the luster of a jewel certainly accords with the actual jewel. Thus, he states [the following] while further supporting the very case of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

"Unreal," and so forth. This is what is being said: if there were a contradiction between error (*bhrānti*) and correspondence (*saṃvāda*), then the proof that error corresponds to a non-existent object would be non-deviant (*avyabhicāra*). But that is not the case.

For the characteristic of error is an unreal appearance (*vitathapratibhāsa*), not non-correspondence. "By its being inseparable from that" means by its being inseparable from the real object (*vastu*).

"Up to the point of 'arising from that'": this correspondence does not depend upon appearance; it does not depend upon an appearance residing in the object itself. For even an appearance that is not [directly] of that object corresponds [to reality] precisely by virtue of being connected to the object. Therefore, it is established that even a verbal cognition, though having a false appearance, [is valid] when there is a connection with the object.
Regarding the phrase "its corroborator":

4. In the investigation of the universal (*sāmānya*), because the universal—which is the object of apprehension when the mind functions toward an entity according to its actual state—is incapable of performing a causal function (*arthakriyā*).

There would be no application [of the word] to that [particular]; if it were applied elsewhere as well, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, if one were to grasp it as possessing that [universal], the futility of the universal and other such faults have already been stated. If it is argued that even when the genus (*jāti*) is grasped, the cognition—due to its connection—proceeds by presenting a fused appearance, then because even that single [genus] is not grasped as having a stable intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the opponent's own doctrine is merely being accepted [by us]. ||66||

(gha) Regarding the objection that recognition would be impossible in the absence of a universal: if it is argued that, since even positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is absent, recognition—which functions by connecting distinct objects through their own nature—would likewise not occur; [we reply as follows].

This is not a fault, provided that— on the other hand— the verbal cognition is held to correspond exactly to the object as it exists. In that case, with respect to the external object, for one whose mind is directed toward the thing "as it is" (*yathābhāvam yathāvastu*), that is to say, for one whose cognition is superimposed [upon the object] by the power of words, such that the cognition arises otherwise than the actual state of the object.

If such engagement [with an object] is admitted, then the universal must be accepted as the apprehended object (*grāhya*) of that verbal cognition, because there is no prompting by a word toward the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). And because that apprehended universal is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), there is no engagement with that universal which is the object of conceptual cognition. "Elsewhere" means elsewhere than the universal, namely, in the individual (*vyakti*).
Even if activity were prompted by the word alone, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for upon hearing the word "cow," activity might arise even toward an individual horse.

If it is argued that this is not the case because there is no relationship between the universal *gotva* (cowness) and the individual horse, we reply: no, for even if a relationship exists, activity is impossible toward what is not prompted by the word; this has already been stated.

Now, it is not merely the universal (*jāti*) that is denoted by the word, but rather that which possesses it (*tadvat*). If, however, the apprehension of that [possessor] is admitted, then the faults such as the uselessness of the universal (*sāmānyavaiyarthyādayaḥ*) have already been stated. It has been said that the universal is useless because the word should be applied directly to the individuals themselves; and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the faults such as infinity (*ānantya*) are included.
[This is] the inclusion. Only the universal (*jāti*) is denoted by the word; however, because that universal is inherent in individuals (*vyakti*), it cannot be apprehended in isolation.
Therefore, it is apprehended as unified with the form of the individual. This very point is stated [in the verse] beginning with "the universal" (*jāti*).

"Appearing as fused" (*śliṣṭābhāsā*) means that the cognition, which appears as a mixture of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal, [occurs] with respect to that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*).

If it is argued that [the word] functions toward the individual (*vyakti*), then at that time, neither the universal (*jāti*) nor its possessor (*tadvat*) is apprehended in its own form—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Why? Because even for a single universal or its possessor, there is a state of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvasthiti*), which is an unmixed form;
yet this is not apprehended by a deluded cognition (*bhrāntabuddhi*) that presents a fused appearance (*śliṣṭābhāsa*). And therefore, from such a deluded cognition...
Because it accepts [the process of] engagement, the view of the proponents of *anyāpoha* is indeed nothing other than the doctrine of the opponents.
"Thus," and so forth, says the opponent. "Of the pervasive" (*anvayinaḥ*) means of the universal (*sāmānya*) which is cognized through multiple individuals.

"This is not a fault," says the proponent (*siddhāntavādī*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [it is meant that] even though there is a difference up to the fetching of water, and even though they are mutually excluded (*parasparavyāvṛtta*), having seen them performing various similar purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) as properties of the thing (*vastudharma*), [one infers] those others—
That which is the separation—the distinct nature—from those effects is the object of certain sounds;

having observed those various purposeful actions, such as the cognition of sound and so forth, which they perform despite their difference, [one acts] together with those sounds whose objects are distinct separations from other things. (100)

This has already been stated. If it is argued that even when there is a difference in the entities, they produce a cognition of identity—such as "this is that"—because they perform similar causal functions, like the eyes and other sense organs;

[we reply: for one who perceives a single causal function such as cognition among them, those very things, by virtue of their own objective nature, produce in relation to others a cognition of identity ("this is that") conjoined with a verbal expression whose object is their exclusion (vyāvṛtti), through the awakening of the latent impressions (vāsanā) from one's own experience.

Otherwise, cognition would not possess both differentiation and connection, as in the case of a staff among staff-bearers. In that case, even though [the person] is joined with one staff, the cognition does not occur elsewhere as "that very same [staff]," but rather as "that [staff] is here. In this way, a person could not, by means of internal verbalizations, join objects together and form the thought, "This is that very same thing."

The word "api" (even/also) is displaced [in the sentence]; its meaning is "even upon seeing something else. The collective sense is this: even when one sees an object different from—that is, distinct from—a previously seen object, one might perform a recognition by superimposing unity due to deception, based on the fact that it performs a similar purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
To the question, "How can things that are distinct perform a non-distinct purposeful action?", he says: "This has already been stated," and so forth.

Because this was previously stated in the verse beginning with: “In the accomplishment of a single purpose, such as a single reflective awareness or a cognition of an object” (1.75). The word "one" (*ekām*) refers to that which is similar for a person perceiving other distinct things;

[the term] "from others" (*anyebhyaḥ*) refers to those entities that exclude [others] by their very nature as objective properties (*vastudharmatayā*) from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the thing, [namely] those that do not perform that function (*atatkāribhyaḥ*).

Not at all. The connection [of the sentence] is: "They produce a false cognition (*mithyāpratyaya*) of the form 'this belongs to you alone. To the question "Of what kind?", he says: "That," and so forth. That which has as its object (*viṣaya*) the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of those things that do not perform that function from other things that do not perform it—namely, those objects that perform a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākārin*)—is that by which [the cognition] is conjoined (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), that is to say, associated (*saṃsakta*), or, in other words, accompanied by verbal expression (*sābhilāpa*).
If they produce [cognition] by virtue of being the nature of things (*vastudharmatā*), why do they not do so at all times? To this he says: "By their own experience," and so forth.

That which is the self-experience of those entities produced previously—the latent impression (*vāsanā*) characterized as a capacity (*śakti*) for the arising of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)—its awakening (*prabodha*) is its orientation toward the production of an effect; and the awakening of that [impression], in turn, is...

Because it arises from the experience of objects of that same class. And since such an awakening does not occur at all times, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not possible at all times. "The difference between the conjoined" (*saṃsṛṣṭabheda*): that by which the difference between the two individuals perceived previously and subsequently is conjoined—that is, unified—is so described. "Otherwise" (*anyathā*): if, by means of their having a single effect or through similarity, oneness is superimposed [upon them], one might erroneously [conceive of] oneness even in the case of things that are distinct.

Recognition is not accepted [as the basis for this]; rather, it is due to the connection with a single universal (*sāmānya*). At that time, [the cognition] would not possess both difference and conjunction. If there were a conjunction of distinct entities, the cognition would not possess a single form; the meaning is that there would be no cognition of a single form regarding many things. For even those who possess a staff are not apprehended as one simply because they are joined by a single staff. He says the same thing: "Just as..."

Regarding the phrase "daṇḍinviti" (in the case of "staff-bearers"): it clarifies the very point that "not [is there identity]. "Therein" means among the staff-bearers. "Elsewhere" means in another staff-bearer distinct from one staff-bearer. That substance which is the staff, having been seen in one staff-bearer, would thus appear here in the second staff-bearer; however, it is not on account of that [substance] that one could say, "This is that very same staff-bearer. Or rather, it is just as when many [people] possess a single staff.

In the same way, there is no such cognition as "this very staff is that [same] staff" with respect to each individual object. This is the consideration of the universal (*sāmānya*) regarding particulars. How can it be that "this is that very same thing"? It is something else. Therefore, even for one who perceives a single thing in many locations, it is not logical [that it is the same], just as in the case of [the notions of] difference and connection. For there is no contradiction if it appears in that way due to the power of delusion (*vibhrama*).

If it is argued that error is not tenable due to the absence of a cause (*nimitta*), [we reply: those very entities which produce a single effect act as the cause through the medium of experience, because by their very nature they are the causes of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which result in error.

This is evident in the case of the delusion of water and the like in mirages; for even though [the rays] are distinct, there arises a reflective cognition (*parāmarśapratyaya*) of a non-distinct form.

Even due to the connection with a single universal (*sāmānya*), there would not be the cognition "this is that very same thing," but rather [the cognition] "that is here. If it is argued, "Let it be so," he replies: "Not so," and so forth. The conclusion is given by the words beginning with "that" (*tad*). "One" means that even for a person who perceives a commonality (*samāna*) across multiple individuals, [the cognition arises] as if there were a connection between differences; that is, the "connection of differences" (*bhedasaṃsarga*) is their having a single form (*ekākāratā*).

In the same way, [the existence of] knowledge is not tenable. However, for the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), this is not a fault; thus he says, "Through delusion," and so forth. This means "by the power of error. If it is argued that—since there is no real, singular universal (*sāmānya*) existing as a single entity that could serve as the cause for recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in its uniform nature—delusion is not tenable; [the author replies: "Those very things" refers to the excluded entities (*vyāvṛttā bhāvāḥ*) which constitute its [the cognition's] object.

They are characterized by the activity of producing a single object such as cognition. Experience alone is the door—that is, the cause—and by its very nature (*prakṛti*), that is, by its own essence (*svabhāva*), it is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) for the fruit of delusion, because it is the cause of the result of error.

Now, one might object: if a delusion such as water were to arise in relation to a mirage and the like even without similarity (*sādṛśya*), there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If similarity is accepted [as the basis for recognition], why is a universal (sāmānya) not also accepted? To this he says: "In the case of mirages, etc. The first word "etc. includes [the perception of] ropes and so forth; the second includes the delusion of snakes and so forth. "Those two alone" refers to the entities in the form of water and mirage, which are the objects of the reflective cognition (*parāmarśapratyaya*) that takes the form of a single, undifferentiated appearance, such as "this is that very same water."

The two causes that produce the experience which serves as the basis for the sign (*nimitta*) are distinct even though they are the originators [of that experience]. What is meant by this is as follows: first, there is no similarity between dissimilar things. Even among similar things, it is their own nature (*svarūpa*), which is similar, that serves as the cause of error; it is not "similarity" itself. For instance, the cognition consisting of the experience of water is, first of all, the form of water—

It deposits a latent impression (*vāsanā*) of conceptual determination (*parāmarśa*). And just as that impression is awakened by the subsequent experience of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of water, so too is it naturally awakened by the experience of the object known as a mirage, because that [mirage] possesses that very nature. Therefore, just as a cognition of conceptual determination in the form of water is said to arise from the experience of water, so it is also from the experience of a mirage. And for this reason:

Those two, known as the water and the mirage, become the cause for the delusion of water by means of the experience of the [actual] object. Nor does this lead to an over-extension [of the principle], because although they are equal in their lack of the nature of water, the specific nature of the mirage arises from its own causes as something possessing similarity;
it is not the case that something becomes similar simply through connection with similarity. This principle was stated in the section on *sāmānya* (universals).

Having thus refuted the view of Uddyotakara and others, he speaks in order to refute the Mīmāṃsaka position, beginning with the words "For not," and so forth. To explain: in the cognition of water, two things appear—the universal of water (*jala-sāmānya*) and its particularity (*viśeṣa*), such as its location and so on.

The cause is that which produces the experience of a sign (*nimitta*). There is no other distinct universal (*sāmānya*) therein that serves as the basis for such a cognition. Or, if it did exist, a cognition apprehending an existent object would not be erroneous.
If it is argued that "superimposition is the attribution of an unreal form," we say no; for that [cognition] apprehends a universal (*sāmānya*).

Whatever form this [cognition] superimposes, that alone is its object. It is impossible to superimpose upon what has not been made an object, just as one cannot superimpose another form [upon something else]. And since that [form] does not exist there, the universal does not exist.
In the sublating cognition that "it is not connected with [that] place," it is the connection with the place and so forth that is sublated, not the generality of water;

therefore, the cognition of water has the generality as its very object. To this it is replied: in those mirages, there is no other distinct generality whatsoever that exists in the form of water, such that the generality of water could be admitted to exist there.
When [the cognition] is being examined, it is a cognition grasping an existent object because it grasps a real universal (*sāmānya*).
Now, it might be argued that the cognition of water has as its objective support the very universal of water residing in other locations and so forth, and thus it is not erroneous.
To this it is said:
"In all cases, the external object of cognition consists of a difference in place, time, and nature.

If it is asked: "How then is the perception of water in a mirage an error? It is because the universal of water, which exists in another place and so forth, is superimposed there," [the author] says this very thing: "Non-existent," and so on. [This refers to] that which does not exist in the mirages.

The error arises from the superimposition (samāropa) of the form of water. "No," and so forth, is the established conclusion (siddhānta). That cognition of water (*jalabuddhi*) which apprehends that generality (*sāmānya*)—namely, the generality of water situated in another location—is not [a valid perception of water]. Why? He says: "And whichever form... and so forth. Whichever form...

The cognition of water superimposes the form of water—which is non-existent—upon those mirages. To the question, "Why is that which is being superimposed an object? he says: "Of that which has not been made an object," and so forth. This means:
at the time of the arising of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), that universal (*sāmānya*) which has not been made an object cannot be superimposed upon it. As for the form...
It is like [the case of] a forest and so forth. For another form, such as fire and the like, is not superimposed there, because at that time it is not an object [of cognition].

And whatever form is superimposed as non-different from the external, that alone appears as the object. Furthermore, that superimposed form of water does not exist in those mirages, because it is sublated; therefore, a cognition of water as a universal does not exist there.

[The opponent argues: "Because it possesses a universal (*sāmānya*). Likewise, even regarding water that does not exist, the cognition of water which superimposes the form of water upon [what is not water]—like a mirage—is non-universal (*asāmānya*).

[The opponent continues: "The word 'existent' (*sat*) and so forth [refers to this]. There is indeed another water-universal; when that is apprehended, there is the superimposition of it, namely the superimposition of water."

Not otherwise. (1) If the superimposition of "water" upon real water were to occur without the apprehension of the universal of water (*jala-sāmānya*), then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);
that is, the superimposition of "water" would occur even with respect to fire and so forth.

When there is the apprehension of the universal, such a superimposition occurs, and not otherwise; for if it were otherwise, there would be an over-extension. This is because [the universal] exists among those things that perform a single common effect.

If it is held that [the universal] is grasped [in the cognition], then once the universal is seen, one must necessarily admit that individual things possess the power to produce their own specific cognitions.

If it is argued that those individuals themselves, being distinct from others, produce such a cognition, then what function does the universal have in that regard? For, according to the nature of things, it is precisely the non-mixed difference [of the individuals] that is perceived; for conceptual constructions arise from ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, an error does not occur without depending on an external object; rather, it is an internal distortion (*viplava*). As stated in the *Siddhāntabindu*: "When there is the perception of real water by those whose nature it is to perform a single function—such as drinking or bathing—is the superimposition of 'water' not accepted? Without a universal (*sāmānya*), how could distinct things produce a single effect?"
If it is argued that there is no such capacity at all, he says: "And necessarily," and so forth. This has already been established in the section beginning with:
"The means of accomplishing a single object, such as a single reflective awareness, a purpose, or a cognition" (verse 3872).

Others, however, explain the passage beginning with "for there is no other generality whatsoever" by taking the word *sāmānya* (generality) to mean "similarity. That interpretation of theirs is not well-founded, because [the word] does not express the idea that "it is perceived as having the nature of water," and so forth. For similarity is certainly not perceived in the form of water.

"Yati" means from that [single cause], i.e., from the power of a single cause. "Ta eva" (those very ones) means that among the aforementioned powers, it is the individual manifestations (*vyakti*) themselves that are joined [to the power], and not the universal (*sāmānya*). "Anyebhyaḥ" means from others, i.e., from those things which do not have that as their effect. "Tādṛśam" means having a single form. "Yathābhāvam" means according to the state of being.

When there is no transcendence of the actual entities (*padārtha*), there is positive concomitance (*anvayībhāva*). For example, since the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) exists devoid of universals (*sāmānya*), why does the conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*) not perceive it as such by transcending them? Why is an unreal universal superimposed there? [The answer is: "In accordance with the entity" (*yathābhāvam*) refers precisely to this, beginning with the word "unmixed" (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*). That which is unmixed does not possess a single uniform nature. (7-78a)

"Endowed with" (*pannaḥ*): that state (*bhāva*) which possesses mutual differentiation (*bheda*) is so described. This is their incapacity regarding the apprehension of things as they truly are. Why? Because they originate from ignorance (*avidyā*). Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the apprehension of reality; since it is the opposite of that, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) itself is ignorance. Thus, "origination" (*prabhava*) is expressed by the word "origin" (*prabhava*).

The meaning is: "by the power of conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*). For the failure to grasp an object as it actually exists is the very nature of conceptual construction, since it is by its very essence erroneous (*bhrānta*); therefore, it is not logical that the delusion of conceptual construction should consist in [the apprehension of] a real universal (*sāmānya*) that is subject to destruction.
As for what was said, beginning with "And not," etc.: here, the very nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is called the internal distortion (*antaro viplavaḥ*).

The meaning is that the nature of conceptual construction itself is such that it becomes an error (*vibhrama*) without depending on any external similarity. An error consisting of the appearance of hair and so forth is the "delusion of hair and so forth" (*keśādivibhrama*); just as that [delusion], being independent of an external object, is an internal apprehension of a non-existent form.

One becomes deluded by relying on a distortion (*viplava*). In the same way, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is also [deluded] because it grasps the form of an unreal universal (*sāmānya*); this is the meaning intended here. This is an error because it arises from an internal distortion, which is the seed of delusion. If it is argued that if [distortion] were due to the arising of ignorance (*avidyā*), then the consequence would follow that the eyes and other [faculties] are also [distortions], we say: no, because of that [ignorance’s specific nature].
Because it has the characteristic of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); for that [ignorance] is indeed conceptual construction itself. By their very nature, those [objects] are inverted.

Sensory cognitions (*indriyajñāna*), however, are not conceptualizing. Nor is this fault applicable even to them, because "non-duality" is not intended here as a mere absence of duality; this will be made clear later.

Regarding the statement "but [it is] due to the arising from ignorance" (*codaka*), by the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is meant precisely the seed of the appearance of duality within a continuum where the obscurations have not been abandoned. Therefore, "arising" (*udbhava*) means production; likewise, even internal distortion (*viplava*) exists at that very time as such a seed. Since all cognitions possess this quality of arising from ignorance, he says: "distortion because of arising from ignorance. (*avidyodbhavād viplavatva*)

And so forth. Because of the arising—that is, the production—of ignorance (*avidyā*), there would follow the consequence that even visual consciousness and the like are erroneous (*viplava*) or mistaken. With the words "No," etc., he states his own intention. "Of that" refers to ignorance; conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the cognition that superimposes a general form (*sāmānyākāra*), because that is its defining characteristic. Thus he says: "For it is indeed conceptual construction," and so forth. "That" refers to ignorance.

"By way of intrinsic nature" means by way of their original character (*prakṛti*). With the words "not thus," and so forth, he refutes the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*): because those [sensory cognitions] are non-conceptual by virtue of having the form of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, they are not erroneous by way of their own nature like conceptual cognitions; rather, for some, delusion occurs due to a disorder of the sense faculties and so forth.

Having explained [the nature of ignorance] according to the system of external objects, he now speaks according to the system of internal cognition, beginning with "And not... and so forth. He says this: "Let it be granted that the meaning of the word 'ignorance' (avidyā) is conceived in whatever form it may be questioned; nevertheless, there is no fault of over-extension (atiprasaṅga), because [such a consequence] is accepted. Nor does this fault of being erroneous apply even to those cognitions of the eye and so forth, for they too are subject to distortion (viplava).

Because of that very fact, he says: "Of the non-dual," and so forth. The self-cognition (*ātmasamvedana*) of the visual and other consciousnesses is indeed non-dual, because one considers that "there is no duality here. For instance, the blue and other objects—which are intended as the apprehended (*grāhya*)—appear as distinct from the consciousness at the same time [as it arises]. Due to their inability to withstand analysis as being either one or many, they do not exist as ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*). Therefore, in dependence upon them...

Furthermore, that which is the exhaustion of consciousness—the nature of the subject as an agent—is also non-existent; however, its self-awareness (*samvedana*) is not [non-existent], because it is directly perceived (*pratyakṣatvāt*). If it is argued that self-awareness is also erroneous because it is not distinct from the erroneous form of the subject, we say no: if it were non-existent by its own nature, there would be no manifestation at all, like a hare's horn. Moreover, even regarding error...

Reality exists by way of its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), for otherwise it would be impossible for it to be an error. Furthermore, cognition whose form is the awareness of its own nature is indeed of the very essence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvid*); how then could there not be reality in that awareness? Alternatively, the appearance of duality is an error, and an error must have reality as its basis, just like the error of [seeing] two moons and so forth. And reality is the opposite of duality; that is non-duality (*advaya*), which is self-awareness.
It is indeed the form itself, and not the absence of duality, because that [absence] is non-existent; so how could it not be known by consciousness?
Thus, regarding the objection stated above...
And those [cognitions] which appear in the form of the apprehended and the apprehender— we shall explain that these too are erroneous in the third chapter.

It should be stated that [this is so] because of the appearance of duality. Furthermore, even if all things are erroneous, the distinction between valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its semblance (*tadābhāsa*) exists due to the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), because of the correspondence with what is intended as capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). This is because, despite being false, it is conducive to tranquility (*praśama*), just like the perception of one's mother and so forth, or the perception of water in a mirage, which differs from that of another.

Even though there is no difference in the arising of the [mental] state or the delusion, there is the arising of that which is capable or incapable of performing the intended purposeful action; thus, as the case may be, there is either correspondence or its opposite. If it is argued that this is because they arise from what is incapable [of such action], [we reply:

for this very reason, although conceptual cognitions—which possess the appearance of duality—are established as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by virtue of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*), they are not established as being "seers of reality" (*tattvadarśin*).

The distinction between valid and invalid cognition. If one asks how this is so, he says: "Of all," and so forth. *Viplava* means error. *Tadābhāsa* means the appearance thereof, i.e., the semblance of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*). The *vyavasthā-vibhāga* is the systematic distinction between these two. The *āśraya* is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is the seed of error; its *parāvṛtti* is the removal of obscurations. The prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*). The *āśraya*— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "The establishment of validity [is due to] the correspondence with what is intended, because of the transformation [of the basis] into that which is capable of all purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

Purposeful action is characterized by the cognition (*vijñapti*) appearing as burning, cooking, and so forth. And that [cognition] is "capable" of it because it is desired by the person; thus, the analysis of the compound is: "because of the correspondence with that [which is] intended. It is precisely because there is correspondence with what is intended—[as stated in the verse]—that [validity is established].

Retention [of validity] does not arise from correspondence alone, because even when there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), correspondence may sometimes be impossible due to a deficiency in the cognitive faculties.

The phrase "because of the non-correspondence with what is intended as capable of purposeful action" is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood to mean "because of the non-correspondence with what is intended in that manner."

In this way, the cause for the establishment of fallacious means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*) has been stated. In the Vijñānavāda, since external objects do not exist, how can there be a correspondence with what is intended as being capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)? This is not a fault, just as in the case of the appearance of water in a mirage.

Because knowledge—which is capable of producing a cognition manifesting burning, cooking, and so forth—is designated by the term "suitable" (yogya). Thus far, the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated for visual and other sensory cognitions, as well as for those produced from signs such as smoke which manifest fire and so forth. Now, however, he speaks regarding the cognition of the non-self (*anātman*) and so on, which is produced from signs such as being produced (*kṛtaka*): "False," and so forth.

The cognition of non-self (*anātman*) and so forth is false because it proceeds by superimposing a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*). Nevertheless, it possesses validity because it is conducive to tranquility (*praśama*); tranquility is the abandonment of passion (*rāga*) and the like. For those who grasp an object through its universal form as non-self and so forth and cultivate it, once that cultivation is perfected, passion and the like are abandoned through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of non-self and so forth. Of what [is this true]?

Furthermore, since it is observed that even in the case of what is false there can be conformity with tranquility (*praśama*), he says: "The perception of a mother," and so forth. Even though the perception of a mother toward one who is not a mother is false, it is a cause for the non-arising of passion. To this extent, this is an illustration based on similarity;

however, the perception of a mother and so forth is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the perceptions of a sister and others is intended.
And the suffix *āyasvati* is used in the sense of the genitive case.
Even when external objects are perceived, since there is no real entity corresponding to a universal (*sāmānya*), if all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is erroneous, then in that case—
just as the conceptualization of water arising from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a mirage, which lacks the universal of "water," is erroneous— [so too is every conceptualization].

Constructions do not arise from necessity; for when a mirage is seen, the delusion of water arises from it. This is because it is produced by an object that distinguishes [itself] from what is not water, by imparting a representation that conforms to its own nature, and thus it does not exist according to that [apparent] nature. Rather, it arises either through a lack of proficiency in perceiving specific characteristics, or through the awakening of one's own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) dependent upon conditions.

Therefore, the conceptual error arising from the birth of distinct entities is a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that "this is that very same thing" due to delusion; it does not arise from the perception of a separate universal (*sāmānya*), for no such separate [universal] exists, as it lacks persistence (*anvaya*), just like the individuals themselves. ||100||
Moreover:

likewise, even from a mass of water that is devoid of the nature of water, a conceptual construction of water arises; because that too proceeds by apprehending what is not that [i.e., water] as being that, it is erroneous. Why is this so? He says: "Because one [cognition] accords with the object, while the other does not... [referring to] a mirage...

"Ketyādi" [and so forth]. "And of another" refers to the cognition of water in a real body of water; because the universal of "water-ness" (*jalatva-sāmānya*) is absent [in a mirage], rays of light and water are distinct entities. Therefore, the connection is: "even though there is no difference in their production [from a common cause]. Furthermore, regarding "astonishment despite the lack of difference": just as in a substance consisting of rays of light devoid of water, there arises a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of water due to the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the universal of water.
Likewise, an error (*vibhrama*) occurs even with respect to water that does not exist;

because it consists in the apprehension of something as being what it is not, it results in unintended causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), such as drinking and so forth. In this regard, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of water is capable [of producing such effects], whereas that of the mirage-rays is incapable. This is due to the cause of their respective origins.
Regarding the conceptual construction of water in a real body of water and in a mirage, there is respectively correspondence and its opposite; "the other" means non-correspondence.

This is because [the mirage] is unsuitable, being the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a mirage. For one would not think that a form which is not water is suitable for the appearance of water.
The refutation begins with the word "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*): [a cognition] is bound to an object insofar as it arises by conforming to the form of that object.

He explains that very point with the words beginning "na hi" (for not...). The term *yathārtham* is an avyayībhāva compound meaning "not exceeding the object. The particle *eva* is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*). The meaning is: for indeed, no perceiver arises that corresponds to the object.
If it is asked, "In that case, how is it said that the cognition of water arises from mirages? he says: "When [the mirage] exists," and so forth.

A delusion arises in the visual consciousness and other cognitions regarding the mirages; when that [delusion] exists, there occurs a delusion of water which superimposes the form of what was previously experienced. Thus, because it arises through a succession [of causes], it is said to arise from the mirage—that is, to arise from the mirage. This is according to its own nature.

As before, this is an *avyayībhāva* compound. A jar or similar object that is incapable of producing the illusion of water is called "non-water" (*ajala*). Therefore, [the term refers to] that which is capable of producing the illusion of water; that is to say, by such an object known as a mirage (*marīcikā*). The connection is as follows: it is called "arising from that" (*tadudbhava*) because it arises according to its own nature (*yathā-svabhāvam*). This is the very meaning of the phrase "according to its own nature. (1)

Regarding the passage beginning with *svabhāvānukāra*: that which imitates the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is called "imitation of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvānukāra*). This refers to the superimposition upon cognition by means of presenting a reflection that conforms to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). To the question, "By what, then, is that [reflection] directly produced?
he says: "That, however," and so forth. "That" refers to the delusion of water; [it arises from] the distinction between water and the mirage.

The definition [of a universal] is the determination [of an object] through its distinction [from others]. Because of a lack of proficiency in that regard, one's own latent predisposition (*svavāsanā*)—which is the seed of the error of water—is awakened; it is produced by that awakening, which acts as a favorable condition. By what kind of factor? By one that depends on a causal condition (*pratyaya*). This "condition" refers both to the perception of a mirage and the recollection of the similarity between that mirage and water. Therefore, this is the conclusion. An entity is distinct from those of a different class. 4. Investigation of the Universal (*sāmānyacintā*).
Even in the case of another's perception, one might perform recognition by connecting [past and present];
yet that cognition does not arise from the universal alone.

For it is not logical to assert that even another person’s cognition is produced from the universal alone; because if there were constant cognition of that [universal] alone, it would follow that the individual is never cognized. If this cognition were to grasp the universal eternally, then by this very knowledge, the individual would necessarily be non-eternal.

Furthermore, regarding the investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*): [text fragment].

If it is thought that cognition does not have an undivided appearance regarding distinct things, it must be said that a single effect is not produced from multiple [causes]. Furthermore, if that [cognition] were established with respect to distinct objects, then cognition would indeed not possess an undivided appearance; for there is no appearance of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) within cognitions that appear as universals (*sāmānya*).

Because those [universals] exist even in the absence of that [particular], and because they appear in one's own cognition through another form; for even that conceptual cognition appearing as a single entity has precisely the form of color, shape, and so forth. Indeed, in that case as well, no other universal form is perceived apart from the forms of color, shape, and the like. Nor is a universal whose nature consists of color, shape, and so forth—

[The syllable] *nyaṃ*. Therefore, the universal (*sāmānya*) does not appear as an objective reality (*vastusthityā*). Nevertheless, according to your own view, that which does not appear exists; it is called a "thing" (*bhāva*) because it possesses efficacy (*sāmarthya*) within consciousness—that is, it is a "thing" because it is that by which an effect is produced (*bhāvyate* / *janyate*). And even though it does appear, there is no efficacy; demonstrating this, he says: *prati-* [etc.].

"Of the luminous," and so forth. They "overflow" (*viplavante*), meaning they depart from being real entities; thus, "overflows" (*viplavāḥ*) refers to things such as [illusory] hairs. This is the analysis of the compound. For these [hairs and the like] appear in the vision of those suffering from ophthalmia and similar conditions, yet they do not exist. As in the previous case, the incapacity of the word "existence" (*bhāva*) is expressed by the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*). [This refers to] the incapacity with respect to the production of consciousness.

This is the meaning. Thus, by showing that even that [single object] possesses causal capacity because it is perceived—that is, because it appears—it has been stated that the [opponent's] argument for causal capacity is inconclusive (*anekānta*).
As it is said: "If those [atoms] could assist that single [object], why would they not produce a single cognition? (1.107).
Regarding what was stated there, he anticipates the opponent’s reply with the words beginning with *abhinna* and so forth. "Non-different appearance" means having a single form.

"In distinct particulars" (*svalakṣaṇeṣu*)—the form of those particulars is "that-form" (*tadākāra*). That cognition in which even that [form] is placed is "such" (*tathā*). And being of such a nature, it is also "possessing a non-different appearance"; for indeed [it is not].

It might be argued that [the cognition] would arise only from heterogeneous things if it were so; however, it appears as non-differentiated. Therefore, it does not arise solely from heterogeneous things, but rather from a universal entity (*sāmānyapadārtha*). He refutes this with the words "No" (*na*) and so forth. This he explains: if particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) were their own forms...

Or rather, it is acceptable [to hold] that they are accepted as the producers of cognitions possessing a generic form (*sāmānyākāra*). But how can there be a cognition with a non-differentiated appearance regarding things that are distinct? That is not the case, because the appearance of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not occur in cognitions that manifest a universal (*sāmānya*). For, in cognitions that grasp a universal, there is no appearance of the particular characteristic.

If this is accepted, there are three possible hypotheses: (1) that the very form in which individuals appear in cognitions of the eye and so forth appears in that same form in cognitions of the universal; (2) that the form which appears in the cognition of the universal is itself the [form] of the particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*);
or (3) that two forms must be admitted for a single individual—that by one of which it appears in cognitions of the eye and so forth.
"By another [means] in conceptual cognitions.

(1) Regarding that, in the first position, just like the cognitions of the eye and so forth, there would be an absence of universal-cognitions (*sāmānyabuddhi*) even in the absence of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
yet this is not the case. Even in the absence of that particular characteristic, those universal-cognitions [persist].
453a And because it would involve the conjunction of manifold forms [and] because of the over-extension [of the consequence].

Therefore, this [cognition], though arising from that [object] and grasping distinct objects, appears as non-distinct. Although it does not manifest that [external object], it causes the world to engage in practical activity through the delusion of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).
However, that form which appears in it does not exist in the objects themselves, except in the case of that which is both distinct and non-distinct.
It is indeed formless. It was stated previously that, having grasped that very form, it errs in such a way.
That [is] because of existence. (2) He states the non-existence of the second position with the words "by another form," etc. [The term] "sāmānya-"...

Because it appears in its own cognition—such as the cognition of the eye and so forth—in a specific, uncommon mode rather than through another mode, form is not merely a universal aspect (*sāmānyākāra*) of individual instances. (3) To refute the third position, he says: "because it is impossible for a single thing to have multiple aspects.

It is illogical for one thing to possess multiplicity, because unity and multiplicity are contradictory; furthermore, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus, the conceptualization of one thing having multiplicity [is untenable].

The meaning is that there would be no unity whatsoever in this [cognition]. Furthermore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear in a cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*). Since this is so, this cognition does not have the form of a universal. While it grasps distinct objects, having been impressed with the forms of those particular characteristics, it appears as if it has a non-distinct form. It arises from those [distinct] entities—that is, it arises from distinct things—but it is nevertheless [based on] the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Relying on a latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by an experience that grasps [an object] momentarily, this [cognition] arises as inherently erroneous. And it is said that, through a causal succession, individual particulars (*vyakti*) are its cause.
If the cognition of a universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) does not manifest the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), how does it cause the world to engage with the specific characteristic?

To this he says: "Even though it does not have that as its manifestation," and so forth. Even though it does not manifest the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because of the error consisting in the determination of an object within its own non-objective manifestation, it causes the world to engage in conventional practice; that is to say, it causes [people] to act by unifying the perceived and the conceptualized. If the cognition of a universal has the form of a universal, then that [universal] would indeed be the ultimate reality.

He says that it will be a universal: "But that [is] in it," and so forth. That appearing form of a universal does not exist in the objects, because it is not perceived as distinct from them, and because, if it were non-distinct, it would lack continuity just like the individual instances themselves.
How, then, is there the appearance of a non-different form among individuals? To this he says: "Other than difference, they are non-different.

Difference is *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others); that very [exclusion] is non-different with respect to each individual. For instance, just as one cow-individual is excluded from non-cows, so too is another.
Thus, by this method, the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves—being excluded from those of a different class—are non-different [from one another] despite their difference.
Thus they are called. Furthermore, this word "anya" is a particle (*nipāta*) that resembles a form ending in a case-suffix;
it has the same meaning as the word "other. It does not, however, end in the suffix *anyatra*, because the sense of the locative case is not intended here. Therefore, the meaning is as follows:
the appearing form is other than the non-distinct [form] from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in the manner already described.

"In objects there is no [intrinsic] difference; rather, difference consists solely in their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). However, a non-difference—consisting in the exclusion of what is of a different class (*vijātīyavyāvṛtti*)—exists everywhere, due to the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of non-difference. And that very difference is the indirect cause of this conceptual determination of non-difference. [Objection: But if a non-different form appears in cognition, how can it be said that it does not exist in objects? To this he says: 'And that...'"

The word "rūpa" is used in the sense of "it is indeed" (*hi-arthe*). For that [mental] form appearing in conceptual construction is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Furthermore, even for one who asserts that the universal (*sāmānya*) is a real entity, the same objection applies: since the individuals (*vyakti*) are distinct, how can there be a difference in the form of the cognition (*buddhyākāra*) directed toward them? It is not the same [objection], if you argue that it is because the universal is non-different (*abhedāt*) in that case. But is it not true that in that case...

Even though it exists, its appearance is not perceived, for that cognition is conceived as possessing color and shape; yet the universal (sāmānya) is not of such a nature. Nor is there, anywhere else than in that [universal], even a form of differentiation.

Even for one who maintains the theory of a natural universal (prakṛtisāmānyavādin), that [universal] would likewise [be non-distinct from particulars], because it is non-different from them, and thus its occurrence in objects—
Because of the difference in their modes (*rīti*), a non-distinct appearance is not tenable;

for it was just stated that it is impossible to establish [them] as distinct in an ultimate sense. Therefore, the cognition which grasps that very form—its arising in that form is itself its "grasping"—is so called because it grasps a form that lacks [external] substance.

It was stated previously that [cognition] "wavers" means it becomes deluded. This incapacity of conceptual constructions has already been explained as being due to their origin in ignorance (*avidyā*).
Having stated the rebuttal of the [opponent's] fault, he now says "Moreover," etc., in order to demonstrate that the same fault applies [to both sides]. It is not...

The opponent says, "It is the same. [The author replies: "In that case," since the cognition of a similar form arises from that very universal (*sāmānya*) with respect to distinct individuals, the objection is not the same. The passage beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*) and so forth is the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*). In that regard, even though that universal exists among the individuals...
The appearance (*ābhāsa*) [of the universal] is not perceived. Or rather, "therein" refers to conceptual and non-conceptual cognition.
It might be argued that it has an appearance within conceptual cognition; to this he says: "For that," and so forth.
For that conceptual cognition is perceived—that is, experienced—as possessing color and shape (*varṇasaṃsthānavatī*). The universal is nothing other than the form of color and so forth.

If it is argued [that there is a universal], he says: "And not," and so forth. "Of such a kind" means having the form of color and configuration, because color, configuration, and the like are qualities (*guṇa*), and because a universal is distinct from a quality. "And not from that" means not from color, configuration, and the like.
Having thus refuted the universal as something distinct, wishing to refute it as something non-distinct, he says: "The configuration..."

And so forth. *Ākṛti* (form) is the similarity that constitutes the very essence (*ātmabhūta*) of the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); that itself is the universal (*sāmānya*). One who holds the doctrine of that [universal] is a *Sāṃkhya*. Or, one whose habit is to speak of that [universal] is a *Sāṃkhya*; he is such [a person]. Because that universal is non-different from the particular characteristic—just like a particular characteristic itself—it does not exist in other objects, namely in the second and subsequent individuals.

The commentary (*vṛtti*) states: For this reason, even that universal (*sāmānya*) has arisen as nothing other than the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, because of the reason of its difference [from the particular], it is not logical for there to be a non-different appearance [of the universal] among the individuals (*vyakti*); this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Thus, having accepted the non-different appearance as stated by Udyotakara and others, [the author proceeds to refute] the distinct... [text fragment ends].
And since a universal devoid of particulars is untenable, it has been stated that this appearance of a single form among individuals is merely an illusion.
Alternatively, let there be an appearance within cognition—
"The appearance of non-differentiation does not [apply] to things that are different," because the appearances of cognitions are distinct, yet they are apprehended as being the same. (109)

Let it be that there is a manifestation [of identity] in cognitions because they are grasped as "similar" despite being distinct. However, there is no non-distinct manifestation within those cognitions themselves, because they are grasped as "similar. Indeed, it is not logical to say that things are "similar" when there is a single manifestation; rather, what occurs is the thought, "This is that very same thing."

If it is argued that [the universals] are [distinguished] because of their connection with two [particulars], we say no; for that which is not already connected cannot enter into a connection, and this would lead to an infinite regress.
If it is argued that they are similar, how is there mutual similarity? If it is argued that it is due to their connection with those [particulars], we say no.
Now he says that there is no single appearance among individuals: "Or rather, let it be," and so forth.

As for what was stated—that a cognition with a non-differentiated appearance does not [arise] toward distinct things—let that be so; the meaning is that this is indeed accepted. For the appearance of cognitions, that is, of universal-cognitions (*sāmānyabuddhi*), is distinct. What is the reason? Because they [the cognitions] are [designated as] "similar" (*samānāḥ*).

[The author] explains by means of the words "not at all," and so forth. "In them" refers to the cognitions of the universal (*sāmānya*). There is a single appearance (*pratibhāsa*) that is non-different.
What is the reason? Because those individuals (*vyakti*) are apprehended as being "similar."

Now, one might object: "If there is the apprehension that [two things] are 'the same,' why is a single appearance not logically consistent? To this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth. What then? It would be simply that "that very thing which was previously seen is now being seen," but not that "this is the same as that previous one," because the conventional usage of "sameness" is based upon a distinction [between the two]. Regarding the phrase "of the two," and so forth: if it were only the universal...

If it were apprehended by those cognitions alone [i.e., the particularizing cognitions], then this fault would indeed arise. However, both the universal and the particular are apprehended by the cognition of the universal. Therefore, because both are apprehended, there is no fault; for it is precisely through that universal that the particulars, being conjoined with it, are apprehended as "similar."
Nevertheless, the Master [Dharmakīrti] says: "Even if the apprehension of a pair is assumed, it would have to be 'that here'.

That is, it would mean that the universal (*sāmānya*) which was previously seen in one individual (*vyakti*) is now seen here in another individual; however, it cannot be said to be "the same," because the universal is absolutely distinct from the individuals. Thus, "that very thing" refers to the cow-ness (*gotva*) and so forth, which are entities distinct from those individuals.

If it is argued that they are "similar" because of a certain similarity (*sāmya*), [the response is: how, and in what manner, can there be a similarity of that [universal] with another, namely the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)? The intention is that it cannot be in any way at all. For instance, one might imagine that the universal is similar to the particulars because it imitates their manifested forms; however, that is not the case, as [the universal] is absolutely distinct from the particulars.
Because the universal is [itself] a universal; nor are other things made similar by this [universal], such that there would be a similarity between them.

For similarity does not arise from the imitation of the form of the individual instances, but rather from their connection with it. [If it is argued: "The universal is the commonality of the individuals because of its connection with the individuals," this is not so. What is the reason? Because that which is unconnected to the individual cannot be a universal.

If it is argued that those [cognitions] grasped by distinct intellects are identical because they have a single effect, is it not the case that their similarity is the cognition itself as the effect? And yet, that [cognition] is differentiated. (110)

Because they are perceived together. In these [individuals], there is an undifferentiated appearance. But is it not the case that there is no undifferentiated appearance in those [individuals]? No, because in the perception of them, there is the appearance of both difference and non-difference; thus they are not identical. [The phrase] "not dependent on them" means "not assisted by them. Because the universal is connected through a relation characterized by inherence (*samavāya*).
If identity (*sāmya*) were admitted, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); even number, conjunction, and effect-substances would possess the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*).

Consequently, due to their connection with those [universals], there would be a uniform appearance (*samānapratibhāsa*) regarding the numbered objects and so forth. "How so? and so on asks the opponent. By the apprehension of them as "identical" (*samānā*), a difference in appearance regarding the individuals (*vyakti*) is established.

(1) And this is contradictory, because it is an exclusive restriction that "individuals possessing identical cognition must be apprehended by distinct cognitions. The meaning is that they would consequently also be apprehended by non-distinct cognitions. For instance, where there is some commonality and some particularity, it is logical to have an apprehension [of them] as "identical"; otherwise, [there would be no distinction between them], like a jar and a cloth.

"There would be an undifferentiated appearance, not 'they are similar'. He explains this with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*). By the phrase "in these individuals," he refers to their specific forms (*viśeṣarūpa*). The word "undifferentiated appearance" (*abhinna-pratibhāsa*) is to be supplied [as the predicate].
And by this, the nature of the universal has been stated.
