Thus, the collective meaning is that through the apprehension of both common and uncommon forms, individuals are apprehended as being identical. Now, does a single or manifold appearance exist among those identical things, such that it can be said thus? If it were so—
It has been stated that there would be the cognition "this is a cow. If it is argued that because particulars possess a generic nature (*sāmānyātmakatva*), they appear as "similar," [we reply:

but in the absence of a recurring appearance (*anugata-pratibhāsa*), how can it be established that a universal exists? Nor is it logical to postulate a universal on the grounds that its similarity would otherwise be inexplicable; for some things arise from their own causes as being inherently similar.

It is not the case that those which are dissimilar [become similar] through their commonality; for it has already been stated that it is not logical for them to possess a uniform nature on account of such commonality.
Therefore, as for what is said by Bhaṭṭa:
Furthermore, no one at all is able to cognize cows and the like— without distinction— as having the nature of an exclusion whose similarity is unestablished.
Furthermore, if the conceptualization of exclusion (apoha) were possible even in the absence of similarity,
why is this "exclusion of non-cow" not also postulated for the cow and the horse?
The difference from a brindled cow is the same for both a black-spotted cow and a horse; since no other universal is admitted, where could the application of "non-cow" (apoha) possibly occur?
If it is argued that even the horses and other things to be excluded are cognized despite the absence of a single common property, [we reply:
no, for it is not by similarity through a single effect alone; rather, there are two aspects in the cognition of an object.
In the case of perception:

when [the object] is not perceived, just as two distinct things are conceptualized, individual entities that perform a single function come themselves to be the objects of conceptualization. Therefore, it is superimposed in that manner due to this deviation.
There is no fault.
Cognition is the effect of those [particulars], and it differs according to them;
likewise, since there is a difference in the individual instances (*vyakti*) of the cognition that manifests them with respect to each substance, how [could there be a contradiction]?

"It cannot be defined; therefore, its exclusion (*apoha*) is not established"—this [objection] is refuted. Even without a universal (*sāmānya*), since cows and other such things arise from their own causes as similar entities, even if one does not accept a "similarity" (*sārūpya*) that exists as a separate entity, they are nonetheless accepted as being similar. And it is by virtue of having such a nature that they...
Since all those [animals], such as horses and so forth, are negated without distinction by virtue of their not being of the nature of a cow, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

However, the Teacher (Dharmakīrti), demonstrating that "though things indeed arise from their own causes as similar, nevertheless the cognition of them as similar does not occur by the power of a universal," says: "Not [so]," and so forth. In the phrase "in the perception of that," it refers to the cognition grasping the individual (vyakti).

In cognition, or in the cognition of a universal; "of the distinct and the non-distinct" refers to the particular and the universal. "Similarity as having a single effect" means that similarity and equality consist precisely in having a single effect; by that alone are individuals perceived as being the same, and not by means of an ultimate universal. Therefore, those for whom similarity consists in having a single effect are precisely those for whom the object is *apoha*.

It is established that they do not have a single effect, for they are [therefore] to be excluded. And how it is that even those things which are absolutely distinct perform a single effect has been explained previously.
To the question, "Why are they not perceived as identical by way of a universal? he says: "For not... and so forth. "In the cognition of the object"—it means:

In the cognition of experience (*anubhavajñāna*), two forms are distinct, due to the conceptualization of two objects and the conceptualization of them as either similar or dissimilar. "The state of being an object of conceptualization" means the state of being the object of a conceptual construction that superimposes unity. "In that way" means by way of having a similar form. "By this conceptualizing intellect" [is the meaning].

The opponent begins with "nanu" (but surely), etc. The portion of the verse consisting of "the cognition of those individuals is the effect, and that [cognition] differs" is recited in reference to the phrase "with respect to each object" (*pratibhāvam*). "With respect to such a state" (*evambhāvaṃ prati*) refers to this. "In the same way," etc., is the explanatory commentary (*vivaraṇa*).

Even for a cognition that manifests those [universals] and even for one that manifests the individual, [the individuals are not identical] because they differ as individuals. How is it that individuals do not have a single effect?
It might be argued: individuals do not have a single effect through the cognition of direct experience (*anubhava-jñāna*), but rather through that conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka*) which is one.

*Ślokavārttika*, Chapter 4: *Sāmānyacintā*. [Objection: Is it not the case that they have a single effect? [Response: That effect of theirs is indeed differentiated. For instance, the fetching of water and so forth belonging to a jar (*ghaṭa*) and other such things constitutes their single effect.

Even that [cognition] is indeed differentiated because it differs according to each individual object. If it is argued that things which are distinct cannot have a single effect, this is not a fault. For it is said: "Because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness, cognition is non-differentiated."
Through the state of being a single cause, there is also non-difference among the individuals. (111)

It has been explained that there is no essential connection between things; therefore, a cognition of a single form is nothing but an error. Objects, being distinct, become the causes of various conceptual constructions (vikalpa) in succession.

Because [the opponent] might think that [the universal] exists in dependence upon those [individuals] through the superimposition of form (*rūpādhyāropa*), he says: "That indeed," and so forth. That is to say, the cognition of experience (*anubhavajñāna*) is the effect of those individuals, but conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*) is not; for the latter exists even in the absence of the individuals. Furthermore, what is the similarity among the individuals with respect to that very conceptualization which arises as "they are similar"? It is [the removal of cold, etc.,] such as the removal of cold by blankets and so forth.

The term *grahaḥ* [is used]. From the avyayībhāva compound *pratidravyam*, there is the substitution of *am* for the genitive case-ending. The meaning is that it is "divided" (*bhidyate*) from the difference of each individual substance—that is, due to the difference in its causes. The Teacher says "no," because [the universal] is the cause of a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*), which is a cognition of a single form regarding its own object.

Whether non-conceptual or conceptual, cognition appears as non-different. This means that because individual entities serve as the cause for a single cognition—one which is determined (*adhyavasita*) to have a single form—those individuals appear as non-distinct.
What is being said is this: although the cognitions grasping the specific nature (*svarūpa*) of each individual entity are indeed distinct...
Nevertheless, their identity is determined through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). And by this similarity of having a single effect, the identity of the individuals is [established].

However, the identity of experiential cognitions is not metaphorically attributed to them on the basis of being the cause of a single conceptual reflection (*parāmarśa*); nor is the identity of individuals metaphorically attributed to them on the basis of being the cause of such experiential cognitions. This is because they are the objects of a non-erroneous cognition (*askhalitapratyaya*).

Because [the universal] exists as a real entity, and because there is no figurative application of a figurative application; furthermore, the meaning of the verse would not correspond to its actual function.
(111) Now, if the determination of identity among individuals occurs through similarity in having a single effect, how then [is this explained] regarding cognitions?

The determination of oneness [is impossible] because there is no single effect. Now, if it is argued that those [universals] produce the determination of oneness by their very nature, then individuals will do the same;
what then is the use of similarity through a single effect?
This has been explained.

This is true: there is no fault, for this was stated precisely according to the intention of the teacher Dignāga. Therefore, unity is accepted based on the determination of unity [of the mental image], but not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). To this end, he says: "It has been explained," and so forth. This is because it was stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.142): "All entities participate in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) by their own nature. In that context, [the term] "therein" refers to those things which are non-associated (*asaṃsargin*).
Regarding the particulars: the cognition that has a single form is indeed an error, because it apprehends as such that which is not so.
Now, it might be argued that without a universal, this error would be impossible; therefore, he says: "But those," and so forth.
Those distinct entities—namely, the excluded particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)—produce that error successively, not directly.

It has been stated that [these causes] produce [the effect]. However, their non-difference consists in the exclusion of a nature that does not produce that [effect], because they bring about some single thing such as cognition.
Furthermore, that [exclusion] is non-different with respect to each substance, because it is by its very nature a cause that does not admit of differentiation. It is non-different.

It is explained as follows: because the cognition and other factors whose object consists in the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the non-difference of causes existing in such a manner [as being identical] serve as the cause, the individuals (*vyakti*) also [do so]. It has been stated repeatedly that by their very nature (*prakṛtyā*), they produce a single cognition whose form is conjoined [with them], which does not involve a superimposition (*anupacarita*) of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the difference in intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
If this is the case, then there is a distinction between things based on their having a single effect.

"By nature" (*svabhāva*) means by its very essence. The particle *ca* serves to draw back the word "it has been explained" (*niveditam*). This too was explained in that very context. Regarding what was stated as "in succession," the explanation is: "being the causes of conceptual construction" (*vikalpahetavaḥ*). Because it is the cause of conceptual construction, experiential cognition (*anubhavajñāna*) is itself a conceptual construction. Thus, they are the causes of that experiential cognition which is the cause of conceptual construction.

This is the meaning. Individual instances produce a cognition of experience, and that [cognition] is an error having a single form; such is the sequence of the argument. He states the meaning of the verse with the words "But this of these," and so forth. The difference (*bheda*) among all entities is *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others). What is its nature? It is the exclusion of what does not perform that function (*atatkāriviveka*). That [difference] is said to be non-different for them. Why? Because of [the uniformity of] cognition and so forth regarding the object.
Because a single [effect], such as the fetching of water by one who possesses sense faculties, is produced in accordance with its cause;

or rather, [one might ask]: "But surely this undifferentiated form belongs only to the cognition—how can it belong to the individuals? To this he says: "That form, however, belongs to these external [objects] because they are perceived in that very way. [Objection: "How is there such a perception? [Reply: "From cognition and so forth."

Because it is produced from a single [cause], that form is called a "differentiation" (*bheda*) or an "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), and not a universal (*sāmānya*). Why? Because it is a distinction from the nature of what does not perform that function.
This is what is meant: by the cognition "this is a cow" with respect to each individual, there is a distinction from the nature of what does not perform that function.

Only a nature that is itself devoid of the nature of performing that [action] is made the object; however, a universal (*sāmānya*) that exists as a separate entity is not [the object], and thus it is called "difference" (*bheda*). This is the explanation of the second half of the verse. (111)

Now, one might ask: "How can there be unity among cognition and the rest? To this he says: "That too," and so forth. This is the explanation of the first half [of the verse]. The connection is as follows: "That effect, such as cognition and the like, also appears as non-different. "By nature" means by its own essence (*svabhāvena*).

"Grasping at non-difference" means having a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of non-difference. By the words "being of such a kind" and so forth, [the author] refers to the individuals (*vyakti*) as well.

He states that [the particulars] are the cause of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) through a causal sequence: "of that in which there exists the determination of non-difference," namely, of the cognition and so forth; because it is the cause—meaning the reason—for the cognition of experience and for the purposeful activity such as fetching water, the manifest individuals (*vyakti*), though distinct, produce a single conceptual cognition (*pratyaya*). This is the connection [of the words]. He asks, "Of what kind? and replies, "having a unified form" (*saṃsṛṣṭākāram*).

"Di-saṃsṛṣṭaḥ" means that by which a single form is superimposed upon individuals; "svabhāvabhedaḥ" is the analysis [of the compound] as: "that whose nature is the ultimate, non-metaphorical [form], which is a distinct essence excluded from others," because conceptual construction (vikalpa) is derived through a lineage via the door of the excluded particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
But has this point not already been stated immediately prior [in the passage] beginning with "Indeed, those things are distinct entities"? True;
and that [exclusion] is the differentiation from what does not produce that effect.
4. Examination of the Universal (sāmānyacintā).
[This applies] to that which follows something other than that [cause],
because it is not observed and because it is excluded;
for it is not the case that a perceptible object does not appear through its distinction, or even if it were so in some instance.
It has also been explained how that which is dependent [on convention] can be a cause of knowledge; even convention is not tenable [as such]. Therefore: "Convention is that which indicates it. (112)

This is indeed correct. This mutual distinction among entities—the convention for the sake of perceiving it—is also real; however, the meaning of the first [point], namely that these things become causes of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) sequentially, has been clarified by this.

To the objection that there might exist a universal (*sāmānya*) consisting of a real entity that is distinct from its individual effects, he says: "And that," and so forth. And that is the state of having a single effect.

Exclusion from those things that do not produce that effect is simply the nature of exclusion itself, not a real universal (*sāmānya*). Why? Because no other persisting, concomitant entity (*anvayin*) distinct from the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is observed apart from the individual manifestations, and because of the refutation previously stated.

He explains [the argument] with the words beginning with "it does not exist" (*na hoti*). Even if a universal (*sāmānya*) were to exist, because it is eternal, it could not have any qualities added to it; therefore, being unattached (*anāśrita*) to any particular individual (*vyakti*), how could it be the cause of cognition? It certainly could not. For it is accepted that its status as a cause of cognition belongs to that which is manifested by its substratum (*āśraya*).
This is the intended meaning. This should also be connected with the phrase "this too has been stated," because this [point] was also mentioned previously.

Since such a universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist, therefore [it is said] "the convention (*saṃketa*) also," and so forth. The word "that" (*tat*) is connected with "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*). "Cognition" (*vit*) refers to the knowledge of that exclusion which is superimposed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) as non-different from its own form (*svākāra*).

The acquisition (*lābha*) is preceded by that [cognition]. The suffix *-vit* denotes that very thing as its object or fruit; thus, it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). The possessive suffix *-ṭhan* is used in the sense of "possessing" (*matvarthīya*), meaning "that which possesses such a convention. The collective meaning is: "for the sake of the apprehension of an external object determined through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Since every undertaking is for the sake of a fruit, the sense of "acquisition" (*vidi-lābha*) is also implicitly included; otherwise, [the purpose would not be established].

Because the formulation of a technical convention would otherwise be purposeless. Now, one might argue that it ought to be a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that which has that as its object"—on account of its brevity (*lāghava*). However, since the possessive sense (*matvartha*) is already expressed by the *bahuvrīhi*, there is no production of the possessive suffix (*taddhita*), and thus brevity is achieved. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "From a *karmadhāraya*..."
Regarding the statement "it becomes a *bahuvrīhi*," and so forth:
this is not a fault. For it has also been stated therein: "In some cases, it is precisely a *karmadhāraya* for the sake of 'all means' (*sarvasādhana*) and so on.

Furthermore, because it belongs to a class of words defined by its form (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the word *sarvasādhana* and so on should be understood there as having the sense of "beginning with that" (*ādyantavidarthika*). (112)
The *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (1913): Being composed, it is indeed fitting that [the treatise] proceeds through discrimination regarding what does not perform that function;
for the scripture exists for the purpose of activity based on non-discrimination.

If the convention does not have that [exclusion] as its referent, then because it does not touch upon it even at the time of linguistic usage, one would not proceed by excluding others. For their distinction from those [others] would not be conveyed by the word;
and such is the nature of verbal cognition.
It appears as having a form identical to that which performs an action and that which does not perform it. ||113||
The intellect has as its object that which is merely the seed of distinctness and is purposeless;

this is the explanation beginning with "this which... and so forth. Since the mutual distinction (*viveka*) of entities is their own nature as excluded from others, even a convention (*saṃketa*), when being applied for the sake of cognizing and determining that [distinction]—within one's own mental reflexion (*svapratibhāsa*) which is superimposed upon an external form—is appropriate.

Because it is logically consistent, [the author] asks: for what purpose is this done? To this he replies: "not performing that" (*atatkārī*), and so forth. It is for the sake of engaging [the agent] by means of distinguishing—that is, excluding—those things which do not perform the intended purposeful action. The meaning is: "let there be no engagement with those things that do not perform that [action]."
Strengthening this very point by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), he says:
"If," and so forth.

If there were no convention for the purpose of cognizing that exclusion of others (*tadanyaparihāra*), then at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahārakāla*), [the word] would not be the cause of that exclusion of others.

Because of the non-contact [with that object]. Or rather, if the convention does not have for its object that [exclusion], but instead has for its object a nature excluded from heterogeneous things (*vijātīyavyāvṛttasvabhāva*), then because one does not contact— that is, does not take as an object via the word— that nature which is excluded from others at the time of conventional usage (not only at the time of the convention), one would not act by way of excluding others.

This is what is meant: when an object is made the focus [of cognition] by way of its positive form (*vidhirūpa*), then the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*) would be perceived. He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "na hi" and so forth. "Distinction" (*viveka*) means a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Of those which perform that function" refers to those [things] from among those which do not perform that function. For if, of that distinct intrinsic nature...

A convention would indeed have been established for the past, and thus it could be expressed by a word even in current usage; and since one would then proceed toward an object by excluding others, it is logical that the convention itself should refer to such an object.
But is it not the case that the cognition produced by a word is false, because it grasps its own internal form by superimposing externality upon it?
And therefore, how can there be correspondence with a real entity for that word which produces [the cognition], and how can it have exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object? To this he says:
"And that," etc. That conventional verbal expression (*śruti*), which exists for the purpose of conveying the exclusion of others, [produces] a cognition...

The connection is: "even though they produce [a cognition]. Of what kind? "Not performing a function" (*akāryakṛti*). [This refers to] its own form, which is not external. "Performing that function" means performing a causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by way of a form identical [to the object]; this is a third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*), meaning "that in which there exists an appearance and determination as if it were a single external form. Subsequently, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is added. 4. Examination of the Universal (*sāmānyacintā*).
Even while producing [a cognition], they do so by virtue of being subordinate factors in the exclusion of what does not perform that function.
And because it relies on the distinction between real entities, it is considered non-deceptive regarding the object;
therefore, its object is the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), since it exists by depending on that which produces it.
Although the Veda produces a false cognition— superimposing a single form upon objects that arise [in consciousness],

whereby it causes one to misapprehend that which does not perform a function as if it were performing a function, having as its sole seed the mere differentiation of things, and resulting in a uniform determination— it nevertheless serves as a means for the exclusion of other things; for, in the ultimate sense, it is not distinct from that [exclusion].
This is what is meant: [the cognition] determines its own internal form—which is not external—to be as if it were external.
By this, the purposeful activity (*pravṛttyarthatva*) of the scripture is explained.
If it is asked, "In the absence of a real entity that is a universal (*sāmānya*), how can there be the arising of that [cognition]?", he says: "The thing," and so forth.

The distinctness of things (*vastūnām pṛthagbhāvaḥ*) is their mutual differentiation (*itaretarabheda*). That which has that alone as its indirect causal seed (*bījakāraṇa*) is described as such. And because it grasps the inclusive form (*anugata-rūpa*) and the excluded form (*vyāvṛtta*) as one, the verbal cognition (*śruti*), even though it produces a non-existent [construct], is not non-concordant (*avisamvādikā*). Why? (1) Because it functions as a factor for the exclusion of what does not perform that function (*atatkāri-parihāra*). [Vijñāna...]
"Because of being the cause for the exclusion of others.

This is what is meant: if the word were to produce a cognition that determines an object as excluded from others, then it would lead a person toward that very particular (svalakṣaṇa) which is excluded from others, and thus it would be reliable (*saṃvādikā*). And at the time of the convention (*saṃketa*)...
The nature [of the object] as apprehended by verbal cognition is indeed mutually distinct, because it is conventionally designated there based on that [nature].

Thus, because it is ultimately based on a distinction between real entities, it is considered non-erroneous with respect to the object; for even at the time of practical activity (*vyavahāra*), it leads to the attainment of only that entity which is excluded from others.
Now, one might object: "Since a thing is determined as having a positive form, how can the scope of the word (*śruti*) be the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*"?

To this, he says: "Therefore," and so forth. Because the word has its basis in the distinction between things through its being an auxiliary factor in the exclusion of what does not perform that function, for that reason its scope is the exclusion of others. He states these two points [of the reason] as follows: "Because of its being based on that which performs it. That is, in that exclusion...

Regarding the status of being an agent (*kartṛbhāva*) and the status of being dependent (*āśritabhāva*): through the expression of its own meaning, the word [indirectly] functions as a factor for the exclusion of what does not perform that function; thus, the status of being an agent belongs to that exclusion (*apoha*) by virtue of the scripture (*śruti*). Furthermore, because it operates at the time of linguistic usage and at the time of the convention (*saṃketa*) by way of relying on the distinction between real entities, the status of being dependent belongs to that exclusion by virtue of the scripture.

With the words beginning with "eka" (one), he states the meaning of the verse. "Tām" (it)—that is, [the cognition] which arises by superimposing and attributing to objects a single form that appears as its own manifestation. And that self-manifestation, because it is a false appearance, does not perform a function.
Yet, although it is of such a nature, [the cognition] determines it as if it were performing a function. By this, the phrase "not performing a function," and so forth, is explained.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is that cognition for which there is merely the distinctness of objects and merely the exclusion of other mental contents. [Objection: Even though the scripture produces a false cognition, why is it called a "false cognition"? To this he says: [it is so called because] it has a uniform determination, that is, a single form.
(Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā 1.115)
"In what objects is it not non-discrepant?
For in those cases, that exclusion (*vyatireka*) is real, because it must be accepted in every respect;
for neither an excluded nor a non-excluded [entity] is possible in any way. When that [exclusion] is applied to a real thing by means of word and cognition—

An object would indeed be utterly cast aside for that which is intended as its referent, because of its own nature, since it does not touch upon any other property of the object whatsoever. For this very reason, that scriptural expression (śruti) is said to have "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) as its object;
for it is applied by specifically taking up a particular exclusion among objects already excluded from others, [thereby functioning] in linguistic usage.

[It is] a determination (*adhyavasāya*). Because it functions as a factor for the exclusion of what is other than that; because it serves as the basis for delimitation by functioning as a factor for the exclusion of anything other than the intended object. In the ultimate sense, that is, in reality, it is said not to be non-concordant with respect to those things that are different from it—that is, those things that do not possess its effect. For instance, the auditory cognitions of "impermanent," "produced," and so forth, [do not deceive] regarding the actual state of what is permanent and so on—

Because they are established by convention based on the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of an excluded entity, even in conventional usage they become causes for attainment by functioning as factors for the exclusion of others. Therefore, since it is not inconsistent with the vision of reality, there is also agreement with verbal testimony (*śruti*).

Alternatively, that verbal expression is designated for a specific exclusion (vyavaccheda) as it truly exists; by this much alone—namely, that the ultimate reality of that [exclusion] has existence among things—it possesses non-contradiction. However, words do not have a necessary connection to the thing itself, as they are dependent solely upon intention, unlike smoke and other such signs.

Establishing precisely its non-contradictory nature, he says: "For it is thus," and so forth. Among those entities, that exclusion—that differentiation—is real (*bhūta*), meaning true. Why? Because even if one accepts a universal in every respect, one must necessarily accept exclusion; otherwise, if there were no excluded intrinsic nature, it would follow that the universal itself does not exist.

Thus it has been stated. If it is argued that [the universal] exists there even though it was mentioned in general terms, he replies with "not one," and so forth. The connection is as follows: for the Vaiśeṣikas and others, the single category of the universal is distinct from the individual (*vyakti*); for the Sāṃkhyas, it is non-distinct; in neither of these cases does it exist [in the manner described]. Why? Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for something that is either entirely distinct or entirely non-distinct.
Because it is untenable due to being sublated, and because it is impossible; for the subverting means of valid cognition has been stated previously and will be stated [hereafter].

Furthermore, if the universal were to be expressed by a word even as it appears [in cognition], then, upon the imposition—that is, the making into an object by a word—of that universal which does not exist in the real thing, or of that universal’s [status as] a means of valid cognition...

If it were admitted that what has been sublated is placed upon an external object, then that object would be utterly discarded—that is, extremely remote. Why? (1) Because of word and cognition; that is to say, because of the word and the cognition expressed by it. Alternatively, it would be cast far away and abandoned by word and cognition. Why? Because of that which is intended as its object—namely, the word and so forth.

Of that which is intended as the object; "of that" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*). Because it does not touch upon—that is, does not apprehend—any other property of the thing (*vastudharma*) or intrinsic nature of the thing (*vastusvabhāva*) distinct from the universal, namely the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); and because it does not apprehend the particular, yet determines it as non-different from its own form (*svākāra*), for that very reason that verbal expression (*śruti*) is said to have the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object. 4. Investigation of the Universal (*Sāmānyacintā*).
And because it functions by excluding others;
for when the meaning of "tree" is apprehended through the exclusion of "non-trees," there is a twofold [dependence]:
they are mutually dependent, such that in the absence of the apprehension of one, there is no apprehension of the other. (116)
"Therefore, some declare that the convention [of words] is impossible;
for if a single tree were distinct from non-trees, it could not be apprehended in that way unless the non-trees were apprehended.
To the objection—"Since the external object itself is determined through a positive form (vidhirūpa), how can it be said that the object is the exclusion of others (anyāpoha)?"—he says:

"Anyetyādi" and so forth. The meaning is as follows: by taking up, without distinction, the difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛttibheda*) among objects excluded from those of a different class—that is, the nature (*svabhāva*) of being excluded from what is dissimilar—and by relying on the mere form of being excluded from the dissimilar, one applies a word to individuals of the same class; that is, one establishes a convention (*saṃketa*). By this, it is explained that the word (*śruti*) is based upon the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). [86a]
"Because it functions by means of exclusion (*parihāra*), the status of the word as the agent with respect to the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) has been stated.

(115) With the words "not a tree," etc., he anticipates the objection of the opponent: for the proponent of the exclusion of others (*anyāpohavādin*), it is said that there is no apprehension of the object "tree" by way of a positive form (*vidhirūpa*), nor is there apprehension of the object "non-tree"; rather, it occurs through mutual exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). In that regard, [the text says] *abū-*...

If it is admitted that the meaning of the word "tree" is grasped as distinct from the exclusion of non-trees (*kṣavyatirekeṇa*), then the grasping of both the tree and the non-tree becomes mutually dependent (*anyonyāśraya*). For, if the meaning of "tree" is grasped by means of the exclusion of the meaning of "non-tree," then the grasping of the tree is accepted as being preceded by the grasping of the non-tree; this is because it is impossible to exclude a non-tree that has not been grasped. [The text continues: *avṛ-*...
Since the apprehension of "non-tree" also occurs through the exclusion of the object "tree," in that case too, the apprehension of "non-tree" necessarily presupposes the apprehension of "tree";

for it is impossible to establish the meaning of "non-tree" by way of its exclusion without first apprehending the "tree. Thus, between the two—tree and non-tree—if there is no apprehension of either one, there is no apprehension of both.

Because there is no apprehension of either [of the two], for that reason some declare that the convention of a word regarding an object excluded from others is impossible. And thus says Uddyotakara: "As long as one does not comprehend the cow, so long is comprehension of the non-cow not possible; and as long as one does not comprehend the cow..."
"In the word 'cow', there is an absence of the cognition of both [the cow and the non-cow].
Bhaṭṭa also states this very point:
"And only an established non-cow could be excluded, for that [exclusion] consists in the negation of the cow."

In that case, only the cow itself should be stated, and nothing else which is being negated. If it were of the nature of the exclusion of the non-cow (*agopoha*), there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). If the cow is already established, then the application of exclusion for the sake of the object to be excluded is futile.
"If a non-cow is not established when a cow is established, then even in the absence of that [non-cow], how could there be a cow?
Therefore, they maintain that a real, ontological universal must be accepted, and that the linguistic convention regarding it is established solely in a positive form.
And the sun is...

As for those who object that a convention is not possible with respect to an object that has not entered the mind—even if it is of the nature of the exclusion of "tree" by one who does not know a tree—because that [exclusion] has not ascended into consciousness; *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (11117) states:

"As for those who object that a convention is not possible with respect to an object that has not entered the mind—even if it is of the nature of the exclusion of 'tree' by one who does not know a tree—because that [exclusion] has not ascended into consciousness;"
Whether those non-trees are excluded from the convention or not, ||117||
And furthermore,
how could those [non-trees] be known as excluded prior to the apprehension of the tree, if there is no thorough cognition [of them]?

For at that time, the cognizer does not fail to know even a tree, nor does he fail to know what is non-tree, since he approaches [the situation] with the desire for that very knowledge in order to understand it. And how could he, being ignorant of that, [understand] the exclusion of the non-tree in the convention?
He explains this with the words "yadi" and so forth. "Tasya" refers to the tree, which is characterized by the exclusion of the non-tree. Thus, first of all, there is no [exclusion] of the tree.

Nor is there apprehension of what is not a tree; thus he says: "By one who has not cognized," and so forth. For a person by whom a tree has not been cognized, [the term refers] to that which has the nature of excluding it—that is, to that which has the nature of excluding the tree—as an object that has not ascended into the mind. If both tree and non-tree were to have ascended into the mind, then there could be a convention regarding the tree by way of the exclusion of the non-tree. But since the tree and the non-tree have not ascended [into the mind], [there can be no such convention].

Regarding the question of how there can be a convention for their meaning, he says "of those" (*teṣām*) and so forth, indicating that this same fault applies equally to the opponent as well. Therefore, the sense is that whatever solution he offers, that very same one shall be mine as well. (116)

He explains this with the words beginning "that which is one," and so forth. When a convention (*saṃketa*) is being established by means of the exclusion of others, there are certain proponents who, having accepted a single entity as a universal (*sāmānya*), raise the objection of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Even in their case, when a convention is being established for a real entity (*vastubhūta*) characterized as "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*), two alternatives arise: [either] non-trees are excluded, or...

"Or not? (117). If they are excluded, then those [exclusions] must be admitted to be known, because there can be no exclusion of what is unknown. And that knowledge is not possible with respect to them. Thus he says: "How," and so forth. How could they be known without the apprehension of the object "tree"?

This much is the portion of the verse (*kārikā*). However, the word "prior" (*prāk*) is supplied by means of the *Miśraka* commentary. The meaning is: prior to the apprehension of the object "tree," those which are not trees are [known] without the apprehension of the object "tree. How are they known? This is the sense. Those, however, who read the word "prior" (*prāk*) in the verse should not read the word "object" (*artha*), for at the time of determining what is not a tree, the object "tree"— [is not present].

The apprehension [of the word] exists because the apprehension of "tree" is preceded by the apprehension of "non-tree. Furthermore, it is not logical to grasp the meaning of "tree" without the ascertainment of "tree," since that too is preceded by the apprehension of "tree. This very point is stated in the passage beginning with "For not... (*na hi*). "Then" (*tadā*) refers to the time of the convention (*saṃketakāla*), when the convention is being made for the sake of the cognizer. To the question "Why does he not know [it]? he replies with the passage beginning with "That" (*tat*).

Because he approaches [the object] out of a desire for that [knowledge], specifically for the sake of knowing the tree and the non-tree, and because of his arrival with the intent to establish a convention—thinking, "How indeed shall I know the tree and the non-tree after the time of the convention?"—or rather, because he proceeds out of a desire for that, meaning out of a desire for the convention; therefore, at the time of the convention, there is no knowledge of the tree and the non-tree for the learner. And that [learner], regarding the tree and the non-tree—

4. [Otherwise] it would not achieve the exclusion of the universal. And if it were not so understood, because of the word "exclusion of what is other than that," there would be no conventional usage for those who employ conventions unless those [other things] were excluded. (11)
There would be no activity by way of excluding that [non-tree], as in the case of the various types of trees.

For it is not logical that, from a word established at the time of convention through the exclusion of others for the sake of another, there should be no activity at the time of usage by way of excluding non-trees, just as in the case of the various types such as *śiṃśapā* and so forth. Now, [if one objects]:
Having neither enjoined nor prohibited anything else, he displayed one [object] standing before him. || 119 ||

How could one who does not know [the exclusion] understand the exclusion of non-trees in a linguistic convention (*saṃketa*)? One would certainly not understand it. And since there is no understanding of the exclusion of non-trees, that which is other than that tree—namely, that which is not excluded from it—is "not abandoned" by it; the application of the convention is toward that object which is a tree, being thus "one in which the other has not been abandoned. [The locative case here is justified] by the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) regarding the seventh case.

This is a compound (*samāsa*). It is a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) in the sense that "it exists in which word. Alternatively, it is formed with the suffix *ṇini* in the sense that "its nature is to indicate that which is not excluded from others" (*aparihṛtatadanya-nirdeṣṭṛ-śīla*). This is because it has been conventionally designated (*saṃketita*) for an object that is not excluded from non-trees—that is, for an object whose specific form is obscured.
There is another way [to explain this]. "Non-inclusion of that other" (*tadanyāniveśa*) means the non-placement of the word in what is other than the tree;
it is a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of "that which is other than the tree" (*tadanya*) and "non-inclusion therein" (*tatrāniveśa*). That [quality] belongs to the word "tree," as before.
Because the referent of the word "tree" is not excluded from what is not a tree, it follows that the word being conventionally designated would also apply to what is not a tree.
The collective sense is: "as in the case of different types of trees.

(118) Therefore, from such a word as 'tree', there would be no directed activity on the part of speakers toward a specific object possessing branches and so forth—by way of excluding that [which is not a tree] and excluding non-trees—at the time of linguistic usage. Rather, there would be activity toward both trees and non-trees without distinction.

There would be [such] activity. How so? Like the case of a particular tree. For, from the word "tree" when devoid of context and other such factors, there is no activity directed toward a specific tree such as the *khadira* while excluding other trees, because at the time of the convention those [specifics] were not distinguished.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "na hoti" (it does not exist). The "time of convention" is expressed by the word "convention" (*saṃketa*). "By way of non-exclusion from others" means by way of the non-exclusion of the object "tree" from what is other than a tree, namely, a non-tree. However, according to the second explanation, it should be interpreted as: "by way of the non-exclusion of the convention of the word 'tree' with respect to another, i.e., a non-tree. [The word is] "established" (*niveśita*).

[The word] "from the conventional" [is used]. The explanation of the phrase "like a tree by excluding that [non-tree], i.e., by excluding non-trees," is "like the particularities such as the *śiṃśapā*.
[The compound] "the particularities themselves are the *śiṃśapā*s, etc. is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). The suffix *-vati* is used in the sense of the locative case.

In the aphorism, however, "tree-particularities" (*vṛkṣabhedāḥ*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). For the particularities such as the *śiṃśapā* are indeed the particularities of the tree; thus, it is entirely appropriate.
Regarding their function: just as the word "tree" does not function by means of mutual exclusion [among its own sub-classes], this has already been explained in the analysis of the sūtras.
With the words "artha" and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's intention; [the phrase] "without prescribing one thing and without negating another" refers to a twofold negation.
If it is argued that even in practical usage one understands the convention "this is a tree" which was established previously, and therefore this is not a fault;
For one who maintains that there is a real universal (vastu-sāmānya), nothing at all is being enjoined. Now,
if it is argued that a convention is established by pointing to a single object standing before one and saying, "This is a tree," then because it was perceived as such at the time of the convention—

If it is argued that the same consequence would apply because one understands [the word] as denoting either the meaning itself or its possessor even at the time of linguistic usage, we reply: it is not the same. For in that case as well, it is like the tree [which denotes both the individual and the universal]. (120)
The undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) does not cease with the word "only" (eva).

Even when presenting a single object by means of two modes—either as "this tree is also that tree" or "this is also that," or "this is only that"—the same fault applies to both. For that which is contrary to what is perceived is easily understood [to be erroneous].

Some read the text as: "Having stated the object in the convention, and not having excluded anything else. This appears to be incorrect, because it is impossible for a word to function apart from affirmation (vidhi) and negation (pratiṣedha). For by stating the demonstration of one thing, an affirmation is necessarily accepted.

Consequently, the two words "not having stated" (*avidhāya*) and "demonstrating" (*pradarśya*) would be contradictory. Therefore, [the reading] should remain as "not having stated" (*avidhāya*) alone.
It is not to be seen as something else. The reading is "without enjoining, having negated another. This means:

without enjoining another object of convention by means of excluding the preceding two, that is, without performing an affirmation preceded by a negation, but rather performing only the affirmation alone. For this very reason, it is said in the commentary (*vṛtti*) that "it is demonstrative," meaning that nothing [is established] through the exclusion of anything whatsoever.
The phrase "it is prescribed" precludes a prescription that is preceded by the negation of something else; however, a pure prescription is indeed accepted.

By the word "one," he indicates a universal (*sāmānya*); thus, he explains that because the convention is established for the universal, it is effectively established for all individual instances. (116)

The phrase "this is a tree" demonstrates the very nature of the convention (*saṃketa*). Whatever object is pointed out when a convention is made is understood even in practical usage (*vyavahāra*). For that reason, this aforementioned point is not a fault for the proponent of the universal as a real entity (*vastusāmānyavādin*). Likewise, the phrase "only the perceived object" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*) with respect to which the convention was made; or "that which is related to it" refers to that which is related to the universal.

[It would be] without a basis. In that case as well—meaning, even when a convention (*saṃketa*) is being made by means of a mere positive injunction (*vidhi*) alone—one who is establishing the convention "this is a tree" would have to establish either "this is also a tree" or "this alone is a tree. In the first alternative, since "treeness" (*tarutva*) is not excluded from anything else, there would be no necessary engagement in conventional usage; thus, that same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains. Now, if...

If [it is argued that] "this very thing is a tree," then the exclusion of the non-tree (*ataru-vyavaccheda*) itself has been accepted. Consequently, since at the time of the convention the [perceiver] would not have cognized trees and non-trees, the same logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains. Thus he says: "the consequence does not cease.
He explains this with the words beginning with "one" (*ekam*): "This is a tree, and this alone is a tree"—[this is] the understanding (*gati*).

"Of those two"—that is, of both these two types. "There is no fault," and so forth, says the opponent. Because that which has been seen—the form of the cloth—is experienced, it is easily known as being the opposite of that, i.e., distinct from it. [4. Sāmānyacintā:
There is no fault because of this nature; for when one sees something single and experiences a cognition that distinguishes its form in another [object], [there is no contradiction].

From that experience, there arises a determination of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-niścaya) regarding what is other than that. Upon discerning that [difference], he is instructed by being shown, "This very thing is a tree. Consequently, wherever he does not see it, he himself realizes that very thing to be a non-tree.
This is not possible under the theory of exclusion (vyavacchedavāda), because the form perceived in one place cannot be concomitant with anything else.
If it is argued that such a cognition would not occur with respect to another [object] when one has already perceived [the universal], then this is equally true in that case as well;
for he explains this very point by means of the introductory statement beginning with "one" (*ekam*) and so forth: "For there is some single universal..."

For a person who perceives a tree and so forth, and who experiences a cognition that distinguishes its form from another distinct object— one devoid of that universal and possessing a different character— the determination of dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇyaniścaya*), which consists in the ascertainment of difference in the form "this is other than what was perceived," arises from that very experience.
By this, the nature of the determination of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-niścaya*) has been stated.
Its function is "the discrimination thereof" (*tadvivecana*), which means the discrimination between objects previously seen and those not seen; it establishes their distinctness.
Since that discrimination is already established by the very expression "other than that," the explicit mention of "discrimination thereof" (*tadvivecanagrahaṇa*) is for the sake of clarity.

In this regard, when such a sequence has occurred, that cognizer—who possesses the certainty of a distinction from his own experience—discriminates an object possessing branches and so forth, which is endowed with a specific universal, from other forms. Having placed that very object before him and demonstrated it by saying "this is a tree," he is taught and made to grasp the convention (*saṃketa*). It is precisely in that [object] where the nature of the universal conforms to that convention...

He sees it; he himself apprehends that very tree without the operation of words. Thus, when a convention is established based on the universal nature—which is itself determined through differentiation from within the internal form—that [convention] becomes established with respect to all individual instances of the same class, because the universal is present everywhere. Furthermore, this is so because of the restriction [expressed] as "this very [thing]" in the convention.

Because that which is contrary to what has been perceived is easily known when [the object] has been established, a determination arises elsewhere that "it is not a tree"; thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply.

If it is argued that this is also the case for the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), he says: "This is not," and so forth. It was perceived at one time during the occasion of the convention (*saṃketa*).

Because its unique form (*asādhāraṇa-rūpa*) does not follow along with or persist in any other individual instance, and consequently, that particular distinction (*bheda*) which was apprehended as "this is a tree" at the time of the convention (*saṃketa*) is not seen elsewhere. Therefore, by reason of the fact that a cognition arises which appears as distinct between the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) seen at the time of the convention and the one seen subsequently—[it follows that] "tree"— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument regarding the impossibility of applying a convention to a unique particular.*

If the cognition [of "tree"] were produced based on two specific trees, then such a cognition as "this is a tree" would not occur with respect to another individual tree—that is, another distinct tree—as well.

For instance, that particular tree-distinct from which was perceived at the time of the convention is different from jars and so forth, and likewise is any other tree-distinct from it. In that case, just as the cognition "this is a tree" does not occur with respect to jars and the like, [it would likewise fail to occur for other trees].
The meaning is that even in the case of a particular tree, there would not be the cognition [of "tree"], but rather the cognition "non-tree" alone would arise.
Thus, by this [argument], the Master [Dharmakīrti] implies that even when a convention is established for a universal in the form of a conceptual construction, [the same fault follows].
If there is a single unifying reflection, then indeed [the cognizer] is established in one place. ||121||
The proponent himself distinguishes the objects that are the causes of that [cognition], [arguing] "this is equal to that. This is the rebuttal of the charge of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
What is meant is this: it has already been established previously that all entities are distinct from their own causes; therefore...

In non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), trees and non-trees appear as distinct entities. Furthermore, the conceptualization of a tree is said to occur toward trees in a purely affirmative form (*vidhi-rūpeṇa*). Likewise, the conceptualization of a non-tree arises toward non-trees by means of the negation of "tree.
Therefore, how could there be any mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*)?

Now, one might object: even if the conceptual cognition of a tree occurs in a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*), nevertheless, because it arises by way of the exclusion of non-trees and so forth, it depends upon the cognition of non-trees and the like; consequently, that very same fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) remains.

This is not so. For the exclusion of non-trees and so forth is simply the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the tree and so forth; thus, it is through the experience of that [nature] alone that the tree and so forth [are cognized].

A conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises, but it does not depend upon the prior apprehension of "non-tree" and so forth; therefore, how could there be a state of mutual dependence? In that regard, within the conceptual construction of a "tree," the form of a tree appears as undifferentiated, despite the individual distinctions such as *śiṃśapā* and other species. And since that [form] is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) prior to linguistic convention because it is of the nature of cognition, it is precisely therein that the word is conventionally assigned.
Therefore, as it has been said by Bhaṭṭa:

Prior to linguistic convention, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is not apprehended by the sense faculties; nor is there linguistic convention elsewhere [than in what is perceived]. Having seen what, then, could that convention be applied?
"Because it is liberated through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), no inference exists here;
therefore, even the experience of its relationship is not possible"— this [objection] is refuted.
He asks, "Why is the rebuttal of mutual dependence equal [to the opponent's]? and replies with the words beginning "Because," and so forth.
"Recognition of a single form" (*ekākārapratyabhijñāna*) refers to a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*); that cognition which has such a designation is described as "that which is thus.
By this, it is stated that even though the individuals (*vyakti*) are distinct, recognition of a single form superimposes unity upon them. And therefore—

It has been explained that the seed for the fact that a convention established with respect to any particular individuals—upon which unity has been superimposed by conceptualizing cognition—becomes established everywhere, is this very point. By the phrase "in one [instance]," he states that the nature of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is restricted to a specific form, being devoid of any reference to heterogeneous objects. Through the exclusion of the forms of heterogeneous objects, [the awareness applies] to homogeneous ones.

The meaning is that he is established in that which is the single unifying cognition (*ekapratyavamarśajñāna*) regarding all things. By this, too, the seed for the differentiation between homogeneous and heterogeneous entities has been stated. For this very reason, he says: by the word "that" (*tat*), a single unifying reflection is grasped; by the word "not-that" (*atad*), its opposite is meant. "That and not-that" constitute *tadat*. The causes of these two are *taddhetu* and *ataddhetu*. He differentiates them as follows: one—

This was already explained previously: certain entities, being distinct by nature, produce results such as knowledge and so forth, while others do not. One perceives them by oneself, having distinguished between those that are causes of that [result] and those that are not. For him—[it is said]: "The entities existing within his cognition appear to the intellect as causes. (122)
The statement "one should perceive various forms as distinct, even though they are themselves devoid of any causal form," is intended to establish distinction. (123)

(While attempting to identify that [object], the intellect) looks toward what [it perceives] as having the nature of branches and so forth, and it distinguishes those things from their opposites by itself through convention;
this was already explained previously: "[The means of establishing a single object consists in] the cognition of a single reflective awareness. (1975)

In this context, because both distinct and non-distinct universals (*sāmānya*) have been refuted and will be refuted, [it follows that] entities differ by their very nature; they are distinct by their own essence. (1) Only some perform [actions such as] cognition and so forth—by the word "and so forth," [actions such as] fetching water and the like are included—not others. (121)

This is so because those [entities] possess by their very nature the character of producing that or not producing that. This cognizer, having himself distinguished—that is, made a division—among those entities even without the operation of words, understands which are the causes of that and which are not its causes. Therefore, how could there be a mutual...?

There is no fault of dependence. For one who himself understands those things which are causes and those which are not causes of that [result], for that cognizer, the phrase beginning with "revolving in that cognition" and so forth is a verbal noun (*karmapada*) dependent upon the verb "he would understand.
That cognition which, having distinguished the causes of that [result] from those that are not its causes, establishes them—that is "that cognition"; revolving in that [cognition] means...
"Established" means appearing—that is, manifesting—as the cause of conceptual cognition (*vikalpikā dhī*).

Because of the connection with the word "as it were" (*iva*), which will be mentioned later, it should be understood as "as if by way of being a cause. However, those things appearing in conceptualization are not actually causes, because they do not exist externally; rather, this is said simply because the cognizer determines them to be so.

The connection here is with the phrase "they appear as if deficient in their form due to the absence of causes. And the application of the word *iva* ("as if") is as before. That is to say, they appear as if deficient in the form of those things which are not the causes for the cognition that reflects upon them as having a single form.

Because of the unification of the perceived object (*dṛśya*) and the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the connection is that they appear as if having a single form together with the external object, even after the time of the initial convention.

Thinking that one should apprehend those entities as distinct from those that do not produce them, a verbal expression—a word—is applied—that is, conventionally designated—to a nature that is excluded from dissimilar classes and superimposed by conceptual thought as non-different from its own form. One apprehends—that is, understands—that aforementioned distinction from that hearing (the word) during practical usage; yet, due to delusion, one perceives it as a conceptual construction (*paridhi*).

It perceives a single entity. The meaning is that the cognition, apprehending that nature—which is excluded from those of a different class—as non-different from its own form, beholds it as if it were a single entity.

Consequently, among all things that are the causes for a single conceptual determination (*ekaparāmarśa*), there arises the cognition "tree"; thus, regarding what was stated concerning apprehension through perception:
The objection that [the universal] would not exist even in another individual has thus been refuted;
and as for what was stated by Bhaṭṭa:
"Because, by their very nature, through the influence of cognition, there is a positive concomitance (anvaya) of the causes of such a conceptual construction."

These [objects], though not actually existing as such, are determined as being so by the conceptual determination (*vikalpa*) of the observer’s intellect; they revolve within that intellect as the causes of its cognition, through the exclusion of everything else, and with the internal and external distinctions undifferentiated.
"But how could horses and other animals not be denotable by the word 'cow' for you?
If it is because the word 'cow' was not observed there at the time of the convention,
then everything other than that single individual body must be [denotable]."

"That it would be [the case that] 'this is water,' and so forth, is not a denotation of a universal"—this too is refuted; for when the word "cow" is applied by convention to a single individual, its object is followed through in another individual, because of the cognition "this is that very same cow. Nevertheless:

He states the meaning of the verse with the words beginning "teṣām" (of these). The connection is as follows: because of the continuity (*anvaya*) of those objects—which are distinguished from heterogeneous things—and which by their very nature (*prakṛtyā*) are the causes of such conceptual constructions (*vikalpaka*). It is "by nature," that is, by their own essence (*svabhāva*), and not because of a connection with a single universal (*sāmānya*). [An objection is raised: "In that case, why do they not all produce reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)? To this he replies: "Because of the conditions (*pratyaya*)."

[The word] "śād" [means]: because the cognition of experience (*anubhavajñāna*) is the conceptualization (*pratyaya*), and through that medium, conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) are generated from them. This is because there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—that is, the presence—of the causes of such a conceptualization, which consists of a single unifying reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśātmaka*). Just as one particular tree, by its very nature, is a cause for such a conceptualization, so too are the second and subsequent ones; it is in this manner that there is positive concomitance, and not merely [the presence of] a single [cause].

The universal (sāmānya) exists as a common essence. Therefore, because of this positive concomitance (anvaya), the ellipsis of the sentence is: "those things which, by virtue of producing a single effect, are fit for a single conceptual determination. "Of the observer thereof" means: of the observer who perceives the production of a single effect among the individuals—[the universals] which are revolving in his intellect but have not yet ascended [into explicit conceptualization].

Therefore, it should be "of the seer" (*draṣṭuḥ*). If it is argued that this is not so because of the prohibition of a genitive compound by the rule *kartari ca* ("and when [the word] denotes the agent"), we say no; for what is intended here is the residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Furthermore, the word *draṣṭṛ* ends in the suffix *tṛn*, and in that case, a genitive is prohibited by the rule *tṛn*. Thus, there is a compound of the form *tat-sādhana-kṛt* ("that which is the instrument of that"), where the word *tat* ends in the accusative. Others, however, [interpret it as] *tat-prayojaka*...

By such indications, they demonstrate that the prohibitive sūtra is not of universal application (*anityatva*). In this manner, similar rebuttals should be stated for other such indications as well. "By being the cause of the knowledge thereof" means by being the cause of that conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*). And "by the exclusion of others" refers to those things which, while being causes for the recognition of a single form, are distinct from those [other] entities of that same nature.

[Conceptual constructions] are causes of conceptualization (*kalpa*). And by way of exclusion from those [external objects], even though they are not real, they are not mounted upon conceptual construction as its causes, because they do not exist externally. For this very reason, their status as conceptual constructions whose form is non-causal is also due to their lack of substantial reality. Thus, they are determined as such; they are superimposed by being the causes of that cognition and by the exclusion of others. By this, they appear—

It has been explained that [the universal] is not devoid of the nature of being a cause for cognition. With the intention that one should understand the causes of that cognition by distinguishing them from others—

having pointed out, in accordance with one's own conceptualization, that these trees appear as a single [universal] in both self- and other-referential conceptualizations— one applies [the term "tree"] to those things that are non-different from the causes of that [cognition].

Then, the intellect (*buddhi*), superimposing that [universal] and proceeding [to grasp it], appears as if grasping a single object solely due to the power of non-deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Even when those [particulars] are seen as distinct, it is by the perception and non-perception of that [universal] that one effects the distinction between "tree" and "non-tree. By this, he explains the phrase "not having a divided external or internal difference" (*avibhakta-bāhyādhyātmika-bheda*) as meaning "having a single form" (*ekarūpa*). It is undivided...

The analysis of the compound is: "those [objects] in which there is a distinction between the external and the internal. The meaning is: grasped by means of the unification of the perceived object (*dṛśya*) and the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The "apprehender" (*pratipattṛ*) is the one for whom the convention (*saṃketa*) is established. "In accordance with the apprehension" means: according to whatever kind of apprehension he has at the time of the convention. Those entities that lack the form of a non-cause but share a single effect are of a single nature; it is in regard to these that this word "tree" is conventionally established.

Thus, these [cognitions] have the form "these are trees" and so forth. Following that [perception], and recollecting that, while abiding in conceptual cognition (*vikalpa-vijñāna*), one understands those aforementioned entities—which are the causes of that cognition—by distinguishing them from their opposites. By means of this [process], how indeed might one understand [them] even at the time of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), upon hearing the word "tree"? Thus it is said.

Generally, the maker of a convention applies it to a nature that is delimited from what is not its cause, once that nature has been made an object of conceptual thought. (123) Now, one might object: the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), being excluded [from others], does not persist at the time of linguistic usage, nor is it an object of conceptual thought.
Because the appearing universal form is non-different from its own cognition, there is no persistence [of it] in another conceptualization.

Nor is there a cognition of that [form] belonging to the speaker by the listener, or of that belonging to the listener by the speaker, because as a property of another's mind it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). And since a convention cannot be established between the person to be informed and the informer unless [the object] is cognized by both equally, he says:

"Regarding 'one's own' and 'another,' etc.: by means of the cause of error characterized by the performance of a single function among the conceptual constructions of both the speaker (the self) and the person to be addressed (the other), one adopts entities that appear as one and which are the objects of linguistic convention.
This is what is meant: just as one person with cataracts, having seen two moons, points them out to another person with cataracts."

One teaches only what has been seen by oneself, not what has been seen by another, because that is not perceptible. And yet, it occurs to that person: "This very thing has been communicated to another by me. And the other person, perceiving the form of two moons occurring within his own mental continuum, thinks: "That very thing which was communicated to me by the communicator has been understood by me. It is just like that.

Although there is a difference between the form of the cognition (buddhyākāra) of the signified and the signifier—both of which are determined as having an external form—there is nonetheless a determination of their identity; thus, the convention (*saṃketa*) is established, and at the time of linguistic usage, it is precisely that [identity] which is cognized through the determination of oneness. The cognition apprehends its own nature, which is excluded from others, by superimposing it as non-different from its own form. "Of that" refers to the scripture (*śruti*). A single entity—
It appears as if it were grasping;
therefore, that which was stated by Bhaṭṭa [is relevant].
“Furthermore, the operation of words and logical marks is not possible if it is devoid of positive concomitance (anvaya).
For that distinct appearance of the branch and so forth cannot be apprehended [as such], just as a staff [is not apprehended] in relation to the person carrying the staff.”
Because that which is not grasped through distinction from another cannot be perceived;

and because a form observed once cannot be seen elsewhere [if it were not distinct], then, regarding the state of being a tree or a non-tree for what possesses that form and what does not, the individual instance (*vyakti*) alone would have to be the tree.
“Granted that in words such as ‘jar’ there is the exclusion of other objects; however, it is not so in sentences such as ‘it is not unknowable.

Without those two [the word and the sentence], there is no cognition of exclusion (apoha), nor is there any positive concomitance (anvaya) with the unique particular (asādhāraṇa). Furthermore, since exclusion itself is unestablished, where can its non-deviation (avyabhicāra) be asserted?”

And [the argument] that "if that [particular] were not present, there would be no validity for those two [word and inferential mark]" is refuted; because, even when one understands the relationship through word and inferential mark with respect to a single particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) excluded from others,
one indeed understands the relationship with other things of the same kind as well, due to the determination of identity— so how could there be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*)?
Regarding the fault [of] "being beneficial" and so forth: a distinction between trees and non-trees is not tenable if one relies upon a universal (*sāmānya*) that is a real entity (*vastubhūta*).

Thus he says: "(1) Not again," and so on. A single entity, the universal, which is perceptible and meets the conditions for apprehension, exists there within the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Just as jars and other things are distinct from the various types of trees, so too are the *dhava* trees and others [distinct].

Even when these distinct things are seen one after another, there must be some universal (*sāmānya*)—by the perception or non-perception of which one would distinguish between "tree" and "non-tree," such that:
"where this universal is perceived, that is a tree; where it is not perceived, that is a non-tree.
Why does he say it does not exist? He says: "of that," and so forth. [This refers to] a universal distinct from the branches and so on.

Because it is not perceived as distinct from its manifestation; for in the case of trees and the like, two manifestations are not observed: one having the form of branches and so forth, and another having the form of non-branches and so forth. Nor can it be said that the universal manifests as being identical to the form of the branches and so forth, because that [universal] would then possess the very form of the branches and so forth. "Like a staff and a staff-bearer" is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Just as...

The staff is perceived as distinct from the person holding the staff; it is not so with the universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, because the universal is not perceived in individual instances (*vyakti*) unless it has been previously distinguished from another object possessing branches and so forth, how could there be a perception of another by means of its own form if it has not itself been grasped? For one who maintains that the universal is not a separate entity from the configuration (*ākṛti*), [the universal is nothing other than the configuration].
Because that which is perceived in one individual is non-different from its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it cannot be seen in the same way in another individual;

therefore, regarding "that which possesses it" and "that which does not possess it": at the time of the convention, the form of a single tree that was observed is "that which possesses it" (*tadvān*);
whereas the distinct tree seen later at the time of linguistic usage, being devoid of the previously seen form of the tree, is "that which does not possess it" (*atadvān*). Of these two—

Just as, when the states of being a tree and not a tree are established by logic, the exclusion (*vyatireka*) is one and the same; thus, it would be the very tree seen at the time of the convention (*saṃketa*), and not something seen at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), because the form seen at the time of the convention is not observed elsewhere. Those who maintain that the referent of a word is the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) have raised the objection that this [theory] lacks pervasiveness (*avyāpitva*); wishing to refute that, [the author provides] merely the direction of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

If it is argued that "since knowability (*jñeyatva*) is not excluded from anything whatsoever, therefore its taking on distinctions [such as 'blue'] consists in its being knowable and so forth," this is not a fault. It is thus: 1. *Ślokavārttika* 4. *Sāmānyacintā*: Since knowability is not excluded from anything whatsoever, therefore its taking on distinctions [such as 'blue'] consists in its being knowable and so forth. This is not a fault. It is thus—
In some cases, for the sake of settling [the matter], having turned back from something [else]. (124)
A word is employed because it determines its own object;
otherwise, its employment would be useless. This applies even to words such as "that" (tat) and "knowable" (jñeya).

In those cases brought forward for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), there is indeed some form of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). [The opponent] says: "Let it be so," and so forth. Why is there no exclusion of other objects (*arthāntara-vyavaccheda*) in that case?
He replies: "For not [is there] the unknowable," and so forth. From what [is it excluded]? From the unknowable. If it is asked why the unknowable does not exist, he says: "Therefore..."
And so forth. One who maintains the theory of exclusion (*anyāpoha*) must admit that the knowable is made an object by way of its distinction from the unknowable;

otherwise, how could there be an exclusion of the knowable from the unknowable? For it is only when the knowable is made an object by way of its distinction from the unknowable that the latter—which is intended to be "unknowable"—is itself established as knowable. Indeed, an exclusion cannot be demonstrated from that which has not been made an object.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of all terms such as "the two collections" (*sarvasamudāya-dvaya*) and so forth. This has been stated by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara: "The claim that the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is incorrect, because it is not universally applicable.
Wherever a duality of categories exists, there one thing is understood through the negation of the other; for example, in the word 'cow,' the non-cow is excluded."
The word *go* is understood [as referring to all cows]; however, this is not the case for every word. For there is nothing whatsoever that is "not-all" which could be excluded by the word *sarva*.
