Now, if you think that "one" and so forth—which are "not-all"—are excluded by the word *sarva*, then the fault of contradicting its own primary meaning (*svārthāpavāda*) would follow.

For if this were the case, a word functioning by excluding "one" and so forth would be meaningless; because the parts are negated and no whole distinct from the parts is admitted. In the same way, all words denoting a collection, functioning by way of negating a single part, would result in being meaningless, since no collection distinct from the members of that collection is admitted.

[They] say: "Since words such as 'two' and so forth have accumulation (*samuccaya*) as their object, when one or more [of those] are negated, the things being negated would not constitute an accumulation; therefore, words such as 'two' and so forth would be meaningless. The Teacher says: "This is not a fault," because [he holds that] the intellect, which possesses expectancy, having been turned away from something by means of some [negation], [is directed toward its intended object].

A certain word is employed by a speaker for the sake of establishing a person who possesses the capacity [to understand] within a specific object. By the phrase "for the sake of establishing," positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is stated; by the phrase "turning away from something else," negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is stated.
For what reason is a word turned away from one thing and established in another? To this he says: "of that object," and so forth.

Because the meaning of a word is determined through exclusion (*avadhāraṇa*). Otherwise, if no object whatsoever were excluded by that word, the employment of the word would be purposeless. Since this is so, in words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*)—the word "etc. (*ādi*) including terms like "all" (*sarva*), "universe" (*viśva*), and so forth—everyone indeed does not transcend [the scope of] these through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Such is its application.

Because it has cessation as its fruit: if this [injunction] were not to cause someone’s cognition to cease from something, then, since one would not cease [from it], one would not engage in any worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) whatsoever due to the lack of such authorization, because engagement is inseparable from determination (*avadhāraṇa*). For example, [the command]: "Bring water with a jar. If [one were to think] "with a jar..."

In the case of "bring water," one would necessarily intend the bringing of water by some means or other; it should simply be stated that one brings water, rather than specifying "with a jar. Likewise, if bringing with the hollowed palms or by some other means were intended, it should have been stated as "bring" without implying a specific instrument or object.

Among those [objects], what kind? Those brought into the sphere of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*). That is, brought for the sake of verbal convention characterized by affirmation and negation; in other words, those situated within worldly usage. Among those factors of linguistic convention, there is some object of exclusion (*vyavacchedya*) in whatever way it may be.

This is what is meant: since it is a principle that "the meaning of a word is that which [the word] aims at," even an affirmative sentence has exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) as its primary aim; therefore, exclusion is also said to be the meaning of the word, and there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
He explains this with the words beginning "For a word... Every person—whether a worldly man or an investigator—[does not fail to understand] for what reason?

He says, "It functions," and so forth. The phrase "because that word has as its fruit the engagement or withdrawal [of an agent]" means that it is for the purpose of engaging someone in something or withdrawing them from something. Otherwise, the employment of words would be fruitless.
He states this with the words "If," and so forth: this speaker would not cause a certain person to be understood to withdraw from something that is undesired.

And in some cases, one who possesses intelligence would not employ a word for that which is intended to be excluded, because it is not authorized as it truly is; this is because prior to the use of the word, the object appears in a completely obscured form to the cognizer, and thus its true nature is not authorized by the word. The meaning is that it is authorized only in some way or another, as such-and-such a thing rather than as it truly is. In all worldly transactions, no speech whatsoever could be employed [if it did not function in this manner].
It would follow [that there is no such thing as a specific means]. What is the reason? Because the linguistic usage of words is inseparable from restriction.

Proving this very point, he says: "Just as," and so forth. For when it is said, "Bring water here," the listener necessarily has an expectation regarding the specific instrument; and for the sake of restriction in that regard, it is said, "with a jar. This [is what is meant by] "this jar is not [the means]."
A word becomes fruitful only by first denoting its own primary meaning, because it implies the exclusion of other instruments;
otherwise, even if the word "water-jar" (*ghaṭa*) were employed, the fetching of water might be performed by means of joined palms (*añjali*), or by some other instrument, in any manner whatsoever.
The intended meaning is that the fetching of water is meant to be done either with a small vessel or a large one. The word "water" (*udaka*) also [denotes] another action—

He says "In that case," and so forth, [arguing] that if [the word] does not incite one toward a qualified action by way of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), then its employment would also be purposeless. [The text continues: "There would be only the bare statement 'Bring'—of what kind? That which has not implied an instrument (*karaṇa*) or an object (*karman*).
That is to say, in the mere statement 'Bring,' there is no instrument called a 'jar' nor an object called 'fetching' upon which unimplied qualifiers depend."

It is not stated as such. A person is directed toward this activity by the word "bring" (*ānaya*). If, by the word "bring," one were not excluded from activities other than bringing, then even the word "bring" would not need to be uttered. 4. Regarding the consideration of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*):
if either bringing, or something else, or some performance or non-performance were intended [by that word], [then it would follow that the word is meaningless].

In that case, even the speaker would not speak, because of the absence of both word and referent. Likewise, for words such as "the knowable" (*jñeya*) and so forth, even when brought into conventional usage, there must be something to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*). For it is impossible to employ a term in the absence of any doubt [regarding its meaning]. In that context, precisely that which is a ground for doubt for a dull-witted person is what must be negated; or else, the listener would simply not entertain any doubt at all.
What need is there for instruction? And how could a speaker who utters what is untrue not be insane?

This very point he states with the words "bringing [the object] in this way," and so forth. Or, "some other performance" means something other than bringing it; that is, (1) the performance of eating and so on. "And non-performance" means the failure to act and the failure to bring it.

If [the object] were already intended [to be understood], then one would not even say the verb "bring. The reading found in some manuscripts, "bringing or something else" (*nayanamanyadvā*), is not correct; for the word "bringing" (*ānayana*) has already been introduced [as the subject]. Therefore, just as there is an exclusion (*vyavacchedya*) for words such as "jar" when they are employed in linguistic usage, so too is there [an exclusion] for those [words] employed in linguistic usage.
Regarding the words "knowable" (*jñeya*) and so forth: there is a certain exclusion, namely the "unknowable" (*ajñeya*) and so on.

"In the absence of the suspicion of another" (*ananyāśaṅkāyām*) means that the suspicion of being unknowable and so forth is the "suspicion of another" (*anyāśaṅkā*); the absence of that is "the absence of the suspicion of another. Thus, the meaning is: when the suspicion of being unknowable and so forth is non-existent. For instance, [one might think]: "Sound is unknowable in its form as impermanent," and so on.

This [definition] is employed when there is doubt, namely that [the object] is to be known through aspects such as impermanence (*anitya*). In that context, it is precisely that unknowability which was suspected regarding the aspect of impermanence and so forth that is excluded. Likewise, in the case of the statement "all things are knowable by the knowledge of the Omniscient One" (*sarvajña-jñāna*), it is precisely that unknowability suspected in relation to the knowledge of the Omniscient One that is to be excluded. Similarly, someone says: "Nir-..."

Because of the absence of other designations (*paryāya*), there is no operation of cognition (*jñāna*) therein; therefore, they are "unknowable" (*ajñeya*). Here too, "unknowability" is merely superimposed, and that alone is what is to be excluded. This is because even non-existence (*abhāva*) is made an object by the statement, "it is not the case that everything is non-existent. The same should be understood regarding the use of the word "knowable" (*jñeya*) in other instances, as well as with the word "object of knowledge" (*prameya*). Likewise [in the case of]: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary."

In this case as well, some might imagine that momentariness belongs only to certain things like lamps and not to everything; [the term "all"] serves to exclude that [limited view] and establish the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Likewise, when there is a doubt as to whether "someone has arrived" or "everyone has arrived," one says, "The entire village has arrived. Here, only that arrival which was suspected for a particular individual is what is being excluded. The same applies to a collective...
By stating that "the five groups of consciousness have a [single] object" (*lambana*) and that they "have a partial object" (*ekadeśālambana*), their having a [single] partial object is negated.
In this way, regarding other terms such as "two" and so forth when introduced into common usage, the specific exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) should be stated according to the context and as appropriate.

This is the collective meaning here: it is not said that a real entity (*vastubhūta*) serving as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), which is apprehended by a distinct cognition and established within two heaps, is what is expressed by the word through "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*). Rather, even when [the object] is such [as it is], the form (*ākāra*) that is superimposed (*āropita*) upon it as being otherwise by the listener—that too is precisely what is to be excluded by the word.

Clarifying this very point, he says: "In that regard," and so forth. That which is the locus of doubt, the object of doubt, for a dull-witted person who is to be instructed—that alone is the purpose of words such as "the knowable" (*jñeya*). If it is argued that no one at all has any doubt, he replies: "Or, not suspecting," and so forth. If he does not suspect anything, then [it would follow that] as it truly is—

This is because words have been established as conventions precisely for the sake of that refinement [of cognition]. Furthermore, words such as "the knowable" (*jñeya*) and so forth, when not brought into linguistic usage, signify nothing at all, since it is only a word situated within a sentence that conveys its meaning. If one asks, "Where is such a word employed?"—in the investigation of the domain of employment, it is said to be "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*).

Regarding the question, "What is the meaning of the word *jñeya* in [the phrase] 'anirdiṣṭaprayogam' and so forth? there is no meaning [to be derived]. Consequently, there is no comprehension whatsoever. Thus, one who possesses such certainty—what instruction would he then require from another speaker? The intention is that he requires none at all. This is because of the absence of expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*).

The "leading" (*nayana*) is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the listener; where that does not exist in a statement, there is no such refinement of the listener. And how could a speaker who utters such a statement not be considered insane? Therefore, the speaker employs a word while desiring precisely to effect the refinement of a listener who possesses an expectation. What is the reason? It is for the sake of that refinement—that is, for the sake of the refinement of the listener alone.

Because words have been assigned conventional designations. Granted that for words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*) and so forth—which reside in sentences and are employed for the sake of practical usage—the exclusion (*vyavacchedya*) is indeed as described; but how is it so for those words such as "knowable" which, not being employed in practical usage, exist in isolation? For [in their case], it is not...
In this regard, since there might be a point of doubt for the listener, he says: “And those not brought into linguistic usage,” and so forth.

The meaning is that there is no expressive word that is not included within sentences (*vākya*). For a speaker, desiring a result, first intends: “I shall communicate this object, connected with a specific action, to this person by means of this word,” and thus [says] “O King... [etc.]

One employs [words] in this manner: "Give! Bring the cow! Therefore, it is only the word-meanings as already connected with the action that are denoted; it is not the case that the word-meanings are first denoted and their connection occurs subsequently. For if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-arising of case-endings such as the accusative in "gām" (the cow) and so forth. Consequently, words are employed only when situated within a sentence. This is precisely what he says: "Of that which resides in the sentence," and so on. Its meaning—
The intention is that [the word] functions as a means of conveying meaning (*pratipādakatvāt*).

As for those words which are recited in groups such as *sarvaviśva* and so forth by the Vaiyākaraṇas, or which are refined through the division of base and suffix, even those are, according to the authors of the *Nirukta*, merely like "line-drawn cows" (*rekhāgavaya*) in comparison to those that stand in the place of actual sentences.

The means [of cognition] are to be regarded as such, but they have no worldly purpose whatsoever. Therefore, only those words that reside within a sentence possess meaning; it is precisely regarding those situated therein that an investigation of meaning is conducted. Thus he says: "But where, etc.
"These" refers to those words residing in a sentence which, when the investigation of the domain of usage proceeds, [reveal that] the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

It is said: [it is called *apoha*] because "by means of this (*anena*), another (*anya*) is excluded (*apohyate*). However, regarding those words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*) which do not occur in actual usage, he states that they lack even the possibility of an object, saying: "without a specified usage," and so forth. The term *nirdiṣṭaprayoga* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is specified (*nirdiṣṭa*, i.e., employed) and is likewise a usage (*prayoga*). Subsequently, the indeclinable particle *na* is used in the sense of non-existence (*abhāva*), according to the rule beginning with "indeclinables [are used] in the sense of case-endings," and so on.

[This is] a *vyayībhāva* compound. Consequently, by the rule "after the locative [ending], there is optionally the substitution of *am* for the locative and instrumental endings," the form *am* is applied. 2. The meaning is that when there is an absence of an expressed usage, the question is: "What is the meaning of the word *jñeya* (knowable) alone, as introduced by the sentence?
Even for words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*), there is nothing [specific]; even that comprehension which arises simply from hearing [the word] within a context is [incomplete].

Because those words have their meanings completed according to the scope of the observed usage, they possess expectancy; yet there is a disruption of that meaning upon the apprehension of words such as "pot" (ghaṭa). Such a phenomenon exists even in words like "knowable" (jñeya) and so forth, exactly as it is observed. Therefore, others maintain that this [word "kim"] is an adverbial modifier for all actions; for the action of questioning is the qualificand, and adverbs modifying an action function as the object (karman).

Regarding the word "tvam" (you): here, if it is a *karmadhāraya* compound, then since it functions as its own constituent meaning (*svapadārtha*), one must explain how it can be qualified by the act of questioning.
Alternatively, if it is a *bahuvrīhi*—meaning that the word "jñeya" (knowable) is that in which the usage is not specified—then even in that case, the word [is qualified].

It is not an action (*kriyā*). However, when such an analysis (*vigraha*) is not specified—namely, that "the question is that in which there is an application"—then it becomes an action. Even then, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "question," the locative case alone is appropriate, as in "the question in which the application is specified. If it is asked why the meaning of the word "knowable" (*jñeya*) does not apply to the word alone, he says: "Therefore... (*tataḥ*).

(1) Therefore, from the word "knowable" (*jñeya*), there is no comprehension of a real entity (*vastu*) anywhere; and since the word "knowable" alone is never employed in linguistic practice (*vyavahāra*), which results in either affirmation or negation, how could there be any comprehension of meaning? When a discussion has begun with words such as "Is that which is knowable impermanent and so forth, or is it unknowable?", and then the word "knowable" is used in isolation, even then—

That comprehension of meaning which occurs by depending on a word that is not isolated arises from the sentence alone, because a word accompanied by other words constitutes a sentence. Therefore, there is no comprehension of the meaning of a word independent of other words;
just as there is nothing expressible by the isolated words "knowable" (*jñeya*) and so forth, so too there is nothing expressible by isolated words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*).
But surely, in the context of the inquiry, "Shall I bring water with a jar or with my cupped hands?", one employs the word "with a jar.

And in that case, even for a listener who has not understood the context, a cognition in the form of a jar certainly arises upon hearing the isolated word "with a jar. How then can it be said that there is no cognition from an isolated word? To this he replies:

"Yāpi" and so forth. That cognition in which the object sought to be known is not fully completed is "one whose object is incomplete. To the question, "In what way is its object incomplete? he says: "In accordance with observed usage. This means: as many [instances] as there are in which the injunctions for actions such as bringing or taking away have been set in motion; in that many instances, the usage of the word "jar" has been observed, and it is in accordance with that [usage].

In preceding sentences, there arises a cognition characterized by expectancy, such as "Is this the intended meaning, or rather that? Because of this state of expectancy, the [cognition] appearing as a form is incomplete in its sense; it is indeed a delusive error. This explains that (1) there is no comprehension of meaning from the mere hearing of isolated words alone, but rather from a word that possesses meaning and has been perceived within a sentence.

The conceit of understanding the meaning arises from hearing the word alone for one whose intellect has been led astray by similarity. Just as there is a confusion regarding the understanding of meaning upon hearing the isolated word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and so forth, following previously observed usage, so it is with words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*)—according to what has been seen and according to the observation of their usage. That is, in as many sentences as the word "knowable" is seen being employed...

In accordance with that, there is indeed a failure of comprehension regarding the meaning upon hearing the word "kevalajñeya" (the exclusively knowable). By this, he states that in every respect words such as "ghaṭa" (pot) and words such as "jñeya" (knowable) are equal.
And as for what was also said: "Functioning by way of excluding 'one' and so forth, [the word] applies to each part of the whole because of the negation of the parts..."

The meaningfulness [of a word] arises from its being withdrawn from certain things and applied to others; this is due to its efficacy. And this application consists in setting aside that from which a given object is distinct. (126)
When that [universal] is differentiated according to the differences [of its instances], it appears as having a uniform form;
and this [differentiation] of that entity is understood through the exclusion of others (anyavyāvṛtti).
"Furthermore, since you do not admit a whole (*aṅgin*) distinct [from its parts], [the term 'whole'] would be meaningless.

This is incorrect; for those things which are the objects of cognitions such as "one" and so forth are different from those which appear as the objects of cognitions such as "collection" (*samudāya*) and so forth.
And it is precisely those things existing in a particular state that are the objects of cognitions such as "collection" who are called the "whole."

This is because the possessor of parts (*aṅgin*) is negated. Furthermore, those [atoms] which are asserted by the opponent to be the initiators of properties such as a "collection" (*samudāya*) are accepted by us as being exactly like that—as the producers of the cognition of a collection and as its objective support (*ālambana*), since there is no contradiction. Therefore, the negation of one and so forth with respect to all terms such as "collection," "duality," and so on, is indeed logically consistent.

"From that," and so forth. Since every sentence is restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇa*), and only those words situated within a sentence possess meaning, "therefore, in the employment of all words" is the conclusion. "Because of its fruitfulness" means because of the fruitfulness of that employment of words. Thus, by the aforementioned method, for all words, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is the expressed meaning.
As stated by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara:
"And is this *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others) intended to be denoted or undenoted?
If it is denoted, is it so by way of a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) or by the negation of another?"
If this [entity] were denotable by way of its positive nature (*vidhyātman*), the doctrine of exclusivity would have to be abandoned;
for it has been stated that the meaning of a word consists everywhere in the negation of other things.
If "exclusion" (*apoha*) is expressed by means of the exclusion of non-exclusion, [then the doctrine of exclusivity is lost].
In each such case, if you maintain this desire, there would be an infinite regress for you.
Moreover, if you maintain that this "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) is indeed inexpressible,
then your statement that "a word effects the exclusion of others" would be contradicted.
"For since the mere aspect of the exclusion of others occurs only in those words with which the negative particle (*nañ*) is joined, whereas elsewhere its own nature alone is understood."
That is incorrect, because it is accepted that the positive injunction (*vidhi*) is the word-meaning, while the negation of other things follows by implication (*arthāt*).

If, then, the positive injunction alone is the word-meaning and the negation of others occurs by implication, how is it that the Master Dignāga stated: "Words express entities as qualified precisely by the exclusion of other objects" (*śabdorthāntaravyāvṛttiviśiṣṭāneva bhāvānāha*), and so forth?

It is not contradictory; therefore, he says: "And the settling [of the convention]," and so forth. By this, he demonstrates that even in the case of a mere convention, a word functions by way of a positive form (*vidhirūpa*), let alone in actual worldly usage (*vyavahāra*). This refers to the object "tree" from which [the convention was established]—*Ślokavārttika*, Chapter 4, *Sāmānyacintā*.
It is said that there is no "part" whatsoever even for this form; nevertheless, through words directed toward it, the exclusion of others is understood. (128)

In that regard, no one is apprehended as distinct or superior to another. "Excluding the non-tree" means being differentiated from things such as jars and the like; the meaning is "having set aside the non-tree. The application—that is, the making of a convention—of the word "tree" should be understood [in this way]. By the phrase "excluding that," it is stated that the word "tree" is not conventionally applied to what is not a tree.

[It is] as follows. Where, then, is that location? He says: "In the difference [of] the trees being differentiated, there is a difference from that which is non-tree; that is, a nature distinct from the non-tree. For just as one particular tree is distinct from that [general category of] 'tree,' so too are all particular trees [distinct from it]."

Therefore, that distinction among them is superimposed as a unity upon all of them by means of conceptual cognition; thus, it appears in an identical form. Upon that distinction—which, though appearing in an identical form, possesses distinct natures—there is the application of the word.
And in the phrase "this very [is it]," the word *ca* (and) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). It is precisely this form appearing in conceptual cognition that is external—
It is distinct. Or rather, that very distinction—characterized by a nature distinct from non-trees—is what was stated by the teacher Diṅnāga.
How was it stated? He says: "By means of the exclusion of others, some part of that entity is understood."
We shall clarify the meaning of this in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
Now, one might ask: why is a portion of reality, distinguished by the exclusion of others, not apprehended in its ultimate sense? To this he says:

"Its form"—that is, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—is nothing at all, because this differentiation, which consists of exclusion (*nivṛtti*), is non-existent. [This refers to] conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)...

And because [difference] appears due to a delusion of the intellect, if difference has no form whatsoever, how then can it be said that "the word expresses entities as qualified by the exclusion of others"?
To this, he says: "In its manifestation," and so forth. Of that aforementioned difference, which is of a different class—
When an excluded nature is understood through a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) from words, the exclusion of others is thereby understood.

For instance, when "tree" is uttered, the exclusion of non-trees is understood by implication. It is by this much alone that being qualified by the exclusion of others is expressed; however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified. Thus he says: "No," and so forth.
In this context, "therein" refers to the word-meaning as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), or to the treatise of the Teacher (*ācāryagrantha*). "Some other" means an object excluded from another.
It is not understood as being qualified by some characteristic consisting of the exclusion of others.
Therefore, that which was stated by Bhaṭṭa [is refuted].
“Furthermore, a unique particular (asādhāraṇa-vastu) is not apprehended as possessing exclusion (apoha);
or else, how could a relationship be conceived between a real entity and a non-entity?”
By its mere existence as its own nature, it would not be any qualifier at all.
Nor indeed is the sound "mutual non-existence" (anyonyābhāva) a producer of duality; such is this [view]. ||129||
The perception of the formless as possessing form is an error of the intellect.

When a word is applied, it excludes everything other than that [referent]; since this exclusion also differs from that which is to be excluded by it, the difference among those things being excluded is indicated as having a common appearance. This is due to the exclusion of other objects.
That by which something is qualified through its own cognition is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa).
Furthermore, from words such as "horse" and so forth, there arises no cognition of apoha;
for in this context, the cognition of the qualified object is desired, and that [cognition] does not occur when the qualifier is unknown.
Nor can one form produce a qualification for a cognition that is of a different nature;
and how could that be called a qualification when the cognition is of a different kind?
Furthermore, in a form that is cognizable through non-existence, there is no substantiality in the qualified object.
"The entity qualified by exclusion (*apoha*) cannot be the denotable object for you"—this [objection] is refuted.
Now, one might ask: how can a single word have two functions characterized by affirmation and negation? He replies:

Nor does a word perform two functions: it performs the two [functions] of denoting its own object and excluding others. What is the reason? It is "mutual non-existence" (*anyonyābhāva*). The word *iti* indicates the reason. Because the meaning of "tree" is the absence of the exclusion of non-trees, and the meaning of "non-tree" is the absence of that [tree], by way of mutual non-existence; therefore, from the word "tree," the meaning of "tree" is understood.
Since the comprehension of the exclusion of non-trees occurs by implication through the word itself, there are not two direct operations of the word. Therefore:
"If this word 'cow' is capable of excluding others..."
Janaka [is perceived] through the cow by means of the cognition of the cow; another sound is sought after.
"Words do not have cognition as their fruit, nor can there be two fruits for one [word];
how then, according to you, can the cognition of both negation and affirmation be the fruit of a single [word]?"—
thus [the objection] is refuted.
If the difference denoted by words were to persist everywhere, then that itself would become the ultimate universal;
therefore, he says: "This" refers to the non-persisting difference which is the object of words. It is formless (*arūpa*), meaning it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Regarding that formless [difference], when speakers and listeners conflate the perceived and the conceptualized, their perception of it as possessing a form is a confusion of the intellect, a delusion (*bhrānti*).
This is the meaning.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "being established" (*niveśyamāna*) and so forth. Because an object such as a tree is differentiated, that [object] is excluded; this is the investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*).

It has been pointed out [by the author] in such passages as, "A certain portion of an object is understood," and "Words denote entities as qualified by the exclusion of other objects. For when that [word] expresses a particular difference, it functions as if it were implying the exclusion of other objects; for the designation of a difference residing in one thing is invariably concomitant with the exclusion of what is other than that.

That very difference is the portion reached through the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of that [other]; for its attainment depends upon that [exclusion] as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). The connection is that "that qualified [entity], having abandoned that [limiting adjunct], is established. To the question "Where? he says: "Of those being differentiated," and so forth. And this has its meaning analyzed in the commentary on the verse (*kārikā*). It is that word by which the exclusion of others is implied.
The analysis: This very distinction, which appears as having a uniform form, has been pointed out by the teacher Diṅnāga.

How so? He says: "By means of the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntaravyāvṛtti*), some part of that real entity (*vastu*) is understood. Likewise, [he says] in the passage beginning with, "In this way, the word denotes only those entities qualified by the exclusion of other objects," and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the reference is] to the object of the word being distinct from others...

The inclusion of such statements as "the scripture, performing exclusion (*apoha*), denotes [the object]" is for the purpose of supporting the very point made in the passage beginning with "for that [word]," and so forth.

For that word "tree," while expressing this specific nature as excluded from non-trees, functions only by implying the exclusion of other objects—that is, of objects that are not trees. What is the reason? Because it is restricted to a single [referent].

Regarding the phrase "of difference" (*bhedasya*), and so forth: Just as specific types of trees, such as the *khadira* and others, are by their very nature distinct from non-trees, so too are non-trees distinct from trees, because difference resides in both [relata]. In that context, the exclusion of what is other than that refers to the exclusion of everything else resulting from the injunction (*codanā*) of that distinct nature—which belongs to one side (the tree), pertains to the object "tree," and appears in a single form—by means of the word "tree."

Because it is inseparable [from it]. Therefore, because it is inseparable from the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of that which is other than the object "tree"—namely, the non-tree—it is in this way that the object "tree" is expressed as having a form excluded from non-trees, provided that the cessation of the object "non-tree" is understood therein. That very thing is the differentiation (*bheda*) appearing in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) for that which is being differentiated from another.

"Differentiated" (*bhinna*) means having a distinct nature (*svabhāva*). By the exclusion of that [nature], that is, by the exclusion of other objects, according to the logic previously stated, a portion of the real entity (*vastu*) is understood through implication; this is the sense of the ellipsis "it is said that [a portion] has been reached.

The intention is that because it arrives via the door of perceiving the excluded object and because it is determined as having the form of the real entity, it is said that "a portion of the real entity has been reached."

This is what is meant: (1) A word conveys in verbal cognition an aspect that appears in conceptual thought (*vikalpabuddhi*)—an aspect which consists in a form excluded from those things that do not produce a reflective awareness of that [object], and which has a unity superimposed upon it that produces such a reflective awareness; this aspect is one in which the distinction between the external and the internal is undifferentiated, because it is precisely that which appears in verbal cognition. And while conveying that [aspect], [the word] conveys the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*).
This implies a boundary (*maryādā*). It is with this intention that the Ācārya stated: "By the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), some part of that entity is understood.

However, no part of an external object is grasped by means of the exclusion of others—which constitutes the word-meaning and takes the form of a qualifier—because such an exclusion simply does not exist. Thus far, [the argument regarding] the other...

It has been established that some part of that entity is understood through exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Now, in order to establish that [the proponent] speaks of entities as being qualified precisely by the exclusion of other word-meanings, he says: "Because of the cognition of that," and so forth. Because of the cognition of that—that is, because of the cognition of the exclusion of others—it serves as its qualifier; since it is the qualifier of the distinction, it is that very [exclusion].

In the sense of "gone," there is no exclusion of other objects (*arthāntaravyāvṛtti*) by which words, like a staff, would be enjoined as qualifiers based on being the cause [of cognition]. Since the difference between two things being differentiated resides in both, even when a difference residing in one is established, there occurs an implication of the other that is inseparable from it.

Therefore, there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified between those two. Even when one exclusion is denoted, the understanding of the exclusion of the other occurs. It is said that by means of the instruction through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the distinction qualified by that [exclusion] is understood; this is according to the Teacher.

Alternatively: (1) because that aforementioned distinction of entities is understood—that is, apprehended—from the word, it possesses that [exclusion] as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), since it is determinative. That exclusion of other things is the limiting adjunct of that apprehension, which is so described because it implies the object.
To be inseparable from the exclusion of other things is precisely what constitutes having that as its limiting adjunct.

This is what is meant: that exclusion of other objects which is understood from the object itself because it is inseparable from it—that very difference, when understood from the word as qualified by the exclusion of others, is said by the Teacher to be "comprehended. Now, one might object: the exclusion of other objects is the basis for the application of the word, by means of which external objects are qualified.

Words such as "cow" are enjoined [to denote their objects] without [the object] being previously perceived. "Like a staff-bearer" is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Just as one is called a "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) by means of a staff, it is not the case that one is [called] "possessing exclusion" (*vyāvṛttimān*) by means of an exclusion. Why is it that exclusion is not a distinct entity? He says: "For of the two," and so forth. Because of the mutual distinction between the two—tree and non-tree—...

The meaning is that because the distinction between the two resides in both—since it resides in both the tree and the non-tree—it consists in a nature distinct from both tree and non-tree. Therefore, even when a distinction residing in one is expressed, although the word expresses the distinct nature of the distinction residing in the tree relative to the non-tree, there occurs an implication of the other (the non-tree) as an inseparable concomitant. This is relative to the non-tree.

There is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of a distinction residing in the tree, characterized by the exclusion of non-trees, even though it does not reside in the tree [itself] when considered apart from the tree; likewise, there is an implication of a distinction residing in non-trees, characterized by the exclusion of trees. The word *iti* indicates the reason. Because of this reason—namely, because they are its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—the phrase "that which is qualified by them has been understood" is to be supplied as an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). [The phrase] "not of those two" means that there is no [distinction] of a difference residing in one [of the two], nor of the exclusion of the other.

The relation of qualifier and qualified. But what is this distinction residing in one [object], and what is that exclusion of others (*tadanyavyāvṛtti*), by means of which there arises from a word the cognition of a distinction residing in one, which is inseparable from the exclusion of others? If this is asked:
It is said: First of all, that which is denoted by the word "tree" is the form possessing branches and so forth, which appears in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*).

Appearing as if it were a non-differentiated form across all trees, and as if distinct from those things that do not possess that form, it is precisely this "exclusion" (*bheda*)—meaning its differentiated nature—that is understood.
In the same way, the exclusion residing in a single [entity] should be seen as what is denoted by words such as "jar. And while establishing that exclusion...
A word conveys by implication the exclusion of dissimilar things, which is characterized as a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*); that is the exclusion of what is other than it.
Now, if a portion of the real entity qualified by the exclusion of others is not being conveyed, for what purpose was it stated [above] that "it is qualified by the exclusion of others"?
To this he says: "In the naming of a single difference," and so forth. And as for this [entity], as it has been divided...

That very same unity and difference is what is expressed by the word; the cognition of that [unity] itself is the understanding of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Furthermore, while demonstrating that words are a constituent part of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), [the author] stated the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in the verse: "It is understood through its exclusion" (*tadvyāvṛttyā gamyate*). For this very reason, in the case of a word, there is no dual operation consisting of both the exclusion of others and the denotation of its own object.

The understanding of the exclusion of others follows simply from the expression of its own referent, because the own referent consists in difference. For there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) for that which lacks exclusion, nor is there exclusion for that which lacks positive concomitance. When there is a single positive concomitance, there is an absence of anything to be excluded; likewise, the understanding of the exclusion of others is the understanding of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Thus, through both positive and negative concomitance, the word possesses a referent.

Thus, by this statement of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it should be understood that while the positive concomitance is stated directly, the negative concomitance follows by implication. By means of that statement, the teacher Diṅnāga, demonstrating that words serve as a constituent of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), said:
"The portion of the real entity is understood through its exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Likewise, he says "or qualified by that," using the term "exclusion."

Exclusion (*vyatireka*) has been stated; by the term "part of the real entity" (*vastubhāga*), inclusion (*anvaya*) is meant. By this, the following is also explained: the meaning is that a word, while effecting the exclusion of other words, expresses its own referent (*svārtha*). In that context, that very difference residing in a single [entity] which appears to conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) has been explained as its own referent; therein, the exclusion of other referents (*arthāntaravyāvṛtti*), namely the exclusion of other referents (*arthāntarāpoha*) characterized as a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), is that [exclusion].
"Performing" means, by implication, "causing [the understanding] to proceed.

Furthermore, if the application of words such as "tree" were preceded solely by the exclusion of others, then the explanation beginning with "by the instruction of positive and negative concomitance" would be redundant.
Therefore, the word-meaning is indeed a positive injunction (*vidhi*).

Precisely because the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) is understood through the force of meaning when a single particular is denoted, it is said "precisely for this reason" and so forth. This is because the object of its own [positive] meaning consists of a particular form.
That which is the referent of the word "tree"—the form possessing branches and so on, appearing in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—is of the nature of a particular.

A thing possesses a distinct nature because it is excluded from that which lacks the form of non-difference. Since the word expresses its own object, which consists of difference, the exclusion of other things is understood by implication; for in this way, the object "tree" is understood precisely as having the nature of being different from non-trees. If, by implication, the exclusion of the tree occurs therein, then the expression of its own object is indeed the function of the word.
The function [of a word] is the exclusion of others by implication; thus, there is not a dual function for the word.
Now, it might be argued that a prescriptive sentence conveys only positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and does not enjoin or prohibit anything else;
likewise, a prohibitive sentence is understood as conveying only negation, and not the injunction or prohibition of anything else. To this, he says:

"For there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*)," and so forth. Positive concomitance is the prescription of a specific object, such as "cut down a tree. In that case, the exclusion of what is not a tree follows by implication; this is negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Where that [negative concomitance] does not exist, there is indeed no negative concomitance. Such a positive concomitance does not exist for me; rather, every [positive concomitance] is necessarily accompanied by negative concomitance.
Therefore, as it was said by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara: "For one who does not accept that the meaning of a word has a positive form (*vidhirūpa*),
there could be no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) either, for the latter is preceded by the former."
1. Slokavārtika:
Because even a rebuttal is fruitless if there is no persistence [of the objection] in any case.

And this distinction is formless (*arūpa*). The perception of it as having form is merely a cognitive error (*buddhiviplava*), which is rejected because it is not desired [as a valid object]. Or, "non-concomitance" (*ananvaya*) means being devoid of concomitance; the connection is that there is no "negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*). In that context, the negation of the specific instance is "negative concomitance. Therein, the understanding of the remainder by implication is "positive concomitance" (*anvaya*). Regarding the phrase "single concomitance," and so forth—

This is not at all tenable. Regarding the phrase "of a single positive concomitance" (*ekānvayasya*): because there would be no fruit in the injunction if there were no object to be excluded—that is, no object to be avoided—the injunction would be purposeless.
If, upon saying "cut the tree," there is by implication no exclusion of what is not a tree, then the employment of the word "tree" [would be redundant].

It would be fruitless. Alternatively, when there is a listener’s desire to know—such as "Which tree shall I cut, or another?"—the prohibition of others is indeed understood when it is said, "Cut the tree"; otherwise, the statement would be purposeless in the absence of anything to be avoided. Likewise, even when a listener who lacks such an inquiry is urged by the words "Cut the tree," [the exclusion of others is still implied]. The tree...
It functions thus and not otherwise. For the speaker employs a word with the intention that "this applies only to a tree and not to anything else.

And sound follows the speaker's intention. Therefore, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) devoid of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), nor is there a negative concomitance devoid of positive concomitance;
the meaning is that this holds for the negation of one thing and the affirmation of the other. This occurs in some cases where [the object] is made the subject of negation.

Because an injunction would be fruitless if there were no persistence of the object [in other cases]. For instance, when drinking that has liquor as its object is prohibited, if there were no persistence of drinking even in something other than liquor, then the specific prohibition of drinking among all prohibited objects would be meaningless. In that case, by the phrase "one drinks liquor," if only the drinking of liquor itself were prohibited—[then the specific mention would be redundant].

Because the sentence has that as its primary purpose, although the drinking of water and so forth is not enjoined by the words themselves, nevertheless, the persistence of drinking anything other than *surā* is not prohibited; thus, the understanding of the connection arises from the sense of the context. Otherwise, the mention of *surā* would be meaningless. Or rather, when the question is asked, "Is *surā* to be drunk like water and so forth, or not?", and it is replied, "*Surā* is not to be drunk," [the implication is] "only *surā*" [is forbidden].

Because it is understood [as such], the injunction to drink water and so forth is not negated by what is under discussion; therefore, in all cases, the meaning of a word consists precisely of the form of either an injunction or a prohibition.
What, then, is the difference between affirmative, prohibitive, and exclusionary (paryudāsa) sentences? There is a great difference. For that which is injunctive...

Having primarily expressed a positive injunction (*vidhi*), [the sentence] implies by implication the negation of other things; and having primarily expressed a negation (*niṣedha*), it implies by implication the injunction of other things. However, a sentence that establishes an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) primarily expresses the injunction of another thing preceded by a negation. Thus, there is indeed a distinction.

[Objection: But surely, if exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is understood through implication, then why is it not accepted that this alone is the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*) of entities, by which they are apprehended as qualified? [Reply: Why, then, is it explained that "it is apprehended as qualified by that" because that [exclusion] has been understood as its adventitious attribute (*upādhi*)?
To this he says: "And this... and so forth. That which is the difference...

The teacher Diṅnāga did not intend for "qualification" (*viśeṣaṇatva*) to have the characteristic of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). This [qualification], moreover, is formless and devoid of intrinsic nature; it is a mere conceptual construct (*sāmānyacintā*), and thus it is not ultimately real. Otherwise, it would not belong to a real entity. (130)
Exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) becomes a real entity (*vastu*), because it is determined as "this is different from that.

For the ultimate reality is form (*rūpa*); if that difference were a form, it would have to be either that very form or not that form. If it were that very form, it would not be different from it. Nor could the form of one thing belong to another.

[This is] the state of being [an entity]. This is because it has no form that is either distinct or non-distinct from it. If it is asked, "In that case, how is there the cognition of the difference of entities from those of a different class? he says: "The mere perception of that difference—by way of its possessing form and by way of its relation to the entity—is a confusion of cognition, an error. The word "mere" [indicates] that such an external [object] does not exist.
The commentary on this verse should also be understood in this way.
Now, one might ask: "If there is perception by virtue of possessing form (*rūpavattva*), how can this be a cognitive distortion (*buddhiviplava*)? To this, he says: "By that alone," and so forth.

By that very perception of difference—which consists in the connection with an entity by virtue of possessing form—it is not ultimately real; that is, it does not exist as a substantial reality (*vastubhūta*).
"Because it exists. "This" refers to the distinction (*bheda*) in its positive form (*prasajyarūpa*). "Otherwise," that is, if this were not accepted:

for the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) belonging to a real entity (*vastu*), namely the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), does not itself become a real entity. Why? Because its distinction [is defined] by being different from this or that.

This is what is meant: if that [exclusion] were a real entity (*vastu*), then the exclusion of non-trees from trees would have to be either non-different or different [from them]. If it were non-different, there could be no cognition of the distinction—namely, "the tree is distinct from this non-tree"—because, being non-different from the exclusion of non-trees in a single *palāśa* tree, the same would apply to *dhava* trees and others; they too would not be non-trees.

There would be no exclusion [of the *palāśa* from non-trees]. Since its nature is that of [the exclusion of non-trees], it would not be present in those [other trees] because of its exclusion [from them], just like the *palāśa* itself. Or, if it were distinct from the *palāśa*, then in that case too, there would be an exclusion of the *palāśa* from the exclusion of non-trees;
and for the *palāśa* which is being excluded from the exclusion of non-trees, it would follow that it has the nature of a non-tree, just like a non-tree. Consequently, from this—

The cognition "this tree is different from that tree" would not occur [if difference were not real], yet it is accepted. Therefore, that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is not a real entity (*vastu*). The phrase "because of the designation 'this is different from that'" means because of its verbal expression; this is also an elliptical indication for including its cognition as well. He explains by the words "for, indeed," etc. "For" (*hi*) means because. What is called "form" (*rūpa*)? It is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); it is the real entity (*vastu*).

[The opponent asks: Is it its own nature (*svabhāva*)? [The author replies: If difference were the form of exclusion from others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), it would have to be its own nature. "That" refers to the form of exclusion from non-trees. "Of that form" means having the nature of that specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *palāśa* tree which is excluded from those [others]. "Or not of that form" means being something other than that;
the meaning is that a real entity (*vastu*) cannot transcend being either identical to or different from [something else].

With the words "tādūpye" (in the case of identity) and so forth, he states the fault in the first position: If identity (*tādrūpya*) means non-difference from the *palāśa* tree, then when that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)—which is the universal by which all distinct trees are seen to be excluded—is admitted to be non-different from the *palāśa*, it follows that the exclusion is simply the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *palāśa* itself; thus, only the *palāśa* would be distinct from non-trees.

Nothing else, such as the *dhava* tree and so forth, attains [that exclusion]. Therefore, it would be distinguished from the non-tree (*avṛkṣa*). He asks: "For what reason? and says: "For not," and so forth. For the exclusion from the non-tree is the very nature of the *palāśa* tree alone; and that nature does not belong to another, such as the *dhava* tree. If that [exclusion] were not the nature of the distinction, then there would have to be a different nature altogether. And consequently, the entity [would be distinct] from that.

It would be excluded; consequently, there would be no difference for it. For that which is excluded from the difference of something else would be identical to that very thing, and thus the principle that "this is its difference" would not hold. Indeed, a difference cannot be a related property of another. Or, if such a relationship did exist, since it would arise from the relation of cause and effect, the form produced by that [cause] would be the difference, and there would be no distinction [between this and any other produced form].

All effects of their respective causes would be exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). Furthermore, if difference were a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), then that [difference] would also have a further difference; thus, because it would possess difference as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it would not be a difference, just like a separate substance.
This would be the case.

The presentation of the second position begins with the words "na tadeva" and so forth. It is not that very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *palāśa* tree itself which is the nature (*rūpa*) of that difference; for "nature" (*rūpa*) is intended here as its very essence (*svabhāva*), and that [essence] is held to be the difference. Therefore, it would have to be something other than the *palāśa*, having the form of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Alternatively, the nature of the difference would be something entirely different. And thus, because it is something else, [the consequence follows].

Therefore, the entity whose nature is "palāśa" would have to be excluded from that which consists of the exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣavyāvṛtti*). For that reason, there would be no distinction of that *palāśa* from a non-tree such as a *ūṣma* tree. Indeed, whatever object is excluded from something—that is, whatever has a distinction from it—it must be that very thing [from which it is excluded]. Thus, it would follow that [the *palāśa*] is nothing other than the exclusion of non-trees.

If the exclusion of the non-tree—which consists in the cessation of the non-tree—were to cease from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *palāśa* tree, then that *palāśa* would be like a non-tree, or it would be as if it were a non-tree.
Alternatively, even if there were no identity between the tree and the non-tree, there could still be no such thing as "this is its difference.
Furthermore, if this difference from the non-tree were other than the *palāśa*, then this difference from the non-tree would not belong to this *palāśa*.

It would not be a "related thing" (*sambandhin*). The passage beginning with "for not... is the justification for this. One distinct thing, being independent, becomes the related thing (*sambandhin*) of another through its nature as a property (*dharma*). Or, "if [it were accepted]"—that is, if the status of being a related thing is admitted—then a relation (*sambandha*) consisting of a cause-and-effect relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) must be accepted; for it is impossible for two distinct things to have a relation without a cause-and-effect relationship. In that case:

Exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is the cause and that which possesses exclusion (*vyāvṛttimat*) is the effect. Thus, the nature of the reason (*hetu*) is indeed a distinct entity produced by that; it is called "differentiation" (*bheda*) because it is produced by that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which possesses exclusion. Therefore, [the word] is given as the name of a separate category (*padārthāntara*), distinct from the category called differentiation (*bheda*) which is intended to be the effect.

Because there is no distinction, in other cases as well, all those effects which are produced by causes would have to be exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) or differences (*bheda*). But this is not so; therefore, let there be no designation of "difference" even in other instances where difference is intended.

Now, it is not said that "the effect is difference," but rather that "difference is the effect. To this, he replies: "And if difference is admitted to be a distinct entity (arthāntara), then this difference, even though it possesses exclusion (vyāvṛtti), must itself have a further difference.
Otherwise, difference would not be a distinct entity at all. Consequently, regarding the difference of a *palāśa* tree from what is not a tree..."

Considering that "the difference from *palāśa* [is] the difference," that difference has difference as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). That difference from *palāśa* has difference as its qualifier; the state of being such is "having difference as its limiting adjunct" (*bhedopādhitva*). Therefore, this difference from non-trees would not be a difference of the *palāśa*, just like any other distinct substance (*dravyāntara*). For example, just as another substance, such as a jar, is not a difference of the *palāśa*. This is the consideration of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*).

For difference is not apprehended as something existing in the same way as the limiting adjuncts of difference; this is because of the specific qualification [in the text]. Consequently, in the absence of the limiting adjunct, there would be an absence of difference itself. Therefore, there is no otherness. Nor is it due to the absence of anything else; for even if something exists, the difference relative to a non-pot is not the difference of the *palāśa* tree, because that [non-pot] serves merely as a limiting adjunct. This is because [difference] is independent, as it has been stated.
Generally speaking: [Objection] Now, even if difference is indeed a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of difference, why does the difference of a *palāśa* tree not [itself] become a difference?
To this, he says: "For not... and so forth. Because of the specific indication "this," namely, "this is the difference from non-trees"; "from this" means—

"From the tree. This must be understood in relation to "of this" (*asya*). Because of this specific designation—"this difference of this *palāśa* is from this non-tree"—and because it is designated through dependence, it is established that the difference is a property (*dharma*) belonging to the *palāśa*. And this designation through dependence is established only if there is no difference [between the difference and the *palāśa*], by way of excluding any other difference; it is not so, however, if [the difference] were a separate entity.

Regarding difference: for if it were a separate entity (*arthāntara*), then because it would have difference as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the difference would not belong to the *palāśa* tree itself—just as [the difference] does not belong to the pot. Consequently, there could be no specific designation such as "this is different from that. Thus, in the case of the position that [difference] is distinct, the difference of difference from non-trees which belongs to the *palāśa* must also possess form; therefore, that too must exist as a difference from its own substratum. And so it continues.

And since all distinctions possess a distinct nature, they would themselves not constitute a distinction of form by virtue of being the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) for distinction; thus, no distinction whatsoever would exist. He states this very point with the words "Consequently," and so forth. "The absence of limiting conditions" refers to that which has the characteristic of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), which is of the nature of a property (*dharma*).

In the absence of a substratum (*pādhī*), because everything would constitute a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāvāntara*) and thus be the subject (*dharmin*), difference itself would be non-existent, since that [difference] has the nature of a subject.
Furthermore, as for the one who thinks: (1) "If exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) were possessed of form (*rūpavatī*), then the alternatives of being identical or different would apply."

The objection that "to whatever extent that [exclusion] is formless, and by it entities are apprehended as qualified," is incorrect. For it has been said: "It is precisely through the cognition of those [entities] themselves, derived from words, that the exclusion of others is understood."

This is because it contradicts the text [of the *Pramāṇavārttika*]: "Nothing superior is apprehended therein by anyone" (*Pra.vā.* 1.128); and because existence is incompatible with that which lacks form (*nīrūpa*), like the horn of a hare. Furthermore, precisely because it lacks form, perception does not grasp it, nor does inference, due to the absence of a [logical] relation (*sambandha*).

Nor can that [universal] be postulated on the grounds that its restricted form would otherwise be inexplicable, because there is no relation [between the particular and the universal]; for restricted forms arise from their own causes alone, as was stated in the passage beginning with "All entities participate in exclusion by their very nature" (PV 1.42).
Nor can that [exclusion] be a qualifier when it has not been apprehended; for indeed, as long as the staff is not perceived, there is no perception of "one who possesses a staff" (daṇḍin).
Nor does it reside anywhere, because it is formless (nīrūpa). Furthermore, that which is unrelated cannot be a qualifier.
Nor does the word "tree" apply to trees and the like preceded by the apprehension of the exclusion of others, since it has already been stated that there is no such apprehension.

Because it is not apprehended as having a non-manifest form, and because linguistic convention does not apply to it, how could it be the object of words? Therefore, it is the ultimate reality (paramārtha). If it is asked: "In that case, when an undifferentiated entity is indicated by a word, since its differentiation from others is [already] present, would not other [words] be redundant? This is not a fault, because:
In the case of the dissolution of a pun on a single meaning, a single resonance (dhvani) operates. ||131||
In that case, there is no mark (liṅga) whatsoever, nor any object, whether distinct or otherwise;
yet, through the power of the object itself, there is comprehension of the whole by means of its designation. (132)

Through the medium of direct experience, the determination arises that "this is a tree, not a non-tree. Thus, the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) is conceptually constructed by means of a negative conceptualization (*pratiṣedha-vikalpa*). Furthermore, when a word is applied to a tree or similar object according to convention, it implies the exclusion of others by implication (*arthāt*). The meaning is that it implies the conceptualization of the exclusion of others. Therefore, the objective portion (*vastubhāga*) is qualified by that exclusion of others.

"It is said that it is understood"—if exclusions (*vyāvṛttayaḥ*), being of the nature of universals (*sāmānya*), are not accepted as external entities, nor is the universal imagined by others accepted, then in this case, it follows that the external object itself must be the denotable. And since there is a fault in that, he asks: "How then?"
This is an illustration [of the problem] when an undivided, partless entity is indicated by a word; it applies equally to its presentation by a logical mark (*liṅga*).

For that very same undivided entity, which is distinct from one thing, is also distinct from another. To explain: by the very same nature through which the word is distinct from the "unproduced" (*akṛtaka*), it is also [distinct] from the "corporeal" and the "impermanent," because that [entity] is partless. Since it is partless...

And when a single distinct difference from the non-produced—that is, a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—is indicated by the word "produced" regarding an object, and when that is established by a logical mark (*liṅga*), there is the comprehension of an intrinsic nature that is distinct from everything because it is present in all [particulars]. In that case, regarding an object that is partless (*anaṃśa*), how could other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as words not be redundant? When the indication is made by one word, what further purpose would other words serve?
There would be redundancy. If [the object] were established by a single inferential mark (*liṅga*), there would be the redundancy of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

He refutes this with the words beginning "because" (*yasmāt*). This objection was already refuted previously by the passage beginning "therefore, whatever specific property is perceived by which [mark]" (1944); however, it is raised again for the purpose of providing further explanation.

The superimposition of another form upon objects is the "conjunction with the object" (arthaśleṣa). And this is manifold, according to the difference in cognition. In that context—referring to the subject (dharmin) appearing in the intellect—they are said to be non-different from the external, because it is precisely the mental form (buddhyākāra) superimposed as being external that is denotable by words. Neither the external object nor the mental form alone is denotable by words, because [either taken individually] possesses the nature of a unique particular (svalakṣaṇa).

In that case, with respect to the subject (*dharmin*), one type of suggestion (*dhvani*) functions through the exclusion of the superimposition of a single object by means of the cognition of its own referent in a positive form;

and the logical mark (*liṅga*) also functions toward the exclusion of the superimposition of a single object. Therein, through the medium of denoting its own referent, [the logical mark effects] the removal of the superimposition.

In other words, the efficacy of words and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) lies in exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). However, there exists no external object as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) distinct from cognition, nor any external object as a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) distinct from the particular characteristic that could be expressed by words. For if such an entity were denoted, one would have access to the entire nature of all things through that single expression. 4. Examination of the Universal (*Sāmānyacintā*).
Therefore, the word, while producing various effects, has a single substratum.

As previously stated, through a cognition that conflates internal and external distinctions, one determines for oneself that which is fit for action; thus, the meaning of the word is employed. By those causes of error, it appears as if its form were conflated.

When [an object] appears, those [words] function precisely therein for the purpose of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) according to convention. For even when there is a single thing to be accomplished, one [word] does not perform the exclusion that another performs, due to the restrictive nature of convention. No excluded entity whatsoever is actually projected; for if it were, then by the mere utterance of a word, there would be a complete comprehension of the object through the power of the thing itself. [This applies to] cognition—

Because it is an object [of cognition], and because in that case there is an absence of the causal efficacy (*vastusāmarthya*) in a non-existent thing (*avastu*). This conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) occurs in such a manner through the power of the real thing (*vastu*) by virtue of the real thing itself; for a word effects exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) by means of its own denotation.
For that reason, by performing various exclusions (*vyavaccheda*), a word has diverse effects while having a single substratum. How so?

By determining (*adhyavasāya*) that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogya*). The meaning is that even though [the object] does not perform causal efficiency, it is superimposed (*adhyasya*) as if it were performing causal efficiency and as if it were the nature of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-rūpa*), namely its own appearance. "In that very place" means in the appearance of the cognition (*buddhi-pratibhāsa*) which has been superimposed as something external. Of what kind [is that appearance]? 96a
Through those various causes of error, it appears as if its form were mixed [with permanence and so forth].
When it manifests as if its form were mixed with aspects such as permanence due to causes of error— such as the arising of similar subsequent moments—
those words "impermanent" and so on function, according to convention, for the purpose of excluding whichever respective superimposition [is present].

How could there be a convention (*saṃketa*) regarding its own appearance? [Words] function for the purpose of excluding each respective counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Explaining that it expresses exactly in accordance with the convention, he says "And not... and so forth. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "for" (*hi*). Since the operation [of words] is according to the convention, therefore another word does not effect an exclusion that is to be accomplished by one word. What is the reason?

Because of the specific restriction of convention: since a word is applied to a mental form—which is undifferentiated from external reality—in order to exclude each [of the other] individual [alternatives], it conveys that very exclusion at the time of practical usage by means of denoting its own object. The mention of "word" is merely illustrative; it should be understood that the same applies to a logical mark (*liṅga*) as well.

[Objection: "But surely, since the object of a word has the form of an external thing superimposed upon it, and since the word thereby apprehends that other-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in its entirety, how is it that other words are not rendered redundant? To this he says, "And not," etc. The particle *ca* (and) functions as an emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). There is no such thing at all that is "severed"—that is, distinct from a portion of cognition—namely, a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) [from] another particular characteristic.

A universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which is distinct [from the particular] and characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti-lakṣaṇa*), is either implied or grasped by means of a word or a logical mark (*liṅga*). If, through the denotation of that [universal], there were a cognition of the thing-in-itself (*vastu*) by the force of the object itself, then because the thing is partless (*niraṃśatva*), there would be a complete comprehension of it in every respect; for properties (*dharma*) are distinct from it. Even if the adjuncts (*upādhi*) are distinct, they are not separate from the capacity that constitutes the factor for the assistance of various adjuncts.

Because it has been stated [in the verse beginning] with *ātmano graha* (1954) that there is no apprehension whatsoever [of external objects], one might ask: "Why is a thing implied by words? To this he says: *śabdānām* and so forth.
This is what is meant: since words determine an internal mental form (*buddhyākāra*) as being external, therefore...

In reality, there are no distinctions or non-distinctions among manifold properties; rather, [the cognition] follows the distortion of appearance. Thus, even though it is bound to that [object], its non-deviation from it is established because, when one who has acted based on that erroneous [cognition] reaches the end [of the process], there is a correspondence of knowledge with an object that is exactly as it was. Furthermore, cognitions and words that grasp distinct forms do not have a single entity as their object, for they possess manifold results.

Sound does not have a single substratum, because that would involve a contradiction. There is no fault, however, if one accepts the basis as the appearance within cognition (*buddhi-pratibhāsa*), as has been described. The meaning is that [words] act as if they were apprehending discrete objects. Furthermore, the "distortion" (*viplava*) of cognition is the grasping of the form of cognition as if it were an external object; this is because words have that [form] as their objective domain. Even when there is a distortion of cognition, there is a complete comprehension [of the object] due to the power of the real entity (*vastu-sāmarthya*) to be expressed.

If it is asked, "Why so? he says: "And therein," and so forth. Therein, in the confusion of the intellect (*buddhi-viplava*), there is an absence of the capacity for a real entity (*vastu-sāmarthya*) because [the object] is not a real entity.

Although the form of the intellect (*buddhy-ākāra*) is a real entity because it is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of cognition, nevertheless, when it is superimposed (*adhyasta*) by words or conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) as being non-different from the external [object], it is indeed a non-entity (*avastu*). Therefore, neither the word nor the conceptual construction has the specific characteristic as its object in accordance with reality.
[This is] because there is no apprehension of either that [external object] or of the form of cognition.

If all words have as their objects only the distortions of the intellect (*buddhiviplava*), how is it that words such as "produced" (*kṛtaka*) and "impermanent" (*anitya*) do not deviate with respect to a real entity (*vastu*) that is of such a nature? To this he says: "Of such a nature," and so forth. [It refers to] that which is distinct from each of those things, such as the unproduced (*akṛtaka*) and the permanent (*nitya*).

The meaning is "by way of the experience of the object. The connection is with the phrase "this conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*). Of what nature is it? [It is] "various and one," and so forth. "Various and one" (*nānaika*) means both various and one. That [is] also a property (*dharma*); thus, there is a *karmadhāraya* compound. Then, there is a three-membered *dvandva* compound with the words "difference" (*bheda*) and "non-difference" (*abheda*). These very differences and non-differences of various and unitary properties appear in the cognition; therefore, they alone are the "appearances" (*pratibhāsa*), and they alone are the "distortions" (*viplava*).
When such a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) exists as an indirect cause of production, there is non-deviation from it;

that is, non-deviation from the real entity (*vastu*). For just as sounds having forms such as "produced" (*kṛtaka*) are deceptive, so too do entities exist in reality in the form of being "produced" and so forth; thus, non-deviation should be understood in this sense.

He says this very thing with the words "from that too," and so forth. From that—namely, from the word which is the object of a cognitive distortion and which constitutes the linguistic convention characterized as inference for others—it is "vitatha," meaning erroneous. At the end of the engagement—that is, upon the completion of the engagement—one arrives at a real entity (*vastu*) that is of exactly that nature, such as being produced (*kṛtaka*), and not of a different nature, such as being unproduced (*akṛtaka*). By this, the nature of non-deviation [is established].

[The word] is "liberated" [from superimposition], because of the correspondence with cognition—that is, because of the arising of a cognition that grasps the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or because of the correspondence between the word and the cognition.

He states that "only in this case of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as the word-meaning is co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) established, but not in the case of a real entity (*vastu*)," by saying "but not different," and so forth.
