"Different forms" refers to universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and so on, which serve as the grounds for the application of words.
Because the cognitions and words that apprehend those [objects] have a single entity as their object; the connection is that "the word has a single substratum.

For if a cognition with distinct forms were to proceed having a single entity as its object, then the word, following that [cognition], would likewise be so. And in that case, there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—that the word, though having manifold results, has a single substratum—but that does not exist.

Because of contradiction. To explain: the two words "blue" and "lotus" must refer to either a single entity or multiple entities. In the first case, since a partless entity would be denoted in its entirety by a single word, there would be no application of a second word; or, if it were applied, the two words would be synonyms, and thus they would not have different results. In the second case, there is no single substratum. 4. Examination of Universals (Sāmānyacintā)
Indicating a break, it occurs by rejecting one [of the two]. ||133||
When one [thing] is pervaded by another and appears as identical with it, then there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), in accordance with the nature of cognition. ||134||
The contact with the property of a real entity is what effects the exclusion [of others] by means of a word,
because, like words such as "jar" or "cloth," it has multiple objects.
Now, if it is thought that (1) the word "blue" denotes a substance qualified by the quality blue, and the word "lotus" also [denotes a substance qualified by the quality lotus]—

He states that it is that very same substance qualified by the genus. Therefore, because there is a difference between the two qualifiers, the word has multiple fruits [meanings], yet because there is no difference in the qualified object, it has a single substratum.
That too is incorrect; for when a substance qualified by the quality of blue is denoted by the word "blue," its entire essence—

It is not denoted [by that word] because it is partless (*niraṃśatva*). Therefore, what other self-nature (*ātman*) of the substance, qualified by the universal "lotus," remains undenoted that could be denoted by the word "lotus"? In that case, there would be synonymy (*paryāyatā*). Alternatively, if the substance to be qualified were different due to the difference in its qualifiers, then there would be no single substratum (*ekādhāratā*). However, for the proponent of Apoha (*apohavādin*), this is not a fault; thus he says:
"Accordingly described," and so forth. That verbal object whose basis is the manifestation of cognition is described as such.

Demonstrating how there is no fault, he says: "Exclusion," and so forth. A single word, *nīla* (blue), while indicating one exclusion—the blue nature excluded from non-blue—also indicates another [exclusion], namely the lotus excluded from non-lotuses.

The meaning is that [the word] functions without rejecting its own nature (*svabhāva*), that is, it does not exclude it. (132) "That" refers to the nature as excluded from non-lotuses. Being pervaded, occupied, and implied by that word "blue," when the word "lotus" is employed, it appears to the intellect as a single unity. This is because there is a dual exclusion of a single substratum (*dharmin*).

Because that which possesses the two properties of a blue lotus appears in conceptual cognition, when this is the case, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by virtue of conforming to the intellect.

This is what is meant: (1) From the employment of the word "blue," the subject (*dharmin*) appearing in cognition appears as having the very form of blue; therein, by implication, that which is non-blue is excluded, but its nature—which is not excluded from being a lotus—is not [excluded]. Furthermore, from the employment of the word "lotus," although it is cognized as having the form of a lotus, that which is non-lotus is excluded, but its nature—which is already excluded from being non-blue—is not [further excluded].

[This is] the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). However, when two words are employed, a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) arises that manifests a single substratum (*ekādhāra*) endowed with the two properties (*dharma*) of "blue" and "lotus"; therefore, since the word has multiple results [but] a single substratum, there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in accordance with that cognition.

Therefore, as it is said by the venerable Dharmakīrti: "For one for whom the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), it must be explained how the exclusions of 'non-blue' and 'non-lotus' can be co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*). On the other hand, for one for whom the meaning of a word is a substance qualified by a genus and a quality—which is positively expressed (*vidhīyamāna*) by the words 'blue' and 'lotus'—and wherein the genus and the quality reside in that substance [co-reference is established]."
[Objection: It might be true that [the word] exists there [in the object], as it is said: "It is not [a word] denoting a single entity. (1.135)
"Because there is the ascertainment of the non-existence of the visible object that appears to the Buddha.
These are the summary verses.
Therefore, words have exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as their domain and the universal (*sāmānya*) as their range. (136)
Words and cognitions [are not real] because these are impossible with respect to a real entity (*vastu*).

For if the real entity itself were made the object of words and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) by way of a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*), then it would follow that all objects are here perceived in every possible aspect. Nor can one [perceive them] after having reflected upon universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth.
The author of the Nyāyaśāstra has specified that these two [terms] have "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) as their object,
and not the exclusion of non-blue and non-lotus; therefore, the claim that there is no meaning of grammatical coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇa) is refuted.

Because it is accepted that the meaning of the word being prescribed [is such]. Furthermore, when it is accepted that a word effects the exclusion of superimpositions by way of denoting its own object— or rather, when it effects exclusion, which consists in making the excluded nature its object— there is, even in a slight degree, a real property of the thing [involved].

There would be contact, characterized by attainment, with the intrinsic nature of a thing as excluded from dissimilar classes. (1) For what reason? Because it exists; for that [nature], being determined, is an excluded intrinsic nature. In that regard, since it is a "thing" (*vastu*), when words denoting a single thing are accepted, there is contact with the property of the thing, which is precisely the universal (*sāmānya*).
Because of the non-existence of a real entity (*vastu*).
If one asks how so, [the text says] "in the cognition," and so forth. This means that because there is no perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility, it is non-existent.
Since such a fault exists in the word-meaning with respect to a real entity, for that reason, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object.

Words and cognitions have been stated by the teacher Diṅnāga to have as their objects the appearances within cognition. What kind of cognitions? The meaning is that they are conceptual (*vikalpikā*) and have universals (*sāmānya*) as their domain. This qualification applies to the cognitions alone and not to the words, because the latter do not deviate from having universals as their object. For what reason? Because these words and conceptualizations [do not apply] to the real entity (*vastu*).
And because of its possibility.

He explains this with the words "If indeed," and so forth. If only the thing-in-itself (*vastu*) were made an object, it would be grasped, but it would not be determined as having a positive form (*vidhirūpa*). This very point—just mentioned—is that all objects [are perceived] in every aspect due to the causal capacity of the thing itself.

The consequence [would be] the cognition [of all things]. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the absence of the qualifier-qualified relationship, the non-operation of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and so forth.
The author is the Master Dignāga. "These two" refers to the cognition and the word. That by which another is excluded is called the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*);
they have that as their object. Thus, if a single entity were made the object by cognitions having different forms—

In that case, it would also be denoted by the word "that. Then, because two words with distinct referents would be applied to a single substance, there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);
however, this is not possible. For instance, the universal denoted by the word "that" is [distinct] from the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
4. Examination of the Universal (*Sāmānyacintā*)
If this is so, since the nature of the object is one, from where could there arise a cognition of diverse forms? (137)
Furthermore, positive and negative concomitance cannot both have a single entity as their object.
If that one thing is partless, how can it be made an object by means of diverse forms of cognition? [Otherwise] there would be a difference in form.

Precisely because it depends upon difference; for that [difference] also arises from the differentiation of the universal (*sāmānya*), since even its own nature shares the same fate as that [universal].
This [dependence] does not exist through the mutual exclusion of their respective objects, because it is impossible for two [cognitions] directed toward the same object to function in such a way.
Furthermore, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth; nor could there be [such properties] within a single ontological essence.
Activity and non-activity are contradictory; nor could activity directed elsewhere constitute a universal.

For it would have to be either different or not different [from the object]. Regarding the first position: since the nature of the entity is one, from what source could there arise a cognition that is diverse in form, appearing as both universal and particular? (136)

And since the universal is not distinct from its own particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the particular consisting of a *śāvaleyā* cow would, because it is excluded from the particular consisting of a *bāhuleyā* cow, entail that the universal "cowness" (*gotva*)—which consists of the *śāvaleyā*—would follow after [be present in] the *bāhuleyā*. Thus, for a single entity, both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) would result in having the same locus. And that is untenable; thus he says: "positive and negative concomitance..."

"Vityādi" (and so forth). Those two positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) whose single object (*gocara*) or domain (*viṣaya*) is such are described as "those [two] whose [object] is thus.

He explains this with the words "that one," and so on. Precisely because of its unity, it is partless, since a single thing lacks parts. It is "formed" (*ākriyate*), thus it is a "form" (*ākāra*), which is the appearance in the intellect. Its "differentiation" (*bheda*) is due to the differentiation based upon it; that is, the multiplicity of the real entity (*vastu*).
If it were apprehended by cognitions of different forms, it would be [itself] distinct. But this is not the case, because such [distinctness] does not exist for that entity (*vastu*).

If it is argued that—since an entity consists of both the universal and the particular—it may be apprehended by cognitions of different forms even though it is a single entity, [the author] replies: "Even with that nature," and so forth. This is because [the entity] shares the same fate (*ekayogakṣema*) as the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), being of the very nature of that particular. [Thus, it is] with the particular...

Because they share the same security (*yogakṣema*), they are likewise non-different. "That" refers to the connection that this [phenomenon], such as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth, would not occur. What is the reason? Because their respective grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) are distinct, which means they exclude one another's referents. This applies to two words that have the same object and reside in the same substance.
Because of the impossibility of subsistence (*vṛtti*).

He explains the portion of the verse beginning with "anvaya" by means of the passage beginning with "na ca. If the very nature of the entity (*vastvātmā*)—the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*)—were one and the same, then, because the particular of a *śāvaleyā* cow would consist of the universal of "cowness" (*gotva*), [the universal] would reside in that very [particular]. In that case, [the following would occur]:...

Furthermore, since its nature consists of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), non-occurrence in that very [locus] at that time is applied; yet that is incorrect, because it involves contradiction and because it is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since the universal (*sāmānya*) is not distinct from the specific characteristic, it does not occur elsewhere at all. If it is argued that, therefore, there can be neither occurrence nor non-occurrence for a single [entity] in a single [locus], he replies with the words "And not," etc., regarding the universal.
And so forth. Therefore, the intention is that there can be neither occurrence nor non-occurrence for a single entity.

The Teacher [Dignāga] says "no," because according to the systems of the Sāṃkhyas and others, there is no difference between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*). Regarding the phrase "that," etc.:
if it is argued that the occurrence of the universal is not the particular, [we say] no, because there is no difference. For that universal is of a single nature.

Or there might be a distinction; for this differentiation is not logical if there is no difference in form, nor—if such a difference exists—would there be non-distinction, as has already been stated. Thus, this [universal] is without division and, though without parts (*niranvaya*), it is not with parts (*sānvaya*).
Even regarding one who asserts that the universal is indeed distinct, in that case too—
Furthermore, linguistic practices regarding non-difference would be without basis if there were [only] difference.
If words, according to their respective [conventions], denoted distinct objects, how could they be the substrata for a single conceptual cognition of one object?
Moreover, since those denoting different objects would be independent, in the absence of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), how could there be the relation of qualifier and qualified?
What is this "being" (bhāva)?
It is the very justification for this [entity]. For that entity, being of a single form and a single nature, must be either a universal (sāmānya) or a particular (viśeṣa).

Because the particular is not distinct from the universal, it would be the universal alone; or else, because the universal is not distinct from the particular, it would be the particular alone. But one thing cannot possess two forms, for this distinction between "universal" and "particular" does not exist when there is no difference in form. Or, if such a distinction were to exist, there could be no non-distinction between the universal and the particular.
It was stated previously that "it might be so. Therefore, this [entity] is the essence of the thing (*vastvātmā*). "Indivisible" (*avibhāga*) means partless (*anaṃśa*).

If it were a universal (*sāmānya*) alone, then it would follow along—that is, it would go toward another individual (*vyakti*). Or, if it were of the nature of a particular (*viśeṣa*) alone, then it would not follow along. The point is that for a single entity, two contradictory properties cannot coexist. He states this very point: (1)
"Nor again," and so forth.

"The one who says" refers to the Vaiśeṣika and others. They assert that the universal (*sāmānya*), which is denoted by words, is indeed distinct from the substance (*dravya*). If a difference between the individual (*vyakti*) and the universals is admitted, then linguistic usages of non-difference—such as the usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the like—would be impossible.
They would be without a basis. "Yathāsvam" (according to each) is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in a distributive sense (*vīpsā*).

For instance, words such as "blue lotus" express their respective universals (*sāmānya*), which are mutually distinct from those of the blue lotus and so forth. Even when the word "blue" is intended to denote the quality of blueness, there is still the expression of distinct objects. That which has a single property-bearer (*dharmin*) as its object or domain—

The term *buddheḥ* [is explained as follows]: it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both one and cognition" (*ekā cāsau buddhiśca*), with the masculine form applied (*pumvadbhāva*). The sense is that how could these be the substrata or causes of this [cognition]? Consequently, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
This would be the case if words such as "blue lotus" were to produce a cognition whose object is a single entity endowed with two qualifiers. In that case—
There would have to be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through the presentation of a single object, but that does not exist. The universal is a different entity from the individual;

those words denoting it do not imply (*anākṣepaka*) the particulars contained within it. Implication (*ākṣepa*) consists in their functioning without abandoning those [particulars], but it is not so in this case.
Why? Because there is no expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*). When the word "tree" denotes only treeness (*vṛkṣatva*), then for that [word]...

Since it [the word "tree"] is devoid of qualification, it is complete in itself by that much alone; how then could it imply *dhava* trees and the like? And since they are not implied, how can *dhava* and the others be the particulars (*bheda*) of the referent of the word "tree"? Furthermore, because they are not its particulars, how can there be the relationship of qualifier and qualified in the expression "the tree is a *śiṃśapā*"? Thus he says: "How... and so forth. [This is] because there is no denotation of a substance qualified by a universal. 4. Examination of the Universal (*sāmānyacintā*).
Since [the entity] is excluded from existence everywhere, these faults do not follow. ||138||
For just as one [individual] is distinct from that [universal], so too is another; thus, the fault of the universal being non-existent due to differentiation does not apply.
The absence of any remaining [category] has already been stated previously. Moreover:
When there are distinct entities that perform a single function, and one is inquiring about that function, [the answer is given]. (139)
Because of respect, incapacity, and futility regarding the expression of difference, the elders have established a common linguistic usage based on the exclusion of what does not produce that effect.
If it is argued that the aforementioned fault remains, we say no; for the answer has already been given: even when a substance qualified by its qualifiers is denoted...

Because the entire meaning is understood from a single word through the inherent power of the thing itself, another word would not apply to that same object; and if it were to apply, there would be no synonyms. Thus, for those who maintain that the referent of a word is a real entity (*vastu*), the possibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth is in no way possible.
It has already been stated that even a universal (*sāmānya*) is not possible for them. For instance, when [the universal] is not distinct from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)...

In that case, the universal would be empty; like a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it would not follow after other individuals and thus would not be a universal (1). Even if there were a distinction [from the individual], how could it be the universal of another? Because of the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and so forth, as was stated previously. However, for the proponent of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), this is not a fault; thus he says "in all cases," etc. These are the faults regarding the universal—

...due to the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth. As it is said, "Just as one... and so on: a single cow-particular, such as a *śāvaleya*, is distinct from that non-cow nature; likewise, another [cow], such as a *bāhuleya* and so forth, is also [distinct]. Therefore, since the nature excluded from heterogeneous things is identical everywhere, the conceptual cognition [grasps] the particular—namely, the nature distinguished from the heterogeneous—as its own form in all cases.

There is no fault of non-universality (*asāmānya*) for that which is superimposed (*adhyasta*) through differentiation. As for the "absence of the remainder," the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth has already been stated [in the verse]: "Indicating a distinction, it functions without rejecting the one" (1.133), and so on. Thus, first of all, there is a single nature excluded from those of a different class, which is everywhere superimposed by the intellect as non-different from its own form.

Now, having established that which is denoted by words, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth, to show that even in the absence of an identical form, a single word is applied to entities that perform a single function. "In the inquiry regarding their effect" (*tatkāryaparicodane*) means for the purpose of inquiring about the state of having a single effect, or for the purpose of inquiring about those things that have a single effect. Among the various distinct entities that have a single effect—even though they lack a single [identical] nature—there is a commonality; that is, a single [conceptual] identity.

The *śruti* (word) is "established" (*kṛtā*), meaning it is conventionally agreed upon (*saṃketitā*) by elders who are experts in linguistic usage. The meaning is that a single word is bound to things that have a single effect based on that exclusion (*vṛtti*) which consists in their differentiation from those things that do not have that effect; that is, a single word is fixed upon things of a single class by way of their exclusion from what is of a different class.
Now, if there is no application of words to a universal (*sāmānya*), then perhaps the application of words would be to the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), since nothing else exists.
[Objection: Nor is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) denotable by words.

[Response: This is not so; for the communicator, intending to establish a convention based on a single effect, takes as his object entities existing in the three times and establishes the convention upon those very things for the purpose of communication at the time of linguistic usage.
Since all entities are established in their own respective intrinsic natures,
that which is the form of a brindled cow does not exist in a black cow. (141)
The exclusion of what does not produce that effect exists for both [the universal and the particular];
moreover, without non-difference in the object, non-difference in the word is not tenable. (142)

Therefore, being its effect is also desired as the distinction from that which is not its effect, just as in the case of the eye and so forth, where there is a certain [cause] that has the singular result of visual cognition. (143)
When it is possible to enjoin its effect without distinction, someone [employs] a conventional expression for the sake of the simultaneous cognition of everything. (144)

Therefore, although entities as they revolve within the intellect are of a universal nature, nevertheless, a single word is applied to many of them when they appear as if external; it is not the case that, while a universal of distinct form exists in all those individuals, a separate auditory expression (*śruti*) is not designated for each individual. Why? He says: "Because of prolixity," and so forth. Because of prolixity (*gaurava*).

(Universal) 1. Because of incapacity and because of futility, there is no common linguistic application (*samā śrutiḥ*) for a universal (*sāmānyam*) that is distinct from its particulars, or rather, for the expression of distinction—that is, for the statement of difference. We shall clarify this in the commentary (*vṛtti*). A common linguistic application is not established for a universal that exists as a real entity (*vastubhūte*). What is the reason? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), that is, the essential form (*svarūpa*), of all entities is fixed and non-confused.

By the statement "the form which belongs to the brindled [cow]," etc., he asserts that [the universal] has a fixed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, the universal is not non-different [from the individual]. Even if it were different, being established in its own intrinsic nature, how could it be the common form of the individuals?

For it has been stated that things are not made common by something else. [Furthermore,] they are the causes of the cognition of forms such as the dewlap, according to the theory of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*).

Exclusion from those [others] is the excluded intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "Of the two" refers to Śābaleya and Bāhuleya. Therefore, it is not contradictory that there is non-difference even among things distinguished by their exclusion from what does not produce that effect. That very non-difference of objects must be accepted as the cause of the non-difference of words, because the non-difference of words is not tenable without the non-difference of objects. How then can there be a single word for many things if there is indeed no non-difference of objects?

To [the objection] that this follows from the process of worldly activity (*pravṛtti*), he says: "Therefore," and so forth. Even that single Vedic word which is desired as having a single effect among many—stated for the purpose of defining it—is to be seen as distinct precisely because of its non-common effect (*atatkārya*). The nature of many [words] is to be seen as distinct precisely because of their non-common effects.

However, there is no such universal (sāmānya) as "being an effect of that. And demonstrating that the application of a single term to distinct things is not contradictory even in the absence of a universal, he says: "In the case of the eye and so forth," etc. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a single result, namely visual consciousness, is the eye and so forth. "At some time" means at that time when they are capable of producing consciousness.
They are intended to be urged. Alternatively, the connection is that one might at some time employ a conventional expression (*sāṃketikī śruti*).

To the question "For what purpose would one employ it?", he says: "Without distinction," that is, generally. This is so when it is possible to manifest to others the collection of causes (*kāraṇakalāpa*) which has as its single common effect visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). However, when [the specific nature] of the eye and so forth is not common—
Even without that form [of the particular], one could produce [the cognition] from a universal that is distinct [from it].

Just as there is a single application of a word across many distinct things because a single operation upon them does not produce a cognition elsewhere, and because if a cognition were produced without such proximity, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); and because when a single word is applied to those [distinct things], there is no objective reality [of a single entity], since there is no assignment to a single object; for if distinct natures were assigned separately, it would be just as [it was] when commanded.

"Because of the lack of knowledge regarding the distinction between those [causes]"—for him as well, the word should be applied by the world as being "only one. And "being an effect" is what is enjoined; the meaning is that, in that case, a single auditory perception (*śruti*) is not conventionally designated for them. This is for the sake of perceiving the entire collection of causes simultaneously (*sakṛt*), at one time. Regarding the phrase "even without," etc.: of those [causes], such as the eye and so forth, of that common form (*sāmānya*)... one—

The meaning is: even in the absence of a distinct universal characterized as "being an effect" (kāryatva). If it is argued that "existence" (sattā) itself is their universal, we say no; for since that [existence] is undifferentiated, it would follow that visual cognition would occur at all times and in all places. "Without a non-distinct object" means without a real entity that serves as a universal. [This refers to] among many individuals such as the brindled cow (śābaleya) and so forth. "Of them" refers to the brindled cow and the others.

Regarding the particulars: if there were a universal belonging to them, then, because the word would be applied to that universal, it would be applied to every particular. However, without a single universal, the application of a single word to many things is not logical. Consequently, when that word is being conventionally designated, it would be designated for only one particular. And thus, the application of a word occurring in one instance would be restricted to that single particular.

Because it does not produce a cognition of a different and distinct kind in other [individuals], a second cow-individual would not be cognized as "cow" from that word, since there would be an absence of a universal (*sāmānya*) based on proximity (*pratyāsatti*). If it is argued that—even in the absence of a conformity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānugama*)—that which is applied to a *śābaleya* (spotted cow) will produce a cognition in a *bāhuleya* (black cow) despite the lack of proximity, he says: "No..."

"And in the case of those that are proximate," and so forth. This is because it would lead to an over-extension (*pratiprasaṅga*); from the word "cow" (*go*), there would be a cognition even of a horse.
Thus far, it has been stated that without a single universal (*sāmānya*), there can be no application of a single word to many things.
Now, having granted [the opponent's position], he states its futility with the words "And in them," etc. For indeed, a single auditory expression (*śruti*) is applied to many things—

[The opponent might argue that] a single word has multiple functions: either to convey a single object, or to convey those very same distinct [objects] without confusion. Regarding these, he states the absence of the first [function]: "Because there is no restriction of a word to a single object. If a word were restricted to a single object, then the conveying of a single object would be possible. He states the absence of the second [function] with the words beginning "distinct," etc.: "[of things] having distinct natures" means [things] that are unmixed.

The phrase "the cognitions of the brindled cow and so forth" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Separately" means in each individual particular. "Upon the application of a single word"—at what point?

Subsequently, at the time of linguistic usage. "Of those as they were enjoined" means for the sake of a non-confused cognition of those things enjoined; because there would be no discernment of their distinction, the application of the word to them would therefore not be fruitful.

For in this way, the application of distinct words to individual specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) becomes fruitful, provided that those specific characteristics are understood without confusion from that word. Since, however, the application of a single word to many [individuals] is actually practiced, the intention is that there must exist a real entity (*vastubhūta*) in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*). 3.

The Master [Dharmakīrti] says "of that too" (*tasyāpi*) and so forth. One alternative is that a word should be applied by the world even without a purpose, simply on the grounds that there exists a single entity as a universal (*sāmānya*). He states the second [alternative] with the words "that" (*tat*) and so forth. "That" refers to the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* (1944).
If it is argued that the object itself, by its own power, brings forth a single word, this is not so.

Rather, one should employ a particular word for a particular purpose. In that case, if multiple things are required for a single purpose, it is proper to designate them there by means of only a single word; for to designate each of them separately would be cumbersome.

It might be so; yet it is not possible to point out a form for this [word] that is not shared by others. In this regard, there is neither complexity nor futility; rather, by this [word], those objects must be indicated therein. If it is argued that the speaker has the freedom here as to whether those [objects] are indicated by a single word or by many, then this single utterance would have to denote many things.

Functioning by virtue of the speaker’s intention (*abhiprāya*), it does not deserve censure. Nor is its operation impossible, because it is dependent upon desire. As for the universal (*sāmānya*), however, it is [manifested] by its own inherent power alone, without depending on human activity; it causes a single phoneme (*śruti*) to resound and arise.

Neither of those two [the object and the means] exists at all, because there is an absence of application (prayoga) without a purpose and human activity. He says "What then is that? and so forth, beginning with "by some purpose. [He explains: "In linguistic usage (vyavahāra), having understood the meaning of these words as the means for achieving that or not-achieving that, one should comprehend it. By this, he states the non-existence of the first alternative.

By the phrase "they are designated," [the reference is] to the second [case]. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "they are designated" (nirdeśyante), meaning they are conventionally established (saṃketyante) for those desiring to engage in worldly discourse (vyavahartukāmaiḥ). In this regard, according to this principle, multiple causes would be employed—that is, they would function—toward a single effect. That [effect] arises from that very collection of multiple causes. In this context, by those desiring to engage in discourse regarding that effect, [the causes] must necessarily...

Furthermore, that which has multiple causes and is characterized by the exclusion of what is not its effect is appropriately denoted by a single word alone, based upon its unity of effect. He states the fault in denoting it by multiple words in the passage beginning with "tasya" (of that), etc. "Pṛthak pṛthak" means by distinct words.
And this has been stated while accepting the application of words to specific individualities (*svalakṣaṇa*).

He states that this very thing is not possible, beginning with "na ca" (and not), etc. "Of this entity" refers to the object. "A form not shared by others" means that which is not shared by others is "not shared by others" (*ananyasādhāraṇa*), i.e., the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Nor [is it possible] for this—namely, for the application of multiple words.
And this is the sequential explanation of [the phrase] "due to prolixity, incapacity, and futility. If one asks, "Why is there futility?

he says: "Only," and so forth. By this [agent], in that particular task, the purpose is merely this much: those things which serve as causes are to be enjoined. However, those things which serve as causes might be enjoined by a single word.

The phrase "or by many" indicates the speaker’s autonomy regarding this expression. Since it is so, this single utterance (*śruti*), proceeding on the basis of the speaker’s intention toward multiple objects denoted, does not deserve to be censured. If it is argued that "a single utterance cannot be applied to many [objects]," he says: "And this," and so forth. This is the single utterance. It is impossible...

The analysis of the compound is "of that which consists of setting [the word] in motion" (*pravarttanamaya*). Why is it not impossible to set [it] in motion? He says: because it is dependent on desire (*icchā*); for that which is dependent on desire cannot be set in motion [by something else]. For if even by one [person], and so forth—it is thus: in that case, regarding the universal (*sāmānya*) imagined by others, the application of a single term does not occur through the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*), but rather through desire alone. 4. Examination of the Universal (*Sāmānyacintā*)

For if the speaker’s intention were not present even in a single instance, how could there be any activity? Or, if such an intention existed, it would be possible [to apply the term] even to many things, since there is no contradiction in the intention. If it is argued that there is no application here because of a lack of purpose, we reply: the purpose has already been stated previously—that it is the cognition of a single entity as distinct from its various purposes.
Furthermore, it is not so because of the unity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Since things established according to their own respective natures do not possess a mutual fusion of forms, how could there be a word based on a single intrinsic nature for things that are distinct? This has been stated previously.
The exclusion from those things that do not have that purpose is not contradictory even for distinct entities; thus, let the non-difference of purpose be the cause of the non-difference of the word.
Therefore, these [words] have that as their purpose, and if so, they are indeed stated to be distinct from those things that do not have that purpose.

Furthermore, there is no other basis for these [words] having that specific function than their distinction from others, just as in the case of the eye, visible form, and the speaker’s intention. If the speaker’s intention were not present, how could this single word be employed even in a single instance?
The intended meaning is: it certainly could not. Thus, even in a single instance, the desire to employ it is the cause, not the actual object.

He says that even in the case of many [objects], there is no contradiction [to the application of a single word] because of its capacity (*śakti*). "Or in the case of desire," and so forth. This means that when a single desire to employ [a word] is postulated as the cause even for one [object], [the same applies to many]. "This single [word]," etc.; "due to the absence of purpose," and so forth. For the application of a single word to many [objects] is not fruitful without a single underlying entity. As was stated previously.

He asks, "What was said? and replies with the words beginning "In the case of distinct [individuals]," etc. This means that although there are distinct individuals such as the *śābaleya* (the brindled cow) and others, there is a cognition from the single word "cow" (*go*) as being distinct from those things which do not serve that purpose—that is, distinct from horses and the like for whom the function or purpose to be accomplished by those cow-individuals, such as carrying or milking, does not exist. Why, then, is a real ontological unity (*ekatva*) not asserted? To this he says:

He said: "Furthermore, it is not because of the oneness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor because of the oneness of a real entity (*vastubhūta*) as a universal (*sāmānya*), that there is a single linguistic expression for diverse things. For that very [universal] is untenable as being either distinct from or non-distinct [from its instances]. Let it be granted that the universal is distinct; even so, it remains unmixed while established within that intrinsic nature."

He says that very thing: "according to their own [nature]," and so forth. Since things are established with natures determined by their respective characteristics, and because there is no mutual commingling of forms, how could a single word—based on a commonality and having a single cause—apply to distinct things? The intention is: it certainly could not. For one thing does not become identical to another through something else. This has already been stated: "All entities, by their own nature..."

Regarding the passage "because of the establishment of their own respective natures" (194.2), [the author] states that for the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), this is not a fault: "But the exclusion from those things which do not have that purpose," and so forth. Since the exclusion from those things which do not have that purpose is not contradictory even among distinct entities, that very [exclusion] constitutes the difference from those things which do have that purpose.

The difference in names arises because that [exclusion] exists everywhere; let it be the cause for the non-difference of words. Furthermore, since a real entity (*vastubhūta*) called a universal (*sāmānya*) cannot in any way be established, it has been stated that these individual cows are distinct from horses and the like which do not serve that purpose—that is, they possess the specific purposes of carrying loads and milking. Thus, they are described as being precisely different from those things that do not fulfill such purposes. (140)

Furthermore, their status as effects of that [cause] is nothing other than their distinction from others; for it is precisely the nature [of things] as excluded from others that constitutes the causal operation of the mind, or rather,
the contact between the self, the sense-faculties, and the mind.

When there is the possibility of a common designation for the causes of the single effect that is the cognition of color— namely, the contact of the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object— one might, for the sake of linguistic brevity despite the resulting complexity, establish some conventional term as the cause of the cognition of color, such as "sara" or "śara," and thus employ such a verbal expression.

Perhaps there might be a simultaneous realization of all those causes; yet, in this case, there is no single recurring form whatsoever. Exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is indeed distinct from those things that do not possess that [excluded] object.
Even though words such as "collection," "continuum," and "particular state" are all applied to them, they have some effect for those [things] despite having such forms.

In that case, since there is no distinction [between them], the injunction of a specific [result] would be futile; therefore, for the sake of enjoining all [the causes] at once, there is no difference between them—this is the meaning. By this, the portion of the verse beginning with "tatkāryatāpi" (it also has that as its effect) is explained.

With the words "yathā" (just as) and so forth, he explains [the passage] beginning with "just as in the case of the eye and so on, [it has] the single result of visual consciousness. [The text continues: "ātma-indriya... [self, sense-faculty...]

The term *tatkāryāṇi* refers to those things for which the cognition of that form (*tadrūpavijñāna*) is the effect; their *sāmānya* is the capacity to produce that single effect without distinction. It is the *codanā*, or manifestation, of this [capacity]. When its possibility exists—[the opponent asks] by what occasion is there the possibility of such a *codanā*? He replies: "From what [does the cognition of form arise]? This means that the possibility of the *codanā* occurs when there is a question posed without distinction regarding the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

The connection [of the passage] is as follows: for the sake of brevity in conventional usage (*vyavahāra-lāghava*), and for the purpose of conveying many things by means of a single word, one should apply a scriptural designation (*śruti-niveśayet*) such as "lake" (*saraḥ*) or "arrow" (*śaraḥ*) to the collection of factors beginning with the eye, which is the cause of the cognition of form (*rūpa-vijñāna*).
With the words "api nāma" and so forth, he explains precisely this brevity of conventional usage. [This refers to] the causes of that [cognition], namely the visual consciousness...

Regarding causes: and it is not the case here—in the eye and so forth—that there exists a commonality (*sāmānya*) such as "existence" (*sattā*) which, by its pervasive form, produces a single visual consciousness. If you argue that such a commonality does exist for the eye and the other [faculties], then because that existence is without distinction everywhere, visual consciousness and the others would arise everywhere. Furthermore, existence does not become differentiated merely through the difference of its correlates.

Because it is eternal, it cannot have any excellence added to it. However, the entities such as the eye and so forth exist solely for the sake of that [consciousness], having the single effect of visual cognition.
Since they are distinct from those things that do not produce visual cognition, their "difference" consists precisely in their exclusion from what does not have that effect.
The non-difference of these [entities] such as the eye is due to the fact that all of them equally possess this exclusion from what does not have that effect. Just as...

There is no difference between the eye and the other [senses], because for all of them, the exclusion from non-causes (atatkāryavyāvṛtti) is equal. Just as a single term is applied to the eye, visible form, and so forth—even in the absence of a single universal—to indicate that they share a single effect; likewise, all things of this kind [are designated by a single term]. Words that denote a collection (samūha), a continuum (saṃtāna), or a particular state (avasthāviśeṣa) are [the basis for] the terms "collection" and "continuum."
These are words denoting specific states. Regarding that, he speaks with reference to a word that denotes a collection, beginning with "those which are combined," and so forth.
Those [qualities] such as color, taste, smell, and so on, which are combined, perform some single effect, such as the fetching of water and the like.

Among those [qualities], such as color and the rest, there is no distinction in their causality toward that effect. For, having established that all of them have a single effect, [they are treated as one].
Therefore, the absence of distinction is stated on account of their having a single effect, but not because there is no distinction in their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
When it is merely necessary to demonstrate the capacity of those [things] to produce a single effect, any mention of a distinction is useless. (Chapter 4: Examination of the Universal) 271.4.
*Sāmānyacintā* (Examination of the Universal)

People employ the single word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) for those [entities]. Although they are no different from others in terms of their distinction from what is similar and what is dissimilar, they are distinguished from others because they serve as the basis for that [specific] purpose; thus, due to that distinction, they are perceived without differentiation. In that regard, even when one says "the color and other qualities of the jar," the color and other qualities are the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the jar. (Example 460b)

"Capable of specific effects and so forth" means: those which are well-known by their own nature as accomplishing general effects—such as the word "form" (*rūpa*) and others—and which are distinguished as being the means for accomplishing specific effects, are thus described.
However, there is no other substance here whatsoever possessing the characteristics as previously described; for such a thing...

Considering that an injunction by means of a word distinct from [the individual] forms and so forth would be fruitless, this world—that is, the linguistic user—employs a single word, "jar," for the purpose of enjoining all [objects] simultaneously at one time toward a certain task; [he does so] with respect to specific forms and so forth that are identical in their function, such as the holding of water. (143)

If it is asked, "But how is it that form and the other [sensory objects], which are indeed distinct, are perceived as non-different from the single word 'jar'? he replies with the words "They too," and so forth. Although there is no difference in their being distinct from similar things like [other instances of] form and from dissimilar things like taste and so on, they are [singled out] because they serve as the cause for that; that is, because they serve as the cause for the specific effect of fetching water and the like. From "those others" means from those things that do not perform that function.

Since they are distinguished from capable things such as cloth and the like, their very difference is their non-difference; therefore, due to that non-difference, all [qualities] such as color and so forth are understood without distinction—that is, by the universal alone—from the single word "jar. If the jar is merely the colors and so forth themselves, and not a substance distinct from them, then how [is it possible for there to be] "of the jar"? (100b)
If it is argued that there is a distinction [between the pot and its qualities] because of the expression "the color and so forth of the pot," he says: "In that case," and so on.

Even regarding the distinction expressed as "the color and so forth of the pot," the meaning is this: the color and so forth have the pot as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and not the cloth or other things.
He explains this very point with the words beginning "of the fetching of water" (*udaka*). The specific quality of fetching water belongs to the pot and not to anything else.

[The word] *dhyātvaṃ* [is used]. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), other effects to be accomplished, such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), are also included. The compound is formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga*: "the locative case is used for that which is capable with respect to that effect" (*tasmin kārye samarthāḥ saptamī*). This is the meaning here: (1) words such as "color-form" (*rūpa*) denote color-forms and so forth without distinction, as being endowed with the capacity for any effect whatsoever to be accomplished by them; however, the word "jar" [denotes] a specific effect—

By means of the application of *śakti*, he speaks of forms (*rūpa*) and so forth as being distinguished by their difference even from those forms that constitute the nature of cloth and other such things. Therefore, through the operation of two words—namely, "of the jar" and "forms"—there arises a cognition in the form of a universal and its particular;
thus, the relationship of universal and particular and the notion of distinction (*vyatireka*) are employed. He expresses this very point with the words beginning with "the universal," etc.
The accomplishment of the general effect—which consists merely of color and so forth—is established by means of that which is well-known as its own nature (*svabhāva*).

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of a characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*), or alternatively, in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). By means of such a form or cause, the words "color" and so forth—being well-established as instruments—[accomplish] a specific effect; namely, that which is to be accomplished by a jar, and specifically the fetching of water to be accomplished by a jar.

[The term] *nādi* [is used]. Its proof (*sādhana*) is established by the fact that "it is proven by this" (*sādhyate 'nena*). That which has such a designation (*ākhyā*) or name (*saṃjñā*) is "thus-named";
they are distinguished by that. These—namely, form (*rūpa*) and so forth—are spoken of in this way.

However, it is not the case here that the conventional usage "this is a jar" refers to the collection (*saṃhati*) of form and so forth, nor does it possess the characteristics as previously described.

Because [multiple things] are not perceived [as a single entity]. The use of the singular number, however, is for the purpose of indicating a single capacity, or it is dependent upon convention (*saṃketa*).

Likewise, those specific causes and effects which accomplish or are accomplished as something "one" are also spoken of—as in the previous case—by means of words such as *vrīhi* (rice) when a convention has been established for the sake of simultaneous cognition.

Even those [qualities] which, whether individually or collectively, are employed at once for the purpose of conveying [the object], [do not prove] a substance distinct from form and so forth—[that is,] such a whole (avayavin) as one distinct from form and so forth. For the whole is held by others to meet the conditions for perception, according to the statement: "Substance is that which is perceptible by sight and touch. Therefore, by that...
The meaning of the sentence is that [the whole] is not perceived apart from form (*rūpa*) and so forth, despite being accepted as having attained the characteristics of perceptibility.
Furthermore, it will be demonstrated in the second chapter that atoms alone are the objects of direct perception, even without a whole (*avayavin*).
If it is argued that if the pot is merely the collection of form and so forth, then how is there the singular number in the expression "one pot" when there are many [constituents]? To this he says:
"The singular number," and so on. Just as among many things a single word serves to indicate a single capacity, so too does the singular number;

it is for the purpose of indicating that capacity which those [constituents], such as form and so forth, possess toward a single effect, namely the fetching of water. This is by virtue of their being performers of a single function.

The meaning is that, having superimposed unity upon those [many things], the singular number is used; however, there is no single potency (*śakti*) existing within them. Furthermore, the singular number is either independent of an external referent or dependent upon convention (*saṃketa*). This has been established by the passage beginning with, "For those for whom words follow the nature of things" (1.66). With reference to words that denote a continuum (*santāna*), he says: "In the same way," and so forth. [He refers to] the cause (*hetu*) and the effect (*phala*).

Regarding cause and fruit (*hetuphala*): the distinction between these two consists in their being related as material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) and in their not having a single substratum within one continuum. The verb *bhū* (to become) is transitive when it signifies "attainment" (*prāpti*). [The compound] is a *dvitīyā-tatpuruṣa* based on the rule *sādhanaṃ kṛtā* (Pāṇini 2.1.33). Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi*: "those for whom the distinction between cause and fruit has become (*bhūta*), i.e., been accomplished (*niṣpanna*). This is because the group beginning with *āhitāgni* is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*).

The word *bhūta* is placed at the end of the compound. [This refers to those things] which accomplish some single [effect], such as the sprout, the stalk, the leaf, and so forth, which together accomplish a single fruit. And they are accomplished by a single [cause], namely, by that very seed which serves as their material cause (*upādāna*). Furthermore, those sprouts and so forth do not consist of a single moment; this is for the sake of understanding them as being perceived simultaneously. Thus, by virtue of this similarity—either through having a single effect or through having a single cause—the term "rice" (*vrīhi*) and so forth is applied.

At the time of establishing a convention, those [terms] which denote a continuum are assigned as conventions; subsequently, at the time of linguistic usage, they are employed for the sake of brevity in communication. This is because, when there is a desire to know the continuity as a single undifferentiated whole, the employment of multiple words—such as "seed," "sprout," and so forth—is fruitless. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), terms such as "human" and so on are also included. By these [terms] as well, [the continuum] is denoted as distinct from the various stages such as "infant," "child," and so on.
Because it denotes a continuum (*prabandha*).

[Objection: But aren't words such as "rice" (*vrīhi*) also merely collective terms (*samudāyaśabda*), since they denote a collection of form and so forth? [Response: True. However, it is stated thus because it denotes a specific cause-and-effect relationship—that is, a continuum of results—and likewise [denotes] a collection.

A word becomes a generic term (*jātiśabda*) in relation to a plurality of aggregates; likewise, a term for a state (*avasthāśabda*) is also such. There is no fault here, as a certain word is called a "term" simply because one intends to express a specific meaning. Just as the form and other qualities of a jar are referred to by the singular "jar" according to a specific basis [of usage], so too should it be understood that the form and other qualities of rice are not referred to by the singular "rice. Therefore...

Thus he says: "It should be stated as before. With reference to the term "states" (*avasthā*), he says: "Even those," and so forth. Even those words that denote particular states, such as "visible" (*sanidarśana*) or "resistant" (*sapratigha*), are indicated by way of a commonality of difference from others. Just as things that have a single effect [are grouped together] when there is an injunction regarding that effect.

When there is an injunction regarding its effect, words for which conventions have been established through the distinction of that [effect] from others, such as a jar, likewise—though manifold with respect to their causes—are expressed by a single term solely for the sake of conventional usage. For example, "the offspring of Śabalā" and "the offspring of Bahulā. [Thus,] sound is produced immediately after effort (*prayatnānantarīyaka*).
"Or is it artificial?
[This refers to: whether the atoms of light, such as blue, yellow, and so forth, are separate—meaning independent of one another—or collective—meaning accompanied by one another.
"In some cases" means either in visual consciousness, in its own location, or in the obstruction of the arising of another, for the purpose of simultaneous cognition.

For the sake of determining many things from a single word: therein, those which are employed in visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and which denote specific states are called "visible" (*sanidarśana*). Those which obstruct the arising of another in their own location are called "resistant" (*sapratigha*).
Now, one might object: "Blue, yellow, and so forth are absolutely distinct; how then can they be expressed by a single term such as 'visible' (*sanidarśana*)? To this, he says:

"By way of the commonality of difference from those others. This means that the very difference from those others—namely, from the non-visible (*anidarśana*) and the non-obstructive (*apratigha*)—is itself [the basis for their being called by a single term].

Because all of them are excluded from that [ultimate particular], for that reason, if it is argued that even words such as "visible" (*sanidarśana*) and so forth are merely collective terms because they denote an aggregation of atoms, we say: no. For even a single atom is denoted by terms such as "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*).

Having explained the application of words by way of their effects (*kārya*), he now explains it by way of their causes (*kāraṇa*). "For the purpose of enjoining that which has a single effect, such as color and so forth"—that is, for the purpose of enjoining that capacity of color and so forth which has a single effect, namely the holding of water; this means "in the injunction of a single power. By its distinction from other things, such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) and the like, the word "jar" and so forth [is applied]. By the inclusion of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*),...

The phrase "the grasping of rice and so forth" refers to the subject at hand: that things for which a convention has been established are communicated [by a word]. Likewise, even with respect to a single cause, multiple objects for which a convention has been established are communicated by a single word; this should be understood as a connection made through a shift in the grammatical construction (vacana-pariṇāma), and it should be seen that this is for the sake of linguistic economy in practical usage. For example, all the offspring of a brindled cow are [designated] by a single term on the basis of having a single cause.

The offspring of *bahulā* are denoted by the word *bāhuleya*, while those of *śāvalā* are denoted by the word *śāvaleya*. Furthermore, whatever sound is produced by human effort as its cause is called "effort-immediate" (*prayatnānantarīyaka*) because it is generated by that same common cause.

The intention "I shall do" is the effort (*prayatna*). That which exists immediately after it, without any interval, is [the meaning of the suffix]; this is derived from the root *grah* and others according to their form.

The suffix *cha* is applied because it denotes a group (*gaṇa*). In that context, the mention of "place" (*deśa*) is not recorded [in the traditional rule]. The suffix *kan* is added to it as a pleonastic (*svārthika*) affix. And this has been stated with reference to a specific cause; however, relying on the cause in general, he says: "or it is produced" (*kṛtaka*). That which has its birth dependent upon causes is "immediately following from effort" (*prayatnānantarīyaka*).
And because it is designated as "produced" (*kṛtaka*) in contrast to everything else;

thus far, it has been stated by way of affirmation (*vidhi*). Likewise, it is stated by way of the negation of its effects (*kāryapratiṣedha*), such as: "sound is not visible," "it is impermanent," and "it is non-self."

By negating its cause, it is said to be "ownerless" and "empty. In the same way, other [terms] are also applied according to their respective contexts. Regarding words such as "empty" and "permanent," having conceptualized the intended form within the intellect (*buddhi*) as described, the designation is made by means of the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of that [form].
For all word-meanings are indicated by the intention of the intellect, since they possess the case-endings assigned [by that intention].

He states it by way of negation, beginning with "tathā" (so too), and so forth. By the negation of that which is the effect of the visual [object], such as blue and so on—namely, visual consciousness—the word "non-visual" (*acākṣuṣa*) is used. It is expressed generally by the term "non-visual" in the sense that visual consciousness is not capable [of perceiving it]. Likewise, the word "impermanent" (*anitya*), when established through the exclusion of the permanent, is also [established] by the negation of its effect.

It is indeed by way of negation. For instance, others always desire that a thing be eternal; however, such a thing, being neither the probandum nor the probans, does not enter the path of conventional discourse. Therefore, the probandum and the probans must be accepted. By the negation of the effect of an eternal entity, there is the non-eternal. Furthermore, the word "self" (*ātman*) is sometimes employed to indicate something independent with respect to a certain effect; thus, the word "non-self" (*anātman*) would function through the exclusion of what is not that effect.

Having thus expressed [the point] by way of negating the effect, he speaks by way of negating the cause, beginning with the words "tad" (that), and so forth. The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: by way of negating the cause of that which possesses an owner and is non-empty, this entity consisting of sound and so forth is proclaimed for the sake of conventional usage as being "ownerless" and "empty. For instance, it is not presided over by an independent self (*ātman*) or the like.

For others, it is held that "having an owner" means being presided over by another. Likewise, even though [the world] is not empty, it is called "presided over" precisely because it is presided over by such a presiding agent;

for the presiding agent's status as a presider consists in his taking possession of that which is to be presided over, otherwise the state of being a presider would be impossible. Therefore, for others, words such as "having an owner" function by way of a cause; they do not apply to entities that perish at every moment, where there is merely a collection of conditions (*sāmagrī*).

There exists some presiding controller whose nature is established as being dependent upon [them], such that the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) proceed in dependence upon him. Therefore, by refuting the aforementioned reasons, they are established as being without an owner and empty. The same applies to other cases as well; that is, [the notions of] suffering, non-emptiness, having no protector, having no refuge, and so forth, should also be understood according to their respective applications. What is the cause for a certain effect? 5–6.

"By negation" means by the negation of certain effects, such as suffering and emptiness; for [the terms] "pleasure," "non-emptiness," and so forth, are established as having the effect of being non-adverse. Furthermore, because everything conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is subject to transformation, it is adverse. Regarding "without a protector, without a refuge," and so on: by the negation of these effects, there is an absence of an independent protector and the like.
Thus, in this way, the fourfold application of words has been explained by means of affirmation and negation regarding cause and effect.
Now, one might ask: "Since there is no object to be excluded, such as 'non-empty' or 'non-eternal,' how can words like 'empty' and so forth express the exclusion of others?
To this he says: "Empty," etc. "As it has been stated" refers to whichever [position] corresponds to the particular philosophical system (siddhānta) adopted.
"By that conceptualization" means having conceptualized—that is, having superimposed upon the intellect—the form of "emptiness," "permanence," and so forth, which is intended and constructed by it.
By means of its exclusion (*tadvyavacchedena*), that is, by the exclusion of forms such as "non-emptiness" imagined by others, the designation "empty" and so forth is made.

He asks, "Why? and replies with the words beginning with "of the intellect" (*buddhi*). The "intention of the intellect" (*buddhisamīhā*) is the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) [in the form]: "I shall superimpose this object. Likewise...
That [word] which possesses such a confusion is "tathā"; its state is "tasmāt. By the inclusion of the term "all" (sarva), he says this: even in that case where [the object] is a real entity...
Thus it is said.

This is what is meant: a word does not, by its own form, enjoin or exclude the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a real entity. [This concludes] the investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*).

The objections raised by those of poor intellect—such as the introduction of faults regarding the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) and so forth—are merely the vacillations of their own minds; therefore, those [objections] are disregarded.
It must indeed be momentary. Furthermore: even if many [entities] were to possess a single auditory perception, provided they occurred in a single momentary occurrence. (145)
It is not only because they are distinct from others that things possessing the same effect are expressed by a single word due to their lack of distinction;

rather, there would be no contradiction even if multiple objects were expressed by a single word through its application to a single function. It has been stated here that if its intended [object] were perceived, it would exist; however, if it were unperceived, it would be non-existent—or, in the case of its being unperceived—[it would follow that it does not exist].
Otherwise, designations, recognition, and so forth, which depend upon the perception of that [object], would not be possible.

All conventional usage regarding affirmation and negation is manifested solely by conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*). Consequently, in words such as "impermanent," there is no counter-correlate (*pratipakṣa*) such as "permanent" to be excluded; thus, the objection regarding the absence of a counter-correlate is raised against that [position].

"Udbhāvanam" means "bringing to light. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the author refers to] the objection that there is a fault of non-refutation even when negating [the opponent's position] by saying "there is no self," and so forth.
These are the "utterances" (*vispanditāni*) or "manifestations" (*vijṛmbhitāni*)—that is to say, incoherent arguments—of those of dull intellect such as Uddyotakara and others.
For one whose intellect follows the path of logic would not bring forward what is incoherent. Therefore, those objections regarding faults are to be disregarded.
The meaning is "not attentive.

The opponent begins with "atha" and so forth. The word "api" (even/also) is displaced in its position. Even because of the occurrence of a single entity, namely the universal (*sāmānya*), there is a manifold diversity of individual instances (*vyakti*). "A single sound" (*ekaśruti*) means one sound; and that [single sound] belongs to this manifold [entity].
"Having a single auditory perception" (*eka-śruti-mān*) means that it would be denotable by a single word.
He considers that there is no distinction whether [the unity] is due to having a single effect, or being a single word, or through a single generality (*sāmānya*). For this very reason, he explains:
"Not only... and so forth. That exclusion (*bheda*) from others—which possess different effects—is itself the non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*) of all those things that have that same effect.

Therefore, they are expressed by a single word. Moreover, even through a single function—that is, by the operation of a single universal—how could there be any contradiction in multiple entities being expressed by a single word? Just as there is no contradiction when a single word is applied to many things on the basis of having a single effect, so too is it the case with a universal that exists as a real entity (*vastubhūta*). Therefore, the postulation of a real universal is also logical.
Such is the meaning.
The Master says, "It has been stated. That universal (*sāmānya*), which is a real entity (*vastubhūta*), is intended [to be] "perceivable by means of its form" (*rūpeṇopalabhyate*).
Since it is intended as such, "perceivability" (*upalabhyatva*) is intended to be expressed as the instrument; thus, the compound is formed according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*.

The meaning of the statement is that because a universal is not perceived apart from its individual instances—even though it has reached the conditions for perception—it does not exist. Or, if its non-perception were admitted, then designations, recognition, and so forth—which depend on the observation of that [universal]—would not occur, as they would depend on the observation of a universal. This is what is meant by the word "it has been said. [Furthermore,] a single word [is applied] to many...

Designation (*vyapadeśa*) is a cognition of an identical form; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such [arguments] as "there would be no application [of words] toward individuals based on a universal.
For designation and recognition, which are based upon perception, do not apply elsewhere when they themselves are not being perceived.
Moreover,

it is not tenable that its mode of existence (*vṛtti*) consists of being located (*ādheyatā*) or manifestation (*vyakti*). Regarding that which, being one, applies a single name to multiple substrata— what is this mode of existence of that [universal] by which it [subsists] in a bowl?

If it is argued that "the jujube fruits exist [in the bowl]," then there would be only a locus (*āśraya*). If it is claimed that there is "manifestation" (*vyakti*) because they are illuminated by those [fruits], [we reply:
a permanent entity cannot be assisted, and thus there can be no locus;
for a locus does not exist where there is nothing to be assisted. For the universal (*sāmānya*) is held to be permanent; if it were impermanent, it would be... [another].

Because origination from another is manifold, and because a single cognition is untenable [for multiple things] as it is for distinct entities; and what could a permanent entity do such that there would be a substratum?
If it is argued that it is a substratum because of its inherence (*samavāya*) therein, then what is this so-called "inherence"? It is not something separate.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "they would not exist" and so forth, other previously mentioned faults are also included.

For things that are distinct cannot be called "possessors of that [common property]" unless they are identical with it; likewise, a universal (*jāti*) is not employed for tasks such as carrying loads or milking, and so forth.

By this, he states the following: there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the postulation of a universal. Therefore, designations and the like are not based upon it. However, since there is no contradiction in their performing a single effect, it is precisely that [the effect] which accounts for the designation and recognition.

"The [argument] regarding sound is not tenable. He states another refutation as well, beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*). One who maintains that the universal (*sāmānya*) is a real entity (*vastubhūta*) must admit that its occurrence (*pravṛtti*) in its own substratum (*svāśraya*) is not restricted to a single instance. For it is not logical that something which does not reside there could be the cause for designations (*vyapadeśa*) and so forth with respect to that substratum. Furthermore, this occurrence of the universal in its own substratum would have to be either its being contained (*ādheyatā*) or its being supported by the power thereof.

Because of its non-abiding. Manifestation (*vyakti*) would have to be either perception by the power of the substratum (*āśraya-bala*) or that [perception] itself as a function (*vṛtti*). Neither of these two is tenable in that universal (*sāmānya*).
He explains this with the words "That which... and so forth: that which is this single, real entity, the universal, residing in many substrata...
The scripture teaches that the universal is one. Having raised the question, "What is this mode of existence (*vṛtti*) of that universal in its own substratum?
[the author] himself states two alternatives, beginning with "and being contained" (*ādheyatā*). Alternatively, the word *kim* is used in the sense of negation;
the meaning is: "What is this mode of existence? None at all. For instance, the mode of existence in its own substratum would have to be either being contained, as for example—

"Plums exist in a vessel"—this is the [example]. Alternatively, the manifestation of that universal might reside in its substratum, because the manifestation is revealed by those substrata. In that case, if "residing" is intended as the state of being contained (*ādheyatā*), then the individuals must be accepted as its substrata. Furthermore, since the universal is admitted to be eternal, it cannot be contained therein prior to the arising of the individual.
Because that which is eternal cannot be assisted by its substrata, the individuals regarded as its substrata are not its support.

He explains this with the words "For that which is eternal," and so forth. Now, if it is not accepted as eternal, then in the case of non-eternality, because of the arising of one after another—the arising of various distinct things—the universal would be manifold; and due to that manifoldness, it would be differentiated among the particulars, just as the particulars themselves are differentiated.

Because a single cognition would be impossible regarding a universal, and because a single [cognition] would be untenable, [the text] connects this with the statement, "The universal is held to be eternal. The intention is that for an eternal universal, what could its substratum (āśraya)—that is, its support—possibly do? It could do nothing at all. For the relationship between the supported and the supporter (āśrayāśrayibhāva) exists only between things that are already established.
[Objection: This would lead to an infinite regress.
[Response: 4. Consideration of the Universal.
We do not admit that something which provides no assistance can serve as a substratum (*āśraya*).

Therefore, relations between entities—such as inherence (*samavāya*) or inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*)—are not distinct from the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). This is because there is no mutual obstruction among things that do not assist one another in any other way, and since that which lacks obstruction cannot be a benefactor, it cannot be a substratum; rather, it is due to the inherence of that universal (*sāmānya*) in its locus.
When [the opponent] objects: "How then does 'cowness' (gotva) subsist in cows? By way of the relationship between locus and located (āśrayāśrayibhāva).

But what is this relationship of locus and located? It is inherence (samavāya). In that case, cowness is the possessor of subsistence (vṛttimat), while subsistence is inherence, because it is the cause of the cognition 'it is here'. [The author], not conceiving of inherence in the absence of a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor, says:
"‘What is this? and so forth;

‘not separate’ and so forth is the opponent’s [position]. Being established as not having separate locations means they are *apṛthaksiddha* (inseparably established). The relation between substratum and superstratum among those [entities] is *samavāya* (inherence)."

"Regarding the passage beginning with *tad* [that], the *Siddhāntavāda* states: We do not conceive that this very nature of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) can belong to a substratum that provides no assistance. Why? Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If the status of being a substratum were admitted for that which provides no assistance, then everything would be the substratum of everything. But this is not the case, because everything is perceived as not inhering in everything else."
