If [you say]: "But surely, in the absence of a contributing factor (*upakāraka*), just as in the case of 'cowness' (*gotva*), because everything would be inherent in everything, there would be no cognition from a single [instance]—this very point is what is being objected to.
All—

Now, this relation characterized as inherence (*samavāya*) is indeed distinct from the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*) and so forth. And since that [inherence] exists here, how can there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)?
It is replied: True; however, inherence occurs only for that which is inherent somewhere. That—its...

And "being inherent" (*samavetatva*) consists in being dependent upon that [substratum]; and for another entity to be dependent upon that [substratum] is nothing other than its arising from it. Therefore, in this case, the relationship between the intellect and its objects is simply arising in a successive sequence (*uparyuparibhāvena utpatti*), not inherence (*samavāya*); thus, the argument based on presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is exhausted. Furthermore, there could be no successive sequence if [the entities] were not related; nor is there inherence of things that do not already inhere, by virtue of which they could possess the state of being inherent.
Because it would follow that [the universal] is inherent in everything everywhere.
Concluding [the argument], he says: "Therefore," and so forth. Inherence belongs to two things that are not established separately, as in the case of the produced and the producer.

Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the connection between two substances that are established separately, as in the case of fire and smoke. Inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*) is inherence in one and the same thing, as in the case of color and taste in a single substance. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the relation of inhering in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamaveta*) is included. The compound *vastubhūtāḥ sambandhāḥ* (real relations) or *sambandhā vastūnām* (relations of things) is either a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) or a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

Or rather, the inclusion of the term "entity" (vastu) is for the purpose of excluding that which is constructed by conceptualization (*kalpanā*). They are not distinct from the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), because they do not exist otherwise due to a lack of connection. Even if there is no mutual assistance among those things inhering in a single object (*ekārthasamavāyin*), [it is because of] the assistance of that one [substratum].
Because the aforementioned fault would otherwise follow regarding existence; therefore, it is explained by means of its own benefit, having first brought about a connection with another.
Thus, even in that case, the relationship is produced solely by the relation of cause and effect.
Consequently, this substratum, not benefiting its own self, being a support for that which is independent, is a "borrowed ornament."
This is the point. [Objection:
But if this is so, how is it that the bowl (*kuṇḍa*) is the producer (*janaka*) of the jujube fruits (*badara*)?
[Response: It is so. Establishing this very point, he says: "mutually," and so forth. Of those things that are mutually beneficial (*upakārin*) to one another—

Alternatively, because there is no dependence on that which is considered the substratum— since it provides no assistance and offers no obstruction— and because there is no connection for that which is unobstructed due to the absence of a causal relationship,
all relations between things do not differ from the relation of cause and effect; this is the connection with the subject at hand.
But surely, if there is assistance [provided] by the substratum (*āśraya*), there can be no mutual relationship of the assisted and the assister between the two things that depend upon it;
so for what purpose is the statement "or from another" introduced?
This is true. However, even though there is no direct mutual assistance, nevertheless, because they are dependent upon a single cause...

The objection is raised that one might postulate a connection even through a succession [of intermediaries]. If it is argued that a mutual relationship of benefactor and beneficiary is not at all intended for those things that coexist in a single object, he replies with the words "Even though," and so forth. This is because, in the absence of benefit from a single substratum, the aforementioned fault would follow. The fault has already been stated as the fear of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since [the benefit] arises from its own substratum.

Since there must necessarily be a mutual benefit between the effect and the two inherent causes, the proponent explains— by means of that benefit which the inherent causes provide to themselves through their own substrate— that they are connected here as "the two inherent causes are related. Thus, having brought together even the second inherent cause by way of that self-benefit, it is made known.

This is what is meant: just as for another [school], there is a relationship between two things inhering in a single object (*ekārthasamavāyin*) despite their being mutually unconnected, because they both inhere in one and the same object; so too, for us, there is a relationship between those two by virtue of having a single effect. Since this is the case, even in that instance of inherence in a single object, the relationship with the substratum (*āśraya*) is produced solely by the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), which is the causal relation existing between them.

Thus, the relation is indeed superimposed by means of that [substratum]. Since the status of being a substratum (*ādhāra*) and so forth occurs only by way of providing assistance (*upakāra*), therefore this individual, such as a *śāvaleyādi* (e.g., a brindled cow), is the substratum. To claim that it is the substratum of the universal—which is independent—while not assisting the universal in its own nature, is merely a vain ornament; for "ornament" (*maṇḍana*) means decoration, as in "one decorates by means of this."

Having formed [the compound] *yācitakamaṇḍana* as a *karmadhāraya*, [the meaning is as follows]: why? Because for a poor man who lacks it within himself, there is a borrowed ornament (*yācitakamaṇḍana*) from another. In the same way, even for that which is the substratum of a universal (*sāmānya*), there is the state of being a receptacle (*pratyādhāratva*) with respect to the universal. Alternatively, it is an instrumental compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) where the suffix denotes the action (*bhāvasādhana*); just as the act of adorning is performed by means of a borrowed ornament.

Likewise, the designation of a substratum for that which has a universal as its locus occurs through being requested by another to serve as a support, and not according to the actual state of things, because there is no benefit [to the universal] from it; thus, [the universal] does not spread out.
The capacity [of the pot] is the production of its effect in that very location, as in the case of a bowl and so forth [producing] cooked rice and the like.

By nature, the property of a heavy substance—which is to produce its effect in the same location as itself—is established by its own continuity. Therefore, the bowl acts as a cooperative cause for that [substance] in its preceding moment, [causing it] to arise in that very place.

It produces the effect of the jujube fruit while serving as its substratum; otherwise, there would be no such activity as "the jujubes are in the bowl," nor would this designation based on that assistance even exist.
If it is asked, "What then is the purpose of producing conjunction?"—it is simply the conjunction of those two, and that too is produced by those two alone.

Inherence [is so called] because of its producing [the effect]. Why does it not inhere in only one [substratum]? Because of its incapacity there. That [inherence] is individually incapable [of producing the effect] because it has not yet been fully produced.

Therefore, the statement that "all real relations do not differ from the relation of cause and effect" is considered to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is with respect to that which spreads forth—that is, that which has the nature of diffusing into other locations.

The production of the preceding entity characterized as a jujube fruit— which serves as the material cause— in that very location where it was previously situated, namely the place connected to the bowl, and not its movement elsewhere: this is the capacity belonging to the bowl and other such things regarded as supports with respect to the jujubes and other such things regarded as supported.

He explains [the verse] with the words beginning "by its very nature" (*prakṛtyaiva*). That which has a location that is unequal by its very nature—that is, by its own essence (*svabhāvena*)—is described as such.

Even though it depends on the word *prakṛti*, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed because it conveys the meaning. And that which is of such a kind and is an effect (*kārya*)—this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. Furthermore, the "effect" refers specifically to the jujube fruit (*badara*) and so forth, as comprised within successive moments. Its production is precisely what constitutes its property (*dharma*).
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a substance such as a jujube fruit (*badara*), which was gathered in a preceding moment, consists in its capacity to produce an effect in the same location;
this state is produced by the support (*ādhārakṛta*). The meaning is that the capacity to produce something in a location identical to its own is brought about by the support.
Precisely because of this, the bowl (*kuṇḍa*) is the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*) for that preceding moment which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the subsequent effect, the jujube fruit.
In that very place, at the very moment of its material cause, the *kuṇḍa* (vessel) is said to be the "support" (*ādhāra*) when it produces the effect, the *badara* (jujube fruit).

By this, it is stated that the relationship of support and supported (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) exists between the moments of the *kuṇḍa* and the *badara*, both of which depend upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*).
Otherwise, if the aforementioned assistance were not rendered by the *kuṇḍa* to the *badaras*, then the expression "the *badaras* are here in the *kuṇḍa*" would not be possible.
There would be no designation [of the container], because a designation that has a fixed substratum is impossible without a cause.

This designation—such as "the jujube fruits are in this bowl"—is produced by the assistance rendered by that [substratum]; that is, it is produced by the assistance rendered by the substratum. What then?
It is produced by the conjunction between the bowl and the jujube fruits.

"What then," and so forth, is the Siddhāntavādin’s response. The intention of the questioner is this: you postulate conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like only if momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) exists; however, if the non-momentariness of entities is admitted, then the very production of conjunction and the like would not occur—this is the meaning. Furthermore, there is even the designation "the conjunction of those two," namely, the bowl and the jujube fruit.
The intention is that there is no causal sign (*nimitta*), because of the absence of the relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary.

Therefore, the capacity for the arising of a particular quality (*viśeṣa*) must come from some other benefit. What is this "benefit" (*upakāra*) that exists between two things that are neither produced nor producers? Since its own nature is already established, it cannot be an effect; and as for the performance of another form, even in that case, there is an absence of benefit.

[This] must be stated. For in either case, that which is inactive is incapable of acting and thus provides no assistance; this has already been explained at length. [The opponent says: "By those two," and so forth. Because conjunction is produced by those two—the bowl and the jujube fruit—their conjunction is accepted. The production of conjunction by both alone is its inherence in both. Having reflected on what was stated by the opponent...

The Siddhāntin says: "That," and so forth. Does that conjunction inhere or is it produced in one and the same vessel or jujube fruit? The intention of the questioner is this: if those two entities called the vessel and the jujube fruit are each individually capable of producing the conjunction or of assuming the state of being its substratum, then why—

"Thus they depend upon one another. If it is argued that those two things, though having distinct referents, are capable only when joined with each other, he replies with the words "That," and so forth. The point is this: whatever entities, such as a bowl and a jujube fruit, are individually incapable, they remain just as incapable even when joined with one another, because they are non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*). However, momentary things, though individually incapable, [become capable] subsequently through their auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).

It is not contradictory to say that things which have undergone specific modifications and are conjoined are capable [of conjunction]. Furthermore, because they do not provide assistance toward the conjunction, the entity known as the "pot-and-jujube" does not possess conjunction as its property. [The opponent replies:
"[Of the conjoined," etc.; because the conjoined pot and jujube fruit provide assistance to one another through something other than that [conjunction]. Therefore...
Whatever is the nature of the jujube fruit as it relates to the bowl, or whatever else is distinct from that bowl as it relates to the benefit of the jujube fruit—
because of the arising of a specific quality for the sake of producing the conjunction of the bowl and the jujube fruit,
or for attaining the state of being a support, the capacity [for this] does not reside in the two things alone.

The Master [Śāntarakṣita] says: "What is this assistance? [This refers to] the case of jujube fruits (*badara*) and bowls (*kuṇḍa*), which stand in a relationship of neither produced nor producer; there is no such assistance at all. If one asks, "How is it that they are precisely not produced and not producers? he replies with the words beginning "intrinsic nature" (*svarūpa*).

The meaning is that since the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the jujube fruit is established by other causes alone, it is not an effect [of the bowl]; thus, the jujube fruits possess neither the state of being produced nor does the bowl possess the state of being a producer. For the opponent does not desire that the essential nature of the jujube fruits and so forth arises from the bowl and such; rather, those fruits are produced solely from their own causes. It is not that the form of the jujube itself is created by the bowl, but rather something else [is produced] from it.

To this [objection], he says: "By its own form," and so forth. Therein, "there" refers to the substratum (*ādhāya*). For an object distinct from another cannot be assisted by an action belonging to that other object. "In both ways" means by way of both its own form and the form of another. This is because, according to the method just mentioned, that which provides no assistance—such as a vessel (*kuṇḍa*) and the like—is of no consequence whatsoever.

This has already been stated for the most part (*uktaprāya*). The word *prāya* signifies "for the most part" or "mostly. Thus, *uktaprāya* means "stated mostly. Because the group beginning with *rājadanta* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the word *prāya* is placed at the end of the compound. And this meaning has been explained in detail in such passages as: "And that effect of theirs, which consists of birth, is what is assisted" (1.10.8). Others, however, take the word *prāya* to mean "similar."

They say: what has been stated is similar to what was previously said; by means of the assistance to the nature of the universal (*sāmānya*) effected by its substratum as previously described, this [discussion] on the universal follows.

Therefore, all relations between entities are established through a distinction based on the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), by virtue of the specific power of assistance belonging only to the producer.

The meaning is that the assistance rendered by the receptacle, such as a pit (*kuṇḍa*), to that which is placed within it is equal [to other causal factors]. The conclusion is provided by the words "all indeed," and so forth. The connection is as follows: all relations between entities are established on the basis of the cause that is the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

If it is argued that there would be no distinction among them, he says: "Of the producer alone," and so forth; or rather, [the distinction is made] through a differentiation from the standpoint of the relation of cause and effect.

They are established through differentiation. To ask how they are differentiated, he says: "Of the producer alone," and so forth. The meaning is: by virtue of that specific assistance (*upakāraviśeṣa*) which the effect receives from the cause. For instance, in the case of a jujube fruit (*badara*) and the like, which have the property of oozing out, there exists a relationship of support and supported (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) through the utility (*upayoga*) characterized by its production in the location of its own material cause (*svopādāna*). And [there is a relationship] brought about by the lamp, consisting in the capacity for generating cognition.

The relationship characterized as that between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) belongs to things such as a jar and a lamp by virtue of the production of their own nature; thus, in other relationships as well, this should be stated according to the appropriate case.
Now, with the words "Indeed, all relationships of entities," etc., [it was shown that] there is no [relationship] characterized as conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Its inclusion is within the category of "being a cause," because it exists only when [the two things] exist at the same time. Now, if [the entity] is non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), the arising of conjunction is not logical; however, in that case, it will occur when [the entity] is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Furthermore, no difference in intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is perceived between the states of being conjoined and not conjoined for a bowl and a jujube fruit. Therefore, conjunction certainly exists even in the case of the non-momentary, because it is so perceived.

As Uddyotakara says: "If conjunction were not a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), then the field, seed, water, and so forth—being indistinguishable [from their previous states]—would always produce effects such as sprouts; but this is not the case. Therefore, because the effect is not produced at all times, the field and other factors depend upon another cause for the production of the sprout, just as the collection of causes such as a lump of clay [depends on a potter] for a jar."

In the case of production, there is dependence on factors such as a potter; however, that which is independent of the field and so forth is established as conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Furthermore, this conjunction is indeed established by direct perception as a distinct entity from those two [substances], because it is perceived as a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*) of the two substances. For instance, when someone is told by another, "Bring the two substances that are conjoined," [he brings] precisely those two substances in which the conjunction exists.

One perceives those very [parts] and brings them forth; it is not merely a substance. Furthermore, for a person standing at a distance, this cognition—which apprehends a forest as being without intervals even when there are intervals—arises as a false cognition (*mithyābuddhi*). A false cognition never arises without the experience of a primary object (*mukhyapadārtha*); for indeed, one who has never experienced the sight of a cow does not have the delusion that "this is a cow" regarding a *gavaya*.

Therefore, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) must necessarily be accepted as primary. Likewise, by the prohibitive statement "Caitra is not wearing earrings," the earring itself is not prohibited, because it exists elsewhere, such as in another location. Rather, what is prohibited is Caitra’s conjunction with the earring. Similarly, by the affirmative statement "Caitra is wearing earrings," [it is not that] Caitra—

Since the production of either of the two atoms (*paramāṇu*) has already been established, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it must be the production of their conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Therefore, conjunction certainly exists.
To this, it is replied: (1) Just as the commencement of conjunction occurs through the attainment of a specific state by the field (*kṣetra*) and other factors...

therefore, conjunction also is included within the very relation of cause and effect. It is merely by excluding other distinctions that there arises the cognition "these two are conjoined" or "this belongs to conjunction," and not due to the force of a real entity called conjunction. For there exists no [cognition] apart from the relation of cause and effect.
The relation is real.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tadayam" (this, therefore): the capacity to produce [the effect] in things such as jujube fruits is itself the substratum (*ādhāra*) for things such as the bowl; this is the relation.
If it is argued that the substratum of the universal must be the substratum by means of the capacity to produce, he says: "No," etc. "That" refers to the capacity to produce.
Regarding the word "here" (atra), it refers to the universal (sāmānya).

He explains this with the words beginning "for not," and so forth. "Arising in the very location of its own material cause" is the specific sense of arising; that which has such arising as its defining characteristic is the state of being a substratum (ādhārabhāva). It is "because of its non-produced nature" (ajanyatvāt), meaning because the universal, by virtue of its eternity, is not produced.

Even though there is no other substratum due to the absence of that [individual], the universal does not abide by virtue of its substratum, because it persists. He explains this with the words beginning "Now" (*atha*). "Of that" refers to the universal; "even in its absence" means even in the absence of the individual, because the universal remains in a place devoid of individuals. For if the universal did not exist in a place devoid of individuals, then...

In that case, if a new individual were produced, there could be no connection with the universal; for it does not come from elsewhere, as it is inactive— this [objection] regarding the universal is indeed untenable, because [the universal] is not a producer.

Because it remains even when that [cause] is absent. For a sustainer would have to be the cause of the prevention of the fall of things subject to falling and destined for destruction; yet, if one does not inquire into the prevention of the fall here as well—if the prevention of the fall were produced by the sustainer, then it would be a distinct entity (*arthāntara*). And if it were a distinct entity, it would reside in that very [entity].
What is the obstruction for that which is falling? Even if there were no falling due to an obstruction, the same inquiry would apply, leading to an infinite regress.
Therefore, how can the absence of falling be produced by anything? If you say it produces an absence, [we reply: 462b.
Nor can an individual situated in a different location be the substratum of that universal, because it occupies a different location.

If it is argued that there is no difference in location for the universal because it is unitary, then it follows that all individuals possessing that single genus must occupy the same location. Furthermore, not all [individuals] would possess the genus; for how could one [unitary thing] be situated in different locations?
If you say "it is you," then let this other fault [of yours] remain.

With the words "subject to falling" (*patanadharman*) and so forth, he states the reason for the accumulation [of faults]. The word *hi* has the sense of *ca* (and). The word *api* is intended to indicate admission (*abhyupagama*). Even while admitting this mode [of existence], it is impossible to establish it in a universal (*sāmānya*). Universal—
This presentation is for the purpose [of showing] that it possesses the nature of not falling; however, it is not possible for that which is not a cause to be a sustainer.

For this very reason, he says "here too," and so forth. Here too, if a proponent of logic were not to inquire into the obstruction of falling when a sustainer is postulated on the grounds of obstructing a fall, then even that which is not a cause would be a sustainer.

The intended meaning is "in accordance with one's own system. Here too, this objection may arise: Is the prevention of falling produced by the stabilizer identical to the object being stabilized, or is it a different entity, or is it merely the absence of falling?
First, it cannot be identical to it, because it is admitted that its nature is produced from something else; nor can it be a different entity, as he says:

If it is accepted that [the support] is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), then the utility of this support—which is a distinct entity—would consist in its being the basis for the connection [that prevents falling]. What, then, would be the obstruction or hindrance to a jujube fruit or the like as it falls? None at all. Consequently, the implication is that even a jujube fruit situated in a bowl or similar vessel would surely fall. [The opponent might argue: "The non-falling of the jujube fruit is due to an obstruction to falling produced by the support, which is a distinct entity."
If it is argued that [the falling] is caused [by another factor], he says: "Because of an obstruction, even though there is no falling," and so forth.

When the non-falling of an object such as a jujube fruit (*badara*) is accepted as being due to what is called an "obstruction" (*pratibandha*), the same objection applies. Is this non-falling produced by the entity called "obstruction" something identical with the nature of the jujube fruit itself, or is it a separate entity (*arthāntara*)? If it were a separate entity, then the utility of this "obstruction" would reside only in that [separate entity].
And so forth. All that has just been stated applies equally here.

Now, if it is argued that the non-falling of the jujube fruit and other such objects is caused by that very factor called "non-falling," he replies that the same objection applies there as well: "And there would be an infinite regress."
With the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth, the third position is presented: How, and by whom, could that absence of falling (*pātābhāva*) be produced?

There is no such thing as an "absence" (*abhāva*) that is an effect (*kārya*). If it were produced by something, it would necessarily be a positive entity (*bhāva*), because an absence is incapable of being produced. Therefore, the expression "he produces an absence" (*abhāvaṃ karoti*) is a designation for the negation of the production of a positive entity.

Likewise, this [object] also, being something to be produced (*prakārya*), must be dependent upon something else. Therefore, because this [other thing] is not dependent on anything else, it would never remain [static]. Consequently, what is called the "prevention of falling" is simply the production of a momentary entity in the same location as its material cause (*upādāna*). Let it be granted that for things subject to falling, such a prevention is non-productive (*ajanaka*).

What kind of "stability" (sthiti) could some [factor] produce for a substance that possesses motion, such that it would be its "stabilizer" (sthāpaka)? For stability is simply the non-deviation from its own nature; and that [non-deviation] does not depend upon a substratum, nor indeed upon anything else.
The sense is that non-existence (abhāva), being a non-entity, cannot be an effect. How, then, is there the designation "he produces non-existence"?

If this is argued, he says: "Non-existence," and so forth. In the designation "it makes non-existence," no effect called "non-existence" is intended. Why? He says: "Of that," and so forth. The intention is that because it would be an effect of that [non-existence], it would necessarily be an existence.

If it is argued: "Just as a cloth does not have the nature of a jar because it is an effect like a jar, so too non-existence will not have the nature of existence because it is an effect like existence," we say: no. For even a jar and the like possess the nature of existence precisely because they have the property of coming into being (*bhavana-dharman*).
Since that [property] exists in non-existence as well, how could it not have the nature of existence? Otherwise, how could it appear as having the nature of non-existence?
If it is argued that [negation] does not have the nature of an entity (*bhāva*), we say no; for there is no appearance of a non-entity (*abhāva*).

Since the mutual distinction between non-entities is perceived—as in "the absence of a jar" and "the absence of a cloth"—it has been stated that the difference between the cloth and so forth [is what is perceived], and not because non-entities appear as a single unity. Therefore, whatever action belongs to an entity, of that...
The instruction of a negation brings about non-existence (*abhāva*).

For this very reason, he clarifies: "it does not bring about existence," which means that whatever is the meaning of this sentence is precisely the same as the meaning of "it brings about non-existence. And likewise, [there is] the non-existence of the obstruction to falling.

Regarding the state of being merely that [support] and thus not being an effect: "this" refers to the bowl (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth; "by that cause" refers to "this," namely the jujube fruit (*badara*) and so forth, which is restricted by some support such as a bowl. If it were not prevented from falling, it would never remain stationary; the meaning is that it would fall at all times. The conclusion is expressed by the words beginning with "therefore. By the word "api" (even), it is indicated even by the designation "the supported" (*ādheya*).

The production of an effect, which is comprised within a subsequent moment and occupies the same location, by means of a substrate (upādāna) comprised within a preceding moment, is what is called [supporting]. Therefore, this mode [of supporting] is also not possible in the case of a universal;
thus, it was stated—having provisionally accepted it for the sake of demonstration—that even that which does not produce [the object] is a "supporter" because it prevents its falling.

In order to demonstrate that very impossibility, he says: "Let it be so," and so forth. Let there be a prevention of falling for things such as jujube fruits—that is, let there be a prevention of their fall—by means of [an agent] whose nature is the non-production [of the fall]. This is because of "the production of that prevention of falling. Now, regarding a substance possessing motion—that is, one with activity—and furthermore, regarding a universal which, being incorporeal, is inactive: what is the characteristic of its "staying" (sthiti)?
One who acts would be a support or an establisher. For there is no falling of a universal, by which it could be obstructed;
because [the universal] is eternal. That too is indeed employed in the investigation of difference and non-difference.
Granted, let it be that the subsistence of the universal is caused by its substratum. Now, is that [subsistence] different from the universal or non-different?

If there is no necessary connection (*apratibaddhatva*) between them, and the substratum alone is what effects its subsistence, then since that [subsistence] would also be unconnected to the universal, what would the universal have accomplished? If, on the other hand, it is indeed connected, then what is the nature of that connection?

Is this what should be said? If it is argued that [the substratum] exists because of the perception of its stabilization (*sthitikaraṇa*), then the same consequence applies there as well, and there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, since the benefit (*upakāra*) cannot be determined, the claim that "that indeed is its stabilization" is unproven. If, on the other hand, [the substratum] is the cause of its arising, then what need is there for a support (*āśraya*) for that which provides no benefit? For "dependence" (*apekṣā*) is indeed dependence upon that—
[The universal] would have stability. However, stability is said to be nothing other than that universal’s non-deviation from its own nature (*svarūpa*).

And that non-deviation from its own nature does not depend upon a substratum, because the universal is eternal. Even granting [for the sake of argument] that it depends on a substratum, it is simply illogical for that stability of the universal to be dependent upon a substratum. This is because there is a difference between the universal and that stability.

"In the analysis of difference" (*bhedavivecane*) means when an investigation into otherness or non-otherness is being conducted. He explains [the verse] with the words "let it be," and so forth. "Dependent on the substratum" (*āśrayahetukā*) means reliant upon the substratum. "It" (*sā*) refers to the subsistence (*sthiti*).
That substratum brings about that very subsistence as something distinct from itself; it does not bring about the universal (*sāmānya*). That subsistence [resides] in the universal.
Therefore, because it is connected through a connection with that which is related, the universal (*sāmānya*) is indeed assisted; thus he says: "And that," and so forth.

"That" refers to the subsistence (*sthiti*) which is a distinct entity. For there is no cause whatsoever for the universal to be connected to that [subsistence]; what, then, would be accomplished by the universal having a substratum (*āśraya*)? This is the ellipsis to be supplied.

If it is argued that a general connection (*sāmānya-pratibandha*) for duration is indeed admitted, he says: "And if there is a connection," and so forth. That is, if a connection is admitted, and if there is an act of causing duration—meaning that the duration produced by the substratum has its own duration produced generally—then that duration produced by the substratum [resides] in the general property (*sāmānya*).

Regarding the term "dependent": even in that case, the same logical consequence applies to the endurance (*sthiti*) that effects endurance. That endurance which is produced generally for an endurance that is dependent upon a substratum (*āśraya*)—would that [general endurance] be identical with the endurance caused by the substratum, or would it be distinct from it? If it were identical, then since it would have been produced by the substratum itself, how could it be produced generally?

And if it were distinct [from the entity], that very same state would be produced by the universal; what then would be produced by the universal for the first state generated by the substratum? Or, if a second state is produced by the universal, that [second state] would be dependent upon the state generated by the substratum. In that case, it must be stated: what is the nature of this dependence? [It cannot be] of that which is produced by the universal...

Because there would be another, third stability produced by the stability generated by the substratum— since the same consequence applies— the result would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, due to this infinite regress, since the assistance rendered by the universal to the stability produced by the substratum cannot be determined, there would be no cognition that "this stability produced by the substratum belongs to this universal."
If "production" is what is under discussion as the bond [of duration], then it is not the case that a further duration is produced for a duration already generated by its substratum;

rather, that very first duration is produced. In that case, the bond of duration would be the general property (*sāmānya*) alone acting as the efficient cause. And since it is illogical for a general property—which cannot possess any added excellence (*atiśaya*)—to be so, it would merely produce [the thing itself].
There is no other substratum that serves as the cause of its persistence.

Since the deity is identical to the universal (*sāmānya*), the very nature of that [deity] is the persistence of that [universal]. And since that [deity] exists eternally, the persistence of this [universal] is not brought about by anything else. Therefore, there is no substratum for the universal; rather, the deity is its substratum.
There is no stability.
Furthermore, if the unmanifest exists as a reality, its manifestation would be the cause for the cognition [of it] by virtue of being manifest;
therefore, even its being a state of stability is not tenable. Why? Because:
That which conforms to another within the self for the sake of making it capable of producing consciousness; 148.
That [cognition] is considered the manifest effect (vyaṅgya), and the capacity (yogyatā) is regarded as its causal agent (kāraka).
Furthermore, since this capacity already exists beforehand, it is not logical for it to depend upon that [agent]. (149)
What could it do by depending on the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*) which is required for its establishment? For dependence upon that which provides no assistance is not logical.

Thus, "dependence" indeed means a connection (*pratibandha*); when one says "there is this dependence of [the universal] upon this object," that dependence is a connection, a state of being contingent upon that which is depended upon. And since that connection, due to [the universal's] permanence, cannot admit of any added excellence (*atiśaya*), [it is impossible].
The sense is this: the claim that "the universal alone, being conjoined, produces persistence" implies there is no other substratum that serves as the cause of persistence;

therefore, the idea that the substratum is the support of the universal by virtue of providing its persistence is untenable. Thus, regarding the analysis of difference and non-difference that was mentioned, the position of difference has first been set aside.

Relying on the second position, he says: "If there is non-difference," and so forth. If it is accepted that persistence (*sthiti*) is non-different from the universal (*sāmānya*), then that very nature (*svarūpa*) of the universal is the form of its persistence.
And since that nature of the universal exists eternally, the persistence of this universal is not produced by any substratum (*āśraya*). Since this is the case, therefore—
"Such as... and so forth. The conclusion is given by "that," etc. "That" means "therefore"; "of this" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*).
Thus, regarding the two positions previously stated—that subsistence (*vṛtti*) is either being contained (*ādheyatā*) or manifestation (*vyakti*)—the refutation of the first has been made.

This is because, [according to that view], the manifestation of the universal by means of its substratum (*āśraya*) would be the making known of the cognition through that substratum, [yet] the substratum is not a cause of the cognition. That alone...

In that case, there would be a subsistence of the universal (*sāmānya*) in its substratum. [To this] the Ācārya says: "No. [The universal consists in] the production of cognition regarding its own object within the self; therein, the universal is the capacity (*yogyatva*), which conforms to other factors for that purpose. That entity which is dependent on other causes is recognized as the manifestable (*vyaṅgya*). And of that [entity], the knowledge of its own object—

That which is the cause of the capacity for production, such as a lamp and so forth, is indeed a producer (*kāraka*)—that is, a generator—of that which is manifested (*vyaṅgya*). This is because it produces a jar or the like that was previously incapable [of producing cognition] but subsequently becomes capable of generating a cognition of its own form.
If, however, the jar or the like were already capable of generating a cognition of its own form even prior to the proximity of the lamp and so forth...

Since that [lamp] is already required for the pot and other such objects due to their perceptibility, there is a dependence upon it; this is the dependence upon the lamp. Because a universal is eternal, how could there be any modification in that which possesses the universal?
There is no distinction whatsoever between a producer (*kāraka*) and a manifester (*vyañjaka*). Furthermore, regarding its own object...
And that very entity, while producing [its effect],
is either dependent upon a homogeneous material cause (upādāna) or independent, insofar as it possesses the capacity to generate consciousness.
"It is called a manifestor" means that,
since the capacity to produce a cognition in another [the object] is not necessarily implied by the produced [cognition], its status as a causal factor consists merely in its production.

For if that from which something acquires the capacity to produce a cognition were not produced by it— since that capacity would already exist as its very nature (svabhāva)— then the production of the cognition would be a modification of the manifested object. Therefore, how could that aforementioned characteristic of being manifested belong to a universal in relation to its substratum?
The meaning is "by no means. "Another" refers to that which produces a state of being distinct from its own continuum; it is called a "manifestor. Of what nature is it?

It is capable of producing a cognition of its own object. "Dependent upon a homogeneous material cause" means dependent upon the preceding moments included within its own continuum. For example, [it is] like a subsequent moment of a jar or similar object situated in darkness, which is capable of generating a cognition while depending upon [its] preceding moments.
The lamp, while producing the momentary jar, is its illuminator.
If it is argued that since the jar is an effect of the lamp, there should be an increase in the jar whenever there is an increase in the lamp—[we reply:
no, because the difference in the effect arises from the difference in the material cause (*upādāna*), not from the difference in the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*). The lamp is an auxiliary cause.

And since the lamp and so forth are the manifestors of the jar, how can there be the contingency of [the jar] possessing largeness and other qualities? Or rather, even if manifestation were being performed, this same contingency would apply; thus, this [objection] is trivial. Furthermore, it is not from the lump of clay that a moment similar to the manifested moment arises, but rather from the lamp and so forth; so how could something of one kind arise from something of another kind?

And [it is] "independent" (*anapekṣa*). For example, an impact (*abhighāta*) produces a sound that is capable of generating a cognition of its own object while depending on a homogeneous material cause (*sajātīyopādāna*). Indeed, before the impact, there is no sound by which the sound could be dependent upon something of the same class.
For it has been stated that sound is also held to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*) by another.

If, then, the producer (*kāraka*) itself is the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), what then is the distinction between the causes of the producer and the manifestor? To this he says: "By another," and so forth. The meaning is: in something other than the manifestor, which is intended to be the producer. The capacity to generate cognition is not implied for the produced [effect]. For the effect is not produced by the producer as something already capable of generating the cognition of its own object.
It is produced by the seed and so forth. Therefore, its status as a causal factor (*kāraka*) consists merely in its production;

however, its status as a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is defined by a specific quality, namely the production of an effect capable of generating cognition of its own object. (147–48) Although the manifested object acquires the capacity for the production of cognition from the manifestor, it is nevertheless not produced [by it].

If this is argued, he says: "If indeed," and so forth. "From which" means from the manifestor (*vyañjaka*). If that [manifested object] is the manifested (*vyaṅgya*), then "its"—meaning of that manifestor—that capacity exists for this manifested object even prior to the proximity of the manifestor; for it does not depend upon it. For if it were something extrinsic (*parabhūta*) to it, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would already exist as such [prior to the manifestor], just as it is established [to be]. That...
Nor is the manifested object produced as something else.
Thus, since it is ineffective, the negation [of its being a producer] follows; therefore, this [claim that smoke is a producer] is contradicted.
Furthermore, smoke and the like are not producers because they are effects; rather, they are manifestors. Indeed, it is true that [the cause] is the producer.

But it does not produce the cognition of fire by depending upon smoke, because such fire is not a direct cause. Rather, in that case, the cognition would arise depending solely upon its material cause (upādāna) and not by the power of the object, since [the cognition] occurs even when that [object] is absent, following the mark through a mediated succession.
Alternatively, even if cognition appears in a general form, it does not have those [individuals] as its proximate object.

It has already been established, and will be further demonstrated, that [cognition] does not arise through the power of an object. Therefore, by way of direct utility, that [manifestation] is the very nature of the manifested. Just as the manifested exists prior [to the manifestation], so too does that which constitutes its nature.

[The term] *yogyatā* [means] that which depends upon it is the manifestor (*vyañjaka*). If it is argued that the manifestor produces a capacity (*yogyatā*) that is distinct from the manifested (*vyaṅgya*), he says: "the other," and so forth. "In this" means in the capacity. That very [capacity] is the [manifested]. "From that" means from the manifestor; there follows the consequence [that the capacity] would persist [even when the manifestor is absent], just like the [manifested object's] state of existence. As it has been said: "(1) If the state of existence were something else, then the substratum would produce that very [state]."
The same [consequences] that apply there would also follow here. "That" refers to the manifested object (*vyaṅgya*). Nor is the cause anything other than the manifested object;
since nothing at all is produced in the manifested object by its production, it is not required [as a cause]. By this, its status as a benefactor (*upakāritva*) is stated.
To deny that status on the grounds that it produces nothing at all is therefore contradictory.
Regarding what was stated—that "the producer itself is the manifester"—he points out its fallibility with the words "tattva" and so forth.
For smoke is not the producer of fire, yet because it is an effect, it is its manifester. By the word "etcetera," examples such as the crane [indicating] water are included.
He refutes this with the words "satyam" and so forth: "But fire does not [manifest itself] by depending on smoke as a logical mark."

It produces knowledge regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Why? (1) Because fire, as it actually exists and as intended to be the object of inference, does not directly produce [the cognition]. Otherwise, since it would possess the form of the particular characteristic of fire, there would be no distinction from its appearance in perception. By the words "merely," etc., he demonstrates that the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) alone is its direct producer. [The cognition] of the mark (*liṅga*)—
[It is] without grasping (*anupādāna*). It is not by the power of the object, nor by the power of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire.
What is the reason? Because even when that fire is absent—having already perished previously—the cognition of fire still occurs. How so? He says: "By way of succession," and so forth.
[It is] by means of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows the mark (*liṅga*), which is the recollection of the mark. For instance, in a certain place for a certain person...

For one who has seen smoke and for whom that smoke has vanished, once a conceptual recollection of smoke somehow arises there, and subsequently a recollection of its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) occurs, the knowledge of fire arises precisely through the sequence: "Smoke was here; therefore, fire was also here," [inferring] fire from smoke produced by fire.

By virtue of its capacity to produce a cognition of its own object, it must necessarily derive its self-acquisition from that [object], for it would otherwise depend upon something else; and this self-acquisition of the universal cannot possibly arise from anything whatsoever. Therefore—
Therefore, it is not manifested from anything whatsoever; nor has the universal attained the fitness for manifestation by an individual.

Now, if the universal exists as inherent in its own substratum, then it was stated that, depending on its inherence in its own substratum, it is the cause of cognition either within itself or elsewhere. In that case, this [inherence] is inherent in the relationship between the produced and the producer, characterized by the relation of substrate and that which resides therein (*āśrayāśrayi-lakṣaṇa*).

What cause of consciousness could depend on inherence? It would have to belong only to that which is produced by it, because the entity that is its cause exists prior [to the effect] and subsequently arises from it. Otherwise, if its existence were eternal, it would follow that consciousness would arise even before the occurrence of inherence.
For an individual is not the manifester of a universal through its own refinement; rather, as stated in the passage beginning, "How then?

Those [cognitions] which grasp it proceed exactly according to the state of things," and as will be demonstrated in the third chapter with the passage beginning, "And because it does not establish existence or non-existence, its capacity is based on appearance," [the individual is the manifester] by way of direct utility.

"By virtue of its capacity to produce a cognition that conforms to its own form"—the word "therein" (*tatra*) refers to the production of a cognition of itself as an object; "another" (*param*) refers to something such as a lamp; "from that" (*tataḥ*) refers to the dependence upon the lamp and so forth.
This is what is meant: not every manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is called a producer (*janaka*), but rather [only one] whose own form...
Only he who receives assistance from another that produces cognition [is manifested]; therefore, there is no deviation [in the rule].

Even a universal (*sāmānya*) depends upon a substratum (*āśraya*) for the production of the cognition of its own form; thus, it is accepted as being manifested. Consequently, the self (*ātman*) must be obtained as something capable of perception through its substratum. And this attainment of the self by the universal does not arise from anything else.
It is possible, because it is accepted as being eternal. "That" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*).
The opponent says, "Not at all," and so forth. The connection [of the sentence] is: "We say that its inherence in its own substratum is the manifestation.

If it is asked, "How is inherence in its own substratum a manifestation? he replies with the words beginning "svāśraya" (its own substratum). "That" refers to the universal. "Elsewhere" means in its own substratum.
The Master has stated: "We do not conceive of this very thing—being a substratum for that which provides no assistance"—and so forth, because he has already said this.

For one who asserts that [the universal] is the cause of cognition when it is inherent in its own substratum, whether in the self or elsewhere, intends the category of the universal to be the cause of cognition by depending upon its inherence in its own substratum.
And therefore, by means of that inherence in its own substratum...

The universal (*sāmānya*) would be the producer of [the cognition of] the produced [particular]. What is the reason? (1) Because its cause—the nature that is the cause of cognition—exists prior to its inherence in its own substratum; and because, once there is inherence in its own substratum, it exists subsequently due to that very inherence in its own substratum as the nature which is the cause of cognition. [This argument is] unestablished because the universal has the nature of producing cognition eternally.

To this he says: "Always," and so forth. "The existence of its own nature" means that even prior to its inherence (*samavāya*) in its own substratum, in a place devoid of manifestation, the universal alone [would produce cognition]; that is to say, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the arising of a cognition having the form of the universal. (148-4)

The opponent [argues]: "No," and so forth. The individual instance (*vyakti*) is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the universal (*sāmānya*); the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is the conferring of capacity (*yogyatādhāna*). For that reason—[as stated] in the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* (1.150)—it is not [the case] because of the refinement of the sense faculty (*indriya*). As for whoever [says this]—
O Queen Añjanā, the refinement belongs to the manifestation, not to the sense organ. || 150 ||

Because the cognition (*pratipatti*) is not different [in its nature] during the times of that [manifestation’s] presence and absence, the sense organ—when refined by collyrium and the like—acquires some excellence (*atiśaya*) in the act of cognition, as evidenced by the distinction between clear and unclear perception; for that which does not produce such [an effect] cannot be its refiner. This is not the case with the manifestation (*vyakti*), as follows:
There is no refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sense faculty, because there is no difference in the cognition [of the object] during the times when that [refinement] is present or absent.
For a refinement of the object would be beneficial by imparting its own particularity even when the sense faculty is unchanged;
it is not, however, a manifester (*vyañjikā*) of the universal, such that the universal would be produced by it. Rather, it is a manifester of the cognizer of that [universal].
"From the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that grasps the universal, [the object] is manifested"—this is the subject under discussion.
"As for the one who... and so forth is said by the Master (Ācārya). "Like collyrium and so forth" is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Just as the refinement of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*) is appropriate from the perspective of collyrium and the like, it is not so from the perspective of manifestation (*vyakti*). Why? Because of cognition—that is, of knowledge—[which is the manifestation].
This is a locative dual [ending] referring to the two times—the existence and non-existence—of the individual (vyakti) intended as the subject.

He explains this with the words "refined" (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: the sense organ, when refined by collyrium and other means, attains a certain excellence that has become its very nature. "In apprehension" (*pratipattau*) means for the sake of the cause of apprehension; that is, for the purpose of producing a specific cognition.

Up to this point: the locative case here is used according to the rule "the connection of an action [occurs] with the cause" (*nimittāt karma-saṃyoga*). If one asks why this is so, he says: "clear," and so forth.

The word "from comprehension" (*pratipatteḥ*) is to be connected by changing its case ending. For instance, a sense faculty impaired by cataracts and the like produces an indistinct cognition; that very same [faculty], when refined by collyrium and other means, is perceived clearly.
A refined sense faculty attains a specific excellence for the sake of cognition. Now,

if there were no difference in cognition resulting from [the application of] collyrium and the like, then those things which do not produce cognition— namely, collyrium and so forth— and those which do produce a difference in cognition would not be its refiners (*saṃskāraka*), because they do not refine the sense faculty, just as [collyrium does not refine] the eye.

The refinement [of the sense organ] does not arise from the manifesting [individual], as it does from the sense organ itself. What is the reason? It is because [the cognition remains the same] during both the time when that [manifestor] is present and the time when it is absent, and so forth. For instance, at a time when the manifesting individual cow is absent, the visual consciousness produced with respect to a tree or similar object is exactly the same even when that individual cow is present; if it were otherwise...
At the time of perception, cognition previously arose unclearly regarding trees and the like; subsequently, a refinement of the sense organ produced by the manifestation of a cow might be admitted.
Even if there were a refinement of the object, there would still be no difference in the resulting cognition regarding other objects; therefore, that [refinement of the sense organ] alone is logical.

If this is argued, he says: "The object," and so forth. Regarding the object—such as odor—and whatever refinement (*saṃskāra*) it may have, even though there is no distinction in the sense faculty itself; that is to say, even if there is indeed no distinction in the faculty with respect to its apprehension toward another object elsewhere, nevertheless, because it bestows a distinction upon that [faculty], it would be beneficial by bestowing a distinction upon the cognition that perceives the refined object. This is the case for the refinements of the sense faculties.
4. Regarding the investigation of the universal (*sāmānya*):

If it is argued that [the universal] is beneficial because it bestows the capacity for perception upon what was previously unperceivable, then why does it not differentiate [its objects], given that cognition arises precisely from the perception of each individual sense-object?

Even if there were a fixed restriction to a single [individual], one would not perceive other universals, because [the cognition] is refined by that individual; and upon perceiving that [one], there would either never be a determination of the universals indicated by it, or there would be another [indeterminate cognition].

Since that [cognition] is undifferentiated, there is no distinction among those [objects]; therefore, the refinement of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*) is not possible for the manifestation [of cognition].
Thus, the connection [of the sentence] is: "The refinement of the sense organ would not be beneficial.
This is what is meant: objects are indeed restricted; they are the means of producing a cognition that possesses only their own form.

This is not the case for that which is associated with another form (*ākāra*). Therefore, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the object is not contradictory, because it produces a specific cognition of its own particular object due to its restricted nature. However, since the sense faculty (*indriya*) is an equal means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) regarding the various objects it perceives, the refinement of the faculty would result in a differentiation of cognition across all those objects it perceives. Thus, there is no differentiation of manifestation (*vyaktibheda*) for the sense faculty.

It deposits a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) for the production of a cognition with a clear form regarding every visible object that is graspable by the sense-faculties. However, if it is argued that the particular individual (*vyakti*) is beneficial [to the cognition] because it bestows the power of vision upon the sense-faculty with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*), which was previously invisible prior to the arising of the individual— then, precisely because of this perception of what is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), the refinement of the sense-faculty is clearly established.
It is understood that what was previously incapable due to the absence of a manifest individual (*vyakti*), becomes capable upon the presence of that [individual].

Thus, how can that which reveals the object called "universal" (*sāmānya*)—which is distinct from individuals and beyond the senses—not be a differentiator of cognition everywhere? The meaning is that it is indeed a differentiator.
This is what is being said: even regarding a visible object, because it bestows the power of perceiving a clear form upon that which is otherwise indistinct, it is—*añjasā*—[the cause of clarity].
The refinement of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*) produced by a lamp is observed everywhere to differentiate the cognition regarding an object perceivable by that sense organ.

What then [is the point]? The implication is that it should likewise reveal other supersensible objects (*atīndriya-artha*), such as atoms (*paramāṇu*). [Objection: One brings about the refinement of the sense organ for the sake of perceiving the universal (*sāmānya*) alone, not for the sake of distinguishing between individuals (*vyakti-bheda*).

If it is argued that there is thus no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he says "one," and so forth. If one accepts that the refinement of the sense faculty (*indriya-saṃskāra*) is restricted to a single universal (*sāmānya*) to be perceived, then the refinement of the sense faculty would be the revealer of whatever other universals— such as existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so on— are inherent (*samaveta*) in that very same particular (*vyakti-bheda*), such as a brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*).

It would not be so; yet it is accepted. If it is argued that the refinement of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*) is for the sake of perceiving all universals (*sāmānya*) inherent in the self, and not for the sake of a single one alone, [the author] says: "And the restriction," etc. "In the perception of those" means in the perception of those [universals] inherent in the individual (*vyakti*).

Regarding the perception of those universals (*sāmānya*) which are manifested by that [particular]: "in those manifested by it" means in those manifested by that particular (*vyakti*). And it is observed that when a substance is seen from a distance, even though there is certainty regarding its being a substance or an object, there is no certainty regarding its being a cow or the like. If it is argued that "the specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*) for the perception of that which is not certain has not been cultivated," he replies: "there would be no certainty of one [thing]."

The connection [is as follows]: the word "one" (eka) has the sense of "other" (anya); it refers not only to that which is not determined, but also to another thing that is intended to be determined, such as substantiality (dravyatva), and so forth.
The *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (1950):
It is illogical for a sense faculty to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

This is because it would fall away from its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), namely, the nature of producing cognition with respect to the manifestation of the universal. Thus, [the sense faculty] is not conditioned.

If it is argued that the arising of consciousness is independent of the sense-faculties [alone], but because it requires the cooperation of conditioned faculties, it is not capable when solitary—then what is the meaning of this "cooperation" for that which is incapable of receiving any added excellence (*atiśaya*)? For entities are impermanent; they depend upon auxiliaries by virtue of obtaining a distinct nature through them. For whatever... [of these]...
The producer-nature (janakātmā) is indeed that very thing which, at that time, arises from that; for the producer-nature is mutually dependent.
How could that intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of a mark (liṅga) which is not established by another universal (sāmānya) be dependent on the sense organs?
For that which is not its intrinsic nature could not possibly exist as such. [This is] the effect of sense organs refined by the individual (vyakti).

There would be no ascertainment. Why? Because that individual, being non-distinct from those universals inherent in its own self, lacks any differentiation among them; for that individual is not proximate to some [universals] and not to others. Consequently, there would either be ascertainment of the universal in its entirety, or none at all—such, then, is the case regarding the sense-contact with the individual.
It has been explained that [the universal] cannot exist as a substrate (*āśraya*).

Now, even granting that it does exist, it is said: "From manifestation," and so forth. Since, according to both positions, the universal has the nature of producing cognition by virtue of its manifestation, [it follows that] from that production of cognition, its own nature— *Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly. The full passage likely continues to argue that once the universal has produced a cognition, it would either have to produce another cognition—which is impossible—or cease to be a cause, thereby losing its status as a universal.*
For it is not logical for that which is already capable to depend on auxiliary causes for its production. That universal whose auxiliary cause is the refined sense organ is described as such;

because of the existence of that [refinement], [the universal would produce]. But since the universal is eternal and cannot have any excellence added to it, what could this "auxiliary" mean? Nothing at all.

By the words "it is impermanent" (*anityā*) and so forth, he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). This is because [the entity] acquires a specific nature from its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). Regarding the word "that" (*tam*): it refers to the auxiliary cause. Why? Because that self (*ātman*) which is the producer of these momentary things did not exist prior to the proximity of the auxiliaries; it exists only at that time of the proximity of the auxiliaries. Therefore, [it arises] from the auxiliary cause.

This is because [the effect] arises from their presence. "Of these" refers to those things that are momentary. Now, one might ask: how can even momentary things depend upon auxiliary causes for the attainment of a specific nature? For among co-existent factors, there is no mutual relationship of benefactor and beneficiary. Furthermore, regarding the moment that is produced, at the time of its existence or non-existence— [The text continues: ...there is no dependence on anything else. Therefore, the production of the effect occurs solely from the specific nature of the cause itself; it does not arise from something other than that. Thus, the capacity of the cause is established as being restricted to its own specific nature. Consequently, the objection that "the capacity would be either eternal or non-existent" is refuted. This is because the capacity is not distinct from the nature of the thing itself. It is precisely this nature that is called "capacity. Since this nature is not different from the thing, it is not eternal. Nor is it non-existent, because it exists as long as the thing itself exists. Therefore, the capacity is established as being neither eternal nor non-existent. As for the claim that "the capacity is not observed," that too is incorrect. For we do observe the capacity in the case of seeds and the like, which produce sprouts and so forth. Thus, the capacity is indeed established. As for the statement that "the capacity is not perceived because it is subtle," that is also untenable. For if it were subtle, it would follow that it could never be perceived at all, just as the universal (*sāmānya*) is never perceived. Therefore, since the capacity is perceived through its effects, it is not subtle. Consequently, the objection that "the capacity is unproven" is refuted. Thus, the capacity is proven by its effects. For we perceive the capacity in the case of fire and the like, which possess the capacity to burn and so forth. Therefore, the capacity is indeed proven. The statement that "dependence consists in being removable" is incorrect, for it is said that one depends on that which is beneficial; this is not a fault. This is stated with reference to existence (*sattā*). Therefore he says:

"Their mutual dependence consists precisely in their being produced. "Without having reached another" means without having reached a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*); [it refers to] its own nature (*tatsvabhāva*).

[It would possess] a capable nature. For that universal, when isolated and devoid of auxiliary causes, its nature—which previously was not to produce cognition—could not possibly arise again. The word "not" (na hi) connects [to this]. The implication is that it is because [the universal] is eternal.
Yan-gar-ba. 4. Regarding the investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*):
since the universal is a cooperative cause, it is the cause of cognition. If this is so, then the universal would be said to be the effect of the individual (*vyakti*) through a mediated succession.
Moreover:
"And if it is maintained that universals possess the state of being possessed of universals by virtue of their manifestors... (151)

A lamp or similar object, being the manifestor of that which possesses "cowness" (gotva) and so forth, would thereby become the possessor of that [universal]. For whatever is a cause of cognition is indeed the manifestor of that [object]; if this were the case for cowness and the like, then even a lamp would be a cause of the cognition of cowness and so forth. This is because the perception of an object by the eye depends upon the refinement [of the sense organ] by light.
Therefore, by that [manifestation], a lamp or similar object would indeed possess the universal "cowness" and so forth.

For there is no manifestation of a universal through an individual other than its being a cause for cognition; this is because it is impossible to impart any excellence of intrinsic nature [to the universal].

Furthermore, (1) since the opponent has accepted that the sense faculty is refined by the individual instance (*vyakti*)—on the grounds that when there is a refinement of the sense faculty by the individual instance, the universal (*sāmānya*) produced thereby [is perceived]—nevertheless, he states [the following] to show that the consequence of being produced by the individual instance still follows: "The individual instance," and so forth. That which acts as its auxiliary (*tatsahakāri*) is the universal, acting as an auxiliary to the sense faculty refined by the individual instance.

If it is accepted that [the individual] is the cause of cognition, then since the sense organ is the effect of the manifestation, it would follow that the universal is an indirect effect of the individual. (146–50) Let it be granted for the sake of argument that the individual is the manifestor of the universal; nevertheless, it is not logical for this [individual] to possess a genus (*jāti*).
He says "lest there be an over-extension" (*tiprasaṅgāt*), beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth.

If it is maintained that the individuals (*vyakti-bheda*) which manifest universals (*jāti*)— that is, generalities (*sāmānya*)— possess those universals, then a lamp or other such manifestor of "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like would, by virtue of being a manifestor, itself come to possess that cowness and so forth, just like a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) or similar individual.
The meaning is that the substratum of "cowness" (gotva) has been established.

He explains this with the words beginning with "yo hi" (for he...). Even for lamps and the like, there exists the state of being a cause for cognition regarding [universals] such as cowness which are to be manifested.
If one asks how this is so, he says: "light," and so forth. Therefore, light possesses the status of being a cause for cognition.

The word "thence" (*tataḥ*) means because it is the cause of cognition. Regarding the phrase "lamps and so forth" (*pradīpādayaḥ*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the refinement of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) and other such factors, since these too are causes of cognition. If it is argued that the manifestation of the universal (*sāmānya*) occurs as something distinct from its individual manifestation (*vyakti*), whereas this is not the case for lamps and the like, he replies with the words "for not," and so on. Even from the individual manifestation, the universal—[is manifested...]

Indeed, there is no manifestation other than that which serves as the cause for cognition. For if the manifestation were to produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the universal, it would not be by means of the individual (*vyakti*), but rather by means of a lamp or the like; in that case, there would be a distinction [between the two], but such is not the case. This is because it is impossible to impart an excellence to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the universal, owing to its eternity—this is the intended meaning. [This applies to] inherence (*samavāya*).
And so forth. Furthermore, the universal "cowness" (gotva) inheres in the individual [cow], not in things such as a lamp; for that [lamp] is not produced by it—that is, not produced by the universal.

In the *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṭṭīkā* (1952), it is stated that if [it is argued that] inherence (*samavāya*) is the manifestation [of the universal], then the answer to that is: "Because of the application and so forth of that inherence. Even for these [universals] which are inherent, there is no possibility of being perceived after [the manifestation], just as before; nothing at all [changes].

The particularity (*viśeṣa*) is not the cause of cognition. If it were the cause of cognition solely by virtue of inherence (*samavāya*), then the same undesirable consequence would apply to lamps and so forth as well.
Therefore, the universal does not possess the property of being "resided in" (*ādheyatā*); nor is it the cause of cognition, because the manifestation (*vyakti*) does not reside in its substratum.
For this very reason—[it is asked] whether the universal (jāti) exists for those [schools] according to whom it is either different from or non-different from the individual (vyakti). // 152 //
How can there be cognitions of a universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) regarding those individuals which are unprecedented?

The word "tu" (but) is used here for the sake of emphasis, [implying] that [the universal] indeed exists as a real entity (*vastusatī*). For it has been stated: "What is this inherence (*samavāya*) between the two producers [of the cognition], each by its own power?"
Granted that it has arisen;

nevertheless, for this universal, there is with the individual only an inherence (*samavāya*) and no other specific quality characterized by the production of cognition. "As before" means as prior to the inherence with the individual.

Even subsequently, although there is no difference whatsoever in the universal even when it inheres in an individual, if it is argued that the production of a cognition of its own object occurs solely by the power of inherence, he says: "Inherence alone," and so forth. When the universal is accepted as a cause of cognition, [it would have to produce the cognition] of that which inheres in it—namely, the substratum (samavāyin) in which it inheres. The universal...

If this were admitted, then for those things—such as color and so forth—which are inherent in atoms, there would follow the consequence of their being visible, even though they are distinct from the universal; for since inherence is a single entity, it is without distinction everywhere. For just as inherence alone reveals the universal, even though it is beyond the senses, so too [would it reveal the other qualities].

Why then does it not also manifest the color and other qualities residing in the atoms? Since this fault exists in the position that [the universal] inheres [in the individual], therefore, in the case of a universal, its status as a manifester is simply its being the cause of cognition. And since this nature of being a manifester is equally present in the case of a lamp and so forth, the same undesirable consequence follows: that [the universal] would be identical with the possessor of that [universal], such as "cowness" and so on. (150–51)

Therefore, because of that, there is no inherence (*ādheyatā*) of the universal in its own substratum, nor is there a manifestation of the individual by its own substratum; thus, the occurrence of the universal in its own substratum does not exist. Consequently, due to this non-occurrence, the universal cannot be the cause of a single-form cognition regarding the diversity of individuals. For that which does not reside in something cannot, by means of its own occurrence therein, [produce such a cognition].
It is joined with the cause of cognition;

for this very reason, because of the non-pervasion of a single universal across multiple instances. Whether the genus is different from the individual or not different—if, for those disputants, [the genus exists] either in individuals that have just arisen now or in those produced later—then [the following applies].

Regarding the phrase "while they are being perceived": the word *tu* (but) is to be understood as following the word *śabda* (sound), serving the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). For this very reason, he says: "it exists indeed," and so forth. This means that for those [Buddhists] for whom the universal (*jāti*) is not substantially real (*vastusatī*), it exists only through its own capacity by way of its own cognition.

"Elsewhere" means while producing a cognition in the difference of individuals (*vyaktibheda*). Of what kind [is this cognition]? It conforms to its own nature (*svarūpānukāriṇī*), that is, it follows a single form (*ekarūpānugatā*). 4. Examination of the Universal (*sāmānyacintā*).

It does not depend on a connection with that [object] except insofar as it produces a cognition that conforms to its own nature; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, for an existing universal, such a connection is impossible under either the view that it is identical to or different from the particular, because what is perceived in one place cannot be perceived elsewhere if it already exists. (153)
