For that cognition which grasps a real entity must pertain to a single existing thing; it would have to leap over to another individual, and in that case, there would be a perception elsewhere of something previously seen.
[But this is impossible] because if there were non-difference, there would be no persistence (anvaya), and even if there were difference, there would be no basis for connection.
There is no production of what does not exist.

That which produces a cognition depends upon a relation with its object; for if it could produce a cognition of its own form without a relation, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). (151–52)

The phrase "it [the connection] also" refers to the connection of a universal (*sāmānya*) that exists—that is, is present—with another individual (*vyaktyantara*). This is impossible under both the view that [the universal and the individual] are identical (*tattvapakṣa*) and the view that they are different (*anyattvapakṣa*). Why? Because it is impossible to perceive in one case a distinction between individuals that is either a separate entity (*arthāntarabhūta*) or not a separate entity (*anarthāntara*), and because such a perception cannot occur in another individual. He proves this very point with the words beginning "for that... (*sā hi...*).
For that cognition, which grasps a real entity and apprehends a real universal, is unitary; having arisen with respect to one particular individual,
it would "leap over" or proceed to another individual— that is to say, it would also grasp that other individual through the form of the universal—
if some real entity were perceived there in that one particular individual as a universal.
"In another place" means that where there is a difference between individuals, it [the universal] must be distributed; and that observation occurs elsewhere.

The connection is that this is not possible for a "real" (*sat*) universal, that is, one that is an ontological entity (*vastubhūta*). What is the reason? Because if it were admitted to be non-different from its substratum, there would be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For that which is not distinct from a single [substratum], being of the same nature as it, cannot be another.

[The opponent] replies: "Even though the universal (*sāmānya*) is distinct from its substratum (*āśraya*), it does not fail to produce a cognition of its own form in another individual (*vyakti*). For the status of being a substratum has already been refuted by the preceding negation of the relationship between locus and located (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*). If, because the universal is distinct [from the individuals], it does not generate a cognition of its own form in another individual due to a lack of connection, then [the same would apply] to the very first individual as well."
If it is argued that [the universal] is similar to the individual, why say "in new individuals" when one should simply say "in individuals"?

Likewise, it must also be stated that "because what is seen in one place cannot be seen elsewhere," for even in a single case, seeing [the universal] is impossible without a relation between the different individuals.

This is true. There is no fault, for this was stated while provisionally accepting that position. Furthermore, as for one who thinks: "(1) In the positions of identity or difference, the perception of something else is not possible for the universal; however, for us, the universal is indeed both distinct and non-distinct. For instance: [as follows].

A universal cannot exist without particularity, for it would be like the horn of a hare. When a variegated object appears simultaneously, it possesses unity with respect to itself and multiplicity with respect to some other aspect.

For intrinsic nature (svabhāva) does not transcend either identity or difference. This is because that which has not become [the other], such as form (rūpa), does not escape being different [from it]. This very difference from form is that wherein it is not itself, unlike any other mode, because there would be no distinction.
And if that were non-different, then it would be that very thing; otherwise, if it were not that, it would follow that it is different, like a distinct entity.
Nor can there be an entry of another individual into the nature of a single entity, because that would entail the consequence of it being a non-individual. Of that [nature]...

"Therefore, from that which is neither distinct nor non-distinct, there can be no cognition of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), nor of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); at that time, all distinctions such as otherness and non-otherness would simply vanish.
To refute that, he says: "For its own nature (*svabhāva*)," and so forth. From its own nature, it is neither identity nor otherness.
The connection is with the word "surpassing" (*laṅghayataḥ*).

Now, one might object: even though there is no difference in terms of place, time, or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), a distinction between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) is nonetheless accepted on the basis of their forms being respectively inclusive (*anugata*) and exclusive (*vyāvṛtta*). To this, he says: "[... of the inclusive form, which is the intrinsic nature, [there is] the exclusionary form which does not belong to that..."

Because one cannot deviate from the distinctness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The meaning is that a universal (*sāmānya*), which is of a pervasive form and distinct from particular forms (*viśeṣarūpa*) that are excluded [from others], must indeed be something else. How is it that being "not of that form" (*atadrūpatva*) is precisely "being other" (*anyattva*)? To this he says: "This very... and so forth. "Wherein that is not" means "that which is not of that form. This alone is the definition of being other.

This is the meaning. [The suffix] *vati* is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), as in the case of "having another form. For instance, suffering is distinct from pleasure; it is considered suffering because its nature is not that of pleasure. By this much, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been stated by means of the characteristic of otherness (*anyattva*) for that which does not possess that nature. And since this characteristic of otherness is without distinction, it applies even to the intended universal (*sāmānya*).

By this, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) has been stated. Now, the formal argument (*prayoga*) follows: Whatever, while being a real entity (*vastutva*), does not have that [specific] form, is necessarily other than it—just as suffering is other than pleasure. Since the universal (*sāmānya*) is accepted as being a real entity while not having the form of the individual (*avyaktirūpa*), its otherness is established through its not having that form; thus, because the conventional usage of "otherness" is what is to be proven, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). In this way, first of all, if the universal does not have that form, it is indeed other.

(1) Now, if otherness is not admitted, then it follows that [the universal] is identical [to the individual]; thus he says: "And that," and so forth. If it were non-different from the individual, then that very thing would be the universal, having the same form as the individual. For if it were not of that nature—that is, if it did not have the form of the individual—it would follow that it is other [than the individual], just like any other distinct entity. This has been stated immediately prior.
"Let it be that the universal is non-different [from the individual]; nevertheless, it will still follow after another individual. To this he says: "And not one," and so forth.
This means that for that which has the nature of a single individual, there can be no entry into or following after another individual—that is to say, no sharing in the nature of another individual.
Why? Because it would follow that the thing being perceived would itself become another individual. If it were variegated (*śābaleya*)...
If the universal were of the same nature as the Bāhuleya cow, such that it were the very self of the Bāhuleya, then the Bāhuleya would be born as nothing other than a Śābaleya;
for, due to its non-distinction from the universal whose nature is the Śābaleya, it would be like a Śābaleya itself. How, then, could it possess the status of being a different individual?
Therefore, [the cognition] is "concomitant" (anvayinī), meaning it follows along, with respect to that universal which is not distinct from the individual.

Because it has no locus anywhere; because there is no other relation—such as the state of being the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), or any other—since even for another [entity], there is no relation with anything else, and because from the absence of a relation, the consequence would follow that it generates cognition [of everything].
Therefore, by perceiving one thing, one who seeks the existence of what occurs in one place in another [place] must seek its identity or its difference.
It is not logical to say that it "overcomes" [the object].
Therefore, this uniform cognition, which is a latent impression (vāsanā) deposited regarding objects despite their actual difference in nature, is nothing but an error.

It has been established that the nature of latent impression (*vāsanā*) is its substratum (*āśraya*). How is it that words denoting effects such as *pradhāna* and *Īśvara* apply non-differently to entities that are distinct from those [effects]?

Nor is it the case—given the subject at hand—that there can be a recurring cognition (*anvayinī buddhiḥ*) based on a universal (*sāmānya*) that is distinct [from the individuals]. Why? Because of that [universal]...

Because a universal (*sāmānya*) that is distinct [from individuals] cannot function in any particular instance without a substratum, since its functioning is impossible without a relation; and because the relation between the manifested and the manifestor, as well as the relation of container and contained, has been refuted by such statements as, "Functioning is being contained and manifestation; these are not tenable in that case. Therefore, the universal must be something else.

If it is argued that "there will be a relation for that which possesses it," he replies with the words "of another as well," and so forth. The word "ādi" (etcetera) in the phrase "vyaṅgyavyañjakabhāvāder" (from the state of being the manifested and the manifestor, etc. functions as an ablative. By the word "ādi," the inclusion of the relation of locus and located is intended. [The meaning is: even for some other relation besides these two previously refuted relations, [the universal] would have a connection toward the manifestation.

Because [the universal] exists. What is the reason? Because it is eternal; since the universal cannot be assisted by any particular individual, there is no restriction [upon it]. For it has been stated that there can be no relation for that which lacks restriction.
By this, the portion of the verse beginning with "even if there is otherness, because of the substratum" (anyattve 'py āśrayāt) is explained. (152–53)

If it is argued that even a universal (*sāmānya*) which lacks a real connection produces a cognition that conforms to its own nature among individuals, he replies with the words "Because of the lack of connection," and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has no connection" (*asambandha*). The meaning is that there would be a cognition of everything everywhere. "That" refers to this [consequence], namely, the universal (*sāmānya*) or the proponent; by the perception of a single universal...
For this reason: that which subsists in one particular individual, such as a brindled cow (*śābaleya*), must also subsist in another individual;

since a universal is intended to be a real entity (*vastu*) distinct from its individuals, its identity with or difference from those individuals cannot be maintained, as there is no other possible mode of existence for a real entity. Furthermore, the fault already mentioned applies; thus, it is untenable [to claim] that [the universal] follows after a universal that is a real entity.
Regarding the term "knowledge":

for this reason, this cognition—which is uniform and of a single form—regarding objects that are mutually distinct, is nothing but an error (*bhrānti*), because it functions by superimposing non-difference upon things that are different. To the question, "From where, then, has it arisen?", he says: "Conceptualization," and so forth. [It arises from] the dissimilar...

That which is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of objects as excluded [from others], which by its very nature gives rise to a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of such a kind, and from which [the cognition] arises—this has already been stated; thus he says: "The differentiation of entities," and so forth. This refers to the differentiation of entities—that is, of their effects—from those that do not have those effects; and it refers to the nature of that latent impression which is deposited by the experience of such [differentiated] things.

And it has been established previously that its own-nature (*svabhāva*) is its basis; in that regard, the difference in existence (*bhāvabheda*) is the cause through a mediated succession (*pāramparyeṇa*).
38ay mala v p pramāṇavāttikasvavṛttiṭīkā.

These [conceptual cognitions] also, being embellished by the latencies (*vāsanā*) within the continuum just like linguistic conventions, function—by means of an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of what is not as it appears—toward an object manifested in conceptual consciousness. This occurs because, upon seeing all objects, they determine them to be such without depending on their actual distinctions; for these conceptual constructions arise through the power of their material cause (*upādāna*).

For in those things that are not as they appear, there is no distinction or non-distinction whatsoever belonging to a universal (*sāmānya*). Nevertheless, through another conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of them as being so, a distinction may arise for cognizers by virtue of their own mental determination (*adhyavasāya*). If it is argued that the universal arises from that very determination, then two things are presented: the latent impression (*vāsanā*) and its nature (*prakṛti*) as direct [causes]. If it is the case that only the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is denoted by words, how then is it...?

Regarding the passage beginning with "dānīm" (now): "Words such as *pradhānakārya* and *īśvarakārya*" refers to the world being the effect of *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and the effect of *īśvara* (the Lord).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of terms such as "the transformation of *śabdabrahman*" and so forth.

"Among entities" (*bhāveṣu*) refers to internal and external things. "Those whose distinctions are not of that nature" (*atadbhūta*) means those whose differences do not consist of the nature of being effects of *pradhāna*, *īśvara*, and so on.

Thus it has been said. Even if there were a distinction among them based on their non-primary effects, then there would be a distinction consisting of their primary effects and so forth; and that very [distinction] is the non-distinction of all things. By means of that non-distinction, which is without a specific cause, they exist everywhere. Yet, according to the view of the proponent of *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others), that [non-distinction] does not exist, because entities consist of non-primary effects and so forth. And therefore, how—

The intention is that they do not indeed function without distinction toward such things; therefore, the point is that the determination of apoha would be non-pervasive. He refutes this with the words "They too," and so forth. The connection is as follows: those words for effects such as *pradhāna* and so on also function toward what appears in conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*). To the question "How? he says: "By convention," and so forth. [This refers to] in the object, which is not thus...
In reality, there is a convention based on the power of desire which designates the world as the "primary effect. By that [convention], the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is deposited;
and although the objects exist within perceptions and experiences, it disregards their difference—that is, the difference from the "non-primary effects" inherent in the things themselves.
Even if the perception of these non-primary effects occurs through the nature of the object, nevertheless, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the thing—
The meaning is "without regard for" (*anapekṣya*). This is because of such a determination (*adhyavasāya*);

that is, due to determining even those entities that are not primary effects as being primary effects according to convention. Consciousness (*caitanya*) is imagined by the Sāṃkhya as a primary effect of that which is not so [i.e., not a primary effect].
By the exclusion of that [consciousness], there are no primary effects. Thus, it refers to the object appearing in that conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*).
The meaning is that this very [word] is "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) by way of the exclusion of heterogeneous things. He asks, "Of what nature are those words?

and answers with the passage beginning "possessing causes" (*sopādāna*), etc. They have arisen from that conceptual construction whose origin or production is due to the strength of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) which is the cause of that conceptual construction.

This is what is meant: even if there is indeed no such real distinction among things, nevertheless, exclusion (*anyāpoha*)—which is merely superimposed by conceptual construction—is the factor for the operation of words; therefore, it does not suffer from the fault of being non-pervasive. [Objection: If words such as "Pradhāna" and "effect" function without distinction, why is a universal (*sāmānya*) that exists as a real entity not accepted in those things?

If it is asked: "Why not? [the author] says: "For it is not," and so forth. The point is that since there is no manifestation (*vyakti*) in those things which are superimposed as being the effects of the *pradhāna* but are not actually so, the universal (*sāmānya*) is absent.

If it is asked why this is so, [the answer is: even by that [universal], a distinction (*bheda*) must necessarily be accepted therein as being inseparable; that very [distinction] constitutes the effect of the universal.

"Enough; thus, the conceptualization of a universal is purposeless. If this increase of a universal does not function as a real object whether entities exist or do not exist—due to its being a cognitive distortion (viplava)—then for the proponent of the exclusion of others (anyāpohavādin), there is no such fault. He says "tathā" and so forth: [this refers to] the conceptualization of [the world] as being the effect of Primordial Matter (pradhāna) and so on.

The meaning is "not so. The distinction—that is, the exclusion—of other effects, such as those that are non-principal, would occur by virtue of the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of cognizers who superimpose upon things the status of being principal effects.
Precisely by virtue of that conceptual determination of the cognizer, there arises the notion of recurrence (*anuvṛttipratyaya*) with respect to [individuals] such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*).
If it is asked, "Why is the universal not the sign?

this is not so. Because even by that proponent of the universal who postulates a universal, a distinction from heterogeneous things within those such as the *śābaleya* cow must necessarily be admitted as being inseparable [from it]; otherwise, the existence of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth would be unestablished.

That very particularity (bheda) alone is capable of being sufficient for the operation of a single term and so forth, which is characterized by non-difference with respect to the universal (sāmānya). Thus, the postulation of a universal is purposeless.
This is what is meant: just as even in the case of entities that are effects of Primordial Matter (pradhāna), [the term "primordial matter" and so on applies] even without a universal—

Words for effects and the cognitions thereof proceed with a single form; likewise, why is it not accepted that in the case of cows and so forth, the words "cow" and so forth, and the cognitions thereof, proceed with a single form? Why [insist] on a real universal, whether imagined or otherwise? For even by others, the occurrence of non-different denotation and cognition among many things is observed even in the absence of a universal.
As it has been stated by Bhaṭṭa Uddyotakara:

"Therefore, the word for a universal (sāmānya-śabda) is based either on the occurrence of one [entity] in many different things, or on the production of a single cognition regarding existence (sattā) and so forth. (Ślokavārttika, Ākṛtivāda, verse 24).

Therefore, this is the meaning: just as the word "universal" (*sāmānya*) and the cognition thereof apply to [categories] such as existence (*sattva*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*), each individually, by virtue of their inherence in multiple objects—even in the absence of a [higher-order] universal—yet the state of inhering in multiple objects is not itself a universal that exists identically both in existence and in substantiality; for it is stated that "universals are devoid of universals."

Nor does the application of those two (the word and the cognition) occur through metaphorical usage, because they are grasped by an unerring intellect. Therefore, just as their application to "existence" and so forth occurs without a universal, so too [is it] with respect to the *śābaleya* and other individuals without a universal:
just as the *śābaleya* is excluded from non-cows, so the *bāhuleya* is excluded from non-cows, and so the *khaṇḍa* is excluded from non-cows. Thus...
The meaning is: why is the occurrence of distinct designations and cognitions not accepted?

It might be argued: (1) a cognition of a universal is indeed desired as the object in all cases; however, without a universal, there would be no non-discrepancy in some instances. To this, he says "yadi" and so forth. The word "yadi" is intended to indicate an admission (*abhyupagama*).

If it is admitted that this [cognition] has no object whatsoever: "when things exist" means when entities excluded from non-cows are present; "when things do not exist" means when entities such as Primordial Matter (pradhāna) or God (īśvara) are non-existent in reality because they are not effects [of anything]. There is no concern for this distinction. In some cases, there is non-discrepancy (avisaṃvāda) of this [cognition] regarding a real entity; thus, there is no grasping of something as it truly is.
This is due to necessity, like the perception of direct experience. We shall demonstrate—and have already demonstrated—that [this cognition] occurs even in the absence of such [external] existence.

Furthermore, although this [cognition] has difference as its object, it frequently arises through the force of perceiving distinct objects, because of the determination of their existence within them. Thus—

The cognition of a universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) is meaningful [only in a conventional sense], because it apprehends what is unreal; for that which is superimposed by it—an undifferentiated form—does not exist externally among external objects. Since this is a distortion (*viplava*) consisting of nothing but error (*bhrānti*), there is no concern whatsoever regarding the determination of an object for this cognition of a universal, which is itself devoid of an object. If every cognition of a universal is erroneous, how...

He states that there is correspondence with reality (*vastu-saṃvāda*) through inference (*anumāna*), beginning with the words "in some cases" (*kvacit*). In some instance, there is non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*) of this cognition from its object, because [the object] is connected as cause and effect, as previously described. And this has already been explained [in verse 1.183]: "Where there is a connection with reality, as in the aforementioned inference... and so forth. It is not [otherwise].

Because such a thing—which is of an undifferentiated nature and graspable by inference—is present through its inclusion within the real entity (*vastu*), there is no discrepancy between the inferential conceptualization and the real entity. "Like perception" is a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). What is the reason?

It is because [the cognition] occurs even when the object is not present in that way; that is, even when the object has passed away, it exists through a succession [of moments] by following the logical mark (*liṅga*).

Or rather, even in the absence of such [external] existence—that is, even in the case of an entity devoid of a universal—the cognition possessing a non-differentiated form exists; thus we shall explain. And this has already been explained previously [in the passage ending]: "The capacity [of a cause] is established because it conforms to the presence and absence [of the effect]. (1)

If a universal cognition (*sāmānyabuddhi*) apprehends distinct entities as non-distinct by superimposing upon them its own form (*svākāra*), thereby conceiving them in a positive manner (*vidhirūpatayā*), how can it be said that its object is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)? To this he says: "By the power of the perception of distinct things," and so forth. This means: by the force of the experience of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as excluded from those of a different class (*vijātīya*).

The word "from arising" (*utpatteḥ*) is to be supplied [to the sūtra]. The inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahula-grahaṇa*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that conceptual cognition (*vikalpa-buddhi*) functions even in the absence of a real entity, as in the case of a "hare's horn" and the like. This is because, among those distinct particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of existence; that is, by means of the non-difference of its own form, there is a determination of its own nature.
The meaning is that activity proceeds by unifying the perceived object and the conceptual construction. This is because, through the power of perceiving a distinct thing...

Cognition does not arise [as something distinct], yet once arisen, it apprehends those very same distinct objects as being non-different from its own form. Therefore, "having difference as its object" means having distinct objects as its object. It is indeed logical that conceptual constructions such as impermanence and so forth—which arise through the gateway of perceiving a real entity—have difference as their object, because they are produced by the power of perceiving a real entity. However, this is not the case where there is no such distinct real entity, as for example:

Regarding the conceptualizations of permanence and so forth, as well as the conceptualizations of a rabbit’s horn and so forth—if it is asked how these can have difference as their object, he says: "In that way, [regarding] existence," and so on. Just as cognitions of impermanence and so forth, which arise through the force of the experience of grasping the intrinsic nature of distinct entities, function by determining their own internal reflections as being distinct existences and thus have difference as their object—in the same way, [the others do as well].

IIIa. Even when there is the conceptualization of an entity (*bhāvakalpanā*), while the conceptualization that determines a distinct external entity occurs within one's own manifestation, and while there is a distinct object, [the term] "elsewhere" (*aparatra*) refers to non-existent things such as eternal *pradhāna*, effects, and so forth, as well as things like a rabbit’s horn. 4. Regarding the investigation of the universal (*sāmānya*): because it exists elsewhere even when there is the conceptualization of an entity, and furthermore, this non-apprehension of universals [occurs] in its own substratum—

Because conceptual constructions (vikalpa) such as the eternal *pradhāna* or the horns of a hare have as their object only difference (*bheda*), they reside solely in the distinction between individual instances (*vyakti*) within their own substratum, and not in a place devoid of individuals. As Bhaṭṭa has said:
"Since a universal (*sāmānya*) is perceived only in individuals and not in the space between them..."
For some do not accept that which is called a "universal" (sāmānya) as being like space (ākāśa). (Ākṛti 25) Since its inherence in each individual is observed, it will not be negated.
And this being so, there will be no multiplicity [of the universal] through a single cognition. (Vana 30)

"Just as a single individual, though perceived again and again even at different times, remains non-different [from itself] while residing in various distinct substrata," so says Uddyotakara: "By whom is the all-pervasiveness of the universal (*jāti*) accepted, such that [it would reside] in a lump of clay..."

Cowness (*gotva*) might exist in a clay cow; however, because its occurrence (*vṛtti*) extends everywhere within its own domain, it is said to be "all-pervading" (*sarvagata*). But what, then, is the own-domain of cowness? It is wherever cowness exists. And where does cowness exist? Wherever cowness—

The cognition of conformity arises from the sign (nimittonuvṛttipratyaya). But where does the universal "cowness" (gotva) produce this cognition of conformity? It produces it in that which is its means of realization (sādhana). But what is the purpose of realizing the cow when cowness is eternal? It is that by which [cowness] is manifested. For there is no manifestation of cowness apart from the object possessing the hump and other [characteristics]. Nor is cowness a separate entity from the individuals, since it is not perceived in the intervals between individuals.
When the Buddhist says "because of apprehension," he should be questioned regarding this "interval between two individual objects" (*piṇḍāntarāla*): what is this interval?

Is it space (*ākāśa*), or rather non-existence (*abhāva*), or perhaps another substance (*dravyāntara*)? If it were space, then "cowness" (*gotva*) would not reside there, for space is not perceived as a cow. By this, [the cases of] non-existence and another substance are also explained.

“Also, because specific cognitions are not accidental. This cognition, which possesses a distinction from the cognition of the whole, arises from another cause. Indeed, it is observed that cognitions possessing a distinction from the whole arise from another cause, as in the case of the cognition of ‘blue’ in leather, cloth, or woolen blankets; and that other cause is the universal (*sāmānya*).”
[Objection: Therefore, the universal (*sāmānya*) is omnipresent (*sarvagata*) because it exists even in a location devoid of individuals (*vyakti*).

Yet, there is no cognition of the universal in that place because of the absence of an individual to manifest it. And only that individual in which the universal is perceived is capable of manifesting the universal; otherwise, the apprehension of the universal would be impossible.
"It is understood as being in those [individuals] and not in others.
Regarding this, Bhaṭṭa says:
"Or rather, even though [the universal] is omnipresent, its manifestation occurs in accordance with the capacity [of the individuals]."

Power is to be inferred from its effects; its manifestation is caused by perception. Alternatively, it would have to be conceived as existing everywhere, like space, even if it were restricted to a single locus.

It does not go there, nor was it there previously, nor does it exist there afterwards; if, at the time when its own substratum alone exists, a jar or the like arises within two positions that were previously empty of a jar, how could a universal residing in a substance located in a different place possibly occur in those [newly arisen jars]? [For] a substance arising from its own previous substance...

It does not go, because it is admitted to be inactive. Since it exists elsewhere, it follows that for something which is immovable and does not pervade the space between two points, conjunction with a substance in a different location is not logical. Furthermore, it was not previously present there;
therefore, the manifestation is seen only where its capacity resides.
And for that very reason, this [universal] is not perceived in all individuals;
for even though they are distinct, some possess the capacity [to manifest it] while others are incapable.
Furthermore, there can never be any objection regarding the inherent power of a real entity.
"Space is the vehicle; what is there to be questioned here?"—

regarding this, between those two positions, if [the universal] resides only in its own substrate, then how could it exist in those substances which arise later in a location different from that of the jar and so forth, in a place devoid of "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and the like at the time of the production of a new jar?

The intention is that there is no possibility [of the universal] in jars and other things produced later. There would be such a possibility if that universal were to pass from the prior substance into the substance being produced later; and that does not exist, as he says with the words "because," etc. "That" refers to the universal; "from the prior substance" means from that wherein it was previously inherent, into the substance about to be produced.

(1) One who wishes for the production [of a universal] must first [admit that] the jar or the like does not move [to another place], because the universal is inactive due to its formlessness. If it is argued that even though it does not move from its previous substance, there will nevertheless be a connection with a different location—just as a reflection appears in a mirror—the author says: "Not indeed," and so forth. This refers to an entity called a "universal" which, existing in a different substance, exists in a substance located in a different place than the substance about to be produced.

Therefore, the connection is as follows: it is not logical for that which does not move from its prior substratum and does not pervade the space between those two—that is, which does not pervade the space between the two [objects] produced in the east and west—to have a conjunction with a substance located in a different place from its own substratum. For who, indeed, would not be considered insane to claim that there is a conjunction of a reflection with a mirror located in a different place? [This occurs] by the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Erroneous cognition arises there, appearing as reflections in a mirror; as it has been said:

"(1) 'In objects such as the surface of a diamond or a mirror, which possess contrary transformations, there is no possibility of the existence of entities whose nature is that of mountains and the like.'"

As for those who maintain that there is the production of a distinct entity (*bhāvāntara*) therein, even for them, there is no connection with the original form (*bimba*); thus, this [position] is trivial. Furthermore, prior to the substance about to arise, the universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist in that location where it is about to arise, because its presence in a place devoid of the individual (*vyakti*) is not admitted. Subsequently, that universal does exist.

In the *Ślokavārttika*, *Akṛti* section (vv. 25–29), the *Sāmānyacintā* states: "Even after [the destruction of the cause], it does not exist; for there too, because of non-arising, it has not come from anywhere.
Thus, due to its inherent dullness (*jāḍya*), who could bear this burden?"
And it does not possess parts. ||154||
It abandons its former substrate and moves to a location different from that where it was about to arise; and between those two,
alas, there is a continuous succession of calamities.

The relationship between two entities existing in different locations must be of two kinds: consisting of multiple parts or consisting of a single essence. Since it is not admitted that there is an individual devoid of the universal when the individual has arisen, [the universal] does not arise in that location together with the individual because of its eternity. Nor is the arising of the universal identical to the arising of the individual, because they are distinct.

Or, if there were non-difference [between the universal and the individual], then the relationship of general and particular would not exist. Furthermore, it has not come from any prior specific individual; this is a restatement by way of conclusion of what was previously said regarding the fact that "it does not go. And in that case, those modes by which the universal might possibly occur in another individual are not admitted.

To claim that "generality is accepted" is a contradiction; and because it is difficult for the wise to endure, it is a burden. For this very reason, he says: "Who would [accept] this," and so forth. For how could a wise person tolerate what is improper? An insentient being (*jaḍa*), however, being incapable of investigating what is proper or improper due to its lack of knowledge, might even tolerate it. As he has stated elsewhere: "Because of insentience."

But surely, even if a universal (*sāmānya*) arises within a substance that is about to come into being, its state of inherence (*samavetatva*) must be understood from perception alone; and that perception of its inherence in the individual (*vyakti*) exists even when the universal has not yet arisen. So what is the use of its arising? Furthermore, the nature of the universal is held to be inherent in the individual; therefore, even if it previously inhered in another substance, it does not deviate from it.

And since [the universal] appears as inherent in substances such as pots, how can it be said that "it does not move" and so forth? This objection is raised because [such appearance] is accepted [by us].
True; this objection—"it appears"—would apply to one who does not accept the appearance of a universal at all.
But for one who considers the appearance of a universal to be unreal (*alīka*), how could there be an objection? [For us,] its unreality...

By means of the passage beginning with "The substance that intends to arise does not go [to the place], nor was it there, nor has it arisen," the Master has demonstrated that even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), a cognition appearing as a universal arises. Furthermore, truthfulness does not follow merely from appearance; for otherwise, it would entail the consequence that even things such as a double moon would be real.

Nor is there a sublation by perception, because sublation by inference is also a form of sublation. If that [substance] were to possess parts, then it would have to pervade, by one part, a substance that previously existed on a different substratum and is now about to arise on another part; or else, being partless, it would have to abandon its previous substratum. He says "And not," etc., to show that neither of these two cases is possible. Previously, the substratum—
The phrase "from a location where it was about to arise" clarifies the mixing [of the two] by indicating a different location. "Of those two" refers to the two substances produced earlier and later.
He explains this with the words "different," and so forth. "It would become twofold" means by way of having multiple parts as its nature. "The former substratum..."
Because of its connection with those two [the eye and the object], like light, a rope, or a bamboo; and not without having parts.

It is not logical for certain things located in different places to exist in one place, because that [entity] lacks a dual nature; for a single essence consists in its relation to those various locations, otherwise such a relation would be impossible. It is contradictory for a single substratum to reside in one place at that very same time and yet not reside in another by that same essence—this constitutes the simultaneous presence and absence of a single entity.

This has been stated because of a contradiction, or else by way of abandonment. First, he states the initial position: "Not one," and so forth. This is stated according to what is established for the opponent; however, it has already been said that a single entity consisting of multiple parts is not admitted. [For] by two distinct parts, which are mutually different—
It is called "dark" because of its connection with that [darkness]. Because of its connection with those two [the rope and the bamboo] which occupy different locations:

for light, being composed of parts, is connected with the pot by one part, and with other things such as the pot by another part; likewise, it is so with the rope, the bamboo, the staff, and so forth, in relation to their respective correlates.
The first [position] has already been refuted. Now, suppose it is maintained that a universal exists in many locations because it possesses parts.

Even so, how could a single entity exist in many places? For [it is argued that] the parts of the universal exist [therein]. And as for those parts of the universal which exist in each individual object, are they of the nature of the universal or not?

If they possess the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*), it follows that a single [universal] exists in many places; yet it is not logical to say that a universal existing in one place is [simultaneously] in many. If, on the other hand, they do not possess the nature of a universal, how can it be said that "the universal exists in many places"?
Furthermore, if the universal were to exist in one part by means of another part, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And it is not [the case that...]

The existence of one thing in many locations is not logical without having parts. Furthermore, if it were partless, it would exist in its entirety within each individual object; consequently, like the objects themselves, it would be unique and could not be a universal. Why? Because that partless universal has a single nature consisting of its relation to one substance; since there is no second nature apart from that, and because it possesses only a single nature—

Because that universal has the nature of a connection consisting in its occupying that same location; [that is,] because it has the nature of being connected with the substance of the jar which occupied the previous location, rather than the location of the jar about to arise. Otherwise, if it had the nature of being connected with the substance at the location where the jar is about to arise, there would be no simultaneous conjunction with a distinct location, because of the impossibility of its being connected with that [new] location and because of the impossibility of its being connected with that previous substance. Therefore—
For a universal whose nature is restricted to a specific individual, there can be no connection at that very same time with a substance located in a different place.

Or, if such a connection were to exist, it would follow that because the universal has a single nature restricted to the previous individual, it would reside in that previous individual while simultaneously not residing in the individual in a different place due to its connection with that other; this is a contradiction, as the author states in the passage beginning, "Of a single substratum," and so forth.
In that context, "abiding" (*sthāna*) refers to the previous individual (*pūrvavyakti*). For at that very time, you have admitted [the universal] to exist in another individual;

and because it is impossible for one thing to be concomitant (*anvaya*) elsewhere without abandoning its previous individual. Therefore, to say that the universal does not abide in that previous individual by means of that very nature restricted to the previous individual is incorrect. What is the reason?
"Abiding in that," and so forth. Because it is contradictory for a single universal, which possesses both abiding and non-abiding natures, to exist simultaneously in that very same individual.
— 4. Examination of the Universal (Sāmānyacintā)

If it is argued that [the universal] exists everywhere, at all times, and in every form as its inherent nature (*sthitātman*), then the cognition based on the perception of that intrinsic nature would indeed arise. Now, just as existence in another location is accepted through the relinquishment of one [part], so too existence in many [locations] is accepted because it is observed to occur through successive parts; likewise, when a universal exists in one place in a certain form, it exists in another place in that very same form at that same time.
Is it not also accepted that this third function exists because it is observed? As Bhaṭṭa has said:
“For there is no restrictive rule that the function [of a word] must be of only two kinds;
for since it is observed to be threefold as well, it may just as well be twofold.
Uddyotakara also says: “Cowness is neither a whole nor a collection; therefore, in that case, there is no [application of the term] *kṛtsna* (entirety) or *eka-* (oneness).”

The two words "deśa" (place) and "śabda" (word) exist [in this context]. If these two words do not apply there, then the question—whether "cowness" (*gotva*) exists in its entirety or by way of a single part—is not tenable. How, then, does cowness exist in cows? By way of the relationship between the locus and the located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*). But what is this relationship of locus and located? It is inherence (*samavāya*). In that case, cowness is that which possesses the occurrence; the occurrence is inherence, [expressed] here as "here [it is]."

Because it is the cause of the cognition [of inherence], its occurrence everywhere—in both the prior substance and the substance about to arise—is precisely inherence (*samavāya*). Therefore, how can it be said that "this is untenable because there is a contradiction between the stationary and non-stationary natures in a single locus"?

He states this very point in the passage beginning with "everywhere" (*sarvatra*): "everywhere," meaning in the prior individual and in the substance about to arise; "always," meaning even while they are arising...

Even when it exists during the production of a substance, it does not abandon that substance; therefore, there is no contradiction between the stationary and non-stationary natures in a single locus because of the absence of a stationary nature. This is incorrect, for being inherent in one [locus] is not the same as being inherent in another individual, since otherwise it would follow that the other would appear there. Therefore, regarding inherence in one and inherence in another...

There is indeed a mutual distinction [between individuals]. Furthermore, if that [universal] were non-different [from its instances], then because it would be inherent in a single [individual], there would be a lack of commonality (ananugama); consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of the universal itself lacking commonality elsewhere. Alternatively, the power of the universal to produce a cognition through its relation to one individual, time, and so forth, does not exist by virtue of its relation to another individual and so forth. Therefore, the power of the universal to produce a cognition resides in one individual—

The power that produces cognition in the [cognition] to be superimposed is opposed [to the object]. Furthermore, power is non-different from the possessor of power, because a real entity is defined by its power. Therefore, the pervasion is established: whatever is a single real entity must reside in only one place. If the universal were a single real entity, how could it reside elsewhere? If it is argued that this is so because it appears as such, [we reply]: no, for the appearance...

A sublater [of a thesis] cannot be that which does not appear [to perception], because even that [non-entity] appears; however, what sublates this [thesis] is the appearance of a real entity (*vastu*), and it has already been stated that no pervasive real entity exists. For this very reason, there is no sublation of the proposition (*pratijñā*) by perception, since the cognition of a universal is merely a semblance of perception.

If it is argued that there would be a circularity—since inference does not proceed as long as this [perception] lacks validity, and as long as inference does not proceed, this perception cannot be classified as a pseudo-perception—[we reply]: no.
For inference proceeds merely by means of a doubt regarding the reality of the object appearing [in the perception]; nor does inference serve as the cause for its invalidity.
In every case, it would possess all forms; and that being so, there would arise the cognition "this is a cow" with respect to a horse, and [the cognition] "this is a horse" with respect to a cow.

Because it is connected with substances while remaining stable in itself, and because it is determined as such through the apprehension of its own nature— since that single [entity] lacks any other form—
it is therefore impartite and cannot be simultaneously placed in multiple locations.

Even if it were to abandon its previous substratum, it is not accepted that it could exist in a different location; for when something existing in one place gives rise to [its effect] in another location, [the cause would have to move]. (155)
Nevertheless, it exists by means of a mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably connected to its own probandum; therefore, it is a sublater of the cognition of a universal.

Consequently, in ultimate reality, there is no single entity that subsists in multiple [loci] at one time. For if it were to so subsist, there would be a direct contradiction between its nature as both abiding and not abiding therein.
The Teacher, however, speaks of the fault even while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position], beginning with the words "of that intrinsic nature" (*tatsvabhāva*), etc.
That condition whose basis is the perception of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) would, in every case—even regarding a substance of a different class—possess all forms.
And this being so, one could say "cow" with respect to a horse, and so forth. What is the reason? He says:

the analysis of the compound is "that whose essence resides in the horse" (*aśve sthita ātmā yasya*). Because it conveys the meaning, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed even with a term in a different grammatical case (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
Alternatively, it is a *kṛdanta* compound meaning "one who stands on a horse" (*aśve sthitaḥ*). Subsequently, with the word *ātman*, it forms a two-membered *bahuvrīhi*.

This is because, through the cognition of its own nature—and specifically through the cognition of a substance whose nature is established as moving—one arrives at such a determination; that is, one determines that "the cow is a substance."

It might be argued: "The cognition 'it is a substance' does not arise from the apprehension of substanceness (*dravyatva*) as inherent in a horse; rather, it arises from the apprehension of substanceness alone. To this, he says: "And of that," and so forth.

And of that—of the single, unperceived, and unapprehended substanceness in the horse—there is no other form apart from its being inherent in the horse, [namely] its non-inherence in what is not a horse.

Because the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is absent. Therefore, one who apprehends a cow as "substance" by means of the generic property of substantiality (dravyatva) which inheres in the horse alone would necessarily perceive it as "horse. On the other hand, for one who holds that the universal of substantiality is indeed distinct from the horse, and who apprehends the cow as qualified by that [universal], he would necessarily perceive it as "horse."

"Therefore" is the conclusion. A partless universal—that which has many locations (aneka-deśa) in many places—is not simultaneously deposited in things such as jars; it does not attain the state of being something that can be contained. By this much, the statement "and not having parts" has been explained.

"He abandons the former substratum"—this is what is explained by the words "the former," and so forth. Furthermore, the abandonment of the former substratum is not intended to apply to the universal (*sāmānya*).
[The phrase] "elsewhere" means that while the universal remains in its previous individual (*vyakti*), it does not move from its own former location, the substratum.
Furthermore, it is highly illogical to claim that a substance which has its birth in a location other than its previous substratum exists there;
for it is highly logical to say that it exists without moving from its own place.
Moreover, whatever state (bhāva) it occupies, it is connected with that very state. (156)
"How is it that this something here pervades that which has a location? This is truly wonderful!"—even for one who maintains that the universal (*sāmānya*) is omnipresent;
these are the summary verses.
If that [universal] were all-pervasive because it is non-different from its manifestation in one instance, then it would be expressed in every case. (157)

The universal (*jāti*) would be perceived everywhere; it has been refuted that there is no manifestation of the universal at any time. Therefore, it must either be eternally visible, independent of any external assistance, or it must be manifested only occasionally; for it remains fixed in its own nature, and not otherwise.
Because an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is never produced from anything whatsoever,
[the author] mocks [the opponent] with the word "mad.
If it is argued that a universal (*sāmānya*), even while not moving from the location of its previous manifestation, pervades a substance in another location, he replies:

"Where," and so forth. In whatever place that entity existing at a later time resides, the universal is not connected with that place, because it is admitted [by you] that the universal is omnipresent within all its own manifestations (*vyakti*). Since it does not reside in the place where the universal is absent, yet it is claimed to pervade the entity residing in that place which exists at a later time, this is something truly marvelous, as it transgresses logic.
He mocks [the opponent] by means of another argument: for it cannot be determined by one who follows logic that "whatever does not exist in a particular place does not pervade that place" (157).
Desiring also to refute the postulation of omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*), he says: "Of whom," and so forth. Of that [omnipresent entity] as well—

If, for the proponent of universals, the universal is omnipresent, then that universal— which is manifested by its manifestation (the individual expression) in a single instance such as a *śāvaleya* cow— would be manifested and revealed even in a location devoid of individuals and even amidst the diversity of heterogeneous individuals, because it is non-different and unitary; thus, it would be perceived even in places where no individuals exist.

This is what is meant: although there is an absence of a manifesting individual instance (svavyakti) both in a location devoid of individuals and in an individual of a different class, nevertheless, because the universal (jāti) exists there in the very form manifested by its own individual instance, it must be perceived;
otherwise, it would follow that the universal possesses a plurality of natures, whereas it is intended to be of a single nature. This is the point. [It is not the case for] the eternal universal...

It has been refuted in the intervening passage [of the *Ślokavārttika*] beginning with "Because there can be no manifestation at any time due to the impossibility of adding any excellence (*anādheyātiśayatva*), 'manifestation' as a form of receptivity (*ādheyatā*) is not applicable to that [universal]" (1.1.46). Therefore, that universal is eternal, independent of any external embellishment, and incapable of having any excellence added to it. If such a thing, by its very nature, were to produce its own cognition—

[If it were] capable, then it would be perceived at all times—both before and after its manifestation. If, on the other hand, it were not capable, then it would never be perceived. Why? Because it would remain in that same state, whether possessing a nature capable of generating cognition or its opposite; the meaning is that it would possess a single form at all times. [But this is not the case, for] it is incapable when the manifestor is absent, yet becomes capable when that manifestor is present.

Even if one were to concede that [the universal] is all-pervasive, since there is no difference in its manifestation when it is manifested in one place, it would follow that it is manifested everywhere; consequently, it would not be perceived even in those regions devoid of the individual instance.
Nor does that [manifestation] depend upon a genus;
for when there is a cognition of the manifestor, the manifested object is not thereby perceived. (158)
Why, then, is the opposite maintained regarding the universal (*sāmānya*) and its possessor (*tadvat*)?

For one who asserts that the universal perishes in regions devoid of its substratum because it depends upon contact with the sense organ of its own substratum—for such a person, contact with the sense organ of its own substratum is indeed a contributing factor; therefore, the observer of it would perceive it exactly as it exists.

Therefore, since there can be neither constant perception nor non-perception of a universal (*jāti*), he says: "In its own nature," and so forth. The meaning is that, because it is eternal, no excellence (*atiśaya*) can be imparted to it. (157–58) If the universal has no manifestation (*vyakti*), why is it said that it is manifested in one place by means of a particular manifestation (*vyakti*) alone? To this [he replies]:

He says: "Even granting [this], etc. Even though the universal (*jāti*) is all-pervading, it is manifested in one substratum; because there is no difference [in the universal] and because the universal is a single entity, it is indeed manifested—that is, revealed—everywhere, even in places devoid of manifestation and in instances of a different class (*vijātīya*).
By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even in places devoid of manifestation," it is implied that it is also [manifested] in instances of a different class. Furthermore, that universal is not...
The meaning is that the manifestor would not depend upon the individual (vyakti), because the individual lacks the capacity to manifest the genus (jāti).
For if the manifestor were to depend upon the individual, then in the absence of the cognition of the manifestor, there would be no cognition of the manifested;
for indeed, in the absence of the cognition of a lamp or similar object, there is no cognition of a jar or similar object. It is the same here as well.

If the individual (vyakti) were not perceived, there could be no perception of the genus (jāti). Why, then, is the reverse—that the universal and its possessor are related as the manifestor (vyañjaka) and the manifested (vyaṅgya)—desired? For indeed, according to the rule that "cognition does not occur with respect to a qualified object (viśeṣya) unless the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) has been apprehended," the apprehension of the universal must be desired first, and through it, the apprehension of the individual. Therefore, [the universal] is the manifestor.
The reversal [of the position] is that the cognition of the universal, which is held to be manifested, is accepted as occurring even without the apprehension of its manifestation.
He explains this with the words "For he who... and so forth. That in which the universal inheres is its own substratum (*svāśraya*).
The sense organ that perceives the universal and the contact between the two—cognition of the universal depending on those is what is thus described. [Universals] devoid of a substratum...

The locations [of a universal] are those occupied by individuals of a different class and those devoid of individuals; in these, [the universal] is not perceived because of the absence of the aforementioned conjunction. For one who argues thus, when an individual is perceived somewhere, the conjunction of the sense organ with its substrate (the individual) certainly exists and serves as an auxiliary for the universal, which resides everywhere. Therefore, due to that cause—the conjunction of the sense organ with its substrate—the observer of that [individual] perceives it.

In some cases, one who perceives the universal (*jāti*) may see the universal as it truly exists, pervading all locations. If it is argued that the essential nature of the universal is visible only where the manifesting individual (*vyakti*) is present and not elsewhere, [the author] replies with the words "Not indeed," and so forth. "In that" refers to the universal. "When a certain individual is being perceived" means when it is being seen in a particular instance; "belonging to it" means related to that universal.

Because it would contradict [the principle that] one thing is both seen and unseen. Thus far, having accepted that the individual is the manifester, the meaning conveyed by the word has been explained. Now, consider the universal (*sāmānya*):
for when that [universal] is being perceived, it is not logical that it remains unseen; such is the case with the universal’s manifestation in the individual.

Because it is something to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*). The argument that [the manifestation] is not observed in places devoid of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) has also been refuted, because in such cases the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor does not exist. A light source, such as a lamp, causes another to perceive after having perceived it oneself; it is the manifestor, not the manifested, in a place devoid of its own form. Manifestation (*vyakti*) is not like this with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*), for the opposite is the case.

For how could it be the manifestor of the universal (*sāmānya*), and yet be visible through the medium of its apprehension? Now, in order to explain [the passage] beginning with "it does not depend on the individual" (*vyakti*), he says: "because it is manifested by the individual" (*vyaktivyaṅgyatvāt*), and so forth.
And its falsity has already been established by what was just stated; for there cannot be both the seen and the unseen for a single thing. Therefore—

This is merely a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) presented while closing one's eyes like an elephant, for the sake of stating another fault. "Of such a kind" means of that which is logical. "Therein" refers to the universal (*jāti*) and its locus (*tadvat*). This is because there is an absence of a logical relationship between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*).

What is the reason? [It is] "its own nature," and so forth. For (*hi*), because, in a place devoid of its own nature—that is, in a place lacking a lamp or similar light—[the manifestation does not occur].

A jar or the like is manifested by its own [manifesting agent]. Manifestation of a universal (*sāmānya*) by a manifestor (*vyañjikā*) is not like this, according to the reasoning already stated. Why? Because of the opposite case: for the opponent maintains that the universal is apprehended first even without having apprehended the individual (*vyakti*), since they admit that the apprehension of the individual occurs precisely through the apprehension of the universal. Therefore, [it is] a manifestor—
Because the manifested [object] is also apprehended through its manifestation, there is a transgression of the properties of the manifestor by the manifestation itself.
This is precisely what he says with the words "For how," and so forth. The connection is as follows: "And that manifestation would be the manifester of the universal.
"By way of the apprehension of that" means by way of the apprehension of the universal. That manifestation is perceptible.

This would be contradictory. "In this way" means by the power of perceiving a universal (*sāmānya*). If the manifestation of the individual (*vyakti*) is admitted, it follows that both that individual and the universal would be manifested; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. "Like a jar by a lamp":
the compound is formed either by splitting the rule *tṛtīyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.30) or by the rule *sup-supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4). Just as a jar [is manifested] by a lamp...

In the same way, the individual (vyakti) is that which is manifested (vyaṅgya) by means of the universal (sāmānya), as this is the meaning of "attainment" (prāpti). This is because, without the cognition of that [universal], the individual would be invisible in form due to the absence of the cognition of the universal. Others, however, say: in the phrase "and that very thing would result in being manifested," the word "and" (ca) includes the idea that the universal is the manifester; therefore, it is similar to the case of a lamp and a jar.

The suffix *vat* should be understood as following from a copulative compound (*dvandva*). Because the rule governing the prior placement [of a word] is subject to exceptions, the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) does not necessarily occupy the first position.

A lamp is like the universal (*sāmānya*), which is the manifester; and a jar is like the individual (*vyakti*), which is the manifested. The meaning of the sentence is that [the universal] is what is logically entailed (*prasajyate*).
By "by this" is meant by the proponent of the universal. Having observed what effect would be impossible without a universal?

"Thus" means according to the method described. "Great effort" refers to that which is a cause of much suffering because it cannot be accomplished. (158-56) Regarding the phrase "mutually," etc.: "other" means different. Because of their difference—that is, because they possess distinct characteristics—in heterogeneous things (*vyatirekin*), which are non-concomitant (*ananvayin*), there is no single uniform cognition (*pratyaya*). The mention of "cognition" is merely an illustration; the same applies to the word. A universal (*sāmānya*)— [...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on a philosophical treatise (likely related to Buddhist logic or Madhyamaka), discussing the impossibility of a single universal existing in diverse particulars.*
Because of the impossibility [of that]. The connection is that the theory of universals (*sāmānyavāda*) has been resorted to.

How so? The Teacher [asks]. For those who do not accept that words such as "cook" (*pācaka*) are based on action (*kriyā*), [the following is said] in response to them—[from the *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (1956)].

In this way, it follows that [the universal] is manifested by something, like a jar by a lamp; for in some manner, it is invisible apart from such cognition. Furthermore, having perceived what is improper in this [position], why has the proponent of the universal (sāmānyavādin) undertaken such great effort? Because [universals] are mutually distinct, a recurring cognition (anvayin-pratyaya) is impossible among individuals that are separate from one another.
How so?
[Because] in the case of "cook" and the like, there is a denotative word even without an object that is non-different [from the action]. (159)

For even in the case of non-correlative terms such as "cook" (*pācaka*) and "designator" (*vācaka*), there is a recurrence of the word and the cognition in the form "cooking" (*pacana*) and "cook" (*pācaka*). Among these, there is no other single, undivided entity by virtue of which they could be cognized in that way through their differences. If it is argued that this is due to the action (*karman*), then rather than that, the cognition itself [should be the cause]; for what has been done by some other action? Indeed, difference...
As it has been said: "Without an undivided object called 'universal' (sāmānya), how could a single word be expressive in the case of [terms like] 'cook' and so forth?

By the mention of the "expressive" (vācaka), the "corresponding cognition" (pratyayānvayin) is indeed already implied, because without that [cognition], the word would not function. For this very reason, he states in the commentary: "There is a recurrence of both word and cognition."

Uddyotakara has also stated: "The recurring cognition regarding cows and the like arises from a cause distinct from the individual bodies and so forth, because specific cognitions are not accidental, just like the cognitions of blue and other colors. That which is the cause [of such recurring cognition] is the universal (*sāmānya*).
Having thus established the proof for the existence of the universal, he himself raised this doubt: (1)

Now, you might think: "Just as words such as 'cook' are recurring [general terms] yet there is no universal called 'cook-ness'—for if it existed, it would have to be manifested at the very moment the entity is produced—so too are there recurring cognitions in the case of cows and the like. This is not so, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the reason [adduced]. For [the opponent has failed to see that] particular cognitions...

The meaning of this reason, "because of its being accidental," is that the cognition [of an object] arises from another cause distinct from the cognition of the individual entity; it does not mean, however, that every recurring cognition arises solely from a universal (*sāmānya*). This being the case, that which is the primary instrument (*sādhana*) for the action of cooking is designated by the word "cook" (*pācaka*); and that primacy belongs to the one who is a cook...

By stating that there is no fault because [the property] exists even in those [individuals], it is indicated by the word *dyotakena* (by the indicator) that the Master [Dignāga] also intended that the application of words such as "cook" (*pācaka*) is accepted even without a universal such as "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*).
With this intention, the Master also said, "How so? and so forth.
Furthermore, it is not logical for the application of words such as "cook" to be based on the action of cooking as the primary cause. Ta...
For if it were based on a causal sign (*nimitta*), the term "primary" (*pradhāna*) would be the recurring one, and not "cook" (*pācaka*). Therefore he says:
"(1) For not... and so forth. "In them" means in those such as cooks. "Other" means distinct from the substance (*dravya*).
Thus, because [the term] is intended to apply to all capacities, by whatever means those cooks and others might be different, they would nevertheless be perceived as such through non-difference.

"By knowledge"—this is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) meaning they would be designated as such. For example, in the case of cooks, there is the activity characterized by placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth; in the case of reciters, it consists of the act of studying; and similarly for others, according to their respective roles. If it is argued that there exists a cause such as a suffix denoting an action (karmaka-pratyaya), then "that" refers to the correlative (anvayin). The mention of "suffix" (pratyaya) is merely elliptical, and the same applies to the word itself. Or, by another [cause], namely, by the cause that is the action (karman).

[The phrase] "by effort, etc. [is used]. He supports this very point with the words beginning with "distinct," etc. The word "that" (*tad*) refers to the external object. "That action" (*tatkarma*)—this is the consideration of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*).
It would not be the cause of a non-distinct cognition; therefore, if you desire a single universal, that [universal] must be non-distinct even for distinct actions.
If [the universal] produces a cognition [of identity], what offense has been committed by the individuals that they are not accepted as such?
If it is argued that because they possess a single form, there would be no cognition of difference—namely, that "it does not possess the specific form of those"—to this we reply:
it has already been stated that even cognitions of specific differences arise from the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntara-viveka*) according to convention. Therefore, regarding the individual...

The word *vā* should be connected [to the preceding]. Because of the distinction between the objects (*karman*) to be cooked, by which fault those individuals are such— that is, they serve as the cause for a non-differentiated cognition.
True, there is no fault; however, it is because those individuals possess a single form.

For instance, a substance has a single form because it is partless. If this very [single form] is the basis for the cognition of non-difference, and there is no other distinct property (*dharmāntara*) separate from it, then the cognition of distinction—such as "the cook-ness of the cook"—would not occur. For it is not the case that [the cook-ness] belongs to that very same [individual].
Therefore, a distinction [from substance] is logical. "Tadākāra" means the form of that non-manifestation (*avyakti*); "atadākāra" means a form other than that, namely the form of non-difference;
"atadākāraviśeṣavatī" means that which possesses a particularity of such a form. The meaning is: having a form other than the form of the substance (*dravya*).
This is what is being said: the cognition "substance" arises from substances themselves with such a form; therefore, it is by something other than [that form]—

If the cognition of "cook" [or the cognition of negation] were caused solely by the substance, then it would be indistinguishable from the cognition of the mere substance. Now, for what purpose are both stated as "possessing a specific form other than that" (*atadākāraviśeṣavatī*)? One could simply say "possessing a form other than that" (*atadākārā*) or simply "possessing a specific form" (*viśeṣavatī*). It is said in reply: when it is stated that "[it has] a form of non-difference," the [opponent's] notion that "there is an absence of the substance" is [refuted].

It might be argued that even a cognition of difference (*bedhapratyaya*) is devoid of that [external] form; however, this [cognition] cannot be accepted by the opponent as being based on another real entity (*vastvantara*), because it is precisely cognitions of particularity (*viśeṣapratyaya*) that are based on a distinct property (*dharmāntara*). Furthermore, when the apprehension of a particularity alone is produced—such as the cognition of Caitra being possessed of a particularity in relation to Maitra—it is not devoid of that form, since it is designated by the name "Caitra" and so forth.

Because it is the substance itself that is being established. However, by the inclusion of both [terms], this meaning results: that cognition has a non-substantial form and yet possesses distinction due to its contact with a real entity (*vastu*). Therefore, in that case, there can be no other cause apart from the substance.

The Master says: "It has been stated. The connection is as follows: it has been stated how there is a distinction (vyatireka)—such as "the cow-ness of a cow" or "the cook-ness of a cook"—and how the cognitions of particulars were just mentioned. To the question "How was it stated?", he replies:

"According to their respective [objects]," and so forth. "Exclusion of other objects" (arthāntaravyavaccheda) means the differentiation from other objects. "According to their respective [objects]" (yathāsvam) refers to whichever word [is concerned].

The meaning is: "from that exclusion which corresponds to the convention. For instance, the word *pācaka* (cook), while denoting the exclusion of non-cooks, does not exclude other distinctions [such as being a Brahmin, etc.], and thus it expresses the substratum (*dharmin*). However, the word *pācakatva* (the state of being a cook) denotes that very same excluded entity while excluding other distinctions; thus, it expresses the property (*dharma*). Therefore, through the conceptualization of the distinction between property and substratum, [one speaks of] "the cooking of the cook"—[and so forth].

The ablative case is employed [in the word] *katva* (the state of being a *kṛt* suffix) to express exclusion (*vyatireka*). Likewise, since the word *dravya* (substance) is conventionally established (*saṃketita*) with respect to an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that excludes what is non-substance (*adravya*), it follows that— in accordance with that [convention], and following the exclusion of the non-substantial— the cognition that conforms to the exclusion of the non-substantial is not the cause for the distinction of its action.

Regarding the cognition of non-difference among cooks and the like: if their cause is the non-difference of the action and the universal (*jāti*), then the universal [cannot be the cause] because it resides in the action. For if a universal, such as "cowness," which is related to one thing (the cow), were the cause of a cognition regarding another thing (the act of going), then [the following would apply]: "going" and so forth [would likewise be universals]. However, a universal is indeed the cause of a cognition regarding another thing only when it is related to that other thing.
Even in the case of cooking actions, there is a universal of action (*karmajāti*); however, those specific actions are not denoted by the word "cook" (*pācaka*). Why is that?
Because [the word denotes] the substance which is the substratum of those actions. Is the universal of action also [denoted]?
No, because it is based on a different cause for its application (*nimitta*).

[The cognition] arises. From the word "cook," however, there arises a cognition that conforms precisely to the exclusion of non-cooks; therefore, a cognition characterized by specific distinctions according to its respective exclusions is not contradictory even in the case of a single [referent], provided it follows convention (*saṃketa*). This has been established in the discussion beginning with "the rejection or non-rejection of other differences."

The conclusion is stated with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth. The connection is as follows: just as there is a difference among individual [cooks], so too, because of the difference in their actions (*karman*), action is not the cause of this non-differentiating cognition (*abhedapratyaya*) such as "cook. Rather, it is that universal (*jāti*) called "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*) which inheres (*samaveta*) in those actions—namely, the actions designated as "cooking"—that is the cause of the non-difference of the cooks.

[The author] refutes [the opponent's view] regarding the cognition of difference with the words "No," and so forth. It is understood from the context that "the universal (*jāti*) is not the cause.
