What is the reason? Because it resides in action (*karma*). That is, because it is inherent in action. Action is a distinct entity from substance; [the universal] belongs to that [action]. The phrase "as a distinct entity" refers to the substance. "Like cowness (*gotva*)" is the illustration. For cowness is not related to individual cows such as Śābaleya and others. Kaka... [text fragment]
Among the various types of horses, there is a cause for the cognition "cow. In the actions called "cooking" (pāka), the universal of action (karmajāti) inheres;
yet those actions themselves are not what are designated as "cooking. The mention of "word" (śabda) is an illustration; likewise, they are distinguished by the cognition of a "cook" (pācaka).
The substance that is the locus of that action called "cooking" is expressed by the word "cook. And it is not the case that therein—
The universal of action inheres in the substance.

Thus far, it has been explained that the designation and cognition of "cook," which have the substance as their object, are caused by the universal of action, based on its relation to something else [i.e., the action]. (1) (159–60)
Now he speaks by way of another method, beginning with "of that" (*tasya*), and so forth. "Another word" (*śrutyantaram*) means a word other than the word "cook" (*pācaka*).

The mention of "word" (*śruti*) is merely illustrative, as it serves as the cause for other types of cognition as well. He states this very "other word": "cooking," and so forth. "From that" (*tataḥ*) means because the class of action (*karmajātiḥ*) is the cause of both the denotation and the cognition regarding the object of action; such is the intended meaning of "from the class of action."

It might be thought: (1) the universal of action (*karmajāti*) does not produce the cognition of "cook," but rather it is the action itself [that produces it] by virtue of being the substratum for that universal of action. To this, he says: "Of that," and so forth. "Of that" refers to the non-differentiated cognition of "cook" and the like. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has action as its cause. It has already been stated [in the verse]: "Like individuals, action is not the cause of this [cognition], because of difference," and so on.

But was it not said that, due to its reliance on a universal (*jāti*), even an action that is distinct [from other actions] becomes the cause of a non-distinct cognition? From that [reliance], there would arise the notion "cooking, cooking," but not "cook. That [notion of "cook"] has been explained as being caused by the action.
Furthermore:
And because there is no persistence of action. || 160 ||

For an impermanent action does not exist everywhere. If that causal condition were the cause of the action, then once the action has ceased, one could not say "the cooker," because the state of acting belongs only to one who is currently cooking. For this very reason—the universal [of the action] exists through a non-connection; it is not illogical, because it is the cause of the word.
Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);

because there is no connection, a universal (*sāmānya*) cannot be the cause of a word, as that would lead to an over-extension—nothing unrelated [can be so]. For that very reason, a universal does not arise from an action, because there is no distinction among actions. A single action is indeed its universal, for there is no action [without] an agent (*kartṛ*). (Ākṛti)
Because of its absence, there is no relation with a substratum (*āśraya*) either. For instance, due to the lack of such a relation, it cannot be the cause of the cognition of the word.

This has already been stated; however, what was said is incorrect. Even in the case of a relation with a universal (*jāti*), the same applies because the action remains distinct. Furthermore, he states the reason for this accumulation [of arguments] beginning with "Moreover" (*kiñca*). If that cognition of non-difference among cooks and the like were admitted to have action as its cause:

When actions have ceased, a person should not be called a "cook. Yet he is so called; this is by virtue of mere capacity (*yogyatāmātreṇa*). Therefore, this designation is not caused by an action that exists as a real entity (*vastubhūta*). If it is argued that there is no fault because even a past action exists, [the author] says: "He is indeed cooking," and so forth. If the past were to exist, it would be perceived just like the present, according to the definition of perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa*).
And it is accepted that action (*karman*) is something attained [by a substance].

Suppose it is thought: (1) the universal of action (*karmajāti*) inheres in action, and action also inheres in a substance; therefore, through a connection with what is connected (*sambaddha-sambandha*), the universal of action is the cause of the cognition "cook" which has a substance as its object. To this, he says: "Precisely for that reason," and so forth.

"From that very [fact]" means precisely because the action has perished, there is no direct connection of the universal with the action; nor is there an indirect connection through the medium of the action with the substance, because of this lack of connection. Therefore, the universal is not the cause of the designation and cognition of "the cooker" and so forth. If it is argued that even something unconnected can be a cause, he says: "No," and so on. This is untenable.
"Connected. The mention of "sound" (*śabda*) is an illustration; the meaning is that an unconnected universal (*sāmānya*) is not the cause of cognition or sound.
Why? (1) Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Even "cowness" (*gotva*) would then be the cause of the cognition of a horse.
(160–61) He explains this with the words "For when [the action] has perished," etc. That universal—namely, the universal of the action—is not present in the action.

Because the *vetaṇta* (the action) does not exist, and because of the very absence of action, [the universal] is not even indirectly inherent (*samaveta*) in the agent, such as a cook; therefore, this universal has no connection with the substance even through a connected connection (*sambaddhasambandha*). "Otherwise" means if it were the cause of cognition and so forth even while being unconnected. As for what was stated, beginning with "and because of the non-existence of the persistence of action," that is [refuted by the following]: "that is past... and so on.
He anticipates another position [by saying]: "The past is that which has perished; the future is that action which will come to be.

Regarding these two—[the objects of] verbal knowledge and expression—the action, though past or future, is non-existent (*asat*); yet it serves as the cause (*nimitta*) for both cognition and designation.

Otherwise, there would be an over-extension [of the principle]. If it is argued that those two [names and designations] proceed by taking the past and future as their causes, then action (*karman*) would likewise be the cause for non-existent knowledge and designation. (161)
It is not a cause (*nimitta*);

for that would entail the consequence of being causeless (*anaimittikatā*). How could that which is devoid of causal capacity (*śakti*) be a cause? [This applies to] that very entity characterized by the performance of an action (*kriyākaraṇa*).

Because it is not perceived, the cessation of past and future karma cannot be the cause for non-perception. Furthermore, since other factors such as individual manifestation (*vyakti*) and so forth are not accepted [as the cause], those two would be without a cause. Consequently, the universal (*jāti*) is not established, because it is accepted as the cause for both cognition and verbal designation. If the capacity (*śakti*) were the cause for words such as "cook" and the like, and not karma—
It is not a universal, nor is it a capacity, because there is no concomitance.
It is a relation. What is the reason? [The text says] "of those two," and so forth; that is, of those two, namely cognition and designation.

He explains [the verse] with the words beginning "asati" (in the non-existent). That by which a thing (*vastu*) is described or manifested is "upākhyā," namely, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*). That from which this has departed is called "non-existent" (*asat*). Since the non-existent is devoid of the capacity for causal efficiency, how could such a thing be the cause of verbal cognition? This is the meaning.

Now, if it is maintained that even a non-existent thing can function as a cause, then it must possess the nature of a real entity (*vastu*) and not the nature of non-existence. Why is this so? He says: "Because of the effect," and so forth. The word *lakṣaṇa* denotes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "That" means for that reason. The past is that whose form has ceased; the future is that whose form has not yet been attained. Furthermore, [the cause] is distinct from the action (*karman*), as well as from the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) and so on, and from cognition (*jñāna*).
The proponent of universals does not accept that [the universal] is the cause of the basis for denotation.

[He holds that] "the individual is the substance which is the locus of action," and by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) and its latent impression (*vāsanā*), as well as their maturation, is intended. The word "those" refers to the word and the cognition. Likewise...

Furthermore, since the words and cognitions such as "cook" (*pācaka*) would lack a basis when considered as following from their objects, the existence of a universal (*jāti*) is not established. From the word *ca* ("and"), it follows that the word and its cognition would either always exist or never exist. Why the universal is not established? He says: "Of that," and so forth. This is because that universal is intended to be the cause for a cognition and a designation that are non-different from itself. For example:

And this applies to objects such as "the cook" and so forth; since those [words] function even in the absence of a [perceptible] cause, by what basis could a universal (*jāti*) be postulated for cows and the like?
With the words "power" (*śakti*) and so forth, he anticipates another position: the power of the substance which is the substratum of the action. The word—
The mention [of "grahaṇa"] is illustrative; the cognition of "cook" and so forth is also caused by a capacity (*śakti*). He refutes this with the words "no," etc.

The capacity of "cook" and so forth is not the cause for the word "cook" and so forth. Why? Because since the capacity is not distinct from the substance, it does not persist [through different instances] just as the substance itself does not; and for an object that does not persist, there can be no persistent cognition or designation.

Because the status of being a cause (*nimitta*) is not admitted; or, if it were admitted, it would follow that the postulation of a universal (*jāti*) is without foundation. For there is no other such thing as a "capacity for cooking" (*pākādi-śakti*) distinct [from the substance], because if there were, it would follow that the substance is useless since the capacity alone would be engaged in the purposeful action of cooking. If its utility lies in that capacity, then what is the function of the capacity? [It is] for the sake of its application to the capacity. (468b)
If one were to admit a separate, distinct power (*śakti*), it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); therefore, it must be said that the substance itself is what is employed.

Consequently, why not accept that it is the substance itself—which possesses the capacity—that is employed in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)? What is the use of an intermediate, purposeless "power"? Thus, it is the substance which is the effect of that [cause] that is the recurring factor there, and not a word [denoting a power].
It might be so, provided that the universal, such as "cook-ness" and the like, existed even prior [to the individual]. (162)
"If it is argued that [the capacity] is manifest, like existence (*sattā*) and so forth, we say no, because there is no distinction later on.

If it is claimed that the capacity is indeed distinct [from the substance], he says: 'Not indeed,' and so forth. For if the capacity were not other than the substance—if it were so—then, by reason of the single capacity being employed for causal functions such as cooking and the like, there would be no utility for the substance which is the substratum of that capacity."

Because it would lead to the undesirable consequence [of infinite regress]. The utility of that substance lies in that power which brings about cooking and so forth. The point is that even in this way, the substance would be utilized in cooking and so forth through a mediated succession. "Why? and so forth is the statement of the established conclusion (siddhānta): there is no purpose whatsoever for a power that is a distinct entity.

For instance, regarding the first capacity that brings about cooking and so forth, there is a substance which is employed by means of that capacity. If that capacity were also admitted to be distinct [from the substance], then, in order for the substance to be employed in the capacity that effects cooking and so forth, one would have to admit another capacity distinct from the substance; this would lead to an infinite regress (*atiprasaṅga*), because yet another capacity would be required for that [second] capacity as well.
The meaning is that another distinct power would have to be postulated for the [first] power, and yet another for that as well, resulting in an infinite regress.

Therefore, it must be stated that even without a separate power, the substance itself is employed in the first power which brings about the accomplishment of cooking and so forth. And thus, when the employment of the substance in the power is intended, that substance [is what performs the function] in the purposeful action.

Why is it not accepted that [the substance] is employed precisely for the purpose of cooking and so forth? What is the use of postulating a "capacity" (śakti) that is devoid of purpose in the interval between the substance and its causal efficiency (arthakriyā)? For this reason, by the phrase "the capacity for causal efficiency such as cooking," it is the substance itself that is being denoted. Of what nature is it?

[The opponent argues: "Because that substance whose effect is cooking and so forth does not persist through other individual instances, there would consequently be neither a recurring word nor a recurring cognition such as 'cook, cook' with respect to that substance. The mention of the 'word' is merely illustrative [of the cognition].
[Our position is that] in substances such as cooks, there exists a universal such as 'cook-ness' (pācakatva), which serves as the basis for the recurring word and cognition."

He says: "If the universal," and so forth. The meaning is this: if a universal such as "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*) is admitted, then it would exist as inherent in the substance at the very moment the substance is produced—that is, even prior to the state of possessing the capacity to perform the act of cooking and so on.

And in that case, the implication is that even an infant born on that very day would become an object of the cognition and designation "cook" and so forth. If not [that is, if the universal does not exist at that time]...
If it existed previously, it would not exist later either, because that substance remains without any change. It exists indeed at all times.

Furthermore, regarding the universal "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*), since it is occasional while its inherence in the object is not occasional, it would be manifested at its very first occurrence, just like existence (*sattā*) and other such universals. The text states that as many properties as belong to the universals of objects, they inhere [in the object] simultaneously with its production.

If there were no distinction even when that [nature] is transgressed, then its inherence (*samavāya*) would not occur later either; for, due to the deficiency in the nature of that which is related to it, such [inherence] would have to occur while that very nature remains present in the absence of its prior non-existence—this is an untenable consequence.
This applies to cases such as "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*) in a substance. However, because it was previously unmanifest, it was not the cause of the word or the cognition; therefore, he says:

"Manifestly" (*vyaktam*) means that it would have already been manifested; [this is] like "existence" (*sattā*) and so forth. Just as existence, substantiality (*dravyatva*), and the like, persist as long as the substance exists (*yāvaddravyabhāvin*); likewise, the substance must already be situated in a suitable location prior to its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). He explains this with the words "even though" (*athāpi*) and so forth: when the object exists—that is, when the locus of the universal (*jāti*) exists—there is the inherence (*samavāya*) of that [universal] in it, which is the inherence of the general property (*sāmānya-samavāya*).
Because it is not occasional—that is, because it exists at all times—he says the following to reinforce this very point: "For as many... and so forth.

Regarding the object (*artha*), which is the locus of the universal (*jāti*): those things which possess the property of inherence (*samavāya*) and are capable of connection are the universals (*sāmānya*). That which is the arising of this object, with that [arising] they inhere. [The phrase] "in this locus of the universal" involves a change in case endings (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*).

The connection is by way of name; that is to say, it is connected with the substance at the very same time as its production. Such is the convention (*samaya*). This is the established tenet (*siddhānta*) of the Sāṃkhyas. As Uddyotakara has said: "Prior to [the cognition of] 'cowness,' this is neither a cow nor a non-cow. What is the reason? Because those two qualifying cognitions do not exist in the absence [of the universal], and there is no qualifier..."

Two conditions do not exist without a relation to a qualificand, nor does an entity exist prior to its connection with "cowness" (*gotva*). Furthermore, that which is non-existent cannot be designated as either "cow" or "non-cow. At the very moment an entity arises, it is simultaneously connected with "cowness. Thus, there is no connection of existence (*sattā*) with what is already existent, nor with what is non-existent; and at the very moment the entity exists, [it is so].
"It is connected with existence. Now,
if one disregards the established tenet (*siddhānta*) and postulates that the universal (*sāmānya*) comes into being later, then upon such a transgression— that is,
a transgression of the established tenet— there is no distinction even later regarding the substance (*dravya*) which is the substratum (*āśraya*) of that universal.

There would be an inherence (*samavāya*) with that [universal]. Therefore, there would be no inherence with that universal. Just as redness does not exist in something whose nature is exclusively that of a fruit at first, but exists later; so too it would be for the universal of "cook-ness" and so forth in the case of a person. To this, he says: "related to that," and so on. Related to that...

Due to a deficiency in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavaiguṇyāt*). That is, due to a deficiency in the intrinsic nature that is related to universals (*sāmānya*) such as "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*). "That" refers to the inherence of the universal (*sāmānyasamavāya*). "Of that" refers to the person. For indeed, for one who remains in an unimpaired intrinsic nature, there would not be an absence of connection with that [universal]. And in that very case, for a substance that remains in an intrinsic nature impaired by the inherence of the universal, the universal subsequently [does not inhere].

"O Vāyu, it will come to be"—this is difficult to follow and difficult to understand. If the fruit, such as a mango, possesses a single nature both before and after [its production], then the same objection applies there as well. At that time, the substance is already connected with the universal; however, it is the universal that manifests [the substance] in dependence upon the assistance of the action. (162–63)
If that which depends on an action for assistance were the manifestor of an unchanging [entity], [it would follow that the entity itself undergoes change]. (163)
Even if there were an excellence [of some kind], how could there be action for this [entity], given its momentariness?

If it is argued that the substance’s state of being a "cook" is manifested by depending on the assistance provided by the action, then since this [state] rests upon the intrinsic nature [of the entity] and does not produce any distinction because no excellence is added, what dependence could there be? Or, if there were an excellence, [the entity would still be momentary] because the action is momentary. (469a)

Since at every moment another distinct excellence (*atiśaya*), which constitutes its very nature, arises, that [entity] too would be momentary. Consequently, for something that perishes at the very place of its own arising, how could there be action, and with respect to what could it be a manifestor?
[Objection: But how can the terms "object" and "cognition" apply to an entity if there is no single underlying substance, as is the case with [the designation] "cook" and so forth?
Likewise:
since that [substratum] does not exist prior [to the action], there is no manifestation of the universal beforehand; therefore, he says: "By the assistance of the action," and so forth.
Action is characterized by cooking and the like. With respect to the universal, it depends on the assistance produced by that [action].
If it is admitted that [the substance] is a manifester, then because that substance is non-momentary and unchanging, it would have no dependence upon auxiliary causes.
Alternatively, if it were to undergo modification, then the substance would incur momentariness due to its excellence (atiśaya). And because of momentariness—

An action is something that perishes immediately after its production; by means of this [action], there would have to be an excellence produced in the universal (*jāti*) which depends upon that assistance for it to become manifest. He explains this with the words "by the assistance of the action" (*karmopakāra*), etc. "Action" (*karman*) refers to the operation characterized by placing [the pot] on the stove and so forth.

The "assistance" (*upakāra*) is the excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by that [action]; depending upon that, how could there be a manifestation of a universal that is stable by nature—since it does not deviate from its prior nature and possesses no excellence?
Because there is no subsequent appropriation [of a new state], what expectation could there be regarding an action that produces no distinction? None at all.

Or, if it is accepted that an excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by an action arises in a substance, then because that action which bestows the excellence is momentary, another excellence—which is of the very nature of that substance being assisted—must likewise arise.

If the excellence produced by an action were not inherent to the substance, then, because that [excellence] would be the production of something else, the substance itself would not be benefited at all. Therefore, since a different excellence inherent to its own nature arises at every moment corresponding to each moment of action, even a substance such as Devadatta must be momentary. "From that" means from momentariness. Its own—

For a person who perishes at the very place of his own birth—that is, one who perishes in the very location where he arose—the action characterized by cooking is performed. That which is required [for that action] would be the manifestor of the substance-universal (dravyasāmānya) such as "cook" and so forth, being dependent upon that action.
Now, if the substance is momentary by way of the first and subsequent moments of action, and in the absence of action, how could it be momentary?

If it is argued that [the universal] is a single entity, we say no; for the meaning is that there is no other action capable of manifesting a universal among those moments produced in connection with a specific action.
Therefore, it remains established that there is no such thing as a real, ontological universal (*jāti*). (163–64)
"How then? and so forth is the opponent's objection.

"Just as... and so forth is the response from the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī). Just as there is no universal such as "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*) in those who are cooks and the like, so too it is not the case that [the universal] exists in them; or rather, "just as in them" means that it has been examined how there is no occurrence [of the universal] in them.

Rather, those two would not exist in the signless (*animitta*). Not in the signless; if you ask why, it is because external reality exists by means of signs (*nimitta*). According to each [individual], from the awakening of whichever respective latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), there arises conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); from that, words arise.
According to each [individual], there is perception. 4
Furthermore, it has already been largely established that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and verbal designation (*abhidhāna*) do not have the existence of a real entity as their basis.

This is because, despite the perception of successive [states] through the manifestation of contradictory forms due to the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one still perceives the continuity of that [entity]. Moreover, in that case, there is no inherent nature (*svabhāva*) anywhere that could serve as the basis for such [designation], since it is impossible for two mutually contradictory things to coexist in a single location.
It would be indeterminate; for if that were causeless, it might exist in some cases and not in others, and thus could not be ascertained.

Furthermore, it has been established that in those cases, the two—cognition and the word—function as concomitants. Likewise, in other instances as well, they would function even without a universal (*sāmānya*).
[The opponent says: "It will be explained later.

[The author replies with] "In that case," and so forth. [The opponent asks: "How can there be the application of inclusive cognition and words in those [cases], such as 'cook' and the like, in the absence of a universal? Therefore, because of the application of inclusive cognition and words even in the case of 'cook' and the like, there must be a universal such as "cook-ness" (pācakatva).
This was considered immediately after [the statement] "it exists. Likewise, a universal such as "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*) and so forth is not possible among them.

If there is no recurring form (*anvayi-rūpa*), then would those words and cognitions now be without a cause? No; this is the *Siddhāntavādī*. There certainly is a cause for those two, which is what the opponent accepts; it is that [cause] which is being rejected. He says that very thing:
"Furthermore," and so forth. A real, external universal (*sāmānya*) does not serve as the cause for those two [conceptual cognitions].

What, then, is their cause? To this he says: "According to their own [respective]... and so forth. From whichever awakening of its own latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) occurs, from that arises the corresponding conceptual cognition (*anvayin* vikalpa). Then, from the arising of that conceptual cognition, [the object appears] in accordance with that conceptualization (*yathāvikalpam*).

Words arise; however, there is no real existence of things (*vastusattā*) corresponding to conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) or designations (*abhidhāna*). It has already been largely explained that [words] depend upon the existence of recurring categories (*anvayipadārtha*). This must necessarily be accepted. For instance, by virtue of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of inherence (*samavāya*) specific to each [system], and in reliance upon their respective tenets, through conformity with the latent impressions of cognition and by way of the imposition of contradictory forms, mutually contradictory forms are superimposed.

By means of the rope, [it is shown that] the effects of Pradhāna, the effects of Īśvara, and the world as mere conventional appearance are without a [real] cause; thus, in all these various distinctions, there is the persistence of those two—namely, cognition and its designation—even when different and successive things are perceived. And "not in that case" refers to those objects conceptualized through mutually contradictory forms, such as being the effects of Pradhāna and so forth.
That which is based upon it is that which is based upon word and cognition. Why does he say it does not exist? He says: "Of two mutually contradictory [things]," and so forth.
The opponent says: "By way of non-restriction," and so forth; [otherwise] every cognition and every designation would be concomitant with everything.
Proving this very point, he says: "For it is not without a cause," and so forth.

[Objection: But has it not already been refuted that these two [the universal and the particular] lack a cause, by the statement beginning with "because conceptual constructions arise from the awakening of their respective latent predispositions (*vāsanā*)"?

Thus, this objection is indeed without foundation. [Response: This is how it is considered: an internal cause alone is accepted for those two, and since there is no proximity or distance for that cause, it would follow that it is the cause of all conceptual constructions everywhere. 4. *Sāmānyacintā* (Investigation of the Universal)

For that [cognition] is not indeed signless (*animitta*), because it has specific latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as its cause; likewise, it has been stated that even when such an external object is not manifested, [the cognition occurs]. Nor is it the case that [the cognition] cannot exist in the absence of that [external object], for conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise in such a manner regarding objects perceived by those who are asleep or suffering from ophthalmia, and regarding specific forms superimposed upon a book. And they do not [arise] merely through the production of that [conceptual construction].
In all places, they exist in all forms; for they are conceptualized as such precisely through their distinct divisions.
Here, by way of a single nature—that is, a single essence—there is the single body of gnosis (*ekajñānakāya*), because existence itself is differentiated in certain respects; this is the summary.
Furthermore:
By which proximity a universal extends over [individuals] despite their being equal in difference. ||164||
"Could it not be that this very [cognition] alone is the basis for verbal knowledge?"—
this is the summary verse.
For in the phrase "arising without a cause," one should understand "without a cause" to mean the absence of an external cause.

"Not in the case of a non-sign" (*nānimitta*) means "not when the sign is undifferentiated," according to the *Siddhāntavāda*. The meaning is that [the two types of conceptualization] do not occur. For this very reason, he says: "Because they have specific latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as their cause. The meaning of the whole passage is this: a latent impression, which has arrived by way of seeing things as they truly are, produces a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that determines that very state in that specific instance, but not everywhere. Thus...

The word "that" (*tam*) refers to the recurring form (*anvayi-rūpam*). And even in the absence of such an external recurring cause (*nimitta*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) must indeed occur; it cannot fail to occur.
He establishes this very point with the words beginning "asleep" (*supta*): in the objects perceived by one who is asleep and one who has ophthalmia (*taimirika*).

In cows and the like, as well as in hair, flies, and so forth, there is respectively the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of inherence (*samavāya*). In non-entities such as the horns of a hare and the like, there is the latent impression of conventional designation (*saṃketa-vāsanā*), by the power of which one superimposes specific forms upon [concepts] such as the "Primal Matter" (*pradhāna*) or "Effects" (*kārya*), according to their respective philosophical tenets. This is because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise accordingly—that is, because conceptualizations that follow a common thread arise. For in these aforementioned things, there is no external, underlying continuum (*anvayi*).
Form exists, because only those things perceived in dreams, by those with cataracts, and so forth, are non-existent. Their non-existence will be demonstrated in the third chapter (3185).

Furthermore, the non-existence of that which is superimposed by philosophical tenets—such as [the claim that] two mutually contradictory things exist simultaneously in one place—has already been established. Nor do those conceptual constructions [apply] to the non-existent things perceived in dreams and the like.

Even without a form that possesses real substantial continuity (*vastubhūtānvayirūpa*), objects arise everywhere in all their aspects; however, they are indeed restricted [to specific ones]. He states the cause for this restriction with the words "only by way of distinction," and so forth. "Of those perceived in that very way" means of those perceived by way of distinction, because conceptualization occurs only by way of distinction. First, in the state of sleep or of *timira* (ocular disorder),...

There is the perception of objects established upon erroneous cognition through their differentiation— such as those superimposed by one's own philosophical tenets at the time of hearing those tenets, and even in cases such as "the horn of a hare" and so forth, at the time of learning linguistic usage like "the horn of a hare" or "the son of a barren woman," because the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of linguistic usage are beginningless. And it has been said in this regard, etc.

In the passage [from the *Tattvasaṅgraha*] stating, "The cognition of a single object, such as 'this is a tree,' is the means of establishing a single referent" (1975), it is further argued that just as *dhava*, *khadira*, and other trees are mutually distinct, so too are cows and other animals. In that case, since the difference is equal, [the Sāṃkhya position fails]. 320.
kha. Refutation of the Sāṃkhya doctrine.
If there were no other continuity of entities apart from cessation, [then... //165//
The effect of one would not belong to another due to their absolute difference.

If these entities were devoid of any nature that persists through others by way of exclusion (*nivṛtti*), then many entities could not have a single effect. For that which has the nature of producing a particular thing does not possess that same nature for another; what exists for one is not what exists for the other.

Janaka: Because exclusion (*vyatireka*) lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). That which is a producer is a real entity (*vastu*). When asked why the property of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*) resides only in *dhava* trees and the like, and not in cows and the like—despite their being producers of the same effect—the opponent must say this very thing:
it is simply the inherent capacity (*bhāvaśakti*) of the *dhava* and other trees by virtue of which they alone are proximate to the property of being a tree, whereas cows and others are not.

In that case, when the object to be distinguished is identical, why does the universal (*jāti*)—by means of the power of being (*bhāvaśakti*), which is characterized by proximity—spread over and pervade a certain mass of objects intended as its own substratum? Let that very power of being be the basis for the recurring word and cognition; what is the use of postulating a "universal" (*sāmānya*)?
Therefore, as it has been said:
"For the arising of cognitions is not held to occur without an object;
because of its distinction [from particulars], they maintain that there must certainly be a universal."
"For those [particulars] would be false if they were produced without that [universal], being devoid of their object;
however, the occurrence of the universal here without another [particular] is not problematic.
This is refuted, for it is not accepted that the occurrence of a universal among certain things takes place without a universal [as its substrate].

In this way, the opponent is compelled to accept that a cognition of a universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) may be admitted even without a real universal. For the opponent’s reply would be that those cognitions, if produced without such a universal, would be false. However, just as for the opponent there is a certain proximity (*pratyāsatti*) by which a universal functions among certain objects even in the absence of a universal, so too [is it here].
There is no fault here in the intended meaning that the cause for the word and cognition of a "succession" (anvaya) is simply error; what need is there for a universal (sāmānya)?
Therefore, this remains established: the succession among entities arises solely from the determination of unity regarding their exclusion (vyāvṛtti), and not from anything else.
On this point, the Sāṃkhya says: "Not cessation," and so forth. "The continuity of entities" (*bhāvānvaya*) means the uniformity of entities.
"The other" refers to that which is a real entity (*vastubhūta*). In that case, whatever effect belongs to one seed would not belong to another, such as the earth.
Why? Because of the absolute difference between those two, the seed and the earth. (165–66)

He explains this with the words beginning "If these," and so forth. "Of these" refers to entities (*bhāva*); for example, from a single seed, there arises a single effect known as a sprout. He establishes that very point with the words beginning "For he who," and so forth: for whatever [effect] arises from that seed by virtue of its nature of producing a sprout, it would not have arisen through anything else.

If that which has the nature of producing a certain [effect] were also the producer of another [effect], then by virtue of that nature it would be non-different from the former; thus, there is a continuity of nature. If multiple [causes] possess a single identity, they would be the producers of a single effect. (166)
The auxiliary causes would be useless;
for if multiple [causes] produce a single effect because they possess a single nature, then their nature is non-different.
Since that nature exists even when only one is present—due to the absence of any deficiency in the causal factors—even a single one should be a producer.
That form does not depart; indeed, it is the particulars that are subject to departure. //167//

For that which has an undifferentiated nature (*abhinnasvabhāva*), there is no distinction even when it relates to another object. If there were such a distinction, its nature would not be undifferentiated; indeed, such [a distinction] does not exist for earth and the like. That which exists is superimposed by the intellect (*buddhyāropita*) and is characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

That [other] is not the producer. Why? Because exclusion (*vyatireka*), which is characterized by the differentiation from others, lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). Therefore, only the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the seed is the producer; and that which has the nature of being a producer is itself the real entity (*vastu*). And that which is the producer is the specific characteristic that produces the sprout. "Elsewhere" means in earth and so forth. Would earth and the other factors produce the sprout?
