The word *hi* has the sense of the particle *eva* (only). "Of that" means of the seed. "Of another," such as earth and so forth—that earth and so forth would, by virtue of that production of the sprout, be non-different from the seed-nature [of the sprout]. Thus, there is a continuity (*anvaya*) of the nature of existence.
Therefore, the statement that "some things, despite a difference in nature, produce a single effect by their very essence (*prakṛti*), like the sense faculties and so forth," is incorrect.

With the words "If," and so forth, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) states: "Even in one [of them]" means that the very nature (*ātman*) by which the collection of causes is held to be the producer [of the effect] exists even in just one cause among those various causes. Since the effect would thus be produced by that single [cause], the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) would be rendered useless.
[Objection: But even for the proponent of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), since all [causes] possess the capacity to produce at the final moment, other causes would be useless.

[Reply: This is not so. It is only when those momentary things are combined that they possess such a capacity, because their presence depends upon causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). For the opponent, however, who maintains the doctrine of permanence, that nature [of producing] exists at all times; thus, there would be no need for other causes.
The name [of the cause] would be meaningless. For this very reason it was stated that "it exists even in one [instance]," meaning even in a state where other causes are deficient.
He explains this with the words beginning "if," etc.: if a manifold entity, by virtue of having a single nature, were the producer of a single effect...

The producer of those things considered to be causes is its own undifferentiated nature; this [nature] exists even when only a single cause is present. Consequently, since the cause is never deficient in any state whatsoever, wherever it may reside, even a single [cause] would be a producer. (166–67)

Strengthening this very point, he says: "Because," and so forth. Even when a single [cause], such as a seed, is present, there is no production of its effect that is non-distinct from the offspring—that is, no universal form. The particulars, which are the distinct individuals, are subject to disappearance (*apāyin*). For it is not the case that [the universal] is lost upon their departure; indeed, it exists even there [in the absence of the particulars]. Thus, even when one [particular] persists, there is no disappearance of that [universal]. As for those particulars...
Because there is no rule for their simultaneous existence, there might be a loss of those various states;
moreover, they are not intended to be the producers [of the effect], since it is accepted that auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) produce [the effect] by virtue of having a single nature.
Therefore, because the producer persists and that which does not persist is not a producer, the effect arises even when [the cause] exists alone.
It might be so, but it is not the case. Therefore:
"Because the effect is absent when even one [of the particulars] is removed, its production arises from the particulars.
An effect that is common to many cooperating causes would not exist even upon the removal of a single particular, let alone upon the removal of all particulars.
It might also be so. But surely, [an effect] does not arise even when the [cause] is entirely non-different in form. For an effect must possess the property of existence derived from something;

that which does exist [must arise] from that [cause], because otherwise it would be deficient. Yet, there is no deficiency in a single, non-different entity even while it persists. Thus, its failure to produce [the effect] while remaining unimpaired indicates its lack of causal efficiency (*ajanakatā*).

Even in earth and other factors—which are distinct from the seed that possesses the nature of producing an effect—there exists a specific quality. Why? Because if there were such a specific quality, the non-difference [of the seed] would be lost. For that very nature, which is intended to be the producer and is held to be non-different, exists even in the seed alone. Thus, even while the one [seed] persists, there is no loss of that non-different form which is intended to be the producer.

There is destruction [of the specific qualities], because the three *guṇas* exist everywhere, at all times, and in their entirety; whereas as for those specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) which are particular states, they may undergo loss due to the absence of a rule for their simultaneous existence. This has been stated while granting the opponent's position; otherwise, there could be no specific qualities distinct from the various states of that which is eternal.

How could there be the destruction even of those [causes]? And why are these specific differences not accepted as being the producers? To this he says: "Of the co-operating causes," and so forth. Therefore, even when a single factor such as a seed is present, because the producer remains in its own state, [the effect would arise] from that non-abiding specific difference. Even when only one [factor] such as the seed is present, the effect—

[The effect] would arise; however, the production of the effect does not occur. Therefore, even though the general [nature] persists and the auxiliary conditions are present, because the result is absent when a single particularity is removed, its arising—the arising of the effect—proceeds from the particularities, not from the general nature. What is that effect, such as the sprout? It is manifold, and so forth. Of the many [particularities], the auxiliary...

"Common to the agents" means produced by multiple auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). "Even upon the removal of one particular [auxiliary]" means even upon the absence of any one of the auxiliaries. By this, he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); by the words "again," etc., he states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Therefore, the positive and negative concomitance of the effect pertains only to the particulars, and not to [the universal].

Regarding the universal (*sāmānya*): he says this [in the verse], "But surely, when not incomplete" (*nanvavikala*). Even when the undifferentiated form is present in its entirety through the presence of a single particular (*viśeṣa*), that effect does not arise. He analyzes this very point with the words beginning "For the effect... and so forth. Arising from something is existence (*bhāva*); that itself is the property (*dharma*). That which possesses it is "that which has the property of existence" (*tadbhāvadharma*). When it occurs at some time or place, that is its production (*janana*).

Due to the deficiency of what? Not of the form that is intended as the producer, because even when one among the auxiliary causes is present, there is a deficiency [among the others]. When that general form is complete, the effect does not arise;
therefore, regarding that general form, the production of the effect occurs precisely through its completeness or deficiency, and the rule is that it arises only when that [general form] is present.

It might be so; for if one were to imagine its production from something other than that, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Therefore, only particulars (*viśeṣa*) are productive, not the universal (*sāmānya*). Consequently, only those [particulars] are real entities (*vastu*). That alone is an ultimately real thing (*pāramārthika-bhāva*) which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*). ||168||

For we shall explain that this very thing is characterized as real or unreal based on its capacity or incapacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). That which is capable of purposeful action is the fit object;
that which does not persist does not give rise to an effect.

Therefore, because it is capable of being the basis for all general conceptual operations, it is not a "real entity" (*vastu*); rather, it is precisely a particular real entity (*vastu-viśeṣa*), since it is from that alone that those [generalities] are produced.

[Objection: If that is so, since the nature of one thing does not persist in another, the form of one thing which is its producer would not exist in the other; thus, the latter would be a non-producer.
He establishes that [the universal] does not possess the nature of a producer.

(167–68) Now, one might object: "It is not the universal alone that is accepted as the producer such that this fault would arise; rather, it was stated that it is a producer by virtue of having a manifold nature. To this, he says: "That which is complete... and so forth. And regarding those particularities whose completeness or incompleteness—
The effect exists like presence and absence [in relation to its causes]. Therefore, the production of the effect is from those very particulars (*viśeṣa*).

"When that exists" means when the particular, which is fit to function as the cause, exists, the effect comes to be. "From something other than that" refers to [the claim that it arises] from a universal (*sāmānya*) other than the particular;
[if this were so], there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that everything would be the cause of everything. Since this is the case, therefore, only the particulars [are the causes].

The producers [are the particulars]. The universal is not a producer; therefore, because it lacks productive capacity, only those particulars are the real entity (*vastu*). This means they are ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). What is the reason? Because an ultimately real thing (*pāramārthiko bhāvaḥ*) means that which is ultimately real;
only that is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*).

He explains this with the words "This very [thing], etc. The definition of a real entity (*vastu*) is its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogyatā*); the definition of a non-entity (*avastu*), however, is its incapacity. The connection [of the sentence] is: "we shall explain [this]"—namely, by the passage beginning with "That which is capable of causal efficiency is here ultimately real" (3.3). An object that is capable of all causal efficiency is...

That which consists of a particular does not persist [through change], because a particular does not follow after other individuals. That which persists consists of a universal; therefore, an effect cannot arise from that which consists of a universal. The conclusion is stated with the words "therefore" and so forth. Because it is unfit for purposeful action—that is, because it is incapable of performing a causal function—[it is not a real entity].

The meaning is as follows: "From that very [cause]" means precisely from the particular [cause], because of the accomplishment of that [effect], namely, the accomplishment of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Thus, it has been demonstrated that what is imagined by others lacks the capacity for production. (168–69) Now, that which was stated by the opponent—"The effect of one would not belong to another due to absolute difference"—is refuted.
He repeats that very objection with the words, "In that case, because there is no concomitance of intrinsic nature," and so forth:
"In the alleviation of fever and the like, some [remedy] acts either together or individually.
If being a producer were the [sole] criterion, then everything would be a producer because there is no distinction [between them].
This is not so;
for even though there is a difference [among things], by virtue of that specific nature, one thing is a cause while another is not. (169)
This is the nature of that which has a single productive essence: all [its instances], being differentiated, must either be equally productive or none at all is productive.

Just as there is no state of distinction among them, so too, despite the lack of difference in their differentiation, some one [instance] is productive and another is not due to some excellence of its own nature (*ātmātiśaya*); for that is its specific nature, and not that of the other.

For regarding the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of things, it is not subject to the objection: "Why does fire burn or is hot, and why does water not? because one must simply accept that "this is its nature. If these were causeless and independent, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of irregularity. Therefore, it is said that its nature arises from its own cause; and for that [cause] as well, its nature consists in the production of that [effect].
This has already been refuted by such passages as the aforementioned; nevertheless, this is introduced again for the sake of providing further elaboration.

Since the nature that is the producer of one thing, such as a seed, does not exist in another, such as the earth, the latter would be a non-producer as a cooperative cause (*sahakārī*). Furthermore, if it were admitted that something possessing a nature distinct from the nature of the producer could nonetheless be a producer...
Since there is no difference in their being distinct entities, everything—even barley seeds and the like—would become a producer of the rice sprout.

He refutes this with the words beginning "This is not so": although there is an absolute difference between the earth and so forth, as well as barley seeds and the like, on one hand, and the single productive rice seed and its nature (*ātman*) on the other, certain causes such as the earth [still function] for the rice sprout.

Nor is anything else, such as a barley seed and so forth. The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of completing the verse, or it has the sense of the restrictive particle "eva. What is the reason? This is the nature of things: all entities that differ from that very nature which is the productive essence of one thing would necessarily follow as being equally productive; or, because there is no distinction in their difference [from the non-producer], none at all would be a producer.
If these [effects] were to arise from a single producing self, this objection would apply; but for those that are distinct, there is no such thing as a non-effect of that.

A specific characteristic defined by necessity regarding production would not be possible; however, it is indeed possible. "Therefore" means because such a specific characteristic is possible. Even though there is no difference in their being distinct entities, due to some internal excellence characterized by a restriction to a particular effect, a certain thing—such as earth and so forth—is the producer of a rice sprout, while another—such as a barley seed and so forth—is not. Why [is this so]? Because of the rice...

The specific nature of the earth and other such auxiliary causes that produce a *ḍakura* sprout belongs to them alone, and not to others such as barley seeds. If it is asked what causes this very distinction, he says: "For indeed," and so forth. One ought not to subject fire to the inquiry, "Does fire burn because it is hot, or does it not burn because it is not hot? for this is established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Only this much may be asked:

It would be logical [to ask]: "From what cause does this have the aforementioned nature? For there must necessarily be a cause for a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because, if it were causeless, then being independent, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of violating the restriction of place and so forth; that is, there would be the consequence of the entity existing everywhere, at all times, and in its entirety. Therefore, its intrinsic nature arises from its own cause, which is considered its cause.

It is said that [the effect] arises from its presence. Furthermore, the fact that this [cause] has the nature of producing that [effect] is due to its being produced by its own cause as having the nature of a cause of such a kind;
and that [nature] is due to another of its own causes, and so on—thus there is a beginningless succession of causes. 4. This is the investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*);
"from another" refers to the beginningless succession of causes.

For there is no other cause for things that are distinct than their own nature (*svabhāva*); thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. However, if they were non-distinct by nature, then destruction and arising would occur simultaneously, because they would be non-different by virtue of their own nature. Just as in the case of one's own self, there would be no production, subsistence, or cessation characterized by various divisions. (471a)

Likewise, because it is characterized by non-difference; for in a homa characterized by both difference and non-difference, there is no contradiction even regarding the single form, whether it is distinct or non-distinct, since there is no contradiction within a single self.
If it is argued that difference is not thus [established] by that [means];

We do not say that there is no distinction between all causes, for if that were so, this [consequence] would follow. Rather, what is its nature? It is neither "different" nor "non-different," because of the distinction [between them]; thus it is not something such as being "inborn" (sahaja) and so forth. For there is no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) that subverts the differentiation of causes for entities that are distinct. He says that very thing: "In the case of the distinct..."

And so forth. "From its own nature" (*svabhāvāt*) means from the actual state of things. He states that there is a subverting argument against their being one, beginning with "But if there were non-difference," and so forth.

The meaning is that because of mutual non-difference, upon the destruction of one, there would be the simultaneous destruction of all; and upon the production of one, there would be the production of all.
He explains this with the words "Because of non-difference," and so forth: because the entire collection of objects (*viśvasya sarvasya padārtharāśeḥ*) is non-different by virtue of its own nature.

Regarding the phrase "distinction in arising," and so forth: there would be no such distinctions as the arising of one thing and the non-arising of another, the persistence of one and the cessation of another, and so on. The phrase "like its own self" means that just as the arising and other states of a single particular condition do not occur through such a distinction, so it would be here. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), one includes such things as the perception of one thing and the non-perception of another.

In the Sūtra, however, the mention of destruction and arising is for the purpose of illustration; for in that very way, through such [characteristics] as division and arising, there is the ascertainment of non-difference by means of illustration. Otherwise, by what would difference and non-difference be characterized? "Even of that which has a single form" means even of that which has an identical form; "distinction" (vyatireka) is division, the state of possessing separate arising and so forth. That is the definition of difference.

Non-distinction (*avyatireka*) means non-separation, the absence of having separate origination and so forth; this is the definition of that non-difference. To the question, "Even if there is separation and the like, why is there no difference? he says: "Of two opposites," and so forth. Because of the contradiction between two opposites—such as origination and non-origination—occurring simultaneously within a single self. It is not that things are absolutely non-different, but rather...
There is also a distinction. As it has been said:
"Indeed, every entity is distinct by virtue of its own form, but not mutually [in its essence];
yet, in relation to their own specific natures, these are mutually distinct."

For that reason, if it is argued that there is no such consequence of simultaneous arising and so forth, he says: "No," and so on, which is the explanation of the first [point]. We certainly do not assert a non-distinction or identity in every respect, by which such a thing as the simultaneous arising of light and so forth would occur. Rather, there is some nature (*ātman*) of this distinction between the external and internal, such as a jar—

The state characterized by a particular condition is distinct [from the substance], yet not other than that which consists of the three *guṇas*; for the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, as well as the nature of being an object, the nature of a substance, and the nature of existence, are found to follow through everything. Therefore, the meaning is this: there is no difference between the state and that which possesses the state.
For thus—the Self does not "abide";
since abiding and non-abiding share a single substratum, what other property could serve as a differentiator? In this way, there is no plurality anywhere.

It would not be so; for it is accepted that there are two objects distinguished by all their aspects. Only the name might not be desired, but the entity itself is not [non-existent], as was stated previously.
Therefore, these entities are indeed distinct, as they do not share the same acquisition or preservation (*ekayogakṣema*).
Therefore, this [destruction] is not a separate entity that remains independent when one thing perishes. (170)

There would be no cognition of it as either a universal or a particular; for although there is no mutual difference between the [universal] and this [particular] because it is produced [from it], yet there is indeed mutual difference between the states themselves. Thus, from the aforementioned definition of states and so forth...
Because of the distinction [between the two].

(166–70) If that is so, then since the universal (*sāmānya*) is eternal, its persistence everywhere is accepted; whereas the destruction of the particulars (*viśeṣa*) is also accepted. Consequently, when one particular perishes, that which remains as the nature of the universal is not [the same as the particular].
The possibility of that distinction [arises as follows]: due to the superimposition of contradictory properties, there would necessarily be a difference between the universal and the particular.

Otherwise, if it were admitted that the locus and the non-locus share a single substratum, then even two contradictory properties would be accepted as residing in one and the same self; and what other property could serve as a differentiator? None at all. Indeed, the properties are not contradictory.

In one place, both [particularity and generality] are accepted because they are distinct due to the difference in their definitions. For instance, particulars are differentiated in every respect through their separate origination and so forth, whereas generality is undifferentiated everywhere because it lacks separate origination and the like; therefore, he says:
"sarvākāra... and so on. This refers to the two objects, particularity and generality, which are respectively differentiated and undifferentiated in all their aspects.

Because of the acceptance [of this]. "Merely a name" means that the expression "the particular and the universal are distinct" is intended as a mere designation and not as a real entity (*vastu*). However, the real entity, which consists of both the particular and the universal, is indeed accepted as being mutually distinct. This has already been stated previously, by means of the passage beginning with: "Or, having accepted a difference in meaning through another name, because it is designated in such a way," and so forth.

The word *tat* means "therefore. These entities—whether particulars (*viśeṣa*) or universals (*sāmānya*)—are indeed mutually distinct. Of what nature are they? They are "not sharing a single fate" (*naikayogakṣema*), which is to say, they are superposed with contradictory properties. For this reason, there would be no cognition of a universal as distinct [from its particulars]; the meaning is that there would be no cognition connecting the universal and the particular to one another.
Furthermore, because of the absence of cognition (*buddhi*), even linguistic designation (*vyapadeśa*) is refuted, since that [designation] is based upon cognition. Therefore:
"There would always be mutual dependence between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*); for particulars depend on the universal, and it [the universal] depends on them. (Ākṛti 6)

—Thus [the objection] is refuted. "Tad" means "therefore. This universal (*sāmānya*) is a distinct entity from the particulars (*bheda*); it does not depend upon the particulars. Why? (1) Because those particulars do not produce that universal. 4. [The section on] the investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*) cannot [be established].
If it is argued that this same undesirable consequence applies even in the case of exclusion (*anyāpoha*), we say: no, it is not the same. For instance:
"Because cessation is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), there is no conceptualization of its abiding or non-abiding. (171)

Regarding [the view that it is] "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), since it is not any positive entity (*bhāva*), there would be no conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of it either, through the conceptualizations of its own-nature, its persistence, or its cessation, which are invariably connected to the nature of an entity. Furthermore, because it is the basis for the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*), it is not subject to that same refutation.
This false cognition is indeed devoid of an object, appearing in various forms because its object does not exist; thus, there is neither persistence nor non-persistence [of the object].
Regarding the second point: this entity, which consists of difference, is a distinct thing from the universal (*sāmānya*); [the cognition] occurs with respect to that universal.

Because it is not produced by that which is independent [of it], and because a permanent entity lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), this particular cannot be designated as "the universal of this particular," nor can the particular be designated as "belonging to this universal."

"This same consequence applies even if the universal is [defined as] the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)," namely: "when one [individual] perishes, the self remains," and so forth. For instance, when a *dhava* or a *khadira* tree perishes, the exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣavyāvṛtti*) certainly remains in other trees.
He refutes this with the words "No" and so on. The meaning here is that the exclusion of others is of two kinds: one is the exclusion of heterogeneous [things]...

In the context of the [cognitive] process (*vṛtti*), that which is superimposed by the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*) through its own distinct form and is made an object by means of a word is precisely that which is the objective domain of purposeful action (*pravṛttiviṣaya*), because it alone possesses causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*). This is not the case for the mere appearance within the intellect, as it lacks causal efficacy. Furthermore, there is another [aspect], namely the mere exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), which is cognized from the [external] object. (170–71)

And since this [negation] is merely the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛttimātra*), it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*); therefore, this objection does not apply. Or, according to what the Master intends, because that [negation] lacks intrinsic nature, it is non-existent—this is the meaning. Thus he says: "Because cessation is without intrinsic nature, there is no conceptualization of possibility or impossibility."

When the particular (*viśeṣa*) perishes, does the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) remain, or does it cease? This conceptualization of its persistence or non-persistence is logical only with respect to that exclusion of others. [The properties] are inherent in its own nature and do not follow the thing itself.
In that case, the conceptualization of the persistence or the departure from its own form would apply to that universal (*sāmānya*) which is superimposed by conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*).

Therefore, he says: "And [it is] a distortion," and so forth. That general form which appears as non-different from multiple objects is a distortion (*upaplava*)—that is, an error—of the cognition of the universal; therefore, even that does not exist externally at all. Precisely because it is thus characterized by being a distortion, the cognition of the universal is "not subject to refutation" (*adūṣaṇā*). The analysis of the compound is: there is no refutation as previously stated in this [cognition].
This conceptual consciousness, which has a single form, is without an object. If it is asked how this is so—since it is a false cognition of a false object—the author says:
"That which," and so forth. Because it has a single form despite having multiple [objects], that conceptual consciousness lacks an object.
There is neither persistence nor non-persistence of the object as a generality. Why? (1) Because that which is the object of false cognition does not exist. (171–72) 4* Skoda 4 % sērs vi
Furthermore, as for this statement: "For that which produces something has the nature of that [thing]—how could a producer other than its produced form be a producer? (172)

Thus we say; however, we do not say that there is no nature (*rūpa*) therein capable of producing another [effect]. What then? We say that whatever is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of one thing that produces it, that is not the nature of another. Another entity also arises by its own essential nature alone, and not by the nature of another, because it is distinct from it. Since they too are each distinct and productive by their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*), what contradiction is there here? [In the case of] a single nature—

That which is deficient [in its causal capacity] would not possess that nature, nor would it be non-producer of that effect. What logic is there in the claim that "by that very [nature], it produces that effect"?
Furthermore, distinct particulars are the producers.
Thus it has been said:
those particulars, too, do not possess mutual connection through that nature [of being identical], because that form which is the producer of one does not exist in the others.
Yet, they are not non-producers for that reason alone. If they were non-different, then it would indeed be true that the particulars are producers; they are also [producers].

Having removed the charge of parity of fault (*samānadoṣatā*), he speaks again—beginning with "But that which..."—in order to resolve the objection raised by another method: "For that which produces it" means that which produces that rice-sprout is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of that rice-seed. And that form of the rice-seed which is the producer of the rice-sprout—from that productive form...

"How can earth and so forth, which are other [than the seed], be the producer?"—the word "therein" (*tatra*) is used for the purpose of introduction; or rather, it refers to the objection being answered therein. We do not say that earth and so forth, which are other than the rice seed, lack the nature of producing that sprout. What then? We say that the nature which is the producer of one thing, such as a rice seed, does not belong to another, such as earth and so forth.

We reply: because entities do not possess mutual continuity (*ananvaya*). "Another [entity] as well" refers to earth and so forth. "Not by way of another's form" means not by way of the form of a rice seed. What is the reason? Because it is not that [same thing], because it does not have that intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatva*). And there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for this, as he says: "those [elements] such as earth, etc., according to their own [nature]"—that which is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of each.

Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that things which are distinct from one another produce a single effect by their very nature, since there is an absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). However, it is not contradictory for earth and other factors—which lack the form of a rice seed yet are considered producers of a rice sprout—to have a rice sprout as their effect; thus he says: "Of a single form," and so forth. Of one...

If the earth and other factors were deficient in that specific nature which is the producer of the rice seed, they would not possess the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the rice seed and so forth; [the rice seed] would not be something that does not produce that effect, but rather it would indeed produce that effect. The analysis of the compound is: "that rice sprout is its effect" (*sa śālyaṅkuraḥ kāryam asyeti*). If, however, the seed alone were the producer of the sprout, there would be a contradiction; but that is not the case. Thus he says: "Therefore..."
"Or [it arises] from the seed," and so forth.
By the words "api ca" (furthermore), he recalls what was stated previously:

"Because the effect is absent when even one [of the causes] is missing, its production must arise from the specific factors (*viśeṣa*). Thus, by the force of this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the specific factors [are established].

It was stated previously that they are "producers" (*janakāḥ*). Therefore, "by that self" means by that nature of being a producer. It is not the case that the specific natures (*viśeṣasvabhāvāḥ*) of a single seed are its producers.
This might be argued: even though they are non-different from it, those [specifics] are non-producers by virtue of that general form (*sāmānyarūpa*).
It was stated [previously] that this follows as a consequence.
4. Regarding the investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*):
[Individuals] are producers because they are conjoined with a single power; therefore, they are said to be non-producers [of anything else].
Because that [non-duality] does not depart; even for one who remains in a single place, the appearance of the production of a result is also a differentiator. || 173 ||
It does not partake of anything else.

Furthermore, sounds are characterized by the distinctions of arising, abiding, and ceasing. For one whose mind [perceives] the distinction between all objects, there would either be no differentiation in the appearance of cognition regarding those things to be grasped—due to the superimposition of contradictory properties—or, if such a differentiation were to exist, it would not be possible.

It would not exist anywhere; and thus, like a single self, this distinction would not occur. Therefore, this [distinction] consisting of a different appearance and so forth is not a difference at all.

The nature of another thing, such as earth and so forth, does not exist [in it]. It is not the case that [the rice seed] is non-productive merely by way of a deficiency in the nature of the rice seed.
"Earth and so forth. "Even non-difference," and so on; the meaning is that even non-difference exists within those particularities.
He explains this with the words beginning "It might be argued that... That very non-different form is a single power; [the particulars] are connected with it.
By that [word], the Master [Dharmakīrti] means: by that non-different form, those particulars are said to be non-productive.
He explains [the point] with the words beginning "Even though... and so forth. By that general form (*sāmānyarūpa*), those particulars (*viśeṣa*) are non-producers.

What is the reason? Because that general form, being eternal, does not perish. And this was stated previously in the passage beginning: "That form does not depart; indeed, the particulars do not perish" (verse 18.167). (172–73)

Having established difference through the superimposition of contradictory properties by means of the verse beginning with “destruction and origination would occur simultaneously” (1.170), he says “Furthermore,” etc., in order to establish it also through the difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*). What kind of difference in appearance?
It is “not shared by others” (*ananyabhāk*), meaning it is distinct for each individual instance. By the word “also” (*api*), the difference in origination and so forth is also included.
The differentiator. And this is merely a restatement of what was previously said.

Furthermore, even one who speaks according to the Vedānta says: "For the apprehension of difference is caused by the apprehension of non-existence, and non-existence is not graspable by perception. Therefore, by perception only existence-in-general (sattāmātra) is grasped, not difference. As it has been said:

Regarding the statement, "Even that which arises in relation to a cow or a horse is not distinguished from direct perception," he says: "The principle (*nyāya*), etc. "Of that" refers to the proponent of non-difference (*abheda-vādin*).

"Difference in the appearance of cognition" means a difference in the form (*ākāra*) of cognition. "Superimposition of contradictory properties" refers to [attributes] such as arising and perishing separately. Even if that [difference] exists...

If one were to admit that there is no difference among entities despite differences in appearance and so forth, then difference would not exist anywhere; yet difference is perceived by the world. Thus, when there is non-difference, this distinction—namely, the distinction in appearance and so forth—is like the case of a single self. Just as there is no difference in appearance and so forth within a single self that consists of happiness, so it is here. Therefore, this external...
Internal difference is indeed a distinction that is mutually distinct. Of what nature is it? (1) It is characterized by a distinct appearance... [text fragment] ...of the parts.

And in this case, there is no perception of non-difference other than that [perception of the object] by whose power the cognition of non-difference arises. Therefore, that object is indeed a particular (viśeṣa) itself;
it is that very object, while its exclusions (vyāvṛttayaḥ) are others.
That which is called the effect and the cause is held to be its own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). ||174||
All human activities have as their fruit the avoidance or acquisition of that [object].

It has been stated that whatever performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*) is alone a real entity (*vastu*); and that [entity] is indeed the particular (*viśeṣa*). As for what is called the "universal" (*sāmānya*), it is merely the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of that very [particular]. For if it were a real object, it would be illogical for its form not to be perceived when the visible [particular] is present.
Because the cognition of non-difference among distinct things is produced by that [non-difference] as a defining characteristic.
Furthermore:
"Just as, despite the lack of distinction between differences, not everything is the means for achieving everything. (175)
Likewise, even though there is no difference in their being distinct, not everything is the means of proving everything;
this begins with "sādi. The analysis of the compound is: that which has a distinct appearance and so forth.
If it is argued that there is also non-difference because a thing consisting of multiple aspects is grasped by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-bodha*), he says:

"And not here," and so forth. "Here" means among the particulars (*bheda*). "The other" refers to the second [type of universal]. "By whose power" means by the power of the non-differentiated appearance. Therefore, there is only a distinction—that is, only a difference—and no non-difference exists. That very distinction is the real entity (*vastu*).
As for those other general properties, such as "being an entity" (*vastutva*) and so on, they are merely conceptualized exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) of that very [particular] entity. (173–74)

"‘That effect,’ and so forth. It is neuter because of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as ‘effect’; otherwise, since the particular (*viśeṣa*) was the subject under discussion, it would have been ‘that’ (*saḥ*). That very thing which is of the nature of a particular is called both ‘effect’ and ‘cause,’ and that same thing is called the ‘particular characteristic’ (*svalakṣaṇa*). ‘Having as their fruit the abandonment or attainment of that’ refers to that very particular, whether it is to be rejected or to be adopted."

Those activities whose results are, respectively, relinquishment and acquisition, are described as such. And that [result] is indeed a particular (*viśeṣa*) capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārī*). The "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) of that very particular from other heterogeneous things is a mere negation; it is not some real entity called a "universal" (*sāmānya*). (174–75)

For if it were to exist, it would be perceived as something distinct from its particular instances, provided it met the conditions for perceptibility. For this reason—since that universal, being an object and a real entity, is visible—it is not logical for there to be a non-perception of its form, that is, a failure to grasp its own nature. Why? Because such perception is produced by the universal; that is, because the perception [of the particular] is brought about by the perception of the universal.
Regarding the cognition of difference among particulars: indeed, that which is not itself apprehended cannot be a cause for knowledge of another thing.

Thus, having refuted the illusory (*prātibhāsika*) universal according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas and others, he says "Moreover," etc., in order to refute the aforementioned inferential [universal] according to the Sāṃkhya view. Just as for the Sāṃkhya, the particulars...

Even when there is a distinction, not everything is the means for achieving everything. Likewise, although there is no difference in the particularity of a Buddhist [cognition], not everything is the means for achieving everything. To which objection, then, does this resolution apply? He says: "As it was stated," and so forth. "[Because it has the nature of producing that]"—this concludes the section on the investigation of the universal (*sāmānyacintā*).

Thus, it would follow that [the cause] produces distinction from its own nature as a producer. As for what was stated—that even if it is a producer, everything would be a producer due to the lack of distinction—regarding this objection:

if [the cause] were without distinction, then just as for one who maintains non-difference on the grounds of "selfhood" (ātmatva), not everything is a producer of everything despite the absence of distinction, so too would it be even in the case of distinction.
Or rather:
for indeed, some [distinction] among the factors of action (kāraka) would exist as a property of the thing itself. (176)

However, two actions would contradict one another in that single [entity], because even though there is no difference in their mere distinction, each has a nature determined by its own specific causes and conditions; thus, only a certain thing would be an agent and not others, because they are characterized by a nature other than that. Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever in this case.
Even if there is identity, it cannot be the case that for that very same thing there is both agency and non-agency;
for even in identity, it is a contradiction for that very same thing to possess both agency and non-agency in that very same respect.
If you argue that there is also a difference [of state] from the action, then the auxiliary causes would not produce [the effect]. (17)
Now, if it is argued that there is no non-distinction among all aspects because distinction exists, then consequently, nothing whatsoever would be an agent.
If that were so, then due to distinction in some manner, a cooperative cause would not indeed be an agent.
Or, if agency occurs successively, does that [agency] belong to that very same entity?

Earth and the other elements are distinct from that which has the nature of producing a rice sprout. Regarding the phrase "of this," it refers to the sprout. If one were to admit its status as a producer, then because distinction [from other things] would be no different, everything would be a producer. To this objection, the answer has already been stated; however, this second point is now being addressed. He asks, "What, then, was said? and replies with the words beginning "If... [referring to the capacity for] producing specific effects.
The distinction characterized by the state of being a producer would not exist.
[Objection: This objection might be raised. [Reply:

He states the meaning of the verse with the words "Just as... and so forth: "In the same way, it will also be the case regarding the particularity (*viśeṣa*); not everything is the producer of everything."

This is the connection [of the passage]: "by way of the nature of things" means by the power of the thing itself. However, if the non-difference of entities were admitted, then for that [nature] which is admitted to be undifferentiated everywhere, both action and non-action would be contradictory in a single instance. (176–77) He explains this with the verse beginning "in mere difference," and so forth. "Cause" (*hetu*) refers to the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*); "conditions" (*pratyaya*) refers to the cooperative causes (*sahakārin*).

"Those whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has been determined and rendered capable of producing a specific effect by their own causes and conditions are described as such. Because of that state [of having such a nature], others—that is, those not intended to be causal factors—would not be causal factors. Why? Because they do not possess that intrinsic nature; that is, because they lack the intrinsic nature for producing that specific effect. Of that [one thing]."

Regarding the three qualities (*traiguṇya*): "in that very same" means in one and the same effect; "in that same way" means by that very same undifferentiated mode. Nevertheless, when a rice seed produces a rice sprout, at that very moment a barley seed does not produce a rice sprout.
Yet, if the essence (*ātman*) of the rice seed were identical to that of the barley seed, it would follow as a logical consequence that the activity of one would occur in the other.
