Moreover, there would be no agent at all, as there would be non-existence. Since everything is utilized everywhere in turn, and because it is utilized through a transformation into another form residing within that [agent], how could there not be a succession for that very same single entity? Or rather, there would be an undifferentiated transformation. Or, if there is some distinction, how could there be oneness?
To say that there is "loss" [of identity] is not at all tenable.
Furthermore:
both absolute difference and non-difference would exist in that underlying entity. (178)

There is indeed a distinction within the triad of qualities (*traiguṇya*) due to their respective arrangements, such as those found in rice seeds and the like. Therefore, if it is argued that because of this distinction some [of them] perform an action, [we reply]: "If there were a distinction, then the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) would not act, because they too are mutually distinct. He explains this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*). [The question is: "Are all forms of cognition [produced] from that single entity alone? The meaning is: "By no means."
Because it is the locus of differentiation; this is the meaning of "of the succession" (*paryāya*).

He explains this with the words beginning with "Now" (*atha*). Because all differentiations (*bheda*) are employed in every effect through succession—that is, in sequence—and because this occurs when the various differentiations, being presided over by the power of the Pradhāna, perform their respective functions through successive transformations (*pariṇāma*).

This view has already been stated. However, when this view holds that the power (*śakti*) of the *pradhāna* itself is employed for the purposeful activity of transformation through various successive forms, then it is said: "or of the power," and so forth. [This refers to] that which is characterized by the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), which was previously situated in things not intended as causal factors (*kāraka*), and which subsequently exists in a different form—that is, in the form of what is intended as a causal factor.

The connection is as follows: by the statement "because of the transformation of that which has matured, there is no one at all who is not an agent," [it is meant that] a modification (*paryāya*) whose basis is diversity—that is, manifoldness—is so described. How could this not apply to a single, non-different entity? The meaning is that it is not logical for a single *śāli* seed to undergo transformation into the form of a barley seed and so forth.
By this, the question "Is it of that very substance? has been explained.

Regarding what was said, namely "or of the power," he says: "Or transformation. How can there be a transformation—or the attainment of another state—of a power that is non-distinct [from the substance], that is, indivisible? Or, if the attainment of other states is admitted...
The attainment of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) is indeed identical with its own nature; therefore, if a distinction is somehow admitted, there would be a loss of the unity of the *pradhāna*.
Having thus refuted the position of transformation (*pariṇāma*), [the author now considers] whether [the effect] is non-different, both different and non-different, or different.

Having accepted the universal (*sāmānya*)— whether as "vertical" (*ūrdhvavṛtti*) because it persists through all successive states, or as "horizontal" (*tiryagvṛtti*) because it persists across all individual instances— the author speaks the words beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*) in order to refute the positions maintained by the Sāṃkhya, Mīmāṃsaka, Naiyāyika, and others.

Therefore, even he who considers himself a Digambara [Jaina] maintains this: (1) it is not held that there exists a single universal (*sāmānya*) in things such as jars and cloths, because they are absolutely distinct (*ekāntabheda*). Rather, it is this very substance (*dravya*), which undergoes transformation (*pariṇāmin*) through successive states designated as "modalities" (*paryāya*), that is called a "universal," because it persists through all those modalities. For instance, having broken a jar made of gold [to make something else], [the gold persists]. [Section 4: Examination of the Universal (*Sāmānyacintā*)]
Or rather, there is a mutual distinction between those two, which consist of similar and dissimilar natures;
that which arises in the form of a primary essence is called "universal" (sāmānya).

When a crown is produced, that very same gold substance, having perished in the form of a jar, persists by way of its own nature as gold; thus, it is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*) through successive states.

Precisely because it is subject to transformation, there is non-difference between the state and the possessor of the state; otherwise, if the state were distinct from the possessor of the state, [the latter would not persist].
Because transformation is impossible [in a single substance]. When the gold-substance perishes in its form as a jar, one who desires a cloth experiences sorrow;

when it arises in the form of a crown, one who desires that [crown] experiences joy; and since there is neither destruction nor arising in its state as gold, one who desires gold experiences equanimity. Therefore, the existent is endowed with simultaneous arising, passing away, and persistence.
Regarding the definition of a thing (*vastu*),
it is said: "A person seeking a jar, a crown, or gold undergoes grief, joy, or indifference— each with its respective cause— upon the destruction, arising, or persistence [of those objects]."

There is no sorrow without destruction, no happiness without arising, and no neutrality without stability; therefore, every entity possesses a threefold nature. One who observes a vow of milk does not eat curd, and one who observes a vow of curd does not drink milk.
Because it does not possess the nature of both [the universal and the particular], the entity is therefore threefold in essence.
It does not arise nor does it perish in its aspect as a universal, because it is clearly perceived through its persistence (*anvaya*).
It perishes and arises through its particularity (*viśeṣa*), for its arising and so forth occur simultaneously with that. Thus, it exists.
That [position] should also be seen as already refuted here, provided that one accepts a real entity (*vastu*) which possesses both the universal and the particular.

In that case, there would be absolute non-difference and difference. Because the universal—characterized by the three *guṇas* and so forth—is not distinct from the particulars such as jars and cloths, the universal would also consist of the nature of the particulars; thus, there would be absolute difference.

Because of the non-existence of a universal (*sāmānya*). Since particulars (*viśeṣa*) are not distinct from the universal, they would be one; thus, there is absolute non-difference because of the absence of particulars. [The opponent asks: "Is there not one thing that consists of both difference and universality? [The author replies: "No," which is what is meant. Now, if it is maintained that there is some kind of difference between the universal and the particular, to this he says: "Mutually," and so forth.

If there were some kind of mutual difference between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), whose natures are respectively similar and dissimilar, then their difference would be absolute, like that of a jar and a cloth. Furthermore, a universal is not perceived as a separate entity. Therefore, no single object exists that consists of both the universal and the particular. Even for the Digambara, if such an object possessing [both aspects] is admitted, then—

There would be both difference and non-difference. When there is non-difference of the universal "goldness" from the various states such as the jar and so forth, then there would be absolute and total difference between the jar, its price, and the like, because of the absence of the universal "goldness. Alternatively, if there is non-difference of the various states such as the jar and its price from the universal "goldness," then there would be absolute non-difference and total unity.

The meaning is that there would be nothing but the nature of gold itself. Now, even though there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between the state and that which possesses the state, if it is maintained that there is a distinction due to a difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), then [it must be admitted that] the nature of the universal (*sāmānya*) "gold-ness" is perceived as persisting through all states.
473a Now,

if [entities] of distinct natures were to possess that [single nature] because they have as their essence a nature non-different from it— which is itself their own self through a non-different identity—
then from what would even their mutual difference arise?
Furthermore, that universal does not possess the nature of that [particular]; therefore, it is also not logical for it to exist in that way [as the particular].
For if it were so, it would possess the properties of that [particular]. Indeed, it is not logical for this one [universal] to have the dual nature of both engagement and withdrawal.
Nor is there non-difference in every respect.

The specific nature (*svarūpa*) of states such as that of a jar is perceived as distinct. Therefore, because there is a difference in definition (*lakṣaṇabheda*) between the state and the possessor of the state, there is indeed a distinction between them.

To this, he says: "Mutually," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of those whose natures are similar and dissimilar": if there were a distinction between the state and the possessor of the state, then there would be a mutual distinction—that is, an absolute distinction—between the two. This is because their forms consist of the inclusive (*anugata*) and the exclusive (*vyāvṛtti*), which are mutually...

Because of their conjunction. Nor is there any other intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) by which those two could be non-different, since the substratum (*dharmin*), which consists of infinite properties (*anantadharmātmaka*), is not perceived [as such]. The connection is: "if entities are distinct. [This means] by a non-different self—whether called *pradhāna* or something else—or by [a common property] such as substantiality (*vastutva*) or goldness (*suvarṇatva*). [This applies] to the very selves of those distinct things, such as jars and so forth.

By being non-different from the existent, they would possess it; that is, they would possess an undivided nature. Of those [entities] such as primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth, the undivided nature is their "undivided-nature"; that which has this as its essence (*ātman*)—that is, its form (*rūpa*)—is the particularity (*bheda*) characterized by jars and the like. That state of having such an undivided-natured essence belongs to that [particularity]. Therefore, how could there be a mutual difference even among those particularities? There is none at all. An-...
It has been explained that there is no absolute non-difference.

Now, that single, identical self (ātman) does not belong to that difference characterized by jars and so forth, because difference possesses a manifold nature in the form of jars and the like. This being the case, by that very self—the nature of difference—it would also [be] a universal (sāmānya).

It is not logical for a category (*padārtha*)—such as that consisting of the three *guṇas* and so forth—to exist in such a way as a universal (*sāmānya*), because since the universal is non-different from its particulars, it would fail to possess the quality of being "common" (*samānatā*). By this, absolute difference is also explained.

For if it were to exist in that manner—that is, if the primary cause (*pradhāna*) and so forth were desired to have the nature of a universal—then the essence of the primary cause and so forth would not possess those properties.

The property of difference would not exist; the meaning is that the possessor of that [property] would not be possessed of a property called "state" (avasthā) that is non-distinct [from it]. In other words, there would be a mutual difference between the state and the possessor of the state. Proving this very point, he says: "For this... and so forth. The connection is: "this single nature is endowed with mere occurrence and cessation. "Staying" (sthāna) means occurrence (pravṛtti).

"Departure" (*vigama*) means cessation (*nivṛtti*). For instance, while the power of the primary cause (*pradhāna-śakti*) remains and the substantiality of gold (*suvarṇa-dravyatva*) and so forth persists, cessation is asserted as the departure from a particular state. By this, [the argument] that "there is a mutual difference between those two," and so forth, is explained.

With the words "No" (*na*) and so on, he anticipates the opponent's intention: it is not the case that there is absolute non-difference between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) in every respect.
"But if there were a difference even between those two—particularity and universality," he explains with the words beginning "na hi" (for not). The connection is as follows:

in a certain substance, there is no absolute difference or non-difference between the universal and the particular. What is the reason? [He says] "by the discerning," and so forth. The universal consists of capacity (*śakti*), goldness (*suvarṇatva*), and substantiality (*dravyatva*); the particular consists of the jar and so forth.
Because they are established through such a distinction. 4. Regarding the consideration of the universal (*sāmānya*):
if there were also a distinction between those two, then neither distinction nor non-distinction would be absolute, because they are established as "universal" and "particular" (*viśeṣa*).
By which nature those two [are characterized]. ||179||
Regarding the distinction [between] "particular" and "universal":

if that distinction exists by way of its own nature, then if that distinction—which is the basis for designating both the universal and the particular as such—exists by way of that very nature, then it is indeed a case of difference (*vyatireka*). For if those two natures of theirs are distinct, then...
It is indeed a case of exclusion (*vyatireka*), for there is a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between the universal and the particular;
for intrinsic nature is the very being (*bhāva*). For it is thus:
there would be only difference, and consequently, there would be a lack of both universality and particularity. (180)

Just as there is no mutual relation between particularity and generality, or among jars and the like; and because, even though there is a distinction between generality and particularity, they lack a mutual connection just as [the parts of] a jar do—
so it has been said, "like a jar and so forth."

Furthermore, the Master [Dharmakīrti] says "by which": by which nature—both excluded (*vyāvṛtta*) and inclusive (*anugata*)—this particularity and this generality among those two are established as "this is the particular" and "this is the generality. If by that nature the generality...
"In that case, the difference between the universal and the particular would be an absolute difference.

He explains this with the words beginning with "yadi" (if). "That self" refers to that which is both inclusive and exclusive. The connection is: "If there were a difference between the universal and the particular by means of that self. Clarifying this very point, he says: "Because," and so forth.

Those two selves which establish the distinction between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are, for those two, their very own selves—that is, they constitute their intrinsic natures. If those two selves are respectively inclusive (*anugata*) and exclusive (*vyāvṛtta*), being distinct (*vyatirekin*) and mutually excluded from one another, then there is only exclusion;
that is, there is only difference. What is the reason? Because of the difference in their intrinsic natures. (176–80)

It might be thought: "Is it not the case that it is precisely the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—which establishes the distinction between the state (*avasthā*) and the entity possessing the state (*avasthātṛ*)*—that differs, and not the entity (*bhāva*) itself? To this he says, "For the intrinsic nature," and so forth. The meaning is that the intrinsic nature is indeed the entity. And "in that case" means:

when there is an absolute difference between particularity (*bheda*) and generality (*sāmānya*), particularity would be devoid of generality, and generality would be devoid of particularity. *(Note: *avasthātṛ* refers to the substratum or the thing that undergoes various states.)*

The connection is that there would be "remainder" (*śeṣatā*). That is to say, the universal would not possess particulars, nor would the particulars possess the universal, because of the absence of a relationship—just as, for example, there is no mutual possession between particular objects such as jars due to the absence of a relationship between them. (181)

He states the meaning with the words beginning "And if there were difference," and so forth. Since there is no relationship between the particular and the universal due to their being neither produced nor productive, yet they are perceived as being related, it is therefore said to be an error, as stated in the passage "there would not be the cognition of the universal and the particular" (11.171). (180–81)………
Placing this self (ātman) at the forefront, this person proceeds.

One who desires the fruit to be accomplished by that [means] considers both difference and non-difference as residing therein: difference from its own nature and similarity through exclusion (vyāvṛtti). (182)
The entity certainly exists, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of [incoherent] activity and so forth.
The formulation of the questions regarding difference and non-difference— such as "Is the cow different from the horse, or not?"—
proceeds on the basis of the premise that every difference is the very nature (svabhāva) of the entity.

For it must be stated that only that [substance] is the expression in that context; for by this [definition], there is no expression of "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and so forth. Just as with the doctrine of the Self, having refuted the doctrine of vertical universals (*ūrdhvasāmānya*) favored by the Digambaras and others, as well as the doctrine of horizontal universals (*tiryaksāmānya*) favored by the Sāṃkhyas and others, through a common refutation, one now proceeds to refute specifically the doctrine of horizontal universals.
He says: "Moreover," and so forth.

This is what is meant: for one who seeks causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), there is no purpose whatsoever in investigating whether a universal (*sāmānya*) is distinct or non-distinct, because it is devoid of causal efficacy. Rather, [one investigates] that nature which is fit for causal efficacy—prior to...

Having made [the object] the focus of his recollection, and possessing a desire for the fruit to be accomplished by it—that is, possessing a longing for that fruit which is to be achieved through that very means—this person proceeds to act. Then, difference (*bheda*) and non-difference (*abheda*), which serve as the basis for that [object] and are the substrata capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), are investigated. And regarding that [object] which is fit for purposeful action, its absolute difference from its own self—that is, from its own nature—is...

There is indeed similarity by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), in the form of being excluded from what is of a different class, through the nature of the determined unity. For one who seeks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), the inquiry into difference and non-difference is exhausted by this much alone. Therefore, why inquire about the difference or non-difference of a universal (*sāmānya*)—which does not perform causal efficiency—with respect to the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)? (181–82)
But surely, for a person seeking causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), what is the purpose of a commonality (*sāmānya*) even through exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), since it is devoid of causal efficiency?

True. It is the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves that are called a "commonality" by way of exclusion; therein, through the word, there is a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of unity.
There is no fault, because activity occurs through the *sāya* [the conceptual synthesis].

Now, it might be argued: "The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself follows after other particular characteristics; what is the use of a postulated exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)? To this he says: "Because particular characteristics are mutually distinct. If the form of a jar were present in a cloth, then one seeking water would [act toward the cloth].

It would also follow [absurdly] for the cloth. Thus he says: "arising and so forth," and so on. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the consequence of [the cloth having] simultaneous arising, cessation, and so on.

He explains this with the words "all indeed," and so on. [He means that] only the particular (viśeṣa)—which is capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) and is called "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva)—is the self...

The meaning is "the real" (*bhūta*). With reference to what state or entity does [a word] function? It is precisely that particularity (*viśeṣa*) which performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). "In that way" means: a word such as "cow" and so forth. For one who seeks causal efficiency employs a word with the intention of conveying the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), having unified the perceived and the conceptualized. The cognizer likewise understands it in exactly that same way.
4. Consideration of the Universal (*sāmānyacintā*):

Because it is designated separately [from the particular], and because the object is not deviant from that [conceptualization], it is therefore a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). This has been thoroughly examined by the Master.

Therefore, when one asks about the object presented by words such as "cow"—whether it be distinct or non-distinct—why should a dual cognition regarding it be produced by the introduction of another object? Consequently, this person, seeking a specific purposeful action, proceeds by taking as his primary focus that essence of the object which is not shared by anything else; for example, [one seeks] a cow for the purpose of carrying or milking, and not anything else.

This refers to a possible sense. Just as when entering a battle, one speaks of it by its own specific name (*yathāsva-śabda*), and not by a universal such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva-sāmānya*). It is understood thus: therefore, this was stated with respect to the operation of words based on the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) of users [of language]. However, since there is no appearance of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-pratibhāsa*) within the word-cognition itself, the particular characteristic is said to be inexpressible; thus, there is no fault.

"But substance and so forth do not [occur] therein" means that when there is an injunction regarding a cow or the like by means of words such as "cow," why is this? Because they—substance-ness and so forth—are denoted separately from the cow and the like by their respective terms, such as "cow-substance" (*godravya*) and so on. If one asks, "In that case, how is it that existence, substance-ness, and so forth are perceived when a word such as 'cow' is employed? he says: "Of the object," and so forth. Of the object...

[This applies] to "cow" and so forth. Because there is no deviation [of the word] from such properties as existence (*sattva*) or substantiality (*dravyatva*), the understanding of universals (*sāmānya*) would follow from that object. However, a particular term (*viśeṣa-śabda*) does not function with respect to a universal. And this has been thoroughly examined by the teacher Diṅnāga in the *Sāmānyaparīkṣā* and other works, namely, that particular terms do not have their application in a universal.

Here an objection is raised: Of what general property (*sāmānya*), then, is there non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) with respect to a particular (*viśe�șa*)? First of all, that which is imagined by others does not exist at all. Furthermore, that which is characterized as the mere exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*)—the purely negative (*prasajya-mātra*)—also does not exist at all.
Nor is there non-deviation between the appearance in conceptual cognition and an external object, because the former is independent (*svatantratva*).

It is said: the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself, when distinguished from those of its own class (*sajātīya*), is the "particular" (*viśeṣa*). That very same thing, when taken non-differently with respect to its distinction from those of a different class (*vijātīya*), is called the "universal" (*sāmānya*). Therefore, because the universal and the particular are in reality one, there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*), just as in the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*). However, due to the difference in the operation of words (*śabdavyāpāra*), [the cognition] is merely verbal in some cases.

Cognition is sometimes called "the object" (*artha*). Therefore, this person [perceives] the object—namely, that which is presented by words such as "cow," brought near by words such as "cow," and which is the locus of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). He is so described because his cognition has two aspects, having the form of both the particular and the universal, due to the presentation of another object, namely the universal. That which is the essence (*ātman*) of this "cow" and so forth...

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The connection with what follows is as stated: "That very intrinsic nature, which is unique and not shared by others, is what is denoted by the word. He explains that object: "one who seeks a specific purposeful action," having placed before him—that is, having taken as his objective—something possessing a dewlap and so forth.
He says "just as," etc.: just as one who seeks the carrying of loads, milking, and so on, proceeds with reference to a cow; [this refers to] those things that are possible in another.

The meaning of the sentence must be supported by the fact that one who desires an object possible in another [animal], such as a horse, does not proceed toward a cow even after placing it before him. To the question "What is the object possible in another?", he says: "such as entering a battle. "According to their respective [denotations]" (*yathāsvam*) means whichever word is the designator of whatever [object].
It is not the universal (*sāmānya*), such as substantiality (*dravyatva*). The word "stated" (*codita*) is used with a change of gender.

The connection [is as follows]: by that injunction—that is, by the injunction of words such as "cow" for things such as cows—and thus, for one who desires a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), [the word becomes] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (1.153)
Because that statement was not intended to be accepted at that time, and because cows and the like do not follow as being identical with it— since they possess a dual nature therein—
it interrogates that very state and its mode in that very context. Even though there is difference in that [state], there is non-difference in terms of substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth.
This is indeed a refutation. For in all cases, one must admit that the universal, which is characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), possesses a difference in its own nature (*svabhāva*).

It has been stated that there is no non-difference for a universal that constitutes the very nature [of things]. If there were non-difference through its own self-nature, then one seeking the activity based upon it would proceed toward both [individuals] equally, because even a single [individual] would possess that nature. For if that [nature] were to perform the function, then anything other than it—

Since that [reason] is equal for the other as well, why does it not also act at the time of engagement? Because the universal such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) is not intended to be attained. This is the connection [of the sentence], with the case-ending changed. But why, again, is the universal such as "substanceness" not denoted by the word "cow" and so forth?
He states what is intended: because of the inclusion of cows and so forth, the word "cow" and the like have been conventionally established (*saṃketita*) in the world for cows and the like.

If it is argued that because the universals (*sāmānya*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) have the nature of cows and so forth, they are denoted by the injunction of "cow" and the like, he replies:

"And of those which constitute its essence. This means that the universals such as substantiality, which have the nature of cows and so forth, are [denoted] just like the cows and so forth themselves.

By means of the reason of non-inclusion (*anvaya*), [it is shown] that "therein"—that is, in that particularity such as a cow and so forth—there is neither a universal nor a particular; the meaning is that it does not possess the nature of either. Consequently, only the particular (*viśeṣa*) is being urged.
He states this very point in the passage beginning with "tameva" and so forth: "And a person seeking purposeful action [perceives] only that entity which is not shared by anything else."

[The opponent] challenges [the position] by means of various modes of difference and non-difference. Even for the proponent of Apoha (anyāpohavādin), a non-difference characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)—such as "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and so forth—is accepted among particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, absolute difference among particulars (*viśeṣa*) is contradictory; hence he says:

"Of that," and so forth. When the difference of that object which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*) is established by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*), [then] that which is characterized by exclusion...

The non-difference of this particular [particularity] from substancehood (*dravyatva*) and so forth is not at all a subverter [of its distinctness], because that [non-difference] is merely conceptualized. Therefore, difference is ultimate (*pāramārthika*). The oneness of individual particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) is thus constructed; and by this method, difference and non-difference are indistinguishable for us. Demonstrating precisely that, he says: "In all cases," etc. Difference by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) [is found] with respect to its own class and other classes...
[The connection is as follows: "And because a universal is admitted to have exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) as its defining characteristic.

If it is argued: "There is no non-difference [of particulars] with a universal in the form of exclusion, but rather only with that which is a real entity (*vastubhūta*," he says: "svabhāva-" [intrinsic nature].]
"Of that which has come to be," and so forth. "Non-difference of the real universal" means [its] non-distinctness from the individuals.

Because they are not separate from the universal, there would be a unity of the particulars; or else, as was stated previously, the universal itself would possess multiplicity just like the particulars. It is not said that the unity of particulars is established by way of the universal; rather, it is this particular...

He says that there is non-difference [of the universal] from the particular itself, starting with the words "by its own self," and so forth. If there were non-difference of cows, horses, and the like by way of their own specific forms (*viśeṣa-rūpa*), then a person desiring a purposeful action—such as carrying or milking—which has that cow-substance as its basis, would perceive the state of being a "cow" equally in both cases; that is, in both the cow and the horse. Because...

For even that object denoted by the word "cow" (gopadārtha), which is intended as the cause [of cognition], possesses that causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) consisting of such things as carrying and milking. [This concludes] the investigation of universals (*sāmānyacintā*).
Now, the refutation of the Jaina position (*jainamatanirāsa*):
By this very [argument], whatever incoherent and vulgar [position] the Digambaras (*ahīka*) have asserted... [183]
They prattle on; that too is rejected because it is possible only in one-sided [extremes].

And this [doctrine] of the naked ones (Digambaras) is somehow improper and indecorous, because it lacks a definitive conclusion regarding what is to be accepted or rejected, such as when they say: "In the lineage, there may be an ocean, or there may not. Those who have spoken thus are also refuted by this very [argument]. By means of existence alone... 474a.
Because of absolute difference; or, if there were a connection with that [difference], then for another as well, it would follow from that.
Because it possesses that intrinsic nature—that is, because its very nature is to perform that specific purposeful action—it performs it.

Since even another substance, such as a horse, would equally possess the nature of performing actions like carrying or milking [if it were a cow], why would that horse not also perform the purposeful action accomplished by a cow? (10) (182–83)

"By this very [means]" refers to the proof of the difference between all things. "Ahnikas" are the shameless Kṣapaṇakas because of their nakedness. He says "something" (*kim api*) because improper speech is contemptible; it is "indecent" (*aślīlam*) and vulgar (*grāmyam*). As for what they prattle—that "everything is of the nature of everything" and yet "everything is not of the nature of everything"—that too has been refuted, because [the relationship] occurs exclusively [in one direction].
Because it is possible for a single end to have the mode of absolute difference [from others].

(183–84) Now, since the Digambaras hold that "everything has everything as its essence" (*sarvaṃ sarvātmakam*) and not that "everything does not have everything as its essence," why is this stated by the Teacher?
True; however, this has already been refuted previously by the passage beginning, "For if there were absolute difference and non-difference, as in the case of perception... (1.178).
As for what was further stated: "Just as, for example, in the case of bracelets, armlets, and so forth, there exists a persisting cognition of gold... (124a) [and so on].

Just as the universal "gold-ness" is postulated [in the case of various golden objects], why is a single universal "substance-ness" not accepted, given that there exists a recurring cognition of "substance-ness" with respect to jars, cloths, and so forth? This statement is intended to show that if one does not accept it in this case— despite the presence of a uniform cognition— one should likewise refrain from postulating a universal in the case of bracelets, armlets, and the like.
It may be a camel, because it is one [with it] in terms of its nature as a substance and so forth. It may not be curd, because the state of being a camel is distinct from the state of being curd.
The explanation that "aślīla" means "improper" (ayukta) is incorrect, because that [explanation] is improper.
The sense is that it is "vulgar" (grāmya) due to its unsuitability for learned people; for "aślīla" is a synonym for "vulgar. O, [Ahe-]!

"Neither to be accepted" means neither to be abandoned nor to be grasped. Why? Because there is no finality [in things]. For if something were determined as a means to happiness and another thing as a means to suffering, then they would respectively be either to be abandoned or to be accepted.
But that is not the case, because everything possesses the nature of everything. And yet, everything does not possess the nature of everything; therefore—
For it is impossible to apprehend even a single instance of such a manifold nature as being distinct from its own essence.
Because everything possesses both natures, when that distinction is negated, [there can be no differentiation]. (184) *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (19185)
If one were told, "Eat curd," why would he run toward a camel?

In that case, even a camel would be curd; nor is that very camel [the same as] by which another might also be a camel, so too curd would be a camel. Nor is that very curd [the same as] by which another might also be curd.

This is because neither of these two [alternatives] exists, nor does the absence of that nature in anything whatsoever; nor is there any non-occurrence of that [nature], nor anything not restricted to itself. If, due to the absence of some particularity, one were told "Eat curd," he might as well eat a camel.
Or, if there is some excellence by which it exists as distinct [from others], [then that excellence must be established]. (185)

This is what is meant: when there is an absolute non-difference between the state and that which possesses the state, yet there is mutual difference between the states themselves, then this fault arises. Thus he says: "Or, in its connection with that. This means: either in the mutual connection of that difference in intrinsic nature; that is to say, because a substance whose nature is curd and so forth would follow after [persist in] camels and other animals by way of identity.

Everything has the nature of being both. The mention of "both" (ubhaya) is for the purpose of indicating multiplicity; for when that [multiplicity] exists, its specific distinction is excluded—namely, that a camel is only a camel and not curd, and curd is only curd and not a camel.
Would a person commanded, "Eat curd," fail to run toward a camel to eat it? For even a camel is [in some sense] curd...

Because of its non-difference from the substance [of the camel] due to its being a substance, it would follow that it is curd; nor yet is it that very same thing. "The camel is indeed the camel" is an extremist view (ekāntavāda). By this, even other things such as curd and the like would become camels, and likewise, curd too would be a camel, because of the curd's connection with identity through the substancehood that is non-different from the camel. Nor yet is it that very same thing, for curd is indeed curd; by which... [the rest of the sentence is omitted in the source].

Curd, such as that from a camel and so forth, would [be the result]. By this, the dual nature of everything is explained. He explains the phrase "due to the exclusion of its specific difference" with the passage beginning "of these two," and so on. In either case, there would be a specific distinction between curd and a camel:
either the absence of the form of curd would exist in the camel, or the form of a camel—which is impossible for curd—would exist in the curd, if the essential nature of the camel were present.
It would necessarily be so. The same should be said regarding curd as well.

First, the impossibility of the former [the universal] is stated by the words "that" (*tat*) and so forth. Thus, the connection is that there is no distinction whatsoever between the two—curd and camel—as they both lack that [universal] form. The phrase "even of one" refers to either the curd or the camel, whichever it may be, because of the absence of that form.
Because there is an absence of the form of a camel and an absence of the form of curd.

He states the absence of the second mode as well with the words "of its own nature" (*svarūpasya*). This refers either to the nature of a camel that does not possess that [curd], i.e., that which does not become curd, or to the nature of curd that does not possess that [camel], i.e., that which does not become a camel; [it refers to] its own fixed nature, the nature of a camel.

Because that which is determined lacks the nature of being determined as curd (184–85). Now, suppose there were some excellence (*atiśaya*) in curd and camel by virtue of which a person, when urged to "eat curd," would engage with it through differentiation; that is, they would engage specifically with the curd while avoiding the camel.
This is what is meant: just as the essential natures (*svarūpa*) of curd and camel are mutually distinct, so too are substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*). [The opponent might argue:
"That very same curd exists here, but it does not exist elsewhere"—this is the experience of both.

Furthermore, if there is some excellence (*atiśaya*) belonging to these two such that [the transformation] is thus enjoined only in the case of curd, which is a modification of milk, [then that excellence must be explained].

It does not occur elsewhere. A specific capacity (*pratiśaya*) is the object of the activity of one who seeks causal efficiency; for it is that very [capacity] which, by virtue of being the material cause characterized by its own nature as distinguished by that result—namely, the nature of curd—is the nature [of the cause]. And such a nature does not exist elsewhere, because there is no activity on the part of the seeker [of that result].
Therefore, the claim that there is an absence of both natures in that case is an extremist doctrine. Furthermore:
"If all things were identical with everything else, then cognition and verbal expression would not be distinct. (186)

If a distinction is asserted based on a difference in characteristics, then that very excellence of intrinsic nature (*svarūpātiśaya*) is what constitutes curd; and that does not exist elsewhere, such as in a camel. Nor does "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) appear as something distinct from curd and the like. By this means, every entity is neither [of the two], being devoid of both generality and particularity; it is merely "the other," while "oneness" is a conceptual construction. Thus it is said: "Of these two..."

[The term] *dadhyuṣṭroḥ* [means]: "Thus commanded" refers to one who is commanded, "Eat the curd. Curd is a transformation of milk; it does not exist elsewhere, that is, not in a camel. That very excellence is the curd. Of what nature is it? It is the object of the activity of a person seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). It is the object of the activity of that person who desires the purposeful action to be accomplished by the curd. What is the reason for this? Because of that—

"Moving," and so forth. That which is to be accomplished by curd is itself distinguished from others; thus, it is a "distinction" (*viśeṣa*). A thing whose nature is characterized by its state as the material cause (*upādāna-bhāva*) or causal state—that very thing is "curd.
And that [nature] is "of such a kind," namely, the aforementioned nature of curd. "Elsewhere" refers to a camel. Why? Because [the camel] desires [milk].
Because there is an absence of activity in the camel (troṣṭra).

(185–86) "The state of being the self of all" means when there is a single form. "Distinct, restricted objects" refers to cognition and sound—that is, knowledge and speech. Due to their absence, there is an absence of distinct cognitions and words. [This concerns] the doctrine of the withdrawal of distinctions. Unity—

The impossibility of the theory of the instrument (*karaṇavāda*). [This refers to] the synthesis or indication as a unity of two things that are perceived or heard as distinct. An example is "curd is sour" (*syāduṣṭo dadhi*), and so forth. He explains this with the words "this is that" (*so'yam*) and so on. In some cases, such as in curd or a camel, there is a single, determinate form—

The connection is: "How could one, seeing [it], be convinced by means of the intellect? To the question "By what kind of intellect?", he says: "Unmixed," and so forth. That object for which there is no other form mixed in is described as such. The intellect that possesses such [an object] is "possessed of an unmixed form"; that is to say, it is precisely that which grasps a distinct object. Or else, how could one express it?
The intention is that [it occurs] by means of a sound (*dhvani*) determined by convention for each respective object. Why would one not be convinced? He says:
"Because that [distinction] does not exist, the doctrine of the synthesis of distinctions is impossible. (125a)
Since that [absence] does not exist, how could there be a desire to conceive of its possibility? For if it were possible, how could the word for it be rejected?
That which is not the object of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) is certainly not the same as what is expressed by words. Who could obstruct the application of words to those [objects]?
(1) An Inquiry into the Words of the Authority (*āpta*).

An inexpressible object is not apprehended by the intellect. It has also been stated that the relation itself is not denoted in its own form. For if it were denoted, it would be presented to the intellect as a related entity, and thus it would not be understood according to the intended meaning.
Even when it is being understood, it exists only in the form of a related entity; therefore, it is not denoted in its own essential nature. Consequently—
Nor does the same consequence apply to the relation [of the word] even when it is non-existent.

Furthermore, how could one who is responding against a proponent of non-existence as the denotable object respond without speaking? Even in this case, how could non-existence not be expressed by the word?
He does not even desire the non-existence of manifestation; therefore, there is no statement [to that effect]. How is it that that very [non-existence] does not exist?

Because there is no differentiation (*vibhāga*) of entities. Thus, the doctrine of their dissolution would not be a doctrine of the dissolution of distinctions, such as "it may be sour milk" or "it may be curd," and so forth.

Furthermore, if one were to apprehend two unmixed entities— a sour milk product (*dadhi*) and a camel (*uṣṭra*)— and then combine them, thinking "there may be a camel" and "there may be sour milk," even then, because the cognition that combines them would have a single form— whether in the form of a camel or in the form of sour milk—

and because it would grasp an unmixed aspect in some camel and in some sour milk, the distinction between those two, the sour milk and the camel, would be produced solely by the difference in their respective appearances.
There is also a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding the phrase "one or many," and so forth: the object of the determination of multiplicity is the difference in appearance;
the determination of oneness [is the object] of the difference in appearance—this is how it should be construed. Furthermore, yogurt and a camel have distinct appearances as their objects.
This being the case, neither the camel nor the yogurt is a single entity that possesses both forms; the analysis of the compound *tadubhayarūpa* is: that whose form consists of both yogurt and camel.
This would indeed be a false statement.

(186–87) "The characteristic of difference" means the characteristic of exclusion; it is precisely the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which are excluded from those of a different class, that are called "the universal.
"By nature" means by their own essence. From the word "etcetera," [it follows that they] have a single result, such as the fetching of water and so forth.
With the words "Let it be so," and so forth, the Master [Dharmakīrti] anticipates the opponent's intention:

"The distinction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) among entities—that is, things—is not at all an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from others within their own intrinsic nature. In that case, regarding those things which are indefinable (*nirupākhya*), how can words have as their object the distinction of intrinsic nature, which is to say, have exclusion as their object?"

One might object: "Since there is no application of words at all toward things that lack any defining characteristic (*nirupākhya*), for what purpose has this doubt been raised? To refute this, the Teacher says: "There must necessarily be an application of words toward those [non-entities], for it is not possible for the proponent of the theory of exclusion (*anyāpoha*) to claim that words do not apply to things lacking any defining characteristic."

The proponents [of the opponent's view] explain that the challenger (codaka) says this because words must necessarily apply to those [entities]. According to them, by this sequence, the negation of space and time is indeed effected for all entities. Likewise, it has been stated that the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the relation is not denoted.
*Ṣaṣṭhamāhnikam* (The Sixth Chapter): Examination of the "da" [syllable].

Furthermore, as for the objection that because an meaningless word is not employed when negating an object, a negative particle (*nañ*) without an object cannot be employed—a response to this will be stated later. Likewise, as for this other point: "because an meaningless word is not employed when negating its referent, a negative particle without an object is not employed."
Regarding this, the passage beginning with “the answer will be stated” would be non-expressive from the perspective of the opponent’s intention concerning what is yet to be said.

Therefore, it is the Teacher himself who establishes the application of words even toward things that lack any defining characteristic (*nirupākhyā*), by means of the passage beginning with “in their case, there must necessarily be the application of words. Why? Because [words] could not otherwise be established as objects of cognition or verbal expression in any way whatsoever.

Because [cognition] applies to all objects that are devoid of any defining characteristic (nirupākhya), whether in the case of affirmation or negation; if, in some instance, there were cognition and verbal designation regarding the negation of a non-existent form, then there would be an affirmation regarding the object consisting in the exclusion of that negated form. And if that were so—meaning, in the absence of both affirmation and negation—then linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) would have as its basis affirmation and negation, which are characterized by positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

He is described as such. He expresses that very nature of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) with the words "hot," and so forth. "Fire has heat as its intrinsic nature" is a convention based on positive concomitance (*anvaya*); "it is not non-hot" is one based on negative exclusion (*vyatireka*). By the word "also" (*api*), he indicates that even this extremely well-known worldly convention would not exist [if there were no exclusion]. For the determination of "hot" occurs through the exclusion of "non-hot."

And since that non-hot thing, characterized by the absence of heat, is established in some way, how could "hot" be established through its exclusion? To this he says: "By another nature," and so forth. The absence of heat itself is "another nature"—that is, something distinct and different from the nature of heat—because it consists in the negation of that [heat]; thus it is called "another nature. For this very reason, the statement "of that which is non-existent" is appropriate.

Now, how can a specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) be established as the object of conceptual cognition or of a word, given that it is not established as such in relation to any other intrinsic nature? Since that which is entirely non-hot is never perceived, it remains unascertained; consequently, the intrinsic nature of fire, which is characterized by the exclusion of that [non-hot], is neither perceived nor ascertained. As it is with the intrinsic nature of fire, so it is with every entity.
Consequently, the world would be deluded and of uncertain nature.

It might be argued: (1) In that case, there is no negation of anything non-existent regarding fire and so forth, such that one could be urged to necessarily act toward a non-entity; rather, it is simply a real entity called "touch" that is not hot, which is indeed a different thing from fire.

"It is negated. [The opponent asks: "How so? and so forth. The Master [Śāntarakṣita] says: From the statement "Being alone," existence is intended; from the statement "it is negated," non-existence [is intended]. And how can there be that which is called both existent and non-existent? The opponent replies with the words beginning with "No" (*na*), etc.: "In that regard, [the absence of] heat in fire..."

Furthermore, by the statement "it does not exist anywhere," we mean that what is non-hot does not exist anywhere. For if it were stated in this way—having first asserted existence and then negating existence—one would be asserting both existence and non-existence in a single locus. However, in our case, we simply state that heat does not exist in fire.

Furthermore, the non-existence of something in a place other than where it exists is not contradictory. And he says: "This very place... [is the negation]. "It does not exist here" is the negation of the location (*deśa*). "It does not exist now" is the negation of the time (*kāla*). "It does not exist in this manner" is the negation of the property (*dharma*). What is the negation of the substratum (*dharmī*)? [He asks: Why? Because when that is negated—that is, when the substratum is negated—the object of that [negation], namely the object of the substratum, [is also negated].

Because a word cannot function in the absence of an object, and because the word for a subject (*dharmin*) would thus not function, the negation (*nañ*) cannot be employed without its object being specified. Here, in the statement "this is not here," an object such as "this" must necessarily be presented for the sake of the negation;
otherwise, it would not be known what the object of this negation is. All of this has been explained by the author of the *Pramāṇavārttika*.
The opinion of Rāma and others has been presented.

Regarding the phrase "sopi" (he too), Ācārya [says]: regarding the phrase "tatrāpi" (even there), Ācārya [says]: even there, by the negation of place, time, and nature, there is a negation of place and so forth, because they exist. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), time is included. Because of the difference in individual manifestations (*vyakti*).

The plural number [is used] because it refers to the property (*dharma*), not to the object (*artha*). In some cases, this is due to the very existence of the entity; however, there is no indication of the locus (*dharmin*) by the word "object" (*artha*), since even the opponent does not desire the negation of the locus itself. It might be argued: "Neither is the negation of place and so forth being made, nor is there a negation of heat; rather, what exists is [the connection] of fire with that which is non-hot."

The Master [Dharmakīrti] refutes the relation with the words "But not... and so forth. Even if that [relation] is negated—that is, even if the relation is negated—the same fault remains, because the relation, like the property (*dharma*), is not negated.
He establishes this very point with the words "If it were non-existent," and so forth. If the relation were non-existent...

There is no application of words. This is because, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is implied that the negative particle (*nañ*) cannot be employed when its object has not been specified. Alternatively, the fault is equal. How so? It should be explained thus: since you yourself negate that negation which occurs regarding something non-existent due to [your own] negation. He asks, "How is there a negation? and replies with the words beginning with "asati. That is, in the negation of this relation (*sambandha*) which is non-existent; "tadvat" means "like that," i.e., like the relation.
There is also the negation of the substratum (*dharmin*).
The opponent replies with "No," and so forth. [The objection is: "It is not that there is no negation of the relation by its own word, namely 'there is no relation'.
What is meant is this: just as there is no denotation of the relation's own nature (*svarūpa*) by its own word, so too...

Even in the case of negation, he says the same thing: "But rather, when there is a statement of negation such as 'there is no jar in this place' or 'not at this time,' the cognition is that this jar has no connection with this place or this time. Likewise, when it is said 'the jar does not exist in this manner,' the cognition is that the jar does not possess this attribute. Such is the cognition [arising] in this way.

[The opponent says: "Even so... [To this] the Ācārya replies with "Not now," and so forth. How is it that the relation is negated by the words beginning with "not now," such that the cognition arises that for this person there is neither a relation nor a property? Here, in the negation "not now," the relation— [The opponent continues: ...is not [negated]. Why? Because the cognition "this is not now" occurs even when a relation exists. For example, one might say, "This is not now," regarding a relation that was previously established but has since ceased. Therefore, the relation is not negated by this [statement]. Furthermore, the cognition "there is no relation" does not arise from the mere non-perception of the relation; rather, it arises from the perception of the absence of the relation. Thus, the relation is not negated here. Moreover, the cognition "there is no relation" does not occur merely because the relation is not perceived at this time; rather, it occurs when one perceives the absence of the relation. Consequently, the relation is not negated here. Furthermore, the cognition "there is no relation" does not arise simply from the non-perception of the relation at this moment; rather, it arises from the perception of the absence of the relation. Therefore, the relation is not negated here. Consequently
The cognition "it does not exist" [is the result]. In the negation "it is not so," the cognition is that "the property (dharma) does not exist.

Now, is it not the case that even the negation of a property is simply the negation of a relation, since it is the relation between the property and the substratum (dharmin) that is being negated? True; however, because there is a distinction in the types of relations—namely, conjunction (saṃyoga) and inherence (samavāya)—they have been stated separately as either "the relation" or "the property."
And it is not the case that there is no relation for this cognition; for if [the object] exists in some way, then the existence of a relation and so forth is possible.

Why? Because of the phrase "in the case of absences" and so on. The word *tathā* (thus) implies the sense of the word *yathā* (as), because of the constant syntactic connection between *yat* and *tat*. Just as when places and so forth exist, there is the absence of the cognition "it does not exist," because the cognition of existence is contradictory to [the cognition of] non-existence.

The same applies to absences (*abhāva*), because it is not admitted that cognition functions with respect to what is non-existent. Therefore, the cognition "this is not here" and so forth does not arise from the cognition of the absence of a relation;
for if there were no cognition of the absence of a relation—that is, in the absence of that [cognition]—it would not occur.
Or, "that" refers to the cognition of the absence of a relation; "in its absence" means in the absence of the absence of a relation. Or, [it may refer to] the cognition itself.

Regarding that non-existence, which is the absence of a relation: for whatever person such a cognition of the absence of a relation exists—that is, for one who possesses it according to how it is cognized—by whom can those words be prevented from occurring, which arise from that cognition of the absence of a relation and have the absence of a relation as their object? The absence of a relation is the object of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), not [directly] of words.
If it is argued that this is not so, he says: "For that very thing," and so forth. That which is not an object of discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) is necessarily not an object of words;
the meaning is that whatever is an object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is inevitably an object of words. And these, when they have arisen, are the discursive thoughts.

[Objection: Is it not the case that regarding blue and so forth situated in front [of one], there is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) such as "this is blue," and yet the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is its object, whereas the particular characteristic is not denotable by words? To this he says: "For not... and so forth. "The inexpressible object" refers to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Because the context concerns conceptual construction, "conceptual cognitions" are understood [by the term *vikalpāḥ*]. "They strive" means they take it as their objective support (*ālambante*). It is precisely of the nature of a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*).

Even when a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is present, the intellect is always conceptual; however, because conceptual and non-conceptual [cognitions] occur simultaneously, this is merely a misconception of those of dull intellect that "conceptualization has the form of the particular characteristic.
This has already been examined by the author of the treatise in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*, so it will not be elaborated upon here.

Now, if it is argued that the absence of a relation must be stated because it is made an object of conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), then in that case, the relation itself would also have to be stated, since it too is made an object of conceptual cognition. Or, if it is accepted [that the relation is indeed stated], then how is it that the Teacher Dignāga stated its inexpressibility? To this he says: "Of the relation," and so forth; "in its own form," etc.

In the form of a relation, the nature of a relation is a mere state of being characterized by mutual dependence—namely, that which relates the related—and it is not a substantial entity (*adravyabhūta*). There is no word that denotes it in that form. For the word "relation" (*sambandha*) must be accepted as its denoter, and when employed, it requires two correlates, such as "of whom? In this case, [it refers to] "the king and the servant."

When "relation" (sambandha) is stated—as in the case of "the king and the servant"—the relation is the cause of that distinction; thus, at that time, the relation is perceived in the form of the related entities (sambandhin). Thus he says: "by means of the designation as being related," and so forth.
When one says "the relation between the king and the servant," [the relation] is extracted from the king and the servant, who are mutually dependent.

Because the relation itself appears in the cognition as the relatum; thus, it is not apprehended according to its intended nature. In the expression "the king’s man," the relation characterized by mutual dependence is not apprehended in that form in which it is desired to be known.
Therefore, although this relation is being perceived, it is [not grasped] by the word "relation" (*sambandha*) according to the method described above.
Since it is of the very nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), it is not denoted by means of a relation. Therefore, the objection that applies to non-existence does not apply to the relation either;

the meaning is that while it must be stated that the absence of a relation is made an object of cognition by the intellect in its own form, such denotability does not likewise apply to the relation itself. For the absence of a relation is indeed made an object of cognition by the intellect through its own nature. In the case of the word—

Nor is it denoted in that very same way. However, the relation is grasped by its own nature; nor is it denoted, because it is both made an object and denoted only when it has assumed the form of the related entities. And so it has been said:
"The relation, being non-substantial, its form is not perceived."
One who has not conquered their own mind is led by others,
like a horse without a bridle.

Therefore, words exist for absences (*abhāva*). If it is asked how there can be a distinction between absences in those cases, [the answer is] that even there, "there is no denotation of a relation by way of its own nature in any way. Consequently, this remains established: the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) must necessarily be expressible. And therefore, if it does not exist...
If the cognition is "there is a relation," then the word arising from that [cognition] would indeed proceed. And thus, it follows that the word has non-existence as its object.
Now, if it is not accepted that the relation is made the object of the cognition "the relation does not exist" so that this fault may not occur; [then...]

In the statement "there is no jar here," what is being negated? (1) It cannot be the location and so forth, because those exist; nor can it be the relation, because that relation is not perceived. Thus, this [objection] is trivial. Furthermore, against one who asserts that non-existence (*abhāva*) is the denotable object, this proponent of the non-denotability of non-existence says: "Non-existence..."

How could one who does not speak—refuting while asserting that "it is not to be spoken"—effect a refutation? For it is not possible for one who utters the word "non-existence" to establish that non-existence is something expressible. Now, if you accept the verbal expression of non-existence, then, since this non-existence is admitted to be expressed, how can it be said that non-existence is unspoken? It is indeed spoken.

If it is argued that non-existence (*abhāva*) is not expressible because it is expressed by the very word "non-existence," or if it is argued that the negation is made by way of restating the opponent's claim that non-existence is expressible— namely,
"Non-existence is not expressible; therefore there is no fault"— [the response follows].

Now, one might ask: even in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), why should non-existence (*abhāva*) not be the denotable object (*vācyatā*), such that this [objection] is raised? Therefore, it is precisely the intended non-existence that is the denotable object. If it is argued that its own nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist at all, and thus because of its non-existence there is no verbal expression of non-existence, he replies: "But rather, non-existence itself," and so forth. "By that" means by the non-existence of non-existence. "Now" means that since non-existence is non-existent, that very thing is non-existence.
How can there be the statement "it does not exist"? There would be no employment of the very word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) in the sense of "it does not exist.

And why would it not be so? Because non-existence itself is not admitted. For non-existence is its [the word's] referent, and that is not admitted. If you argue that this is a negation of a non-existence imagined by another, then at least the object of non-existence is accepted.
[This is] sound. Therefore, by one who in some way initiates the conventional usage of non-existence, cognitions and words whose object is non-existence must necessarily be admitted.
As for what was further stated: [that] because when there is a negation of an object, words that are meaningless [with respect to it] are not employed, [therefore] that which is without an object...

Regarding the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*), the answer will be stated later with the passage beginning, "established by conceptual constructions arising from beginningless latent impressions" (1.2.07).
The word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) serves as a conclusion. By this much of the text, that which was stated—that there must necessarily be the application of words toward those [entities]—is established.
This very point has been established by the Master [Dignāga].

Here, an opponent says: "If words also exist with respect to non-entities (abhāva), how could there be a distinction in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*)—which serves as the cause for the application of those words—by virtue of which words expressing non-entities would have exclusion (*apoha*) as their object? [End of] *Śabdacintā*.
Because that [nature] does not exist, [the object] is impossible;
since an entity lacks form, words are denotators of form. (187)
Those words which express exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) are established as being beyond doubt.
Regarding the functions of words toward objects, there might be a doubt as to whether the expressed form is the [positive] nature itself or rather a distinction (*bheda*);
however, the "exclusion" (*prabhāva*) is precisely characterized by differentiation (*viveka*), because it consists in the exclusion of some form that is to be rendered causeless.

[This is] because [an entity] cannot be absent when that [other entity] is present, or because existence is characterized by that [absence]. Therefore, there is a distinction within that very same object. One might suspect: "Are those words which manifest such an existence not without a basis, since their object is a distinction? Therefore, all words and conceptual constructions have distinction as their object.

[The opponents’ position is] established. Therefore, even though [cognitions] follow a single entity, they are differentiated by specific distinctions as conceived according to their respective particularities.

To this, the Master (Ācārya) gives the reply beginning with "tatrāpi" and so forth. Because of the absence of form—that is, because of the absence of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*)—non-existence [is such].
Words that denote form and grasp intrinsic nature cannot even be suspected [to apply to non-existence], since those words have non-existence as their object.

Words that express exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) or the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) are indeed established [as having such a referent]. This is what is meant: just as words whose objects are absences have exclusion as their object, so too do those whose objects are positive entities.

Because words do not grasp the essential nature of an entity, they have exclusion (*apoha*) as their sole object. (1) Some words have an entity as their object because they determine an entity; some [have an entity as their object] because they determine a non-entity.

Those [cognitions] are said to have non-existence as their object. A doubt might arise as to what the denoted form of those words whose operation or function pertains to a real entity (vastu) is: is it apprehended as a positive entity (vidhi-rūpa), or is it determined as a distinct nature (svabhāva) excluded from others? However, since non-existence is characterized by differentiation (viveka), it is defined by the absence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-viraha); why [then would it be otherwise]?

Regarding the form (*rūpa*) that is to be established as threefold, which is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity: for in the absence of that [exclusion], the existence of that form would be impossible. "The existence of that form" (*tad-bhāva*) means its very presence; that which has this as its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is described as such.

This alone is the primary distinction (*viveka*), the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). However, other things, such as the objects of words like "cow," are called "exclusion" (*apoha*) because they serve as the cause for exclusion. (127a)

It is practiced as having the characteristic of being devoid of all [intrinsic] entities. "Of that discrimination" (*tasya vivekasya*) refers to that which makes known the state of things as they truly are; thus, it denotes the nature of discrimination. The connection is as follows: "having discrimination as their object" means that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), whose objects are the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), have discrimination as their object.
Those are the words and the conceptual constructions. A single entity serves as the basis for the exclusion. Regarding each...

Those words and conceptual constructions for which the battle is the locus are so described. For instance, that very object which is the locus of the word "produced" and its conceptual construction—by way of the exclusion of the unproduced—is the same locus for the words "impermanent," "selfless," and so forth, as well as their respective conceptual constructions. Thus, even though they are of such a nature, they are indeed distinct in their objects; this is the connection [of the argument].

"Why 'according to their respective [objects]' and so forth? That from which a differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*) is established is the limit (*avadhi*) of that [differentiation]. For example, for the exclusion termed 'produced' (*kṛtaka*), the non-produced (*akṛtaka*) is the limit; likewise, for the exclusion characterized by impermanence (*anityatva*), the permanent (*nitya*) is the limit, and so on. By means of those various limits, the impermanent is fashioned or constructed as distinct."
In the seventeenth week of Alet (19318),

[it was stated] that because [the objects] appear as distinct within the intellect— just as in the *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* of Deśika— and because they are presented as such, they have difference alone as their object.

Therefore, even though it is the very nature [of the thing] that constitutes the relationship between the probandum and the probans, there is no actual conjunction (*saṃsarga*) between the probandum and the probans;
consequently, the reason (*hetu*) would not be a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*). This is not so. And this has been stated precisely regarding the reason:
"The nature [of the thing] is either dependent on a distinction of conditions (*upādhi*) or it is absolute (*kevala*). (18)

It is said: for the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*), [the property of being produced] is like [the properties of] perishability, effectness, and existence. For that which, upon the completion of its own nature, possesses the state of depending on the operation of another is "produced" (*kṛtaka*). Therefore, this term "produced" serves as a distinction (*bheda*) among the various specific differences (*viśeṣa*) of things such as sound for those who possess discernment. By means of these [distinctions], [the object] appears as if non-different within the conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*).

When the substrata (*dharmin*) appear, because of the presentation of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding the distinctions and differences of those words, there is a sequential association [of them] as the denoter (*vācaka*) and the designator (*grāhaka*). But is it not the case that there is no difference in limit (*avadhibheda*) between "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*), since that which is unproduced is of the very nature of being permanent? 3.

And consequently, the reason (hetu) would be merely a part of the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā). This is not a fault, because there is indeed a distinction in their limits (avadhibheda): for prior non-existence (prāgbhāva), though unproduced, is impermanent; whereas posterior non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva), though produced, is permanent. Alternatively, [it refers to] the fact that sound is not produced by a cause.

By the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa*), that which is produced is called "impermanent" through the exclusion of the superimposition of persistence in the second and subsequent moments; thus, there is indeed a distinction of limits (*avadhibheda*). Therefore, by means of this aforementioned distinction of exclusions (*vyāvṛttibheda*), even though in a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) the essential nature itself constitutes the relationship between the probandum and the probans, there is no conjunction or identity between the probandum and the probans. And so, as for what was stated:

He states that the fault—namely, that if the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) would be a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*)—does not apply. He says, "That is not so" (*tan na*). "That" (*tat*) means "therefore. The connection is: "And this is the intrinsic nature. "Intrinsic nature" refers to a property (*dharma*) that is non-distinct [from the subject]. That may be existence (*sattva*) or something else. Even though existence exists in what is produced (*kṛtaka*), [it does not constitute a part of the proposition].

And although existence (*sattva*) is indeed produced by causes, when there is the intention to express only this much—that "this intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is produced by a cause"—then "being produced" (*kṛtaka*) is stated as the reason (*hetu*), but not when there is an intention to express its [logical] capacity (*sāmarthya*), as in the case of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth. And when there is the intention to express only this much—that "capacity exists"—then "existence" (*sattva*) is stated as the reason; but not when there is the intention to express that it is produced by a cause. (187–88)
Therefore, what was said—(1) “Existence is found in that which is produced, and there is no deviation from its impermanence;

so why is it qualified by a distinction of conditions?”—is refuted, because the capacity [of the reason] is not intended in cases such as ‘being produced’ (*kṛtakatva*). When stated as being adduced as a logical reason (*hetu*), it is a qualification dependent upon a distinction of conditions.

"Dependent on a distinction" (*bhedāpekṣa*) means independent of an adjunct (*upādhi*). This is stated for the purpose of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*). When "impermanence" is the probandum, "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is dependent on a distinction of adjuncts, whereas "existence" (*sattva*) is independent of it. By the words "dependent" and so forth, he states that "being produced" is dependent on a distinction of adjuncts. For the opponent, who considers [the cause] to be a non-reason (*ahetu*), the very capacity to produce is the operation (*vyāpāra*). [This is established by] positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Prescription (*vidhāna*) itself is dependence (*apekṣā*). A thing is "produced" (*kṛtaka*) when, for the sake of the accomplishment of its own nature, it requires the operation of another as the cause for that accomplishment. Because the suffix *-kan* is prescribed in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), this word "produced" (*kṛtaka*) is a technical term (*saṃjñā-śabda*). For even when a word expresses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it implies an extrinsic condition (*paropādhi*). By this, [the arguments such as] the difference according to the difference in conditions (*pratyaya-bheda-bhinna-tā*) and so forth are explained.
