Thus, the essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is said to be dependent upon a distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhibheda*) in some cases, while in other applications it is said to be independent. For example, existence (*sattva*) is invariably impermanent. In some instances, it functions by way of grasping a distinction within a property that constitutes the essential nature itself.
Just as [the production] occurs in that very [case], so too should it be understood in other divisions of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) by this same method.
If the reason is the nature of existence (*sattāsvabhāva*), how could existence not be established? (189)
For the non-concomitance (*ananvaya*) of particulars between the reason and the probandum is contradictory.
If existence (*sattā*) itself is indeed impermanent and serves as the essential nature of the reason (*svabhāvahetu*), why is it not intended to be proven?
In that case, it becomes qualified by the primary [property], and a particular cannot be proven because of its lack of concomitance (*ananvaya*).

Thus, although this scriptural statement regarding "being produced" (kṛtaka) expresses an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it implies an intrinsic nature that possesses an external condition (paropādhi) as its ultimate qualifier. By the word "etena" (by this), there is the demonstration that the property of being produced depends upon a distinction in conditions; the term *pratyayabhedabheditva* refers to the state of having the nature of being differentiated by a difference in causes (*pratyaya*), such as the articulatory places (*sthāna*) and the producing organs (*karaṇa*).
The word differs because of its difference [from others]. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), properties such as being produced immediately after an effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) are explained.

The conclusion is made with the words "In this way," and so forth. In some applications, it is independent of a distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhi*). For this very reason he says: when the probandum (*sādhya*) is simply "impermanent" in general, [the reason] is "existence" (*sattva*); and this is both a property (*dharma*) and an essential nature (*svabhāva*).

By the inclusion of that [term], it is stated in the present context that in some cases *svabhāva* (essential nature) is called a reason (*hetu*). For example, in that very same case, when "impermanence" is the probandum (*sādhya*), "origination" (*utpatti*) is the reason. And origination is not something other than that which possesses origination; for if it were, it would follow that non-existence (*abhāva*), being unproduced, lacks origination.

It is merely imagined as a distinct entity by way of being a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*); thus, the meaning is: "because of its having origination" [is said] by means of that [imagined] origination. This—

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) should be understood as being dependent upon conditions (*upādhi*). In cases such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), the distinction is merely this: that [the nature] is either a distinct attribute (*parabhūta*) when devoid of conditions, or an essential attribute (*ātmabhūta*) when not so devoid. "By this direction" means by the method of distinguishing between causes that depend on conditions and those that do not. (186)
If the reason is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) called "existence"—that is to say, existence itself—then why is the existence of primordial matter (pradhāna) and so forth not established?

If, on the other hand, what is to be proved is existence in general, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā). Therefore, it must be a specific instance of existence that is to be proved;

yet, if that specific instance were to be proved, the example would lack the probandum (sādhyaśūnya), because the specific property does not persist in the example. Consequently, existence as such is not what is to be proved.

In that case, even if existence (*sattva*) were present in the reason (*hetu*), because the specific property (*viśeṣa*) would not be concomitant (*ananvaya*), the example would be devoid of the probans (*sādhana*). Thus he says: "(1) *Ananvayo hi*," and so forth. "The contradiction regarding the particulars" (*bhedānām viśeṣāṇām*) refers to the fault in the reason and the probandum (*hetu-sādhyayoḥ*). The meaning is: [contradiction] in the reason and in the probandum; and "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) means in [the case of] non-self (*anātman*), etc. "That" (*tat*) refers to existence (*sattvam*). The word "kila" is used in the sense of what is not intended (*anabhimata-arthe*).

"Thus being established" means that by such [arguments] as "the Pradhāna exists," it becomes a specific [entity] through its connection with the characteristics of the Pradhāna; yet, it is not a specific [entity].

As it has been said: "Because of the lack of knowledge regarding the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And this is the distinction: the probandum and the reason are not contradicted in some cases. What then? Because the same fault applies even to the reason. For a reason that lacks positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) is not a factor for establishing [the conclusion]. Therefore, because it remains in a state of doubt, that too is not a fault. Thus—
But when there is the mere apprehension of an entity, [it occurs] in a subject characterized by the generality of the probandum. || 190 ||
No object whatsoever would be established, and such [an object] would remain unrefuted.

In proving existence in every respect, no specific quality is established; for when something qualified merely as "being" is proved in some subject, its specific nature remains unspecified, since there is no denial of mere existence in any case.

This is not a negation of the proof of existence here; rather, when one says "it exists somewhere" in this manner, how can it fulfill its own purpose without taking account of some other specific [qualification] regarding that "somewhere"?
Therefore, by this very fact, the probandum (sādhya) is already implied.
If this specific appropriation (upātta) were the probandum, the reason would be one lacking positive concomitance (ananvaya). ||191||
It cannot be established because of its lack of logical concomitance (*ananvaya*). As the teacher Dignāga said:

"That which was stated by the Sāṃkhya—namely, that 'by the statement "the Pradhāna exists," the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the Pradhāna itself is being established'—is contradicted and rendered faulty, because of ignorance regarding the object of inference as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for inference has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, whereas [the specific characteristic] has the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object."

But rather, (1) because the same fault applies even to the reason (*hetu*). He states this very point: "For it is not the reason," and so forth. That which lacks positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is "non-concomitant" (*ananvaya*); it is not a constituent part of the proof of the probandum (*sādhya*) by the probans (*sādhana*). Why? Because of the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason.

Existence (*bhāva*), meaning being (*sattā*), is the basis (*upādāna*)—that is, the qualifier—of the subject (*dharmin*), and [the reason] applies only to that. Precisely because it applies only to that, it is a universal (*sāmānya*).

If the property to be proven (*sādhya*) were restricted to two forms, nothing at all would be established for the Sāṃkhya, because that which is characterized by the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) and so forth would remain unestablished.

And such [a thing] is not refuted. "Such" means merely a generality (*sāmānyamātra*). By this, he states that [the argument] suffers from the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). (190–91)

He explains by means of the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*) and so forth. "In the proof of existence" (*sattāsādhane*) means for the sake of establishing existence; "having existence alone as its qualifier" (*bhāvamātraviśeṣaṇaḥ*) means having mere existence as its qualifier. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose specific nature (*svabhāva*) is not specified. "Not here" (*neha*) refers to when there is a proof of the mere thing (*vastumātra*). This is a negation of the proof of existence. However, that proponent [does not intend] it thus in the case of a universal (*sāmānya*).

"Someone" (*kaścit*) refers to one who does not attend to—that is, does not touch upon—a certain distinction or particularity (*viśeṣa*) of this subject (*dharmin*), such as its eternality and so forth.

"By this" means by the proponent (*vādin*). "Having taken up a distinction" (*upāttabheda*) means having taken up a particularity (*viśeṣa*). In this case, when the subject (*dharmin*) is *pradhāna* and so forth, and the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is something like "consisting of the three guṇas" or "eternal," the reason would be "lacking positive concomitance" (*ananvaya*). This is because [the reason] does not possess that which is to be proven.

Because there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the example that qualifies the property (*dharma-viśeṣaṇa-dṛṣṭānta*), there is a lack of concomitance (*ananvaya*). For this reason, (1) by means of that [example], a distinction would be established regarding existence (*sattā*) as the probandum (*sādhya*).

Others, however, having later explained the passage beginning with "in existence" (*sattāyām*) as referring to the property (*dharma*) and so forth, explain the first half-verse beginning with "the difference already mentioned" (*upāttabheda*) and so on.
Later, they explain: 5. Regarding the investigation of sound, if existence (*sattā*) were the probandum (*sādhya*), then a specific property (*viśeṣa*) would be established.

For that subject (*dharmin*)—whether it be characterized by the primary [qualities] as a single entity consisting of eternal bliss and so forth, or otherwise in any way whatsoever—[would be established].
The specific nature [of the subject] would have to be established; yet that does not follow in such a manner.

Indeed, nothing at all is established by that which is established as merely following upon existence (*sattāmātrānvayin*). There is no such consequence regarding fire and so forth; for even there, there is no dispute concerning the existence of fire. [Rather, the dispute concerns] what is intended as the qualification of a particular locus. (7-476a)

There is no lack of proof because of the connection with the locus (*sthāna*). For that [locus] does not qualify [the subject]; rather, it qualifies it by excluding non-connection with it, as has been stated and will be stated again.

He explains [the verse] beginning with "sa hi" and so forth. It is "one" because there is no differentiation within the root-prakṛti; it is "eternal" because there is no destruction that leaves no trace (niranvaya-vināśa); it is "consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion" because its nature is that of the three guṇas. "Or else it is other" means it is endowed with agency and so forth. "In any way whatsoever" means as has been stated: distinguished by all or by some of these attributes either collectively or individually.

"Of that nature" means having a nature characterized by the aforementioned qualifications. And that subject (*dharmin*) does not "conform" to such a qualified nature in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), because a subject possessing such a nature is unestablished in the example. "Not by that which is established" means not by mere existence; for there is no dispute regarding mere existence. (161–92)

The opponent begins with "nanu" and so forth. Thus, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) is that which was stated regarding existence (*sattā*) through the alternative of being either a universal (*sāmānya*) or a particular (*viśeṣa*). As it has been said:
"(1) 'In the case of a universal, there is an absence of the concomitance of particulars; [thus] what is already established is being proven.'"

Because even in that case, regarding the things to be proven such as fire and so forth, there is no dispute concerning the existence of fire itself, since mere fire is already established. Nor is anything achieved by that which is already established, because it is not a factor for initiating action. For it is fire qualified by a specific location and so forth that is a factor for action, not mere fire. Therefore, he says that it is precisely that [qualified fire] which is the object to be proven: "the qualified substratum."

That in which fire and so forth are established is the qualification; that fire and so forth which possesses such a qualification is the "qualified substratum" (*viśiṣṭādhāra*). [The opponent says: "There is a lack of proof because there is no concomitance in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) for that which is intended as the probandum. The Teacher says: "No; for even though that substratum is apprehended by way of being a qualification, it does not qualify that fire."

[The author] provides [the reason]: "by which there would be a positive concomitance (*anvaya*). What is the reason? "Because of its non-connection," and so forth. This means that by way of excluding (*vyavacchedena*) that non-connection of the property (*dharma*) with that subject (*dharmī*) which was suspected, [the subject] is qualified. And this has been stated in the section on "the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) [at 1.13], and will also be stated in the fourth chapter [at 4.146].

But is it not the case that at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), fire delimited by non-connection with a specific location is unestablished? Or, if it were established, what would be the purpose of following the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)? How is it unestablished? Because when one realizes the pervasion—"wherever there is smoke, there is fire"—fire delimited by non-connection with the intended location is indeed implied by way of generality (*sāmānya*).
Now, it is only for the sake of producing a specific cognition such as "there is fire in this place" that the pursuit of positive concomitance (anvaya) is desired. 70.
*aṅka-sa-pamama-sadv-te-madhe-me-me-me-me-me-plage*.

Therefore, in that case [of the proof of existence], it is the universal itself that is established by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*); it is not so in this case anywhere.
The proof of existence [is as follows]: Since the object denoted by words such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter) does not exist at all, that existence is indeed devoid of any specific qualities.

How could it be cognized, expressed, or determined? Thus, even that [existence] is already established. Therefore, let there be the establishment that "the knowable exists. Even so, what would be established? [It would be established] elsewhere than that—
In that case, it is established that the commonality with fire is not proven;

for even there, a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with a generality that is devoid of connection to that [fire] is certainly not established. Indeed, no one establishes a concomitance with such an object. Therefore, by one who intends to inform another, wherever—
"In that case, smoke is the fire"—meaning smoke, which is invariably concomitant with fire and inseparable from fire, must be observed.

Being thus established as pervaded by fire in general, it produces the cognition of fire precisely where it itself is seen. In this context, "therefore" (*tasmāt*) is the conclusion; "there" (*tatra*) refers to the location and so forth; and "by the exclusion of non-connection with that" (*tadayogavyavacchedena*) means in that very location and so forth.

Is it because, by excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) with the subject (*dharmin*), one proves the generality of mere fire as the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)? If so, there is no fault of lack of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Nor is there the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because the exclusion of non-connection with the specific location (*pradeśa*) is unestablished. If it is argued that, in subjects such as *pradhāna* and the like, mere existence is to be proven by means of the exclusion of non-connection, [the author] says: "Not so," and so forth. "In some cases" refers to *pradhāna* and so on.

"In the case of a property-bearer (*dharmin*). Why? Because the very object denoted by terms such as "primordial matter" (*pradhāna*)—that is, the object characterized by the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) and so forth—is non-existent. That existence (*sattā*) is indeed without qualification, because there is no substratum (*ādhāra*) that could serve as a qualifier.
"How? and so forth asks the opponent. "How is that property-bearer itself to be cognized? And having cognized it, how is it to be expressed by a word?"

It must be maintained; it has been stated that it is to be ascertained by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, because it is an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and so forth, it is indeed established.

In that [object], existence (*sattā*) as a universal (*sāmānya*) is being proved. Now, would the establishment of the Pradhāna follow merely from the fact that there exists an "object of knowledge" without further qualification? For the meaning of the Pradhāna would then be merely the meaning of "object of knowledge," which is nothing but the form of a word-meaning (*śabdārtha*), and not [the actual Pradhāna].

[The opponent objects: "The Pradhāna is established as being endowed with qualities such as permanence, and other properties will be established by other means of valid cognition. To this he replies: "Even so, what would be established by [the reason] 'being an object of knowledge' and so forth? (1) There would be no establishment of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the Pradhāna as it is intended, because this [reason] has the nature of a word-meaning (*śabdārtha*). If that were the case, even in the inference of fire—"

He says that if it were established as merely "fire," it would be unprovable; however, in another case, that very same thing—restricted to a specific substratum of fire—is not established in that particular place, and thus it is proven [there].

Now, even in that case, [it is qualified] by "being devoid of non-connection with that"; "non-connection" (*ayoga*) is the absence of connection with that location, and "devoid of that" (*tad-viraha*) means being free from such non-connection.

The meaning is that there is a connection with a specific location (*pradeśa*). That universal (*sāmānya*) which possesses this [connection] is described as such; by that, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not established.

He refutes this with the words "Not so" (*na*) and so forth: indeed, no one who knows logic establishes a pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of a fire-universal (*agni-sāmānya*) that is related to a specific location in that manner. Therefore, for one who is demonstrating smoke to the opponent (*paravādin*), [the following applies]:
That which is invariably concomitant with fire—that which is inseparable from fire—must be shown; namely, "wherever there is smoke, there is fire.

That smoke is established as being pervaded by fire alone through the demonstration of a universal pervasion (*sarvopasaṃhāra-vyāpti*) in this manner: "it is so. There is no purpose whatsoever in [showing it] in a specific location. Since it is observed there, the desired [conclusion] is established merely by the declaration of the relationship.

And if that [fire] were not specified, how could there be a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with that which is qualified by it? This [smoke], established as being invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) with fire, by implication excludes the non-connection of fire with the location. Therefore, it is that very [smoke] which is stated as the probandum (*sādhya*) in that manner;

however, the positive concomitance is not preceded by such a formal statement of the probandum, because the explicit mention of the probandum is not a constituent part (*anaṅga*) here. This applies to that which follows that stage.
Someone might remove [the fault] by means of establishing the proposition; and thus it has been said:
"Even when there is no deviation elsewhere, one should indeed show the property as the reason;
by that means, it will cause the subject, which possesses established [status], to be understood."
Therefore, just as it is not possible to establish fire, so too it is not possible to establish existence.
Furthermore, a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is certain and non-deviant must be well-known in that regard;
by means of that pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*), it will cause one to understand the subject (*dharmin*).

The subject (*dharmin*) is perceived by itself in its own form, and it is precisely therein that it generates the cognition of fire. Therefore, since the cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) arises through the capacity of this [perception], there is no purpose whatsoever in stating the probandum (*sādhya*); for the establishment of the probandum occurs even without it.

This very point he states with the words "therein," etc. Therein, because of the observation of the mark (*liṅga*) in the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*), there is merely the declaration of the [invariable] relation.

Because there is no statement of the probandum (*sādhya*)—which consists of the combination of property and locus—and since it is not stated, how could there be a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of that [locus] as qualified by the property to be proven? There would be none at all; for this reason, the fallacy of non-concomitance (*ananvaya*) would occur.
Therefore, because this smoke is established as being inseparably connected with fire, by the very force of that [establishment], [the presence of fire] in that location—
It does not exclude non-application; therefore, the aggregate is said to be the probandum (*sādhya*).

For if there were no fire there, there would be no smoke at all—this is the logical capacity (*sāmarthya*). However, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) should be shown by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) alone, and not by the aggregate of the property to be proven and its locus (*dharmin*); for that [aggregate] is unestablished in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Because [the pervasion] is established by the whole, and because there is no purpose in demonstrating the pervasion by means of the whole; for this very reason he says: "But not 'of this [subject] in that way,'" which implies that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is preceded by the presentation of the subject as qualified by a specific location. What is the reason? Because at the time of demonstrating the positive concomitance, the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is not a constituent part (*anaṅga*); or rather, if the positive concomitance were intended to be preceded by the indication of the probandum, it would simply not be so.
Someone might, on account of the statement regarding wealth, set aside the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*).

Therefore, it is established that: (1) one must state the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), even without first indicating the subject (*pakṣa*). And thus said the Master Dignāga: "The non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the logical mark, such as smoke, from the property to be proven..."

It should not be shown elsewhere than in the general [subject], nor in the mere locus (*dharmimātra*). And the logical mark (*liṅga*) must be ascertained as non-deviant therein; being thus established in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), it—being conjoined with that pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*)—will cause one to understand the subject of the thesis. Therefore, the conclusion begins with "tasmāt" (therefore). Just as the proof of fire is faultless because it does not involve the apprehension of a particular [fire], so it is not [faultless] in the case of existence (*sattā*).

The proof is faultless because the specific [reasons] are not unestablished. Thus, since it would result in proving what is already established and because there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the existence of *pradhāna* and so forth cannot be proven.
The feet were swollen with wind,
and the woolen garment was torn because of illness.
In the *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (1994): "But when proving the mere existence of an entity... [192]

The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the probandum (*sādhya*), which pervades only that [specific category], is not impaired. Even when the existence of the probans (*sādhana*) is present, there is no contradiction of the positive concomitance regarding the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) that pervades the mere entity (*vastumātra*), provided that one does not insist upon a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*).

For in that case, there is no necessity for the act of grasping a specific qualification; because even when the probans relies on mere existence (*sattāmātra*), its status as a probandum is established by its own capacity [to prove], since [specifying a qualification] would be futile.
Moreover—
A property of existence does not exist in what is unestablished; that which depends on both [existence and non-existence] is inconclusive. ||193||
How can that existence (*sattā*), which is a property (*dharma*) contradictory to non-existence, be established?

If existence is what is to be proven, its logical reason (*hetu*) is a cognition (*pratyaya*) found everywhere; thus, he says "unperceived," etc., in order to demonstrate that all such means of proof (*sādhana*)—belonging to the three classes of fallacies known as the inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and so forth—are indeed unestablished (*asiddha*).

"Untouched" means unappropriated; that is, the distinction [of the subject]. When a proof is formulated with respect to that mere entity, which is mere existence, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not obstructed. Of what? Of the probandum (*sādhya*) that pervades that alone—that is, that pervades mere existence. Explaining this very point, he says: "In the case of a property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) that pervades the mere entity, there are no specific individual natures (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*)."

Furthermore, when existence (*sattva*) is taken as the logical reason (*parigraha*), there is no contradiction with the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). The meaning is that the example is not devoid of the probandum (*sādhya*).

"For not there" means: even when existence is the means of proof (*sādhana*), that is, even when mere existence is adopted as the reason; however, it does not follow that there is no reliance on specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) of existence when [existence] is the probandum. Why? [Because...]

(1) Because it is fruitless (vaiphalyāt) [to prove existence], he states another fault when "existence" (*sattā*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), beginning with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). Since the primary cause (*pradhāna*) and so forth, which serve as the locus (*dharmin*), are unestablished (*asiddha*), a positive property (*bhāvadharma*) does not exist therein; thus, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished. As for that property which rests upon both existence and non-existence, it...

When "existence" (*sattva*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), even that property of non-existence which is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to deviation becomes contradictory (*viruddha*) when existence is the probandum, because it proves only the absence of existence. Whatever reason (*hetu*) is adduced for the probandum, which is the existence of Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth, none of them escapes these three faults. How can that existence be proven? And here, the established nature of the reason is accepted...

Having set aside the faults of contradiction (*viruddha*), inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), and non-deviation (*anantikatva*), it has been stated that these two [faults] are impossible when there is a failure to establish the reason (*hetvasiddhi*).

(192-63) Now, one might object: "Since the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhatā*) and so forth is equally applicable even when the existence of an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) and the like is the probandum (*sādhya*), how can their existence be established?"

This is not a fault. Whatever is taught is preceded by knowledge, just as is the case with anything else. And the Four Noble Truths are taught; therefore, they too must be preceded by knowledge. We accept him as omniscient who possesses that knowledge; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. "The cause of that" means the cause of its existence. "The threefold [Veda]"...

The class of fallacies (*doṣajāti*) does not exceed the three types of fallacies consisting of the three members [of the syllogism]. He states this: "unestablished" (*asiddha*), and so forth. It does not go beyond the contradiction regarding the word. In that case, even if a property of an existent (*bhāvadharma*) is adduced as a reason (*hetu*), how could it be unestablished with respect to something whose existence is not proven?
For how could one who desires a property of an existent there not also desire the existent itself? At some point, for that which lacks its own nature—

In relation to the subject (*dharmin*), a property (*dharma*) is indicated as if it were distinct; however, it has been stated that among words expressing a property or a subject, there is no difference whatsoever regarding their referent (*vācyārtha*), which is exclusively the object of determinative cognition (*niścayajñāna*). Just as both are called "properties," for when a real entity is relied upon, there is no contradiction even in the absence of mere negation, because there is no opposition.
Just as "not being material" (amūrtatva) would apply even to that which is indefinable (nirupākhya) because it is not material;
if, on the grounds that the indefinable lacks existence, it cannot be the object of negation, then what could be the object of affirmation?
If you say that this too does not exist, how then is it not the object of negation? For negation consists in the cessation of affirmation.
[This would result in] contradiction. In that case, how could a property of an existent (*bhāvadharma*) be established in something whose existence is unestablished?

It might be argued: "The property of an existent is established in *pradhāna* and so forth, but not the existent itself. To this he says: "He who," and so on. For how can that proponent [who] desires a property of an existent such as *pradhāna* to be the reason (*hetu*) in that *pradhāna* and so forth...

One should not desire for existence (*bhāva*) to be established as a non-existence (*abhāva*). Therefore, existence itself is the property (*dharma*). If it is asked, "In that case, how is it said that 'this is a property of existence'? he replies: "Sometimes by way of dependence. By means of a definition that excludes other distinctions, a property is indicated as if it were distinct, as if it had a separate form from the substratum (*dharmin*). For example, its "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*).

Thus, it is said that an entity (*bhāva*) is merely that which is excluded from what is not produced (*akṛtaka*). He states that it is not the case that one distinct property (*dharma*) is expressed by the word "property" and another distinct substratum (*dharmin*) is expressed by the word "property. For, as the verse beginning with "na hi" and so forth indicates: when a person, independent of the exclusion of others, desires to know the exclusion of a word from only one thing, such as "the unproduced," then it is said, "this [word] has the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*)."

When one, desiring the exclusion of other [properties], seeks the exclusion from just one [property] such as "being unproduced," then it is said that "sound is produced. And this has already been stated previously, by means of the passage beginning with "the rejection or non-rejection of other distinctions," and so forth.
Now, if one were to state that the property (*dharma*) is the cause for both existence and non-existence, how could a single property belong to both existence and non-existence?
For a property is an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and how could that which is the intrinsic nature of an existent belong to a non-existent? To this he says:
"Without depending," and so forth. That in which there is no real entity, but merely a negation (*vyatireka*)—of that [negation]...

There is no contradiction even in the absence of that which is conceptualized as a property consisting of mere negation (*pratiṣedhamātra*). To explain how there can be a mere exclusion (*vyatirekamātra*), he says: "by way of a non-exclusion (*aparyudāsa*), that is, by way of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). An exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is a positive injunction (*vidhi*) where the negation is subordinate;
and that is not relied upon here. For example, in the case of "it is not corporeal," incorporeality is merely the cessation of corporeality, even while [the entity] exists.

[The opponent says: "It would apply even to consciousness, which is indefinable, and even to non-existence. [The author] states the dependent [nature]: "Because that which is indefinable and non-existent cannot be the object of negation, [negation requires] a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth."

That which is endowed with causal capacity (*śakti*) may be the object of someone's cognition; but how could that which is "indefinable" (*nirupākhyam*), being devoid of all capacity, be an object? Now, since its status as an object of negation has been refuted, could it be an object of affirmation? But that which is "indefinable" is merely the absence of exclusion (*avyavacchedamātram*). Its status as a means of cognition (*gamakatva*) consists in the exclusion of the suspicion that it might reside in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣavṛttiśaṅkāvyavacchedena*), regardless of whether it pertains to existence or non-existence.

How could it be possible for one to make [the property] one's own? And he, by his own words, while asserting that both properties [belong to existence], speaks of its occurrence elsewhere than in what exists, stating that there is a statement of non-deviation regarding existence; how then is there no deviation? For in this case of a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*), the property of non-existence regarding existence is a statement of a cause for the exclusion of an object that pervades mere being.
It may be so; for that entity, because it is absent in some places, there exists the exclusion of its non-existence (*prabhāva-bhāvavyavaccheda*).

Therefore, even though this property (*dharma*) is of three kinds, there is no other way [to establish it] except by means of proving existence (*sattā*), which is the basis for the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*). Consequently, existence itself is not what is being proven. Here, the general proof of a positive property (*bhāvadharma*) that pervades that [existence] alone—

Even when the substratum (*dharmin*) has its existence established, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*). And if the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with that property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is somehow ascertained, [one might object]: "The scope of positive affirmation (*vidhi*) does not apply to that which is indefinable (*nirupākhya*), because it would otherwise fall into the domain of contradictory deviation (*viruddhavyabhicāra*). If this is so, then how is it that non-existence (*abhāva*) is not the object of negation (*pratiṣedha*)? [For it is] positive...

For it is precisely by the negation of being an object [of affirmation] that it becomes the object of negation. What is the reason? Because negation consists in the cessation of an affirmation (*vidhi*). Therefore, how could this aforementioned mere non-exclusion (*avyavacchedamātra*)—which is possible in both existence and non-existence—bring about its own status as a means of proof (*gamakatva*) when existence is the probandum (*sādhya*)? Of what specific nature is this means of proof?

"Regarding the passage beginning with *vipakṣe* (in the dissimilar instance), etc.: [it means] the presence of the reason (*hetu*) in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), the suspicion regarding that, and its exclusion—none of these are obtained. Furthermore, since there is no exclusion of the mere property of both [sides] from the dissimilar instance, how could one appropriate for oneself the capacity of that [reason] to prove? And that proponent, by his own words or by the words of another, [asserts] the dual nature of the reason that proves existence."

When one speaks of the presence of this probans, which possesses both properties, elsewhere than in the subject (*sādhya*) even though it is absent there, and since that very [presence] is the basis for its non-deviation— and thus its capacity to prove— when existence is the property to be proven, how is he not insane to claim these [probans] are non-deviant?

For this proponent who asserts that non-existence (*abhāva*) is the cause of existence (*sattā*), there would be a contradiction, because he is proving non-existence (*asattva*), which is the opposite of existence. Furthermore, what is the property (*dharma*) of this very non-existence? He says: it is exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). Of what kind is this exclusion? It is that which pervades mere existence and is characterized by capacity; its exclusion is necessarily [the exclusion] of non-existence alone.
It exists [as a property], but there is no exclusion of corporeality and so forth, because that very [property] possesses both characteristics. Why is it contradictory? He says:
because that exclusion of an object which is pervaded by mere existence is absent in some cases where existence occurs, yet present in all cases where non-existence occurs;
thus it is contradictory. Therefore, this property—whether of three types and related to existence, non-existence, or both—is [the subject] for the proof of existence (*sattā*).

The definition of the reason (*hetu*) has been stated. Furthermore, there is no other possible state or mode apart from the three types of non-existence (*adharma*); therefore, existence (*sattā*) is not established [as the probandum]. This is because, when this existence functions as a means of proof (*sādhana*) or as a logical mark (*liṅga*), it is taken in a general sense without its specific qualifiers being applied. Thus, there is no lack of establishment (*asiddhi*) regarding a subject (*dharmin*) whose existence is already proven, provided that what is to be proven is a real property (*vastudharma*) such as impermanence and so forth. Of what kind [of subject] is it?

It pervades that alone; and by means of that property to be proven (sādhyadharma), there is the pervasion (vyāpti) of the logical mark (liṅga). As for the phrase "in some way," this does not entail the non-existence of both [the pervader and the pervaded] through the force of positive concomitance (anvaya). For if the pervasion, or its locus in the subject (dharmī), were not ascertained, then because of its being of that nature, nothing at all would be a prover (gamaka). Therefore, it is established that [the mark] is pervaded by its own property.
The essential nature (*svabhāva*) must be stated as that which makes [the object] known.
For a lamp is not an illuminator by virtue of its luminosity alone; if that [luminous] form were not perceived, it would not perform its own causal function (*arthakriyā*).
An established essential nature is the indicator, provided its pervader (*vyāpaka*) is ascertained. (194)
Precisely because of the ascertainment of that property [in the subject].

For when there is an ascertainment of pervasion, the property of that subject has the nature of being the object to be understood; thus, even upon its own cessation, it causes that [pervaded property] to cease. This is the pervading property of that [subject]; by ceasing itself, it causes the cessation of that property which is pervaded.
If, in the absence of this [reason], that [consequence] would not occur, then in this way its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established.

Therefore, by means of this definition of a prover (*gamaka-lakṣaṇa*), whether through the method of agreement (*anvaya*) or the method of difference (*vyatireka*), the defining characteristic of both types of formal proof (*sādhana-prayoga*) is ascertained. There is neither contradiction (*virodha*) nor deviation (*vyabhicāra*); there is no state of being contradictory (*viruddhatva*).

Or, [the reason] may be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Thus, for this reason, this [logical fault] does not possess the characteristics of being unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

However, when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the mark (*liṅga*) by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is uncertain, or when its subsistence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—that is, its reliance upon the locus—is uncertain, then that which is intended to be the prover by virtue of having a nature consisting of the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) ascertained through its own essential nature [is not so].

No such reason would be indicative [of the probandum]. For this very reason, one must state that the essential nature of the reason—which is pervaded by its own property (svadharma), namely its own form as the probandum—is established and ascertained in the subject of the probandum (sādhyadharmin).
To reinforce this point, he says: "For not," and so forth. [This refers to] not illuminating jars and other objects by way of luminosity—that is, by way of being radiant.

Whenever it exists within the interior of a jar or the like, then, while its own form is not perceived and luminosity is being perceived, it does not indeed perform its own causal function, which consists in the illumination of the jar and so forth.
Having stated the nature of the signifier (*gamaka*), he now states the nature of the signified (*gamya*) with the words: "it is pervasive of that. This is the aforementioned signifier.

The pervaded (*vyāpya*) is its own nature (*svabhāva*), while the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is its own nature ascertained as the object of comprehension (*gamya*). He explains this with the words "of that property" (*taddharma*) and so forth. The property of the subject (*dharmī*) is the object of comprehension; what kind of property? It is one ascertained as the pervader of that which is intended to be the means of comprehension (*gamaka*). But how is it ascertained as the pervader? To this he says:
"From the very ascertainment of that property" means from the very ascertainment of the pervading property (*vyāpaka-dharma*).
By this much, the essential nature of the object to be understood (*gamya*) and the means of understanding (*gamaka*) has been shown.
He now states the essential nature of the excluded (*nivartya*) and the excluder (*nivarttaka*) as well, beginning with "of that," etc. "This" refers to the pervading property.

"When its own [absence] is established, it is the negator of that pervaded [property]"—this he explains with the words "of that" (*tasya*) and so forth. The connection is as follows: this pervading property (*vyāpaka-dharma*), while itself being absent, is the negator of that pervaded property (*vyāpya*). What is the reason? Because, in this way, this property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) is the pervader of it.
It becomes established: if, in the absence of this pervader (*vyāpaka*), the pervaded (*vyāpya*) were not to exist. The word "that" (*tat*) is used as an introductory particle for the statement.
It should be understood that what has been stated [is as follows]:

for there are two kinds of formal argument (*prayoga*): namely, that which possesses similarity (*sādharmya*) and that which possesses dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). As others have said, [the former is] the positive concomitant (*anvayin*) and...

They say there are two [types of inference]. Between these two, apart from the difference in their formal connection (saṃyoga), there is no difference whatsoever in terms of their actual meaning (artha).

Even when using the method of similarity (sādharmya), the understanding of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) follows by implication; for if that [dissimilarity] were absent, there would be no positive concomitance (anvaya) between the probandum (sādhya) and the reason (hetu).
Thus, there would be an understanding of positive concomitance through similarity. And if that [positive concomitance] were absent, there would be an absence of the probandum.
We shall explain in detail that there would be doubt in the absence of a logical reason (*hetu*). An example is as follows:
(1) Destruction is without cause; for instance, in the case of impermanence, whether it be an effect or a non-effect, [destruction] occurs in that which is not subject to destruction. (195)

By this, the illustration of these two has been stated. Among them, the positive concomitance (*anvayin*) is as follows: "Whatever is produced is all impermanent," such as a jar and so forth; and sound is produced. Thus, by this immediately preceding [statement], through the demonstration of the relationship between the follower and the followed (*anuvarjyānuvarttakabhāva*), as well as the relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*nivartyanivarttakabhāva*), [the positive concomitance is shown].

The definition of the indicator (*gamaka*)—that is, the definition of its capacity to prove the probandum (*sādhya*)—should be understood as having been stated for both types of formal argument (*sādhana-prayoga*), namely those based on similarity (*sādharmya*) and those based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
He explains this with the words "For it is of two kinds," and so forth. "As some say" refers to the Naiyāyikas; they maintain that [the argument] is based on similarity alone.
For the formal application (*prayoga*) is indeed either characterized by positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or by negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Now, if it is argued that in a formal application based on similarity (*sādharmya-prayoga*), there is both the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and likewise in a formal application based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-prayoga*), there is both the property of being a feature of the subject and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), then it follows that the logical mark (*liṅga*) possesses two forms. To this he says: "Not of these two," and so forth. "Of these two" refers to positive concomitance...

In reality, from the perspective of ultimate truth, there is no difference whatsoever between two reasons that are purely negative (*vyatirekin*), because both possess both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). This is the case except for a difference in their formal conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Therefore, those very same positive and negative concomitances are sometimes demonstrated through the application of similarity (*sādharmya*) and sometimes through the application of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*); thus, only the formal application (*prayoga*) differs, but not the actual meaning. What is the reason?

For even in a formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya*), it is by implication—that is, through the force of the argument—that the exclusion of the reason from the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*) is understood as its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). He states that very same force [of the argument] with the words beginning "asati" (when it is non-existent), etc. "In that" refers to the dissimilar instance. For in this way, regarding the probandum—

A reason would not be "concomitant" (*anvita*) if it did not exist in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*). Such is the case with "dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya*) in the application of dissimilar instances.

Regarding that [term] "in that" (*tasmin*) in the context of positive concomitance (*anvaya*): for if there were a positive concomitance of the reason with the probandum, then this [reason] would cease upon the cessation of the probandum. We shall explain this further in the investigation of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). (194–95)

Just as with impermanence, for example, "the state of being produced" exists only in what is impermanent; this is an example of a positive concomitance (*anvayin*). Alternatively, "that which is not a product" [is] "indestructible"; this is an example of a negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*). By this, the meaning is as follows:
(1) in that which is indestructible—that is, in the absence of destruction—"the state of being produced" does not exist. He states that very point:

"By this," and so forth. "Of these two" refers to the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*). "Whatever" is stated as being pervaded by a universal synthesis; thus, even the word [itself] becomes impermanent simply through the force of stating its produced nature (*kṛtakatva*).
Therefore, the subject (*pakṣa*) need not necessarily be explicitly mentioned. For this is a formulation based on positive concomitance (*anvayin*).

Regarding the phrase "also in the case of negative concomitance" (*vyatireke 'pi*): it means that in the absence of impermanence, there is an absence of being produced (*kṛtakatva*). Since sound is produced, its nature is established. When that [impermanence] is absent, the absence of being produced does not occur; and since its presence is declared in the case of sound, the presence of that very nature is established by implication. Thus, the previous statement of the proposition, "sound is produced," is established.

The positive concomitance (anvaya), however, is established through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). For that which is restricted to a particular nature necessarily ceases when that nature ceases. Having established this restriction, the cessation must be stated;
and if that cessation is established, it implies—by the force of presumption—the restriction to that nature, and thus the positive concomitance is established.

By the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the exclusion of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) from the eternal is stated by implication; thus, there is the cognition of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). The statement "and sound is produced" is the declaration of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). To the question "Why is the subject (*pakṣa*) not explicitly stated?", he says: "Of the produced," and so forth.
When "producedness," which is pervaded by impermanence, is stated by means of sound, then it necessarily brings its own pervader (*vyāpaka*) into proximity.

By the very force of the statement "it perishes," it follows that sound is impermanent. Therefore, [the author says] "not necessarily" and so forth. Thus, having stated the syllogism based on similarity (*sādharmya*), he states the syllogism possessing dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). [He says] "even in the case of exclusion" (*vyatireke’pi*) and so forth. And this is not a non-effect, nor is it perishable...

This is the explanation of that [verse]. Here too, there is no statement of a thesis (*pratijñā*). This is because, by means of the nature of being established—which is determined as having the nature of permanence—acting as the reason, when its absence occurs—that is, when impermanence is absent—and when the existence of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) in sound is declared, meaning when its presence is stated, then for that which exists as such a self-nature...

Thus, since producedness—which possesses the nature of impermanence—is present in sound, it is established by implication that "sound is impermanent. "As before" means as in the formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya-prayoga*).

[Objection: But in this formulation based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-prayoga*), the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has not been stated. To this he says: "But the positive concomitance," and so forth. The positive concomitance—

The non-occurrence of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) without [the presence of the probandum] is presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*). What is the reason? [It is stated: "For indeed," and so forth. Because it is not restricted to that nature—that is, because it is not tied to the nature of impermanence—its cessation, namely the cessation of impermanence, would logically entail its own cessation. Since this is so, one must establish by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the necessary connection (*niyama*) of the reason with the probandum through either identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).
Having established [the pervasion] by means of the exclusion of the probandum (*sādhyavyatireka*), the exclusion of the reason (*hetuvyatireka*) must be stated for the sake of the deluded person.

Therefore, that which is said—(1) “If the restriction has been established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what is the use of a fruitless statement of exclusion? Or how could one not understand the restriction? But it is not the case that there is an exclusion [of the reason] upon the exclusion [of the probandum]”—is refuted.

Others, however, explain it differently: having established [the rule] from the word and its meaning, there is a statement of implication; thus, the meaning is that after having established the restriction and implied the restriction through the force of the meaning, the exclusion (*nivṛtti*) must be stated. Exclusion must be stated by means of such a statement.

The statement of exclusion (nivṛttyukti) implies a restriction by virtue of its own logical force (sāmarthya). For this very reason, he says: "And that," and so forth. That is, the exclusion which implies the restriction is established for the opponent, provided it is manifested by such a statement. If that were so, then how could it be said: "How is it that [the property] 'produced' necessarily entails 'impermanent'? Thus—

Because destruction has [the entity itself] as its cause, it is necessarily connected to the thing's own nature. For a perishable entity does not depend on a further cause for its destruction, since perishing things arise from their own causes as such.
Therefore, whatever is produced is perishable by its very nature.

For indeed, the real entity—by the necessity of its own nature and by the necessity of the nature of the probandum—implies [the other] through the force of the statement and the meaning. For this reason, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established.
"How so? and so forth asks the opponent. "Now," [refers to] when the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader has been ascertained; [only then is] the logical reason (*hetu*) a prover.

The meaning is: "given that [the relationship] is accepted as necessary. How—that is, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is it to be understood or ascertained that "whatever is produced is necessarily impermanent," such that you may say: "Sound is produced; sound is impermanent; whatever is produced is impermanent"? Being thus questioned, he says "Because... and so forth, in order to demonstrate the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the scope of the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Because...

The "inseparability" (*anubandhitā*) of destruction—characterized by the property of cessation—from its own nature (*svabhāva*), that is, from its mere essential form (*svarūpa*); or alternatively, *bhāva* means "that from which something comes into being," and *svabhāva* means "one's own state of being," which is to say, one's own cause (*svahetu*). It is precisely from that [cause] that there is the inseparability of destruction, meaning its existence within the entity; therefore, what is produced is impermanent. Why? Precisely because it lacks a [separate] cause for that [destruction].

Since there is no cause for destruction other than the cause that produced [the thing], it follows as a matter of its own nature. This is the summarized meaning here: immediately after the operation of a mallet, two things are perceived—the cessation of the jar and the potsherd. Furthermore, these two are perceived in the form of destruction. Among these, because the cessation of the jar is devoid of any positive form (*nīrūpa*), it is not an effect.

He will say "from you" (*tvāt*). However, the cognition [of it as such] would be nothing but an error, because it is its effect. Or, if it were an effect, it could not have the nature of the cessation of the jar, since it would be produced in relation to the jar. Furthermore, there would be no cognition of it as having the form of destruction, because the jar still exists. Even though the potsherd is an effect of the mallet, it is not a destruction.

[The opponent argues: "It is the nature of form (rūpatā), because the jar has not ceased," as he will state later. And if that is so, how can there be a cognition of this [jar] as having the nature of destruction? However, if destruction were causeless, the jar would cease by its own inherent nature; in that case, the hammer and other factors would act as auxiliary conditions merely for the sake of producing shards, since they do not initiate similar moments [of the jar]. Thus, the cessation of the jar occurs immediately after the operation of the hammer, and the shards—

Since those two [the pot and its destruction] exist as real entities, and since destruction is of the nature of their cessation, and since destruction possesses a cause, it is indeed appropriate for those of dull intellect to conclude that [destruction is caused],
because the continuity of the series is severed immediately after the operation of the hammer. Therefore, how can there be an acceptance of destruction being without a cause?
It is argued that there is a contradiction with common experience regarding [the permanence of] things. He states this very point in the passage beginning with "na hi" (for not).

Those things for which destruction is observed—namely, those produced things (*kṛtaka*) that are perishing—are "those that perish. In their existence—that is, in their perishable nature—their own essence does not depend on any cause other than that which produces it. Why? Because those things that are perishable by nature and subject to cessation arise from their own causes alone.

Because of this [independence], since entities are independent with respect to their perishable nature, therefore whatever is produced is perishable by its very own nature. (195–96) 5. Investigation of Sound:
For it is observed that for those entities which are dependent, there is no necessary occurrence. (196)
The destruction of things is likewise independent; for if it were dependent [on other factors], some things such as jars might even be eternal. As it is said:
"Even if [the cause] is abundant, there may still be non-occurrence in certain cases."

In some cases, non-destruction might occur. If there is an abundance of causes for destruction, since even those depend on the presence of their own specific conditions, their presence is not necessarily guaranteed; thus, it may be that nothing at all perishes. For causes do not necessarily produce their effects, due to the possibility of deficiency or obstruction, and because they may instead result in other effects.
By this, the inconclusiveness [of the reason] has been stated,
because the destruction of all things is not established as having a cause, for those who maintain that destruction possesses a cause.
This is an intermediate verse (antarashloka).
An entity that is independent with respect to its own existence is necessarily restricted to that existence; for example, this [entity] which possesses all its causes.

If destruction were caused by a cause, it would not be necessarily occurring; thus he says: "Of those things which depend [on causes]," and so forth. For (hi) because things that depend [on causes] do not have necessary occurrence, therefore an entity that is independent regarding its destruction possesses a perishable nature. For if there were dependence on a cause, then among things such as jars, some would—

It might also be so for those for whom the cause of destruction is not present. If it is argued that because the causes of destruction are numerous, there is no place where they are absent, he says "by which," etc. The connection is as follows: "of that cause" means that even for those causes of destruction, there is not necessarily a presence [of the object to be destroyed]. Why? Because of its own... [condition].

Because its presence depends on [other factors], and because those [factors] are present only for their own causes; and since the causes [of destruction] are not present everywhere until the moment of the cause of destruction, something might not even perish due to the non-presence of the cause of destruction. Even when the cause of destruction is present, destruction is not certain, because it is not necessarily [the case].

Causes possess effects; that is, they possess the effect known as destruction. Why? (1) Because there may be a deficiency in the proximity of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), or an obstruction consisting in the encounter with a contrary factor. By this, it is stated that for that which is dependent [on other factors], there is no necessary occurrence, and thus its [the cause's] capacity is subject to deviation. (195–66)

Regarding those causes that are adduced as the marks (*liṅga*) for the destruction of all things that have destruction as their cause: why? (1) Because the effect is not established; that is, because there is no rule regarding the production of the effect characterized as destruction. For those who maintain that destruction has a cause—those who assert that destruction possesses a cause—[it follows that] since destruction is causeless, therefore this entity [is momentary].

"Independent regarding its being"—that is, independent regarding its nature of perishing. "Necessarily determined to be that"—meaning it is fixed in its character of having the property of cessation. He states an example for this [with the words] beginning with "impossible," etc. That causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) in which no [other factor] is possible—that is, not dependent [on anything else]—is "complete" (*sakala*), meaning it is accompanied by auxiliary conditions (*sahakāripratyaya*) and the transformation of the continuum (*santānapariṇāma*).

The meaning is "complete. The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: Whatever is independent with respect to the existence of a certain thing is necessarily restricted to its absence. For example, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is subject to possible obstructions in the production of its effect.

If it is argued that even in some cases where certain factors are independent, their presence is not necessarily required—just as a sprout does not invariably arise despite the collection of soil, seed, and water—we say no. For even in those cases, the causal factor itself is dependent [on other conditions].
Existence (*bhāva*), however, has no such dependence whatsoever. Even in that case, regarding the production of the effect by the final causal complex (*hetu-sāmagrī*), there is nothing intervening.
It is indeed fruitful; however, among those [transformations], that very one is the cause of the sprout, while the others are merely prior transformations for its sake.
And no one is able to obstruct it there, because no modification arises in what is already established, or because if it were to arise, [the obstruction would be impossible].

"The causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) possesses the capacity for the production of an effect when there is no obstruction; and a produced entity (*kṛtaka-bhāva*) is destruction independent of anything else—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). (196–97) With the words "But surely" (*nanu*) and so forth, [the opponent] raises the objection that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*): [namely,] regarding certain effects, even those things which are independent..."

He states that the presence of causes does not necessarily entail the existence of the effect, beginning with the words "the ground" (*bhūmi*) and so forth. For that [ground] is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) required for the production of the effect; yet, even when that complex is absent—such as at a time when there is an obstruction—the sprout does not arise. Furthermore, this has been stated with the determination of the continuity (*santāna*) as a single entity.

He refutes [the objection] with the words "no," and so forth. In that regard, within the aforementioned causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the continuum, characterized by the arising of a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because [this transformation] is dependent upon that [complex], the reason "because of being independent" does not apply there.
He says that even for a produced thing (*kṛtaka*), there is a dependence on a later time regarding its destruction; therefore, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). "Not at all"—[he says].
"Thus, etc. He will state that for a produced entity (*kṛtaka-bhāva*), there is no dependence on any other time (*kālāntara*) for its destruction.

It might be argued: "The earth, seeds, and so forth possess only a single nature; how then can they depend on a transformation of their continuum (*santāna-pariṇāma*)? Therefore, the logical reason (*hetu*) is indeed inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*). To this he says: "In that case too," and so forth.

This is what is meant: the soil, seed, and so forth do not possess a single, unchanging nature, for otherwise it would follow that the effect would be produced even before [the final moment], just as it is later. Rather, they are distinct through successive transformations (*pariṇāma*). "Therein" means within that causal complex (*sāmagrī*) which is differentiated by the transformation of the continuum; that which is the final causal complex is that which is not separated from the production of the effect by any other characteristic.

How can there be inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) regarding the reason that [the cause] must possess the fruit? It might be argued: "Even though the preceding causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is productive, it is not determinate. To this he says: "That very [complex]"—namely, the final causal complex; among those [preceding complexes], it alone is the cause of the sprout, and no other whatsoever. For what purpose, then, do those seeking a sprout [employ] the preceding [complexes]?

He says, "The causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is appropriated," and so forth, beginning with "But others... The "prior transformation" refers to a specific preceding state; its very purpose is the purpose of the final causal complex (*antya-sāmagrī*) which is capable of producing the sprout. Therefore, it is appropriated by those seeking that [result], and it is determined (*adhyavasīyate*) as being of the nature of a [specific] form (*rūpa*).

It might be argued: (1) even for the final causal complex (*sāmagrī*), an obstruction is possible; therefore, there would be a loss of its unity. For, as long as the cause has not fallen away from its own nature, there is no power [to prevent it] in that which does not produce an obstruction to its arising. Indeed, barley seeds and the like are not dependent [on other factors] for the production of a rice sprout. Its production—

If it is argued that [the seeds] are independent because the conditions are sometimes present even there, how can they be independent? For how could it be that the very same rice seed possesses the nature of production? Since that [nature] would be absent [without conditions], there is a dependence upon that nature.

If that is so, then among certain produced things or existing things, that which is perishable does not exist at all. Therefore, because they depend upon that [perishable] nature, they are not perishable.
For the nature of rice seeds and the like arises from their own causes; indeed, that which is not their cause cannot be their nature. 479a

Regarding the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for that effect to be produced: "existence in one [moment]" refers to the final moment. Alternatively, if there were the arising of a transformation (*vikāra*), the final moment would lose its singularity, because the preceding moment would perish and a second moment called "transformation" would arise. Consequently, that [final moment] would not be the final one.

Now, if it is not admitted that the final [moment] deviates from its nature as a producer, then, for that which has not deviated from its own nature— that is, its nature as a producer— it would follow that there is no deficiency regarding the production of that effect; for an obstructing cause, by failing to produce an obstruction, would not act as a hinderer.

Again, he anticipates a deviation [from the rule]: "Barley seeds and the like are not dependent [on anything else]—in what respect?—with regard to the effect to be produced, namely, the rice sprout. Why? Because the conditions for its production are sometimes present even in that case, such as the barley seed itself. [The opponent argues: "Even though they are independent, they do not produce a rice sprout; thus, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)."
"Thus it is.

How so? [The Siddhāntavādin says: "They are indeed dependent"—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "of these": the specific nature (*svabhāva*) of rice seeds and the like, which consists in the production of that [rice], namely the production of a rice sprout—that very nature does not belong to these [barley seeds and the like].

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: "dependence on that intrinsic nature" means dependence on the intrinsic nature of producing a rice sprout. At what time and in what manner would there be independence? Such is the objection of the opponent. Furthermore, among certain things that are produced or certain things that exist, there is no such intrinsic nature as that which is perishable. Therefore, because of the dependence on that intrinsic nature...
Because they depend upon a perishable nature, [the claim that] they are not perishable constitutes a reason that is unestablished (*asiddha*).
He begins to refute this with the words "The rice seed," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), barley seeds and others are included.
That nature—namely, the nature of producing or not producing an effect other than the one intended—is due to its own cause; for whatever is a barley seed...

The rice seed and so forth are not its cause; that is to say, they are not the cause of that [other sprout] which has rice seeds as its cause. That [other sprout] is "of a different nature," meaning it lacks the nature of producing a rice sprout.
Now, one might object: "Could it be both not the cause of that and yet possess that nature? To this he says: "and having a restricted capacity," and so forth. Restricted...
That which possesses a specific, determinate capacity is thus [described]; it is the cause, having the nature of producing rice or barley seeds.
It is perceived through direct perception by its own distinct, differentiated nature.
And that cause, possessing a determinate capacity, is indeed perceived by its own nature; nor is there even a doubt regarding its intrinsic nature.

In the case of objects, [change] would be accidental; for that which is independent cannot have a fixed determination of place, time, or substance. Thus, here too, a cause for restriction must be stated, by which some things are born with a perishable nature. And yet, there is no restrictive cause here in the form of an inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

If, because impermanence is established for all living beings, the very nature of those who are born is perishable, [we reply: birth is certainly not the cause for the nature of destruction. Nor is there a restriction of nature without a cause. Therefore, in this case, there is no differentiation of nature anywhere based on a cause. Since that [cause] is absent, it is incorrect to say that the effect either exists or does not exist; thus, this [argument regarding] destruction is unequal [to the argument regarding production].

Indifference [to conditions] at some place or some time is incompatible with existence; thus, it establishes the non-existence of that [existence]. For one might argue: "The differentiation of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities is not produced by causes, but rather the very nature of some is such, while that of another is otherwise. To this he says: "And not," etc. [It would be] accidental (*ākasmika*).

Thus, [the arising] would be without cause. For that which is independent and lacks a cause, there would be no restriction regarding the nature of producing a rice sprout in a particular place, at a particular time, or from a particular substance such as a rice seed; rather, it would occur for everything, at all times, and in all places, due to the absence of dependence. Therefore, the restriction that occurs in dependence on place and so forth must possess a cause.

It is understood as follows: just as there is a restriction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaniyama*) in the case of rice seeds and the like, so too must a cause for restriction be stated here regarding things produced (*kṛtaka*) or those that exist (*satsv*), by virtue of which restrictive cause some things— whether produced or existent— are born with a perishable nature and others are not.

It might be argued: "Even if a determining cause cannot be shown, it is nevertheless possible. To this he says: "And here in the world, there is no determining cause for a perishable nature; that is to say, none is even conceivable. This is because destruction is observed to be established for all things that possess birth. Destruction would thus have no fixed cause.
This means: if the destruction of all living beings is established in this way, then the reason "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). To this he says:

"That which possesses birth," and so forth. Destruction is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of those things that possess birth, not of those that do not possess birth, such as space (*ākāśa*) and the like.
The opponent thinks that [existence] belongs even to things that exist. The Master says: "Indeed, not by birth.

For the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity does not arise by virtue of its birth; therefore, birth is not the cause of destruction. Furthermore, he says "nor... and so forth, because existence is not found in space (*ākāśa*) and the like. There is a restriction of intrinsic nature—that is, a restriction of essential form—for causeless things such as space, due to their lack of dependence on place, time, or material cause (*prakṛti*).

This is due to the necessity of logical connection (*niyama*). Since the destruction of all living beings is established and the non-existence of [entities] such as space is proven, there can therefore be no differentiation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) among produced things or existing things based on whether a cause produces what is perishable or imperishable.

Because that [differentiation of causes] does not exist, and because there is an absence of a differentiation of causes, there can be no differentiation of the effect—whether it be something produced or something existent—into the perishable and the imperishable.

"It does not exist" is dissimilar to the case of barley seeds and the like. This independence of destruction with respect to a certain entity at a certain time is incompatible with the existence of that destruction; it brings about its non-existence. Regarding its [the entity's] existence at a certain place and at a certain time, it is independent of its own nature, yet dependent on the time and substance for its existence at that particular place and time, because it is dependent upon those.

Thus it has been stated that [the entity] would not be independent at all. Since non-destruction is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would be causeless because of its independence from that [cause];
for it arises in such a way precisely from the very state of being the cause of existence. For, according to you, existence belongs only to an entity of that very kind [which is already established].

If it is argued that existence does not necessarily arise from anything, then existence itself would be accidental; thus, this [existence], by its very nature as existence, does not establish the absence of destruction for anything at any time—meaning, it establishes existence everywhere and at all times. What is the reason? "For he who," and so forth. "Dependent upon that time and substance" means in which...

It has already been stated previously that since [destruction] occurs at a certain time or with respect to a certain substance, it depends upon that time and substance; thus, it could not be entirely independent.
Now, one might object: "The independence of destruction consists in its not depending on a cause of destruction, but not in its not depending on time and so forth."

(1) How then can it be said that destruction is "dependent on time and substance," such that it would not be independent? For if destruction were independent of time, there would be no destruction in the second moment either, because it would depend on that [specific] time.
And if it were independent of substance, of what then would there be destruction?

He thinks as follows: (1) because of the statement that "for that which has arisen, its destruction occurs without dependence on anything else," destruction takes place in the very second moment and not in any other moment. Furthermore, this applies to everything that has arisen, not to a specific substance alone. Therefore, if destruction does not depend on a substance, of what indeed would there be destruction?

This is refuted: if destruction were to exist at another time and in a particular substance, then that other time and that particular substance would themselves be the causes of destruction, because destruction exists only when they exist. Therefore, if it were dependent on that time and substance, it could not be said to be independent.
"From that," says the opponent. "No," says the Master. Because of the very existence which is the cause of being, there arises such [a nature];

that is, because there arises a perishable nature. He clarifies this very point: for when something exists—that is, when it attains being—there occurs only such a state as that, namely, a perishable nature. It is not necessarily the case that a thing which exists...

If it is argued that an entity arises from some cause, the opponent maintains that some things, though existing, are not subject to origination, such as space and so forth. "Accidental" means causeless. This existence would never cease for any object, at any time, or in any substance.

But surely, if the existence of jars and other things is restricted by their own causes, how can there be the consequence that space and so forth must exist?
