True; however, the meaning of the statement "it would not cease for anything" is as follows: some say that there is no entity whose nature this [space] and so forth would not be, for it would follow that it is composed of everything. That is incorrect.

For if the form of a jar or the like were to exist in space, it would be causeless, because it would exist even without a lump of clay or other such causes. Therefore, this existence does not belong to space or similar entities. [If it did], it would cease for some entity—such as the self—at some time, in some place; yet it never ceases at any time or in any place. Therefore, this [existence] belongs to nothing at any time. For whatever [entity], wherever, there is something...
It is not unconnected. If this existence were unconnected to anything, it would not be subject to restriction.
Therefore, this existence is not accidental in any respect.
If it is asked, "How then was destruction said to be causeless? [the answer is: because once something has arisen, its becoming that [destruction] does not depend on anything else.
Because [it is] non-existent. And here there is no such thing as "destruction"; for destruction is indeed the entity itself.

For that very thing, having arisen, persists for only a single moment. Therefore, the dull-witted determine its nature only after that moment and not before, because even though it is perceived, there is a lack of clarity—this has been stated. By the power of that [lack of clarity], ignorance [arises] through its influence.

Like the destruction of one whose vision has been struck down by knowledge, it must subsequently be destroyed. Thus, this destruction would cease to exist apart from existence itself; the meaning is that it would not be restricted by space, time, or substance.
Strengthening this very point, he says: "For that," and so forth. For that entity would somehow dissolve or depend [upon something else].
That which is dependent or contingent upon something else—such as its production and so forth—is not found to be non-contingent with respect to that thing.

If this existence (*sattā*) were non-contingent with respect to anything at all, it would lack restriction in relation to substance and time. Consequently, there would be no such distinctions as "this existence belongs to space and not to the self," or "the existence of the self does not belong to time," and so forth. And because—
Therefore, this existence is not accidental even in those things considered eternal.
If it is argued that since destruction arises from the very cause of existence, how can it now be said that destruction is causeless? Thus he states the contradiction.

He refutes [the objection] with the words beginning "of that which is born" (*jātasya*). For that which is born—that is, that which has come into existence—there is no dependence on anything other than its cause for its state of perishability (*vinaśvaratā*) were it not to exist;
thus, destruction is said to be causeless. And it was stated previously in this context that what is called "destruction" is not something distinct [from the entity itself].
Some [hold] that destruction is [distinct from] existence; however, destruction is indeed existence itself.
To the objection—"But surely destruction is non-existence through annihilation (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*); how can it have the nature of existence?"—he says:
"For that very thing," and so forth. Since it has arisen from its own causes as something lasting for only a moment, therefore existence itself is destruction.

It has been said: that which has the nature of remaining for only that single moment which is the time of a thing's existence is so described. It does not, however, remain for even a moment after having arisen. We shall explain later that if it were to remain, it would never cease. If a thing that lasts for only one moment perishes, why does it not do so even before the interruption of its continuity?

He says that because it is not ascertained [at first], that [entity] is non-momentary: "In darkness," and so forth. Due to the persistence of ignorance from beginningless time (*āsaṃsāra*), the dull-witted ascertain that nature of destruction belonging to this jar and so forth only at the time when the continuity of the stream has ceased, and not previously, at the time of its existence. "Even upon seeing" means even though there is seeing of the perishable nature; they do not ascertain it at the time of seeing.
It belongs to that [moment]. Because of the arising of another [moment] similar to it, there is an absence of clarity in perception.

And since the certainty of its nature as destruction is established at the time when the continuum is interrupted, therefore, by virtue of that, the conceptualization of the word "certainty" does not depend on anything else; thus, it pervades that [destruction]. If it is asked: "How can this [destruction] be understood as independent of a cause of destruction?"

Because that cause lacks efficacy, and because activity that produces a manifestation is prohibited, how much more so in the case of a word? If it is asked, "How is there a lack of efficacy?"—it is because once an entity is established, an agent does not produce it. An action directed toward something else does nothing to that [already established] thing; since an agent acts upon what is either of that nature or not of that nature, that which is of a different nature (the already established) does not require anything, even if that [agent] does nothing for it.

If it is asked how there can be a negation of action: for they consider "destruction" to be the non-existence (*abhāva*) of an entity. Thus, it follows that this cause of destruction produces non-existence. In that case, if non-existence were some kind of effect with an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would simply be an entity and not a non-entity. Therefore, to say "it produces non-existence" is to say [it produces] an entity.

By virtue of [this]... "Afterwards" means that at the time when there is the ascertainment of the nature of destruction, it is precisely that temporal condition (*kālopādhi*) which is established as the nature of destruction of that entity. He states an example: "In the case of a transformation," and so forth.
Just as a poisonous substance, even though it has been taken, was not previously identified by ignorant persons due to the presence of delusion, afterwards—
Just as poison is determined by observing the transformations produced by it, such as the salivation and so forth, so too is this case. This illustration is based on this much alone;
it is not that the power to kill is first apprehended and only later ascertained—this is the meaning of the illustration.
"Tad" means "therefore"; the connection is that "this is destruction. Apart from the existence (*sattā*) of the entity, there is nothing else.

"It depends on some cause of destruction; therefore, it pervades that [destruction] and pervades existence. "How so? asks the opponent. "And because of incapacity," is the reply. "Of that cause" means of the cause of destruction.
[The word] "and" implies "and because of being a non-agent. Explaining this very point, he says: "of that which produces non-existence," meaning of that which produces non-existence.

And because it negates the agency of that action which is intended [by the opponent]. That which is intended to be a non-substantial agent (*avastukārī*) is in fact an agent (*kāraka*) itself. To demonstrate its lack of capacity, he says: "For when [the entity] is established," and so forth. Would the cause of destruction produce a destruction that is non-different from the entity, or one that is different from it? First of all, the first position is not tenable; for when the entity is already established, an agent...

The cause of destruction does not bring about the non-existence [of the entity], precisely because that [non-existence] is already established. Nor is the second position tenable; for no action whatsoever can be performed upon an entity by another [cause], since it remains in its very same state. Regarding the phrase "having that form or not having that form," etc.: since destruction is either of the nature of the entity itself or something other than it, a cause of destruction is ineffective against it and thus is not required.
There is no lack of capacity [in our position].

But how is there a negation of action? To this he says: "For those who maintain that destruction has a cause (hetumannāśavādinaḥ) consider destruction to be the non-existence (abhāva) of an entity (bhāva). By us, however, it has been stated that destruction is the very intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the entity. Therefore... (tad iti tasmāt).

Without compassion, it would follow that the cause of destruction brings about destruction, which is to say, it brings about non-existence (*abhāva*). This being the case, if there were some intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) called "non-existence" that were an effect, then, because it is an effect—like a sprout or similar things—it would be an existent (*bhāva*) and not a non-existent. Now, just as a jar is an effect in the form of a jar and a cloth is an effect in the form of a cloth, but not...

Because it is an effect, a pot becomes a cloth; likewise, an existent (*bhāva*) would be an effect in the form of an existent, and a non-existent (*abhāva*) would also be an effect in the form of a non-existent. It is not the case, however, that only an existent comes into being. That is incorrect, for if [one says] "it does not become," then the negation of its activity—namely, "it does not act"—would be established. Even so, why is it that [an entity] which initially performs some action [is later said not to act]?

It is turned back. Thus, it is established that an entity is independent with respect to its destruction. Therefore—due to the incapacity of its cause [to produce destruction], it occurs by its very nature. (198)
And since it is non-existence, non-existence is the opposite of existence.

Nor is it of the nature of non-existence simply because it appears as having the form of non-existence; for if it were of the nature of existence, there would be no appearance at all of it as having the form of non-existence—this is precisely what is being questioned.

Furthermore, there is no manifestation of absences as having mutually distinct forms. Since an absence, being devoid of form (*nīrūpa*), is not an effect, the statement "one produces an absence" would have the meaning that "one does not produce an entity. Consequently, this cause of destruction would merely result in the negation of an action. Even so, despite the negation of action, this cause of destruction remains [ineffective].
[Objection: Why is destruction not dependent upon an entity? Thus, it is established that an entity is independent with respect to its destruction.

[Reply: But even if destruction is causeless, how can an entity be independent with respect to its destruction? For this is its very nature, by virtue of which it ceases upon encountering an opposing factor—just as the stream of other things [ceases] upon encountering a hammer or the like. Therefore...

If it is argued that momentariness cannot exist because there is no cessation as long as the opposing factor is absent, that is incorrect. For if the nature of the entity depends upon an opposing factor such that it does not exist even previously, then its prior and subsequent forms would be distinct, and thus it would be permanent. On the other hand, if that nature exists even previously, then its cessation must have occurred even before.

It might be argued: "In that case, since there is no opposing factor (virodhin) at that time, [the nature] does not cease. How then can it have a nature dependent upon an opposing factor? It has such a nature only when the opposing factor exists, because its nature as being dependent on an opposing factor occurs then and not at other times. If the opposing factor does not assist the entity, how can the entity depend upon it? Or, if there is assistance, then [the entity would exist] even when the opposing factor is present.

If there were the arising of another state, the preceding state would be seen remaining in its original condition, because it would not cease due to the absence of proximity with that which is opposed to it. Or, if it does cease, then the cessation of the state is not dependent upon the opposing factor. Furthermore, if it does not destroy the state, how can it be an opponent? Moreover, for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*), [the state] does not exist at the time of the presence of the opponent.

Existence (*sattā*) does not cease; rather, it simply does not arise. For instance, a jar, while undergoing cessation, depends upon auxiliary causes such as a mallet and, by way of producing shards, ceases to initiate similar moments [of its own continuum]. Thus, there is a non-arising of the continuum, but the stream does not cease by depending on an opposing factor. And because, by means of the preceding continuum, the entity that is about to arise...

Because there is no arising of the continuum when an opposing factor is present, dull-witted people consequently form the determination that destruction has a cause, and they likewise determine that the hammer and so forth possess the quality of opposition; thus, everything is well-established. Therefore, precisely because it is independent, wherever destruction is observed by you to occur, it happens there solely by way of its own nature.

Surely, even if destruction were causeless, it would only be causeless at the very moment when the destruction of a jar or the like is perceived, and not prior, because it was unperceived before; for a jar and so forth arise with the property of persisting for only a single moment. [Objection: But just as there is no arising from its own causes with the property of persisting for only a single moment, so too there could be arising with the property of persisting for many moments. [Response: Causes possess diverse potencies.
For causal complexes are indeed observed; among them, there might even be one that would produce an imperishable nature. Thus he says:
"In the case where [a cognition] arises from this [sound], it would likewise arise elsewhere by its own nature. (Verse 366, Section 5: Investigation of Sound)

Thus, this [reason] might be a *svabhāva* (essential nature) in some cases because it is independent of the perception of existence; likewise, in other cases as well, it would be a *svabhāvabhāvī* (invariably concomitant with its own nature), since there is no distinction [between them].
Regarding the phrase "from this" (*asmāt*) and so forth: and from this fact of being merely the presence of the essential nature, even in another place separated by space and so on—
[In the case of] what is seen; likewise, when it is seen [to perish], because of the presence of an opposing factor, destruction occurs by its very nature even previously.

This is how it is thought: for those things whose destruction is observed, if their destruction did not occur at every moment, then the cognition of destruction would not occur at all. For instance, if the entity were to persist in the second moment—

Then it would have to exist for all time; for even in the second moment, it would possess a nature that persists for two moments. Consequently, it would have to persist for another two moments thereafter. Since in each subsequent moment it possesses a nature that persists for two moments, it would necessarily continue to exist in every further moment—thus [the entity] would endure as long as saṃsāra lasts.
[There would be] persistence.

Now, if in the first moment the nature of the entity is one that lasts for two moments, and in the second moment it is one that lasts for a single moment, even so, because of the difference between those two natures, there would be momentariness. But even if this were the case, in the first moment of the entity—

Because it has been stated that non-momentariness would follow from a nature that persists for more than a single moment, as this would entail the consequence of its remaining [in existence] until the end of saṃsāra.

Now, one might argue: "Even in the second moment, although the entity does not persist into subsequent moments, since it remains in the first moment with an undifferentiated form, it indeed possesses a duration of two moments. (1)
No; for this is the very nature of an entity that it abides in one moment and will abide in another moment.

If that same nature persists in the second moment, then it would likewise abide in one moment and abide in two moments in the next; this should be understood to apply to each subsequent moment as well, and thus there would be no destruction of the entity.
And it is observed that, therefore, because destruction cannot otherwise be accounted for, there is an inference of momentary destruction.
But how, then, can there be an inference of momentary perishability regarding unobserved produced things, since their destruction is not even seen?
This is not a fault, because even for those [unobserved things], if the very same nature that exists in the first moment persists in the second and subsequent moments—

At that moment, its coming into being would be like the first moment; or else, in the first moment there would be only its birth and no duration, while in the second moment there would be only duration and no birth. Even so, momentariness would still result, because there is no difference between the birth and the thing born, nor between the duration and the thing enduring. Furthermore, duration without birth in the second moment is not logical. Birth...

If it is argued that there is stability [of the entity], that is not so, because such stability would occur in the second and subsequent moments; and since the same would apply in the second moment and beyond, there would be nothing but origination everywhere and no stability—thus, momentariness is established. Furthermore, because the connection with successive times, which is distinct from one another, is non-different from the produced entity itself, momentariness alone follows.

With the words "this" (*ayam*) and so forth, he states the meaning of the verse. "This" refers to destruction. "In some cases," such as with a jar or similar object when a hammer or other instrument is present;
"and likewise elsewhere" means even prior to the presence of the hammer. Thus, in any case concerning an entity, whether regarding place and so forth, inference is of only two kinds. (199)

Because the relationship between those two [the probans and the probandum] is restricted by their presence or absence in relation to their own respective probanda, inference regarding an existent object is of only two kinds: that which has an effect as its mark (*kāryaliṅgaka*) and that which has an essential nature as its mark (*svabhāvaliṅgaka*).
This is because, as previously stated, there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between those two alone with respect to the specific, pervading probandum (*liṅgin*).
(3) Consideration of Non-apprehension:
What is the validity of non-apprehension?
Because activity is preceded by cognition, [non-apprehension is valid] when there is no perception of its existence. || 200 ||
It has been stated that [an object] should not be engaged with because of its non-apprehension; thus, non-apprehension possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As for the third reason, it is said that non-apprehension, without distinction, is an indicator (*gamaka*) of some object. For in the negation of the certainty of existence, of verbal expression, and of conventional usage, every kind of non-apprehension is indeed a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Even when there is an intervention.

(168–66) Concluding that which was previously set forth—that "there are two [types of] means of proving a real entity"—he says: "Therefore" (*tataḥ*), meaning for that reason, whatever inference has an existent thing as its object is of only two kinds, by virtue of the two types of logical marks (*liṅga*) consisting of effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*). Why? Because of those two.

Because there is a necessary restriction of the relationship between the effect and the essential nature themselves with respect to their own respective probanda (*sādhya*). "Effect" is the logical mark (*liṅga*) of that inference; likewise, "essential nature" is the logical mark of that [other inference]. This is the analysis of the compound. In each case, with respect to the pervading probandum—the cause being the pervader of the effect, and the essential nature being the pervader of the essential nature—it is with respect to that probandum, which is the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), [that the relationship holds].
This is because of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between those two very marks (*liṅga*), namely the effect (*kārya*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), he says "from activity" (*pravṛtteḥ*), and so forth. Because activity—characterized by the determination of existence and the linguistic usage [based on it]—is preceded by cognition and preceded by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, when there is no apprehension of its presence, that is, of the object of such activity...

When an entity is not apprehended through perception and inference, a discerning person should not act [regarding its existence]; by this much, the status of non-apprehension as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated even for that which has an invisible object. The connection is as follows: the third reason is said to be the indicator of non-apprehension "without distinction," meaning that setting aside the qualification "having a visible object," it applies generally to some object.

Regarding the probandum (*sādhya*): by the words "certainty of existence" (*sanniścaya*) and so forth, he demonstrates that very same point. The conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as "existent" is the certainty of existence. The verbal expression "existent" (*sad-dhvani*), which is the word "existent" (*sat-śabda*), follows immediately after that [certainty].

Likewise, the practical application of "existent" is the conventional usage of "existent" (*sad-vyavahāra*). For, when these are negated, [the non-apprehension] pertains to every object, whether it be perceptible or imperceptible.

[Objection: Was it not stated in the *kārikā* that "activity" (*pravṛtti*) [is the definition of a means of valid cognition]? How then is it explained in the *vṛtti* as "from the ascertainment of existence" (*sanniścayāt*) and so forth?

[Response: He says: "Because from the ascertainment of existence," and so on. Since linguistic conventions (*śabdavyavahāra*) proceed from the ascertainment of things (*sat*) that exist, therefore they are said to be "activity.
Thus, because linguistic conventions proceed from the ascertainment of existing things, they are called "activity."

For it has been stated that the non-existence of non-existent things consists precisely in their non-apprehension. And that [non-existence] is stated from the perspective of the cognizer, not from the perspective of the object itself. As long as there is no cognition of something here, so long its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) does not exist here; for even if it were existent, it would not perform its function. In reality, however, that which is not being apprehended is neither existent nor non-existent, because even among existing things, there may be a deviation from their intrinsic nature, etc. [480b]

Because it is not perceived after being drawn [toward the senses], and because that [non-perception] is equally present even when things exist; since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the perceiver [to establish its existence], this "existence" characterized by perceptibility, upon its cessation, causes the verbal conventions (*śabdavyavahāra*) based on its own causes to cease.
Therefore, even this non-perception of things that have reached the conditions for perceptibility is itself of the nature of non-existence in reality.

Because it is fit for purposeful activity (*pravṛtti-yogyatvāt*). Its validity regarding this object is equal [to that of the other two]. Although its result is not the ascertainment of existence (*asanniścaya-phalā*), nevertheless, all three—the word, the linguistic convention (*śabda-vyavahāra*), and the person’s activity—proceed because they are auxiliary factors for purposeful activity, being directed toward the person’s engagement.
It has been stated that activity [of the world] proceeds from friendship; therefore, there is no contradiction between the Sūtra and the Vṛtti.

What, then, is the reason that the conventional usage of "existence" ceases when perception ceases? For it was previously stated that non-perception itself—both types without distinction—is non-existence. And that non-existence applies to non-perception that is remote.
This has been stated from the perspective of the cognizer. For the cognizer determines that what is not perceived does not exist; it is not due to the nature of the object itself.

For instance, regarding a remote object, both its existence and non-existence are doubtful. Therefore, for that cognizer, a remote entity does not exist as long as there is no cognition of it. Why? Because even if it exists, due to its remoteness—

Because that object is not produced for the person by means of an unperceived, inferred object; since it does not produce any effect for that person, even though it exists, it is as if non-existent. In reality, however, that which is not being perceived is neither existent nor non-existent. Why? Because even among existing things, there is no certainty of non-existence due to the occasional non-perception resulting from remoteness of nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth; nor is there a certainty of existence [in such cases].
Because non-apprehension is equal even in the case of non-existent things. "Tad" means "therefore. The connection is with the word "this existence.

Of what nature [is this]? It is characterized by non-apprehension and remote in terms of place and so forth, because for the cognizer there is an absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Its cessation occurs due to the absence of perception and inference, not due to the force of the object itself. What does it do? It produces verbal conventions based on its own causes.
He turns back from [the existence of] those [entities].
Others read "characterized by perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇam*). The meaning is that existence itself is perception through metaphorical designation; thus, such existence has ceased.

For this very reason, this non-apprehension—(1) of what? Of those things that have reached the conditions for apprehension; (2) which is, by its nature, an absence even in reality (*vastu*), the word "even" (*api*) implying that it is so also by virtue of the cognizer; for what reason? Because it is unfit for engagement and because it is fit for the conventional usage of "non-existent. This [is the definition] of that non-apprehension as well.

The validity [of this non-apprehension] is equal [to that of other means of knowledge] in its function of negating the conventional usage of existence regarding this object. This non-apprehension, which is characterized by the absence of perception, results in the ascertainment of non-existence.

This ascertainment of non-existence occurs when, despite all other causes being present, something that possesses the characteristics for perception—that is, something capable of being perceived—would not be apprehended if it were actually existent.
Nor, however, does it prove prior non-existence;
for there are many supersensuous matters that are irrelevant to the subject matter of the treatise. (201)
And how can they be said to be without marks (*aliṅga*), given that their nature is not perceived?

If it were established by mere non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) alone as proving their absence, then for all objects, [the absence of the three means of valid cognition] would be established through the cessation of the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatraya*).
However, the cessation of that treatise (*śāstra*) does not prove its absence, because it functions within a specific domain of application.

For a treatise proceeds by relying on some means for accomplishing the goals of human life; otherwise, it would be an incoherent prattle and thus lack authority. In this regard, even within a specific treatise, not all matters necessarily need to be set forth, such as the mental dispositions of individuals which are restricted to each person.
The functions of certain [cognitions] arise from indeterminate causes, like the various substances used as supports for objects situated at a distance in space and time;
this is the analysis of the compound *phalaṃ yasyāḥ*.

He explains this with the words beginning "asattāyām" (in the case of non-existence): because even when there is non-existence, or even when there is no certainty, [the cognition] does not indeed exist.

"Occurrence" (*sambhava*) refers to a thing that is capable of being perceived; if, while all other conditions for perception are present, it is not perceived despite existing, then its non-perception constitutes proof of its non-existence. However, the aforementioned non-perception of a remote object does not establish non-existence.

For non-perception is characterized precisely by the cessation of perception through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*). In this context, it is scripture (*śāstra*) that has jurisdiction in this treatise.

In this context, "unconnected" means those many things which are not invariably concomitant (anāntarīyaka) and are remote by nature and so forth, and thus are not treated in the treatise; that is to say, they are not even objects of perception, as he says they are "beyond the senses" (atīndriya). Nor are they objects of inference, because they are "without marks" (aliṅga); that is, there is no mark for them, hence they are "without marks. Of those objects beyond the senses, [there is no cognition] by the three means of valid knowledge—
How can there be non-existence on the basis of the non-apprehension of that which is characterized by cessation? [The opponent replies: "Not at all.

This is the proponent's view. Regarding "of all objects," this refers to those things remote in terms of place, time, or nature. "By the cessation of the three means of valid cognition" means by the cessation of perception, inference, and scripture. "Of that" refers to the treatise (*śāstra*) in certain cases where it does not lead to human goals (*puruṣārtha*).

Because activity [would occur] even in the absence of an application [of the scripture] when there is no qualification for the sake of a Yoginī; for the scripture begins with "Since... and so forth. "Otherwise" means if the scripture were to proceed by relying on a matter that is not conducive to the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*); for a scripture that utters incoherent talk—that is, one which expresses what is irrelevant—lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*).
This might be so: [the opponent argues that] all objects whatsoever are useful for the purposes of man (*puruṣārtha*). To this, he says: "In that context," and so forth.
"In that context" means in the introduction to the investigation of the purposes of man. "Fixed for each individual" means fixed for every person.
By this, he states that because persons are infinite, the mental fluctuations (*cetovṛtti*) are also infinite. [The phrase] "to arise from an indefinite cause" [is used].
The analysis of the compound is "those whose [nature] is virtue" (*śīlam yāsām*). By this, even though there is only one person, plurality is expressed due to the diversity of causes.

Such mental states (*cetovṛtti*) do not necessarily have to be specified in their entirety for every single instance, because that would be impossible. Furthermore, specific substances—whether separated by time or space—that are of no utility for human goals need not necessarily be specified; therefore, there is no investigation of words (*śabda-cintā*) regarding them.
That treatise does not take it as its object; nor is there an absence of the power to produce knowledge regarding such a remote thing due to the non-application of its own capacity.

And that [power] must necessarily exist by which one infers even in the absence of the perception of an effect; yet those [means of knowledge] are excluded by the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It does not possess the capacity for certainty. Therefore, every non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is not a means of establishing the certainty of an absence (*nivṛtti*). Rather, this [non-perception] makes its own object known. And those mental modifications (*cetovṛtti*), as well as those specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), are referred to in the masculine gender [by the pronoun *tān*].
Having made the man the remainder [of the compound] in the expression “pumān striyā” (man with woman),
he states that they are not objects of perception, saying “na ca” and so forth. Likewise, regarding things that are remote— namely,

those remote in terms of space and so on— there is no capacity to produce cognition because of the non-proximity of their own nature (*svarūpa*), due to the lack of the application of their own causal power.

By this, the statement "they are beyond the senses" has been explained. He further states that they are not even objects of inference, beginning with the words "And that [inference] necessarily... and so forth. "Of these" refers to those things obstructed by space and other factors. "By which" refers to the perception of an effect. And "not those" refers to the remote objects.

The phrase "of all" refers even to the non-perception of the imperceptible (*adṛśyānupalabdhi*). "Of the certainty of cessation" means of the certainty of non-existence. "Since it is thus, therefore"—that is, for this reason—this non-perception of the imperceptible does not have the result of a certainty of existence; that is, it is not the cause for the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of "existent. Nor does it have the result of a certainty of non-existence, because of doubt. For this reason:

It might be argued that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) lacks the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because the result of a means of valid cognition is ascertainment (*niścaya*). For all means of valid cognition have ascertainment as their result; even perception (*pratyakṣa*), though it grasps all aspects (*sarvākāra*), brings about ascertainment only with respect to those aspects for which it produces such certainty.
[The opponent objects: "But surely non-apprehension would be a means of valid cognition for the negation of activity. To this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth. "This" refers to non-apprehension.

The analysis of the compound *niḥśaṅkaparicchedam* is: "that cognition whose determination (*pariccheda*) is free from doubt (*niḥśaṅka*). The meaning is that it does not produce a mind that is certain in the sense of thinking, "Since there is doubt, one must certainly not act. For even from doubt, people such as farmers sometimes do engage in activity. [Objection: How then is its status as a means of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) stated to have non-engagement as its result? To this [the author replies]:...

He says: "In that case, 'that' and so forth. In that manner—that is, in that form—this cause for non-engagement called non-perception (*anupalambha*) would be faultless and blameless, provided that someone were to employ it preceded by certainty; that is, one would initiate such engagement with what exists based on valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By means of this method, this non-perception of the unobservable is said to have non-engagement as its result, [referring to] the certain engagement with what exists and so forth.

It is taught that [the means of knowledge] have negation as their result; however, since the conventional usage of "existent" and so forth remains doubtful and is not negated, human activity still occurs.

Regarding the phrase "possessing the state of an excellence of the mark" (*liṅgātiśayabhāvinī*): the "mark" (*liṅga*) is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*); its "excellence" (*atiśaya*) is its specific qualification, namely the fulfillment of the conditions for apprehensibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*).
That [non-apprehension] in which this "state of being" (*bhāva*), i.e., its actual presence, exists is so described. It is like [the term] *liṅgaviśeṣavat*.
Or else, there would be the absence of the result consisting in the ascertainment of the true and the false, or else there would be invalidity. (202)

Furthermore, this non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the fruit of all means of valid cognition is determinate ascertainment (*vyavasāya*). This [non-apprehension] does not even constitute a mind that has reached a fearless determination regarding the prohibition of activity, since activity sometimes occurs even from doubt. If that were the case, one would act only after such faultless certainty; therefore, it is said that its result is the absence of activity.

There may also be a certain type of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arising from a specific excellence of the logical mark (*liṅga*). In this context, every non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) that possesses a specific characteristic of the mark is also a valid cognition, as was illustrated previously.
This applies even to one who maintains that there is no valid cognition regarding that which is not apprehended.
This principle has been illustrated regarding the ignorance that fails to recognize intrinsic nature. || 203 ||
Whatever thing is non-existent merely because it is not perceived due to its excellence in terms of its own nature,

its object, or other factors— as was stated previously— even if a supersensuous object or a specific nature is rejected due to the absence of a cognizing mark (*liṅga*), such as [the claim that] there is no dispassionate mind, or no state of being a particular deity, or [the denial of] giving, non-violence, and so forth.
The meaning is: "it exists. This amounts to saying that there is a non-apprehension of what has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*).
He explains this with the words "here," and so forth. "Here" refers to the ascertainment of cessation. "As was previously illustrated" refers to [the verse] beginning with:
"A certain [non-apprehension], depending on a distinction of causes, results in the cognition of non-existence," and so on.
Furthermore, as for what was stated—that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*)—that should not be understood without qualification;

rather, it refers to cases such as "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) and so forth. [In this context,] "intrinsic nature" refers to that which is remote in terms of space and so on, while "indicative mark" (*liṅga*) refers to that which makes known. Regarding the lack of knowledge of these two, it is said:
"This principle has been illustrated by the absence of knowledge of intrinsic nature and the indicative mark" (1.203).

"When non-existence is the probandum, there is no [valid] means of cognition. Non-cognition of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the cessation of perception (*pratyakṣa*); non-cognition of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is the cessation of inference (*anumāna*). This principle has been illustrated regarding the cessation of both perception and inference with respect to an imperceptible object;
such is the collective meaning.

He explains [the verse] with the words beginning with *yasya* ("of which"). "Of some," such as a *piśāca* or other [supernatural being]. "That" refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "By the mere non-perception of that" means by the mere non-perception of that object; this is the cessation of perception in the form of [the statement] "non-existent. As was stated previously: "Because even existing things are sometimes not perceived," and so forth. By this, the ignorance of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvājñāna*) has been explained.

He speaks [the passage beginning with] "And whoever," etc., in order to explain the non-cognition of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). The term "of the indicator" is an elaboration of "of the mark" (*liṅga*). An object beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) is rejected, such as, for example, "there is no dispassionate mind," and so forth. Likewise, it is not merely the locus (*dharmimātra*) that is rejected, such as, for example, "there is no giving," and so forth; for giving consists in the abstention from violence.

Thus, it is a *dvandva* compound. The volitions (*cetanā*) have that as their object; that is to say, the volitions of giving and the volitions of abstaining from violence. Furthermore, there is no status as a cause for higher rebirth (*abhyudaya*) or the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) for [mere] sounds or for the volitions of abstention, because even in the case of an object that is perceptible, that fruit does not occur immediately. One might even deny it due to a misconception based on the dissimilarity with those fruits. However, one cannot [deny it] merely by that much... [481b]

Because the production of those fruits is observed for the sake of those very causes, their non-existence [cannot be established]; it is like the case of a rat or a mad dog exhibiting symptoms of poisoning. Since there is no contradiction when that [cause] is present, mere non-perception here is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).

If there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding existence, then doubt alone is appropriate; it is only because a means of valid cognition is possible that [existence] is rejected. By the cause of prosperity—that is, by the cause of results such as heaven—the intrinsic nature of these volitions is not rejected.
Because it is directly perceived. However, it is said that there is no specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that serves as the cause of prosperity (*abhyudaya*).

[Objection: But since the cause of prosperity is also directly perceived in conscious beings, because it is of the same nature as them, how can there be any delusion regarding the fact that it is indeed directly perceived? And so forth.

The connection [of the sentence] is: "Even regarding an object that is directly perceived, one who is mistaken might even deny it. To the question "In what way is he mistaken?", he says: "Because of their having non-those fruits," and so forth. Those specific conscious states which are observed to be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and have non-those fruits—that is, those whose fruits are not spiritual elevation (*anabhyudaya*)—[he denies them].

This is due to their similarity (*sādharmya*). To the question "How exactly is there this similarity?", he says: "Because there is no immediate succession of the fruit," and so forth. Whatever other...

Volitions do not have that [specific] result; nor do those volitions which have that result, for in both cases the immediate succession of that result is not observed. It is not by the mere non-observation of the immediate succession of the result that its absence—that is, the absence of the result—is established. Why? Because of the phrase "of those that are separated," and so forth. [The result arises] from the cause at a later time, characterized by a successive transformation of states.
This is because we observe results that are temporally remote. It is like the toxic transformation caused by a rat, a snake, or a mad dog;

for that transformation does not occur at the very moment the poison enters the body, but rather it comes about when the presence of a specific auxiliary condition (sahakārin) is met. It is not, however, as if there were some entirely different cause involved in that case.

It might be argued: (i) since the transformation caused by the poison of a mouse or similar creature is observed at a later time, its existence is indeed logical. However, the fruit of giving and so forth is never observed; how, then, can its existence be established? To this, he says: "That," and so on. "The existence of that" means that there is no contradiction regarding the existence of those two things—the fruit of giving and so forth, and the supersensible entity.

In this regard, the opponent argues that mere non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) for establishing either the fruit of giving and so forth or its supersensible nature (*atīndriyabhāva*).
If there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), there is no negation; however, as for its existence (*bhāva*) or presence (*astitva*), what proof is there?
Therefore, it is not logical to determine its existence. This is the opponent’s position.

"Therefore," says the Teacher: since there is an absence of both proving and refuting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object that is utterly beyond the senses, doubt is appropriate for a discerning person. Or rather, when an entity cannot be rejected and yet no proving means of valid cognition appears for it, such a possibility is appropriate: "Perhaps a proving means of valid cognition for this [object] might exist."
In this regard, it is because of the lack of proficiency in perceiving certain objects, intrinsic natures, and causes.

Because there is no certainty regarding the production of an effect, the indicator is unestablished. Its absence is not proven by this much alone, since for some things it may still be manifested through a transformation (*paryāya*). However, in the case of an effect, the non-cognition of its cause is indeed a proof of its non-existence.

For someone who possesses creative intuition (pratibhā), there is no rejection [of the possibility of omniscience] due to doubt regarding the object or doubt regarding the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Others, however, having explained that "for one whose mind is detached, it is for this very reason a cause of worldly prosperity," maintain that there is doubt because of the absence of both proving and refuting means of valid cognition. Thus, they hold that there is no rejection of the idea that a detached mind might be a means of valid cognition for omniscience.
And they explain that this means of valid cognition will be discussed in the second chapter;

for it is precisely because of this that the production of an effect occurs even from something remote. Therefore, although the sequence of the text here is "among the supersensible [objects], of certain objects and of certain natures," nevertheless, the connection is made according to what is appropriate.

For some intrinsic natures, such as those that are causes of prosperity and so forth, there may be a lack of proof for the indicator (*jñāpaka*). How so? (1) Due to the absence of clarity in perception; because of the incapacity of the experience regarding those objects to produce a determination of their nature exactly as it was apprehended, in the case of certain things such as those whose minds are dispassionate.
The effect, characterized by perception and inference, is absent because there is no indicator (*jñāpaka*) for it.
To the question, "Why is such an effect absent?", he says: "Of the causes," and so forth. For indeed, the causes—
There is no rule that an action which necessarily indicates its own agent must be undertaken by every person as something to be grasped.

Others, however, explain it differently: for certain natures that are proponents of prosperity as their cause, and for objects such as a detached mind and so forth, there may be a non-establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that serves as an indicator or a determiner. Why? (1)

Because of the lack of clarity in perception. This is what is meant: perception itself is the indicator of some object, and because it is not sharp, it does not produce a determination of all its aspects. Furthermore, there is no necessity for causes to produce their effects; therefore, immediately—

Because their effect is not observed. Even by way of their effects, it is impossible to deny that they are causes of prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Likewise, because the perception of supersensible objects—which is characterized as mental cognition (*manovijñāna*)—is not sharp, they are not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Indeed, there is no determination of these [objects] by way of their effects, because there is no necessity regarding the production of effects by causes; for it is not the case that by means of causes...

The rule is that an effect which is subordinate and indicative of [the existence of] the self must be produced in another continuum; therefore, neither perception nor inference exists for them. It is not the case that the non-existence of those supersensible things follows merely from the absence of such an indicator as described; for: [The original Sanskrit text continues: *na hy adṛṣṭimātreṇa tadabhāvasiddhiḥ |* For the non-existence of something is not established by mere non-perception. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *yasmāt* Because: [The original Sanskrit text continues: *na hi dṛśyādṛṣṭir evābhāvasya sādhikā, kiṃ tarhi? dṛśyādṛṣṭir upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyaiva |* For it is not the mere non-perception of the perceptible that proves non-existence; rather, it is the non-perception of the perceptible only when it has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). [The original Sanskrit text continues: *na caivam atīndriyāṇām upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptiḥ sambhavati |* And in this way, the attainment of the conditions for apprehension is not possible for supersensible things. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *tasmād adṛṣṭimātreṇa na teṣām abhāvaḥ siddhyati |* Therefore, their non-existence is not established by mere non-perception. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *yadi punar manyeta—yady api na pratyakṣato nānumānataḥ siddhiḥ, tathāpi śabdād āgamāt siddhir bhaviṣyatīti |* If, however, it should be thought: "Even if there is no establishment through perception or inference, nevertheless, establishment will occur through verbal testimony (*āgama*)," [The original Sanskrit text continues: *tad apy ayuktam | āgamasyāpi pratyakṣānumānapūrvakatvāt |* That too is incorrect, because even verbal testimony is preceded by perception and inference. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *na ca tābhyām atīndriyārthasiddhir astīty uktam |* And it has already been stated that there is no establishment of supersensible objects by means of those two. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *tasmād āgamād api na teṣām siddhiḥ |* Therefore, there is no establishment of them even through verbal testimony. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *atha syāt—yady api na sākṣāt siddhiḥ, tathāpy arthāpattyā sidhyanti |* Now, it might be argued: "Even if there is no direct establishment, they are established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). [The original Sanskrit text continues: *tad apy asat | yasmāt* That too is false, because: [The original Sanskrit text continues: *na hy anyathā nopapadyate iti kṛtvā sarvasyānyathānupapannatvād arthāpattiprasaṅgaḥ |* For if it were on the grounds that "it is not otherwise possible," then since everything is otherwise impossible, there would be the unwanted consequence of [everything being established by] presumptive testimony. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *tasmād yathoktajñāpakābhāve 'pi na teṣām abhāvaḥ |* Therefore, even in the absence of the aforementioned indicator, there is no non-existence of those [supersensible things]. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *kiṃ ca* Furthermore: [The original Sanskrit text continues: *na hi vayaṃ sarvajñābhāvaṃ sādhayāmaḥ, kiṃ tarhi? yasya yasya jñāpakaṃ nāsti tasya tasyābhāvaṃ brūmaḥ |* We do not establish the non-existence of every omniscient being; rather, we state the non-existence of whichever [person] lacks an indicator. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *na ca buddhasya bhagavato jñāpakaṃ kiṃcid asti yena sarvajño bhaved iti |* And there is no indicator whatsoever for the Blessed Buddha by which he might be [proven to be] omniscient. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *tasmāt sarvajñābhāvo na siddhaḥ |* Therefore, the non-existence of an omniscient being is not established. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *api ca* Moreover: [The original Sanskrit text continues: *na hi dṛṣṭamātreṇa sarvasya sarvajñatvaniṣedhaḥ śakyate kartum |* For it is not possible to negate the omniscience of everyone merely by what is seen. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *na hi vayam ekapuruṣam eva sarvajñaṃ pratiṣedhayāmaḥ, kiṃ tarhi? sarvāneva puruṣān |* We do not negate only one person as being omniscient; rather, [we negate] all persons indeed. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *tatra yasya yasya jñāpakaṃ nāsti tasya tasyābhāvaṃ brūmaḥ |* In that regard, we state the non-existence of whichever [person] lacks an indicator. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *buddhasya ca bhagavato nāsti jñāpakam iti pūrvam evoktam |* And it has already been stated previously that there is no indicator for the Blessed Buddha. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *tasmāt sarvajñābhāvo na siddhaḥ |* Therefore, the non-existence of an omniscient being is not established. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *yasmāt* Because: [The original Sanskrit text continues: *na hi dṛṣṭamātreṇa sarvasya sarvajñatvaniṣedhaḥ śakyate kartum |* For it is not possible to negate the omniscience of everyone merely by what is seen. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *tasmād yathoktajñāpakābhāvamātreṇa na teṣām abhāvaḥ |* Therefore, there is no non-existence of those [supersensible things] merely due to the absence of the aforementioned indicator. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *api ca* Moreover: [The original Sanskrit text continues: *na hi vayaṃ sarvajñābhāvaṃ sādhayāmaḥ, kiṃ tarhi? yasya yasya jñāpakaṃ nāsti tasya tasyābhāvaṃ brūmaḥ |* We do not establish the non-existence of every omniscient being; rather, we state the non-existence of whichever [person] lacks an indicator. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *na ca buddhasya bhagavato jñāpakaṃ kiṃcid asti yena sarvajño bhaved iti |* And there is no indicator whatsoever for the Blessed Buddha by which he might be [proven to be] omniscient. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *tasmāt sarvajñābhāvo na siddhaḥ |* Therefore, the non-existence of an omniscient being is not established. [The original Sanskrit text continues: *api ca* Moreover: [The original Sanskrit text continues: *na hi dṛṣṭamātreṇa sarvasya sarvajñatvaniṣedhaḥ śakyate kartum |* For it is not possible to negate the omniscience of everyone merely by

For even certain objects that have not been perceived through perception or inference may later, in turn and by way of sequence—such as objects situated behind a wall or in an opening—be manifested and cognized through perception or inference. Thus, in the case of remote objects, the non-perception of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) is not a proof of their non-existence, nor is the non-perception of their effect (*kāryānupalambha*). 5. Investigation of Sound (*śabdacintā*).

When the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the probandum, non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is said to be not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*); however, the non-apprehension of causes (*kāraṇānupalambha*) is indeed a means of valid cognition. For it is not the case that the effect of many causes can possibly come into existence [if those causes are absent].

But surely, even when the cause has perished, the persistence of the effect is not observed. We do not say that the effect exists at the same time as the cause; nor is the persisting entity its material cause in that sense. Rather, it is the effect of that [cause] through a succession, because of the assistance rendered to the continuum.

This is the designation. It has been stated that if an entity arises in the absence of a cause, it cannot be said to exist. If its non-existence could somehow be established, then it would be certain that the effect does not belong to it.
He states that the non-perception of the cause is also a means of proving non-existence in that case, beginning with the words "But in the case of the effect," etc. But in the case of the effect...

Even when [an object] is remote in terms of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, the non-cognition of the causal factor (*kāraka*)—namely, the non-apprehension of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*)—is indeed a means of proving non-existence.

He explains this with the words "intrinsic nature" and so on: when the non-existence of an intrinsic nature whose object is remote is to be proven, the non-apprehension of the intrinsic nature itself is said to be non-authoritative (not a means of knowledge), whereas the non-apprehension of the cause is indeed authoritative.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of a remote object, the non-perception of the cause itself is impossible to ascertain; how then could it establish the absence of the effect? [Reply: True. However, this much can be stated: that in a case where no cause has been specified, the effect necessarily does not exist. It is for this slight reason alone that this [argument] is presented. For this very reason, he states it in general terms: "No..."
"‘It exists yesterday,’ and so forth.

‘But surely,’ and so forth, says the opponent: because smoke is observed even when fire has perished, as in the case of a house or a cave; thus, since an effect is seen even in the absence of its cause, there is a deviation [from the rule]. An effect would not exist if its cause were absent—"

By that statement, it is meant that the effect exists at the time when the cause is present; we do not say that "as long as there is existence of the cause, so long is there existence of the effect," for if we did, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that [the effect would persist] even upon the destruction of the cause and so forth would follow. Rather, he states what is actually expressed by this sentence: "devoid of a cause," and so on.

Thus far, it has been stated on the assumption that [the cause] is stable. However, if [the cause] is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), once the cause has perished, there is no possibility at all for the effect to remain; so how could there be any suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? For instance, that moment of smoke produced by fire does not exist at all once the fire has perished, because it perishes due to its momentariness. As for the smoke that remains later, [it is not produced by that specific fire].

That [smoke] has smoke alone as its cause, not fire. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "And not in that way," and so forth. "Abiding in that manner" means persisting for a later time even when the initial cause has perished. "Having that as its material cause" means having the previously ceased cause as its material cause.

How, then, can even subsequent smoke be said to have fire as its cause? To this he says: "By way of succession," and so forth. First, fire alone produces the initial moment of smoke; that moment of smoke produces another, and that one another—in this manner, by way of succession. Clarifying this very point, he says: "Because of the assistance [rendered] to the continuum" (*santānopakārāt*). This refers to the initial production of the series.
Therefore, there is the designation of that as its effect. Consequently, even if it occurs later, that which is the cause is designated as such by the fact that it has this as its effect.
(Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā 1.206)
And there is the non-perception of the intrinsic nature when the intrinsic nature of the object is the probandum. (204)
In the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the non-perception of that very intrinsic nature regarding the subject (*liṅgin*) is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
If the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) were itself established as its intrinsic nature— just as [the non-perception of] a tree [is established] for a *śiṃśapā*— then [it would be valid].
That state would be cognized if it were established by some reason; that is,
if the absence of this [subject] and its pervading nature were established from some indicative reason.

By the very absence of that [probans], it would not be excluded from its own effect or from the pervaded; for even if it were excluded when the absence of that [probans] is unestablished, there remains doubt.
(Kha) How can there be proof of the non-existence of an entity through the non-perception of its own nature, given that the entity itself is not perceived?
When there is no possible cause for the non-perception of the visible object, || 205 ||
The non-existence of an entity is cognized when that entity is not perceived.

[This applies to] place. If the non-existence of a certain cause is established by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it is determined that its effect—the effect of that cause—does not exist.

This was stated with the intention of establishing the non-existence of a subject that has been specifically indicated (*uddiṣṭa-viṣaya*). However, regarding a subject that has not been specifically indicated (*anuddiṣṭa-viṣaya*), this is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it results from a logical connection (*pratibandha*).

[The passage beginning with] "svabhāva" and so forth [means]: by the non-existence of the object—that is, the pervader (*vyāpaka*)—within the indicator-bearer (*liṅgin*) whose nature is non-different [from it].
It was previously stated that the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) and the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) are means of proving non-existence.

[The author] explains this with the words beginning "the absence of essential nature" (*svabhāvābhāva*). The word "some" (*kaścit*) refers to the non-perception of the pervader. If the pervader were established as the essential nature of this pervaded while it is not being perceived, then it would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [This concerns] the cause (*kāraṇa*).

And the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) would be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) if the absence of those two—the cause and the pervader—were to be cognized by some reason known as the "non-apprehension of essential nature" (*svabhāvānupalambha*). With the words beginning with "yadi" (if), he states the meaning of the verse: "If the absence of this causal factor were established."

The connection [is as follows]: there is the absence of the pervading nature (*vyāpaka-svabhāva*). This is due to some indicative reason (*gamaka-hetu*), namely, non-perception of that which has met the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta-anupalambhāt*). Thus, this [reason], being either a producer (*kāraka*) or a pervader (*vyāpaka*), being established as non-existent, successively causes the cessation of the effect (*kārya*) and the pervaded (*vyāpya*). If its absence is not established, then when the absence of the producer or the pervader is not established, even if [the other] is to be negated—[this is the point regarding] the investigation of sound (*śabda-cintā*).

For if an entity were indeed perceived by its respective perceiver, it would necessarily be perceived when obstacles to seeing, such as screens and the like, are present. However, that which is not perceived is determined to be non-existent, because perception is never absent [when the object is present]. This same reason is to be understood to apply even in the case of the absence of a cause or a pervader.
Non-apprehension itself is non-existence;
for when a contradictory entity exists, it subverts the existence of that [other].
Upon the apprehension of what is contradictory to it, there occurs the ascertainment of its non-existence.
Because there is doubt regarding the effect and the pervaded.

(204-5) If it is argued that when the absence of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is to be proven, its non-perception alone is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then how is the non-existence of an entity such as a jar established through its own non-perception?

He states the reply: "Of the perceptible," and so forth. The meaning is that non-apprehension as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated regarding an object that is remote (*viprakṛṣṭa*) in its nature and so on, but not regarding an object that is perceptible. "Of the perceptible" refers to an entity (*bhāva*) that is not remote in its nature and so on, which, while existing, is not apprehended. The non-existence (*abhāva*) of the being (*sattā*) of that entity is cognized. When? When there is an absence of causes for the non-perception [of the entity].

The cause for the absence of perception is the deficiency of other causes; this means that when there is a completeness of all other conditions for apprehension (*upalambha-pratyaya*). The passage beginning with "for existence" (*bhāvo hi*) is an elaboration: if an entity were not remote from its own nature and so forth, as it is in its own case...

"By means of the apprehender as the instrument" means that whatever is the apprehender of a given object—that sense faculty—by means of it, that entity (bhāva) must necessarily be perceived, as has been stated. This is provided that there are no obstructions to its perception, such as "obstructions and so forth"; by the word "and so forth," deficiencies, impediments, and the like are included. That is to say, provided that the conditions for perception (*upalambha-pratyaya*) are present. (205.6)

Thus, that which is not perceived as it actually exists is determined to be non-existent. What is the reason? Because for such a thing—that is, for an existing entity that has reached the conditions for perceptibility—perception is invariable. This very reason should be understood as that which was stated [in the verse] beginning with "the perception of the visible" (*dṛśyasya darśana*) for the sake of determining the absence of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For what probandum (*sādhya*)?

"Even in the absence of the cause and the pervader, [there is certainty] regarding the probandum; and likewise in the case of the perception of that which is contradictory [to the probandum]," and so forth. When there is the perception of that which is contradictory to that whose absence constitutes the probandum, there would be the ascertainment of non-existence—that is, of the absence of the object to be negated. What is the reason? Because of the presence of a contradictory entity.

"Because its existence is sublated" means because the existence (*sattā*) of that which is intended to be negated is sublated. The phrase "For he who... and so forth is the explanation. To the question "Why does it not remain? he says: "Of those two," and so forth. This refers to being the locus of the mutual deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) between those two contradictory things when they are both adopted, as in the case of cold...

The meaning is that one [of the two] is the substratum for the deficiency of the hot material cause of the other, and vice versa. For that reason, two contradictory states do not coexist simultaneously; because there is a contradiction in their production when they serve as mutual substrata for deficiencies in their respective material causes. Even when one of those two contradictories exists, there is the absence of the other, as was stated previously.
Therefore, difference must be established by non-apprehension alone; for it is from that very [non-apprehension] that contradiction is understood, and from contradiction that non-existence is proven.
Let it be granted that the cognition of non-existence arises from such a non-apprehension. How could it not be so? [Consider] the example—

Because there is an absence of expectation; for in this [state], there is no existence whatsoever. If it is asked, "Why is it not like a sky-flower, which is called 'non-existent'?", that is not a valid example. How is it to be understood that "this is non-existent," such that it would be so? If it is by means of non-perception itself, then in that case as well, how can the proof of non-existence be established without an example? Or, if there were an example, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Likewise...

Because there is a contradiction in the simultaneous commencement of two [opposites] in one place; for even when one of those two opposites exists, there is the cognition of the absence of the other, as was stated previously regarding the divisions of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*): "There is no sensation of cold here because of fire," and so forth.

Although the term "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) is not explicitly heard here, nevertheless, this logical mark (*liṅga*) called "contradiction of essential nature" (*svabhāvaviruddha*) is not stated as something separate from non-apprehension. Why? Because the cognition of contradiction arises precisely from that non-apprehension, and it has been stated that the proof of absence proceeds from contradiction.
Let it be granted that the cognition of an entity arises from such a non-perception of the perceptible; however, how could that [cognition] not be inference?
It is not at all inference, but rather a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). This is the sense.
To the question "How could it not be so?", the Teacher [responds]:

"An example," and so forth, says the opponent. For inference depends upon an example because it possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). He states precisely this dependence on an example with the words "Not indeed... (*na hi*). "In this" refers to non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). "Why not? asks the Teacher (*ācārya*).

The opponent says "that," etc. That [refers to] things such as a sky-flower. How, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is it to be understood that they are non-existent, so that this might be the case—that there would be no example? If it is argued that "in that case," things such as sky-flowers are to be understood as non-existent through the very mark (*liṅga*) of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), then how can their non-existence be without an example—devoid of an illustration?

Success! Or, if there were an example, it would entail the fault of infinite regress; for in that case, one would have to posit yet another [example] for that one as well. And thus, while such an infinite regress exists, there is no comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*). Furthermore, since the fault of infinite regress arises regarding the example, therefore the establishment of the non-existence of an indefinable entity must be made without an example. Just so in other cases as well: "There is no jar here..."

The Master [Dharmakīrti] states, "Even though one hears it," because even in such formulations as "due to the non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension," there is no dependence on an example, non-apprehension is not an inference. This has been stated more than once; for instance, in the case of the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), it is not a non-existence.

"But it is established that there is the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of non-existence. Even while hearing this, the "beloved of the gods" (the fool) does not comprehend it; his lack of discernment and his reflection are non-understanding. Therefore, just as with the proof of the "indefinable" (*anupākhyasiddhi*), because there is no requirement for an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) elsewhere either, this is not an inference (*anumāna*).
Even while hearing this, the "beloved of the gods" is not intent on comprehension. [He fails to grasp] the cause (*nimitta*) of the conventional usages of words such as "existent" (*sat*).
Because it is accompanied by apprehension (*sopalabdhi*), every example here involves the presence of the conjunction of its own causes and conditions (*svanimitta-sāmagrī-yoga*).

Here, non-existence itself is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). For this very reason, since this is characterized as an inference of the effect from the cause, we shall explain that it is included within "inference based on its own cause" (*svahetu*).

Even when the linguistic convention of "existence" is negated, because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has ceased, sprouts and the like are also [negated] due to the deficiency of their cause. Thus, even though an example exists, its non-establishment is urged. He begins to demonstrate that very example with the words "For the cause... and so forth. The "perception of what is perceptible," which is the non-perception of the visible, is the cause—the reason—for non-existence.

[This refers to] the linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*). "That" means non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*); by its own presence—that is, by the presence of itself—it establishes these linguistic conventions of non-existence, which have as their cause that very non-apprehension. This being so, it serves as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) in all cases. Of what nature is it? It is one whose presence is capable of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of its own causes; that is, the causal complex of its own [constituent] causes.

That for which there is a suitable presence in that [locus], such as a sprout and so forth, is what is thus described. Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever has its entire causal complex (*nimitta*) present without obstruction must exist there, just like a sprout and so forth. And the state of being the cause for the conventional usage of non-existence regarding things that have reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is present in the case of non-perception; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Why is it that here only the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of non-existence is established, and not non-existence itself? He says: "Non-existence," and so forth.

Here, in the case of the non-perception of the perceptible, non-perception itself is existence, as was stated previously. Therefore, non-existence is not being established. Precisely because the conventional usage of non-existence is established here, this non-perception is [established] by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*).

The connection is that [it] is included within the reason (*hetu*). Having first indicated the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) in a general sense—as "that which has as its defining characteristic the inference of the conventional non-existence of an effect from the non-perception of a perceptible cause"—the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is subsequently applied.
Furthermore, since the inference of an effect from a complete cause is an inference of capacity (*yogyatā*), it is included within the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
We shall explain this in the fourth chapter.

[The opponent asks: "Let there be an example for the non-perception of what is perceptible; but how can there be one for the non-perception of what is imperceptible? To this he says: "In the case of the word 'existent,' etc. When the negation of the conventional usage of "existent" is to be proven regarding objects remote in space and so forth by means of the cessation of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [there is no example] because of the absence of a cause.

The non-existence of the effect is what is to be proven; therefore, in this context, the example is not only that which is "indefinable" (*nirupākhya*), but also sprouts and the like, which do not exist due to the deficiency of their efficient and material causes. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: (1) Whatever has its causes deficient does not come into being, just as a sprout devoid of a seed; and in the case of the non-perception of the perceptible, the practical usage of existence is likewise deficient in its causes.

This is the non-perception of a cause. Furthermore, as for what was said: "How is that which is non-existent and indefinable to be apprehended?"—in that case too, with respect to the example of the indefinable (*nirupākhya*), this activity characterized by the conventional usage of ignorance is prohibited; it is not [prohibited] on account of non-perception.

The existence [of the object] is being established. What is the reason? [It is] because of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), and so forth. The example is a rabbit’s head as distinct from horns and the like. For it is not merely something devoid of any designation (*nirupākhya*). Even regarding that which is devoid of designation, this very [conceptual] activity is what is negated.

The non-existence of that which is characterized by non-apprehension is established. Having accepted the absence of a cause, one who subverts both engagement and withdrawal [from activity] establishes there—according to what has been accepted—that which is indefinable or something else.
Non-apprehension is simply the apprehension of a head and so forth, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*). That very thing is the characteristic of the "hare's horn" [and the like].
Non-existence is indeed established by that [non-perception].

It might be argued: (1) when non-existence has been established as the object in the case of the non-perception of the imperceptible, the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of "non-existent" based on that [establishment] is also already established; so what is the use of this linguistic usage of "non-existent"? [For] even in the case of the non-perception of the imperceptible, there is the linguistic usage of "existent"...

Since the absence of the cause for verbal designation (*hāranimitta*) entails that linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) does not occur, this is already established; therefore, what is the point of proving it even by means of the negation of the usage of "existent"?

Likewise, there is nothing further to be gained regarding non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) even by means of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) characterized by the presentation of a previously established object.

To state the purpose [of this], he says: "This very [thing]," and so forth. That is to say, this is established for the sake of one who is deluded. Having accepted non-apprehension of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) as the cause for the conventional usage of "non-existent" in some cases, [the opponent] acts contrary to the engagement in that conventional usage of "non-existent"—that is, he fails to do so. Furthermore, regarding the non-apprehension of the imperceptible (*adṛśyānupalabdhi*), [he denies] its absence, which is the cause for the conventional usage of "existent" and is [established by] valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Having accepted its non-existence and yet contradicting the cessation of the conventional usage of "existent" by not acting accordingly, you are being made to understand that it must be established in accordance with what has been accepted.
