Since the conventional usage of "non-existent" was applied elsewhere by you on the basis of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), that same [basis] exists here as well; therefore, you are being made to understand: "Perform the conventional usage of 'non-existent'. Likewise, by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as the basis, you...

In some cases, the conventional usage of "existent" is established; therefore, it is also not [established] here in the case of the indefinable (*anirupākhyam*). Consequently, it is demonstrated that one should not engage in the conventional usage of "existent. How so? Like the indefinable. Just as the conventional usage of "non-existent" occurs in the case of a rabbit's horn and the like because of the presence of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), which is the cause for the usage of "non-existent," so it is here as well.

"Or otherwise": just as the very cognition of a sprout and so forth when their causes are present constitutes the linguistic usage of "existence," and just as the cessation of the linguistic usage of "existence" occurs in the case of the indefinable (*nirupākhya*) due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
or as there is a cessation of the effect in another case where the cause is deficient— so too, in the case of remote objects, there is a cessation of the linguistic usage of "existence."

Thus it is established. First of all, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that very non-apprehension called "non-perception" (*anupalabdhi*), which is the absence of apprehension, established?

(1) It is not by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because there is a contradiction in [perception] having absence as its object. Nor is it by inference (*anumāna*), because the latter is preceded by direct perception. Nor...

Uddyotakara and others maintain that non-apprehension of a connection with a location cannot serve as a reason for non-existence, because non-existence, being devoid of form (*nīrūpa*), cannot possess the status of being related. Furthermore, if the location itself is not apprehended, the property (*dharma*) [of non-existence] cannot be established, rendering the reason one whose locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*); thus, non-apprehension does not possess the characteristic of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharman*).

To this, he says: "We shall explain this later. [The opponent asks: "In that case, since there is a perception qualified by that [non-existence], how is its non-perception established? We shall explain this later as well.

Furthermore, even in other forms of inference, when one intends to establish a pervading property (*vyāpaka*) as the probandum (*sādhya-dharma*), why should the positive entity itself be what is made known?
Because the pervader is established simply by the mention of the pervaded;

and if it is argued that the purpose of the example is for the sake of recollection even for one who has already ascertained the relationship between the meanings, then this is equally applicable here as well.
Thus, this conceptualization of the conventional usage of "power" (*prabhāva*) based on mere non-perception elsewhere is intended here to produce a memory for the sake of the deluded.

And how is it that [one says], "Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) and the like do not exist because they are not perceived"? In that case, how could the establishment of the conventional usage of "power" be possible?

How could there be a negation of the conventional usage of "existence"? For if that object [existence] were negated, the term denoting the substratum (dharmin) would not be employed, and a negation without an object is impossible. Therefore, this non-perception is established by perception itself. As for what was further stated regarding non-perception, what is the example?

He says, "By perception," and so forth, including "even elsewhere" and so on. Even in an inference that establishes a positive proof (*vidhisādhana*), why must the person to be convinced be made to understand by means of an example the probans—such as "being produced"—which is pervaded by the pervading property that is the probandum?
For what reason? Because the pervading probandum-property is understood from the very indication of the reason (*hetu*) which is pervaded by its respective probandum.

[This is] because of its establishment. For one who possesses a certain knowledge of the object characterized by the relation, [the statement] serves the purpose of a reminder for someone who is confused.

This very production of a reminder for a confused person regarding this non-apprehension is illustrated by the example. He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "This is that," and so forth. "In other cases as well" refers to things such as a hare's horn. (205–6)

Now, regarding that which was stated by Ācārya Diṅnāga and others—"Primal Matter (pradhāna) and so forth do not exist because they are not perceived"—in that formal argument, the Teacher (Ācārya) asks: "And how could it not be so? The opponent states his own intention with the words beginning "tadartha... (for the sake of that). This means: when there is a negation of its object, namely the object that is Primal Matter...

Because there is no employment of a designation that expresses properties such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and so forth; for there is no employment of a denoter in the absence of a denoted object. And when words such as *pradhāna* are not employed, then only the word expressing the negation remains, namely "they do not exist. Furthermore, if the objects of negation are not mentioned, that negation would be without an objective referent (*nirviṣaya*).

Because there is no employment of a word expressing negation; and thus, since neither of the two members of the proposition—namely, "the Pradhāna and so forth do not exist"—is employed, where and what would be proven? Therefore, the application of a means of proof is futile, as it is unperceived. Furthermore, because the Pradhāna and so forth, which constitute the subject (*pakṣa*), are non-existent, the logical reason (*hetu*) would have to be a property of that non-existent subject. Or else, [it would apply] to the two members of the proposition... [the opponent].

Furthermore, there is a contradiction: for instance, from the usage "the primal matter (pradhāna) and so forth," there is the presence of those objects; yet, from the statement "they do not exist," there is their absence. And these two—presence and absence—are contradictory when occurring simultaneously in one and the same place.
¹Run. bahi-phyir. (Because it is external.)
This is not a fault; for it is thus:
"It is established by conceptual constructions arising from the non-abiding [state]. (207)
The object denoted by a word is a threefold subject (dharmin) based on existence, non-existence, or both.
When that [subject] is to be proven as not being the basis for existence, its non-apprehension [serves as the reason]. (208)

Thus, the reason is not the non-existence of that very [particular] because of the employment of words. It has already been explained how these words do not have the particular (svalakṣaṇa) as their object; rather, they appropriate as their own object the thing appearing in a conceptual construction (vikalpa) produced by beginningless latencies (vāsanā).

For both the speaker, who possesses that conceptualization, and the listener, it is possible to determine that the object appears as such through the application of the means of communication intended to convey the object,
because it generates a conceptualization having that form.
However, it cannot be determined as such by virtue of being an object appearing in the form of a material cause (*upādāna*) or an effect-cognition (*kāryapratyaya*).

"This is not a fault," is the rebuttal. Because the meaning of a word (*śabdārtha*) is established and mounted upon a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises from beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and because it is a threefold property (*dharma*) since it rests upon existence, non-existence, and both;
in that case, when it is to be proven that the word has "non-existence as its material cause" (*bhāvānupādāna*), meaning that external [objects] such as *pradhāna* are not its material cause.

"Of this" refers to the subject (*dharmin*) such as *pradhāna* and so forth, which circulates within the intellect. "In that way" means that non-perception is the logical reason (*hetu*) for its not being perceived as having an external *pradhāna* or similar entity as its material cause (*upādāna*). Here, non-perception consists precisely in its being perceived as having mental impressions (*vāsanā*) as its material cause. It is not the non-existence of that very subject established by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that is being proven. Why? Because [the term] "pradhāna" and so forth...

[This is] from the perspective of linguistic usage (*prayoga*). For if that [particular] were negated, there would be no linguistic usage at all, because [the word] would lack an object. He explains this with the words "it has been explained" (*niveditam*), and so forth. For if the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) were the denotable object, then upon the negation of the particular, the referent of the word would be negated, and consequently, the word expressing it could not be used. However, as has been explained—

This is how these words do not have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object; rather, they appropriate as their object that thing which appears in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) whose origin or production is from beginningless mental impressions (*anādivāsanā*). Why is it that they take as their object only that thing which is the domain of conceptual construction? He says: "Because the speaker possesses that conceptual construction."
Thus, he states the cause for those who possess conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that take on a general form (*sāmānyākāra*) based on existence, non-existence, or both: "Just as," and so forth.

Because words are employed through the desire to communicate in accordance with the object as it appears—that is, without overstepping the appearing object—therefore, words take as their objects only those things that appear within conceptual construction.

Likewise, the connection is that [words] also possess those conceptual constructions of the listener. What is the reason? Because they generate conceptual constructions having that form. And because they generate conceptual constructions of a general form based on existence, non-existence, or both, words take as their objects only those things that appear within conceptual construction.

It might be argued: "Even if that were so, why is it that words do not have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object, given that there is a cognition of the particular characteristic? To this he says: "And not... and so forth. "Appropriation" (*upādāna*) and "effect" (*kārya*)—these two are the conditions (*pratyaya*), that is, the cognitions; therein [lies] the investigation of words (*śabda-cintā*).

That conceptual construction, however, is said to have existence as its nature because it arises from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by cognitions of the forms of the existent, the non-existent, and both, and because it functions through the determination of the form appearing therein.

Therefore, having taken that subject (dharmin) as the basis here, how could they deliberate upon its existence or non-existence— thinking that this object appearing from the word "pradhāna" is not based on a real entity? When its lack of being based on a real entity is to be proven, that very [subject] is not to be rejected, because it is personally experienced by each individual.

Nor can it be said that this [cognition] itself is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). For when an object has not yet been reached or has already ceased, its form—which does not appear [to the cognition]—cannot be determined as being the object of that [cognition]. In this context, the "appropriating condition" (*upādāna-pratyaya*) is the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consisting of the speaker’s desire to communicate, because it is the cause of the word. The "resultant condition" (*kārya-pratyaya*) is that which arises from the word.

The conceptual construction belongs to the hearer. For that which does not appear in the cognition of a word is not the meaning of the word; nor does the particular (svalakṣaṇa) appear therein, because it is devoid of a clear form.
But how [can it be so], since the absence of conceptual construction would follow from its being produced by an object, given that it rests upon the absence of conceptual construction? How...

Nor can non-existence be the basis [of conceptualization], because non-existence is not a cause. Furthermore, how could a single thing be the basis for both, given the consequence that it would be without a cause?
To this, he says: "But that... and so forth. Conceptualization has the form of existence, non-existence, or both; it is the cognition of existence, non-existence, or both.
The latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) deposited by that [cognition] is its source—that is, its origin—and thus it is so described. For this reason, [it arises from] existence and non-existence.
It is called the "nature of fear.

He states the second reason: "In that," and so forth. The determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the aspect (*ākāra*) appearing in that very conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as being existent, non-existent, or both, and by virtue of that [determination], it is called the "nature of existence, non-existence, or both."

This is what is meant: a mental state (*bhāva-dharma*) is said to be "determined" (*adhyavasāyin*) as having the form of existence because it arises from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by previous cognitions of existence. The same should be understood for the two [other] categories, non-existence and both.

Precisely because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "existent" and so forth arise from latent impressions deposited by successive prior cognitions of existence and so on, they are beginningless (*anādi*). Therefore, they are not produced by external entities (*bhāva*) and the like.

Since the referent of a word (*śabdārtha*) is threefold, for that reason, persons established upon this referent as the locus (*dharmin*)—standing as the basis of dispute—contemplate the existence or non-existence of *pradhāna* and so forth. How do they contemplate? He says:
"Is this object, which appears in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) following the utterance of the word 'pradhāna,' based upon an external *pradhāna*?"

Whether [it] exists or not: if that appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pratibhāsa*), such as the primary cause (*pradhāna*) and so forth, has existence as its material cause (*upādāna*), then when "existence" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), that very appearance of conceptual construction is the subject (*dharmin*) for the purpose of non-rejection; this is because it is of the nature of cognition (*buddhi-svabhāva*), is personally experienced (*pratyātmavedya*), and is established by self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*).
[Objection: But surely that very object appearing in conceptual construction is the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it is determined as having the nature of a particular.

And therefore, [it follows that] *pradhāna* and so forth are established by perception, and words also have the particular as their object. [Reply: To this he says, "And not that very [object]," and so on. It cannot be said that that very object appearing in conceptual construction is an external particular. Why?
Because they exist in regard to things through an adherence to erroneous forms, as well as in regard to the cognitions of those belonging to other schools;
[therefore], when there is a single-pointed focus on the ultimate reality, words are without a basis. (209)

There would be no engagement with objects that differ according to various philosophical systems, nor with those that are past or yet to be born; furthermore, there would be no falsity regarding the object. (210)
"Of whatever speech"—this [statement] is considered to have as its object a conceptualized entity (*bauddhārtha*).
Thus [end] the summary verses.

And just as in that case, when it is to be proven that the intended form is not apprehended, so too here, because of the property of non-apprehension (*anupalambhadharmatva*), it is not [the case that...].

This is the non-establishment of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). However, it is not that the object appearing as a reflection in the word (*śabdapratibhāsyartha*) is denied here; for the word is employed precisely to present that [object] to the intellect, since it would be impossible [to employ the word] in its absence.

Furthermore, the cause [is as follows]: because that appearance of conceptual construction does not cease even when its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has not been reached, has not yet arisen, or has already ceased. Moreover, regarding an object such as a jar, there are contradictory aspects, such as permanence and impermanence, which are mutually exclusive.

Those who have the habit of adhering to those [entities]—namely, the proponents of other systems (*tīrthāntarīya*)—possess such dispositions; it is because of their existence that there is the appearance of objects as words.
And that very object is not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); this is the connection with the subject at hand. (209–10) Words are without a basis.

To summarize this very point, he says: "The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); that which has its activity situated in a single location therein is the state of being such (*tattva*).
When that exists, [conceptions] are devoid of a basis in ultimate reality."
There would be no application [of words] to objects that differ according to other systems of philosophy (*darśanāntara*), nor to objects distinguished by differences in tenets (*siddhāntabheda*).

Furthermore, there would be no application of words to past and future things; likewise, for some speech, there would be neither truthfulness regarding actual facts (*bhūtārthatā*) nor falsity. Therefore, for the reasons stated above, this speech has as its object a conceptual entity (*bauddhārtha*).
The object appearing in conceptual construction is considered the [actual] object.

(210–11) "Of that" refers to the appearance in conceptual construction such as [the notion of] *pradhāna* and so forth. "A form corresponding to what is intended" means a form such as an external *pradhāna* as it has been imagined; this is when it is to be proven that it lacks such a basis (*anupādānatva*). "Non-perception in that manner" means as it was intended...

The meaning is that, since non-apprehension exists by virtue of its being the appropriation of a beneficial form, there is no failure to establish the property of the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*), nor is the reason (*hetu*) a non-property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*).
Furthermore, in this formal argument (*prayoga*), it is not the case that "this very sound," and so forth; rather, it refers to the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which arises from the sound.
The meaning of the statement is refuted. What is the reason? (1) Because that object appearing in conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pratibhāsy-artha*) is established in the mind of the listener;

[this is] the investigation of words (*śabda-cintā*). [Note: The Tibetan fragments provided—"bsgrub-par-bya-bahi-chos" (the property to be proven), "bskyed-pahi-phyir" (because of being produced)—are integrated into the logical structure of the Sanskrit sentence.]
When the negation of the word and its object is to be proven, the substratum of the property is thereby rejected. || 211 ||
The composite whole would not be the object of proof, nor would the property alone be established;

for if the substratum—the subject (*dharmin*) expressed by the principal term—were rejected through the denial of the very meaning of the word, there would be an absence of a locus for the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*). Therefore, this [subject], which does not depend on the exclusion of its own substratum, is not the point of contention.
It is certainly not even to be proposed; moreover: "By those who do not deny the referents of words, through the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence," [212]
Only that entity is investigated upon which the arising of the fruit depends;
for those who seek it, what is the use of investigations into that which lacks the capacity for causal efficiency? (213)
What is the use of examining whether a eunuch is handsome or ugly?

For an unreal object of a word does not obstruct any human goal, nor does a real one accomplish it; for [the former] lacks reality according to one's attachment, while [the latter] lacks stability according to the true nature of things.

Because the word is employed for the purpose of establishing [the object]; "in its absence" means in the absence of an object appearing as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); "because that is impossible" means because the employment of the word would be impossible.
Furthermore, if the negation of the word's object were being proven, then, when the negation of the word's object is the probandum (*sādhya*),...
Since the substratum (dharmin) characterized as the referent of the word— the locus of that property to be proven (sādhyadharma), namely non-existence— is negated,

the composite consisting of both the property and the substratum could not be the object of proof (sādhya). Furthermore, the property to be proven alone would already be established, because mere non-existence is established in some cases.

The passage beginning with "yadi" is an explanation. "Tat" means therefore this property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is independent of that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*)—which is a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) by the locus (*ādhāra*) consisting of its non-existence. For this reason, it should not be introduced at all during the time of debate. By the distinction between existent and non-existent positions—that is, by the distinction between existent and non-existent theses—it is considered as a substance alone by those who do not deny the referent of words.

By those who seek the performance of a chariot and are discerning [people], because the arising of the result is bound to this entity (vastu). Even if that were so, why should the meaning of words not be investigated? To this he says: "The meaning," and so forth.

What is the purpose for seekers of results in investigating the meaning of words—that is, in investigations as to whether it exists or does not exist—which is incapable of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*)? (1402)

He provides an illustration for those seeking action, beginning with "of a eunuch" (*ṣaṇḍhasya*), and so forth. For one who lacks masculinity, what is the point of examining the beauty or ugliness of form in that regard, since he is a woman desiring sexual union?
(213–14) The explanation begins with "for not," and so on: for a non-existent meaning of a word does not obstruct or prevent any human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
The word *yati* [should be understood] as "he composes" or "he performs," to be connected accordingly. What is the reason?
Because a person adheres to—that is, determines—that object of a word as being external in accordance with his attachment;
therefore, this [cognition], proceeding in that manner, always disregards the appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) when investigating existence and non-existence.
That very object upon which this human purpose depends without regard for anything else is made the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

For example, in the case of "the warding off of cold by fire," there is no power of the word's meaning (*śabdārtha-śakti*) [to produce that result] here; for even when that experience is attained, [the purpose] is absent. This, then, is the meaning:

It is not appropriate for one who seeks a result to apply critical inquiry toward that which is incapable of producing it; for a woman in heat does not concern herself with examining the beauty or ugliness of a eunuch.
(dha) Non-perception of the imagined.

Furthermore, as for that which was stated—that a phenomenon (dharma) is an object of non-perception through investigation—it is conceptually constructed by virtue of being an object of conceptual cognition regarding the referent of a word. (214)

The proponent of logic has stated that for this [property], there is the non-establishment of its locus in reality (*vastu*). Because it is an object of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the referent of the word is itself merely imagined. For his intention is that it is a property (*dharma*) because no locus in reality is perceived for it.
Because it exists [as a conceptual construct] yet is non-existent [in reality], or because it is intended according to its true nature;
for the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—whether that of the object or of cognition—as it actually exists, is not made an object by the word.
Since this is so, this person, when engaging in the investigation of existence and non-existence, always disregards conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Appearance (*bhāsa*), which disregards the manifestation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), takes the real thing (*vastu*) itself as its basis and makes it its object—that real thing in which this human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) is bound up. "In fire" means in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire; by the inclusion of the word "etc.," burning, cooking, and so forth are meant.

It might be argued that such a purpose is also accomplished by the object of a word; to this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth. "In this context" refers to the warding off of cold and the like. Why? Because even when there is the attainment of the experience of that [word-object], there is an absence of that [purpose]. That is, even when there is the attainment of the experience of that word-object, there is an absence of that [result], such as the remedy for cold. Therefore, this person is one who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

It is not appropriate for one who intends to engage with a word-meaning that is incapable of performing that [intended] purposeful action to apply focused attention to it. For a woman desiring sexual union does not, even if she is attentive, fix her attention on examining the beauty or ugliness of a eunuch who is incapable of engaging in intercourse.

The author asks [the following] in order to refute the objections raised by others: "As for that which was stated by the teacher Dignāga, 'of that which is imagined,' etc.—what is the meaning of this? He provides the answer:
"The object of a word," etc. Because it is the object of conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*), the object of a word—such as *pradhāna* and so forth—is [as follows].

The meaning of the word: By resorting to a conceptualized external object characterized as "primordial matter" (*pradhāna*), the non-establishment—that is, the non-apprehension—of this referent of words such as "primordial matter" is stated by the Master Dignāga, the author of the *Nyāyamukha*, as a property (*dharma*) serving as a logical mark (*liṅga*), when it is to be proven that [the word] does not have existence as its material cause (*bhāvānupādānatva*). 6. Examination of Scripture (*Āgamacintā*).
6. Consideration of Scripture (Āgama):

As for what was stated—that even upon the cessation of the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the non-existence of an entity is not established—that would not apply to the cessation of other means of valid cognition, because those two [the remaining two] lack the capacity to encompass all objects. It does not pervade anything...

[One] attains [it]. If it is argued that its cessation is like [the word] "gamika" [which does not function as a verb], it has already been stated here that in the Āgamas there is no application to all objects, because it does not fall within the relevant context. Moreover:
Because there is no necessary connection between words and real entities. (215)
In that case, there is no establishment of the object, for words indicate the intention of the speaker;

indeed, the application of words does not occur according to the actual state of things, whereby the nature of the object could be determined from them. This is what was stated by Uddyotakara and others: "If the Primal Matter (pradhāna) is postulated as existing by means of a valid means of cognition..."
How can its property of non-apprehension be understood? If it is conceived as non-existent, even so, how can its property of non-apprehension be established, given that it is non-existent?
That is refuted because, since it is an object of conceptual cognition, it is merely a conceptualized meaning of a word; it is not [ultimately real].

By means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the external *pradhāna* is conceptualized as existing; [the phrase] "of that" refers to the fact that the referent of the word *pradhāna* is not found to be based upon an external *pradhāna*-entity. This is the intention of the teacher Dignāga. (214–15) As for the words "what was said," etc., the opponent [states]: the three types of valid cognition characterized by perception, inference, and scripture; other valid cognitions...

"In their cessation" means in the cessation of perception and inference; "cessation" refers to [the non-perception] of things remote in space and so forth. "Of those two" refers to perception and inference.
"It does not pervade anything" means it takes everything as its object. "The cessation of that" is the cessation of scripture (āgama).

"It has been stated here" refers to the Siddhānta-dīpa. "Because it does not fall within the context" means because it is not applicable to the introduction of the inquiry into the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). This is because it was stated in the intervening passage (1.201) that "many matters are unrelated to the scope of the treatise."
This was stated while accepting the authority of scripture (*āgama*) regarding external objects;

now, [the author] says "Moreover," etc., to show that there is no authority for external objects at all. Because there is no necessary connection (*avinābhāva*), that is, no inseparable relation, between words and real entities (*vastu*)—namely, particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)—no cognition of those [entities] can be established from those words.

There is certainty regarding external objects because those [sounds] indeed indicate the speaker’s intention. Even though a word such as "cloth" may arise from the desire to speak of a "jar," it nonetheless arises directly from the impact of the articulatory places and organs; thus, since there is no deviation in its production, it is not causeless. And that which is produced by the desire to speak of a jar—

One perceives the word "jar. From that [perception], there is an inference of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) regarding a cloth based on the word "cloth"; and such perception [of the word] and inference of the intention certainly exist for people through context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth. Thus, there is indeed no deviation (*avyabhicāra*) in the inference of the intention.

Because they reside in the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), they would be indicators by virtue of being invariably concomitant with that very intention. If every object desired by a person were not of such a nature [i.e., not residing in his intention], then for that which does not have its own nature dependent on it, nothing else could be an indicator.
Thus, it has been stated that scripture is indeed inference, based on the commonality of being a report of what has been attained and being non-discrepant (*avisamvāda*).

If it is asked how that is so: this person is not capable of acting without relying on the authority of scripture (*āgama*). This is because one hears of great benefits and sins resulting from engagement and withdrawal, which have perceptible fruits, and because no contradiction is observed in their absence.

Therefore, since one must indeed act when there is something to be done, he asserts its authority through such an investigation, thinking, "I have acted in this manner. And that [authority] is as follows:

"According to the state of being" (*yathābhāvam*) means according to its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇam*). "From which" (*yataḥ*) means that from the occurrence [of words] according to the state of being, the nature of the object—the intrinsic essence of the meaning—would be determined by means of words. "Those" refers to the words. They are so described because their occurrence is due to the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*). "Inseparable from it" means inseparable from that very intention to speak. That very intention to speak is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

It does not exist without [a connection]; therefore, he says that there is indeed an non-deviation of words from their objects, beginning with "And not... Those whose nature it is to exist in accordance with the object—that is, in accordance with the thing—are so described. He says that for one whose defects are exhausted and who is compassionate, all [words] exist in accordance with the object. If it is argued that even a word not bound to an object will cause the object to be understood, he says: "No."
And so forth. That linguistic characteristic (*śabdalakṣaṇa*) whose nature is not restricted to that [external] object— namely, that to which it is not restricted—
if there were no validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the word regarding the external object, then this non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*) of the speech of a reliable person (*āptavāda*)...

By way of generality: whatever is the word of an authoritative person (*āptavāda*) is non-discrepant (*avisamvādī*), such as the statement, "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary," and so forth.
And since this [word] regarding even an extremely imperceptible object is the word of an authoritative person, it too is non-discrepant; thus [is established] the authoritative person.

Because the treatise (*vāda*) possesses the common quality of non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*), it is an inference (*anumāna*) due to its being non-discrepant; thus, the Teacher Dignāga stated that scripture (*āgama*) is an inference with respect to external objects. How is that so? By this [phrase], he states the contradiction of what has been accepted (*abhyupetabādhā*). He refutes it with the words beginning "This is not... and so forth. How is this...

The author [Yati] does not state that scripture possesses intrinsic validity (*bhāvikam prāmāṇyam*) and is therefore a form of inference; rather, he speaks with respect to human activity. For this person, desiring to act, is not capable of acting without relying on the validity of scripture. Why is this? Because for some people who possess results that are either perceptible or imperceptible, there is the cessation of activity...

The word "of these two" (*tyoḥ*) is to be connected as appropriate: because it is heard in scripture that the cessation of intentional acts such as violence toward objects of cognition results in great benefits, such as heaven; whereas the engagement in specific intentional acts of violence results in great sins, such as hell. Furthermore, there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operating by the force of the nature of things (*vastubala*) that could establish this independently of scripture.
The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) proceeds;

nor is there any subverting factor (bādhaka) by which it might be turned back. He states precisely the absence of such a subverting factor: "In the existence of that," meaning that since no contradiction is observed in the occurrence of desired or undesired results through the aforementioned engagement and withdrawal, one acts according to one's desire.
And this [scripture] proceeds by the force of tradition; therefore, when it is appropriate to proceed, one should do so.
6. An investigation of scripture: that which is connected, provides a suitable means, and expresses the goals of human endeavor. (216)

A statement subject to examination is indeed a connection, for the utility of sentences lies in their convergence upon a single meaning; otherwise, it would reveal the deficiency of the speaker. Like the "ten pomegranates" and so forth, it would be entirely incoherent. Treatises whose fruits and means are impossible [to achieve] are likewise useless.

For one who desires a result would not care to investigate that which has results not conducive to human goals, such as the instruction to use the crest-jewel of Takṣaka for the purpose of neutralizing poison, or like an examination of a crow’s teeth. On the contrary, it is a treatise that possesses a feasible means and speaks of human goals that is investigated, as is the case with the concluding summary.

Because it is simply unreasonable to disregard [the scripture] otherwise. When examining that [scripture], if it is found to be non-contradictory, it is better to act after having thus examined the scripture; for this reason, the Master [Dignāga] stated that the authority of scripture is established through examination.

Furthermore, not every treatise (*śāstra*) is subject to such examination; rather, it is that treatise which [begins with] "And that... and so forth, concerning the mutual [relationships] of categories (*padārtha*).

"Connected" means being related [to a human goal]. "Having a suitable means" refers to that [treatise] in which the means for accomplishing the result is capable of being realized; thus, "connected and having a suitable means" is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). Even if it is such [a treatise], if it expresses a human goal, then that statement is subject to critical examination (*parīkṣā*). Therefore, any other statement than one possessing the aforementioned nature—

Having established this in the examination, he explains it with the words "connection" (*sambandha*) and so forth. The connection between sentences is their mutual assistance through their integration—by way of the relationship of subordinate and principal—with respect to a single object characterized as either something to be enjoined or something to be prohibited. This integration (*upasaṃhāra*) consists of their being brought together (*mīlana*). Anu-...

Regarding the benefactor (*pakāraka*), he asks: "Of what [is he the benefactor]? and says: "Ten pomegranates," and so forth—namely, the sentences beginning with "ten pomegranates, six cakes, a skull, a deer-skin, minced meat," and so on. For there is no unification of meaning among these, because they lack mutual connection. Since they are meaningless and disconnected, it constitutes a deficiency in the speaker or the author of the treatise, as the [sentences] are incoherent.

One should clearly manifest the state of being expressible. Those [treatises] for which the means are impossible are "those whose means are impossible. Those treatises for which the fruits are of such a nature—fruits that are infinite and have impossible means—a person seeking those fruits would not care to investigate them.
This is the explanation by way of contrast (*vaidharmya*) for the phrase "possessing a compatible means" (*anuguṇopāya*).

Those treatises for which the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is the fruit are described as such; others than those have fruits other than the human goal. One should not take the trouble to investigate them.
An example of that which has an impossible means or fruit is "poison," and so forth. For instance, his poison is pacified only if—

"The ornament is made with a jewel placed on the ear of Takṣaka, the king of nāgas"— this is an impossible undertaking. It is an example of that which does not result in a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), like the examination of a crow's teeth.

By the opposite of that—that is, by the reverse of those three aforementioned [factors]—it is like a summary. By this, the term "connected" (*sambaddha*) is explained; and by the term "feasible means" (*śakyopāya*), the "concordant means" (*anuguṇopāya*) is explained. Elsewhere, one who proceeds with connection and so forth appears beautiful. 2.
What, then, is its non-contradiction? It is the absence of sublation by both types of valid cognition: perception and inference. (217)

The non-contradiction of this [scripture] regarding both seen and unseen objects is the fact that those objects intended as perceived exist in that very way, which constitutes their non-sublation by perception—

just as in the case of cognitions such as blue and so forth, pleasure and pain, the apprehension of their causes, and attachment and so forth; whereas for those [cognitions] that do not exist in that way...

And there is non-perceptibility, as in the case of pleasure and so forth which are manifested in the form of sound and other [sensory objects], just like substance, action, generality, and so on. Likewise, it would be so for those things intended as the objects of inference that do not depend upon scripture (*āgama*), just as in the case of the four [truths] being devoid of the three [times]. "Attention" (*avadhāna*) means respect (*ādara*). "That" refers to the treatise (*śāstra*) endowed with the three aforementioned qualities.
When there is investigation, it does not become subject to contradiction. A person who applies himself to that scripture which is free from contradiction shines forth.
But what is the non-contradiction of this scripture? He says: "By means of direct perception," and so forth; the first word [of the verse] is *arthaḥ* (the object).

The first [term] refers to the object (*vastu*); the second refers to the domain (*viṣaya*). Therefore, the meaning is as follows: the non-contradiction of this treatise is its lack of sublation—respectively by means of perception and inference, both of which function through the power of real entities (*vastubala-pravṛtta*), and that which relies on scripture (*āgama-āśrita*)—with respect to the two kinds of objects, seen and unseen, which are the respective domains of perception and inference. (216–17)

He explains [the passage] beginning with "pratyakṣa" (perception). In the treatise, the "being such" (*tathābhāva*) of those objects accepted as perception—that is, their status as perception—is the non-sublation by perception.

With the words "yathā" (for example) and so forth, he shows that, according to his own established doctrine, the object accepted as perception is comprised within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

By the phrase "blue and so forth," he refers to the five objects, such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest; by this, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is stated. "Pleasure and pain" refers to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*). "The discernment of signs" (*nimittopalakṣaṇa*) means the perception of signs, such as the characteristics of male and female; by this, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*) is indicated. By the mention of "attachment and so forth," the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is indicated. From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the other afflictions are understood].

The inclusion of hatred, delusion, and so forth [is implied]. By the mention of "intellection" (*buddhi*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is meant. The compound consists of: blue and so forth, pleasure and pain, the apprehension of signs, passion and so forth, and intellection. Thus, according to the treatise, those things considered to be perceptible are indeed perceptible; for blue and so forth are perceptible by visual consciousness and the like, while pleasure and so forth are [perceptible] through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

Because it is perceptible. The connection with the subject at hand is as follows: the non-perceptibility of those objects that are not intended to be such, and of those objects intended to be imperceptible, is determined by perception. The word "yathā" (just as) serves to indicate the object of comparison. It refers to the non-perceptibility of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, which have the nature of being disposed in the form of sound and other [sensory qualities]. [This applies to] pleasure, pain, and so on, whose intrinsic nature consists of sound and the rest.

Because delusions are not perceived through direct perception, this was stated as a refutation of the Sāṃkhya system. As a refutation of the Vaiśeṣika and other systems, he says: substance is of two kinds: substance without constituent parts (*adravya-dravya*), such as space (*ākāśa*)—this is the investigation of scripture (*āgama*).

The Noble Truths. Their suchness is not to be inferred, just as that of the self and so forth. Even inference depends upon scripture; for, having accepted that desire and the like exist and arise from those [truths], there would be no instruction on bathing, fire-sacrifices, and so forth for the sake of abandoning them.
This is the purity—that is, the non-contradiction—of the entire object consisting of the determination of sound.
Because it shares the common quality of being non-contradictory with the speech of a reliable person, it possesses the nature of inference. (218)

Because it is impossible for the intellect (*buddhi*) to function otherwise even regarding an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), this very destruction of defects—which is of such a nature—is established through its general non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*), despite the fact that deviation has been observed in cases such as [the perception of] fire and so forth.

Furthermore, substance (*dravya*) is that which consists of multiple substances, such as a composite substance (*avayavidravya*). Action (*karman*) is [motion] such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth. Generality (*sāmānya*)...
Existence (*sattā*), cowness (*gotva*), and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including [qualities such as] disjunction (*vibhāga*) and the like.

For there is no perceptibility of anything else apart from the five [categories] such as blue and so on, because nothing is perceived apart from them. Inference proceeding by the force of real entities (*vastubalapravṛtta-anumāna*) is inference that does not depend on scripture (*āgama*). That which is intended as its object—

The non-existence of a thing in a manner other than [its perceived state] does not constitute a sublation by inference, because such a thing is not an object of inference. Furthermore, there are the four Noble Truths, which will be explained later. The non-existence of things that are not inferable constitutes their non-inferability, which is non-sublation by inference. For example, the self (*ātman*) and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *pradhāna*, *Īśvara*, and others is intended. Indeed, there is no logical mark (*liṅga*) for these.

By means of which [reasons] they would be inferable. This too will be explained later. When the two types of objects have been purified and regarding the object of scripture (*āgama*) which is entirely beyond perception (*atyantaparokṣa*), that inference which proceeds with respect to something by way of investigating it for internal contradiction is also dependent upon scripture (*āgamāpekṣamanumāna*). "Non-sublation" (*abādhana*) is the subject under discussion.

He explains what that non-sublation (*abādhana*) is like: having accepted as unrighteousness (*adharma*) that which consists of passion and so forth—that is, the nature of attachment, aversion, and delusion—and having also accepted as unrighteousness the physical and vocal actions produced by them, namely those originated by passion and so forth; for the sake of abandoning that, i.e., for the removal of that unrighteousness, [one performs] bathing, the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and so on. Through bathing at sacred sites (*tīrtha*), the destruction of evil occurs. [This is done] with reference to whom [the following is said]: "In the fire..."

There is no instruction to the effect that "by offering ghee and so forth into the fire, the destruction of one's sins occurs," and so on; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), fasting and other such practices are included. For indeed, bathing and the like do not remove sin, because there is no contradiction between them and passion (*rāga*) and the rest, which are the causes of sin.

This is the characteristic of sublation regarding the entirety of an object that can be determined and ascertained through the two kinds of inference and direct perception just mentioned. This is because of the general principle of non-discrepancy: just as the word of a reliable person (*āptavāda*) is non-discrepant with respect to an object that can be determined, so too is it non-discrepant even with respect to an absolutely imperceptible object, precisely because it is the word of a reliable person.
Furthermore, the teacher Dignāga has stated that the cognition of non-discrepancy arising from the mark characterized by authoritative testimony is inferential (217–18).
This [cognition] occurs even regarding an object beyond perception—that is, even regarding the domain and subject matter of this treatise which is entirely beyond perception. It is that [cognition].
For it is impossible to act toward something entirely beyond the senses in a manner not previously stated by another; and even if such activity were to occur,

it would be better to have understanding regarding an object accessible through perception or inference, because [scriptural cognition] depends upon that [perception and inference], just like any other understanding [based on them] when there is no contradiction.
It is not an object of inference.

Therefore, even though it originates from words, like verbal cognition (*śābda*), it does not merely communicate an intention; rather, because it is non-contradictory, it is also an inference (*anumāna*).

Alternatively, it must be stated that [the Buddha's teaching] is indeed an inference, because of its non-contradiction regarding the abandonment of afflictions, due to the establishment of the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted along with their means. (219)
"Or else, inference [is established] regarding another [subject] because of the non-contradiction with the primary object;
thus it is 'engaged'.
The phrase "of that," and so forth, is the explanation: of that scripture, the status of being an inference was indicated by the teacher Dignāga.
Of "this" [the treatise], which has been examined by us through its connection with the words "suitable means" and so forth; for this very reason he says:

"(1) Of such a one," meaning of that which is endowed with qualities such as connection and so on. Because there is a commonality of non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*) regarding that object cognizable through perception and inference, and because of the cause of being non-contradictory, [it serves as] a refutation of the exception consisting in observed deviation.

Regarding an object that is not accessible through perception or inference, the non-discrepancy of the cognition—that is, the understanding—arising from the statement of a reliable person (*āptavāda*) is inferred. Why? Because it is based upon that; for its basis in the statement of a reliable person is established through the instruction of the lineage of teachers, just like any other such understanding regarding an object other than the extremely remote (*atyantaparokṣa*), namely, an object within the domain of perception or inference.

Like [the cognition] of practice (*pratipatti*). Therefore, regarding an object that is extremely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), the cognition based on the aforementioned scripture—though it arises from words, even though it is produced from words—is not like other verbal cognitions (*śābdavat*) which communicate merely the intention (*abhiprāya-mātra*). This cognition does not communicate the intention alone; this is the function of the particle *eva* (only).

Because the order [of the argument] has been broken. What then? Even inference—though an object that is not accessible through perception or inference is [in fact] non-discrepant due to the reasoning just stated—is [accepted] by a person desiring action on account of his intention; however, in reality, words are not inference.
[The word "api"] is used because there is no connection [to the preceding].
The word "api" is also intended to clarify this very point; showing that the non-discrepancy of the authoritative person's speech occurs in another manner, he says:

"Or else," and so forth. That which is to be abandoned is all suffering (*sarvaduḥkha*). That which is to be adopted is nirvāṇa, which is the abandonment of all afflictions (*sarvakleśaprahāṇa*). Of these two—

Reality (*sattva*) is the non-erroneous nature of the truth of suffering and the truth of cessation. That which exists together with the means constitutes the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with its means. The means for what is to be abandoned is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*); the means for what is to be adopted is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). This reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, together with its means, as shown by the Blessed One, [is established] by the power of the thing itself (*vastu-bala*).

By that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), through its established certainty, [it is proven]. In the word of the Blessed One, there is no contradiction regarding the primary subject matter characterized by the Four Noble Truths. The subject matter characterized by the Four Noble Truths is primary because, by realizing it, one attains *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, because of this non-contradiction regarding the primary subject matter, the knowledge arising from the word of the Blessed One [is authoritative] even with respect to other matters. Thus ends the investigation of scripture (*āgamacintā*).

Non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) is the absence of discrepancy regarding the things to be avoided, the things to be adopted, and the means thereto as taught by him— just as in the case of the Four Noble Truths according to the principle that will be explained later. Because this [teaching] which is useful for human goals and worthy of application is non-contradictory, its status as being likewise [non-contradictory] in other domains is accepted and does not lead to deception, since there is no obstruction to the speaker’s [reliability].

Because stating something purposelessly is futile, and since that [purposelessness] is impossible in either case, it has been established that scripture is indeed a form of inference (*anumāna*). If one acts based on scripture, one must act accordingly; and if this is so, then this inference is certainly not fallible regarding its objects.

It has been stated: "Because words lack an invariable concomitance [with their objects]. Others, however, maintain that [the truthfulness of words] depends upon the excellence of the person [who utters them]. (220)

This point is accepted: if there were such an excellence that a person endowed with the quality of seeing things as they truly are and free from afflictions could be known, then the composition [of a scripture] by him would indeed constitute non-contradiction; so say others. For every person who acts with deliberation and desires to engage [in an activity] seeks out either a traditional scripture (āgama) or a non-scripture (anāgama), and not otherwise.
Inference or verbal testimony regarding even an object that is extremely beyond the senses is intended here as an alternative to the previously mentioned method.

The "means to those two" refers to the means for what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and what is to be adopted (*upādeya*). The compound *tadupāyau* is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound consisting of: what is to be abandoned, what is to be adopted, and the means to them.
When these—taught by that authoritative person (*āpta*) and examined through inference—are found to be non-erroneous, [they constitute valid knowledge].

"Suchness" (*tathātva*) is non-deceptiveness, as [was established] regarding the four Noble Truths, such as suffering and so forth, in the second chapter by means of investigation according to the method that will be explained. "Of this"—that is, of that which was previously indicated by the Blessed One and is now being analyzed—refers to that which has the characteristic of the fourfold truth. Of what nature is it? It is "useful for the human goal" (*puruṣārthopayogin*). The human goal is...

Nirvāṇa is that [goal]; "that which has it as its cause" means that for which it serves as the instrumental cause. Precisely for this reason, because there is no contradiction regarding the application and the practice toward that which is worthy of such application, there is an acceptance of the same nature even with respect to other objects not accessible through perception or inference. Thus, the acceptance based on non-contradiction does not lead to deception; it does not result in being contradictory. What is the reason? [It is] because of...

Because it is not sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, having not deceived a person regarding the primary object characterized by the Four Truths, any subsequent false statement in the third instance is purposeless, as it would be futile.
If it is argued that such a statement might occasionally occur there even due to ignorance, he says: "That," and so forth; in both ways...

"By the manner indicated in the two verses beginning with *pīti*": the connection [of the sentence] is that this very scripture has been described as inference (*anumāna*) out of necessity (as there is no other way). It should be understood as "inference" because it is the cause of inference. When activity proceeds from scripture, it is better to proceed from a scripture that is thus logically consistent, rather than from one that is contradictory regarding an object accessible through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
486a [Dīti:
Even by the method thus stated, knowledge based on scripture (*āgama*) is not an inference that is infallible or faultless. Why?

(1) It has been explained that words do not possess an invariable concomitance (*anāntarīyakatva*) with objects, nor do they possess non-deceptiveness (*asaṃvādatva*) regarding them—by means of the passage beginning with "because there is no invariable concomitance of words with things" (1.213). Furthermore, the excellences of a person cannot be established through [mere] attachment (*vyasana*). For it might be possible [to say]: "Having understood what is to be practiced from this [scripture], one who acts accordingly becomes successful. However, such is not possible.
Because it is a cognition that is non-contradictory upon observation, it would indeed function as valid even in other cases, since worldly convention is generally of this nature.
(1) If [the Veda] were of human origin,
then only a statement composed by an extraordinary person (*puruṣātiśaya*) would be a means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, if activity were to proceed based on an examination of the person, there would be no activity at all; for such a person is impossible to know, not because of an undesirable consequence, but because those [reliable persons] speak nothing that is untrue. To explain:
Whether this [person] is thus or not, another [person] does not know whether there are faults or faultlessness. ||221||

Others know that [the Buddha's teaching] is difficult to understand because valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) are rare. Other proponents know—that is, they understand—that whatever statement depends upon one whose faults have been exhausted and so forth is "in accordance with reality" (*yathārtha*). "In accordance with reality" means seeing and knowing exactly as things are established according to their actual state; this is "knowledge in accordance with reality. That which has this as its beginning—namely, compassion, detachment, and so forth—[is the cause].

For example, [it consists of] the vision of reality and so forth. A person endowed with that very quality is an *āpta* (reliable authority); by him it is composed, and thus the word of an *āpta* is the non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*) of scripture (*āgama*), according to others.
(220–21) Regarding the phrase "is desired" (*iṣṭa*) and so forth, the author of the *Siddhāntabindu* states: "This matter just mentioned is desired by us; however—"
It might be possible to know [the excellence] through the determination of the person, as is the case with excellence characterized by vision and so forth;

however, he explains this with the words "all indeed," and so on. Every person who acts with foresight seeks out and examines whether there is a tradition (āgama) or no tradition; desiring to act by means of a tradition while abandoning what lacks one, and not out of mere addiction or attachment.

He says "not even the desire for activity," and so forth. The word "api" (even) implies "how indeed might it be? Thus, having understood from scripture (*āgama*) that which is to be performed—the object that must be directly realized—a person, having set out [with the thought], "May I become one who possesses the goal, that is, one who possesses the fruit," searches for that object. Regarding that object which is accessible through perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), there is the possibility of seeing it, which is to say, there is certainty.

Non-contradiction is the absence of conflict with perception and inference. That very cognition is the basis [of activity], and by means of it, one proceeds toward other objects as well, even those not accessible through perception and inference. What is the reason? Because worldly convention is generally of such a nature.
"In this way" means proceeding toward another object by observing non-contradiction in one part; "generally" (*prāyaḥ*) means for the most part (*bāhulyena*), in that which possesses this quality.

In worldly convention, he is described as such. However, if one were to assume that activity proceeds from an examination of the person, then no activity at all would occur. Why? Because for such a person—one who possesses qualities such as seeing things as they truly are—there would be no activity due to a lack of desire [to act]. It is not that there is simply no activity because of a lack of desire.

The word "might be" (*syāt*) is connected [to this]. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: it is not the case that there would be a total lack of activity because persons endowed with qualities such as seeing things as they truly are are not accepted as speakers of non-false statements. What is the reason? Because such persons—those endowed with qualities like seeing things as they truly are—are speakers of non-false statements, since they reveal objects exactly as they exist.

Furthermore, what is the reason that such a person cannot be known? To this he says: "For thus," and so forth. [The question is: Is this very person possessed of such faults, or not? Is he possessed of such faults, or rather is he faultless? In this way, both the presence of other faults and the state of being faultless are subject to investigation through scripture (*āgama*).

Those persons who, due to their mental qualities and dispositions, are either rightly or wrongly disposed, would be beyond the reach of the senses; they must be inferred from the bodily and verbal activities originating from themselves. Furthermore, such activities can generally be performed otherwise even with prior intention, because they proceed according to human will and because those intentions are manifold. Therefore, this...
How could one, failing to ascertain [the truth] through the refinement of the *liṅga* (logical mark), attain it?
Or rather, is there no such person who is entirely free from defects?

"Because all [things] possess their opposites, others know that [the Buddha's nature] is difficult to understand, as it relies on the absence of excess. (222) Regarding the term "faultless" (*nirdoṣatā*), there is a designation in the singular number and feminine gender as "difficult to understand" (*durbodhā*) with reference to this [state of faultlessness]. However, with reference to "other faults," there is a modification by means of the masculine plural number as "difficult to understand" (*durbodhāḥ*).

A name must be given. Why? (1) Because of its difficulty of comprehension and because of the difficulty of attaining [the truth] regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that determine the virtues and faults of others.
He explains this with the words "from those mental [factors]" and so forth. Right and wrong activity consists of the actions of body and speech.

Those men who possess such characteristics are likewise [described]. Mental factors (*caitasāḥ*) are those qualities and defects that exist in the mind. From mental qualities—such as causes like compassion, detachment, and awakening—there arise correct activities, which are activities in accordance with reality. From mental defects—such as attachment and so forth—there arise false activities, which are contrary activities. And "those" refers to the mental factors of others.

Virtues and faults, being properties of the mind, are beyond the reach of the senses; therefore, they are not accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor are they accessible through inference (*anumāna*), because, precisely due to their being beyond the senses, a natural mark (*svabhāva-liṅga*) is unestablished. Rather, they are to be inferred by means of the mark of an effect (*kārya-liṅga*), namely, bodily and vocal action, which originates—that is, arises—from those virtues and faults themselves. And that [action] does not exist [in the case of the Buddha].

Because conventional practices (*vyavahāra*), characterized by the actions of body and speech, are for the most part—or in great measure—capable of being performed otherwise through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) based on prior intelligence (*buddhipūrva*). For instance, even those possessed of passion (*sarāga*) display themselves as if free from passion (*vītarāga*), and those free from passion appear as if possessed of passion. What is the reason? Because they proceed according to the will of persons (*puruṣecchāvṛttitvāt*).

The analysis of the compound is: "those whose activity or occurrence (*pravṛtti*) is according to the will of persons. Even if linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) are indeed occurrences that follow the will of persons, he asks: "In that case, why are they not performed otherwise?
He replies: "And because those persons possess diverse intentions—that is, diverse purposes—therefore linguistic conventions are [established] according to their desire."

Since conventional transactions arising from virtues and faults proceed in such a manner, there is no definitive discernment [of their true nature]. Therefore, because the signs are conflated and the signs deviate [from their objects], this person who infers—failing to reach certainty—being one whose defects have not been exhausted, how could he understand the author of the scripture? The conclusion must be: "He certainly could not."
Now, as for the passage beginning with "Then why," etc.: Is there no such person at all who is faultless, being free from defects such as passion?
To demonstrate that there is such a person, he says: "Of all [beings]," etc. When the antidote is present, there occurs diminution—that is, decrease.
The outflows (*āsrava*), which possess qualities that can be surpassed, may be abandoned somewhere through the cultivation of their opposites once those opposites have become internalized; however,
one who has abandoned the outflows is difficult to know, for the faults are...

[They] establish the increase and decrease [of qualities], like a flame and so forth. For those [qualities] arise from conceptual construction; even when their material cause (*upādāna*) is present, they may diminish through the cultivation of certain mental virtues. When that [cultivation] reaches proficiency, they would possess the nature of being destroyed without leaving a trace. Furthermore, those [defilements] such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, which resort to excellence and accumulation when their counteragents (*pratipakṣa*) are not present, do not rely on excellence [inherently].

Because they are all adverse to it; and that very thing which, through its presence or absence, causes them to undergo excellence or deficiency, is their adversary (*vipakṣa*)—that is, the subverter—and because it exists together with that, it is "with an adversary" (*sadvipakṣa*). The state of being so is "adversariality" (*tattva*); therefore, [the term refers] to that which, by virtue of being a subverter, [removes] the defects. And by which subverter... of the defects.

Through the repeated and continuous production of that which possesses an antidote—the practice of the subverter—there arises a state of naturalization (*sātmībhāva*), which is its invincibility and identification with it. Therefore, due to this naturalization of the subverter, the *āsravas*—attachment, aversion, and so forth—would be diminished; they would be exhausted. This occurs in a certain mental continuum where the antidote to the defects has been naturalized, for the subverter of the defects is selflessness (*nairātmya*).

He will demonstrate that [the term] refers to "knowledge. Therefore, it is not that such a person is not accepted; rather, we say only this: he is one whose outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted and who is difficult to know.
The passage beginning with "for the fault" is an explanation. For the faults are passion and so forth. Of what nature are they? (1) They are characterized by decrease and increase—

[These] phenomena, possessing the nature of decrease and increase, establish and demonstrate the increase and decrease of the overcoming of the opposing factors—that is, the increase and decrease of that overcoming, which is the subjugation or disparagement caused by the opposing factors. By this, the meaning is as follows:

(1) those things characterized by cessation establish the increase of the overcoming of opposing factors; [this occurs] through the increase of the overcoming of the subverting [factors], [which results in] the [decrease] of defects.

Those things possessing the property of excellence (*atiśaya-dharman*) establish the diminution of the suppression by an opposing factor (*bādhaka-abhibhava-apakarṣa*), because they possess the property of excellence due to the weakness of the suppression by the opposing factor, like a flame and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of cold and hot touch and the like.
Just as flames and the like, when there is an increase or decrease of an opposing factor such as water, possess the property of excellence.

Just as [the elements] successively establish the overcoming and increase of water and so forth, so it is here. Now, one might object: "Since passion and the like are dependent upon external objects, and since external objects are always present, how can there be an eradication of passion and the rest? To this, he says: "For those... and so forth. The word *hi* has the sense of "because. Those passions—

Attachment and the other [afflictions] arise from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The analysis of the compound is as follows: "those whose arising (*prabhava*)—that is, their production (*utpāda*)—proceeds from conceptual construction characterized by improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*). For it is thus: even when external objects exist, attachment and the rest do not arise without improper mental attention; yet, when that [improper attention] is present, they arise even in the absence of an object. Therefore, attachment and the rest arise from conceptual construction. Consequently, even if...

Regarding the "appropriation" (*upādāna*) characterized as previously described, this locative case is used here in the sense of disregard. [The meaning is: due to the cultivation of a certain mental quality characterized by the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya*), they become "diminishing," that is, subject to decrease.
This is what is being said: although there is no constant eradication of the cause of the defects (*doṣa*), because of the presence of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*)—

Because they lack extreme intensity; nevertheless, due to the practice of the antidote, the capacity of the appropriation that causes decline is weakened, and thus the defects become increasingly diminished—by this, the reason has been stated. However, when there is reflection on the aforementioned [teaching], like a flame and so forth, by that means it may indeed be free from defect. (224)

How can it be called "faultless" when, even though it has become the very nature of the antidote to faults, there is still the arising of an antidote to that which is the nature of faults? [One might argue: "The arising of faults occurs according to conditions; this is not a fault. To this we reply: No, because [the Buddha's nature] is the essence of reality, free from affliction, and contrary to [the conditions for faults]. (223)

There is no sublation [of the cognition], even when effort is exerted, because of the partiality of the intellect toward that [object]. Since the mental quality [of the impression] reaches a state of proficiency by existing at the limit of the intensification of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), when there is proficiency in that mental quality— given that the "concomitant" (*anvaya*) arises from it, in the sense that a defect (*doṣa*) follows from it as its seed of affliction— [there is no sublation].

That destruction in which no continuity remains is "destruction without continuity" (*niranvaya-vināśa*). Those defects which possess that quality are "possessing the quality of destruction without continuity. The meaning is that they have the nature of being destroyed along with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), like a flame and so forth. Just as flames and the like are subject to absolute destruction when there is an increase of their opposites, such as water, so too are these [defects]. Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

Those things which, by the presence of a certain factor, undergo diminution, possess the nature of being utterly destroyed without leaving a trace when that factor reaches its ultimate increase due to the suppression [of the former].

For example, flames and the like [diminish] upon the increase of the suppression by water. Since defects (doṣas) possess the nature of diminution through the presence of the vision of selflessness (nairātmyadarśana), this is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu).
Since this is so, for that reason, it might be that someone is indeed faultless. [The opponent asks: "How so? and so forth.

The particle *yāvat* here functions in the sense of *yat*. "Like the arising of the antidote in one whose nature is characterized by faults" means: for a person whose nature is characterized by faults, the arising of the antidote is the arising of the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*), due to practice over beginningless time.

Even though the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*), which is the antidote to these defects, has become one's own nature (*sātmatva*), the arising of defects may still occur according to conditions (*yathāpratyaya*) and according to the presence of causes (*yathākāraṇasannidhāna*). "This is not so," says the Master (*ācārya*): because it is free from all the calamities of saṃsāra, it is "without affliction" (*nirupadrava*). It is the opposite of what is unreal (*bhūtaviparīta*).

The term *bhūtārtha* (the real object) refers to that which has as its object a thing (*artha*) characterized by impermanence and so forth. Precisely because it grasps the real object, the path is the very nature of the mind. Since this [path] is both free from affliction (*nirupadrava*) and a real object (*bhūtārtha*), it is a *karmadhāraya* compound containing within it another *karmadhāraya*: namely, "the real object that is free from affliction. Of such a real object that is free from affliction...

When [the path] has reached the state of being naturalized through repeated practice because it is the true reality, there is no longer any affliction by the defects—characterized as being contrary to the three aforementioned [factors], accompanied by calamities, unreal, and having the nature of non-reality—which are the opposites of the antidote to the mind’s own nature.
The meaning is that the defects do not arise by overcoming the path once it has become naturalized. What is the reason? Because of the presence of effort.
"Affection and so forth," etc. This is what is being said: for one who has made the path his very nature (*sātmībhūta*), even the effort to produce a fault is impossible.
Nevertheless, it is stated [hypothetically], assuming such an effort toward the production of a fault: (1) "Because of the mind’s partiality toward that [path]";
that is, because of the high esteem resulting from partiality toward that faultless path of selflessness (*nairātmyamārga*), which serves as the antidote to faults. [Thus, no] fault—
For this intrinsic nature cannot be turned away without that [cause], just as the aversion of a Vedic scholar toward a Kāpālika cannot be removed.

And effort would be exerted toward the removal of one's own nature or the attainment of another only by perceiving their respective defects or virtues; however, such perception regarding defects is not possible for a person whose nature consists of the absence of opposing factors, because he is free from affliction.

Because of the abandonment of all defects; because of the seclusion from suffering, which is bound to the outbursts and rebirth; and because of the lack of agitation regarding the essence of the bliss of tranquility—indeed, even that which arises through the power of grasping at unreal objects would not exist for the continuum due to the grasping at the opposite.

Having set aside effort toward producing the true object (*bhūtārtha*) by means of the power of real entities (*vastubala*), [one proceeds] because effort is applied specifically to the counteragent of faults through partiality toward virtues (*guṇapakṣapāta*); this is the meaning.
First, he explains the word "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*): for intrinsic nature does not have the characteristic of the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*).
It cannot be turned back by a person established in the self through its counteragent without great effort,
just like the aversion of a Vedic scholar who has become a Kāpālika.
Just as that aversion which existed in the state of being a Vedic scholar when he becomes a Kāpālika cannot be removed without exertion, so it is in this case.
