And the effort being made to turn away from the intrinsic nature of the path would be undertaken by seeing the virtues of that which is to be attained—the intrinsic nature of passion and so forth—and by seeing the defects of that which is to be turned away from—the intrinsic nature of insight (*vipaśyanā*). And that perception of defects occurs for a person whose self is characterized by the opposite of the defects, through the antidote to those defects. Likewise, that perception of virtues—
It is not possible for faults to exist in one's own position.
But why is it that seeing faults in the counter-position is not possible? He says: "Of that," and so forth.
Because that counter-position is free from affliction (*nirupadrava*). For there are three kinds of affliction, by the absence of which the path is free from affliction.

For instance, the cause for the mind being bound is the affliction of the faults (*doṣa*), by which the mind becomes bound and does not engage in the perception of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*).

The affliction of suffering and mental distress is the cause of physical and mental anguish. Furthermore, because contaminated pleasure (*sāsrava-sukha*) is not tranquil, there is agitation even when it is experienced.

In that regard, he states the absence of the first calamity with the words "due to the abandonment of all defects. This means because of the removal, that is, the disappearance, of every defect such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth.
He states the absence of the second [calamity] with the words beginning "obsessive outbursts" (*paryavasthāna*): the manifestation of passion and so forth is what constitutes an obsessive outburst.

There are two types: the affliction (*paryavasthāna*) and birth (*janma*). Suffering is dependent upon these two; it arises from their separation. At the time of the arising of passion and so forth, the suffering characterized by the burning of body and mind is dependent upon the afflictions, whereas the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and so on, is dependent upon birth.
He states the absence of the third calamity with the words beginning "praśama" (tranquility). Tranquility is *nirvāṇa*, characterized by the absence of passion (*rāga*) and so forth.
The "taste" (*rasa*) is the savoring of that untainted bliss (*anāsrava-sukha*) within it; because there is no revulsion toward that [bliss], and because it causes one not to turn away from it.
Furthermore, passion and the like have unreal objects—that is, they have non-existent things as their domain. The connection is that [passion] would not exist [in the presence of such bliss].

If it is asked how that which has an unreal object can arise, he says: "It exists through the power of grasping (*upādāna*)," referring to false conceptualization (*vitathavikalpa*). Furthermore, unreal objects are not defects for one who possesses the nature of the antidote (*pratipakṣasātmya*). Therefore, even when effort is made, there is no further arising of defects;
for in the case of an intelligent person who inclines toward the side of virtue, because they apply effort specifically toward the antidote through investigation, [defects do not arise].
Of the evil-minded one.
[The commentary states: "The view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the cause of the afflictions.
Furthermore, what is the source of these afflictions, through the cultivation of the antidote to which they are abandoned?
The origin of all classes of defects arises from the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
That [view] is ignorance; through it there is attachment, and from that, the emergence of hatred and the rest.
For indeed, for one who perceives "I am not" and "this is not mine," there is no attachment anywhere in the absence of grasping, nor is there any lack of affection.

It arises through the power of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). Thus, because the continuum of consciousness—which serves as the substratum for the seeds of such passion and so forth—is grasped by the appropriation of error, the antidote characterized by the reversal of passion and so forth would not exist, nor would it arise. However, it would not be the case that it does not have the true object as its non-erroneous domain; rather, it certainly would exist. What is the reason? The power of the real entity (*vastubala*).

Because it arises through the power of the object as it actually exists; for one who remains even while defects are congenial to them, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which grasp the aspects of impermanence and so forth, bring about the path that is the antidote—how much more so for one who is established in self-insight (*vipaśyanā*)? Furthermore, defects such as passion and the like are unreal objects; [and] the self—

Because their activity is directed toward objects superimposed by ignorance, those [afflictions] do not become habitual—that is, they do not become the very nature—of one who has accumulated the true reality that is their antidote. Precisely because this is so, there is no further arising of defects for those whose defects have been abandoned. Even when an effort is made to produce a defect, because the intellect’s partiality is toward virtue, one applies effort specifically toward the antidotes to passion and the other afflictions; such is the nature of exertion.
Because of this [reasoning]. For whom? For one who possesses discernment, who investigates through logic, and who remains even amidst the habitual nature of the faults;
specifically, for one of uncorrupted mind who, with excellence and intensity, applies effort toward virtues alone, remaining established in the nature of their antidotes.
Furthermore, what is the source—the cause of origination—of these faults? It is so called because from it they "originate" (prabhavanti), that is, arise.

He states the subsequent [verse]: "Of all," and so forth. Regarding the various types of defects—that is, the categories of defects—their origin (*jāti*) or production arises from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), that is, from the persistent attachment to a self and what belongs to a self.
[Objection: But surely it is stated in the scriptures that the afflictions (*kleśa*) have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their cause; so how is there no contradiction? [Response: He says:

"That ignorance" means that very view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is ignorance. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, by what sequence does the arising of the faults from the view of a self-identity occur? He says: "In that regard," and so forth. In that regard, [one] conceives [of things] as "self" and "mine"...

Regarding the object [of attachment], there is affection for it; that is, affection for the self and what belongs to the self (*ātmātmīya*). From that affection for the self and what belongs to the self, hatred arises; such is the sequence. He explains this with the words beginning "not indeed," etc. "Not I" is the negation of the aspect of the self; "not mine" is the negation of the aspect of what belongs to the self.

For a person who perceives [the aggregates] through the aspect of non-self and the aspect of non-belonging-to-self, there is no aversion toward anything without prior grasping. This is because [aversion] is absent in that which does not obstruct the self or what belongs to the self, and is absent even in that which opposes such obstruction.
Therefore, the view of self, born from the repeated practice of its own kind, gives rise to the grasping of "mine," and those two [grasping and view] produce attachment to it.
"From hatred and so forth" means that all faults are born from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). That very thing is called ignorance (*ajñāna*).
Therefore, delusion (*moha*) is declared to be the primary cause of the faults.
(225) Elsewhere, it is stated that the view of a self-identity is abandoned through the abandonment of that [ignorance].

He states that delusion (*moha*) is the primary cause of the afflictions (*doṣa*), because afflictions do not arise in one who is free from delusion. Furthermore, elsewhere [in the scriptures], the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is mentioned as such. That would be the case if it were presented as the principal [cause]; for the afflictions cannot have multiple origins simultaneously, as their simultaneous arising is contradictory. It is not [delusion] that consists in grasping by conceptualizing [the aggregates] as "self" and "mine" or as being "beneficial to the self"; for without that [conceptualization], there is no grasping toward any object whatsoever.

Affection (*sneha*). Furthermore, for one who lacks passion—that is, for one devoid of affection toward the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*)—there is no aversion (*dveṣa*) anywhere, because such [aversion] does not exist without prior attachment (*anunaya*). What is the reason? [It is] "toward the self and what belongs to the self," and so forth. [This refers to] that which does not obstruct or act contrary to the self and what belongs to the self; that is, in the case of the neutral party (*udāsīna-pakṣa*). Because of the absence of that [attachment], there is an absence of that aversion.

And [it is] "obstructive and resistant. Obstruction (*uparodha*) refers to the affliction of that which has been grasped as "self" and "mine"; "resistant" means acting to counteract or prevent that. This is because such [affliction] is absent in the case of the friendly side, due to the absence of hatred. Alternatively, it refers to that which stands in opposition by way of conflict with the objects of attachment toward self and what belongs to self; hatred exists precisely toward that which remains adverse. Therefore—

There is no hatred without attachment to self and what belongs to the self (*ātmātmīya-sneha*). Therefore, with the words beginning "tasmāt" (therefore), the conclusion is stated: "yata evam tasmāt tau ca" (since it is so, therefore those two as well).

The connection is made by modifying the verbal construction to "ātmadarśanātmīyagrahau snehaṃ prasuvāte" (the view of self and the grasping at what belongs to the self produce attachment). And that attachment produces—that is, generates—hatred and the other afflictions.

He states the cause for those two—the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*) and the grasping at "mine" (*ātmīyagraha*)—in the passage beginning with "homogeneous," and so forth. "Homogeneous" refers to the view of a self belonging to the same class [of beings]. Its "cultivation" (*abhyāsa*) is its repeated production over beginningless time; there is also the "latent predisposition" (*vāsanā*) resulting from that.
From that [predisposition], the view of a self is born, which gives rise to the grasping at "mine. Therefore, all afflictions (*kleśa*) are born from the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
In our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it is said that the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) itself is ignorance (*avidyā*).

For this very reason—that the view of a self-entity is indeed ignorance—it is stated in another Sūtra that delusion (*moha*) is the source, the primary cause, of all afflictions such as attachment and the rest: "All defilements have ignorance as their cause."

Thus, it is stated in other sūtras that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the cause of the afflictions (*doṣa*). Why? Because when that is abandoned—that is, when the view of a self-identity is abandoned—the afflictions are abandoned. The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have said that delusion (*moha*) is the cause of the afflictions, the source of the afflictions. Why? Because for one who is not deluded, who is devoid of ignorance, the afflictions do not arise. Furthermore, in another section:
They say that the cause of the fault of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is this very causality of delusion (*moha*).

Since both [delusion and the view of a self-identity] are primary in the Buddha’s word, the mention of each one individually when they are both primary is merely a matter of emphasis. There is no contradiction in mentioning either one in either case.

Furthermore, its predominance is due to its being the basis [for them]; for when it is abandoned, the defects are abandoned. Therefore, it is possible for the abandonment of the defects of those born with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) through the cultivation of the realization of selflessness (*nairātmya*), which is its antidote.
(1) General refutation.

Because the defects that cause the falsity of speech reside in persons, some declare that what is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) possesses true meaning. This would be so when there is a statement of a reason, not merely a statement of the reason itself. What is the reason? Because from many [causes], such as the objects of the senses...

Since those defects whose birth arises from the complex of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) are incompatible with the arising of even one of them— namely, delusion (*moha*) and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)— it is understood that, although other causes may exist, the causality of delusion and the view of a self-identity is stated by taking their predominance.

If delusion (*moha*) were one thing and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) another, and both were equally predominant, then there would not be a singular designation for each of these two—delusion and the view of a self-identity. The meaning is that sometimes only delusion is mentioned, and sometimes only the view of a self-identity; it does not possess excellence or beauty, but rather results only in the speaker’s lack of skill.

...up to: furthermore, when there is no difference in intrinsic nature between these two, then there is no contradiction in designating a single entity by way of synonyms through both the term "delusion" (*moha*) and the term "view of a self-entity" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), according to their predominance. Moreover, the predominance of the view of a self-entity is due to its being the basis for those [other] defects, just as it is the basis for the [root] afflictions; and that [predominance] has just been explained immediately below.
This has been established, and it will be further demonstrated in the second chapter.

Furthermore, when that view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned, there is primacy [in its abandonment] because of the abandonment of the defects (*doṣa*). Since this is so, for those defects whose birth arises from that view of a self-existent body, [the abandonment of] that view of a self-existent body... [145b]
The antidote to [the view of] seeing is the vision of selflessness; through its cultivation, [that view] is abandoned.

That person whose faults have been destroyed is difficult to follow and difficult to understand—meaning that one who desires to engage in practice would rely on the instruction of such a person whose faults are destroyed. One should carry out the purpose taught by him.

Let it not be that scripture (*āgama*) is a statement dependent upon a person or caused by a person. Why? Because, according to the reasoning just stated, the author of scripture is difficult to trace; because he is difficult to understand;
and because of those defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, which are the causes for the falsity—that is, the deceptive nature—of words and speech.

And this genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). "Resorting" (*āśrayaṇa*) is "resort" (*āśraya*). The compound is *puruṣasyāśrayaḥ* ("the resort of the person"). Furthermore, the genitive case after the word *puruṣa* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Nor does the rule "when both [agent and object] are possible, the genitive is used for the object" apply here; for there is an option provided by the rule *śeṣe vibhāṣā*. …… them.

For that person who has exhausted all defects is difficult to follow; it is by following his instruction that one attains [the goal]. Let it not be the case that a word based on a person is not considered authoritative scripture (*āgama*), because such a person is difficult to follow.
Therefore, the meaning is as follows: (1) because it is grasped by a person through defects that are false causes;

or alternatively, the genitive case in "of the defects" (*doṣāṇām*) is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*), meaning because the defects are grasped—that is, taken up—by a person as their locus.
Some Mīmāṃsakas hold that non-human speech has true meaning because of the absence of defects, which are the cause of falsity.
They explain as follows:

what is meant is this—in the context of debate (*vāda*), the threefold lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*), characterized by falsity (*mithyātva*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), and doubt (*saṃśaya*), simply does not exist. This is because the nature of words is twofold: innate (*nisargasiddha*) and adventitious (*aupādhika*); therein, the innate...

That which is established is the capacity to convey the object as it truly is; conversely, the capacity to convey what is not as it truly is is adventitious (*aupādhika*), because its nature depends upon the person [who utters it]. Thus it has been said:
"It is established that the arising of defects in speech depends upon the speaker."
"Their absence [of defects] occurs in some cases because the speaker possesses excellence;
for it is impossible for those qualities to be transferred into the word when they are inferior to those [excellences].
Alternatively, due to the absence of a speaker, there would be no defects, as they would lack a substratum. (62–63)

Therefore, indeed, upon the cessation of the person, there is the cessation of falsity. Nor is non-authoritativeness characterized by non-arising, because meaning is understood from the Veda. Nor is non-authoritativeness characterized by doubt, because when the meaning is apprehended from the Veda, no doubt appears. Thus he says:
Thus, for the Veda which produces knowledge in such a manner,
both its erroneous nature and doubt regarding it have been refuted by the Bhāṣya.

Since the three grounds for invalidity have been excluded, and since the Veda possesses an intrinsic nature characterized by the communication of its meaning as established by its very origin, therefore its validity is inherent (*svataḥ*) because it communicates meaning. Furthermore,
since in ordinary speech the defect characterized by sublation or a defective cause can occur due to the fault of a speaker, [this does not apply] to the Veda.

When the person [who produced the cognition] has ceased [to exist], there is the cessation of defects by their own nature. Because the causes of sublation and the knowledge of the defectiveness of the instruments [of cognition] have ceased, there is no suspicion of invalidity. At that time:
"In that case, the removal of sublation is rendered effortless due to the absence of a speaker."
Therefore, the Veda does not even incur the suspicion of being invalid;
however, the validity of that which is of human origin depends upon the existence of other means of knowledge. (Ślokavārttika, Codanā-sūtra 68)

2. Ibid., 7. An Investigation into the Non-Personal Origin (*apauruṣeya-cintā*): Not all scripture (*āgama*) can indeed be suspected of being deceptive, because the defects that cause deception reside in persons.
Some maintain that what is non-personal in origin must have true meaning; for the absence of a cause establishes the absence of an effect.
Against those who speak thus:
1. Refutation of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣanirāsa):
Because qualities such as truthfulness, meaningfulness, and reasoning in words depend upon a person [as their locus]. (227)
Others declare: "Why should that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) be false?
But in the absence of such [human authorship], that [falsity] would never be observed in the Veda;
therefore, there is no contradiction between the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

By that very [cognition] it would possess the status of a valid means of knowledge; otherwise, it would be a mere restatement. Furthermore, how can the sublation by that very cognition—which occurs through inference against one who asserts a contrary state of the Vedic injunction—be prevented? (81)
"If you argue that there is no sublation because that [Vedic meaning] is false, then you have fallen into a circular argument;
for you have no sublator other than inference.

(60) Furthermore, the non-existence of the Vedic meaning cannot be established by other means of knowledge in the same way as [the non-existence of] taste and so forth. Now, if [you say it is like] taste and so forth being [known] by another cognition of taste...
Just as the validity of the cognition of taste [arises] from a prior perception, so too will it be with the meaning of the Veda. Thus he says:
Nor can the non-existence of an object be established by other means, as is the case with taste and so forth;
for if the cognition of the object occurs through that very [non-perception] itself, then it will be just like that.
If you say, "This is unestablished for me," [we reply: when the comprehension has arisen from the Veda...
"It is not fitting for one who speaks the truth to speak out of mere hatred.

(61.92) He explains the meaning of the verse with the words "Not indeed," and so forth. "All" refers to both that which is of human origin and that which is not of human origin. "Possibility of deception" means that deception, or contradiction, is possible—that is, it is to be expected. However—

Only that which is of human origin can be suspected of deception, because the defects that cause deception— the causes of contradiction— reside in persons. (227) Some, however, maintain that what is non-human in origin possesses true meaning, because in the Vedas the causes of falsity reside in persons.

The absence of a name establishes the absence of falsity in the effect [of the Veda]; thus, it is non-human (apauruṣeya) and possesses true meaning. (2) Against those Mīmāṃsakas who argue in this way, others speak as follows; indeed, the author of the treatise himself speaks through the mouth of another: "Since those qualities which are the causes of the truthfulness of words depend upon persons, they cannot exist in that which is non-human."

Since the quality that is the cause of truthfulness ceases when the author of the sentences is removed, the effect—truthfulness itself—also ceases; therefore, why would a non-human (apauruṣeya) sentence not be false?
(1) This is what is meant: since truthfulness and falsity in speech depend upon the person, if...
When people manifest light, they are granted tranquility for men and women; if there is transmission within this art, it is a vast assembly.
Mayor modeled on 19., his father giving him a payment and with that... [text corrupted]... dem.

It is argued: "If the person (*puruṣa*) is excluded, why is truthfulness not accepted [as the criterion], while falsity is not? To this it is replied: In ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), however, since both truthfulness and falsity are excluded by the exclusion of the person, they are rendered purposeless; therefore, invalidity is characterized precisely by non-origination (*anutpatti-lakṣaṇa*).
By that—(1)

"If [the opponent argues], 'This is unestablished for me'—this cannot be said by one who speaks the truth out of mere malice, regarding the cognition arising from the Veda; for such cognition does not arise from the Veda by its own nature. (62, 63) This is refuted, because cognition of the meaning does not arise from the Veda through its own inherent nature.

(2) Furthermore: (1) since phonemes (*varṇa*)—whether individually or collectively—are non-expressive by nature, and the Veda consists of the form of phonemes, how can there be knowledge of meaning from it?
[Objection: Even for one who has not grasped the linguistic convention (*samaya*), upon hearing a sentence uttered, there arises the doubt, "Has some meaning been expressed by this?"
It is observed.

And this would be so if the word possessed by its very nature the power to convey a meaning. In that case, however, its lack of authority—characterized by doubt—would arise, because the capacity to illuminate both a desired and an undesired object is possible. If...

Moreover, since that capacity belongs to it by its very nature, what is the use of convention? If it is argued that just as a lamp, though capable of illuminating an object, requires the sense organ, so too a word requires convention—this is not so; for while it is logical that there is mutual dependence between the lamp and the sense organ because neither can illuminate the object in the absence of the other, such is not the case with the power of the word.

Regarding the two types of convention (*saṃketa*): since the cognition of an object arises through mere convention alone, a word is therefore not inherently capable of conveying an object; thus, its lack of authority is characterized by its non-origination [from an intrinsic nature].
(3) Now, in sentences such as "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra*," regarding the *agnihotra* and so forth—

Since it is indeed perceived that [the Agnihotra and other rites] are means for achieving heaven and so forth, how can there be invalidity characterized by non-origination? True, this is so; however, perception is a sublater of non-perception, but not of falsity, because falsity is also perceived. Therefore, do these sentences present the Agnihotra and other such rites as being non-means for achieving heaven, while [in fact] being means?

Furthermore, since it is shown that [the Veda] is indeed a means [to knowledge], the suspicion of its falsity does not cease at all. This is because there is an absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against its being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), and because there is no contradiction between its authorlessness and its having false content. Indeed, even things that are authorless are observed to be causes of erroneous cognition; for example, moonlight and the like are causes of the cognition of yellow in a white cloth and such. Therefore, regarding the meaning of the *codanā*—

Since the state of being otherwise is established through inference, how could there be sublation by that cognition? However, in the case of cognitions of taste and so forth, because their validity is ascertained from the very beginning through the non-discrepancy of their effects, such as satisfaction, it is logical that at other times their validity is ascertained intrinsically (*svataḥ*) through repeated practice and so on; thus, no suspicion of falsity arises. In the Veda, however, there is never any non-discrepancy [with reality].

If it is argued that [the Veda] is "practiced" (pratipanna), how can there be a determination of its intrinsic validity at other times as well? Therefore, even when cognition exists, just as the status of being a means of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) belongs to intuition (*pratibhā*) and the like by virtue of their own independence, so too should it be seen in the case of the Veda.
Furthermore: (1) because the cognition of the meaning of an injunction (*codanā*) consists in the apprehension of what is non-existent, it is false. Likewise... 407
7. An Inquiry into the Non-Personal (Apauruṣeya):
Just as a person overcome by passion and the like is seen to be a speaker of falsehood, so too one endowed with compassion, the nature of dharma, and so forth, is a speaker of truth.
Thus, just as the falsity of speech arises from its dependence on a person, so too does its truthfulness [arise therefrom]. Therefore, when that [person] is absent—

If [words] were to turn back even that [intended meaning], they would be purposeless; or else, there would be the opposite [of what is intended]. For words do not possess meanings by their own nature (*prakṛti*); rather, the manifestation of meaning from them occurs through convention (*samaya*), just like bodily gestures and the like. Compatibility (*yogyatā*), however, consists in non-contradiction, because convention is established according to human will. It is impossible for that which is established by nature to be communicated by the power of will; therefore, those [words] would be meaningless.

For the authority of the Veda is accepted only with respect to what is to be accomplished (*kārya*). And that which is to be accomplished is precisely that which is to be performed; since it exists as something yet to come into being, it does not exist at the time of the cognition arising from the injunction (*codanā*). Therefore, how could the cognition arising from the injunction not be false, given that its object is non-existent? Furthermore, since it has already been established that all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have non-real things as their objects, for that reason as well—
The knowledge derived from the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is indeed false. Furthermore, the phonemes and words in both the worldly and the Vedic [languages] are identical;

only a difference in sentence structure is admitted. In the world, the meaning of words is determined by convention (*saṃketa*). Since the meaning of worldly words is the same as that of Vedic words, the relationship between the word and its meaning is purely human in origin. And by means of the worldly word-meanings, the Vedic...

Since the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs [in this way], it is indeed of human origin, just like an ordinary worldly sentence. Furthermore, because words in the world have multiple meanings, the possibility of multiple meanings for a Vedic sentence also exists; thus, the doubt regarding a contrary meaning does not cease.
Consequently, the Veda possesses the characteristic of uncertainty, which constitutes its lack of authoritative validity (*apramāṇya*).

He explains the meaning of the verse with the words beginning "yathā" (just as). "Overcome by passion and so forth" means possessed of passion and the like. "Compassion" (*dayā*) means *karuṇā* (pity); that very [compassion], when it has become one's own nature, is the *dharmatā* (essential nature). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), wisdom, faith, and others are included; [the person] is endowed with these. Therefore (*tattasmāt*), just as the falsity of a statement arises from its dependence upon a person, so too does its truthfulness arise. "He" refers to the person. That [truthfulness] as well...

It does not turn [the Veda] away from having truth as its object; it does not [turn it away] merely from having falsity as its object. Thus, upon the cessation of the person, there would be a cessation of both truthfulness and falsity—those two attributes of his—and consequently, the Veda would be purposeless. If, on the other hand, truthfulness is maintained even upon the cessation of the person, then falsity would be the opposite of truthfulness.

Or it might be thought: "The meaningfulness of words does not depend upon a person, but rather arises from their very nature. To this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth. [Words are] meaningful by *prakṛti*, that is, by their own nature. What is the reason? Because of convention (*samaya*).

[It arises] from convention (*saṃketa*). Therefore, because meaning is expressed by words—that is, because the object is cognized—it is like the "gesture of the body" (*kāyasaṃjñā*) and so forth. Gestures of the hand, winking of the eyes, and the like are called "gestures of the body. Just as in those cases, the comprehension of a certain meaning occurs through convention, so it is here. If, on the other hand, words were by their very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*) revealers of meaning, they would not depend upon convention. Therefore, it is not [the case that they reveal meaning inherently].

The capacity of words to illuminate their own objects does not consist in that; rather, the capacity of words is simply their functioning according to convention, which is their non-opposition [to the intended meaning]. Why is this? Because at the time of the convention (*samaya*), when the maker of the convention intends to employ them, words are produced according to his will, and thus they function accordingly. If, on the other hand, they were established by nature (*nisargasiddha*), [they would not function according to convention].

If words were established by their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*) with respect to some object, then, since they are established by nature, they would be subject to human desire as one pleases. [In that case], they would possess meaning through human refinement (*saṃskāra*). And it is precisely this capacity for refinement that constitutes their being "human-made" (*pauruṣeya*), not their production; for it is from that [refinement] alone that the deception regarding the object arises. Even if produced otherwise, it does not obstruct [the truth], just like other qualities of a person.

Therefore, this [word], when it ceases, causes the manifestation of the object—which arises from its own established convention—to cease. How, then, could there be truthfulness of meaning through its cessation?
Furthermore, if being produced by a person (*pauruṣeyatā*) consists solely in origination and not in the communication of a convention—even so—

For convention (*saṃketa*) is the cause for making an object known, and it has its basis in persons. Since it is impossible to convey an object through convention [without such a basis], words are inherently devoid of meaning; being thus meaningless by nature, they [acquire meaning] through the refinement of persons, that is, through the conventions of persons. (228)
[The words] possess meaning. Now, lest they be meaningless, their meaningfulness is accepted with respect to the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person.

In that case, they would necessarily be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). For it is logical that the very fact of these words being refined by that [person], which is indeed the refinement of the person, constitutes their being of human origin; it is not their production from a person. What is the reason? Precisely for that [same reason].

Deception regarding the object arises solely from the convention of a person, that is, from contradiction; it does not arise from the production [of the word] by a person. For even though a word is produced by a person, it is "conformed" (*samita*) otherwise—that is, it is designated (*saṃketita*) according to the state of things—without contradiction to its true meaning. Thus, it is not obstructive nor deceptive. "Different from that" means different from the word; it refers to the manifestation (*unmeṣa*), which is a quality of the person.
Just as blinking and so forth, though in themselves meaningless, do not deceive when associated with a person according to the actual state of things, so it is here.

Concluding, he says: "Therefore" (tad). Therefore, this person, by desisting from his own convention, also causes that manifestation of meaning—that is, the cognition of the object—to cease, which has its origin (sambhava) or production in that convention. Thus ends the section.
Therefore, by the cessation of what would there be a cessation for that person? [If it were so], its status as having a real object would not exist; rather, it would simply be meaningless.
By this, that which is said—
Having refuted that which is asserted by opponents as a proof for the prior and posterior limits [of the world],
the proponents of the Veda have accomplished their purpose.
The claim that the prior limit of the Veda is characterized by being of human origin, while its subsequent limit consists in destruction— and that its eternity is simply the absence of such [limits]—
is refuted; for even if the Veda were of non-human origin and eternal, it would be purposeless and thus fail to achieve its intended aim.
(6) Furthermore, if "being of human origin" (*pauruṣeyatā*) consists solely in the act of production— and not in the communication of a convention or the making of a linguistic agreement—
then the implication is that the Veda is authoritative precisely because it is not of human origin.
Even so, the convention, which is the cause for making the meaning known and the cause for manifesting the meaning, depends upon persons and conforms to human will.
Therefore, even if words were not of human origin, the possibility of falsehood remains.
For what does it matter that they are not of human origin, since the comprehension of meaning arises from convention (*samaya*)?

That convention could be of human origin and might even be erroneous. [For example, one might state] "virtuous conduct is the means for attaining heaven," and then, through another convention, reverse it.

(1) Because it is possible for that [word] to manifest even what is not in accordance with reality, that same fault remains; namely, that words do not necessarily correspond to reality when their non-human origin is asserted. Therefore, [it depends on] human intention—
The possibility of falsity arises from a dependent convention (*saṃketa*).

(7) The explanation beginning with "Why... [is as follows]: "Of this" refers to the Veda; for since the understanding of meaning—the manifestation of meaning—arises from a convention (*samaya*), that convention is of human origin, and therefore it may even be false or untrue, because of its independence [from reality].

And therefore, for that heaven which has morality as its means and cause—such being that heaven characterized by the summit of Mount Sumeru—the statement regarding it in the Veda should not be subverted or rendered otherwise in another system (*samaya*). One should not make it have the opposite meaning, such as defining heaven as "supreme pleasure," nor should one make it have the opposite meaning by asserting that it is achieved through means such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice; for that reason, this—

Since it is possible for [the meaning] to be revealed even for that purpose, the same fault applies as was stated regarding human compositions: "In the case of human compositions, deception is possible because of the faults of the person. (228)

(8) But surely the relationship between word and meaning is non-human (apauruṣeya). For instance, just as contemporary elders teach the relationship between word and meaning exactly as it was previously established, so too did the elders of preceding generations; thus, due to its beginninglessness, the relationship is indeed non-human. As it has been said:

“Excluding the beginninglessness of words and their meanings, there is no other cause for the beginninglessness of the relationship [between them]; therefore, in the Veda, no beginning of the relationship is found. And that relationship is established by three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance: (1) by someone [acting] so that a listener may understand the meaning;...

When a word is employed by an elder, another person standing nearby, who is the cognizer, perceives through direct perception both the speaker and the denotative capacity (*vācaka*) of the word. Furthermore, he understands the listener’s state of comprehension by means of his subsequent activity. And, through the fact that the cognition of the object would otherwise be inexplicable, he understands the power of denotation and denoted residing in the word and its meaning; thus, it possesses exactly three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The connection [is as follows]. Thus it has been said:
In this context, one perceives through direct perception both the word and the referent denoted by the elder; one perceives the listener’s comprehension through inference based on their behavior;
and one understands the capacity residing in both [the word and the referent] through the principle of "otherwise it would be impossible" (*anyathānupapatti*).
"And they understand through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that the one who establishes the relationship is an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
— *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (1.230)

Even if [the Veda] were not of human origin, it would lack authority; for if the relationship [between word and meaning] were not of human origin, there would be no cognition for one who lacks [prior] knowledge [of that relationship]. (229)

It might be argued: (1) words are indeed unrelated to their effects, and they are not arbitrarily misinterpreted by persons regarding those objects; therefore, there is no fault. [But then] what is the use of convention (*saṃketa*) now? For that relation is that from which the cognition of an object arises. This [relation] would not depend upon convention. How can relations be based on non-cognition?

The postulation of something else is incapable of manifesting [the relation] through convention. Indeed, even if a relation exists, it cannot be the cause of cognition if it is unmanifested. Since convention itself now serves as the manifestor of this [relation], why is it being nourished without reason as if it were something already established?

Regarding this, he says: "If the relation between word and meaning were non-human-made," and so forth. If the relation between word and meaning is accepted as being non-human-made (*apauruṣeya*), there would be comprehension—that is, the understanding of the meaning—even for one who lacks *saṃvit*. *Saṃvit* is the knowledge of the convention (*saṅketa*). For one in whom that does not exist—namely, those words whose relation to their objects is *akārya*, meaning not produced or generated by persons—those words [would still convey their meanings].

Because they reveal the objects as they truly are among those things to be expressed by persons, they are not made to be causes of false cognition by being otherwise than their own nature; therefore, due to that absence of error, there is no fault characterized by non-correspondence. Now, if the relationship is non-personal (apauruṣeya), what is the purpose of a convention (*saṃketa*)? For that [relationship] is indeed the connection between word and object.

If the relationship that causes the comprehension of meaning were non-human (apauruṣeya), then a person, while understanding the meaning from a word because the relationship is established by nature, would not depend upon convention (*samaya*), just as one does not with a lamp or similar objects. Yet, he does depend upon convention; therefore, there is no non-human relationship between words and their meanings, unlike the insignia of a king or similar things.

(6) It might be thought: "The relationship itself is indeed non-human (apauruṣeya), but it is independent of convention (*saṃketa*) and is the basis for comprehension. To this he says: How can that which is not the basis for comprehension—or rather, how can that which is the basis for the comprehension of meaning—be a relationship? It is not so at all. For a relationship is postulated because comprehension would otherwise be impossible. In the absence of comprehension, how could there be a relationship? Now, [if one were to argue...]
For a relation, being indicative in nature, requires knowledge of its own self;
therefore, even though it exists, it does not manifest [its object] if it is not itself apprehended.
[This applies] to all [relations] that have not been manifested by preceding speakers.
"The relation is established; thus, no relation or such exists.

To this, he replies with the words beginning "by convention" (*saṃketa*). When that relation is manifested by convention, the postulation of a relation other than convention is both incapable [of producing the manifestation] and fruitless.

This is what is meant: since the cognition of an object arises when there is a convention (*saṃketa*) and does not arise when it is absent, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the convention alone is the cause of the cognition of the object; what need is there for any other relation?

He explains this with the words beginning "no" (*na*). [The convention] is the cause of the cognition of an object when it is unmanifested—that is, when it has not been made known. "This" refers to the relation (*sambandha*).

The connection is "that [is] this. When the communication of meaning is established through convention (*saṃketa*) alone, that which has the nature of being present is [the word]. This is the inquiry into the non-human origin (*apauruṣeya-cintā*).
Now, is not the function of this [word], namely the production of cognition regarding an object, such a limited relation that it is accomplished by convention itself?
For convention is not capable with regard to what is unfit. If fitness (*yogyatā*) is the relation, then is that [fitness] the word itself, or is it something else?

Let it be so. For the capacity (*yogyatā*) of a word is its form (*rūpa*), just like the capacity for performing an action. If that [capacity] were a different entity from the word, then a relation must be stated as to how it belongs to the word. If it is argued that there is assistance (*upakāra*) by way of capacity, we say no; because that which is eternal is without degrees of excellence (*niratiśaya*), there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of such assistance even in that case. Furthermore, since assistance is not established in the case of capacity...

If [the word] is inherently capable [of denoting the object], why is the object itself not accepted? Why is a relation maintained as causeless and for what reason is it nourished when it is fruitless?
(10) He states its very fruitlessness with the words beginning with "nanu" (but surely), etc. "This much" means only this much: that which [is required] regarding the object to be expressed.

The production of cognition is the generation of comprehension (*pratīti*). Since that generation of comprehension is accomplished through convention (*samaya*), the [intrinsic] relationship is fruitless.

Convention is not capable regarding what is unfit. Rather, it is precisely that word which is understood by the speaker as being capable—on account of the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the comprehension of the meaning—in which respect convention is effective. Thus, if fitness (*yogyatā*) is the relationship, it has been said:
"For the relation is indeed power (*śakti*), and no difference in it is perceived; for since it is to be inferred from its effects, it conforms to their differences. (Saṃbandhaparīkṣā 28).
Here [the author] says: "What then," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: A single power does not reside in both the word and its meaning; rather, the expressive power resides in the word, while the expressed power residing in the meaning is quite another. But when the power of the word is the relation itself, then it follows that the relation is identical with the related entity. Thus he asks: (1) "In that case, let the word itself be the relation."
Now, one might object: "The capacity (*yogyatā*) is indeed one thing, and the word (*śabda*) is another; how then can the word be the relation? To this he says:

Because the very form of the word, in its capacity to convey a meaning, is its fitness (*yogyatā*). It is like the fitness between cause and effect. "Fitness for producing an effect" means the capacity for bringing about an effect; it is as if it were the very essence of the cause.

It is just like that. If "that" refers to fitness (*yogyatā*), then if it is something other than the word, one must state the relationship between the word and the fitness—otherwise, it would not be established that "this is the fitness of the word. If it is argued that the word assists that fitness which is a distinct entity, [it follows that] an assistance to the fitness is being performed by the word.
The point is this: because it is produced by sound, it is called the "fitness" (*yogyatā*) of the word. There is no assistance rendered to fitness by the word;

why? Because fitness, being eternal, is incapable of receiving any enhancement (*niratiśayatvāt*). If, on the other hand, it is argued that even for fitness, a distinct assistance is produced by the word, then [one must consider] that assistance created by the word...

It must be stated what the relationship is with respect to fitness (*yogyatā*). If it is argued that even in that case, another assistance is produced through fitness, then, by the aforementioned method, one would have to postulate a further and further assistance for that assistance as well; this leads to an infinite regress (*atiprasaṅga*).
Consequently, since no assistance is established due to this infinite regress, the very relationship of the word with fitness remains unestablished. Furthermore:
A word, while assisting a distinct capacity, assists by its own nature alone, not by the nature of another. For a word does not possess another form.
The newspaper says that my brother Ambang has died and is buried.

There can be no relation between established entities that are unmixed, because that would entail their non-distinction, and because they are independent of one another. [Objection: If that is so, how then is the convention (*samaya*) the relation between word and meaning? [Response: Because it exists within persons.

Therefore, it is the *explanation of the relation* (*sambandhākhyāna*) that constitutes the convention (*samaya*), because the capacity to convey meaning is established through the explanation of the relation; it is not the relation itself.
Speech is impelled by a desire to communicate a specific object; thus, for one who knows "this [word] refers to this [object]," the object appears as manifesting its own cause.
Regarding the term "indicates": the relationship between the cognition-form and the vocal intimation is that of producer and produced.
Therefore, from that sound, there is comprehension due to their invariable concomitance.

Because it would follow that [the word] provides no assistance. Furthermore, regarding that capacity (*yogyatā*): if the word is by its own nature inherently capable, why is it not accepted that the meaning itself is the very nature of the word, fit for generating cognition? That is to say, why resort to an indirect process? Therefore, capacity is neither the relation nor the cause of the cognition of the meaning; for the cognition of the meaning arises from inherence (*samavāya*) alone.

If that is so, how can the convention (*samaya*) of a Buddhist be the relationship between word and meaning? And why would it not be [such a relationship], since it resides in persons? Convention is the statement of the meaning: "This [word] is the designator of this [object]. And that resides in persons, not in the word and the object. Furthermore, a property belonging to one thing cannot be the property of another, just as the property of a horse is not the property of a cow.

(1) But the Teacher [Dignāga] says that there is not only no convention (*samaya*) as a relation, but that no other real relation (*bhāvika-sambandha*) exists either. He says "No," and so forth. For instance, the relation between entities would have to be either a fusion of their forms (*rūpa-śleṣa*), or dependence (*pāratantrya*), or mutual requirement (*parasparāpekṣaṇa*). Among these, for things that are unmixed—that is, mutually distinct—there is no relation whatsoever.

The relation characterized by the fusion of forms would entail their non-difference, resulting in the consequence of their becoming one. Furthermore, for established or perfected forms, there can be no relation characterized by dependence, because dependence is incompatible with what is already established. He states that even a relation characterized by mutual dependence does not exist, saying: "And because of the absence of dependence."
Because that which is established is independent of everything.
(2) [Objection: If, then, there is no relation between word and object, how is there the cognition of the object from the word?
And how is verbal knowledge included within inference? Or, in that case, what is the purpose of the convention (*samaya*)? (1)
He says: "A specific object," and so forth. A specific object is that which has been made the focus by the intention to communicate.

The striving for that is the desire to communicate. Speech, impelled—that is, produced—by that [desire], indicates or reveals the object as it appears in its own cause. The cause of speech is the intention to communicate. Of what does that [speech] reveal?

It indicates [this]. "For one who knows 'therefore this'": for that wise person who understands that this speech has come forth from the intention to explain; thus, there is a relationship characterized by the produced and the producer between the mental cognition in the form of an intention and the vocal intimation. Therefore, comprehension arises from the word through invariable concomitance. (1) Therefore...
The comprehension of meaning arises from a sentence due to the relationship of produced and producer.

Therefore, as for what was stated: "(1) Although the cognition of meaning from a word is inference, the comprehension of meaning from a sentence is a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because the [necessary] connection is not grasped; and here, inseparable concomitance (avinābhāva) is of no use.
