That is rejected, because the relationship between signifier and signified cannot exist without invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
As for what was also asked— (1) how there can be comprehension of meaning from words, and how verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*) is included within inference— that has been answered.

kha. Now he states the purpose of *samaya* (convention): "The exposition of that," and so forth. *Samaya* is the exposition of that [invariable concomitance] (*avinābhāva*), because it is by means of this that [the concomitance] is explained. "From that" means from the *samaya*; it refers to the establishment—that is, the cognition—of the characteristic of invariable concomitance, which is the means of communication and a factor for the presentation of the object. Through metaphorical usage, it is called the connection of the *samaya*.
The designation of a "relation" [between word and meaning] arises from its manifestation; however, that convention (*samaya*) itself is not the primary relation. Therefore, as it is said:
"Is the convention established for each individual person, or indeed for every single utterance?"
(1) The view that "the world was created at the beginning by some single agent once and for all" has been refuted.

[Ga: Now, if the cognition of an object from a word occurs through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), then the word’s communication of its meaning would not be by way of denotation (*vācakatva*), but rather like smoke’s communication of fire. And if it is argued that the relationship between word and meaning is established through convention (*samaya*) rather than through [invariable] existence...
The connection with convention (*samaya*) is now stated. [Objection: "In that case, there would also be a convention between fire and smoke.

[Response: This is not a fault, because when one intends to convey a meaning, having superposed the state of being denoted upon the object and the state of being a denoter upon the word—thinking, "I shall convey this meaning even by means of a word for which no convention has been established"—it is at that time [that the relationship is established]. When the word...
When [the effort] is applied, there is then the production of the word itself in its expressive form.

[Objection: But surely it is only phonemes (*varṇa*) that are produced with the intention of conveying a meaning, and phonemes are not accepted as being the expressive [word]. So how can it be said that "from the intention [of the speaker], the expressive word is produced"?

(1) It is true that, solely because the speaker and the listener have the conceit (*abhimāna*) that [the phonemes] are expressive with respect to the phonemes themselves, it is said that the expressive [word] itself arises. Therefore, for a deluded person, the communication of this very inseparable relation—which is characterized by the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*)—is called the "convention" (*samaya*) as the relationship between word and meaning. However, not every communication of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is [so called].

Convention (*samaya*): (1) Therefore, the connection [of a word] with smoke and so forth is not called convention (*samaya*). Although there is a difference between the time of the initial agreement (*saṃketa*) and the time of practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the relationship between word and object, nevertheless, because of their similarity, people proceed by superimposing identity upon them.
For this very reason, whatever relationship between word and object the speaker has previously apprehended, that very same one the listener [apprehends].
He practices accordingly; therefore, that which is said—
Furthermore, that relation must be either distinct for each instance or it must be one.

If it were one, it could not be produced; if it were distinct, there would be a cognition of difference. (From *Saṃbandhaparīkṣā* 14) Due to the difference between the cognitions of the speaker and the listener, linguistic usage is not impaired.
For the relationship [of a word] for the speaker is one thing, while that for the listener in his cognition is another.

Or, let it be that the relationship is indeed something else, eternal; nevertheless, if words were restricted to a single meaning by that [eternal relationship], there would be no comprehension of any other meaning. (230)

For it is not logical that there should be a cognition of an object through a relation with which it is not connected, because that would result in the relation being purposeless. Since a convention is established by the power of observed desire, everything can illuminate everything. When there is a connection with multiple objects, the possibility of contradictory manifestations arises.
If it were not so— that is,
if all words were denoters of everything— then there would be no contradiction with what is perceived;
however, because of the confusion of cause and effect, when a specific means is intended for a specific purpose, [all things] would be the means for everything.
"What relationship does the speaker establish for the listener and the act of speaking?
For that which was previously perceived by him, he does not produce for the listener; and that new thing which he produces is not something already perceived by the communicator. (1)

That is refuted; for in all cases, people act by determining the identity of the various relations between the signified and the signifier, even though they are distinct. Nor is there any beginninglessness to them, because recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatvāt*).
(226) Or, let it be that there is indeed another, eternal relation between word and meaning, distinct from the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). By that—

If there were a restriction of words—that is, of sounds—to a specific effect by means of a [fixed] relation, then, due to the force of convention (*samaya*), there would be no comprehension (*gati*) regarding another meaning where that word has not been restricted. Why? Because it is not logical for there to be a cognition of an unrelated meaning through a relation fixed to a single object; for what reason? Because it would result in the uselessness (*vaiphalya*) of that relation.
"It is not the case that there is no comprehension at all there," he says:
"It is observed," and so forth. The lamp is the illuminator because its convention has been established by the power of human intention.
"By many [meanings]," and so forth: if it is accepted that a word has a connection with multiple meanings, then [if one were to argue] by way of the restriction to a single meaning...
The proponent of the convention (*samayakāra*) brings about manifestation. At that time, he does so only with respect to the intended object and not with respect to any other contradictory one;

thus, there is no fixed rule, and consequently, the manifestation of a contradictory [object] is possible. It is even conceivable that a contradictory meaning might be manifested instead of the intended one.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "atha" and so forth: (1) If there were a restriction to a single meaning, then the observation that multiple meanings are conveyed by virtue of convention would be contradicted; therefore, so that this observed fact is not contradicted, all words are denoters of every object.

With the words "tathā" and so forth, there is the presentation of a contradictory instance (*viruddhavyakti*). Just as it is accepted that all [words] are denoters of everything, so too must this necessarily be accepted: (1) that not every object is the producer of every effect, because this is established by logic (*nyāya*). And he states that logic: "Because of confusion (*saṃkara*)," meaning because the relationship between cause and effect is restricted.

In this regard, given this principle, there is a specific and distinct entity that serves as the means (*sādhana*) or cause for a desired object to be established (*sādhya*), such as heaven and so forth. With respect to that [object] which has become the domain [of the word], what kind of word [is involved]? (1) 7. An Inquiry into Non-human Origin: How is it known that the author of the convention (*samaya-kāra*) establishes only the manifestation of the visible form (*dṛṣṭa-vyakti*) as common to all means of proof? 489a
That which is unrestricted obtains its restriction from a person; otherwise, the postulation of its being authorless would be purposeless. (231)

Thinking, "May I indeed understand the meaning as it is mixed," the confusion caused by human agency is evident. In that regard, although certain [words] used by people in some instances are mixed, even such words, being common to all, are restricted by them to specific meanings. This is due to a lack of knowledge of the true nature [of the word], arising from their very disposition (*bhāva*).

If it is argued that Vedic words are fixed by their very nature, then they would not require instruction; otherwise, they could not be made manifest through convention, and there would be no possibility of alternative explanations. Regarding the possibility of alternative instructions in the case of instruction, [the text says] "all" and so forth. This refers to all things to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and all effects (*kārya*), and their respective means (*sādhana*) or causes (*kāraṇa*).

Since that word is common [to many meanings] by virtue of its denotative capacity, why should it be held that the author of the convention effects its manifestation only in the intended object—that is, as manifesting that specific meaning which is accepted as having the particular property to be proven?
This is what is meant: even if a certain object is, by the nature of things, a means to attaining heaven, it is only in that very [object] that the author of the convention [establishes it].

There is indeed doubt as to whether the word *agnihotra* and so forth is manifested [in its true sense], or whether, due to intellectual dullness, it refers to something else entirely that is contrary to the means for attaining heaven.
The word "sa" (he/that) is unrestricted in its denotative capacity across all things; [only] through a person does it become restricted to a particular object.

One understands [the meaning] from convention (*saṃketa*). And that person might establish a convention even for a contradictory object. In that case, not only would the possibility of expressing a contradiction exist, but this very postulation of the Veda’s lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatā*), which is intended [by you], would become useless. The phrase "api nāma" means "how indeed. "Unmixed" (*asaṃkīrṇam*) means not conjoined with what is unintended; it refers only to the intended object.

Thinking, "May I understand [the truth] from words that are not of human origin," the cause of confusion— the intermingling of the desirable and the undesirable— is excluded from Vedic words by being attributed to humans. Such being the case,
those words which are considered to be of human origin are confused when a person employs them for some intended meaning.

This is due to the possibility that they express a definitive conclusion (*niṣṭhā*). Indeed, even those words considered to be authorless (*apauruṣeya*) are common to all possible meanings; however, they have been restricted by those persons to a specific meaning according to their own whim through convention (*samaya*). What is the reason? It is because those persons lack knowledge of the true nature of reality (*tattva*). By their very nature—that is, by their inherent essence (*svabhāva*)—Vedic words are restricted.

If it is argued that, because [the words] are directed toward a specific object, there is no fault caused by human refinement, then in such a case they would not require instruction for the manifestation of the meaning; yet they do require it, because there is no cognition of the meaning from them by their own nature (*svataḥ*). Furthermore, if they were restricted to specific objects by their very nature, then how could they, having been assembled once for some particular object, ever again [be used] in any other way?

Otherwise, they would not manifest a different meaning through a different convention; yet they do manifest it. Therefore, it is not seen that [words] exist by way of their own nature (*prakṛti*). [If it were so,] understanding would occur [naturally]. Thus, since there is no non-deception (*avisaṃvāda*) by way of intrinsic nature, the claim of being non-human (*apauruṣeya*) is futile.
External objects are the cause [of verbal cognition] because a relationship between distinct entities is established;

external objects are not the form of the word, nor is the word the form of the objects. For if they were of non-different nature, there would be an inseparable connection (avinābhāvitā)—as in the case of "produced" and "impermanent"—even when there is a difference in their conventional designations.

Nor are intentions (vivakṣā) manifested by words that are produced by the lack of intention to speak, nor are they manifested by those that are unproduced; nor are they dependent upon external objects. They are restricted by their effects. Furthermore, if there were a natural restriction to a single meaning, then the various alternative explanations and the differences between successive interpretations by commentators regarding Vedic sentences would not exist, because of the fixed determination to a single meaning. Yet, such [diversity] does occur.
And therefore, unlike human utterances, Vedic words are not restricted to a single meaning.
Now, it might be argued that their teaching is indeed restricted to a specific meaning; to this, he says: "Of the teaching," and so forth.
That Vedic sentence in which there is a conceptualization of multiple possible meanings due to different interpretations is described as such.

In the case of Vedic sentences that admit of alternative interpretations, the instruction given by commentators lacks correspondence with the intended meaning; for there is no certainty that "this is its meaning" or "that is its meaning," and thus it might even be something else. For this reason, the non-human origin [of such texts] is useless, because even after assuming that, the suspicion of error is not removed.

Furthermore, he who maintains that there is a relationship between word and object must state the reason for the establishment of that relationship—that is, for the determination of the relationship. [The question is: of what things? Of distinct things—of words and objects that are mutually different. First of all, the relationship between word and object cannot be characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), because objects...

External objects such as jars and cloths are neither the form nor the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the word. For if jars and so forth were of the nature of the word, they would be non-existent; nor is the word the form of objects, for if they possessed the form of the object, it would follow that they lose their status as being of the nature of the word—by virtue of which they might share an identical essence and thus be inseparable (*avinābhāvitā*). This remains true even when there is a distinction in their conventional designations (*vyavasthābheda*).

Even though there is a distinction between the probandum and the probans based on a difference in their exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), what is it like? It is like "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*).
Just as, despite a difference in the exclusions of producedness and impermanence, there is an inseparable connection (*nāntarīyakatā*) due to their being of one nature, so it is here.
(2) He states that even the relationship characterized by "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*) does not exist, beginning with the words "nor... (*nāpi*). This is what he says:

Or [is it] by means of the external? (ka) First of all, it is not the first position; because these Vedic sounds are not admitted to be born from the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*). The analysis of the compound is: "those whose birth is from the desire to speak. This is because their eternity is accepted. They are unborn—
Nor are [these] cognitions unarisen, for they are not manifested by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), since that would entail the loss of their eternity;
as was stated previously, that which is manifested is something produced.
(kha) Nor is the second position tenable; thus he says: "They are not dependent on objects. That is to say, they are not dependent on external objects.
Precisely because they are eternal.

Others, however, compose and explain them as a single text: since [words] do not arise from the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*), nor are they of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*), how could they establish their connection with that [intention], which is to be accomplished through specific determination? Nor is there any proof for such dependence.
Because it could not be modified by persons, it would be entirely useless. ||232||
"When one resorts to linguistic convention (*saṃskāra*), it would be primarily like an elephant's bath.
This is the summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*).
Furthermore, the relationship between word and meaning must be either eternal or non-eternal. If it were non-eternal, [it would depend on] a person...

Activity (*pravṛtti*) is either the operation (*vṛtti*) of desire (*icchā*) or [its manifestation]. If it were not dependent on persons, then since places and other factors could exist otherwise than according to the intentions of persons, there would be no bringing about [of those factors] therein. Furthermore, even in the case of desire, that which is independent [of a person] cannot occur at any time, just like mountains and the like.
They are manifested by that [word]. Therefore, in both ways, Vedic words are not dependent on meaning, nor are they connected to external objects.

And because they are not dependent on meaning, for that reason—[the word] "now" [implies] in the absence of a connection—how could those words establish the concomitance, that is, the existence, of that object? They could not establish it at all. Of what kind [is that object]?

That [cognition] is to be established by means of a specific restriction [of words]. That is, it is to be established by that specific restriction of words which, with respect to that external object, arises through identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from it (*tadutpatti*). This is because there would be an absence of restriction due to a lack of connection (*apratibandha*) with the external [object]. (232) 3.
He summarizes the very point already stated in a verse: "By way of being unconditioned," and so forth. (1) All—

Thus it is said: if words were not created by persons with the intention of conveying meaning, nor even conventionally designated, then, because they would be incapable of being refined by persons—this being the reason—the Vedic words would be devoid of meaning. Since the truthfulness or falsity of words depends upon their refinement by persons, in the absence of that [refinement], they would necessarily be meaningless.

(2) Furthermore, if one were to resort to the refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*) in order to avoid the charge of pointlessness (*nirarthatā*), there would also be the charge of falsity (*mithyārthatā*); thus, this would become like the "bathing of an elephant. For an elephant, having bathed to remove mud, again besprinkles itself with mud. Since there is no other possible state for a real entity (*vastu*)—namely, that it must be either eternal or non-eternal—[this position is untenable].

(3) [Objection: Its activity might occur by the power of human will, like contraction and so forth; or it might be inactive, as in the case of sprouts and the like, for its activity does not depend on human will. In that regard, under the view that [the world] is impermanent and dependent on humans, there would be a change of place and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), time and state are included. For humans, [there would be change] through the alteration of place and other factors.

"According to intention" means that it would not be possible for a person to convey by means of a word exactly how they wish to convey it; this is the connection [of the sentence]. What is the reason? Because even when a person has the desire to convey something, since the word is independent [of that desire], it might at some time fail to be employed, and thus it could never be made subject to the person's control.

The meaning is "like the sun. It is like mountains and so forth; for example, just as mountains and the like are not dependent on persons, and thus cannot be employed at will even when there is a desire [to do so], so it is with this. Furthermore, it is observed that through the shifting of place and other factors, the communication [of meaning] occurs according to one's intention. Therefore, the relationship is not dependent on persons.
iii iii iii

This very same objection applies even if [the cause] were eternal, because such a stable entity could not otherwise function [differently]. Since it would abide equally in all cases, there would be no specific restriction; consequently, as before, there would be no cognition of distinctions.
This leads to an undesirable consequence: since the operation [of the word] depends on human will, there is the suspicion of deception.
Furthermore:
"Because the relata are impermanent, the relation cannot possess permanence. (233)
Because the relationship between those two is employed [only] when there is a dependence on another related substrate;
and that substrate is impermanent. Upon the departure of this [substrate], the relationship would also necessarily depart. Otherwise, it would not depart.
Furthermore, the purpose of having such a substrate must be stated.

If this aforementioned defect—namely, that the relationship is not dependent on a person—applies to an eternal relationship, it is the very same defect that applies even to a non-eternal relationship. Why? Because that relationship, being of a stable nature, cannot undergo transformation through the change of place and so forth; otherwise, such a transformation would be impossible, just as in the case of space.
4. ka. Now, [it might be argued that] the word is connected to all objects. To this, he replies with the verse beginning "samam" and so forth.

Even if it were imagined that the connection exists simultaneously (*saman*)—that is, at one and the same time—with respect to every object, because there would be no restrictive determination (*pratiniyama*) regarding the specific intended object, there would consequently be no cognition of that particular intended object from that which is common to all objects.

Thinking that this might be the case, one must admit that even though a word is connected to multiple meanings, it attains a restriction to a desired meaning through the mental refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person;

however, in that regard, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) as before applies, which was stated [in the verse] beginning with: "When there is a connection with multiple meanings, and the possibility of expressing contradictory [meanings]... (1.231). Thus, first of all, whether the relationship is eternal or non-eternal—

The defect in [the relation's] dependence on a person has already been stated. Furthermore, since the occurrence of the relation depends on human will, there is the suspicion of deception, because one must admit that the person is the cause of any discrepancy.
Also, "Moreover" (*api ca*), etc.: therein he states another objection. For the object of words is of two kinds.

"Directly, it is the genus (*jāti*), and the individual (*vyakti*) is characterized by that. Regarding this, if [the relation] were with the individual, he says: "Because the objects denoted, which are the relata, are impermanent; when they perish, the relation—which depends upon them—also perishes. Thus, the relation has no permanence. 'Dependent on another' (*parāśraya*) means dependent on the other relatum."

This is because [the relationship] has that as its substratum (*āśraya*). For when there is no obstruction to the relation between two related things, it is impossible for those two related things not to possess their state of being related; indeed, no one becomes possessed of something by means of that which is unconnected, just as a cow is not possessed of a horse. Furthermore, that substratum of the relationship between word and object is impermanent, because objects are impermanent. Upon their disappearance...

Upon the destruction of the substratum, that which is dependent upon it must also cease to exist, just as light ceases when the lamp is extinguished. Otherwise, if it were maintained that the dependent does not depart even when the substratum is destroyed, then the relation—which is held to reside in the substratum—would itself not be dependent. Therefore, because it perishes along with the destruction of its substratum, the relation is not eternal. 7. An Inquiry into the Non-Personal Origin (Apauruṣeya-cintā).
Because that which is eternal cannot be assisted, it cannot be a substratum if it performs no action.

If it is argued that there is no fault because the universal (*jāti*) is what is denoted, we say no; for it has already been thoroughly examined that there is no purpose in denoting that [universal]. Furthermore, since a universal is impossible in all cases, usage occurs [only] in the case of arbitrary terms that denote individuals.

Furthermore, there can be no application [of a word] at all when there is an injunction regarding a genus (*jāti*), because it would be impossible to function while excluding other specific differences. Therefore, the relation belongs only to an entity that possesses both presence and absence—that is, one which is characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Consequently, this [relation] is to be refined for words by persons through their intellect. (234)

Furthermore, the meaning of its "substratum" (*āśraya*) must be explained. One must state by what kind of purposeful object that relation is supported; for the meaning of a substratum is the meaning of providing assistance. But such [assistance] does not exist here. Why? Because a permanent relation cannot be assisted, as it is incapable of having any excellence added to it; and that which is intended to be the substratum, failing to provide assistance, is not a substratum.
It might be so.
This would be the case if the individual (*vyakti*) were the denotable object; then the fault just mentioned would apply.

However, since it is the eternal universal (*jāti*) that is the denotable object, there is no fault; for even with the disappearance of the related individuals, the relation does not incur the fault of being non-eternal.

If it is argued that [the universal] does not exist, the reply is "No," and so forth. This has already been thoroughly examined in the *Anyāpoha-cintā* (Investigation of Exclusion of Others), on the grounds that there is no purpose in employing such a statement regarding a universal. (3155)

In this context—namely, that "a person acts only after having cognized things capable of purposeful action"—and because a universal (*jāti*) is impossible in every instance of denotation, the application of a universal is untenable. Just as in the case of arbitrary names (*yādṛcchika*) denoting individuals, "arbitrariness" (*yadṛcchā*) is the desire to employ a word without any external cause; [the universal] would reside in that [desire].
[These are] arbitrary. Regarding those words such as "Devadatta" and so forth, which denote individuals:

(234) 5. According to the view of some, there is a fourfold application of words—namely, genus-words (*jātiśabda*), quality-words (*guṇaśabda*), action-words (*kriyāśabda*), and arbitrary-words (*yadṛcchāśabda*). It is with reference to their opinion that this was stated; for even a word such as "Devadatta" [is an arbitrary one].

If it is maintained that a word denotes a genus (*jāti*) by means of a distinction of locus (*sthābheda*), then, since the denotation of the genus would have to be accepted at all times, it would be impossible for the word to apply to a specific intended individual while excluding other particulars and abandoning other individuals; thus, there can be no denotation of the genus. This is observed in common usage: when a cow-owner says, "Bring the cow," it is understood as excluding cows belonging to others.

The activity for the purpose of bringing a cow would indeed be restricted; and that [restriction] could only occur if, by means of context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, the word "cow" were to function with reference to a specific [individual]. Furthermore, since there is no bringing of the universal "cowness," there would likewise be no cognition of the sentence-meaning.
Therefore, the universal is not denoted in all cases. For this reason, a real relationship (*vāstavaḥ sambandhaḥ*) is not tenable. [End of 15 Ia]
Of distinct [entities]. Therefore, for a positive entity that possesses both presence and absence— which is intended as the effect—
the very relationship consisting of its presence and absence by way of the presence and absence of that which is intended as the cause is the relation of producer and produced (*janyajanakabhāva*).

Relying on those very same existence and non-existence, even though they are unmixed, they appear as mixed to a person due to the mental habituation (*bhāvanā*) of conventional usage; thus, the conjunction of entities is a product of human agency.
Furthermore, because the relationship [between word and object] perishes when its substratum perishes, that word is not joined with the former [object].

Because [entities] would be unrelated; in that case, entities as they arise one after another would be inexpressible, because there is an absence of an established relationship. Furthermore, even in the case of arising simultaneously with their objects;
When it is not being conceptualized,
the inversion of intrinsic nature is not applicable to words.

Now, lest there be non-existence in another object upon the destruction of the related entity, or lest words become inexpressive of objects, it is held that the relation belongs to those things that are non-different; this is the sense.
For this reason, therefore, the person (*puruṣa*) is the relation between words—which are effects—and their objects, which serve as the causes.
The relationship between word and meaning is established by the intellect through the agent's cognition; for a word is employed when an object exists and is not employed when it does not exist.

Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that the relationship between word and meaning is established by the intellect by relying on the existence and non-existence of the word, which correspond to the existence and non-existence of the object.

6. He explains this very point with the words "those two indeed," and so forth. Relying upon the existence and non-existence of a word by way of its object, the word and the object—which, though by their own nature unmixed and unrelated, appear as mixed and connected—appear to a person; that is, they manifest in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*). Why? (1) From the cultivation of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra-bhāvanā*) since beginningless time.

Because of the habitual practice of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), for this reason, the connection—the relation—between things and words is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). This is because it is established by the force of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of linguistic usage.
He states "Furthermore," and so forth, to show that there is another fault if one were to accept a real, ontological relation (*vastubhūta-sambandha*): [if] in the state of being denotable...

Because the substratum of what is intended [to be expressed] has perished, even though the relationship has not itself perished—that relationship which was intended as its signifier—is no longer present. On the grounds that this relationship does not exist, its absence means that, due to that lack of relationship, it could not again be joined with a new object of expression. Consequently, all things that arise as they arise would be inexpressible, being devoid of any relationship.

For this reason: how could there be a relation for those things that are themselves unrelated? (1) Because no relation is established; for among those various things that arise, no relation exists prior to their arising, since it is impossible for a relation—which by nature resides in two entities—to exist in the absence of its relata. Regarding the phrase "there too," and so forth: even in that case, when a relation arises together with those very objects as they successively arise, [the same difficulty persists].
If every object that arises were to arise as possessing a relation [to a word], then even though the relation has arisen, it would not exist in the word.

For it is impossible for that which lacks the nature of being related to acquire that state without a reversal of its own nature. Furthermore, because a relation that arises simultaneously with the word cannot reside in the word—which, having been established from elsewhere, provides no assistance to the relation.

If that [permanent cause] were also a cooperative factor for its production, it would follow that it must produce [the effect] eternally, because it is independent and because there is no benefit to be conferred upon a permanent entity. Even if it lacks the capacity [to produce], it could not acquire power later, because it does not abandon its own nature.
This fault is not raised [as applicable] if a relationship [between the cause and the effect] is postulated. ||235||

For a relation characterized by dependence on that [other entity]—which appears through the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of persons and depends upon the conjunction of entities—is not possible when it is merely being postulated.

It is not logical for there to be a change in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of words; for that nature which constitutes the relation with an object arising later did not exist previously due to the absence of the relation, yet it comes into existence afterwards.

There would be a reversal of the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of words; and that is not tenable because of their permanence. The explanation beginning with "artha" [is as follows]: when the previous related object has perished, the word whose connection [to that object] has been destroyed suffers a deficiency—that is, a lack of connection—regarding another object that arises subsequently; and from that, regarding objects arising subsequently...

Lest it be the case that [the object] is not denotable by a name, even if an object were to arise as something possessing a relation yet without having grasped that relation as it arises, even so, the relation—though arisen—would not belong to the word; the word would not possess that relation through that [relation]. Why? Because that word [is not connected] with that relation which arose subsequently.

Because it is impossible for that which lacks the nature of a related entity to possess the state of being related to it; that is, because by means of that relation, it is impossible for it to have the nature of a related entity.

At what time? (1) Without the reversal of its own nature—that is, without abandoning its prior nature as a non-related entity. He states another fault [regarding] a relation that has arisen simultaneously with the object and is established from something other than the word, [namely] in that which provides no assistance:
And because the word does not serve as its basis, it is simply impossible for that [connection] to exist. (234) 490b Now,
even if that word were a cooperative cause for its production, it would be a cooperative cause with respect to the production of the connection.

If [the word] were being produced at a specific time (*ritve kalpyamāne*), it would follow that a capable word is produced at all times, and it would follow that the relationship [between word and meaning] is generated at all times. What is the reason? Because it does not depend on auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). Furthermore, there is no dependence because a permanent word cannot be assisted by auxiliary causes. Alternatively, if it were incapable [of producing the relationship], it would produce it only through dependence on auxiliary causes; in that case, prior to [that dependence], the relationship—
Even if there is an incapacity regarding the production of a cognition, there is likewise an incapacity at a later time—that is, at the time of its presence. What is the reason?

Because it does not abandon its prior nature of incapacity. This fault exists when the relation is a real entity (*vastubhūta*); it does not exist when the relation is conceptualized (*vikalpita*), being merely indicated by the intellect.

The explanation begins with "it does not exist" (*na hoti*), and so forth. Their mutual dependence (*parasparāpekṣā*) is in relation to those entities, arising from some cause imagined by the intellect (*buddhiparikalpita*). That connection, characterized by such [dependence], appears as a mental cultivation of the person (*puruṣabhāvanāpratibhāsī*).
This is because its nature is to appear within that conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) which possesses the repeated practice of mental cultivation regarding the person. It is that [connection].
And thus, a human-made relationship does not depend upon the conjunction of entities; for "conjunction of entities" means mixing, and it does not depend on that.
O you who learn the Brahma that pleases!

Thus, even though he does not alter the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of eternal things, he might himself conceive of something from somewhere and construct it; yet, by that much, those things do not become subject to the law of decay (*cyavanadharmāṇaḥ*).
As was stated previously: [an entity] is impermanent because the relationship between the substratum (*āśraya*) and the dependent (*āśrita*) is destroyed through the destruction of the substratum.
In this regard:

"If it is accepted that there is no destruction even when the substratum perishes because [the quality] is eternal, then what is the efficacy of the substratum in the case of eternal things, by virtue of which that [substratum] is desired as a support? (236)

It is heard that, regarding the impermanence of what is born from a source, there is no simultaneous destruction [of the quality] with its substratum; however, in the case of eternal things, we observe this through the capacity of the substratum, by which it would have a substratum. This is because there is no production of what has already been produced, and because a causal agent is independent.

If it is argued that the manifestation (*vyakti*) [of a universal] occurs through its substratum (*āśraya*), its genus (*jāti*), and its relation (*sambandha*), and that these are the basis for its benefit; [we reply:

because all entities, due to the difference in their intrinsic natures (*prakṛti-bheda*), abide in their own essential forms (*svasvarūpa*) by virtue of their connection with auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) which produce cognition—this person [is merely] eternal.

Nor does he transform his own inherent nature into that of another, nor does he remove a stable related nature while failing to assume another related nature. Why? Because one observes the existence of something when that [other] exists, or because of the ripening of the internal latent impression (*vāsanā*) for such conventional usage; or because a person, having himself reflected, might construct this connection here, thinking, "This is the relation. Thus, the person...

Through the practice of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), even those things regarded as eternal would become so; they would possess relations constructed by persons. Yet, for that reason alone, they do not undergo a change in nature from their previously established state of being unrelated.
This is what is meant: the relation imagined by the intellect is [distinct from] the relation imagined by you.
This is not contradicted even if [the substrata] are assumed to be eternal; therefore, it is proper to accept that very [connection], and not one that is real.

As for what was stated previously—that the connection is impermanent because the connection of the supported perishes due to the departure of the support—if, in response to that objection, it is argued that the connection is not destroyed even upon the departure of the support because it is eternal, just like a universal (*jāti*);...

It is said: "Just as [a universal] is not destroyed even when its substratum is destroyed because it is eternal, so too is the relation. (235) To this, he replies: Even in the case of universals and the like, which are considered eternal and are bodies [of their own], what efficacy does the substratum have? For that reason, the substratum is held to be of no assistance. This is the explanation beginning with "it is heard," and so forth; it is heard...

By this [statement], he says that this is merely a conventional designation and lacks any real entity. (1) [The universal] depends on individuals. In the case of universals (*jāti*) and so forth, which are exclusively eternal, we do not perceive any capacity of the substratum—that is, any benefit produced by the substratum—by virtue of which that which is intended as the substratum would actually be a substratum.
What is the reason? Because there is no cause for that which has already been produced and possesses an established nature; for that which is unproduced, there can be no agent.

And because the substratum is independent. (236) If it is argued that from the substratum there arises the manifestation—which is the appearance—of the universal and its relation, and that this very manifestation is the capacity [for cognition]; and that this alone is the benefit conferred by the substratum, and for that reason the category is called the "substratum" (*āśraya*).

He states the reply: "By knowledge," and so forth. The manifestation (*vyakti*) of the auxiliary causes—such as lamps and the like, which are the causes for the production of cognition—is held to be their arising with the capacity to produce that [cognition]. (237)

Even in the case of jars and other such objects, since there is no difference for those who know the reasoning—that these objects are unchanging—how could any purpose be served by their manifestation through their respective manifestors, given that they are held to exist [even before being manifested]? (238)

Because it depends upon the material cause (*upādāna*) in relation to its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), the very production of another moment is what constitutes the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of jars and other things with respect to the generation of cognition. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that cognition would be generated even without depending on that assistance. Furthermore, since that which produces capacity is the producer itself, because the capacity is of the same nature as that [entity]. If it were not of the same nature as the object, there would be no assistance. (491a)
Because it would follow [absurdly] that, due to the capacity for the arising of cognition, jars and other objects would never be perceived.

Since cognition arises from the connection with light and from their being situated in a suitable location— by virtue of their fitness for producing that [cognition] and their capacity to produce a cognition corresponding to themselves—
that very arising, even in the case of manifestable objects such as jars, is what is called "manifestation" (*vyakti*) by those who know logic and understand the principles of reasoning.

[The universal] is manifested. However, since the universals (*jāti*) and so forth—which are the objects manifested—are eternal and unchanging, they possess no distinction [from their previous state] relative to the manifestor. Consequently, there is no production of a capacity for generating cognition. What benefit, then, is conferred upon those universals by their respective manifestors? None at all. For it is precisely because of this that those universals and so forth are considered to be "manifested" by those manifestors. (237)

He explains [the passage] beginning with "from the co-operating causes" (*sahakāriṇaḥ*). From what kind of co-operating causes—namely, from lamps and so forth—which depend upon their material cause (*upādāna*), does [the effect arise]? The preceding [moment], characterized as a jar or the like, is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) for that which is capable [of producing knowledge].
This is because the jar, characterized as such, depends upon [its own] material cause. It [produces] another moment that is fit for generating a cognition of its own object.

The very production of jars and other objects is their manifestation; otherwise, if jars and the like did not acquire the capacity for generating cognition from a source such as a lamp, then it would follow that cognition of jars and so forth could arise even without depending on the assistance— that is, the assistance— of the lamp.

Now, if it is maintained that a lamp or the like confers capacity upon a manifested object that was previously incapable, then, because the lamp and such—which confer this capacity—are the producers of the jar and so forth, for what reason? (1) Because that capacity is of the same nature as that [object], being of the nature of the manifested itself; therefore, upon the production of that [capacity], the jar and so forth themselves would have been produced.

Now, lest this fault should arise, it might be maintained that the capacity produced by a lamp or similar cause is a different entity from the object to be manifested. But if the capacity is admitted to be a distinct entity, it follows that there would be no benefit conferred upon an existing thing, such as a jar, by the lamp and so forth; for when something is done to one thing, another is not thereby benefited, as that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

Furthermore, if the capacity produced by a lamp or other such factors were a distinct entity from the jar, then because the capacity for the cognition of the jar and so forth would arise from that [distinct entity], the capacity itself would have to be apprehended at all times. Consequently, it would follow that jars and the like—which do not produce a cognition of their own object—would never be apprehended; yet, the apprehension of jars and the like is indeed accepted. Moreover, even in that case, it would follow that they could be apprehended without depending on light, since they would be apprehended independently of light.

The meaning is that it would follow as a consequence that jars and other such objects would be perceived [even in darkness]. If one asks how it could be so without depending on light, he says: "Without depending...
[from the *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* 1.236].

[Otherwise] there would follow the consequence that [the sense organs] would grasp [objects] without dependence [on anything else]. This is because independence implies no benefit to the self. Therefore, these [senses], while depending on something else for the production of the cognition of their own objects, thereby acquire a specific excellence of their own nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*). Consequently, they are indeed produced by that [other factor]. However, because they attain the form of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), through the power of cognition, they are designated by a term expressing a specific excellence of the effect; thus, their distinction is proclaimed.

That is called "suggested" (*vyaṅgya*). It is not so with genus (*jāti*), relation (*sambandha*), and the like, because they cannot in any way be benefited [by manifestation]. That which does not confer a benefit cannot logically be manifested.
Furthermore, for a relation, there would have to be a real entity; otherwise, it would merely be a variety of cognition (*buddhicitratā*).
And this relation, being a real entity (*vastu*), necessarily does not transcend difference and non-difference from the word and its object.
For it has been stated previously that "otherness" (*anyatva*) is indeed the non-identity (*atattva*) of that nature (*svabhāva*).
And since this [relation], while being perceivable by the eye, does not appear in its own cognition as a form distinct from other things through a process of exclusion (*viveka*), how...

Regarding the passage beginning with *kṣeti* and so forth: this contingency—that jars and the like do not depend upon light—arises because there is no benefit to their own nature; that is, because the lamp and such do not provide any benefit to the nature of the jar and the like.
For by producing a capacity that is distinct [from the object], the lamp and so forth would provide some assistance to the jar and the like.

[Objection: They are helpers (*dupakāra*). [Response: Therefore, since these [objects] depend upon [the lamp] for the production of the cognition of their own objects, they [the lamp, etc. acquire from that other [cause] a specific nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*), a form capable of producing cognition. For that reason, those things considered to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*) by the lamp and so forth are indeed produced (*janya*). If they are produced...
He asks: "Why are they designated as 'manifested' (*vyaṅgya*)? and answers with the verse beginning "having the form of the object of knowledge" (*jñeyarūpa*), etc.

Because of the reason that one obtains—that is, acquires—the form of the object of knowledge (*grāhyarūpa*) from a manifestor such as a lamp, there necessarily arises a cognition having that [form] as its object. Therefore, by virtue of that cognition—by means of a term denoting an excellence of the effect (*kāryātiśaya*)—the effect, which is the cognition, [is established], even when the cognition has not been previously grasped.

The term "manifest" (*vyaṅgya*) refers to that which possesses excellence, expressed by words such as "manifested. This is for the purpose of distinguishing [these effects] from those effects whose cognition is not grasped.

When a cognition is necessarily produced, even though it is something generated (*janya*), it is called "manifested"; whereas that which is not of this nature is called merely an "effect" (*kārya*). Thus, the meaning is that things are designated as "manifested" for the sake of establishing this conventional distinction. It is not otherwise.

"Jāti-sambandha-ādayaḥ" means those for which genus (jāti) and relation (sambandha) are the first [members]. By the word "etc. (ādi), other things also considered eternal that are dependent [upon a substratum] are included. This is because they cannot be assisted in any way by that which is considered their substratum. Therefore, the connection is as follows: it is not at all logical for them to be manifested by that which provides no assistance.

And in order to show that the relation is not established by three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "If the relation were a real entity (*vastu*), then because the relation is distinct from its two relata, a third entity called 'relation' would have come into being. And if that [third entity] were capable of being perceived (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), then there would be a diversity of cognition based upon three objects. But this [relation] between word and meaning..."

A relation, being a real entity (*vastu*), necessarily does not transcend—nor does it go beyond—difference and non-difference from the word and its object. If it is argued that there might be a mode distinct from difference and non-difference, he says: "For its nature" (*rūpaṃ hi*).

Since "nature" (*rūpa*) means intrinsic being (*svabhāva*), it has been stated previously that for an entity, its "non-being as that" (*atattvam*)—that is, its not being that very thing—is precisely its "otherness" (*anyattvam*). [This concludes] the section on the investigation of the non-human origin (*apauruṣeya-cintā*).

It might be so; for the existence of non-discrimination (*aviveka*) and non-perception (*adarśana*) depends upon the presence of discrimination (*viveka*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that they could not persist. If it is argued that there is no fault because these two are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and thus do not appear [to consciousness], just like the sense organs and so forth—

No; for that would entail the consequence of non-comprehension [of the object], and because only that which is already established can serve as a communicator. If it were communicated by mere proximity, then even those who are unlearned would comprehend it. Nor is there comprehension through inference, because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and the failure to establish an example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Even in that case, [it would fail] because of its being a sense faculty (*indriyatva*).
In this context, [it is said]: "Because an existing thing does not deviate from its otherness.

This very relation, being perceptible by the senses, exists within one's own cognition which takes that relation as its objective support. It is said to be "in the exclusion of what is other than that," because the relatum is not manifested as a distinct object with a different form through its separation from that relation.

How could it be so? How could its form be distinct from others? What is the reason? (1) Because there is no distinction, that is, no separation, of the perceptible object from direct perception; and because non-perception [of it] is, respectively, the basis for the existence of distinction and its opposite. The opposite of distinction is the absence of distinction; its basis is the non-distinction from the perceptible.

The basis for the error regarding existence and non-existence is the non-perception of that which is perceptible. Therefore, the meaning is this: (1) whatever is not perceived as distinct from something else is not other than that; that is to say, whatever is perceptible yet is not perceived does not exist.
"Otherwise" means: if a thing is accepted as being a different entity from another and is perceptible, yet there is no perception of it while it remains undifferentiated from that [other thing].

Furthermore, if both distinction (*viveka*) and existence (*sattā*) are postulated, then it follows that there can be no established determination of their persistence and their absence of distinction. For indeed, the non-perception of the non-distinction of the perceptible is the cause of this determination. If these two—the distinction and its absence—are not accepted as the means of proof, then that determination is destroyed, because the relation [between them] is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
If it is argued that there is no fault as previously stated even though the relation does not appear in the cognition separately from its relata, just as the sense organs do—
meaning that just as the sense organs such as the eye do not appear in the cognition separately from forms and so forth, yet they exist as distinct entities,
so too will the relation exist.

No, says the Teacher: the relationship is not supersensuous. For it would follow that the object could not be apprehended from a supersensuous relationship. What is the reason? Because that which is unestablished—that is, not ascertained in its own form—cannot be a signifier.
Indeed, it is not logical for there to be a cognition of something by means of another with which it has no perceived relationship.
Now, he says that the relation, even if unknown, makes the meaning known just like a sense organ: "By mere proximity," and so forth.

If it were admitted that the relation makes the meaning known by its mere proximity—that is, by its mere existence—then even those who have not mastered the relationship between word and meaning would have the realization: "This is the designator of this meaning."
It might be thought: (1) there certainly is a perception of the relation through its distinction [from the relata]; however, that is not obtained from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). I.153a.

(From the *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* 1.236): [The opponent argues: "If it is argued that [the existence of] the sense faculties and so forth is established in the same way because they depend upon a means of proof (*sādhana*), [we reply: No, because those are inferred in another manner. [Namely,] cognition [is perceived] in certain..."

In the case of [the senses], because they possess both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it establishes that [cognition] cannot arise from those [objects] alone and demonstrates its dependence upon their absence. Thus, the senses are established by way of their effect. This is not the case for the relation (*sambandha*), because that very relation is unestablished; for there is no cognition of its effect. Indeed, neither the form of the word nor the object is the logical mark (*liṅga*).

Because both are suitable in all cases, there is no cognition [of the relationship] through the communication that serves as the basis for the apprehension of a specific object; rather, it must be from inference. To this he says: "There is no comprehension of the relationship through inference. Why? Because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
For there is no logical mark whatsoever that establishes the relationship. Nor is the apprehension of the object itself a logical mark.

Because the example is unestablished. For nowhere has the cognition of an object as the effect of a relation been apprehended in an example. Why? Because even in that which is adduced as an example, a means of proof (*sādhana*) is required, since the relation is by nature beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). And no such means of proof exists, because there too the example remains unestablished.

If it is argued that this lack of a corroborating example is the same when an inference is being made to establish the existence of the sense organs and so forth, which are beyond the reach of the senses; we say it is not the same. Why? Because those sense organs and so forth are inferred in another way. For no specific form of the sense organs and so forth—which are [already] perceived—is established as "this is it," by which the fault would be equal.

However, knowledge, being an effect, is perceived as possessing positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with respect to certain factors such as light; it possesses negative concomitance in states such as when the eyes are closed, and positive concomitance in states such as when the eyes are open.

Such knowledge, being an effect, cannot arise from those [factors] alone. For it is observed that even when those [factors] are present, [knowledge] does not arise [if other conditions are absent], and therefore it cannot originate from those alone.
It establishes the non-arising of the self and its dependence on what is distinct from it;
and as for that dependence on what is distinct, it establishes both the dependence on causes distinct from the proximate cause and the dependence on causes other than those.

"There must be some other cause. Therefore, from the aforementioned positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the sense organs are established by means of their effects. In this context, sprouts and the like—which cannot occur in the absence of other causes—serve as the illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). However, there is no inference of the connection [of the sense organs] through the exclusion of the effect (*kāryavyatireka*) in the same way as with the eyes and so forth, because it is an inference based on specific characteristics (*viśeṣānumāna*). For instance, [the inference is simply]: "The connection exists."
Whatever is an inference is an inference of that very particular [object].

And that is incorrect. Why? Because, while that very relationship remains unestablished, there is an absence of the cognition of that effect—the effect which is the relationship itself. If it is argued that "the word-meaning is the logical mark (liṅga)," he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.

For in that case, neither the form of the word nor the object is a logical mark (*liṅga*) for a specific relation. What is the reason? Because both the word and the object are everywhere capable; because every word is capable of being expressive of every object, and every object is capable of being expressed by every word. Furthermore, the cause of the cognition of a specific object is the relation—

There is no specific relation for that [cognition], which is the basis for the cognition of a specific object, because words and objects are not restricted [to one another] since all words are capable of being denotable in every case. [Added: In the investigation of the non-human origin [of the Veda], for if there were no specific relation, that [cognition] would not be logical; or if that [cognition] were without a cause, its specificity would not be established.

Why is it not accepted that the teaching of words, even when provided with restrictive rules (*niyama*), is itself without a causal basis (*animitta*)? Consequently, that indicative mark (*liṅga*), being similar [to all others], would lead to the cognition of a connection without distinction. Therefore, there would be a cognition of every object without distinction.
Thus, for the sake of establishing the connection and the resulting cognition of the object, no one would have any need for traditional transmission (*sampradāya*).

If it is argued that [the word] possesses the status of a *liṅga* (inferential mark) only when accompanied by tradition (*sampradāya*), then what is the use of this succession? Why does that very [word], dependent on tradition, not itself bring about the cognition of the object? Because it does not produce cognition [on its own]. Or, if it were to produce cognition, then in the absence of any distinction [between one word and another], there would be no comprehension of all objects through the perception of a relation with every [word].
It might be so; but it is not thus. Therefore, there is no cognition of this relationship through words and objects that are themselves indeterminate.

Furthermore, if a specific relationship between words and objects were established along with [their] general relationship, then in some cases there would be a cognition of that specific relationship. For indeed, in the absence of the establishment of a relationship between words by means of a specific relationship, [such a cognition would not occur].
That cognition of a specific relation is logical.
However, if it is instead maintained that there is a cognition of a specific relation from a word even in the absence of a [prior] relation, then,
since that cognition of the specific relation is desired to have the cognition of a relation as its cause, the specific nature of that [relation] must be like the necessity of the cognition itself.
Why is it not accepted that the communication of meaning by words is likewise without a specific cause, just as there is a fixed restriction regarding the cognition of particularities?

That nature of the word and its object is a mark (*liṅga*) that is similar and equal in all connections. Consequently, if the word were to bring about a connection with everything without distinction, then there would be a cognition of every object without distinction for everyone. For every person—
Whether the convention has been grasped or not grasped, there would be comprehension of all meanings. Therefore,

since the comprehension of meaning arises through the establishment of the relationship by the aforementioned logic, no person would depend upon tradition or the instruction of another for the comprehension of meaning.

If it is argued that it is not the word alone that functions as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the establishment of the relationship, but rather the word together with its traditional transmission (*saṃpradāya*), then what is the point of this succession? What is the use of this sequence: first the traditional transmission, then the word’s status as a logical mark, then the cognition of the relationship, and finally the communication of the object?
