Why does a word, being in itself devoid of any real-world relation and depending solely upon tradition, not bring about the cognition of its meaning—such that another relation would have to be postulated?
For this very reason, the postulation of a relation in the form of a "power" (śakti) based on the otherwise inexplicability of the comprehension of meaning is also refuted. [Power...]

Since the comprehension of meaning is possible through the power of convention alone even without [an eternal] connection, that which is asserted— namely, "the relationship is established by three means of valid cognition"— is thereby refuted. This is because the specific cognition of those [meanings] is restricted [to their respective conventions], just as in the case of [specific] objects.
B. ca—added. B.
the relation is equal. 4B. because of its existence.
All-tök: The Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā (1.236)

And that word, when observed to be employed with certain intended meanings and not otherwise observed, produces a cognition through the two processes of observation and non-observation—just like smoke and so forth. This is the relationship known as "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*). Nor do we perceive the efficacy of anything else in this regard.

Furthermore, the relationship between word and object belongs to no other; since there is no difference [between them], they are themselves that [relationship]. There is no other way for a real entity [to exist]. (239)

Because the establishment of another state is based on a difference in form, that very form would remain the same; however, there may be a difference in attributes according to the sequence previously described, and that is indeed non-contradictory, but it is not a difference in the substance itself. There is no other possibility for a thing apart from difference and non-difference.

Because that object possesses its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and because this [word] does not transcend conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, that word is observed to be employed by persons with a specific intention—that is, with the intention of communicating a particular meaning—at the time of convention (*samaya*); it is not observed otherwise. Thus, it is not observed when employed in a manner contrary to the intended meaning. These—
Positive and negative concomitance have not been explicitly stated.
(238) Thus, through the aforementioned observation and non-observation, it produces the cognition of that object, just like smoke and so forth.
That very relationship between word and meaning, known as inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), is indicated by the terms "observation" and "non-observation. It is not...

Furthermore, we do not perceive the efficacy of any other real (vastubhūta) relation—apart from the aforementioned invariable concomitance (avinābhāva)—in producing cognition here. Nor do we perceive any means of establishing, nor any ground for the establishment, of such a relation.
Thus, having stated the fault in the admission of a distinct relation between the two related entities, [the author now addresses] the admission of their non-distinction as well.

He states the fault: "Now," and so forth. "By those two" means that when there is no difference between the relation and its relata, then those two relata alone are the word and the object; thus, there is no such thing as a "relation. If it is argued that the relation will therefore be something devoid of both identity and difference, he says: "Not from this," and so forth. From this, [the alternatives of] identity and difference...
There is no other possible state for a thing than this.

The explanation begins with "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth. "Difference in form" (*rūpabheda*) means difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*). This is because another determination is based upon that;
that is, it is the basis for the determination of another intrinsic nature. As for that which is not of a different form, but rather has that very form as its related form—
The entity called "relation" is precisely what is desired by us; it must be that very thing itself. It must have the very nature of the related entities and nothing else.
If one asks, "How then does the cognition 'the relation of these two' arise?", he says: "But the distinction between properties (*dharma*) would be merely conceptualized.

This is based on the distinction between exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), following the previously mentioned sequence established through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). And that distinction between exclusions—

That which is constructed by conceptual thought is not contradictory even in a single entity; however, a real distinction (*vastubheda*) is not non-contradictory in one place, but is indeed contradictory. Because multiplicity is impossible for a single thing in the ultimate sense, there is no other way for a real entity (*vastu*) than difference and non-difference. [B] Statement: 7. Consideration of the Non-human Authorship (*apauruṣeya-cintā*).
Because the nature of a real entity is distinct, the relationship is created by conceptual construction;
this was stated previously. For a relationship characterized by conjunction is not possible between entities that are not conjoined.
Nor does the relationship between those two constitute a separate entity. Thus—
How could that which is dependent on another be a real substance, or how could it be the relation of something else? (240)

For that which is already established does not depend on another; nor is a relation independent [of its relata]. What is called "substance" is an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). How could that be a conjunction with an extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*)? There is no such thing as one thing being conjoined with another through the existence of a different intrinsic nature. If it is argued that while there may be no conjunction with what is unjoined, there might be conjunction with what is joined, we say: no.

For one who would conjoin those two, conjunction with them is impossible for that very [entity]. Therefore, if these two were to be conjoined by means of another object (arthāntara), how could that be so? Because that entity is characterized by form (rūpa) and characterized by intrinsic nature (svabhāva). And because this form does not transcend conceptual construction (vikalpa)—that is, it does not transcend the conceptual constructions of difference and non-difference—the nature of the entity is distinct from the referent of a word (śabdārtha).

Regarding the essential nature [of the relation]: it has been stated previously that the relation characterized by conjunction (*śleṣa*) is not real (*bhāvika*), but is rather produced solely by conceptual construction (*kalpanākṛta*).

This was expressed in such passages as: "Due to the habitual practice of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), even though those two are unconnected, they appear as connected; on account of this, the establishment of the relation occurs," and so forth. For a relation characterized by conjunction is not a state of mutual intermingling between the two related entities.

A relation is possible only among word-meanings that are distinct and unconnected. Because the forms of words and their meanings are fused, he says that the relation is a third entity, a different thing altogether. Regarding the phrase "And not," etc. (236):
since that other entity would have to be already established, how could it be dependent on anything else? How could it be dependent upon a relation?

Furthermore, a relation is held to be dependent upon [the related terms], because it resides in two things (*dviṣṭhatvāt*). Nor is it logical for a relation to be a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), since a relation consists in the mutual contact (*paraśleṣa*) [of those entities]. Thus he says: How could a substance or a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) be the relation of another related thing? (154a)
By this, both points asserted by the opponent—that the relation, being a distinct entity, is dependent upon the related terms and that it consists in a mutual conjunction—have been refuted.
To the question, "Even if it were a distinct entity, why would it not be dependent on others? he says: "For not," and so forth; because it is not...

For that which is already established does not depend on another, because that which is already accomplished has no further expectations. Since it is independent, there can be no relation with anything else.

Nor is it logical for a relation to be a separate entity (*arthāntara*), because "substance" (*dravya*) is said to be an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and thus it is said to be a distinct category of thing (*padārthāntara*). How then could it be a conjunction of two related things belonging to other natures?

It might be so; it could not be so at all; nor does it serve as a cause for conjunction. What is the reason? Because by the existence of a third intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), no other nature of the two related entities becomes what is called "conjoined. An entity that is unjoined—that is, unrelated—cannot become conjoined by means of something called a "relation" which is itself unrelated. If it is argued that it would become conjoined by means of something that is already conjoined:

This is not so. What is the reason? Because that very thing called the "relation" would then be conjoined with those two related entities; thus there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since there is no distinction [between the relation and the relata]. Furthermore—
Since phonemes are devoid of meaning when conceived as parts of words and so forth, how can there be an operation upon a real entity by means of this relation to that real entity? (241)

For that which possesses the capacity to denote would be a denoter by virtue of its verbal component. Even if phonemes (*varṇa*) were denoters, the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*) does not exist among them, because if that relationship were to reside in them, it would entail the loss of their own essential nature (*svarūpahāni*).
If it is argued that the phonemes themselves are the denoters through a specific sequence (*kramaviśeṣa*), [the following applies].

Because of [the impossibility of] establishment: if a relation, once created, were to join those two related entities, then there would be the consequence that "this is that," and so forth. If the two related entities were joined by a third entity as a different object, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for everything would be joined with some third thing, since there is no distinction. For it is not the case that only that which is intended to be related [is joined] with another object-entity, and not anything else.
There is no distinction whatsoever in the case of their being related.

Furthermore, those phonemes which exist as real entities are first of all devoid of meaning; therefore, they are not expressive, and consequently, the operation of the relationship between the signified and the signifier does not occur therein. Since words and so forth possess meaning, the operation of that relationship occurs there.
He says: "It will be so. [The opponent argues: A word or a sentence—constructed from parts such as words, the word "etcetera" (ādi) implying this—might be the expressive signifier.

And when that constructed word or sentence is a non-entity (*avastu*) whose nature is that of a non-entity, how could there be the operation of a real entity (*vastu*), characterized by the relationship between the signified and the signifier, which possesses the nature of a real entity? It could not be at all.

The phrase "he is the designator" (*vācaka*) and so forth is the explanation. For the designator would possess that [meaning]—that is, he would be possessed of the relation—by means of the factor of speech, namely the cause of expression, which is the relation itself. Even though the phonemes (*varṇa*) exist, they do not individually convey the meaning because they lack simultaneity (*sāhitya*). Furthermore, it is observed that no comprehension of meaning arises from phonemes uttered by multiple speakers.
The expressers [of meaning] say:

"Therefore" (*tat*) means that, for that reason, the relationship of signifier and signified does not exist among those phonemes; nor does it exist in their occurrence—that is, in the occurrence of that relationship within those expressive phonemes.
For if there were a [separate] *vṛtti* (function), it would follow that the capacity of the relation to serve as the expressive agent (*vācakatva*) would be lost.

Therefore, it is the phonemes themselves—employed by a single speaker according to a specific order, that is, a specific sequence—that are the expressers; hence, [there is no need for a separate function].
If it is argued that the aforementioned fault remains, it has been said:
"However many letters there are, of whatever kind they are, and whatever capacity they possess for conveying a particular meaning, they convey that [meaning] in exactly that way. (Sphoṭasiddhi 66)
This very point is clarified [by the following verse]:

"Regarding those phonemes which have become subordinate, their conjunction for the purpose of conveying meaning, as well as their sequence and having a single agent, is intended [to be significant]. (Sphoṭasiddhi 70). 7. An Inquiry into the Non-human Origin [of the Veda].

No; for sequence is not a distinct entity [from the things themselves] and thus cannot serve as a differentiator. Since that nature [of the sequence] remains unchanged even when the order is reversed, the cognition would be identical. Furthermore, the claim that sequence is a distinct entity will be refuted later.
And when there exists a sequence based on the nature of the agent and the object,
that observation of sequence by the elders which they employ as a regulator [is the authority].
"Just as things that have been observed to possess efficacy simultaneously are not capable [of acting] in succession,
so too things that are capable in succession would not be capable [of acting] simultaneously.
Furthermore, with respect to the communication of meaning:
"Proximity to something is always necessarily present;
yet, by that alone, the others do not cease to be constituent parts simply because they have departed."
Just as the visarga has no capacity [to cause elision] when there is an intervention,
so too it is not at all capable;
indeed, they are seen to be incapable.
In the same way, the capacity [to denote] others does not exist in mere immediate succession. (Sphoṭasiddhi 71)
"And it is not the case that where there is incapacity in each individual part, there is incapacity for all of them together;
for indeed, the parts of a chariot are seen to be capable of drawing [a load] and so forth.
(86) He states the refutation with the words beginning "No," etc.: "This is not so, because the sequence is not something other than the letters."

Or there may be a difference in meaning. In that regard, in the first position, because sequence is not a different entity, it is non-differentiating—that is, it does not produce distinction—since that which is not distinct from something else cannot serve as a differentiator of its own nature. Consequently, the form of the sequence consisting of the phonemes [in the word] *rasa* is the same as the form in the other sequence *sā*.

Since there would be no distinction [in the letters], the comprehension of meaning would be identical. If, then, the sequence were distinct from the letters, he says: "Even as a different entity. This is because the claim that the sequence is a different entity from the letters will be refuted later; for [the sequence] does not belong to letters that have arisen simultaneously.

Sequence does not exist [as a separate entity], because it is not perceived. Even for things that arise non-simultaneously, sequence is not a distinct entity, because the very fact of non-simultaneous arising constitutes the nature of sequence.
For instance, when people in the world speak of "sequence," they are speaking precisely of non-simultaneous arising.

Therefore, sequence is nothing other than non-simultaneous arising. Furthermore, sequence is not a property (*dharma*) of one of two things that have arisen non-simultaneously, [since it is not perceived] in the cognition of the single [item].

Because sequence is not perceived [as a distinct entity]. Nor is it a property (*dharma*) of both [the preceding and succeeding moments], because both do not exist simultaneously; and how can there be a property of that which is non-existent?

Therefore, he will state that sequence is simply the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the two entities, the prior and the posterior. And even if sequence consists of the forms of the prior and posterior, syllables still do not become the cause for the comprehension of meaning through sequence, because each [syllable] individually does not convey the meaning.
Because of [their] individuality; because of the absence of coexistence; and because it is impossible for things occurring in a fixed sequence to act in combination due to their non-simultaneity.
And [there is] incapacity in all [of them]. B. And.
B. There is no [difference] among the colors.
It might be argued: just as a seed, though not a cause for a sprout by itself, [becomes so] when there is the presence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), [so too...]

Because it is distinguished, it possesses causal efficacy (*kārakatva*). Likewise, although individual phonemes are incapable [of producing meaning], when they are distinguished by a specific sequence (*ānupūrvī*), they become causes for the cognition of meaning.
This is incorrect; for when the final phoneme is uttered—whether accompanied by other phonemes or alone—[the meaning is not perceived].
What is the distinction such that the presence or absence of the cognition of an object would depend upon it?
Is it not the case that this very distinction is whether they are combined or uncombined?
True; however, their combination indeed consists in their performing an effect. And when they exist, they do not [simply] exert activity—
[This is] because [the letters] are individually incapable of producing the cognition [of the word], nor because they do not exist at the time of the other letters.

If you say that this is the distinction—namely, that in some cases there is a prior apprehension of the preceding letters, while in others there is not—this too is not sound. For a prior apprehension of the preceding letters, even if it has occurred, cannot affect the final letter, since [at the moment of the final letter's production] it does not exist.

Furthermore, in a case where there is no distinction regarding an effect, if the individual phonemes lack the capacity, then even when combined they likewise lack it—just as blind people cannot see the sun. Therefore, the argument that "where there is no capacity individually," and so forth, is refuted; for it is only when a specific transformation has occurred in the parts of a chariot that [they produce the effect].

In the state of their combination, there is capacity for conveying [meaning] through the process of carrying [the cognition]; otherwise, just as with each individual letter, there would be no capacity even in their combination.

Nor is there a mutual relationship of cause and effect between the letters such that the preceding letters could be capable of contributing to the comprehension of meaning through a traditional succession. Nor is it the case that the final letter, accompanied by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding letters, [comprehends the meaning].

The preceding phonemes possess efficacy through a successive causal chain; for the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the experience of the phonemes serves as the cause of recollection only with respect to those very phonemes, not with respect to the object. Indeed, a latent impression deposited by the experience of a cow does not produce a recollection of a horse.

Nor can it be argued that the preceding phonemes are the cause [of the cognition of the object], because the cognition of the object is observed only when there is the perception of the final phoneme accompanied by the latent impressions deposited by the preceding phonemes.

Because there is no cognition of meaning in the absence of convention (*saṃketa*). And since convention has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, not the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phoneme (*varṇa*), how could phonemes be expressive through a particular sequence?
Furthermore, if a single phoneme alone does not convey meaning, it cannot do so even when accompanied by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

That might be so; however, since no distinction [between the letters] arises, how can it be said that one letter is capable of conveying the meaning directly while another is so only through a succession? As for what has also been said:
"In this way, there is either a simultaneous existence of those letters grasped in sequence, or..."
"Therefore, she [the phoneme] would be the eternal cause for our cognition of meaning.
Thus, because the phonemes perceived in succession are eternal and all-pervading, their simultaneous existence in the locus of space is precisely the instrumental cause for the cognition of meaning.

That is incorrect. For it is the perceived [word] that conveys the meaning of a word, not its mere presence; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of conveying the meanings of all words simultaneously. Furthermore, simultaneity does not appear among words produced by a single agent, nor is it logical for them to possess eternality and omnipresence, as he will explain later; thus, this argument is devoid of substance.
And as it is also said:

"Alternatively, that subsequent cognition of all the phonemes which occurs after the preceding [phoneme] has been perceived among those not previously known, is the cause of the cognition of their meaning."
And in that cognition, the simultaneity of the phonemes is perceived;
yet it need not necessarily arise through simultaneity residing in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

That cognition which has all the phonemes as its object—arising from the subsequent [cognition] "that which follows" through the reflection upon the preceding and succeeding [phonemes]—is the comprehension of the meaning.
The "sign" (nimitta) would be the communication of the meaning; that is to say, the communication of the meaning could occur even by another [means] through simultaneous cognition—this is the sense.
This too is incorrect, because sequence is indeed brought about by the speaker, not simultaneity. It is brought about by the speaker...
Furthermore, since meaning is understood from both stationary and fleeting phonemes, there could be no simultaneous comprehension of meaning [from them].

Moreover, if there were a simultaneous apprehension of phonemes that occur in succession, it would result in the fallacy of error; yet such simultaneity does not exist for them, as it is incompatible with their eternity.

"Furthermore, some say that this cognition is multiform (*citrarūpā*) and has both existent and non-existent phonemes as its object— that cognition by which the final phoneme is grasped at every word" (Sphoṭasiddhi 11).
That cognition by which the final phoneme of each word is grasped [is so called] because it has as its object both the proximate and non-proximate phonemes.
Some say that it has both forms, consisting of both recollection and perception;

but that too is incorrect, because it is contradictory for a single cognition to have both perceptual and non-perceptual forms. Furthermore, perception alone cannot have both existent and non-existent things as its objects, because that would contradict its having non-existence (*abhāva*) as an object. Nor can it be of the nature of recollection regarding a present [object].
Because it is not desired as an object [of cognition]. For this very reason, the cognition that grasps the word and so forth would have a constructed (kalpita) object.

Others, however, maintain that when the final phoneme is fully cognized, there arises a recollection—produced by the awakening of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) deposited by the experience of the preceding phonemes—which causes the meaning to be understood with respect to all the phonemes. Thus he says:

For they all maintain that when consciousness reaches its final moment, there occurs a simultaneous recollection of all the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) produced by them. If it is asked how there can be a simultaneous recollection of things experienced sequentially, he says: "In this way, for all objects, there is a mental [recollection] according to all proponents. (155)
A simultaneous cognition of the collection [of phonemes] is desired, even though cognitions of them occur sequentially.
(Sphoṭasiddhi 113) Therefore, although there is first a sequential cognition of the phonemes by means of the ear and the mind, subsequently a simultaneous recollection occurs.
If phonemes were not expressive, then the word (*pada*) and so forth would have to be the expressive unit.
(Refutation of the Grammarians' position:
That being the case, if phonemes were not expressive, then the word and so forth would have to be the expressive unit; yet that [word] is nothing [in itself]. [Because it is] distinct—
Because identity and difference are mutually exclusive,

therefore that locus which appears as a single manifestation— consisting of the error of conceptual appearance based on the appropriation of homogeneous latencies and following upon the distinctions of sensory cognition— is indeed false, because unity and plurality are incompatible. [This applies] to a cognition that is manifold.
"The classes [of sounds] mounted upon that [phoneme] are not far from the comprehension of meaning;
therefore, the cognition of meaning arising from the word is designated as 'conventional' (laukika) by worldly people."

This too is incorrect; for since [words] convey meaning only when employed by a single agent, they convey meaning only when occurring non-simultaneously. Furthermore, simultaneity is not apprehended among the phonemes that are objects of memory, because they are remembered only in a fixed sequence. Nor is there a clear grasping of the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the phonemes through memory, as occurs in perception.

Because there is no appearance [of external phonemes], and because it is impossible for a single [cognition] to possess multiple forms—both clear and unclear—it is merely by means of memory that phonemes, which are inherently unclear and consist of their own internal forms, are determined (*adhyavasāya*) as non-different from external phonemes; thus, it is said that external phonemes alone are the signifiers (*vācaka*). And regarding those phonemes which are not external, through the determination of them as external phonemes, [the status of] words (*pada*) and so forth [is established].
This is accepted by us as being merely imagined (*parikalpita*).

Thus, in the Mīmāṃsaka position, once the expressiveness of phonemes (*varṇa*) has been refuted, the word (*pada*) and so forth are likewise refuted, because the word and so forth do not exist apart from the phonemes and the like. As it has been said:
For there exists no word distinct from the phonemes (varṇa),
nor does anything exist as a sentence distinct from both phonemes and words.

Now, in order to refute the position of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*) that words and so forth exist apart from the phonemes (*varṇa*), he says: "That is non-existent" (*tadasat*). The word "that" (*tat*) is used for the purpose of introduction, or it carries the sense of "therefore. If the phonemes were not expressive, then the word and so forth would be the expresser; however, that word and so forth do not exist at all. What is the reason? Because [the word] is distinct from the phonemes...
Because there is a contradiction between being distinct and non-distinct: if it were distinct, there would be the perception of it as a separate entity, since it is perceptible;

even if it were imperceptible, it would lack the capacity to signify, because that which is not apprehended cannot function as a communicator. Furthermore, if it were non-distinct, the consequence would be a lack of signifying power, just as in the case of individual phonemes.

Therefore, for this reason: auditory consciousness—which is a specific type of sensory cognition, more acute in its grasping of sequential phonemes, and which follows upon that [sensory perception] having arrived by way of the experience thereof—has as its material cause (*upādāna*) a homogeneous latent impression (*sabhāgavāsanā*), meaning a capacity for a conceptualization of a similar kind.
It is called such because it is a conceptualization whose material cause is a homogeneous latent impression. And of that [conceptualization]...

The delusion of appearance: the very error of manifestation—the word and the sentence appearing as a single unit—is indeed false, because sequential apprehension is impossible. It cannot be grasped by a single [cognition], since it is apprehended according to the sequence of phonemes.
Even in the apprehension of a single phoneme, there is an intermingling of multiple cognitions, because cognitions are momentary; for a moment—

This is what is meant: the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which arises subsequent to the experience of the letters in their sequential order, determines those letters as having a single nature in the form of a word (*pada*) and so forth; thus, the conceptual construction (*parikalpita*) of a word and the like is indeed false.
Now, one might object: since the letters are experienced only as distinct from one another, how can a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arise that manifests as a single word or the like?
And it does arise. Therefore, one must experience the phonemes as a single word and so forth.

This is not a fault. For at the time of establishing the convention, the communicator—having already understood the sequence of phonemes in the form of a single word and so on—establishes the convention for another person by saying, "This is this word," and so forth. And at that time, for the other person as well, regarding that sequence of phonemes...

A cognition superimposing a single word arises. And for that person, whose mental impression (*saṃskāra*) has been deposited by the experience of a single form superimposed upon that single word and so forth, there occurs at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), upon hearing the sequence of phonemes, the production of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a single form, such as "this is one word" or "this is one sentence. In this way, from successive speakers, there is the attribution of unity to the sequences of phonemes.
Since cognition occurs in this manner, the linguistic usage of words and so forth is beginningless (*anāditva*).

For this very reason it is said: "The delusion consisting of the appearance of conceptual construction, which possesses beginningless homogeneous latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is false; the word and the sentence appear as a single [entity]. And their falsity consists in the fact that distinct phonemes (*varṇa*) are perceived in the form of a single word and so forth.
Because it appears in the cognition of the battle, and because it is impossible for that [cognition] to possess both unity and multiplicity due to their mutual contradiction.
Now, it might be argued: "Since a single word or the like is grasped by direct perception, how can it be false?

This is incorrect. For a word or the like is not indeed a single entity. Why? Because it is impossible for it to be grasped sequentially by a cognition that apprehends the sequence of multiple phonemes. For if it were a single entity, it would be grasped all at once by a single cognition; it could not be grasped by a single cognition [only] sequentially.

If it is argued that "the apprehension of words and so forth occurs through cognition," he replies: "Not by a single [cognition]," and so on. That [word and so forth] is not to be grasped by a single cognition.
What is the reason? Because words and sentences are apprehended according to the sequence of phonemes—that is, by means of the succession of phonemes.

[Objection: "In that case, a word would be graspable by a single cognition because it consists of a single phoneme. To this, he says: "Even a single phoneme," and so forth. Even at the time of the production of a single phoneme, it is not [grasped] by a single cognition, because multiple cognitions pass away [in that interval]. For instance, when "bhāg" is uttered, the vowelless letter *ga* is perceived as lasting for half a mora (*mātrā*), whereas the letter *ga* with its vowel is perceived as lasting for one full mora. Thus, how [could it be grasped by a single cognition]?

There exists no word-form consisting of phonemes (*kavarṇya-rūpa*) that could be grasped by a single act of cognition. Therefore, it is said: "Even with the slightest effort, when a sound is uttered, the intellect either does not grasp it at all, or it grasps the phoneme entirely and clearly."

And [the claim] that "the parts of a phoneme are nowhere perceived separately" is refuted; for, by the reasoning already stated, a phoneme possesses parts. Furthermore, there can be no simultaneous apprehension of the successive portions of a phoneme by a single cognition, because cognitions are momentary.
And because it takes the time required to traverse a single atom, there would be no end to the division of that which possesses parts, even if [the atoms] were increased.
Because the time required for the production of an extracted phoneme (*varṇa*) consists of the duration of many atomic displacements and eye-blinks, memory also belongs to that same duration;
for memory occurs in accordance with the experience, and since no distinction is perceived between the sequence of experience and the sequence of memory, a single word or the like does not exist.
This is because cognition appears as non-different, and because its multiplicity will be refuted later. Therefore, it is not a real entity (*vastu*).
It might be argued: "In as much time as it takes for the completion of the phonemes (*varṇa*), that duration constitutes a single moment (*kṣaṇa*);
therefore, the apprehension of the word (*pada*) will occur by means of a single cognition. To this, he says: "Because a moment... and so forth.
A moment is so called because its duration is equal to the time it takes for one atom (*paramāṇu*) to pass beyond another atom; it is thus devoid of further division.

And that time is logically equivalent to the duration required for the passing of a single atom. For if one were to accept a *kṣaṇa* longer than the aforementioned time, it would be impossible for a *kṣaṇa*—which possesses division and is susceptible to division—to serve as the ultimate limit of time.
Therefore, even a single, most subtle phoneme (*varṇa*) is produced over many *kṣaṇas*. What is the reason? Because [it consists of] many...
And so forth. A "moment" (*nimeṣa*) is one in which there is a displacement—that is, a transgression—of many atoms (*aṇu*).

Because it is simultaneous with that [moment], even the final phoneme (*varṇa*), such as the letter *ā*, is completed. Therefore, a word whose form consists of a single phoneme is not grasped by a single cognition; nor is a word consisting of multiple components grasped by memory. What is the reason?

Because recollection occurs according to the experience; just as the experience of the phonemes occurs in a sequence, so too does the recollection occur sequentially therein, and thus the recollection is also simultaneous with that [experience]. This is because its time is the very same as the time of the sequence of the experience.
And this has been stated with reference to another type of activity; however, in an activity characterized by practice (*abhyāsa*), even for those things experienced in sequence...

Although the simultaneous recollection of the phonemes occurs, nevertheless, because no distinction is perceived between the sequence of experience and the sequence of recollection, there is not a single word or the like. Therefore, this is the meaning: (1) since no distinction—that is, no difference—is perceived between the sequence of phonemes that appears in experience and the sequence of phonemes that appears in recollection, how could it be one?
It is said that a word or the like is grasped by a single cognition;

nor is it many. What is the reason? Because the cognition appears as non-different. Since the cognition, which takes the form of a word or a sentence, appears as non-different—that is, as a unity—this is so when a word or a sentence is uttered.
The common worldly understanding is that this [phoneme] is both a word (*pada*) and a sentence (*vākya*).
Therefore, it is said:
"Because of its rapidity and because the difference between them is slight, that [notion of being a word] might indeed occur in the case of the word 'cow' (*go*)."

The claim that "in words such as *devadatta*, a clear difference [between the phonemes] is perceived" (*Sphoṭasiddhi* 121) is refuted; for it is only after the experience of the individual phonemes that a cognition arises which superimposes them onto a single word, and because the multiplicity of those [phonemes], as well as the multiplicity of words and so forth, will be negated later on.

Because it does not transcend these conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), how could a real entity (*vastu*)—which is the relation—be its substratum? For that which is to be supported would be impossible. Thus, it would be without a substratum; and if so, it would be without a relation.
Therefore, the relation between word and meaning is not intrinsic (*svābhāvika*). [It is] produced from the application of the speaker's intention (*tad-abhiprāya*).

Or, if the word is manifested, its relationship with that [meaning] is one of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). And whether that [relationship] is based on origination or manifestation, since it rests upon non-deviation and is dependent on a person (*pauruṣeyī*), the relationship is indeed personal (*pauruṣeya*). Furthermore, regarding the communication of meaning by words through that [relationship], there is no fixed necessity; thus, even if [the Veda] were impersonal (*apauruṣeya*), that same deception would remain.

A word or the like is not indeed manifold. "That" means therefore: because it appears as both one and many, and because being one and many is contradictory and thus impossible, the word or the like is not a real entity (*vastu*). Alternatively, that word or the like is not a real entity; the sense is that it is impossible for it to be either one or many. What is the reason? Because that real entity cannot transcend these two alternatives. For a real entity is of a single nature.

It would have to be of multiple forms, or it might at some time be [one way], but it cannot be of both forms due to contradiction. Furthermore, the opponent maintains that the relationship between word and object is a real entity (*vastu*); how then could that [relationship] have those [words and objects] as its substratum? It would have to have words and sentences—which are non-entities—as its substratum. This is the analysis of the compound: "that which has those words and sentences as its substratum. What is the reason? Because, due to their non-existence, words and so forth are unfit to serve as a substratum. Thus—

In the absence of a basis for that [relation], the relation would be without support; and thus, due to its lack of support, the relation would be non-existent, because it lacks dependence upon the relata. Since this is so, the relation between word and meaning is neither innate nor non-human (apauruṣeya); rather, it is human (pauruṣeya).

This very [relation] is to be understood as follows: because the word arises from that—namely, from the "activity at the end of the utterance" (prayogānta-parispanda) of one who intends that, i.e., who intends to convey a meaning;

this has been stated according to our own view. Or, if it is held that the word is manifested, this has been stated according to the view of others. It is non-deviant; that is, it is non-deviant in conveying the meaning. Thus, by virtue of its being such, it is the reality (tattva).

The relationship of this word is its being produced by the intention to convey a meaning, because a word is employed with the intention of conveying a meaning. And that [intention], whether as the production or the manifestation of the word, is the basis for the non-deviation of the word toward the conveying of meaning; it is the cause of non-deviation, being human—meaning created by a person. Thus, the relationship is indeed human-made.

Regarding the word and its meaning: since there is no restriction on words in conveying a meaning through that [connection], namely, by means of the aforementioned relationship, even if words are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), this same deception—that is, inconsistency—remains. Thus, the implication is that the postulation of the non-human origin of words is indeed useless. (241–242)

The Mīmāṃsakas also maintain that the Vedic sentences are of non-human origin (apauruṣeya), on the basis of the mark (liṅga) of the non-recollection of any authors or composers of the Veda. The word "kila" is used to indicate that this [position] is improper.
The explanation beginning with "yāpi" [is as follows]: the author of many things is not remembered; yet they do not [cease to exist] merely because of that.
[These are] things that have been produced, such as ruined wells and the like. In the same way, this authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatā*) is also illogical due to the deviation of the reason (*hetu*).
Jaimini describes it [as being so] because no author of the Vedic sentences is remembered. For such a matter as this, there are indeed [objections], such as... [text fragment].
ga. Not [the case] that it is not of human origin.
Indeed, even its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatā*) is asserted on the grounds that the authors are not remembered;
for this very reason—that the authors of the Vedic sentences are not remembered—it is described as such.
"There are also secondary consequences for this"—fie on such all-pervading darkness! || 242 ||

Our minds are filled with both wonder and compassion as we consider how such a lapse in wisdom could have occurred even for him. Furthermore, others say that the world has been cruelly overrun by predatory beasts; what fault is there in a living being who desires its own welfare?
For instance, the Buddhists remember the authors of the *Aṣṭaka* and other texts, while the followers of Kaṇāda remember Hiraṇyagarbha.

If you argue that their [traditions] are false because they acknowledge such authors, then who now [denies] that those who repeat [the Vedas] do so despite their being of human origin? What is there to say here? It is simply a pervasive darkness; for indeed: (1)

Our mind is filled with both wonder and compassion regarding Jaimini, who—on account of the non-recollection of an author—asserted that [the Veda] is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). How could such a lapse of wisdom have occurred even for him? Thus, our mind is moved by wonder and compassion. It is filled with wonder because even one so learned can exhibit such a play of ignorance; it is filled with deep... [compassion].

It is not out of compassion that [the author] says "sentient beings are not tormented by the bond of ignorance"; rather, it is said out of ruthlessness toward those others, such as Kumārila and his followers, who nowadays consider themselves investigators and thus repeat this very point. "By which darkness the world—the universe—is pervaded" refers to that which is thus described; "fie upon that all-pervading darkness! For here, it is ignorance alone [that is meant].

Reproach is appropriate for the speaker, not for the living being. For what fault is there in the living being who, though thus addressed, was deceived by a desire for his own welfare—that is, deceived by the desire to attain what is beneficial—and was thereby contradicted? Rather, this is the fault of ignorance alone. Furthermore, what lapse of wisdom is there on the part of one who speaks in such a manner?

Because this proof is both unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Regarding that which is unestablished, he says: "For thus," and so forth. Buddhists remember the authors of the Veda, such as Kaṇṭhaka and others; by the word "and others" (*ādi*), [he refers to] Vālmīki, Vāmadeva, Viśvāmitra, and so on. Hira...

The followers of the Nyāya school remember Brahmā as the author of the Veda, while the Vaiśeṣikas remember Hiraṇyagarbha. Consequently, the [Buddhist] argument that "there is no recollection of an author" is unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, for those Buddhists, this doctrine of recollecting an author of the Veda is a false claim.

If you argue that it is because of the reason for its establishment [that the Veda is not human], then what other word besides the Veda is now considered of human origin? None whatsoever is of human origin.
This is the meaning: "In this way" means if the doctrine of the author's recollection were false. Clarifying this very point, he says:

"In the *Kumārasambhava* and so forth," etc. In works such as the *Kumārasambhava*, when Kālidāsa and others designate themselves or another as the author or composer (*praṇetṛ*), if they were thus refuted (*prativyūhyeran*), [they would be rejected]. Refuted...

17. What is the refutation (*prativyūha*) regarding the consideration of [the Veda] being non-human-authored (*apauruṣeya*)? It is as follows: those who designate themselves or another as the author (*praṇetṛ*) in works such as the *Kumārasambhava* would offer a refutation in this manner. If you argue that in such a refutation there is a contradiction with what has been accepted (*abhyupeta-bādha*), then is it not precisely this very [point] that has been accepted?

What objection is there to the phrase "pagamaṇḍagam" (the circle of tradition)? That [objection] applies equally to the other [party] as well. If it is argued that there is no fault because that [tradition] is accepted [by us], then from where did this acceptance of his originate, being itself devoid of any authoritative basis? Furthermore, why would he, who accepts it so abruptly, ever require a formal proof—such that he would trouble himself with considerations of whether [the source] is human or non-human in origin?

Therefore, if one seeks to avoid the contradiction of contradicting what has been accepted [by oneself], then this applies equally to the other case as well; thus, there is no valid objection. [The objection] "Your claim is false, for you are not the authors [of these works]"—in that regard, regarding the refutation of an author for works such as the *Kumārasambhava*, there is the contradiction of contradicting what has been accepted, because works like the *Kumārasambhava* have been accepted as being of human origin.

Objection: But surely this very fact—that there is no recollection of an author—is a factor (*aṅga*) and a proof for accepting the non-human origin [of the Veda] according to the aforementioned reasoning; and since that [lack of recollection] exists in the *Kumārasambhava* and so forth, how can the *Kumārasambhava* and other such works be intended by you to be of human origin?
What, then, sublates what? Response: Even though the reasoning is equal, if one maintains that an author for the *Kumārasambhava* and so forth is denied...

This constitutes a contradiction of what has been accepted. This very contradiction of what has been accepted applies equally to the opponent, even the proponent of the Veda, regarding the rejection of an author for the Vedic sentences. Since that proponent of the Veda accepts the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedas, there is no fault even in rejecting an author, because authorlessness is what he accepts. If it is argued that there is no fault of contradicting what has been accepted, [the question remains: from where does this [fault] arise?

For the proponents of the Vedas, prior to the examination of whether the Veda is based on a source or an author, there was this very position—the acceptance—that "the Veda is indeed not of human origin. This was without proof, being devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, when the non-human origin of the Veda is accepted, the lack of remembrance of an author is stated as the proof; however, since the defect just mentioned applies to that [lack of remembrance], it is without proof.
This is the *Iṣṭi* [chapter].

Now, the proponent of the Veda (*vedavādin*) has accepted the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Veda without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, who indeed is this Mīmāṃsaka who grasps things arbitrarily—that is, a grasper who acts without reasoning—and how much less could he possibly distinguish between that which is human-originated and that which is non-human-originated?

At the outset, a proof requires a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By stating "that which... and thus introducing the consideration of whether [the Veda] is of human or non-human origin, he establishes himself through the presentation of arguments for its being either human or non-human. For if one were to accept whatever is illogical, let him proceed in that very manner in all cases; why should he trouble himself by introducing means of valid cognition in some instances? This is the general meaning.

Therefore, since the Vedavādin accepts the authorlessness of the infinite Veda as his reason, even when he refutes the existence of a creator of the Veda, there occurs a sublation of what is not [otherwise] accepted; and for that very reason, the same applies to anyone other than the Mīmāṃsaka.

For one who maintains that the doctrine beginning with "the birth of the Puruṣa from Kumāra" is authorless (*apauruṣeya*), the same refutation applies even when rejecting its author; thus, it is not a valid objection. The meaning is that in that case of rejecting [the author], there is no such objection as "contradiction of what has been accepted.

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "one who perceives no excellence," this refers to [arguments] such as "because the author of such types [of works] is not remembered," and so forth, which [support] the authorlessness—

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: he perceives no distinction between the sentences of those who assert that [certain works] are human-authored and those who assert they are not, even though both types possess the same defects of proof (*ruṣayatvasādhanānām*).
For instance, just as there is a non-remembrance of the author for many human-authored works whose authors have long since passed away, so it is with these.

Furthermore, this person, who perceives no excellence [in the Vedas], yet accepts some excellence in certain sentences— whether in the form of proofs for their non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) or as properties of their effects— is acting without conviction.
If it is argued that even those who are diligent perceive artificial [works] whose traditions of practice and constituent parts have been interrupted, we say no; because there is no such rule.
For even elsewhere, perception or non-perception may occur due to the instruction of another, and thus non-perception does not constitute certainty [of non-existence].

Because it is the cause; because it demonstrates that [the Veda] was composed by itself; and because it is impossible to reach a definitive conclusion [regarding its origin]. Thus, the Mīmāṃsaka, perceiving no excellence in the arguments—such as the non-recollection of an author—presented within the Vedic sentences themselves, is one who perceives the distinction [of the Veda's uniqueness]. Or, the properties of words produced by persons are "properties of effects" (*kāryadharma*), following the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with persons.
Observing no distinction among those functional properties— such as being maintained and so forth— in either worldly or Vedic sentences,

this proponent of the Vedas nevertheless accepts a certain excellence or peculiarity in some Vedic word characterized by its non-human origin, yet not in others. Since there is no means of proof for such an acceptance, his conduct is like that of one who speaks without conviction, as if it were merely the wind.
Thus, according to the method stated, the reason "because the author is not remembered" is unestablished (*asiddha*). He also states that it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*):

"And they are seen," and so forth. *Sampradāya* means a lineage of instruction. Those words such as *vaṭe vaṭe vai śravaṇa* for which the lineage of practice and the lineage of human authorship have been interrupted are like that. By this, [the reason] being unremembered—

[The opponent] asserts [the existence of] an author: "They are both produced and of human origin. Therefore, since the non-remembrance of an author exists even in the case of a sentence that is of human origin, this reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). "Those"—meaning those whose tradition of performance has been interrupted—"produced words," [people] who exert effort perceive a person [thinking], "These were made by him. This is not so. What is the reason? Even for one who exerts effort...

Because there is no rule that one must remember the author, and since even one who exerts effort does not necessarily perceive the author, there remains only doubt. Furthermore, in other cases—even regarding words held to be non-human (apauruṣeya)—the author is not perceived; thus [the argument] is inconclusive.
Regarding the perception [of an author]: there is no certainty regarding the perception of an author for this non-human [Veda] derived from any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Rather, it is from the instruction of another—what kind? From one that is untrustworthy and lacks valid authority. And because such an instruction is incapable of determining whether an author is perceived or not, [it cannot establish an author]. This applies even to one who says, "I have composed these Vedic sentences."

The claim that the absence of an author is determined regarding Vedic sentences because no such author is perceived is also not tenable. This is because we observe even those who have composed their own words denying their authorship; having composed words themselves, people are seen to repudiate them, saying, "These were not made by me. In such cases, there is no way to reach a definitive conclusion as to whether these [Vedas] were composed by this person or by another.
Because that is impossible.
(242) Thus, having refuted the reason "because the author is not remembered," there is another proof as well:
"All study of the Veda is preceded by the teacher's own study."
Because it is denotable by the study of the Veda, its study now is like [the study of] the past. (1) 7. Examination of the Non-human Origin:
A. Not Eternity;
(ka) Also not [eternal] because of being preceded by the teacher's study.
Just as this person, without having heard it from another, is not capable of uttering this sequence of syllables and words, so too is any other person whatsoever. (243)
Even regarding the claim that it is "human-made" despite being non-human-made, that very same response would apply. For instance:
"What other work composed by others has been seen, apart from oral tradition, which could be cited such that this [Veda] too might not be inferred in the same way? (244)

He introduces [the following] in order to refute [the opponent's position], stating: "Indeed, there is no basis for [asserting] the non-human origin [of the Veda] other than the capacity [for understanding] derived from the instruction of contemporary people;
and that capacity is equal in another work composed by a single person. Therefore, everything following that [instruction] should be inferred in the same way.
This is introduced with the words "Just as," and so forth. Just as this contemporary student of the Veda [derives his knowledge] from another...

Having heard this sequence of phonemes from someone else's presence, one is not capable of either speaking or studying the sequence of phonemes and words; likewise, any other person who is considered an author of the Veda also requires instruction from another, and that person from yet another—thus, due to its beginninglessness, its non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) is established. Thus says someone. For one who speaks in this manner, that very same [point applies].

This was stated [in the previous section] regarding the non-remembrance of an author. Thus, even if [the Veda] is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) according to the manner just described, would it now follow that every human sentence is also not of human origin? For even in the case of another [text], such as the *Kumārasambhava*, its beginninglessness could be established by proving that its study is preceded by prior study. If you say that establishing this [beginninglessness] for other texts would contradict what has been accepted [by us], [we reply:]...
Is this not indeed the very basis for acceptance? All that has been said [is intended] for this purpose; the word "etcetera" (ādi) is employed to include this very point.

Demonstrating the extreme consequence (atiprasaṅga), he says: "For instance," and so forth. Or another work composed by a person, such as the *Kumārasambhava* and others, [would also be authoritative] even without tradition—that is, without the instruction of others—[if it were] proclaimed or seen by others.
Not even a single instance has been observed. For that reason, since it too is a text other than the Veda, how can it be inferred to be thus—authorless?
He explains this with the words "Certainly not," and so forth: "Certainly not; for there is no basis for authorlessness in anything that possesses authorship."

Furthermore, regarding the signs of accomplishment (*siddhinimitta*), there is no teaching for people of the present day; thus, there is an incapacity for recitation in that regard. Indeed, it is accepted that the Vedic sentences are non-human (*apauruṣeya*) because one is not able to recite this Veda without the instruction of another. And that incapacity for recitation without instruction applies elsewhere as well, even in those works claimed to be human, such as when one person has composed [a work] and another student—
Ślokavārttika, Vākya, 366:
Since this is indeed true, it is thus established.
Nor is there anyone [who would object], because that is not desired by him; and so on, it has been stated: "Because it is desired as its substratum," and so forth. Moreover:
Whatever kind [of effect] is established from whatever [cause], that [cause] is understood to be indistinguishable [from others of its kind], like wood;
even another [instance] whose cause is unperceived is likewise understood to be indistinguishable. (245)

It is not called "causeless" merely because the cause is not perceived; for even those entities whose causes are unperceived are inferred to be of that same nature, as they experience no difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) from others of that kind.
Now, if that nature were not excluded even upon the exclusion of the form of the cause, then there would be a transgression of the property of being an effect.

"Following that" means: whatever [reason] one follows as a proof for non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) because of the inability to teach or recite [the Veda], by that very reason every word—whether worldly or Vedic—is to be inferred as being of human origin. Or rather, no Vedic word [is exempt], because there is no distinction [between them]. This is because, in such cases as "that worldly sentence," it is not established as being of non-human origin. 5

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the sublation of what has been accepted (*abhyupetabādhā*) is included; this was stated immediately prior [in the commentary]: "Because it is the locus of what is intended, because it is the locus for proving the lack of human authorship," and so forth.

(243–244) Furthermore: whatever belongs to a certain class is of the same class as that substance; for which reason, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are established.

By means of two [reasons]: it is understood that even another [instance] which is not distinguished from that by belonging to the same class, though its cause is unperceived, does not arise from that [same] cause.

How so? Like fire and wood. Just as when one fire is perceived arising from fuel, another [fire] of a similar nature, though its cause is unperceived, is likewise understood to have a cause identical to that [first one]. By this, the [status of] the Veda—
He states the sublation of the proposition by inference (*anumāna-bādha*) in the proof of [the world] being a human creation.

He explains [this] with the words beginning "No" (*na*). Because a cause is not observed, it is not called "causeless. The analysis of the compound is: "those for whom no cause is seen" (*adṛṣṭo hetur eṣām iti*). Even though such entities exist, their nature is [different] from other things whose causes are observed.

The meaning is that they are "of similar form" (tulyarūpāḥ) because they do not experience any difference [from one another]. By the phrase "of such a kind" (tathāvidhāḥ), those things which have the same causes as them are inferred.

This is the collective sense [of the passage]: by means of a worldly word, a Vedic word would also possess the same property; thus, like the worldly word, it would either be caused by a person, or else nothing at all [would be so caused].

Now, if it is maintained that even when the form of the cause—that is, the causal nature—has ceased, that form which is identical to the word "person" (*puruṣa*) has not ceased in the case of Vedic speech, then there is a violation of the property of an effect. For this is the property of an effect: that it ceases when its cause ceases. But when, even though the person has ceased, human [agency] persists in Vedic words...

If it were form (*rūpa*), then by that [fact] the property of being an effect (*kāryadharma*) would be excluded. Consequently, due to the exclusion of the property of being an effect, [the argument] beginning with "because of being a means of proof" (*sādhanatva*) and so forth [would fail]. [This concludes] the investigation into the non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

Therefore, one should not say "it would not exist," nor should one point out any specific characteristic of form (*rūpaviśeṣa*) that would correspond to this reason, by which there would be no reversal of the desired and undesired [outcomes].
For even when the intrinsic nature of the cause has ceased, if there were no difference among things, that difference would have to be accidental; thus, it is not [the case].

In some cases, it might cease. Therefore, whatever is observed to arise from a particular nature does not, when occurring elsewhere as well, deviate from its own essence in being an effect of that [nature], just like fire and fuel.
Consequently, there would be no statement whatsoever that is not derived from a person; thus, no worldly word exists in that manner by virtue of being non-human (apauruṣeya).

It must be stated: either a specific feature of form belonging to human [compositions] must be shown as distinct from the Vedic, such that this specific feature of form would conform to the cause known as "person"; by which distinction there would be no reversal of the desired and undesired—namely, that the Veda is desired as being non-human (apauruṣeya) while the worldly [text] is undesired as being human (pauruṣeya), respectively.
Or it may be you yourself [who asserts this]. Furthermore, it has been stated that there is no difference whatsoever in the essential nature (*svabhāva*) between worldly and Vedic [words].
Moreover, even when the nature of the cause called "person" (*puruṣa*) ceases, there is no distinction between the genitive and locative cases;
for example, as in "the branch on the tree" (*vṛkṣe śākhā*) and "the branch of the tree" (*vṛkṣasya śākhā*). Thus, [there is no difference] between Vedic sentences and human sentences.

If it is admitted that they possess an identical nature despite their distinctness, then that distinction among those worldly sentences—this specific quality produced by a person—would be accidental (*ākasmika*), meaning it would be causeless; for that same distinction exists even in Vedic sentences independently of a person. And if that were so, it would never cease, as in the case of space and the like. Therefore, it is not thus. Consequently, that which...

"Nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to that from which something arises; the analysis of the compound is "that of which [something] has its birth from this. Even in other cases where a cause is not perceived, when it is not being differentiated—that is, when it is not being separated from the effect whose cause is perceived—it is seen as having attained the status of being that effect. Existing thus, it does not transcend that status of being its effect by its own nature, by its own form. How so? As in the case of fire—

Like fuel and fire; "fire-and-fuel" (*agnīndhana*) refers to that which is similar to them, meaning like that. Just as fire, which possesses an unobserved cause, does not transcend its status as an effect of fuel when it is perceived as distinct from the observed cause that is the fuel, so too [is the case here]. (244) This being the established principle, one who fails to demonstrate the distinction between worldly and Vedic sentences—[being] ignorant...
Those reasons which are set forth to prove the quality of being authored by a person (*pauruṣeyatva*) are stated in detail, as follows: "Because no author is remembered;
the study of the Veda is preceded by the study of a teacher. (1)

Because it is denotable by the term "Vedic study," the present study is like [past and future studies]. (Vākya-pada 366) Past and future time are devoid of an author of the Veda, because they are time, just as the present time is observed to be.
B. It would not be so;
for in that case, one would not have demonstrated the distinction [between things] by merely observing the commonality of their effects.
All those reasons that are set forth are fallacious. ||246||
Just as the first fire produced by a traveler is preceded by another flame—because it is a fire produced by a traveler—and not preceded by the friction of wood, like a subsequent fire;
how then can there be a deviation regarding the fire produced by a traveler? For [the argument] relies upon the capacity for the emergence of flames, thereby excluding other causes.
It is rejected. For if it were to exist even without fire, it would also exist in other things;

thus, in the absence of a relationship of sublated and sublater between the birth of the flame and that of other things, the fact of being produced from a flame could occur otherwise as well. In this way, regarding two properties in a single object, one should understand that Brahmā and others are not the authors of the Vedas.

"Because of reasons such as being composed by a person (*puruṣatva*), just like ordinary men"—all these reasons are indeed fallacious and inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*, *anaikāntika*). This is because of the observation of a commonality of effect;
for one observes in Vedic words a commonality equal to that of words produced by human effort.
He says that [the arguments] are exclusively based on hearsay: "For example," and so forth;

or rather, "therein," meaning in this formal argument (*prayoga*): "That which is the study of the Veda is preceded by the study of the Veda. "Without showing the difference" means without showing the distinction from a person who is devoid of the manifestation of Vedic activity. Now, the study of the Veda...

In this way, by observing the general nature of the effect characterized as "the study of the Veda"—namely, that it is preceded by the study of the Veda, or likewise by something else—these various types of reasons are elaborated; yet they are all fallacious (*vyabhicārin*). For example, another fire produced by a traveler is not preceded by a previous flame because its cause is unseen, but rather it is preceded by the friction of wood. Why? Because on the road...
Like fire. What is it like? Like fire produced immediately [after another], meaning like fire seen when produced from another flame.
How so, and so forth? Because one relies upon the capacity for the arising of a flame, that is, from the presence of a flame—
Relying on the capacity for a bad birth (*durbhava-sāmarthya*), the alternative cause—the churning of fire-sticks—is rejected in the case of a fire produced by a traveler.

Why? Because if this fire were to exist without a flame, it would also exist in this case; that is, even at the site of the traveler's fire which was preceded by a flame, it would exist without a flame. In that regard, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) in this proof.

[The opponent] is released [from this objection]. How so? Because the production of a flame from something other than a flame—namely, its production from the friction of fire-sticks (*araṇi*)—and the production [of another flame] from that [other flame], these two productions do not stand in a relationship of sublation and sublated with respect to the common nature of fire. For what contradiction is there here that "it would be fire, yet not preceded by another flame"? This being the case, the state of being produced from a flame...
B. Because of their equality [with other causes], there arises the consideration of whether [the Veda] is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

It is suspected that there would be deviation (*vyabhicāra*), such that a particular object—whether it be the fire of a traveler's hearth or something else—would not be restricted to a single [cause]. To this it is replied:
"The introduction of properties that are mutually distinct is not contradictory within the generality of things (*vastusāmānya*). Thus it is said; it is not a matter of [changing] states.

Or [it may refer to] a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*). For it is contradictory that the partless self (*niṣkala-ātman*) could possess that [distinction] or its opposite. Furthermore, there is no relationship of sublated and sublater (*bādhyabādhakatā*) between a flame and something other than a flame in the case of a fire on a road, because there is no absence of the possibility of the latter being produced from the former’s flame. Thus, while it might be the case that a particular fire on a road is produced from a flame, this is not true for all fires; for in that case, it is impossible to exclude the specific distinction.

The form [of fire] might otherwise exist even from the friction of kindling wood (*araṇi-nirmathana*). Thus, since both of these—which possess such characteristics and are capable of arising—are possible within the single object of fire in general, whether it be that fire of a traveler or another, such as the study of the Vedas, [the latter] is restricted to a single [cause], namely, being preceded by flames; whereas the study of the Vedas [is not].

One might suspect that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the claim that [the first fire] must necessarily be preceded by the study of the Veda; for there could be the study of the Veda without it being preceded by the study of the Veda. Likewise, there could be a traveler’s fire (*pathikāgni*) that is not preceded by a flame, because there is no contradiction [in such cases].
One might object: "If [fire] produced from a flame is not produced from the friction of fire-sticks, how is there no contradiction?

To this he says: "That too," and so forth. That mutual exclusion—the occurrence of two mutually contradictory properties characterized as being produced from a flame and being produced from the friction of fire-sticks—is not contradictory within the generality of a thing (*vastu-sāmānya*).

It is said: [this] is not stated to be non-contradictory with respect to a specific fire that undergoes different states, whether it be the production of a flame or its production from the friction of fire-sticks;

rather, it is indeed contradictory. What is the reason? (1) Because there is a contradiction between being that [nature] and not being that [nature] regarding the nature of the partless and undivided self (*ātman*). For, in the case of the production of a flame, its being preceded by a flame and its not being preceded by one are contradictory.

The fact that fire produced from friction must be preceded by the friction-block (araṇi) and cannot be otherwise is contradictory; and even in the case of the general category of "traveler's fire," these two [contradictions] are present. Thus he says: "And not... and so forth.

Regarding the production of a flame and the production of fire by rubbing the friction-blocks—namely, the arising of the traveler's fire within the general category of traveler's fires—there is a relationship of sublation and being sublated. What is the reason?

(1) Because there is no absence of that impossibility which consists in the non-existence [of fire] apart from the production of a flame—that is, apart from the arising of a flame—[it is not the case that all fire arises from a flame]. The meaning is that it exists even from the friction of fire-sticks (*araṇi*) apart from the arising of a flame. However, while such a thing as "the production of a flame" may exist, not every fire occurs without distinction [in that manner].
