• B. Therefore, he says:
* B. "Flame" (*jvāla*)—omitted. B.
"The state of being" (*bhāvatā*).
And because there would be no restriction on its arising in that same state. If it could exist even without the flame, it would have to exist elsewhere as well.
If the causal complex by which it arises were present, then it would necessarily arise. Having demonstrated its existence...
One might describe the absence of intoxication, or demonstrate the presence or absence of a flame therein.

Therefore, the fact that the study of one person was preceded by another does not prove that the same is the case for everyone, because there is no impossibility of its being otherwise. For such a thing would only be so for one who is devoid of fear regarding the performance of that action; thus it is—
Only that which is real should be stated; it is not easy to state something that, while lacking specific qualification, could potentially possess such qualifications.
How is the possibility of a specific distinction established, given that even those persons possess only limited power?

What is the reason for this? (1) In the case of fire, which is differentiated by various causes, there is the rejection of a specific distinction [based on] the particularity produced by the friction of fire-sticks.

Because it is impossible to deny [the causal relationship], for a specific quality produced by the fire-drill (*araṇi*) is possible, and because there is no rule that such a thing must remain in its original state. Furthermore, since there is no necessity regarding the state characterized by being produced from a flame, as it was said: "If the first fire of a traveler were to exist without a flame, then a flame would also exist elsewhere."
"Even in a secluded place, it would occur.

To this it is said: (1) It certainly does occur, provided that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by the friction of the fire-drills (*araṇi-nirmathana*)—by which that traveler’s fire is produced—is present. However, if there were no possibility of such a causal complex...

Having demonstrated the absence of that [smoke], one would state the absence of fire; or else, in a place where the aforementioned causal complex is possible, one would point out a flame. In that case, there would indeed be the property of being preceded by a flame, but this is not so. Therefore, it is not the case that every instance of a traveler's fire is preceded by a flame; thus, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Since this is so, it is not observed that the study of a single person who lacks the power of knowing or performing the Veda is preceded by another—that is, preceded by a teacher—[as if such a rule applied] to everyone; for even in the case of the study of Hiraṇyagarbha and others, their being preceded by another establishes that very state of being preceded by another.
What is the reason? Because there is no possibility of that study occurring otherwise than by being preceded by another.

The meaning is that it would not be possible for one to study [the Veda] after having composed it oneself, because while the capacity for composing the Veda exists in the case of Hiraṇyagarbha and others, there is a contemporary person who is devoid of such capacity— one who is unable to study the Veda after having created it himself. For such a person, who is lacking in that creative power (pratibhā) regarding the act of composing the Veda, the composition of the Veda [is impossible].

The meaning is: "of one who is devoid of a capable intellect. For such a person, whatever study there may be, it would be so—that is, it would be preceded by another study—on this basis. "Of that nature" means: for one who lacks the capacity for Vedic action, whatever study there may be, that alone [is meant]. Thus, the statement should be expressed as being preceded by another study, and not without qualification. As for that study, however...
B. *Tada*—added. 7. Regarding the investigation of the non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*):

[it is] like [the case of] persons. (In this regard) there is no observation of any contradiction between the two capacities; therefore, the application of the non-perception of a contradictory rule is not a means of proof. For it has been stated that there is no cognition of contradiction regarding supersensible (*atīndriya*) matters. Nor is this...
The application (*prayoga*) differs from the previous one:
"If persons were capable [of creating the world], then those of the present would also be so.

This would hold true only if a distinction [between past and present persons] were impossible; however, that is difficult to prove. Where there is the incapacity of one person, [there is no capacity for others].

The claim that "all men possess [the capacity for] such power" is also fallacious, as before. Even in the case of the *Mahābhārata* and other such works, since it is possible for contemporary individuals to be persons of extraordinary excellence, there is the possibility that they composed them themselves and then studied them; thus, the statement that "all study is preceded by another study" without qualification is not established as a universal rule (*vyāpti*) and, being fallacious, does not cast its shadow [of certainty].
[The author] maintains [the position], because it does not establish the intended probandum.
"How so? and so forth is the opponent's question. Having himself established the particular [point], [he asks]: how is the possibility of study by those outside the Veda [accounted for]?
The word *yāvatā* means "at which time" (*yadā*). Even for those persons who are considered to be the authors of the Veda, the Veda—
"Incapacity for composition follows from being a human being, like contemporary humans.

Regarding this, the Ācārya says "atrāpi" (even here). That is, even in this syllogism, there is no observation of any contradiction between the capacity to compose the Veda and the status of being a human being. And therefore—

The fact that Brahman and others possess the nature of a person is stated as a reason [for their authorship] because it is not contradictory; it does not remove their capacity to compose the Veda. Therefore, this is not a contradictory formulation. A formulation of what is not contradictory in a given application of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*)—such an application of non-perception is not a means of certain knowledge (*gamaka*). He asks: "How is there an absence of contradiction? and answers with the words beginning "For not... regarding supersensible (*atīndriya*) objects.

Regarding Brahman and other such entities that are entirely beyond perception, there is no cognition of a contradiction characterized by non-coexistence (sahānavasthāna), precisely because they are supersensible (atīndriya). Nor is there a cognition of a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion (parasparaparihārasthiti), because capacity and incapacity, as well as being a person and not being a person, are mutually contradictory; [therefore], there is no capacity—160a.

The argument is: "Whichever person [is a human], he is incapable of composing the Veda, just like a person of the present day. Nor is this formal argument (prayoga) distinct from the previous one. For the argument—"Whatever study of the Veda there is, it is preceded by a prior study of the Veda, just like the study of the Veda at present"—differs from that previous formulation. Therefore, the intention is that the inclusion of both [formulations] is indeed redundant.
Furthermore, as for what is said: "If men of former times were capable of composing and studying the Veda themselves, then those of the present day would also be so.
To this it is replied: This [objection] would apply only if there were no distinction among men; and that [distinction] exists.

Because there is no possibility of distinction among persons, [the proof] that what is difficult to accomplish can be accomplished is unestablished, since there is no subverting evidence. Therefore, in the proof that "where one person lacks capacity, all persons lack capacity, because they possess the nature of being a person," the logical mark (*liṅga*) of "personhood" is fallacious, just as in the previous case with "being a student" and so forth. What is the reason? Because even in the case of the *Bhārata* and other such works...
Even if contemporary persons lack the capacity regarding those works claimed to be of human origin, the capacity of someone such as Vyāsa may still be established;
for even when some are incapable, the power of another may be proven.
Therefore, one who analyzes the causes must demonstrate a difference in nature (*svabhāvabheda*) between objects that arise from those [causes] and those that do not.

In the absence of that [common nature], everything would either become identical with it or nothing at all. Furthermore, we do not perceive any difference in intrinsic nature between worldly and Vedic sentences; for when such a difference is absent, only their commonality is observed. Thus, when one analyzes some property of one [sentence], [it must be understood] as being possible within its own intrinsic nature.
Fearing a charge of inconsistency, the following argument is made:

"Is there not a distinction characterized by reality between the Veda and what is non-Veda? True. But this distinction exists not only between those two; it also exists between the *Ḍiṇḍika-purāṇa* and other [works]. And yet—
To that extent, a difference in name does not invalidate the illumination of the non-difference of one's own nature, because such a consequence would apply elsewhere as well;
for excellence is established through power.
Therefore, by one who discriminates the causes [of speech], the operation of the palate and other organs of Vedic sentences [is to be understood].

By removing the cause [of confusion], one must demonstrate the difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) among words—both worldly and Vedic—with respect to their objects. Of what kind are these? They are those produced from that [cause] and those not produced from that [cause]. One must show the diversity of intrinsic nature as follows: "The intrinsic nature of causes such as the palate is of this kind, while the intrinsic nature of those that do not have those as their causes is of another kind. In this way, the plurality of intrinsic natures must be demonstrated.

That by which the state of being produced from that or not from that arises through differentiation—if that were absent, and there were no distinction in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*), then everything would be of the same nature as that [cause].
Consequently, every word would be human-made (*pauruṣeya*), or else not even any worldly word at all.
Now, one might argue: "There certainly is a distinction in the intrinsic nature of those two. To this, he says: "And not here," and so forth. Here...

In this world, we observe a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between worldly and Vedic sentences. If that essential distinction did not exist, then since one would perceive only the commonality— the identical form characterized by the sequence of phonemes— between worldly and Vedic sentences, one could not distinguish any specific property belonging to either a worldly or a Vedic sentence.

Establishing the distinction between human authorship (*pauruṣeyatva*) and non-human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*), a person who entertains doubts is described as one whose discourse is subject to deviation (*āśaṅkya-vyabhicāra-vāda*). He is so called because he is a person whose speech is open to doubt. By whom is this [distinction] established? By that which is possible within its own nature—that is, by the arrangement of phonemes and words found in both worldly and Vedic sentences.

By means of the general characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). That is to say, one who asserts the authorlessness of the Veda—which possesses properties identical to those of human compositions—is shown to be fallacious.
Now, it might be argued that there certainly exists a distinction between the Veda and non-Veda characterized by their being the same or different entities; therefore, from that distinction—

The opponent maintains that there will be a distinction between the worldly (*laukika*) and the Vedic (*vaidika*), namely that the former is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*) while the latter is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).
The Teacher [Dharmakīrti] says, "True. But is such a distinction not the very proof for their being of human origin and not of human origin?
For this distinction does not exist only between these two—the worldly and the Vedic; what then? [It exists elsewhere as well, such as in the case of] a *ḍiṇḍika*...

Regarding both the *pūrva* and the *itara*: by the *Ḍiṇḍika* naked teachers, who have composed both the *pūrva-purāṇa* and the *itara-purāṇa*. If such an inquiry into the non-human origin [of the Veda] were conducted—if men were unable to produce such a composition, or if one could distinguish a produced work from its intended convention—then it would be clear that the Veda is non-human (authorless).

But surely, the power to compose mantras belongs only to human beings. We shall examine this further below. Moreover, that which is called a "mantra" is not something distinct; rather, it is the speech of those possessing the power of truth and austerity for the accomplishment of their desired aims. Even today, such a thing is indeed observed among human beings, by virtue of the power of one's own truthful resolve (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).
Because of the neutralizing of poisons, fire, and the like; because of the [neutralizing] of certain Śavaras through the use of mantras;

and because we observe the ritual manuals of mantras belonging to non-Vedic traditions such as the Buddhists and others—and since these are the work of human beings—how could that which is not the work of a person (apauruṣeya) be infallible? For instance, in the Buddhist and other ritual manuals of mantras...

There is indeed a distinction. However, that much does not undermine the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Veda on account of a difference in names or designations (*saṃjñābheda*)—which are merely conventional constructs intended for practical usage and which illuminate the differences in their own internal systems. What is the reason? Because otherwise, it would follow that other Purāṇas are also non-human in origin, since a difference in names exists among the Purāṇas other than the *Ḍiṇḍika*.

If, however, men were unable to produce such an arrangement of letters and words as is seen in Vedic sentences, or if one who has not previously established a convention could distinguish—merely upon hearing—an arrangement of letters and words that has been composed or produced, thinking, "This is preceded by a person," then it would be evident that the Veda is authorless (*apauruṣeya*). [But this is not the case. It is not distinguished.

Since it composes that arrangement, how could the Veda be non-human (apauruṣeya)? [The opponent replies: "But surely," and so forth. We shall examine later that even the mantras are indeed composed by persons. Furthermore, what is called a "mantra" is not something entirely different; rather, it is—as in the passage beginning with "truthful" (*satya*)—that which is according to reality.

Truth is *khyāna* (manifestation). The restraint of the senses and the mind is *tapas* (asceticism). The power (*prabhāva*) of these two refers to the capacity for such things as paralyzing poison; those men who possess this are "those endowed with truth, asceticism, and power. For such men, whose truth, asceticism, and power are present, their very speech is the means of accomplishing their desired goal—that is the definition of a *mantra*. This characteristic of a *mantra* is indeed observed even today among men. What is the reason?

For it is observed that by the power of their respective resolutions regarding truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*), there occurs the neutralization of poison, fire, and so forth, as well as the impairment of their potency; likewise, even today, certain Śabaras who abide by their own observances (*svaniyama*) are indeed still able to compose mantras by means of causes endowed with the power to remove poison and other such things. This is also the case for those outside the Vedic tradition.

"Of others than the Vedas," such as the Buddhists and so forth—by the word "and so forth" (ādi), [the text refers to] the Ārhata, Gāruḍa, Māheśvara, and other mantra-kalpas. This is because of the observation of both mantras and mantra-kalpas. Mantras are the syllables of knowledge (vidyā);
the instructional treatises on the methods for accomplishing them are the mantra-kalpas. And of those mantra-kalpas belonging to the Buddhists and others...
Because they are produced by persons—that is, because they are created by persons—therefore there is no difference in nature between the worldly [mantras] and the Vedic ones.

Regarding the passage beginning with "In that case" (*tatra*), the opponent argues: even in the case of the ritual manuals for mantras belonging to the Buddhists and others, if one were to assume their lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*), how...
Now, while every non-human (apauruṣeya) statement is indeed non-false, it might nevertheless have a false meaning. For instance, [it is said:
"Violence, sexual intercourse, the view of a self, and so forth, are causes for the lack of spiritual welfare," yet they are described otherwise. How then can there be no contradiction?
Could it be that two [properties] reside in one place as a reality?

In that case, if one postulates a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), that would apply equally elsewhere as well. Furthermore, due to such a determination of the object, no individual manifestation (*vyakti*) whatsoever would exist. Consequently, even the apprehension of its being authorless (*apauruṣeyatva*) would be entirely useless.

If it is argued that the status of being a *mantra* does not exist at all for the Buddhists and others, then one must likewise undergo the ordeal of drinking from a vessel (*kośapāna*) in other cases as well.
For even Buddhists are seen to perform rites involving poison and the like; yet even there, the status of being a *mantra* is not prohibited.
Ritual actions are performed through gestures (*mudrā*), mandalas, and meditations (*dhyāna*) that are non-verbal; nor are these [Buddhist practices] of non-human (Vedic) origin.
This is appropriate;

this very point makes it clear: for in the Buddhist ritual manuals (*mantrakalpa*), violence, sexual intercourse, the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*), and—by the word "and so forth"—false speech and the like, are described as causes of non-prosperity and causes of suffering. However, in the other [non-Buddhist] ritual manuals...
For indeed, acts such as violence and their opposites are described as causes for worldly prosperity; and if all ritual manuals (*mantrakalpa*) were of non-human origin,
then how could these two mutually contradictory statements both be true within a single non-human work?

It might be argued that in the Buddhist ritual manuals (*mantrakalpa*), words such as "violence" (*hiṃsā*) have entirely different meanings than those established in the Vedic ritual manuals, and thus they are not in contradiction with them. To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth. That is to say, when one imagines a meaning other than the one established in the Buddhist ritual manual, that imagined alternative meaning would apply elsewhere—in other words, in non-Buddhist [traditions].

Since it is considered equal in the Vedic *mantrakalpa*, and because in all *mantrakalpas* there is no possibility of postulating a different meaning due to the lack of a definitive determination of meaning, there would be no comprehension or performance of the action regarding the meaning established by them. And thus,
in the absence of performance due to the uncertainty of meaning, even an authorless (*apauruṣeya*) statement would be useless with respect to human goals.
If it is argued that Buddhist and other [non-Vedic] mantras do not possess the nature of mantras at all, he says: "Regarding the non-mantra-status of Buddhist and other [mantras].

(161a) Therefore, even in cases other than those Buddhist and other mantras—namely, in order to establish the status of mantra in Vedic mantras as well—one must undergo the ordeal of drinking from a vessel (*kośapāna*). The intention is that there is no individual instance [of a mantra] that exists [which lacks this status]. Furthermore, this [position] contradicts what is observed.

"Buddhist and other [mantras] are not mantras. For indeed, even among Buddhists, mantras are observed that perform acts such as the administration of poison when they carry out the ritual of poisoning and so forth. Therefore, in those Buddhist and other ritual manuals (*mantrakalpa*), the status of being "non-mantra" is also contradicted; for by way of performing acts such as the immobilization of poison, even Vedic [texts] are established as mantras. Nor is there [a lack of efficacy in] the immobilization of poison...
Because of its connection with supernatural powers (*disāmarthya*), it is logical that the Vedic statement possesses a superiority over worldly statements and is therefore authorless (*apauruṣeya*).
For instance: a *mudrā* is a particular arrangement of the fingers; a *maṇḍala* is a specific configuration of deities and so forth;

and *dhyāna* is the mental visualization of the forms of deities and so forth. By means of these—which are non-syllabic and non-verbal in nature—one performs one's own rites, such as the removal of poison and the like.

Characteristics are being established. And it is not logical that those mudrās, maṇḍalas, and meditations are non-human (apauruṣeya). This might be argued: "The capacity of men to perform actions exists only in the case of mudrās and the like, but not in the case of mantras consisting of sequences of phonemes. [Response: Regarding the consideration of their non-human origin—if the performance of those actions is possible, what obstacle is there to the composition of syllables? Therefore, nothing is impossible.
[The efficacy] of these [mantras] is being established.

And how could those two—the mantra-formula arising from truth (*satya*) and that which arises from power (*prabhava*)—be mutually contradictory? Indeed, they do not both arise from truth in every case; there are also those characterized by the declaration of a person endowed with power (*prabhāva*). That power is a specific attainment (*siddhi*) of movement (*gati*).
It might also be the case for both [the Veda and the Purāṇas].
If mantras were of human origin, then why are not all men composers of mantras? [The answer is] because of their deficiency in the means for performing those actions.

If, however, they were endowed with such truthfulness, austerity, and so forth; furthermore, if it were the case that "a person composes poetry," then every person would be a composer of poetry. That is not the case in this context, because when the possibility of action exists for those [signets] such as seals, there is the composition of syllables by those possessing truthfulness and the like.

What obstacle is there for men, given the absence of any distinction? Therefore, there is nothing impossible for these men to accomplish, by which a person, perceiving some uncreated excellence, might postulate a difference in nature between worldly and Vedic [mantras].
If both the Buddhist and other mantra-systems are human compositions and originate from truth, they are non-false.

[The two systems] have arisen from a person who is their designator. How, then, is it now logical that these very two—the Buddhist and the other [non-Buddhist] mantra-systems—should originate from the same source yet be mutually contradictory? For in one case, acts such as violence are shown to be causes for the absence of prosperity (*anabhyudaya*), while in the other, they are shown to be causes for prosperity (*abhyudaya*).

He refutes this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*). It is certainly not the case that those two types of mantras and ritual procedures (*mantrakalpa*) everywhere derive their power solely from truth (*satya*), such that this contradiction would arise.

Rather, those two types of mantras and ritual procedures also have the character of being the assertions of persons endowed with supernatural power (*prabhāva*). By a person possessing such power, it is declared: "For whoever practices this arrangement of syllables and words and performs its prescribed rite, for him I shall [fulfill] the purpose as promised."

The two mantra-calculation systems (mantrakalpa) also possess the characteristics of that vow, "I shall accomplish [this]. Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that even one who speaks otherwise may indeed produce mantra-calculation systems endowed with power (prabhāva). If it is asked, "Since truth (satya) is absent, from what does that power arise?", he says: that power may also arise from specific attainments (gati) and accomplishments (siddhi), as well as from merit (puṇya). From attainment—
That specific excellence is indeed such a particular accomplishment of mantra (*mantrasiddhi*) acquired through the assistance of deities and others, by which such a power comes to be.
If mantras were of human origin, then, because they are human, why would not all men be creators of mantras? (1)

And they do not do so; therefore, the intention is that even those persons who are desired [as composers] did not create the mantras. Regarding the passage beginning with "tat" (that), the Siddhāntavādin states: because of the deficiency in those mantras of the means for accomplishing the action—such as truthfulness, austerity, power, and so forth—not all persons are creators of mantras.
Furthermore, if such persons were endowed with the causes of mantras, such as truthfulness, austerity, and so forth, then they would indeed produce mantras.

"Whatever one has not done oneself, nor even anyone else could ever do"— such is this unprecedented turn of phrase!

True. [It is true that] people do not produce mantras through a deficiency in the performance of ritual acts (*mantrakriyā*). Yet, we do not perceive such completeness (*sākalya*) in anyone, because all persons possess identical characteristics (*samānadharmatva*).
It has been stated in this regard: what is called a "mantra" is nothing other than a statement consisting of a proposition (*pratijñā*) endowed with truthfulness and so forth.
Furthermore, these [qualities] are observed only in certain individuals;

yet it is not certain that all persons are devoid of them, because there is no contradiction in their possible existence. Moreover, non-perception is not a cause for determining the non-existence of things whose nature is perceptible. Nor is there [non-perception of] memory, intelligence, or discernment...
The capacities for truthfulness exist everywhere as potentialities.

Furthermore, if one were to argue that a person creates poetry because they possess the creative intuition (*pratibhā*) for its production, then every person—even one devoid of such creative intuition for its production—would become a poet, by virtue of the commonality of being human. Or, if [poetry] were not produced [by everyone], [then the reason would be inconclusive].

No one else whatsoever would do it either; it is just like that, like a person incapable of composing poetry. This is an unprecedented logical argument (*apūrvā vāco-yuktiḥ*), meaning it is fallacious (*vyabhicāriṇī*). The opponent replies with "True," and so forth: persons who lack the means for the performance of mantra-rites do not perform those mantras.
We do not see that completeness of the mantra, ritual action, means, truthfulness, and so forth, belonging to any single person here;
for all persons possess equal characteristics.
"It has been stated" refers to the *Siddhāntavāda*. Here, the answer to the objection has been stated. What was stated? That it is not the mantra...

"Name," and so forth. "Speech" (*vacana*) and "convention" (*samaya*) form a *dvandva* compound. This is because speech accomplishes the desired aims of persons endowed with truthfulness and other virtues; likewise, it is because of the convention characterized by the pledges (*pratijñā*) of persons possessed of truthfulness and the like that mantra is not something other than names. And those mantras, which are characterized by the specific attainments of truth, austerity, and realization, are the means for accomplishing the ritual actions of mantra.
They are seen only in certain individuals.
It might be argued: "Whosoever is devoid of the means for performing mantra-rites, such as a common street person;
and this person intended as a mantra-author is indeed a person. Even in that case, all persons are likewise devoid of those [means].

The phrase "devoid of the accomplishment of mantra-practices" is also [not a valid reason], because there is no contradiction between the possibility of that—namely, the possibility of the accomplishment of mantra-practices—and being a human being. "Indecision" means lack of certainty. If it is argued that the nature of the accomplishment of mantra-practices is ascertained in the person precisely through the non-perception of its own nature, he says: "And not," etc. "Beyond the senses"—

The meaning is: "in those things whose nature is entirely beyond perception" (*atyantaparokṣa*), that is, in those whose nature has transcended the senses. Non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is not a cause for the ascertainment of non-existence. If it is argued that because one does not perceive the means of mantra-rites, such as recollection and so forth, within oneself, their non-existence is also ascertained in others, he says: "And not... and so on. [This refers to] the recollection of past lives and so forth.

Memory (*smṛti*); knowledge of the minds of others (*mati*); penetration (*prativedha*), which is the vision of the true nature of things not previously perceived; truthfulness (*satya*), which is the state of speaking without deviation; and power (*śakti*), which is sovereign influence (*prabhāva*). These are the causes of the mantras, and they exist in all [mantras]. Regarding the consideration of whether [mantras] are non-human (*apauruṣeya*): just as there are differences in the traditions of their means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), there may also be means for accomplishing other qualities. Nor is it the case that even if [the cause] exists, it exists in its entirety in all [mantras].

It is possible to perceive [this]; therefore, there is no denial of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). Nor is there anyone among men who can obstruct the quality of the mind that desires to arise. This is because the relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) is not established, since the sublated is unperceived. By this, the refutations of an omniscient being and so forth have been answered. In that regard as well, this is the tradition for proving it: [The text continues: ...the tradition for proving it is this...

How could it be logical to claim that for others as well, such a state does not exist? Nor is it correct to say that [memory] is not a cognizer of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). These [mental states] occur within a continuum (*saṃtāna*); therefore, just because they were not perceived by oneself, they should not be rejected in other cases either.
Now, he explains the occurrence of memory and so forth in a particular person alone, with the words "the proof of that" (*tatsādhana*), etc. Of those...
The means (*sādhana*) for the aforementioned [qualities] such as mindfulness (*smṛti*) is their cause of origination; the tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is the instruction regarding that.

Its distinction (*bheda*)—that is, its specific character—is that it occurs only in certain scriptures (*āgama*), not everywhere. Similarly, there may also be means for accomplishing other qualities (*guṇa*);
these would exist only in certain individuals. "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) is the means. Those which are the effects produced by the causes of mindfulness and so forth—

The other qualities consist of memory and so forth. Their means of accomplishment—that is, their production—would occur only in a particular person, due to the performance of the causes of memory and the rest. If it is asked, "If memory and the rest were a means [of perceiving another's mind], why is it not seen?", he replies with the words beginning with "nor" (nāpi). Even though it exists—that is, even though it is present—the mental quality residing in another continuum cannot be perceived.

It cannot be accomplished by a mere person. For this very reason, there is no denial or rejection of the existence of the mental quality (*manoguṇa*) belonging to another unseen continuum (*santānāntara*). Nor is there any sublater (*bādhaka*) who can obstruct the arising of a mental quality that is about to arise in persons, such that it would follow that no one possesses a mental quality superior to other qualities. [This is because of] their humanity (*puruṣatva*).

If it is argued that only a [contrary] property (*dharma*) can be a sublater (*bādhaka*), we say no. Why? Because that quality (*guṇa*) which is to be sublated exists in another continuum (*santāna*), and it is not perceived by a mere person (*puruṣamātra*). Furthermore, the relationship of sublated and sublater cannot be established on the basis of a property such as "being a person" (*puruṣatva*). And that which is not a sublater cannot be rejected.

By this internal statement, there is a negation of that knowledge which pertains to every object. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the negations of those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*) and so forth have already been explained.
Just as omniscience and other such qualities cannot be rejected by means of signs such as being a speaker, so too—in that case as well—is one who is free from passion...
The logical principle that such a person—one endowed with qualities such as freedom from passion (*vītarāga*)—is indeed a negation of [the self] and so forth, is correct.

Of what nature is he? He is one for whom the tradition of the means to achieve those [qualities] is impossible; this is the analysis of the compound: "one whose tradition of the means to achieve those [qualities], such as freedom from passion, is impossible. He is devoid of the methods consisting of the means to achieve freedom from passion and so forth.

The meaning is that the logical principle does not apply such that one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) and so forth cannot exist. Nor is it correct to say, "That which has an unperceived indicator (*jñāpaka*) is not of that nature merely by being seen. This means: it is also improper to state that for one whose indicator—such as the mark (*liṅga*) of being free from passion—is unperceived, he is "not of that nature" merely through observation; that is, his nature would be devoid of qualities such as freedom from passion. For it is not the case that [the absence of the indicator] is merely a non-perception of the indicator.

It is logical that there is an absence of what is to be made known by a series [of signs]. What is the reason? Because it is possible for certain existing things not to initiate an effect that would serve as a sign. Even if an effect were initiated by those supersensible things, it might still fail to manifest due to the intervention of a contrary nature.

Because it is possible for even the wise not to undertake a task, and because [the Veda] cannot be seen due to its remoteness in nature (*svabhāvaviprakarṣa*), the argument that "study is preceded by another study" based on the reason "because of study" is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*). As for the *Bhārata*—
[The opponent argues: "Because [the study] exists when there is meditation (*dhyāna*).

If it is argued that there is no fault because of the qualification 'study of the Veda' (*vedādhyayana*), then what is the excellence (*atiśaya*) of the Vedic study such that study otherwise would not be possible? For a qualification that is not incompatible with the contrary (*vipakṣa*) does not exclude the reason (*hetu*) from that contrary."
Because two non-contradictory things can coexist in one place. If it is argued that this is because people of the present day do not study [the Vedas], the answer to this has already been stated.
If it is argued that this is due to their non-appearance, this too has already been refuted previously. Moreover, mere non-perception does not establish non-existence;
thus, there is indeed a logical fallacy (*vyabhicāra*). Therefore, the qualification does not possess any additional force, and thus it is equivalent to being unmentioned (*anupāttasama*).

Whatever study of the Veda there may be, all of it is preceded by another study of the Veda; such is the pervasion (vyāpti), because it is impossible to perceive through direct observation that "this is the effect of those [specific individuals]. Therefore, it remains established that it is impossible to ascertain that the deficiency in the means for performing the mantra-rites belongs to one person in the same way as it belongs to everyone else.

Since this is so, therefore, in the proof that "study is preceded by another study, just like the study of other [texts]," the logical mark (*liṅga*) "because of being study" (*adhyayanāt*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*). This is because in the case of the study of the *Mahābhārata* and similar works, there exists the state of being a study of something of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). [Objection: There is no fault, because [the reason] is qualified by "Veda. For it is only the study in general that is inconclusive, not that which is qualified by "Veda."
The intention is that it would be [possible] for the study of the Veda. But what [is the reason], and so forth, asks the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*).

What excellence does the study of the Veda possess, such that that study of the Veda could not be undertaken by oneself after having first performed it otherwise? There is no excellence at all. Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that there might be study of the Veda and yet it would not be preceded by [another] study; thus, he [states] that.

Thus there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*). For the qualification "being a Veda" is not incompatible with the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), namely, "not being preceded by another recitation. Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is excluded from that counter-example. What is the reason? Because the two non-contradictory properties—"being a Veda" and "not being preceded by another recitation"—are both possible in a single Vedic sentence. Which...
There is no contradiction here in the claim that there may be Vedic study which is not preceded by another study [of the Vedas], because people of the present day do not engage in such study;
rather, their study is necessarily preceded by another study. This has already been answered. The same applies even to the study of the *Bhārata*.

This follows as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). For even that [study] is nowadays learned solely through the instruction of others. Consequently, the very first study intended by him would—like the Veda—be non-human (*apauruṣeya*) by virtue of being preceded by another study. If it is argued that "the study of the Veda is necessarily preceded by the study of the Veda because no author is observed," this too has already been refuted and rejected previously. For [authors] are indeed observed...

[The traditions of] practice have been interrupted, as indicated by the phrase "and [the Vedas] are products," and so forth. Furthermore, since mere non-perception does not necessarily establish non-existence, there is indeed a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the reason "because of being the study of the Veda. Therefore, the property of being a Veda (*vedatva*)—as a qualification of the reason, namely the act of studying—is not a factor of excellence; it does not contribute any specific distinction. This is because it is not incompatible with the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
Because it does not exclude the opposite by its very nature, even a qualification that has been employed is equivalent to one not employed.

Furthermore, the claim that "whatever study of the Veda there is, all of it is preceded by another study," which establishes the non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*) of the Veda, fails because it is not proven that everything is of such a nature. Rather, it would follow that only that specific instance is so, for which the cause [of being preceded by another study] is observed.

For when a specific feature is perceived as being caused by that [general property], the apprehension of the general property through the exclusion of that specific feature is indeed fallacious— just like the case of white matter for proving fire.
By this, the arguments using speech and so forth to prove passion and the like are also refuted.
Or let there be study; this [scripture] is preceded by such study.
In every way, it would be established as beginningless, and thus not dependent on a non-human [source].
Therefore, if it were authorless, there would be yet another [logical] dependence. (247)

For it is the person alone who either composes [the words] himself or [causes them to be composed] by another. Since those sounds do not themselves resound when their instruments are inactive—by which means they might be considered non-human (apauruṣeya)—even if the reason is specified, pervasion (vyāpti) is not established. This is because, due to the absence of a subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) regarding the contrary case, [the reason would apply to] all of the Vedas...

For the establishment of such a state of recitation is not proven to be preceded by another instance of recitation. However, when a particular kind of recitation is observed to be caused by another instance of recitation for one who is unable to perform it themselves, then that [recitation] would indeed be preceded by another instance of recitation. This applies to the recitation of one who is unable to study by themselves, which is observed to be due to specific causes such as dullness.

In the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), it is by way of being caused by that—that is, by way of being caused by a previous study of another [text]. By the abandonment of that, meaning by the abandonment of that study which is caused by dullness and so forth, just as in the case of the abandonment of a perceived particularity. Alternatively, "by way of being caused by that" means by way of being caused by capacity (*śakti*). When the particularity has been seen and understood, having performed it oneself in the form of study, by the abandonment of that—of that particularity...

By abandoning that [specific instance], if one were to grasp the general property of being Vedic study—arguing that "all Vedic study, whether by a capable person or an incapable person, is preceded by another instance of Vedic study because it possesses the general property of being Vedic study"—this would indeed be fallacious. How so? It is like [the argument] for establishing fire: just as possessing a pale substance (*pāṇḍudravyatva*) is used to establish fire; for instance, when smoke—which is produced by fire—is present, that which is pale...

The meaning is as follows: a distinction has been observed; therefore, the commonality of the white substance (*pāṇḍudravyasāmānya*), which is being taken up by the exclusion of that [distinction], is fallacious (*vyabhicārin*) for the purpose of proving fire, just like that.
By this aforementioned demonstration of fallaciousness, [the argument] beginning with "speech" (*vacana*) [is refuted]. From the word "etc. (*ādi*), [one understands] the person (*puruṣa*).
The [objections] beginning with "you" have been answered: namely, that those [reasons] are also inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*).

With respect to what probandum? In the proof of passion and so forth; that is, in the establishment of passion and so forth. For, when one abandons a specific kind of speech observed to be produced by passion and so forth, there is an inconclusiveness regarding the general property of being a speaker (*vaktṛtva-sāmānya*).

Even granting that "let it be so," he says: even by doing this in every respect, the beginninglessness of the Veda would be established; however, only its being devoid of a beginning would be established, not its non-dependence on a person (*apuruṣāśraya*). Thus, its authorless nature (*apauruṣeyatva*) would not be established.
If, on the other hand, authorlessness is desired based merely on that absence of a beginning, then there would be another worldly convention as well.

Because it proceeds from sounds such as *hāra* and so forth, it does not have a person as its substratum; it is non-human (*apauruṣeya*). For a person indeed either learns it by himself through his own inference and mental construction, or learns it having heard it from another. In the case of those persons whose organs are unimpaired—that is, whose palates and other vocal organs are not obstructed—it [the Veda] exists by itself...
A is must-1/0/-! 34a.
Even if [the Vedas] were not of human origin, if there were a beginning of humans, even then they would not be established as being preceded by something else, because of the absence of a teacher.

The first student of that [Veda] would necessarily be its author. Therefore, this [Veda], which has proceeded from the demonstration of what came before and is beginningless, is like the dust raised by children...

Human linguistic usage might be like play and so forth; it would not be non-human (apauruṣeya). Since it is beginningless, if it were non-human, then by now there would be much more that is non-human. And thus, [this would apply] to the usages of barbarians and the like, as well as to the words of nihilists.
Due to beginninglessness, there is such a state [of things] because of the continuity of prior formative predispositions. || 248 ||
Even certain practices of the Mlecchas, such as marrying one's mother and the like, as well as festivals like the Madanotsava, are beginningless;
yet these words merely "resound" (dhvananti), that is, they manifest their own form. By this very act of resounding, they would not [thereby] become non-human (apauruṣeya).
Rather, because these Vedic words are made to resound through human activity, they possess only a human origin (pauruṣeyatva), just like worldly sentences.
Furthermore, these [Vedic texts] might be non-human-authored; their non-human authorship is conceivable only if there were a beginning of human beings.

However, since study is beginningless, even then, the study of the first person cannot be established as being preceded by another—that is, preceded by a prior act of study. Why? Because of the absence of any other person to teach him. Therefore—

The first student of that Veda, being the first student, would have to be the author of the Veda himself, having studied it through his own inference. Therefore, this worldly practice characterized by the study of the Veda—where one, having studied from one person, teaches another, and he too [teaches] yet another—is a human activity that is beginningless, proceeding from the observation of each preceding generation; thus, this [Veda] is indeed [the work] of men.

Just as children (*ḍimbhaka*) play with dust, so too is the human convention (*puruṣavyavahāra*) beginningless because it has proceeded from [time] immemorial, as in the previous example. By the word "beginningless" (*ādi*), activities such as eating and so forth are included.
Regarding the phrase "because of being beginningless," etc.: if the Veda is accepted as being authorless (*apauruṣeya*) due to its beginninglessness, then [the same would apply to] the Mlecchas...

Regarding "divine practices" (*divyavahāra*): because those practices transmitted through one's own family lineage—characterized by such things as marriage with one's mother and so forth—are beginningless, they would likewise possess that status [of being beginningless], and thus, like the Veda, would be non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of beginningless noble practices (*āryavyavahāra*) is intended.

Similarly, even the words of nihilists (*nāstikya*), which proceed from the denial of dharma, adharma, and the next world, would likewise possess that status [of being beginningless] due to their beginninglessness.

It would be non-human in origin (*apauruṣeyatva*). If one asks how they could be beginningless, he says: "Because of the continuity of prior formative impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*)," meaning because they proceed as a continuum by the power of prior formative impressions. The linguistic practices of barbarians (*mleccha*) are beginningless. If one asks what these are, he says:
"When the father has died, the son must perform the marriage of his mother. Such is the practice of those barbarians.

This refers to conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such usages as the killing of elders for the sake of liberating them from *saṃsāra*, and so forth.
He states what is included by the word "etc.": "Madana," etc. On the thirteenth lunar day of the month of Madana, there is the festival of Madana (*madanotsava*).
Here too, by the word "etc.," there are also beginningless festivals such as those for the birth of a son. [This refers to] the Lokāyata of the nihilists.

Furthermore, the words of an atheist—which consist of denials of the unprecedented [karmic results] and the next world—cannot indeed be set forth by another person who has not been instilled with the necessary mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). For even those who have constructed their own conventions based on their own imagination proceed only by means of a conceptualization of the meaning according to what they have heard. Therefore, some [knowledge] must have come from somewhere; it must originate from a single teacher.

Because it does not exist as a continuous stream, it is said to be "not preceded by another. Worldly conventions, whether correct or incorrect, proceed precisely according to how they were previously observed.
It is not maintained that conventions such as those concerning bodies and so forth—which were previously unobserved among the Kalpikas—arose only later. No.
Even for those who are protected by other formative forces (*saṃskāra*), [the impressions] awaken according to their respective conditions.

And what are their words? They are those that deny the prior world, the subsequent world, and so forth. What kind [of denial]? They are denials and rejections of a "prior" [world], namely merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), as well as a "subsequent world. Those too are beginningless. [The gender] has been changed.

The connection is by way of name. (248) But how is it that worldly transactions among barbarians (*leccha*) and others are beginningless? To this he says: "For not... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "those transactions and those nihilistic utterances," [the rule] "a neuter [word] with a non-neuter [word] becomes one [in form], optionally" (*napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccānyatarasyām*) applies.

This is a *ekaśeṣa* compound of neuter nouns; thus, the meaning is as follows: (1) Modern people—whose mental impressions have not been instilled by others and whose intellects are unrefined—do not engage in those conventional practices nor utter those nihilistic words.
Rather, it is only those whose intellects have been refined who do so. Since this applies to them and to others, and to yet others still, the beginninglessness (*anāditva*) of these is established.

Even those who compose original poetry and the like proceed by means of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by another; thus, even the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) established by them is beginningless. Stating this, he says: "By their own intuition," and so forth. For even those persons whose conventions—characterized by poetry and the like—are composed by their own intuition, that is, by their own intellect, [they still rely] on what has been heard from another.

Whether the meaning is taken as a whole or individually, the "withdrawal" (*saṃhāra*) of those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) means their collection together in one place—that is to say, their categorization—because it is produced by means of that very same method found in previously existing works and so forth. Even a work composed from one's own creative intuition (*svapratibhā*) is, in reality, preceded by others. To the question, "How then can it be called 'one's own creation'? he says: "That poetry and so forth [is] another..."
The connection is that it is said to be "preceded by another. It is said to have been composed by someone himself. For what reason?

Because [the author thinks] some collection of meanings has come from a certain teacher. This is because a single teacher does not exist continuously [throughout time]. Thus, even a treatise composed through one's own intuition is, in the ultimate sense, preceded by another; how much more so [in the case of those based on tradition]?

What, then, are those that proceed according to what is seen? Those for whom engagement and withdrawal occur from others exactly as they have been seen are so described. (163b) They are those whose engagements and practices are both correct and false; those worldly transactions whose engagement and conduct (*ācāra*) are correct and false are so described. Among these, correct engagements consist of honoring those worthy of honor and so forth; false engagements are those associated with sensual desire.
[The words] "and so forth" [are used]. And these [beings] are clearly preceded by others.
Here, one raises the objection of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with the words "But surely," and so on. Those who exist in the first eon are the "primordial-eon beings" (*ādikalpika*).
458. *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (11246).
If it is argued that let there be the lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) for all [scriptures], then even if such a lack of human authorship were established, what benefit would there be?
It may be granted that the lack of human authorship is desired because it implies non-contradiction; however, [what of] those certain [texts] which are nonetheless contradictory?
Since it is beginningless, why [assert] its lack of human authorship on the grounds that "it exists"?
Even if it were beginningless, there would be doubt due to differences in the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding the meaning;
or, even if the Vedic sentences themselves were indeed without human authorship, [doubt would remain].
Furthermore, doubt arises from observing differences in both meaning and grammatical refinement. ||249||

Even if it were non-human in origin, if it produced only a specific intuition of its meaning, confidence would be possible; however, linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) are not observed in them, for they are held to be the very first [of their kind], since no conventions were perceived by those who preceded them.

He refutes this with the words "teṣām api" and so forth: Even for those men of the first eon, whose latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) were deposited through the conventional usage seen in previous successions of births—impressions deposited by the conventional usage previously observed—their subsequent activity proceeds from awakening [of those impressions] according to conditions, that is, according to the proximity of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). Therefore, they too are not preceded by anything else. (248a.b)

If it is argued that because they are beginningless, all worldly conventions such as those of the Mlecchas and others must be non-human (apauruṣeya), [we reply: even if the non-human status of all conventions were established by such mere beginninglessness, what benefit would there be? None at all. For instance, it is the fact of being non-human that is desired so that [a convention] might be non-contradictory; and that—

Since even some worldly conventions that are deceptive possess the quality of being human-authored (*pauruṣeyatva*), authorship is not a prover of non-falsity due to its deviation; therefore, what is the use of postulating this "non-human-authorship" (*apauruṣeyatva*)?
If, on the other hand, it is intended that only Vedic sentences are non-human-authored, then [the argument applies] only to those Vedic sentences.

The meaning is that even when that [authorlessness] exists, there is once again—*bhūyaḥ*—only doubt regarding the objects expressed by those [Vedic texts]. This implies that even after postulating authorlessness, doubt remains. What is the reason? Because various interpretations (*arthabheda*) of the Vedic meanings, consisting of alternative explanations of the Vedas, are observed according to the difference between teachers.
He explains by means of the passage beginning with "yadī" (if).
Even if [the Veda] were not of human origin, if the Vedic sentence were to produce for each person a specific intuition of its own respective meaning— that is,
a mental engagement directed toward the object expressed by the Veda— then there would be an absence of the superimposition of contrary meanings.

There might be consolation for debate, and the person would find a place to dwell; however, that does not exist. Why? Because [the term] "as desired" (yatheṣṭam) means by means of superimposition (samāropa) or denial (apavāda), that is to say, by the addition of extra words or the concealment of other words.
Those who practice according to contradictory scriptures are the etymologists (nairukta). By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of the Grammarians (vaiyākaraṇa) and others is intended.

Vedic sentences are seen being dissected by the Mīmāṃsakas and others, who produce various meanings; yet those mutually contradictory meanings brought about by different interpretations do not fail to cohere within those Vedic sentences—they indeed do so exist. This is the meaning. 7. Regarding the consideration of the authorless nature [of the Veda]:
however, the Mīmāṃsakas and others, according to their own whims, dissect the Vedic sentences through the imposition of superimpositions and the denial of [actual] negations.

They are observed, yet they do not [necessarily] belong to those [words], because it is not possible [to determine them solely by grammar]. This is because a single sentence, due to the predominance of convention (*samaya*), can give rise to multiple alternative meanings; because verbal roots (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) are taught with multiple meanings; because even conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is not admitted as absolute; because there is an abundance of words that lack conventional meaning; and because the meaning of such [words] depends upon human instruction. Regarding that instruction...
Therefore, because its occurrence depends upon [divine] will, there is indeed no certainty regarding the meaning of the sentence.

(ga) Refutation of the eternality of letters and sentences: Furthermore, this person, while establishing the lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*), must establish it either for the letters (*varṇa*) or for the sentence (*vākya*). In that regard: (1)
If there were no distinction between the phonemes (*varṇa*) in other [Vedic] cases, what would be the result of establishing them?
For the phonemes are not different in the world and in the Veda; even though there is a difference [in usage], there is no difference in their recognition. Therefore, they are one.
What is the reason? Because the application of meaning—functioning as the denotation of an object—is dependent primarily upon convention (*samaya*).

Because [words] are bound by convention (*saṃketa*). Since even a single sentence can give rise to various conceptual constructions of multiple meanings according to the agreement [of speakers], there is indeed doubt. Furthermore, because Vedic sentences are explained by following the rules of roots (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*), and because those [roots and suffixes] have fixed meanings, it is also false to claim that the possibility of conceptualizing multiple meanings does not exist within Vedic sentences. What is the reason? (1)

Because it is possible for both roots (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) to be listed with multiple meanings—since even a single root is recorded in various senses, and likewise a suffix—the doubt remains exactly as before, due to the distinction in the formation of meaning according to one's intended purpose. It might be argued that, by relying on conventional usage (*ruḍhi*), there is no doubt regarding the multiple meanings of roots and suffixes because the meaning of the Veda is explained [in that way]. 164a.

The claim that "there is no doubt even regarding the reading" is also incorrect. Why? Because [the author] himself does not accept, nor acknowledge, that conventional usage (*ruḍhi*) is absolute. Why is this so? Because of the abundance of non-conventional words. Those very words that are non-conventional in common worldly usage are seen in great number in the Veda, such as *jarbhurāṇa* and others. Therefore, there is no conventional usage (*ruḍhi*) in those cases.

Determination arises from words; yet, in that regard, for the determination of the meaning of those [words]—that is, the meaning of words whose referents are not self-evident—one must depend upon the instruction of a person who explains them.

And because both that [instruction regarding the word-meaning] and the instruction of the person follow the person's will, there can be no certain determination at all regarding the meanings of Vedic sentences, since they follow the whims of the person. (246)
Moreover, this [argument] establishing the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) must establish it either for the phonemes (*varṇa*), or for the sentence (*vākya*).
By means of the same alternative applied to the sentence, the designation of the word (*pada*) should also be understood.
(1) With reference to the alternative regarding the phonemes, he says "In that case," and so forth. "Because there is no difference from others" refers to the worldly...
[The opponent asks: "From which [perspective] would there be no distinction for the Vedic [words] among the phonemes? What result would be obtained by proving that phonemes are not of human origin?
(1) None at all. He explains this with the words beginning with "For it is not," etc.: because it is not the case that the phonemes in worldly sentences and Vedic sentences are different.

Because it would entail the consequence of [the Vedas] being established [by human agency], because no difference [between them and other speech] is perceived, because recognition [of the letters] would lead to the consequence that they are not established [as eternal],
and because [such eternality] is not accepted; furthermore, if their lack of human authorship were to be proven, they would be the same in all cases— so what is the point of this?
Thus, it remains as a residue that all linguistic usage is of human origin and yet not all of it is false; therefore, this labor is in vain.
Or else, [it might be argued that] a sentence is intended to be non-human in origin.
A sentence does not exist as something distinct from its phonemes, because it is not perceived [apart from them]. (250)

For we do not perceive in the words and sentences such as "Devadatta" any manifestation other than the appearance of the letter *da* and so forth, apart from the appearance of the second letter, as if it were something distinct. Nor is that which is manifesting intended as an object of apprehension (*grāhya*) in the act of grasping;
rather, just as the vowels *a* and so forth are non-different according to the Vaidikas, so too are the worldly ones [non-different] in their oneness.

Because they are recognized [as identical]. Even though recognition exists, if one were to maintain that there is a difference between worldly and Vedic phonemes, then even given that difference, it would follow as a consequence that the unity of Vedic *a*-sounds and so forth—which is established through recognition at each utterance—is not proven. Why? Because there is no distinction in their recognition.

The meaning is: since the recognition (pratyabhijñāna) observed in the distinction between worldly and Vedic phonemes is no different regarding the Vedic phonemes themselves, how can the oneness of the Vedic phonemes be established based on a recognition that deviates from oneness? Furthermore, the Vedic phonemes are not established because their difference [from worldly ones] is unperceived; that is, because no difference between the worldly and the Vedic is perceived.

Now, it might be argued that in the case of Vedic syllables, recognition is indeed a valid means of knowledge because they are identical, whereas elsewhere it is not a valid means of knowledge because it is an error due to similarity; to this, he says: "Because it would follow that there is no cognition [of momentariness] through recognition.
If it were invalid elsewhere, then it would follow that even in the case of jars and the like, there would be no cognition of their momentariness on account of recognition.

Precisely because they are different; for you Mīmāṃsakas do not accept a distinction between the phonemes (varṇa) of the worldly and the Vedic. Furthermore, if those phonemes are accepted as being established by proofs for their non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva), then since those phonemes are identical everywhere—in both the world and the Veda—what remains to be established by this Mīmāṃsaka who thus proves non-human origin? What has been left over?

That which is devoid of the collection of phonemes would be something produced by a person (*pauruṣeya*). Likewise, if worldly and Vedic phonemes were indeed not produced by a person (*apauruṣeya*), then all verbal usage—both worldly and Vedic—would be non-personal; yet not all would be non-erroneous, nor would all have a true meaning, because even in the case of being non-personal, there is the possibility of having a false meaning. For this reason, [the argument] is futile.
The labor involved in the hypothesis of the non-human origin [of the Veda] is [thus shown].
(2) Now, with the words "Or rather" (*atha*) and so forth, the second position is introduced: "Alternatively, it is accepted that the sentence (*vākya*) is non-human in origin.
That is incorrect. For instance, a sentence does not exist as something distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*). What is the reason? Because [the sentence] is not perceived apart from them..."
[This is] because of perception.

He explains [this] with the words beginning "na hi" (for not...). For indeed, in sentences such as "devadatta," we do not perceive a word consisting of other phonemes, setting aside the manifestation of the phonemes *ba*, *ka*, *ra*, and so forth, which occur within the words "devadatta" and the like, or within the sentences themselves.

7. Regarding the inquiry into the non-human origin [of the Veda]: it is impossible to determine whether there exists something else or not, just as in the case of other forms. If it is argued that an effect which is impossible for anything else to produce serves as a means of cognition, then this would only be so if that effect did not occur even when those phonemes were present.

If it is argued that [the word] does not exist because, despite the lack of distinction among those [phonemes], it is absent in other words and sentences—[we reply: no, for their lack of distinction is unestablished. If it is argued that their lack of distinction is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)—[we reply:

no, for we do not perceive the appearance of a sentence in cognition, just as [we do not perceive it] in the case of the appearance of a second phoneme; just as in the case of the appearance of the phoneme *da*.

At the very same time as the perception [of the first phoneme], a second phoneme does not appear. In the same way, a word or a sentence does not appear. And that which does not appear cannot be determined to exist as something that has attained the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*) as an object of apprehension within the grasping cognition. Likewise, it cannot be determined whether [the word or sentence] is other than the phonemes or not. This is because [the word or sentence] is not... [connected].

[End of section: Since existence has been negated, otherness is also necessarily negated. Nevertheless, the mention of both is for the purpose of establishing absolute non-existence, just like [the case of] another form. Just as when one form is appearing, there is no other visible form not appearing therein that is distinct from it, so it is here.

"Impossible in other [factors]," and so forth. [This means] impossible in other phonemes (*varṇa*). If it is argued that the characteristic of the body [of speech] which causes the cognition of meaning is the indicator (*gamaka*) of a word or sentence distinct from the effect [of the phonemes], then indeed non-comprehension is observed in the case of words and sentences such as "Devadatta. And this [non-comprehension] does not arise from the phonemes themselves, because they are individually meaningless. At the time of one phoneme, the other—
Because of the absence of phonemes and because of the absence of totality, it is understood from this that there exists that word or sentence from which this comprehension of meaning arises.
With the words "It might be," etc., he provides the rebuttal: "The word and so forth might be something other than the phonemes, if [it were perceived] within them..."

Even though the phonemes are present, the effect characterized by the cognition of that meaning would not occur. This might be the case if the cognition of the meaning did not arise from as many phonemes as have been conventionally designated for the purpose of conveying that meaning; however, it certainly does arise.
As it has been said: (1)

"But the impossibility of [the cognition of] meaning otherwise does exist; that very [impossibility] would be its cause, according to the principle: 'That which arises immediately after something is the cause of that thing. (Sphoṭasiddhi 65) The opponent says: "It does not occur," and so forth. "The cognition of meaning does not arise from the phonemes. What is the reason? Because of them..."

Because, even though there is no difference in the phonemes (*varṇa*), the cognition of meaning within words and sentences would be impossible. For if the cognition of meaning were to arise from the phonemes alone, then the cognition of meaning in the word *sara* would be exactly the same as in *rasa*, since the phonemes are identical in both cases. The same should be understood regarding sentences that contain similar phonemes. And yet, [this is not the case].

[The opponent argues: "Therefore, the effect characterized by the cognition of meaning does not arise from the phonemes. [The author] refutes this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*). For those phonemes are not established as being without distinction across different sentences; for indeed, those phonemes which exist in one sentence are not the very same ones in other sentences, because the phonemes differ in each sentence due to the difference in human effort (*puruṣaprayatna*).
Because they arise only from those that have already been produced.
From the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṟtti-ṭīkā* (19250):

Because of its deviation and because it is not an illustration, even if there were a difference in the phonemes (*varṇa*), since there is no difference in the sentence (*vākya*), there would have to be a difference in cognition and a difference in the effect arising from the sentence; yet that [sentence] is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), so how could it exist? [It cannot,] for it exists merely by way of proximity (*sannidhi*).

It would follow that this [cognition] would occur even for one who has not mastered the formation of words. Therefore, if it is argued that there is no such thing as a "sentence" distinct from the phonemes—since the identity of the phonemes in every sentence is established through the recognition (pratyabhijñā) that "this is that very same phoneme," and thus their non-difference and lack of distinction are proven;
[we reply:]...

This is not so. What is the reason? Because that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is fallible. For it is observed that in the case of hair that has been cut and grown back again, even though it is different, there arises a recognition in one who is deceived by the apprehension of similarity.

And the apprehension of similarity is the apprehension of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of what is similar, not the apprehension of "something similar to another. This is because [the object] is non-demonstrable (*anidarśanatvāt*).

Furthermore, because recognition lacks a supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is not a valid inferential mark (*aliṅga*). For there exists no single instance recognized by both proponent and opponent that could serve as an example. Nor is it possible for a perceptual recognition (*pratyakṣa-pratyabhijñāna*) to grasp the speaker’s identity at every moment, because the connection with the previous time is not apprehended due to its current non-proximity; or, even if it were apprehended by the auditory organ—
It would have to appear clearly, like [an object of] knowledge; yet it does not so appear. Therefore, it is not a grasper of the salt from the previous time.

Since that which is being perceived belongs to the present time, how could a nature connected to the present time be connected to the previous time? Because the previous and subsequent times are mutually contradictory, how could its reality be established by perception?

Perception is said to have a proximate object; however, such proximity is not possible for a phoneme because it consists of parts. Furthermore, at the time of the final part of a phoneme, the preceding parts no longer exist. Therefore, perception in the form of recognition that grasps the oneness of a phoneme in each word is not possible.

Therefore, this remains established: in every sentence, the phonemes (*varṇa*) are indeed distinct; it is from the distinction of these very [phonemes] that the cognition of meaning arises, hence the term "distinction" (*bheda*).
Now, it was stated that phonemes are devoid of meaning; how then can it be said that the distinction [of meaning] arises from the distinction of those very [phonemes]?

True. The [actual] phonemes (*varṇa*) are devoid of meaning; rather, it is only the universals (*sāmānya*), which are the objects of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), that are distinct in every sentence.

Or rather, it is the particularities of the phonemes (*varṇasvalakṣaṇa*), superimposed as distinct, that are held to be the denoters. Therefore, it is said that the distinction in the cognition of meaning arises from the very distinction between the phonemes. However, if this distinction in the cognition of meaning is not admitted to arise from the distinction between the phonemes...

But even though the phonemes are indistinguishable, there is a difference in the cognition of meaning due to the difference in the sentence—which is distinct from those [phonemes]. That very thing would be the difference in the effect. And that cognition of meaning must arise from the sentence; moreover, that sentence is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), because it does not appear in sensory cognition apart from the phonemes. How, then, could this be so? From the sentence.
That cognition would not occur, because the relationship has not been apprehended.
To this it might be argued: (1) even though that sentence is imperceptible, it produces cognition by its mere presence, just like a sense organ;
and the postulation of the sentence follows from the fact that the cognition cannot otherwise be explained. To this he says:

If it is admitted that a sentence produces cognition by its mere presence, then— just like the sense organs and so forth— it would be unlearned (*avyutpanna*). Consequently, since that [quality of being learned] is absent, the claim that the letters of the Veda are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) is refuted in the first position, as they are no different from those [ordinary letters].
Furthermore, let there be a sentence as a distinct entity; it must consist of multiple parts or be partless.

If it consists of multiple parts, those parts would be individually meaningless. Even if those many parts of it were by their very nature individually meaningless, [the whole could not convey meaning].
And the attribution of that nature to what lacks it is a conceptual construction, like [the attribution of] "lion-ness" and so forth. (251)

The sentence is indeed meaningful as a whole, yet its constituent parts are themselves meaningless. In those [parts], that whole would have to be superimposed through conceptual construction, just as "lion-ness" is [superimposed] upon a youth and so forth; thus, it would be merely human in origin.
Now, if one were to think: "Let this fault not occur"—
Even if each [word] were individually meaningful, there would be the false assumption of multiplicity;

furthermore, there would be comprehension of meaning from a sentence even for a person who has not established a convention, yet this does not occur. Therefore, because the comprehension of meaning arises from the phonemes solely through the power of convention, [the sentence is the unit of meaning].

How else could a sentence be postulated through the principle of "otherwise it would be impossible"? Therefore, there is no distinct entity called a "sentence" apart from the phonemes, whose authorlessness (apauruṣeyatva) could be established. Since that [sentence] does not exist, and thus the sentence itself is absent, only the phonemes remain; and these are indistinguishable everywhere.

In establishing their lack of human authorship, one would have to establish the lack of human authorship even for those worldly phonemes (*varṇa*) whose forms are distinct from [Vedic] cognition. And regarding this, in the first position—the thesis that seeks to prove the non-human origin of phonemes—it has already been stated: "This effort is in vain."

"Moreover," and so forth. If it is postulated that a sentence consists of multiple constituent parts (*avayava*), [the author] explains with the words "those parts," etc., whether those parts are individually meaningless when taken separately. Those many parts of that sentence, by their own nature, separately—

If, by its very nature, [the parts] were meaningless, then the sentence as well—being a collection of multiple components—would likewise be meaningless. Consequently, "not having that form" means that within the aggregate of parts, which lacks the form of a signifier due to being meaningless, there would be an attribution (*tādrūpya*) of the form of a signifying sentence, that is to say, meaningfulness;
this would be merely imagined or superimposed, like "lionhood" and so forth. For example, as in "The boy is a lion."
