In such figurative usages as these, [the word] "lion" and so forth is superimposed upon boys and others who do not possess that nature; it is like that. He explains by means of the passage beginning with "possessing meaning": the self indeed possesses meaning; the sentence is a nature that is exclusively expressive;
those parts of the sentence are themselves meaningless. And while those parts are themselves meaningless, that [sentence] which is meaningful—within those parts—is [the expressive whole].

Or would the self be something superimposed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), like "lion-ness" and so forth in the case of a young boy and the like? For this reason, that word denoting the self, being fashioned by conceptual construction, is indeed of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). (251) Now, lest this fault should occur, it might be maintained that each individual component of a sentence possesses meaning in relation to the sentence-meaning.
34b 165b A Fragment from the Life Story of Padmasambhava (PE 12)
Or whether he enters into the state of *poligt* (the state of being one with the object), he finds no falling away or any signs of effort; he remains as he is,
and thus finds [liberation].
And through the comprehension of a single constituent part, the understanding of the meaning of the sentence may occur. ||252||

For a sentence is a form of speech whose meaning is complete; and since those constituent parts (*avayava*) are likewise [complete] individually, each one of them would be a sentence. And thus, a sentence would not consist of multiple parts, and because the meaning of the sentence would be understood through the comprehension of a single part, there would be no dependence on other parts nor any lapse of time. This is because that [sentence] is partless in nature.
Because, in a single moment, through the arising of a single cognition, there is a complete understanding [of the whole] via comprehension;

thus, if each individual member were meaningful on its own, the false assumption of multiplicity would be erroneous, since even a single member would contain the completed meaning, and therefore dependence on other members for the sentence would not be logical—this is the sense. And when, by the apprehension of a single member...
Or rather, upon the apprehension of even a single constituent part of a sentence, there would occur the cognition of the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.
Now, it might be argued: "Even through the understanding of a single part, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning indeed occurs in a general way.
As Bhartṛhari said: "All [parts] possess individual meaning-possessiveness, because the entire meaning is fully completed in every word."

Likewise, it has been said: "When the very first word is employed—which already encompasses the meaning of all forms—the other words are understood as being based on restriction (*niyama*) or restatement (*anuvāda*). How then can it be said that the postulation of multiplicity is useless?
This is not a fault, because this is stated with reference to the specific intended meaning (*vivakṣitārtha-viśeṣa*).
Even if each [word] were individually meaningful, there would be the false assumption of multiplicity;
furthermore, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning would occur through the cognition of only a single constituent part. This [is the case] regarding the specific action—

Nor is it logical that some constituent part of a sentence expresses a specific *kāraka* while another expresses something else, for it is appropriate that each constituent of a sentence possesses its own meaning and efficacy;
because it is impossible to express a specific *kāraka* that is not connected to a specific action, whereas if one were to express it as already connected to that [action], it would be redundant.
The fault regarding the conceptualization of a single [unitary] nature and so forth remains exactly as it was.

He explains this with the words "having a completed meaning" (*parisamāptārtha*) and so on. That which has a completed meaning belonging to a certain verbal form is "of such a kind. And those components situated within the sentence are likewise; thus, they are "of a completed-meaning nature" individually, each one separately. So it is said.
For this reason, it follows that each individual member [of a sentence] would be a sentence; and thus, a sentence would not consist of multiple members.

The meaning is that a single sentence joined by multiple members would not exist. Furthermore, if each member were meaningful in itself, then through the comprehension of a single member, the comprehension of the entire sentence-meaning would occur, rendering the other members purposeless with respect to that sentence-meaning.

There would be no dependence on a listener, nor would there be a delay in time; the meaning is that through the lapse of time, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning would not occur. What is the reason? Because that sentence-meaning, being partless and indivisible by nature, is apprehended in a single moment. Why is this so? Because when a single cognition arises, that sentence-meaning—[is apprehended]...
Because of the remaining scripture;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with [the doctrine of] oneness.
Furthermore, if all [the parts] were heard at once, a difference in time would not be possible.

Lest there be a loss of the sentence's possession of multiple parts—since the meaning of the sentence would be established from a single part alone without waiting for the other parts—it must be accepted that all parts are heard simultaneously. Even then, a lapse of time [would still be required].

It is simply not tenable: (1) because all [phonemes] would be heard at the very moment a single constituent part is perceived; and because, if they were heard sequentially, since those possessing distinct meanings would have their purpose accomplished by just one of them, the others would be redundant; furthermore, when heard simultaneously, such [distinct meanings] are never observed.

The meaningfulness of individual capacities is not established. [Objection: There is no fault, because meaning is observed when they are combined. [Response: No; for that which lacks form individually cannot exist even in combination, and because no distinct entity is produced. Others, however, explain it differently: and if the meaning of the sentence were understood through the cognition of each individual part, then—

And there would be no delay for that part. What is the reason? Because that part, being partless by nature, is apprehended in a single moment. Why is that? Because when a single cognition arises, that partless part is understood in its entirety.

"Otherwise" means that if the apprehension of everything were not possible by a single moment of cognition, then there would be a contradiction regarding the identity between the nature of what is apprehended and what is not apprehended; for it is impossible for two contradictory things to be one. (252) Now, if it is maintained that there is simultaneous hearing so that this fault may not arise, then in the case of simultaneous hearing, all [of them]— [The text continues: ...would be heard simultaneously. But since they are not heard simultaneously, the claim that there is a single cognition of all things is untenable. Furthermore, if it is argued that the object is perceived as a continuum (*saṃtāna*) rather than as a single entity, then because the continuum is a mere conceptual construction (*prajñapti*), it lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*). Therefore, it cannot be an object of cognition. Consequently, the apprehension of all things by a single cognition is not established. Thus, the proof of the existence of a single omniscient being is refuted. This concludes the section on the refutation of the omniscient being. Now follows the refutation of the existence of Īśvara. To begin with, the following objection is raised: "If the Lord (*Īśvara*) does not exist, then how is it that the world, which is characterized by diversity, arises? For it is observed that whatever possesses diversity is produced by an intelligent agent, just as a house and the like are produced by a builder. To this we reply: No, because the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). It is seen that even without an intelligent creator, diverse things such as mountains, rivers, and the earth arise through the power of their own causes. Therefore, the reason is not proven. Furthermore, if the Lord were the cause of the world, he would have to be either permanent or impermanent. If he were permanent, he could not produce effects sequentially, because a permanent cause would lack the capacity for change. If he were impermanent, he would be subject to dependence on other causes and thus could not be the independent creator of the world. Moreover, if the Lord were the sole cause, then all effects would arise simultaneously, which is contrary to observation. Therefore, the existence of a Lord as the creator of the world is not established. This concludes the refutation of the existence of Īśvara. Now follows the refutation of the existence of the Self (*ātman*). Some maintain that the Self exists as the substratum of the qualities of pleasure, pain, and the like. However, this is untenable. If the Self were eternal and unitary, then the experience of pleasure and pain would occur simultaneously, which contradicts experience. Furthermore, if the Self were omnipresent, it would follow that the pleasure and pain of one person would be experienced by all others. Since these faults arise, the existence of the Self is not established. This concludes the refutation of the existence of the Self. Now follows the refutation of the existence of Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*). The Sāṃkhyas assert that the world arises from Primordial Matter, which consists of the three *guṇas*. But this is also untenable. If Primordial Matter were the cause, then the world would be devoid of consciousness, as Primordial Matter is insentient. Furthermore, since the world is clearly conscious, it cannot be derived from an insentient source. Moreover, if the three *guṇas* were eternally in equilibrium, no manifestation of the world would ever occur. If they were not in equilibrium, then Primordial Matter itself would be subject to change, and thus could not be eternal. Therefore, the doctrine of Primordial Matter is also refuted. This concludes the refutation of the existence of Primordial Matter. Now follows the refutation of the existence of atoms (*paramāṇu*). The Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that the world is composed of atoms. But this is also untenable. Atoms must be either spherical or non-spherical. If they were spherical, they could not combine to form larger objects, as there would be no contact between them. If they were non-spherical, they would possess parts and thus would not be atoms. Furthermore, if atoms were eternal, they would never cease to exist, and the world would be eternal. If they were impermanent, they would be subject to causes and conditions, and thus could not be the ultimate constituents of matter. Therefore, the existence of atoms is not established. This concludes the refutation of the existence of atoms. Now follows the refutation of the existence of the Person (*puruṣa*) as taught in the Yoga system. They assert that the Person is eternal, unchanging, and the enjoyer of experiences. But this is untenable. If the Person were eternal and unchanging, it could not undergo transformation or experience pleasure and pain. Moreover, if it were unchanging, it could not be an agent. Since these contradictions arise, the existence of the Person as described is not established. This concludes the refutation of the existence of the Person. Now follows the refutation of the existence of the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*) according to the Buddhist tradition. Some argue that an omniscient being exists who knows all things directly. But this is untenable. If one were to know all things, one would have to know the minds of all beings simultaneously. However, since the mind is momentary, it is impossible for a single cognition to encompass all things at once. Furthermore, if the omniscient one were to know everything, he would necessarily know suffering and its causes, and thus would be subject to the same afflictions as others. Since this is absurd, the existence of an omniscient being is not established. This concludes the refutation of the existence of the Omniscient One. Now follows the refutation of the existence of the Buddha as a supernatural being. Some claim that the Buddha possesses miraculous powers and can transcend the laws of nature. But this is untenable. If the Buddha were to possess such powers, he would have to be either eternal or impermanent. If he were eternal, he could not act or change. If he were impermanent, he would be subject to birth and death, and thus could not be a transcendent being. Furthermore, if his powers were real, they would have to be produced by causes and conditions, and thus would not be supernatural. Since these contradictions arise, the existence of the Buddha as a supernatural being is not established. This concludes the refutation of the existence of the Buddha as a supernatural being. Now follows the refutation of the existence of the Veda as an eternal authority. The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the Veda is eternal and self-evident, requiring no author. But this is untenable. If the Veda were eternal, it would be devoid of meaning, as it would be like the sound of the wind. Furthermore, if it were eternal, it could not convey new knowledge, as it would always be present. Moreover, if the Veda were eternal, it would be impossible to determine its truth, as there would be no way to verify its origin. Since these faults arise, the existence of the Veda as an eternal authority is not established. This concludes the refutation of the existence of the Veda as an eternal authority. Now follows the refutation of the existence of the Soul (*jīva*) in the Jain tradition. They assert that the soul is eternal, pervasive, and the agent of actions. But this is untenable. If the soul were pervasive, it would occupy the space of all things, and thus the experiences of one being would be shared by all. Furthermore, if it were eternal and unchanging, it could not perform actions or undergo rebirth. Since these contradictions arise, the existence of the soul as described is not established. This concludes the refutation of the existence of the soul. Now follows the refutation of the existence of the Self (*ātman*) in the Upaniṣadic tradition. They assert that the Self is the ultimate reality, identical with Brahman, and that it is the witness of all phenomena. But this is untenable. If the Self were the witness, it would have to be distinct from the objects witnessed. However, if it were truly one with Brahman, there would be no distinction between subject and object. Furthermore, if the Self were the witness, it would be subject to the limitations of perception, and thus could not be the ultimate reality. Since these faults arise, the existence of the Self as the ultimate reality is not established. This concludes the refutation of the existence of the Self. Now follows the refutation of the existence of the Void (*śūnyatā*) as the ultimate truth. The Madhyamikas assert that all phenomena are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature. But this is untenable. If all things were empty, then even the teaching of emptiness would be empty, and thus could not lead to liberation. Furthermore, if there were no intrinsic nature, then the distinction between truth and falsehood would vanish, and ethical conduct would become meaningless. Since these faults arise, the doctrine of universal emptiness is not established. This concludes the refutation of the existence of the Void. Now follows the refutation of the existence of the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as a real entity. Some maintain that there are unconditioned phenomena, such as space and cessation, which exist independently of causes and conditions. But this is untenable. If these were real entities, they would have to be either conditioned or unconditioned. If they were unconditioned,
"When the [sentence] is being analyzed as consisting of *yava* [syllables], a delay in time is not appropriate.

(252) He explains this with the words "lest it be so" (*mā bhūt*) and so forth. On the grounds that the meaning of the sentence is established from a single constituent part alone—without waiting for other constituent parts—and because the meaning of the sentence is thus ascertained, the sentence would forfeit its status of having multiple constituent parts. Therefore...

It is maintained that all the members of a syllogism must be heard at once; even then, a delay in time is not at all appropriate. Why? Because [the meaning] of all the members would be heard at the very same time as the comprehension of a single member. Yet, hearing is observed to occur sequentially. And when the members are heard sequentially, they each possess their own individual meanings; from just one member—

Because the meaning of that [sentence] is established through the establishment of the sentence-meaning, any other constituent part would be redundant; this has been stated immediately prior. Now, pointing out a further fault when all constituents are heard at once, he says: "If it is admitted that all constituents are grasped simultaneously upon a single hearing, then for those constituents whose capacity to express their respective individual meanings has not been observed..."
Furthermore, meaningfulness is not established even for [phonemes] when combined.

It might be argued: (1) since meaning is perceived because the meaning is seen in the parts when they are combined, the individual parts must possess the capacity to generate the cognition of meaning; therefore, this is not a fault.

That is not so. Why? Because the nature of form—which consists in the communication of meaning—that does not exist in those parts individually and separately, cannot possibly exist when they are combined.
The form of the parts taken alone is entirely different from the form of those same parts when assembled, which is capable of communicating meaning.
For the Mīmāṃsakas, this is not a fault at all; for even parts that are individually incapable [of producing the effect] can, through a specific mutual assistance—
Because those possessing excellence are employed for specific effects. If each individual part were capable [of producing the effect], the postulation of anything else would be redundant.
Alternatively, the sentence might be a single, partless entity. In that case:

For even if there were oneness, since it is impossible for that which is non-different to undergo sequential apprehension, a distinction in time is not tenable. Indeed, the sequential cognition of a single entity is not logical, because there is no difference between what has been grasped and what has not been grasped; for if they are non-different, the state of being grasped and ungrasped cannot exist. Yet, the sequential comprehension of a sentence is observed in all cases.

Because the time required for the hearing and recollection of the words—including the insertion of ellipses—is completed through a sequence of many moments and eye-blinks; and because the nature of the word (*śabda*), which does not touch upon the form of the individual phonemes (*varṇa*) and appears as a single cognition, does not manifest [as such]; and because the perception of the sequence of phonemes is established, [the opponent] says: "And because no other entity arises," meaning that from a preceding, inefficient form, no other efficient entity [arises].

And because of the non-arising of form; the sense is that phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal. He asks: "Is this fault not also applicable to the proponent of impermanence? To which he replies: "Regarding the arising of sound," and so forth. For the proponent of the arising of sound, this fault just mentioned does not apply at all. Why? Because for that proponent, [the phonemes] are individually incapable.

Even for those [sounds] which are individually incapable, there arises—due to a specific assistance produced by human effort in their state of conjunction—an excellence characterized by the capacity to convey meaning; thus, being possessed of this excellence, they contribute to the specific effect characterized by the cognition of meaning. For the proponent of eternality, however, since the meaning would be cognized from even a single part when each part is individually capable, the other parts would be useless.
This is the conceptualization of a sentence as having parts.

Thus, the fault has been stated regarding the position that a sentence possesses parts. Now, however, let it be that the sentence is indeed one and partless. For even if the oneness of the sentence is accepted—
Regarding the [object] being cognized: since it is partless and indivisible, a sequential progression—that is, a gradual movement—is impossible;
because such a progression is impossible, a distinction of time is not tenable. For it is not logical for a single entity to be apprehended sequentially. Why?
Because there is no difference between what has been grasped and what has not been grasped. Indeed, there exists no other nature for it apart from its already-grasped nature.
[The opponent might argue: "Let there be the apprehension of the sentence in a non-successive manner. To this, he says: "And [it cannot be] successively," and so forth.

What is the reason? Because the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahārakāla*) for the entire sentence—for both the speaker and the listener—is completed through a sequence of many moments (*kṣaṇa*) and eye-winks (*nimeṣa*). It consists of many moments...
In that very moment of a blink of an eye (*akṣinimeṣa*), there are many moments and blinks; their sequence is the succession (*paripāṭi*), and it is because of that succession—
the cause of their arising—
that time and the time of recollection [are established].

If it is argued that this apprehension of phonemes occurs sequentially, whereas the apprehension of the sentence occurs without sequence, [the author] says: "The phonemes," and so forth. This is because there is no manifestation of a verbal essence (*śabdātman*) that does not touch upon the form of the phonemes—that is, something distinct from the form of the phonemes—appearing in a single moment of cognition.
Why is this so? Because the sentence is perceived precisely through the sequential perception of the phonemes. [This concludes] the *Apauruṣeya-cintā* (Investigation of the Non-human Origin).

(1) Regarding the sequence of phonemes (*varṇānu-*): even though there is no difference in those [phonemes] themselves, the cognition of a sentence possesses a specific sequence because the sentence is produced through a sequence.
If it did not depend on sequential assistance, then any kind of sentence would be cognized even when they are uttered in an arbitrary order.

Alternatively, even without phonemes (*varṇa*) possessing a sequence, a sequence [of meaning] is functional; for it is impossible to express [meaning] without sequence, and because there is no other alternative. If it is argued that "in a sentence, phonemes do not exist at all, but rather a single unitary word-form appears as if divided into sequential phonemes due to the influence of the manifesting [articulation]," this is not so, because [that form] does not possess a sequence.

For no sequential appearance other than that produced by the phonemes occurs in auditory cognition apart from the sequential appearance of the phonemes themselves. Furthermore, there is no appearance of a sentence that lacks sequence; because, even though those phonemes are indistinguishable according to your view, the perception of a distinct sentence possessing a sequence does not arise, since the difference between sentences is produced by the sequence of the phonemes.

[The cognition] would occur simultaneously [with the utterance], provided it did not depend on the assistance provided by the sequence of phonemes. If the sentence were not to depend on the assistance produced by the sequence of phonemes, then any kind of sentence whatsoever would be understood from those phonemes, even when they are employed in some arbitrary order or in a different order;
for instance, when "rasosti" is uttered, one would understand "rasostīti. This is because [the cognition] does not depend on the assistance of the phonemes.
Alternatively, a sentence might be perceived even without the phonemes. Nor does the perception of a sentence depend upon assistance rendered by the phonemes.

Why? Because it is impossible for these phonemes, which possess a sequential order, to provide assistance to this sentence. If those [phonemes] possessing a sequence were to produce an assistance that itself possesses a sequence, then the assisted [sentence] would likewise have to possess a sequence; however, this is not accepted.

If it is argued that the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves, though lacking sequence, will serve to assist the sentence, he replies with the words "And [if] without sequence," and so forth. This is because it is impossible to utter or pronounce phonemes without a sequence. Furthermore, since there is no other mode besides assistance provided through either sequence or non-sequence, and since there is no alternative possibility, the phonemes do not provide assistance.
It is established that this applies to the sentence (*vākya*). There are no phonemes (*varṇa*) in a sentence, nor is a sentence composed of phonemes.

Rather, a sentence is a single linguistic form (*śabdarūpa*) distinct from the phonemes. The manifesting sounds (*dhvani*), which possess a sequence, manifest [the sentence] through a specific order and not through a disordered one. As it has been said:
"Just as there is a fixed sequence in the transformation of milk and seeds,
so too is the order in cognitions fixed for those who perceive.
(1) Therefore, the objection beginning with "if it is employed in any way whatsoever" is not a fault.
Due to the sequence of its manifestors, that single sentence, though unitary, appears as if it possessed a sequence because of the sequence of its manifestations.

Because the sounds (*nāda*) in the form of phonemes (*varṇa*) are perceived without distinction from the nature of the *sphoṭa*, it appears to a person as if divided into phonemes, even though in ultimate reality it is devoid of both sequence and the division of phonemes. As it has been said:
Because sound is produced through a sequence, it is neither prior nor posterior;
though itself without sequence, it arises as if possessed of division by means of a sequential form.

The manifestation of a sequence by means of a manifestor has been refuted, because of the contradiction between the manifested and the unmanifested. Furthermore, in the case of sentences consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*) or parts of phonemes (*bhāga*), there would be no comprehension of the sentence, because a single [phoneme] lacks all [parts].
Therefore, in the case of phonemes, sentences, words, and so forth, which are non-distinct in time—
"And the nature of the sound and time is differentiated according to the differentiation of the *nāda*.

To this, he states the reply: "Possessing a sequence," and so forth. He thinks as follows: manifestation is either of the nature of determination (*avadhāraṇa*) or of the nature of non-determination. If it is of the nature of determination, then for a sentence that is without sequence (*akrama*), [manifestation] would be—

[The objection] is answered and rejected by [the argument that] the manifestor occurs sequentially. What is the reason? Because there is a contradiction in the coexistence within a single [entity] of two forms—one manifested and one unmanifested, or one determined and one undetermined. For there is no other undetermined form distinct from the determined form belonging to a single [entity], such that it might be manifested later. Therefore, as for what is said: "By the first phoneme, [the word] is manifested... [this is refuted].

The claim that "because there is no determination [of the word] from the previously mentioned [letters], other letters function for the sake of determination" is refuted; for the manifestation has already been accomplished by the very first letter in the form of a determination. He will state the answer later, beginning with "in the manifestation which is not of the nature of determination, all the letters... and so forth.
Now, it might be argued: "The sentence appears as something entirely distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), and not as merged with the sounds (*dhvani*);
for it has been said by some that 'the *dhvani* is imperceptible, while by others it is postulated as independent'."

Regarding this, he says: "If it were devoid of phonemes," and so forth. This means that if one were to accept a sentence in which parts consisting of phonemes do not exist, then for a person who does not perceive all [phonemes] at once—that is, for a listener who hears the sequence of all phonemes only in fragments—there would never be a comprehension, i.e., an auditory perception, of the sentence as a whole. What is the reason?

(1) Because there is no single sentence apart from its phonemes, as it lacks parts due to the absence of divisions; yet in the world, upon hearing a few phonemes, there arises the cognition of having heard a prior portion of the sentence. Now, if it is accepted that the sentence possesses parts by means of its phonemes, then upon hearing a few phonemes, the hearing of a prior portion of the sentence is intended.

That is incorrect. (1) Because a sentence is a single unit, if there were hearing of its prior portion, then there would be hearing of the whole, that is, hearing of the sentence in its entirety, since it is not distinct from its prior portion. Alternatively, if there is no hearing of the whole, then there would be no hearing of anything at all; for there would be no hearing even of the prior portion, because it is part of the sentence.
Regarding the phrase "because of being distinct":
by this, that which is stated by Maṇḍana—"And because of the similarity of the manifestors, there is the misconception of grasping the essence [of the word] in the sentence;
therefore, there is neither non-hearing nor hearing of the whole"—is addressed.

That is rejected. At the time of perceiving the portions of all or some of the phonemes, there is no perception of a partless sentence; nor is it the case that a sentence is determined by a final cognition possessing the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of all the phonemes. This too is false, because nothing whatsoever that does not touch upon the form of the phonemes is ever perceived at any time.

[This is] not so; for there is no similarity between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), because they are dissimilar by virtue of consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*) and non-phonemes (*avarṇa*). Therefore, how could there be the conceit of grasping the nature of phonemes in a sentence? This is trivial. Others, however, explain it otherwise: "Now, even though [the sequence] is illogical due to the absence of a relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary, it is nevertheless sequential..."

It is accepted that a sentence, which is itself partless (*akrama*), conforms to its manifestors; consequently, it follows that there would be no hearing of the whole [sentence]. To this, he says: "The whole," and so forth. Even for a listener, there would be a hearing of the entire partless sentence in its fragments. If that is not accepted, then it would not belong to any person at all; nor would it belong even to one who has heard all the phonemes.

There would have to be an audition of the partless word, because even in its final stage, since the letters are not heard simultaneously, it is only a portion that is heard. Now, it might be argued: (1) just as a verse, when revealed once, is not fully grasped, but is [grasped] upon a subsequent revelation...

It becomes capable of being ascertained; indeed, it is ascertained through repeated manifestation. Likewise, a sentence, though not yet manifested by the preceding sounds, has not been ascertained. Therefore, at the time of hearing the final phoneme, it is ascertained by means of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the manifestations of each preceding word-sound, which serve as the causal conditions for the ascertainment of the sentence. Thus, by the [final] phoneme—

The manifestation of a sentence that is inherently sequential through a process that appears non-sequential is indeed logical. As it has been said: "Just as a section of a recitation (*anuvāka*) or a verse (*śloka*) attains mastery through repetition, yet that is not called a 'repetition of the text' [but rather mastery of it]."
When the word is manifested by means of imperceptible phonetic elements that are conducive to its apprehension, its true nature is then ascertained.
"When the intellect has had the seeds sown by the preceding sounds and its ripening is completed, the word is apprehended together with the final sound."

He says this very point in the passage beginning with "samasta" and so forth. That cognition (*buddhi*) in which there exist impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by all the phonemes (*varṇa*), either collectively or individually, preceded by the manifestation of the sentence, is described as such.

The notion that the apprehension of the partless sentence occurs through that final cognition—which possesses the impressions of all the phonemes and has the final phoneme as its object—is also false. 167b

What is the reason? (1) Because that sentence, which does not touch upon the form of the phonemes (*varṇa*) and is devoid of contact with the form of the phonemes, is never perceived by the auditory cognition of any person at any time; the meaning of the verse is that there is no appearance [of such a sentence] upon the utterance of each individual phoneme, whereas there is an appearance of the utterance of the verse itself.
Now, it might be argued: (1) since a sentence consists solely of phonemes, it must therefore be an object of sensory perception; to this he says:

"Since phonemes are not perceived without a sequence, how can there be such a thing as a non-sequential [sentence] graspable by a single cognition? Nor is there [grasping] upon the perception of the final phoneme..."

We perceive the nature of sound as something else, namely as a whole that exists above [the individual phonemes]; nor does the speaker himself discern this. If it were the case that the word, its purpose fulfilled, appears in the final cognition, then it would be well; yet the dull-witted man, out of a desire for what is auspicious, merely dreams this.

For even when words and sentences are being remembered, the phonemes are not perceived as having a specific sequence, because there is an absence of priority and posteriority in the mental cognition (*buddhi*). Furthermore, the distinction between different words and sentences would not be produced by that [sequence].
Nor has it been stated that we perceive the form of the word as a sequence of phonemes.

Since phonemes cannot be apprehended out of sequence, and because they are apprehended only in a specific order, how could a sentence— which is supposedly grasped by a single cognition— exist? Now, it might be argued that after the apprehension of the final phoneme, there is a mental cognition [of the sentence] as a partless whole.

If it is argued that there is indeed such a determination [of the word], he says: "And not," and so forth. This means that after the cognition of the final phoneme, we do not perceive any essence of sound (*śabdātmāna*) that is distinct from the phonemes—meaning something complete, indivisible, and without parts.
Nor does the speaker himself apprehend such an essence of sound as previously described. For even then, [he perceives nothing other than the phonemes].

While apprehending a sentence, one apprehends it merely as a sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*) in their external form; one does not, however, apprehend a sentence that is distinct from the phonemes or devoid of division. This speaker [thinks]: "If only this word, complete in its parts as spoken by me, were to appear in the final cognition in such a way, it would be well for me"—this is the auspicious [hope].

*Kāmatā* is the longing for a desired object. By means of that, one of deluded intellect "dreams"; even while not actually sleeping, he behaves as if his self were situated within a dream. Regarding the rule *adhikaraṇācca iti vaktavyam*, [it is stated] that the suffix *kyac* is applied even after a word ending in the locative case. Some maintain that this should also be recorded as a traditional rule (*smṛta*) regarding the prescription of *kyac*. Others, however, say: [in the case of] *svapnavān*— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

Or rather, it is due to the metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abheda-upacāra*). Alternatively, because the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is prescribed by the rule beginning with *arśas* (Pāṇini 5.2.127), it is expressed by the word "dream" (*svapna*). Thus, the *kyac* suffix is applied based on the agent himself being the object of comparison; that is to say, "he acts as if asleep" (*svapnāyate*). By this, he mocks him.
If it is argued that words and sentences are grasped in a sequential order by means of recollective cognition (*smaraṇajñāna*), he replies with the words "For not," and so forth.

For even in the case of words and sentences being recollected, the phonemes (*varṇa*) belonging to them do not establish the distinction between different words and sentences if they are presented without a specific sequence; for they are not manifested within a single cognition that is itself without sequence, but rather [they appear] just like the sequence of their original experience.

Recollection also occurs only in a sequence; that is to say, if the letters of words or sentences were perceived in a non-sequential final cognition without a specific order, then, because there would be no priority or posteriority in that non-sequential cognition, the letters would be perceived simultaneously. Consequently, there would be no distinction between those various words and sentences, or between the different words themselves.

Furthermore, there would be no distinction—that is, no difference—caused by that [sequence], which consists in the appearance of the preceding and succeeding order of phonemes. If such a sequence of phonemes exists, it must be either non-eternal or eternal. If it were non-eternal, being produced through effort, how could it not be of human origin?

For that which is necessarily impermanent must arise from some cause; it has already been stated that if its possession of such causality were accidental, there would be no restriction regarding place and so forth.
Furthermore, this is observed in the case of things produced by effort with unimpaired instruments, and not otherwise. Likewise...
Because one observes that the properties of the cause [are essential], human effort alone is the cause; therefore, [the Veda] would be of human origin.
Even if [the Veda] were eternal, there would be constant perception, because an obstruction is impossible. (254)

Now, if that form of sound were eternal and possessed the nature of being perceptible, then since that nature of it would never depart, it would be perceived eternally, provided it did not lose its capacity for anything whatsoever. In this way, indeed, it would be eternal, because its capacity to produce cognition consists in its very nature of production; [otherwise] there would be a difference in essence.
This is because it has already been refuted.
The meaning is that the mutual distinction between words and sentences arises solely from the manifestation of specific [phonemes]; in the absence of that, such distinction would not exist.
Nor is it "without sequence," and so forth; that form of speech in which no sequence of phonemes exists is "without sequence" (*akrama*).

It has been stated [in verse 16] that we perceive nothing other than the phonemes (*svara*); for it has been argued that there is no apprehension of anything whatsoever that does not touch upon the phonemes' own form.

Furthermore, the theory of the *jāti-sphoṭa* is refuted precisely because of the non-existence of a universal (*jāti*). Or, even if such a universal were to exist, it would reside in the sequence of phonemes.
Regarding the nature of sound: that nature of sound must be either impermanent or permanent, for there is no other possibility for a real entity (*vastu*).
If it were impermanent, then being produced by human effort, how could that sentence not be of human origin? It would necessarily be of human origin.
For whatever is impermanent is necessarily produced, arising from some cause of its own. This is because, if it were accidental (*ākasmikatve*), [it would follow that it arises without a cause].

If it is admitted that sound is devoid of a cause, then there would be no restriction regarding place and so forth; by the word "and so forth," it is stated that there would be no restriction regarding time or substance.
And that statement [is made] for those persons whose sense organs are impelled by human effort and are free from defects.

[Objection: But it has been observed that [the production of a sentence] does not occur otherwise, provided there is no desire to speak or a defect in the instruments. [Reply: It has indeed been observed; for the causal property characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with human activity is seen in relation to the sentence. Therefore, human activity alone is the cause of the sentence;
thus, because of this cause, the sentence is also of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). (253)

Now, if that sentence were eternal, then its eternity being admitted, there would have to be constant perception of the sentence. What is the reason? (1) Because for that which is eternal, an obscuration is impossible; that is, because of the absence of obscuration. The explanation beginning with "arthat" [is as follows]: Now, if that nature of sound consisting of the sentence were eternal, it would be perceived—

And its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The analysis of the compound is: "its intrinsic nature is perceivable. (1) Since that perceivable intrinsic nature of that statement never departs nor diminishes, it would necessarily be perceived at all times.
Furthermore, because there can be no obscuration of the perception of that which is of the nature of being perceivable, even though it exists...

For it is impossible to deny the capacity of that which does not destroy itself; indeed, in such a case, that which is incapable of producing any excellence cannot be said to perform any function at all. And it has already been largely examined whether an obscuration is something that performs no function or something else entirely.
This is accepted [as the case].

We do not say that nothing excels [the preceding moment]; rather, not all pot-moments are causes for everyone's sensory cognition. However, when the object, the sense faculty, and the light are conjoined with one another, they become causes for cognition because they produce a distinct subsequent moment characterized by excellence, since it is impossible for an effect to follow without dependence on [its causes], given that their nature is efficacious.

It has been stated that for something else, there would always be either constant production or non-production. And since that [permanent entity] is not obstructed by anything else, it would remain eternal; it could not fall away from its capacity—even that characterized by the production of cognition.
Why? Because that capacity to produce cognition is of the very nature of that [entity], being the inherent essence of the eternal sound.
Nor is the capacity for producing cognition from sound a distinct entity, because the status of being a distinct entity has already been refuted [in the passage]:
"Because it would follow that it does not assist the existent," in the intervening section.
If it is argued that they are not perceived constantly because they are obstructed by still air, he replies: "Nor... and so forth.
For that external object, which is of a perceivable nature and visible, some obstruction to its perception is impossible;

for there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish such an obstruction. Or, even if an obstruction were to exist, it would be incapable of obstructing its capacity to produce cognition, because it could not deviate from that nature—the nature of the eternal word—which remains unimpaired. This is because it is impossible for [an obstruction] to suppress the power [of the word] to generate knowledge.

Because it is impossible for existence [to be an obscuration]. For in that case, something considered an obscuration which does not produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the nature of the word cannot be said to perform any function at all.

And what object that performs no function could be an obscuration of anything, or an impediment to knowledge, or otherwise a cause of harm? This has been thoroughly examined; this has been essentially investigated.

Previously, the opponent stated that "obscuration is observed even for that which effects nothing," saying "walls and so forth" and so on. Do walls and the like produce some excellence (*atiśaya*) in jars and such, or do they destroy some excellence of their capacity (*sāmarthya*), by virtue of which they are desired to be obscurations? Therefore, just as they [are considered obscurations] without producing any excellence in jars and the like—
[Objection: "Obstructions will be required. The intention [of the opponent] is that even for an eternal sound, there must be some kind of obstruction.

[The author] refutes this with the words "We do not say," and so forth. We do not say that walls and such things "surpass" some object like a jar—that is, they produce a distinct nature [in it]. Then he asks: "In what sense, then, are they called obstructions? He replies:

"However, not all [of them]," and so forth. Not every moment of a jar is a cause for the sensory cognition of every person. Rather, the object, the sense organ, and the light, when combined with one another, become causes of consciousness because they produce distinct subsequent moments through mutual interaction. What is the reason? Because that which is not assisted [by others]...

Because it is impossible for that which cannot have any excellence added to it by others to be independent of others; and that which cannot have any excellence added to it by others must possess a potent nature. [This concludes] the consideration of the non-human origin [of the Veda].
[The letters] are mutually assisting one another without interval, because they possess the capacity for proximity and act as auxiliaries to one another. Of these, the mutual—

Because of the production of a specific excellence (*atiśaya*). When there is an obstruction, due to the absence of the cause, there is no production immediately after the capable moment; thus, consciousness is not produced. Therefore, because of the cessation of the previously arisen capable [moment], and because when a wall exists, another [moment] that is about to arise does not arise due to the absence of its cause, there is no production of the cognition of the effect and cause; hence, walls and the like are "obstructions" (*āvaraṇa*).
They are to be known [as such], but not prior to their connection.
Alternatively, because the capacity of causes and conditions is inconceivable, the mutual assistance of momentary entities cannot be understood by anyone who is not omniscient.

Therefore, that which exists as an obstruction between the sense-faculty and its object might either diminish that [obstruction] according to the degree of deficiency in the production of consciousness, or it might be of a nature incapable [of producing it]. In that case, for that which is of a capable nature, there would be the constant production of the effect; otherwise, there would be non-production.
It was stated previously that for that which is of an incapable nature, [the effect] would not arise. And those [factors] are the objects, the sense-faculties, and so forth.
When they are not separated by an obstructing object such as a wall, they then become mutually beneficial.
What is the reason? "Because there is no separation," and so on. That location for which no separation exists is "unseparated" (*avyavahita*).

The "place of occurrence" (*dhānadeśa*) for that [pot] is its fitness (*yogyatā*), because it possesses the capacity (*sāmarthya*) through the cooperation of those factors such as the object and so forth, due to the arising of mutual excellence among them. However, when there is an obstruction caused by a wall or the like for those factors such as light, because the cause characterized by fitness regarding an unobstructed place is absent, no other capable moment arises; for this reason, [the pot and so forth...]

There is no arising of cognition. Since, in this way, there is no persistence of a single nature at all times among momentary things, the capable moment of the sense organ and so forth that arose previously ceases by its own inherent nature (*svarasataḥ*).

Furthermore, when there is an intervening obstacle such as a wall, another capable moment that is about to arise does not arise due to the absence of the aforementioned causes; thus, cognition [does not occur].

Therefore, it is due to a deficiency of causes (*kāraṇavaikalya*). Because cognition does not arise with respect to jars and the like when they are obstructed by walls and such, walls and so forth are called "obstructions" (*āvaraṇa*). It is not, however, because of an impediment to a jar or the like that was previously capable of producing consciousness. What is the reason? Because that jar or the like remains in its own capable nature even in the presence of a wall or similar object.

Even when its nature (*svabhāva*) has not fallen away from its state of being capable, that which is capable remains indeed capable; it is impossible to effect any alteration in it. Thus, regarding momentary entities, even that which does not produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) according to the aforementioned method is called an "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*).
Now, he states that obscuration occurs precisely through the production of an excellence, beginning with the words "Alternatively," etc. Even though [an excellence] is possible for an entity...

Regarding momentary things such as jars and the like, there is mutual assistance even when that assistance is provided by a wall or similar object, because there is no dispute regarding assistance rendered by a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). However, an obstruction is remote from both the sense faculty and its object. How, then, does it assist the sense faculty and the object? To this he says: "Because it is inconceivable," and so forth. It is not possible to conceive of it in this way [as being distant].

How can a spatially remote obscuration be beneficial to its object? [It is so] because even though it is far away, iron is attracted by a magnet. The "cause" (hetu) is the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa), while the "condition" (pratyaya) is the auxiliary cause (sahakāri-kāraṇa); the power of these two is inconceivable for one who is not omniscient—that is, for one who lacks all-knowing wisdom.
In the *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (1.254),

it is stated that because of the difference in the covering [of the auditory organ], one observes a dullness or acuity of hearing regarding sound and so forth; otherwise, [the covering] would be ineffective.

Because even presence is equivalent to absence, the application [of the relation] "this belongs to that" would be merely constructed by conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and not based on a real entity (*vastu*).
Furthermore, causal functions do not follow upon superimposition (*samāropa*); for a boy does not perform cooking simply because the term "fire" is metaphorically applied to him.
Therefore, even if conceptual construction exists, entities would remain exactly as they are established by their own nature, not turning away from that [nature].
For this reason, whatever obstruction stands between the sense faculty and its object— that very [obstruction]— the sense faculty and...
[He] might even cause it to surpass [the previous state]. By what means? (1) By the degree of deficiency in the production of cognition.
The word "even" (*api*) is used in the sense of possibility; this matter is possible, for there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka*) here.
[Objection: But surely, by the immediately preceding obscuration, that substance is produced as incapable of generating cognition in the second and subsequent moments.

(1) But it is not [the case that there is no assistance] at the very moment of contact, because there is no assistance [at that time]. Consequently, in the first moment, that substance would be visible even when an obstruction is present, since the capacity for producing cognition is unimpeded.
This is not a fault; for that which is observed to be the producer of the moment of the obstruction is also [the producer] of the moment of the object being obstructed.

It is observed that even that which is incapable is indeed a producer, as in the case of the second and subsequent moments. Therefore, at the very beginning, the moment that produces the moment of obscuration would produce the obscured moment as something incapable. For this very reason it is said: "Because the capacity of causes and conditions is inconceivable. Consequently, how could there be perception of the substance in the first moment when an obscuration is present?
And this meaning has been demonstrated regarding the perception of degrees of intensity: (1) in the first moment, a deficiency is produced even in the cause of the object's obscuration;
in the second and subsequent moments, that obscuration acquires an excellence [of that deficiency].
This might be so: the capacity for producing a deficiency in the obscuration is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
He says that [the object] must be reached, yet neither positive nor negative concomitance exists, beginning with the words "by means of the difference in obstructions" (*āvaraṇabhedeneti*).

This refers to the differences in the intervention of cloth, canvas, walls, and so forth, regarding sound and the rest—that is, sound, odor, and touch. The mention of "hearing" (*śruti*) is for the purpose of illustration;
therefore, because one observes the dullness or sharpness of hearing, seeing, and so on, the efficacy of obstructions is inferred. Otherwise...

If no distinction is produced by the obscuration, then that proximity of the obscuration— which is incapable of performing any function— is equivalent to its non-proximity. Consequently, the attribution "this is the obscuration of this sound," or the relationship [between them], would be merely constructed by conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and would not have a real entity as its basis.

If it is argued that [the object] will be the basis for causal efficiency (arthakriyā) as superimposed by conceptual construction (vikalpa), he says: "And not," and so forth. And causal efficiencies do not conform to superimposition—that is, they do not have as their basis objects superimposed by conceptual construction—because they have real entities (vastu) as their basis. For a youth does not perform the act of cooking merely because of the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) "The youth is fire" based on the metaphorical application of the term "fire."

It is applied or directed toward the object to be proven (*sādhya*). Since this is so, even though conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) exists, entities do not have a reversal from that [object]. Those whose reversal is caused by that conceptual construction are "those characterized by such [reversal]. Because of the absence of that, they do not have a reversal from that; rather, they would simply function according to their own nature (*yathāsvabhāvavṛtti*). The analysis of the compound is: "those whose functioning is according to their own nature. 7. Examination of the Non-human Origin (*apauruṣeya-cintā*)

Even if that obscuration were present, the sense organs and so forth would still make [the objects] known; however, this is not the case. Therefore, they must be made known as such by means of a specific quality imparted [to them] by that [sound].
This might be argued: even if eternal words exist somewhere in this manner, it is certainly not so for those that are eternal.
When something exists, there is a loss of excellence in sounds.

That is to say, if their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) were to produce cognition, they would either produce cognitions of their own objects all at once for everyone at all times, or else they would never produce any cognition at all; this is the inevitable conclusion.
[Objection: Non-hearing may occur due to the deficiency of some auxiliary cause.

It might be argued that the non-hearing of eternal sounds is not caused by an obscuration; rather, there is a certain specific auxiliary cause for their perception, which sometimes occurs for someone, and it is this [cause] that produces their [non-hearing].
If it is argued that there is occasional hearing [of the Veda] somewhere, then let there be no expectation of desire; however, this contradicts the restrictive rule. || 255 ||

Indeed, we do not deny that there are auxiliary causes for causal factors; rather, those factors certainly depend upon them. Therefore, if no specific quality were imparted by the obstruction, then even when the obstruction is present, the sense organs and other such factors would still cause cognition—that is, they would simply produce knowledge. But this is not the case. Consequently, a specific quality must be imparted by that obstruction.
It is understood that the specificities of birth consist of the sense organs and so forth.
Indeed, for eternal sounds, there can be no loss or production of any excellence (atiśaya) when some particular obscuration is present.

The word "tat" means "therefore. If those eternal sounds have the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of producing cognition, they would produce all cognitions of their respective objects for every person at all times simultaneously. If, on the other hand, they do not have the inherent nature of producing cognition, then they would never produce any cognition for any person whatsoever.

This is an absolute certainty. If it is argued that even for an eternal word, there is no hearing at all times because of the deficiency of some auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*), he explains this with the words "It might be so," and so forth:
"However, in the apprehension of these eternal words, something [is required]..."
The causal sign for the realization [of these sounds] is a specific auxiliary factor. For some [sound], there exists a certain object that is fixed by its very nature as a condition;
that is the auxiliary factor. It is because of this that, at a certain time, the hearing of a particular sound occurs in a certain place;
thus, the occasional and localized hearing of these sounds is produced by an auxiliary cause. (254)

"Kāmam" and so forth [is from] the *Siddhāntavādī*. "Kāmam" means "let it be so. Let there be the waiting (*pratīkṣā*) for another auxiliary cause; that is not being prevented. However, the restriction (*niyama*) is contradicted. The sound remains in its very same prior nature. This restriction—that it [remains] as it is—would not exist because of the necessity of depending upon an auxiliary factor.
With the words "Indeed, not for you," and so forth, he explains this very point: that [the opponent] does not reject the auxiliary causes of the causal factors.
In that case,

there would be a confused apprehension, because the auxiliary— which assists [the cause] in its specific state— is required for the effect that is to be obtained from it; and the refutation of this will be stated hereafter.

Likewise, if sound were to produce an effect in dependence upon something else, it would not be restricted to its prior nature; for through that dependence on auxiliary causes, it would acquire a different nature. It has been stated previously that dependence is impossible in the absence of the acquisition of some excellence (*atiśaya*).

It does not receive any assistance from something that is a distinct entity; thus, its lack of relation and so forth has been stated. Furthermore, it would follow that this [word] is unknowable, because cognition arises from an assistance [received from an external object].
Therefore, this word is neither a sense organ, nor a contact, nor the self, which is the basis for the arising of another cognition.
It requires something for the production of its own cognition.
Moreover: "If those [atoms] were non-pervasive, there would be non-perception everywhere."

Those sounds must be either pervasive or non-pervasive. If they were non-pervasive, then there would be no perception of them everywhere. How could one situated in a place devoid of them perceive that which exists in only one location? [Objection: But causes indeed depend upon auxiliary factors (*sahakārī*); what kind of entity is it that assists them in that state?
For what reason [is this so]?
Because the excellence (*atiśaya*) obtained from those auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) is employed—that is, functions—in the production of the effect to be produced.
Likewise, if even a Vedic word, depending on some auxiliary cause, produces an effect which is a cognition having itself as its object...

[He] would act; let [him] act—who is there to prevent it? However, the claim that [the entity] is restricted to its previous intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and thus remains in that very same previous intrinsic nature would not hold. Why? Because that previous intrinsic nature has fallen away, and because, through dependence upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), another, previously non-existent, intrinsic nature is acquired.

Because dependence is illogical in the absence of the acquisition of some excellence (*atiśaya*). For it has been stated previously that [a thing] does not depend on anything else if no such excellence is produced. Now, if the word receives an assistance (*upakāra*) from its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) that is distinct from itself, then [the question arises regarding] that assistance...

And if [the assistance] were a different entity, the existence of a relation—expressed as "this is the assistance of that"—would have to be stated. By the word "etcetera," the following is also stated:

if, for the sake of establishing the relation, an assistance produced by auxiliary factors is postulated for the assistance produced by the sound, then there would be the fault of infinite regress (anavasthā), where yet another [assistance] would be required for that, and yet another for that, and so on. Furthermore, it follows that the sound itself would be unknowable.

What is the reason? Because cognition arises from an assistance produced by auxiliary causes that is distinct from [the object] itself. Since this is so, this sound is not the sense organ called the ear, nor is it the contact between the sense organ and the object, nor is it the self. This has been stated according to what is established for others. "And other" refers to [factors] such as effort. Of what nature is it? [It is] the investigation into whether [sound] is unauthored by a person (*apauruṣeya*).

If it is argued that this fault does not apply to the position that [the sense organ] grasps what has not been reached, we say no; for even in that case, it must depend on the specific condition of being situated in a suitable location, as in the case of a magnet and the like. Otherwise, there would be no distinction between clear and unclear hearing. Furthermore, if the conditions for perception were present, things would be perceived equally in all locations. Therefore, [the sense organs] are not non-pervasive.
It requires a basis for the arising of cognition and a cooperative cause for the arising of cognition in order to produce its own cognition. What is the reason?
(1) Because, if [the word] were eternal, it would be of no use to anyone there. Furthermore, etc.: if it were non-pervasive, then those words would not be perceived in all locations.
It might be argued as follows: "How could a person situated in a place devoid of sound perceive a sound located in another place?

If it is claimed that there is no such fault under the view that perception occurs without contact (*aprāptagrahaṇapakṣe*), then since the sound would be perceived by the auditory organ even without reaching the location of the ear, a person standing in a place devoid of sound would likewise perceive the sound; therefore, the fault of non-perception everywhere does not arise."
It is not so. What is the reason? Even in that case, according to the position that [the sense organ] grasps what it has not reached, the grasping of something obstructed is not possible.
What is the reason? Because as long as that sound remains in a suitable location—

Because the sense organ depends on a degree of proximity (*stāratamya*). What is it like? Like a magnet (*ayaskānta*) and so forth. Just as a magnet, although it attracts without reaching [the object], does not attract iron situated in an unsuitable location, so it is in this case. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), a venomous snake (*āśīviṣa*) or similar creature is understood when it causes harm to a lamp or the like. "Otherwise" means if sound were suitable...

The sense faculty does not disregard the location of the object; for if it did, there would be no distinction between clear and unclear cognitions based on the differences in the degree of proximity to a suitable location. Yet such a distinction does exist. Therefore, there is a dependence upon a suitable location.
Even though sound is apprehended while remaining at a distance from a suitable location, there is still a difference in its manifestation as clear or unclear.

He says: "It might be so. And if the conditions for perception—characterized by the activity of the palate and other organs—were present, then sounds would be perceived equally in all locations, whether near or far. But this is not the case; therefore, they are not non-pervasive. However, the Buddhists do not maintain that sound is apprehended by the sense organ without having reached the location of that organ; how then could there be a distinction between its clear and unclear audition?

As it has been said: "For those who hold that this sound is perceived by the ear even without being reached, there would be an equality of non-reachability in the cases of sounds that are distant, obstructed, and so forth."

"In that case, for one situated at a distance or nearby, there would be equality in both perception and non-perception; there would be no succession [of cognitions], nor would there be the possibility of intensity, dullness, and so forth.
Thus he thinks: "For whom all cognitions, whether appearing clearly or unclearly, are indeed non-erroneous..."
This fault does not apply to the Buddhist, because it is admitted that cognition with an indistinct appearance is erroneous.

Furthermore, since the sound is perceived as it arrives through successive productions in different locations, its sequence is apprehended; and if it were all-pervading, everyone would simultaneously perceive it in the region of the ear with equal intensity. (256)
If there were pervasion everywhere, there would be simultaneous perception; for sound is not absent anywhere.
Thus, it would be perceived simultaneously by all people situated in all locations, because the sense organs are capable, the object is present, and there is no factor causing non-perception.
And if there is the perception of a conditioned [sound], who is the conditioner of that which is subject to modification?
There is no fault whatsoever in the fact that the production of a sound—whether faint or otherwise—gives rise to variations such as intensity or dullness.
This might be argued: (1) just as a form is perceived from a distance as being mixed with dust, mist, and so forth, but in close proximity it is perceived as being without them;...
This is clear. Likewise, sound too is perceived as distinct or indistinct according to the distinction between being distant or near;
this is incorrect, because if the perception of the mixing of form with dust, mist, and so forth occurs in those two cases...

If they were perceived separately, then for two persons situated at a distance and nearby, the appearance of the form would be identical, because it would be perceived through its own nature as it actually exists. Alternatively, if they were perceived as one—that is, perceived as being conjoined—how could that cognition, having an indistinct appearance, not be erroneous? Furthermore, since distinct things are perceived as one, how can there be a single form possessing multiple aspects?
It is an appearance. As it has been said:
"Since the basis for cognitions is indeed different for each [cognition] regarding that single object, how can its form appear in diverse aspects?"

But surely our words do not pervade space and time? [We reply: Because the permanence of sound is established by auditory recognition, and its omnipresence is likewise established; who then could maintain the opposite?
The claim that [the object] is distinct due to the difference in location is inferential, whereas the perceptual cognition "that very same [object]" is its sublater;
for just as in the world, even one who travels through different locations in succession [recognizes them as the same].
Just as Devadatta does not undergo division, so too sound does not undergo division.
Therefore, that unity which exists at all times and in all places,
established through direct perception and recognition, serves as its sublater.

"Therefore, sounds are all-pervasive. To this, he replies: "If those sounds were all-pervasive, there would be a simultaneous perception of all sounds by all persons; for no sound exists in any particular place, but rather every sound exists everywhere."
7. An Inquiry into Non-Personal Origin (Apauruṣeya):
It might be argued that even though it exists, not every sound is perceived, because a refined [sound] is perceived only by one who is refined.

In that case, there is no perception of a [perceptual] refinement (*saṃskṛta*), because it is impossible to refine that which cannot undergo modification. However, if the sense faculty were to be refined, one would hear everything. (257)

In that case, if perception occurs only through a refined [organ], then one whose sense organ is not refined would not perceive; and for one whose sense organ is refined, the undesirable consequence—that they would hear all sounds simultaneously—remains unavoidable. If it is argued that there is a restriction to a single object because the refinement differs [for each sound], [the response follows:]
How can there be auditory perception of a cacophony consisting of a multitude of various sounds? (258)

Moreover, if the refinements (*saṃskāra*) of sounds were restricted [to specific locations], then because those refinements would be restricted by something [else] due to their pervasiveness, for this reason, all sounds would be perceived simultaneously and would be perceived by persons situated in all places. What is the cause? (1) Because persons possess functional sense faculties, and because the object characterized as sound [is pervasive].

Because that which exists eternally is always present everywhere due to its pervasiveness; and because, precisely due to its eternity, it is incapable of having any excellence added to it, as well as because of its continuity.

Regarding the phrase "of the conditioned" (*saṃskṛtasya*) and so forth: the genitive case is used either in the sense of the object (*karman*) or the agent (*kartṛ*). By this, the meaning is as follows: [due to] effort...

If it is admitted that sound, which has been refined by the striking wind, is perceived only by a sense organ that has likewise been refined, then the aforementioned fault does not apply. To this, he replies: "Who is the refiner of the mutable sound? None at all."

He explains [the argument] with the words "It might be so," and so forth. Although sound exists at all times, it is not perceived by every person. What is the reason? Because sound, when refined, is perceived only by a sense organ that has been refined by air struck by effort. In this regard, between those two [possibilities], there is first of all no perception of sound as something already refined.

What is the reason? Because sound, being incapable of undergoing modification (*anādheyavikāra*), cannot be subject to refinement (*saṃskāra*). However, since the sense organ is impermanent and susceptible to receiving specific qualities, its refinement could occur through the air impelled by effort. As it has been said:
"The air within the chest, impelled by effort, moves forth; of this there is no doubt" (*Ślokavārttika*, *Śabdanityatā* 122).

Having reached the space of the ear, it imparts its power to the auditory organ. The power of the sense-organ is postulated because the perception of the form of sound would otherwise be impossible; and this power is held to be of the nature of a *saṃskāra* (latent impression).
Regarding this, he says: "Even that sense organ, when refined, would hear every sound without exception.

He explains this with the words beginning with "In that case" (*tatra*). If it is held that the perception of sound occurs only through a refined sense organ, such that a person whose organ is not refined does not perceive it, then that person for whom the refinement of the sense organ has been performed [would hear] all sounds.
The previous objection—that one would hear [all sounds] simultaneously—remains unrefuted.

Now, it might be argued: (1) Just as the postulation of a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sense organ is necessary because the perception of sound cannot otherwise be explained, so too the refined sense organ is the perceiver of only a certain [sound], and thus there is no simultaneous hearing of all [sounds]. [Regarding this] refinement...

If a restriction of auditory perception to individual [sounds] were admitted, there would be no hearing of a "cacophony" (*kalakala*) consisting of a multitude of sounds. For that which is called a "cacophony" is not a single sound, since it is heard simultaneously as things of distinct natures,
and because the determination of difference is based upon a difference in nature.

If it is argued that the simultaneous perception [of the parts] is an illusion because the duration is brief, [we reply that this is not so], for even in the case of a flute or similar instrument, there is a synthesis of the constituent parts of the *svara*, *dhārā*, and *gama*.
Likewise, the postulation of specific latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) is necessary because the cognition of the particular sound could not otherwise be explained. As it has been said:

In the same way, its particularity would also arise from hearing a specific [sound]. Therefore, due to the difference in mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)—because the sense organ is distinct for each respective object—there is a restriction to a single object; that is, there is the apprehension of only one sound. (258)

If this were so, how could there not be an auditory perception (*śruti*) of a tumultuous sound (*kalakala*), which consists of a collection of many sounds and is composed of a multitude of diverse sounds? Yet, such perception is observed.
He explains this with the words beginning "But even... (*athāpi*): those refinements (*saṃskāra*) of the sense organ are specific to each respective sound.

In this regard, if there were such a specific determination of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), then a sense organ conditioned by a particular impression would be the perceiver of only a certain sound, and thus all sounds would not be heard simultaneously. If, in this way, a restriction of the auditory perception of the sense organs were admitted based on a specific latent impression, there would be no hearing of a "cacophony" (*kalakala*), which is a conglomeration of many sounds.

For a single sound does not constitute what is called "clamor" (*kalakala*). What is the reason? (1) Because in a clamor, sounds of different intrinsic natures—such as those of the flute, the drum, the recitation of poetry, and singing—are heard simultaneously. Nor is there non-difference even when there is the apprehension of different intrinsic natures, because the establishment of difference is based upon the difference in intrinsic nature.

But surely, when multiple sounds are heard, since that hearing of multiple sounds would otherwise be inexplicable, one must postulate multiple refinements (*saṃskāra*) of the sense organ; therefore, the hearing of multiple sounds is indeed not contradictory.
This is what is thought: those refinements which are produced by the air-currents impelled by effort—if they [belong] to the sense organ...

If [the sense organ] were non-different [from its impressions], then how could there be a multiplicity of impressions? Since the sense organ is one, [it would follow that there is only one impression].
Alternatively, if they are different, then how is the sense organ "conditioned" by them? Furthermore, the relationship—that "these are the impressions of that"—is not established.

Moreover, those [impressions] which come into being once [the organ] is already produced, how could they have that [organ] as their nature, given the superposition of contradictory properties? Therefore, the impressions are neither identical nor different [from the organ].
This claim that "it is not logical" is trivial. It is not the case that multiple sounds are perceived simultaneously in a cacophony;

rather, each individual sound is heard there only in succession. Furthermore, those auditory cognitions are of rapid occurrence. Therefore, if it is argued that because of this rapid occurrence, there is the illusion of simultaneous hearing even though they are being grasped in succession—then [we reply]: [The argument continues: ...then [the following applies].

In the continuous flow of notes such as *vaṃśa* and others, there are various musical modulations (*gamaka*), which are specific types of notes; because even their constituent parts are withdrawn through a rapid occurrence and unified, the resulting perception would be a confused mass. It would not, however, possess the sequential order of the unmixed parts of the modulations.
Therefore, since the capacity for apprehension is restricted, the multi-faceted cacophony (*kalakala*) is not heard by the sense organ when it perceives [the sound].
