If it is argued that only *dhvanis* (sounds) are heard there and not the expressive [words], [we reply]: in a tumultuous noise (*kalakala*), phonemes, words, and sentences are not heard, because only the *dhvanis* themselves are perceived. Furthermore, the sense organ has a fixed capacity for the expressive [word], but not for the *dhvanis*.
That there exists something distinct from the sounds is a claim to be accepted [only] when it is not intended to be expressed. // 259 //

We do not perceive sound (*dhvani*) and the word (*śabda*) as denotative to be distinct in form; rather, when the sequence of phonemes is heard at once, we determine them to be a single essence of the word (*śabdātman*). Therefore, how could we engage in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), which is preceded by such determination, if we did not do so? Consequently, it is the specific sound itself that is designated as the "phoneme" (*varṇa*).
Moreover: while other sounds persist, how can the expressive [word] be heard?
Therefore, the resonance (*dhvani*) is not distinct from its form, whether as a unity or separately. For when an object is directly perceived, the instruction of another is not authoritative.

It might be so; however, a refutation of this will be stated here in the third chapter [of the *Ślokavārttika*] with the words, "If there were [a capacity] in the utterance of two short vowels," and so forth (3.463).
Since this is the case, the sense-faculty possesses a manifold nature due to the specific restriction of capacities within the scope of a single word. It is not manifold—

The nature of sound as a confused clamor is not heard; yet it is heard. Therefore, there is no refinement of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*), but rather the production of sound by means of the vocal organs and so forth. Consequently, as many sounds as are produced, so many are heard; thus there is the perception of a confused clamor. If it is argued that in that case only the resonances (*dhvani*) are heard and not the expressive words (*vācaka-śabda*), [then...]
He explains by means of the words "not... not," and so forth: in a tumultuous noise, expressive phonemes, words, and sentences are not heard.
Why? (1) Because there, only non-expressive sounds (*dhvani*) are heard. (258)
If it is asked, "How can there be simultaneous hearing of sounds even if their capacity for a single mode of movement is restricted?", he says:

"In the case of the expressive word," and so forth. We maintain that the sense organ has a restricted capacity with respect to the expressive word (*vācaka*), but not with respect to the sounds (*dhvani*) themselves or the words that are not expressive.

He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "In that regard" (*tatra*). For it is the sounds themselves, specifically in the form of phonemes (*varṇa*), that are the expressive agents (*vācaka*).

The claim that there exists a distinct entity called "word-form" (*śabdarūpa*) separate from them which expresses meaning—this is something to be believed with great difficulty, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend its existence. What is the reason?

For we do not perceive that there is a non-expressive *dhvani* and a separate, distinct form of the expressive word (*śabda*) whose nature is different from the *dhvanis*. Rather, at the time of hearing the sequence of phonemes one by one, we determine that there is only a single essence of the word (*śabdātmāna*), characterized by that very sequence of phonemes. How, then, could the word be something distinct from the *dhvanis*?
Determining and delimiting themselves; preceded by resolve—that is, preceded by certainty—from sounds... [text missing] ...Egy 13 watts • From the commune Bak 7.
When other [causes] remain present but are obstructed, one hears the sound alone; thus, there is a collection of conditions for its perception.
If [the conditions] were capable of producing something other than that [specific effect], then that other thing would be perceived as being produced by them.

How could conditions that possess such an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) initiate another object within a cacophony of sounds? Indeed, a difference in the effect is not logical when there is no difference in the cause; for that would entail the consequence of the effect being without a cause, as was stated previously.

Is it not the case that in a cacophony there is no designator? It is not heard, because one cannot perceive the divisions of words and sentences. How can we set in motion a distinct form of sound that is without a basis? Therefore, it is a specific resonance (*dhvani*) itself, existing in the form of *a*, *kā*, and so forth, which is called a "phoneme" (*varṇa*). The analysis of the compound is: "that whose designation is 'phoneme' and so forth. By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the other phonemes are meant].

This refers to the inclusion of words, sentences, and so forth. Furthermore: (1) If the sounds in a clamor are not expressive [of meaning], then what happens when one person speaks while many other speakers remain silent, even though other sounds persist?
If that single [word] is heard, how can there be a designator?

Now, if it were argued that "in that case, the sound (*dhvani*) is also perceived," he says: "The sound is not distinct from the designator; therefore, it is not heard separately from that designator. If it is argued that "it is indeed heard apart from the sounds (*dhvani*)," he says:

For an instruction from another is not more authoritative than what is directly perceived; for by means of one's own discernment, even without hearing [the teacher], one understands the hearing of the sound as distinct [from its meaning] merely from your words. Therefore, while other speakers remain present, this listener hears only the word itself, entirely distinguished from the sounds of other meanings.

One perceives the lack of capacity in the conditions for perceiving that [object], such as the completeness of the sense organs belonging to the speaker, which are the conditions for perceiving sound. In what respect? In the production of something other than that;
that is, in the production of the resonance (*dhvani*) other than the sound (*śabda*) being heard. What is the reason? If those conditions for perceiving it were...

If they were capable of producing [the sound], then that form of sound (*dhvani*) established by those causal conditions consisting in the perception of the word-sound would be perceived. Yet it is not perceived.
Now, it might be argued: "In a tumultuous noise (*kalakala*), those [sounds] initiate the *dhvanis*. To this he says: "Having that nature," and so forth.

Furthermore, how could the conditions for the perception of sound—whose very nature is to produce sound devoid of resonance (dhvani)—produce another effect, namely resonance, while abandoning their own effect, sound, even when many people are speaking in a clamor? They certainly would not produce it.
For it is not logical that there should be a difference in the effect when there is no difference in the cause; a difference in the effect must reside in that very same cause.

It is not logical that [the sounds] are characterized as mere *dhvani* (vibration/noise). Why? Because it was stated previously that if the distinction between effects were independent of the distinction between causes, it would follow that the distinction [of effects] would be causeless. Therefore, in a cacophony (*kalakala*), it is only the expressive words (*vācaka*) that are heard, not the *dhvanis*.
Now, if it is admitted that in a cacophony there are only expressive words, how then [can one hear them] from a distance?
"Merely hearing the sound" means hearing the sounds of expressive words that are situated nearby.
1. Don-gshon-du. 483.
7. An Inquiry into the Non-human Origin [of the Veda].
Or else, how could there be a perception of distinct sounds due to the restriction of capacity? ||260||

Although these sense organs possess specific capacities, they do not hear various forms that are restricted to individual sounds; thus, their [non-hearing] regarding sounds is due to their being distinct from the expressive [words]. Since they are sometimes heard as distinct from the expressive words, for even though the sense organs have specific capacities regarding the expressive words, there is very little difference in their [capacity] regarding the phonemes (dhvanis), which are distinct from them.

This is the portion [of the word]. For this is the course of all the articulated sounds (*dhvani*s). Indeed, it does not coincide with a single portion of the articulated sounds, because the sentence would otherwise have no stability. Thus, it is established that the nature of the word (*śabda-rūpa*) exists without succession. True. Only those [sounds] produced by effort which are expressive, through their mutual friction, initiate the articulated sounds (*dhvani*).
(1) As for the question "Which [is it]?", there is no fault in this: in a tumultuous noise, some perceive only the sound (*dhvani*), while others perceive both; thus, there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, as to what was said—that even for one standing nearby, in a tumultuous noise, only sounds (*dhvanayaḥ*) are heard and not the expressive words (*vācaka-śabdāḥ*)—that too is incorrect.

That too is incorrect, because in a cacophony, the designator (vācaka) is not heard; rather, it is indeed heard. What is the reason? Because words, sentences, and their divisions are perceived. Furthermore, how could there be the perception of distinct sounds (*dhvani*) from a sense faculty that is restricted to a single power? [If it were so], there would be no apprehension of multiple sounds at all.

He explains this with the words beginning with "tāni" (those). Although those sense organs possess specific capacities, they do not hear various sounds simultaneously. Of what kind [of sounds]? (1) Those restricted to individual sounds (*pratiśabdaniyatān*).

That is, they are restricted as manifestors (*vyañjaka*) with respect to each individual sound. But since they do not hear these sounds simultaneously, what [capacity] do these [organs] have regarding sounds?

Disgust for [words] is a turning away by which one does not hear them; nor can it be said that the capacity of things is such [as to prevent hearing], because sometimes even many speakers are heard. Regarding what was stated [in the verse beginning with] "yad uktam" and so forth, the opponent [argues]: as has been stated by the Buddhist, [the word] exists as distinct from the letters, words, and sentences that constitute the speaker.

"Speech-sounds (*dhvani*) are not established. How are they not established? They are indeed established. What is the reason? Because the meaning is understood from speech; that is, because the expressed object is cognized from the uttered sound. Furthermore, this cognition of the meaning cannot possibly arise from speech-sounds.
[The opponent] asks: What is the reason? For indeed, there is no cognition of meaning from a portion of sound (*dhvani*) that is smaller than that which manifests a phoneme (*varṇa*).

Even a single phoneme is generally meaningless; how much more so a smaller portion of sound that manifests it? If it is argued that [phonemes] together are the conveyors [of meaning], he replies: "And that [small portion] does not join with another," referring to that very small portion of sound.

Because of its momentariness, it meets—that is, it coalesces—with another part of the sound that arises at a subsequent time. Therefore, this comprehension of meaning occurs in a designator (*vācaka*) in which the parts exist in their entirety and completeness as words and sentences; such [comprehension] is not possible in sounds (*dhvani*). In what kind of sounds? In those whose parts are incomplete and uncoalesced.

Because of its momentariness, that portion of sound which has already arisen does not persist until the second portion of sound occurs; therefore, it is established—by the fact that the comprehension of meaning would otherwise be impossible—that the nature of sound is non-sequential (*akrama*). That form of sound whose nature is non-sequential is thus described; that is to say, it is partless (*nirvibhāga*). Sound, on the other hand, is sequential and possesses parts, being distinct from the expressive [word].

The face [of the argument] is "X. This is because succession has already been refuted by the preceding [argument] regarding the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of that which possesses succession; likewise, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since one subsequent division of action does not connect with the previous one, and because there is no cognition from a single part alone. Therefore, it is excluded from that...

In the case of hand gestures and the like, the cause of comprehension must be admitted to consist of the totality of its form and action, just as in the case of a word. It is logical that the distinct phonetic components or action-components, which arise in succession through the employment of their respective instruments, produce the cognition of an object according to convention, by means of being sequentially the objects of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
(1) The analysis of the compound is: "that which has parts possessing a sequence.

He refutes this with the words beginning with "tatra" [therein]. This aforementioned [position] is not possible. Why? Because the sequence belongs to the phonemes (*varṇa*) that possess it; there is no word (*śabda*) called "sequence" distinct from them. For we do not [perceive] Devadatta or other such words...

This is because it has already been refuted previously by such arguments as: "In these [phonemes] like 'da' and so forth, apart from the appearance of the individual letters, we do not perceive any further appearance.

Furthermore, if one were to postulate that the nature of the word exists simultaneously (without sequence) because the cognition of meaning is impossible if the sounds occur in non-composite parts, [the following would apply].

Furthermore, if this were postulated, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For instance, regarding the actions of the hands and so forth that indicate going, coming, and the like according to convention: because those parts [of the action] are momentary, the preceding part of the action does not connect with or join with the subsequent part of the action; and because it is not perceived as a single unit from a single [part]. From one—

Furthermore, because the object characterized by going, coming, and so forth—which is the conventional agreement (*saṃketa*)—is not understood from a smaller portion of the action, [the action] must be distinct from those portions; that is, it must be other than the constituent parts of the action. For example, there are hand gestures and the like according to convention;

by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), nodding the head and so forth are included when there is comprehension of meaning. In these cases, one would have to admit that the cause of the comprehension of meaning consists of the entire nature of the action.
It is just like the case of sound (*śabda*). It is like the conceptualization of a "sound" distinct from its resonance (*dhvani*).

Furthermore, as it was stated by Maṇḍana: "When the elders learned in the three Vedas accept that objects such as hand gestures have specific universals (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) denotable by terms such as 'throwing upwards' (*utkṣepaṇatva*), then what is this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*)? [That] action (*karman*) has a single essence."
"It must be admitted [that there is a universal].

This is incorrect; for if a single action in the form of upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) were established, and likewise downward throwing (*apākṣepaṇa*) and so forth were also established, then the universal "upward-throwing-ness" (*utkṣepaṇatva-sāmānya*) would subsist in each of those many instances of upward throwing.

But that very [universal] is not established, because there is no continuity (*ananvaya*) among the preceding and succeeding parts of the action. Furthermore, in the absence of particularity (*viśeṣa*), there can be no existence of a universal (*sāmānya*).

Nor is there a cognition of each part of the action as having the form of "throwing upward" (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth; rather, they are cognized as having the form of those [specific] parts. Therefore, how could the universal "throwing upward-ness" be admitted in those parts?

Or, if [you] were to accept [this], then even from a single action-part (*karmabhāga*) there would be the comprehension of an object characterized by movement and so forth, because of the existence of a universal (*sāmānya*) that denotes the object; thus, this [argument of yours] is trivial. And just as there is no distinct essence of action (*karmātman*) apart from the action-parts, likewise there is no distinct essence of sound (*śabdātman*) apart from the sound-parts (*dhvanibhāga*). How then [is the object understood]?
Furthermore:

"Those who maintain that certain phonemes (*dhvani*) are non-expressive due to specific defects—how could those same defects not apply to this expressive word when it is manifested by those very phonemes? (261)

The expressive [word] (*vācaka*), manifested or revealed by the sequential parts of sound produced in order, expresses [its meaning]. You [the opponent] say that even that [expressive word] is not perceived; to this he replies: "They exist only in succession," and so forth. According to their respective [causes], whatever is the organ—such as the palate and so on—for each [sound], its employment is its activity; from that, the distinct parts of the phonemes (*varṇabhāga*) arise, or rather, the parts of the action (*karmabhāga*) according to their respective organs.
Because of application. This should also be connected to the statement: "Because of the application of the cause, which is action, those [parts] belonging to action are distinct.

Those aforementioned parts of phonemes or parts of actions, having sequentially become objects of conceptualizations that follow the sequence of direct experience and cognition from the domain of conceptualization, produce the comprehension of meaning precisely according to convention.

It is logical [to say that]. Because it is devoid of reason (*yukti*), he states another fault as well: by means of whatever faults—such as the fact that each preceding portion of sound (*dhvani*) is not reconnected with each succeeding portion of sound—and so forth, those sounds [are rejected] by the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*).

[The opponent objects: "Words are traditionally held to be non-eternal. Since this [word] is manifested by those sounds which occur sequentially, why is it that the defects inherent in sounds—which are distinct from the word—are not present in that expressive [word]? They certainly do exist.
[For] surely, according to the reasoning previously stated, neither individual nor collective sounds are the conveyors of meaning."

However, you maintain that each individual *dhvani* is a manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*) of the expressive word (*vācaka*). Since the expressive word manifested by a single *dhvani* is not definitively apprehended, it is apprehended through the awakening of the varying degrees of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by other [successive] manifestations.
Thus, even when the expressive word is being manifested by the *dhvanis*, how could those defects [you alleged] apply? As it has been said by Maṇḍana:
“For those who maintain the theory of *sphoṭa*, neither a sentence nor a word consists of multiple parts;
for even though it is a single, indivisible entity, its manifestation is shown to occur sequentially.
This is incorrect. For manifestation is indeed cognition (*jñāna*), and there can be no cognition without the apprehension of the sounds (*śabda*).

It is accepted by you that [the word] is manifested; therefore, what is called "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*) is in fact nothing but "ascertainment" (*niścaya*). Furthermore, the ascertainment of the expressive word does not occur immediately after the first sound. If it is said that [the word] "appears," how then can there be its manifestation?
Therefore, this remains established: just as the sounds, whether individually or collectively, are incapable of conveying the meaning, so too [is the case here].

Regarding the phrase "in the manifestation of the denoter": the explanation beginning with "succession" and so forth [means that] the denoter, which is the nature of the word (*śabdātman*)—being non-successive (*akrama*)—is said to express the meaning when manifested, that is, revealed, by the successive parts of sound (*dhvani*). It does not do so by mere proximity. (261)

Furthermore, those sounds do not manifest that essence of the word—which is distinct from the sound itself—all at once. Why? Because those parts of the sound occur sequentially. Nor does a single part of the sound manifest the word.
They manifest [the word] all at once, because there is no succession [of parts]. Nor is it the case that only a single part [is manifested], for that would entail the uselessness of the others;

moreover, at the time of the manifestation of a single phonetic portion, the whole is not perceived. Therefore, this perception—which apprehends the entire [word] as a non-composite unity—establishes its object through the totality of its perception, just like the perception of a sound (*dhvani*).

How could it be established? For what difference is there between an existent and a non-existent thing when both are absolutely unperceived in matters that are to be established through perception? Nor is there establishment by mere proximity, because [perception] depends upon the manifestation of the individual instance (*vyakti*). Since [perception] occurs sequentially for both the existent and the non-existent, its utility is equal; thus, it cannot be established by means of sounds (*dhvani*). In that case as well, it being so, there is no need for anything else.

Therefore, there is no lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatā*) regarding the phonemes (*varṇa*). (gha) Regarding the consideration of the sequence of phonemes: if it is argued that the sentence is the sequence of phonemes, [we reply] no, because phonemes are indivisible.

No. It determines [the contrary]. For what reason? Because it would follow that the other portion of sound (*dhvani*), which is intended to be the manifestor, would be rendered useless. Furthermore, no single portion of sound is the manifestor of the entire word, because at the time of a single phonemic portion, the form of the entire expressive word is not perceived.

"Therefore" (*tad iti*) means for this reason this nature of sound (*śabdātmā*). Because it is manifested sequentially by parts of sound (*dhvanibhāga*) that occur in succession, the nature of sound is such that its complete apprehension (*sakalopalambha*) is not joined together—that is, it is not synthesized. How could such a nature of sound accomplish its objective, which is characterized by the illumination of its own denotable meaning, an objective that is to be achieved through the totality of its apprehension?

(1) It would not establish [the object] at all. Why? Like sound (*dhvani*). Just as, according to your view, the parts of sound do not manifest the meaning because they are not connected with what precedes and follows, so it is here.
With the words "For who... and so forth, he supports this very point: for when objects are to be established through perception, who indeed—whether existent or non-existent—is absolutely...

When there is non-apprehension, there is no distinction whatsoever. For just as momentary parts of a sound are incapable because they do not exist at the time of the subsequent parts and thus lack complete apprehension, in the same way, even if the nature of the word exists as something non-sequential (*akrama*), it is likewise incapable if its complete apprehension is not admitted. Furthermore, this nature of the word is not independent of apprehension.

It is the means for accomplishing the cognition of the object through its mere presence. Why? Because it depends upon that [presence]. And this manifestation occurs sequentially; it belongs to both the existent and the non-existent—the existent being the nature of the word (*śabdātman*), and the non-existent being the portion of the sound (*dhvanibhāga*).
Since it occurs sequentially, it is of equal utility and, by virtue of having an equal result, it accomplishes what cannot be accomplished by the sounds alone.
Whatever effect has the characteristic of the cognition of meaning—in that case as well, it is the same; even when the nature of the word is manifested by *dhvanis*, it remains the same.
It is simply impossible to establish [the Veda] otherwise; therefore, enough with this imagined word distinct from *dhvani*.
Consequently, there is no non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatā*) in the phonemes, nor in the sentence; such is the conclusion.

If it is argued that a sentence is not something distinct from the phonemes, but rather that the sequence of phonemes constitutes the sentence, and that this [sequence] is non-human (apauruṣeya); [we reply: If the sentence, as a form of sound, were non-human insofar as it is something other than [the phonemes], what then? It is the sequence of phonemes.
If it is argued that our sentence is the definition [of the Veda] and that it must be proven to be non-human (apauruṣeya), we say:

no. Because there is no difference in the sequence of the phonemes (varṇas). This [sequence] is not a distinct entity from the phonemes. For if it were perceptible, it would follow that it would be perceived as distinct [from them]; if it were imperceptible, it would follow that it could not be cognized; and because it cannot be defined. 17. Difference... 504b.
Furthermore, regarding the influence of the sequence [of phonemes], the consequence is as before: only the phoneme remains.
Moreover, there is no fixed arrangement for them, as it would contradict other sequences.
If the sequence of phonemes were inherent, and if those [phonemes] were not many of the same class, then by whatever [means they might be perceived],...

[The letters] would have a fixed order, while others [the words] would undergo transpositions according to one's whim. What then? [If you say] that there is only one form in the three worlds, that is not so. What is the reason? Because it is non-different from the sequence of the phonemes (*varṇa*). Is the sentence—an eternal (*apauruṣeya*) verbal form—something entirely distinct from the phonemes? No; rather, it is the sequence of the phonemes.
For our definition [of scripture] is the statement of those named Mīmāṃsakas. If it is argued that this must be proven to be non-human (apauruṣeya), we say no;

because there is no difference between the phonemes and their sequential order. This sequential order is not a distinct entity from the phonemes. Why? Because if one were to accept that this sequential order exists as something perceptible yet fails to be perceived—thus meeting the criteria for non-apprehension—[it would follow that it does not exist].

There can be no distinction among the *varṇas* (phonemes) through sequential order (*ānupūrvī*), because that would entail the consequence of their non-perception. Furthermore, since they are not perceived, one must state a "non-perception of the intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) in order to establish their non-existence. If, on the other hand, you claim that the sequence is imperceptible (*adṛśya*), then, while the sequence is imperceptible, there would follow the consequence that meaning is not understood from the sequence. Moreover, perception (*pratyakṣa*) cannot be the grasper of a perceptible sequence, precisely because [in this case] it is imperceptible.

O King, nor can there be inference, because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*). Since there is no sequence (*ānupūrvī*) distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), the mere phonemes remain indistinguishable everywhere—in all worldly and Vedic sentences—and thus the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) applies, as stated in the passage beginning with "What would be left over by this? and so forth.
Now, it might be argued: "The sequence of phonemes is merely a property (*dharma*) and not a separate entity; therefore, there is no fault. As it has been said:
"This [sequence] is held to be a mere property of them and not a separate entity.
Thus, phonemes, when cognized in succession, become the means of comprehension."
Furthermore, the sequence is not something produced, because it is adopted from what was already established;
for no speaker adopts a sequence independently,
but rather intends to express it exactly as it has been stated by another.
"Even for one who exists [now], another [person] likewise possesses a connection [to it], and thus there is beginninglessness.
(1) Therefore, he says this regarding the claim that the sequence of phonemes—which has come down through the observation of successive elders—is indeed non-human (apauruṣeya):
"And there is no fixed arrangement of them"; that is, those phonemes do not possess a fixed sequence. What is the reason?
(1) Because it is contradictory for another action to arise from a single [cause] that is already determined.
173a ma—
These are the [following]:
i www.

The same applies to the letter *ga*. In that case, it would be "agni" (fire) and not "gagana" (sky), because the prior-posterior relationship between the letter *a* and the letter *ga* is fixed. Even for produced things that possess a fixed causal magnitude, a reversal of sequence can be effected; as for example:

This applies to seeds, sprouts, stalks, and so forth, as well as to seasons, years, and the like. How much more so, however, for those things under discussion which possess an unchanging essential nature and remain in some fixed state; for it is impossible for them to become otherwise without abandoning their prior state. And if they were to abandon it, it would follow that they undergo destruction—this being especially true in the case of an eternal sequence (*ānupūrvī*) at every step.

He explains by means of the words beginning with "yadi" (if). If the sequence of phonemes were something produced (*kṛtaka*), and if those phonemes were not many and of the same kind—such that the Vedic phonemes would have a fixed order, while others, being worldly, could be reversed at will; for "reversal at will" refers to those whose application occurs through a change in order according to one's desire.
[Objection: But rather, is it not the case that in the three worlds there is only one form for the letter *ga*? As it has been said:
"Even though there is a difference in place, time, and speakers, the phoneme *ga* and others do not possess difference, since recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is perfectly clear in that regard."

And when this is so, since the sequence of the phonemes (*varṇa*) is fixed, there would be only "agni" and not "gagana. What is the reason? Because the prior-posterior relationship between the phoneme *a* and the phoneme *ga* is fixed.

The meaning is that the phoneme *a* is established as preceding the phoneme *ga*, and the phoneme *ga* is established as following the phoneme *a*. This [fixed order] does not apply in the case of "gagana."
The vowel *ā* would follow after the letter *ga*; thus, there would be no other sequence [of letters].

Strengthening this very point, he says: "Even of those things that are produced," and so forth. Let us set aside for now the consideration of unproduced things—those whose alteration cannot be brought about in any way whatsoever. Even of those things that are produced...

Now, what is the transformation of causes for entities that possess a fixed causal transformation? It is the attainment of successive states. Therefore, the "rule" (niyama) is the existence of the effect immediately following the cause. Those things which possess this are so described. Even for them, it is impossible to reverse the sequence, as in the case of the seed, sprout, and so forth. Seed—

Just as after being born, the stalk arises from the sprout, and from that stalk the flowers and so forth arise without reversal; likewise, there is a fixed sequence for the seasons, years, and so forth—namely, the seasons characterized by winter and the rest, the years such as Śauka and Bārhaspatya, and by the word "and so forth," the planets, lunar mansions, and so on. Furthermore, what is this immovability?

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "of those uncreated phonemes whose nature consists of states that are immovable in their sequence and so forth. How is it that they are established in some way? It is by means of a fixed sequence;
for since it is impossible for there to be a change of state without the relinquishing of the preceding state, it is impossible for them to exist in any other order.
Furthermore, if the abandonment of their prior state were admitted for the years, it would entail the consequence of their destruction; for even in the case of letters,
a reversal of sequence cannot occur without the abandonment of their prior state, especially since their sequential order is eternal.
Alternatively, there would be an abundance of phonemes due to the production of new ones whenever the phonemes differ. And this is not what is intended.
Furthermore:
"If the sequence of phonemes constitutes the sentence, it is not so, because the phonemes themselves are without distinction. (262)
There is an absence of spatial and temporal sequence because [phonemes] are described as all-pervasive and eternal. Furthermore,
this sequential order of phonemes must be either spatially produced, like a row of ants, or temporally produced, like a seed, a sprout, and so forth.
This [temporal sequence] is impossible in two ways among the phonemes (*varṇa*). For spatial priority and posteriority consists in existing by way of mutual exclusion of location;

but because everything is equal in relation to everything else, that is not possible among phonemes. Just as with wind and sunlight, or as with the self and the sky, so too temporal priority and posteriority consists in existing by way of mutual exclusion of time. When one [phoneme]...

That [distinction] does not exist because other [phonemes] are present at that time. Furthermore, that [distinction] is not possible in the case of eternal [phonemes] and so forth, because everything exists at all times.
And there is no other alternative. Therefore, how could a sentence consisting of the sequence of phonemes be established as non-human (apauruṣeya)?
This difference in sequence would occur only if there were a difference in the phonemes for each word; however, even if the phonemes were eternal, they would be distinct for each word.

Having considered this: because new phonemes (*varṇa*) are produced at every step, there would be an increase in the number of phonemes; or else, there would be a difference in their sequence. And both of these [consequences] are unacceptable to the Mīmāṃsakas, because phonemes are unitary and eternal. (262)

Furthermore, with the words *api ca* and so forth, he states another refutation: How can there be a non-eternal nature for that sequence which is produced by space and time? This is because [the opponent] describes [sound] as being pervasive and eternal. As it has been said: "Moreover, the eternity of sound is established by auditory recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)."
"Since its omnipresence is established, who could determine its contrary?

Because it is described as being all-pervasive like space, there is no sequence produced by location (*deśakṛta*). Because the phonemes are eternal, there is no sequence produced by time (*kālakṛta*).
He explains this with the words "And this," and so forth: "And this sequential order of the phonemes would have to be either produced by location..."
Just as there is a sequence among ants and the like standing in a row by virtue of their mutual exclusion from one another's locations;

or there may be a sequence produced by time, as in the case of the seed, the sprout, and so forth—where when the seed exists, the sprout does not, and when the sprout exists, the leaves and so forth do not—this sequence is of two kinds: that produced by location and that produced by time. [Such a sequence] is not possible among phonemes (*varṇa*).

Why? (1) Because of [their] pervasiveness and permanence. In that regard, a spatial sequence of phonemes is first of all impossible. This is because spatial priority and posteriority consist in the existence of entities by way of excluding one another's locations. Such a priority and posteriority is not possible among phonemes. What is the reason? Because, due to their pervasiveness, every phoneme [occupies] the same location as every other phoneme.

Because they occupy the same location, like wind and sunlight; this is a worldly example (*laukiko dṛṣṭāntaḥ*). He states a scriptural example (*śāstrīya*): "like the self and so forth" (*ātmādivat*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), space and other [entities] are included. Likewise, there is no temporal sequence among the phonemes.
(Kumārila, *Ślokavārttika*, *Vanityādhikaraṇa* 47)
In this way, it assists in establishing [the impermanence];
however, the fault regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*) has already been stated previously. (1.263)

Now, lest this fault arise, one might maintain that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are impermanent and non-pervasive; however, those two positions have already been refuted previously, so this is not a solution. Furthermore, a sentence is not an order of manifestation (*vyakti-krama*), because manifestation has already been refuted.

It is possible. Because "temporal sequence" (*kālapaurvāparya*) is the occurrence [of things] in relation to one another through the exclusion of time. Why is this so? [It is because of the phrase] "at which time," and so forth. At the time when one [phoneme] does not exist, the other exists; for that reason. Furthermore, that temporal sequence is not possible among phonemes (*varṇa*) that are eternal, because every phoneme exists at all times. And it is not...

There exists a sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*) that is distinct from the sequence produced by space and time; this is the "mode" (*gati*). How then could you establish that a sentence—which consists of the priority and posteriority of phonemes—is non-human (*apauruṣeya*)?
Furthermore, a sequence of phonemes that arise simultaneously cannot be produced by sounds (*dhvani*), because that would entail their being impermanent.
As it has been said: (1) "Because sequence is an effect of impermanent sounds, it is therefore perishable; and its dependence upon the person arises by virtue of their desire to speak. 1.

Therefore, the meaning is this: (1) because phonemes are all-pervading, they are simultaneous; thus, succession is incompatible with all-pervasiveness, and all-pervasiveness is incompatible with succession. If succession is admitted for phonemes, then the recognition that grasps their pervasiveness would be erroneous. And in that case, since phonemes would be distinct due to differences in location, time, and speaker, [the recognition would fail].
If it is an effect, how can there be beginninglessness of the sequence?
Therefore, as it has been said:
"Nor is the sequence an effect, because it is adopted from what was previously established."

"For no speaker indeed adopts a sequence independently; rather, he intends to speak it exactly as it has been stated by another. And since another [speaker] does likewise, this [sequence] is beginningless, like the relationship [between word and meaning]. (1)

That is refuted; for if there were identity [of the phoneme], the recognition of the oneness of the phoneme would lack authority, because the phonemes would be produced anew with each utterance, and because the sequence is not something distinct from them. Furthermore, sequence is not a property (*dharma*) of the sequential items (*dharmi*);
for if it were, then due to the difference between a property and its possessor, the sequence would appear as a distinct entity in auditory cognition. Yet it does not so appear.

Therefore, entities are indeed produced non-simultaneously; this is what constitutes "sequence. Consequently, because there is a difference in the production of phonemes at each utterance, there is also a difference in their sequence. The recognition that "this is the very same sequence as previously perceived" is based on similarity.
It is not the case that recognition is based on similarity; furthermore, it will be demonstrated that recognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
How, then, can it be said that the sequence is non-human (apauruṣeya) because it is beginningless?

(263) A sentence is not the formal sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*). What then? It is the sequence of their manifestation. Since that [manifestation] occurs through the sequence of the conditions for the manifestation of its respective phonemes, it is possessed of sequence; thus, it is also the case that the sequence is the sentence.

This is false; for its [existence] among eternal things has already been refuted. "Being an effect" (kāryatā) is simply a specific causal operation consisting in the production of a cognition through the immediate mediation of the mother-of-pearl substrate. This has been explained as being what is called a "capable individual" (samarthavyakti).
Since that [capacity] is established precisely through the operation, the status of being an effect belongs to the instruments (karaṇas). || 264 ||

Indeed, when a form is perceived from a particular [source], the world designates it as an effect based solely on that perception which is inseparable from its own perception; and that [perception] exists in the case of phonemes (*varṇa*). Since that very [basis] exists elsewhere as well, there is no distinction in its being the basis; how then, given that the grounds for acceptance are equal, could phonemes not be considered effects? They are not.

This establishment of "being an effect" is based on its apprehension; what else could it be? It is simply that [the effect] occurs only when [the cause] exists. Now, if a Vedavādin should desire that phonemes (*varṇa*) be both non-eternal and non-pervasive so that this fault might not arise, then the fault regarding their non-eternality and non-pervasiveness has already been proclaimed previously.

He explains [the objection] with the words beginning with *atyādinā*. Thinking, "Let there not be this fault of the absence of a fixed sequence (*varṇānupūrvyabhāva*) among the phonemes," the Vedavādin might postulate that the phonemes are impermanent (*anitya*), non-pervasive (*avyāpin*), and perishable (*naśvara*). He does so thinking that their temporal priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) is due to time because they are impermanent, and their spatial priority and posteriority is due to space because they are non-pervasive. However, those two positions—of being impermanent and non-pervasive—have already been refuted previously [by the statement]: "That which is impermanent, produced by effort... and so forth.

"How could that [word] not be of human origin? and so forth; and by the statement "there would be non-perception everywhere," etc., these [objections] have been refuted in due order, and thus there is no [valid] rebuttal.

(264) The manifestation (*vyakti*) of phonemes is their revelation (*abhivyakti*); even the sequence of that [revelation] does not constitute a sentence when it resides in the action (*karma*). When...
The meaning is that, at that time, since there is no manifestation of action (*kriyā*), nor the sequence of the manifestation of the phonemes (*varṇa*) as its object, it cannot be a sentence either.
Why? Because of the refutation of the manifestation of eternal [phonemes].

He explains this with the words "not" (*na*) and so forth: "It is not the case that the sequence of the forms (*rūpa*)—that is, the sequence of the intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*)—of the phonemes is the sentence, by which..."
No fault: rather, it is from the manifestation of that [word]. A sentence is that sequence (*ānupūrvī*) which is characterized by the manifestation of the forms of the phonemes (*varṇa*).

Demonstrating this very point, he says: "No," and so forth. That manifestation occurs according to the conditions for the manifestation of its own phonemes; namely, those operations of the palate and other articulatory organs which are the conditions for the manifestation of each respective phoneme, occurring in their sequential order.

To claim that "the sequence of those manifested phonemes, taken as a sequence of *kāma-yoginīs*, is the sentence"—this too is false. Why? Because that [sequence] has already been refuted in the section concerning the investigation of universals (*sāmānya*) versus manifestations (*vyakti*) among eternal [phonemes]. Recalling that very point, he says: "Because it is an effect," and so forth. [This refers to the sequence] being produced by the manifestor (*vyañjaka*).

By means of the direct imposition of the power of production. It has been explained that for things such as jars, which are incapable of producing cognition, "manifestation" is merely a specific effect. Furthermore, because those phonemes are perceived only through the operation of the articulatory organs, such as the palate and so forth, it follows that those phonemes possess the status of being effects; for this reason.
If one says that...

If existence (*sattā*) is dependent on various [causes], from what is that existence established, by which it might establish [the status of] being an effect? For this is not the case when it is itself unestablished.
It exists. Therefore, the establishment of existence is the means of proving that [object]. And that is nothing other than perception.
True; this would be so if its existence were not already established prior to it. For that establishment of existence is preceded by the establishment of the effect.
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "Whatever form (*rūpa*) is perceived from a particular [cause], the world designates that form as being an effect.

Regarding the phrase "from whatever it is perceived," the word "whatever" (*yat*) refers to that which has been indicated; its perception is "that-perception," and this relies upon a perception that is necessarily concomitant (*tad-anantarya*) with it—the particle *eva* (only/just) is placed out of its logical order. That aforementioned perception—
Because of the perception of color.
This [perception] exists even with respect to colors, precisely because it is invariably concomitant with the perception of the operation of effort;
and that perception occurs elsewhere as well, in an object established as an effect. Its basis is the basis for the conceptual designation of "being an effect."
There is no distinction greater than this. Therefore, since the basis for accepting causal efficacy (*kāryatā*) is [the fact that they are] equal, why are the phonemes not considered effects?

"No," and so forth, says the opponent. "Nor is this [causal relation] based on perception. The establishment of causal efficacy is not based on the perception of one thing being invariably concomitant with the perception of another. What then? It is that which occurs only when [the cause] exists; in which..."

"That which exists when [something else] exists"—thus, the status of being an effect (*kāryatā*) is based upon existence (*sattā*). And it is held that for phonemes (*varṇa*), there is no existence arising from their production organs, but rather only perception; this [perception] is what the Teacher calls "existence. That the designation of being an effect belongs only to that which has existence as its basis—this is false. It is merely...

From what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that existence established, by which it might prove this state of being an effect? For when that existence is unestablished, it cannot be said: "When this exists, that comes to be. It is only when this [existence] is present that one can say: "When this exists, that comes to be. Therefore, the establishment of existence is the means of proving it; that is, the means of proving that state of being an effect. That establishment is indeed apprehension (*upalabdhi*), for establishment is knowledge.

Because it is their very nature. And thus, it is established that whatever exists whose perception is invariably concomitant with another is the effect of that [other]; and since this is the same in the case of phonemes as well, why are phonemes not effects? [The opponent replies:
"True," and so forth. It is indeed true that if the perception of sound arises solely from the operation of the articulatory organs, then it is an effect of those.
It might be so, provided that the existence of that word were not established by the operation of the palate and other vocal organs;

however, it is indeed established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, in a person who has previously heard the word "cow" (*gośabda*), upon hearing the word "cow" at another time, there arises a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) grasping its identity, such as: "This is that very same word 'cow'. Such grasping of identity would not be possible otherwise, if [the word were not established]. If...

By means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the existence of the sound prior [to its perception] is indeed established, on the grounds that there would otherwise be no sound in the interval between the times of its preceding and succeeding auditions. Nor is it the case that an establishment preceded by another establishment serves as the proof for its being an effect; rather, that establishment of existence is the very basis for the designation of "being an effect," which is itself an established fact. For example, [the existence] of a jar that was previously non-existent [is established] through the activity of the potter and so forth.
Success comes only from the other side, that is, from what follows.

[The opponent asks: "But surely," and so forth—the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) says this: he is stating that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) will not first be established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, how can its existence be established? Let it be granted for the sake of argument that the existence of the word is prior.

[The opponent replies: It is established. [The proponent asks: Even so, that form of the word is unestablished. Which is that form? He says: That which is useful for the uninterrupted production of such cognition. [The opponent objects: But surely that form is indeed unestablished, since it is not useful due to the deficiency of other factors. [The proponent asks: If this is the case, how can there be no difference between what is useful and what is not useful? Now, regarding the investigation into the non-human origin [of the Veda]: Is it not true that that form is simply unestablished, insofar as it is useful for the uninterrupted production of such cognition? If it is argued that it is indeed established, yet not employed because of the deficiency of other factors—then how can there be no distinction between what is employed and what is not employed?

Nor can difference be something that does not touch upon the intrinsic nature [of the cause], because it is precisely that excellence (*atiśaya*) whose utility is established; for otherwise, it would follow that the cause lacks causal efficiency. Indeed, it is logical that only that in whose presence the probandum is established is what is useful in that context. Even if one argues that the cause is useful through the excellence of that [excellence], the same consequence follows. Therefore, it is only through the excellence itself that the capacity for immediate efficacy is employed as a state.

If it is argued that the distinction [of the manifestor] from other conceptual constructs is not applicable, that has already been refuted. Furthermore, since that [manifestation] is established solely through the operation of the instrument (*karaṇa*), it possesses the same properties as every other effect. If such a [manifestor] were to manifest one thing, then everything would be manifested; or else, nothing at all would be manifested, because there is no distinction [between them]. To illustrate:
That which, through its own cognition, causes the understanding of another, is considered a manifestor (vyañjaka) when the object is already established.

Regarding the passage beginning with *vidhi*: the analysis of the compound is "that whose nature (*śīla*) is employed through mediation by such a cognition in which the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound appears. For if such a form were established beforehand, then there would be a constant perception of sound.
If it is argued that the form of that sound as described is indeed established, but due to the deficiency of another auxiliary cause, it was not employed as a cause for auditory consciousness;
then, if this is so, that [form] which is subsequently employed in its own cognition upon the presence of the auxiliary cause, [arises] from effort.

The state prior [to utterance] is that of being unmanifested; these two states are mutually contradictory. How, then, can there be non-difference between these two contradictory states—the manifested and the unmanifested? On the contrary, there is indeed difference. Consequently, because of this plurality, such an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the word would be something produced, and thus the word would necessarily be an effect.
Now, it might be argued: "That excellence which occurs is not the very essence (*ātmabhūta*) of the word, but rather a distinct entity (*arthāntara*);
therefore, this [word] has not fallen away from its prior nature. To this he says:
"Nor is there a difference [of the word] from its state as a non-agent."

The excellence (*atiśaya*) characterized by the state of being a causal factor (*kāraka*) does not touch upon the intrinsic nature of the word; that is to say, it is not distinct from the intrinsic nature of the word. For if it were distinct, then since the utility of that very excellence would be established in the cognition of the word, its status as the cause would be established, which would result in the absurdity of the word itself being non-causal. To explain further:

Only that in whose presence the proof of the probandum is established is appropriately useful for the probandum there, and nothing else. While excellence (*atiśaya*) is directly useful for cognition, the word is useful for excellence; thus, even the word is indeed indirectly useful for cognition. To this, he says:

"Excellence (*atiśaya*) and so forth": even if one assumes that a word is employed for the sake of an excellence, there follows the same consequence as with cognition (*jñāna*). Just as when a cognition is to be produced, a word is not employed for an excellence that is a distinct entity (*arthāntarabhūta*), so too, when an excellence is to be produced, another excellence existing as a distinct entity must be postulated. And thus, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

There may be an excellence (*atiśaya*) [of the word] that is non-different from the word; and because it is non-different from it, therefore it must indeed excel the nature of the word in producing a cognition of its own object, by means of a difference in its own form (*svarūpa*). [This is] some unmediated capacity (*sāmarthya*).
*Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (1.265) 1752. [End of section]

Whether it be like a lamp or otherwise, what distinction is there between this [manifestor] and an agent? (265) In the world, a manifestor is established as a cause for the cognition of another by means of its own cognition, just like a lamp and so forth. If that [manifestor] were already established beforehand, then because it is established as having a material cause (*upādāna*) of a similar kind, there would be no cognition of any excellence (*atiśaya*) belonging to that very [manifestor].

Because that cause is conditioned by its own causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Furthermore, those factors which are perceived as unestablished are merely producers, like a potter and so forth in relation to a jar; even the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of these parts does not fulfill the definition of a [valid] reason (*hetu*).
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "use" (*upayoga*) refers to a specific state (*avasthābheda*) whose capacity is immediate.

Now, it might be argued: (1) "The state that produces cognition does not arise at all because [the entity] is eternal; rather, it produces cognition in dependence upon the palate and other such factors.
To this, he says: "Of the excellence," and so forth. It means that there is no excellence produced by auxiliary causes for this [eternal entity], hence it is "non-excellent" (*anatiśaya*).

The dependence of a permanent entity (*śāśvata*) upon auxiliary causes has already been refuted. Furthermore, since that sound, which is the nature of the producer, is established solely through the operation of the instrument (*karaṇa*), it possesses all the properties common to every effect. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has all effects possessing common properties.
If the manifestation of such a sound—one whose properties are identical to those of all effects—is desired, then everything, even sprouts and the like [would be manifested].

There would either be something manifested (*vyaṅgya*), or there would be nothing manifested at all. Furthermore, the word (*śabda*) itself would be an effect, because there is no distinction [between it and other effects].

To explain: (1) An object is considered a manifester (*vyañjaka*) when, by means of its own cognition as an instrument, it becomes the cause of another's understanding. When? At the time of its establishment. If that object is manifested, it must have acquired its existence from a cause, just like a lamp or a potter.

When the bell is established, that which causes the knowledge of it is its manifestor (*vyañjaka*). Or otherwise, even if the manifested object were unestablished prior [to manifestation], what distinction would there be between this manifestor and a causal factor (*kārakahetu*)?
He explains by means of the passage beginning with "its own apprehension" (*svapratipatti*), etc.: "Its own apprehension itself is the door, the means; by that instrument—"

In the world, that which is established as a manifestor (*vyañjaka*)—such as a lamp—is the cause for the cognition of a jar or similar object. If that [manifestor] were itself a manifested entity (*vyaṅgya*), it would have to be already established prior to the operation of the manifestor.
But is it not the case that even a lamp or the like produces a momentary state of the jar that was previously unestablished and yet capable of being perceived? What then—?
"If that [cause] were already established prior [to the effect], it would be released [from the charge of being unproven].

To this he says: "Of the same kind," and so forth. If that prior moment of a jar or the like—which is capable of being perceived and which is of the same kind as its material cause—is established prior to the operation of the manifesting agent, then for that reason...

It is said that [the capacity] must be established beforehand (*prāk-siddha*). This does not mean that the excellence (*atiśaya*), which is the cause of cognition and is obtained from the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), is established beforehand. What is the reason? Because that aforementioned excellence exists in its own causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Because it has a causal condition (*pratyaya*). The analysis of the compound is: that collection of manifesting factors (*vyañjaka-sāmagrī*) is its condition, that is, its cause. Furthermore, since they bring about the perception of what was previously unestablished prior to their own operation, they are indeed producers (*kāraka*). How so? Just as a potter and others are the causes for the perception of a jar and the like; similarly, the causes for the perception of sound are equivalent to those such as the potter. Sound, too, is like a jar—
The same applies to the effect [of the word].

Now, when a word heard at one time is heard again at another time, there is the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) "this is that very same one," which is a matter of perception. As for the claim that some subsequent cognition [of the form] is [the proof], it is not so, because it is not perceived. That [subsequent cognition] has an object non-different from the previous one.

[The opponent argues: "That [argument] beginning with 'dityādi' is also not capable of proving the non-difference of the two specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), because their own nature (*svabhāva*) is unestablished. It is perceived through a universal (*sāmānya*). And since the cognition of that [universal] would otherwise be impossible, it is certain that sound also exists prior to the operation of the palate and other [articulatory organs]. Therefore, how could the palate and so forth be the perception of something already established? Thus, they are manifestors (*vyañjaka*)."
Thus they are joined.

He thinks as follows: in the first moment there is the perception of sound; in the second moment there is the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the previously perceived sound;
then in another moment there is the recollection of the sound; and then, in the fourth moment, when that [sound] has vanished...

How could the recognition "this is that very same word 'ghaṭa'" be a case of perception, given that its object is not present? Nor is it possible for a person whose latent impressions have been previously awakened to have a recognition grasping the phonemes, because it has already been stated that a phoneme possesses parts; and at the time of the final part of the last phoneme, the earlier parts of the phonemes do not exist, so [the recognition of] the final one as well—

Because the phoneme (*varṇa*) is not present [simultaneously]. For this very reason, perception as recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is also impossible for words and sentences, because they are aggregates of phonemes;

furthermore, at the time of the final phoneme of a word or the like, the preceding phonemes no longer exist, and perception is held to have a present object. Therefore, there is no perception as recognition regarding phonemes, words, or sentences.
It is possible that [the cognition] grasps the true nature [of the object]; for this very reason, it was not rejected by the Ācārya.

Or, let there be recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) regarding them as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); nevertheless, since the grasping of the true nature cannot otherwise be accounted for, it is not logical to postulate the existence of sound prior to the operation of the palate and other [articulatory organs]. For the grasping of the true nature can also occur through the perception of a similar subsequent [instance].

If it is argued that because [the object] exists, the non-apprehension of a similar subsequent [moment] is unestablished as a pervader (*avyāpyasiddha*), then surely even oneness is not established. If it is argued that it is established through the apprehension of identity (*tattva*), we say no; for identity is observed even in the case of distinct hairs that have been cut off and grown back again. Therefore, there remains only doubt. How, then, could it be established by presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*)? Priorly...

The conceptualization of a sentient being (*sattvakalpanā*). Now, because sound is recognized as being the same [before and after], it is eternal; for if it were non-eternal, it would be manifold, and thus there could be no recognition at all. Likewise: that which is employed for the sake of another must exist prior to its employment.
Just as an axe or similar tool is employed for the purpose of cutting, so too is sound employed for the purpose of communicating to others;
therefore, one might argue that it must also exist prior [to its utterance].
To this, he says: "Recognition," and so forth. These [reasons] also do not establish the eternal existence of sound.

They nourish the definition of the reason (*hetu*). For indeed, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is observed even in the case of impermanent things such as a lamp; therefore, this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Likewise, application is seen even in the case of momentary action (*karma*); thus, the reason "because it is being applied" is also strictly inconclusive.

Whatever mark (*liṅga*) is adduced to prove the oneness of the word— namely, that the subsequent cognition of the phoneme *a* which occurs later has the same object as the preceding one, meaning it has the same object as the prior cognition of the phoneme *a*—
it is thought that by this proof of the oneness of words, their eternity is established. This refers to the "cognition of the phoneme *a*."

How simple it is for us to conceive that there is no contradiction even between two cognitions of different objects occurring at the same time; and as for two cognitions of the same object, their relation of priority and posteriority—

[It] proceeds from the production and non-production [of an effect] due to the proximity or non-proximity of the cause; for even when [the cause] is present, that which has not yet arisen lacks the status of being its cause.
Thus, those two possess entirely distinct causal conditions. In that case, even if there is no difference in the single [cause], the potent [cause] does not wait [for anything else].
[This is] not [the case], because it contradicts reason that two successive cognitions should have the same object.

(1) The cause for the appearance in cognition is as follows: "in the same way" means "just like the cognition of the previous form," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), one includes the fact that in the states of fast, medium, and slow [utterance], there is the cognition:
"this very same phoneme *ga*, etc., is indeed this phoneme *ga*, etc., though distinguished by the differences of fast and so on."

(1) The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognition of the letter *a* there is, it has an object non-different from the previously occurring cognition of the letter *a*. For example, the previous cognition of the letter *a*; and the subsequent cognition of the letter *a* is also a cognition of the letter *a*. This is a counter-example of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). However, even that proof is not capable of establishing the non-difference between the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the preceding and succeeding letters *a*. Likewise...

The reason "because of the cognition of the letter *a*" may be stated either specifically, as "because it consists in the cognition of a preceding form," or generally, as "because it is merely the cognition of the letter *a*. In the first case, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). Why?
Because its nature as such is unestablished—that is, because its being a cognition of a preceding form is unestablished. Or, if the reason is stated specifically regarding the subsequent form—

"Because it has the nature of cognition"—this too is not a valid proof. Why? Because its being of that nature is unestablished; that is, because its being of the nature of the probandum is unestablished.
The meaning is that there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) due to the non-establishment of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Furthermore, when the mark (*liṅga*) is stated in a general sense, there is no contradiction even if it has different objects. And there would be a cognition of the letter *a*; what contradiction is there in that [this] cognition of the letter *a* has an object distinct from the object of the previous cognition? Others, however, hold that the commonality (*sāmānya*) is the state of being a cognition of the letter *a*, just as it is in those two cognitions; likewise, the state of having the letter *a* as its object—
They explain that [the object] is obstructed.

Furthermore, regarding two cognitions having the same object—that is, two cognitions occurring at earlier and later times whose objects are established as having a single form—their relation of priority and posteriority (being first and being after) is contradicted. What is the reason?

(1) Because the effect arises and does not arise respectively according to whether the causes are present or absent; and if the causes were indeed present, those two [cognitions] would have to exist simultaneously. Now, if it is argued that even when the cause is present, only the prior form-cognition arises and not the subsequent one, then the subsequent one would never arise either. What is the reason? Because [the conditions for both] are the same before and after...

Even when the causes for cognition are present, the subsequent specific cognition of a later form has not arisen because it does not have those [same] causes; the meaning is that the cause of the cognition of the previous form is not its cause. Therefore, those two cognitions, occurring in prior and posterior succession, possess entirely distinct causes; the analysis of the compound is: "those two whose entire cause is distinct."

It might be thought: (1) that for those two cognitions of the letter *ra*, the sound alone is the single cause, while the sequence of production arises from the sequence of the presence of auxiliary conditions.
To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth. "In that" (*tatra*) means at that time of the production of the preceding and succeeding cognitions of the form; of one...

Even if there is no difference in the essential nature of the cause, the two cognitions would necessarily occur simultaneously. Why? Because that single, potent cause does not await auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). Consequently, it is logically contradictory for the two successive cognitions to have the same object.

By all of this, it has been stated that the thesis is contradicted by inference (*anumāna-bādhitatva*) when it is to be proven that the cognition of the subsequent form has an object non-different from the cognition of the preceding form. The inference is as follows: whatever occurs successively does not have a single object, just like the visual and auditory cognitions occurring successively; and the cognitions of the preceding and succeeding forms occur successively.
The state of having a single object is pervaded by non-sequential occurrence, and since sequential occurrence is its opposite, it is indeed a contradiction of the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha*).
Now, one might argue that because this [subject] is sublated by the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the inference cannot even arise.

If [you say] no, [we reply]: that is not so, because the cognition "this is that very same thing" has as its object a relation between earlier and later times, and therefore has difference as its object;
for being related to an earlier time is one thing entirely, and being related to a later time is another thing entirely. Otherwise, [it would follow that...]

Alternatively, if there were no difference between its relation to a later time and its relation to a prior time, then because the entity exists now, there would be no manifestation of that entity as having existed previously;
nor would there arise the cognition "this is that very same thing," but rather [the cognition] "it is not that.
Or, if there were no difference between its relation to a prior time and its relation to a later time, then there would have been no manifestation of it previously.
Furthermore, there would arise the cognition "this is that very one," rather than "this is that.

Therefore, that which is connected with a prior time is not connected with a subsequent time, and that which is connected with a subsequent time is not connected with a prior time; thus, by virtue of having as its object things connected with prior and subsequent times—
Since [recognition] has difference as its object, how can there be no sublation of the thesis on the basis of recognition?

Umbeka, however, says: "Even if 'this is that very same one' is a single experience, it is nevertheless perceived as apprehending the state of being the object of past cognition and immediate presence within a single substratum. Or, even if this is two cognitions—[the cognition of] grasping..."

It is of the nature of recollection. Nevertheless, there is a distinction between the recollection of a jar and the perception of a cloth, which arise in immediate succession, because they appear as having distinct mutual objects. For in recollection, the object appears precisely as something present (aparokṣa) by way of being qualified by a past cognition; whereas in direct perception, the object of that past cognition appears as something present. Thus one says, "I remember this."

Because [the object] appears [as such]. Therefore, for a person whose vision is unblinking, the very determination that [the object] persists as devoid of arising and destruction is the sublater of the inference that proves momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
That is incorrect; for successive perceptions have, respectively, as their objects the successive differences in the states of the subsequent entities.

Because the superimposition of identity—that "this is that very same thing"—is erroneous due to its lack of certainty. For instance, in the perception of one who sees for the first time, the present state appears directly, not the state that was the object of past cognition. This is likewise for one who sees it repeatedly. Furthermore, the object exists in its current form, not in its former form; and while the form remains constant, the former form—

Destruction is simply non-existence. Just as in the state of old age, the former form of childhood and previous cognitions and actions have passed away, while the present form is directly perceived; yet, that which was seen in states such as childhood [is no longer present].

Since the *puruṣa* is recognized in states such as old age, how could the status of being the object of past cognition and the state of being directly perceived appear as residing in a single substratum? Or else, how could the object, while being directly perceived, appear in memory as qualified by a past cognition?
It is said, "it shines forth," and so on.

Even in a case where there is a continuous determination for one who has been looking with an unblinking gaze for a very long time, the object's state of being directly present (*aparokṣatā*) arises through its connection with the present perceptual cognition; [this is so] because, due to the absence of past cognition, there is no status as the object of a past cognition.

If it is now argued that destruction is simply non-existence, how can it be said that "the very determination of persistence, which is devoid of arising and destruction, is the subverter of the inference of momentariness"?
Furthermore, as for what is said: "For one who asserts that there is difference at every moment, this [determination] is a subversion based on recognition."

If non-difference [of the cause] from the effect were established merely by the recognition of the essence (*tattvāvagama*), then even for that which has perished, such an essence would be perceived; this is like the recognition of a dead person. Thus, that [argument] is also refuted, because non-difference itself does not exist. Nor can there be non-difference between the perished and the unperished, due to their contradiction. Furthermore, non-difference cannot be proven by the necessity of explaining the recognition of the essence otherwise, since the recognition of the essence can occur even through similarity.

Because it is possible for it to have the nature of recollection; furthermore, the portion "that" (saḥ) is not perceptual, since its object is not present. Nor does this [cognition] grasp an object previously seen, because there is an absence of a clear manifestation. This is due to its being a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāyaka*) of a previously seen object.

A portion [of the object] is held to be perceptible; however, the identity between memory and perception is contradicted. Therefore, with respect to an object situated before one—which is devoid of being the object of a previous cognition—one superimposes the status of being the object of that previous cognition upon it by means of similarity, and thus the mental cognition grasps it as "this is that very same thing. And by the force of this superimposition, the state of being the object of a past cognition and the state of being directly manifest coexist within a single substratum.

They appear [as one], like the recognition of water in a mirage. However, in the absence of superimposition (*āropa*), these two appear as having distinct substrata, like the recollection of water and the perception of the mirage.
Therefore, this is established: because it is erroneous and because it is not a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), [the object] is not momentary by virtue of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Therefore, what is stated [by others] is based solely on similarity:
"For even when there is a difference in speed and so forth, the completed [word] is not perceived as distinct."
"A distinct cow-individual, clearly separated from other cow-individuals, [is perceived];
therefore, due to the oneness of the phoneme, a single cognition arises.
The existence of a cognition of difference would be due to the difference in the manifestors. (1)

Even when there is a difference in nature, it is illogical to claim that they have the same object simply because their names are identical; for this would lead to the absurd consequence [of identity] even in the case of jars and the like.
If you argue that [the reason] is not a valid means of proof in those cases because it contradicts what is accepted, [we reply: by what is the absence of contradiction established here as well?
As long as the fact of being denoted in such a way is not proven to be pervaded by the non-difference of the objects, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) remains doubtful. (35b)

That is refuted; for it is said that a phoneme (*varṇa*) is nothing other than a particular sound (*dhvaniviśeṣa*). Therefore, particular sounds uttered rapidly are called a rapid manifestation (*drutā gavyakti*); those uttered at a medium pace are a medium manifestation (*madhyagavyakti*);
and particular sounds uttered slowly are a slow manifestation (*vilamvitā gavyakti*). But [the phoneme] does not [arise] from the manifesting sounds (*vyañjaka-dhvani*).
The letter *ga* does not appear [as a single entity]; rather, among those instances, one perceives only the identity of the name, namely, "the letter *ga*, the letter *ga*.

Likewise, there is no single form among the short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*) vowels. For it is only specific sounds (*dhvani-viśeṣa*) employed for the duration of one measure (*mātrā-kāla*) that constitute the short vowel *o*.
