Similarly, other specific sounds [employed] for the duration of two measures...

When it is uttered for a long duration, it becomes the *dīrgha* (long) vowel; when uttered for a duration of three morae (*trimātrā*), these specific sounds become the *pluta* (protracted). Thus, the difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the short, long, and protracted vowels appears in this way; however, the letter *a* does not appear as undifferentiated among them. Rather, it is the very same letter *a* that is being articulated for durations such as one mora and so forth.
Since short, long, and protracted [vowels] are perceived, it is merely sound alone that exists. Therefore, as it has been said:
"In the doctrine of eternality, an inherent distinction between short and so forth is contradictory;
according to the sequence..."

How can that which exists at all times be itself composed of morae (*mātrika*)? Therefore, let its pronunciation be understood as lasting for the duration of one or two or three morae; the word itself is not composed of morae. (1)

That too is refuted; for the cognition and the designation "the vowel *a* [or *u*]" do not apply across short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*) durations. Furthermore, it might be argued that because the cognitions occurring at the earlier and later times share the same name, they must have the same object.

Therefore, he says: "Dependent upon," and so forth. There is a difference in the appearance (*pratibhāsa*) between the preceding and succeeding cognitions of the letter *a*, by virtue of their being prior and posterior in form. There is a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), through distinctions such as fast, medium, or slow [articulation]. Even though there is this difference in cognition, appearance, and intrinsic nature, it is illogical for them to have a single object simply because of the identity of their name, namely, "cognition of the letter *a*. What is the reason?

(1) Because it would lead to the absurd consequence [of identity] even in the case of jars and the like. For the cognition of a jar that occurs first and the cognition of another jar that occurs later—since both are "cognitions of a jar"—would have the same object due to the identity of their names. And if that were so, it would follow that a single jar exists everywhere. In that case, if one were to attempt to prove the oneness of jars and so forth, there would be a contradiction with what is observed, as jars and the like are [in fact] manifold.

If it is argued that because [the difference] is perceived, there is therefore no proof of oneness in that case, then here too—in the proof of oneness regarding the sense organs (*varṇas*)—by what means of valid cognition is the absence of contradiction with perception established? Here too, the distinction of the instruments [of cognition] as distinct for each person is indeed established;
the point is simply that, as in the case of hair that has been cut and grown back, there is a determination of oneness due to similarity.
• Ma-th Monit

If it is argued that sound, having a distinct nature, is established as manifold because it enters into the auditory perception through a diversity of instruments, why is this not also the case for jars and other objects? For in those cases too, one could likewise object that the difference in appearance arises from the difference in manifestors;
[this is untenable] because [objects like jars] are perceived through the operation of a complete collection of causal instruments.

And [the property of] being an effect belongs necessarily [to the word], because that [property] is impossible in a manifestor. (266) For it is never the case that words are not perceived when the instruments [of perception] are unengaged; nor does the operation of a manifestor necessarily cause perception, since in some cases a jar or the like is not perceived even when there is light. This is the necessity.

"Because of the operation of that [word] upon its arising, there would be no perception [of the object], since it is impossible for that [object] to be established through the operation of one who is not its agent.

(1) He states that this reason—"because of the identity of name"—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), beginning with the words "as far as... and so forth. "Being denotable in such a way" means by way of non-difference in meaning.

The state of being denotable through the identity of names—such as the cognition of the letter *ra* following the cognition of the letter *a*—is not established by pervasion through the unity of the object; thus, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) remains doubtful. Furthermore, there may be both identity of name and difference [of the objects]. Moreover, with respect to each difference of instrument, sound possesses a distinct nature for each difference of instrument according to the difference of persons.

If, while entering into or ascending upon the hearing of an auditory cognition (*śrotravijñāna*), the oneness of the word-sound (*śabda*) is established, why are jars and other objects not also established as being of a single form? Let them too be so established! Or else, some distinction must be stated.
If it is argued that even though the word-sound is one, there is a difference in appearance due to the difference in its manifesters (*vyañjaka*), [the author] says: "In that case also—"
And so forth. Even in that case, when a jar or the like is distinct, one might still object that the difference in appearance is due to a difference in the manifesting conditions (*vyañjaka*).
Furthermore, [the effect arises] necessarily from the operation—characterized by movement and so on—of the complete collection of causes.

From the very perception of sound, its status as an effect is established. Why? Because that [perception] is impossible when the cause is merely a manifestor; for it is impossible to perceive the manifested object invariably [while the manifestor is present].
He explains this with the words "for not," etc.: indeed, while the sense organs are active, there is never a non-perception of sounds.

But it is indeed perception [that occurs]. And the operation of a manifestor does not necessarily cause the object to be perceived or grasped. Why? Because in some places devoid of jars and the like, even when there is light characterized by lamps and so forth, jars and the like are not perceived.
Therefore, for a person who possesses the auxiliary causes for the production of unimpaired cognition, this [perception] of sound arises from its operation.

If there is a necessary perception [of sound] following the operation of the instruments, then that must occur upon the production [of sound] from the operation of the instruments. Consequently, sound is indeed something produced (*janya*), not something manifested (*vyaṅgya*).

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that a causal factor (*kāraka*) is defined merely by its capacity to produce, whereas that which produces [an effect] through making it fit for the arising of cognition is precisely a manifester (*vyañjaka*)?"
Thus it has been said. Therefore, it is logical that the palate and other such organs are merely manifestors (*vyañjaka*).

This is not a fault, because it was stated that something is a "producer" (*kāraka*) by virtue of mere production with respect to the effect in general, whereas it is a "manifestor" by virtue of its fitness for producing cognition; this is not, however, with respect to a visible effect. For instance, [the cause] possesses its auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) in their entirety—

Since the person who is the cause [of perception] is necessarily the producer of the lamp and so forth, and thus the producer rather than the manifestor, there is no fault. If it is argued that there is the apprehension of pervasiveness and eternity [in the case of the Veda], then what assurance can there be now regarding jars and other such things?

If it is argued that this is because they do not accept [the existence of such a thing] in that way: (1) Is sound accepted? Is it something possessing those same properties? And it has been stated that there is no excellence whatsoever in it. Furthermore, its pervasiveness and eternity have been refuted.
As for jars and the like, there is no fault because other manifestors are possible; for light is indeed their manifestor.

Established is this: (1) when [factors] such as the potter act as manifestors (*vyañjaka*), they appear as exactly that [manifestor], yet they excel because of their excellence as manifestors; thus they are indeed causal agents (*kāraka*), since there is no other possible mode for one who provides assistance.

This is the same in the case of sounds as well; for there too, due to the excellence of the instruments [of articulation] arising from factors such as the suitability of the location for the sense organ, [the sounds are produced].

(1) Furthermore, because the property of being an agent, as seen in the case of jars and other objects, is observed in the instruments [of action], such as a lamp, with respect to a different object; and yet, sound is not its agent. Since it is impossible for that which is established to arise through the operation of an instrument belonging to one who is not its agent, sound cannot be so established. Therefore, sounds are pervasive and eternal; thus, because of the pervasiveness and eternality of sounds—

Because of the operation of the manifesting instrument (*vyañjaka-karaṇa*), there is perception everywhere. However, jars and the like are neither all-pervasive (*vyāpin*) nor eternal; therefore, they are not necessarily perceived through the operation of the manifesting instrument.
If this is so, what confidence can there now be regarding jars and the like? [The answer is: certainty (*niścaya*). Just as they are neither eternal nor—178a—[all-pervasive].

Regarding the term "all-pervasive": let it be that these [atoms] are also eternal and all-pervasive. If it is asked, "How is it that they are not perceived at all times?", this is equally true for sounds as well. Whatever rebuttal applies there [to the case of atoms], that will apply to jars and the like as well. If it is argued, "Because those jars and the like are not accepted as being all-pervasive and eternal," [then we reply: sound is [accepted] as being all-pervasive and eternal.

[Objection: Why is it desired? [Response: Because it possesses the same properties as that. [Objection: It possesses the same properties as a jar and so forth; however, since pervasive permanence has been refuted previously, this is trivial.
[The opponent replies: "Of jars and so forth," etc. There is no fault, because there exists another manifestor distinct from the causal agent (*kāraka*).

There is no fault of the consequence of [the pot] being equal to the word. Demonstrating that it is indeed another manifestor, he says: "For illumination," and so forth. For in the world, illumination is established as the manifestor of these things such as pots, not the potter and others. If the potter and others were manifestors, they would be exactly like lamps and the like, and not otherwise.

They invariably bring about the perception of a jar, because even when there is illumination, the jar may be absent. If that were so, potters and the like would also [be causes]; but it is not thus. Furthermore, potters and the like possess a distinction [from mere illuminators], because a jar and such always exist whenever the activity of the potter and others occurs. Therefore, [the cause] is distinct from a manifestor, because it functions as something different from a manifestor. [It is] a causal...

Who, then, are the potter and others? What is the reason? Because there is no other possible mode for that which provides assistance; for there exists no other category apart from being either a producer (*kāraka*) or a manifestor (*vyañjaka*). Since manifestor-ship has been refuted in that context, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), the potter and others must be producers. It is not so with sound, for after stating its production, no other manifestor [is found].

It is established that by which very means [the cognition of] sound is conceived as its instrumental cause (*kāraka*). Therefore, because of its distinction from jars and the like, sound is indeed manifested (*vyaṅgya*).
To this, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntavādin*) replies with the words "That," and so forth: this possibility of other manifestors is equal even in the case of sound.

Because there is no other manifester (*vyañjaka*) for anything [other than sound], their causes would have to be the manifesters of those [sounds]. Therefore, it is not [the case that they are manifesters].

The manifestation (*vyakti*) of a sound consists either in its production by means of the [articulatory] organs, or in the sound possessing an excellence (*atiśaya*), or in the removal of its obscuration, or in cognition, since there is no other possible alternative. Among these, it cannot be the production of an excellence, because that would entail the consequence of the sound being non-eternal (*anityatā*). Nor can it be the latter [production].
(1) Because it is characterized by the loss of a prior form and the arising of a subsequent one;
or (2) if their manifestation is the disappearance of those obstructions to that form.

Because even in that case of sound, there is a superiority of the instruments [of production] due to their being situated in a location suitable for the auditory faculty from the perspective of the auditory faculty, as well as from the words "hundred" and so forth—where the word "and so forth" includes mental attention—and due to the excellence of the instruments themselves. If it is asked how there is such excellence, he says:

"In the case of a jar," and so forth. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "hi" (because). It refers to those complete causal factors (*kāraka*) of the jar and so forth, such as the potter and others.

That property which invariably initiates its own effect is observed in the case of instruments; for they too, being pervaded [by that property], invariably produce sound. Therefore, they too are indeed causal factors (*kāraka*), just like a potter and others.
And if, because there is no other manifestor of sound, the instruments are intended to be its manifestors, then—

For that very manifestor, such as a lamp, and for any other object, such as rasa and so forth, there is no other manifestor like a lamp; therefore, due to the absence of another manifestor, their causes— the causes of the lamp and so forth—
would themselves have to be the manifestors of those lamps and so on.

Since this is so, manifestation is not the function of the articulatory organs; rather, it is simply production. Alternatively, if manifestation were to occur from the articulatory organs, it would be of three kinds: (1) manifestation would consist in the sound possessing an excellence through the abandonment of its prior state;
(2) or it would consist in the removal of the obstruction to its perception; (3) or it would consist in the cognition having the sound as its objective support.
Alternatively, manifestation (*vyakti*) is cognition (*jñāna*). This is because there is no other possible way [to explain it] apart from these three modes.

Among these, manifestation is not the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the sound, because that would entail its impermanence. If it is asked, "Let there be the production of an excellence; but how does that entail impermanence?", he says: "Of that production of excellence, which [is the cause] of the previous form..."
Because it is characterized by the production of another, subsequent form, which is its disappearance.

(2) He states the second position: "Now," and so forth. Those obstructions of that sound—which consist of the conjunctions of the particles of stagnant air and which obstruct its perception—are the factors that impede its apprehension; their removal [is what constitutes its manifestation].
If you, a Mīmāṃsaka, hold that the separation [of the air] by the wind impelled by effort constitutes the manifestation (*vyakti*) of sound,
it has been said:
"The air within the chest, struck by effort, undoubtedly moves forth."
And that [air] follows along with the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other [articulatory organs].
And because it possesses momentum (*vega*), it necessarily persists for as long as that momentum lasts.

Furthermore, due to its movement, conjunctions and disjunctions between its constituent parts and the still air inevitably arise. (Ślokavārttika, Śabdanityatā 122–24) 7. Non-human Origin (*apauruṣeya*)
Why would the capacity of the collection [of causes] not exist?
For indeed, instruments that do nothing to remove an obscuration cannot be called "capable. Furthermore, disappearance is non-existence.

And it has already been explained that non-existence is not an effect. Nor can there be any capacity for an obscuration of an eternal sound, as has been stated. Therefore, there is no application of instruments toward an obscuration; nor is there an incapacity [of the organs], because sound is not perceived when those [instruments] are absent. Consequently, it is illogical that these [organs] should produce sounds.
Otherwise,
because there is no distinction in the word [itself], the manifestation of other things would also follow as a consequence.

If that were accepted, all causes would be rendered purposeless. (268) How could that manifestation be produced? Since the removal of an obscuration is a non-entity, how could the collection of instruments—the assemblage of causal factors—possess efficacy toward that non-entity which is not an effect in any way? It certainly could not.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "na hi" (for not...). This is what he says: (1) when the nature of the obscuration has been established, the causal factors (karaṇas) are indeed incapable of acting; they do not possess efficacy. Even upon the removal of the obscuration, they lack efficacy. Why? Because...
It has already been explained in the investigation of capacity (*sāmarthya-cintā*) that disappearance is non-existence, and that non-existence is not an effect.
Furthermore, this was stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position]. Now he says "nor indeed," etc., to show that [this too] does not exist.
Because an eternal word cannot have any excellence added to it (*anādheyātiśayatvāt*), there is no such thing as an obscuration; therefore, the removal of an obscuration cannot be its manifestation.
It might be so. What is the reason? It has also been stated that this is because that obscuration lacks the capacity with respect to an eternal entity.

Therefore, there is no application of causal instruments (*karaṇa*) toward the obscuration. The meaning is that one should not put forward the claim that "the causal instruments effect the removal of the obscuration of sound."

Nor is it the case that the causal factors lack the capacity for sound altogether. Why? Because when their activity is absent—that is, when the activity of the instruments is absent—sound is not perceived. Therefore, it is logical that these activities of the instruments should produce sounds.
Otherwise, if instruments were not producers (*kāraka*) but merely manifestors (*vyañjaka*), then, since there is no distinction regarding sound [as being produced],

it would follow that other things as well, such as jars and the like, would be manifested by potters and others. Now, if it is further maintained that those jars and so forth are indeed manifested by potters and others, then in that case—

If [the manifestation of an already existing entity] is admitted, all causes would be rendered purposeless. For instance, with respect to an object that is to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*), a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) would have to be either a producer of an excellence (*atiśaya*), a producer of the absence of an obstruction, or a producer of cognition; yet neither excellence nor the nature of manifestation itself can be an effect.
Therefore, all manifesting agents (*vyaktikāraka*) and agents that produce intrinsic nature (*svarūpakāraka*) would be rendered purposeless.
The explanation begins with the words "If... and so forth: if the instruments of sound are its manifesters, what kind of things are they?
If even those possessing the same properties as all other causes were manifesters of the cause and so on, then no effect whatsoever would exist at present.

This might be so; however, this is not tenable because an entity cannot have a specific quality added to it (*anādheya-viśeṣatvāt*). Since the absence of an obscuration (*āvaraṇābhāva*) is not an effect, its cognition is established in the very same way as the entity itself. If something were to act as a causal factor (*kāraka*) with respect to that cognition, then by the consequence that other things would likewise become such factors, it would follow that everything would be an effect.

Therefore, this collection of factors intended as agents would be useless with respect to the manifestation, rather than the action itself; and if that were so, this world would be devoid of activity, lacking both the benefactor and the beneficiary.
This would also be the case if the word were eternal.

(1) "Possessing common properties with all causes" (*sarvakāraṇasamānadharmāṇi*): the analysis of the compound is "those things which have the same properties as all causes. In that case, not even a jar or the like would now be the effect of anything such as a potter, because there is no distinction regarding the word [used to denote them]. If it is argued that "the manifestation (*vyaṅgyatva*) of everything is intended," this is not tenable.
What is the reason? (1) Because it would follow that all causal factors, which are intended to be manifestors, would be rendered purposeless. To explain:

there are three possible alternatives regarding manifestors; a manifestor could exist by producing either an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the manifested object, or the absence of an obscuration (*āvaraṇābhāva*), or [the production of] cognition (*jñāna*).

A manifestor does not function by producing an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the manifested object. What is the reason? (1) Because a thing that possesses a fixed nature cannot have an excellence added to it. Nor does it function by removing an obscuration; for the absence of an obscuration is not something produced as an effect. Nor does it function as a manifestor by producing cognition; what is the reason? Precisely because [the object] is a thing, just like any other entity.

For even the cognition whose object is that [entity] is established according to the Satkāryavāda view. Now, if it is held that cognition is produced as something previously non-existent (*asat*), then if some [agent] is desired to be the causal factor (*kāraka*) with respect to that cognition, it would follow by extension that other factors such as the potter—who possess the same properties as those [causal factors]—would likewise be [regarded as] causal factors with respect to the cognition. Consequently, they would also be causal factors with respect to jars and the like.

Because it would follow that everything would be an effect by virtue of this [same] consequence; or else, a distinction must be stated whereby [the cause] possesses the status of a producer (*kārakatva*) with respect to cognition, but not with respect to jars and the like. Furthermore, no other mode of manifestation (*vyakti*) is possible.
Therefore, this collection of objects intended as causes is of no use whatsoever for the manifestation of a jar or anything else.

Because manifestation is precluded by the fact that an entity cannot possess an added particularity (*ādheya-viśeṣa*), nor is it applicable to action, since the acceptance of a causal effect (*kārya*) is not admitted; thus, [the postulation of such a thing] would be entirely useless.
And "in that case" means: when there is a deficiency of causal factors (*kāraka*), this world would be devoid of growth and inactive. Why?

(1) "Real" (*bhūta*) means that which is neither assisted nor assisting. The analysis of the compound is: that in which neither an object of assistance (*upakārya*) nor an agent of assistance (*upakāraka*) exists.

Furthermore, when the permanence of sound is to be proven, the proof (*sādhana*)—namely, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), non-application (*aprayoga*), and so forth—is that which is accepted as intended.
For example, sound is eternal because it is recognized as being one and the same. As it has been said: (1) "Because of the absence of number.

For people say, "The word 'cow' has been uttered eight times," and not, "There are eight 'cow'-words. By this, [the eternity of sound] is understood. 7. An Inquiry into the Non-human Origin [of the Veda].
The means of proof is recognition, which is held to consist of the application of what truly exists and so forth.
There is no example [of persistence] for all entities because of their momentary destruction.

(269) For it has been stated that all entities are indeed momentary, since destruction is without cause; and it will be stated later that origination does not come from another, because it is impossible for existence to be accidental. Therefore, this recognition is not [valid] because of its application to existing things...

In some cases, [the cognition] follows after [an object] that is stable and of a single nature; however, in the case of lamps and the like—which possess successive transformations of their own nature—it is observed that people recognize them through *pratyabhijñā* (recognition). This is because it is applied to what exists (*sataḥ prayogāt*). Whatever is employed [as an instrument] must exist prior [to its operation], just as an axe and so forth exist prior to the act of cutting. And since a word is employed for the purpose of conveying meaning, it too must exist prior to its employment.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of [the reason] "because it is uttered for the sake of another" and so forth is intended. As it has been said: "(1) But [the word] must be eternal, because its manifestation is for the sake of another. 'Manifestation' (*darśana*) means utterance (*uccāraṇa*); that is for the sake of another in order to convey a meaning.
If the word were destroyed as soon as it was uttered, it would not be able to convey the meaning from that point; therefore, it is not for the sake of another [if it perishes]."

"Let it be released" means it is without an example; that is, it is without an illustration. For there is nothing eternal upon which this proof could operate. What is the reason? Because all entities are subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
Explaining this very point, he says: "For [entities] are momentary," and so forth. [This refers to] the non-production of destruction...

This has been stated previously and will be explained later as well. Having demonstrated impermanence by way of destruction, he now demonstrates it by way of origination as well, saying "origination," and so forth. Since entities possess origination from an external cause, they are therefore not eternal. Why is it that they originate from another? Because it is impossible for existence (*sattā*) to be accidental.

It has already been stated that if things were accidental, there would be no restriction of place and so forth. Therefore, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)—which consists of the application of a real object and so on—is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) for a thing that is stable and of a single nature, serving as its similar instance (*sapakṣa*). It does not follow [as a concomitant] in any such case; rather, it is a transformation or arising through various distinct natures, just as in the case of waves and the like, where recognition occurs only among those very [successive states].

Since it is observed that [the object] is pervaded by the distinction of characteristics such as different cognitions, this is indeed contradictory. Nor is there here a recognition based on a universal such as "lamp-ness" and so forth, because the universal has already been refuted.
[The opponent replies: "No," etc.; the recognition is not contradictory. For what reason? Because of the non-differentiated, stable, and unitary form...

For one whose birth is non-different—that is, for recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) which has a single birth—there is the occurrence [of recognition] regarding lamps and the like due to delusion (*bhrānti*).

If it is asked, "How is there delusion? [the answer is: because of deception through similarity; that is, because one is deceived by the similarity between the preceding and succeeding moments. This explains that non-delusory recognition serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*).
Furthermore, that [property] does not exist at all in the case of lamps and the like.
The Master [Dignāga] stated, "[Recognition is] a cognition of non-different birth. On what basis, on what authority, is it said that recognition is a cognition of non-different birth?
Because a permanent entity lacks causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*). And this [same argument applies] even to the recognition of perception.
If it is argued that the refutation of [the opponent's] cognition should be seen as follows—namely, that because that which is being recognized appears as non-different—[we reply:
no, for that very non-difference must be examined in all cases, even in the case of bricks and stones, by means of their temporal sequence;
thus, [your claim] is indeed contradictory.

(1) It is not [the case that identity is established] because of the deception caused by similarity in things of non-different origin; for since [identity] exists even in the case of lamps and the like due to delusion, on what basis is it asserted that there is no difference in origin? For that very non-difference must be considered in all cases through the sequence of priority and posteriority.
If it is argued that the same applies to difference as well, then let there be doubt precisely because of that. And there is no establishment [of a conclusion] from what is doubted.

If it is argued that there is oneness due to the non-perception of distinction, we say no; for existence and non-existence are established by the temporal sequence of cognitions. This is because there exists a distinction in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
Is the nature of the *bimba* and so forth the very same afterward as it was before, or is it something else entirely? It is merely due to similarity that there is [the appearance of] oneness.

This notion that there is an error, as in the case of lamps and the like, must be examined. If it is argued that just as the non-difference [of a gem] in diamonds and such is to be examined, so too is its difference, then this must also be investigated: does difference appear through a sequence of before and after?

The teacher says: "By that very [fact]. Since neither difference nor non-difference can be determined with absolute certainty, let there be doubt due to that very lack of determination. Let there be doubt regarding difference and non-difference in objects that are being recognized. If it is argued that "from doubt alone, because of the state of being recognized, there is a determination of difference," he replies: "And not from what is doubted—that is, from an object of doubt."
If it is argued that the oneness of sound is established by the mark of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*),

and that because no distinction is observed between the preceding moment and the succeeding moment— and because no distinction appears— the oneness of the entity across preceding and succeeding times is proven; [we reply:]...

"No," and so forth, is the reply. By this, the meaning is as follows: for an entity (*bhāva*), its manifestation at this very moment is its manifestation as a moment (*kṣaṇa*), because it does not manifest as being connected with prior and subsequent times. And the manifestation of a moment by way of its own nature is indeed a manifestation distinguished from prior and other moments; it possesses a distinct manifestation, but not one that is non-distinct (*avinābhāvin*).
Because of the existence of the preceding moment appearing [in consciousness], that distinction alone is not apprehended;
for that purpose, inference is employed. Regarding this, he says: "There is no non-perception of non-distinction in the case of diamonds and so forth. What is the reason?

Because the existence and non-existence of the diamond and so forth are established through the sequence of cognitions of the diamond and so forth, by way of their being prior and posterior. For instance:

The subsequent cognition having the diamond and so forth as its object establishes the prior non-existence of its own specific cause; and since it exists subsequently, its existence [is established]—thus, through the temporal sequence of cognitions, the existence and non-existence of the diamond and so forth are proven. This is because of the presence of distinction (*viveka*), that is, the presence of difference (*bheda*).

Clarifying this very point, he says: "If," and so forth. If other cognitions arising at a later time were to have their causes present at the earlier time of the preceding cognition, they would indeed have already arisen, just like that preceding cognition. But this is not the case. Therefore, those cognitions being unarisen at the earlier time indicate a deficiency in their own causes.

Otherwise, if their cause were already present even previously, it would have to be either capable or incapable [of producing them]. 7. Regarding the consideration of the non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*):

if other cognitions were produced with their causes already present, just like the preceding cognition, they would indeed have arisen. However, those that have not arisen indicate a deficiency in the causes; for while a capable cause produces [its effect], an incapable one does not produce it again.

Because capacity has not been acquired, and because even when acquired, stability is impossible; therefore, this so-called "application" (*prayoga*) is in fact merely the production [of the result] by virtue of the agent's capacity, for if [the object] were itself capable, that [application] would be useless. Furthermore, what is called "application"—such as the application of an axe or similar tools—is simply the production of that which is capable of accomplishing the desired goal, whether it depends on a homogeneous material cause (*upādāna*) or does not.
It is spoken of as being like the application of [the term] "action" (*karman*) and so forth.

For one who thinks: "Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) occurring in the presence [of the object] is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*); therefore, from that very perception, stability (*sthairya*) must be capable of producing [the effect] even previously. What is the reason? Because that which is capable produces [the effect]. Or, what if it is incapable?

Nor would it produce [the effect] later. Why? Because even for that which is incapable, since no excellence can be imparted to it, how could it ever acquire capacity from anything else? If, on the other hand, it were to acquire capacity from something, then, upon the acquisition of that capacity, its stability would be untenable; for there would be the loss of its prior nature of incapacity and the emergence of another nature of capacity.
Because of its arising [from that], cognitions occur sequentially; therefore, they also establish the sequence of their own objects.
Thus, since the distinction between all entities is established, their impermanence is proven. As for the cognition "this is that very same thing," it is caused by the perception of similarity.

Since this is so, even that second reason which is stated—namely, "this is a correct application" (*satprayoga*)—also refers only to the production of the word. What is the reason? Because of the capacity of the word [to arise] from the speaker;
the meaning is that the word acquires its capacity for performing the intended effect [only] from the speaker. Otherwise, if [the speaker's] activity...

If the axe and so forth, or the sound itself, were capable of their own effect even prior to [human] employment, then, because its own capacity would render the user useless, there would be the spontaneous operation of the axe and other tools independently of persons. But this does not occur.
Therefore, there is also "employment" (prayoga), which is the means for accomplishing the desired or intended object, such as cutting.
In this context, "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) refers precisely to the production of that which has a capable nature, such as an axe or similar tool. What kind of production is it?

It is "dependent upon a homogeneous material cause" (*samānajātīyopādānāpekṣa*), meaning it depends upon a preceding momentary cause that is of the same class or similar; this is like the application of an axe or similar instrument. In the case of cutting and so forth, the axes and other tools being employed [are of the same kind].

Because it depends on a preceding moment of the same kind, or because it is independent of a material cause (*upādāna*), like the production of sound through action and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of sounds such as those from a lute is intended. For when actions and the like are first employed, there is no dependence on a preceding similar moment.
The opponent thinks: "Let there be no recognition as inference because it is fallible;

rather, that recognition which occurs when an object situated before one is perceived is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, the stability of entities is established from this very means of valid cognition, direct perception. We shall refute that as well later on.
In this manner, the fallacious reason (kuhetu) adduced for the purpose of establishing stability is to be understood; for no such [stability] exists at all,
because it is merely a mental construction.
Regarding "accomplishment" (*siddhi*): we shall refute that as well later on.
Any other fallacious reason (*kuhetu*) is also to be refuted;
for there is not a single property (*dharma*) that follows after something of the same class (*samānajātīya*), because all properties are established in this very manner.
Furthermore, because the claim of universal stability contradicts reasoning as it has been stated, other eternal causes are also subject to the faults of verbal expression.
[This applies] when the intellect is held not to reside in the person, for there is sublation by what is accepted, by perception, by what is known, and by inference. (270)

If the individual cognition (*vyakti-buddhi*) is the sentence, then its sequence (*ānupūrvī*) is the sentence; yet in establishing its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*), [the doctrine] is contradicted, because it is admitted that cognitions are qualities of persons (*puruṣaguṇatva*). Indeed, this is even perceptible (*pratyakṣa*): if those cognitions [arise] from what are reckoned as persons, namely from the qualities of persons...
Or [they arise] from mental attention (*manaskāra*) and so forth. Furthermore, what is called "being an effect" is nothing other than the distinction between existence and non-existence.
There is no proof for the stability of wealth or merit that would follow a stable, unitary entity of the same kind. Why? Because all phenomena (*dharma*) are subject to this very condition.
Because it possesses the nature of the destruction and arising of successive intrinsic natures, and because all recognition of stability contradicts reasoning and contradicts inference. How so?
According to the explanation; that is, just as the proof of momentariness has been explained and will be explained in this treatise, so too does it contradict reasoning.
For this reason, other grounds for establishing permanence imagined by others are also to be stated as defects of expression.
Thus, having begun with the premise that "the word is not manifested," manifestation has been conceived as threefold:
the production of an excellence in the word, the removal of its obscuration, and cognition. Among these, because [the word] is eternal—

[The opponent argues: "It is neither the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the object, nor is the removal of an obscuration (*āvaraṇavigama*) the manifestation (*vyakti*), because the absence of an obscuration is not something produced.

When these two alternatives have been rejected, it remains that cognition (*jñāna*) is the manifestation. And in that case, a sentence is either the manifestation itself, or it becomes the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) of cognitions.

And this is not logical, because a sentence does not have cognition as its intrinsic nature. Nevertheless, it is stated for the sake of argument. Furthermore, if the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of a sentence consisting of a sequence of manifest sounds is to be proven, then the non-human origin of cognition itself would be what is to be proven. In that case, if the non-human basis—that is, the non-reliance upon a person—is being proven regarding cognition, there is a contradiction of the thesis (*pratijñābādha*). By whom?

[The opponent argues: "That which is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), that which is known through verbal commitment (*abhyupeta*), and that which is inferred (*anumita*)—all these occurring simultaneously with what is committed to, accepted, directly perceived, and inferred; the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) of those is the sequence of cognitions (*buddhi*), and that [sequence] is not something other than the cognitions themselves. Therefore, in establishing the non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*) of that sequence, it would be the non-human origin of the cognition itself that is established. To this, [the author replies]: "In that case..."

Furthermore, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of this Mīmāṃsaka is contradicted. Why? Because, according to his own established doctrine, cognitions are admitted to be qualities of the person (*puruṣaguṇatva*).
Demonstrating the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), he says: "Indeed, this is directly perceived, if those cognitions [are] mental attentions (*manaskāra*)."

"Arising from those [causes]"—by the inclusion of "etcetera" (*ādi*), the sense faculties (*indriya*) are included. From what kind of [causes], such as mental attention (*manaskāra*)? It will be stated that [this is] the "investigation of the non-human" (*apauruṣeya-cintā*).

Furthermore, that existence (*bhāva*) is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*); even non-existence (*abhāva*) is established by the efficacy of direct perception characterized by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

Maḥ! Therefore, the fact that cognitions are the result of human effort is to be inferred from this [cognition] because it possesses positive and negative concomitance as its logical mark; furthermore, the difference of the sequence from the phonemes has been examined by means of the *sphoṭa*.

How could that [sequence] be superimposed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), or how could it be based on a person (*puruṣāśrayā*)? The sequence distinct from the phonemes has already been refuted in the course of the analysis of the *sphoṭa*. Nor is it of the nature of the phonemes, because the nature of the phonemes cannot escape these alternatives. [If it were not of their nature,] it would be of a nature other than theirs in things that do not possess that nature.

The term "person" (*puruṣa*) is used for the sake of linguistic brevity, having been established as a convention among those who have made such an agreement; this is stated according to [the author's] own view. Alternatively, the phrase "or from the qualities of a person" (*puruṣaguṇebhyaḥ*)—transgressing [the usual order] by saying "from the qualities of a person"—is stated according to the view of others. Therefore, since the fact that cognition (*buddhi*), which arises from mental attention (*manaskāra*) and other factors, is an effect is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), when its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) is to be proven, [this serves as] a counter-example.
[Objection: "There is no sublation by perception because the state of being an effect (*kāryatā*) is not perceptible. To this, he says: "But surely," and so forth.
These two specific instances of presence and absence are: the existence [of the effect] only when that which is considered the cause exists, and its non-existence when that [cause] is absent.
There is no other "state of being an effect" for an entity than these two; that aforementioned entity is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If it is asked, "But how is its non-existence established by direct perception when that [entity] is absent? he says: "Non-existence, too. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose characteristic nature (*svabhāva*) is precisely non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). We shall explain later that this too is established through the power of direct perception.

Perception, by establishing the very nature of an entity as being distinct from others, implies non-existence through its own force; thus, the term "force" (*sāmarthya*) is employed. Furthermore, since the existence and non-existence of cognition follow the existence and non-existence of mental attention (*manaskāra*) and so forth, it is precisely because cognition occurs when those [factors] are present that the fact that cognitions are produced by human effort is to be inferred. What is the reason? [It is] positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
Because this status as an effect is established through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), by this [statement] the sublation by inference (*anumāna-bādha*) has been stated.

Now, it might be argued: "The sentence is not the manifestation (*vyakti*); rather, the sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*) is the sentence. To this he says: "Furthermore," and so forth. [He means: there is no difference between the sequence and the *sphoṭa* apart from the phonemes themselves, according to what was previously stated regarding the *sphoṭa*.
Even if it were not distinct [from the phonemes], it would have been refuted even earlier; for there is no other possibility for a real entity (*vastu*) except difference or non-difference.

Furthermore, in that case, the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) of the all-pervading phonemes would have to be something superimposed through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Moreover, how could it then be independent of a person (*apuruṣāśrayā*)? It would necessarily be dependent upon a person (*puruṣāśrayā*).

He explains this with the words beginning "from the phonemes" (*varṇebhyaḥ*). The sequence (*anupūrvī*) is distinct—that is, of a different nature—from the phonemes. It has already been refuted by the very same order of investigation into the *sphoṭa* mentioned previously, through such criticisms as: "The sentence does not exist as something separate from the phonemes, because it is not perceived," and so forth; [this applies] to the sequence as well.
It is rejected;
nor is it of the nature of color, because that would entail the consequence of a difference in cognition such as "sara" and "rasa.
Nor can it be inexpressible in terms of identity or otherness, because the nature of a real entity does not transcend these two alternatives. Identity and otherness—
So...
"Tirulporn apa Rasa Ngentot" (What is the taste of sex? d...

This notion that there is a sequence would be an error of the intellect appearing as a superimposition; and how could that intellect be non-human (apauruṣeyī), given that it arises from the manifestation of mental construction?

(Ṅa) Destruction is causeless: furthermore, since no eternal intrinsic nature exists whatsoever, your sound must be non-eternal. And that [non-eternality] would have to be either causeless or caused by something else; it could not arise from human effort. (1)
Therefore, it is of human origin.
How is it known that sound—or any other entity—is not eternal?
Because destruction is necessarily concomitant with mere existence, sound is impermanent.

For the destruction of entities does not arise from anything whatsoever. Therefore, that [destruction] must be the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the entity itself, because it exists as a property belonging to the entity arising from its own causes;
this is because one cannot transcend conceptual construction. Consequently, with respect to phonemes—which lack that form and are devoid of a real, distinct sequential order—that form—

This delusion—that there is a "succession"—would belong to a cognition that manifests as a superimposition, specifically one that manifests as a superimposition of succession. And how could that succession be non-human (apauruṣeyī)? It is indeed human (pauruṣeyī). Why? Because it is established by the activity of the Buddha’s manifestation; for it has been demonstrated [by him].

Moreover, because there is no such thing as an absolute or eternal intrinsic nature, the sound or word that exists for you must necessarily be non-absolute and unstable. Furthermore, that sound would have to be either causeless, or it would have another cause distinct from the person—that is, it would be caused by something else. In that case, if it were causeless, it would be eternal; otherwise—

Because it is independent [of other causes]. If, however, it were caused by something else, it would not arise from human activity; yet it does arise from human activity. Therefore, it is understood to be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).
"How so? and so forth says the opponent: sound, or any other non-existence such as that of earth and so on, is not eternal.
How is this understood? The Master [Dignāga] says: "Because destruction is invariably concomitant with mere existence, sound is impermanent due to its cause;
for destruction occurs simply by virtue of being existent and does not depend on any other cause. And sound is existent. Therefore..."

"Permanent" is the meaning of the aggregate [of terms]. Why? Because destruction is invariably concomitant with mere existence; thus he says, "For not," and so forth. For there is no separate entity called "destruction" that arises for things from some cause of destruction.
Since this is so, (1) therefore destruction must be the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity. Why is this?

Because the entity itself, possessing that property—that is, the property of perishing—arises from its own causes. To say "destruction" is simply to mean the state of having the property of existing for only a single moment; and that [property] arises precisely from causes. [Section on] Destruction Without Cause.

Nor can it have the nature of a specific entity, because that will be refuted later. Therefore, it must have the nature of mere existence. By this, it is established that every entity—whether it be sound or anything else—that partakes of existence is non-eternal.

It is not established, because that very destruction is not proven to have another birth. For instance, causes of destruction for entities are observed, such as "wood by fire" or "a jar by a staff. Those who know the definition of cause and effect state that the characteristic of a cause and its result is the conformity with presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
(1) It is not [the case that destruction occurs] because when the preceding [moment] ceases by its own nature, another arises modified through dependence on specific conditions.
For only those things that are produced undergo destruction, not other existing things. As it has been said: "That which exists and is without cause is eternal."
And so forth. Furthermore, the destruction of no particular entity has [itself] as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Why? Because that [destruction] will be refuted later. Therefore, destruction would have the nature of being merely an entity;
it would have the nature of mere existence (*sattā*). For that reason, sound or any other entity whatsoever is a vessel for existence.
"Existing" means being the substratum of existence (*sattā*). "Not ultimate" is established. [The opponent says:
"It is not established. For what reason? Because the birth of that very destruction from another [cause] is not established.
"Birth from another" is *parajanma*; "not birth from another" is *aparajanma*. Because that is not established—since destruction is without cause.
This means "because of [the establishment of] proof.

For instance, it is observed that fire is the cause of destruction for wood, as in "the wood is burnt by fire," and a staff is the cause of destruction for a jar, as in "the jar is broken by a staff. Thus, when fire and the like are present, there is the destruction of the wood and so forth; when they are absent, there is not.

Furthermore, there is no positive or negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the destruction of destruction itself. And this, they say, is the definition of cause and effect—that which possesses the cause (*hetumat*). As it has been said:
"The presence of the conditions for destruction—such as impact, contact with fire, and so forth—"

"Without [contact], they do not undergo destruction, even in the absence of jars and the like"— this he refutes with the words "not so," and so forth. In the world, fire and the like do not cause the destruction of wood and such things without [contact].

Causes are indeed perceived; however, when each preceding moment of wood and so forth ceases by its own nature—that is, through spontaneous cessation—another subsequent moment, in the form of ashes or the like, arises. Thus, fire and other factors are recognized as the causes for the destruction of the wood and so forth, but not because they produce destruction. For how could there be a transformation of that [destruction]?

He says that its production [occurs] through the following: "qualified," and so forth. A qualified cognition, such as fire and the like, acts as a cooperative cause (*sahakārī*) by depending upon that [fuel].
Even granting this, we say: (1) let it be granted that fire is the cause of the destruction of the wood; yet that destruction [is not produced by fire]. 181b.
Or let it be that fire is the cause of the destruction of the wood; yet is that destruction produced from the fire the wood itself, or is it something else?
If fire were to arise from something else, there would be the perception of wood [even after the fire has arisen].

If it is argued that because it does not perish, "that very thing" is its destruction, how can this be? For when one distinct entity arises from another distinct entity, how could it be said that the wood has ceased to exist? Or, if it is not perceived, then there would be an over-extension of the principle.

If it is argued that "it remains thus," and that "this very thing is its destruction": (1) if that non-existence is indeed produced from fire, then because it has not [previously] come into being, it is not perceived.
Let it be granted that this is its name, "non-existence"; nevertheless, how can one thing be the destruction of another? For it is not so.

It is reasonable that a piece of wood is not consumed merely by the naming of some object; nor can it be [the cause of its own destruction], because that would lead to the absurdity (atiprasaṅga) of mutual destruction. Since there is no distinction [between them], it would follow that, as a separate entity (arthāntara), it would be a real thing distinct from others. [The compound] "born from wood" (*kāṣṭhaja*) is analyzed as "that of which the birth is from fire" (*agnerjanma yasya*). Is this simply the wood itself, or is it something other than the wood? In that regard, [the question concerns] the fire—
(1) Regarding the destroyer:

if destruction were to arise from the cause as a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), there would be the perception of the wood. Why? Because [the wood] would not have perished. What [would happen] to the wood if destruction, as a distinct entity, were to arise from that distinct entity which is the wood?
When there is birth, wood that was non-existent is said to have perished; that is to say, it is not at all non-existent.
If it is argued that even if it has not perished, it is nonetheless perceived through the arising of another entity, [the author] says: "Or else it is not seen" (1).
Why is it not seen? It is indeed seen. If, however, by the arising of one entity another entity has perished—

Or it is not seen; in that case, there would be this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): by the arising of just any other object whatsoever, everything would become non-existent, or else nothing would be seen. That very entity [fire] is born from fire, not everything; for this wood is perceived in the world as having the nature of destruction—this is what is meant.

He explains this very statement of the summary (*grahaṇaka-vākya*) with the words beginning "yadi" (if). If that very destruction of the wood, which is born from fire, is its non-existence; then, for that reason (*tad*), because this wood has become non-existent—that is, because it has perished—it is not seen.

He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "Let it be," and so forth: "Let this thing produced by fire have the name or designation 'non-existence' (abhāva). Even so, how can one thing be the destruction of another merely by way of a name? For it is not logical that wood should cease to be seen simply because a certain thing produced by fire has been given the mere name 'destruction.'"
Now, one might object: "Since this is well-known in the world, it is simply destruction itself; to say 'it is not its destruction' is a mere matter of naming.
To this, he says:
"And one entity cannot be the destruction of another, because that would lead to an over-extension [of the definition]. [Otherwise] all entities would be the destruction of the wood."
Destruction would [occur]. This recalls exactly what was just stated above.

If it is argued that "destruction caused by fire is a specific nature (*svabhāva*) and not universal," then what is the connection with "wood"? If it is the relationship of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), no; for that will be refuted later. If it is the relationship of produced and producer (*janyajanakabhāva*)—

If it is argued that there is no fault because the production [of fire] does not depend on wood and so forth—which are already existent—[we reply: what dependence can there be for that which acquires no excellence (*atiśaya*)? Or, if there is an acquisition [of excellence], there would have to be the birth of another piece of wood; otherwise, the cause of the non-disappearance of the previous [wood] would be seen exactly as before. If it is argued that the previous fire is destroyed by that very [new wood], then what is the relationship between this [new fire] and the previous one?

He thinks as follows: Just as all entities are not perceived as being of the nature of the destruction of the wood because they are distinct entities, so too, that which is produced by fire would not be perceived as being of the nature of the destruction of the wood, since it is also a distinct entity.
This might be the case if, on account of being a distinct entity, that thing produced by fire were not of the nature of destruction; [but then] the same would apply to smoke.

"In that case, there would be no such thing as 'the effect of fire' [produced by fire], because it would be a different entity (*arthāntara*), like a jar. Yet, it does exist; and even though there is no difference in its being a different entity, the destruction of the wood will take the form of something produced by fire.
To this he replies: "Because there is no distinction," meaning that for that real entity produced by fire, there is no difference from the wood.

Because there is no distinction between this [non-existence] and other things such as jars; the point is that how could it have the nature of destruction, since destruction itself consists in the form of cessation? As for smoke, even though it is a different entity, its being an effect of fire is perfectly logical, because there is no contradiction between a different entity and being an effect of fire—thus, this [objection] is trivial.
If it is argued that the nature produced by fire in the wood is destruction, and since this applies to all things such as pots, there is no over-extension [of the definition], then we ask:

what is the relationship between the wood and this destruction produced by fire in the wood? Since they do not stand in a relationship of mutual benefit (*upakāryopakāraka*), there is indeed no relationship at all.

Wood is the support; that which has this support is the supported, namely destruction. If it is argued that there is therefore a relationship between the support and the supported, this is not so, because that relationship between support and supported will be refuted later.

Is destruction produced? Wood is its producer. Therefore, if there is a relationship of produced and producer between destruction and wood, then what of fire? What is meant by saying that destruction occurs from fire? What is the reason?

(1) Because that destruction arises from the wood itself; since destruction arises from the wood in dependence upon fire—that is, in dependence on it—there is no fault. If you argue that the fault previously stated—that there would be no destruction produced by fire—does not apply, [we reply as follows].
What dependence could there be on fire for a piece of wood that has already acquired its excellence from the fire? None at all.

If the wood were to acquire excellence from the fire, then there would have to be the production of a second, distinct piece of wood designated as "excellence. In that case, the original wood would be something whose cause of destruction does not exist; it would not [be subject to] decay.
The analysis [of the compound] is "there is a threefold cause. It is observed in that very way, as before.
This might be the case: since from that very fire which possesses excellence there is the birth of a second piece of wood, from that same fire...
What is there in the Sarībhakāpaḍa marsh?
Thus, that same consequence remains unresolved:
fire, while assisting toward a subsequent excellence (*atiśaya*) that is fit for connection with destruction, must necessarily produce something entirely new (*apūrva*);

otherwise, the wood would be perceived remaining in its previous state. Furthermore, what is called the "destruction of the wood" is simply the non-existence (*abhāva*) of the wood. It is not [an entity].

Furthermore, it has been stated that non-existence cannot be an effect, and thus that which produces it would be a causal agent itself; consequently, it would not require anything else. Moreover, if there were a difference between the nature of existence and non-existence, then for existence to be excluded from that [non-existence], its very nature as existence would be established; how then could it be called "non-existent"?
Therefore, (1) there can be no mutual destruction; why then is the wood not seen?
(If it is argued: "It is the destruction of the previous wood. (273)
What connection does this destruction produced by fire have with the preceding wood? That is precisely the same objection. It was stated immediately after that what the connection with "wood" is;
furthermore, if one resorts to a relationship such as that of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), then that [relationship] will be refuted later, and so forth.
Furthermore, since everything would undergo transformation, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress.

Therefore, because fire assists toward a subsequent excellence in the wood that is capable of being connected with destruction, it produces an entirely new piece of wood; thus, the previous wood would have to be seen remaining in its former state—this is the conclusion.
Furthermore: "The destruction of wood" is said to be the non-existence of the wood. And non-existence is not an effect.

For if it were accepted as an effect by way of a positive affirmation (*vidhi*), it would follow that it is an existent entity (*bhāva*). Therefore, the statement "one produces non-existence" means "one does not produce an existent";
it is merely a negation of action. Thus, one who performs that [action] is indeed a non-producer, for the negation of action is itself non-production.

On the grounds that [the destruction] is a mere negation (*pratiṣedhamātratvāt*), it was stated in the section examining the relationship between the locus and the located (*ādhārādheya*) regarding the general property (*sāmānya*) and its possessor (*tadvat*), that fire and so forth need not be depended upon for the destruction of wood.
Furthermore, as for the non-existence— that is, the destruction— of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of wood and the like, from that...

If a distinction from the intrinsic nature of wood and so forth is admitted, then, because there is no non-existence apart from that [wood], the entity consisting of wood and so forth would be excluded from non-existence. Consequently, for that wood and so forth which is being excluded from non-existence, its very intrinsic nature would be established; for it follows that for that which is excluded from non-existence, existence itself is established. Thus, how could [the effect] be produced by fire and the like?

By destruction, wood and so forth are called "non-existent. Since this is the case, there is no destruction of one thing by another; the meaning is that one distinct entity is not the destruction of another distinct entity.

Even granting this, we say: (1) Let there be another destruction distinct from the wood; since that other entity is produced by fire, why is the wood not perceived to remain in its very same state? Proving this very point, he asks: "What is this contradiction? What contradiction is there between the occurrence of a separate entity and the perception of the wood, given that destruction is causeless?
If it were [an obstruction] by virtue of being grasped by that [other object], then there would be no non-obstruction by it;

for if it were grasped by that other object, the wood would not be seen. It would follow, then, that this [other object] is the obstruction of the wood. But this is not logical, because an obstruction would hinder the seeing [of the object], whereas it does not hinder its striking and so forth.
The potencies of substances [are such that] there is a total obstruction. Regarding the existence of a distinct entity called "destruction" produced by fire, and the continued perception of the wood—
[if these were the case], then the wood would be seen remaining in that very same state.

Now, [it may be argued]: "That entity which is a different thing (*arthāntara*) produced by fire is the destruction of the wood, because it is perceived as having the nature of destruction. And destruction is non-existence (*abhāva*); that which is the non-existence of the wood is produced precisely as something having a nature opposed to the wood. But since this is a different thing, like a jar, is it not impossible to produce it as something having a nature opposed [to the wood]? (1) For it is not like a jar, as a different thing... [182b]

Because it is a distinct entity, smoke is not the effect of fire. Therefore, just as smoke—though being a distinct entity—is produced by fire, so too is destruction, which is of a contrary nature, produced [by it]. And since there is a contradiction between two things by way of mutual exclusion, the non-perception of one occurs precisely when the other exists; how then could destruction, designated as a distinct entity produced by fire, [be the case]?
Śaṅkara says: "It is stated that there would be the perception of wood when its opposite exists.

This is incorrect because (1) there is no contradiction between being a different entity (*arthāntara*) and being an effect of fire; even though smoke is a different entity, its status as an effect of fire remains entirely uncontradicted. However, for a different entity produced by fire, the property of coming into existence—

By that [reasoning], it possesses the nature of an entity (*bhāva*). And how could that which is an entity be a non-entity (*abhāva*) for you? Because of contradiction, destruction (*vināśa*) is held to be a non-entity; therefore, destruction is contradictory to an entity that is a different thing (*arthāntara*). Nor does this apply even to a different thing, because it does not appear as having the form of destruction. For the destruction of wood and such things consists in their cessation by their own inherent nature (*svarasanirodha*), which is the cause.

If it is argued that [destruction] appears as a distinct entity, then, provided that its cessation by its own nature is not admitted, how could even a different entity appear in the form of destruction?

For it has already been stated at the very beginning that this is because [the entity] is of the nature of an existent. So how can it be said that there is a contradiction with a different entity called "destruction"?

[Objection: "Because it has been produced, the wood is not seen. [Reply: However, if destruction were formless (*nīrūpa*), there would be a contradiction between it and the entity (*bhāva*) with which it coexists. But even then, because it is formless, it could not be a distinct entity (*arthāntaratva*) nor could it be produced by a cause.
Therefore, if fire were to produce a distinct entity, the wood would be perceived in its original state.
If it is argued that the wood is not seen because it is grasped— that is, appropriated— by that other entity produced by fire,
then it follows that this other entity is an obscuration of the wood. But that is not tenable,
because an obscuration of the wood by that other entity is impossible.

He explains with the words beginning "yadi" (if). By that other object produced by fire; "that" refers to the other object produced by fire. Nor is it logical for this [non-perception] to be imagined as an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*). For an obscuration would indeed obstruct the seeing of the object being obscured; it would not, however, obstruct the capacities of substances, such as striking and so forth. Darkness—
It is necessary to meditate on the suffering of the three lower realms after having generated bodhicitta.
"Lal"— [one might object] that by this very [process], the substance would be destroyed; for, due to the loss of all its powers, there would again follow an infinite regress, as in the case of fire.

Or, even if its capacities for impact and so forth have not fallen away, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be desired by it through another existing entity. Furthermore, if wood is not seen because of the apprehension of an object called "destruction" arising from fire—[then the following applies].
There would be the non-destruction of destruction, and from that,
the wood would be seen again; for that which possesses arising must necessarily be destroyed by destruction, and when that [destruction] has been destroyed, the wood [would reappear].
There would be emergence [from non-existence]. Furthermore, upon the killing of a killer, there is no further rebirth for Caitra.

This is because we observe the striking and so forth of jars and other things that have already come into being. In that case, it is the obstruction of another's arising in its own location [that constitutes destruction].

[The word] "destruction" [is used]; by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of odor, taste, and so forth is intended. Now, if one were to attribute all causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) to the obstruction itself, then, while that total impediment is admitted, the wood would not be consumed by this very obstruction, nor would it be consumed by fire. What is the reason? Because by that very [obstruction], all the capacities of this wood would have been displaced.

From the forest [of arguments]. And that being so, there would again be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even in that case, destruction would be caused by something other than fire—just as in the case of fire itself.

Whatever fault was stated at length regarding fire in relation to the destruction of wood would apply when the destruction of wood is brought about by another entity produced by fire. And thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). By that other entity produced by fire, through destruction—
If one were to postulate another ultimate destruction, that too would require another, leading to an infinite regress.
Now, if this fault is to be avoided, then the capacities of the wood for being struck and so forth must remain unimpaired.
But even if those capacities of the wood for being struck and so forth remain unimpaired, by what other [cause]—whether existing or otherwise—would fire...

183a. What is destroyed by the fire produced from wood, such that it would act as an obstruction [to the wood] and yet the wood could still be seen? As for the phrase "if... and so forth: the analysis of the compound is "that from which fire arises. The meaning is: because of the grasping of the object by means of the destruction produced by the fire. In that case, there would be the destruction of destruction itself. What is the reason?
(1) Because it has an origin. Since it possesses an origin, its destruction, like that of wood, would also be destructible;
that is to say, from the destruction of that destruction, the wood would be seen once again.
He explains this with the words beginning "necessarily" (*avaśyam*): since the destruction of the wood exists as something possessing an origin, it must necessarily—
It must be considered: when that destruction of the wood has occurred, there would again be the emergence of the wood and so forth;
its manifestation would take place. [The opponent] raises a further objection with the words "hanta ghāta" and so on: just as when the killer of Caitra is killed...
The non-reappearance of the destroyed Caitra is not his non-arising again. If it is argued that here too, even when wood is destroyed, there is likewise a "non-reappearance" of the wood, [we reply:
destruction is without cause.
If it is argued that "it is the same here as well," [we reply: because the killer does not die.

Even when the destruction of destruction occurs, there is no restoration of the entity. If you say, "For even when the killer is killed, the one who possessed him [the victim] does not return to life," we say: No; for the killer is the cause of that [victim's] death. We do not say [that the destruction itself is destroyed].
When the cause—such as fire or a staff—is absent, there must be the presence [of the effect]. What then?

It is the absence of that [effect], characterized by absolute non-perception. When that [cause] is absent, what other course remains for the persistence of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? Indeed, the death of Caitra is not like a staff; rather, it is like a staff. For his death is the cause of destruction.
Upon the cessation of that, there would indeed be no further rebirth for him.
If destruction were non-different [from the thing], then the wood itself would be the agent; because it exists, it would follow that it is causeless. There is no other possible course.
(276) He refutes this with the words beginning "the killer" (*hantuḥ*), etc.: this solution is not tenable. What is the reason? Because of the killer...

Because of its nature as destruction (*raṇatvataḥ*). For the killer is not of the same nature as Caitra’s death; rather, he is the slayer (*mārayitā*). Therefore, it is logical that when that [slayer] perishes, Caitra does not come back to life. However, if death itself has not ceased, there would necessarily be a coming back to life.
He explains this with the words beginning "vināśa" (destruction): even upon the destruction of destruction, there is no restoration of the entity.

[The opponent claims: "It is a return to a previous state; for even when the killer has been killed, the one who possesses that [karma] does not come back to life because of being killed by that killer, the person. This rebuttal is not tenable. Why? Because the person who kills is the cause of that death;
it is because he is the cause of Caitra’s death. However, that killer is not of the nature of death itself.

Clarifying this very point, he says: "Not," and so forth. We do not say that when the causes of destruction—such as fire or a staff—have ceased to function, an entity that has already perished must come into existence once again. If one were to assert such a thing, this [objection] would indeed be a valid rebuttal. Rather, what is it? It concerns that non-existence (*abhāva*) which is produced by fire and other factors in relation to an entity such as wood; of what kind of [non-existence] is this?

(1) Regarding that which is characterized by absolute non-apprehension: here, apprehension consists in action residing in an object. By the negation of that [action], absolute non-apprehension is said to be the absence of all causal capacity. When there is the cessation of such a non-existence, what other course remains for an entity than its abiding in its own nature? It is simply the abiding in its own nature.
This refers to the "course" [of rebirth].

However, it is not logical for there to be a renewed existence once the killer has perished; for the killer of Caitra is not like a destroyer, but rather like a staff or similar instrument—being equal to a staff and so forth because he is a cause of destruction. For his [the victim's] destruction is like that caused by a staff...
If death were to cease— that is, if that death which is like a destruction were to cease— then this Caitra would certainly undergo rebirth.
Thus far, the fault has been stated regarding the case where destruction is a distinct entity.

With reference to the state of being non-different [from the entity], he says: "Even if there is no otherness," and so forth. Even if the destruction of the thing were non-different from it, the destruction would simply be the wood itself; for that wood, having arisen from its own causes, exists. [It is not... nothing at all.
The destruction of wood is not something different from the wood itself; it is that very thing which becomes [the destruction]. And that [destruction] already exists beforehand.
For what purpose would there be efficacy for [the causes] such as the seed and so forth? Therefore, because they do not provide assistance to it, the effect does not depend on them in any way;

nor is it possible for a relationship of "this belongs to that" to exist, since such a relationship is based upon the provision of assistance, otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Even in the case of indirect assistance, this conceptual dilemma necessarily follows: is that which is assisted a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), or is it that very same thing? If it is a distinct entity, then the inquiry as to how it can belong to that [original thing]—namely, whether it constitutes an "assistance" and so forth—remains unresolved.
