The same applies if it is not distinct. Therefore, since an existing form cannot transcend being either identical to or different from [the original], [the problem persists].

Because the production of an effect is characterized by the accomplishment of a form, that which is devoid of such activity is not a "doer" at all; thus, something must be produced by fire and other such factors. Consequently, destruction—which is of that very nature—is without a cause. Therefore, for destruction as a property of a real entity, there exists no other possibility than these two alternatives: identity with the thing or difference from it.

He explains [the point] with the words "not a different thing" (*anarthāntara*), and so forth. When destruction is not a different thing from the wood, then it exists even prior to that [destruction]; in this case, one should consider what efficacy fire and the like could have regarding the wood and other such things to be destroyed. In some places, the reading is "of the staff and so forth" (*daṇḍādīnām*); however, that should be explained by taking the jar and other such things as the primary referents.

Therefore, because it follows that [nature], since there is no assistance rendered to the wood and so forth by the causes of destruction, those causes of destruction do not depend in any way whatsoever—by any form—upon that wood and so forth. Nor is it possible for this fire and so forth to possess a relationship with the wood and so forth such that "this is the cause of destruction of that. Why? Because [the status of being a cause] is based upon the rendering of assistance.
Otherwise, if one were to postulate a relationship in the absence of any benefit (*upakāra*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); everything would then be related to everything else.
One might argue: "Fire and the like do not directly benefit wood and the like, but rather [they are related] because they produce a benefit that is related to them."

Therefore, he says: "By way of a succession," and so forth. An assistance that is related to the wood and other such things is produced by the forest and so forth, not directly. Even when such assistance is conceived as occurring through a succession, this conceptual construction necessarily follows along [with it]. Is that assistance, even by way of succession, a different entity (*arthāntara*), or is it that very thing, such as the wood?

[Objection: In that case, even if the assistance (*upakāra*) is a distinct entity from the wood and so forth, what is the relationship such that "this is the assistance belonging to that wood"? In this regard, one must inquire how that assistance produced by fire acts as an assistive factor (*upakāraka*) toward the wood and so forth, since there is no relationship [between them] without such an intermediary. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is implied that if another assistance were postulated for that [assistance] as well—

This includes the inclusion of faults such as the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Likewise, even if [the effect] were different [from the cause], the same objection would apply regarding the assistance [rendered], namely that which was stated by the words "destruction would be just like wood" and so forth. Therefore, because an existing form cannot transcend being either identical to or different from [its cause].

This might be the case: since an existing entity cannot transcend being either identical to or different from itself, the production of an auxiliary effect brought about by a cause of destruction is simply non-existent. Therefore, destruction is without cause;
and that which is without a cause does not depend on anything. Consequently, it is established that this entity is by its very nature such that it perishes spontaneously.

If it is argued that because destruction is causeless, it follows that existence and destruction must coexist due to its permanence—[we reply: how can there be permanence for that which is non-existent?
(277) This might be the case: even if destruction is causeless, it must necessarily be permanent; therefore, existence [would be] non-existence...

(ba) "And destruction occurs together with its own nature. This is not so, because it would lack the properties of a permanent entity; for such a conceptual construction is impossible when [the object] is non-existent. This is because both [existence and destruction] are properties of a real thing (*vastu*), whereas destruction itself is a mere nothingness (*akiṃcit*).
Indeed, co-existence could only occur with something [existent]; yet destruction does not exist as such. Therefore—
It is faultless.

Nor is it logical that there would be the consequence of the destruction of an existing entity (*sattva*) [by non-existence], because the destruction of an entity is not held to occur through its own destruction.
Therefore, he says: "In the case of assistance," and so forth. This is because [assistance] has the characteristic of producing a form (*rūpa*), namely, the production of an existent form.

Because [the cause] is not [the agent]. Consequently, that entity possessing [the property] must either be produced by that destroyer or something else; and in both cases, the aforementioned fault applies. Therefore, a cause of destruction that lacks the capacity for such action cannot be an agent; thus, it is not the cause of anything. Furthermore, a non-cause—such as a staff or the like—is not required by a perishable object, such as a jar. Therefore, this entity [perishes] by its own mere existence.
"That which has that as its nature" means having a perishable nature.

Having taken "destruction" to mean non-existence through annihilation (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), he anticipates the objection of the opponent: "Even if it were causeless," and so forth. For if it were causeless, it would have to be eternal; and because it would be eternal, destruction would exist even at the time of the entity's existence—such is the [opponent's] conception regarding the entity and its destruction.

If it is argued that this leads to the consequence [of their] coexistence, this is not a fault. Why? Because how could there be permanence for a destruction characterized by annihilation, which is non-existent?

He explains this with the words "It might be so," and so forth: Even if destruction is causeless for the proponent of momentariness, it must necessarily be eternal; thus, existence would be characterized by that absence [of destruction], having the nature of the cessation of destruction, while destruction would be characterized by the absence of that [existence], having the nature of the cessation of existence. These two would coexist in a single entity.

This is not so. Why? Because that non-existence, being a non-entity (*avastu*), cannot possess properties such as permanence and so forth. For when something does not exist, the conceptual distinction between permanent and impermanent is impossible; this is because those two [categories] are properties of entities. Furthermore, destruction, which is characterized by the cessation of an entity, is a mere nothingness.
Furthermore, since for you [the opponent] that which is arising exists eternally, it would have coexistence with something;

yet no destruction occurs. Rather, this is merely a negation of activity, to the effect that an entity whose nature is to abide for only a single moment simply does not exist by itself. Therefore, the fault just mentioned does not apply.
Furthermore, he anticipates the opponent's intention: "If destruction is admitted to exist, then [the following occurs] regarding that destruction...

How could non-existence destroy an entity? Therefore, the claim that "the entity would thus be perishable" is also a mere impossibility, because it is not admitted that the destruction of an entity results from [its own] destruction. For how could one who says that "destruction" is simply "nothing at all" desire the destruction of an entity on account of that?

How, then, can an entity be said to be "destroyed" if destruction does not exist? For entities do not depend upon a destruction that is non-existent during their state of being present; indeed, one who possesses something is designated or perceived as such by virtue of that thing, just as a horse is [designated] by its horn. It is certainly not the case that destruction does not exist at all.

But there is no [entity] that becomes the destruction of an entity; rather, the entity itself, characterized by momentary duration, is the destruction. It has been stated that, discerning this nature of it at a later time, people designate "destruction has occurred for this" according to their conventional perception. For nothing whatsoever ever happens to an entity; it is simply that very [entity] itself.

If [destruction] exists, it follows that existence would be subject to destruction; however, this consequence—that an existent thing would not possess destructibility—is also untenable. This is because we do not maintain that the destruction of an existent thing is brought about by a separate entity called "destruction.
He explains this with the words beginning "How? (katham): "How could a non-existent destruction cause an existent thing to perish? For there can be no operation of what is non-existent..."
Because of [this] connection, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that an entity must be indestructible. What is the reason?
Because one does not admit the destruction of an entity by means of a "destruction" that is a distinct entity from itself.
The author supports this very point with the words beginning "For whoever... and so forth: for whichever proponent says that "destruction" is nothing at all.

How could one desire the destruction of an entity from that destruction which is itself devoid of intrinsic nature? [The opponent asks: "How so? and so forth. If destruction is non-existent—that is, not present—how can an entity be said to be destroyed? It would simply not be destroyed. For instance, in the state of being presently arisen, there is no destruction; those things for whom there is no destruction [in that state]...

This is the analysis of the compound. For those [entities] that have perished are not counted [as existing]. And when there is no destruction of an entity, how can it be designated by that [destruction] as "possessing destruction"? Indeed, an object that does not possess a certain intrinsic nature—that is, one that lacks a connection with it—is not designated by that unrelated thing as being "possessing it" through the word. It is designated by the word as "possessing that."
Or it is perceived by means of cognition.
He refutes this with the words "No," and so forth: "Indeed, it is not that the destruction of an entity does not exist at all; rather, destruction certainly exists.
How then is it said that 'it does not exist'? It is because that destruction which belongs to the entity does not [inherently] exist."

If destruction does not exist, how then is it said that "destruction exists"? To this he replies: "But existence itself, having the property of momentary duration, is destruction as it lasts for only a single moment.
If existence itself is destruction, how then does the world designate it by saying "the destruction of existence has occurred"?

Therefore, he says: "In darkness," and so forth. [They] discern—that is, they ascertain—this entity's nature of abiding for a single moment, which is characterized by the deception of the production of a similar subsequent [moment], by means of non-perception at a later time when the continuum has been interrupted, through the realization of its non-abiding; [they ascertain it] according to the cognition that "the destruction of this entity has occurred."

It was stated previously that worldly people designate [things] as "persons. Now, regarding destruction without a cause: such [destruction] arises from its own causes. Therefore, it has not been destroyed by anyone; rather, it is simply its very nature (*svabhāva*) by which it is called "destroyed."
How then is it said that destruction is now causeless?
That [statement] was made in order to indicate that a perishing entity does not depend on anything else.
The state [of destruction] has been described as being without a cause by the mind, having superimposed a distinction upon it.

An entity that has arisen does not obtain destruction from another; for such an entity arises by itself. Thus, in order to negate any other property dependent on something else, and by making known its own nature, the property is presented by the mind as if it were a separate entity from the substratum.
For indeed, no other form whatsoever—whether called "destruction" or anything else—ever arises in an entity that has already been produced.

That very entity, having arisen from its own causes in such a manner, exists for only a single moment. Therefore, it is not by some occurring thing called "destruction" that the entity is said to be destroyed; rather, it is its very nature (*svabhāva*).

Thus, this entity has the nature of abiding for only a single moment, by which it is said that the entity is "destroyed. Otherwise, if it did not possess that nature of its own, there would be no destruction even in the absence of another cause. If destruction is nothing at all, then how can it be said that destruction occurs without a cause?

By you [it must be admitted]. For how can one even consider whether that which lacks an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is causeless or has a cause? Furthermore, how could there be a distinction such as "the destruction of an entity" (*bhāvasya nāśa*)? He answers this with the verse beginning "naśyan... (while perishing...). An entity, while perishing, does not depend on another—that is, it does not depend on a separate cause of destruction.

This is because it does not depend [on anything else]. It is not for the sake of making known—that is, not for the sake of making known its independence from another. That state of destruction has been described by us as being without cause. Having superposed (āropya) a distinction—that is, a difference (vyatireka)—between that state of destruction and existence by means of the conceptualizing mind (vikalpabuddhi), [one might object].
This is what is meant: (1) the destruction of an entity occurs without a cause; the meaning is that its destruction does not possess a cause.
He explains this with the words "no," and so forth: an entity, having arisen, does not [require] destruction from another cause of destruction.

[He] obtains [it]. What is the reason? Because for that which is of such a nature—namely, precisely that which has a perishable nature (*naśvara-svabhāva*)—arising occurs from its own cause of existence itself. For this reason, it does not depend on another, imagined cause of destruction; thus it is "independent of another" (*aparāpekṣa*). And such is this phenomenon (*dharma*), namely that which is called "destruction. [The compound *aparāpekṣadharma*] is for the purpose of negating that [dependence on another].

This means: for the purpose of refuting destruction that has a cause. "By making known its intrinsic nature" means by making known the perishable nature of the entity (*bhāva*). This is to be connected with the phrase "its very nature is stated thus. "Stated thus" means it is stated that its destruction occurs without a cause. This is said when there is sometimes a desire to know that [nature] alone, [namely] that the entity [arises] from something other [than itself].

When there is merely the desire to know whether destruction occurs or not, in what manner is it said [to occur]? By mentally distinguishing—through the intellect—a property called "destruction" as if it were a separate entity from the substratum, one makes the division, thinking, "this is the destruction of this entity. Thus, according to the aforementioned method, because it is non-existent, it is not distinct [from the entity itself].
When there is a desire to know that [nature] alone after having analyzed [the object], it is the very nature itself that is thus described. However, those of dull intellect—

deceived by mere sounds because they have seen things in such a way elsewhere— superimpose upon that [nature] a quality of destruction, whether with or without a cause, and thereby confuse themselves with reflections on existence based on an unestablished reality.

If this dilemma regarding whether non-existence exists by itself or not is the same [for us], then surely, even if destruction occurs after [the entity], for you this dilemma of whether it is identical to or different from the entity remains equal—since it must arise from the entity itself. In that case, why is the entity not perceived when there is a separate existence [of destruction]? And even if it were not separate, that very thing would simply become that [destruction].
Since nothing at all has happened to it, how can it be said to have perished?
Indeed, in this case: "Nothing happens to it; it simply does not exist. (250)

The connection is as follows: although it has been established that [the self] is by its very nature devoid of destruction, those of dull intellect and the intoxicated, having superimposed upon it the quality or attribute of destruction, cause themselves to become agitated.
To the question, "Why, then, do they agitate themselves in this way? he says: "In some cases," and so forth; for example, "the king's man."

Because such usage is observed in cases like "the separation of two related things" (*sambandhinor vibhāga*) where the ablative case of separation (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) is employed; and because here too,

people are deceived by the mere proclamation that "the destruction of an entity occurs," having superposed upon the entity a quality or attribute (*guṇa-dharma*) called destruction that is distinct from it, and then [superposed] the existence (*bhāva-sattā*) of that imagined quality.

Having superimposed that quality called "destruction"—whether it be with or without a cause—through various modes of perception, by means of a conceptualization of things as possessing real existence;
of what nature is this? It is a conceptualization in which reality is not established. By means of such [conceptualization], they agitate themselves.
With the words "even from itself" (*svataḥ api*), etc., he anticipates the opponent's intention: even for one for whom destruction occurs spontaneously and without a cause,

if the existence of that very non-existence— namely, destruction— is admitted even from itself, then this conceptual alternative (*vikalpa*) characterized as "identity" or "otherness" arises in the mind.

He explains with the words beginning with "nanu" (surely). The meaning is that there is neither posteriority nor anteriority even in the case of causelessness. Regarding the destruction of an entity (*bhāva*), which is a real thing (*vastu*), since it occurs by its own nature (*svata eva*), this dilemma of identity or difference is equal:
is destruction a different entity from the thing, or is it the thing itself? In that regard, if it were a different entity, then what [would be the consequence]?

If destruction were something distinct from the entity, then its existence (bhāva) would not be perceived while the entity exists. Alternatively, if destruction is not distinct from the entity, then even in the case of non-distinction, that very thing—the jar or whatever it may be—would be what is called "destruction. Therefore, since nothing at all has happened to this object, how can it be said to have been destroyed?

He refutes [the objection] with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely). Regarding this context, what was said? He says: "There is no existence of that. It was stated previously that [destruction] simply does not exist. It was stated that destruction is causeless;
for he says that this destruction, or anything else, does not come into being. What then?

"That very entity does not exist. For if one were to speak of the existence of something, the entity would not have been negated by this [statement]. Thus, while the cessation of existence is the subject at hand, one would have stated something entirely irrelevant; for indeed, no entity ever ceases to exist by virtue of another entity's existence. It would only then be "non-existent" if it did not exist of its own accord. And the phrase "it does not exist" is a *prasajya* [negation].

Clarifying this very point, he says: "For indeed," and so forth. For this proponent of causeless destruction does not claim that for an entity produced from its own causes, there exists some property—whether of the nature of an entity, the nature of a non-entity, or something else such as destruction, or alteration while persisting (*sthityanyathātva*). Rather, he maintains that the entity itself simply does not exist; this is the cessation of the entity (*bhāvanivṛtti*).

He states the mere measure [of the definition]. By this, the meaning is as follows: (1) in the first moment, an entity comes into being that was previously non-existent; in the second moment, there is neither the existence nor the non-existence of that [entity]; nor does it undergo destruction by its own inherent nature (*svarasa*); rather, it simply ceases of its own accord.
Furthermore, if one were to assert through the term "destruction" the existence or arising of some property (*dharma*), then for this proponent, the entity [would not be destroyed].

It would be turned back; that is to say, the cessation of existence has not been stated. And thus, while the cessation of existence is the subject under discussion, by the prescription of another thing—a different matter—only something irrelevant would have been said. What is the reason?
For there can be no existence [of anything] through the production of some non-existence called "destruction," or through the form of the cessation of existence.

An entity is not something that is non-existent [in itself], by virtue of which its own cessation would occur through such a designation. This is what is meant: just as when there is the cognition of an entity, the entity itself does not cease, but rather that cognition alone becomes related to it; likewise, if one accepts that the cessation of an entity occurs, that very [cognition] is the cessation.
The property called "cessation" would be related to that [entity], but the entity itself would not cease; how, then, could its cessation occur?

Therefore, at that time, that entity would not have become ceased unless it had ceased of its own accord. Consequently, as for what is said: "If even the non-occurrence of the entity does not happen, then there is no destruction."

Now, it follows that [non-existence] must be either different from or non-different from that [existence]. In either of these two positions, there would be the perception of existence at all times, because of its indestructibility. Therefore, there is no destruction of non-existence. How then is existence not perceived at all times?
It is because of the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

That is rejected; for the existence of a perceptible object is pervaded by its being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, from the absence of that [cognition], there is an absence [of the object].

Or, if it exists, it must necessarily be an object of valid cognition; so how can there be non-apprehension? If, on the other hand, its existence is due to its being of an imperceptible nature, then in that case there is a cessation of its perceptible nature. And is that [cessation] different from the entity or not different? (1)

The objection that there would be a perception of the existence of an entity in both states remains exactly as it was. Therefore, even the non-becoming of an entity does not occur; nor is there the fault of indestructibility, because [the entity] ceases by way of its own nature.
If it is argued that, since the cessation of an entity is formless (*nīrūpa*), it must be distinct from the formal entity (*rūpin*):

Now, for that which has no form at all, how could there be otherness? Might it then have identity? That too does not exist, because it lacks form. Therefore, in relation to an entity, one merely negates its being either identical to or different from it, just like the horn of a hare.

...185b This is a negation (*pratiṣedha*), not an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). Now, even in this case, if something were to exist, there would be no difference in form between negation and exclusion, because in both instances the affirmation (*vidhi*) is primary. Or rather, [there would be a difference] from the negation of something.

Even exclusion (*paryudāsa*) would not occur in any case. For if something were to be negated, then that which is distinct from it would be conditioned by means of that exclusion. But that is not so, because when "negation occurs everywhere" is said, there is the cognition of some positive entity itself. And for them, by that [statement], only the existence of a different thing would have been expressed; there would be no mutual distinction between those two.

Furthermore, in the case of isolation (*viveka*), there is no relative negation (*paryudāsa*). Thus, since there is an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*) would also not exist. Even if [the entity] were thus unitary, how could it be maintained that its existence does not occur in the second moment? For if it exists in the second moment, how can it be maintained that it does not exist there? Because of the contradiction. If, on the other hand, it does not exist, then how can it be an existent thing?
"It is said that 'it does not exist' because of its non-existence;

that is incorrect. For even in the first moment, it is commonly expressed in the world that 'an entity comes into being. And in that case, if it is an entity, how can it be said to 'come into being'? Therefore, in all instances, affirmation and negation are applied by taking the entity as it exists within the intellect."
This so-called "conventional usage" is trivial;
therefore, it is established that: "At that time, that entity would not have existed if it did not exist by itself."

[Objection: But does not this sentence, "it is not self-existent," also state that the non-existence of an entity occurs by itself? And in that case, the same fault remains. To this, he says: "And [the phrase] 'it is not'... and so forth. The word "and" (*ca*) is used because...

Regarding the meaning: because it is said that "existence does not exist," this is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (non-affirming negation), not a *paryudāsa* (affirming negation). Where there is merely the cessation of what was expected to occur, without any contact with a positive entity, that is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*.
However, where the negation of one thing results in the affirmation of another, that is a *paryudāsa*. Otherwise, even here in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*, [there would be] some...

In the sense of "stuti" (praise), when there is an injunction (*vidhāna*), there would be no difference in form or difference in essential nature between a negation (*pratiṣedha*) and an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
By the word "negation," the *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) is meant. What is the reason? Because in both cases—both the *prasajya* and the *paryudāsa*—the injunction is predominant.

And if there were a positive injunction even in the case of a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), then negation itself would not exist. And thus, because there would be no negation of anything, there could be no exclusion (*paryudāsa*) anywhere either. What is the reason? For if some entity were to be excluded from something, then it would be distinct from that; [that is,] it would be distinct from the entity being excluded.

It would be touched [by the exclusion]. By the exclusion of that—namely, by the exclusion of what is to be turned away—just as in the case of "Bring a non-Brahmin," there is contact with a Kṣatriya or the like through the exclusion of a Brahmin; yet, in that case, there is no turning away of anything at all. What is the reason?
Even when it is said that "in every case there is the cessation of something," the exclusion of an existing entity (*bhāva*) is not perceived in anything.
Moreover, since even by the word "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) some kind of entity (*bhāva*) alone is perceived, this proponent— who, while speaking of the cessation of an entity,
has not actually stated a mere cessation but rather must have stated the existence of another entity—

cannot establish a mutual exclusion (*parasparaviveka*) between those two things of which one is said to be distinct from the other through a relative negation (*paryudāsa*). And if that [exclusion] does not exist...

In this case, there is no *paryudāsa* (presuppositional negation). This is because *paryudāsa* is characterized by the apprehension of one thing through its distinction from something else (*tadanya-viveka*). Thus, destruction is not causeless, since it is characterized by the persistence of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
And that persistence could only occur if there were the exclusion of something other than that [nature]. And that...

If it were non-existent, the world would be devoid of both engagement and withdrawal. Therefore, when it is said that "for whom there is no destruction," it must mean that he himself does not exist. Indeed, a rule observed in one context cannot be applied everywhere merely because of a similarity in sound; for just because a person is given the name "donkey" (*gardabha*), it does not follow that they possess the characteristics of a donkey (*bāleya*).

[These points] are to be applied accordingly. Likewise, in the case of "Caitra does not have a son," even though there is a negation of an affirmation (*vidhi*), it is observed [that this is not a case of non-existence], because of the contradiction [involved].
Thus, even when expressed in this way, the purpose has already been explained. Therefore:
"For this alternative would apply only to an existent thing, since affirmation conforms to a real entity."

In the manner described, because there is an absence of exclusion (*vyatireka*), there would also be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*). The meaning is that *anvaya*—the following along with or the affirmation of some object—would not exist. What is the reason? Because that *anvaya* is characterized by the persistence of a single nature. And since that persistence is the persistence of a single nature, [this would follow] when there is the exclusion (*parihāra*) of anything other than that.

It might be so; however, according to your own view, that exclusion of others (*tadanyavyatireka*) does not exist. Consequently, the world would be devoid of activity and cessation based on words, and there would be an absence of the linguistic practice of affirmation and negation.
Since this is not the case, one must necessarily admit that the denotation of a word consists solely in the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of something.

And since this is so, therefore, when it is said that "the destruction of a given entity occurs," what is meant is that the entity itself does not exist; (1) it is not, however, that some other distinct property called "destruction" is predicated of it. Just as there is a real distinction in the case of "Caitra’s son," so too in the case of "the destruction of an entity," because of the use of the ablative case [to express separation].

To [the objection] that [this is so] because of similarity, he says: "No," and so forth. Indeed, it is not on account of mere sound—that is, by virtue of the similarity with the expression "Caitra’s son"—that a real affirmation (*vidhi*) seen in another context applies here. The real affirmation seen in the case of "Caitra’s son" is fit to be applied even here, in the case of "destruction of an entity," provided it is not based merely on the application of words to the thing.

Because it is illogical. He states this very point with the words "for indeed not," and so forth. Since a certain person has been given the name "Gardabha" (Donkey), the qualities of a *bāleya*—that is, the qualities of a donkey—are certainly not to be applied to that human being. Likewise, [the statement] "Caitra's son exists"—
In that sentence, since the prescription of another thing—the production of a son—is observed, it should not be applied to the destruction [of the father].
Even in the case of the statement "the destruction of an entity occurs," destruction must be prescribed as something distinct from the entity. What is the reason?
Because of contradiction. It has been stated that because destruction is of the nature of non-existence, and non-existence is contradictory to coming into being (*bhavana*).
If destruction is not a distinct entity, why is it said that "destruction occurs for an existent"?
To this he says: "And thus," and so forth. Even when one speaks of "the destruction of an existent," the purpose has already been explained.
When, having mentally separated the property from the substratum as if it were a distinct entity, there arises a desire to know that [property] alone, its own nature...
This has been explained by such statements as, "Thus it is said," and so forth.

Therefore, since non-existence (*abhāva*) is nothing at all, the conceptual distinction between identity and difference is not applicable to it. Consequently, for an existent (*bhāva*), another existent necessarily depends upon it [for its arising], and that [dependent] is precisely its own-nature (*svabhāva*). For that which lacks own-nature...

Because there is no inclusion [of such a thing] in any activity—since "activity" is indeed the arising of a nature of such a kind—how could that belong to something devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)? How, then, does the conventional usage "the horn of a rabbit is non-existent" and so forth come to be? Indeed, it is not said that the horn of a rabbit is some kind of thing; rather, it is described in this way for its sake.
"It does not exist" is merely a negation of its being. Furthermore, speakers, by means of some context, present this very thing as if it possessed activity through superimposition;
however, it is not so in reality. For in that case, the truth consists in the discernment of all objects, wherein neither identity nor difference exists.
This conceptualization of identity or difference would apply only if there were the production of a real entity (*vastu*). What is the reason?
Because production is an affirmation that conforms to a real entity.
[Objection: But even in the case of the arising of an excellence (*atiśaya*), it is simply that very same thing which has arisen as an excellence; so how can it be said to have perished?

Therefore, in that state, this [entity] is not what is called "destroyed" by virtue of ceasing to exist of its own accord; rather, it is said to be "destroyed" because another thing has arisen. For it is not the case that something is said to have ceased to exist of its own accord simply through the arising of some excellence (*atiśaya*), since non-existence (*abhāva*) is characterized by the exclusion of all properties of existence (*bhāvadharma*) due to the cessation of all designations of excellence. Furthermore, existence involves the occurrence of origination.
Because it is momentary.

He explains by means of the words "existence" (*bhāva*) and so forth: existence (*bhāva*) is becoming (*bhavana*), that is to say, arising (*utpāda*). That [arising] necessarily depends upon that which is becoming; it depends upon an agent of becoming (*bhavitṛ*), because there is no becoming in the absence of an agent of becoming. And that existence...

In the case of an activity (*vyāpāra*), it is simply the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) itself; it is indeed the thing (*vastu*) itself. What is the reason? (1) Because that which lacks intrinsic nature cannot have any occurrence, and so forth, since there is no possibility of its being present [in a locus]. Furthermore, because there is no relation [to such a locus]. Nor is what is called "activity" a separate entity.
Rather, "activity" is the arising of a specific intrinsic nature characterized by the arising of an intrinsic nature as it actually exists. That [is what activity is].
How could there be the destruction of that which is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) at its very arising?

If that which lacks intrinsic nature cannot possess the engagement of an activity (*vyāpāra*), how then does the conventional usage "the rabbit's horn is a non-entity" occur, given that it involves the activity characterized by "becoming," as in "the rabbit's horn becomes a non-entity"?
The meaning is "in common usage. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of such statements as "the son of a barren woman becomes a non-entity" is intended.
He refutes this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*). Indeed, it is not stated by way of a positive injunction that "the rabbit's horn is some kind of non-entity or something else";

rather, it is by means of this sentence—"the rabbit's horn is a non-entity"—that [it is understood] of this [horn]... *(Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available text.)*

The non-existence of a horn is such that it is not an existence; thus, a negation of existence is being made. And these people who engage in worldly discourse, by means of some particular context, superimpose upon things like the horns of a hare as if they possessed activity, and show them, saying: "In this way, the horn of a hare and so forth become non-existent. Is it the case that the horn of a hare and so forth become non-existent? Or not?

[The phrase] "it comes into being" is used by way of reference to conventional discourse; however, that [entity], such as a rabbit's horn and the like, does not actually possess such activity even through mere linguistic usage. For the reality (*tattva*) regarding a rabbit's horn and so forth consists in the discernment of all objects—that is, the absence of any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in all objects—and there is no inclusion therein of any non-existent coming-into-being or the like. (Chapter 6: Investigation of the Person)
There is a certain [logical] inclusion here. Indeed, destruction does not exist in this way within a real entity because that entity still persists.

Even if speakers were to describe it in such a manner, it would not itself be so; rather, it is simply accepted that "nothing at all has ceased to exist. Therefore, an inherent nature that exists by itself cannot escape two alternatives: it must be either identical to or different from the reality.
Now, regarding the investigation of the person (*pudgala*):
the difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indeed not a reality. For even in the case of color and taste, their mutual difference is not something other [than the things themselves].

If it is argued that "difference is the non-connection of intrinsic natures," then what is this so-called "connection" (*pratibandha*), by virtue of which that [non-connection would constitute difference]?

[If it were argued: "It cannot be that [the cause] is not other [than the effect]," [we reply: if it were "unborn" (*ajanman*), there would be a mutual ineffability (*avācyatā*) between all causes and effects.

And in that case, since everything is in some way useful for everything else, nothing would be "other" than anything else. If it is then argued: "In this way, even destruction which has an ineffable cause will occur in such a manner," he says: "No," and so forth. Thus, like a rabbit's horn...
Furthermore, destruction is held by others to have the characteristic of being devoid of all entities. What is the reason?
Because that destruction arises—that is, comes into existence—within the entity itself. And how can that which comes into existence be a non-entity? Because it is a contradiction.
If, on the other hand, this destruction were indeed devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it would merely be described by speakers as "occurring in this way."

It is described as if it were something possessing a further shore (*pāravat*), yet it does not itself possess the nature of becoming such, because it is devoid of form (*nīrūpatva*). Thus, even for one who asserts that "non-existence comes into being," it is indeed intended that "nothing at all comes into being," since this statement consists merely in the negation of action. Therefore, [this applies] to some entity by way of a form that is not superimposed upon it in its own right.
An intrinsic nature does not transcend the two alternatives of identity or difference, because there is no other possibility.

If it is argued that the person (*pudgala*), whose intrinsic nature consists of the aggregates such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, is neither identical to nor different from form and the rest—and therefore its intrinsic nature indeed transcends identity and difference—[we reply: [This is not so. Because there is no third category beyond identity and difference, the intrinsic nature of the person must necessarily be either identical to or different from the aggregates. Since it is observed that the person is neither identical to nor different from the aggregates, it follows that the person lacks an intrinsic nature. Thus, the person is merely a conceptual construction (*prajñapti*). Just as a chariot is designated based on its parts, so too is the person designated in dependence upon the aggregates. Therefore, the person is not substantially existent (*dravyasat*), but exists only as a designation (*prajñaptisat*). Furthermore, since the person is not perceived apart from the aggregates, it is established that the person is a mere conceptual construct. Thus, the person is devoid of intrinsic nature. This concludes the refutation of the person's substantial existence.
That is not so; for (1) "otherness of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvānyatva*) is simply the state of not being that [very] intrinsic nature, which is precisely its non-reality as that.

If the person (*pudgala*) does not have the aggregates (*skandha*) as its intrinsic nature, then it must be something other than the aggregates. For even in the case of form (*rūpa*) and taste (*rasa*), which are well-known to be distinct, their mutual otherness is not something separate from them; rather, it is simply the state of not having the intrinsic nature of the other.

Since that [nature] exists in the person (*pudgala*) as well, the person too must be accepted as being distinct from the aggregates (*skandhas*). If it is argued that distinctness consists in the absence of mutual essential connection (*svabhāvāpratibandha*) even when there is no identity of nature, [we reply: that connection does exist between the person and the aggregates; therefore, despite the lack of identity of nature, the person is not distinct from the aggregates.
Regarding the phrase "of the neck":

he refutes this with the words beginning "What is this," and so forth. What is this so-called "bond" (pratibandha) of the person (pudgala) with respect to the aggregates (skandhas), by virtue of which bond [the person would exist]? And since that [bond] would not exist, the person would neither have the nature of the aggregates nor have a nature other than that.
The analysis [of the compound] is: "its intrinsic nature is other than the aggregates.
If it is argued that the birth of the person from the aggregates is itself the obstruction to birth, [we reply: no. 186. *Bīja-vāda* (The Theory of the Seed).

Even the statement "the Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā" would merely express the very same relationship of cause and effect through different words; there is no difference in meaning. We maintain that "otherness" (anyatva) consists in the non-concomitance of intrinsic natures (svabhāva). This otherness certainly exists between things possessing intrinsic natures, for they do not share a common nature. Nor does this [otherness] arise from the characteristic of being produced from that [cause].

There is no connection other than the essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), because that which is not dependent [on another] cannot be subject to deviation, and because it would otherwise contradict [the nature of] the property; furthermore, there is a difference in their characteristics.
If it is argued that the connection is one produced by cognition (*jñānakṛta*) and thus distinct [from the essential connection], [we reply: (1)

It might be argued: "Since a cognition that is inseparable from the apprehension of X necessarily manifests X when that [cognition] is understood, even though it possesses both that form and a non-that form, it is inexpressible [as being either].
This is not so; for it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). Its own nature is either that very [X] itself, or it is distinct [from it].

That which appears [as such]—for if it did not have that nature, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its appearing as if it did; and since it does appear, if this were the case, the person (pudgala) would be intended as being inexpressible in terms of identity or difference from the aggregates (skandhas) because of its being an effect.
And if that were so, there would be mutual inexpressibility among all causes. "And if that were so" refers to the case where inexpressibility follows from being an effect.

Everything is somehow useful for everything—whether directly or through a succession of causes; thus, the relationship of cause and effect exists everywhere, and nothing whatsoever could be other than something else. Therefore, even by one who asserts "ineffability" according to the definition of ineffability just mentioned, it would be merely the relationship of cause and effect expressed by another term; there is no difference in meaning whatsoever.

But difference (*anyatva*) is certainly not negated; for we define difference as the mutual non-concomitance and non-mixture of two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). And since that non-concomitance of intrinsic natures exists among all things that possess such natures, there is indeed mutual difference between them. Nor is there any other connection (*pratibandha*) between the person (*pudgala*) and the aggregates (*skandhas*), because [the person] is not born...

Apart from [the relation of] definition (*lakṣaṇa*), birth (*janman*), and essential nature (*svabhāva*), there is no other such thing as a "relation" (*pratibandha*). What is the reason? Because that which is not dependent lacks a causal connection; thus, it is not bound to that [other thing]. Consequently, any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to it is not contradictory. Therefore, due to the lack of a relation, the person (*pudgala*) is distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*). Furthermore, they are distinct because of the difference in their properties (*dharma*); for instance, [the person] possesses the quality of being inexpressible (*avācyatva*).
The distinction between phenomena (*dharma*) is that the person (*pudgala*) is a phenomenon, whereas the aggregates (*skandha*) possess mutual denotability.
If it is argued that although there is no causal connection (*pratibandha*) based on origination, there is nevertheless a connection between the person and the aggregates based on cognition;

The phrase "it might be," and so forth, explains this very point: for whatever form (*rūpa*) or other object there is a cognition—that is, a cognition of which—there is a knowledge that is *nāntarīyaka*, meaning inseparable (*avinābhāvin*), from the cognition of that person. Because, when those [objects] are apprehended—that is, when the form and so forth are apprehended—that person necessarily appears [in consciousness]. Thus, there is a connection established by cognition; for instance, in the case of form, sound, and so on—

By the very apprehension [of the aggregates], the apprehension of the person (pudgala) is intended, because the person is cognizable by the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth. Therefore, due to the connection established by that cognition, that entity called "person" is inexpressible as being other than the aggregates; even though it does not possess their form and lacks the intrinsic nature of the aggregates, it is thus designated.

He refutes this with the words "no," and so forth. There is no cognition of a person that is inseparable from the apprehension of form and so on. Why? Because the object of observation—the person—does not exist; and even if it were observable, such a cognition would not have that [person] as its nature. Thus, for whom would there be a dependent apprehension? Furthermore, when something has an apprehension dependent on another, its own manifestation as a self-nature does not perish, just as [the manifestation of] light depends on [an illuminator].

[It would be] like [the relation between] cognitions and blue objects and so forth. Or what is its proximity (*pratyāsatti*) therein, such that when that which is not its own nature is being perceived, it itself presents itself?

For in this way there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that "it is because that which is being perceived is the material cause (*upādāna*) of that [which presents itself]," then who—

The meaning is that it is easy to grasp. There is no relationship of cause and effect, for neither upon the removal nor upon the acceptance [of one] do the cause and effect mutually establish their own cognition. If it is argued that the very proximity consisting in the necessary concomitance (*tannāntarīyakatā*) of the cognition itself [constitutes this relationship], [we reply:
The reason is that, having abandoned the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and so forth, that person (*pudgala*) is itself devoid of intrinsic nature.
For that which appears as the form of form and so forth is indeed its very intrinsic nature.
Now, if the person were of a nature other than form and so forth, then, given that this person lacks the nature of form and so forth, it would not [be perceived] as such.

Because it would follow that the person (*pudgala*) must appear separately, like form (*rūpa*) and other [sensory objects]. Yet it does not so appear; therefore, the person does not exist at all, because that which is perceptible but does not appear is non-existent. Now, if the person is held to be imperceptible—then even if the person is held to be imperceptible, there would be no cognition of its nature, meaning there would be no cognition having the aspect of the person. Of what, then, would it be?

On what does cognition depend? The meaning is that the cognition of a person (*pudgala*) is not invariably concomitant with the cognition of form and so forth. Thus, the implication is that there is no connection established by cognition. If it is argued that the person does not appear separately precisely because its cognition depends on form and so forth—(1)

He says: "And not," and so forth. The connection is as follows: when a thing (*vastu*) has a cognition dependent upon another, and its perception is restricted to that [other], then there is only the manifestation of its own nature (*svabhāva-pratibhāsa*), and it does not perish. Why? He says: "Manifestation," and so forth. Just as in the case of blue and other objects whose cognitions are restricted to light, even when light is manifesting, their own manifestation does not [cease].
It perishes, because they appear apart from light; the same would apply to the person (pudgala) as well.

Furthermore, what proximity or connection does that person have with that aggregate? By what cause of proximity would it establish itself— meaning, it causes one to grasp itself— as being present within that aggregate which is non-self in form and lacks the intrinsic nature of a person, even while appearing therein?

For in this way there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If, when something unrelated is appearing, the person (*pudgala*) were necessarily to appear, then the meaning would be that even when anything whatsoever appears, something absolutely unrelated would also be perceived. [Objection: There is a proximity (*pratyāsatti*) consisting in the fact that the perceived person has those [colors, etc. as its material cause (*upādāna*), just as [the person] has color and so forth as its material cause.

If [it is asked], "What is this meaning of 'appropriation'?"—it cannot be the relationship of cause and effect between the person (*pudgala*) and form (*rūpa*) and so forth, respectively; for that is not admitted. Or, even if the relationship of cause and effect were admitted, there would not necessarily be the perception of the person upon the perception of form and so forth. What is the reason? Because they are not cause and effect, nor are they mutually...
Regarding the establishment of cognition: just as there is cognition of a cause from an effect, there is no such cognition of an effect from a cause. [Objection:
Is it not said that this is not tenable unless there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*)? [Response: There is no necessary connection whatsoever between what is not an effect and its cause.
And it has been said: that cognition which is inseparable from the apprehension [of an object] would also exist only when that [object] is known.

For there can be no cognition of something that does not appear in a consciousness whose own nature is free from association [with other things]. Due to its absence, the "ineffability" (avācyatā) characterized as the form of the object is not established. Therefore, that entity must, in reality, partake of either identity with or difference from [the cognition].
But for that entity which, upon perishing, becomes nothing at all,
it has been stated by him that "an entity does not come into being," and likewise, "non-existence comes into being.
Even when he says that this non-existence of an entity comes into being, that too is simply stated as "the entity does not come into being."

For in this way, it is turned back; because when there is a negation, a positive injunction is impossible. Therefore, for its destruction, there is no cause whatsoever. For instance, [the meaning is] that it comes into being. It is not that the person (*pudgala*) is invariably concomitant with form and so forth, but rather, the cognition of the person—
[If it is argued: "That [inseparability] belongs to her; inseparability from form and so forth is that very proximity. [We reply:
But is that not precisely the person's inseparability from form and so forth, provided there is no obstruction [to their cognition]?
It is said that this is not logical.
[One might argue: "There will be a connection even between a person (pudgala) and form (rūpa) and so forth, despite their being neither cause nor effect.
To this he says: "It has been stated more than once that there is no real connection whatsoever between things that are neither cause nor effect," which—

As for what is said—that knowledge which is the "concomitant of the cloth" (paṭāntarīyaka)—that would occur if there were a cognition of a person (pudgala) distinct from form and so forth. But that does not exist. For, regarding that [person] which does not appear by way of its own nature in the cognition of the person—the meaning being that it does not appear through a non-connection with anything else because it lacks connection with its own nature—there is no cognition of it whatsoever; such is the connection [of the argument].

Due to the absence of that—that is, due to the absence of the aforementioned cognition—the characteristic of inexpressibility of the object-entity called the "person" (pudgala) is not established. Therefore, in reality and from the perspective of ultimate truth, that [object] must in some respect possess the nature of being either identical to or different from something; for there is no other possible mode of existence for a real entity. However, for the proponent of momentariness, when [an entity] is perishing—

Nothing at all happens to the entity; rather, it is held that the entity itself simply does not exist. Therefore, even by one who says "non-existence comes to be," only a negation—that "the entity does not exist"—is expressed, and there is no affirmation of anything whatsoever.
Consequently, it is considered that for the proponent of momentariness, there is no room for the conceptual alternatives of identity or difference with respect to non-existence.

He explains with the words "Even though... and so forth: Even though this proponent of momentariness expresses, by means of a word that seems to involve a positive injunction, that "the non-existence of an entity comes about," what he actually says is simply that "it is not an entity. For in this way, an entity is negated only if nothing [positive] is enjoined. What is the reason? Because [negation is] a prohibition.

Because a positive injunction is impossible when there is merely the exclusion of an entity, and because no real property whatsoever belongs to an entity that is perishing, for that very reason there is no cause for the destruction of this entity. To explain: a separate cause of destruction would have to be required by the entity in the process of perishing. And if [this were so]... [the investigation of the person].

If there were any effect whatsoever, another would depend upon it; but since no such entity exists, what could possibly depend on anything? (282) For it is only when an effect exists that there can be an agent; and it has already been stated that for a perishing entity, there is no effect whatsoever.
Therefore, that which is called the cause of destruction does nothing at all to the entity; thus, being ineffective, it is not to be depended upon.
(1) How can there be no excellence produced? If the entity remains in that very same state, how can it be said to have perished?
It cannot.
Therefore, there is no attribution of existence to anything else within non-existence.

By this, the objection that the fault of "non-perishing existence" would follow—on the grounds that even in the case of causeless destruction, there is the state of perishing after having not existed—is refuted. (283)

Furthermore, as for the one who thinks: (1) "Even if destruction were causeless, since it comes into being after not having existed, its existence and impermanence would be difficult to deny; moreover, the claim that 'coming into being after not having existed, it becomes causeless' is also contradictory"—he too is refuted by this very same [argument]: if that [destruction] were to exist, some effect of the entity would have to be produced; however, no such effect exists.
Therefore, a cause of destruction is ineffective. And whatever thing is ineffective, why would it be depended upon by anyone? It is not depended upon at all.
He explains this with the words beginning "when existing" (*sati*). For a causal factor (*kāraka*) exists only when there is something to be produced; and [in the case of] that which is perishing...

It has been stated that an entity possesses some effect. Therefore, whatever is called a cause of destruction does nothing to the entity; being thus ineffective, a cause of destruction is not to be depended upon.
To this, the opponent asks: "How so? and so forth. If no excellence (*atiśaya*) whatsoever arises in the perishing entity, how—

"Now, it has not produced any excellence (*atiśaya*). The analysis of the compound is: "one for whom no excellence has arisen. A thing (*bhāva*) that is said to have perished is merely in that state—that is, in its previous form.
[The opponent asks: "But surely," and so forth—the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) replies—[that] an excellence arises in the thing from the cause of destruction.

Even if this [destruction] were admitted, that very excellence of it which is called "destruction" would be nothing other than its own nature. How could an entity that has arisen be said to have perished? For the destruction of one thing cannot occur through the existence of another. Since this is so, for that reason, this entity remains in its own state and is not what is called "destroyed. Rather, it is called "destroyed" because it does not exist by itself, and not because of some other distinct entity.

It was stated immediately prior that [this occurs] "due to the arising of that which is called destruction. For it is not the case that an entity, by the arising of an excellence (atiśaya) called destruction, becomes something that has not existed before. What is the reason? Because all excellences of non-existence are characterized by causal capacity (sāmarthya), and through the cessation of those designations (upākhyā)—that is, verbal expressions—there is the cessation of all capacity and designation.

The meaning is "by means of its function. This is because it is characterized by the *viveka*—the separation or absence—of every property of existence (*bhāvadharma*), that is, every property whose nature is to come into being; and because existence (*bhāva*) is characterized by the occurrence of origination (*utpatti*). For that which comes into being is called "existence" (*bhāva*); therefore, existence is that which is connected with origination. And since this is so, there can be no [destruction] of existence—that is, of destruction—without something else.
Existence (*bhāva*) is the projection of the end of becoming; the meaning is that there is no becoming for anything whatsoever. 27280355... [text fragment] ...and the companions.
It has been refuted, because no entity whatsoever is admitted [to exist].
Just as hostility is desired by some among those subject to rebirth,
so too would it be if the nature of destruction belonged only to entities and not to those that are unproduced. (284)

Now, it might be argued: (1) Let it be granted that this destruction is indeed the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these entities, which have the property of existing for only a single moment; however, it will belong only to those things that possess origination. For it is not the case that everything must have an intrinsic nature simply because it is called "intrinsic nature," just as the quality of resistance (*pratighātmatā*) is not the intrinsic nature of everything.
Even so, it is indeed true.
From the restriction of the cause’s intrinsic nature comes the restriction of the effect’s intrinsic nature;
for in that which is impermanent, there is no differentiation of form, due to the absence of differentiating factors. (285)

"By this" means by the demonstration of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Even if destruction were admitted to be causeless, that destruction would first be non-existent and then come into being; thus, because destruction comes into existence after having not existed, it would possess existence (*sattā*), just like a sprout or other such things. Furthermore, regarding "the state of being destructible": the objection that follows from the faults of [both] existence and destructibility has been refuted.

By this very [point], he explains with the words "And even," etc. Even if destruction were causeless, because this destruction comes into being after not having existed (*abhūtvā bhāvāt*), its existence and permanence would be difficult to avoid. Furthermore, it is contradictory to say that something which comes into being after not having existed is causeless, since that which occurs only occasionally (*kādācitka*) must have a cause.

Because there is no contradiction. That objection regarding a fault has also been refuted by this very demonstration that destruction is formless (*nīrūpa*). What is the reason? Because it is not admitted that any property exists at the time of destruction.

Just as, while the status of being a real entity (*vastutva*) is equal, only certain things that possess birth—that is, those subject to origination—have what is called "resistance" (*pratigha*) in their own location.

The characteristic of being an obstacle to the arising of another is not accepted by all [schools]. Likewise, let the nature of destruction belong only to those entities that possess arising, and not to non-arising things such as space (*ākāśa*). In this way, the principle that "whatever exists is momentary" would be subject to deviation (*vyabhicārin*).
He explains by means of the words beginning with "artha" [meaning]. Let it be so. This is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities;
what is this intrinsic nature? He says: "Those which have the property of momentary duration. The analysis of the compound is: "those for whom the property is momentary duration.
However, that intrinsic nature of momentary duration will belong only to entities that possess origination, and not to those that do not originate.
This refers to space and so forth.

For it is not the case that everything becomes the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of everything simply by virtue of being an intrinsic nature. The meaning is as follows: just as the nature of resistance (pratighātmatā), although it is the intrinsic nature of a real entity, does not belong to everything, so it is in this case as well.
The Master says: "It is true. It is indeed true that everything is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of everything else.

Nevertheless, because there is a restriction of intrinsic nature based on the cause, there is a restriction of intrinsic nature regarding the effect: "this is the producer of this [which possesses resistance], and this is not.

However, among things produced (*kṛtaka*), which are impermanent, there is no difference in their form (*rūpa*) with respect to impermanence by virtue of which one would not [be impermanent] while another is. [This concludes the] investigation of the person (*pudgala*).

Neither resistance nor any other intrinsic nature (svabhāva) can be restricted by necessity without a cause; rather, whatever the state of the capacity of its own cause may be, such is the result that arises. Thus, from the restriction of the intrinsic nature of the cause, there follows the restriction of the intrinsic nature of the result. Even if this [restriction] were said to be accidental, the same fault [previously stated] would apply; for the nature of resistance is not [accidental], just as the restriction of the intrinsic nature of the cause is not.

We perceive an entity whose nature is specifically determined by its production, such that it would be thus at birth and not otherwise; for we observe the destruction of all things born in every manner.
[Objection: But even this is uncertain, namely, that "all things born in every manner perish," because their destruction is not observed in its entirety.

[Objection: Various causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) are indeed observed to possess diverse powers. Among them, there might be one whose nature is imperishable and not that of anything else. [Response: What is the reason? Because there is an absence of causes that differentiate an impermanent nature; that is to say, because everything is produced with an imperishable nature.

Now, the objection raised was: "If it is argued that the destruction of entities is their very nature, then this cannot apply to those things that are unproduced. Furthermore, the response given—"In that case, there is no difference in the nature of the impermanent, because there is an absence of differentiating factors"—is not tenable. For the perishable nature of space and so forth is not produced by its own causes, precisely because they are unproduced. Therefore, how can it be correct to say [that there is no difference]? Thus, the argument is untenable.

He thinks as follows: (1) Just as "existence" (*sattva*) was stated to be inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), one might suspect that even among "produced things" (*kṛtaka*), some are perishable while others are not. Therefore, there is no fault in stating "existence" (*sat*) and so forth at the very beginning in order to first eliminate the inconclusiveness of "being produced."

He explains [the verse] with the words "no," and so forth. "Other" refers to that which is visible (*sanidarśana*) and so on. "Accidentally" means without a cause (*hetu*). "In some cases it would exist, in others not" refers to the fact that the capacity of a cause—which produces properties such as resistance—is restricted to specific objects. Such a restriction of capacity belongs to the power of the cause.
Since the effect is of a corresponding nature, the determination of the nature of the effect is accepted as following from the determination of the nature of the cause.

However, if it were accidental—that is, if it were causeless—the aforementioned fault regarding the determination of the nature of the effect would apply; namely, that a restriction by place, time, and intrinsic nature would not be logical. Therefore, resistance (*pratighāta*) is its essence, and that is its nature.

It is like specific determination (*pratiniyama*). We do not perceive a nature in an entity that is restricted to the production of what is perishable—that is, an entity whose nature is specifically determined toward the production of the perishable such that only some [cause] produces what is perishable, and not everything. The analysis of the compound is: "that entity which possesses a nature specifically determined toward the production of the perishable. By means of which causal restriction, its birth arises; that is, its birth occurs from the cause of producing what is perishable.
That which is such would be perishable, and not that other which has an origin from causes possessing different characteristics. What is the reason?
(1) Because destruction is observed in all things produced from every kind of cause. The analysis of the compound is: "those things whose birth is from causes of every kind.
[The opponent objects: "But," and so forth; those entities whose birth is from causes of every kind are destroyed—

This too is indeed indeterminable. What is the reason? Because those causal complexes (*hetu-sāmagrī*) cannot be seen in their entirety by those of limited vision, as they do not perceive them exhaustively. If it is argued that, because some complex producing perishable things has been observed, other such [complexes], though unobserved, are determined to be of that same nature on account of belonging to that class; [we reply:]...
One should not produce [the following] view:

that those objects of knowledge which, having been known by someone, at some time, or somewhere, are no longer known, undergo destruction as a necessary consequence of their existence. We maintain that it is precisely these produced things that are proven to be impermanent; for this is not [the case].

It is possible that those [causes], which possess the nature of producing cognition, would not produce it again if they were not destroyed, provided they depended on something else, because their nature for producing that [cognition] has been brought to completion. Nor is it the case that [cognition] does not arise from them; for there is no instance where the cognition of anyone regarding anything ever ceases at any time. Furthermore, nothing exists that is of such a nature, since everything is cognized by someone at some time. Cognition—

Furthermore, because it lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it would not exist as a real entity (*vastu*). To explain this: he states that "a real entity has that [causal efficiency] as its characteristic," and so forth, beginning with the word *vicitra*. The analysis of the compound is: "those which possess diverse capacities. Such causal complexes (*sāmagryaḥ*) are observed.
Among those causal complexes possessing diverse capacities, there might even be some complex that produces an imperishable entity.
[The opponent argues that] it would produce itself.
[The author] refutes this with the words "No," and so forth. Furthermore, this refutation applies to the destruction of entities, not to those things that lack production.
This should also be understood in response to the objection beginning with "If," because it is common to both cases. Why is this not a fault?
(1) Because of the context of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).

Clarifying this very point, he says: We maintain that for those objects which, having been known by some person at some time and in some place, are no longer known, there is a destruction that follows their continuity (*santāna*). And as for those [objects] which remain unknown...

Whether they are known or, having been known, are no longer known—those very things are established as being produced and impermanent. By this, it is stated that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being produced" by "momentariness" is ascertained through [the reason] "existence" (*sattva*), and so forth.
Now, one might object: even if, once known, they are no longer known, how can their impermanence be established?

Therefore, he says: For it is not possible that those things which possess the nature of producing cognition, having previously existed and subsequently not perished, should remain in that very same nature and yet fail to produce [the cognition].
If it is argued that they do not produce it because of the absence of auxiliary causes (sahakārin), (1)
He said: "They would not depend on anything else. For there is no possibility of its [arising]—this is the connection. What is the reason?
Because that which has the nature of producing it has already been accomplished.
Now, it might be argued: "Even though they do not depend [on others], knowledge of some thing will occur at some time."

Therefore, he says: "And if those [senses], which are established as having the inherent nature of producing cognition and are independent of auxiliary causes, were such for any person, then at some time some cognition would never cease; rather, they would produce cognitions of their respective objects for everyone at all times. But this is not the case, because cognition is observed only occasionally. And therefore, cognition—"
It is understood that [these things] do not produce [anything], because they have fallen away from the nature of a producer.
As for that which is unknowable—whether produced or unproduced—it will not be like this.
To this, he says: "No," and so forth. There is nothing whatsoever that is unknowable in such a manner. What is the reason? Everything—

Because this object is known by some person at some time; otherwise, if that cognition were not produced, we shall refute the opinion of Kumārila. Furthermore, its existence is invariably connected with its destruction.
For this very reason, the eternality of their relation must also be rejected;
and for this same reason— that destruction is invariably concomitant with the mere entity as previously stated— the eternality of the relation must likewise be rejected, just as in the case of sound.
(c) Refutation of Kumārila’s View (a) Faults in the Theory of Non-Authorship: Furthermore,
that capacity of words called "semantic fitness" (*yogyatā*), which is described by the followers of Jaimini as the basis for the comprehension of meaning, [is untenable].
It is not indeed a different entity. For it has been explained previously that "capacity" is simply a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) of the nature of things.
Or, let it be a different entity; even so:

The power of the word (*śabdaśakti*) has already been undermined by the defects of the relation previously mentioned. (286) For indeed, many kinds of defects have been stated in the discussion regarding the relation as having a distinct object; since that very [power] is thereby undermined, it is not stated again. Moreover:

If it were incapable even of the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of mere cognition, then that entity would not exist at all, being devoid of such capacity. For we shall state that the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of an entity is its capacity for causal efficiency. Furthermore, since an entity capable of causal efficiency—which performs that efficiency either successively or simultaneously—is invariably subject to destruction, and since destruction is causeless, [the entity] must possess existence (*sattā*).

The destruction [of the relation] is established. Precisely for this reason—namely, from the aforementioned proof of the momentariness of all entities—the eternity of the relationship between word and meaning must also be rejected; it is to be refuted. [The author] explains this with the words "not" (*na*) and so forth. Precisely for this reason, because destruction follows immediately after the aforementioned [existence of] mere entities...
Because of its being a bond. Like sound: (1) just as the permanence of sound has been rejected, so too the permanence of the relation must be denied.
Thus far, the fault has been stated by assuming the relation to be distinct; now, [it is stated] by assuming it to be non-distinct.

Thus, [the opponent] says that such a connection is not tenable. Furthermore, that verbal power called "fitness" (*yogyatā*), which is described by the followers of Jaimini as the basis for the comprehension of the meaning designated by the term "fitness"—that fitness is not something distinct from the word-meaning itself. For instance, in the case of entities—

It was stated previously that fitness (*yogyatā*) is precisely an excellence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*) which is capable of performing the intended purposeful action, as expressed in the passage beginning with, "For the form of a word that is capable is its fitness.
Therefore, the point is that if the word is impermanent, its fitness must also be impermanent, because there is no distinction between them.
The mere fact that [a text] is not of human origin does not establish it as a means for knowledge of things as they truly are;
for fire and the like are seen to be otherwise [i.e., misleading] due to the defects of a person, even when they are themselves unimpaired. (287)

Granted that Vedic words may be non-human (apauruṣeya), nevertheless, it is quite possible for them to be the cause of erroneous cognition. For it is not only through the imposition of human defects that confusion regarding objects arises; even for things devoid of such [defects], like lamps and the like, there is the production of false cognitions regarding blue lotuses and so forth. Therefore, these words are independent of mental impressions (saṃskāra).

By their very nature, [words] would not be causes for the manifestation of objects (1), due to a specific intrinsic character (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*), like fire and so forth; and they would necessarily manifest what is false. If it is argued that this is incorrect because there is no cause for such restriction, then what is the cause for the restriction of manifesting what is not false? Therefore, just as there is a restriction regarding the manifestation of things as they truly are, by nature there is the manifestation of things as they are not.

Or, let it be that fitness (*yogyatā*) is something other than the word; even so, the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*) must be understood as refuted. By what? By the previously mentioned defects of the relation (*sambandhadoṣa*).
He explains this with the words "For it has been said," and so forth, regarding the doctrine that the relation is an entity distinct from the related terms.
