Various types of defects have been stated [in the passage] beginning with:

"Because the relata are impermanent, there is no permanence in the relation. Since the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*), which is postulated as being of the nature of that very relation, is also refuted by those same previously mentioned defects, it need not be discussed again.
The fault is stated separately. Thus, the Veda is not of non-human origin. Even if it were of non-human origin, its truthfulness could not be ascertained; because—

On the grounds that it is of human origin, the Vedic word is not a means for the knowledge of things as they truly are, nor is it a cause for non-erroneous knowledge of objects; because it is seen to be corrupted by human faults— that is, by the defects of persons— just as fire and so forth (the word "and so forth" including moonlight and the like) are seen to be otherwise, serving as causes for false cognition.

He explains by means of the words "let it be" (*bhavatu*) and so forth: "Granted that Vedic words may indeed be non-human (*apauruṣeya*), nevertheless, it is quite possible that these Vedic words are causes of knowledge that does not correspond to reality (*ayathārtha*). For [the falsity of knowledge] does not arise solely from the imposition of human defects—that is, from the imposition of human defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like—but rather from the [Vedic] impressions (*saṃskāra*) themselves."

Regarding objects to be known, there is a confusion of knowledge—that is, a perversion of knowledge—on the part of the words that serve as the means of cognition; for it is possible, even by their very nature, for them to produce false knowledge. This is because even in the case of those [words] devoid of that [defect], and even when they are free from the imposition of human defects, such as in the case of a lamp—

Because [words] such as "lamp" produce knowledge of objects associated with them; by the word "etcetera," [the inclusion of] moonlight and so forth is intended—[for example], in the case of blue lotuses and the like. For instance, at night, a lamp is the cause of a cognition appearing as red in a blue lotus;
moonlight is the cause of a cognition of white in a yellow garment. Therefore, these Vedic words are devoid of human refinement.

The connection is that they would be "indifferent" (*upekṣāḥ*). And by their very nature (*prakṛtyā*) and essence (*svabhāvena*), they would be the causes of cognition—that is, the causes of knowledge—regarding objects.

What is the reason? Because of a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣāt*), that is, a specific intrinsic form (*svarūpaviśeṣāt*). Like what? Like fire and so forth. [This is the refutation of Kumārila’s view: Why is such a restriction not postulated? Or rather, like fire and so forth, there would be the state of being a cause for both types of cognition regarding objects.

For even non-human [authorless] things such as fire and the like, though they are causes of correct cognition in one instance, do not function in that same way everywhere. Likewise, even if words were authorless, both [properties—being a cause of correct cognition and being otherwise] would apply.
Let it be that for fire and the like, because they are produced (*kṛtaka*), there is a change in other instances according to the conditions; however, this is not the case for eternal things.
This [property] exists in words.
But surely, such a property exists there as well; for even they, by the power of convention (*saṃketa*), exclude other [objects].
Since their nature is established as producing an effect, there is no dependence on convention or the like. Therefore, there is cognition of objects [from words].
It would have to exist for everyone at all times; yet it does not. Therefore, words do not possess an enduring intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, the manifestations [of meaning] would be false; that is, the cognitions of meaning derived from those words would necessarily be false.

[Objection: There is no reason for the rule that Vedic words always possess false manifestations (*vitathavyakti*). Therefore, since there is an absence of a cause for such a rule, the conceptualization that "Vedic words possess only false manifestations" is untenable. [Response:
For you, the Mīmāṃsaka, as well, there is no reason for the rule that "Vedic words are causes of non-false cognition."

What is the cause for the restriction of a matured and non-false manifestation? None at all. Therefore, according to your own view, since there is a restriction to manifestation that accords with the object, why is it not postulated that by nature—that is, by its very essence—there is a restriction to manifestation that does not accord with the object?
Or else, just as fire and other things [are restricted] toward objects such as jars and blue lotuses, respectively, whether real or unreal—

Likewise, Vedic words would be causes of both types of cognition—namely, as causes of false cognition and as causes of non-false cognition—with respect to their objects. For even non-human (apauruṣeya) things such as fire and the like, or moonlight and the like, are not [uniformly] so;
for while they are causes of true cognition regarding a jar or similar object during the day, they are likewise [causes of false cognition] regarding a blue lotus or similar object at night. Thus...

They become causes of knowledge that is either true or false. Likewise, even though Vedic words are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), both [states] would apply: they would be causes of both true and false knowledge.
"Let it be so," etc., says the opponent. Because fire and other such things are produced (*kṛtaka*), according to their cause, for whomever...
Whatever is the cause of error, by virtue of that, there occurs a deviation from reality—that is, the state of being a cause for false cognition—in other cases such as the blue lotus;

however, this [state of being a cause for false cognition] does not exist in the case of eternal sounds through the power of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*). This is because it is impossible for eternal things to function otherwise through the power of auxiliary conditions.

"Is it not so? and so forth, says the Siddhāntavādī. "Of such a kind" means that there certainly exists a property characterized by transformation into something else in objects [of meaning] through the power of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). "In that case too" refers even to Vedic words. What is the reason?
Because even those Vedic words undergo transformation otherwise through the power of convention (*saṃketa*), which conforms to human will.
The meaning is that [they] do not produce cognition otherwise.

Now, if it is maintained that there is no exclusion (*parāvṛtti*) of those [Vedic words] from their objects by the force of convention, but rather that Vedic words, due to their eternity, possess by their very nature the essence of generating cognitions of their own objects; then, regarding the effect, which is the cognition of its own object—
If that [cause] were considered uncreated, it would not even possess the status of being a cause for cognition. *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* (19288) 1.2538.
For nothing whatsoever has an origin from eternal things by virtue of their inherent capacity.

(2885) If sound were unproduced, there would be no cognition of objects at all; for it is impossible to conceive of a capacity for producing cognition in that which possesses an identical nature both at the time when cognition arises and at other times. Thus, one [sound] is not a producer in this way, while the other is.

Because there is no difference in the nature of that which is to be distinguished [as permanent]. It is not logical that what is a non-producer of this [cognition] should be exactly the same as what is a producer;
moreover, dependence upon anything else has already been refuted. Therefore, eternal things possess no capacity whatsoever for producing cognition.
For if they do not produce it at some time, it would follow that they never produce it at all. Furthermore, because a continuity of effects is not observed, how could they [be causes]?

It was stated previously that they are "transformers. This is because, regarding those Vedic words which possess a generative nature and abide therein, there is an absence of any other unobservable cause—such as convention (*samaya*) and so forth; the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes other causal operations such as [linguistic] activity. Therefore, from the Vedic [words]...

If the cognition of objects were produced from the [Vedic] words themselves, then every person would always have cognition of all objects; yet there is no such universal cognition of objects for everyone at all times. Therefore, Vedic words do not possess a nature established for the production of cognition of objects, but rather they necessarily depend upon convention (*samaya*) and so forth. Consequently, those [words] are also causes of false cognition, and thus the same defect remains.

Furthermore, (1) if that sound is held to be unproduced (*akṛtaka*), it could not even be the cause of cognition. For nothing whatsoever— whether it be cognition or anything else— is produced from eternal entities by way of their objective capacity (*vastusāmarthya*), that is, through the capacity of imparting their own form (*svarūpopadhāna*).

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "If [it were] unproduced" (*yadyakṛtaka*). If the Vedic word were unproduced, then there would be no cognition at all regarding its objects. Why? [Because of the passage beginning with] "cognition," etc. The analysis of the compound *itaradajanmājanma* is "the other" (*itarat*) and "non-arising" (*ajanma*). Because the time of those two—the time of cognition and the other time—is of an identical nature due to [the word's] eternity, and because it is of a single form, [there would be no distinction in] cognition.

Because the possibility of efficacy is impossible at a time other than its birth; for there is a contradiction in that which is the productive form of a thing at the time of its birth remaining in that very same nature while being non-productive. What is the reason?
It is because one must distinguish [the two cases] separately as follows: "In this form, this [entity] considered to be eternal is productive; in this [other] form, it is not productive."
Because there is no difference in the nature of this fixed form, nor any difference in its intrinsic essence; for that which is eternal is of one and the same form at all times.

If it is argued that even though it has a single nature, it might be a non-producer previously and become a producer later, [the author] says "no," and so forth: the very same nature that this eternal thing possesses as a non-producer is precisely the same nature it possesses as a producer.
This is not tenable, because [the cause] is of a single nature. The claim that it produces [the effect] later after obtaining an additional auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*) and so forth is false;
for dependence on another—namely, dependence on an auxiliary cause—is already precluded in the case of what is eternal.
Therefore, how could eternal words possess the capacity to produce cognition in a person regarding certain objects?

(1) A cause [would entail] the undesirable consequence of eternal non-production, because if it sometimes fails to produce a cognition, it would follow that it must always fail to produce it, given that its nature remains the same even afterwards. (2) Now, if one were to maintain that this fault shall not occur and thus the cause always produces its own effect— [this is the refutation of Kumārila’s position].
Furthermore, those cognitions directed toward space and so forth, which are considered eternal, do not possess that [eternal] nature as their own essence;
for they are produced from the latencies of conceptual construction and have superimposed objects as their domain.
Cognitions arise therein that have exclusively the [particular] as their object and not the external thing itself;

for a cognition whose domain is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) necessarily conforms to the presentation of its own capacity. When that [specific characteristic] exists, its cause possesses that very capacity. Thus, if it were the case regarding the specific characteristics of eternal entities...

If knowledge were to belong to someone, it would have to belong to everyone at all times. For it is logical that particular effects, which are manifested entities, depend upon specific things as the cause for acquiring a superior capacity for their production, since they are utilized in some way or another in certain places. However, it is not so [logical] that an eternal entity, which is not a particular effect, should be perceived by someone while remaining unproduced by that [perceiver].
If its apprehension were produced by something dependent upon an effort, it would be logical that it be perceived by that very same [effort];

yet, because it possesses a stable nature, even that [effort] does not exist. Furthermore, because no continuous production of its effect—namely, the cognition of its own object—is observed, those sounds are in no way whatsoever agents; this has already been stated previously.
It might be argued: (1) "Cognitions indeed arise even from eternal things such as space and so forth, for someone at some time.
To this he says: "Even those cognitions which are perceptions occurring with respect to space and so forth, which are considered to be eternal—"

It is maintained that they will perish; yet even those [perishing things] do not have their birth dependent on the nature of space and so forth, for it is contradictory for eternal entities to perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) either successively or simultaneously.
What, then, is the cause for their production? (1)

He said: "It is not," and so forth. "Beginningless" means that which has been deposited by a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of a similar kind; it is the latent impression (*vāsanā*), the capacity, from which [these cognitions] have arisen or emerged. They have gone—meaning they merely appear—as having as their object a superimposed form such as space (*ākāśa*) and so on, in accordance with scripture. In that regard, [they appear] toward space and so on, which are imagined as being external.
They arise; however, those cognitions do not have objects as their domain, nor do they have the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of space and so forth as their objects.

He explains this with the words beginning "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*). For a cognition whose object is a specific characteristic necessarily follows upon the presence—that is, the proximity—which is the capacity or efficacy of that specific characteristic; it exists only when that [specific characteristic] exists.

Having established this principle: when the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—the cause that is suitable and capable—is present as a fit cause, that cognition necessarily arises. This being the logical state of affairs, if there were to be the knowledge of any person regarding the specific characteristic of eternal entities, then, because the cause would be eternally present, it would belong to every person at all times.

Nor can it be said that eternal things produce knowledge at some time or place through dependence on auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*); for an effect is produced by those individual instances (*vyakti*) which possess specific qualities brought about by auxiliaries. How then could those very instances, being restricted by certain places, times, and states, and being employed toward a particular effect while assuming the status of its cause, bring about the production of that effect? [If they were eternal, such restriction would be impossible.]
Regarding the statement "it arises": it would either be perceived as identical to everything, or not perceived by anything at all. Since it is seen by someone, it is not eternal.

Something might be beyond the senses; however, this is not the case. Therefore, [words] do not depend on the capacity of an external object, but have superimposed entities as their domain. Relying solely on internal material causes—the awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of conceptual construction—they are nothing but errors devoid of external objects, occurring for everyone regarding space and so forth. Consequently, words do not possess properties that function otherwise. (1)

Or [if you say] it is in reality; from what [source] do you know that these are indeed non-erroneous cognitions? For it is not the case that in statements such as "Fire is the remedy for cold," everything is necessarily so, because the capacity of fire to counteract cold is merely made known [by the word], since worldly usage proceeds according to conventions established by people's own whims. Why is this so? Because of the world... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
The "excellence" (atiśaya) that is suitable [for the cognition] is inherent in it; the phrase "cause of its apprehension" means a specific object acting as a cooperative cause (sahakārin).

"In the same way" means like impermanence. If an eternal entity, which is a specific effect incapable of having any excellence added to it by anyone, were to produce its own apprehension for a person while being perceived—provided it depended upon that cause, namely, dependence upon the cooperative cause of apprehension.

It is logical that it should be apprehended by that very person and not by another, due to the specific restriction of its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). Furthermore, such production in dependence upon auxiliary causes is impossible for that which is eternal. Why? Because its intrinsic nature is fixed; that is to say, because no excellence (*atiśaya*) can be imparted to an eternal entity by an auxiliary cause.

Furthermore, because it would be eternally established in the nature of producing [cognition], it would be perceived by every person at the same time; or else, because it would not be a producer for anyone, it would not be perceived. In that case, since that very nature belongs to it, it would never be perceived by any person whatsoever. For this reason, if an existent, eternal entity were perceived by some yogi—

Nor was anything eternal perceived at that time; for there could be no eternal object beyond the senses, since everything must necessarily be perceived by someone. Furthermore, such an entity would have to be eternally perceptible by the senses of all persons, because its capacity to produce cognition would be indistinguishable with respect to every person. Yet this quality of being perceptible to all persons does not belong to an eternal entity. Therefore, [the existence of an eternal entity] cannot be established through the power of the object.

The [cognitions] independent of the causal capacity of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of space and so forth have superimposed objects as their domain; that is to say, they appear in the forms of space and so forth as superimposed according to tradition (*yathāgama*). Relying solely on an internal material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), what kind of awakening of conceptual impressions (*vikalpa-vāsanā*) is there? It is the beginninglessness of the conceptualization of space and so forth—the impression (*vāsanā*) which has been deposited.

Its "awakening" is its orientation toward the production of an effect. Precisely because it does not depend on the causal efficiency of an external object, it is for this very reason that, being devoid of external objects, such errors arise for every person regarding space and so forth.
Thus it is established: (1) there is no production of effects from eternal things. However, [such production] is observed from words at times—

Therefore, words do not have the property of non-reversal (*aparāvṛtti*) as their effect upon cognition. The analysis of the compound is: "those whose property is precisely non-reversal when there is a single form.
However, cognitions, with respect to each object, necessarily possess distinct modes of operation.
If, on the other hand, they were eternal and possessed a single form, then—whether that [single form] is accepted as their true nature (*tattva*) or as their single form—[the following would hold].

How is it known that Vedic words exist solely for the purpose of conveying meaning? The analysis of the compound is: "those from which an unerring cognition of meaning arises. (2) Refutation of Kumārila’s view:
There is a doubt as to whether one cognizes in this way merely by following one's own convention, or rather due to the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the words. (1) [The worldly desire...]

As for the claim that words, even when being reversed, are seen again elsewhere in a different manner, this alteration is indeed possible even when following worldly convention (*lokaprasiddhi*). Therefore, even if the non-perversity of some [words] is observed, it is not established that all [words] are likewise [non-perverse].
(kha) Furthermore, there are defects even if [words] were produced:

for even if they possessed an unproduced nature (*akṛtaka-svabhāva*), some might still be restricted to false objects; thus, due to the lack of complete knowledge of their nature, doubt would arise in every case.
It might be thought: "Because Vedic statements such as 'Fire is the remedy for cold' are non-false, all [Vedic statements] must be non-false.
To this, he says: "For not... and so forth. For it is not the case that in statements such as "Fire is the remedy, the counteragent, for cold," and so on...

In the Vedic sentences, the capacity of fire to ward off cold is made known even prior to the [Vedic] statement itself, according to convention and as it is well-known in the world; thus, every Vedic sentence, even regarding unseen matters (*adṛṣṭārtha*), becomes so—that is, it becomes non-false. For in the case of a matter well-known in the world, the usage of people is observed to follow convention. Therefore—

Because of the convention established by the world’s own whim, and because of the subsequent usage at the time of linguistic practice, there arises precisely a doubt: does this world, following its own convention— that is, conforming to it—
understand from such sentences as "Fire is the remedy for cold" that fire possesses the capacity to dispel cold?

Or rather, one determines that because the word abides in its own nature as *śabda*, it leads to such a cognition solely through the restriction of its capacity by its very essence or *prakṛti*. And when the inherent power of a Vedic word to convey meaning even regarding an object already perceived is itself doubtful, then the sense is that it is all the more impossible to conceive of such a power regarding an object that is entirely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*).

[Objection: Surely, the meaningfulness of Vedic words is established simply by conforming to the conventions well-known in the world, and no doubt appears there regarding this; [to this, the author] says: "Being turned back according to the will of the world, and being applied to objects again according to convention... (191a)

It is observed that words, when being applied by shifting their meaning to another object through a change of place and so forth, appear differently. For this reason, even if one accepts conformity with worldly convention, a transformation— and thus a falsity— of these Vedic words is indeed possible, because convention itself is not fixed.

Therefore, even if one observes the correctness of some Vedic statement such as "Fire is the remedy for cold," it does not follow that all Vedic statements possess such a nature—that is, that they are true in meaning.
If it is argued that their truthfulness follows precisely from their being uncreated (*akṛtakatva*), [we reply: (1)
Falsity is observed only in things that are produced; therefore, speech that is unproduced [is true].
If [it is argued that] the exclusion of the probandum is pervaded by the opposite of the reason because of the contradiction [between them],

then— since all speech that is false is produced, and because the exclusion of the probandum is pervaded by the exclusion of the reason and cannot occur elsewhere— it would follow that what is unproduced is true, even without a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

For when something is not pervaded by another, the absence of that [pervader] might be suspected in its regard. However, there is no possibility of two contradictory things existing in one place; and since such a possibility does not exist, there is no other alternative for a heterogeneous entity. Consequently, the desired object is established, because the logical mark (*liṅga*) serves as its means of proof.
"The observation of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is useless, because the [conclusion] is established by negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone.
This is true, provided that the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between the two counter-examples were established; however, that is not established.
He says: "For if these Vedic words were of an uncreated nature (*akṛtakasvabhāvatva*), then even though they are restricted to false objects, someone..."

There would be doubt regarding every word. For this reason, because one cannot ascertain the nature of words through discrimination—such as "this has a true meaning" and "this has a false meaning"—due to a lack of thorough knowledge of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there would be doubt concerning every word. This is because, when the argument is formulated as "The Vedic sentence has a true meaning because it is uncreated," there is an absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

He states the formulation by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words beginning "falsity" (*mithyātva*). The connection is as follows: "If speech that is unproduced (*akṛtaka*) were to have a true object, because falsity is observed only in things that are produced. What is the reason? Because the negative concomitance pervades the contradictory [of the probandum]. The negative concomitance of the reason "unproducedness" is "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*); by means of that, the state of having a true object—[which is the probandum]—is pervaded.

Because [the property of] falsity, which is the opposite of truth, is pervaded by the absence of the reason; here, the genitive case in "vyatirekasya" (of the exclusion) is used in the sense of the agent.
This is because falsity, which is opposed to having a true object, is pervaded by the absence of the reason, namely "being produced.
Since the Vedic word is not produced, when "being produced" is excluded, falsity is also excluded; thus, its having a true object is indeed established.

He explains by means of the words beginning with "yathā" (as follows): whatever speech has a false object, all of that—without exception—is "made" (*kṛtaka*). This is on the basis of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*)—namely, truthfulness—from the absence of the reason (*hetu*), namely, being unmade (*akṛtakatva*), by means of its opposite, being made (*kṛtakatva*). The probandum is truthfulness; its absence is falsity. [The pervasion is] of that [falsity] elsewhere, in that which is unmade, [where there is no] false object.

Because of the impossibility of that [falsity] in it, the Vedic word must be uncreated and true even without a positive concomitance (*anvaya*). This means that in the formal argument—"The Vedic word is true because it is uncreated"—although there is no positive concomitance, it is nonetheless established even without one. For, in a case where the property of falsity is not pervaded by the property of being created, [the absence of the reason in the dissimilar instance is sufficient].

When falsity is present, how could one suspect that its non-pervader—the property characterized as "being produced" (kṛtakatva)—is absent, thinking, "this too might exist in falsity"? For such [absence] does not exist here, because being produced is pervaded by falsity. Nor is there the possibility of a contradictory [property] existing where a contradictory is pervaded; for it is not the case that...

Since it is possible for both "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "not being produced" (*akṛtakatva*) to be false in one and the same thing, there is no other alternative (*gatyantara*) besides truthfulness and falsity regarding the object. Therefore, because falsity—which belongs to a different class—is impossible in that which is not produced, it must be true by virtue of its being unproduced; thus, [the Veda] is established as having a true meaning through its non-produced nature.
For this reason: (2) Refutation of Kumārila’s view: Even if the reason is not stated because it is impossible, the existence of that [non-existence] can still be established.
Because even contradictory things may be observed to coexist with a common pervader.

(291) If the absence of the reason in the counter-example of the probandum were established, then the exclusion of the reason would pervade the exclusion of the probandum. However, we do not see any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its impossibility in that case; nor is there a positive instance of non-contradiction.

It is not logical for a proof to function as a negation, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is it the case that what is observed in one place must necessarily exist elsewhere, since we observe even mutually contradictory things coexisting in different instances. Furthermore, just as with the property of being impermanent, there is no need for positive concomitance (*anvaya*) when establishing the nature of a statement’s truth—namely, its correspondence with reality—since the inferential mark (*liṅga*) is intended to establish that very object. Thus, the purpose of the [statement] is achieved.

Furthermore, since the logical mark (*liṅga*) is a means of proof, the observation of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is useless. Why? Because, according to the method already stated, the probandum (*sādhya*) is established by the mere absence [of the reason] in the heterologue (*vyatireka*) alone. "This is true," says the Teacher; for when the exclusion of the reason from the heterologue is established, the probandum is established.

This is true. If the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between falsity and being produced—the two counter-examples (*vipakṣa*) to truth and being unproduced—were established, then the unproduced would be excluded from falsity, which is pervaded by being produced.
However, that relationship of pervader and pervaded between the two counter-examples is not established. Why? Because [if] in falsity there were no being produced...

When the impossibility [of the reason] is not established—that is, when no subverting reason (*bādhaka-hetu*) has been stated to account for that impossibility—the existence (*bhāva*, *sattva*) of even that which is unproduced (*akṛtaka*) can be possible in its falsity (*mithyātva*). For it could be both unproduced and have a false object.
(290ab) But surely, falsity is observed in the case of being produced; and where there is being produced, how could there be non-production?
To this he says: "Of contradictory [things]," and so forth. Even for contradictory categories of entities, there is pervasion by virtue of observing a single pervader (*ekavyāpaka*).

For example, there is the pervasion of things produced through effort (*prayatnāntarīyaka*) and things not produced through effort (*aprayatnāntarīyaka*), both of which are impermanent, by means of the single property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*).

He explains this with the words beginning "yadi" (if). If the absence of the reason called "uncreatedness" (*akṛtakatva*) in the counter-example of the probandum—that is, in the state of having false objects (*mithyārthatva*)—were established, then the negation (*vyatireka*) of the probandum, namely falsity (*mithyātva*), would be pervaded by the negation of the reason; that is, the negation of the reason "uncreatedness," which is called "createness" (*kṛtakatva*). And yet, that [negation] of uncreatedness does not exist there.
We see no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the possibility of the Veda having a false meaning.
If it is argued that, precisely because the Veda is uncreated (*akṛtaka*), it cannot function as something with a false meaning—[the author] replies:
"And not," and so forth. [This refers to] the fact that being uncreated, which is not incompatible with having a false meaning, [is present in the case of] the injunctions having a false meaning.

The proof of a negation is logical. Why? Because of the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For in this way, by the affirmation of anything whatsoever, the absence of anything whatsoever would be understood.
If it is asked: "How can falsity, which is observed in what is produced (*kṛtaka*), apply to what is unproduced (*akṛtaka*)? [the answer follows].
He said: It is not the case that what has been observed as falsity in one instance of something produced cannot possibly occur again in another instance of something unproduced;
rather, it is indeed possible. What is the reason? Because [the properties] that occur separately, in opposition, or together [can exist] separately.
Because it is not perceived, its non-existence alone [is established].
For it has been stated that (1) there is no proof of non-existence because of its non-apprehension in every respect.
The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful regarding the existence of the subject (*masattā*).
For this person is not merely a human being capable of perceiving everything, such that by the cessation of his perception [of something], it would follow that [that thing] does not exist.
Only one whose knowledge never deviates from the existence of the object of knowledge would shine by speaking thus; [but] not one who [speaks] on the basis of non-perception.

He praises [this]: "Therefore, these [entities], being separated by nature, place, and time, would be imperceptible. For instance, who—whether an omniscient person or another—is capable of determining the correspondence or otherwise of a statement, whether it be unauthored or otherwise, regarding an object that is absolutely beyond perception? And this has already been established: even for objects perceived as such in some instances, [there is no certainty] again..."

Occasional transformation occurs, as for example in some regions where nimba fruits are sweet; this is because one observes the coexistence of contradictory properties in a single individual due to differences between individuals. Just as impermanence [is established] by means of being produced immediately after an effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*), so too, for that which is other than what is produced immediately after an effort, the other—namely, not being produced immediately after an effort—is [established] by means of impermanence.
It is observed together with the state of being necessarily concomitant with non-effortful observation.
If it were thus [that falsity is absent], then because falsity is not observed in that which is uncreated (*akṛta*), it would follow that it does not exist;
to this he says: "And it is not the case that such a thing..."—meaning that simply because falsity is not observed in something that exists as uncreated, it does not follow that it is non-existent.

For it was stated previously that the non-existence of the reason (*hetu*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) cannot be established through non-perception in all cases. Consequently, since the non-existence of the reason in the counter-example remains unestablished, there is an exclusion (*vyatireka*) from the counter-example that is merely doubtful. He explains this with the words beginning "for not" (*na hi*), etc. One who perceives only this [limited] person (*puruṣamātraka*) is incapable of seeing all things.

By means of which [cognition] it would not be so for this person through the cessation of perception; that is, he would not perceive [it]. For, (1) in the case of a person whose cognition does not deviate from the existence of the object of knowledge—such that his cognition operates toward every object of knowledge simply because it exists—his cognition, being pervasive of the object of knowledge, causes the object of knowledge to cease as well when it itself ceases.

Therefore, one who says "it does not exist" on the grounds of its non-perception would be justified; it is not the case that "all [of it is unperceived]. Consequently, these entities, though existing, would be imperceptible and thus subject to exclusion (*apohya*). How so? By way of remoteness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), place (*deśa*), and time (*kāla*). The analysis of the compound is as follows: *svabhāva*, *deśa*, and *kāla*—the remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) by means of these, which is to say, their separation (*vyavadhāna*).

Even the seven [elements], though separated by space, time, and intrinsic nature—like a *piśāca* or similar beings—[are not non-existent]. Now, one might argue that it is logical for things separated by time—the past and the future—to be non-existent precisely because they are absent due to their very non-existence. True; however, although the past and future are not perceived at present, their existence has occurred at some time, or will occur at some time.

"Consciousness will exist"—this is the absence of non-perception. This very point is made clear by the words "for thus," and so forth. For who, indeed, is not all-seeing? Regarding an object that is absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), how can there be corroboration of an unauthored statement? And regarding an object that is absolutely beyond the senses, how can there be non-corroboration of any other, authored statement? Or rather, [it is] the other [that is] non-corroborative.

(1) Is it capable of being cultivated or ascertained? No. (2) It has been stated that there is no contradiction with what was produced by another; thus, two points have been mentioned. Refutation of Kumārila’s view: Now, those [critics] who hold such a view should not reject these [arguments]. Therefore, we perceive a contradiction in the claim that something could be both unproduced and false in its object.

And [it is observed that] *āmalakī* fruits [ripen differently] due to a specific transformation (*saṃskāra*). It has been stated that this non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) does not establish an invisible nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, because there is no certainty that "whatever is false is entirely of human origin," there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). For instance: [The argument: "Whatever is produced by human effort is false, like the Veda. [The counter-argument: "Whatever is produced by human effort is true, like the treatises on medicine (*cikitsā-śāstra*). Since both [the truth and falsity of human-made works] are observed, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, since the Veda is not perceived as being composed by a person, its authorship remains unestablished. Thus, the reason is also unestablished (*asiddha*). Moreover, the Veda cannot be proven to be eternal through inference (*anumāna*), because it is not perceived in its entirety. Nor can it be proven through scripture (*āgama*), because there is no authoritative person (*āpta*) to attest to it. Consequently, the Veda is not established as eternal. Whether it be positive concomitance (*anvaya*), negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), or presence (*sattva*) in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), these constitute a means of proof (*sādhana*) only if they are established by cognitions that result in their ascertainment.
And thus it has been said: "Only that which expresses what is ascertained by both [parties] is a proof or a refutation, and not otherwise. (293) (1)

It might be argued that because one Vedic sentence is seen to be consistent [with perception], there must be consistency throughout the entire Veda. To this he says: "And this has already been established previously during the investigation of *śeṣavat* inference. He asks, "What was established? and replies with the words beginning "In some cases," etc. "In some" means in some place or time; "in that way" means by this manner.
The alteration of objects previously seen is their becoming the opposite of the form in which they were first perceived. This very point is stated [by the verse beginning] "Just as," etc. [It means:

due to a particular preparation (*saṃskāra*) characterized by the addition of milk, honey, and so forth; and the *āmalakī* fruits are sweet in certain regions—this is the connection. "Not now by one who does not see that" means: not by one who does not perceive the sweetness of the *nimba* fruit and other such things.

Those sweet neem fruits must indeed be rejected. Likewise, even if the falsity of the Vedic statements were observed, it still could not be rejected. Therefore, we see no contradiction between being uncreated and having false meaning; that is, between being uncreated and having a false object.

Now, one might object that since non-artificiality (*akṛtakatva*) is not observed in cases of falsity, its absence [in falsity] follows; to this he says: "For it has been stated previously that this non-perception does not establish the absence of a thing when that thing is of an invisible nature or possesses a nature that is not perceptible. Since, therefore, the absence of non-artificiality in falsity is not established, whatever is false is all of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).

Thus, there is no pervasion (avyāpti) of falsity by the property of being produced. What is the reason? Because of uncertainty. The meaning is that there is no certainty regarding the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the property of not being produced with falsity. Furthermore, the probandum cannot be established from a reason for which the negative concomitance is uncertain.

For instance, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason (*hetu*) with its own probandum (*sādhya*) consists either in positive concomitance (*anvaya*), or in negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), which is the exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), or in the existence of the reason in the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*); this is the meaning of "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*). And if these three characteristics are established by cognitions through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then what kind of certainty regarding that triad of characteristics constitutes its result?

The analysis of the compound is: "those for which certainty is the result. In that case, those three forms become the means of proving (*sādhana*) the intended probandum (*sādhya*). As stated by the Master Dignāga: "For that alone which expresses what is certain to both [parties]—that is, which expresses a matter established by both the proponent and the opponent and endowed with the characteristics of a valid reason (*hetu*)."

A word that expresses a matter characterized by such defects as being unestablished (*asiddha*) and so forth, when employed by the opponent with the intent to refute, is a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). A term established for only one of the two parties, or a doubtful statement— namely, a word that expresses something established for only one of the two, or something doubtful for both— is not a means of proof (*sādhana*), because it is not accepted by both the proponent and the opponent.

"It is well-known that [a reason] which expresses something doubtful requires further proof. For who could deny the possibility of an unseen contradiction? Thus, this negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not a means of proof because it involves doubt;
furthermore—

Where the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the counter-example to the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*) is described, that very thing would be its similar instance (*sapakṣa*); therefore, every reason would be positive (*anvayin*). [For example:
"Whatever has a false object, all that is of human origin. [In this case,] by means of the counter-example to the reason, [the counter-example to] the probandum...

Pervasion (vyāpti) would be established through the proof of its absence when that [probandum] is absent, because for you, pervasion by means of that [absence] is impossible. Furthermore, the very establishment of the exclusion of two heterogeneous things is itself the state of positive concomitance (anvaya), since it is characterized by the exclusion of the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).
Nor is there any refutation [of this]. Why? Because it depends upon further proof for the sake of ascertaining what is not yet certain.

Furthermore, because it depends upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor is a contradiction between "being unauthored" (*akṛtakatva*) and "falsity" (*mithyārthatva*) established, such that the absence of falsity in what is unauthored would be proven.
Now, if it should be argued: (1) "Falsity does not occur in the Veda precisely because it is unauthored," then—

He says: "For who," and so forth. For what reason? Because what conscious person would deny the possibility of falsity—which is contradictory to the unseen [result]—in the Vedic statements on the grounds of their being unauthored (*akṛtaka*)? Therefore, this aforementioned negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason "being unauthored" is not a proof. Why? Because of doubt. And the other [reason] is also characterized by negative concomitance.

To show that the reason does not exist [in the counter-example], he says "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth. In whatever subject (*viṣaya*) the negative concomitance (*vyatirekitā*) of the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*) is described—that is, the falsity (*mithyātva*) which is the opposite of the probandum, namely truthfulness (*satyārthatva*)—[the formulation is]: "Whatever is not produced (*kṛtaka*) is not false."
Whatever is the object of the exclusion of falsity (*mithyārthatva-vyavaccheda*), that alone would be the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) for this produced reason (*kṛtaka-hetu*).

For this reason, every reason is positive (*anvayin*); that is, it is both positive and negative (*anvaya-vyatirekin*), because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is the subject under discussion. The meaning is that it is not merely negative (*vyatirekin*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) is defined as an object that shares the same nature as the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), and is thus called an example based on similarity (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*)? Since such an object does not exist here, how can it be said that this very [object] is its similar instance? [Response: True. It is precisely the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by virtue of being a similar instance—that which is to be proven—that is called the "similar instance. For this very reason, he says: "Every..."
"The reason is not concomitant" (*heturatonvayī*).

He explains this with the words beginning "whatever," etc.: "Whatever has a false object, all that is of human origin. In this way, there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason—non-artificiality (*akṛtakatva*)—by its opposite, artificiality (*kṛtakatva*), which is the pervasion of the opposite of the probandum, namely falsity (*mithyātva*).

That [concomitance] would exist when, in the absence of that [producedness], there is the establishment of the absence of falsity. What is the reason? Because for falsity, which exists in the absence of producedness, there can be no logical pervasion (*vyāpti*) by that [property of being] produced. Therefore, one who desires pervasion must accept that the cessation of falsity follows from the cessation of producedness. And that very [cessation]—

The exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of falsity and being produced—which belong to different classes from the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*)—is established. This serves to refute the position of Kumārila through the negation of "being produced. Furthermore, from a double negation, a positive affirmation (*vidhi*) is established. What, then, is the establishment of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) that lacks both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)? Therefore, there is no such thing as a "probans lacking positive concomitance" (*ananvaya*), because the exclusion of one [class] is inseparable from the establishment of the other dissimilar class (*vijātīya*).
The same would apply even in the case of the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of impermanence, selflessness, and so forth.

(40b) This is because the exclusion of a negative counterpart (*vyatireka-vyavaccheda*) is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa*); it is not [the case that] when there is an exclusion of the nature of a positive entity, there is no positive entity.

Concomitance (*anuṣaṅga*): the exclusion of non-existence necessarily entails the presence of existence. Since existence and non-existence consist in their mutual differentiation, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), which is of the nature of non-existence, brings existence to mind when it is itself being excluded. The form "falsity is excluded" is precisely this: it is the establishment of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the cause "unproducedness" with truthfulness.

This is the establishment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). What is the reason? Because the property to be proven—namely, the state of having a real object—is characterized by the exclusion of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

The dissimilar instance consists of falsity; therefore, it is because the state of having a real object is characterized by that exclusion or absence of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) from what is not produced (*akṛtaka*).

Furthermore, (1) falsity consists in the negation of truthfulness. When that falsity is negated in that which is uncreated (*akṛta*), then a double negation occurs. Because of this double negation—which takes the form of the exclusion of truthfulness—the affirmation of truthfulness is established; for this reason, it is devoid of both non-concomitance and concomitance.

Since the pervasion of the probandum's absence—namely, falsity—with the absence of the probans—namely, being produced—is established by means of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), there is no establishment of pervasion through positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Therefore, there is no such thing as a "positive-only" reason; rather, every [valid] reason possesses both positive and negative concomitance. 193a

What is the reason? (1) Because the exclusion of falsity from that which is uncreated is inseparable from the establishment of its opposite; for the establishment of "truthfulness," which is the opposite of "falsity," is necessarily concomitant with it.
If the exclusion of one thing is necessarily concomitant with the establishment of its dissimilar counterpart, then even in the case of the exclusion of non-momentariness,
selflessness, and so forth— where "and so forth" includes suffering and the rest—
the same would apply when an exclusion is made in some instance, such as a rabbit's horn; that is, it would likewise be concomitant with the exclusion of falsity.

Just as there is the establishment of [the properties] such as being true, so too there would be the establishment of [properties] of a different genus, such as being eternal, possessing a self, and being pleasurable; yet this is not desired. [The opponent thinks: "In that case, let it not be so here either. [The author] refutes this with the words beginning with "No" (*na*). This fault does not apply. Why? Because of the exclusion of the opposite (*vyatireka-vyavaccheda*).

Because it has the nature of an existent (*bhāva*). Negation (*vyatireka*) is non-existence (*abhāva*); and since the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), which is the cessation (*nivṛtti*) of that non-existence, has the nature of an existent, the point is that the establishment of an existent occurs through the cessation of non-existence. By this, the definition of an existent has been stated. From this very statement, the following is also implied by implication: because the exclusion of an existent has the nature of non-existence.

Thus, by this, the definition of both existence and non-existence has been stated. In that regard, showing that when one thing is excluded there is no consequence of existence, and when another is excluded there is a consequence of existence, he says: "Not existence," and so forth.
When the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of existence is excluded, there is no consequence of existence—that is, no implication of existence. Existence does not occur.
Selflessness and so forth do not arise from a specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For the self (*ātman*) is dependent, being the locus of activity and enjoyment;
thus it is "selfless" (*nirātman*), because the characteristic of a self is independence.

That form of selflessness is not merely the cessation of a self; otherwise, since [a mere non-entity] is indefinable (*nirupākhya*), properties such as being produced would be impossible, and [selflessness] could not follow from that.

If it is argued that the establishment of selflessness would be faultless because one apprehends a thing as "selfless" by means of the exclusion of a self, [we reply: since there is contact with a real entity through a relative negation (*paryudāsa*), that very nature of the entity itself becomes "selflessness. For a negation is only possible of that which exists; however, mere absence, whose nature is the exclusion of non-existence, [cannot be so established].
That which, by necessity, brings about the presence of an entity through the exclusion [of its opposite] is the "implicator" (*ākṣepaka*) of that entity. What is the reason?
Because it has the nature of the mutual distinction (*viveka*) or separation (*viraha*) between existence and non-existence; that is to say, because it has that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This means that the distinction from existence has the nature of non-existence, and the distinction from non-existence has the nature of existence.

Having thus explained how the exclusion of existence and non-existence does not entail or exclude [the other], he applies this to the subject at hand with the words "But that which has the nature of non-existence," and so forth. As for the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of truthfulness, which is characterized by falsity—that exclusion has the nature of the absence of truthfulness. Being excluded, it ceases along with the cessation of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), and thus [it] establishes existence.
It establishes the characteristic of having true meaning in that which is uncreated.

However, if the opponent were to accept that "having true meaning" consists in having a non-erroneous form, then in the case of Vedic statements—where the quality of being created is excluded—there would be only falsity and not true meaning; consequently, they would be purposeless.

He will say: "Therefore, truthfulness must necessarily be of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*). A property characterized by falsity (*mithyārthatā*) must be admitted; and that, being distinct [from truthfulness], establishes the existence of truthfulness. It is not so for selflessness (*nairātmya*) and the like, which are of the nature of absence (*viraharūpa*). Why? Because of the distinction in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*). For selflessness is indeed a specific intrinsic nature."

He says that very thing: action (*kriyā*) is the performance of what is auspicious and inauspicious; enjoyment (*bhoga*) is the experience of pleasure and pain; and their locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the appropriation [of them]. In this regard, the self (*ātman*) is not independent, for it is subject to another; its own nature (*svabhāva*) is "selfless" (*nirātman*). The word *ātman* is a synonym for *svabhāva*.
What, then, is the reason why such a nature is selfless? He says: because of its dependence on that— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "tatsvātantrye-".]
And so forth. Because that which is sovereignty over that locus of activity and enjoyment is its defining characteristic;

and because it is of the very nature of the self [as opposed to] what is imagined by others. Therefore, the intention is that by contrast with that, that which is non-sovereign in nature is "selfless" (*nirātman*).
Since it is thus, therefore "form" is the intrinsic nature [of things], which is selflessness (*nairātmya*), and not merely the cessation of a self. Otherwise,
if selflessness were merely a cessation, then, due to its lack of intrinsic nature, it would be utterly indefinable.

And because a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*), such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*)—the word "etc. (*ādi*) implying "being immediately subsequent to effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) and so forth—is impossible in the case of that which is indefinable (*nirupākhya*); therefore, from the reason of "being produced" and the like, there is the comprehension of selflessness (*nairātmya*), that is, the establishment of selflessness, and not merely the exclusion of a self (*ātmavyavacchedamātra*).
B. It is precisely the state of having a false object. B. [The nature of] form.
B. The refutation of the doctrine of Kumārila regarding independence (svātantrya).

Even for one who holds that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not of the nature of non-existence, there would be the establishment of a positive entity (*bhāva-siddhi*) upon the exclusion of a positive entity;

thus, there would be no connection with positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Likewise, even in the case of selflessness (*nairātmya*), there would be no establishment of a positive entity, as in the argument:
"This living body is not devoid of a self, because it possesses breath and so forth. [In such cases,] between the two counter-examples (*vipakṣa*), there is no pervaded-pervader relationship...

In the consideration of the state of being a product (*pakabhāva*), selflessness (*nairātmya*) is observed only where there is the absence of breath and so forth; and since it does not exist in the absence of those [breaths], even though it does not itself come into being, it does not establish the proof of breath and so forth in the self.

This might be so. And yet, [selflessness] is accepted [by us]. Therefore, for the Buddhist, selflessness is not merely the absence of a self (*ātmavirahamātra*); it is not a mere negation (*vyavacchedamātra*).

If it is argued: "It is indeed intended [to be expressed], but because a thing (*bhāva*) that is selfless (*nirātman*)—through the exclusion of a self—is referred to and denoted by the word 'selfless,' the understanding of selflessness does not fail to arise from [the reason] such as 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*); therefore, this is not a fault. Even so, since there is contact with the real entity (*vastu*) through the negation of a self, that very thing which we have called the "form of the real entity" (*vasturūpa*) is the nature of the thing (*bhāvasvabhāva*).
Selflessness has been established through the exclusion [of self]. Furthermore, when one entity is excluded, there is no necessary implication of another entity.

Therefore, for the Buddhists, even though selflessness is excluded in the case of things such as a rabbit’s horn, this does not establish the existence of a self. Consequently, what was stated—that "the same would apply to the exclusion of impermanence and selflessness"—is refuted.

Even for the Naiyāyika and others, the self (*ātman*) is not an exclusion (*vyatireka*) of the nature of an entity; rather, it is simply the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvābhāva*). Therefore, by the exclusion of the non-self (*nairātmya*)—which, for the Naiyāyika and others, is itself an entity—the existence of a self as a positive entity would not be established. For this reason, even when the non-self is excluded in the case of a rabbit’s horn and the like, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the self.

The term *dhānuṣaṅgaḥ* means that there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya-anugama*) with the self. Just as in the case of a rabbit's horn and the like, even though there is the exclusion of selflessness (*nairātmya-vyavaccheda*), there is no positive concomitance of a self; likewise, in a living body, even though there is non-selflessness—that is, the absence of selflessness—the existence of a self would not be established.

Alternatively, it is explained otherwise. In the context of refuting the "negative-only" (*vyatirekin*) inference as stated by the Mīmāṃsakas, [the author] says "Of whomsoever... and so forth, in order to refute the negative-only inference as stated by the Naiyāyikas as well. For whomsoever—such as the Naiyāyika and others—the self (*ātman*) is not of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*) as a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); rather, what is it? It is simply the nature of existence (*bhāvasvabhāva*) itself, namely, selflessness (*nairātmya*).

For a Naiyāyika who speaks in this manner, there can be no establishment of the existence of a self (*ātman*) through the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of a selflessness (*nairātmya*) that is itself of the nature of an entity (*bhāvarūpa*). This is because when an entity is excluded, there is no implication of another entity [in its place]. For this reason, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) such that "wherever there is possession of breath and so forth, there is a self. And just as there is no positive concomitance, so too it is with respect to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).

Even when there is selflessness (*nairātmya*), and even upon the cessation of selflessness, the existence of a self (*ātman*) would not be established. Demonstrating this very point through a formal argument (*prayoga*), he says: "Just as," and so forth. "This living body is not devoid of a self (*nirātmaka*), because it possesses breath (*prāṇa*) and so on. Here, "breath" (*prāṇa*) refers to inhalation (*āśvāsa*); by the word "and so on" (*ādi*), exhalation (*praśvāsa*) and the rest are included.

In this formal argument (*prayoga*), the possession of a self (*sātmakatva*) in a living body is the probandum (*sādhya*), and it is not established for both [the proponent and the opponent]. Since that self, which constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*), does not exist [for the opponent], positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not considered. Rather, one considers the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between the two counter-examples (*vipakṣa*)—namely, the absence of a self (*nairātmya*) and the absence of breath and so forth (*aprāṇādimatva*)—which correspond respectively to the probandum, the self, and the reason, the possession of breath and so forth (*prāṇādimattva*).
When [the reason] is being applied, it is only when there is the possession of breath and so forth that selflessness (*nairātmya*) is observed;
in its absence, [selflessness] would be excluded by breath and so forth even in the case of the probandum (*sādhya*), because breath and so forth are absent in selflessness.

Therefore, breath and so forth serve only to exclude selflessness; they do not establish a self (*ātman*) therein, because the existence [of a self] is unestablished. Nor does the exclusion of selflessness [itself constitute a self].

[The opponent claims: "There is proof [of the negative concomitance], because even when one observes the absence [of the reason] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there is the consequence [of proving the positive concomitance]. [Reply: That is not so;

for if the pervasion by the contrapositive (*viparyayavyāpti*) is not established, then the establishment of that [negative concomitance] is itself the establishment of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Furthermore, even if the non-establishment [of the reason in the counter-example] and the establishment of the exclusion of its absence are proven, that [positive concomitance] remains unestablished; thus, the same consequence applies to the probandum (*sādhya*) as well. Therefore, that is not [the case].
There is a negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) without positive concomitance (*ananvaya*):

namely, that where there is an absence of "sentience" (*mattva*), there is the pervaded "selflessness" (*nairātmya*). This follows from the logical principle that [selflessness] does not exist in that which possesses breath and so forth. Although selflessness itself is not present [in the subject], it does not establish the presence of breath and so forth—which are intended as the reasons—within the "self," which serves as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

[The opponent] replies: "Even when there is an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of selflessness (*nairātmya*) as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), there is no implication (*anākṣepa*) of a positive entity characterized by non-self (*anātma*). Therefore, even though there is a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), because there is no connection with a positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the vital breaths (*prāṇādi*) and so forth are purely negative reasons (*vyatirekin*).
By this much of the text, it has been shown that the Naiyāyika’s desired conclusion is not established.

He states the fault in this acceptance, beginning with "tathā" and so forth: Just as non-selfhood (*nairātmya*), which is excluded from breath and so forth by the exclusion of the absence of breath and so forth, does not establish its presence in the self— which serves as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)— so too, in the case of the subject, the living body, non-selfhood is being excluded by the reason consisting of breath and so forth.
It might exist as such, but it does not establish the self.

Clarifying this very point of the introductory statement (*grahaṇakavākya*), he says: "Because of the absence [of breaths, etc. in the case of selflessness," and so forth. Since breaths and the like are absent in the state of selflessness (*nairātmya*), breaths and so on—by negating that [selflessness]—exclude only selflessness and do not establish a self.

[They are] fallacious. What is the reason? Because in that case, [if the subject] possesses a self (*sātmaka*), the existence of breath and so forth is not established. Nor is there an establishment of a self through the exclusion of selflessness (*nairātmya*), which is the opposite of a self, from a living body. What is the reason? Because even if one demonstrates the absence of breath and so forth from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—namely, selflessness—there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that breath and so forth would be established in the similar example (*sapakṣa*), namely, a self.

Since this is so, there is no pervasion by the contrary (*viparyaya-vyāpti*). The meaning is that the pervasion between "possessing a self" (*sātmakatva*) and "possessing breath, etc. (*prāṇādimattva*) is not established, because [the two] are absent from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), namely, from "selflessness" (*nairātmya*). When? At the time when the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of breath, etc., from selflessness is not established. For in this way, the probandum's dissimilar instance, which is selflessness, would be [conjoined] with the reason's dissimilar instance, which is the absence of breath, etc. (*aprāṇādimattva*).

The establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) would occur if selflessness were excluded from breath and so forth. And that exclusion would occur only if there were a positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Thus he says: "(1) And the very establishment of that," and so on. The very establishment of that negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is the establishment of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), because the latter is inseparable from the former. Thus, the establishment of the positive concomitance is stated as being nothing other than the establishment of the negative concomitance.

Now, if the establishment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not accepted, then, given that positive concomitance is unestablished—even though the occurrence of its absence (*vyatireka-vṛtti*) is established—there is the non-establishment of that [absence]. That is, even if the exclusion of selflessness (*nairātmya*) from breath and so forth is established, there is the non-establishment of that self which serves as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). Consequently, since the self is unestablished, there would likewise be no selflessness in the living body, which is the subject of the thesis (*sādhya*).

1B. [Regarding] the characteristic of a self: (2) Refutation of Kumārila’s position: Although falsity is excluded from that which is non-human (apauruṣeya) because it is pervaded by being human-made (pauruṣeya), this does not entail truthfulness, since another alternative is possible. This would only be the case for words if they were restricted to two categories, because if one category is excluded, there would be no other way [for them to exist].
But since they might still be meaningless, the desired conclusion is not established.

(1) If it is argued that they are not meaningless because a meaning is understood, this would not be a human activity; it would be like the conceptualization of other objects—for example, just as others interpret the deeds of Bharata, Urvaśī, and so forth in a different way even though they do not have that [specific] purpose.

They say this; and in accordance with that, for some there is such a cognition, whereby this conceptualization of meaning in [words] that are devoid of meaning would be produced by a person (*puruṣakṛta*), not produced by the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the word. Furthermore, because it depends upon human instruction (*puruṣopadeśāpekṣaṇāt*), it is just like other distinct objects (*arthāntaravat*). For indeed, even when the primary function (*prakṛti*) has ceased, there is no consequence of the non-establishment of the self (*ātman*). Therefore, for that reason, those [words] which are devoid of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and non-concomitance (*vyatireka*) are not...

The meaning of "negative pervasion" (*rekavyāpti*) is that there is no pervasion between the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the opposite of the probans (*sādhana*). However, we say this even while granting [the opponent's point]. Let it be granted that there is a negative pervasion consisting of non-concomitance (*ananvaya*); nevertheless, from the living body, upon the exclusion of soullessness (*nairātmya*), there follows the possession of a soul (*sātmakatva*) for the living body, because there is no other alternative.
However, this method is not possible when "non-artificiality" (*akṛtaka*) is the reason for proving "truthfulness. Thus he says: "But [regarding] falsity," and so forth.

Even if falsity—which is the opposite of the probandum—is excluded from non-artificial speech because of its pervasion by authorship (*pauruṣeyatva*), which serves as the reason, truthfulness would still not be established for that which is non-artificial. What is the reason?

Because there exists another possibility for meaninglessness apart from having truth as its object? This would be the case for words only if there were two categories: having truth as their object and having falsity as their object. For if falsity as their object is excluded, they must have truth as their object. Why? Because when one is excluded—namely, when falsity as their object is excluded—there is no other alternative besides having truth as their object.

Because [the two categories] exist, there is indeed no duality of classes, since another possibility for their movement exists; therefore, those words might even be devoid of meaning, so that neither the desired proof nor the proof of their having true referents is established.
If it is argued that they are not meaningless because meanings are cognized from words, this cognition of meaning is not inherent to them.

However, this would be a human activity (*puruṣavyāpāra*). The convention (*saṃketa*) is a human activity; because it is the fruit of that [activity], it is stated as non-different from it, meaning "it would arise from human activity. Like what? Like the conceptualization of another object from a well-known object.
He explains this very point with the words "Just as," and so forth. By the Jaiminīyas, through a desired object, such as the lineage of Bharata...

Although the *baritā* and other [melodic modes] do not have that as their primary meaning, they refer to the life-story of Bharata, the life-story of Urvaśī, and—by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)—the life-stories of others such as Purūravas. Regarding the second "etcetera," others explain that it refers to specific states of being and so forth, distinct from the life-stories of Bharata and the others; these they interpret differently from the meanings well-known in the world according to the Mīmāṃsakas. Bharata...
"The sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the *urvarśī* vessel, the fire-drills (*araṇi*), and so forth.
If it is argued that comprehension of the meaning does not occur at all from what is imagined by the commentator, he says:
"In accordance with that," and so on. That is, in accordance with the meanings imagined by the commentators, for some listeners...

The cognition indeed occurs as "it is so," just like the explanation of words such as *bharata*. Even though Vedic sentences are meaningless by their own nature (*svabhāva*), the conceptualization of meaning would be produced by persons; it would not be produced by the nature of the word itself. What is the reason? Because [this is] in the case of Vedic [words].

Fire and other such things depend upon light for their manifestation; however, it is logical that a person teaches by explaining his own conventional usage. Since both human-composed and natural [teachings] require instruction, and because there is no other distinguishing feature, it is difficult to determine which one is natural and which one is human-made.

If it is argued that there is a distinction because [the Veda] accords with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃvāda*), we shall refute this later; for there is no operation of another means of valid cognition regarding objects that are entirely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*). If the distinction between two things possessing common properties consists merely in their accord with other means of valid cognition, then now a great many things would be authorless (*apauruṣeya*). Indeed, there exist things produced by persons...

Since some of those sentences are also of this kind, the same objection applies to them as well. Consequently, their possession of an intended meaning would likewise be human-made and dependent upon means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because, in order to understand the meaning, a person such as Jaimini must rely upon instruction. What is it like? (1) [It is] like another meaning—

Ravadeva [says]: The meaning is that it is like the case where words such as "Bharata" or "Urvaśī" are subject to alternative interpretations of their referents. Furthermore, the claim that even though words naturally convey meaning, they must nevertheless depend upon human instruction, is false. For fire and other such things, which illuminate objects by their very nature or inherent character (*prakṛti-svabhāva*), do not depend upon human instruction. A person, however, [requires] his own application of convention (*samaya-vyāpāra*).

By means of the power of convention (*saṃketa*), one teaches another by declaring: "This word has been employed by me with reference to this meaning"—this is logical. However, it is not logical that there should be instruction by a person regarding the manifestation of meaning through the word's own nature (*prakṛti*).
Now, if even the Veda—which is established by nature like an object prepared by a person—requires instruction by a person regarding its meanings, then [the same would apply].

Whether a word is conventionally established by human agreement (*puruṣa-samita*) or its meaning is established by nature (*nisarga*) through its own inherent essence (*svabhāva*), there is no distinction between these two insofar as both depend upon human instruction. Furthermore, there is no other distinguishing feature by which one could be recognized as "human-established" and the other as "naturally established. For this reason, one [type of] Vedic meaning cannot be considered natural.

In the expression *nisarge bhavaḥ*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied because it belongs to the class beginning with *adhyātma*. Any other worldly word regarding its meaning is of human origin; thus, [its authority] is difficult to maintain and difficult to understand, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its distinction [from Vedic words].
There is, however, some correspondence with the means of valid cognition in the case of the Vedic word established by nature (*nisargasiddha*). Proof—

[There is] no subsequent following [of the author]. If it is argued that "that which is not thus [i.e., not dependent on a person] is *pauruṣeya* (human-made)," we shall refute this later with the passage beginning, "There is no operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object beyond the senses," and so forth. Furthermore, since worldly and Vedic [utterances] share common characteristics such as depending on human instruction, there is only the distinction of agreement with a means of valid cognition in one case—the Vedic—[while the other lacks it].

If [the Veda] were to be postulated as being of human origin, then one would now have to postulate that a great many worldly single-sentence utterances—which are in agreement with valid means of knowledge—are likewise not of human origin. For there exist certain sentences composed by humans, such as "Alas, conditioned phenomena are impermanent," and others like them, which are of this kind—that is, which are in agreement with valid means of knowledge. Thus, on the grounds that they are in agreement with valid means of knowledge...
In those cases, it would follow that they are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).
If, on the other hand, even worldly speech that accords with valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃvādin*) is held to be of human origin, then by that same logic, these Vedic [utterances] would also be so.
Thus ends the refutation of Kumārila’s position in the *Dharmapada*.
Furthermore, we observe that this [position]—namely, that "mantras are not of human origin"—is contradictory. For instance:

For if mantras were based on convention (*samaya*), it would be logical for them to accomplish some specific purpose, provided that these mantras are a convention for someone— just as this composition of mine, which binds together desired objects, is a statement that enjoins one to employ it with such-and-such a meaning. [This would be so] by virtue of its devotion to the welfare of others, rather than [arising] from another source.
