Or it might arise from some other cause; in that case, the accomplishment of the result would be possible at times through the application of the mantra, as is the case for reciters due to the conventions of poets and the like.
However, if there were an inherent power (*bhāvaśakti*) [in the mantra], it would exist without distinction elsewhere as well. (295)
Nor is the accomplishment of a purpose from mantras due to human convention; rather, this is the very nature of things (*bhāvasvabhāva*).

If they were not fixed in any [particular way], they would not yield results. Furthermore, if the capacity of words to convey intended meanings were a product of human agency, it could not be consistent with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor could it be in harmony with those means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, we perceive no distinction between Vedic words and worldly ones.
Showing that Vedic words are non-human (apauruṣeya) precisely because they are mantras, he says "Moreover," and so forth.
"Contradictory" means mutually opposed. For instance, if it were asserted that mantras are the conventional agreements of some person—

When there is a formal establishment [of efficacy], the accomplishment of an effect is logical; that is, the attainment of the desired effect through the application of mantras is logical. The explanation begins with the words "If these... and so forth. The connection is as follows: "If these mantras were the convention (*samaya*) of some powerful agent," as will be stated later. They are called "conventions" because they are established by convention.
But how was this convention established? He says: "For the sake of others," and so forth. "Devotion to the welfare of others" means having the welfare of others as one's primary concern;

that is to say, out of compassion. Or else, it might have been established for some other reason, such as fame and the like. What kind of convention is this? He says: "Just as," and so forth. "Just as this statement was composed by me..."

(1) What is it that has come into being? It is that which provides the connection to the intended object. The "intended object" of the mantra's author is a specific ritual procedure characterized by [acts such as] invocation and dismissal; that sentence in which this serves as the "connection"—that is, the factor for engagement—is so described. Thus, by means of this sequence, it enjoins—that is, employs—the person who acts with this purpose, which is the person’s own intended aim.

The convention (*samaya*) would be: "I shall endow [the practitioner] with the fruit. Then, through the application of the mantra, upon the completion of the ritual procedure at some point, the accomplishment of the desired object would occur, just as in the case of a literary convention (*kavisamaya*). For example, suppose someone, having composed a poem, establishes such a convention: "To whoever recites this poem composed by me, I must give this [reward]. Therefore, that which was performed by him—
Just as for those who recite poetry there is the accomplishment of the intended meaning, so it is here.

Now, as for the power of the *bhāva*, that is simply such an inherent power of the word itself by which the desired result occurs, and not from a human convention as one might intend. If that were the case, it would occur elsewhere as well; [for instance,] from a word employed in some way—

Furthermore, what is the reason? Because there is no distinction in a mantra whose essence consists of phonemes (*varṇa*). This is the explanation beginning with "no" and so forth. Indeed, the accomplishment of a purpose from mantras does not arise from the convention of a person;
rather, this is the very nature of a mantra, which is an entity consisting of the form of phonemes: that if [the mantras] do not belong to anyone...
In that case, since the phonemes (varṇas) of the form are indistinguishable everywhere, the result would follow even from a mantra employed in any manner whatsoever;
for the mantras are indeed nothing other than the phonemes themselves.
If it is argued that "the sequence is what is intended," [we reply:
the fact that sequence is a distinct entity has already been refuted.
It has been demonstrated that there is no sequence other than the phonemes themselves; and if there is no distinction, then it is simply the phonemes.
And those mantras are undifferentiated everywhere; thus, they should always yield their fruit.

However, an obstacle is observed even from the slightest deviation in the sequence [of ritual], due to the non-performance of some part, the incomplete presence of the deity, and its violation. But in the case of a total failure, it is due to the non-performance of some specific rule (*samaya*).

O Lord of lords, those [deities] who have been appointed according to the ritual rules bestow the fruits [of practice]. Regarding that very point, it is said in the *Siddhāntavāda*: "Therefore, that which is called 'mantra' is the form of the phonemes (*varṇa*) in their entirety—"
In this regard, it is argued that [the result] would be no different even when used at an improper time, or when applied with inverted order and so forth;

that is, even from a mantra employed by disregarding the prescribed sequence and ritual injunctions, the desired fruit might still arise. For the reason that the mantra is nothing other than the phonemes themselves, and there is nothing whatsoever distinct from the phonemes.
If it is argued that the sequence of phonemes is what constitutes the word, and not the phonemes themselves—

this is incorrect; for the claim that the sequence is a distinct entity from the phonemes, namely that "the sentence is the succession of phonemes," has already been refuted previously in this very context.
The explanation begins with "No," and so forth. If there were no distinction between the sequence [of sounds] and the phonemes (*varṇa*), then the phonemes themselves would be the mantras;

and since those phonemes are indistinguishable everywhere—even in cases such as reciting in reverse order—they would grant results whenever they are employed in any way whatsoever. Yet, they do not grant results. Not only do they fail to grant results when there is a deviation from the prescribed rule, but on the contrary, they lead to misfortune.

He says that they indeed become performers [of their effects], starting with the words "upaplava" and so forth. "Upadrava" means a calamity; "upaplava" likewise. The word "tu" (but) indicates an emphasis.

It is observed that [failure occurs] even from a slight deviation from the sequence of ritual procedures. And this [deviation] is logical if mantras are of human origin (*puruṣasamaya*), but not if they are of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*).
If it is asked, "Even if it is a [prescribed] occasion (*samaya*), how can there be a disturbance (*upaplava*)?", he says: "Of someone," and so forth.

Among the procedures (*vidhi*) prescribed by the author of the mantra, through the performance of one particular procedure, the presence (*sannidhi*) of the deity occurs. Then, due to that presence, because another specific procedure is not fully accomplished—that is, not performed in its entirety—[there is a disturbance] of the deity.

From violation and from causing distress, there will be an affliction. In that regard, a deity who has not transcended passion brings misfortune upon herself when she is displeased; however, one who has transcended passion does not do so herself. It should be understood that other deities and such, who are well-disposed toward him, are the ones who act [to bring about misfortune].

Regarding the question of how it is when no ritual procedure whatsoever is prescribed for a mantra, he says: "In the case of the failure of all procedures," and so forth. [This refers to] a certain commitment (*samaya*) established by the author of the mantra. Furthermore, whether the sequence is a distinct entity from the phonemes or not a distinct entity, [the mantra consists of] the phonemes themselves or that which has the nature of their sequence.
Because it is uncreated for the sake of its object, that which is eternal is eternally present.
The accomplishment of that purpose would be eternal;
for since the production of the fruit arises from the power of the entity (*bhāva*), and that power is unimpaired, there would be no deficiency in the fruit.
Indeed, it is not logical for there to be a deficiency in the effect when the causes are complete, as that would entail the consequence that the cause is not a cause at all. Not only...
If it is argued that the accomplishment of the desired goal through the application of mantras and so forth depends upon their specific ritual procedures, [we reply:
there is a lack of inherent capacity in the case of such dependence. (296)

For if they were to acquire some excellence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*) from the mantra or from something else in any way whatsoever, then that [cause] would be capable and thus not neglected; however, it has been stated that this does not occur in the case of eternal things. Therefore, why would that which is incapable be neglected? Thus, being independent, they would either always produce [their effect], or never at all, since there is no change in their nature.
Because the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is performed, there is no presence of a deity, and thus it is meaningless.

With the words "Furthermore," etc., he states another defect. The idea that the sequence (*krama*) has a meaning distinct [from the phonemes] has been refuted. Or, let it be that the sequence is either distinct from or non-distinct from the phonemes. In that case, if the sequence is non-distinct from them, its nature would be that of the phonemes themselves.

A mantra is simply the nature of the phonemes (*varṇa*). If it were something other than that, it would consist of their sequence—that is, its essence would be the sequence of phonemes. Since such a mantra—whether consisting of the phonemes themselves or their sequence—is eternal because it is not produced by causes for the sake of some purpose, and because it is eternally present, there would be the constant accomplishment of its purpose. From those...

The accomplishment of the human goal would arise from the mantras. What is the reason? Because, since the fruit to be accomplished by the mantra arises from that very power of the entity (*bhāva-śakti*) which is the power of the mantra, that power of the entity is unimpaired; thus, there would be no deficiency in the fruit. For when the completeness of the cause is present, there can be neither deficiency nor non-existence of the effect.

This is logical. What is the reason? Because it would follow that even a complete cause which does not produce its effect would still possess the status of being a cause. Furthermore, even if mantras were eternal, the accomplishment of the desired goal does not arise from the mere application of the mantra; rather, it arises from the connection with the mantra. If you argue that this is because the mantra depends upon the prescribed ritual procedure (*vidhāna*), that is incorrect.

Because, if it were admitted that a mantra depends upon its ritual injunction (*vidhāna*), then that which is depended upon—the injunction and so forth—would lack efficacy with respect to the mantra, since no excellence (*atiśaya*) can be imparted to the mantra by them.
He explains this with the words "If indeed," and so on. By means of the injunctions and other factors, the mantra is [determined as] the ritual procedure (*kalpa*); therefore—

Or else, from some auxiliary cause—such as a particular location or the like—they might acquire or obtain some excellence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*). In that case, the auxiliary would be capable and thus worthy of being disregarded regarding that excellence of intrinsic nature to be produced in the mantra. However, it has already been stated previously that such production of an excellence does not exist in eternal things. Therefore, what [is the point]?

If it is argued that mantras are required because [the causal complex] is incapable of producing an excellence in the co-operative cause (*sahakāri*), then mantras would either always produce the effect— since they are not required—
or else they would never produce the effect at all.
(ga) If the capacity of an entity were such as you describe, then all things would be the means of proof for everything;
furthermore, dependence on a difference among users is not logical for that which cannot be modified. (297)

If mantras were to bestow success solely by virtue of their own inherent power (*bhāvaśakti*), they would not exclude anyone— neither the sacrificer nor another; for an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not become non-existent with respect to another, since it cannot be diminished by that other,
nor can it be enhanced by another, as there is no possibility of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between them due to proximity or distance.
Because of the absence of a seer (*ṛṣi*), and for this very reason because it cannot be refined (*asaṃskārya*), there is no performer (*prayoktṛ*) either, from whom one might obtain the fruit.
For even in the case of an entity to be refined, a difference in the object itself is what causes the distinction;
this is because its own nature remains always identical.
Furthermore, those mantras are not the cause of results for every person, even one joined with sins and the like.

[They] would [be so]. If such an inherent power (*bhāva-śakti*) of mantras were independent of convention (*samaya*), then it might be argued that they grant results only when employed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

To this, he says: "The distinction (*bheda*) or specific quality (*viśeṣa*) of the employer—that is, the state of being the sacrificer—and the dependence upon that [quality] do not apply to one who is not subject to ritual refinement (*asaṃskārya*)."

It is logical for the mantra [to function] thus: if mantras were to grant results solely through their own inherent power (*bhāvaśakti*) without depending on the observance of rules (*samaya*), they would not exclude any person from granting those results—not even others such as *śūdras* and the like. For it is not the case that the nature of mantras—which is to perform an action—would cease to be its own nature and become non-productive with respect to another who is not a sacrificer (*ayajamāna*).

The state [of being a Brahmin] comes into existence. What is the reason? Because that nature which produces [the status] has neither been diminished by that non-Brahmin—meaning it has not been impaired—nor has it been enhanced by another, such as a sacrificer and so forth. For this reason, there is a relationship of cause and effect between the mantras and a certain person; and because of that lack of connection, [the results follow] in their respective order.
Since there is no distinction of proximity or remoteness between one Brāhmaṇa and another regarding mantras, it would follow that anyone could accomplish [the ritual] through them.

For this very reason, because this mantra is eternal and thus not something to be refined (*asaṃskārya*), there is no one—whether a Brāhmaṇa or another—who acts as its "employer" (*prayoktā*) in the sense of being an agent who enjoins it toward a task; for if such an employer existed, he might enjoy or obtain the fruit to be accomplished by the mantra.

Only a Brāhmaṇa, and no other. For just as one such as a Śūdra who has not studied does nothing and is therefore not an agent, so too is the Brāhmaṇa [if he lacks the necessary preparation]. Therefore, because of the failure to acquire the refinement (*saṃskāra*), even for an entity that possesses an excellence derived from the Veda, there is indeed a difference in the object based on a difference in its cause.

For there is no ultimate ontological difference between Brāhmaṇas, Śūdras, and others; the distinction between a Brāhmaṇa, a Śūdra, and so forth is merely created by worldly convention. Therefore, a restriction based on the difference among the users—such as Brāhmaṇas and others who are distinguished by worldly convention—is not possible regarding the power of a mantra, such that only a Brāhmaṇa would obtain the fruit and not a Śūdra. 557

(2) Refutation of Kumārila’s View: Restriction [of meaning] arises from the difference in the speakers, not from [innate] capacity; it would pertain to convention (*samaya*). Since there is no external eternal entity to be imparted as a specific quality, and because its cause possesses a distinction in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [the word's power] is thereby acquired—

Otherwise, they would be different in other cases due to their distinct nature; for there can be no non-difference when there is a difference in the cause, since the effect would then lack distinction.
Furthermore, it has already been largely established that if there were such a distinction, that [cause] would result in being causeless.
Therefore, these mantras yield results through a specific excellence of their own nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*); even though they are effects, they do not [function] when employed by Śūdras and others.

Otherwise, they would not be so; for there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of two persons designated as "Śūdra" and "Brāhmaṇa. Indeed, there is no alteration in the objects associated with distinct intrinsic natures merely because of a difference in names and conventional designations that follow a person's whim. If it is argued that there is a difference of caste (*jāti*) between the two, that [difference] is certainly accepted only when there is a difference in form, quality, and capacity, as in the case of a cow and a horse.
Furthermore, the world accepts this [position] as being without foundation. We do not perceive any fixed quality whatsoever in these two;

so where, then, could such a restriction exist? To this he says: "It would exist in the case of a convention (*samaya*). When a convention is a mantra, then the maker of that convention does not depend upon the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things.

He establishes a convention (*samaya*). Just as in the world, there might be a restriction that "I shall grant the fruit only to those well-known Brahmins who are the performers [of the ritual], and not to others," so it is here.

The explanation begins with the word *ādheya*: those entities (*bhāva*) which possess a particular quality (*viśeṣa*) to be produced (*ādheya*) or brought into being (*janya*) are the causes of that [convention].

When there is a difference in intrinsic nature due to a specific cause, then, because an excellence has been acquired from that specific cause, it might be of one kind in one place and of another kind elsewhere due to other causes; however, if there is no difference [in the cause], there can be no change in the effect. Why? Because when there is no distinction in the cause, there is no distinction in the effect.
Now, if there is a distinction in the effect despite the absence of a distinction in the cause, then, even if such a distinction in the effect is admitted,

it follows— almost as has already been stated— that this distinction would be causeless. Therefore, these mantras, though they are effects and though they are impermanent, [possess their specific nature] due to a difference in their causes.

Even for a donor who is capable of bestowing results, [the rituals] would not become otherwise—that is, they would not fail to yield results—even when performed by a Śūdra or others. What is the reason? Because there is no difference in the nature of the intellect, the sense organs, and the body between those two persons whom one designates with the names "Śūdra" and "Brāhmaṇa. If it is argued that there is a distinction of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) in each individual, we say no; because of that...
This is because [the distinction] occurs even among Brahmins on a per-individual basis; it is simply said that there is no distinction based on genus (*jāti*).

[Objection: But surely in the world there is a difference in names, such as "this is a Brahmin" and "this is a Śūdra," and likewise a difference in treatment, such as honor and so forth; from this, a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is inferred. [Response: If you say this...

He says: "It is not so," and so forth. Because there are distinctions in names such as *brāhmaṇa* and others which conform to human desire, and because there are distinctions in conventional usage such as honor and so on, there is a change in the nature of things that are followed by a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—that is, things that are accompanied by a difference in intrinsic nature produced according to their respective causes. For it is not the case that there is no difference in intrinsic nature; this is the connection [of the sentence].

If it is argued that there is a difference in caste between those two persons, the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra, then how could we perceive that difference when we do not see it? How indeed could we establish a distinction?

Furthermore, as for this difference in cognition in the world that follows from a difference in names, even though a difference in genus (*jāti*) exists, it is not due to that [genus] alone; rather, it is due to the operation [of the word]. To explain why: "For indeed," and so forth. Since the universal (*sāmānya*) has been refuted, the genus itself is indeed refuted; [the following] is stated merely by way of concession. Even if such a difference in genus were to exist, it is held to be threefold: [namely] configuration (*ākṛti*), quality (*guṇa*), and...

When there is a difference in capacity (*śaktibheda*), it is like the case of a cow and a horse (*gavāśvavat*). Just as in the case of a cow and a horse (*gavāśvasya iva gavāśvavat*): therein, the difference in form (*ākṛtibheda*)—that is, a specific configuration (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*)—is found to persist even among individual cows that differ from one another, but not among individual horses. The difference in qualities (*guṇabheda*)—consisting of the differences in taste, potency, post-digestive effect, and so forth, regarding milk and the like—is likewise [found] among members of the same class.
It is observed to follow after individuals, but not among those of different species; it is characterized by the capacity for effects corresponding to a specific difference in power.

For example, the capacity for milking and so forth belongs to cows, but not to horses. Thus, since differences such as generic form (*ākṛti*) are perceived as following after individuals of the same class, let there be a distinction of genus (*jāti*) in the case of cows, horses, and the like; however, it is not so with respect to Brāhmaṇas and others.

There exists a specific distinction in form and so forth by which a difference in genus (*jāti*) might be postulated. Furthermore, once a person has learned [the distinction] regarding cows and the like, they perceive this difference in genus even across differences of place, time, and so on, without further instruction—thinking, "This is a cow" and "This is a horse. However, one does not perceive the distinction between Brahmins and others in such a way without instruction. It is just like that.

Like that of a cow and a horse: we do not perceive any fixed quality whatsoever belonging to these two—the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra—residing only in individuals of the same class. (The mention of "quality" is illustrative. Likewise, we do not perceive any fixed difference in form or difference in capacity. And failing to perceive such differences in form and so forth, how can one maintain a difference in caste between a Śūdra and a Brāhmaṇa?
We shall not undertake it; that is to say, we will not do so. For indeed, every distinction such as study, purity, and conduct is subject to deviation.
Furthermore, the specific physical characteristics that are postulated—such as having a fair complexion and reddish-brown hair—are absent even in some Brāhmaṇas, yet they are present in some Śūdras.

If there is no difference in caste between a Brahmin and a Śūdra, how then does this distinct cognition arise from hearing words such as "Brahmin" and so forth? To this he says: "Even that which... and so on. This connection with the difference in names is caused by specific designations such as "Brahmin" and the like. Even this...

The distinction in cognition—the distinction in understanding such as "this is a Brāhmaṇa" and "this is a Śūdra"—would arise from the performance of specific activities, that is, from the performance of specific rites such as recitation (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*), even in the absence of a difference in birth (*jāti*). It would also arise from lineage (*anvaya*), meaning from being born into a family that performs such activities. This applies to designations such as "physician" or "merchant."

Just as among Śūdras of the same caste, designations such as "physician" and so forth arise from the performance and mastery of specific professional activities, yet no difference in caste results therefrom; so too it may be in the case of Brāhmaṇas and others.

[This would apply] in the case of a specific performance. Furthermore, it could be so by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), as in the case of the designations "physician" or "merchant," and so forth.
Thus, these mantras, when employed by a distinguished [person], attain that very same undistinguished nature;
therefore, they would grant results without distinction. However, when the results proceed from them due to a convention (*samaya*) and the like, then this fault does not arise.
Because the production of a result is determined by the intention (*ruci*) of the agent of the convention (*samayakāra*), entities function according to their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
it is through that [nature] that they are subject to logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). They do not function according to human desire, for they do not function in any way based on that.
Furthermore, the statement "the performer enjoys the fruit" refers to the production of something capable of accomplishing the intended purpose; [this occurs] within the continuum (*saṃtāna*)—
Or do we perceive a transformation? That [transformation] would have to arise from a specific difference in those two;
otherwise, for things that cannot have any excellence added to them, what could an instigator possibly do, by virtue of which one person would enjoy a certain fruit while another would not?

The word "tad" means "therefore": these mantras, when employed by anyone without distinction—such as Brāhmaṇas, Śūdras, and so forth—attain a nature that is likewise undifferentiated from that of the Brāhmaṇas and others. For that reason, the conclusion is that they would yield results for Śūdras and others equally, without distinction. Thus, there is no such defect regarding the production of results through the inherent power (*bhāva-śakti*) of the mantras.

But when a result is desired from these Vedic mantras, or from others, according to the aforementioned convention of persons (*puruṣasamaya*), then they would grant the result without distinction; this is not a fault. What is the reason? Because the production of the result is restricted by the intention (*ruci*) of the author of the convention, the composer of the mantra. It was thus intended by the author of the convention that such a Brāhmaṇa—

One who observes such a rule becomes entitled to this designation; for one who has such an inclination, thinking, "I am present for him alone through the connection with the fruit, and not for others," there is a restriction regarding the fruit. This is the challenge [to the opponent]. For indeed: (1) entities that function by their own nature (*svabhāvavṛtti*) act as effects by the very state of things (*vastusthiti*), independent of human activity; they [act] through that, namely by way of their own nature.

They are subject to the charge of over-extension (*prasaṅga*). For example, one might ask: "Why does it not happen here in this case as well, given that there is no difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? However, entities do not function according to the whims of persons, and thus they do not admit such a charge of over-extension. What is the reason? Because those persons, who act according to their own desires, may proceed in any manner whatsoever.

As for the claim that a distinguished practitioner obtains the fruit of the mantra, even there we observe that the "application" (prayoga) has this very characteristic: namely, the production of that essential nature of the mantra which is suitable for the human goal desired;
and, once produced, the transformation of its continuum through the production of ever-increasing excellence, or else its alteration—both of these constitute it.

[The production or transformation [of a mantra] would occur only when a distinction arises—that is, when a specific excellence is produced. Otherwise, if no distinction were produced, for mantras that cannot have any excellence added to them, what could the prompter do? Nothing at all.
He explains this with the words beginning "by which," etc.: by which reason, from that application of the mantra, some prompter...

A Brāhmaṇa enjoys the fruit [of the rite], while another, such as a Śūdra, does not. If it is maintained that the "application" (*prayoga*) of mantras is not their production but rather their manifestation (*abhivyakti*), then that manifestation has already been refuted in the general discussion. If application is indeed manifestation, that has already been rejected previously. (299)

For it has been stated that there is no manifestation whatsoever of eternal things, such that a speaker could be the manifester. Furthermore: "If cognition, which is manifestation, is connected with results because of its cause, then the connection with the result would belong to the hearer, for the speaker is merely the cause of manifestation. (300)

For the manifestation of a word is neither a transformation of its own nature from something else, nor the removal of an obscuration; rather, it is the cognition of it as its object, because that which is not being heard is designated as "unmanifested. In that case, if the speaker were the cause of the cognition, then the same would apply to the listener as well; he too, like the speaker, would experience the result. For there is no distinction for the speaker... [text fragment ends].

If it is argued that the nature of one thing exists elsewhere because it is the cause of the cognition of that [other] thing, and that there is a distinction in that the listener’s cognition of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) does not belong to the speaker—then what is the utility of the speaker to the listener such that the adjunct is postulated? If it is argued that this is because the hearing of the sound [occurs] from that [speaker], we reply: surely this very point is being questioned. How can it be "from that," given the lack of a connection, since the object is not presented [to the listener]?

He explains this as follows: It has already been stated that for eternal entities, there is no manifestation whatsoever, on account of which a speaker could be the manifester of a word. Or, let there be manifestation; however, since it is eternal, that manifestation would merely be a capacity. But—

Furthermore, if the individual—the cognition whose object is the word—is joined with the fruits of the mantra because of the person who utters it, then there would also be a connection with the fruit for the listener. For one who merely hears a mantra being recited by another, there would be a connection with the fruit of that mantra, and not for the speaker alone; since the speaker is indeed the cause of the manifestation [of the sound].

And for this reason, that which is the cause of knowledge is connected with the result; and since that quality of being the cause of knowledge regarding the object of the mantra is equal for the listener as well, why is he not also connected with the result, just like the speaker?
He explains this with the words "For it is not," and so forth: for there is no modification of the essential nature of an eternal word from any other cause.

Manifestation (*vyakti*) is not a change in the essential nature (*svarūpa-anyathātva*) of the name; nor is manifestation the removal of an obscuration, because an obscuration is impossible for that which is eternal. Rather, manifestation is the cognition or mental apprehension (*pratīti-buddhi*) having that [word] as its object. What is the reason?
Because the designation "unmanifest" applies when the word is not being heard. For a word that is not being perceived is never said to be "manifested."

This being the case, if the speaker were the cause of the cognition whose object is sound, then the listener would also possess that nature of being a speaker which is the cause of the cognition having sound as its object; consequently, the listener too, like the speaker, would obtain the desired result produced by the application of the mantra. For there is no state other than that of being a speaker—namely, the state of being a speaker—that distinguishes the speaker from anyone else.

Because it is the cause of that cognition; because it is the cause of the cognition of sound. Therefore, since there is no distinction between the speaker and the hearer in being the cause of the cognition of sound, the connection with the result would be equal for both. The other is the speaker. That cognition which has an external factor (*upādhi*) as its cause is "cognition with an external factor"; this belongs to the hearer, not to the speaker, whose cognition does not have an external factor [in this specific sense]. Thus, there is a distinction between the speaker and the hearer based on this reason.

If this is argued, what then is the utility or capacity [of the speaker] with respect to generating cognition in the listener, by virtue of which he would be its hearer? And that is not possible, because there is no transformation of it (the listener's mind) in any way whatsoever.

(The modifications of the sense organs and so forth have also been discussed. If it is argued that there is a distinction between the speaker and the listener because of two cognitions—namely, "He makes me hear" and "I hear"—this is merely an illusion regarding that which neither benefits nor is benefited. Therefore, if that were the case, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since such cognitions are seen through illusion even in other instances. Furthermore, this is so because there is no benefit whatsoever [in the latter case].

Likewise, such a condition is not logical, because it would lead to the same consequence for all things in relation to one another. If it is argued that even error is accepted by the speaker as a limiting adjunct (upādhi) arising from some cause, and that consequently the hearing of the word—the perception of the word—occurs for the listener on account of the speaker, and therefore that speaker is the limiting adjunct; [we reply: no.
Is it not precisely this that is being questioned: how does the hearing of the word by the listener arise from the speaker?
And how could it not arise from him? Because of the absence of a relationship; because of the absence of the state of being the benefactor and the beneficiary.
Demonstrating that very absence, he says: "By bringing the object near—that is, by placing the object in proximity—this speaker is the one who causes this listener to hear."

It might be so; it would become a communicator. However, that presentation [of the sound] is not possible for that sound, because it is eternal and thus incapable of undergoing transformation in any way, and because there is no possibility of its becoming otherwise.
[The speaker] would have to proceed by either effecting a refinement of the listener's sense organ or by accomplishing the removal of the sound's obscuration.

If it is argued that [the speaker] speaks to the cow, that is not so; for the refinement of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*) and other such factors have already been mentioned and refuted by the passage beginning, "The sense organ would undergo refinement, and it would hear everything," and so forth. Furthermore, the cognition of the listener is: "This speaker is making me hear."

If it is argued that the speaker has the cognition, "I shall cause this listener, who possesses intellect, to hear," and therefore, due to these two cognitions, there is a distinction between the speaker and the listener as appropriate—
[the author] refutes this with the words beginning "anupakārya" (not being assisted). [The notions] "He makes me hear" and "I am making [him] hear" are merely delusions.

This is not so. Of what nature is that which is "neither beneficiary nor benefactor"? A beneficiary is the listener; a benefactor is the speaker—that in which these do not exist is described as such, being merely an error. Furthermore, since an eternal word is in no way operative in the production of cognition in a person, the absence of the relationship between beneficiary and benefactor has been established. Therefore, from such a state of mere error—
If there were no distinction between speaker and listener, there would be an over-extension [of the argument]. This would apply to everyone who does not hear, even those who do not listen at all.

What is the reason? Because even in other cases, such as with a madman, one observes cognitions such as "I am hearing" arising through delusion even without hearing a sound. Therefore, since there is no assistance whatsoever, such a cognition as "I am making [you] hear" and so forth [is untenable].

A cognition is not tenable. Why? Because for all things that are mutually neither benefactors nor beneficiaries, there would follow the absurd consequence that "I hear this from that," and so forth. If it is argued that, just as a cognition arises through delusion regarding those who are insane, so too might it arise regarding eternal entities, [the author] says: "Delusion," etc. Even that delusion which occurs to a person who is insane...

Even that [cognition] occurs elsewhere through some form of proximity when, during a state of normalcy, a benefit has been received from a certain person and a corresponding conviction has arisen; this being so,
it would not exist even indirectly.
Therefore, since there is no distinction between the speaker and the listener regarding their being the cause of manifestation, the connection with the result would be equal for both. Moreover,
the purpose of the vocal organs is the manifestation of sounds that have not yet been manifested.
Or else, mental recitation would be useless, for sound is indeed within the range of the ear. || 301 ||
Because if one were to overstep the definition of sound as that which is apprehended by the sense of hearing, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Now, even so, does this not lead to the same problem regarding universals (*sāmānya*)?
We do not say that it is *only* sound [that possesses this definition]; rather, sound necessarily possesses that definition, since no other definition for it exists.

In that case, if the reciter—the one who mutters or the one who performs mental recitation—is the cause for the manifestation of mantras whose nature is sound, then by virtue of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), this occurs even in another state such as madness, and even when there is no speaker;

this happens through some proximity or some similarity. Yet, since mantras are eternal, that [manifestation] is an error, for it provides no benefit whatsoever, even indirectly, to those things which are permanent.
It would not be so.

Therefore, with the words "tasmāt" (therefore) and so forth, he concludes the subject under discussion. If, according to the method stated, [the mantra] were the cause of the manifestation for both the speaker and the listener, then—since there would be no distinction in its being the cause of the cognition of the word—the connection with the fruit of the mantra would be equal [for all]. [This applies even] regarding eternal [words], in terms of manifestation—
Even causality does not exist at all; this is stated merely by way of concession.

Furthermore, with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth, he states another refutation: those organs, such as the palate and so on, by which sound—which is unmanifested—is brought within the range of the auditory faculty are "organs that do not manifest sound. The purpose of those organs is—

The phrase "the completion [of the recitation] would be in vain" is to be connected by changing the grammatical gender (*liṅgavipariṇāmena*). The meaning of the sentence is that where the *upāṃśu-japa* (whispered recitation) is performed merely by the movement of the lips and so forth, it would be useless. Where there is not even movement of the lips and so forth, but only the mental contemplation of the mantra, that is *manojapa* (mental recitation). The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction; thus, the *manojapa* as well is useless.

It might be argued as follows: Since sound is the object of the ear, only that which is grasped by the ear is sound; and a mantra has the nature of sound. Now, because there is no grasping by the ear in the two types of recitation—namely, the whispered (*upāṃśu*) and the mental (*mānasa*)—they lack the quality of being sound. And because they lack the quality of being sound, they lack the status of being mantras. How, then, could one who recites them obtain a fruit? "Grasping" (*grahaṇa*) means that which is grasped (*gṛhyate*). [Thus, it is] "grasped by the ear."
This is the meaning. That which has that very [definition] as its characteristic is described as such. Otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If, setting aside sound as that which is apprehended by the auditory organ, one were to accept that things consisting of cognition—such as mental recitation (*manojapa*) and so forth—are "sound," then taste and the other [objects of sense] would also have to be considered "sound."

[Objection: Even so, if that which is within the range of the auditory organ has the nature of sound (*śabda*), then it follows that the universal "sound-ness" (*śabdatva-sāmānya*) must also have the nature of sound. [Reply:
No, says the Siddhāntavādī. We do not say that only that which is within the range of the auditory organ is sound; rather, sound is necessarily...

We say that it has the characteristic of being perceived by the sense of hearing (*śrotra-grahaṇa-lakṣaṇa*). Why? Because it is not logical for that *mantra* to have the fruit [of its recitation] if it lacks the quality of being graspable by the sense of hearing (*śrotra-grāhyatva*). For at that time, we do not perceive any object with the ear;
nor is a *mantra* something whose nature is non-verbal.
If it is argued that even that cognition is a manifestation of that [word], because it is produced from it through a traditional succession, [we reply:

for one who is merely meditating with the mind, there is no cognition appearing as a mantra without hearing [it]. Therefore, since it originates from sound, that too is indeed a manifestation of sound. In this way, there would be an infinite regress regarding the conceptualizations of word and meaning.
If it is argued that they too would be so because there is a continuous production through a lineage,
then if they exist for that purpose, [the reason] is unestablished due to the presence of conceptual construction.

Because there is no other characteristic [for it] apart from being released. In this regard, if within this specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound, a person is intended as the agent who utters—that is, the cause for the manifestation of mantras whose nature is that of sound, and the cause for the cognition that grasps the form of the sound—and with whom the connection to the fruit [of the action] resides; then, for those [mantras] whose objects of hearing have not yet been manifested, the word "object of hearing" (*śrutiviṣaya*) refers to the sound.

The analysis of the compound is: "by those causes through which [the mantra] is not manifested. The *prayoktā* of those causes is the one who sets them in motion merely by the movement of the lips and so forth. One who mutters silently (*upāṃśujāpī*) is not joined with the fruit of the mantra; nor would one who mutters mentally be joined with the fruit of the mantra. For at that time—during the silent muttering while observing a vow of silence (*mauna*)—no object whatsoever is perceived by the ear.
We maintain that what is called "sound" (śabda) is what we perceive.
He states that even mental recitation is a mantra; for a mental conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that is not of the nature of sound cannot be a mantra.
This is because sound is accepted as being perceptible by the ear, as being unauthored (*apauruṣeya*), and as eternal, whereas a conceptualization is the opposite of that.

[The author] anticipates the opponent's objection with the words "pāramparyeṇa" (by way of tradition), etc. Even that cognition or intellect which is a mere semblance of the mantra at the time of silent mental recitation (*upāṃśu-manojapa*) is also a manifestation of that [mantra]. It is the knowledge of the manifestation of that sound. Why? (1)
Because it is produced through a lineage; because it is born from sound. For instance, first there arises the cognition of the sound;
then, for one who has been infused with a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) by that cognition, there arises in due order the appearance of the sound during mental recitation (*manojapa*).
He explains [this] with the words "not," and so forth: "For even for one who is mentally meditating or reciting, the cognition which is the appearance of the mantra..."

That [consciousness] is devoid of hearing; that is, without the hearing of sound. Therefore, because it arises from sound—which is the source of sound—that cognition at the time of mental recitation (*manojapa*) is indeed the manifestation of sound, which is to say, it is the very knowledge of sound. Consequently, since mental recitation and the like possess the nature of mantra, the practitioner shall be endowed with the fruit; this is the intended meaning. Thus, even though [the mantra] is a mantra only through a traditional succession (*pāramparya*),...
This would be the case.

He states this very point with the words beginning with “śabda” and so forth. From a word characterized as a mantra, there arise conceptual constructions of meaning—namely, conceptual constructions of the word and its meaning. For instance, when it is said, “Svāhā to Agni,” [there arises the thought] that fire has a form that is blazing, radiant, and so forth.

Conceptual constructions arise at certain times; since even these have their origin in words through a continuous succession, those conceptual constructions would likewise be applications characterized by the manifestation of mantras. Even though they originate from words, that which has them as its object—*El Padre* 199a.
We do not say that every cognition arising from words is its manifestation (*vyakti*). Rather, that which has that [particular] as its object is its manifestation.

It is unestablished that mental conceptualization (*manovikalpa*) has the word as its object; for we shall demonstrate that conceptualizations do not operate upon particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

For these [cognitions] arise from the awakening of their respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of conceptual construction, without depending on the proximity of an external object; this is because they exist even when external objects are absent or have not arrived. Indeed, how could that which does not depend upon the presence of something else be its cause? It would be neither a cause nor a non-cause. Therefore, the conceptual construction of the mind is not the manifestation of the word, such that one who possesses it could be the user (*prayoktā*) of that word.

The cognition produced by that [word] and having that as its object is the manifestation (*vyakti*) of that [word]. The agent who employs it is its substratum (*āśraya*). In this context, the analysis of the compound *tadviṣayā* is: "that which has that word as its object (*artha*)," referring here to the auditory organ (*śrotra*). If that very cognition is the manifestation of the mantra, and not those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of meaning which have words as their objects—[the Siddhāntavādī says] "it is unestablished" (*asiddham*); the conceptual construction of the word is unestablished because of the nature of the word itself.

[The cognition] has the [universal] characteristic as its object. What is the reason? Because it follows from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). This is because it has conceptualizations of similar classes as its cause.
Mental conceptualizations have only superimposed forms as their objects.
He explains this with the words "no," etc.: "We do not say that every cognition arising from a word is a manifestation of that [particular]."

"Manifestation" (vyakti)—but what is this? It is the conceptual cognition (*vikalpa-buddhi*) which has that [object] as its domain or has the word as its domain; that is the manifestation of that word.
This is incorrect, because it is unestablished that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has that [external object] as its domain or has the word as its domain. For—

For we shall demonstrate that words do not function with respect to particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). If external objects are not the cause of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), how then do they arise? [The answer is:
their cause is [the latent impressions].

He says: "For those," and so forth. For those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise according to their respective [causes], that is, from the awakening of whichever latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) is established within consciousness; they arise from the awakening of the predispositions for conceptual construction. The analysis of the compound is: "those by whom the proximity—that is, the presence—of an external object is not required. Why? [He says: "External," and so forth.

Cessation is the absence [of arising]; non-arising is non-occurrence. This is because, when external objects cease and do not arise, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) no longer exist. Since these [constructions] occur even in the absence of an object, they do not have the object as their cause. What is the reason?
(1) For that which does not depend upon the presence or the proximity of existence of something else—that which is independent—is not the cause of that [other thing], since it is being disregarded.

And how could it not be the object of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)? Since conceptual construction is thus not the object of words, therefore the mental conceptualization—characterized by "mental recitation" (*manojapa*) and so forth—is not the manifestation of sound (*śabdavyakti*). For that reason, a person possessing that [conceptualization], i.e., one who possesses mental recitation, would be a practitioner of mantra; however, he certainly would not be [such a practitioner]. This is the sense.

Even while accepting the manifestation of sound, he states a fault: "The cognition produced by sound and having that as its object is the manifestation of sound; since the person is the locus of that manifestation, he is therefore the 'employer'. This has also been stated regarding this position. What was stated? "It would follow that the ear is the employer," for the hearer also [produces the cognition] born from sound.

And it has been stated that this leads to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). In that case, the person exerts effort toward the sound, not toward the cognition, because [the effort] produces that cognition. The person does not exert effort toward the sound, because there is no benefit to the sound by means of that [effort]. Thus, the claim that "the person is the user (*prayoktṛ*) of words" is an unconventional (extraordinary) usage.
In every respect, since the attainment of the fruit results from the employment of mantras whose intrinsic nature is sound, mental recitation (*manojapa*) is useless;
for conceptual thought does not touch upon the actual form of the sound. (Gha) A distinction in the fruit [is obtained] through the utterance of those who established the convention (*samaya*).

By intending to express the single nature of specific and general properties, the authors of the conventions have stated that there is no contradiction; this does not apply to the actual entity itself. (303)

For those who establish conventions (*samayakāra*)— having, according to worldly usage, synthesized the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the object of the sense faculties, and the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which is the appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpapratibhāsa*)— proclaim the convention (*samaya*) as that which brings about this [result] in accordance with the convention;
and since it is the basis for the cognition directed toward that [object] arising within one's own continuum, so too is it [the basis] for the fruit of the mantra.

[Yoga: It may be so. Furthermore, the application (*prayoga*) of eternal mantras does not consist in the production of some excellence; rather, the application is the knowledge regarding them. And when that knowledge is accepted as the application, the word operates upon the person. How [does it operate]? Upon that person—

Because it generates cognition; the person does not exert activity upon the word. Why? Because there is no benefit whatsoever to the person by the eternal essence of the word—that is, its own self. And yet, that "the person is the user of words" is an extraordinary convention; for in the world, he who exerts activity toward something is the user of that thing.

It is said: the conclusion is expressed by the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*) and so forth. Whether the cognition produced directly from the word is the "word-cognition" (*śabdabuddhi*), or whether it is [produced] through a succession, in either case, because of the employment of mantras whose intrinsic nature is that of sound (*śabda-svabhāva*), there arises a cognition having them as its object.

If the attainment of the fruit is desired, mental recitation (*manojapa*) is useless. Why? Because the conceptualization characterized as mental recitation does not touch upon the nature of the sound [of the mantra]. Even for one who holds that the fruit [arises] from the conventional agreement (*samaya*), why would mental recitation not be useless? To this he says: its own intrinsic nature (*svasvabhāva*).

The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound is the form appearing in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which has the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*). With the intention of expressing these individual and universal natures as a single entity—by unifying the perceived object and its conceptual representation—the author of the convention (*samayakāra*) composed the mantra. Thus, there is no contradiction in the fact that mental recitation (*manojapa*) would otherwise be useless; for by fulfilling the intention of the author of the convention, the fruit [is attained].

Because [the result] would follow [absurdly]. However, there is no lack of contradiction regarding the real entity (*vastu*); rather, there is indeed a contradiction. To explain: (1) if the fruit were obtained from the real entity that is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound, then mental recitation (*manojapa*) would be useless, because it does not touch upon the real entity.
He explains this with the words beginning "by convention" (*samaya*). The specific characteristic of sound is the object of the auditory faculty, and the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)...

They proceed by synthesizing [the sequence] conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), according to worldly usage, as a manifestation of conceptual construction (*vikalpapratibhāsa*) that does not transcend worldly conventions. Thus, there is no fault regarding mental recitation and the like. However, if the production of a result were to arise from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the thing itself, it would not occur upon contact with that which lacks such an intrinsic nature. As it has been said: "The sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) is not something other than the phonemes (*varṇa*)."
If it is argued that, in the absence of sequential order, there would be no difference in the effect produced when hearing the words "sara" and "rasa"— for indeed,
there is no difference whatsoever in the phonemes within such words as "sara" and "rasa"— [we reply: no.
(Ṅa) Regarding the consideration of the fruit of the sequence of phonemes:

it is not something distinct [from the phonemes] such that there would be a difference in the effect. Yet, we observe a different manifestation (*pratibhā*) for those two, as well as an unequal sequence (*anupūrvī*). And it is not logical for there to be a difference in the effect without a difference in the cause. Therefore—
Since that [cognition] possesses differentiation, there is a difference in its apprehension. True;
it exists as something residing in the person. (304)

By means of a conceptualizing intellect, having unified the perceived object and the conceptualization—the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sound and its universal form (*sāmānyākāra*)—one should announce the convention (*samaya*). One should declare: "For whoever performs the verbal and mental recitation of this mantra composed by me, this mantra shall accomplish his purpose according to the convention. Then, for one who [performs] this mantra with speech and mind...

One speaks [the mantra] for him and should accomplish the purpose at the appropriate time; thus, there is no fault in mental recitation (*manojapa*) and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of whispered application (*upāṃśuprayoga*) and other such methods is intended. However, if it were maintained that the production of fruit arises from a mantra by virtue of its own nature as sound, then in the case of mental recitation and the like—where there is contact with that which does not possess the nature of sound—there would be no fruit.

With the words "As for what was said," etc., he anticipates the opponent's intention. Regarding what was stated in the intervening passage, "(1) 'The mantras are indeed just the phonemes,' [and] there is no sequential order (ānupūrvī) other than the phonemes," it is replied to that: if there were no sequential order, [the word] "sara" [would not be distinguished from "rasa"].

If it is argued that although the sound "rasa" is heard [in both cases], there should be no difference in the resulting cognition characterized by a difference in apprehension— because there is indeed no difference whatsoever in the phonemes within words such as *sara* and *rasa*; for the very same phonemes that are in the word *sara* are also in the word *rasa*.

Nor is there any other distinct word from which a difference in effect—characterized by a difference in cognition—could arise; yet a difference in effect does exist, since we perceive a different cognition (pratibhā) and intellect (*buddhi*) for those two words *rasa* and *sara*, even though they consist of the same letters. Furthermore, we observe that the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) of the two is unequal and different, while the phonemes (*varṇāḥ*) themselves remain the same. And it is not [the case] of the cause...

It is logical that there should be a difference in the effect—characterized by a difference in cognition—even when there is no difference in the phonemes. Therefore, although the phonemes are identical, there exists a distinct and differentiated comprehension for each word; this is what is meant by "sequence" (*ānupūrvī*). For it is due to this sequence, which differs for each word, that there arises a difference in apprehension—a difference in cognition—regarding words such as *sara* and so forth.
"Truth," says the Siddhāntavādin. "It is true that there is a sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) characterized by difference in every word; however, this is merely a refutation of Kumārila’s position.

For the sound (*dhvani*) which arises from the cognition that produces the manifestation of a particular phoneme (*varṇa*), that [sound] is perceived through hearing as having that [cognition] as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). (305)
He possesses knowledge produced by that [prior] knowledge, yet his hearing is unskilled in the sacred revelation (*śruti*). For instance:
that sequential order (*sānupūrvī*) resides in the person and is thus human (*pauruṣeyī*); it is indeed non-different from the phonemes (*varṇa*), and the phonemes [are non-different] from each word.
I believe that others also arise due to the difference in their causes; it is only because of their similarity that those of dull intellect determine them to be one. 523a

Demonstrating this very point, he says: "For it is thus," and so forth. Herein, the collective meaning is as follows: by means of the preceding preceding mind that originates each successive phoneme residing in the speaker, a subsequent subsequent mind that originates the next phoneme is produced; thus, due to the sequence of the originating minds, there is a sequence in the arising of the phonemes originated by them. And by means of the phonemes produced in succession, [the cognitions] of their respective objects...

Auditory cognitions are produced directly only in a sequential manner, and recollections having phonemes as their objects are likewise produced only sequentially, though indirectly. Therefore, that which is the state of being an effect in a sequence—arising from the sequence of the cognitions that give rise to the phonemes—and that which is the state of being a cause in a sequence with respect to the cognitions of their own objects, is established as "succession" (*ānupūrvī*). 4.
Now the meaning of the term *avapada* is analyzed. The connection is: "the sound (*dhvani*) which is produced.

For example, in the word *sara*, there is the vowel *a* following the letter *sa*. From what is it produced? It is produced from the cognition arising from the cognition of the origination of that letter. The letter existing at the preceding time is the letter *sa*. And that which is this letter is "that letter" (*yad-varṇa*).

That which is the cause for the arising of a phoneme (*varṇa*), in the sense that "by this it arises," is "the arising of a phoneme. [The compound] *yadvarṇasamutthāna* is a *karmadhāraya* meaning "that which is both the arising of a phoneme and knowledge. The knowledge produced from that is "the knowledge born from the arising of a phoneme" (*yadvarṇasamutthānajñānaja*).
It arises from that knowledge. From that knowledge which is the producer of the letter *sa*—from that...

The meaning is that the cognition which gives rise to the form (ākāra) arises, and by that [cognition], the form is produced. In the same way, it should be applied to other cases as well: each subsequent phoneme (varṇa) is produced from the cognition arising from the production of each preceding phoneme. Thus far, it has been stated that the phonemes possess the nature of being effects because they arise sequentially, following the sequence of the motivating cognition (samutthānajñāna) residing within the continuum of the speaker. And those...

Showing that those [sounds] which arise in succession become the causes, in turn, for the cognitions of their own objects residing in the continuum of the hearer, he says: "That qualified by it," and so forth. That which has the preceding phoneme as its specific qualification (upādhi) is described as such. That [latter phoneme], namely the subsequent phoneme, is "ascertained" (samavasīyate)—that is, grasped—by hearing, i.e., by auditory cognition.
But surely, the preceding phoneme does not exist at the time of the succeeding phoneme; how then can the succeeding phoneme be perceived as having that as its adjunct (*upādhi*)?

To this he replies: "by means of the cognition produced by the cognition of that. This means: by means of the cognition produced by the cognition which has the preceding phoneme as its object, [the subsequent phoneme] is... its own...
The analysis of the compound is: "that whose object is knowledge.
Having depended upon that [prior] recollection, it subsequently establishes a recollection within itself. (306)

Thus, this very causal relationship among the cognitions that grasp those causes is what is called "sequence" (ānupūrvī) with respect to the phonemes; for it is indeed dependent upon human agency. (307)

Vocal intimation arises from the mind; it consists of phonemes, words, and sentences. In this context, "arising from the letter *sa*" means the following: when the auditory consciousness has the letter *sa* as its object, at that very moment, the letter *a* is produced by a mind arising from the letter *sa*; thus, the letter *a* is both produced by the letter *sa* and has the letter *sa* as its objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). These two are simultaneous.

[This refers to] time. In that context, the meaning is as follows: by means of the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) which has a specific form as its object and acts as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), the final phoneme—producing a cognition of its own object while being conditioned by the preceding phonemes—is said to be "perceived. Thus, the subsequent phoneme—having produced a self-cognition through the cooperation of the preceding cognition—is of what nature at the time of hearing? [It is] one whose hearing is not clear...

When a phoneme is articulated very slowly and gradually, then there is an auditory cognition (*śruti*)—that is, an auditory perception—of that sound which is "imperfect" (*apaṭu*); it is slow-moving and perceives the phonemes as distinct. This means that it is in this state that the distinct phonemes are discerned. However, when it is being articulated too rapidly...

This is for the purpose of demonstrating how a sequential recollection arises from the non-discrimination of distinct phonemes; [the text mentions] "imperfect auditory apprehension. He asks: "How does such a phoneme act?
[The answer is: "Depending upon that recollection—namely, the recollection of the preceding phonemes—it subsequently deposits [the effect]; that is, it generates recollection."
"In itself" means in its own object; it should be understood as being "successively.

By this, it is stated that phonemes (*varṇa*) are the causes, in a sequential manner, for the cognitions of their own objects. This causal relationship occurs according to the sequence just described. "In the phonemes" means having the phonemes as their substratum—that is, belonging to the phonemes.
The same applies to human [utterances]. In common worldly usage, it is said that "the sequence is indeed produced by a person.
With reference to what, then, do the phonemes possess the status of being effects and causes? To this he says: "of the cognitions apprehending their causes.

This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "causes" (*hetavaḥ*) and "apprehenders" (*grāhīṇi*). Then, there is a genitive *ṣaṣṭhī* compound: "apprehending the causes of those phonemes" (*teṣāṃ varṇānāṃ hetugrāhīṇi*).

Subsequently, there is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) with the word *cetas*. If the minds are the causes of the phonemes in their respective order, then by virtue of their connection, the phonemes possess sequential causality; for the phonemes are produced by those minds. Furthermore, regarding those minds which grasp those phonemes, by virtue of their connection, the phonemes possess sequential causality [of the minds]; for the minds [are produced] by those phonemes.

Because [these] are produced by minds that grasp [objects], he explains by means of the words "citta" and so forth. That vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) for which the mind is the originating cause is described as such. Speech itself is the intimation because it makes others understand; and it says that this is of three kinds in the world. [It consists of] phonemes (*varṇa*).
The analysis of the compound is as follows: that whose designations are "letters" (*varṇa*), "word" (*pada*), and "sentence" (*vākya*). Among these, "letters" are the phonemes (*akṣara*).

A collection of letters delimited by meaning is a "word. A collection of words is a "sentence. Regarding the phrase "therein," etc., [it refers to] the word *sara*. (1) In the margin. (2) Refutation of the view of Kumārila.

By means of the mind as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), the consciousness that gives rise to the letter *a* is produced; likewise, there are successive conditions for the production of the letters *ra*, *visarga*, and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the syllable, there is the phoneme *sa*, followed by the letter *a*, then the letter *ra*, then the letter *a*, and what follows that.

Regarding the term *visarjanīya*: therein, the cause for the arising of the letter *s* is that mind; by means of that mind acting as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). The inclusion of the term "immediately preceding" is for the purpose of excluding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). [This refers to] the mind that gives rise to the letter *a*; that is, the mind by which the letter *a* is raised up or produced. That [mind] is thus produced. In the manner already stated, [the same applies to] the letter *r*. 200b... [repha-akāra...]

The *visarjanīya* is produced by those mental states which are preceded by prior conditions. The analysis of the compound is: "those for which each preceding mental state is the condition (*pratyaya*)—that is, the cause. In that process, the letter *repha* arises from the mental state that produces the letter *a*; the letter *a* [arises] from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which is the mental state that produces the *repha*; and the *visarjanīya* [arises] from the mental state that produces the letter *a*.

Regarding the phrase "it is produced": surely, a word is uttered with the intention, "I shall utter this word. Therefore, the sequence of phonemes is uttered by means of that single intention alone; it is not the case that each individual phoneme is preceded by a separate intention, because such is not perceived. How then...

It is liberated [from that]. Since the mind that originates the letter *a* and so forth is produced by the mind that originated the letter *sa* and so forth, it is considered as follows: first, this very sequence applies to the utterance of phonemes (*varṇa*); likewise, this same sequence applies to the utterance of words (*pada*). For instance, one utters the letter *sa* with the intention of uttering *sa*, and so on for each subsequent [phoneme].

One utters each successive phoneme with the intention of expressing that particular phoneme. However, some maintain that in the utterance of a word through practice, the sole cause is the intention to express the word itself. Others, however, hold a different view: that in the utterance of a word, there is only a single intention [to express the word] as the cause.

This is true; however, at the time of the utterance of the syllable *sa*, the mind must necessarily exist, otherwise the consequence of death would follow. That very mind is said to be the arouser (*samutthāpaka*) of the syllable *sa*, because the syllable *sa* arises immediately thereafter. In this same manner, the quality of being the arouser of the mind should be understood for each subsequent phoneme. And in this regard, [the text says] "the arouser of the syllable *sa*..."

By the passage beginning with "by the mental consciousness as the immediately preceding condition," it is stated that the sequence of phonemes has a single author as its cause for the cognition of meaning, and not a plurality of authors. Therefore, as Maṇḍana says: "If the sequence [of phonemes] is the causal relation between effect and cause, then it belongs to the cognitions that apprehend it."

The argument that "therefore, even in the case of a speaker, there would be a cognition of the individual self (*ātmabheda*) as its cause" (Sphoṭasiddhi 31) is refuted; for it is not admitted that the existence of cognitions apprehending phonemes produced by different agents is the cause of the comprehension of meaning.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by Maṇḍana: "Even if the comprehension of meaning occurs through the sequence of phonemes [arising] from the sequence of the motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*), nevertheless, that sequence, being a signifier (*jñāpaka*), depends upon cognition. Moreover, the knowledge of meaning is observed to arise from words uttered by a speaker who is concealed or obstructed; and in such cases, no one perceives a causal relationship with the motivating mind."

It ought to be determined: for if the eye were unitary, it would be determined even without the cognition of sound. Nor is that [eye] concealed; these phonemes (varṇas), being causes of one another and born from their own causal sequence, at the time of hearing—even when they proceed slowly—require the auxiliary cognition of the preceding phoneme for their own cognition.

When they produce [cognitions], they then dissolve into such memory precisely by depending upon a prior recollection. [The opponent claims: "There is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the oneness of the speaker, even when [the cognitions] are separated by distinct causal conditions and intervening factors.
This is incorrect; because even in a state where [the speaker] is concealed or obstructed, the oneness of the speaker is indeed ascertained by some.

For instance, in the world, activity is seen to be preceded by such a cognition as, "Devadatta calls me, not Yajñadatta. Where there is no such ascertainment, there is no activity; thus, our desired conclusion is indeed established. Furthermore, for the proponent of *sphoṭa* as well, how could there be the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* in states where it is obscured and so forth, given that it is manifested [by sounds]?

"Because it cannot be determined that the various phonemes (*varṇa*) have a single creator, and because the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* must necessarily be accepted there—otherwise, the comprehension of meaning would not occur—this has been determined by some. This is trivial. "Therefore (*tat*)," [it is said,] "these phonemes have distinct causes; that is, each one is produced by a different motivating mind (*citta*)."
"Those whose birth is in sequence" means those phonemes that occur sequentially according to the order of their causes. By this much, the following [verse] has been explained:
"(1) That sound which is known from the cognition arising from the cognition of the production of a particular phoneme..."
Explaining the phrase "[it is determined by hearing]," he says "śruti" and so forth.

"Even at the time of hearing" means even at the time of listening; "when they proceed slowly" means when they are pronounced not too rapidly. Those phonemes which depend upon that very cognition having the preceding phoneme as its object—which serves as a cooperative condition—are described in that way.
Being thus constituted, what do they do? (1) They produce their own cognition, which has itself as its object, namely, auditory consciousness.

For instance, at the very same time that auditory consciousness has the letter *sa* as its object, the letter *a* is likewise produced by a mind that originates the letter *a*; therefore, the letter *a* and the cognition having the letter *sa* as its object exist simultaneously. Thus, the letter *a*—
By means of the knowledge having *sa* as its object acting as a cooperative cause, it produces a cognition of its own object; this same principle should be applied to the other phonemes as well.
"Then" (*tadā*) refers to when they have produced the experiential cognition of their own objects; at that time, there arises a recollection of the previous phoneme's object.
They dissolve into memory—that is, they ascend into memory—precisely by depending upon that [preceding cognition].

The meaning is that they are remembered in the very same sequence in which they were experienced. This is connected to the statement: "this is the nature of phonemes, characterized by their non-simultaneity.
To the question "Of what kind is it?", he says: "distinct," and so forth. Because they are produced by preceding preceding cognitions, their state as effects is distinct.

Because they serve as the causes for each subsequent cognition, those cognitions that give rise to the [articulations] beginning with *sa* possess a distinct causal relationship; these very [cognitions] are the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the causes (*hetu*). From them arises that which has the nature of being produced and the nature of producing distinct [effects]; for that is the intrinsic nature of the phonemes (*varṇa*), differentiated by the distinctions in human articulation (*puruṣasaṃskāra*), and it is sequential.

Thus it is said: "The form of those phonemes, whether in words or non-words, is indeed something else; accompanied by the agent's mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), it produces a difference in the effect. (308)

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *dharmma* is that which has *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) as its *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic), and that [nature] is precisely its *utpatti* (origination). By this, it is stated that letters possess the status of being effects (*kāryatva*) in relation to the cognitions that cause them;

conversely, it states they possess the status of being causes (*kāraṇatva*) in relation to the cognitions that apprehend them. This refers to the production of a distinct effect, namely, consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that very dharma which has production (*janana*) as its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the phonemes. Such an intrinsic nature of the phonemes, differentiated by the distinctions in human articulation—that is, differentiated by the distinctions in human effort—is called "sequence" (*krama*). Now, an objection may be raised: sequence is a property (*dharma*) of the phonemes; how then can that which is such an intrinsic nature of the phonemes be called "sequence"?

He thinks as follows: (1) There is no sequence for those things that arise simultaneously, because such a sequence is not perceived. Therefore, the sequence belongs only to phonemes (*varṇa*) that arise sequentially. If it were maintained that phonemes arise non-simultaneously, then that very [sequence] would be the sequence in the world, and it would not be something distinct from the phonemes themselves, because it is not perceived as such. Nor is their sequence a single property (*dharma*), because they do not exist together.
