Nor is each individual phoneme the sequence, because a sequence is not perceived [in isolation]. Therefore, it has been stated that it is only phonemes produced non-simultaneously that are called a "sequence. This conventional usage of "their sequence" is merely conceptual.

Furthermore, the very sequence that is perceived in the world in the word *sara* is not the same as that in the word *rasa*; nor is there any sequence distinct from the preceding and succeeding phonemes.

[This is] the intrinsic nature [of phonemes]. Therefore, the intrinsic nature of phonemes in each word is indeed different. And the world certainly perceives the difference between the word *sara* and the word *rasa*;
thus, that which was stated by Maṇḍana—
“Let the proponents of the production [of sounds] maintain that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are distinct;
however, their specific difference is not the cause for the cognition of meaning. (Sphoṭasiddhi 30).
This is because that [difference] is not determined at the time of the convention (*saṃketa*), and because it has not been perceived then. (1)
That is rejected; for it is precisely the difference in the sequence of phonemes that is perceived when the sequence "sara" is distinguished from the sequence "rasa.

Nor do phonemes appear apart from their sequence. Therefore, the determination of a difference in sequence is itself the determination of a difference in phonemes. It is only that, due to similarity, the difference between one word "rasa" and another word "rasa" is not perceived.

Therefore, because it was perceived at the time of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), it is logical that [the word] conveys the meaning of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); the same applies to any other word—thus, this [objection] is trivial.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "It is something else," and so forth. For the nature of the phonemes (*varṇa*) is as previously described: their sequence...

It is said for that reason: "that" refers to the form which, although determined as one due to its similarity, is yet a different word for every word (*pratipadam*). What is the reason? Because it is distinct from the mental impression of the agent (*kartṛ-saṃskāra*).
Since the mind that originates [the speech] is the agent, it is distinct due to the difference in its capacities. "Combined" means according to the preceding and succeeding sequence.

Therefore, it is certainly not the case that there is only a single nature for the phonemes within words, because they differ according to the distinctions in the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the agent and the mind.
That [nature], when accompanied by one another, is the cause of the diversity of effects.

And that sequence of phonemes occurs as a product of composition, because there would be a contradiction in the established order of those [phonemes] whose realization is not obstructed by desire. (309)

It has been stated that the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) of phonemes is a specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) produced through the causal conditions of action and cause. And since that [order] is produced by the human conceptualizations and deliberations (*vitarka-vicāra*), the sequence is not fixed. Because it possesses a proven status that is not contradicted by desire, it is uttered through action; thus, it produces a distinction in the effect, namely, it effects a distinction in cognition (*buddhi*).
Furthermore, it was already established previously that "phonemes are devoid of meaning" (1.241); how then can it be said that the nature of the phonemes, when combined, produces a specific effect?
On this point, some hold the view: the nature of the phonemes in each word is distinct and is the human-made signifier; it is not [the case that they are] non-human.
As for what was said, "I would be angry," [the response is]: "True; it exists, but it resides in the person.

That is incorrect, because phonemes—whether combined or uncombined—are incapable of conveying meaning. Therefore, the intended meaning is this: if the sequence of phonemes were to exist in an ultimate sense, then that [sequence], by way of being a single word and so forth, [would convey meaning].

It would be the signifier of an imagined object. And because the sequential phonemes, having been made objects by a single conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), are the signifiers—precisely because they appear within a single conceptual construction—it is said that the combined form of the sequential phonemes produces the specific effect; thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, since the difference [arises] from the difference in their originators, therefore it is not...

The nature (*svabhāva*) of phonemes (*varṇa*) is indeed one and the same in words such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*. What is the reason? Because there is a distinction [in their nature] due to the difference in the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the producing mind. The producer is that [mind] which knows [the phoneme]; the difference in its mental impression consists in a difference in capacity (*śakti*) due to the difference in the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). Therefore, because of this difference in the nature of the phonemes, that [nature] is distinct for each individual word.

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of a sequence because it is mounted upon a single conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Accompanied by one another, it is the cause of the differentiation of effects—that is, the differentiation of cognitions regarding objects.
And this causal sequence, which is characterized as a specific order (*lakṣaṇānupūrvī*), is the very sequence of phonemes that has arisen and proceeded.

"From the person who is the creator of the arrangement" (*racanākṛtaḥ*); that is, from him who "makes the arrangement" (*racanāṃ karoti*). To the question "From what [does it arise]?", he says: "By the will," and so forth. This is because there is a contradiction with the established sequence of those phonemes whose establishment is not obstructed by the will of a person.

He explains this with the words "the effect," and so forth; the analysis of the compound is: "those which are both causes and effects, and which are also cognitions" (*kāryakāraṇabhūtāś ca te pratyayāś ca iti vigrahaḥ*).

The minds that give rise to the articulated sounds (*varṇa*) are described in this way. For these [minds], in relation to the preceding consciousness, are effects, while in relation to the subsequent consciousness, they are causes. The specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṇa*) produced from them is called "succession" (*ānupūrvī*).
And since that succession is produced by the initial and sustained mental applications (*vitarka-vicāra*) of a person, the articulated sounds do not possess a fixed order.

*Vitarka* is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the form of deliberation, such as "Is this it, or is that it? *Vicāra* is a conceptual construction in the form of ascertainment, such as "This alone is it. Why is the sequence not fixed? [The answer begins with] "By desire," and so forth. A sequence whose accomplishment is not contradicted by desire is one of "accomplishment uncontradicted by desire" (*icchā-aviruddha-siddhi*). Those sequences for which there is accomplishment uncontradicted by desire are described as such. (2) Refutation of Kumārila’s View.
It is like a sequence of specific distinctions.

For indeed, it is not possible to arrange the sequence of space and time, or the order of the Himalaya, Vindhya, and Malaya mountains, or that of seeds, sprouts, and so forth, according to one's own will. Therefore, [this applies] to the sequence of the various conceptualizations enumerated as the attributes of the person (*puruṣa*).

Because [the effect] exists when [the cause] exists and does not exist when it is absent, the relationship of cause and effect is established for men and the sequence of phonemes; thus, every sequence of phonemes arises from men, just like the relationship between fire and fuel. (310)

If it exists, it burns in its function of combustion; yet, because of its non-existence [in the absence of fuel], it does not burn. For even that which has visible fuel is not without fuel, since a restriction of place and time would otherwise be impossible. When such a restriction exists, that very thing constitutes the fuel; therefore, fuel is the material cause (*upādāna*) of burning, and its existence depends upon it. To illustrate: (1) just as the sequence of letters is established according to one's will—what is it like? It is like the arrangement of the phonemes *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*.

(1) Like the sequence of specific actions. Just as there is a sequence for specific actions such as contraction and so forth because their occurrence is determined by volition, it is the same in this case.
With the words "for not... and so on, he states the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Regarding the phrase "of place and time," it refers to that which is situated in space.

The connection is that it is not possible to perform such an arrangement. For indeed, by human will, it cannot be made that "let the Vindhya mountain be in the place of the Himalaya, or let the Malaya mountain be in the place of the Vindhya," nor can it be made that "first let there be a sprout, and afterwards let that which produces it [the sprout] arise from the seed."
It is impossible to reverse the [order of the phonemes]. However, the phonemes (*varṇa*) can indeed be reversed at will. Therefore, the phonemes do not possess a fixed order.
Consequently, when there is a sequence of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that stands in the relation of cause and effect, the phonemes—[Vākya-kārikā 2]—...

Because sequence exists, and because there is no sequence of conceptual construction, there is an absence of a sequence of phonemes [independent of an agent]. In worldly sentences, the causal relationship between the person and the sequence of phonemes is established: the person is the cause, and the sequence of phonemes is the effect. Therefore, from the establishment of this causal relationship, all other Vedic phonemes as well [are likewise produced by an agent].
3. Thus, just as it is logical that every burning is preceded by fuel, so it is here.

He explains this with the words beginning "when existing" (*satī*). When burning is occurring while fuel exists, "burning" (*dāha*) is stated to be the very act of burning—that which burns—because burning cannot exist when fuel is absent. This is so provided that, in some cases, the relationship of cause and effect between burning and fuel is established.
Even for that fire whose fuel is not perceived, since its fuel is unobserved, it would follow that—
because a spatial restriction and a temporal restriction would be impossible for such a causeless fire— it would exist everywhere and at all times. Or else, if it were indeed restricted...
[Lines are missing.

Furthermore, because it possesses characteristics [of being produced], just as in the case of Mārupe; likewise, if this sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) were not dependent upon human effort (*puruṣaprayatna*), then it would be without a basis (*nirālamba*).

It would manifest by itself; even with effort, it could not be manifested, because that [effort] would be excluded from it. If it were possible in some cases, then everything would be so, since there is no distinction. And if that which exists only when the other exists—which is indistinguishable [from it]—were not produced by it, then the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) would be rejected everywhere, for its definition consists in positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). Its definition...

Nor should any distinction be asserted [between them], for it would follow that all things, such as jars and the like, whether artificial or non-artificial, are [identical], since such a conceptualization is possible even in those cases and because there is no difference [between them]. Therefore, these too must be preceded by the observation of others.

It is accepted that [fire] occurs in certain places and so forth. If it is maintained that there is a restriction regarding place and so forth for fire, then that very place and so forth would constitute its fuel.
Why? Because of the passage beginning with "of fire," etc. For if fire were independent of its material cause (*upādāna*), a restriction of place and time would be impossible.

Likewise, if this sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) were not to depend upon human effort as its cause, then—being without support, without basis, and independent of human effort—it would manifest by itself. Even when a person exerts effort with the thought, "I am uttering the sequence of phonemes," it would not be possible for that sequence of phonemes to be manifested. Why? Because of that... [text fragment]

If, on the other hand, the sequence were produced by a person, then if some capacity [for efficacy] were admitted in that sequence, the entire Vedic sequence of syllables would likewise be of human origin.

Why? Because there is no difference between the sequence of syllables in common worldly usage and that in the Vedas. [This is so even regarding] the characteristics such as the removal of poison and so forth.
Because such a specific quality is observed even among worldly people;
furthermore, since a person who possesses that state [removes poison, etc.
by means of worldly phonetic sequences and so forth—

And regarding the specific Vedic sequence of letters (*varṇakrama*), which is produced by something other than that [human agency]—that is, produced with excellence (*prakarṣeṇa kṛtau*)—the phrase "in all cases" implies that even where human authorship is accepted, the relationship of cause and effect would likewise be refuted. Why? Because of the rule beginning with "in the presence of" (*anvaye*). "Presence when that exists" (*tadbhāve bhāvaḥ*) is positive concomitance (*anvaya*); "absence when that is absent" (*tadabhāve 'bhāvaḥ*) is negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Since [causality] is defined by these two...
If it is not accepted that "of that" [the Veda] there is the state of being an effect,
then another definition of the causal relation— distinct from the principle of "arising when that exists"— must be stated, by the absence of which the [causal status] of the Vedas for a person...
There would be no causal relationship with effort. Nor is there any other definition of causal relationship.

Now, if the definition of causal relationship were the same [in both cases], it would follow that the conventional sequence of phonemes is artificial, whereas [the sequence] of the Vedas is not; such consequences would ensue. What is the reason?

In that case as well, since such a conceptualization is possible regarding jars and other objects—just as there is a conceptualization regarding the sequence of Vedic words—just as it is conceptualized that "that very Vedic sequence is manifested by human activity," so too are jars and the like. [Objection: Someone else creates them; [Reply: In that case, some have unknown creators, or perhaps all [objects] are [created] by the processes of certain [beings].

Let it be so established. Therefore, because the sequence of phonemes and the relationship of cause and effect are well-known, and because they do not transcend the nature of real entities, all [such sequences] are created by persons;
for that very reason.
And the uniqueness of men who act in succession is established by their knowledge and power, because these are absent in others. (311)
If one were to think that this specific sequence of phonemes is capable of destroying poison and so forth, while no other is, then it would be understood as such;

for there is no difference [in the case of the sequence] because it is likewise [dependent on human effort]. If it is argued that there is indeed a distinction between this [sequence] and things like a jar due to its conformity with human activity, [the author] says:
“Those,” and so forth. Even those [objects] such as pots—the construction of pots and the like by others, namely previous potters and so on—was previously observed.
The meaning is: “having indeed seen them. A subsequent person, such as a potter, also produces them;
not without instruction. And for those whose understanding is preceded by the instruction of another, if their [Vedas] were of non-human origin...

[The opponent says: "The sequence beginning with the Vedas is accepted as being non-human (apauruṣeya) because its author is not remembered. If that is so, then even jars and the like are sometimes of unknown authorship.
Jars and such things are seen in places shrouded by vast periods of time, yet their author is not remembered. Therefore, since [the case of the Vedas] is equal to that of human beings—"
If the Vedic sequence were non-human (apauruṣeya) in its conformity with activity, then there would be no creation of all things such as jars and the like;
or rather,
just as there is no creation of the Vedic sequence due to the non-recollection of an author, so too there would be no recollection at any time of certain things such as jars.

Let there be for the agents an adherence to non-action. But this is not the case; therefore, the connection is that neither this worldly nor the Vedic sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*) is created by a person. Why? He says: "Because it is well-known," and so forth.
Well-knownness is the relationship of cause and effect...

This is a possessive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). Their property (*dharma*) is the conformity to the presence and absence of their own causes; this is because they do not transcend that [conformity]. Precisely because these mantras are of human origin, they possess a distinctiveness that is not shared with ordinary persons.

Accomplished! For whom? (1) For those men who perform the sequence known as mantra—those who carry out the sequence of phonemes designated as "mantra"—for them, by what [means] is there the thorough knowledge of this [reality], which brings about the fulfillment of desired aims? 203a.

"Power" (*śakti*) means influence (*prabhāva*). Why? Because it is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) compared to others; thus he says: "Because of the absence of those two—knowledge and influence—in other ordinary persons (*prākṛta-puruṣa*) and so forth.
He explains this with the words beginning with "this": "This sequence of syllables is capable of destroying poison and so forth, but no other."

If any other ordinary person (*prākṛtapuruṣa*) were to know [this] through such a distinction, then he too would understand that sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) in that very same way by means of that distinction. But this is not the case. Therefore, although this sequence produces its effect by its own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), it is only someone who knows it who becomes a person who perceives an imperceptible object (*parokṣārthadarśin*). For it is not the case that this [sequence] is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); indeed, it is not possible [to say so].
Because a specific characteristic that is unconfounded [with the opposite] is not established;

because, through perception alone, one cannot distinguish between what is a mantra and what is not a mantra when they have not been pointed out; and even if they were pointed out, because their distinction by way of intrinsic nature is not perceived in any other respect, except through the correspondence with their effects—and because that effect [is not yet present] prior [to the application].

Because it is impossible to perceive [it directly], this sequence does not function as a causal agent by its own nature, since the purification of one occurs only after a long time for another; thus, one would neither practice what is to be established, nor would one establish it in such a way. Therefore, this is called "mantra."

Even if the Mīmāṃsakas admit that the sequence of phonemes produces an effect by virtue of its own nature, nevertheless, since only a certain person endowed with a transcendental distinction of power has cognized it, there exists a person who perceives supersensible objects— one who knows the mantra, its efficacy, and its performance.

Although it has been stated that a "mantra" is speech that accomplishes a desired object for those possessing the power of truth and austerity, nevertheless, this is said even while granting [the opponent's position]: a mantra is a producer of effects by its very nature.
By means of either the production of an effect through a mantra or the knowledge of the potency for the fruit of a mantra, an excellence of the person is established; this is known through inference.

Regarding the claim that there can be no one who perceives the imperceptible because of the lack of knowledge concerning what is a mantra and what is not a mantra, he says: "Not indeed," and so forth. The meaning is this:
(1) while a particular sequence of phonemes is capable of removing poison and the like, this [other] sequence of phonemes is not so capable.
Thus, it is not possible to ascertain [the efficacy] through a logical mark (*liṅga*). Why? Because [the distinction between] mantra and non-mantra is not mixed up.
Because the specific characteristic [of the mantra] is unestablished.

Now, one might argue that since both mantras and non-mantras consist of the nature of phonemes (*varṇa*), their capacity to bestow results is also grasped through perception, because it is not distinct from them. (1)

Therefore, he says: "Of two [things] perceived directly," and so forth. "Of two that have not been taught" means of those that have not been described as "this is a mantra" or "this is not a mantra," because they are not recognized as such. This is due to the lack of certainty regarding whether "this one is capable of removing poison and the like, while this one is incapable.
"Even when there is instruction" means even if it should happen that someone instructs: "This is indeed a mantra; it is thus..."

Regarding the phrase "one who performs the task": even so, because there is no perception—and thus no certainty—of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the mantra through any means whatsoever, the instruction lacks authority. Only through the correspondence with the result elsewhere would there be the certainty that "this is the mantra," by virtue of attaining the effect to be accomplished by that mantra. And regarding that mantra which is to be accomplished...

"Prior to the performance of the rite" means prior to the execution of the mantra, because [the mantra] cannot be perceived at that time; the sense is that it exists then. Furthermore, the performance of a mantra that has not been ascertained is impossible. Therefore, the Mīmāṃsaka must necessarily accept a person who perceives supersensuous objects (atīndriyārthadarśī), who distinguishes between what is a mantra and what is not a mantra.

(1) Otherwise, the practice of mantras would not be possible. Furthermore, this sequence of phonemes called a "mantra" does not, by its own nature, effect the removal of poison and so forth; rather—(2) [this is] the refutation of Kumārila’s position.

Furthermore, because others require the practice of vows and so forth; because we observe that from even a single action, both benefit and harm may arise for different individuals; and because even efficacious mantras sometimes fail to produce their results—this kind of variation is not logically consistent with an inherent nature (*svabhāva*), since an inherent nature is uniform everywhere. A person, however, acts according to his own will, [varying] by virtue of factors such as his similarity in character (*sattvasabhāgatā*).
Or it is logical that [the Lord] favors one person over another due to the excellence of their service.

If success or failure were established by nature for those whose essence consists of merit and demerit, following the accumulation of merit and demerit through the violation of vows and so forth, then [the Lord's role would be redundant].
Nature—
It is due to the convention of persons (*puruṣasamaya*). What is the reason? Because for one person who performs a mantra, there is success with that mantra quickly;

whereas for another who performs the same mantra-rite, success occurs only after a long time. For if the mantra were to grant its fruit by itself, this distinction in time would not be logical, since no excellence or lack of excellence could be produced in the mantra by anyone. [This applies] to another person [relying] on the mantra.

Because the accomplishment of the fruit depends upon the practice of vows and so forth, the mantra is not an agent by its own nature. "Vow" (vrata) refers to the restriction prescribed in the ritual manual of the mantra; its "practice" (caryā) is its performance.
By the word "also" (api), the inclusion of fire-offerings (homa) and other rites is intended. For, by its own nature... [203b]

Regarding the granting of results: what is the need for the performance of vows, practices, and so forth, since no excellence arises from them? Likewise, even when two persons perform the same ritual procedure based on a single mantra—such as recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and so on—one may observe success while the other observes failure; therefore, the result does not arise from the inherent nature [of the action].

In that case, the causal efficiency (*arthayoga*) would be equal in the granting of the result. Even for those [mantras] that "carry" [the result], meaning even for those mantras that perform the removal of poison and so forth, there is again, at another time, a failure to produce some effect when they are employed by that same person, due to their non-performance. For this kind of behavior is not consistent with the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing. Why? Because of the intrinsic nature...

Because it is equal in all cases, such as with respect to persons and so forth. For that which is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of something does not become its nature by depending on anything else. However, when the fruit is held to result from a convention (*samaya*) established by a person, then this fault does not apply. For instance: (1) a person is the creator of the mantra-convention; acting according to his own will, he bestows favor upon a certain person.

"It is logical that there is no other [birth]"—for what reason? Because of a specific similarity (*sabhāgatā*) among sentient beings. There is a similarity between the practitioner of the mantra and the originator of the mantra, by virtue of identical conduct, behavior, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of ritual offerings and the like is intended. This is due to the influence of that [similarity], or due to attachment to it, or due to a specific type of service through recitation (*japa*), fire-oblations (*homa*), and so on.

Or rather, it is because of the specific service consisting of the propitiation of a deity that [the Lord] bestows grace upon a certain person, and not upon another being who lacks the commonality of nature (*sattvasabhāgatā*) and so forth. With the words "vratena" and so on, he anticipates the following objection: the practice of a restriction is *vratacaryā* (the performance of a vow); and *vratacaryā* is a vow—

The term *virūpaikaśeṣa* (an irregular collective compound) refers to "the failure of conduct" (*caryābhraṅśa*) and so forth. The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is connected with each [term]. The meaning is: by means of the practice of vows (*vratacaryā*) and so forth, and by means of the failure of the practice of vows (*vratacaryābhraṅśa*) and so forth. The connection is that when there is an accumulation of merit (*dharmopacaya*) through the practice of vows and so forth, there is accomplishment (*siddhi*). Likewise, there is accomplishment for a person who is by nature (*prakṛtyā*) virtuous by their very essence (*svabhāvena*). [The compound] ends with "failure of the practice of vows."

However, when there is an accumulation of demerit (*adharma*) through [the recitation of] the *śādi* [mantra], or because the person is by nature of a demeritorious self, the non-attainment of success (*asiddhi*) occurs; this is how the meaning of the sentence should be construed. The opponent thinks that even if the fruit is produced from the mantra by its very nature, the distinction between success and non-success will occur in the manner already described.

No; for even those things contrary to the Dharma—such as cruelty, theft, sexual union with two organs, and an abundance of base actions—are seen in the *Ḍākinī* and *Bhaginī* Tantras and so forth. This is because through these too, there is a specific accomplishment of mantra (*mantrasiddhi*). And such [a path] is not non-Dharma.
We shall explain what is meant by "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) at the appropriate time.
Why is it that for those who possess mantras, purity, and dharma, there is the non-attainment of some [result] precisely because of those very factors, while attainment occurs through their opposite?
Furthermore, it is not logical for both dharma and adharma—which are mutually contradictory—to arise from a single form of action. How then, regarding adharma...

He refutes [the opponent's view] with the words "no," and so forth: the accomplishment of the fruit does not arise from a mantra that depends upon *dharma*. What is the reason? Because in the *Ḍākinītantra*, the *Caturbhaginītantra*, and others—indicated by the word "and so forth"—vows (*vrata*) that are causes for the accomplishment of mantras are seen even though they are contrary to *dharma*, such as those involving theft, the *kambu* [conch], and so on.

Because they are seen in the *Kinnī-tantra* and other such works. But what are those things that are contrary to the Dharma? He says: "Cruelty," and so forth. Cruelty (*kraurya*) is the killing of living beings. Theft (*steya*) is robbery. Sexual intercourse (*maithuna*) is the union of the two organs. Base actions (*hīnakarma*) include [acts] such as [the killing of] cats and the offering of impure smoke; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), other things contrary to the Dharma are also included. Those [actions], beginning with cruelty—

Those vows which are numerous and abundant are referred to as "many. And by means of those aforementioned vows, there is a specific accomplishment (*siddhi*) of mantra. For instance, in the *Ḍākinī-tantra*, the rule of commitment (*samaya-vyavasthā*) is as follows: when one kills and eats a living being, then one attains the accomplishment of mantra. Likewise, in the *Kambukinī-tantra*, there is the practice of theft (*steya*).
If it is argued that in some other [time] there might be a convention [that] cruelty and the like would indeed be dharma, he says:
"And not," and so forth. This means that such a nature of dharma, characterized by cruelty and the like, is as follows—
"We shall inform you of the day later. Thus far, it has been shown that success is attained even through unrighteousness (*adharma*).

It is now stated that success is not seen even through righteousness (*dharma*): "Loving-kindness" (*maitrī*), and so forth. Loving-kindness is the contemplation of the welfare and happiness of sentient beings. Purity (*śauca*) is twofold: external and internal. External purity consists of bathing and the like; internal purity consists of [abstaining from] theft and the like.

Cessation [is the goal]. Dharma is the favoring of others through giving and other such means. Those for whom friendliness, purity, and dharma are the supreme gifts are described as such. For persons who are of that nature, taking precisely that—friendliness and the rest—as the cause, there is the non-attainment of a certain perfection; that is, the non-attainment of that perfection which would otherwise be obtainable through the reversal of friendliness. And by way of reversal...

Furthermore, because [the result] is accomplished through hatred and so forth, the accomplishment of the fruit does not arise from a mantra that depends upon the accumulation of merit (*dharma*). Even cruelty and the like, when originated by hatred and so forth, become merit (*dharma*) itself when performed according to the injunctions of the mantra;
therefore, he says "And not," etc. For, from an action characterized by a single form, such as killing and so forth—

That dharma which is opposed to that [unwholesome state] is necessarily opposed to the non-dharma; and as for non-dharma, it is not appropriate [to claim it arises] from anything other than the injunction of mantras, because non-dharma arises precisely from acts such as violence. For dharma does not arise from a cause of non-dharma, due to their contradiction. To explain: by the very same intention of hatred and so forth with which one performs acts such as violence outside of the injunction of mantras, non-dharma occurs. By that same [intention]—

(2) Refutation of Kumārila’s View: One obtains the desired fruit of dharma through one's own vows and so forth; yet this desired fruit of those vows and so forth is not their maturation (*vipāka*), but rather that of previously committed acts such as the killing of a Brahmin performed during the execution of the ritual injunctions. Even though violence and the like are practiced in the performance of the ritual procedures for the *vāśīya* [mantra], how can it be considered a constituent part (*aṅga*) of dharma? [The opponent argues: "One obtains the desired fruit of dharma through one's own vows and so forth; yet this desired fruit of those vows and so forth is not their maturation, but rather that of previously committed acts such as the killing of a Brahmin performed during the execution [of the ritual]."
It is like the support of a village for a tree. However, the future fruit of that vow, whose nature is faith and dharma, is not desired [as the direct result].
Rather, that application of mantras and so forth is a ripener of that action which has a desired fruit, because it provides assistance in some manner;
for the power of assistance is manifold.
Dharma is a phenomenon whose maturation depends upon a specific person as its locus; thus, what is performed by such a person bears fruit through that very propitiation.

If it is argued that because it is produced by hatred and the like, cruelty and so forth—even when carried out according to the ritual injunctions of mantras—are indeed *adharma*, then how can there be [merit] from vows and the like which are themselves of the nature of *adharma*? This refers to the previously mentioned [point]: from a vow characterized by cruelty and so forth. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), [other qualities are included].

How can a practitioner of recitation (jāpī) enjoy—that is, partake in—the fruit of Dharma, characterized by desirable enjoyment and so forth, arising from an inferior and impure practice such as the offering of incense?

[The answer is] "No," and so forth, according to the established tenet (siddhānta). Furthermore, that desired fruit does not arise from a vow (vrata) or the like whose nature is unrighteousness (adharma).

Maturation (*pāka*) is the fruit of karma. However, regarding the maturation of previously performed wholesome karma, he asks: "In what way? He replies: It is like the command for the killing of a Brahmin, which results from its execution or accomplishment, just as in the case of obtaining a village.
For example, someone might employ another person, saying: "Kill this Brahmin; I will give you a village."

By carrying out that instruction, he obtains the village; yet this is not the fruit of the murder of a Brahmin. Rather, it is his own previous auspicious karma that bears fruit in such a way, having encountered as a cooperative cause the person who was propitiated by the performance of that Brahmin-murder.

He then states what the fruit of that unrighteous vow (*adharmātman* vrata) is: "But for that vow characterized by cruelty and so forth—which is unrighteous in nature—the future fruit, pertaining to a subsequent birth, is undesirable, such as hell and the like. [Objection:
If the fruit of virtuous action (*śubha-karma*) is desirable, why is there a need for this unrighteous application of mantras and so forth?
If it is argued that [the result] comes from that, he says:

"But he is one whose nature is unrighteousness (*adharma*)," [referring to] the employment of *ḍākinī*-mantras and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the employment of vows such as cruelty and the like.
"[Of] that action which has a desired fruit": the analysis of the compound is "that action for which a desired fruit exists."
In some way, by some manner, through assistance, the ripener is the giver of the fruit.

But how can the unwholesome be an assistant to the wholesome? To this he says: "Because the power of assistance is manifold. For the state of being a cooperative cause is indeed manifold; sometimes [the unwholesome serves as such].

An unwholesome [action] has a wholesome [action] as its auxiliary cause; likewise, a wholesome [action] has an unwholesome one. For example, for one who performs extremely noble wholesome deeds, an unwholesome karma that would otherwise result in the suffering of the hells and so forth does not bear fruit; having encountered a wholesome auxiliary cause, it is exhausted in this very life by yielding nothing more than the suffering of illness and the like. This applies even to the employment of spells and such, which are of an unrighteous nature, regarding a karma that somehow yields a desired result.

It has been stated that [the mantra] is an auxiliary (*upakāraka*). Demonstrating in what manner and by whom the assistance is rendered, he says: "A particular person is the author of the mantra; because he has performed the ritual action whose nature is to produce the result through the application of that mantra, [the mantra is an auxiliary]."

If it is argued that the result arises from the benefit of that very [object] even without a special person (*puruṣaviśeṣa*), this is not so. For it would follow that the person’s specific form, nature, conduct, and resolve (*adhimokṣa*) are useless. If that too were to provide benefit, then a special person with extraordinary qualities (*asādhāraṇaguṇa*) is established; for it is precisely through resolve toward him that [the efficacy of] rites such as those involving poison and so forth occurs.

Because of this [dependence], even those mantras composed by humans do not yield results by their own inherent nature independently of their application. (c) Regarding the consideration of authoritative persons (*āpta*): even some experts in the Tantras who compose certain mantras [do so with such dependence].

That which has such a basis (āśraya) is the ripening (vipāka); that very phenomenon (dharma) whose intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is the granting of a fruit is "one whose ripening-dharma has the person as its basis" (puruṣāśrayavipākadharmā). "Dharma" here refers to a specific kind of merit (puṇya). "By him" means performed by that person in a previous birth. "In that manner, through propitiating him" means that the dharma [was produced] in that way through the practice of cruelty and so forth; "through propitiating him" means through propitiating the person who composed the mantra.
"It bears fruit.
Explaining this very point, he says "that," and so forth. By that person who composed the mantra, there was the performance of vows and other practices joined with cruelty;
by that [performance], there was assistance. It is the nourishment of the action. Through that, the maturation—the giving of the fruit—is the *dharma*.

Of that very thing which has such an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [it is said] "of that fruit. Because of the performance of an action that has a desirable fruit as its cause, it bears fruit through propitiating that [deity], even without a person who composed the mantra, due to the assistance provided by that [deity]. [This occurs] simply through the recitation (*japa*) and so forth of that very *yantra*.

If it is argued that the fruit arises from the mantra through its function (*vyāpāra*) as an auxiliary cause, then the opponent considers the previously stated view—that the fruit results from propitiating a person—to be incorrect.

[The author replies: "No," and so forth, stating the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). This is not so. Why? Because of the words beginning with "person" (*puruṣa*), etc., referring to the one who composed the mantra.

The "form" (*ākāra*) of the person consists of his complexion, physical configuration, and so forth; his "nature" (*svabhāva*) consists of being peaceful, fierce, and so on; and his "conduct" (*caryā*) consists of activity characterized by the operations of body and speech.
Since there would otherwise follow the consequence of their futility, there must be a resolve (*adhimukti*) regarding these forms and other qualities.

If the person who is the empowerer (*adhiṣṭhātā*) of the mantra does not exist, for what purpose would one resolve upon his form and other attributes? If, on the other hand, such a person is accepted [to exist]...

Furthermore, regarding the assistance provided by that person: if it is admitted that even the person who composed the mantra provides assistance toward the attainment of the result from the mantra, then that specific person is established as possessing extraordinary qualities (*asādhāraṇa-guṇa*). The analysis of the compound is: "one whose qualities are extraordinary. What is the reason? Because it is precisely through faith in him (*tad-adhimukti*) that [the result arises], which has the nature of the form of that specific person.

Because it is precisely through the practice and conviction [of the practitioner] that the performance of rites such as those involving poison and so forth occurs; therefore, even though mantras are composed by persons, they do not—by their own nature or essence—bestow results independently of the application of those [mantras], nor independently of the application of a specific person. Rather, they depend exclusively upon the application of a specific person.

If only a person possessing extraordinary qualities (*asādhāraṇaguṇa*) is the author of a mantra, how is it that those who know the tantras (*tantravid*) recite mantras even though they are devoid of such specific powers and so forth? [In response: "The speech of those [tantra-knowers] is authoritative (*āptaprabhāṣa*), because their conduct proceeds according to the principles taught by him [the Buddha]. (312)

If it is argued that even some common people on the street who are experts in the Tantras perform certain rites with mantras composed by themselves, and thus there might be another author of a mantra who is not possessed of extraordinary powers (*atiśaya*), we say:
no. This is because they [the common people] act under the influence of the presiding power of those [Tantras]. For, while observing the convention (*samaya*) established by them, they—
And they function through a portion [of their power], because they possess efficacy independently of instruction regarding that specific occasion (*tatsamayopadeśa*).

Even in those cases, it is precisely through the application of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and so forth bearing that particular form (*ākāra*) that they act. Therefore, that [power] should be inferred as being based upon that very [meditative state].
Furthermore, for this reason he says: "Those which... and so forth. These are the treatises (*śāstra*) and tantras bound by mantras (*mantrapratibaddha*).

Those who know [the systems] are the "knowers of the tantras" (*tantravidah*). Even today, some among them compose certain unprecedented mantras. This lack of capacity belongs not to them alone, but rather to the extraordinary person—the Lord, the Master—who is the author of the tantra upon which they rely; it is his power and efficacy. Why? Because they proceed according to the principles taught by him.

Therefore, because they follow the rule—beginning with the covenant—that was taught to them by the Lord, the Lord is pleased and consecrates even the mantras composed by them; this is the intended meaning. He explains the meaning of the verse, preceded by the presentation of the prima facie argument, starting with the words "rathyāpuruṣa" (the man in the street). The man in the street...

The word "even" (*api*) implies that even certain ordinary persons, such as snake-charmers and others who possess knowledge of the characteristics of mantras and tantras, perform some action characterized by the pacification of poison and so forth; yet they are not distinguished [from commoners] because of their practice of drinking liquor and other such acts.
Likewise, another person—the composer of a mantra who is considered to possess power—might also lack any extraordinary excellence (*anatiśaya*). On the street...
And [the opponent] thinks that there would be a person devoid of excellence who is the author of mantras; thus, it is held that a powerful person is not established.
He refutes this with the words "No," and so forth: "The composition of mantras does not belong to those devoid of power; as for those who are mere street-urchins..."

Even those who compose mantras possess the power to do so only through the influence of the author of the tantra and his empowerment; it is by virtue of this that they have the capacity to create mantras.

Demonstrating this very point, he says: "For it is produced by that," and so forth. This means that those who maintain and protect the convention established by that person endowed with extraordinary power, and who proceed according to the instruction of that person endowed with power, are capable of performing mantra-rites. Why is this so?

Regarding the passage beginning with *tat* and so forth: "by its power" refers to the *samaya* (pledge/observance) and the instruction (*upadeśa*). This is because men who are independent [of such guidance] lack the capacity for the composition of mantras. In that context, *samaya* is that by the transgression of which one must undergo re-entry into the maṇḍala and so forth. Therefore, the distinction between these two is that the other consists of the instruction regarding the ritual procedures (*vidhāna*). "In that case too" means even in those [mantras] composed by ordinary people on the streets.

In the case of mantras, it is solely due to meditating on their form; and in the case of a person possessing power, it is likewise due to meditating on their form. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of meditation on essential nature and conduct is intended. Because of that—namely, through the application and activation of the mantra—for this reason, that [result] must be inferred and understood as being precisely that very empowerment, namely, the empowerment of a powerful person.
As for the claim that they perform rituals with mantras composed by themselves,
such a person would indeed possess extraordinary power; because of possessing a capacity not shared by others, he would be established as a superhuman being (*puruṣātiśaya*).

Mantras that are created and composed by human beings must be recited by one who desires a result; for the employment of those not so created is impossible, and no fruit arises from those that are not employed. Thus, since fruits are observed to arise from the employment of mantras whose fruits would otherwise be impossible without the supervision of a person, one desiring a result through their employment [should recite them].
They [the Vedas] must be declared to be produced and of human origin, like poetry composed under a conventional agreement;
by this very [argument], the proof for the incapacity of men has been refuted. ||313||

For it has been established that mantras are created by persons, and they yield results through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of those [persons]. Furthermore, by asserting that "some who know the tantras compose mantras," one would be acknowledging a superior person (*puruṣātiśaya*). This is because such a knower of the tantras, being the author of the mantra, must necessarily possess great power (*prabhāva*), unlike others.

This is because those who know the tantras possess extraordinary power. Furthermore, since the fruit of mantras is obtained only when they are presided over by a person, therefore mantras should be described as being produced and human-made (*pauruṣeya*) if one desires their fruit.
One who seeks the fruit from a mantra should not consider mantras to be eternal, but rather produced; for even though they are produced, they grant the fruit [only through such agency].
The two terms "produced" (*kṛtaka*) and "human" (*pauruṣeya*) are employed to demonstrate the two meanings of being independent of a person.

He explains this with the words beginning "for not," etc.: for indeed, the application—that is, the utterance—of eternal Vedic mantras is impossible, because they cannot have any excellence added to them (*anādheyātiśayatvāt*). And since there is no fruit from mantras that are not applied, [the Vedas must be human] on account of their application.

Mantras that produce results should be said to be created [by someone]; they are human in origin and, being presided over by a person, they should be said to bestow results. What is the reason? Because it is impossible for mantras—which have results that cannot arise from anything else such as the inherent power of the thing itself—to produce results without the superintendence of a person; for it is only through the superintendence of a person that their result is observed. And it is not by way of the inherent power of the thing that [they produce results].

The production of results from mantras has been established in this way by [the verse] beginning: "If the power of entities were such that they would become the means for accomplishing everything" (1.267).
Furthermore, he provides an illustration: "I must accomplish this purpose for whoever shall recite my poetry and so forth in this manner."

Thus, a convention (*samaya*) has been established regarding that poetry and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including the arts (*śilpasthāna*) and the like. That poetry and so forth is "one for which a convention has been made" (*kṛtasamaya*). Just as in that case, [the mantras] are "like that" (*tadvat*); the meaning is that just as there is a result for those who recite such poetry and so forth due to being presided over by a person (*puruṣādhiṣṭhāna*), so it is with the mantras as well. [The opponent's position is: "Human beings lack the power (*śakti*) to perceive objects beyond the senses (*atīndriyārtha*). Thus, [this is] the [argument of] incapacity.

Whatever proof for the lack of efficacy is asserted by the Mīmāṃsakas, all of that has been refuted by this very [work] which establishes the excellence of the knowledge and power of those who employ mantras.
He explains [this] with the words beginning "For it has been established," etc.; for it has been established that mantras are produced by persons.

It has also been established that mantras bestow their fruits through [divine] empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Furthermore, not all persons are capable of either composing or empowering mantras. Therefore, there exists some person of superior excellence who is the author of the mantra. Moreover, the arguments for the rejection of such a person of superior excellence are also [to be examined] in the *Āptacintā*.
Thus, the arguments for refuting the claim that "someone possesses excellence" have also been countered.

As for the proof described—such as [the possession of] intellect, sense organs, speech, and masculinity—that is a fallacy of the semblance of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*); for there is no inference based on the method of residue (*śeṣavat*). ||314||

As for the argument beginning with "because of the mention of the sense organs, intellect, and masculinity," which is intended as a proof for the rejection of any excellence in a person—that is indeed unscriptural (*āgamakam*), because it is impossible to establish a general rejection [of such excellence]. For a rejection of those who perceive supersensible things is not possible; this is because, even though these things exist, they are unknown [to us]. Therefore...

Thus, because contradiction is unestablished, and because it has been stated that there is no contradiction in the possibility of non-contradictory [properties] existing in one place, the [opposing] arguments have been refuted. By this, it is not the case that the "non-deviant contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritva*) is being raised against the proof for the refutation of excellence as asserted by the opponent; rather, it is the proofs for the refutation of human excellence that are [addressed as] real entities.

This is stated under the pretext that [qualities] derived from the power of things simply do not exist; for there is no means of proof whatsoever capable of negating a superior person (*puruṣātiśaya*) who is established by the force of reality. [Objection:
But surely this exists: the person intended [as the subject] does not possess excellence, because he possesses intelligence, and because he possesses sense faculties, [just like us].
Because of [the presence of] speech and because of [the presence of] masculinity; "like a man on the street"—to this he says:
"Intellect, sense-faculties," and so forth. This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of intellect (*buddhi*), sense-faculties (*indriya*), speech (*ukti*), and masculinity (*puṃstva*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), qualities such as possessing vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the like are included. As for that which is described as the means for refuting the excellence of a [supernatural] person (*puruṣātiśaya*):

All of that is "pseudo-means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāsa*), meaning it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). What is the reason? Because, due to doubt regarding its presence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), everything is "possessing a remainder" (*śeṣavat*); for that which is "possessing a remainder" is inconclusive. Thus, there is no comprehension of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) through a conclusion that is contrary to the actual state of things.

He explains with the words beginning "As for that which... The connection is as follows: "That proof which is intended to refute the excellence of a person is indeed not a means of cognizing reality. Furthermore, that proof consists of [the argument] beginning with "Because of the conjunction of the intellect and the senses," and so forth. He asks, "Why is it not a means of cognition? and answers with the words beginning "Refutation and generality... "Refutation" (*pratikṣepa*) and "generality" (*sāmānya*) constitute "refutation-and-generality" (*pratikṣepasāmānye*); [it is not a means of cognition] because it is a proof of those two.

Because those two [alternatives] are impossible. To explain: by means of a proof such as "possessing intelligence" (*buddhimattva*), either (1) the negation of a superior person would be established—that is, that no superior person exists—or else, that which is this superior person would be established as being identical to ordinary persons on the street, thereby establishing his commonality with other men.

In this context, by the words "there is not" and so forth, he states the absence of a proof for refutation. For a refutation by one who does not perceive supersensuous objects is not possible regarding objects that transcend the senses. What is the reason? Because even though these supersensuous objects exist, they are unknown to those of limited vision. Therefore, there is no refutation based on mere non-perception.
This is the state of affairs.

Nor is there a rejection of the excellence of the person (*puruṣātiśaya*) due to the prescription of a contradictory [attribute], because for that very reason—namely, precisely because of its being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*)—the two kinds of contradiction are unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the excellence of the person by means of such reasons as "being an intellect" (*buddhitva*). There is no contradiction.

And it was stated previously that there is no contradiction in the possibility of a person's excellence [consisting] in both [qualities such as] being a speaker and so forth occurring in a single individual.
Nor is the establishment of the universal [sāmānya] possible through the other [particular], because it is possible to know the impossibility of [the existence of] particulars;
for the non-perception [of the particular] has already been rejected as a logical reason.

It has also been stated previously that even when there is equality regarding such factors as masculinity, one observes a certain excellence in some cases; thus, even when a particular distinction is possible, the general rule is not established.
In such instances...

Therefore, even if the presence [of the reason] in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is not observed, this inference is as incapable as the "remainder" (*śeṣavat*) type because of the doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Furthermore, the followers of Jaimini who speak in this manner undermine their own position;
for words do not say, "This is the meaning, and this is not the meaning."
This object must be conceptualized by persons, and those persons are possessed of passion and other such afflictions. ||315||
"How is the distinction made that 'he alone knows reality and no other'?

By the words 'nor even,' etc., he states the absence of any means for establishing a generality (*sāmānya*). Nor can there be an establishment of a generality—that is, an establishment of equality—of that person possessing excellence by another person who is one of limited vision. What is the reason? Because [the former possesses] the perception of supersensible objects and so forth."

Because it is impossible to know the occurrence of a specific characteristic, and because such things as the perception of supersensible objects— which reside within the mental continuum of another person and are not perceptible to ordinary individuals— cannot be established; whatever non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) one might employ to prove their impossibility, that non-perception has already been rejected as a valid reason (*hetu*).

Furthermore: (1) even though masculinity and so forth are common [to all], since we observe an excellence such as wisdom in some due to their respective cultivation, it is possible for another [excellence] to exist in others as well. Therefore, men are those in whom excellence is possible; for if excellence were impossible, the general category of "other men" could not be established—this has also been stated previously.
Therefore, this is an inference *śeṣavat* (by elimination), which demonstrates the impossibility of a superior person on the grounds of [his] being a speaker and so forth,
even though no occurrence [of these qualities] in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is observed.
Even if indeed no occurrence of being a speaker and so forth is seen in the dissimilar class— that is, in a superior person— nevertheless, there is a subverting [reason].

Because there is doubt regarding its exclusion from existence, [the argument] is ineffective. Furthermore, for those who speak thus—namely, Jaimini and others who maintain that "there is no person who perceives supersensuous objects"—how could there be an understanding of the meaning of the Veda from someone like Jaimini, who possesses some degree of excellence? Thus, [the author] returns to the position of accepting human excellence, stating that there is no [person who perceives] supersensuous objects.

By this statement, "any person who knows the meaning," they [the Mīmāṃsakas] undermine and refute [the existence of] a person of superior insight, because it is impossible for one to determine the meaning of the Veda [without such a person]. For instance, the Vedic words themselves do not say, "This is our meaning; this is not the meaning. Therefore, whatever meaning is intended for the words regarding the *agnihotra* must be postulated [by someone].
[If it is argued that] the meaning [of the Veda] is established by certain persons, that too is not the case; for those persons are possessed of passion and other such afflictions (*rāgādiyuktāḥ*).
Therefore, an object imagined by them is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Now, if it were assumed that someone such as Jaimini himself is the knower of that Vedic meaning, then regarding that single person—
And just as [the attainment of] thought was reached, so too, in the state of manhood, why is it that some knower has not somehow arisen among you? (316)

The Vedic words do not cry out, "O venerable Brahmins, this is our meaning that must be accepted and no other. Rather, the scriptures fall upon us with their meanings and specific relations unmanifested; in that state, one person imagines a certain meaning, while another imagines something else.
Furthermore, there is no inherent restriction of nature among words by which one would perform a specific function regarding a single object while another would not;

rather, they are seen to enter into various [meanings] by virtue of convention (*samaya*). It is not logical for someone—being ignorant and afflicted by some defect—to declare that the true nature (*tattva*) of those words, whose restriction of meaning is unknown, is due to an "entry into direct perception" (*pratyakṣāveśa*), and not due to the word *apa*.

The meaning intended [by the author] is this: what is the basis for the claim that no person other than Mīmāṃsaka knows the true essence of the Veda? There is no reason for this here, because there is no difference in their being human beings; thus, the implication is that either everyone knows it, or no one knows it at all.

Now, even though there is equality in terms of being human and so forth, if it is assumed that someone such as Jaimini—who possesses extraordinary powers—is the knower of the relationship between Vedic words and their supersensible objects, then [the opponent might argue]: "Just like Jaimini and others, although equal in terms of being male or human, how could another person, despite being entirely without cause, also become a knower? [This would be impossible.]

[He is] possessed of excellence. Why? Because it would follow that there would be another person possessing knowledge [of everything], just like Jaimini and others—this is what is meant by "not so," etc., which he explains as follows: "Come here, sirs, you Brahmins; this is our purpose."

Vedic words do not cry out or declare, "They are to be grasped by these [means] and not by others," by which means there might be a comprehension of their meaning from them. The word *kevalam* is used for emphasis. It is only when their connection with specific meanings remains unmanifested that they strike upon—that is, ascend to—the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*). "Unmanifested" refers to the connection or relation with a specific meaning.

The analysis [of the compound] is "yeṣām" (of those). In that regard, when words whose connection to their meanings is unknown are being heard, one person imagines some meaning according to his own whim, while another person imagines a different meaning; thus, there is simply no determination of the word-meaning. 17

[The opponent argues: "The relationship between words and their meanings is innate; therefore, there will be a restriction to a single meaning. To this, [the author] says: "No," he says. There is no innate restriction of words by way of their own nature (*svabhāva*), nor is there an essential connection (*prakṛti*) with a meaning by virtue of which, even when multiple meanings are postulated, they would enter into that specific meaning as the denotable object solely by the power of convention (*samaya*).

They are seen giving [gifts]. It is not logical that among those Vedic words, one person explains the true meaning while another does not; this is the connection [of the sentence]. Of what kind [are they]? "Of those whose rules of meaning are unknown"—this is the analysis of the compound (*aviditārthaniyama*). What is the reason? Because of the penetration of supersensuous [objects]. [This refers to] heaven and so forth, which are beyond the senses.

Because one makes the meaning of the means [of knowledge] one's own by taking it as an object; for a person of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*) is not capable of knowing the fixed relation between a word and its supersensible (*atīndriya*) referent. In that regard, someone who is ignorant—such as Jaimini or Śabarasvāmin, who is overwhelmed by defects such as passion—declares the true nature of those words, saying, "The meaning of this [word] is precisely this."

Now, if someone [claims] that he alone, and no one else, knows those objects through the sense-faculties and so forth, from what source does he possess this excellence of supersensuous knowledge? Likewise, is it impossible for another person to be a seer of objects remote in space, time, or nature?

It has been observed that no means of refutation whatsoever apply to this [position]. Even if such means were possible, it would be more appropriate to remain free from dogmatic attachment, thinking: "Just as this person possesses this particular quality, so too might another.
He whose speech accords with valid cognition—that person should know the truth.
For indeed, there is no possibility for a means of valid cognition regarding things that are absolutely beyond the senses. ||317||

Nor is there another [alternative]. For it is not logical to establish a distinction based on the claim that another person—such as Jaimini and others—is no different [from us] yet does not teach the truth, because such a position lacks justification.
Now, from what [source] do the intellect, the sense organs, and so forth—the word "and so forth" including repeated practice—[arise] from that indefinable form?

On account of this excellence as a cause, it is maintained that Jaimini and others alone understand the meaning of the Veda, and no other ordinary person does. In that case, from what source does this Jaimini and his peers derive such an excellence of knowledge regarding that which transcends the senses— the true nature of the Vedic meaning— given that they are no more distinguished than others whose true nature remains unknown?
Or let it be granted that from the time of Jaimini onwards there has been a person who is a knower of objects beyond the senses;

likewise, let it be granted that there may be another superior person, as intended by the Buddhists and others, who is a seer of things remote in space, time, and nature. Is this impossible? Why is such a person not observed, such that he might be rejected? He too is... [beyond the senses].

Let it be accepted that [the author] is one who perceives the objects of the senses. If not, then let even Jaimini and others, though they are desired [as authorities], not be so. For there are no arguments for refuting them; indeed, there exist no arguments such as "being a human being" (*puruṣatva*) and the like—which are intended to refute the excellence of a person as accepted by the Buddhists and others—that would refute Jaimini and his followers, who distinguish the meaning of the Veda.

They do not rely [on them], nor do they take them as objects; rather, they certainly do rely [on them], because they too possess the quality of being persons (*puruṣatva*) and so forth. Now, even if the means of proof such as *puruṣatva* are possible, if a distinction is desired for Jaimini and others, then just as this [is the case for him]—

The distinction of this [system] from that of Jaimini and others is characterized by the discernment of the meaning of the Vedas through the senses; even though the means for that [discernment] is possible. That is to say, even if the means—such as the quality of being a human being (*puruṣatva*) and so forth—which serves to reject the claim that there is a person who perceives supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*), were indeed possible, it would follow that other persons as well could perceive supersensible objects. Thus, you Mīmāṃsakas simply lack any firm conviction [regarding the existence of such a person].
It is logical:

it is not on the grounds that he perceives supersensuous objects that Jaimini and others accept the knowledge of the Vedic meaning; rather, if a person is accepted as a knower of the Vedic meaning because his words accord with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇasaṃvādin*), then he is so regarded.
The opponent maintains that the statement of Jaimini and others, who analyze the meaning of the Vedas, is consistent with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
To this, Ācārya [Śāntarakṣita] replies: "No. This response is not tenable, because regarding the meanings of the Vedas—which are entirely beyond the senses, such as heaven (*svarga*)—...

There is the possibility of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the directions and the means of knowledge (*ghanatva*). [This] may be the "Investigation of the Authority" (*āpta-cintā*). It might be argued: "We are not attached to the authority of any person whatsoever in the interpretation of the Veda. What then? [We rely on it] because of its correspondence with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Among many commentators, he who possesses the means of valid cognition, such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth..."

"He brings them into connection; he approves"—this is not correct. For, regarding invisible things (*adṛṣṭa*) and other objects beyond the senses, other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) do not operate. Indeed, it is precisely because they do not operate that the scripture (*gama*) is requested for the sake of cognizing them. Otherwise, even if that [scripture] existed, if there were no operation of another means of valid cognition, [cognition would still not occur].
Because there would be no comprehension [of it]. Consequently, scripture would be a non-prover (*asādhana*) of that which is to be comprehended solely on its own.

If it is argued that there is no comprehension of supersensible objects even from something else [than scripture], then how can something be both supersensible and yet an object of perception and the other [means of knowledge]? Furthermore, those [perception and so forth]—even regarding their own objects—are dependent upon scripture...

If it were only by depending on [human] agents that [the Veda] were established, then there would be no cognition of fire and so forth from smoke and the like, as it would lack a source of authority (*āgama*). He explains this with the words, "Indeed, this would not be the case in the *Āgama*," and so on. We are not intent upon the explanation of the Vedas by some person such as Jaimini who is an authority; rather, we accept the explanation because of its correspondence with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

They are deeply attached [to this]. He clarifies this very point: even among many commentators on the Veda, that commentator who, in explaining the meaning of the Veda, harmonizes and coordinates it with means of valid cognition such as perception—that kind of commentator is approved and accepted, and no other.

He refutes this with the words "That is not so," and so forth. Merit and demerit constitute the *adṛṣṭa* (the unseen force); by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he includes other supersensible factors that bring about results such as heaven.

Since no other means of valid cognition, such as perception, operates regarding these, there is no statement concerning the subject matter of the Veda that is corroborated by any other means of valid cognition. This is precisely because such corroboration is impossible; for perception and the other means of valid cognition cannot function regarding that which is absolutely beyond the senses.
For indeed, scripture is requested—that is, it is sought—for the sake of cognizing that which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).

"Otherwise" means: if the ascertainment of an object occurred solely through corroboration by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even regarding an object accessible through scripture, then, even when that scripture exists, if there were a non-operation of another means of valid cognition regarding the object accessible through it, then [there would be no certainty] due to the non-operation of that other means of valid cognition.

Because there is no comprehension from verbal testimony alone; and for that reason, since there would be no comprehension of an object devoid of traditional scripture (āgama) from other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) alone, scripture itself would not be a means of proof. This is because the existence or non-existence of the comprehension of an object depends precisely upon the presence or absence of other means of knowledge. Furthermore, there is comprehension of supersensuous objects even from other [means] such as perception, independent of scripture.

If it is argued that the cognition of supersensuous objects arises from perception and other means of knowledge when accompanied by scripture (*āgama*), how is this so? [The Siddhāntavādin asks: How indeed can that which is supersensuous—such as the means for attaining heaven and the like—be an object of perception and other such means, given the contradiction?

It might be thought: (1) it is not the case that perception and the other means of knowledge establish an object that is entirely beyond the senses; rather, those very means—perception and the rest—are established as valid even with respect to their own respective objects only by depending upon scripture (*āgama*). Thus, the opponent maintains that the authority belongs to scripture alone.

Regarding the passage beginning with "anāgama," the Siddhāntavādin states: "That in which there is no scripture (āgama) is 'anāgama'; thus, the cognition of fire and so forth would not arise from the mark of smoke.
[Objection: "Once [cognition] has occurred, another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is sought; however, it is simply that the occurrence of that very scripture is not known."

For one who is already capable of establishing [an object] by themselves, what excellence does the introduction of scripture (āgama) provide? On the other hand, one who is incapable will not succeed even in the application of scripture. Furthermore, since that application of scripture is connected with an object beyond the senses (atīndriya), how could that supersensible application be established by another means?

Furthermore, the definition of scripture would be as follows: "That speech which is composed by one whose words accord with valid cognition is scripture. Thus it follows that the quality of being authorless (*apauruṣeyatā*) is meaningless. (318)

Even though the claim regarding scripture (*āgama*) is equal [to other means of knowledge], since scripture also functions as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for certain objects by virtue of its own force, the definition of scripture would be "a statement that accords with other means of valid cognition. It is not "that which is not produced by a person" (*apuruṣakriyā*). For even though that [non-human origin] is equal across all objects, [scripture does not apply to them all]; such is the opponent's view. Indeed, when scripture operates regarding objects beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), the means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) do not [apply to it].

[The opponent] seeks [an answer] to this, lest this fault should occur. And consequently, scripture (*āgama*) would not be a means of valid cognition (*sādhana*) for understanding at all, because it would function independently. However, that very activity of scripture even with respect to supersensible objects (*atīndriya*) is not known. If it is argued that the operation of scripture depends upon perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of knowledge, [we reply: [This is the opponent's position: "Scripture is sought after by those who desire to know the truth regarding matters such as dharma and adharma, which are beyond the reach of the senses. For one who desires to know the truth about such things, scripture is indeed a means of valid cognition. This is because it is a statement made by a trustworthy person (*āptokti*). A trustworthy person is one who possesses direct knowledge of the true nature of things and speaks without deceit. Therefore, since scripture is the word of a trustworthy person, it is a means of valid cognition for those seeking to know the truth concerning dharma and so forth. [The author's response: This is not so. Even if scripture were the word of a trustworthy person, it could not be a means of valid cognition for those seeking to know the truth regarding dharma and so forth. Why? If it is argued that its being the word of a trustworthy person is established through inference (*anumāna*), we say no; for there is no inferential mark (*liṅga*) that establishes it. Nor can it be established through another means of valid cognition, because there is no other means of valid cognition apart from inference. Furthermore, if it were established through another means of valid cognition, then scripture would become redundant. Moreover, if scripture were established as the word of a trustworthy person through inference, then scripture itself would not be a means of valid cognition for those seeking to know the truth regarding dharma and so forth, because it would depend on inference. If it is argued that scripture is established as the word of a trustworthy person through perception (*pratyakṣa*), we say no; for perception does not apply to supersensible objects. Regarding the reply beginning with "by itself" (*svayam*), when perception and the other means of knowledge are themselves capable of establishing supersensible objects, what excellence does the proximity (*upadhāna*) of that scripture— its presence— confer upon perception and the rest, such that it causes them to function toward supersensible objects by making known the scripture?

Now, perception and the other means of knowledge are incapable [of establishing] that which is beyond the senses (atīndriya). Furthermore, perception and the others, even if they were capable, would certainly not establish the application of scripture (*āgama*), because that application of scripture is itself beyond the senses. For just as the means for achieving heaven and so forth is beyond the senses, so too is that application of scripture related to an object that is beyond the senses. How, then, could it be established by another means of knowledge, such as perception? It certainly cannot.
This is established; for it is a triviality to say that perception and the other means of knowledge are sought for its sake.

Furthermore, if one were to say, "Among many commentators, the statement of whoever correlates [the subject] with the means of knowledge such as perception is accepted," then because of its human origin, this definition of scripture would be something other than the true characteristic of scripture. He states this very point:
