"Thus, indeed," and so forth. For that person whose speech accords with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it follows that the speech composed and refined by that person is *āgama*. And the refinement of speech is the demonstration that its meaning is supported by valid cognition. This is another definition of *āgama*. Furthermore, in this way, authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatā*)—which is claimed as the defining characteristic of *āgama*—is rendered meaningless and useless.

He explains this with the words beginning "tulya" (equal). When there is the assertion of the non-human origin [of scripture], even though two objects— one imagined by a person whose speech accords with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the other imagined by another— are equal, if one accepts that scripture possesses the status of scripture regarding some object that accords with valid cognition due to the force of valid cognition, then [this applies] to sentences such as those concerning the *agnihotra* sacrifice.

The definition of scripture (*āgama*) would be its correspondence with valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃvāda*), not its non-human origin. Non-human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) could not be the definition of scripture. Why? Because even though that non-human origin is identical in respect to all things taught by persons—whether they be accepted or unaccepted—it is because [scripture] is not sublated by valid cognition that it is accepted as a source of understanding. Thus ends the consideration of [the definition of] scripture.

Because it is not sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in its apprehension; and because, even when that [means of cognition] exists, it is undesirable in other cases where there is corroboration by another means of valid cognition. Furthermore:

if the possibility of knowledge independent of scripture (*anāgama-jñāna*) were to occur regarding an object that is absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), [it would follow that such knowledge is possible everywhere].
It might be intended that there exists someone who knows objects beyond the senses. || 319 ||

If it is maintained that a person’s cognition of an object beyond the senses possesses its true nature independently of scripture (*āgama*), then it would follow that there exist persons who perceive objects transcending the senses; for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) preceded by perception is impossible in the absence of such vision, since perception does not operate [in that domain]. Since no other means of valid cognition is possible regarding them, scripture is the means of valid cognition for cognitions that do not have those [objects] as their objective support.

If the operation of another means of valid cognition were to draw upon perception, then the existence of a superhuman being (puruṣātiśaya) would be unavoidable. Therefore, there is no operation of another means of valid cognition regarding that which is beyond the senses; for this very reason, the operation of scripture (āgama) with respect to specific objects is not fully understood—whether it be by Jaimini or anyone else.

This is what is meant: the meaning is that the comprehension of the content of scripture is desired because it is in conformity with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Even if that [conformity] were absent—that is, even if the quality of being authorless (*apauruṣeyatva*) were equally present—it is not desired to comprehend a matter that does not conform to valid cognition elsewhere; therefore, conformity with valid cognition would be the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of scriptural statements.

If it were possible for knowledge independent of scripture to arise regarding an object that is entirely beyond the senses— that is, if knowledge not reliant on scripture were possible— then one might maintain one's own preferred position that there exists someone who knows objects beyond the senses.

This would be the case if, for instance, a person such as Jaimini, who expounds the meaning of the Veda, [possessed such knowledge] regarding an imperceptible object, namely the means for achieving heaven and the like.

The true nature of knowledge, which is its non-erroneousness, is held to depend upon [the absence of] pride. In that case, one would have to accept that other persons as well—just like Jaimini and others—are perceivers of supersensible objects.
This might be argued: "One does not know a supersensible object through direct perception, but rather teaches it after having known it through inference."

This is not so; because inference and the other means of knowledge are preceded by perception. When there is no perception of that [object]—that is, when the supersensible is not perceived by that perception—he clarifies this very point with the words "by perception" and so forth. Among those [objects], the supersensible...

Because other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) preceded by perception cannot occur with respect to those objects for which perception does not function, [the scripture] is understood as having that which is not the object of those [perceptions] as its objective support (*ālambana*). "Not having that as its objective support" (*atadālambana*) means that it has as its objective support what is not the domain of perception and the other [means of knowledge]. It is sought after for the sake of certain determination (*niścaya*) regarding that which is not the object of perception and so forth; thus, the scripture is investigated.

[The opponent replies: "A necklace! But the operation of other means of knowledge, such as inference and the like, regarding supersensible objects, draws upon and establishes the supersensible object by means of perception; for inference and the like are preceded by perception. For this reason, a superior person who perceives supersensible objects would be unavoidable for the Mīmāṃsakas. Yet he has been refuted. Therefore, it is not [the case that...]"

The operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) applies to objects beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). For this very reason— namely, because the operation of scripture (*āgama*), that is, the Veda, upon a specific object characterized as the means to attaining heaven and so forth (which is beyond the senses) is not certain due to the non-operation of other means of valid cognition— is it Jaimini or someone else, such as Śabarasvāmin?
One who possesses passion and other defects does not understand the meaning of the Veda by himself, nor from another; nor does the Veda itself make it known.
How, then, can there be any comprehension of the Veda's meaning? ||320||

For every speaker is a human being who has not transcended defects and error; he does not himself know that specific restriction regarding supersensuous objects, nor does another person make it known to him, for the same consequence applies to that person as well. Indeed, one blind man being led by another blind man does not find the path. Nor does the Veda itself explain its own meaning.

Because it would follow that instruction is rendered useless. Therefore, this [person], whose meaning is not fully understood, is like a useless tumor of words; thus, like a thorn bound by the sinews of false views, it is difficult to extract and brings about suffering.
Regarding the Vedic revelation stating, "One who desires heaven should offer the Agnihotra," what is the authority for the claim that its meaning is not "one should eat dog-meat"? (321)

Regarding some particular matter, a person such as Manu—who lacks proximity [to the source] regarding [injunctions] like "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice"—does not know the meaning of the Veda by himself, that is, independently of the instruction of others, because he possesses passion and other such defects.
Possession of passion and so forth is the cause of non-comprehension; for this reason, he does not know the meaning of the Veda even from another source.

Because this person possesses defects such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth, the Veda itself does not know—that is, it does not reveal—the meaning. Therefore, how could there be any comprehension of the Veda’s meaning? There is no comprehension at all. For the analysis of the compound is as follows: "one whose delusion (*viplava*), which is error (*bhrānti*), has been produced by defects such as attachment and so forth, has not transcended [these defects] in every respect. Regarding the word *tam* (it), it refers to the Veda's cognition of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*).

He does not himself know that "the meaning of this [scripture] is precisely this, and not otherwise," nor does another person who possesses passion and other defects perceive him. This is because the same logical consequence applies to that other person as well; that is to say, due to his possession of passion and so forth, he too is ignorant.
For indeed, a blind man being led by another blind man who himself does not know the path does not find the way. Nor does he [find it] by himself...
The Veda reveals its own meaning independently of human instruction. Why? (1) Because it would follow that [human] instruction would be useless;
because it would follow that the exegesis of Jaimini and others would be fruitless.
Therefore, this thing called the Veda, whose meaning is not fully understood, is a mere verbal tumor—a lump of flesh between the forehead and the skull.

It is called a "goitre" (gaḍu) because it is fruitless; likewise, even a Vedic word is a "goitre" because it is fruitless due to its meaning being unknown. It is like a goitre in that there is doubt as to whether this is its meaning or that; thus, for one who has faith in it, it becomes a thorn—a cause of suffering—and consequently, it brings suffering and establishes that person who has accepted the Veda in a state of pain. Of what kind is this non-existent...?

The sinews are indeed the veins; bound by them, he is difficult to extract even by someone wishing to remove him out of compassion—thus [the author] mocks [the opponent]. By the word "thereby" (tena), because the meaning is not understood, [he mocks] the Vedic statement in the *agnihotra* injunction: "One desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra*. In the [Vedic] text, one might as well say "eat... [implying a similar absurdity].
Regarding the statement "dog-meat," this is not its actual meaning; what then is the proof that another intended meaning is meant here? There is no proof whatsoever.
We see no great difference between the injunction "one should throw ghee or the like into a particular sacrificial fire" and the injunction "one should eat dog-meat.
We accept the words of those whose teachers are beyond our perception exactly according to their intended purpose.

Or is it the opposite? This same consequence would not apply everywhere, because a teacher’s own intention can be revealed through their instruction; for this [consequence] does not apply to words that are not taught by an instructor.

And one who speaks with the intention of convincing the world maintains the conventions established by the world; from that [convention] as well, there may be comprehension of that [meaning]. This is not the case for words that are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), because in their case, there is an absence of any speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
He explains this with the words "in some cases," etc., citing: "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice."

Because a real relationship— whether characterized by proximity to the intended meaning of a sentence or by the absence of remoteness from the unintended meaning— is denied in every case, both [proximity and remoteness] are absent. For example, in the case of a specific element such as fire,
the intended meaning is "one should pour clarified butter purified by mantras and so forth," and not the meaning "one should eat dog meat."
Thus, we do not perceive any superiority [in this].

But surely, this is as previously stated: the same consequence applies everywhere, even in the case of human-authored scripture (*pauruṣeya-āgama*). Demonstrating that very point, he says: "The teacher who speaks is beyond perception; those words and scriptures which are spoken by him—[one must consider] their meaning..."

"According to intention" means according to what is intended by the teacher. Since there is no fixed rule, one must consider whether contemporary persons who have not seen the teacher follow [the teaching] correctly— understanding it as the teacher intended— or rather in the opposite way, contrary to the teacher's intention.

One might think that there is doubt in every case; he refutes this with the words "No," and so forth. This undesirable consequence does not apply everywhere, because [the author] first reveals his own intention to those listeners present at that time by clarifying the intention of the teacher and the author of the scripture.

"This is the meaning of this statement," they say; those listeners, in turn, reveal it to others, and they to yet others. Thus, because a tradition of succession is possible within the teacher's instruction, this characteristic of expressing an intended meaning cannot belong to Vedic words, which are non-human (apauruṣeya) and lack an instructor, precisely because of the absence of an instructor.

Furthermore, in the case of human compositions, since the occurrence of well-known meanings is possible—because the author of the scripture speaks with the intention of informing the world, thinking "I must make the world understand"—he maintains and protects the established usage of a word for whatever meaning it has in the world; otherwise, his disclosure would be fruitless. Therefore, too...

The establishment of that meaning would also result from following the conventions well-known in the world; the establishment of the meaning of a scripture composed by a person would [also] result [from this]. By the word "also" (api), it is implied that [this follows] from the previously mentioned possibility of a tradition. There is no establishment of meaning for non-human (apauruṣeya) words in the manner described above. What is the reason? Because, regarding those Vedic words, for someone...
Because a person lacks the capacity for such exertion, and because there is an absence of the intention to speak— the cause of verbal expression— it has been stated that,

given the possibility of [relying on] oral tradition and so forth, there is no equal application of the same logical consequence regarding the possibility of understanding the meaning of a human-authored scripture.

Moreover, it is precisely by adhering to reason that the wise engage in what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with their respective bases; they do not act on mere rumor. Thus, the [alleged] consequence is not the same. We shall demonstrate this in its proper place.
This is established.
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that even an object such as the arrangement of the world, though beyond the scope of logical reasoning, [is known] from the word of a reliable person?
No, because there is no conviction [regarding such a person]. For it cannot be that because there is doubt in one instance, it must be so in all cases.
Now, he states "Moreover," etc., to show that the ascertainment of the meaning of human-authored texts occurs precisely through the application of logic.

Adhering strictly to logic and reasoning, the wise Buddhists, acting with circumspection, engage themselves in what is to be abandoned and so forth. They strive for the abandonment of that which is to be abandoned along with its basis, and for the acquisition of that which is to be acquired along with its basis. In this context, that which is to be abandoned is suffering (*duḥkha*), and that which is to be acquired is liberation (*mokṣa*). Their respective bases are, in order, karma and the afflictions (*kleśa*), and the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

This is what is meant: (1) even though words may have multiple meanings, the followers of the Sugata determine the meaning of the scripture only as that which is logically consistent and conducive to the goals of human beings, and not merely by the instruction of others. Therefore, this is not a fault;
he states this very point with the words, "not by mere report. This means it is not [determined] by mere report from the elders; thus, it is not the same [as other traditions].
This is a consequential argument (*prasaṅga*). Furthermore, we shall later demonstrate how the engagement with scripture must be preceded by the adherence to logic (*nyāya*) on appropriate occasions.

If the determination of the meaning of scripture occurs through the adherence to logic regarding that which is entirely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), then [the following applies] regarding the meaning of scripture:

He says that the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) would not exist, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*), etc. "The arrangement of the world and so forth" (*lokasanniveśādiḥ*) refers to the arrangement and so forth of the earth and other elements, as it has been stated: (1)

"In that regard, they maintain that the configuration of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) begins with an incalculable wind-circle (*vāyumaṇḍala*), sixteen hundred thousand [yojanas] in thickness," and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [is meant] the giving of desirable or undesirable fruits by volitions such as generosity and non-violence, and so on.

Even an object that is beyond the scope of logic—due to being remote in terms of place, intrinsic nature, and so forth—is understood by you, the wise, because of the speech of a person who is worthy of trust. Why? Because of the words of a person whose speech is non-contradictory regarding objects accessible through perception and inference;
the speech of such a person in a third category [of objects] is considered probable as being true in its meaning. Therefore, it is [to be accepted as] probable.
[The opponent argues: "In that case, since a meaning is understood from the word of a person, the engagement with the meaning of scripture would not be preceded by the observance of logic;
thus, he considers the same undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) to apply.
[The author] refutes this with the words beginning with "No" (na). An object that is absolutely beyond the senses is not understood from the word of a person. Why?

[Objection: Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that object due to a lack of conviction, [the object] remains uncertain. [Response: It is false to claim that because there is correspondence (*saṃvāda*) regarding objects such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), correspondence is thereby determined even for that which is extremely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*); for it is not established anywhere that the engagement [of scripture] with its object is pervaded by correspondence simply because it is seen through direct perception. This definition of scripture (*āgama*) has been observed as a last resort (*agatyā*).
Therefore, there is no certainty; thus, it was stated previously that scripture (*āgama*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The knowledge of the meaning of words that are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) does not arise from tradition, nor from reasoning, nor even from common worldly usage.

For it is not reasonable that there should be a lack of comprehension in this regard. If that well-known worldly discourse were the cause of such understanding, [then it would be a source of knowledge].
If it is a well-known worldly expression,
then it is the cause for the cognition thereof.
In that regard, there is one who perceives objects beyond the senses.
By whom this meaning has been discerned among words that have multiple meanings. ||322||

For this worldly convention does not arise from a relationship between word and meaning that is not of human origin. Rather, it is because [the convention] is seen to be unerring regarding its object due to its correspondence with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) based on a formal agreement (*samaya*), that everything taught by him—even if not accessible through reasoning—is accepted as being so. What is the reason? "Because of the activity of that," and so forth; [it refers to] the activity of the speech of that superior person.

Because the contrapositive is established through pervasion by means of non-contradiction with the [perceptual] experience of the thirteen [points], there is an absence of any subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

Now, you too have accepted that the definition of scripture consists in its non-contradiction in at least one respect, as stated in [verse 1.218]: "Non-sublation by both perception and the two kinds of inference," and so forth.

Therefore, he says: "And because there is no other way," and so forth. The definition of scripture (*āgama*) is that it is a statement which, through its non-contradiction regarding objects accessible to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is also non-contradictory even with respect to extremely remote objects; this is accepted as the definition of scripture because, when one must act on the basis of scripture due to the lack of any other recourse, acting in such a manner is preferable. However, from such a scripture as described above, there is no certain determination of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*), because it lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*). Therefore, for that reason, it is not [the case that...].

It was stated previously that scripture (*āgama*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the knowledge of the meaning of words that are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) arises from the tradition of the teachers, because there is no [human] instructor [to provide such knowledge]. It does not arise from reasoning (*yukti*), because the means of valid cognition do not operate with respect to an object that is entirely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*). Nor does the comprehension of the meaning arise from the world (*loka*), for the world—

Because there is an absence of formal application for the sake of communication, it is impossible to follow worldly convention [in such cases]. Therefore, in the case of non-human (apauruṣeya) words, it is logical that there is simply no comprehension of their meaning. Even in the case of Vedic words, the established worldly usage is as follows:
for example, from words such as "fire" (agni), people proceed toward objects capable of burning, cooking, and so forth. 3.

If it is argued that worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*) is the cause for understanding the meaning of the Vedas, he states the reply beginning with "In that case" (*tatra*). In that regard, since worldly convention is characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*), what person could be a seer of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*)? For, by means of such a seer of supersensible objects—who would otherwise be able to establish a restriction to a single meaning among words that possess multiple meanings—one might [otherwise] suspect various specific meanings.
Among the Vedic [texts], there is no such person who has discerned this supersensuous meaning, or who has distinguished it, saying, "This is its meaning, not that. (1)

He explains by means of the words "it does not exist," and so forth: "For this [usage] is not like the worldly convention of non-human, unauthored treatises—such as the linguistic usage of Pāṇini and others—because it depends upon instruction. It is not [the case that it is independent].

In that which is non-human (apauruṣeya), instruction is not tenable because it cannot be known by anyone; for it is beyond the senses (atīndriya). If it were within the range of the senses, it would follow that it could be apprehended by oneself, like color and so forth. Furthermore, regarding instruction, since there is no established non-contradiction in the instructions of independent persons given according to reality, there can be no confidence in them.

If it is argued that, like the Vedas, its commentary is authorless (*apauruṣeya*), having come down through an uninterrupted tradition, and therefore the meaning is established from it—no; for even that, being of the nature of words, is subject to the same inquiry: "How was its meaning known?
For a person can indeed teach the meaning of words he has himself mastered to one who is ignorant, even by pointing directly at each term (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*).
It does not arise from a relationship between the word and its object; rather, it arises from convention (*samaya*), which is characterized by the expression of intention.

How so? "As in the case of the authors of their own treatises," and so forth. It is like the linguistic usage of terms such as *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* among those who follow that convention—namely, Pāṇini and others—based on the convention (*saṃketa*) of the authors of their respective treatises. What [is the point]?
The reason [is] (1) because it depends upon instruction.
For if even worldly linguistic usage were established by nature (*nisargasiddha*), then it would not depend upon the instruction of others.

Furthermore, the comprehension of meaning from an authorless [Vedic] connection does not occur in the same way as the comprehension of meaning from a conventional connection, which depends upon instruction.

The comprehension of the meaning of the Veda arises solely from the relationship [between word and object] which depends upon instruction; for, since that Vedic relationship between word and object is not of human origin, an instruction by another person is not tenable therein. What is the reason? Because no person whatsoever knows that meaning of the Veda, and because the meaning of the Veda is beyond the reach of the senses for those who do not know it. As it has been said:
"For it is from the Veda alone that this [action] is eternally understood as a means to the highest good (*śreyas*);
and because its nature as *dharma* consists in being such [a means], it is therefore not within the range of the sense organs.
For the highest good is the pleasure of the person, and that [pleasure] is [brought about] by substances, qualities, and actions."
"Therefore, dharma is to be established by means of those [means] characterized by injunction (*codanā*).

For if it were admitted that the meaning of the Veda is perceptible by the senses, it would follow—just as in the case of color and so forth—that the meaning of the Veda could be cognized even without instruction; that is, just as color and other such objects are cognized without instruction because they are perceptible by the senses, so too would the Vedic meaning be.

Now, if it is accepted that instruction is required even regarding the supersensuous meaning of the Veda for the sake of certainty, then, regarding that very instruction—since those men who instruct on the meaning of the Veda are independent [agents] and, due to being overcome by passion and other defects, lack perfect knowledge and act according to their own whims—their instruction cannot be established as non-contradictory with reality; thus, there is no confidence and no certainty regarding the meaning of the Veda. Not so.

If it is argued that ignorant persons are incapable of teaching according to reality, and that individuals do not teach according to their own whim, but rather—just like the Veda—the commentary on the Veda is also authorless (*apauruṣeya*), having come down through an uninterrupted tradition characterized by a succession of instruction; and therefore, the meaning of the Veda is established from such a commentary on the Veda as described: (1)

He states the reply: "Of that too," and so forth. If that commentary on the Veda is also of the nature of sound—that is, if its intrinsic nature is that of sound—then the same objection applies as it does to the Veda: "How is the meaning of this non-human (apauruṣeya) commentary on the Veda known? From what, then, could the determination of the Veda’s meaning arise from it? However, this fault does not apply to a human scripture (*āgama*), because a person [is the source].

(Ślokavārttika 1.1.4, verse 14) Furthermore, for human compositions, there is concern regarding the means by which their meaning is understood. But an authorless word does not act in this way; nor is anyone anywhere capable of knowing its fixed relationship [to a meaning]. Thus, there would be a total lack of comprehension regarding its meaning.

Furthermore, (1) regarding the fact that the Veda or its commentary, when being taught by one person to another, continues to follow an unbroken tradition— here too, convention (*samaya*) is the refuge. This is because those who cause the corruption of the scripture do so either out of arrogance, out of hatred for that philosophical system, out of a rogue’s desire to humiliate its adherents, or for some other reason.
Because it is possible for the arrangement [of words] to be otherwise due to some cause;
moreover, out of attachment to your own doctrine, you have surely forgotten your own position here:
"A person afflicted by passion and other defects might speak even what is untrue; therefore, his word is not a valid means of knowledge. Why, then, is this not the case here as well?

One examines whether [the meaning] is possible or not. That very person, teaching without error, [teaches] the Veda and the meaning of the Veda; he makes known to an ignorant person who does not yet understand—by way of "seizing by the horn" (definitively)—that "this is the meaning of this word," among the words that have been mutually agreed upon by those assembled together. Thus, there exists in human words a capacity for conveying meaning.

In the case of knowledge, there is no means [of comprehension] for those [Vedic words] that are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). For instance, a word that is not of human origin does not act in such a way as to say, "This is my meaning;

it should be grasped by one possessed of passion and so forth. Nor is any person such as Jaimini or others, being possessed of passion and so forth, capable of knowing or establishing the rule of connection for this non-human word regarding any object beyond the senses.
There is simply no comprehension of its meaning—that is, the meaning of the Veda.

Furthermore, even if the Veda and its commentary were indeed non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*), nevertheless, when taught by a person possessed of passion and other defects to another person, it would continue to persist today only as an unbroken tradition (*anaṣṭasaṃpradāya*). (In this case too...)

"Because there is a lack of authoritative evidence, oaths and the like are the refuge for those who cause the destruction of the tradition"—by such statements, he establishes the very possibility of a different composition through the interruption of the lineage. The connection is as follows: "For men who cause the destruction of the tradition, [there is] otherwise," because a composition is observed that is contrary to the previous composition. He states the cause for this alternative composition:
Regarding the phrase "out of self-aggrandizement" (*āhopuruṣikayā*) and so forth: "out of self-aggrandizement" means by way of ego-inflation (*ahaṃmānitva*).

For example, Mādhaba, the destroyer of Sāṃkhya, composed a distorted version of the Sāṃkhya tenets; this was because a distorted composition could not have occurred except through hatred for that system. Or, for example, those who were hostile to the Mahāyāna composed other sūtras that were mere counterfeits of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of humiliating those who have adopted that [view]": it means that for the person who has adopted that philosophical system (*darśana*), there is the possibility of constructing [the argument] otherwise in order to humiliate him. How exactly does this humiliation of those who have adopted it occur? Through the vice of being a rogue (*dhūrta*).
This vice of rogues is the thought that another must be humiliated, or else for some other reason such as the acquisition of profit and so forth.

Moreover, regarding this determination of the meaning of the Veda, you either know it or do not; yet, for the reason that you are attached to your own doctrine, you merely describe your own "mukhavarṇa"—that is, you embellish your own face.
You have surely forgotten your own admission, since you request the determination of the Veda’s meaning from persons defiled by passion and other such flaws.

With the words "The person" (*puruṣa*) and so forth, he explains the flaw of the speaker. Since a person is afflicted by passion and other [defilements] and is thus deluded, he might even speak what is untrue; therefore, the word of this person is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). (1 | 322) *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* (1 | 322).

Or he might teach it otherwise; for indeed, certain other recensions (*śākhāntara*) are heard to have been recovered by some individuals from what had been lost. Even now, some [recensions] have few students. Just as that is possible, so too the destruction of those with many students could have occurred at some time or another. Furthermore, this is established through the trustworthiness of persons who are considered reliable.
Furthermore, because there is the possibility of frequent encounters with them;

and because it is possible that those propagators of the teachings—who may have forgotten what they studied—or others might give a distorted instruction due to fear of losing their reputation and so forth; and because, through trust in them, their devotees accept [the teaching] without inquiry even when many [contradictory views] exist.

Why is it that even here, in the sequence of the tradition of the Vedic meaning being established by persons such as Jaimini, one does not examine whether it is possible or not? For that very person, being subject to passion and other defects, might teach the Veda or the Vedic meaning otherwise due to the influence of passion and so forth; thus, it would be false.
A doubt is not at all dispelled;

rather, [the author], demonstrating the very causes for such doubt, says: "For it is heard," and so forth. By certain persons, such as Yājñavalkya and others, those [Vedic branches] which had been lost (*utsanna*) were recovered (*uddhṛta*). "Lost" means interrupted; there exist other branches of the Veda (*vedaśākhāntara*).

The [verses] have been extracted; having remembered them again and again, they have been reconstructed. And what is the proof here that these were extracted after being remembered according to their true nature? Even now, certain other recensions (*śākhāntara*), such as the Āhūraka and others, are seen to have few students and very few readers. Those few—
What is the proof that the students do not teach by superimposition?

It is observed that other branches (śākhās) have few students; likewise, even for those other branches that currently have many or very many students, there is the possibility within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) that at some point in the past they had few students.
Because of the impossibility of their being considered [authoritative]. For there is no evidence that they were widely studied even previously.
To the question, "How then are they widely studied now?", he says: "Again," and so forth.

That is, due to the conviction—that is, the authoritative status—of a person who has been considered trustworthy at another time, [there arises] the study by other persons who were not previously considered trustworthy.
There is uncertainty because it is possible that those students who have been withdrawn [from other branches] by way of reversal might become numerous— that is, reach a great abundance.
Furthermore, as for those men who have become rare— the propagators of the various other branches— their propagation...
The connection is that "there is the possibility of teachers teaching otherwise. And thus, the intention is that there would be a lack of confidence [in their teachings].

Of what kind of teachers? Of those who have at some time forgotten what they had studied. They are so described as those by whom the study, though once learned, has been forgotten. The meaning is that, being forgetful of what was studied, they might expound it in a manner other than it was originally taught.

He asks: "For what reason? and says: [It is] out of fear of the loss of that great esteem which others—those who are devoted to it and those who study it—have for him as their teacher. [He thinks: "If I were to teach otherwise, they would surely abandon their well-founded confidence in me. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [he refers to] pride (*āhopuruṣikā*) and so forth; [otherwise...]

[The validity of the word] arises from its origin in a [particular] place. Furthermore, there is the consideration of what has been attained: because it is observed that understanding [of the meaning] occurs frequently based on a person who is considered reliable; yet even from such a person, deception can somehow occur.
Furthermore, (1) we hear from you as well that there is merely a succession of limited human commentators.
In that regard, there might be someone who is among those who are hostile, ignorant, or deceitful; thus, there is no confidence.
Therefore, the meaning of the Veda is not established through non-human commentary, nor through conventional worldly usage.

Even if [the connection] were not based on convention (*asāmayikatva*), since words with multiple meanings are observed in common usage, and because one observes the re-acquisition of meaning for certain words whose meanings are unknown or unestablished, the suspicion that this might apply everywhere does not cease.
Furthermore, even if all [words] were restricted to their respective referents, since they produce cognition according to convention without deficiency, [the desired result is achieved]. Desired—

"Let them indeed propagate [the Veda] otherwise; nevertheless, the students would not understand it in that way," he says with the words beginning "tad" (that). Because of trust in that person who is held in high esteem, those who have confidence in the author of that [work] would study and understand the Veda without critical inquiry, thereby resulting in a different tradition. [This concerns] the person—

Establishing that activity [toward an object] occurs precisely because of its validity, he says: because in the world, among many students, activity is frequently observed to arise from a person who is considered reliable (*sambhāvita*). Now, one might object: "If understanding arises from a reliable person, there is necessarily a correspondence (*saṃvāda*) [with reality]. To this, he replies: "Even from such a reliable person..."

From a person, somehow—by some cause such as the fear of losing one's reputation—there arises the possibility of *vipralambha*, that is, deception. He states the reason for this accumulation [of faults] with the words "Furthermore," and so forth: "And those persons who have been explained are limited..."
In this matter of explaining the Veda, we hear only a tradition from you Mīmāṃsakas.

Among those [tradition-holders], one might be a commentator on the Veda who is one of those characterized by hatred and so forth; another might be hostile toward the vision of the Veda and thus teach otherwise; likewise, some might be ignorant or deceitful. Consequently, there is a lack of confidence in the explanation of the Veda.

Since this is so, the meaning of the Veda is not established through an authorless (apauruṣeya) commentary on the Veda, nor is the meaning of the Veda established through worldly usage, which is conventional and based on social convention; for the world is afflicted by passion and other defects. Or, let it be granted that Vedic words are innate and independent of convention; even so, they would remain non-conventional—

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: even if [the non-eternality of words] were admitted, since words such as "cow" (*go*) are seen to have multiple meanings in common usage, the suspicion regarding them would not cease even in the case of every Vedic word. This means that the suspicion of multiple meanings would not be removed.
If it is argued that only worldly words have multiple meanings and not Vedic ones, he says: "Of any [word]," and so forth; for that [Vedic word] too...

Regarding some Vedic word whose meaning is not well-known: whether it be a case where the word is well-known but its meaning is not, or where the word itself is unknown, a person must determine the meaning by demonstrating its etymology once again. And this being so, does the person teach the meaning of the Vedic words exactly as it stands, or otherwise?

Because the doubt that [words] have multiple meanings persists everywhere, it is also incorrect to claim that Vedic words, even when employed for an unintended object, do not produce a cognition of that [intended] object; for there is no distinction between the two cases. Since these words are indistinguishable with respect to all objects, one who does not possess supersensuous vision cannot perceive a single specific meaning among them through a connection that is not supersensuous.
Who could distinguish [the specific] from the general category of "person" on the basis of worldly convention? Moreover, even this [proponent] does not himself follow established usage in all cases;
for instance, words such as "heaven" (*svarga*) and "Urvaśī" are seen to denote conventional meanings.
Being described by this very [passage]:
"Heaven is the abode of a person who transcends humanity, a locus of superhuman pleasures, and possesses various implements; the celestial nymph dwelling there is named Urvaśī. (1)
Disregarding worldly convention (lokavāda), this person constructs a different conceptualization of the object; how then could he validate what is well-known regarding other words?

If it is argued that there is acceptance [of the convention] because there is no contradiction in those cases, we say no; for even here, in the case of supersensible objects, contradiction is established.

For, even though all words—both worldly and Vedic—are employed according to their actual referents, there is an *avyayībhāva* compound with *yathārtham* used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). This is because, despite the fact that a convention (*saṃketa*) has been established for each specific referent, a cognition is produced in each respective case exactly as agreed upon and as per the convention, without any deficiency. Furthermore, there is no production of an unintended or contrary cognition; for...

Because there is no distinction in the production of cognition regarding desired and undesired objects due to the absence of proximity or remoteness, all Vedic words—which are indistinguishable with respect to all objects—would have only a single meaning. What kind of specific [meaning] would it be? It is that which has a connection with the word that is beyond the range of perception (*atyakṣasaṃyoga*). For one who does not perceive what is beyond the senses—that is, for a person of limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*)—[this would be the case].

Who could distinguish [the meaning] in a general sense? No one at all could distinguish it, since the understanding would derive from common worldly usage. Moreover, this Mīmāṃsaka himself does not follow established consensus regarding the entire Veda, by which the comprehension of the Vedic meaning might proceed from the well-known worldly discourse. What is the reason? Because [he rejects] heaven, the lineage, and so forth—

And there is the word "heaven" (svarga). The word "urvarśī," and by the word "etcetera" (ādi), words such as "Nandanavana" and so forth are observed to be explained and interpreted by this proponent of the Veda as denoting either a conventional meaning or an unfamiliar meaning. For instance, it is described as the abode or dwelling place of those superior persons who transcend ordinary men.

It is a bliss transcending that of humans, a superhuman bliss; it is the locus, the support, of that superhuman bliss. There is a diverse report: the worldly rumor is that the celestial nymph named Urvaśī, who dwells in heaven, resides there. Disregarding that worldly rumor, heaven is simply unsurpassed delight among human beings; and Urvaśī is the lower fire-drill (*araṇi*), the vessel.

By the words "or" (*vā*) and so forth, [the author means]: how could this Jaimini and others, who construct a conceptualization of meaning entirely different from that which is well-known in the world, rely upon common usage as a valid authority when determining the meaning of other terms such as *agnihotra*? The sense is that they would certainly not rely upon it as a valid authority.

If it is argued that in the case of words such as *agnihotra*, one accepts the very meaning as it is understood because there is no contradiction in postulating a meaning well-known in the world, whereas in the case of words such as *svarga* (heaven) and *urvaśī* (the nymph), one does not accept the well-known meaning because it contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)— this is what the opponent thinks. [This concludes] the "Investigation of the Authoritative Person" (*Āptacintā*).

Furthermore, because non-contradiction is difficult to establish even in other cases, one might not even perceive that the attainment of heaven from the Agnihotra sacrifice is contradicted by slowness and so forth. Moreover, contradiction and non-contradiction consist in the operation of subverting and proving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and those two are not admitted in the case of what is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
Therefore, how could there be a cognition [of such a result] on the basis of them?

Nor is mere verbal consistency itself non-contradiction, because that would lead to over-extension (*prasaṅga*) elsewhere as well. If the scripture were not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), its meaning would be established through its proclamations; however, if one were to investigate contradictions therein, there would be a lack of confidence in the scripture. [The author] states "even though it exists" and so forth, referring to the proponent of the tenet (*siddhāntavādī*). It is appropriate [to speak of] the distinction just mentioned, because even here, heaven—
When words such as *vaśyā* (a type of plant) are accepted as having meanings well-known in common worldly usage, there is no contradiction with any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),

for in these cases there exists neither perception nor inference that could subvert them. However, this principle cannot be easily extended elsewhere— that is, even to words such as *agnihotra*— because it is difficult to maintain the absence of contradiction when assuming meanings based on common worldly usage, given the lack of any supporting evidence (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*).
Because it is difficult to understand.

Proving this very point, he says: there is doubt that perhaps even someone like Jaimini and others might not perceive the attainment of heaven from the Agnihotra sacrifice, even though it is contrary [to reason] yet well-known as established by tradition. Furthermore: (1)
Furthermore, contradiction and non-contradiction are not two separate entities; rather, they are the operations of subverting and proving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Contradiction is the operation of the subverting means of valid cognition called "non-perception" as previously described. Non-contradiction is the operation of the proving means of valid cognition, namely perception and inference. These two possess the intrinsic nature of contradiction and non-contradiction, respectively. [End of fragment on] the subverting [means].

[The words] function as means of valid cognition for the prover [of the object], but not with respect to an object that is beyond the senses (*atyakṣa*) and transcends the faculties. For indeed, regarding things remote in space and so forth—such as the means for attaining heaven and the like—neither a subverting (*bādhaka*) nor a proving (*sādhaka*) means of valid cognition operates. And since this is so, how could it be "not by virtue of that"?
[This refers to] by virtue of contradiction or non-contradiction. By virtue of contradiction, there is the cognition of the well-known meaning in words such as "heaven" (*svarga*).
Furthermore, the comprehension of the well-known meanings in words such as *agnihotra* occurs by virtue of the absence of contradiction.

Now, it might be thought: (1) "Non-contradiction does not consist in the operation of a validating means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding a supersensible object; rather, non-contradiction is simply the occurrence of the scriptural statement known as *āgama*, such as that concerning the *agnihotra*, in its capacity as a denoter of meanings well-established in the world."

Therefore, he says: "And not," and so forth. The very fact that the statement regarding the *agnihotra* and other rites proceeds by expressing meanings well-established in the world constitutes non-contradiction; and why is this? Because otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-contradiction even in the case of other words such as "heaven" (*svarga*) and "Urvaśī," since they too proceed by expressing [entities] such as heaven. For instance, the words "heaven," "Urvaśī," and so on—

In the world, [the word] is seen to be applied specifically to places, celestial nymphs (*apsaras*), and so forth; therefore, since there is no distinction [between these meanings], let the term be accepted as having its meaning established in both ways. Nor is it restricted to only one.
Furthermore, the scripture known as the Veda is not of human origin, and it does not reveal its own meaning by itself.

However, it is accepted that the establishment of the meaning of that scripture [is based] on worldly consensus. In that case, even if one accepts a jar as established by worldly consensus, if an investigation into contradiction were to be carried out, there would be a lack of confidence in every scripture, because it is impossible to determine whether there is a contradiction or not in regard to supersensible matters.
Establishing that there is indeed no confidence, he says: "Even though that [Veda] exists," and so forth.

Even though that non-human (apauruṣeya) [Veda] exists, because its meaning is not as it appears, it does not function as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the object; furthermore, other [meanings] may also be suspected [of being false].
As it has been said: "In the injunction 'One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra,' there is the teaching of eating dog-meat."
"Let it not be non-conceptual"—this [objection] does not hold, because the meaning is stated in other passages in that same way.
(1) It is not due to a lack of understanding of its meaning, for even in other passages, such a conceptualization of the meaning cannot be prevented.
For if this collection of words were non-human (*apauruṣeya*) and its meaning were known in some instance, then from that [collection], the cognition of the meaning [would follow].

[If one were to argue that] there would be [such a thing as a "universal"], then even though they are numerous, all of them would indeed be blind, and thus they could be led about at will. Therefore, (1) regarding other words of a similar nature, let the conceptualization be exactly like that of the sentence:
"One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra. (322)
Moreover:

"The consensus of people is a discourse, and that is not accepted as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding scripture (āgama), because the referent of words such as 'heaven'—namely, heaven and so forth—is not [as it appears]. 'Tathābhāva' means being thus (tathātva)."

(1) Just as in the world there is the apprehension of the meaning "heaven" (*svarga*) based on common usage because it is not otherwise, so too there is the apprehension of an unfamiliar meaning; consequently, even other words such as *agnihotra* and the like are subject to doubt. Is the meaning of this [word] precisely that which is well-known in the world, or is it something else entirely, just like the word "heaven" and so forth? Why is this so? Because of the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For in this case, if one were to accept the meaning as it is well-known in the world...

"The means of valid cognition functions," [says] the opponent regarding what was stated, and so forth. As for what was stated: "In the sentence 'One should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice,' let there be an option—that is, a conceptualization—of the injunction to eat dog meat. That fault does not apply.

It occurs. What is the reason? Because, in another section of the Veda itself, it is stated that "one should pour ghee and so forth into such-and-such a specific substance"; thus, this is due to the investigation of the meaning of the *agnihotra* and other such passages, that is, from the [Vedic] explanation.
"No," and so forth, is the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*). This response is not tenable, because of that [statement] which stands in another section.

Because the meaning of the sentences that serve as explanations is not fully understood; and consequently, because there would be an assumption of such meanings even in other sections that serve as explanations—since the assumption of eating dog meat would be unavoidable. This [passage beginning with] "If... is a justification for that very point: for if this collection of words called the Veda, which is purportedly non-human (apauruṣeya), were in some place...

If, in another passage, their meaning were known, then from that other passage whose meaning is known, there would be a comprehension of the remaining meaning. However, since those Vedic words, despite their abundance, are entirely like blind men because their meaning is not understood, they are composed and explained by humans according to their own whims.

Since this is so, therefore, regarding "similar other words"—that is, those sentences serving as explanations such as "one should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice" and so forth—let the same kind of interpretation apply. What kind [of interpretation]? He says: just as the interpretation was made for the sentence "one desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra*," the same applies even to the interpretation of eating dog-meat in another context.
It means "it does not exist.

Furthermore, common renown (*prasiddhi*) is not something entirely different; rather, it is the discourse (*vāda*) of men (*nṛṇām*, i.e., *puruṣāṇām*). [This concludes] the investigation of authoritative testimony (*āpta-cintā*).
Furthermore, regarding the understanding of further objects: "Is this [understanding] twofold?

(323) Not so; for 'common renown' (prasiddhi) is nothing other than public report (janapravāda). And all those people, being overwhelmed by ignorance such as passion and the like, are incapable of speaking with words that correspond to reality. Therefore, their report is not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa)."

For indeed, in the absence of correct practice by anyone at all, even a great number [of people] does not become meaningful, as in the case of the Persian custom regarding their mothers. Furthermore, if the comprehension of an imperceptible object arises solely from the words of those very persons, how can that same [comprehension] occur simultaneously?
[The object] may be loathsome or desirable;
there is no basis for conceptual construction that transcends established usage regarding an object.
Since established usage is not an independent means of valid cognition, what would be the basis for grasping it [otherwise]? (324)

The engagement in something else through the reversal of what has been attained is consistent with the observation of merits and defects; this is known as *anvaya* (logical concomitance). Yet, you do not accept that such discourse is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because all persons are afflicted by passion and other defilements. The word "again" (*bhūyaḥ*) means "furthermore. Consequently, since popular worldly discourse has been previously established as non-authoritative, the understanding of the meaning of the Vedas cannot arise from it once more.

How can this be simultaneously desired and disliked? For that very same object which is disliked because it lacks authoritative validity (*apramāṇatva*) is again desired and longed for as the cause of its own apprehension; thus there is a mutual contradiction.
What is called "common renown" (*prasiddhi*) is not something other than public report (*janapravāda*); rather, public report itself is common renown. And those...

All people possess speech whose reality is inconceivable; that is, those whose speech possesses a reality (*yāthātathya*) that is inconceivable and non-erroneous—this is the analysis of the compound. What is the reason?
(1) Because they are overcome by passion and ignorance; because they are pervaded by passion and ignorance. Therefore, for them...
The common talk of people is not an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Even the claim that "the talk of people is authoritative because of their great number" is false; for, among many people, if there is not even a single individual who possesses correct practice (*samyakpratipatti*), then [the talk] of the world— [is not authoritative].
Abundance becomes meaningful and purposeful. For example, [the case of] the Persians and so forth:

just as it is not right because many Persians practice sexual intercourse with their mothers, likewise, even if there is abundance, the statement of those possessed of passion and other defects regarding supersensible objects is simply not authoritative.

Now, it might be argued that from the speech of those very persons possessed of passion and other defects, there is again a comprehension of an object beyond the senses, such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice, which is denoted by words. But how can that same [word] be simultaneously appropriate as both something to be hated and something to be desired?

To disregard and abandon the meaning in which words such as *agnihotra* are well-known in common usage (*lokaprasiddhi*), and instead to postulate another meaning—such as the eating of dog meat—is without foundation or cause. Therefore, the claim that "only what is well-known should be accepted" is also untenable; for since common usage is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), if one were to accept it, [it would lead to error].

If it is argued that [the phrase] "not even anything whatsoever" (*naiva kiñcit*) is used so that there might not even be an apprehension based on what is commonly known (*prasiddhi*), we say no. This is because attainment (*prāpti*) is characterized by the operation of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For the mention of "anything whatsoever" implies an understanding through that [common knowledge] while treating it as non-authoritative; thus, since attainment is negated by logic (*nyāya*), the conceptual constructions of self and other are equal [in being negated].
Since the operation [of the word] occurs in both ways, what regard is there for common usage?
Moreover,
this very doubt regarding the determination of the word’s meaning is produced by that very [usage] which is commonly accepted.

Because the polysemous nature of words is observed therein, (325) there is no determination of a single meaning for words based on common usage alone, since doubt arises from that very fact. For words are seen in the world to have multiple meanings, and worldly discourse is based on conventional understanding; thus, they possess multiple meanings. Therefore, there can be no restriction [of meaning].

He first explains the first half [of the verse] with the words beginning "prāptyā" (by means of attainment). It is logical that, when one perceives defects in a well-known meaning and perceives virtues in another, one should proceed toward that other meaning by abandoning the former through its reversal—that is, by rejecting it—since it is not well-established elsewhere. This would be the case if there were a perception of defects in the well-known meaning of the Agnihotra and other terms, and a perception of virtues in what is not so established. However, no such perception of defects exists in the well-known meaning of the words "Agnihotra" and so forth.

If it is argued that, once [the object] is established, there is the perception of its qualities, and therefore from that very establishment follows the "concomitance" (*anvaya*) or following after it—[the author] refutes this with the words beginning with "no. This is an explanation of the second half of the verse. It is not so. Why? Because "attainment" (*prāpti*) is characterized by the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For attainment of an object occurs through a proving means of valid cognition.

Since it is said that [an object] "is ascertained," it follows that attainment (*prāpti*) is the defining characteristic of the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, common consensus (*prasiddhi*) is not itself a means of valid cognition, such that an object established by it would be one attained through logical necessity (*nyāya*). Consequently, for the Mīmāṃsaka who does not regard this very consensus as a means of valid cognition, whatever understanding he has of the referent of words such as *agnihotra* by way of that consensus is merely arbitrary.

[The opponent argues: "Because there is no authoritative means of knowledge [for it], its apprehension is merely arbitrary; that is to say, the meaning of words such as *agnihotra* is not established by logic (*nyāya*) as it is well-known in common worldly usage. Thus, because the attainment of the meaning as it is known in the world is precluded by logic, the meaning of words like *agnihotra* is determined by mere whim."

It is to be conceptually constructed. In that regard, regarding both of these conceptual constructions— namely, the meaning of words such as *agnihotra* as characterized by burning substances and so forth which is constructed by the Mīmāṃsakas,
and that characterized by the eating of dog-flesh which is [constructed] by the other— if [it were] well-known in both ways...

Furthermore, whether there is preservation [of a conventional meaning] or non-preservation, since there is an absence of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*), the mode of operation would be the same if one were to accept [meanings] according to mere whim;

thus, what established usage (*prasiddhi*) is there by which a specific meaning could be postulated based on that established usage? Moreover, if the meaning of all words were determined solely by established usage, then this very doubt regarding their having multiple meanings would arise.
[Objection: What is the reason? Because the application of words such as "fire" (*agni*) to [other] objects is not observed in common usage (*prasiddhi*).
He explains this with the words beginning with "not" (*na*): there is no determination of a single meaning for Vedic words based on common usage.

What is the reason? (1) Precisely because it is established from that very source, doubt arises. For instance, words such as "fire" are seen in common usage to have multiple meanings. And this observation of multiple meanings is worldly discourse, worldly tradition, and conventional cognition; therefore, it is not tenable [to claim] that [the word's meaning] is restricted to one alone. Thus, the inquiry begins.
"Since there is no impossibility otherwise, the sound itself does not possess multiple powers;
therefore, those who do not perceive a restrictive factor must necessarily entertain doubt.
(326) This is an intermediate verse (1).

Therefore, since Jaimini— having determined a single meaning for words whose distinctions of referents are unknown, which are beyond sensory contact, and which involve a superimposition lacking a basis—
expounds them under that pretext, we perceive no distinction between him and other founders of philosophical systems (tīrthakara).

For instance: (1) The designation of something that is devoid of the activity of expressing that [specific] meaning by superimposing it upon it does not surpass one's own statement. Since a person who acts thus merely illuminates his own false pretension of discipline and the fact that he follows worldly conventions, there is no restriction to a single meaning for Vedic words based on those worldly conventions.

This is not tenable. Strengthening the point that the meaning is indeed indeterminate, he says "otherwise," and so forth. Because there is no possibility of it being otherwise for *dhvani*—that is, for sound—which by its own nature possesses various capacities and is capable of conveying multiple meanings; [it would follow that] from the intended meaning, another meaning [would arise].

Otherwise, there would be a different mode of operation (*vṛtti*). Since that other mode of operation is impossible, there is "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathā-asambhava*), because of its absence. This means that by means of two negations, an affirmation is accepted, since [the word] could also exist in another way. Consequently, in the case of Vedic words whose operation concerns supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*), there must necessarily be a suspicion of multiple meanings (*anekārthavṛttitva*). For whom, then, is there a restrictive factor?

For those persons who perceive [the world], there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes specific objects; for those who do not perceive it—since this is so—the analysis of the compound is as follows: "those for whom the distinction between objects is unknown.
Among those words for which the distinction between objects is unknown, one might intend a single object; what is its nature? It is that which has a connection beyond the senses (*atyakṣasaṃyoga*).
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "atyakṣatīndriyasaṃyoga" means that for which there is a connection with a word that transcends the senses. "Ālambana" refers to that very [connection];

thus, one for whom there is a superimposition (samāropa) that lacks such a basis—being without a means of valid cognition (niḥpramāṇaka) due to the absence of that [connection]—is described in that way.

Having ascertained the actual fact, Jaimini, while explaining it, says "by way of that" (*tadvyājena*), meaning he expresses his own view under the guise of the Veda, saying "the Veda itself speaks thus. However, another teacher (*tīrthakara*) speaks thus without such a pretext, saying "I myself speak this. Therefore, there is no distinction between this Jaimini and that other teacher.
We see this. Establishing precisely the lack of distinction, he says: "For it is thus," and so forth. That which is both "that" and "the object" is "tadartha" (that-object);
its manifestation is the statement (*vacana*). In that regard, the operation is the capacity; [he refers to] the Veda being devoid of—that is, lacking—that [capacity]. Its superimposition...

By superimposing the activity of manifesting an object through the word "pena," the designation "he speaks thus" is merely his own statement; that is to say, it is his own word regarding one who performs that [act] while being devoid of the actual operation of speech.

By superimposing upon [the Veda] the operation of manifesting the meaning of what is seen, the Jaiminīyas would merely be revealing their own lack of logical consistency; there would be no distinction between this [Veda] and a human statement. 604.
It would be so.
Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā (1.327): For instance, someone might say, "This is a post; this is the path."
The distinction between these two— [the one who says] "another [speaks]" and the one who says "I myself speak"— should be examined.

(327) Whether one attributes speech to an inanimate post as having activity devoid of intention, or whether one teaches an independent [agent], there is no difference whatsoever in accepting the statement of its own function, except for the dullness of comprehension on the part of the insentient.

Furthermore: If one were to know this through the restriction of meaning (*arthaniyama*), then how could there be such a restriction for a word that is capable [of expressing] every object, in the illumination of a single meaning?
For no object of a word is restricted by its own nature (*svabhāva*), because it is capable of [expressing] everything. Therefore—

Furthermore, because that [nature] does not deviate, and because it is impossible for persons—who are not subject to its command—to bring about or remove anything in any respect, he says the following to clarify this very point: "For instance," and so forth. When asked, "Which is the path leading to Pāṭaliputra?", a certain man replies: "I do not know myself; I can only say that this post is the way."
Thus, one person, devoid of the capacity to instruct on the path, points out the way under the guise of a post. But another says:

"The post has no power of speech; it is I myself who, having known this path, am saying so. While these two are speaking in this manner, let their difference in speech be examined by oneself—whether it exists or indeed does not exist; such is the intended meaning.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "without intention" (*nirabhiprāya*). Intention (*abhiprāya*) is the volition, "I shall do this and that. The activity (*vyāpāra*) is the effort preceded by that [volition]. [The compound] refers to that in which intention, activity, and speech do not exist; such is what is described. Upon such a pillar as this, sit down after superimposing the quality of being a guide for the path.

The connection [of the sentence] is: "either for one man who is independent, or for another who teaches the path while being independent of a post. Between these two men, if they both accept their own statement, there is no distinction whatsoever, except that the dull-witted listener lacks comprehension; it is only the dull-witted listener’s lack of comprehension that is distinguished. Because of this intention and so forth—

One understands that the speech of an empty post is uttered by the post itself. In the same way, when Jaimini expresses his own view under the guise of the Veda, the dull-witted person, due to their lack of discernment, understands it as "the Veda speaks thus. Furthermore, if a Vedic word were restricted to a single meaning, then Jaimini [would have to acknowledge] this restriction to a single meaning.

One should understand this as follows: since a word, as a signifier capable of denoting any object whatsoever, possesses the fitness to illuminate any single object, why is there not a restriction [to one specific object]? For no object is restricted to a word by its own nature through innate establishment.
What is the reason? Because the word possesses the capacity for every object that can be expressed.

Furthermore, if the word were not capable of signifying every object, then, because that incapacity does not depart—since an eternal word cannot deviate from its own nature of incapacity—it would be impossible for persons to apply it, as a signifier, to any particular object, nor could they withdraw it once applied; for such a word is not subject to human control and is independent of them. Now, this [word]...

Because it is impossible for a word to be a signifier [on its own], and because [a speaker] exists, therefore in all cases the word is the signifier. [Thus: "Who, other than through the expression of intention (*vivakṣā*), could know supersensible things? (328).
For when a word is produced by a person, it is sometimes [understood] by someone through a particular intention.

Even if one intends to convey [a specific meaning], a restriction of meaning for words preceded by such intention might still be perceived. However, in the case of that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), how can a restriction of meaning be known even if it exists? This is because there is no difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, if such a difference were present, it would follow that it must be perceived directly (*pratyakṣa*) by itself. Even if it were not directly perceived, it would be impossible for anyone to know it. And yet, it does not exist—

There is a certain distinction: for all words are devoid of proximity or remoteness with respect to all objects. Therefore, (1) the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) is the cause for restricting them [to a specific object], and linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) is that which reveals it.
"In that which is not of human origin, that [intention] does not exist; how then could there be its [the Veda's] status as having a single meaning?

(329) Thus, there is no manifestation of a single meaning. Or, even if there were a restriction to a single meaning for the Vedic [words], a person would still be unable to know that restriction of meaning, which transcends the senses.

[The opponent] is capable [of this objection]. He states that very point: By what person could supersensuous objects be known? For the Mīmāṃsaka does not accept anyone as a seer of supersensuous objects. Without the expression of the intention to speak—that is, without speech which makes the intention to speak manifest—supersensuous objects are certainly not [known] by anyone at all, even in the absence of stating the speaker’s intention.
The meaning is "one who knows.

He explains this with the words beginning with "puruṣa" (person). When a word has been composed and uttered by a person with a certain intention (*vivakṣā*), that person might at some time communicate that intention to a certain listener, [saying]: "This was intended by me as the thing to be expressed (*vācya*)."

Regarding the word "that": while a restriction regarding the meaning of words preceded by a speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) may indeed be understood, how could a restriction of meaning be known—even if it existed—in the case of a non-human (Vedic) word that has not been employed by anyone with such an intention? Not at all.
Why? Because there is no difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*). For a Vedic word possesses no particular intrinsic nature [to distinguish it].
That [difference] which is distinct must be restricted to a single intended object, because it is through the perception of that [difference] that the cognition of the desired object occurs.

Alternatively, even if there were a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), that difference in intrinsic nature would have to be either perceptible or imperceptible. It cannot first be perceptible; for what reason? Because an intrinsic nature that is perceptible does not depend on verbal instruction, and thus it would follow that it is cognized by itself.

[The word] "gāt" [is used]. Now, as for that which is not perceived (*apratyakṣa*): even though it is not perceived, because there is an absence of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it cannot be known by anyone who sees only the immediate (*arvāgdarśana*). This was stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position]. Furthermore, there is no particular distinction whatsoever that is restricted to a single object; [rather], all—
For words are devoid of both proximity and remoteness with respect to all objects.

Indeed, certain words are not inherently proximate or remote toward any particular object; rather, since those words are by their very nature equal with respect to all objects, the cause for restricting them to a single meaning is the speaker’s intention regarding the thing (*vastu*) and the convention (*saṃketa*).
"Manifestation of that" means that the convention (*saṃketa*) is the manifestation of that intention to speak (*vivakṣā*).

For it is understood from the convention that "this is the meaning intended by him. And since that intention to speak does not exist in a human-made word, [it is said: "For a word is restricted to meanings by intention, not by its own nature. Regarding that... *Note: The provided Sanskrit fragment appears to be a commentary on the relationship between linguistic convention, speaker-intention, and the non-arbitrary nature of word-meaning.*

Because there is an equality in the connection [of all words] everywhere; and even where there is a connection, there is no necessity for its specific designation, which would result in the undesirable consequence that the word "all" would apply to all instruments of cognition. Therefore, a convention (*saṅketa*)—characterized by the communication of intention—is established in order to manifest the speaker's desire to speak (*vivakṣā*). But in that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), there is neither the desire to speak nor a convention, because there is no intention of anyone [to speak].
There would be neither a restriction [of usage] nor knowledge of that [restriction].
(15) If there were a restriction by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-niyama*), it could not be applied again elsewhere.
Furthermore, if a word were inherently attached to objects independently of convention (*saṃketa*), it has been said in this regard:

(1) It is "determined" because there is no obstruction. Furthermore, if the relationship between the signifier and the signified were inherent (*svābhāvika*), it could not be directed at will by a speaker's intention, and convention (*saṃketa*) would be purposeless. (330)
From where does that aforementioned singularity of meaning of that non-human (apauruṣeya) word come? Not at all.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "for there is the intention to speak" (*vivakṣā*). By the intention to speak acting as the cause, the word is restricted to objects such that "this is the designator of this very object. But it is not so by way of its own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*). What is the reason? Because of that word...

Because, due to the absence of a connection—namely, the lack of a necessary bond (*apratibandha*) with respect to any given object—the word is identical in meaning everywhere. Even in cases where there is a bond for the word with respect to the places of articulation (*sthāna*) and the producing organs (*karaṇa*), since words arise from or are manifested by them, there is still no fixed rule for the denotation of those organs by all words; for indeed, not all words [denote] the organs.

Furthermore, while words that denote instruments might convey those very instruments, the inclusion of the term "all" [in the definition] is intended to show that words can also denote other things. Since this is the case, a convention (*saṃketa*) is established for the purpose of manifesting the speaker's intention. Of what nature is it? It is characterized by the communication of intention; that is, it is characterized by the manifestation of the speaker's intention. However, in the case of a word that is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), there is no such thing.

The intention to speak is the regulator; nor is convention the revealer of that [intention]. Why? Because, since there is no cessation of persons and because no particular intention exists [to govern them], there is no restriction to a single meaning for Vedic words.
