Or, even if such a restriction were to exist, no one would possess knowledge of it—that is, knowledge of the restriction to a single meaning. For [Vedic words] are by their very nature restricted to a single meaning.
Vedic words do not depend upon the speaker's intention.
Thus, when their inherent restriction is accepted, that word is not dissociated from its other meaning by that intention.

He explains by means of the words beginning with *yadi*. If it were logical for a word to be inherently attached to objects independently of convention (*saṃketa*), the answer to this has already been stated: "(1) because there is no necessary connection (*apratibandha*) to any particular object, [the application] would be indeterminate. Furthermore, if the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*) were accepted as being natural (*svābhāvika*) or established by nature (*nisargasiddha*), then—

Furthermore, by the desire to speak, a word is employed at will for another meaning. For it is not possible to employ the eye—which is restricted by its own nature to the illumination of form—for the illumination of sound. Yet, a word is employed at will; therefore, it is not restricted by its own nature, just like a hand gesture or other signs. If words were restricted to their objects by their own nature, there would be no need for convention (*saṃketa*). This concludes the *Āptacintā*.

It might be so. For a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) is not accessible to the senses in its own cognition in such a way that it depends on linguistic convention (*paribhāṣā*) and the like, as is the case with the distinction between blue and other colors. However, those cognitions which depend on [convention] do not pertain to the intrinsic nature of things; rather, they are like royal insignia or signs of authority. This is because that which is conventional and restricted by intrinsic nature is logically impossible, since it would function according to mere whim.

Precisely because of this convention (*saṅketa*), how could there be a restriction regarding the manifestation of a specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*)? Convention functions according to one’s own will; it can be established here and not elsewhere, as there is no obstruction [to doing so]. Since it is created by persons according to their own will, there is no restriction that it must manifest that very intrinsic nature and not another.
"Where there is freedom for the will, what indeed is restriction? Therefore, a convention would only manifest its intended fitness. (331) — this is an intermediate verse.

It would be meaningless and fruitless; for a distinction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) or a specific characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) is not accessible to the senses through its own cognition via technical terminology (*paribhāṣā*) and so forth. "Technical terminology" means convention (*saṃketa*). By the word "and so forth," the recollection of conventions and other such factors are included.
How is this so? Like the distinctions of blue and so forth. Just as the specific qualities of blue and so forth [are perceived] in their own cognition [without depending on] convention and the like.

They do not depend on it in that way. However, those cognitions which depend upon it—namely, those cognitions which depend upon convention—are not the intrinsic natures of things; they are not properties of a thing established by its very nature (*nisargasiddha*). Rather, they are conventional, produced by convention. How so? Like royal insignia and the like. Just as banners and such are designated by a king for his own recognition...

The various types of signs include hand gestures and so forth, as indicated by the word "etcetera. It is logical that a conventional sign is restricted by its own nature; it is not logical for it to be established by nature alone. Why? Because that conventional sign functions according to the will of the person.

If it is argued that "in the case of a Vedic word, a specific inherent nature is fixed by its very essence regarding its meaning, but that [nature] is merely manifested through convention," he replies with the words "For this very reason," and so forth. Because its operation is based on desire, for that very reason...
"How can there be a restriction [of a word] to the manifestation of a specific nature fixed to a single object by convention?

(1) He explains this very point: convention operates according to one's own will; it can be established for this intended object alone and not for another—there is no obstruction [to this], nor is there any [intrinsic] denotative power [in the word]. Therefore, that convention is established by the person according to their own will.

When being employed, [a word] manifests only that specific nature restricted to a single meaning and not any other; thus, there is no fixed rule. Since there is freedom of will regarding the convention (*saṃketa*), what kind of restriction could there be in that case? The meaning is that there is no restriction at all. For this reason—namely, because of this lack of restriction—the intended object of this Vedic word is indeed established as desired.
[The opponent argues: "Convention would not indicate that very fitness [of the word for its object].
Thus, it has been demonstrated that being authorless (*apauruṣeyatva*) is not the defining characteristic of scripture (*āgama*).
(608) Refutation of Jaimini’s view:
If [the Veda] were authoritative only because it accords with a portion of the Veda, then not all of it would be authoritative;
for another person has said: "Indeed, such a statement as 'fire is the dispeller of cold' is true because it is a part of the Veda; therefore, other statements are also [true]. (332)
But another, rejecting the definition of scripture as being non-human in origin, desiring to establish the authority of the Veda in another way, says:

"The Vedic statements are non-false regarding that which is not [otherwise] understood, because they are part of the Veda, just like the statement: (1) 'Fire is the remedy for cold,' and so forth. (1)
This [inference] of his—(1) because it possesses a similar form like that of flavor, and because it is like cooking in a single vessel;
yet, because it is subject to deviation, it has been cast aside as a pseudo-reasoning by those who know logic. (333)

The Teacher himself, having thus raised the objection that the Naiyāyika’s *śeṣavat* inference is fallacious, now presents the following argument in order to refute the definition of scripture (*āgama*) as being "non-contradictory in one respect" (*ekadeśāvisamvādana*). He begins with the words "Because," etc.
The particle *kila* indicates the speaker's intention. Fire is "the dispeller of cold," meaning it is the remover of cold. By this—

"Just as the statement 'Fire is the remedy for cold' is true, so too another statement such as 'One should offer the Agnihotra and so forth' is not false; this is the probandum (*sādhya*). 'Because it is a part of that same [Vedic] collection' is the reason (*hetu*). Thus spoke another elder Mīmāṃsaka. He said:

He explains [the passage] beginning with "But another," and so forth. "Another" refers to a Mīmāṃsaka. Because [the Veda] is afflicted by the aforementioned defects, he—having rejected the definition of scripture as being authorless (apauruṣeya)—desiring to establish the validity of the Veda in another way, says:
"Not false," and so forth. "Where there is non-comprehension" means those Vedic sentences regarding which the Buddhist has no comprehension of their being non-false.

By the statement "these [scriptures] are false," the specific [quality] is made the subject (*pakṣa*). As for the phrase "because they are a part of the Veda," since the general property is taken as the reason (*hetu*), the reason does not constitute a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*). This is just as in the sentence "Fire is the remedy for cold," where it serves as a counter-position, and so forth. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the twelve months [are included] as the year.
This includes such statements as these. He provides the answer with the words "of that," and so forth. This proof (*sādhana*) of that proponent is *śeṣavat* [an inference based on remainder]. Why?
Because it is fallible (*vyabhicāritvāt*). Such an inference was [rejected] by the master Dignāga, the knower of logic, in his *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.
The connection is with the word "rejected" (*pratikṣiptam*). To the question "In what way is it like the *śeṣavat* [type of inference]?", he says: "Like the *rasavat*, etc.
For example, because an un-eaten fruit is of the same nature as a tasted fruit, the un-eaten fruit is likewise [tasted]; this kind of inference is *śeṣavat*.

In the same way, even unobserved grains of rice are cooked because they are cooked in the same vessel as those that have been observed to be cooked; this is like the cooking in a single vessel. Just as such an inference is *śeṣavat* (based on what remains), so too is it stated by the Mīmāṃsaka.
The explanation beginning with "by himself" (*svayam*) shows that such an inference was declared by the Teacher himself to be no means of proof; thus ends the refutation of Jaimini’s position.

Because the fruits are of an identical nature, it is like the means for producing an identical taste; and because they are contained within a single vessel, it is like the means for cooking rice that is unseen, just as one has seen [the process]. Thus, its lack of probative power has been stated. Furthermore, the reasoning regarding that lack of probative power has already been explained. Moreover, this definition of scripture (*āgama*) has been stated by us: it concerns every object that is capable of being investigated.

Just as, when a person has been purified by the application of the respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding injunctions and prohibitions—even though there is no necessary connection (*nāntarīyakatā*) between words and their objects—their activity proceeds with respect to those objects despite the presence of doubt; for in such cases, non-contradiction is possible at some time.
Therefore, the activity of a person who has observed the sublation of a means of valid cognition elsewhere [proceeds] in this manner. Furthermore, as for one whose object is ordinary...
Connection: [This occurs] in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, where the Naiyāyikas' inference based on the "remainder" (*śeṣavat*) is exposed as being fallacious. How so?

Just as fruits that have not yet been tasted are inferred to possess a taste equal to one that has been tasted, by virtue of their identical form acting as the probans—just as there is a means of establishing an identical flavor—and because they have entered into the same vessel. And so forth.

By means of a reason (*hetu*): like the cooking of unperceived grains of rice by means of the cooking of perceived ripe grains; and the illogicality of its being a non-prover—this refers to the illogicality of that "inference based on remainder" (*śeṣavat-anumāna*) not being a prover. For it has already been stated previously [in the passage] beginning with, "Because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is demonstrated merely by non-perception," and so forth. Now, however: (1)

By stating, "Because of the commonality of non-contradiction with the words of a reliable person, [scripture] is an inference" (*pramāṇavārttika* 1.218), the Master Dignāga has also indeed stated that the definition of scripture (*āgama*) consists precisely in its non-contradiction with respect to a portion [of reality]. (1)
He says: "And this has been stated," and so forth. And this has been stated [in the passage]:

"(1) 'The definition of scripture (*āgama*) is that which is non-contradictory in at least one part. We are not capable of remaining here without relying on the authority of scripture. This is the intermediate point.

In this regard, the definition of scripture (*āgama*) does not consist merely in non-contradiction with respect to one part, nor does it depend on the truth of a single object that is already universally established; rather, the definition of scripture as reality (*tattva*) is that which can be determined through valid cognition by limited vision (*avagdarśana*). Its entire domain [is thus established].

The analysis of "the object of all that can be analyzed" (*sarvasya śakyavicārasya viṣayasya*) is as follows: it is that of which an analysis is possible. Just as there is the establishment [of things] through their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whether by way of affirmation or negation, so too is there "perceptuality" for those things intended as objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) within the treatise, once they have been purified. This is as in the Buddhist tenets regarding the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth; likewise, regarding the thing-in-itself (*vastu*).

Those things intended as objects of inference based on authority (*āptānumāna*) are actually objects of inference based on the force of real entities (*vastubalānumāna*), such as the Truth of Suffering and so forth.

Likewise, those intended as objects of inference dependent on scripture (*āgamāpekṣānumāna*) are also of that same nature. The establishment of the existence of these three types of objects occurs through their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The state of being an object of perception and so forth is what constitutes the nature of perception and the other [means of valid cognition].

The establishment of negation occurs through its respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, when affirmation and negation have been established, regarding those remaining objects that are absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), even though there is no internal consistency among words and no [perceptible] relation, it is better—given the lack of any other recourse—that a person who is in doubt should act toward them. Therefore, in all such matters, there is no observed deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in scripture (*āgama*).

Because non-contradiction is possible at times. [Objection: "But not elsewhere" means: in whatever scripture there is trust (*śraddhā*) regarding the subject matter as it has been described, even with respect to objects such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth.
The statement regarding the capacity of fire to ward off cold is for the sake of truth; indeed, this entire treatise speaks for the sake of truth.

Even though its subject matter is capable of being determined, it contains much that is unreasonable due to contradiction with valid cognition—for instance, [the claims] that an eternal person is an agent, that things are eternal, and that there are supersensible objects.
One who asserts that the causes of entities are irregular,

or that their existence is irregular, or that their cessation is established by means other than the two valid cognitions, or that it falls outside their scope, or who speaks in contradiction to scripture or to inference based upon scripture; (334–335)
Without resolving contradictions and without demonstrating the meaning of the scriptures,
he who claims to know the true meaning might as well overcome a harlot through sheer audacity.

(336) [He argues that] the Person, whose nature is neither subject to falling away nor produced, and who is without prior or posterior states, is the agent of actions and the enjoyer of the fruits of those actions in succession.

Or rather, a contradiction has been observed by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). We have thus stated the definition of scripture (*āgama*) as that [text] by which the activity of a person is not justified.
Furthermore, regarding the Mīmāṃsakas and others who [assert] the cold-removal power of fire, which is the object of ordinary persons—
The statement "Fire is the remedy for cold," which is a portion of the Veda, is true in its meaning.
Having presented this as an example, [the author] states that the entire scripture characterized as the Veda is true in its meaning. What kind of scripture?

Even regarding a subject that is determinable and accessible through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is such that, although much within it may be illogical due to contradiction with the means of valid cognition, it remains so.
The connection is with what will be said later: "One who professes a treatise, such as a Mīmāṃsaka and so forth, might out of audacity win over a harlot.
Showing that [the opponent's position] is even more improper than what has already been stated, he says: "Of the eternal," and so forth. The word "asserting" (*vadat*) is to be connected everywhere.
He asserts the agency of an eternal person, namely: "There exists an eternal agent, a Person (*puruṣa*). Thus, he asserts the agency of an eternal being.

The treatise speaks thus of eternal entities; it speaks of objects that are beyond the senses and imperceptible as being perceptible by the senses. Likewise, it speaks of discordant causes for entities; likewise, it speaks of the discordant persistence and the discordant cessation of entities. And this is clear in the commentary.

We shall [refute it]. Or rather, a thing other than what has been stated, which has a "dispersed scope" (*vyastagocara*). That is to say, it is so described because its scope—its range or opportunity—is dispersed, that is, rejected. By what is its scope dispersed? He says: by the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*); that is to say, it is impossible [for it to exist] according to these two. Thus, one who speaks of such a thing [is refuted], as well as [one who relies on] scripture (*āgama*).

A scripture that contradicts inference based on observation is [unreliable]. Thus, a proponent who asserts as true a scripture that expresses many such irrational points would, out of sheer audacity, "conquer a harlot.
To the question, "Without doing what does he assert this? he says: "Contradiction," and so forth. This refers to a case where the object is capable of investigation.

Without resolving or setting aside the contradiction with the treatise (*śāstra*), and without demonstrating the cause for the engagement of persons with the treatise and the purpose of the treatise—characterized by the means conducive to the connection and the human goal—he makes his formal proposition (*pratijānānaḥ*).

He explains this with the words beginning "apracyuteḥ" (due to non-decline), etc. [The meaning is: the former nature is not lost, and the latter nature is not produced. This is the refutation of the view of Jaimini.
The Veda states that the enjoyer [is the self] because of his status as the substratum of the inherent cause;

however, that is largely shown to be untenable. Furthermore, the eternality of certain entities is untenable, as it would involve transgressing the essential nature of things, which is non-momentary. Moreover, universals and the like, though not themselves perceptible, are [claimed to be] perceived [through their instances].

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: it refers to one for whom there is birth (*janman*), subsistence (*sthiti*), and cessation (*nivṛtti*); who is subject to uneven (*viṣama*) conditions; who, being incapable of having qualities superadded (*anādheya-viśeṣa*) and previously a non-agent, becomes a producer through dependence on another; whose subsistence, being of a non-product nature (*niṣpatti-akārya-rūpa*), occurs by virtue of a support; and whose destruction occurs without a cause. Such a person, they say, is the sequential agent of good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta-karma*). Karma—

And [the self] is the enjoyer of fruits. In what manner is it both the agent and the enjoyer? With respect to the cognition of pleasure, pain, and so forth produced by prior karma, the self is the enjoyer of the fruits of karma by way of being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). As it has been said:
"The state of being an enjoyer consists in the inherence of the cognition of pleasure, pain, and so forth."
In the performance of auspicious and inauspicious actions, the self is the agent through its status as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for knowledge, effort, and so forth.
As it has been said: (1) "The connection with knowledge and effort is declared to be its agency."
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," the status of the self as an enjoyer is understood even though it is insentient in nature, due to its association with consciousness. As it has been said:
"(1) And the enjoyer is so because of association with consciousness, not by virtue of its own essential nature."

Thus, the Veda speaks of [the world] as being due to the state of being an inherent cause, a locus, and so forth; and this has already been shown to be untenable by the author of the treatise himself, who demonstrated that a causal relationship is impossible for eternal things. This should be connected with the statement: "The Veda declares the eternality of certain entities, and that too is untenable. Why?

(1) It is logical [that the non-momentary is unreal], because it transgresses the nature of a real entity by contradicting causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through either succession or simultaneity. For a real entity is that which is capable of causal efficiency; yet such causal efficiency is impossible for the non-momentary, and thus it is simply non-existent. How, then, could it possess the properties of a real entity? [The phrase] "universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth" refers to those things which are indeed not perceived. (1) "And so forth"—

The Veda declares that actions, qualities, and so forth are directly perceived through words; and the Veda speaks of the birth, subsistence, and cessation of entities, which are diverse. Because of this diversity of birth, the object is stated in the Sūtra to be the cause of entities.

He states that very same flawed reason: "of that which is incapable of having anything added to it," and so forth. Because it is eternal, it cannot have any excellence added to it; thus, it was previously a non-producer during its state at the time prior to causal efficiency. Yet, [the opponent] claims it becomes a producer later through dependence on others—that is, dependence on auxiliary causes. This is what the Veda asserts. And this is untenable, as has been demonstrated in detail.

With the words beginning "Because of its production" (*niṣpatter*), he states that the Veda expresses an unstable state. Because it is produced from its own causes—that is, because it is already established as an entity whose nature is not something to be further produced—the Veda asserts the persistence [of things] by virtue of a substratum. However, this is improper;
for it has been previously established that that which is entirely independent cannot persist through the power of another.
Demonstrating that cessation is inconsistent, he says: "And from a cause, which is a reason for destruction, [the non-existence] of entities... and so forth.

Furthermore, other things—such as the capacity of the *agnihotra* sacrifice and the like to purify sin—which are established through perception and inference, are sublated by an inference based on scripture (*āgama*) that contradicts their established status.
While the Veda speaks in this manner, he— without resolving the contradictions with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) throughout the entire body of the treatise,

and without demonstrating the characteristics of a treatise (*śāstradharma*), namely its connection [to a goal], its suitability as a means, and its declaration of human aims— desires to establish its faultlessness within a depth difficult to fathom even for those of superior intelligence, by merely enumerating subjects that are extremely well-known.
The Veda says that there is destruction; and that is incorrect, as has been demonstrated regarding the destruction of duality.
The Veda also says that other such things are existent. Of what nature [are they]? They are the opposite of what is commonly established: non-existence.

For [the Veda] is the subverter of existence. The meaning is: for that which has a well-established subversion, by what means—namely, by perception and inference—does the Veda state its existence? [The Veda states] the capacity of the *agnihotra* and so forth; by the word "and so forth," it refers to bathing at sacred sites (*tīrtha*) and the like, stating their power to purify sin. Here too, by the word "and so forth," [it refers to] the accumulation of merit (*dharma*) and so on.

It is sublated by an inference based on common experience (*gamāśraya*). For instance, the established position of the scriptures (*āgama*) is that non-dharma consists of passion and the like, as well as the karma produced therefrom; yet neither of these two is negated by the *agnihotra* sacrifice and similar rites. How, then, could there be purification of non-dharma through it? Or how could there be an increase of dharma from it? This is because dharma has the nature of non-greed and the like, as well as the karma produced therefrom.
Because bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and the like do not possess that nature; by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), other similar improper assertions are also to be understood.
For that very proponent, regarding the Veda in all cases—even in the threefold domain of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth—[.... 1].

Without resolving—that is, without removing—the contradiction with valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the subject matter to be established by the treatise (*śāstra*), and without demonstrating those properties (*dharma*) which constitute the necessary factors for engaging with the treatise;
what then are those properties? He says: "The connection," and so forth. It is the mutual coherence of the meanings of the constituent terms.

The relationship (*sambandha*), the feasible means (*śakyasādhana-upāya*), and the appropriate means (*anuguṇopāya*). That which is taught in the treatise as a means for achieving the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*)—namely, that it can be accomplished by a person—is what is meant. The goals of human life are prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). "Relationship," "appropriate means," and "goals of human life" form a *dvandva* compound. The expression [refers to] their designation...

Not so. For has it not already been stated that the scripture is unacceptably because its internal contradictions have not been resolved? What is the point of stating this by way of failing to demonstrate the properties of the scripture?

He thinks as follows: (1) Having demonstrated that [the means of knowledge] are pure regarding the objects of perception and inference, he might at some point say something regarding another object that is devoid of a [logical] connection and so forth; therefore, it was stated that there is no demonstration of the characteristics of a treatise (*śāstradharma*) for such a purpose. Likewise, by stating the [logical] connections and so forth, without demonstrating the characteristics of a treatise, [he intends to establish] the truth of the meaning in an extremely well-known subject matter.
"By the mere statement of that" refers to the capacity of fire to dispel cold, which is an extremely well-known object;

"by the mere statement of truth" means by the mere statement of that [capacity] as it truly is. Because it is difficult to fathom even with the excellence of wisdom, there is a "seizing of the excellence of wisdom. For that very reason, it is "profound"; that is to say, even regarding such an object, one that is entirely beyond the reach of perception. (3) Refutation of the view of Jaimini.

Even a courtesan may overcome [her husband] through audacity. It is said that a certain courtesan was caught by her husband himself in the act of misconduct and rebuked. She replied to him: "Look, mother, at the perversity of this man;
instead of placing his trust in me, his lawful wife, he places it in the water-bubbles called his own eyes."

"Even though she was solicited by that Jaratkāṇa, a rustic wood-gatherer, she did not unite with him. Out of passion for his beauty and virtues, she said, 'I desire the son of the chief minister. Desiring thus to establish the lack of harm from cold, the truthfulness of this matter, and its validity, that Mīmāṃsaka, with such audacity, [spoke] even to a harlot."

He triumphs by means of boldness (*dhāṭya*). He demonstrates with the words "whatever kind of unchaste woman (*bandhakī*) he triumphs over" and so forth. An "unchaste woman" is one of loose conduct. Having been seen by her husband himself at the scene of an infidelity, and having been reproached while in that state of infidelity, saying, "You have consorted with another man," she [confronts] that husband.
He replied. Regarding how he replied, it says: "Behold," and so forth.
The women standing nearby are addressed by the word "mātaḥ" (mothers): "O mothers, behold this man."
"The reversal of my master—look indeed! This [form] ends in the second person plural of the imperative (*loṭ*).

Consequently, it is also appropriate for the word *mātṛ* to be in the plural, namely *mātaraḥ*. Regarding this, some maintain that there exists a word *mātaḥ* which has the same meaning as the vocative singular form *mātṛ*, and that its accentuation is...
According to the maxim that "particles (*nipāta*) are like their counterparts," and because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), it retains the same form across all cases;
thus, even when connected with the plural word *paśyata*, it is employed as *mātari* alone. Others, however, read:
*paśyata mātaraḥ puruṣasya*. [The term] *dharmapatnī* means a wife who is a means for accomplishing *dharma*. This is the middle [explanation].

This is an elided compound (*padalopī samāsaḥ*). The context is that he places his trust not in me, his lawful wife, but rather in these two things called eyes, which are like water-bubbles arising from his own [body]. The analysis of the compound is: "those whose designation (*abhidhāna*) is 'eye'. He states the reason why he does not associate with other men, beginning with the words "by him," etc. He was old...

"Kāṇaśca" means "jaratkāṇaḥ"; that is to say, by one who is old and blind. In this context, by the mention of "old" (*jara*), the deficiency of age is expressed. Since the eye is the supreme locus of form, the mention of "blind" (*kāṇa*) expresses deformity due to its deficiency. By the mention of "rustic" (*grāmya*), the deficiency of qualities such as wit is expressed. By the mention of "wood-gatherer" (*kāṣṭhahāraka*), poverty is expressed because of a life of hardship.

Thus, although she had been requested for the sake of union by a man endowed with qualities such as old age, she did not previously unite with him out of attachment to his form and qualities. "Form" (*rūpa*) refers to physical beauty; "qualities" (*guṇa*) refers to attributes such as cleverness. "Attachment to form and qualities" (*rūpaguṇānurāga*) means the longing for them, and by that cause [she did not unite]. [She united instead] with the son of the chief minister (*mantrimukhyadāraka*), the preeminent counselor...

"A young boy" (*dāraka*) means a son; the analysis of the compound is "he who is both a chief minister and a boy. How can it be possible that I should desire such a boy? In this regard, by way of the reversal of the four defects beginning with old age, the four qualities of the chief minister's son are stated: by the mention of "form" (*rūpa*), his comeliness (*prāsādikatva*) is indicated; by the mention of "qualities" (*guṇa*), his wisdom (*vidvattva*) is indicated.

[The mention of] "the prime minister and so forth" refers to sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). The mention of "the son" refers to the quality of age. And this [statement] was merely prompted by the audacity of the harlot;
it is her own word alone and is not logically consistent. For it is only beauty and such qualities that are the cause of desire—this is from the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* (1.337).

By means of the word of a reliable person (*āpta*), even for an object that is entirely beyond perception, there is an inference of non-contradiction, provided that [the word] is established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding matters where it does not contradict perceived means of knowledge.
If this is so, what is not a valid means of knowledge here?
For indeed, among a person who speaks much, there is never not a single word that possesses a true meaning. (337)
Just as this statement of absolute truth is extremely difficult to achieve, so too is the statement of absolute falsehood. In that case,

if one single statement were somehow found to be consistent with reality, then there would be no person who could not be considered authoritative (*āpta*) regarding the remainder of that body of speech.
But it is not [due to] old age and so forth.

With the words "of such a kind" (*evaṃjātīyaka*) and so on, he applies the example to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). "Of such a kind" means similar to the reply of a promiscuous woman. This is the inference of the Veda’s non-contradiction regarding an object that is entirely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*). (1)

Of what kind of Veda? Of one whose subject matter is capable of investigation and which contradicts perceived means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The analysis of the compound is: "that of which there is a contradiction with a perceived *pramāṇa*. An inference is established by the example of [the statement regarding] cold-removal: by the statement that fire is a remedy for cold. Just as the sentence "Fire is the medicine for cold" is non-contradictory, so too is another [statement] of the Veda.

"Speech is non-contradictory. In this context, the Veda stands in the place of the lawful wife; the statement regarding the agency of a man who is constant despite contrary appearances stands in the place of the eyes; and perception and inference stand in the place of the eyes. Furthermore, the word of a wife whose conduct has been observed to be deceptive is not authoritative.

Having seen the misconduct of that person by whom [the Veda was composed], one should not treat one's own view as authoritative, but should instead accept his word as being true to fact. Thus, having rendered the two means of valid cognition that contradict the meaning stated in the Veda to be invalid, one would [accept] what is extremely beyond the senses from the word of that which stands in the place of a wife to the Veda, even though its deviation has been observed.
"Let us proceed.

(336) Here, he states another fault: "It would be established," and so forth. "In this way" means that if the entire Veda were established merely by the statement of a single perceived truth, then every person—[all] men—would be [an authority].

This would then be the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For it is not the case that among the many words spoken by a person there is not even a single word whose meaning is true; rather, such a word certainly exists.
He explains this with the words "just as," etc.: namely, this state of being an utterer [of truth], which is absolute truthfulness.

It is extremely difficult for the intellect, because it is performed with extreme hardship. Likewise, in that very same way, the declaration of truth is extremely difficult for the intellect; such being the case according to this principle (*nyāya*), how could there be any correspondence—even by the *kākatālīya* (coincidental) principle—with even a single statement? It is by means of that [correspondence], which consists in having a true object, that [truth is established]. Therefore, from that non-discrepant word—

Regarding the phrase "of that mass of speech characterized by the [single] sound": this refers to the mass of speech belonging to that person whose single statement has been observed to be non-contradictory. If one were to accept such a state—that is, its non-contradiction—then there would be no person who is not authoritative;
rather, everyone would be authoritative. But this is not the case. Therefore, [it is not established] on the basis of non-contradiction in a single part...
• [Validity] (prāmāṇyam). (3) Refutation of Jaimini’s view:
Sound does not possess the nature or the effect of things [it denotes] within the speaker;
nor is there any non-deviation (avyabhicāritā) for that which is distinct from those two. ||339||

Speech is neither the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the things expressed, nor is it their effect (*kārya*); for it occurs even in their absence, arising merely from the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). Furthermore, there is nothing else that is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*). Since a deviant thing can occur otherwise than its cause, the cognition of those [objects] based on its existence is untenable.
If it is argued that the activity of signifiers is caused by the perception of the signified,
then in that case, the sentence would have only an instrumental purpose (*kārya*), because the signifier functions through the perception of the signified. This being so—
Furthermore, whatever indeed makes something known must do so by being either of the same nature as it or produced from it;

it cannot do so otherwise. Nor is this sound (*dhvani*) of the same nature as the objects intended to be expressed. Why? Because sound resides in the speaker; for that which is of one nature cannot exist in another. [This applies] to objects.
Or [it is] an effect: (1) this sound is not [an effect]. What is the reason? Because the sound arises from the speaker’s cognition (*mati*).

Therefore, the meaning is this: because it is dependent solely upon the speaker’s intention and not upon an external object—this is the sense. And [the phrase] "not distinct from that" means that there is no non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) regarding an object that is distinct from both intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*).
The practice exists.

He explains by means of the words beginning with "no" (*na*). The word "first" (*tāvat*) indicates sequence. This speech residing in the speaker is neither the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the objects to be expressed, nor is it their effect (*kārya*). What is the reason?

Even in the absence of that—that is, even in the absence of real entities—because [the word] arises from mere intention (*vivakṣāmātra*), there is no cause other than the effect or the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that is non-deviant for anything. And since there is deviation, the word may occur otherwise than that; therefore, "otherwise than the external object" means even when the external object is present.
Because of its occurrence—that is, because of the occurrence of that word—and because of the existence of that word, the cognition of it, namely the cognition of an external object, is untenable.
This might be argued: even though the expression is a distinct entity from the thing expressed, nevertheless, [it is related] to that which is expressed...

"Only the effect" means only the indicator. For the activity—whether it be the production or the manifestation—of expressive words is caused by the perception of the signified object. That is, it is caused by the seeing of the signified meaning. For when the signified exists, there is the seeing of it; from that seeing comes the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*); and from the desire to speak comes the speech. Thus, it is through this succession.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that speech has purposeful action as its object.

He explains this with the words "it might be so" (*syād etat*) and so forth: "Therefore, since a denotative word functions by means of the perception of the denoted object, how could it have mutually contradictory objects in a single instance? (340)

If this rule— that a word does not function without a corresponding real object (vastu)— were strictly maintained, then there could be no occurrence of contradictory natures being attributed to a single object within different doctrines. For it is impossible for a single word to denote both eternality and non-eternality without distinction.
Therefore, since cognitions that differ from the object are not in any way invariably concomitant with it, how can a determination of the object be established on their basis? ||341||

An ignorant person seeks the authority of scripture for the sake of understanding what it indicates; this is because those who have realized the true nature of reality do not depend on instruction, and because [the ignorant] lack the capacity to discern a person whose qualities transcend the senses.
He refutes this with the words "If that were so," and so forth. "If that were so" means: if all [words] proceed solely by the force of their meaning...
The activity of speech regarding a single object of expression would have mutually contradictory meanings due to the differences in scriptural traditions (*āgama*).
How could such an activity of speech exist? It could not exist at all; the meaning is that it would be one and the same in all doctrines.
He explains this with the words beginning "If" (*yadi*), etc.: "If this restriction [were such that] the object to be expressed were not distinct from the other object to be expressed..."

Since a word does not function without [a referent], then, because they express mutually contradictory meanings regarding a single entity amidst various divergent doctrines and systems (*siddhāntas*), there would be no operation of speech through the synthesis or superimposition of a nature that is both eternal and non-eternal. For it is impossible that a single word [should denote such a thing].

"Without alternative" (*niḥparyāya*) means "without another mode. [The phrase] "it would be both eternal and non-eternal" is intended as an illustration; by this, even a jar or the like would be both eternal and non-eternal without alternative. But it is simply impossible for something to be both eternal and non-eternal. Furthermore, there is the occurrence of the notion that for some, such as the Sāṃkhyas, sound is eternal, while for others it is non-eternal.
"Endowed with a self," "devoid of a self," and so forth.
Therefore, there is no connection between words and external objects. For this reason, for the person who understands [them], the scriptures are not invariably concomitant with real entities.

Those things which are invariably concomitant [do not in any way establish themselves for the cognizer]; therefore, from those scriptures (*āgama*) that do not have the thing as their internal essence, how can there be certainty, or rather, is there no certainty? [The scripture is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): it is not everyone who investigates it, but rather the ignorant person.
For what purpose does he investigate it? It is for the sake of understanding the object indicated by it. By that scripture, the [object] indicated—

For the sake of understanding the meaning. What is the reason that only the ignorant person investigates and not another? He says: because those who have realized the true nature of things—the non-erroneous form of entities—have understood the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and thus do not depend on the instruction of others.
Furthermore, as for the ignorant person by whom [the truth] must be sought, his qualities are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).

The quality of the sense of hearing (1) is first [established], and subsequently, there is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) with the word "person" (*puruṣa*). For that person—who understands the functioning of sentences even in the absence of the existence of the intended object—there must necessarily be doubt as to whether the speech of such individuals, whose words have not been observed to deviate from reality, is indeed true or not. Therefore, it is not logical [to claim] by means of this...
It is impossible for anyone to ascertain anything at all regarding this.
Therefore, even through the cessation of that [cognition], the non-existence of the entity is not established.

As it has been stated: because scripture has all things as its object, and because it functions without contradiction when a thing exists, non-apprehension characterized by the cessation of that [thing] will establish its non-existence. And this quality of having all things as its object belongs to it;
it would exist if there were no obstruction by another thing. Therefore, it was said that for one who desires to understand, the intended goal is established. 12
Therefore, non-apprehension that results in the certainty of non-existence is not established.

Therefore, even when the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are absent, there is no certainty regarding remote objects. This is because one lacks the capacity to make such a distinction as: "The Veda is authoritative," "Someone [is its] author," "There is a desire for merit in bathing," "There is pride in the doctrine of caste," "This person is omniscient," "He is not [omniscient]," or "He is a speaker of falsehood. Thus, that—

Having ascertained that such speech, composed by a person of that [reliable] kind, is an authoritative scripture (*āgama*), one proceeds [to act upon it]. Furthermore, not all words of everyone function in accordance with reality; for a cognizer who perceives the occurrence [of a word's application] even in the absence of the existence of that object which is desired and intended by others— [The text continues: ...the person... [is not necessarily led astray]. Thus, since there is no contradiction regarding the fact that the cognition produced by a word arises from its own cause, and because the object is established by the very nature of things (*vastubalapravṛttānumāna*), the word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the statement that "words are not a means of valid cognition" is refuted. This concludes the section on the examination of scripture (*āgama*). Now follows the examination of comparison (*upamāna*). Regarding this, the following is said: "Comparison is the cognition of similarity based on the perception of a remembered object. That is to say, having perceived a cow (*go*) and remembering it, when one perceives a similar object elsewhere, the cognition that arises—"this is similar to that"—is comparison. For example, just as one who has seen a cow and remembers it, upon seeing a gavaya, forms the cognition: "This is similar to that cow. However, this is not a distinct means of valid cognition. Why? Because it is included within inference (*anumāna*). How so? It is because it is produced by the power of the relationship between the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the pervaded (*vyāpya*). That is to say, the similarity to a cow is the pervader, and being a gavaya is the pervaded. Since the gavaya is established by the perception of the pervaded, it is nothing other than inference. Therefore, comparison is not a separate means of valid cognition. This concludes the examination of comparison. Now follows the examination of presumption (*arthāpatti*). Regarding this, the following is said: "Presumption is the postulation of another entity when a perceived or heard object is otherwise inexplicable. That is to say, when a perceived or heard object cannot be explained otherwise, the postulation of another entity is presumption. For example, when Devadatta, who is alive, is not seen in his house, the postulation of his being outside is presumption, because his being alive is perceived and yet he is not seen in his house. However, this too is not a distinct means of valid cognition. Why? Because it is included within inference. How so? It is because it is produced by the power of the relationship between the pervader and the pervaded. That is to say, the non-perception of Devadatta in his house while he is alive is the pervader, and his being outside is the pervaded. Since the being outside is established by the perception of the pervader, it is nothing other than inference. Therefore, presumption is not a separate means of valid cognition. This concludes the examination of presumption. Now follows the examination of non-apprehension (*abhāva*). Regarding this, the following is said: "Non-apprehension is the cognition of the non-existence of an object through the non-perception of that which is perceptible. That is to say, when an object that is capable of being perceived is not perceived, the cognition of its non-existence is non-apprehension. For example, when a jar is not perceived on a spot of ground where it could be seen, the cognition "there is no jar here" is non-apprehension. However, this too is not a distinct means of valid cognition. Why? Because it is included within inference. How so? It is because it is produced by the power of the relationship between the pervader and the pervaded. That is to say, the non-perception of a perceptible object is the pervader, and the non-existence of that object is the pervaded. Since the non-existence is established by the perception of the pervader, it is nothing other than inference. Therefore, non-apprehension is not a separate means of valid cognition. This concludes the examination of non-apprehension. Now follows the examination of tradition (*aitihya*). Regarding this, the following is said: "Tradition is the report of 'thus they say' (*iti ha*). That is to say, the report of "thus they say" regarding an object that is not currently perceived is tradition. For example, "There is a yakṣa at the crossroads," or "There is a treasure-trove at the foot of the tree. However, this too is not a distinct means of valid cognition. Why? Because it is included within inference. How so? It is because it is produced by the power of the relationship between the pervader and the pervaded. That is to say, the report of "thus they say" is the pervader, and the existence of the object is the pervaded. Since the existence of the object is established by the perception of the pervader, it is nothing other than inference. Therefore, tradition is not a separate means of valid cognition. This concludes the examination of tradition. Now follows the examination of probability (*sambhava*). Regarding this, the following is said: "Probability is the determination of a part based on the whole. That is to say, when a large quantity is perceived, the determination of a smaller portion contained within it is probability. For example, when a hundred is perceived, the determination that ten is present is probability. However, this too is not a distinct means of valid cognition. Why? Because it is included within inference. How so? It is because it is produced by the power of the relationship between the pervader and the pervaded. That is to say, the large quantity is the pervader, and the smaller portion is the pervaded. Since the smaller portion is established by the perception of the pervader, it is nothing other than inference. Therefore, probability is not a separate means of valid cognition. This concludes the examination of probability. Now follows the examination of non-existence (*abhāva*). Regarding this, the following is said: "Non-existence is the cognition of the non-existence of an object through the non-perception of that which is perceptible. That is to say, when an object that is capable of being perceived is not perceived, the cognition of its non-existence is non-apprehension. For example, when a jar is not perceived on a spot of ground where it could be seen, the cognition "there is no jar here" is non-apprehension. However, this too is not a distinct means of valid cognition. Why? Because it is included within inference. How so? It is because it is produced by the power of the relationship between the pervader and the pervaded. That is to say, the non-perception of a perceptible object is the pervader, and the non-existence of that object is the pervaded. Since the non-existence is established by the perception of the pervader, it is nothing other than inference. Therefore, non-apprehension is not a separate means of valid cognition. This concludes the examination of non-apprehension. Now follows the examination of inclusion (*prasaṅga*). Regarding this, the following is said: "Inclusion is the demonstration of an undesired consequence for the opponent. That is to say, when one demonstrates an undesired consequence for the opponent, it is inclusion. For example, if a Vaiśeṣika were to say, "Sound is eternal," one might respond, "Then it would follow that sound is not produced by effort. However, this too is not a distinct means of valid cognition. Why? Because it is included within inference. How so? It is because it is produced by the power of the relationship between the pervader and the pervaded. That is to say, the property of being produced by effort is the pervader, and the property of being non-eternal is the pervaded. Since the non-eternality is established by the perception of the pervader, it is nothing other than inference. Therefore, inclusion is not a separate means of valid cognition. This concludes the examination of inclusion. Now follows the examination of the remainder (*śeṣavat*). Regarding this, the following is said: "The remainder is the cognition of what remains after excluding the perceived and the heard. That is to say, when some objects have been perceived or heard, and others remain, the cognition of those remaining is the remainder. For example, when among a group of five people, three are perceived to be Brahmins and two are heard to be Brahmins, the cognition that the remaining two are also Brahmins is the remainder. However, this too is not a distinct means of valid cognition. Why? Because it is included within inference. How so? It is because it is produced by the power of the relationship between the pervader and the pervaded. That is to say, being a Brahmin is the pervader, and being of a certain class is the pervaded. Since the class is established by the perception of the pervader, it is nothing other than inference. Therefore, the remainder is not a separate means of valid cognition. This concludes the examination of the remainder. Now follows the examination of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Regarding this, the following is said: "Direct perception is the cognition that is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpodha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*). That is to say, the cognition that is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous is
There must necessarily be doubt regarding the speech of such a person: "Is this speech true, or is it not? Regarding whose speech?

Even regarding the speech of those whose words have never been observed to deviate from the truth—those for whom even when the object is subject to investigation, their words have not been seen to be erroneous—even regarding the speech of such persons there is doubt;
by the use of the word "even" (api), it follows that there is all the more doubt regarding the speech of those whose words have been observed to deviate.
Because it is impossible to ascertain any given object through the word of some person, and because there is no certainty,
the non-existence of the entity intended to be negated is not established by the cessation of that cognition, nor even by the cessation of its arrival.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "yad uktam" (as it was stated). As was stated previously: (1) because scripture has all things as its object, and because it does not fail to correspond when a thing exists; therefore, non-apprehension characterized by the cessation of that [scripture]—that is, non-apprehension characterized by the cessation of scripture—will establish the non-existence of even an object remote by nature and so forth. That—

The establishment of the certainty regarding its non-existence does not belong to this scripture at all; for this scripture does not possess omniscience, because it does not take as its object those things that are unrelated to human goals. Even granting [for the sake of argument] that the scripture has everything as its object, [if... 217b.
And "Rambha" for the removal of sin—these five are the signs of dullness in those whose wisdom has been destroyed.

(The commentary on the first chapter of the *Pramāṇavārttika*, composed by the great logician Ācārya Śrī Dharmakīrti— the lion for his prowess against the elephants that are the disputants of the entire earth, whose sweet fame pervades all directions— is hereby completed.
May there be auspiciousness!)

If there were a functioning [of the scripture] with respect to another object while it was obstructed [by that other], then non-perception—characterized by the cessation of the scripture's occurrence—would be determinative of its absence;
but that is not the case, because the scripture functions even with respect to another object.
This being so, for a person desiring to understand a specific intended object from a scripture that deviates regarding that object, [the scripture cannot serve as a valid means of knowledge].

It has been stated that "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) [occurs]. For that reason, in the case of remote objects, the linguistic convention of "non-existence"—which has the result of determining non-existence—is not established.
Therefore, even when the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are absent, [the absence of] the three means of valid cognition known as perception, inference, and scripture [is not established].

The conclusion is that even when [a means of knowledge] has ceased to function, there is no certainty regarding objects remote in space, time, or nature. Demonstrating just a portion of the improper assertions of the various non-Buddhist schools (*tīrthika*), he says:
"(1) The Veda," and so forth. Here, the word *iti* and the word *vāda* should be connected with what is to be stated below.
Therefore, the meaning is this: [the phrase "vedaprāmāṇya... jāḍye"] is the logical mark (*liṅga*).
Now, one might object: since there is a prohibition against a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with a quality word (*guṇa*), it ought to be "the validity of the Veda" (*vedasya prāmāṇyam*).
This is not a fault, because in that context only those qualities well-known in common usage are understood by the term "quality. And of this—
The designation "the mark [is] in the sense of locus and extent" and so forth refers to this.
(2) Furthermore, the claim of certain Naiyāyikas and others that God is the creator of the principles (tattvas) and so forth is also a mark of their dullness.

(3) The desire for dharma through bathing at sacred sites (*tīrtha*) is a mark of dullness, as is the physical and vocal action produced by others. Dharma is the opposite of that; how, then, could dharma be attained from a bath characterized merely by contact with water? This doctrine of bathing at sacred sites has been refuted in detail by the Teacher.
This is not elaborated here by Subandhu and others.
[2] Even when lacking qualities such as moral conduct (*śīla*) due to delusion, the arrogance consisting in the conceit "I am a Brahmin" based on the claim of birth is pride (*darpa*).

This is a sign of dullness because it is illogical; for if one were to grasp [the definition], there would be an arrogant adherence to the doctrine of a universal (*jāti*). Alternatively, one might rely on that which is produced by a Brāhmaṇa father in the womb of a Brāhmaṇī mother. In that regard, the former position is not tenable because a real, ontological universal (*sāmānya*) has been refuted. Nor is the latter [position tenable], because of the [distinctness of] the bodies of the Brāhmaṇa and the Brāhmaṇī.
Because its nature is pure, it is no different from other bodies.
(5) The tormenting of the body through fasting and so forth is "suffering" (*santāpa*); the undertaking or practice of that is for the sake of destroying sin.
Of sin...

...J4 The mark [of its futility] regarding dullness is as follows: (1) Greed, hatred, and delusion are the cause of all evil. Since the undertaking of penance is not inconsistent with these, how could there be purification from evil through it?

These five signs [indicate] dullness (*jāḍya*). In what kind of dullness? In that which is characterized by "destroyed wisdom" (*dhvastaprajñāna*). That dullness in which wisdom—the cognition based on the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—has been destroyed is so described. The meaning is that it is devoid of knowledge that follows right reasoning (*nyāya*). It is said to be "five" because they are taken according to their respective contexts.
These are the marks. ||0||
Those who possess great discernment regarding Bhaṭṭa Uddyotakara and others, whose minds are deeply immersed in the ocean of Dharmakīrti— the mine of true reality—
and whose memory is fully capable of investigating the sequence of earlier and later [statements], and whose wisdom is likewise preeminent.
Whatever has been said here will be understood by those who are truly skilled.
In the successive excavations of its meaning, there is a great clarity of speech; therein is perceived the excellence of the eloquent sayings of others,
as well as the destruction of the doctrines of all rival sectarians who are puffed up with pride.
How could this commentary not be captivating for those whose intellects have been awakened by its most distinguished characteristics? ||0||
In the *Pramāṇavārttikavṛtti* composed by Karṇakagomin.
